I call heaven and earth to witness against you today: I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. So choose life, that you and your descendants may live,

loving Yahweh your God, listening to his voice, and holding fast to him. For he is your life and the length of your days, so that you may dwell in the land Yahweh swore to give to your forefathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”

notes.text: Or “bring you back from captivity.”
The Septuagint begins this verse, “If you hearken to the commandments of the Lord your God, which I command you this day” (Brenton, modernized), a clause missing from the traditional Hebrew text.

verses.text: Then Moses went and spoke{a} these words to all Israel.
And he said to them, “Today I am one hundred twenty years old; I can no longer go out and come in, and Yahweh has said to me, ‘You shall not cross this Jordan.’

Yahweh your God is the one who will go across in front of you. It is he who will wipe out these nations before you so that you take their place. And Joshua will lead you across, just as Yahweh has said.
And Yahweh will deal with them as he dealt with Sihon and Og, the kings of the Amorites, and with their land, which he destroyed.
Yahweh will hand them over to you, and you must treat them exactly as the command I have given you requires.
Be strong and brave. Do not fear them or tremble before them, for it is Yahweh your God who goes with you. He will not let you go or abandon you.”

Then Moses called Joshua and said to him in the sight of all Israel, “Be strong and brave, for you will go with this people into the land Yahweh swore to their forefathers to give them, and you will divide it among them as their inheritance.
Yahweh himself goes before you; he will be with you. He will not let you go or abandon you. Do not be afraid or dismayed.”
Moses wrote down this law and gave it to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of Yahweh’s covenant, and to all the elders of Israel.
Then Moses gave them this command: “Every seventh year, at the set time of the year when debts are released, during the Feast of Booths,{b}
when all Israel comes to appear in the presence of Yahweh your God at the place he will choose, you shall read this law before all Israel, in their hearing.
Assemble the people, men, women, and children, and the sojourner in your gates, so that they may listen and learn to revere Yahweh your God and be careful to observe every word of this law,
and that their children, who have not known it, may listen and learn to revere Yahweh your God as long as you live in the land that you are crossing the Jordan to possess.”

Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Your time to die is drawing near. Summon Joshua, and both of you take your stand in the tent of meeting, and I will give him his charge.” So Moses and Joshua went and stood in the tent of meeting.
And Yahweh appeared at the tent in a pillar of cloud, and the pillar of cloud stood over the entrance of the tent.

Yahweh said to Moses, “Soon you will lie down to rest with your forefathers, and this people will rise up and go whoring after the alien gods of the land into which they are going. They will abandon me and break the covenant I made with them.

My anger will be kindled against them on that day, and I will forsake them and conceal my face from them; they will be consumed, and many disasters and distresses will befall them. And they will say on that day, ‘Have not these disasters come upon us because our God is not in our midst?’
On that day I will indeed turn my face away from them, on account of all the wickedness they have committed by turning to other gods.
“Now therefore write this song for yourselves, and teach it to the Israelites; put it in their mouths, that this song may be a witness for me against the Israelites.

For I will bring them into the land flowing with milk and honey that I promised on oath to their forefathers, and when they have eaten until they are full and have become fat, they will go after other gods and serve them, scorning me and breaking my covenant.

And when many evils and troubles have found them, this song will testify against them as a witness, for it will not be forgotten from the mouths of their offspring. For I know the plans they are forming even today, before I have brought them into the land I swore to give.”
So Moses wrote this song down on that day and taught it to the Israelites.
And Yahweh{c} commissioned Joshua the son of Nun and said, “Be strong and courageous, for you shall bring the Israelites into the land that I swore to them, and I will be with you.”
When Moses had finished writing the words of this law in a book, to the very end,
he gave this command to the Levites, the bearers of the ark of Yahweh’s covenant:
“Take this book of the law and put it beside the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God, so that it may stay there as a witness against you.
For I know how rebellious and stiff-necked you are. If even today, while I am still alive among you, you have been rebels against Yahweh, how much more after my death!
Gather to me all the elders of your tribes and your officials, that I may speak these words in their ears and call heaven and earth to witness against them.

For I know that after my death you will act very corruptly and turn aside from the way I have commanded you. Disaster will meet you in later days, because you will do what Yahweh regards as evil, and anger him through what your hands have made.”
Then, while the whole assembly of Israel listened, Moses spoke the words of this song from beginning to end:

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “Moses finished speaking” (Brenton), and a Qumran manuscript is reported to agree; the difference involves two similar Hebrew words.
Held in the seventh month, Tishri (September–October).
Hebrew “he”; the context shows that Yahweh is meant. The Septuagint makes Moses the subject.

verses.text: “Give ear, you heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.
Let my teaching fall like rain, my speech settle like the dew, like fine showers on new grass, like heavy rains on the green plants.
For I will proclaim the name of Yahweh; give greatness to our God!
“The Rock—his work is perfect; all his ways are justice. A God of faithfulness and without wrong, righteous and upright is he.
Acting corruptly toward him, they are no longer his children, because of their blemish;{a} a perverse and crooked generation.
Is this how you repay Yahweh, you foolish and unwise people? Is he not your father, who acquired you,{b} who made you and established you?
“Remember the days of long ago; consider the years of generations past. Ask your father, and he will inform you, your elders, and they will tell you.
When the Most High{c} gave the nations their inheritance, when he divided the descendants of Adam,{d} he fixed the borders of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.{e}
For Yahweh’s portion is his people, Jacob his allotted inheritance.
“He found him in a desert land, in an empty, howling waste. He encircled him and watched over him; he guarded him like the pupil{f} of his eye.
Like an eagle that rouses its nest and hovers over its young, he spread out his wings and took him up, bearing him on his pinions.
Yahweh by himself was his guide; there was no alien god beside him.
He made him ride on the heights of the land, and he ate the produce of the field. He fed him honey from the rock and oil from the flinty crag,
curds from the herd and milk from the flock, with the fat of lambs, rams of Bashan’s breed and he-goats, with the choicest kernels of wheat; and you drank wine, the foaming blood of the grape.
“But Jeshurun{g} grew fat and kicked— you grew fat, you grew bloated and gorged— he abandoned the God who made him and scorned the Rock of his salvation.
They made him jealous with strange gods; they angered him with detestable things.
They sacrificed to demons that were no god, to gods they had never known, to new gods lately arrived, whom your forefathers never dreaded.
You neglected the Rock that begot you, and forgot the God who gave you birth.
“Yahweh saw it and spurned them, provoked by his sons and his daughters.
He said, ‘I will hide my face from them; I will see what their end will be, for they are a perverse generation, children with no faithfulness in them.
They roused my jealousy with a no-god; they angered me with their empty idols.{h} So I will rouse their jealousy with a no-people; I will anger them with a nation that lacks sense.
For fire has flared up in my anger, and it burns down to the depths of Sheol;{i} it consumes the earth and its harvest and sets the roots of the mountains ablaze.
“ ‘I will pile up evils on them; I will spend every arrow I have against them.
They will be wasted by hunger, devoured by plague and bitter pestilence. I will send the fangs of wild beasts against them, with the venom of things that glide in the dust.
Outside, the sword will bereave, and in the inner rooms, terror, for young man and virgin alike, for the nursing infant and the gray-haired man.
I said, “I will scatter them,{j} I will erase their memory from among mankind,”
but I feared the taunting of the enemy, that their foes might misjudge and say, “Our hand has prevailed; Yahweh did not do any of this.” ’
“For they are a nation void of counsel, and there is no understanding in them.
If they were wise, they would grasp this; they would see what their end will be.
How could a single man pursue a thousand, and two drive ten thousand into flight, unless their Rock had sold them, unless Yahweh had given them up?
For their rock is not like our Rock— even our enemies are judges of that.
For their vine comes from the vine of Sodom and from the terraces of Gomorrah; their grapes are full of poison; their clusters taste of bitterness.
Their wine is the venom of serpents, the cruel poison of vipers.
“ ‘Is this not stored away with me, sealed up in my treasuries?
Vengeance and recompense are mine,{k} for the time when their foot shall slip; for their day of calamity is at hand, and their doom comes swiftly.’
For Yahweh will judge his people and relent concerning his servants, when he sees that their power has vanished and none remain, whether bound or free.
Then he will say, ‘Where are their gods, the rock in which they sought refuge,
who ate the fat of their sacrifices and drank the wine of their drink offerings? Let them get up and help you; let them be a shelter over you!
“‘See now that I, even I, am he, and there is no god beside me; I am the one who puts to death and gives life; I have wounded, and I myself heal, and none can deliver from my hand.
For I raise my hand to heaven and say, As I live forever,
once I whet my lightning sword and my hand grasps judgment, I will pay back vengeance to my foes and repay those who hate me.
I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword will feed on flesh, with the blood of the slain and the captives, from the heads of the long-haired leaders of the enemy.’{l}
“Shout for joy, you nations, over his people,{m} for he will avenge the blood of his servants. He will pay back vengeance to his foes and make atonement for his land and his people.”{n}
Moses came and recited all the words of this song in the ears of the people, he and Hoshea{o} son of Nun.
When Moses had finished speaking all these words to all Israel,
he said to them, “Set your hearts on all the words I testify to you today, so that you may command your children to take care to do every word of this law.
For this is no empty word for you; it is your very life. Through this word your days will be long on the soil you are going over the Jordan to possess.”
That same day Yahweh spoke to Moses:
“Go up this Abarim mountain range,{p} to Mount Nebo, in the land of Moab across from Jericho, and look at the land of Canaan, which I am giving to the Israelites for a possession;
and die on the mountain you are about to ascend, and be gathered to your people, as your brother Aaron died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people,
because you both broke faith with me among the Israelites at the waters of Meribah-kadesh{q} in the Wilderness of Zin, by failing to uphold my holiness among the Israelites.
You will see the land from a distance, but you will not go into the land I am giving to the Israelites.”

notes.text: The Hebrew of this line is obscure. The Septuagint reads “spotted children” (Brenton).
Or “created you.”
Hebrew ‘Elyon, a title of God meaning “highest.”
Or “humankind”; Hebrew “the sons of Adam.”

So the traditional Hebrew text (MT). A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran (4QDeut-j) reads “the sons of God,” and many scholars regard that as the earlier reading. The Septuagint reads “the angels of God” (Brenton), and some Greek manuscripts are reported to read “the sons of God.” The difference bears on whether the nations are allotted to heavenly beings under the Most High (compare 4:19; 29:26). This needs scholarly review.
Hebrew “the little man of his eye.”
Jeshurun means “upright one,” a poetic name for Israel. The Septuagint reads “So Jacob ate and was filled, and the beloved one kicked” (Brenton).
Hebrew hebel, “vapor” or “breath.”
Sheol is the realm of the dead.
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “cut them in pieces” or “blow them away.”
The Septuagint reads “In the day of vengeance I will recompense” (Brenton). Romans 12:19 and Hebrews 10:30 quote this line as “Vengeance is mine; I will repay.”
Or “from the heads of the enemy’s leaders.”
Or “Praise his people, you nations.” The traditional Hebrew wording is brief and can be read several ways.

This verse is much longer in other ancient witnesses. The Septuagint reads (Brenton, modernized): “Rejoice, you heavens, with him, and let all the angels of God worship him; rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people, and let all the sons of God strengthen themselves in him; for he will avenge the blood of his sons, and he will render vengeance, and recompense justice to his enemies, and will reward those who hate him; and the Lord shall purge the land of his people.” A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran (4QDeut-q) is reported to have a longer text than the traditional Hebrew as well, including a call to the heavens to rejoice and to the gods (or heavenly beings) to bow down to him. Hebrews 1:6 and Romans 15:10 appear to draw on the longer form. This needs scholarly review.

Hoshea means “salvation,” the earlier name of Joshua (Numbers 13:16). The Septuagint reads “Joshua” (Brenton, “Joshua the son of Naue”), and it also begins the verse, “And Moses wrote this song in that day, and taught it to the children of Israel.”
Abarim means “regions beyond,” the range east of the Jordan facing Jericho.
Meribah means “quarreling”; see Numbers 20:1–13.

verses.text: Here is the blessing which Moses, the man of God, spoke over the Israelites before he died.
He said: “Yahweh came from Sinai, and rose from Seir upon them; he shone forth from Mount Paran, and came with ten thousands of holy ones;{a} at his right hand was a flaming fire{b} for them.
Truly he loves the peoples;{c} all his holy ones are in your hand. They sit at your feet, each receiving your words.
Moses gave us a law, a possession for the assembly of Jacob.
And there was a king in Jeshurun, when the heads of the people gathered, the tribes of Israel together.
“Let Reuben live and not die, though his men be few.”
And this he said for Judah: “Hear, Yahweh, the voice of Judah, and bring him in to his people. With his own hands he fights for his cause;{d} be his help against his foes.”
For Levi he said: “Your Thummim and your Urim{e} belong to your faithful man, whom you tested at Massah, with whom you strove at the waters of Meribah;
who said of his father and of his mother, ‘I regard them not’; he did not acknowledge his brothers, nor know his own children. For they have observed your word and kept your covenant.
They teach your rulings to Jacob and your law to Israel; they set incense before you{f} and whole burnt offerings on your altar.
Bless, Yahweh, his strength, and take pleasure in the work of his hands. Smash the loins of his attackers, of those who hate him, so that they rise no more.”
For Benjamin he said: “The one Yahweh loves dwells in safety beside him. He shelters him all day long, and he rests between his shoulders.”{g}
For Joseph he said: “May his land be blessed by Yahweh with the choicest gifts of heaven, the dew, and of the deep that crouches below,
with the choicest yield of the sun and the rich produce of the months,{h}
with the finest things of the ancient mountains and the wealth of the hills that last forever,
and with the choicest gifts of the earth and its fullness, and the good will of him who lived in the bush. May they come on the head of Joseph, on the brow of the prince among his brothers.

His firstborn bull has majesty, and his horns are the horns of the wild ox; with them he shall gore peoples, every one, to earth’s farthest limits; they are the ten thousands of Ephraim, and they are the thousands of Manasseh.”
For Zebulun he said: “Rejoice, Zebulun, as you go out, and you, Issachar, in your tents.
They will summon peoples to the mountain; there they will offer right sacrifices, for they will draw on the wealth of the seas and the treasures hidden in the sand.”
For Gad he said: “Blessed be the one who makes Gad’s land wide! Gad lies in wait like a lioness and tears off arm and scalp alike.
He chose the first part for himself, for a ruler’s portion was kept for him there. He came with the heads of the people; he carried out the justice of Yahweh and his rulings for Israel.”
For Dan he said: “Dan is a lion’s whelp that springs out from Bashan.”
For Naphtali he said: “Naphtali, filled with favor and full of Yahweh’s blessing, take possession of the sea{i} and the south.”
For Asher he said: “Asher is blessed above the other sons; let his brothers look on him with favor, and may he bathe his feet in oil.
Your bolts will be of iron and bronze, and your strength{j} will last as long as your days.
“There is none like God, Jeshurun, who rides the heavens to your aid, and the clouds in his majesty.
The God of old is your dwelling place,{k} and underneath are the arms that last forever. He drove out the enemy before you and said, ‘Destroy!’
So Israel dwells in safety, the spring of Jacob undisturbed,{l} in a land of grain and new wine, where the heavens drip with dew.

How happy you are, Israel! Who is like you, a people saved by Yahweh, the shield that helps you and the sword of your triumph? Your enemies will come cringing to you, and you will tread upon their high places.”{m}

notes.text: Or “from Ribeboth-kodesh,” perhaps a place name. The Septuagint reads “with the ten thousands of Kadesh” (Brenton, “Cades”).
Hebrew uncertain. The written Hebrew has a single obscure word; it is traditionally read as two words, “fire of law.” The Septuagint reads “on his right hand were his angels with him” (Brenton).
Or “his people.” The Septuagint reads “he spared his people” (Brenton).
Or “his hands are enough for him.”

The Urim and Thummim were the priestly lots used to seek God’s will; the names may mean “lights” and “perfections.” The Septuagint begins, “Give to Levi” (Brenton), and a Qumran manuscript is reported to read similarly.
Hebrew “in your nostrils.”
Or “and he dwells among his slopes,” perhaps a reference to the temple hill in Benjamin’s territory.
Or “moons.”
Or “the west.” Hebrew yam can mean “sea” or “west”; here perhaps the Sea of Galilee.
Hebrew uncertain; the word may mean “strength” or “rest.”
Or “refuge.”
Or “alone.”
Or “trample on their backs.”

verses.text: Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the summit of Pisgah, which faces Jericho, and Yahweh showed him the whole land: Gilead as far as Dan,
all of Naphtali, the land of Ephraim and Manasseh, all the land of Judah up to the sea in the west,{a}
the Negev,{b} and the plain of the valley of Jericho, the city of palm trees, as far as Zoar.

Then Yahweh said to him, “This is the land I swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob when I said, ‘To your offspring I will give it.’ I have shown it to you, and you have seen it, but you yourself will not go over there.”
So Moses, the servant of Yahweh, died there in the land of Moab, as Yahweh had said.{c}
And he buried him{d} in the valley in the land of Moab opposite Beth Peor; but his burial place is unknown to this day.
Moses was 120 years old when he died. His sight had not grown dim, and his vigor had not left him.
The Israelites mourned for Moses in the plains of Moab thirty days, until the days of weeping in mourning for Moses were complete.
Now Joshua son of Nun was full of the spirit of wisdom, since Moses had placed his hands upon him, and the Israelites obeyed him and did what Yahweh had commanded Moses.
Never since has a prophet arisen in Israel like Moses, whom Yahweh knew face to face,
none like him for all the signs and wonders Yahweh sent him to perform in Egypt against Pharaoh and against all his officials and his whole land,
and for all the mighty deeds and all the great and awesome acts that Moses did in the sight of all Israel.

notes.text: That is, the Mediterranean.
Negev means “dry land,” the arid south of Judah.
Hebrew “at the mouth of Yahweh.” Later Jewish tradition read this as “by the kiss of Yahweh.”
That is, Yahweh buried him. Or “he was buried.” The Septuagint reads “they buried him” (Brenton).

books.name: Joshua
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls of Joshua (4QJosh-a and 4QJosh-b). The Old Greek of Joshua often differs from the Hebrew. It is shorter in many places, it places the altar on Mount Ebal (8:30–35) after 9:2, and it adds material, most notably after 24:31 and 24:33. The major differences are given in the footnotes. Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a places the reading of the Law (8:34–35) right after the Jordan crossing, before 5:2. This was checked against published descriptions of the scroll (Ulrich), and other scroll readings are stated in general terms. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible. Measurements are given in modern US units, and calendar dates with their modern-month equivalents, with the originals and metric figures in the footnotes. Place names whose meaning is known or likely have a note at their first appearance.

verses.text: After the death of Moses the servant of Yahweh, Yahweh said to Joshua{a} the son of Nun,{b} Moses’ assistant,
“My servant Moses has died. So now get up and go across this Jordan,{c} you and all these people, to the land I am about to give them—to the Israelites.
Every place on which the sole of your foot treads I have given to you, as I promised Moses.
Your territory will stretch from the wilderness and this Lebanon{d} to the great river, the Euphrates—the whole land of the Hittites—and west to the Great Sea{e} where the sun goes down.
No one will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you or forsake you.
Be strong and courageous, for you will cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.
Just be strong and very bold, and take care to carry out the whole law that my servant Moses commanded you. Do not stray from it to the right or the left, so that you will prosper{f} wherever you go.

This book of the law must not depart from your mouth, but you are to meditate{g} on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will succeed.
Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be terrified or dismayed, for Yahweh your God is with you wherever you go.”
Then Joshua commanded the officers of the people, saying,

“Go through the camp and give the people this order: ‘Get your provisions ready, because in three days you will cross this Jordan to enter and take the land Yahweh your God is giving you as your possession.’”
To the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,
“Remember the word that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, saying, ‘Yahweh your God is giving you rest and will give you this land.’
Your wives, children, and livestock may stay in the land Moses gave you east of the Jordan,{h} but all of you who are mighty warriors must cross over armed{i} ahead of your brothers and help them,

until Yahweh gives your brothers rest as he has given you, and they also take possession of the land that Yahweh your God is giving them. Then you may return to the land of your possession and possess it, the land that Moses the servant of Yahweh gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise.”
They answered Joshua, saying, “All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.
Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may Yahweh your God be with you as he was with Moses.
“Anyone who rebels against your order and will not obey your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Just be strong and courageous.”

notes.text: Hebrew Yehoshua‘, “Yahweh is salvation” (or “Yahweh saves”). His earlier name was Hoshea, “salvation” (Numbers 13:16). The Greek form of the name is Iesous, “Jesus.”
Nun may mean “fish.” The Septuagint spells it Naue.
Hebrew Yarden, probably “the one that goes down,” fitting the river’s steep descent to the Dead Sea.
Lebanon means “white,” perhaps from its snowy peaks or limestone cliffs. The Septuagint reads “Antilibanus.”
That is, the Mediterranean Sea.
Or “act wisely”; so in verse 8.
Hebrew hagah, to murmur or read in an undertone (compare Psalm 1:2).
That is, east of the Jordan.
Or “in battle formation”; the Hebrew ḥamushim is related to the word for “five,” perhaps describing an army in five divisions.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun secretly sent two men as spies from Shittim,{a} saying, “Go, look over the land, especially Jericho.”{b} So they went and came into the house of a prostitute{c} whose name was Rahab,{d} and lodged there.
It was told the king of Jericho, “Look, men from the Israelites have come here tonight to search out the land.”
Then the king of Jericho sent this message to Rahab: “Bring forth the men who came to you, the ones now in your house, for they came to scout out all the land.”
The woman, however, had taken the two men and hidden them. She replied, “True, men did come to me, though I had no idea where they were from.
At dark, when the gate was about to close, the men left. Where they went I do not know. Chase after them quickly, and you will catch them.”
But she had brought them up to the roof and hidden them under the stalks of flax that she had laid out on the roof.
The men chased after them along the road to the Jordan, toward the fords, and as soon as the pursuers had gone out, the gate was shut behind them.
Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof
and said to the men, “I know that Yahweh has given the land to you, that dread of you has fallen on us, and that everyone living in the land is melting away because of you.

For we have heard how Yahweh dried up the water of the Red Sea{e} before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.{f}
When we heard it, our hearts melted, and no courage remained in anyone because of you, for Yahweh your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
Now then, please swear to me by Yahweh, since I have dealt kindly with you, that you also will deal kindly with my father’s house, and give me a sure sign,
and that you will let my father, my mother, my brothers, my sisters, and everyone belonging to them live, and rescue our lives from death.”

The men said to her, “We pledge our own lives for yours, even to the death!{g} If you do not reveal this business of ours, then when Yahweh gives us the land we will treat you with kindness and loyalty.”
Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was in the town wall, and she lived in the wall.
She said to them, “Go into the hill country, so that the pursuers do not meet you. Hide there three days until the pursuers have returned, and afterward you may go on your way.”
The men said to her, “We will be free from this oath of yours that you have made us swear,

unless, as we enter the land, you fasten this cord of scarlet thread to the window by which you lowered us, and bring your father, mother, brothers, and all your father’s household together into your house.

Anyone who goes out from the doors of your house into the street will have his blood on his own head, and we will be free of blame. But for anyone with you in the house, his blood will be on our heads if any hand is laid on him.
But if you tell this business of ours, then we will be free from your oath that you have made us swear.”
She said, “According to your words, so be it.” Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
They went and came into the hill country and stayed there three days, until the pursuers returned. The pursuers searched all along the way but did not find them.
The two men then came back down from the hill country, crossed the river, and came to Joshua son of Nun, and reported to him everything that had happened to them.
They said to Joshua, “Truly Yahweh has given all the land into our hands, and all the inhabitants of the land melt away before us.”

notes.text: Shittim means “acacia trees” (Numbers 25:1).
Jericho may mean “moon city,” from yareaḥ, “moon,” or “fragrant place,” from reaḥ, “scent.” The meaning is uncertain.

Hebrew zonah. Josephus and the Aramaic Targum understood her as an innkeeper, but the Hebrew word means “prostitute,” as the Septuagint (pornē) and the New Testament (Hebrews 11:31; James 2:25) take it.
Rahab means “broad” or “wide.” She appears in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Hebrew ḥaram, to give something over completely to Yahweh, usually by destroying it. See the note at 6:17.
Literally “Our life in place of yours, to die.”

verses.text: Early in the morning Joshua got up, and he and all the Israelites set out from Shittim and came to the Jordan; there they stayed before crossing over.
At the end of three days the officers went through the middle of the camp
and commanded the people, saying, “When you see the ark of the covenant of Yahweh your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you are to set out from your place and follow it.
There must be a space between you and it of about 3,000 feet,{a} measured out. Stay back from it, so that you will know which way to go, since you have not traveled this way before.”
Joshua said to the people, “Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow Yahweh will do wonders among you.”
To the priests Joshua said, “Lift up the ark of the covenant and cross over ahead of the people.” They lifted it and walked ahead of the people.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so that they may know that as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.
You yourself are to command the priests carrying the ark of the covenant: ‘When you reach the edge of the Jordan’s waters, stand still in the Jordan.’”
Joshua said to the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of Yahweh your God.”

Joshua said, “By this you will know that the living God is among you, and that he will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.
Look, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth goes ahead of you into the Jordan.
Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one man from each tribe.

When the soles of the feet of the priests who carry the ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan will be cut off, the waters coming down from above, and they will stand in one heap.”
So when the people set out from their tents to cross over the Jordan, with the priests carrying the ark of the covenant before the people,
and when those carrying the ark reached the Jordan and the priests’ feet touched the water’s edge (the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the harvest season),{b}

the waters flowing down from upstream stopped and stood up in a single heap, a great distance away at Adam,{c} the city next to Zarethan,{d} while the waters running down to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea,{e} were entirely cut off, and the people crossed over facing Jericho.

The priests who carried the ark of the covenant of Yahweh stood firmly on dry ground in the Jordan’s middle while all Israel crossed over on dry ground, until the entire nation had finished crossing the Jordan.

notes.text: Hebrew “two thousand cubits,” about 900 meters.
That is, the barley and wheat harvest in spring (April–May), when the Jordan was swollen with rain and melting snow from Mount Hermon. Compare 4:19.

Adam means “red” or “earth,” perhaps from the color of its soil. It is probably Tell ed-Damiyeh, about 18 miles (30 kilometers) north of Jericho. Medieval Arabic sources report that landslides there blocked the Jordan in A.D. 1267, and an earthquake did so again in 1927. The Hebrew reads “at Adam,” following the qere (the reading tradition); the written text has “in Adam.”
The location of Zarethan is uncertain.
That is, the Dead Sea.

verses.text: When all the nation had finished crossing over the Jordan, Yahweh said to Joshua,
“Take for yourselves twelve men from the people, one man from each tribe,

and tell them: ‘From this spot in the middle of the Jordan, where the priests’ feet stood firm, pick up twelve stones for yourselves, carry them across with you, and set them down in the place where you will stay tonight.’”
Then Joshua called the twelve men whom he had appointed from the Israelites, one man from each tribe.

Joshua said to them, “Cross over before the ark of Yahweh your God into the middle of the Jordan, and each of you lift a stone on his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the Israelites,
so that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, ‘What do these stones mean to you?’

you are to tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of Yahweh. When it crossed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones are to be a memorial to the Israelites forever.”

The Israelites did exactly as Joshua had ordered: they picked up twelve stones from the Jordan’s middle, matching the number of the tribes of Israel, as Yahweh had told Joshua, carried them to their campsite, and set them down there.
Joshua also set up twelve stones in the middle of the Jordan,{a} in the place where the feet of the priests carrying the ark of the covenant had stood, and they are there to this day.

The priests who carried the ark stayed standing in the Jordan’s middle until everything Yahweh had commanded Joshua to tell the people was done, in keeping with all that Moses had ordered Joshua. And the people hurried across.
When all the people had finished crossing over, the ark of Yahweh and the priests crossed over before the people.
The Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed over armed before the Israelites, as Moses had told them.
About forty thousand armed for war crossed over before Yahweh for battle, to the plains of Jericho.
That day Yahweh made Joshua great in the eyes of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him all his life, as they had of Moses.
Yahweh said to Joshua,
“Command the priests carrying the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan.”
So Joshua commanded the priests, saying, “Come up out of the Jordan.”

When the priests carrying the ark of the covenant of Yahweh came up from the middle of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests’ feet were lifted up onto dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and ran over all its banks as before.
The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month (in March–April),{b} and they camped at Gilgal{c} on the east border of Jericho.
As for the twelve stones taken from the Jordan, Joshua set them up at Gilgal.
He said to the Israelites, “When your children ask their fathers in time to come, ‘What are these stones?’
then you are to let your children know, ‘Israel crossed over this Jordan on dry ground.’
For Yahweh your God dried up the waters of the Jordan before you until you had crossed over, as Yahweh your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up before us until we had crossed over,
so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of Yahweh is mighty, and that you may fear Yahweh your God forever.”

notes.text: Or “Joshua set up the twelve stones that had been in the middle of the Jordan.” The Septuagint reads “other twelve stones,” and the Latin Vulgate also speaks of a second set in the riverbed.

Hebrew “in the first month,” counted from the spring new year of Israel’s religious calendar (Exodus 12:2). It was called Abib and later Nisan. Because the Hebrew months were lunar, it fell in March–April. The tenth day was the day the Passover lamb was chosen (Exodus 12:3).
Gilgal means “circle,” probably a circle of stones. Joshua 5:9 links the name with galal, “to roll away.”

verses.text: When the kings of the Amorites on the Jordan’s west side, together with all the kings of the Canaanites by the sea, heard how Yahweh had dried up the Jordan’s waters in front of the Israelites until we{a} crossed over, their hearts melted, and they had no spirit left to face the Israelites.
Yahweh said to Joshua at that time,{b} “Make yourself flint knives and circumcise the Israelites a second time.”
So Joshua made flint knives for himself and circumcised the Israelites at Gibeath-haaraloth.{c}
This is the reason Joshua circumcised them: all the people who came out of Egypt, the males, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they came out of Egypt.
All the people who came out of Egypt had been circumcised, but none of those born in the wilderness on the journey out of Egypt had been.

The Israelites had walked in the wilderness forty years, until the whole nation—the men of war who left Egypt—died out, because they had not obeyed Yahweh’s voice. Yahweh had sworn to them that he would not let them see the land he swore to their fathers to give us, a land flowing with milk and honey.{d}
Their sons, whom he raised up in their place, were the ones Joshua circumcised, since they were uncircumcised, not having been circumcised during the journey.
When they had finished circumcising all the nation, they stayed in their places in the camp until they were healed.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “This day I have rolled off{e} you the disgrace of Egypt.” That is why the place is named Gilgal to this day.
While the Israelites were camped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month (in March–April),{f} at evening, in the plains of Jericho.
The day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate unleavened bread and roasted grain{g} from the produce of the land.
The manna stopped the next day, when they ate the land’s produce; the Israelites had no more manna, and that year they ate from the crops of Canaan.

When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and there was a man standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. Joshua went to him and said to him, “Are you for us or for our adversaries?”
“No,” he said, “but I have just now come as commander of Yahweh’s army.” Joshua fell with his face to the ground, worshiped, and asked him, “What does my lord have to say to his servant?”
The commander of Yahweh’s army said to Joshua, “Take off your sandal from your foot, for the place where you are standing is holy.” And Joshua did so.

notes.text: So the Hebrew written text (ketiv). The qere (the reading tradition), many Hebrew manuscripts, and the ancient versions read “they.”

The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a (about 150–50 B.C.) is arranged differently here. In it, the end of the account of the reading of the Law (8:34–35) comes right before this verse, linked by a transitional sentence not found in other witnesses. In that order, the covenant reading, and perhaps the building of the altar, took place at Gilgal right after the Jordan crossing. Josephus (Antiquities 5.16–20) also places an altar soon after the crossing. Compare the note at 8:30.
Gibeath-haaraloth means “hill of the foreskins.”
In verses 4–6 the Septuagint has a different text. It says that some of those who came out of Egypt had been uncircumcised, and that Israel wandered forty-two years in the wilderness.
Hebrew galal, which sounds like Gilgal; see the note at 4:19.

Hebrew “on the fourteenth day of the month,” that is, the first month of the spring-start religious calendar (4:19). It was called Abib or Nisan and fell in March–April. The exact correspondence varies from year to year with the lunar calendar.
The Septuagint lacks “on the day after the Passover.”

verses.text: Now Jericho was shut up tight because of the Israelites. No one went out and no one came in.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “See, I have given into your hand Jericho and its king, the mighty men of valor.
You are to march around the city, all the men of war, going around the city once. You are to do this for six days.
Seven priests are to carry seven rams’ horn trumpets{a} before the ark; on the seventh day, march around the city seven times, with the priests blowing the trumpets.

When they make a long blast with the ram’s horn, as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, all the people are to shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat,{b} and the people are to go up, each man straight before him.”
Joshua son of Nun called the priests and told them, “Pick up the ark of the covenant, and have seven priests carry seven rams’ horn trumpets in front of Yahweh’s ark.”
He{c} told the people, “Advance, and march around the city, with the armed men going ahead of Yahweh’s ark.”

Just as Joshua had spoken to the people, the seven priests carrying the seven trumpets of rams’ horns before Yahweh went forward and blew the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of Yahweh following them.
The armed men went before the priests who blew the trumpets, and the rear guard went after the ark, with the trumpets blowing continually.
But Joshua commanded the people, “You are not to shout or let your voice be heard, nor let a word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you are to shout.”
So he had Yahweh’s ark carried around the city once. Then they went back into the camp and spent the night there.
Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of Yahweh.

The seven priests with the seven rams’ horn trumpets walked ahead of Yahweh’s ark, blowing the trumpets without stopping, with the armed men in front of them and the rear guard behind the ark, while the trumpets sounded without stopping.
On the second day they marched around the city once and returned to the camp. They did this for six days.
On the seventh day they rose at daybreak and went around the city in that same fashion seven times; only on that day did they circle it seven times.
On the seventh circuit, as the priests blew the trumpets, Joshua told the people, “Shout! Yahweh has given you the city.

The city and all that is in it belongs to Yahweh, set apart{d} for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute will live, along with everyone in the house with her, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.
As for you, stay away from what is set apart for destruction, or you will set it apart and then take some of it, making Israel’s camp subject to destruction and bringing trouble{e} on it.
But all silver and gold, and vessels of bronze and iron, are holy to Yahweh. They are to go into the treasury of Yahweh.”

So the people shouted when the trumpets sounded. When they heard the trumpet blast, they gave a great shout, and the wall collapsed where it stood. Then the people went up into the city, each man straight ahead, and took it.
They devoted to destruction all that was in the city, both man and woman, young and old, and ox, sheep, and donkey, with the edge of the sword.
Joshua instructed the two spies, “Go to that prostitute’s house, and from there bring the woman out with everything that is hers, as you swore to her.”

The young men who had been the spies went in and brought out Rahab, with her father, mother, brothers, and everyone belonging to her; they brought out all her family and placed them outside Israel’s camp.
They put the city to the torch with all it contained; the silver and gold, however, along with the bronze and iron vessels, they deposited in the treasury of Yahweh’s house.

Joshua spared Rahab the prostitute, her father’s household, and everyone belonging to her. She has lived among the Israelites to this day, because she hid the messengers Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.

At that time Joshua put them under an oath: “Cursed before Yahweh is the man who gets up and builds this city, Jericho. He will lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn, and set up its gates at the price of his youngest.”{f}
So Yahweh was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.

notes.text: Hebrew shofarot hayyovelim, “ram’s-horn trumpets”; the word yovel, “ram,” also gave its name to the Jubilee (Leviticus 25).
Literally “will fall in its place.”
So the qere (the reading tradition), the Septuagint, and other witnesses. The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “They.”
Hebrew ḥerem, something given over completely to Yahweh, which could not be used by people. In war this usually meant its total destruction; so throughout this book.
Hebrew ‘akhar, “trouble”; compare the Valley of Achor in 7:26.

The Septuagint adds, “And so did Hozan of Bethel. He laid its foundation with Abiron his firstborn, and set up its gates with his youngest surviving son.” Compare the fulfillment in 1 Kings 16:34, where the builder is Hiel of Bethel and his sons are Abiram and Segub.

verses.text: But the Israelites acted unfaithfully in regard to the devoted things, for Achan{a} the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi,{b} the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of Yahweh burned against the Israelites.
Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai,{c} which is near Beth-aven,{d} east of Bethel,{e} and said to them, “Go up and spy out the land.” So the men went up and spied out Ai.

They went back to Joshua and told him, “There is no need for all the people to go up. Send up two or three thousand men to attack Ai. Do not wear out all the people by sending them there, for the people of Ai are few.”
So some three thousand of the people went up, but they ran from the men of Ai.

The men of Ai struck down about thirty-six of them, and chased them from before the gate as far as Shebarim,{f} and struck them down on the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became like water.
Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell on his face to the earth before the ark of Yahweh until the evening, he and the elders of Israel, and they put dust on their heads.

Joshua said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us? If only we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!
O Lord, what can I say, now that Israel has turned their backs before their enemies?
For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it, and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?”
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?

Israel has sinned! They have violated the covenant I laid on them; they have taken some of the things set apart for destruction, and they have stolen, lied, and hidden them among their own possessions.

Therefore the Israelites cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted to destruction. I will not be with you anymore unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.

Rise, consecrate the people, and tell them, ‘Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow, because Yahweh, the God of Israel, says this: “Things set apart for destruction are among you, Israel. You will be unable to stand against your enemies until you remove those things from your midst.”

In the morning you are to come near by your tribes. The tribe that Yahweh takes{g} is to come near by clans, the clan that Yahweh takes is to come near by households, and the household that Yahweh takes is to come near man by man.
Whoever is found with the things set apart for destruction shall be burned with fire, along with all he owns, because he broke the covenant of Yahweh and did a disgraceful thing{h} in Israel.’”
Joshua got up early the next morning and had the tribes of Israel step forward one at a time, and the tribe of Judah was taken.
He had the clans of Judah come forward, and the Zerahite clan was taken. Then he had the Zerahite clan come forward man by man,{i} and Zabdi was taken.
He brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.
Then Joshua said to Achan, “My son, give glory to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and give praise to him.{j} Tell me now what you have done. Do not hide it from me.”
Achan answered Joshua, “Truly I have sinned against Yahweh, the God of Israel, and this is what I did:

Among the plunder I saw a lovely robe from Shinar,{k} about 5 pounds of silver,{l} and a bar of gold of about 20 ounces,{m} and I wanted them, so I took them. Look, they are buried in the ground inside my tent, with the silver under it.”
So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent, and there it was, hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.
They took them from the middle of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the Israelites, and they laid them out before Yahweh.

Then Joshua, and all Israel with him, took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons, his daughters, his oxen, his donkeys, his sheep, his tent, and all that he had, and they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.
Joshua said, “Why did you bring trouble on us? Today Yahweh brings trouble on you.” Then all Israel pelted him with stones; they burned the rest in the fire and pelted them with stones.

Over him they piled a great heap of stones, which is still there today. Then Yahweh turned back from the fierceness of his anger. For this reason that place has been called the Valley of Achor{n} to this day.

notes.text: The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 2:7 call him Achar, “trouble,” which makes a wordplay with the Valley of Achor (verses 25–26).
The Septuagint has Zambri; 1 Chronicles 2:6 has Zimri.
Ai (Hebrew ha‘ai, always with the article) means “the ruin” or “the heap.”
Beth-aven means “house of wickedness” (or “of nothingness”). Hosea 4:15 later uses the name mockingly for Bethel.
Bethel means “house of God” (Genesis 28:19).
Or “the quarries”; the Hebrew word means “breakings.”
That is, the tribe that is selected, probably by casting the lot.
Or “a disgraceful folly” (Hebrew nevalah).
Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and the Syriac read “by households,” as in verse 14.
Or “and make confession to him.” This was a formula calling someone to tell the truth under oath (compare John 9:24).
That is, Babylonia. The Septuagint reads “an embroidered cloak.”
Hebrew “200 shekels,” about 2.3 kilograms.
Hebrew “50 shekels,” about 575 grams. Literally “a tongue of gold,” that is, a wedge-shaped ingot.
Achor means “trouble.” Compare Hosea 2:15 and Isaiah 65:10, where the valley becomes a place of hope.

verses.text: Yahweh said to Joshua, “Do not be afraid or discouraged. Take the whole army with you and go up to Ai. Look, I have handed over to you the king of Ai, his people, his city, and his land.
Do to Ai and its king what you did to Jericho and its king; but you may keep its plunder and livestock for yourselves. Set an ambush behind the city.”
So Joshua and all the men of war arose to go up to Ai. Joshua chose thirty thousand mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.
He commanded them, “Listen, you are to lie in wait behind the city; do not go very far from it, and all of you stay ready.
I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. When they come out against us as at the first, we will flee before them.
They will come out after us until we have lured them away from the city, for they will say, ‘They are running from us, as before.’ So we will run from them.
Then you are to rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for Yahweh your God will give it into your hand.
When you have taken the city, you are to set the city on fire. You are to do according to the word of Yahweh. See, I have commanded you.”
So Joshua sent them out, and they went to the place of ambush and stayed between Bethel and Ai, west of Ai. But Joshua spent that night among the people.
Early in the morning Joshua assembled the people, and he and the elders of Israel went up ahead of them to Ai.
All the men of war who were with him went up and drew near and came before the city, and they camped north of Ai, with the valley between them and Ai.
He took about five thousand men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, west of the city.
So the people took their positions, the main camp north of the city and its rear guard to the west. And that night Joshua went into the middle of the valley.{a}

When the king of Ai saw this, he and his whole people, the men of the city, hurried and got up early to meet Israel in battle at the appointed place{b} facing the Arabah; but he did not know that an ambush lay behind the city.
Joshua and all Israel let themselves be beaten before them and fled by the way of the wilderness.
All the people in the city{c} were summoned to chase after them, and as they chased Joshua they were lured away from the city.
Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel{d} who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.
Yahweh then said to Joshua, “Hold out toward Ai the javelin{e} in your hand, for I am giving it into your hand.” So Joshua held out toward the city the javelin in his hand.
As soon as he stretched out his hand, the men in ambush sprang up from their place and ran. They went into the city, took it, and quickly set it on fire.

The men of Ai turned and looked behind them, and saw the city’s smoke rising to the sky; they had no strength to run either way, for the people who had been fleeing toward the wilderness turned on those chasing them.
Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had taken the city and that smoke was rising from it, so they turned around and attacked the men of Ai.

The others from the city came out to meet them, so that the men of Ai were caught in the middle of Israel, with some on one side and some on the other. Israel cut them down until no one was left alive or escaped.
But the king of Ai they took alive and brought him to Joshua.

When Israel had finished killing all the people of Ai in the open fields and the wilderness where they had chased them, and every one of them had fallen by the sword to the last man, all Israel went back to Ai and put it to the sword.
All who fell that day, both men and women, were twelve thousand, all the people of Ai.
For Joshua did not pull back the hand that held out the javelin until he had set apart all who lived in Ai for destruction.{f}
Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as plunder for themselves, according to the word of Yahweh that he commanded Joshua.
Joshua burned Ai and made it a mound{g} forever, a waste to this day.

He hung the king of Ai on a tree until evening, and at sunset Joshua gave the order, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the city gate. Over it they raised a large pile of stones, which is still there.
Then Joshua built an altar{h} to Yahweh, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,{i}

just as Moses, Yahweh’s servant, had commanded the Israelites and as it is written in the book of the law of Moses: an altar of uncut stones that no iron tool had touched. On it they offered burnt offerings to Yahweh and sacrificed peace offerings.
There, in the presence of the Israelites, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.

All Israel—the foreign resident as well as the native-born—with their elders, officers, and judges, stood on both sides of the ark facing the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, half toward Mount Gerizim{j} and half toward Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of Yahweh had earlier commanded for blessing the people of Israel.
Afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the book of the law.

Of everything Moses had commanded, there was not a word that Joshua failed to read before the entire assembly of Israel, including the women, the little children, and the foreign residents living among them.

notes.text: Some Hebrew manuscripts read “spent that night” (compare verse 9). The Septuagint lacks most of verses 11b–13; it does not mention the second ambush of five thousand men.
Hebrew mo‘ed; or, with a small change, “at the descent.” The Septuagint lacks this phrase.
The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “in the city”; the qere (the reading tradition) reads “in Ai.”
The Septuagint lacks “or Bethel.”
Or “scimitar” (Hebrew kidon); a curved sword is possible. The Septuagint reads “spear.”
The Septuagint lacks this verse.
Hebrew tel, a mound of ruins, the word that gave its name to the archaeological “tell.” The name Ai means “the ruin” (see the note at 7:2).

The Hebrew text places the altar and the covenant reading on Mount Ebal (verses 30–35) here. The Septuagint places them after 9:2. The Qumran scroll 4QJosh-a apparently placed at least the reading of the Law (verses 34–35) right after the Jordan crossing, before 5:2 (see the note there). These different placements suggest that the passage was positioned differently in different early forms of the text. Compare Deuteronomy 11:29; 27:1–26.
Ebal may mean “bare” or “stony.” Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim stand on either side of Shechem.
Gerizim may mean “those cut off.” The Samaritans later regarded it as the chosen place of worship (compare John 4:20).

verses.text: When all the kings west of the Jordan heard about this—those in the hill country, the lowland,{a} and along the whole coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon: the Hittites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites—
they gathered together with one accord to fight against Joshua and Israel.{b}
But when the inhabitants of Gibeon{c} heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,
they also acted craftily. They went and disguised themselves as envoys,{d} and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins that were worn-out, torn, and mended,
with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet and worn-out clothes on them. And all the bread of their provisions was dry and crumbly.
They went to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, “We have come from a distant country. Now therefore make a covenant with us.”
The men of Israel replied to the Hivites, “Maybe you live among us; how then could we make a covenant with you?”
They told Joshua, “We are your servants.” But Joshua demanded, “Who are you, and from where have you come?”
They answered, “Your servants have come from a very distant country because of the name of Yahweh your God, for we have heard news of him, and of all he did in Egypt,
and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon king of Heshbon and to Og king of Bashan, who was at Ashtaroth.
So our elders and everyone living in our land told us, ‘Take provisions for the journey, go meet them, and tell them: “We are your servants; so now make a covenant with us.”’
This bread of ours was still warm when we took it from our houses as food for the journey on the day we left to come to you; but now look, it is dry and crumbling.
These wineskins were new when we filled them, and see, they are torn. And these clothes and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey.”
So the men took some of their provisions, but they did not ask counsel from the mouth of Yahweh.
Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore an oath to them.
At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.
So the Israelites set out and came to their cities on the third day. Their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.{e}
But the Israelites did not strike them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by Yahweh, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation grumbled against the leaders.
But all the leaders said to all the congregation, “We have sworn to them by Yahweh, the God of Israel, and now we cannot touch them.
This is what we will do: we will let them live, so that no wrath will fall on us because of the oath we swore to them.”
The leaders added, “Let them live.” So they became woodcutters and water carriers for the whole congregation, as the leaders had decided concerning them.
Joshua called them and said, “Why did you trick us by saying, ‘We live very far from you,’ when you actually live among us?
Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you will never cease to be slaves, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God.”

They answered Joshua, “Because it was clearly told to your servants that Yahweh your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land before you, we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.
Now, see, we are in your hand. Do to us whatever seems good and right in your sight.”
So he did this to them: he delivered them out of the hand of the Israelites, and they did not kill them.
That day Joshua made them cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of Yahweh, to this day, at the place that he would choose.

notes.text: Hebrew shephelah, the low foothills between the hill country of Judah and the coastal plain.

Here the Septuagint has the account of the altar on Mount Ebal and the reading of the Law (Hebrew 8:30–35), as 9:2a–f. In it the passage begins, “Then Joshua built an altar to the Lord, the God of Israel, on Mount Gaibal.” See the note at 8:30.
Gibeon means “hill” or “hilltop place” (from giv‘ah, “hill”). It is probably el-Jib, about 6 miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

The Hebrew word is uncertain. With a one-letter difference, some Hebrew manuscripts and the ancient versions read “they took provisions” (compare verse 12). The Septuagint reads “they made provision and prepared themselves.”
Kiriath-jearim means “city of forests.” Beeroth means “wells,” and Chephirah may mean “village” or “lioness.”

verses.text: When Adoni-zedek{a} king of Jerusalem{b} heard that Joshua had captured Ai and devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and that the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,
he{c} feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were mighty.
Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent word to Hoham king of Hebron,{d} Piram king of Jarmuth, Japhia king of Lachish, and Debir king of Eglon,{e} saying,
“Come up and help me attack Gibeon, because it has made peace with Joshua and the Israelites.”
So the five Amorite kings—the kings of Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, and Eglon—joined forces and marched up with all their armies; they camped by Gibeon and attacked it.

The men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp at Gilgal, saying, “Do not withdraw your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who live in the hill country have gathered against us.”
So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.
Yahweh said to Joshua, “Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hand. Not a man of them will stand before you.”
Joshua came against them suddenly, after marching all night from Gilgal.

Yahweh threw them into a panic before Israel, and he{f} struck them with a great slaughter at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon,{g} and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.

As they ran from Israel down the slope of Beth-horon, Yahweh hurled huge stones from the sky on them all the way to Azekah, and they died; the hailstones killed more of them than the Israelites killed with the sword.

Then Joshua spoke to Yahweh on the day when Yahweh gave the Amorites over to the Israelites, and he said in the sight of Israel,{h} “Sun, be still{i} at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon.”{j}

And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on its enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?{k} The sun stopped in the middle of the heavens and did not hurry to go down for about a whole day.{l}
There has never been a day like it, before or since, when Yahweh heeded the voice of a man; for Yahweh was fighting for Israel.
Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.{m}
These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.
It was told to Joshua, “The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah.”
Joshua said, “Roll great stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them.
But do not stop there. Chase your enemies and attack them from behind; do not let them reach their cities, for Yahweh your God has handed them over to you.”
When Joshua and the Israelites had finished a very great slaughter of them, until they were finished off, and the survivors had reached their fortified cities,
all the people returned safely to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. No one moved his tongue against any of the Israelites.
Then Joshua said, “Open the mouth of the cave and bring out to me these five kings from the cave.”
They did so and brought out to him these five kings from the cave: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.

When they brought these kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, “Come near, put your feet on the necks of these kings.” So they came near and put their feet on their necks.
Joshua told them, “Do not be afraid or discouraged; be strong and courageous. This is what Yahweh will do to all the enemies you fight.”
After that Joshua killed them and hung them on five trees, and they remained hanging there until evening.

As the sun was setting Joshua gave a command, and they lowered them from the trees and threw them into the cave in which they had hidden; over its mouth they placed great stones, which remain to this very day.

Joshua captured Makkedah that day, put it and its king to the sword, and set every person in it apart for destruction, leaving no survivor. The king of Makkedah he treated just like the king of Jericho.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.
Yahweh also gave it and its king into Israel’s hand. Joshua put it to the sword along with everyone in it, leaving no survivor there, and he treated its king as he had treated the king of Jericho.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish, and camped against it and fought against it.
Yahweh handed Lachish over to Israel, who captured it on the second day and put it and everyone in it to the sword, just as he had done to Libnah.
Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish, and Joshua struck him and his people until he left him no survivor.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon, and they camped against it and fought against it.
On that day they took it and killed everyone in it with the sword; he set every person in it apart for destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron, and they fought against it.
They captured it and put it, its king, its towns, and everyone in it to the sword; he left no survivor, just as at Eglon, and set it and every person in it apart for destruction.
Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir{n} and attacked it.

He captured it, its king, and all its towns, put them to the sword, and set every person in it apart for destruction, leaving no survivor. What he had done to Hebron, and to Libnah and its king, he did to Debir and its king.

So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country, the Negev,{o} the lowland, and the slopes, and all their kings. He left no survivor, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, as Yahweh, the God of Israel, commanded.
Joshua conquered them from Kadesh-barnea{p} to Gaza, and the whole region of Goshen up to Gibeon.
Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because Yahweh, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.
Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.

notes.text: Adoni-zedek means “my lord is righteous” (or “my lord is Zedek,” a divine name). Compare Melchizedek, king of Salem (Genesis 14:18). The Septuagint reads Adonibezek (compare Judges 1:5–7).
The meaning of Jerusalem is uncertain; it is perhaps “foundation of Shalem,” the name of a god, though it was later understood as “city of peace.”
Hebrew “they.”
Hebron may mean “alliance” or “association.” It was earlier called Kiriath-arba (14:15).
The Septuagint reads “Dabin king of Odollam” (that is, Adullam) here and in verses 5 and 23, though it has Eglon in verses 34–37.
That is, Joshua (or Israel).
Beth-horon probably means “house of Horon,” a Canaanite god, or perhaps “house of the hollow.” The road climbed from the coastal lowland through Upper and Lower Beth-horon.
The Hebrew can also mean “and he said, in the sight of Israel.” The Septuagint reads only “and Joshua said.”

Hebrew dom, “be still, be silent,” or “stop.” Some interpreters take the poetry as a request that the sun stop shining (cease its scorching heat, or be darkened by the storm of verse 11) rather than stop moving. The lines are poetry, and the prose that follows takes them literally.

Aijalon means “place of deer” (from ’ayyal, “deer”). The valley lies west of Gibeon, so the sun stood over Gibeon to the east and the moon over Aijalon to the west, which may suggest an early morning scene.

Jashar means “the upright one.” The Book of Jashar was an early collection of poetry, now lost, that is also cited in 2 Samuel 1:18 (David’s lament). The Septuagint lacks the question “Is this not written in the Book of Jashar?” here. The Septuagint of 1 Kings 8:53 cites a “book of song,” which may be the same work under a slightly different name.
Literally “as a complete day” (Hebrew keyom tamim). The time is not given in hours.
The Septuagint lacks this verse, which anticipates verse 43; verse 21 places the camp at Makkedah.
Debir means “back room” or “inner sanctuary.” It was earlier called Kiriath-sepher, “city of the book” (15:15).
Negev means “dry land,” the arid region in the south of Judah.
Kadesh-barnea means “holy place of Barnea”; it was the main oasis of the Sinai wanderings (Numbers 13:26; 32:8).

verses.text: Jabin{a} king of Hazor{b} heard of these events and sent messages to Jobab king of Madon, to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,
and the kings in the northern hill country, in the Arabah south of Chinneroth,{c} in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor{d} to the west,
the Canaanites to the east and west, the Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, and Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites at the foot of Hermon in the land of Mizpah.{e}
They came out, they and all their armies with them, a great people, as many as the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.
All these kings met by appointment, and they came and camped together at the waters of Merom{f} to fight against Israel.
Yahweh told Joshua, “Do not fear them; about this time tomorrow I will hand them all over to Israel, killed. You are to cut the hamstrings of their horses and burn their chariots in the fire.”
So Joshua and all his fighting men came against them suddenly at the waters of Merom and attacked them.
Yahweh handed them over to Israel, who defeated them and pursued them to Great Sidon, to Misrephoth-maim,{g} and east to the Valley of Mizpeh, striking them down until none were left.
Joshua did to them as Yahweh told him. He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
At that time Joshua turned back, captured Hazor, and killed its king with the sword; Hazor had formerly been the head of all those kingdoms.
They put to the sword every person in it, setting them apart for destruction; nothing that breathed remained, and Hazor itself he burned with fire.
Joshua captured all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, and put them to the sword, setting them apart for destruction, as Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded.
Yet Israel burned none of the cities standing on their mounds,{h} apart from Hazor alone, which Joshua burned.
The Israelites took for themselves all the plunder of these cities, and the livestock; but they put every person to the sword until they had wiped them out, leaving no one alive who breathed.
Just as Yahweh had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that Yahweh had commanded Moses.
So Joshua took all that land, the hill country, all the Negev, all the land of Goshen, the lowland, the Arabah, and the hill country of Israel and its lowland,
from Mount Halak,{i} which rises toward Seir, all the way to Baal-gad{j} in the Valley of Lebanon at the foot of Mount Hermon. He captured all their kings, struck them down, and put them to death.
Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.
There was not a city that made peace with the Israelites except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.
For it was Yahweh’s doing to harden their hearts so that they would meet Israel in battle, and so be set apart for destruction without mercy, being wiped out as Yahweh had commanded Moses.

Joshua went at that time and eliminated the Anakim{k} who lived in the hill country—in Hebron, Debir, and Anab, and in the entire hill country of Judah and of Israel; he set them apart for destruction along with their cities.
There were no Anakim left in the land of the Israelites. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.
Thus Joshua took the entire land, just as Yahweh had told Moses, and gave it to Israel as an inheritance, divided among their tribes. Then the land had rest from war.

notes.text: Jabin may mean “he understands” or “he discerns.” A later Jabin king of Hazor appears in Judges 4.
Hazor probably means “enclosure” or “settlement.” It was the largest city of Canaan, north of the Sea of Galilee.
That is, the Sea of Galilee; Chinnereth may mean “harp-shaped.”
Or “the heights of Dor,” a coastal town south of Mount Carmel.
Mizpah means “watchtower” or “lookout”; so also Mizpeh in verse 8.
Merom means “height.”
Misrephoth-maim may mean “burnings at the water” (perhaps lime kilns or salt pans), or “hot springs.”
Hebrew tel; see the note at 8:28.
Halak means “smooth” or “bare.”
Baal-gad means “lord of fortune,” or “Baal of Gad” (a god of luck).
Anakim probably means “people of the neck,” that is, long-necked or tall. They were remembered as giants (Numbers 13:33; Deuteronomy 2:10–11).

verses.text: These are the kings of the land whom the Israelites defeated and whose territory they took across the Jordan to the east, from the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon, including the whole eastern Arabah:

Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley, and half of Gilead, as far as the river Jabbok, the border of the Ammonites,
and the Arabah as far as the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and as far as the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, eastward toward Beth-jeshimoth, and on the south below the slopes of Pisgah;{a}
and the territory of Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim,{b} who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei
and ruled in Mount Hermon, in Salecah, and in the whole of Bashan, to the territory of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over the half of Gilead reaching the border of Sihon, king of Heshbon.
Moses the servant of Yahweh and the Israelites struck them, and Moses the servant of Yahweh gave it as a possession to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh.

These are the kings of the land that Joshua and the Israelites defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon as far as Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir. Joshua then gave their land to Israel’s tribes as a possession, divided into portions,

in the hill country and the lowland, the Arabah and the slopes, the wilderness and the Negev: the land of the Hittites and the Amorites, the Canaanites and the Perizzites, the Hivites and the Jebusites:
the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;
the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;
the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;
the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;
the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;
the king of Hormah,{c} one; the king of Arad, one;
the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;
the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;
the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;{d}
the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;
the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;
the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;
the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;
the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim{e} in Gilgal, one;
the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.{f}

notes.text: Pisgah means “cleft” or “peak.” From its summit Moses viewed the land (Deuteronomy 34:1).
The Rephaim were an ancient people remembered as giants (Deuteronomy 3:11). The word is also used for the shades of the dead.
Hormah means “devotion to destruction” (from ḥaram; Numbers 21:3).
Or “the king of Aphek in Sharon.” The Septuagint reads “the king of Ophek of Aroc.”
Goiim means “nations.” The Septuagint reads “Gei of Galilee,” which suits the northern setting (compare Isaiah 9:1).
The Septuagint lists twenty-nine kings, with differences in several names.

verses.text: Joshua was now old, well along in years, and Yahweh said to him, “You have grown old and are well along in years, yet a great deal of the land is still to be taken.
This is the land that still remains: all the regions of the Philistines and all those of the Geshurites
