(from the Shihor,{a} east of Egypt, north to the boundary of Ekron, counted as Canaanite; the five rulers{b} of the Philistines were those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and the Avvim
in the south; all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, as far as Aphek, to the border of the Amorites;
and the land of the Gebalites,{c} and all Lebanon toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath.{d}

All the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, all the Sidonians, I myself will drive them out from before the Israelites. Only allot it to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.
Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh.”
Together with the other half of Manasseh,{e} the Reubenites and Gadites received the inheritance Moses gave them east of the Jordan, just as Moses the servant of Yahweh had given it to them:
from Aroer, which sits on the rim of the Arnon gorge, and from the city in the gorge’s middle, with the entire tableland{f} from Medeba to Dibon,
and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the border of the Ammonites,
and Gilead, and the territory of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan as far as Salecah,
the whole realm of Og in Bashan, who had reigned at Ashtaroth and at Edrei; he alone remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Moses had defeated these and driven them out.
But the Israelites did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, and Geshur and Maacath live in the midst of Israel to this day.
Only to the tribe of Levi did he give no inheritance; the fire offerings to Yahweh, the God of Israel, are their inheritance, as he had told him.{g}
To the tribe of the Reubenites, by their clans, Moses gave an inheritance.
Their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;
Heshbon and all its cities that are in the tableland: Dibon, Bamoth-baal,{h} Beth-baal-meon,
Jahaz, Kedemoth, Mephaath,
Kiriathaim, Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,
Beth-peor, the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,

all the cities of the tableland and the whole kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who ruled in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated along with the chiefs of Midian—Evi, Rekem, Zur, Hur, and Reba—the princes of Sihon who lived in the land.
Balaam also, the son of Beor, the diviner, the Israelites killed with the sword among the rest of their slain.
The border of the Reubenites was the Jordan and its region.{i} This was the inheritance of the Reubenites according to their clans, the cities with their villages.
Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of Gad, to the Gadites, according to their clans.
Their territory was Jazer and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, as far as Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,
and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim{j} to the territory of Debir,{k}

and in the valley, Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth,{l} and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, with the Jordan as its boundary, as far as the end of the Sea of Chinnereth, beyond the Jordan eastward.
This is the inheritance of the Gadites according to their clans, the cities with their villages.
Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was for the half-tribe of the Manassites according to their clans.
Their territory was from Mahanaim, all Bashan, all the kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all Havvoth-jair,{m} which are in Bashan, sixty cities,
and half of Gilead, with Ashtaroth and Edrei, cities of the realm of Og in Bashan. These went to the sons of Machir, Manasseh’s son—to half of Machir’s sons, by their clans.
These are the inheritances Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, east of Jericho across the Jordan.
But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance. Yahweh, the God of Israel, is their inheritance, as he said to them.{n}

notes.text: Shihor means “black” or “the pool of Horus,” probably an eastern branch of the Nile or a stream on Egypt’s border.
Hebrew seren, a Philistine word for the rulers of their five cities; it may be related to Greek tyrannos.
That is, the people of Gebal (Byblos), on the coast north of Beirut.
Or “to the entrance of Hamath.”
Hebrew “With it,” referring back to the half-tribe of Manasseh in verse 7.
Hebrew mishor, “level land,” the plateau east of the Dead Sea; so throughout this chapter.
The Septuagint adds, “This is the division that Moses made for the Israelites in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan, by Jericho” (compare verse 32).
Bamoth-baal means “high places of Baal.”
Or “The border of the Reubenites was the Jordan, as a boundary.”
Mahanaim means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2).
Hebrew Lidbir, perhaps the same as Lo-debar (2 Samuel 9:4).
Succoth means “booths” (Genesis 33:17).
Havvoth-jair means “tent villages of Jair” (Numbers 32:41).
The Septuagint lacks this verse.

verses.text: These are the inheritances the Israelites received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar{a} the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of the families of the Israelite tribes distributed to them.
Their inheritance was by lot, as Yahweh had commanded through Moses, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe.
For Moses had given the inheritance of the two and a half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.
For the descendants of Joseph formed two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. The Levites received no share in the land except cities to live in, along with pastureland for their livestock and goods.
The Israelites did as Yahweh commanded Moses, and they divided the land.

Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. Caleb{b} the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite{c} said to him, “You know what Yahweh said to Moses the man of God at Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.
I was forty years old when Moses the servant of Yahweh sent me from Kadesh-barnea to scout the land, and I reported to him what was in my heart.
But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt, while I wholly followed Yahweh my God.
On that day Moses swore, ‘The land your foot has walked on will surely be your inheritance and your children’s forever, because you have followed Yahweh my God fully.’

And now, see, Yahweh has kept me alive, as he said, these forty-five years since the time that Yahweh spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, see, I am today eighty-five years old.
I am as strong today as on the day Moses sent me; my strength now equals my strength then, for fighting and for going out and coming in.

So now give me this hill country about which Yahweh spoke that day, since you heard then that the Anakim were there, in great fortified cities. Perhaps Yahweh will be with me and I will drive them out, as Yahweh said.”
Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.
Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Hebron’s name was formerly Kiriath-arba;{d} Arba{e} was the greatest man among the Anakim. Then the land had rest from war.

notes.text: Eleazar means “God has helped.”
Caleb means “dog,” perhaps in the sense of a loyal servant. Some connect the name with kol-lev, “whole heart,” in light of verses 8–9 and 14.
The Kenizzites were a clan related to Edom (Genesis 15:19; 36:11). Caleb’s family had been joined to the tribe of Judah.
Kiriath-arba means “city of four” or “city of Arba.”
The Septuagint reads, “The name of Hebron formerly was the city of Argob; it is the mother city of the Anakim.”

verses.text: The portion for the tribe of Judah, by their clans, extended south to the border of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the far south.
Their southern border ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward.
It went out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim,{a} passed along to Zin, went up south of Kadesh-barnea, passed along by Hezron, went up to Addar, and turned about to Karka.
It passed along to Azmon, went out by the Brook of Egypt,{b} and the border ended at the sea. This will be your southern border.
The eastern boundary was the Salt Sea, as far as the Jordan’s mouth. The northern side’s border began at the sea’s inlet, at the mouth of the Jordan.
The border went up to Beth-hoglah and passed along north of Beth-arabah. The border went up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.

From the Valley of Achor the border went up to Debir and then north, turning toward Gilgal, which faces the ascent of Adummim,{c} south of the valley. It continued to the waters of En-shemesh{d} and ended at En-rogel.{e}

Then the border climbed by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom{f} along the Jebusite’s southern ridge (which is Jerusalem). From there it ran up to the peak of the mountain that stands opposite the Valley of Hinnom on its west side, at the far north end of the Valley of Rephaim.

Then the border was drawn from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah,{g} went out to the cities of Mount Ephron, and the border was drawn to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).
The border turned about from Baalah westward to Mount Seir, passed along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), went down to Beth-shemesh,{h} and passed along by Timnah.
The border proceeded to the ridge north of Ekron, bent around to Shikkeron, went across Mount Baalah, and reached Jabneel; its end was at the sea.
The western border was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the border all around the people of Judah according to their clans.
To Caleb the son of Jephunneh he gave a portion among the people of Judah, according to the command of Yahweh to Joshua, Kiriath-arba (Arba was the father of Anak), that is, Hebron.
Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.
He went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher.{i}
Caleb said, “To the man who attacks Kiriath-sepher and takes it, I will give my daughter Achsah{j} as his wife.”
Othniel{k} son of Kenaz, Caleb’s brother, took it, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as wife.
When she arrived, she urged him to ask her father for a field. She dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb asked her, “What do you want?”
She replied, “Give me a blessing.{l} Since you have given me land in the Negev, give me springs of water also.” So he gave her the upper and lower springs.
This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans.
The cities at the farthest limits of the tribe of the people of Judah, toward the border of Edom in the Negev, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,
Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,
Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,
Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,
Hazor-hadattah and Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),
also Amam, Shema, and Moladah,
also Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, and Beth-pelet,
also Hazar-shual, Beersheba,{m} and Biziothiah,
Baalah, Iim, Ezem,
Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,
Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,
Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon—twenty-nine cities in all, with their villages.{n}
In the lowland there were Eshtaol, Zorah, and Ashnah,
along with Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, and Enam,
also Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, and Azekah,
and Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, and Gederothaim—fourteen cities and their villages.
Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,
Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel,
Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,
Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish,
Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages.
Libnah, Ether, Ashan,
Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,
Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages.
Ekron with its towns{o} and its villages;
from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.
Ashdod, with its towns and villages; Gaza, with its towns and villages, up to the Brook of Egypt; and the Great Sea with its shore.
In the hill country: Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,
Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),
Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,
Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages.
Arab, Dumah, Eshan,
Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,
Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior—nine cities and their villages.
Also Maon, Carmel, Ziph, and Juttah,
then Jezreel, Jokdeam, and Zanoah,
Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah—ten cities and their villages.
Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,
Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages.{p}
Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim) and Rabbah: two cities with their villages.
In the wilderness: Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,
Nibshan, the City of Salt,{q} and En-gedi:{r} six cities with their villages.
As for the Jebusites living in Jerusalem, the people of Judah were unable to drive them out, and so the Jebusites have lived with the people of Judah in Jerusalem to this day.

notes.text: Akrabbim means “scorpions.”
Hebrew naḥal Mitsrayim, the Wadi el-Arish in northern Sinai.
Adummim means “red (places),” probably from the red rock along the road from Jericho to Jerusalem.
En-shemesh means “spring of the sun.”
En-rogel may mean “spring of the fuller” or “spring of the foot.”
Hebrew Ge ben-Hinnom. The Hebrew Ge-Hinnom later became the Greek Gehenna, a name for the place of judgment (Matthew 5:22).
Or “the spring of Me-nephtoah.” Nephtoah may mean “opening.”
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.”
Kiriath-sepher means “city of the book” (or “city of the scribe”). The Septuagint reads “city of letters.” Verse 49 calls it Kiriath-sannah.
Achsah means “anklet.”
Othniel may mean “God is my strength” (or “lion of God”). He became Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9–11).
That is, a gift.
Beersheba means “well of seven” or “well of the oath” (Genesis 21:31).

The names listed in verses 21–32 number more than twenty-nine. Some names may be combined (for example, Ain and Rimmon, which are one place, En-rimmon, in Nehemiah 11:29), or some may have been added to the list later.
Hebrew “daughters,” that is, dependent towns; so throughout these lists.

The Septuagint adds another district of eleven cities here: “Tekoa, Ephrathah (that is, Bethlehem), Peor, Etam, Culon, Tatam, Thobes, Carem, Gallim, Bether, and Manocho: eleven cities with their villages.” This district is missing from the Hebrew text, probably through an accidental omission by a copyist whose eye jumped from one “with their villages” to the next.
Hebrew ‘Ir-hammelaḥ.
En-gedi means “spring of the young goat.”

verses.text: The lot for the descendants of Joseph ran from the Jordan at Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, through the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country of Bethel.
Then it went from Bethel to Luz{a} and passed along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites.
Then it went down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, and to Gezer, and it ended at the sea.
The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.
The territory of the people of Ephraim{b} according to their clans was this: the border of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon,
and the border went out to the sea. On the north was Michmethath. Then on the east the border turned around toward Taanath-shiloh and passed along beyond it on the east to Janoah.
Then it went down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, touched Jericho, and went out to the Jordan.
From Tappuah the border ran west to Brook Kanah{c} and ended at the sea. This was the inheritance of the tribe of Ephraim’s descendants, by their clans,
along with the cities set aside for the Ephraimites within the inheritance of Manasseh’s descendants—all those cities and their villages.
But they did not drive out the Canaanites living in Gezer, so the Canaanites live among the Ephraimites to this day, serving as forced laborers.{d}

notes.text: Luz means “almond tree.” It was the older name of Bethel (Genesis 28:19), but here the two seem to be distinguished.
Ephraim means “doubly fruitful” (Genesis 41:52).
Kanah means “reed.”

The Septuagint lacks “and they have become forced laborers.” Instead it adds, “until Pharaoh king of Egypt went up and took it and burned it with fire, and the Canaanites and Perizzites and those living in Gaza they destroyed, and Pharaoh gave them as a dowry to his daughter.” Compare 1 Kings 9:16.

verses.text: This was the allotment for the tribe of Manasseh,{a} for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, because he was a man of war, were allotted Gilead and Bashan.

Portions were also allotted to the rest of Manasseh’s descendants, clan by clan: the descendants of Abiezer, of Helek, of Asriel, of Shechem, of Hepher, and of Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh son of Joseph, by their clans.
Zelophehad son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, only daughters, whose names were Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.

They approached Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the leaders, saying, “Yahweh commanded Moses to give us an inheritance among our brothers.” So, at Yahweh’s command, he gave them an inheritance among their father’s brothers.
So ten portions fell to Manasseh, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan across the Jordan,
since Manasseh’s daughters received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead went to the rest of Manasseh’s descendants.
Manasseh’s territory extended from Asher to Michmethath, east of Shechem; then the border ran south toward those living at En-tappuah.
The land of Tappuah{b} belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the border of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim.

Then the border went down to the brook Kanah. South of the brook, these cities belonged to Ephraim among the cities of Manasseh. The territory of Manasseh lay on the north side of the brook and ended at the sea,
The land to the south belonged to Ephraim and to the north to Manasseh, with the sea as its boundary. On the north it touched Asher, and on the east Issachar.
In Issachar and Asher, Manasseh also held Beth-shean and its towns, Ibleam and its towns, and the inhabitants of Dor, En-dor, Taanach, and Megiddo with their towns; the third being Naphath.{c}
Yet the Manassites were unable to take those cities, because the Canaanites were determined to stay in that land.
When the Israelites grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.
The descendants of Joseph said to Joshua, “Why have you given me only one lot and one portion as an inheritance, when I am a numerous people whom Yahweh has blessed until now?”

Joshua answered them, “If you are so numerous, go up on your own to the forest and clear land for yourselves in the country of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too small for you.”

The descendants of Joseph said, “The hill country is not enough for us, and all the Canaanites living in the valley lands, in Beth-shean and its towns and in the Valley of Jezreel,{d} have iron chariots.”
Then Joshua spoke to the house of Joseph—Ephraim and Manasseh—saying, “You are a numerous people with great power; you will not have just one lot,
for the hill country will be yours. Though it is forested, you will clear it and own it to its farthest limits. You will drive out the Canaanites, even though they have iron chariots and are strong.”

notes.text: Manasseh means “making forget” (Genesis 41:51). Parts of this chapter (verses 1–5 and 11–15) are preserved in the Qumran scroll 4QJosh-b (about 50 B.C.), which agrees closely with the Hebrew text.
Tappuah means “apple” (or another fruit tree); so also En-tappuah, “apple spring,” in verse 7.
Or “the three heights.” The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint lacks Ibleam and En-dor here and reads “the third part of Napheth.”
Jezreel means “God sows.”

verses.text: The whole congregation of the Israelites gathered at Shiloh{a} and set up the tent of meeting there, with the land under their control.
Seven tribes among the Israelites still had not received their inheritance.
So Joshua told the Israelites, “How long will you delay entering to take possession of the land that Yahweh, the God of your fathers, has given you?
Choose three men from each tribe, and I will send them out to travel through the land. They are to write a description of it according to how they will be inherited, and then return to me.
They are to divide it into seven parts. Judah will stay in its territory to the south, and the house of Joseph will stay in its territory to the north.
You are to write a description of the land in seven divisions and bring it here to me. I will cast lots for you here before Yahweh our God.

For the Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of Yahweh is their inheritance. And Gad and Reuben and the half-tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of Yahweh gave them.”

The men set out, and Joshua instructed those who went to describe the land in writing: “Go and walk through the land, write a description of it, and come back to me. Here at Shiloh, before Yahweh, I will cast lots for you.”
So the men went and traveled through the land, and they recorded it in a book, city by city, in seven divisions. Then they returned to Joshua in the camp at Shiloh.
Joshua cast lots for them at Shiloh before Yahweh. There Joshua apportioned the land to the Israelites according to their divisions.
The lot for the tribe of Benjamin’s descendants{b} came up, by their clans, and the territory assigned to them lay between the descendants of Judah and of Joseph.
Their northern boundary started at the Jordan, climbed to the slope north of Jericho, then went up west through the hill country and ended at the wilderness of Beth-aven.
From there the border crossed south toward Luz, to Luz’s slope (that is, Bethel), and descended to Ataroth-addar, on the hill south of Lower Beth-horon.

Then the boundary turned and curved along the west side toward the south, from the hill facing Beth-horon on the south, and finished at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city of Judah’s descendants. That was the western side.
The southern side began at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. The border went out westward{c} and went to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.

The border descended to the foot of the mountain facing the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim, ran down the Hinnom Valley along the Jebusite’s southern slope, and reached En-rogel.
Then it bent in a northerly direction, going out to En-shemesh, and from there to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it went down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,
passed on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah,{d} and went down to the Arabah.
The border continued north of the slope of Beth-hoglah and ended at the Salt Sea’s northern inlet, at the Jordan’s southern end. That was the southern boundary.
The Jordan bounded it on the east. This was the inheritance of Benjamin’s descendants by their clans, with its boundaries all around.
The cities of the tribe of Benjamin, by their clans, were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, and Emek-keziz,
also Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, and Bethel,
also Avvim, Parah, and Ophrah,
and Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, and Geba—twelve cities and their villages.
Gibeon, Ramah,{e} Beeroth,
Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,
Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,
Zela, Haeleph, the Jebusite city (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeath,{f} and Kiriath{g}—fourteen cities and their villages. This was the inheritance of Benjamin’s descendants, by their clans.

notes.text: Shiloh may mean “place of rest” or “tranquility.” It became the site of the sanctuary through the period of the judges (1 Samuel 1–4).
Benjamin means “son of the right hand” or “son of the south” (Genesis 35:18).
Or “to the west.” The text is difficult; the Septuagint reads “to Gasin.”
The Hebrew reads “to the shoulder opposite the Arabah.” Some ancient witnesses read “Beth-arabah,” as in 15:6.
Ramah means “height.”
Gibeath means “hill.” This is probably Gibeah, Saul’s town (1 Samuel 10:26).
Hebrew Qiryat, “city.” Some propose reading Kiriath-jearim, but 18:14 assigns that city to Judah.

verses.text: The second lot fell to Simeon,{a} to the tribe of Simeon’s descendants by their clans, and their inheritance lay within the inheritance of Judah’s descendants.
Their inheritance included Beersheba, Sheba,{b} and Moladah,
also Hazar-shual, Balah, and Ezem,
also Eltolad, Bethul, and Hormah,
also Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, and Hazar-susah,
also Beth-lebaoth and Sharuhen—thirteen cities and their villages;
Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan: four cities with their villages,
as well as all the villages around these cities up to Baalath-beer, Ramah in the Negev. This was the inheritance of Simeon’s tribe, by their clans.
Simeon’s inheritance was taken from Judah’s territory, because Judah’s portion was too large for them; so the Simeonites received their inheritance within Judah’s.
The third lot came up for Zebulun’s descendants,{c} by their clans. Their inherited territory extended to Sarid.
Then their border went up westward and on to Maralah, touched Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam.
From Sarid it went in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the border of Chisloth-tabor. From there it went to Daberath, then up to Japhia.
From there it crossed eastward, toward the sunrise, to Gath-hepher and Eth-kazin, and continued to Rimmon, where it curved toward Neah.
Then on the north the border turned about to Hannathon, and it ended at the Valley of Iphtahel,
with Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem{d}—twelve cities and their villages.
That was the inheritance of Zebulun’s descendants by their clans—these cities and their villages.
The fourth lot fell to Issachar,{e} to Issachar’s descendants by their clans.
Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,
Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,
Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,
Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, and Beth-pazzez.
The border also touched Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and their border ended at the Jordan: sixteen cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Issachar’s tribe by their clans—the cities and their villages.
The fifth lot fell to the tribe of Asher’s descendants{f} by their clans.
Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,
also Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it reached Carmel{g} and Shihor-libnath.
Then it turned east toward Beth-dagon, reached Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel, and went north to Beth-emek and Neiel, continuing north to Cabul,
Ebron,{h} Rehob, Hammon, and Kanah, as far as Great Sidon.
Then the border turned toward Ramah and the fortified city of Tyre.{i} It then turned to Hosah and ended at the sea; there were also Mahalab,{j} Achzib,
Ummah, Aphek, and Rehob: twenty-two cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Asher’s tribe by their clans—these cities and their villages.
The sixth lot fell to Naphtali’s descendants,{k} by their clans.
Their border ran from Heleph and the oak at Zaanannim, with Adami-nekeb and Jabneel, to Lakkum, and ended at the Jordan.
Then the border turned westward to Aznoth-tabor and went from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun on the south and Asher on the west and Judah{l} at the Jordan on the east.
The fortified cities were Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,
Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,
Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor,
Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh: nineteen cities with their villages.
That was the inheritance of Naphtali’s tribe by their clans—the cities and their villages.
The seventh lot fell to Dan’s tribe{m} by their clans.
Their inherited territory included Zorah, Eshtaol, and Ir-shemesh,
also Shaalabbin, Aijalon, and Ithlah,
also Elon, Timnah, and Ekron,
also Eltekeh, Gibbethon, and Baalath,
also Jehud, Bene-berak, and Gath-rimmon,
and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa.

When the territory of the Danites slipped from them,{n} the Danites went up, fought against Leshem, took it, and put it to the sword; they occupied it and lived there, and they called Leshem “Dan,” after the name of their ancestor Dan.
That was the inheritance of Dan’s tribe by their clans—these cities and their villages.
After they had finished distributing the lands as inheritances, the Israelites gave Joshua son of Nun an inheritance among them.
By command of Yahweh they gave him the city that he asked for, Timnath-serah{o} in the hill country of Ephraim. He rebuilt the city and settled in it.

These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the family heads of the tribes of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh, before Yahweh, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they completed the dividing of the land.

notes.text: Simeon means “heard” (Genesis 29:33).
Or “Shema,” as in 15:26 and 1 Chronicles 4:28; the list totals thirteen only if Sheba is a repetition of Beersheba.
Zebulun may mean “honor” or “dwelling” (Genesis 30:20).
This is a Bethlehem in Galilee, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) northwest of Nazareth, not Bethlehem of Judah.
Issachar sounds like the Hebrew for “there is a reward” (Genesis 30:18).
Asher means “happy” or “blessed” (Genesis 30:13).
Carmel means “garden land” or “orchard.”
Some Hebrew manuscripts read Abdon (compare 21:30).
Tyre (Hebrew Tsor) means “rock.”
Hebrew “from Hebel”; the reading Mahalab, a town known from Assyrian records, involves a slight change.
Naphtali means “my wrestling” (Genesis 30:8).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint lacks “and Judah.” The phrase may refer to Jair’s towns east of the Jordan (1 Chronicles 2:21–23), or the text may be damaged.
Dan means “he judged” or “judge” (Genesis 30:6).

Literally “went out from them.” The Septuagint has a different text in verses 47–48. It says that the Amorites pressed the Danites into the hill country and did not let them come down into the valley, that the Danites took Lachish (the Hebrew has Leshem) and called it Lasendan, and that the Amorites stayed in Edom and Shaalbim until Ephraim made them pay tribute. Compare Judges 1:34–35; 18:27–29.

Timnath-serah means “portion that remains” (or “extra portion”). Judges 2:9 calls it Timnath-heres, “portion of the sun,” and Serah may be a deliberate reversal of the letters. The Septuagint spells it Thamnasarach.

verses.text: Then Yahweh spoke to Joshua, saying,
“Speak to the Israelites, saying, ‘Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses,
so that the manslayer who strikes any person unintentionally, without knowing it, may flee there. They are to be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.{a}

He shall flee to one of these cities, stand at the entrance of its gate, and state his case to that city’s elders. They shall then bring him into the city, give him a place, and he shall live among them.{b}
If the avenger of blood pursues him, they are not to give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor without knowing it and did not hate him in the past.

He must live in that city until the assembly has judged his case, and until the high priest serving at that time has died. Only then may the killer return to the town from which he fled, to his own home.’”
So they set apart Kedesh{c} in Galilee{d} in the hill country of Naphtali, Shechem{e} in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.

On the east side of the Jordan, opposite Jericho, they set apart Bezer, in the wilderness on the tableland, belonging to Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, belonging to Gad; and Golan in Bashan, belonging to Manasseh.

These were the cities set aside for all the Israelites, and for the foreign resident among them, so that anyone who killed a person accidentally could flee there and not be killed by the avenger of blood before standing trial before the congregation.

notes.text: Hebrew go’el haddam, the nearest relative, whose duty was to take responsibility for a family member’s death. The same word go’el means “redeemer” elsewhere (Ruth 4:1–6).

The Septuagint lacks verses 4–6 and the phrase “without knowing it” in verse 3. In verse 3 it reads instead, “until he stands before the congregation for judgment.” The longer Hebrew text echoes Deuteronomy 19:1–13, while the shorter Greek text echoes Numbers 35:9–28.
Kedesh means “holy place.”
Galilee (Hebrew Galil) means “circle” or “district.”
Shechem means “shoulder” or “ridge,” perhaps from its position on the saddle between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim.

verses.text: Then the heads of the fathers’ houses of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the Israelites.
At Shiloh in the land of Canaan they told them, “Yahweh commanded through Moses that we be given towns to live in, with pastureland for our livestock.”
So by command of Yahweh the Israelites gave to the Levites from their inheritance these cities and their pasturelands.
The first lot fell to the Kohathite clans. The Levites who were descendants of Aaron the priest received thirteen cities by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin.
The remaining Kohathites received ten cities by lot from the clans of Ephraim, from Dan, and from half of Manasseh.
The Gershonites received thirteen cities by lot from the clans of Issachar, Asher, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan.
The Merarites, by their clans, received twelve cities from Reuben, Gad, and Zebulun.
The Israelites gave these cities with their pastures to the Levites by lot, as Yahweh had commanded through Moses.
From the tribes of Judah and Simeon they gave these cities, listed by name,
which went to Aaron’s descendants, of the Kohathite clans of Levi’s descendants, since the first lot was theirs.
They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba was the father of Anak), that is, Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, with the pasturelands around it.
The fields around the city and its villages, however, were given to Caleb son of Jephunneh as his own.
To Aaron the priest’s descendants they gave Hebron, a city of refuge for the killer, with its pastures, along with Libnah and its pastures,
Jattir with its pasturelands, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands,
Holon with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands,
Ain,{a} Juttah, and Beth-shemesh, each with its pastures—nine cities from these two tribes.
Then out of the tribe of Benjamin: Gibeon with its pasturelands, Geba with its pasturelands,
Anathoth{b} with its pasturelands, and Almon with its pasturelands: four cities.
Altogether the cities of Aaron’s descendants, the priests, were thirteen cities with their pastures.
As for the remaining Kohathite clans of the Levites, their allotted cities came from the tribe of Ephraim.
They were given Shechem, a city of refuge for the killer, with its pastures in the hill country of Ephraim, and Gezer with its pastures,
Kibzaim with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Dan: Elteke and Gibbethon, each with its pastures,
Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the half-tribe of Manasseh: Taanach and Gath-rimmon,{c} each with its pastures—two cities.
In all, the cities for the clans of the remaining Kohathites were ten, with their pastures.
To the Gershonites, a Levite clan, they gave from the half-tribe of Manasseh: Golan in Bashan, a city of refuge for the killer, and Be-eshterah,{d} each with its pastures—two cities.
From the tribe of Issachar: Kishion and Daberath, each with its pastures,
Jarmuth with its pasturelands, En-gannim with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Asher: Mishal and Abdon, each with its pastures,
Helkath with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Naphtali: Kedesh in Galilee, a city of refuge for the killer, Hammoth-dor, and Kartan, each with its pastures—three cities.
Altogether the cities of the Gershonite clans were thirteen, with their pastures.
To the rest of the Levites, the Merarite clans, they gave from the tribe of Zebulun: Jokneam and Kartah, each with its pastures,
Dimnah with its pasturelands, Nahalal with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Reuben:{e} Bezer and Jahaz, each with its pastures,
Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands: four cities.
From the tribe of Gad: Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge for the killer, and Mahanaim, each with its pastures,
Heshbon and Jazer, each with its pastures—four cities in all.
All the cities allotted to the Merarite clans, the rest of the Levite families, came to twelve.
The cities of the Levites in the midst of the possession of the Israelites were in all forty-eight cities with their pasturelands.
Each of these cities had pastureland surrounding it; this was true of all of them.{f}
So Yahweh gave Israel all the land he had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it.
Yahweh gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for Yahweh had given all their enemies into their hands.
Of all the good promises Yahweh had made to the house of Israel, not one word failed; every one came true.

notes.text: Ain means “spring.” The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 6:59 read Ashan.
Anathoth was later the hometown of the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:1).
The repetition of Gath-rimmon from verse 24 is probably a copying error. 1 Chronicles 6:70 has Bileam (that is, Ibleam), and the Septuagint reads Iebatha.
Be-eshterah is probably a contraction of Beth-ashtarah, “house of Astarte.” 1 Chronicles 6:71 has Ashtaroth.

Verses 36–37 are lacking in many Hebrew manuscripts and in some printed editions of the Hebrew Bible, though the edition followed here includes them. They are present in the Septuagint and in 1 Chronicles 6:78–79, and the totals in verses 7 and 40 (twelve cities) require them.

The Septuagint adds, “And Joshua finished dividing the land by its borders. And the Israelites gave a portion to Joshua by the command of the Lord. They gave him the city that he asked for, Thamnasachar in the hill country of Ephraim. And Joshua built the city and lived in it. And Joshua took the flint knives with which he had circumcised the Israelites who were born in the wilderness on the way, and put them in Thamnasachar.” Compare 19:49–50 and 24:31 (Septuagint).

verses.text: Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh
and said to them, “You have kept all that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, and you have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you.
All these many days, up to this day, you have not abandoned your brothers, but have kept the charge Yahweh your God gave you.

And now Yahweh your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn now and go to your tents, to the land of your possession, which Moses the servant of Yahweh gave you beyond the Jordan.

Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of Yahweh commanded you, to love Yahweh your God, to walk in all his ways, to keep his commandments, to hold fast to him, and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul.”
So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.

To one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given land in Bashan, while to the other half Joshua gave land alongside their brothers west of the Jordan. When Joshua sent them home to their tents and blessed them,

he said to them, “Go back to your tents with great wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with very many garments. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers.”

So the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh left the Israelites at Shiloh in the land of Canaan and went back to Gilead, the land they owned, which they had taken by Yahweh’s command through Moses.

When they reached the district{a} of the Jordan in the land of Canaan, the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh built an altar there beside the Jordan, an altar that was impressive in size.
The Israelites were told, “The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh have built an altar at the border of Canaan, in the Jordan district, on the side that faces the Israelites.”
When the Israelites heard this, the whole congregation of Israel assembled at Shiloh to go to war against them.
Then the Israelites sent to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas{b} the son of Eleazar the priest,
and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the fathers’ houses of each of the tribes of Israel, every one of them the head of a fathers’ house among the clans{c} of Israel.
They came to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them,

“This is the word of the whole congregation of Yahweh: ‘What is this unfaithfulness you have shown toward the God of Israel, turning away today from following Yahweh by building yourselves an altar and rebelling against Yahweh today?
Was the iniquity of Peor{d} too little for us, from which we are not yet cleansed to this day, though a plague struck the congregation of Yahweh,
that you too must turn away this day from following Yahweh? If you too rebel against Yahweh today, then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.

Yet if you find the land you hold to be unclean, then cross to Yahweh’s own land, where his tabernacle stands, and settle among us. But never rebel against Yahweh, nor make us rebels, by raising an altar for yourselves apart from the altar of Yahweh our God.
Did not Achan son of Zerah act unfaithfully regarding what was set apart for destruction, so that wrath fell on the whole congregation of Israel? He was not the only one to die for his iniquity.’”
The Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh answered the heads of the families of Israel:
“The Mighty One, God, Yahweh! The Mighty One, God, Yahweh!{e} He knows, and Israel too shall know! If this was rebellion or unfaithfulness toward Yahweh, do not save us today
by building an altar to turn away from Yahweh. And if our purpose was to offer on it burnt offerings, grain offerings, or peace offerings, may Yahweh himself require an account.
No! We acted from a worry that in days to come your children would say to our children, ‘What business do you have with Yahweh, the God of Israel?
For Yahweh has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you Reubenites and Gadites. You have no portion in Yahweh.’ So your children might make our children cease to fear Yahweh.
That is why we said, ‘Let us get ready to build an altar—not for burnt offering and not for sacrifice,

but to be a witness between you and us, and between our generations after us, that we do serve Yahweh before him with our burnt offerings, our sacrifices, and our peace offerings; then your children will not be able to tell our children in days to come, “You have no share in Yahweh.”’

And we thought, ‘If they ever say this to us or to our descendants in the future, we will reply, “See the likeness of Yahweh’s altar, which our fathers built, not for burnt offerings or sacrifices, but as a witness between you and us.”’

Far be it from us that we should rebel against Yahweh and turn away this day from following Yahweh by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of Yahweh our God that stands before his tabernacle!”
When Phinehas the priest, with the leaders of the congregation, the heads of Israel’s families who were with him, heard the words spoken by the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites, it pleased them.

Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest told the Reubenites, Gadites, and Manassites, “Today we know that Yahweh is among us, since you have not committed this act of unfaithfulness against Yahweh. You have now rescued the Israelites from Yahweh’s hand.”
Phinehas son of Eleazar the priest and the leaders then turned back from the Reubenites and Gadites in Gilead and returned to Canaan, to the Israelites, and gave them the report.
The report pleased the Israelites, and they blessed God. They said no more about going to war to destroy the land in which the Reubenites and Gadites lived.
The Reubenites and Gadites named the altar Witness,{f} saying, “It is a witness between us that Yahweh is God.”

notes.text: Hebrew gelilot, “circles” or “districts,” possibly a place name, Geliloth; so in verse 11. The Septuagint reads “Galaad” (Gilead).
Phinehas is an Egyptian name, probably meaning “the Nubian” (Numbers 25:7).
Hebrew “thousands,” a term for clan divisions; so in verses 21 and 30.
See Numbers 25:1–9.
Hebrew El Elohim Yahweh, three names for God, repeated as a solemn oath.

Hebrew ‘ed, “witness.” The name is not in the standard Hebrew text, which reads “called the altar, ‘For it is a witness…’” Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac supply it. The Septuagint reads, “Joshua gave a name to the altar… and said, ‘It is a witness in the midst of them.’”

verses.text: Long afterward, when Yahweh had given Israel rest from all their enemies around them, and Joshua had grown old and was well along in years,
Joshua called together all Israel—its elders, heads, judges, and officers—and told them, “I am old and well along in years.
You have seen all that Yahweh your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is Yahweh your God who has fought for you.
Look, I have assigned to you, as an inheritance for your tribes, the nations that remain, as well as all the nations I have cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea on the west.
Yahweh your God himself will thrust them out from before you and drive them away from you, and you will take possession of their land, as Yahweh your God promised you.
So be very strong to keep and do everything written in the book of the law of Moses, without turning from it to the right or to the left,
so that you do not mingle with these nations left among you, mention the names of their gods, swear by them, serve them, or bow down to them,
but you are to cling to Yahweh your God just as you have done to this day.
For Yahweh has driven out great and mighty nations ahead of you; as for you, up to this day no one has withstood you.
A single one of you chases a thousand, because Yahweh your God is the one fighting for you, as he promised you.
Be very careful, therefore, for your own sakes, to love Yahweh your God.
For if you turn away and hold fast to the survivors of these nations that remain among you, and intermarry with them and mix with them and they with you,

know for certain that Yahweh your God will not go on driving these nations out ahead of you. They will become snares and traps for you, whips on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land Yahweh your God has given you.

“I am now about to go the way of all the earth. All of you know in your hearts and souls that not one of all the good things Yahweh your God spoke concerning you has failed. Everything has come true for you; not one of them has failed.

But just as every good thing Yahweh your God promised you has come to you, so Yahweh will bring on you every evil thing until he has wiped you out from this good land that Yahweh your God has given you,

if you break the covenant of Yahweh your God that he commanded you, and go serve other gods and bow down to them. Then Yahweh’s anger will burn against you, and you will quickly perish from the good land he has given you.”{a}

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks the last sentence of this verse (“Then the anger of Yahweh…”).

verses.text: Joshua assembled all the tribes of Israel at Shechem{a} and called for the elders, heads, judges, and officers of Israel, and they stood before God.

Joshua told all the people, “Here is what Yahweh, Israel’s God, declares: ‘In ancient times your fathers lived on the other side of the River,{b} namely Terah, the father of Abraham and the father of Nahor, and they served other gods.
But I took your father Abraham from beyond the River, led him through the whole land of Canaan, and multiplied his offspring. I gave him Isaac.
To Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau; to Esau I gave Mount Seir’s hill country as a possession, while Jacob and his sons went down to Egypt.
Then I sent Moses and Aaron, and I struck Egypt with what I did in its midst, and afterward I brought you out.{c}
I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. The Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.

When they cried out to Yahweh, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians, and brought the sea down over them and covered them. Your eyes witnessed what I did to the Egyptians. Afterward you stayed for many days in the wilderness.
I brought you into the land of the Amorites who lived east of the Jordan; they fought against you, but I handed them over to you, and you took their land, and I destroyed them ahead of you.
Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. He sent and called Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,
but I refused to listen to Balaam, so he actually blessed you, and I rescued you from his hand.

You went over the Jordan and reached Jericho; Jericho’s leaders{d} fought you, and so did the Amorites, Perizzites, Canaanites, Hittites, Girgashites, Hivites, and Jebusites, but I delivered them into your hand.
I sent the hornet{e} ahead of you, and it drove out the two kings of the Amorites{f} before you—not by your sword or your bow.
I gave you a land you had not tilled and cities you had not built; you now live in them and eat from vineyards and olive orchards that you never planted.’
“So now fear Yahweh and serve him with integrity and faithfulness. Throw away the gods your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve Yahweh.

But if serving Yahweh seems wrong to you, choose today whom you will serve: the gods your fathers served beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you are living. As for me and my household, we will serve Yahweh.”
Then the people answered, “Far be it from us that we should forsake Yahweh to serve other gods,

For it is Yahweh our God who brought up both us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, who performed those great signs before our eyes and kept us safe throughout the journey we made and among every nation we passed through.
Yahweh also drove all the peoples out ahead of us, namely the Amorites who lived in this land. We too, therefore, will serve Yahweh, for he is our God.”
But Joshua said to the people, “You are not able to serve Yahweh, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God. He will not forgive your transgressions or your sins.
If you forsake Yahweh and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good.”
The people said to Joshua, “No, but we will serve Yahweh.”
Then Joshua said to the people, “You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen Yahweh, to serve him.” And they said, “We are witnesses.”
He said, “Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to Yahweh, the God of Israel.”
The people answered Joshua, “We will serve Yahweh our God and obey his voice.”
That day Joshua made a covenant with the people, and at Shechem{g} he set statutes and ordinances before them.
Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the oak{h} that was by the sanctuary of Yahweh.
Joshua told all the people, “Look, this stone will witness against us, for it has heard all the words Yahweh spoke to us; it will witness against you if you are false to your God.”
So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.
After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died, being 110 years old.{i}
They buried him within his own inheritance at Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.{j}
Israel served Yahweh all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that Yahweh did for Israel.{k}

Joseph’s bones, which the Israelites had carried up from Egypt, were buried at Shechem in the parcel of land that Jacob had purchased from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred pieces of money;{l} it became an inheritance for Joseph’s descendants.
Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and he was buried at Gibeah,{m} the property of his son Phinehas, who had been granted it in Ephraim’s hill country.{n}

notes.text: The Septuagint reads Shiloh here and in verse 25. Shechem was the site of Abraham’s first altar in the land (Genesis 12:6–7) and of Jacob’s burial of foreign gods (Genesis 35:4).
That is, the Euphrates; so in verses 3, 14, and 15.
The Septuagint has a shorter text in verses 5–7. It lacks “I sent Moses and Aaron” and some other phrases.
Hebrew ba‘ale, “the lords” or “citizens.”
Or “panic” or “terror” (Hebrew tsir‘ah). Compare Exodus 23:28 and Deuteronomy 7:20.
The Septuagint reads “twelve kings of the Amorites.” The Hebrew “two kings” refers to Sihon and Og (2:10).
The Septuagint reads “at Shiloh, before the tabernacle of the God of Israel.”
Or “terebinth,” a large tree. Compare Genesis 35:4, where Jacob hid foreign gods under the oak near Shechem.
An age of 110 years was considered the ideal life span in Egypt. Joseph died at the same age (Genesis 50:26).
Gaash may mean “quaking” or “shaking.”

The Septuagint places this verse before Joshua’s death (as verse 29). After the burial account it adds that Joshua’s flint blades, used to circumcise the Israelites at Gilgal once he had led them out of Egypt, were laid beside him in his grave, just as the Lord had commanded, and that they remain there to this day. Compare the Septuagint addition at 21:42.

Hebrew “for a hundred qesitah,” a unit of uncertain value, perhaps a weight of silver; it appears elsewhere only in Genesis 33:19 and Job 42:11. The Septuagint reads “for a hundred ewe-lambs.” Compare Genesis 33:19; Acts 7:16.
Gibeah means “hill.” The Septuagint reads Gabaar.

The Septuagint adds a longer ending: “On that day the Israelites took the ark of God and carried it around among them. And Phinehas served as priest in place of Eleazar his father until he died, and he was buried in his own place, Gabaar. And the Israelites went away, each to his own place and to his own city. And the Israelites worshiped Astarte and Ashtaroth and the gods of the nations around them. And the Lord gave them into the hands of Eglon king of Moab, and he ruled over them eighteen years.” This addition links the book to Judges 2:6–13 and 3:12–14.

books.name: Judges
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls of Judges (4QJudgᵃ, 4QJudgᵇ, 1QJudg). The Septuagint of Judges survives in two quite different Greek forms: the “B” text (represented by Codex Vaticanus) and the “A” text (represented by Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts). Septuagint readings cited in the footnotes were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation, which mainly follows the B text; A-text readings are cited only where Brenton’s notes or published scholarship confirm them, and otherwise are stated in general terms. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which agrees with the Hebrew in Judges. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes.

verses.text: After the death of Joshua,{a} the Israelites asked Yahweh, “Who will go up first for us against the Canaanites, to fight against them?”
Yahweh said, “Judah will go up. Look, I have given the land into his hand.”

Then Judah said to Simeon his brother, “Come up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanites. Then I also will go with you into your allotted territory.” So Simeon went with him.
Judah marched out, and Yahweh delivered the Canaanites and Perizzites to them. At Bezek they killed ten thousand men.
At Bezek they located Adoni-bezek{b} and fought him; the Canaanites and Perizzites were routed.
Adoni-bezek fled, but they pursued him, caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his big toes.

Adoni-bezek confessed, “Seventy kings, each missing his thumbs and big toes, scavenged leftovers beneath my table. God has paid me back exactly what I did to them.” They led him to Jerusalem, and he died in that city.
The men of Judah fought against Jerusalem and captured it. They struck it with the edge of the sword and set the city on fire.
Afterward the men of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites who lived in the hill country, in the Negev,{c} and in the lowland.
Judah then advanced on the Canaanite inhabitants of Hebron (its older name was Kiriath-arba{d}), and struck down Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai.
From there they went against the inhabitants of Debir. (The name of Debir was formerly Kiriath-sepher.{e})
Caleb declared, “Whoever assaults and takes Kiriath-sepher, I will give him my daughter Achsah as a bride.”
Othniel{f} son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, took the town, and Caleb gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife.
On her wedding day she persuaded Othniel to request a field from her father. She dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb asked, “What would you like?”
“Grant me one more favor,” she told him. “You have placed me in the dry southland, the Negev, so give me springs as well.” Caleb then gave her the upper pools and the lower pools.{g}
The Kenite’s descendants,{h} kin of Moses’ father-in-law, left the City of Palms{i} and went with Judah’s people to the Judean desert in the Negev near Arad, where they settled among the people.
Judah marched with his brother tribe Simeon, and together they defeated the Canaanites of Zephath and put the town under the ban.{j} The town was renamed Hormah.
Judah also captured Gaza with its territory, Ashkelon with its territory, and Ekron with its territory.{k}
Yahweh was on Judah’s side, and Judah occupied the hill country. But they failed to expel the people living on the coastal plain, since those people owned iron-clad chariots.{l}
They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said, and he drove out from there the three sons of Anak.
But the Benjaminites did not drive out the Jebusites who lived in Jerusalem, so the Jebusites have lived with the Benjaminites in Jerusalem to this day.
The house of Joseph also went up against Bethel, and Yahweh was with them.
The house of Joseph sent spies to Bethel. (The name of the city was formerly Luz.)
The scouts saw a man leaving the town and told him, “Tell us the way in, and we will treat you mercifully.”
He showed them the way into the city, and they struck the city with the edge of the sword, but they let the man and all his family go.
The man went to Hittite country, built a town there, and called it Luz, the name it still bears today.

Manasseh did not dispossess the residents of Beth-shean with its dependent villages,{m} or of Taanach with its villages, or of Dor, Ibleam, or Megiddo and their villages, because the Canaanites stubbornly held on to that territory.
When Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but they did not drive them out completely.
Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites lived among them in Gezer.
Zebulun failed to evict the people of Kitron and Nahalol, so the Canaanites lived among them as forced laborers.
Asher failed to dispossess the residents of Acco, Sidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob.
So the Asherites lived among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land, for they did not drive them out.

Naphtali failed to evict the inhabitants of Beth-shemesh and of Beth-anath, so Naphtali settled among the Canaanites already native to the land. Even so, those two towns’ people were reduced to servitude as forced laborers for Naphtali.
The Amorites forced the tribe of Dan up into the hills and refused to let them descend onto the lowland.
The Amorites held firmly to Har-heres,{n} Aijalon, and Shaalbim, but the tribe of Joseph overpowered them and made them forced laborers.
The border of the Amorites{o} ran from the Ascent of Akrabbim,{p} from Sela and upward.

notes.text: The Septuagint of Judges survives in two main Greek forms, the B text (Codex Vaticanus and related manuscripts) and the A text (Codex Alexandrinus and related manuscripts). They differ often in wording and sometimes in sense; significant differences are noted. Joshua means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Adoni-bezek means “lord of Bezek.”
The Negev is the dry southern region of Judah; the word also means “south.”
Kiriath-arba means “city of Arba” or “city of four.” Hebron perhaps means “alliance.”
Kiriath-sepher means “town of the book” or “town of the scribe.”
Othniel perhaps means “my strength is God” or “lion of God”; the meaning is uncertain.
Or “Gulloth-illith and Gulloth-tahtith”; gulloth means “basins” or “pools.” Compare Joshua 15:16–19.
The Septuagint (B text, as in Brenton) names him: “the sons of Jothor (Jethro) the Kenite.” Compare 4:11, which calls Moses’ father-in-law Hobab.
That is, Jericho (Deuteronomy 34:3).
Hebrew charam, to give over completely to God, usually by destruction. Hormah sounds like the word for “devoted to destruction.”

The Septuagint reads the opposite: “But Judah did not take possession of Gaza and its territory, nor Ashkelon and its territory, nor Ekron and its territory, nor Ashdod and the land around it.” This agrees with verse 19 and with the later history of the Philistine cities.
Hebrew rekeb barzel. The Septuagint (B text) takes rekeb as a name: “because Rechab prevented them.”
Hebrew “daughters,” the usual term for the smaller towns dependent on a city; so throughout this verse.
Har-heres means “mountain of the sun.” Compare Ir-shemesh (“city of the sun”) in Joshua 19:41.
Some Septuagint manuscripts and many scholars read “Edomites,” which fits the location of the Ascent of Akrabbim.
Akrabbim means “scorpions.” Sela means “rock.”

verses.text: Yahweh’s messenger came from Gilgal up to Bochim.{a} He announced, “I led you out of Egypt and into the country I promised your ancestors. I told you, ‘I will never annul my covenant with you,
and you must make no covenant with the inhabitants of this land; you must tear down their altars.’ But you have not obeyed my voice. What is this you have done?
So now I say, I will not drive them out before you, but they will become thorns in your sides,{b} and their gods will be a snare to you.”
When Yahweh’s messenger finished speaking to all Israel, the people broke into loud weeping.
So they called the name of that place Bochim, and they sacrificed there to Yahweh.
Joshua dismissed the people, and the Israelites each went to occupy their own allotted land.
The people served Yahweh all the days of Joshua and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work that Yahweh had done for Israel.
Joshua son of Nun, the servant of Yahweh, died at the age of a hundred and ten years.
They buried him within the boundary of his inheritance at Timnath-heres,{c} in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash.
And all that generation also were gathered to their fathers. Another generation arose after them who did not know Yahweh or the work that he had done for Israel.
The Israelites did evil in Yahweh’s sight, worshiping the Baals.{d}

They abandoned Yahweh, the God their ancestors had worshiped, who had rescued them from Egypt. They followed other gods, those of the neighboring peoples, bowing before them and making Yahweh furious.
They abandoned Yahweh and served Baal and the Ashtaroth.{e}
Yahweh’s fury blazed against Israel, so he surrendered them to raiders who looted them. He turned them over to the enemies surrounding them, and they lost all power to resist.
Whenever they went out, the hand of Yahweh was against them for harm, as Yahweh had said and as Yahweh had sworn to them. And they were in great distress.
Then Yahweh raised up judges,{f} who saved them from the hand of those who plundered them.

Still, they would not even heed their judges. They chased after other gods like a prostitute, and bowed to them. They swerved quickly from the road their ancestors had followed, which was obedience to Yahweh’s commands. They did not follow it.

Whenever Yahweh appointed a judge for them, he stood with that judge and rescued them from their enemies throughout the judge’s lifetime. Yahweh took pity on them as they groaned under their oppressors and tormentors.

But whenever the judge died, they turned back and acted more corruptly than their fathers, going after other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. They did not give up any of their practices or their stubborn ways.
So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he said, “Because this nation has broken my covenant that I commanded their fathers and has not obeyed my voice,
I in turn will no longer drive out before them any of the nations that Joshua left when he died,
in order to put Israel to the test through them, to see whether they would follow Yahweh’s path as their ancestors did, or not.”
This is why Yahweh let those nations remain; he did not hurry to dislodge them, and he never handed them over to Joshua.

notes.text: Bochim means “weepers” (verse 5). The Septuagint adds “and to Bethel and to the house of Israel.”

Hebrew “they will be sides to you.” “Thorns in” is supplied from the similar warnings in Numbers 33:55 and Joshua 23:13. The Septuagint reads “they will be distresses to you,” and the Latin Vulgate “enemies.”
Timnath-heres means “portion of the sun.” In Joshua 19:50 and 24:30 the name is Timnath-serah (“remaining portion”), with two letters reversed.
Baal means “lord” or “master,” the title of the Canaanite storm god. The plural refers to the local forms of his worship.
Ashtaroth is the plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess of fertility and war.
Hebrew shophetim, leaders who delivered Israel and governed it, not only judges in a court of law.

verses.text: Now these are the nations that Yahweh left in order to test Israel by them, all who had not known any of the wars of Canaan.
It was only so that the generations of the Israelites might know war, to teach it to those who had not known it before:

These were the five Philistine lords,{a} every Canaanite, the Sidonians, and the Hivites who made their home in the Lebanon highlands, stretching from Baal-hermon’s mountain to the approach to Hamath.{b}
They were left to test Israel by them, to know whether they would obey the commands of Yahweh, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.
So the Israelites lived among the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites.
They took their daughters as wives for themselves and gave their own daughters to their sons, and they served their gods.
The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh. They forgot Yahweh their God and served the Baals and the Asheroth.{c}
So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Cushan-rishathaim{d} king of Aram-naharaim,{e} and the Israelites served Cushan-rishathaim eight years.
When the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, Yahweh raised up a savior for the Israelites, who saved them: Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.
The Spirit of Yahweh came upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to war, and Yahweh gave Cushan-rishathaim king of Aram into his hand, and his hand prevailed over Cushan-rishathaim.
So the land had rest forty years. Then Othniel son of Kenaz died.
Again the Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh strengthened Eglon{f} king of Moab against Israel, because they had done what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.
He gathered to himself the Ammonites and the Amalekites, and he went and struck Israel, and they took possession of the City of Palms.
And the Israelites served Eglon king of Moab eighteen years.

Then the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, and Yahweh raised up a savior for them, Ehud{g} son of Gera, the Benjaminite, a man who was left-handed.{h} The Israelites sent tribute by him to Eglon king of Moab.
Ehud made himself a sword with two edges, about a foot{i} long, and he strapped it under his clothes on his right thigh.
He presented the tribute to Eglon king of Moab. Now Eglon was a very fat man.
When Ehud had finished presenting the tribute, he sent away the people who had carried the tribute.
But he himself turned back at the carved images{j} near Gilgal and said, “I have a secret message for you, O king.” The king said, “Silence!” And all who stood by him went out from him.
Ehud came to him as he was sitting alone in his cool upper room. Ehud said, “I have a message from God for you.” And he rose from his seat.
Ehud reached with his left hand, took the sword from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly.
The handle also went in after the blade, and the fat closed over the blade, for he did not pull the sword out of his belly. And the dung came out.{k}
Then Ehud went out to the porch{l} and shut the doors of the upper room behind him and locked them.
When he had gone out, the king’s servants came, and they saw that the doors of the upper room were locked. They said, “Surely he is relieving himself{m} in the inner room of the cool chamber.”
They waited so long that they were ashamed, but he still would not unlock the upstairs room. Finally they fetched the key and unlocked it, and there lay their master, sprawled dead on the floor.
Ehud escaped while they delayed. He passed beyond the carved images and escaped to Seirah.
When he arrived, he sounded the ram’s horn in the hill country of Ephraim, and the Israelites went down with him from the hill country, with him at their head.

He said to them, “Follow me, for Yahweh has given your enemies, Moab, into your hand.” So they went down after him and seized the fords of the Jordan against Moab, and they did not allow anyone to cross.
At that time they struck down about ten thousand men of Moab, all strong, all able men; not one escaped.
So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel, and the land had rest eighty years.
Next came Shamgar, Anath’s son,{n} who killed six hundred Philistines using a cattle prod. He, too, rescued Israel.

notes.text: Hebrew seren, a Philistine title, perhaps related to the Greek word tyrannos.
Or “the entrance of Hamath.”
The Asheroth were wooden poles or images associated with the goddess Asherah. The Septuagint reads “the groves.”
Cushan-rishathaim means “Cushan of double wickedness,” probably a mocking form of a foreign name.
That is, “Aram of the two rivers,” upper Mesopotamia.
Eglon sounds like the Hebrew word for “calf” (egel).
Ehud perhaps means “where is the glory?”; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “restricted in his right hand.” The same expression is used of the Benjaminite slingers in 20:16. Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”
Hebrew gomed, a measure found only here, perhaps a short cubit of about 13 inches (33 cm). The Septuagint reads “a span” (about 9 inches, 23 cm).
Or “the stone quarries” (also in verse 26). Hebrew pesilim usually means carved idols.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word parshedon is uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) lacks this clause.
The meaning of the rare Hebrew word misderon is uncertain; perhaps “vestibule” or “latrine.”
Hebrew “covering his feet,” a polite expression.
Anath was a Canaanite goddess of war; “son of Anath” may refer to Shamgar’s town (Beth-anath) or describe him as a warrior.

verses.text: After Ehud died, the Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.
So Yahweh sold them into the hand of Jabin{a} king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor. The commander of his army was Sisera, who lived in Harosheth-hagoyim.{b}
Then the Israelites cried out to Yahweh, for he had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had oppressed the Israelites harshly for twenty years.
Now Deborah,{c} a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth,{d} was judging Israel at that time.
She held court beneath Deborah’s Palm, between Ramah and Bethel in Ephraim’s hill country, and Israelites came to her for rulings.
She summoned Barak{e} son of Abinoam from Kedesh in Naphtali and told him, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, commands you: Go, assemble at Mount Tabor, bringing ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.
I will lure Sisera, Jabin’s army commander, to the Kishon wadi to meet you, with his chariots and soldiers, and I will give him to you.’”
Barak said to her, “If you will go with me, I will go, but if you will not go with me, I will not go.”{f}

She said, “I will certainly go with you. Nevertheless, the road you are taking will not lead to your glory, for Yahweh will sell Sisera into the hand of a woman.” Then Deborah arose and went with Barak to Kedesh.
Barak summoned Zebulun and Naphtali to assemble at Kedesh. Ten thousand men marched out behind him,{g} and Deborah went along as well.
Heber the Kenite had split off from the other Kenites, who descended from Hobab, Moses’ brother-in-law. He had set up his tent far off, by the great tree at Zaanannim,{h} close to Kedesh.
When Sisera was told that Barak son of Abinoam had gone up to Mount Tabor,
Sisera called out all his chariots, nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people who were with him, from Harosheth-hagoyim to the Kishon River.
Deborah urged Barak, “Go! This very day Yahweh hands Sisera over to you. Isn’t Yahweh marching ahead of you?” So Barak descended Mount Tabor, ten thousand men behind him.
And Yahweh threw Sisera and all his chariots and all his army into panic before Barak by the edge of the sword. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled on foot.
Barak chased the chariots and the troops as far as Harosheth-haggoyim, and Sisera’s whole army was put to the sword. Not a single man survived.
But Sisera fled on foot to the tent of Jael,{i} the wife of Heber the Kenite, for there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.
Jael went out to greet Sisera and told him, “Come in, sir, come in with me; have no fear.” He went into her tent, and she hid him under a blanket.
He asked her, “May I have a sip of water? I am parched.” She opened a milk skin, gave him a drink, and covered him up again.
He said to her, “Stand at the entrance of the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is anyone here?’ say, ‘No.’”
Then Heber’s wife Jael took a tent peg and a mallet. She crept up to him and hammered the peg through his skull into the ground, as he lay in a deep sleep of exhaustion. And he died.{j}

And just then, as Barak was pursuing Sisera, Jael came out to meet him and said to him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are looking for.” So he went in with her, and there was Sisera lying dead, with the tent peg in his temple.
So on that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites.
The Israelites’ grip on Jabin, the king of Canaan, grew steadily stronger, until at last they wiped him out.

notes.text: Jabin means “he understands.” A king of Hazor of the same name appears in Joshua 11:1.
Harosheth-hagoyim perhaps means “woodland of the nations” or “cultivated land of the nations.”
Deborah means “bee.”
Or “a woman of fire” or “a fiery woman.” Lappidoth means “torches,” and may be a name or a description.
Barak means “lightning.” Abinoam means “my father is pleasantness.”
The Septuagint adds: “for I do not know the day on which the angel of Yahweh will give me success.”
Hebrew “at his feet,” that is, following him; also in verse 15 of chapter 5.

Or “the oak of Zaanannim.” The Septuagint reads “the oak of the covetous ones.” Hobab is perhaps the same person as Jethro (Exodus 3:1) or a son of Reuel (Numbers 10:29); the Hebrew word for “father-in-law” can also mean “brother-in-law.”
Jael means “mountain goat.”
Or “he was fast asleep and exhausted. So he died.” The Hebrew is difficult. The Septuagint reads “and he fainted away, and darkness fell upon him, and he died.”

verses.text: Then Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang on that day:
“When locks hang loose{a} in Israel, when the people offer themselves willingly, bless Yahweh!
Hear, O kings; listen, O rulers! I, to Yahweh I will sing; I will make music to Yahweh, the God of Israel.
Yahweh, as you came out of Seir, as you strode from Edom’s fields, the earth shook, the skies poured rain, the clouds dripped water.
The mountains quaked{b} before Yahweh, the One of Sinai,{c} before Yahweh, the God of Israel.
In Shamgar son of Anath’s time, in Jael’s time, the main roads stood empty,{d} and caravans took the byways.
Village life{e} ceased in Israel; it ceased until I, Deborah, arose,{f} until I arose, a mother in Israel.
They chose new gods; then war was in the gates.{g} Was a shield or a spear to be seen among forty thousand in Israel?
My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel, those who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless Yahweh!
You who ride on white{h} donkeys, you who sit on rich carpets,{i} and you who walk on the road, tell of it!{j}

Louder than the voice of the archers{k} at the watering places, there they recount the righteous acts of Yahweh, the righteous acts of his villagers in Israel. Then the people of Yahweh went down to the gates.
“Awake, awake, Deborah! Awake, awake, sing a song! Arise, Barak, and take your captives captive, son of Abinoam.
Then the survivors came down to the nobles; the people of Yahweh came down for me against the mighty.{l}
From Ephraim came those whose root is in Amalek;{m} after you, Benjamin, with your kinsmen. From Machir came down commanders, and from Zebulun those who carry the officer’s staff.{n}
Issachar’s chieftains marched with Deborah, and Issachar stood by Barak; they plunged into the valley on his heels. Among Reuben’s divisions there was much soul-searching.{o}
Why did you linger among the sheep pens,{p} listening to shepherds pipe to their flocks? Among Reuben’s divisions there was much hesitation.
Gilead remained across the Jordan; and Dan, why did he loiter near the ships?{q} Asher stayed on the seashore and lingered in his harbors.
Zebulun’s people risked their lives, facing death; and Naphtali too, on the open hills.
“Kings came; they fought; then the kings of Canaan fought at Taanach, by the waters of Megiddo. They took no plunder of silver.
From heaven the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.
The river Kishon carried them off, that ancient{r} river, the Kishon. Advance, my spirit, with might!{s}
Then the horses’ hooves hammered with the galloping, the galloping of his mighty steeds.
‘Curse Meroz,’{t} said Yahweh’s messenger, ‘curse her people bitterly, for they never came to aid Yahweh, to aid Yahweh against the warriors.’
“Most blessed of women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; of women in tents she is most blessed.
He asked for water; she gave him milk; in a bowl fit for nobles she brought him curds.
She put her hand to the tent peg and her right hand to the workman’s hammer. She struck Sisera; she crushed his head; she shattered and pierced his temple.
At her feet he crumpled, collapsed, and lay still; at her feet he crumpled and fell; right where he crumpled, he lay dead.
