“At the window she peered out and cried, Sisera’s mother, from behind the lattice: ‘Why is his chariot delayed? Why is the sound of his chariot wheels so late?’
The wisest of her ladies answer her; indeed, she repeats her own words to herself:

‘Are they not finding and dividing the spoil? A girl, two girls{u} for every man; spoil of dyed cloth for Sisera, spoil of dyed cloth embroidered, dyed cloth, doubly embroidered, for the neck of the plunderer?’{v}
“So may all your enemies perish, O Yahweh! But may those who love him be like the sun when it rises in its might.” And the land had rest forty years.

notes.text: Or “When leaders take the lead.” The Hebrew phrase bifroa‘ pera‘ot is one of many difficult expressions in this ancient poem. It may refer to warriors letting their hair hang loose as a sign of dedication (compare Numbers 6:5), or to leaders taking command. The Septuagint (B text) reads “When a revelation was made in Israel”; other Greek manuscripts understand it of rulers taking command.
Or “flowed” or “melted.” The Hebrew may come from a verb meaning “quake” (as the Septuagint, “were shaken”) or from one meaning “flow.”
Or “this is Sinai,” or “even Sinai.” Many scholars take Hebrew zeh sinai as an ancient title, “the One of Sinai” (compare Psalm 68:8).
Or “caravans ceased.”
Or “Warriors.” The meaning of Hebrew perazon (also in verse 11) is uncertain; it may mean the people of unwalled villages, or rulers or warriors. The Septuagint (B text) reads “the mighty men.”
Or “until you arose, Deborah, until you arose.” The Hebrew form qamti can be read as an old second-person form, which the Septuagint follows (“until Deborah arose”).

The Hebrew of this line is very difficult. The Septuagint (B text) agrees with “They chose new gods”; some translators read “God chose new leaders.” The second clause is also uncertain (“then there was fighting in the gates,” or “then there was bread of barley”).
Or “tawny.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “at noonday,” taking the Hebrew word as tsohorayim.
The meaning of Hebrew middin is uncertain; perhaps “saddle blankets.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “on the judgment seat,” relating it to the word for “judgment.”
Or “consider it!” or “sing of it!”
Or “of those who divide the flocks,” or “of the musicians.” The meaning of Hebrew mechatsetsim is uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) reads “from the noise of disturbers among the drawers of water.”

The Hebrew of verse 13 is difficult and has been read in several ways. The Septuagint (B text) reads “Then the remnant went down to the strong; the people of Yahweh went down for him among the mighty from me.”
The meaning is uncertain; perhaps Ephraim had settled in land once held by Amalek (compare 12:15). The Septuagint (B text) reads “Ephraim rooted them out in Amalek.”
Or “the staff of the scribe,” or “the rod of the marshal.” Hebrew shebet sopher.

Hebrew chiqqe-leb, “decisions of heart.” Many Hebrew manuscripts and the parallel line in verse 16 read chiqre-leb, “searchings of heart,” a difference of one letter. The Septuagint (B text) reads “great pangs reached to the heart.”
Or “saddlebags” or “campfires.” The meaning of Hebrew mishpetayim is uncertain.
Or “why did he serve as an alien on ships?” The Hebrew verb gur means to stay as a resident alien.
The meaning of Hebrew qedumim is uncertain; perhaps “ancient,” or “onrushing,” or “of battles.”
Or “You trampled the strong, O my soul!” The Septuagint (B text) reads “my mighty soul will trample him down.”
The location of Meroz is unknown.
Hebrew “a womb, two wombs,” a crude soldiers’ term for captive women.

The Hebrew of the last line is difficult; some read “for my neck as plunder,” or “for the neck of the queen.” The Septuagint (B text) has “he will surely be gracious to every man … they are the spoils for his neck.”

verses.text: The Israelites did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh gave them into the hand of Midian seven years.
The hand of Midian prevailed over Israel. Because of Midian the Israelites made for themselves the dens that are in the mountains, and the caves and the strongholds.
For whenever Israel had sown seed, Midian and Amalek and the people of the east would come up and attack them.
They would camp against them and destroy the produce of the land as far as Gaza, and they left no sustenance in Israel, neither sheep nor ox nor donkey.
They arrived with their herds and tents, as numerous as locusts. They and their camels were beyond counting, and they invaded the land to devastate it.
So Israel was brought very low because of Midian, and the Israelites cried out to Yahweh.
When the Israelites cried out to Yahweh on account of Midian,{a}
Yahweh sent a prophet to the Israelites, who told them, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I rescued you from Egypt and freed you from the house of slavery.
I rescued you from the hand of the Egyptians and from the hand of all who oppressed you. I drove them out before you and gave you their land.
I told you, “I am Yahweh your God; do not worship the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you live.” But you ignored me.’”

The messenger of Yahweh arrived and sat beneath the oak tree in Ophrah, a town of Joash, from the clan of Abiezer. Joash’s son Gideon{b} was threshing wheat inside a winepress, to keep it out of Midian’s sight.
The angel of Yahweh appeared to him and said to him, “Yahweh is with you, mighty warrior.”

Gideon replied, “Please, sir, if Yahweh is with us, why has all this disaster come upon us? Where are the marvels our ancestors described to us, saying, ‘Didn’t Yahweh lead us out of Egypt?’ But now Yahweh has deserted us and handed us over to Midian.”
Yahweh turned to him and said, “Go, with all the strength you possess, and deliver Israel from Midian’s grip. Am I not the one sending you?”
He said to him, “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Look, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house.”
Yahweh answered him, “I will be with you, and you will defeat Midian as though it were a single man.”
He said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes, then give me a sign that it is you who are speaking with me.
Please stay here until I come back with my gift and set it down in front of you.” He answered, “I will wait until you come back.”

So Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, and unleavened cakes from about three-fifths of a bushel{c} of flour. He put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and brought them out to him under the oak and presented them.
The angel of God said to him, “Take the meat and the unleavened cakes, put them on this rock, and pour out the broth.” And he did so.

Then the angel of Yahweh reached out the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened cakes. Fire went up from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened cakes. And the angel of Yahweh vanished from his sight.
Then Gideon saw that he was the angel of Yahweh. And Gideon said, “Alas, Lord Yahweh! For I have seen the angel of Yahweh face to face.”
But Yahweh said to him, “Peace be to you. Do not be afraid; you will not die.”
So Gideon built an altar there to Yahweh and called it Yahweh Shalom.{d} To this day it still stands at Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
The same night Yahweh instructed him, “Take your father’s second bull, a seven-year-old,{e} Demolish your father’s altar to Baal, and chop down the Asherah pole{f} beside it.
Then build an altar to Yahweh your God on the top of this stronghold, laid out in proper order. Take the second bull and offer it as a burnt offering with the wood of the Asherah that you cut down.”
So Gideon took ten men from his servants and did as Yahweh had told him. But because he was too afraid of his father’s household and the men of the city to do it by day, he did it by night.
When the townsmen got up early next morning, they saw Baal’s altar demolished, the Asherah pole beside it hacked down, and the second bull offered on a newly built altar.
They said to one another, “Who has done this thing?” When they had inquired and searched, they said, “Gideon son of Joash has done this thing.”
The townsmen demanded of Joash, “Hand over your son for execution! He demolished Baal’s altar and chopped down the Asherah pole next to it.”

But Joash said to all who stood against him, “Will you contend for Baal? Will you save him? Whoever contends for him will be put to death by morning. If he is a god, let him contend for himself, because someone has torn down his altar.”
So on that day Gideon was called Jerubbaal,{g} that is to say, “Let Baal contend against him,” because he tore down his altar.
Then all of Midian, Amalek, and the eastern peoples joined forces, crossed the Jordan, and encamped in the Jezreel Valley.
But the Spirit of Yahweh clothed{h} Gideon, and he sounded the ram’s horn, and the Abiezrites were called out to follow him.
He dispatched messengers across the territory of Manasseh, calling its men to arms behind him. He also sent word to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and those tribes marched out to join them.
Then Gideon said to God, “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have said,

watch, I will put out a wool fleece on the threshing floor. If dew gathers only on the fleece while the surrounding earth stays dry, I will be sure that you plan to save Israel through my action, as you promised.”
And so it happened. He got up early the next day, wrung out the fleece, and squeezed out a bowlful of dew.

Gideon pleaded with God, “Please don’t be furious with me, but let me ask once more. Allow me one more test with the fleece: this time let the fleece alone stay dry, and let dew cover the ground around it.”
God did that during the night. Only the fleece was dry, while the ground all around was covered with dew.

notes.text: The Dead Sea Scroll 4QJudgᵃ, one of the oldest surviving manuscripts of Judges, lacks verses 7–10; its text passes directly from verse 6 to verse 11. Many scholars regard these verses, which are present in the Masoretic Text and the Septuagint, as a later addition to the story.
Gideon probably means “hacker” or “one who cuts down” (compare verses 25–32). Joash means “Yahweh has given.” Ophrah perhaps means “fawn.”
Hebrew “an ephah,” about 22 liters (L).
Yahweh Shalom means “Yahweh is peace.”

The Hebrew is difficult; perhaps “the young bull of your father, and a second bull seven years old.” The Septuagint (B text) agrees with the Hebrew: “the young bullock … even the second bullock of seven years old.”
A wooden pole or image associated with the goddess Asherah; also in verses 26, 28, and 30.
Jerubbaal means “Let Baal contend.” In 2 Samuel 11:21 the name is changed to Jerubbesheth, replacing Baal with bosheth, “shame.”
That is, took possession of him; Hebrew “put on Gideon like a garment.”

verses.text: Early next morning Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) and his whole army set up camp at the spring of Harod.{a} Midian’s camp lay to the north, beneath Moreh hill,{b} in the valley.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “The people who are with you are too many for me to give Midian into their hand, or Israel would boast against me, saying, ‘My own hand has saved me.’

So now, proclaim in the hearing of the people, ‘Whoever is fearful and trembling, let him turn back and leave Mount Gilead.’”{c} Then twenty-two thousand of the people turned back, and ten thousand remained.

Yahweh told Gideon, “You still have too many men. Lead them down to the water, and I will sort them out there for you. Of anyone I say, ‘This man goes with you,’ that man goes; of anyone I say, ‘This man does not go with you,’ that man stays behind.”

So he brought the people down to the water, and Yahweh said to Gideon, “Everyone who laps the water with his tongue, as a dog laps, you shall set by himself; likewise everyone who kneels down to drink.”
The number of those who lapped, putting their hand to their mouths,{d} was three hundred men, and all the rest of the people knelt down to drink water.
Yahweh said to Gideon, “With the three hundred men who lapped I will save you and give Midian into your hand. Let all the rest of the people go, each to his home.”

So they took the people’s provisions in their hand, and their ram’s horns, and he sent all the rest of the men of Israel each to his tent, but he kept the three hundred men. The camp of Midian was below him in the valley.
That same night Yahweh said to him, “Get up, go down against the camp, for I have given it into your hand.
If you are afraid to attack, go down to the camp with your servant Purah.
You will listen to their talk, and after that you will find the nerve to attack the camp.” So he and his servant Purah crept down to where the armed sentries were posted at the camp’s edge.
The Midianites, Amalekites, and all the eastern peoples had spread across the valley like a swarm of locusts, and their camels were as countless as the sand along the seashore.

When Gideon arrived, there was a man telling his comrade a dream. He said, “Look, I had a dream, and there was a round loaf of barley bread tumbling into the camp of Midian. It came to the tent and struck it so that it fell, and turned it upside down, and the tent collapsed.”
His companion replied, “That can only mean the sword of Gideon, the Israelite son of Joash. God has delivered Midian, and the entire army with it, into his power.”
When Gideon heard the dream described and explained, he knelt in worship. He went back to Israel’s camp and called, “Rise! Yahweh has put the Midianite camp in your power.”
He split the three hundred men into three divisions. He gave every man a ram’s horn and an empty jar, with a torch burning in each jar.
He said to them, “Watch me and do the same. When I come to the edge of the camp, do as I do.
When I and all who are with me blow the ram’s horn, then you also blow the ram’s horns all around the camp and shout, ‘For Yahweh and for Gideon!’”

Gideon and his hundred men reached the camp’s perimeter at the start of the middle watch (about ten at night),{e} just after the sentries had been changed. They blew their horns and smashed the jars they were holding.

The three companies blew the ram’s horns and broke the jars. They held the torches in their left hands and the ram’s horns in their right hands to blow, and they cried out, “A sword for Yahweh and for Gideon!”
Each man stood in his place around the camp, and all the camp ran; they cried out and fled.

When the three hundred horns sounded, Yahweh turned every man’s sword against his fellow soldier throughout the camp. The army fled toward Beth-shittah and on to Zererah, to the border of Abel-meholah near Tabbath.
Israelites from Naphtali, Asher, and all of Manasseh were called up and joined the chase after Midian.

Gideon dispatched messengers across Ephraim’s hill country with this order: “Come down and attack Midian! Seize the fords of the Jordan before they reach them, as far as Beth-barah.” All the Ephraimite men were called up, and they held the fords as far as Beth-barah, and the Jordan itself.

They captured two Midianite commanders, Oreb and Zeeb.{f} Oreb they killed on the rock that bears his name, and Zeeb at the winepress called after him. They kept chasing Midian, then carried the heads of Oreb and Zeeb across the Jordan to Gideon.

notes.text: Harod means “trembling” (compare verse 3).
Moreh means “teacher” or “one who gives oracles.”

Gilead lies east of the Jordan, far from Gideon’s camp; many scholars suspect an early copying error, perhaps for Mount Gilboa, or take the Hebrew verb (found only here) to mean “and hurry away from Mount Gilead.”

In the Hebrew the words “putting their hand to their mouths” stand in verse 6 with those who lapped; the Septuagint (B text) agrees. Some scholars think the phrase originally belonged at the end of verse 5 with those who knelt.
Hebrew “the middle watch.” In the Old Testament the night was divided into three watches: evening (until about 10 p.m.), middle (until about 2 a.m.), and morning (until about 6 a.m.).
Oreb means “raven,” and Zeeb means “wolf.”

verses.text: The Ephraimites demanded of Gideon, “Why did you treat us this way? You never called us when you set out to fight Midian!” They berated him harshly.
He said to them, “What have I done now in comparison with you? Is not the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the grape harvest of Abiezer?
God handed Midian’s commanders, Oreb and Zeeb, over to you. What could I possibly accomplish next to you?” When he said this, their resentment cooled.
Gideon came to the Jordan and crossed over, he and the three hundred men who were with him, exhausted yet pursuing.
He said to the men of Succoth,{a} “Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me, for they are exhausted, and I am pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna,{b} the kings of Midian.”
But the officials of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?”
Gideon said, “Because of this, when Yahweh has given Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, I will thresh{c} your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
From there he went up to Penuel{d} and spoke to them in the same way, and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.
He warned the men of Penuel, “When I return victorious, I will demolish this tower.”

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their army with them, about fifteen thousand men, all who were left of the whole army of the people of the east; for those who had fallen were a hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword.
Gideon took the caravan route east of Nobah and Jogbehah and attacked the enemy camp, which was off its guard.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled, and he pursued them. He captured the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and threw the whole army into panic.
Then Gideon son of Joash returned from the battle by the Ascent of Heres.{e}
He captured a young man of the men of Succoth and questioned him, and the young man wrote down for him the officials of Succoth and its elders, seventy-seven men.

Then he came to the men of Succoth and said, “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, about whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna already in your hand, that we should give bread to your exhausted men?’”
He seized the town’s elders, gathered thorn bushes and thistles from the wilderness, and used them to give the men of Succoth a painful lesson.{f}
He tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of the city.
Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men were they whom you killed at Tabor?” They said, “As you are, so were they, each one resembling the son of a king.”
He said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As Yahweh lives, if you had let them live, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether his firstborn, “Get up, kill them!” But the young man did not draw his sword, for he was afraid, because he was still a young man.

Zebah and Zalmunna replied, “Do it yourself, strike us down, for a man’s strength matches his years.” Gideon stood up, killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and removed the crescent ornaments from their camels’ necks.
The Israelites told Gideon, “Be our ruler, you, then your son, and then your grandson, since you rescued us from Midian’s power.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you. Yahweh will rule over you.”
Then Gideon told them, “I have one request: each of you, hand over the earrings you took as plunder.” (The enemy wore gold earrings, as Ishmaelites did.{g})
They said, “We will gladly give them.” So they spread out a garment, and every man threw on it the earrings from his spoil.
The gold earrings he had requested weighed about forty-three pounds,{h} not counting the crescent ornaments, pendants, and purple robes worn by Midian’s kings, or the chains around the camels’ necks.
Gideon made it into an ephod{i} and put it in his city, in Ophrah. And all Israel prostituted themselves after it there, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house.
So Midian was subdued before the Israelites, and they did not raise their heads again. And the land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jerubbaal son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons, his own offspring,{j} for he had many wives.
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.{k}
Gideon son of Joash died at a ripe old age and was buried in his father Joash’s tomb at Ophrah, the town of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon died, the Israelites turned again and prostituted themselves after the Baals, and they made Baal-berith{l} their god.
The Israelites did not remember Yahweh their God, who had rescued them from the hand of all their enemies on every side,
and they did not show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal (that is, Gideon) in return for all the good that he had done for Israel.

notes.text: Succoth means “booths” or “shelters.”
Zebah means “sacrifice,” and Zalmunna perhaps “protection withheld.” The names may be deliberate distortions of the kings’ real names.
Or “tear.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and the Barkenim,” keeping the Hebrew word for “briers” as a name.
Penuel means “face of God” (Genesis 32:30).
Or “from the battle before sunrise.” Heres means “sun.”
So the Hebrew, “made to know.” Many scholars read “threshed” (compare verse 7), a slight difference in the Hebrew letters; the Septuagint (B text) reads “tore.”
Here a general term for desert traders. Compare Genesis 37:25–28, where Ishmaelites and Midianites are mentioned together.
Hebrew “1,700 shekels,” about 19.5 kilograms (kg).
An ephod was a priestly garment (Exodus 28:6–14), but here it seems to be an object used in worship or for seeking oracles.
Hebrew “who came out of his thigh.”
Abimelech means “my father is king.”
Baal-berith means “lord of the covenant.” Compare El-berith in 9:46.

verses.text: Abimelech, Jerubbaal’s son, traveled to Shechem, to his mother’s brothers, and addressed them and his mother’s whole extended family:
“Put this question to all of Shechem’s leaders:{a} ‘Which would you prefer, rule by seventy men, all of Jerubbaal’s sons, or rule by a single man? Remember that I am your own flesh and blood.’”
His mother’s brothers repeated his proposal to every one of Shechem’s leading citizens, and their loyalties swung toward Abimelech, since they reasoned, “He is our own flesh and blood.”
They gave him seventy pieces of silver{b} from the house of Baal-berith, and with it Abimelech hired worthless and reckless men, who followed him.
He went to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men, on one stone. But Jotham,{c} the youngest son of Jerubbaal, was left, for he hid himself.
Then all the leaders of Shechem and all Beth-millo{d} gathered together and went and made Abimelech king by the oak of the pillar{e} at Shechem.
When Jotham was told, he went and stood on the top of Mount Gerizim and raised his voice and called out to them: “Listen to me, leaders of Shechem, so that God may listen to you.
The trees once went out to anoint a king over themselves. They said to the olive tree, ‘Reign over us.’
But the olive tree said to them, ‘Should I give up my rich oil, by which gods and people are honored, and go to sway over the trees?’
Then the trees said to the fig tree, ‘You come and reign over us.’
But the fig tree answered, ‘Am I to abandon my sweet, rich fruit and go off to wave above the other trees?’
Then the trees said to the vine, ‘You come and reign over us.’
But the vine said to them, ‘Should I give up my new wine, which cheers gods and people, and go to sway over the trees?’
Then all the trees said to the bramble, ‘You come and reign over us.’

And the bramble said to the trees, ‘If you are truly anointing me king over you, then come and take refuge in my shade. But if not, let fire come out of the bramble and consume the cedars of Lebanon.’
“Now consider: did you behave honestly and sincerely when you crowned Abimelech? Have you treated Jerubbaal and his family fairly, and repaid him in keeping with what he did?
for my father fought for you and risked his life and rescued you from the hand of Midian,

and you have risen up against my father’s house today and killed his sons, seventy men, on one stone, and have made Abimelech, the son of his slave woman, king over the leaders of Shechem, because he is your brother—
if you have indeed dealt honestly and sincerely with Jerubbaal and his family today, then enjoy Abimelech, and may he enjoy you too.
If not, may fire blaze out from Abimelech and devour Shechem’s leaders and Beth-millo, and may fire blaze out from Shechem’s leaders and Beth-millo and devour Abimelech.”
Then Jotham ran away and fled and went to Beer,{f} and he lived there because of Abimelech his brother.
Abimelech ruled over Israel three years.
Then God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the leaders of Shechem, and the leaders of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech,

This was to bring retribution for the violence against Jerubbaal’s seventy sons, laying their blood on their brother Abimelech, who murdered them, and on the Shechemite leaders, who had backed him in killing his brothers.
The leading men of Shechem stationed ambushers for him along the mountain summits, and they plundered every traveler on that route. Abimelech was told about it.
Gaal, Ebed’s son,{g} arrived with his brothers and settled in Shechem, and the city’s leading men came to trust him.
They went to the countryside, harvested their vineyards, trampled the grapes, and held a celebration.{h} In the temple of their god they feasted, drank, and cursed Abimelech.

Gaal son of Ebed said, “Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him? Is he not the son of Jerubbaal, and is not Zebul his officer? Serve the men of Hamor, the father of Shechem! But why should we serve him?
If only I commanded this people! I would remove Abimelech.” He taunted Abimelech,{i} “Build up your forces and come out to battle!”
When Zebul the ruler of the city heard the words of Gaal son of Ebed, his anger burned.
He sent messengers to Abimelech in secret,{j} with this message: “Gaal, Ebed’s son, and his brothers have arrived in Shechem, where they are turning the city against you.
So now, get up by night, you and the people who are with you, and lie in ambush in the field.
At sunrise tomorrow, be up early and storm the town. When he and his men march out against you, deal with them as the opportunity allows.”
So Abimelech and all the people who were with him got up by night and lay in ambush against Shechem in four companies.
Gaal son of Ebed went out and took his stand at the town gate’s entrance. Abimelech and his troops emerged from their hiding place.
Gaal spotted the troops and said to Zebul, “Look, men are descending from the mountaintops!” Zebul answered, “Those are just the shadows of the hills, which look like men.”
Gaal spoke again and said, “Look, people are coming down from the center of the land,{k} and one company is coming by the way of the Diviners’ Oak.”{l}
Zebul retorted, “Where is your big talk now? You asked, ‘Who is Abimelech, that we must serve him?’ Aren’t these the very men you sneered at? Go on out and fight them.”
So Gaal went out at the head of the leaders of Shechem and fought against Abimelech.
Abimelech chased him, and he fled before him, and many fell wounded, up to the entrance of the gate.
Abimelech remained in Arumah, and Zebul expelled Gaal and his kinsmen from Shechem, so that they could no longer live there.
On the next day the people went out into the field, and Abimelech was told.
He divided the troops into three companies and hid them in the fields. When he saw the citizens emerging from the town, he sprang up, attacked them, and cut them down.
Abimelech and the companies that were with him rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the city gate, while the two companies rushed upon all who were in the field and struck them down.
Abimelech fought against the city all that day. He captured the city and killed the people who were in it, and he tore down the city and sowed it with salt.
When all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem heard of it, they went into the stronghold{m} of the house of El-berith.{n}
Abimelech was told that all the leaders of the Tower of Shechem had gathered together.

So Abimelech went up to Mount Zalmon,{o} he and all the people who were with him. Abimelech took an axe in his hand, cut down a bundle of brushwood, lifted it up, and put it on his shoulder. He said to the people who were with him, “What you have seen me do, hurry and do as I have done.”

Each of the soldiers likewise chopped down a branch and followed Abimelech. They piled the branches against the tower and set it ablaze with the people inside, so that everyone in the Shechem Tower died, about a thousand men and women.
Then Abimelech went to Thebez, camped against Thebez, and captured it.
Inside the town stood a fortified tower, and every man and woman, the town’s leaders included, fled into it, locked the door behind them, and climbed onto the tower’s roof.
Abimelech came to the tower and fought against it, and he drew near to the door of the tower to burn it with fire.
But a certain woman threw an upper millstone on Abimelech’s head and crushed his skull.
He shouted urgently to his armor-bearer, “Pull out your blade and finish me off, or they will say about me, ‘A woman killed him!’” The servant ran him through, and Abimelech was dead.
When the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they went each to his home.
In this way God paid Abimelech back for the crime he had committed against his father by murdering seventy brothers.
God also paid back the Shechemites for all their wickedness, and Jotham son of Jerubbaal’s curse fell upon them.

notes.text: Or “citizens” or “lords”; Hebrew ba‘ale, plural of baal, “owner, lord.” So throughout this chapter.
Hebrew “seventy of silver,” probably shekels, about 1¾ pounds (800 grams, g).
Jotham means “Yahweh is perfect.”
Beth-millo means “house of the fill,” probably a fortified structure built on an earth platform.
Hebrew elon mutstsab. The Septuagint (B text) reads “by the oak of the station” and adds a second rendering of the same Hebrew word (“of the finder”); the A text lacks the addition.
Beer means “well.”
Gaal perhaps means “loathing,” and Ebed means “servant” or “slave.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “Gaal son of Jobel.”
Hebrew hillulim, a festival of praise held at the grape harvest. The Septuagint (B text) keeps the Hebrew word (“made ellulim”); the A text reads “made dances.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “I would say to Abimelech.”
Or “at Tormah.” The meaning of Hebrew betormah, found only here, is uncertain; some read “at Arumah” (verse 41).
Hebrew “the navel of the land.”
Hebrew elon me‘onenim. The Septuagint (B text) keeps the Hebrew words as a name; the A text translates them, “the way of the oak of the seers.”
Or “inner chamber.” The meaning of Hebrew tseriach is uncertain; also in verse 49.
El-berith means “God of the covenant.” Compare Baal-berith in 8:33 and 9:4.
Zalmon means “dark” or “shady.”

verses.text: After Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, son of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar, came forward to deliver Israel. He lived in Shamir in Ephraim’s hill country.
He judged Israel twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried at Shamir.
After him rose Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel twenty-two years.
He had thirty sons who rode on thirty donkeys, and they had thirty towns,{a} which are called Havvoth-jair{b} to this day; they are in the land of Gilead.
And Jair died and was buried at Kamon.

The Israelites went back to doing evil in Yahweh’s sight. They worshiped the Baals and Ashtaroth and the deities of Aram, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and Philistia. They deserted Yahweh and no longer served him.
So the anger of Yahweh burned against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of the Philistines and into the hand of the Ammonites,
and that year they crushed and battered the Israelites. For eighteen years they tyrannized all the Israelites east of the Jordan in Gilead, the Amorite country.
The Ammonites also crossed the Jordan to fight against Judah, against Benjamin, and against the house of Ephraim, so that Israel was in great distress.
Then the Israelites called to Yahweh for help: “We have wronged you; we have forsaken our God and worshiped the Baals.”
And Yahweh said to the Israelites, “Did I not save you from the Egyptians, from the Amorites, from the Ammonites, from the Philistines?
The Sidonians, Amalek, and Maon{c} oppressed you, and you cried out to me, and I saved you from their hand.
Yet you have abandoned me and served other gods; therefore I will no longer save you.
Off with you! Call on the gods you picked yourselves. Let them rescue you when you are in trouble.”
The Israelites pleaded with Yahweh, “We have sinned. Treat us however you see fit; only deliver us today.”
So they put away the foreign gods from among them and served Yahweh, and he could no longer bear the misery of Israel.{d}
Then the Ammonites were called to arms, and they camped in Gilead. And the Israelites gathered together and camped at Mizpah.
The people, the leaders of Gilead, said to one another, “Who is the man who will begin to fight against the Ammonites? He will be head over all the inhabitants of Gilead.”

notes.text: There is a play on words in the Hebrew: ‘ayarim means both “donkeys” and “towns.”
Havvoth-jair means “villages of Jair” (compare Numbers 32:41).
The Septuagint reads “Midian.”
Hebrew “his soul was short with the misery of Israel,” that is, he became impatient with their suffering.

verses.text: Jephthah{a} the Gileadite was a great warrior, though he was the son of a prostitute. His father was Gilead.

Gilead’s wife also bore him sons. When his wife’s sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out and said to him, “You will not have an inheritance in our father’s house, for you are the son of another woman.”
Jephthah ran away from his brothers and settled in Tob. A band of outlaws gathered around him and joined his raids.
After some time the Ammonites fought against Israel.
When Ammon went to war with Israel, Gilead’s elders hurried to fetch Jephthah from Tob.
They told him, “Be our commander, and we will battle the Ammonites.”
But Jephthah said to the elders of Gilead, “Did you not hate me and drive me out of my father’s house? Why have you come to me now, when you are in distress?”
Gilead’s elders replied to Jephthah, “That is exactly why we are back. Come with us and fight the Ammonites, and you will govern everyone who lives in Gilead.”
Jephthah answered Gilead’s elders, “If you take me home to fight Ammon, and Yahweh delivers them to me, will I truly become your head?”
Gilead’s elders replied, “Yahweh is our witness; we will certainly do what you have said.”
So Jephthah went with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him head and commander over them. And Jephthah spoke all his words before Yahweh at Mizpah.
Then Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites, saying, “What is there between you and me, that you have come to me to fight against my land?”

The king of the Ammonites said to the messengers of Jephthah, “Because Israel took away my land when they came up from Egypt, from the Arnon as far as the Jabbok and the Jordan. So now restore it peaceably.”
Jephthah again sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites
“This is what Jephthah says: Israel never seized Moabite or Ammonite land.
For when they came up from Egypt, Israel went through the wilderness to the Red Sea{b} and came to Kadesh.

Then Israel sent messengers to the king of Edom, saying, ‘Please let us pass through your land,’ but the king of Edom would not listen. They also sent to the king of Moab, but he was not willing. So Israel stayed at Kadesh.

Next they traveled through the desert, skirting Edom and Moab, reached the territory east of Moab, and encamped across the Arnon. They stayed out of Moabite land altogether, because the Arnon marked Moab’s frontier.
Israel then sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, king of Heshbon, and Israel said to him, ‘Please let us pass through your land to our place.’
But Sihon did not trust Israel to pass through his territory. So Sihon gathered all his people and camped at Jahaz and fought against Israel.
Yahweh, Israel’s God, delivered Sihon and his entire army to Israel, who defeated them. So Israel took over every acre belonging to the Amorites who lived there.
They seized the whole Amorite region: the Arnon marked its southern edge, the Jabbok its northern edge, the desert lay on the east, and the Jordan on the west.
So now Yahweh, the God of Israel, has dispossessed the Amorites before his people Israel; and are you to take possession of it?
Will you not possess what Chemosh your god gives you to possess? And all that Yahweh our God has dispossessed before us, we will possess.
Are you any better than Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab? Did he ever pick a quarrel with Israel, or go to war with them?
Israel has lived in Heshbon and Aroer and their dependent villages, and in every town along the Arnon’s banks, for three centuries. Why have you made no effort to retake them in all that time?
I have not sinned against you, but you are doing me wrong by fighting against me. May Yahweh, the Judge, decide today between the Israelites and the Ammonites.”
The Ammonite king, however, ignored the message Jephthah had sent him.
Then Yahweh’s Spirit took hold of Jephthah. He crossed Gilead and Manasseh, came to Mizpah in Gilead, and from there advanced against the Ammonites.
Jephthah made Yahweh a vow: “If you truly hand the Ammonites over to me,
then whatever{c} comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites will belong to Yahweh, and I will offer it up as a burnt offering.”
So Jephthah crossed over to the Ammonites to fight against them, and Yahweh gave them into his hand.
He cut them down over a stretch from Aroer to the vicinity of Minnith, twenty towns, then on to Abel-keramim,{d} inflicting enormous losses. In this way Ammon was brought low beneath Israel.
When Jephthah reached his house in Mizpah, out ran his daughter to greet him, dancing and playing a hand drum. She was his only child; he had no son and no other daughter.

When he saw her, he tore his clothes and said, “Alas, my daughter! You have brought me very low, and you have become one of those who trouble me. For I have opened my mouth to Yahweh, and I cannot take it back.”
She told him, “Father, you made a promise to Yahweh; do to me what you vowed, since Yahweh has avenged you on your enemies the Ammonites.”
She added, “Grant me this one request: let me be for two months, so I can roam{e} the hills and mourn my virginity with my friends.”
He said, “Go.” And he sent her away for two months. She went with her companions and wept over her virginity on the mountains.
Two months later she came home to her father, and he fulfilled the vow he had sworn. She never had relations with any man.{f} From this arose a custom in Israel
that the daughters of Israel went year by year to commemorate{g} the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite four days in the year.

notes.text: Jephthah means “he opens” or “he sets free.”
Hebrew yam suf, literally “Sea of Reeds.”
Or “whoever.” The Hebrew can refer to a person or an animal. Houses of the time often sheltered animals on the ground floor.
Abel-keramim means “meadow of vineyards.”
So the Hebrew, “go down.” Many scholars, with a small change of the Hebrew, read “wander.”

Some interpreters, ancient and modern, understand verses 39–40 to mean that Jephthah dedicated his daughter to lifelong virginity rather than offering her as a sacrifice; the plain sense of verse 31 is a burnt offering.
Or “to lament” or “to recount the story of.” The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain.

verses.text: The Ephraimite men were mobilized and crossed to Zaphon.{a} They confronted Jephthah: “Why did you march against the Ammonites without summoning us to join you? We will set fire to your house with you inside it!”
Jephthah answered, “My people and I were locked in a bitter struggle with the Ammonites. I appealed to you for help, but you never rescued me from them.
When I saw that you would not save me, I took my life in my hand and crossed over to the Ammonites, and Yahweh gave them into my hand. Why then have you come up to me this day to fight against me?”
Jephthah mustered all of Gilead’s men and fought Ephraim. Gilead’s men defeated Ephraim, who had taunted them: “You Gileadites are deserters from Ephraim, living between Ephraim and Manasseh.”{b}

The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan against Ephraim. Whenever any of the fugitives of Ephraim said, “Let me cross over,” the men of Gilead would say to him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he said, “No,”

they told him, “Say ‘Shibboleth,’”{c} and if he said “Sibboleth,” unable to pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the Jordan crossing. At that time forty-two thousand{d} Ephraimites died.
Jephthah judged Israel six years. Then Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.{e}
After him Ibzan of Bethlehem{f} judged Israel.
He had thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage outside his clan and brought in thirty daughters from outside for his sons. He judged Israel seven years.
Then Ibzan died and was buried at Bethlehem.
After him Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel. He judged Israel ten years.
Then Elon the Zebulunite died and was buried at Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
After him Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.
He had forty sons and thirty grandsons, who rode on seventy donkeys. He judged Israel eight years.
Then Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite died and was buried at Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.

notes.text: Or “northward.” Zaphon was a town in the Jordan Valley (Joshua 13:27).
The meaning of the Ephraimites’ taunt is uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) makes it the escaped Ephraimites who say, “You are of Gilead in the midst of Ephraim and in the midst of Manasseh.”

Hebrew shibboleth means “ear of grain” or “flowing stream.” The Ephraimites’ dialect evidently lacked the “sh” sound, so they said “sibboleth” with an “s.” The Septuagint (B text) translates the word as “ear of grain” (Stachys); the A text translates it as “watchword.”
Or “forty-two units”; on the Hebrew word elef (“thousand,” perhaps also “clan” or “military unit”), compare 20:2.
So the Hebrew, “in the cities of Gilead.” The Septuagint reads “in his city, in Gilead.”
Probably the Bethlehem in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15), not Bethlehem of Judah.

verses.text: The Israelites again did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and Yahweh gave them into the hand of the Philistines for forty years.
There was a man from Zorah, of the Danite clan, named Manoah.{a} His wife was infertile and had no children.
The messenger of Yahweh appeared to the woman and told her, “You have never been able to bear a child, yet you will conceive and give birth to a son.
Now take care that you drink no wine or other liquor, and avoid every unclean food,

You will become pregnant and bear a son. A razor must never touch his head, because the boy will be a Nazirite{b} consecrated to God from birth, and he will begin delivering Israel from Philistine power.”

Then the woman came and told her husband, saying, “A man of God came to me, and his appearance was like the appearance of the angel of God, very awesome. I did not ask him where he came from, and he did not tell me his name,

yet he told me, ‘You are going to conceive and bear a son. Starting now, avoid wine and other liquor, and eat nothing unclean, because the child will be a Nazirite, consecrated to God from birth right up to the day of his death.’”
Then Manoah prayed to Yahweh and said, “O Lord, please let the man of God whom you sent come to us again and teach us what we should do for the boy who will be born.”
God listened to the voice of Manoah, and the angel of God came again to the woman as she was sitting in the field. But Manoah her husband was not with her.
So the woman ran quickly and told her husband, saying to him, “Look, the man who came to me the other day has appeared to me.”
Manoah got up and went after his wife. He approached the man and asked, “Are you the one who spoke with my wife?” “Yes,” he said.
Manoah asked, “When your promise comes true, how should the boy be raised, and what will he do?”
The angel of Yahweh said to Manoah, “Of all that I said to the woman let her be careful.
She may not eat anything that comes from the vine, neither let her drink wine or strong drink, nor eat anything unclean. All that I commanded her let her observe.”
Manoah told Yahweh’s messenger, “Let us hold you here while we cook a young goat for you.”

Yahweh’s messenger told Manoah, “Even if you urge me to stay, I won’t touch your food. But should you want to prepare a burnt offering, present it to Yahweh.” (Manoah did not realize he was speaking with Yahweh’s messenger.)
Manoah asked Yahweh’s messenger, “What is your name, so we can honor you when your word comes true?”
And the angel of Yahweh said to him, “Why do you ask my name, seeing it is wonderful?”{c}
So Manoah took the young goat with the grain offering and offered it on the rock to Yahweh, and he{d} did a wonderful thing while Manoah and his wife were watching.
As the flame rose from the altar toward the sky, Yahweh’s messenger ascended in it. Manoah and his wife saw this and fell face down on the ground.
The angel of Yahweh did not appear again to Manoah and to his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of Yahweh.
Manoah told his wife, “We are certain to die, because we have seen God.”

But his wife said to him, “If Yahweh had wanted to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering from our hands, nor shown us all these things, nor now announced to us such things as these.”
The woman bore a son and called his name Samson.{e} The boy grew, and Yahweh blessed him.
Yahweh’s Spirit began to move him at Mahaneh-dan,{f} between Zorah and Eshtaol.

notes.text: Manoah means “rest.”
Nazirite means “one consecrated” or “separated” (see Numbers 6:1–21). The Septuagint (B text) keeps the Hebrew word (Nazir); the A text reads Naziraios, a form close to the wording of Matthew 2:23.
Hebrew pil’i, “wonderful, beyond understanding”; compare Isaiah 9:6.
Hebrew “and he did wonderfully,” referring to the angel. The Septuagint (A text) reads “offered it to Yahweh, who does wonders.”
Samson (Hebrew Shimshon) is related to shemesh, “sun,” perhaps meaning “little sun” or “of the sun.” Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” lay near Zorah.
Mahaneh-dan means “camp of Dan” (compare 18:12).

verses.text: Samson went to Timnah, and in Timnah he noticed a young Philistine woman.
He returned and told his parents, “At Timnah I saw a Philistine woman. Get her for me as a wife.”

His parents objected, “Can’t you find a wife among your own relatives or in all our people? Must you take one from the pagan Philistines?” But Samson insisted to his father, “Get her for me! She is the one who pleases me.”
His parents did not realize this was from Yahweh, who was looking for a pretext to confront the Philistines, since they were then Israel’s rulers.
Samson and his parents went down to Timnah, and as they approached the vineyards there, a young lion suddenly came roaring at him.
Yahweh’s Spirit seized him, and bare-handed he ripped the lion apart as if it were a kid. But he said nothing to his parents about what he had done.
He went down and spoke with the woman, and Samson found her pleasing.
After some days he returned to take her, and he turned aside to see the carcass of the lion. And look, there was a swarm of bees in the body of the lion, and honey.

He scraped it out into his hands and went on, eating as he went. He came to his father and mother and gave some to them, and they ate. But he did not tell them that he had scraped the honey from the body of the lion.
His father visited the woman, and Samson held a banquet there, as young men customarily did.
When they saw him,{a} they brought thirty companions to be with him.
Samson told them, “Let me pose a riddle for you. If you solve it and give me the answer before the week-long feast ends, I will award you thirty linen shirts and thirty sets of fine clothing.
If you are unable to solve it, the thirty linen shirts and thirty sets of fine clothing will be mine.” They answered, “Go ahead, tell us your riddle, and we will listen.”
He said to them, “Out of the eater came something to eat, and out of the strong came something sweet.” And for three days they could not solve the riddle.
On the seventh day{b} they said to Samson’s wife, “Entice your husband to tell us the riddle, or we will burn you and your father’s house with fire. Have you invited us here to impoverish us?”

Samson’s wife sobbed against him and said, “All you feel for me is hatred! There is no love in you. You gave my countrymen a riddle and never told me the answer.” He replied, “I haven’t even told my own parents, so why would I tell you?”
She sobbed in front of him throughout the feast’s seven days, and on day seven, because she badgered him so, he gave her the answer. She then explained the riddle to her countrymen.

And the men of the city said to him on the seventh day before the sun went down,{c} “What is sweeter than honey? What is stronger than a lion?” And he said to them, “If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle.”

Then Yahweh’s Spirit came powerfully over him. Down to Ashkelon he went, struck dead thirty of its men, stripped them, and handed their clothes to the guests who had solved the riddle. Furious, he returned to his father’s house.
And Samson’s wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man.

notes.text: So the Hebrew and the Septuagint. With different vowels the Hebrew could be read “Because they feared him.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and some other ancient versions read “the fourth day,” which fits better with verses 14 and 17.
Hebrew harsah, “toward the sun” (a rare word for the sun). Many scholars, with a change of one letter, read “before he went into the bridal chamber.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “before sunrise.”

verses.text: Some time later, around wheat harvest (in May–June),{a} Samson visited his wife, bringing a kid goat as a gift. “I am going to my wife’s room,” he said. But her father refused to admit him.
Her father explained, “I was convinced you despised her, so I gave her to the man who stood as your best man. Isn’t her kid sister prettier? Have her instead.”
Samson said to them, “This time I shall be blameless toward the Philistines when I do them harm.”
So Samson went and caught three hundred foxes{b} and took torches. He turned them tail to tail and put a torch between each pair of tails.
He lit the torches and released the foxes into the Philistines’ ripe grain, burning up the stacked sheaves and the standing crops, along with the vineyards and olive orchards.

Then the Philistines said, “Who has done this?” And they said, “Samson, the son-in-law of the Timnite, because he took his wife and gave her to his companion.” And the Philistines came up and burned her and her father with fire.
Samson answered them, “Since you have behaved this way, I swear I will take revenge on you. Only then will I quit.”
He attacked them savagely, slaughtering many,{c} then went down and took refuge in a rocky crevice at Etam.
Then the Philistines came up and camped in Judah and spread out at Lehi.{d}
And the men of Judah said, “Why have you come up against us?” They said, “We have come up to bind Samson, to do to him as he did to us.”

Then three thousand men of Judah went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson, “Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? What then is this that you have done to us?” And he said to them, “As they did to me, so have I done to them.”
They said, “We came down to bind you and deliver you into Philistine custody.” Samson replied, “Promise me you will not kill me yourselves.”
“No,” they answered, “we only mean to tie you and give you to them. We swear we will not put you to death.” They fastened him with two new cords and led him up from the rock.
As he arrived at Lehi, the Philistines rushed toward him shouting. Yahweh’s Spirit came upon him with power, and the cords binding his arms turned to burnt flax and dropped from his wrists.
He found a fresh jawbone of a donkey, put out his hand, took it, and with it he struck down a thousand men.
And Samson said, “With the jawbone of a donkey, heaps upon heaps,{e} with the jawbone of a donkey I have struck down a thousand men.”
When he had finished speaking, he threw away the jawbone from his hand. And that place was called Ramath-lehi.{f}
Burning with thirst, he cried out to Yahweh, “You granted this tremendous victory through your servant. Must I now perish from thirst and land in the hands of these pagans?”

God then split open a hollow in the earth at Lehi, and water gushed out. Samson drank, his strength came back, and he revived. That is why the spring is called En-hakkore,{g} and it remains at Lehi today.
And he judged Israel in the days of the Philistines twenty years.

notes.text: The wheat harvest followed the barley harvest and came in late spring, roughly the Hebrew month Sivan (Pentecost/Shavuot), in May–June.
Or “jackals.”
Hebrew “leg upon thigh,” an idiom for a crushing defeat.
Lehi means “jawbone.”
Hebrew hamor homoratayim, a play on words: hamor means “donkey,” and homer means “heap.” The Septuagint reads “I have utterly destroyed them.”
Ramath-lehi means “height of the jawbone.” The Septuagint (B text) understands it as “the lifting (or throwing away) of the jawbone.”
En-hakkore means “spring of the one who called.” The Septuagint (B text) reads “Well of the invoker.”

verses.text: Samson visited Gaza, where he noticed a prostitute and went in to spend the night with her.
The people of Gaza heard, “Samson is here!” They encircled the town and waited in ambush at the city gate all night, staying quiet and thinking, “At first light we will kill him.”

But Samson stayed in bed only till midnight. Then he rose, grabbed the town gate’s double doors with both posts, tore them loose along with the bar, hoisted them onto his shoulders, and hauled them up to the summit of the hill facing Hebron.
After this he loved a woman in the Valley of Sorek,{a} whose name was Delilah.{b}

The Philistine rulers approached her and said, “Coax him. Find the secret of his tremendous strength and how we can overpower him and tie him up to subdue him. Each of us will pay you eleven hundred silver coins.”{c}
Delilah asked Samson, “Tell me, what is the secret of your great strength, and how could you be tied up and subdued?”
Samson told her, “If anyone binds me with seven fresh bowstrings,{d} still damp and unused, I will lose my strength and be like everyone else.”
Then the lords of the Philistines brought up to her seven fresh bowstrings that had not been dried, and she bound him with them.

She had men waiting in ambush in the next room. She shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” But he snapped the strings like a flax thread that singes in a flame. His secret remained undiscovered.
Delilah accused Samson, “You made a fool of me and lied to me. Now tell me honestly how you can be tied up.”
He told her, “If anyone ties me firmly with new ropes that have never been used, I will lose my strength and be like everyone else.”
Delilah took fresh ropes and bound him, then screamed, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” The ambushers lay waiting in the next room. But he snapped the ropes off his arms like so much thread.
Delilah complained to Samson, “So far you have mocked me and lied. Say how someone might tie you up.” He said, “Weave the seven braids of my hair into the loom’s fabric.”{e}
She secured it with the pin and shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” He woke up and yanked out the pin, the loom, and the fabric.
Then she said, “How can you claim to love me when your heart is elsewhere? Three times now you have made fun of me, and you still have not revealed what makes you so strong.”
Day after day she nagged him with her pleading until he felt sick enough to die.

So he opened his whole heart to her: “A blade has never been used on my head, since I have been set apart for God as a Nazirite from the day of my birth. Shave my head and my strength will drain away; I will turn weak and become like any ordinary man.”

Delilah saw that he had finally told her everything, so she sent word summoning the Philistine rulers: “Come one more time; he has confided in me completely.” The rulers came to her, carrying the silver.
She made him sleep on her knees. And she called a man and had him shave off the seven locks of his head. Then she began to humble{f} him, and his strength left him.
She shouted, “Samson, the Philistines are on you!” Waking from his sleep, he thought, “I will break free as before, with a shake.” He had no idea that Yahweh had abandoned him.
And the Philistines seized him and gouged out his eyes and brought him down to Gaza and bound him with bronze shackles. And he ground grain in the prison.
But the hair of his head began to grow again after it had been shaved.
The Philistine rulers assembled for a great sacrificial feast to their god Dagon{g} and for rejoicing, saying, “Our god has put Samson, our enemy, in our hands.”
When the crowd saw him, they praised their god: “Our god has put into our power the foe who ravaged our land and killed so many of us!”
When their hearts were merry, they said, “Call Samson, so that he may entertain us.” So they called Samson out of the prison, and he entertained them. They made him stand between the pillars.
Samson said to the boy leading him, “Place my hands on the pillars that support the building, so I can lean on them.”
The building was crowded, full of men and women. Every Philistine ruler was present, and some three thousand more were up on the roof, watching Samson perform.
Samson prayed to Yahweh: “Lord Yahweh, remember me! Give me strength just this one time, God, so that with a single blow I may repay the Philistines for my two eyes.”
Samson felt for the two central columns that supported the building. He braced himself against them, one under his right hand and the other under his left.

And Samson said, “Let me die with the Philistines!” Then he bent with all his might, and the house fell upon the lords and upon all the people who were in it. So the dead whom he killed at his death were more than those whom he had killed during his life.

His brothers and his father’s whole house came down, collected him, carried him back, and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the burial place of his father Manoah. For twenty years he had been Israel’s judge.

notes.text: Sorek means “choice vine.” The Septuagint (B text) keeps the Hebrew as a name (Alsorech); the A text reads “the brook of Sorek.”
The meaning of Delilah is uncertain; it may be related to dallah, “hair, threads,” or to dalal, “to be weak, small.”
Probably shekels; 1,100 shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). Hebrew “a thousand and a hundred of silver.”
Or “cords” or “sinews”; Hebrew yetarim, used of bowstrings and tent cords.

The Hebrew here appears to be shorter, perhaps because a scribe’s eye skipped between similar words. The Septuagint has a longer text: “If you weave the seven locks of my head with the web and fasten them with the pin into the wall, then I shall become weak and be like any other man.” And in verse 14: “And while he slept, Delilah took the seven locks of his head and wove them into the web.”
Or “to afflict” or “to subdue.” The Septuagint reads “and she began to humble him”; some scholars read “he began to grow weak.”
Dagon was a grain or storm god worshiped in Mesopotamia, Syria, and Philistia.

verses.text: There was a man of the hill country of Ephraim whose name was Micah.{a}

He said to his mother, “The eleven hundred pieces of silver{b} that were taken from you, about which you uttered a curse and also spoke it in my hearing—look, the silver is with me; I took it.” And his mother said, “Blessed be my son by Yahweh.”

He returned the eleven hundred pieces of silver to his mother. And his mother said, “I solemnly dedicate the silver to Yahweh from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a cast image. So now I will return it to you.”
When he gave the silver back to her, she took two hundred shekels of it to a silversmith, who fashioned a carved idol and a molten one. These stood in Micah’s house.
This Micah owned a shrine.{c} He had an ephod made, and household idols,{d} and appointed{e} one of his own sons to be his priest.
In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.
There was a young Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, belonging to the Judah clan, who was staying there as a resident foreigner.
He left Bethlehem in Judah to live wherever he could find lodging. On his way he reached Micah’s house in Ephraim’s hill country.
Micah asked him, “Where are you from?” He said, “I am a Levite of Bethlehem in Judah, looking for a place to stay.”
Micah said to him, “Stay with me, and be to me a father and a priest, and I will give you ten pieces of silver{f} a year and a set of clothes and your food.” So the Levite went in.
The Levite agreed to live with Micah, and the young man became like a son to him.
Micah ordained the Levite, and the young man became his priest, and he was in the house of Micah.
Micah concluded, “Now I am certain that Yahweh will do me good, since a Levite is my priest.”

notes.text: Micah (here Hebrew Mikayehu, verses 1 and 4; elsewhere Mikah) means “Who is like Yahweh?”
Probably shekels; 1,100 shekels weighed about 28 pounds (12.6 kilograms, kg). Verse 4’s two hundred pieces weighed about 5 pounds (2.3 kg).
Hebrew “a house of God” (or “of gods”).
Hebrew teraphim, small household idols, perhaps also used in divination.
Hebrew “filled the hand of,” an idiom for installing a priest; also in verse 12.
Probably shekels; ten shekels weighed about 4 ounces (115 grams, g).

verses.text: At that time Israel had no king. And at that time the Danite clan was still seeking a place to settle, because it had not yet received an allotment among Israel’s tribes.

From their clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, the Danites picked five capable men to scout and map the land. Their instructions: “Go, survey the country.” They reached Ephraim’s hill country, arrived at Micah’s house, and spent the night.
Near Micah’s house, the young Levite’s accent gave him away to them. They stopped and asked him, “Who brought you here? What is your business in this place? What is your stake here?”
He explained, “Micah made an arrangement with me. He pays me, and I serve as his priest.”
They said, “Ask God, so we can learn whether our mission will succeed.”
The priest told them, “Go in peace. Yahweh is watching over the mission you are on.”

The five men left and reached Laish. They watched the people living there: they were secure, like the Sidonians, calm and trusting, wanting nothing the earth could supply, and prosperous.{a} They lived far from Sidon, with no ties to anyone.{b}
When the five returned to their kinsmen at Zorah and Eshtaol, the kinsmen asked, “What did you find out?”
They answered, “Let’s march against them! We saw that land, and it is excellent. Why are you sitting still? Don’t hesitate; go and capture the country.
When you arrive, you will find a trusting people and a wide-open country. God has delivered it to you, a place that lacks nothing the earth can provide.”
So six hundred men of the clan of the Danites, armed with weapons of war, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol,
They went up and pitched camp at Kiriath-jearim in Judah. For that reason the spot has been named Mahaneh-dan{c} ever since; it lies west{d} of Kiriath-jearim.
And they passed on from there to the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah.
The five men who had scouted the Laish region said to their kinsmen, “Did you know that one of these houses holds an ephod, household idols, a carved image, and a cast idol? Think about what to do.”
And they turned aside there and came to the house of the young Levite, at the house of Micah, and asked him about his welfare.
The six hundred Danite men, equipped for battle, stood beside the entrance to the gateway.

The five men who had scouted the land went inside and removed the carved idol, the ephod, the household gods, and the molten idol. Meanwhile the priest was standing by the gateway’s entrance with the six hundred armed warriors.
When these went into Micah’s house and took the carved image, the ephod, the household gods, and the cast image, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
They told him, “Silence! Cover your mouth with your hand, and come along as our father and priest. Would you rather serve one man’s household as priest, or serve a whole tribe and clan of Israel?”
The priest was delighted. He took the ephod, the idols, and the carved image and joined the Danite company.
Then they turned and left, placing the children, the livestock, and the baggage ahead of them.
They were some distance from Micah’s house when the men living in the neighborhood were rallied, and they caught up with the Danites.
Calling out to the Danites, who looked back at them, they asked Micah, “What is wrong? Why have you brought such a crowd?”
He replied, “You carry off the gods I made, along with my priest, and leave. What do I have left? And you ask me, ‘What’s wrong?’”
The Danites warned him, “Keep your voice down around us, or some hot-tempered men may attack you, and you and your family will lose your lives.”
Then the Danites went their way. And when Micah saw that they were too strong for him, he turned and went back to his home.
They carried off Micah’s handiwork and his priest, and reached Laish, a calm and unsuspecting people. They slaughtered them with swords and burned the town to the ground.

No one came to rescue the city, because it lay a long way from Sidon and had no dealings with outsiders. It was situated in the valley by Beth-rehob. The Danites reconstructed the city and made it their home.
They renamed the town Dan after their ancestor Dan, Israel’s son; its earlier name had been Laish.

And the Danites set up the carved image for themselves, and Jonathan son of Gershom, son of Moses,{e} he and his sons were priests to the tribe of the Danites until the day of the captivity of the land.{f}
They kept Micah’s carved image for themselves all the time God’s house stood at Shiloh.

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew of this clause is uncertain.
So the Hebrew and the Septuagint (B text). The A text, followed by some scholars, reads “with Aram” (Syria), a difference of one letter in Hebrew (adam, “anyone,” and aram).
Mahaneh-dan means “camp of Dan.”
Hebrew “behind,” that is, west.

Most manuscripts of the Hebrew text read “Manasseh,” but the letter n (nun) is written above the line, raised or “suspended” between the other letters, the only suspended nun in the Hebrew Bible. Without it the word reads “Moses.” Jewish tradition (Talmud, Bava Batra 109b) explains that the scribes added the nun to spare Moses the shame of a grandson who served as an idolatrous priest, while marking it as an addition. The Septuagint A text and the Latin Vulgate read “Moses”; the B text reads “Manasseh.” Gershom was the son of Moses (Exodus 2:22).

So the Hebrew and the Septuagint. Some scholars, with a slight change of the Hebrew, read “the captivity of the ark” (compare 1 Samuel 4:11, 21–22). The captivity of the land may refer to the Assyrian deportations in 734–732 B.C. or 722 B.C.

verses.text: In those days Israel had no king. A certain Levite was living in a remote corner of Ephraim’s hill country, and from Bethlehem in Judah he took a concubine.
His concubine became angry with him{a} and left, going back to her father’s home in Bethlehem in Judah. She remained there four months.

Her husband set out to follow her and win her over, so she would return. He took along his servant and two donkeys. She brought him into her father’s home, and when the young woman’s father spotted him, he welcomed him gladly.
His father-in-law, the young woman’s father, persuaded him to stay, and he lodged with them for three days, eating, drinking, and sleeping there.
On the fourth morning they got up early and he was ready to leave, but the girl’s father urged his son-in-law, “Refresh yourself with a bite to eat, then you can go.”
The two men sat down together to eat and drink. Then the young woman’s father urged the man, “Won’t you agree to stay the night and enjoy yourself?”
When the man stood to leave, his father-in-law pressed him, and he stayed another night.
On the fifth day he rose at dawn to leave. But the young woman’s father urged him, “Eat something first and wait until the afternoon.” So the two of them dined together.

When the man, his concubine, and his servant stood to go, his wife’s father, the young woman’s father, told him, “Look, evening is coming on and the day is nearly gone. Stay one more night. See, the sun is setting. Spend the night here and enjoy yourself. You can get up early tomorrow, begin your trip, and head home.”
But the man refused to stay another night. He rose and left, and reached a point across from Jebus (that is, Jerusalem). His two saddled donkeys were with him, along with his concubine.
By the time they were close to Jebus, the day was nearly gone, and the servant suggested to his master, “Let’s turn off to this Jebusite town and stay the night there.”
His master answered, “We won’t detour into a foreign city whose inhabitants are not Israelites. We will continue to Gibeah.”
He told his servant, “Let’s try to reach one of these towns and stay the night in Gibeah or Ramah.”
So they passed on and went their way. And the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin,
and they stopped there to spend the night in Gibeah. He went in and took a seat in the town’s public square, but nobody offered them a home for the night.
Then an old man came along from his work in the fields that evening. He was originally from Ephraim’s hill country and was living in Gibeah, though the townspeople were Benjaminites.
The old man looked up and noticed the traveler in the town square. “Where are you headed?” he asked. “Where did you come from?”

He answered, “We are traveling from Bethlehem in Judah toward a remote corner of Ephraim’s hill country, which is my home. I had gone to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I am heading to the house of Yahweh,{b} but nobody has invited me into a home.
We carry our own straw and feed for the donkeys, plus bread and wine for me, for your servant woman, and for the young man traveling with us. We need nothing else.”
The old man replied, “You are welcome. Whatever you require, I will provide. Just don’t sleep out in the open square.”
He led them to his house and fed the donkeys. The travelers bathed their feet, then ate and drank.

While they were enjoying themselves, a gang of the town’s scoundrels{c} ringed the house and hammered on its door. They shouted to the elderly owner, “Send out the man who has come to your house, so that we can have sex with him.”
The owner of the house stepped outside and pleaded with them, “No, my friends, please don’t do such a wicked thing. This man is my guest; don’t commit this outrage.
Here are my daughter, a virgin, and his concubine. Let me send them out. Abuse them and treat them however you like, but do not commit such an atrocity against this man.”
The men refused to heed him. So the man grabbed his concubine and shoved her outside to them. They raped her and tortured her throughout the night until morning, and at first light released her.
And as morning appeared, the woman came and fell down at the door of the man’s house where her master was, until it was light.
When her master rose that morning and opened the house door to continue his journey, there lay his concubine at the entrance, her hands stretched out on the threshold.
“Get up,” he told her, “we are leaving.” She did not respond.{d} He loaded her on the donkey and started for home.
Once inside his house, he picked up a knife, took hold of his concubine, cut her body apart into twelve parts, and sent them to every part of Israel.
Everyone who saw it said, “Never has such a deed been done or witnessed since the day Israel left Egypt. Think about it, discuss it, and speak up!”

notes.text: Hebrew “played the harlot against him” (zanah). Some Greek manuscripts read “was angry with him,” perhaps reflecting a different Hebrew verb; the Septuagint (B text) reads “departed from him.”
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “to my house,” which fits verse 29; the Hebrew may have arisen from a misread abbreviation.
Hebrew beliya‘al, “worthlessness.”
The Septuagint adds “for she was dead.”

verses.text: All Israel, from Dan down to Beersheba and from Gilead too, marched out, and the community gathered as one person before Yahweh at Mizpah.
The leaders of every tribe of Israel took their positions in the gathering of God’s people: four hundred thousand{a} infantrymen carrying swords.
(The Benjaminites heard that the Israelites had gone to Mizpah.) The Israelites demanded, “Explain how this wicked deed came about.”
And the Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered and said, “I came to Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.
During the night the lords of Gibeah attacked me, surrounding the house. They intended to murder me, and they raped my concubine so savagely that she died.
I took my concubine, cut her into pieces, and sent them across Israel’s whole territory, because they have done a vile and shameful thing in Israel.
Look, you Israelites, all of you, give your advice and counsel here.”
The entire people rose together and swore, “None of us will return to his tent or go back to his home.
But now this is what we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot,

We will pick one man in ten from all Israel’s tribes, one in a hundred, and one in a thousand, to gather food for the army. Then, once the troops arrive, they will punish Gibeah in Benjamin for the disgraceful crime it committed in Israel.”
So the men of Israel assembled against the town, united as a single body.
The tribes of Israel sent envoys to every clan of Benjamin with this question: “What is this crime committed among you?
Surrender those scoundrels in Gibeah, so that we may execute them and cleanse Israel of this evil.” But the Benjaminites refused to obey their fellow Israelites.
Then the Benjaminites came together out of the cities to Gibeah to go out to battle against the Israelites.
On that day the Benjaminites recruited from their towns twenty-six thousand{b} swordsmen, in addition to seven hundred elite troops from Gibeah’s population.
Among all these troops were seven hundred select men who were left-handed;{c} each could sling a stone at a hair’s width and never miss.
The men of Israel, not counting Benjamin, numbered four hundred thousand sword-bearers, every one a seasoned warrior.
The Israelites set out for Bethel and asked God, “Which of us should march first against the Benjaminites?” Yahweh answered, “Judah goes first.”
Then the Israelites rose in the morning and camped against Gibeah.
The men of Israel marched against Benjamin and took positions opposite them at Gibeah.
The Benjaminites came out of Gibeah and destroyed on that day twenty-two thousand men of the Israelites.
But the Israelite soldiers rallied their courage and again assembled in the same location they had occupied the day before.

The Israelites went and wept in Yahweh’s presence until evening, and they asked Yahweh, “Should we once more march out to battle against our kinsmen the Benjaminites?” Yahweh said, “March against them.”
So the Israelites came near against the Benjaminites the second day.
And Benjamin went against them out of Gibeah the second day, and destroyed eighteen thousand men of the Israelites. All these were men who drew the sword.

Then all the Israelites, the whole army, went up and came to Bethel and wept. They sat there before Yahweh and fasted that day until evening, and offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before Yahweh.
And the Israelites inquired of Yahweh (for the ark of the covenant of God was there in those days,

Phinehas, Eleazar’s son and Aaron’s grandson, served before it in those years). The Israelites asked, “Should we go out to battle against our kinsmen the Benjaminites once more, or give up?” Yahweh replied, “Attack! Tomorrow I will hand them over to you.”
So Israel set men in ambush around Gibeah.
On the third day the Israelites again marched against the Benjaminites and took up positions facing Gibeah, as they had done before.

The Benjaminites advanced against Israel’s army and were lured away from the town. Just as earlier, they began wounding and killing Israelites along the roads, one leading to Bethel, another toward Gibeah, and in the fields, about thirty Israelites in all.
And the Benjaminites said, “They are defeated before us, as at the first.” But the Israelites said, “Let us flee and draw them away from the city to the highways.”
All Israel’s men left their positions and formed their line at Baal-tamar,{d} while the ambush force burst from its cover west of Geba.{e}
Ten thousand picked soldiers from throughout Israel advanced on Gibeah, and the fighting was fierce. The Benjaminites had no idea that catastrophe was approaching.
Yahweh gave Israel victory over Benjamin, and on that day Israel killed 25,100 Benjaminite swordsmen.
The Benjaminites realized they were losing. Israel’s soldiers had retreated before them, counting on the troops they had hidden near Gibeah.
The ambushers raced into Gibeah, spread out, and put the entire town to the sword.
The agreed signal between the Israelite army and the hidden troops was a tall column of smoke rising from the town
was the cue for Israel’s troops to turn and fight. Benjamin had started to wound and kill some thirty Israelites. They told themselves, “We are beating them just as in the first battle!”
But when the column of smoke started to climb from the town, the Benjaminites looked back, and the whole town was rising in flames to the sky.
Then the men of Israel turned, and the men of Benjamin were dismayed, for they saw that disaster was close upon them.
They turned away from the Israelites toward the desert, but the battle caught up with them, and men from the towns cut them down in the middle of the fight.
They encircled the Benjaminites, chased them down, and trampled them from Nohah{f} to a point east of Gibeah.
Eighteen thousand men of Benjamin fell; all of them were men of valor.
The survivors turned and ran for the desert, to the rock of Rimmon. Along the roads five thousand of them were cut down,{g} and the pursuit pressed on as far as Gidom, where two thousand more fell.
So all who fell that day of Benjamin were twenty-five thousand men who drew the sword, all of them men of valor.
But six hundred men turned and ran into the wilderness to Rimmon’s rock, where they stayed for four months.
