Abigail hurried to gather two hundred loaves, two skins of wine, five sheep ready for cooking, about a bushel of roasted grain,{i} a hundred raisin clusters, and two hundred fig cakes, and she loaded these on donkeys.
She said to her young men, “Go on before me; look, I am coming after you.” But she did not tell her husband Nabal.
And as she was riding on the donkey, going down in the shelter of the hill, there came David and his men descending to meet her, and she encountered them.
Now David had said, “It was all for nothing that I kept watch over everything this man owns in the wilderness, so that not a thing of his was lost; and he has paid me back evil for good.
God do so to David,{j} and more also, if I let remain until daybreak a single male{k} out of all that are his.”
When Abigail saw David, she got down quickly from her donkey, threw herself face down before David, and bowed to the ground.
Falling at his feet, she said, “Upon me, my lord, upon me let the iniquity rest. Let your handmaid, I pray, speak in your hearing, and listen to the words of your handmaid.

Please, my lord, pay no attention to this worthless man Nabal, for he is just what his name says. Nabal is his name, and folly goes with him. But I, your servant, did not see the young men my lord sent.

Now, my lord, as Yahweh lives and as you yourself live, since Yahweh has held you back from bloodguilt and from winning the victory by your own hand, may your enemies and all who seek to harm my lord be like Nabal.
And now this gift{l} which your servant has brought to my lord, let it be given to the young men who follow my lord.
Please forgive the trespass of your handmaid. For Yahweh will certainly make my lord a sure house, because my lord is fighting the battles of Yahweh, and evil shall not be found in you all your days.

Should a man rise up to chase you and to seek your soul, yet the soul of my lord shall be bound up in the bundle of life{m} with Yahweh your God; but the souls of your enemies, them he will hurl away as out of the pocket of a sling.
And when Yahweh has done to my lord according to all the good that he has spoken concerning you, and has appointed you prince over Israel,

my lord shall have no cause of grief or stumbling of heart, either for having shed blood without cause or for my lord having saved himself. And when Yahweh has dealt well with my lord, then remember your handmaid.”
David said to Abigail, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who sent you this day to meet me!
May you be blessed for your good judgment, and may you be blessed, because you have kept me today from bloodguilt and from avenging myself with my own hand.
As surely as Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, who has kept me from harming you, if you had not come quickly to meet me, not one male would have been left to Nabal by morning.”
Then David received from her hand what she had brought him, and he said to her, “Go up in peace to your house. See, I have listened to your voice and have lifted up your face.”{n}
Abigail went back to Nabal, who was holding a feast in his house, a feast fit for a king. Nabal was in good spirits and very drunk, so she told him nothing at all until dawn.
In the morning, when the wine had gone out of Nabal, his wife told him these things, and his heart died within him, and he became as a stone.
About ten days later Yahweh struck Nabal, and he died.

When David heard that Nabal was dead, he said, “Blessed be Yahweh, who has defended me against the insult from Nabal and kept his servant from doing wrong. Yahweh has returned Nabal’s wickedness on his own head.” Then David sent a message to Abigail asking her to be his wife.
When David’s servants came to Abigail at Carmel, they spoke to her, saying, “David has sent us to you to take you to him as his wife.”
She arose and bowed with her face to the earth and said, “Look, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
Abigail got up quickly and rode off on a donkey, with five of her maids going with her. She followed David’s messengers and became his wife.
David had also taken Ahinoam from Jezreel,{o} and the two of them were wives to him.
Saul had given Michal his daughter, David’s wife, to Palti{p} son of Laish, who was of Gallim.

notes.text: So the traditional Hebrew text. The Septuagint reads “Maon” (Brenton), as in verse 2.
This Carmel (meaning “garden land” or “orchard”) was a town in Judah near Maon, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) south of Hebron, not Mount Carmel in the north.
Nabal means “fool” (see verse 25). The word suggests a person who is morally senseless.
Abigail means “my father is joy” (uncertain).

Or “according to his heart”; the Hebrew letters can be read either way. Calebites were descendants of Caleb, who had received the region of Hebron (Joshua 14:13–14). The Septuagint reads “a man of a dog-like nature” (reported), playing on the name Caleb, which is similar to the word for “dog.”
The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “to the living one.”
A feast day, the time of sheep-shearing.
Hebrew “a son of Belial.” Likewise in verse 25.

Hebrew “five seahs,” about 33 quarts (37 liters); a seah was about a third of an ephah. The Septuagint reads “five ephahs of fine flour” and “one homer of dried grapes” (Brenton, modernized) instead of the hundred clusters.
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “So God do to David”). The Hebrew reads “to the enemies of David,” apparently a scribal change to avoid a curse falling on David himself.
Hebrew “one who urinates against a wall,” a coarse expression for a male. Likewise in verse 34.
Hebrew “blessing.”
An image of a person’s life kept safe like a precious thing tied in a bundle.
That is, “granted your request.”
Ahinoam means “my brother is pleasantness.” This Jezreel was a town in Judah (Joshua 15:56), not the northern city.
Called Paltiel in 2 Samuel 3:15. Palti means “my deliverance”; Paltiel means “God is my deliverance.” Gallim was a town near Gibeah (Isaiah 10:30).

verses.text: Then the Ziphites came to Saul at Gibeah, saying, “Is David not concealing himself on the hill of Hachilah, which faces Jeshimon?”
So Saul rose and went down into the wilderness of Ziph, having with him three thousand picked men of Israel, to search for David in the wilderness of Ziph.
Saul pitched his camp beside the road on the hill of Hachilah, opposite Jeshimon. David was staying in the wilderness, and he saw that Saul had followed him into it.
David therefore sent out spies and learned for certain that Saul had come.{a}

Then David rose and came to the place where Saul had camped. David saw where Saul was lying, and Abner son of Ner,{b} the captain of his host; Saul lay inside the camp ring,{c} and the troops were camped round about him.
David asked Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai{d} son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, “Who will go down into the camp with me to Saul?” “I will go with you,” said Abishai.
So David and Abishai came to the people by night, and there Saul lay sleeping inside the camp ring, his spear stuck in the earth at his head, and Abner and the people lying around him.
Then Abishai said to David, “God has shut up your enemy into your hand this day. Now let me pin him to the earth with the spear in one stroke. I will not need to strike him twice.”
But David said to Abishai, “Do not destroy him. For who can put forth his hand against Yahweh’s anointed and be guiltless?”
David said further, “As Yahweh lives, Yahweh himself shall strike him: or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish.
Yahweh forbid that I should put forth my hand against Yahweh’s anointed. But now take, I pray, the spear that is at his head and the jug of water, and let us go.”
David took the spear and water jug from beside Saul’s head, and they left. No one saw it or knew about it, and no one woke up; they were all asleep, because Yahweh had put them into a deep sleep.
Then David crossed over to the far side and stood on the top of the hill at a distance, with a wide space between them.
And David called out to the people and to Abner son of Ner, “Will you not answer, Abner?” Abner answered, “Who are you that call to the king?”

Then David said to Abner, “Are you not a valiant man? And who in Israel is your equal? Why then have you not kept watch over your lord the king? For one of the people came in to destroy the king your lord.

This thing that you have done is not good. As Yahweh lives, you deserve to die,{e} because you have not watched over your master, Yahweh’s anointed. And now look about: where is the king’s spear, and the jug of water that was at his head?”
Saul recognized David’s voice and said, “Is this your voice, my son David?” David said, “It is my voice, my lord the king.”
He went on, “Why does my lord pursue his servant? What did I do? What is the wrong on my hands?

Now therefore, I pray, let my lord the king hear the words of his servant. If it is Yahweh who has stirred you up against me, let him accept an offering;{f} but if it is the sons of men, cursed be they before Yahweh, for they have driven me out this day so that I have no share in the inheritance of Yahweh, saying, ‘Go, serve other gods.’
Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth away from the presence of Yahweh. For the king of Israel has come out to seek a single flea,{g} as one hunts a partridge in the mountains.”

Then Saul said, “I have sinned. Come back, my son David, for I will no longer do you harm, because my life was precious in your eyes this day. Look, I have acted the fool and have erred very greatly.”
“Here is the king’s spear,” David answered.{h} “Let one of the young men cross over and take it.
Yahweh rewards each man for his righteousness and faithfulness. Yahweh delivered you into my hands today, but I refused to raise my hand against Yahweh’s anointed.
And see, just as your life was valued highly this day in my eyes, so may my life be valued highly in the eyes of Yahweh, and may he deliver me out of every distress.”
Then Saul said to David, “Blessed are you, my son David! You will both do great things and surely prevail.” So David went his way, and Saul returned to his place.

notes.text: Or “had come to Nacon” (uncertain); the Hebrew word can be read as a place name.
Abner means “my father is a lamp” (uncertain). Ner means “lamp.”
Or “within the circle of wagons.” Likewise in verse 7.
Ahimelech means “my brother is king.” Abishai means “my father is a gift” (uncertain). Zeruiah, David’s sister (1 Chronicles 2:16), was mother of Abishai, Joab, and Asahel.
Hebrew “you are sons of death.”
Literally “let him smell an offering,” that is, let him be appeased by a sacrifice.
The Septuagint reads “to seek your life” (reported) instead of “a single flea” (compare 24:14).
So the traditional Hebrew reading (qere). The written text (ketiv) reads “Here is the king’s spear.”

verses.text: David said to himself, “One day Saul will surely kill me. The best thing for me is to flee quickly to Philistine territory. Then Saul will stop looking for me within the borders of Israel, and I will be out of his reach.”
So David set out with his six hundred men and crossed over to Achish son of Maoch, king of Gath.
And David lived with Achish at Gath, he and his men, every man with his household, David with his two wives, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the Carmelitess, Nabal’s widow.
When it was told Saul that David had fled to Gath, he sought him no more.

Then David said to Achish, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, let them give me a place in one of the country towns, that I may live there. For why should your servant live in the royal city with you?”
That day Achish gave him Ziklag.{a} That is why Ziklag belongs to the kings of Judah to this day.
The number of the days that David lived in the country of the Philistines was a year and four months.{b}
David and his men went up and raided the Geshurites, the Girzites,{c} and the Amalekites, who had lived in the land since ancient times, in the region stretching toward Shur and as far as Egypt.
Whenever David attacked a district, he left no man or woman alive; he took the sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels, and clothing, and then returned to Achish.
When Achish asked, “Where have you raided today?” David would say, “Upon the south of Judah,” or “Upon the south country of the Jerahmeelites,” or “Upon the south country of the Kenites.”{d}
David left no man or woman alive to bring word to Gath, thinking, “They might tell on us and say, ‘This is what David did.’” This was his practice all the time he lived in Philistine territory.
And Achish trusted David, thinking, “He has made himself utterly odious to his people Israel; therefore he shall be my servant forever.”

notes.text: Ziklag was a town in the Negeb, in the south of Judah; its exact location is uncertain.
Hebrew “days and four months”; “days” here means a year. The Septuagint reads “four months” (reported).
So the traditional written text (ketiv); the margin reads “Gezrites.” Some Septuagint manuscripts lack this name (reported).
Hebrew “the Negeb,” meaning “dry land,” the southern region of Judah.

verses.text: About that time the Philistines mustered their armies to make war on Israel. Achish told David, “You must understand that you and your men will march out with me in the army.”
David answered Achish, “So be it; you shall learn what your servant will do.” And Achish replied to David, “So be it; I will make you keeper of my head{a} for all time.”
Now Samuel had died, and all Israel had lamented him and buried him in Ramah, his own city. And Saul had driven out of the land those who called up the dead and those who consulted spirits.{b}
So the Philistines were gathered together, and they came and pitched at Shunem;{c} and Saul assembled all Israel, and they pitched at Gilboa.{d}
When Saul saw the army of the Philistines, he was afraid, and his heart trembled greatly.
When Saul inquired of Yahweh, Yahweh did not answer him, neither by dreams, nor by Urim, nor by prophets.
Saul said to his servants, “Find me a woman who is a medium,{e} so that I can go and consult her.” “There is a medium at En-dor,”{f} they told him.

Saul put on other clothes to disguise himself and went with two men. They came to the woman by night, and he said, “Please practice divination for me by a spirit, and call up the person I name to you.”
The woman answered him, “You surely know what Saul has done: he has removed the mediums and spiritists from the land. Why are you laying a trap for me, to get me killed?”
But Saul swore to her by Yahweh, “As Yahweh lives, no punishment shall come upon you for this thing.”
Then the woman asked, “Whom am I to bring up to you?” He answered, “Samuel; bring him up to me.”
When the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. And the woman spoke to Saul, saying, “Why have you deceived me? You are Saul!”
The king told her, “Have no fear. What do you see?” The woman answered Saul, “I see a divine being{g} rising out of the earth.”
He said to her, “What form has he?” She said, “An aged man is coming up, covered with a mantle.” Then Saul perceived that it was Samuel, and he bowed with his face to the ground and did homage.

Samuel said to Saul, “Why have you disturbed me by calling me up?” Saul answered, “I am in deep distress. The Philistines are fighting against me, and God has turned away from me. He no longer answers me, either through prophets or through dreams, so I have called on you to let me know what I should do.”
Samuel said, “Why ask me, now that Yahweh has turned away from you and become your enemy?{h}
Yahweh has done to you{i} just as he spoke by me. Yahweh has torn the kingdom out of your hand and given it to your neighbor, to David.
Because you did not listen to the voice of Yahweh, nor execute the heat of his anger upon Amalek, for that reason Yahweh has done this thing to you this day.

Moreover, Yahweh will also give Israel along with you into the hand of the Philistines, and tomorrow you and your sons shall be with me. Yahweh will give the army of Israel also into the hand of the Philistines.”
Then Saul fell at once full length on the ground and was greatly afraid because of the words of Samuel. And there was no strength in him, for he had eaten no bread all day and all night.
The woman approached Saul and saw how terrified he was. She said, “Your servant has obeyed you; I took my life in my hands and did what you told me.
Now please listen to your servant. Let me put a bit of food in front of you so that you can eat and regain your strength for the journey.”
He refused and said, “I will not eat.” But his servants, together with the woman, pressed him, and he listened to their voice. So he rose from the ground and sat on the bed.
Now the woman had a fattened calf in the house, and she hurried and slaughtered it, and she took flour and kneaded it and baked unleavened bread from it.
She served it to Saul and his servants, and they ate. Then they got up and left that same night.

notes.text: That is, “my bodyguard.”
Hebrew ʾovot and yiddeʿonim, those who claimed to consult the spirits of the dead. Likewise in verse 9.
Shunem was a town in the territory of Issachar, on the slope of the hill of Moreh.
Gilboa was a mountain ridge south of the Jezreel Valley.
Hebrew “a woman who is mistress of a spirit” (baʿalat ʾov).
En-dor means “spring of the dwelling” (uncertain), a town north of the hill of Moreh.
Or “a godlike being” or “divine beings” (Hebrew ʾelohim, with a plural verb). The Septuagint reads “gods ascending out of the earth” (Brenton).
The Hebrew word ʿar is uncertain; perhaps “adversary” (an Aramaic sense). The Septuagint reads “is with your neighbor” (reported).
So many Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (reported); the traditional text reads “to him,” that is, to David.

verses.text: Now the Philistines gathered all their forces to Aphek,{a} while Israel was camped by the spring that is in Jezreel.
Now the lords of the Philistines were marching past by hundreds and by thousands, and David and his men were marching past at the rear with Achish.

Then the princes of the Philistines said, “What are these Hebrews here for?” And Achish answered the princes of the Philistines, “Is not this David, servant of Saul the king of Israel, who has been with me these days, or these years? I have found no fault in him from the day he went over to me until this day.”

But the princes of the Philistines were angry with him and said to him, “Make the man go back, so that he returns to his place that you appointed him. He shall not go down with us to the battle, lest in the battle he become an adversary{b} to us. For with what could this man win back the goodwill of his lord? Would it not be with the heads of these men here?
Is not this the David of whom they answered one another in the dances, saying, ‘Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands’?”

So Achish called David and told him, “As Yahweh lives,{c} you have been honest, and I would be pleased to have you serve alongside me in the army, since I have found no fault in you from the day you came to me until now. Even so, the other rulers do not approve of you.
So turn around now and go back in peace, so that you will not offend the Philistine rulers.”

David said to Achish, “But what have I done? And what have you found in your servant from the day that I came before you until this day, that I may not go and fight against the enemies of my lord the king?”
Achish answered David, “I know that you are as good in my eyes as a messenger{d} of God. Nevertheless, the commanders of the Philistines have said, ‘He shall not go up with us to the battle.’
So get up early in the morning, together with your lord’s servants who came with you,{e} and leave as soon as it is light.”
So David set out early, he and his men, to leave in the morning and return to the land of the Philistines. But the Philistines went up to Jezreel.

notes.text: Aphek was a town in the Sharon plain, the gathering place before the battle of 4:1.
Hebrew satan, “adversary.”
A Philistine king swearing by Yahweh may reflect courtesy toward David.
Or “angel.”
The Septuagint adds “and go to the place where I appointed you, and entertain no evil thought in your heart, for you are good in my sight” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: On the third day David and his men arrived at Ziklag. The Amalekites had raided the Negeb and Ziklag; they had struck Ziklag and burned it down,
and had taken captive the women and everyone else in it, young and old. They had killed no one, but had carried them away as they went on their way.
When David and his men came to the town, there it was, burned with fire, and their wives and their sons and their daughters taken captive.
Then David and the people who were with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no more strength to weep.
David’s two wives also had been taken captive, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the widow of Nabal the Carmelite.

And David was in great straits, for the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was bitter, each man for his sons and for his daughters. But David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God.
David said to Abiathar the priest, son of Ahimelech, “Bring the ephod here to me, I pray.” So Abiathar brought the ephod to David.
David asked Yahweh, “Should I chase this raiding party? Will I catch them?” “Chase them,” he answered, “for you will certainly catch them and rescue the captives.”
So David went, he and the six hundred men who were with him, and they came to the brook Besor,{a} where those who were left behind stayed.
But David pursued, he and four hundred men, while two hundred stayed behind who were too faint to cross the brook Besor.
They found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David. They gave him bread, and he ate, and they gave him water to drink.
They also gave him a slice of fig cake and two raisin cakes. After he ate, his strength returned, for he had eaten no food and drunk no water for three days and three nights.
David said to him, “Whose are you? And from where do you come?” He said, “I am an Egyptian lad, a slave of an Amalekite man. My master abandoned me three days ago, because I fell ill.
We made a raid on the Negeb of the Cherethites,{b} on the territory of Judah, and on the Negeb of Caleb, and we burned Ziklag.”
David said to him, “Will you bring me down to this band?” He said, “Swear to me by God that you will not kill me or deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will bring you down to this band.”

When he had brought him down, look, they were scattered over the face of all the land, eating and drinking and feasting, on account of the vast plunder they had seized out of the Philistines’ land and out of Judah’s land.
And David smote them from the dusk until the evening of the following day,{c} and not one man of them escaped except four hundred young men who mounted camels and fled.
David recovered all that the Amalekites had taken, and David rescued his two wives.
There was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither plunder nor anything they had seized. All of it David brought back.
David also took all the flocks and the herds, which they drove before those other livestock, and they said, “This is David’s spoil.”{d}

Then David came to the two hundred men who had been too faint to follow David, whom they had left at the brook Besor. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him. When David came near to the people, he greeted them.

Then answered all the evil men and the base fellows{e} among the men who had gone with David, and said, “Since they went not with us, we will give them nothing of the plunder that we have rescued, but only to every man his wife and his children, that they may lead them away and go.”
But David said, “You shall not do so, my brothers, with that which Yahweh has given to us, who has kept us safe and has delivered the raiding band that came upon us into our hand.
And who will hearken to you in this matter? For as his portion is that goes down to the battle, so shall his portion be that remains with the baggage. They shall share alike.”
And from that day forward he made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel, to this day.
When David reached Ziklag, he sent part of the plunder to his friends, the elders of Judah, with this message: “Here is a gift{f} for you from the plunder taken from Yahweh’s enemies.”
He sent to them in Bethel, and to them in Ramoth of the south, and to them in Jattir,
and to them in Aroer, and to them in Siphmoth, and to them in Eshtemoa,
and to them in Racal, and to them in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to them in the cities of the Kenites,
and to them in Hormah, and to them in Bor-ashan,{g} and to them in Athach,
and to them in Hebron, and to every place where David himself and his men had been accustomed to go.

notes.text: Besor was a stream (a wadi) south of Ziklag, flowing west to the Mediterranean.
The Cherethites were a people related to the Philistines, perhaps from Crete. Some of them later served in David’s bodyguard (2 Samuel 8:18).
The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “from the twilight until the evening of their morrow.”
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Hebrew “men of Belial.”
Hebrew “blessing.”
So many Hebrew manuscripts (reported); others read “Cor-ashan.” Bor-ashan means “smoking pit.”

verses.text: Now the Philistines were fighting against Israel, and the men of Israel fled before the Philistines and fell slain on Mount Gilboa.
The Philistines closed in on Saul and his sons and killed Saul’s sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua.{a}
The battle pressed hard against Saul, and the archers, the men with bows, found him, and he was badly wounded by the archers.{b}

Then Saul said to his armor-bearer, “Draw your sword and run me through with it, lest these uncircumcised come and run me through and make sport of me.” But his armor-bearer would not, for he was greatly afraid. So Saul took the sword and fell upon it.
When his armor-bearer saw that Saul was dead, he also fell upon his own sword and died with him.
So Saul died, and his three sons, and his armor-bearer, and all his men, on that same day together.

When the Israelites on the other side of the valley and across the Jordan saw that Israel’s army had fled and that Saul and his sons were dead, they abandoned their towns and ran away, and the Philistines moved in and settled there.
The next day, when the Philistines came to strip the slain, they found Saul and his three sons fallen on Mount Gilboa.
They cut off his head and stripped off his armor and sent them round about the land of the Philistines, to proclaim the tidings in the temples of their idols and among the people.
They put his armor in the house of the Ashtaroth,{c} and they fastened his body to the wall of Beth-shan.{d}
But when the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead heard what the Philistines had done to Saul,
all their brave men set out and traveled all night. They took Saul’s body and his sons’ bodies down from the wall of Beth-shan, brought them to Jabesh, and burned them there.{e}
And they took their bones and buried them under the tamarisk tree in Jabesh, and they fasted seven days.

notes.text: Abinadab means “my father is generous.” Malchi-shua means “my king is salvation” (uncertain).
Or “he was greatly afraid of the archers.” The Septuagint reads “he was wounded under the ribs” (Brenton, modernized).
The plural of Ashtoreth (Astarte), a Canaanite goddess. The Septuagint reads “the temple of Astarte” (Brenton). First Chronicles 10:10 adds that they fastened his head in the temple of Dagon.
Beth-shan means “house of quiet” (uncertain), a city at the junction of the Jezreel and Jordan valleys.
Burning the bodies was not the usual Israelite practice. Some have reported that the verb here may mean “anointed with spices” (scholarly review). First Chronicles 10:12 does not mention the burning.

books.name: 2 Samuel
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where 2 Samuel is called 2 Kingdoms) and against the Dead Sea Scrolls of Samuel, chiefly 4QSam-a, the largest of them. In Samuel the traditional Hebrew text has suffered more copying damage than in most books, and the Septuagint and 4QSam-a often preserve an older or fuller wording; the most important differences are footnoted (for example, in David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan, the list of David’s mighty men, and the census account). Every Septuagint reading cited in the footnotes was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation (quoted in modernized wording). Readings of the Dead Sea Scrolls are stated in general terms (“is reported to read”) until they can be checked against the critical editions. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (18:33; 19:1–43), a footnote says so. Measurements are given in modern US units, and times and dates use modern equivalents, with the originals in the footnotes.

verses.text: Now it came about after the death of Saul, when David had returned from striking down the Amalekites, that David remained two days in Ziklag.
On the third day, look, a man came out of the camp from Saul, with his garments torn and earth upon his head. And as he came to David, he fell to the ground and did obeisance.
David said to him, “From where do you come?” He said to him, “Out of the camp of Israel I have escaped.”

David said to him, “How did the matter go? Tell me, I pray.” He answered, “The people fled from the battle, and many of the people also have fallen and are dead; and Saul and Jonathan his son are dead too.”
Then David said to the young man who was telling him, “How do you know that Saul and Jonathan his son are dead?”

The young man who brought him the report said, “I chanced to come upon Mount Gilboa, and look, Saul was propped upon his spear, and look, the chariots and the masters of horse were following hard upon him.
When he looked behind him, he saw me and called to me. And I answered, ‘Here am I.’
He said to me, ‘Who are you?’ I answered him, ‘I am an Amalekite.’
He said to me, ‘Stand over me, I pray, and kill me, for dizziness{a} has seized me, though my life is still whole in me.’

So I stood over him and killed him, because I was sure that he could not live after he had fallen. And I took the crown that was on his head and the band that was on his arm, and I have brought them here to my lord.”
Then David seized his clothes and rent them; likewise every man that was with him.
They mourned and wept and fasted until evening for Saul and for Jonathan his son and for the people of Yahweh{b} and for the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword.
David said to the young man who told him, “Where are you from?” He answered, “I am the son of a sojourner, an Amalekite.”
David said to him, “How were you not afraid to put forth your hand to destroy Yahweh’s anointed?”
Then David called one of the young men and said, “Go near and fall upon him.” And he struck him so that he died.
David said to him, “Your blood be upon your own head, for your own mouth has testified against you, saying, ‘I have killed Yahweh’s anointed.’”
Then David lamented with this lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son,
and he said it should be taught to the sons of Judah: the Bow.{c} Look, it is written in the Book of Jashar.{d}
“Your glory,{e} O Israel, is slain upon your high places! How are the mighty fallen!
Tell it not in Gath, and do not proclaim it in Ashkelon’s streets, or the daughters of the Philistines will celebrate, and the daughters of the uncircumcised will gloat.
You mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew nor rain upon you, nor fields of offerings!{f} For there the shield of the mighty was defiled, the shield of Saul, not anointed with oil.{g}
From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, the bow of Jonathan turned not back, and the sword of Saul returned not empty.
Saul and Jonathan, beloved and lovely! In their lives and in their death they were not divided. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions.
You daughters of Israel, weep over Saul, who clothed you in scarlet with delights, who put ornaments of gold upon your apparel.
How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies dead on your heights.
I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan; you were dear to me. Your love for me was more wonderful than the love of women.
How are the mighty fallen, and the weapons of war perished!”

notes.text: The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain; perhaps “cramp” or “agony.” The Septuagint reads “a dreadful darkness” (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “for the people of Judah” (reported).
The Hebrew is uncertain. “The Bow” may be the title of the lament (see verse 22). The Septuagint lacks the word (Brenton, “he gave orders to teach it the sons of Judah”).
Jashar means “upright.” The Book of Jashar was an ancient collection of poems, now lost (see also Joshua 10:13). The Septuagint reads “the book of Right” (Brenton).
Or “The gazelle.” The Hebrew word tsevi can mean either “beauty” or “gazelle.”
The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “nor fields of first-fruits” (Brenton).

Leather shields were rubbed with oil before battle. The Septuagint likewise reads “the shield of Saul was not anointed with oil” (Brenton). Some read the phrase as referring to Saul himself, “no longer anointed” (scholarly review).

verses.text: After this David inquired of Yahweh, saying, “Shall I go up into any of the towns of Judah?” Yahweh said to him, “Go up.” David said, “To where shall I go up?” And he said, “To Hebron.”{a}
David went up there with his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, the widow of Nabal of Carmel.
And David brought up his men who were with him, every man with his household, and they settled in the towns of Hebron.
Then the men of Judah came, and there they anointed David king over the house of Judah. They told David, “It was the men of Jabesh-gilead who buried Saul.”
So David sent messengers to the men of Jabesh-gilead and said to them, “Blessed be you of Yahweh, because you have shown this kindness to your lord, to Saul, and have buried him.
Now may Yahweh show steadfast love and faithfulness to you. And I also will do you good, because you have done this thing.
So now strengthen your hands and be sons of valor; for Saul your master is dead, and me the house of Judah has anointed as king over them.”
Meanwhile Abner son of Ner, the commander of Saul’s army, had taken Saul’s son Ish-bosheth{b} and moved him across to Mahanaim,{c}
and he made him king over Gilead and over the Ashurites{d} and over Jezreel and over Ephraim and over Benjamin and over all Israel.
Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, was forty years old when he began to reign over Israel, and he reigned two years. But the house of Judah followed David.
The number of the days that David was king in Hebron over the house of Judah was seven years and six months.
Abner son of Ner and the servants of Ish-bosheth son of Saul went out from Mahanaim to Gibeon.
And Joab{e} son of Zeruiah and the servants of David went out and met them by the pool of Gibeon. They sat down, the one band on the one side of the pool and the other on the other side of the pool.
Abner said to Joab, “Let the young men arise now and contend before us.” Joab said, “Let them arise.”
Then they arose and went over by number, twelve for Benjamin and for Ish-bosheth son of Saul, and twelve of the servants of David.
Each man caught his fellow by the head and thrust his sword into his fellow’s side, and they fell down together. Therefore that place was called Helkath-hazzurim,{f} which is in Gibeon.
And the fighting grew exceedingly hard that day, and Abner was beaten, and the men of Israel with him, before David’s servants.
The three sons of Zeruiah were there, Joab and Abishai and Asahel.{g} Asahel was as light of foot as one of the gazelles in the field.
Asahel pursued after Abner, and in going he turned neither to the right hand nor to the left from following Abner.
Then Abner looked behind him and said, “Is that you, Asahel?” He answered, “It is I.”
Abner said to him, “Turn aside to your right hand or to your left, and lay hold of one of the young men and take his gear for yourself.” But Asahel would not turn aside from following him.
Abner told Asahel again, “Turn aside from following me! Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I hold up my head before your brother Joab?”

Yet he refused to turn aside. So Abner smote him in the belly with the hinder end of the spear, and the spear went out behind him; and he fell there and died in his place. And every one who came to the spot where Asahel fell and died halted.
But Joab and Abishai chased after Abner. And the sun went down as they reached the hill of Ammah, that lies before Giah by the road to the wilderness of Gibeon.
The Benjamites rallied behind Abner and formed a single group, taking their stand on the top of a hill.
Abner called out to Joab, “Must the sword go on devouring forever? Surely you realize this will end in bitterness. How long before you tell your men to stop pursuing their brothers?”
“As God lives,” Joab answered, “if you had not spoken up, the men would not have given up pursuing their brothers until morning.”{h}
So Joab blew the trumpet, and all the people stood still and pursued Israel no more, nor did they fight any more.
All that night Abner and his men traveled through the Arabah. They crossed over the Jordan, passed through the whole Bithron,{i} and came to Mahanaim.
Joab gave up the chase after Abner and assembled all his troops. Nineteen of David’s men were missing, besides Asahel.
But the servants of David had struck of Benjamin and of Abner’s men three hundred and sixty men, and they died.
They took up Asahel and buried him in the tomb of his father, which was in Bethlehem. And Joab and his men went all night, and the day broke upon them at Hebron.

notes.text: Hebron was the chief city of Judah, about 19 miles (31 kilometers) south of Jerusalem. Its name perhaps means “association” or “alliance.”

Ish-bosheth means “man of shame.” His original name was Ishbaal or Eshbaal, “man of the lord” (1 Chronicles 8:33); scribes replaced “baal” with “bosheth” (“shame”) to avoid the name of the god Baal. The Septuagint reads “Jebosthe” (Brenton). Likewise throughout.
Mahanaim means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2), a town east of the Jordan.
So the Hebrew. Some ancient versions read “Geshurites” (reported); others suggest “Asherites.”
Joab means “Yahweh is father.”
Helkath-hazzurim means “field of flints” or “field of blades” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “Portion of the Treacherous ones” (reported).
Asahel means “God has made.”
Or “If you had not spoken, the people would have given up the pursuit of their brothers only in the morning.” The Hebrew can be read either way.
Or “the whole morning”; the Hebrew word bitron may be a place name or mean “ravine.”

verses.text: Now the war between Saul’s house and David’s house was long. And David went on growing ever stronger, but the house of Saul went on growing ever weaker.
Sons were born to David in Hebron. His firstborn was Amnon,{a} by Ahinoam the Jezreelitess;
his second, Chileab,{b} whose mother was Abigail, formerly wife of Nabal of Carmel; and the third, Absalom{c} son of Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur;
the fourth was Adonijah{d} son of Haggith, the fifth Shephatiah{e} son of Abital,
and the sixth Ithream,{f} born to David’s wife Eglah. These sons were born to David at Hebron.
During the war between Saul’s house and David’s house, Abner kept strengthening his own position in Saul’s house.
Now Saul had had a concubine whose name was Rizpah,{g} the daughter of Aiah. And Ish-bosheth{h} said to Abner, “Why have you gone in to my father’s concubine?”

Then Abner was very angry over the words of Ish-bosheth and said, “Am I a dog’s head that belongs to Judah? To this day I keep showing loyalty to the household of your father Saul, to his kinsmen and to his companions, and I have not handed you over into David’s hand; and yet you charge me today with a fault concerning this woman!
So may God do to Abner and more also, if I do not accomplish for David what Yahweh has sworn to him,
to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and to set up the throne of David over Israel and over Judah, from Dan to Beersheba.”
And Ish-bosheth could not answer Abner another word, because he feared him.
Abner sent messengers to David on his own behalf{i} to ask, “To whom does the land belong? Make a covenant with me, and I will lend you my support in turning all Israel over to you.”
“Good,” David replied. “I will make a covenant with you, but I demand one thing: you will not be admitted to my presence unless you bring Saul’s daughter Michal with you when you come to see me.”
Then David sent messengers to Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, saying, “Give me my wife Michal, whom I betrothed to myself for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines.”
So Ish-bosheth had her fetched from her husband, Paltiel son of Laish.
But her husband went with her, weeping as he went behind her as far as Bahurim. Then Abner said to him, “Go, return.” And he returned.
Now Abner had held counsel with Israel’s elders, saying, “Both yesterday and the day before you were seeking to have David as king over you.
Now then do it. For Yahweh has spoken of David, saying, ‘By the hand of my servant David I will save my people Israel from the hand of the Philistines and from the hand of all their enemies.’”
Abner also spoke in the ears of Benjamin. And Abner went to speak in the ears of David at Hebron all that seemed good to Israel and to the whole house of Benjamin.
When Abner came to David at Hebron with twenty men, David made a feast for Abner and the men who were with him.

Abner told David, “Let me go at once and gather all Israel to my lord the king, so that they may make a covenant with you and you may rule over everything you desire.” David let Abner leave, and he went away in peace.
Just then David’s servants and Joab came back from a raid, bringing a great deal of plunder. Abner was no longer with David at Hebron, because David had dismissed him and he had left in peace.
When Joab and all the army that was with him came, they told Joab, “Abner the son of Ner came to the king, and he has sent him away, and he has gone in peace.”
Then Joab came to the king and said, “What have you done? Look, Abner came to you. Why is it that you have sent him away, and he is quite gone?
You know Abner the son of Ner, that he came to deceive you, and to know your going out and your coming in, and to know all that you are doing.”
When Joab had gone out from David, he sent messengers after Abner, and they turned him back from the well of Sirah;{j} and David knew nothing of it.
When Abner returned to Hebron, Joab took him aside into the midst of the gate to speak with him quietly, and there he smote him in the stomach, and he died, for the blood of Asahel his brother.
Afterward, when David heard of it, he said, “I and my kingdom are guiltless before Yahweh forever of the blood of Abner the son of Ner.

May it whirl{k} upon the head of Joab and upon all his father’s house. And may there never be lacking from the house of Joab one who has a discharge, or one who is leprous,{l} or one who leans on a staff,{m} or one who falls by the sword, or one who lacks bread!”
So Joab and Abishai his brother killed Abner, because he had put their brother Asahel to death at Gibeon in the battle.
Then David said to Joab and to all the people who were with him, “Tear your clothes, and gird yourselves with sackcloth, and mourn before Abner.” And King David followed the bier.
They buried Abner in Hebron. And the king lifted up his voice and wept at the grave of Abner, and all the people wept.
Then the king chanted a lament over Abner, and said, “Was Abner to die the death of a fool?
Your hands were not tied, and your feet were not chained. You fell as a man falls before criminals.” And all the people wept over him once more.
Then all the people came to cause David to eat bread while it was yet day. But David took an oath: “God do so to me, and more as well, if I taste bread or anything else before sunset!”
All the people noticed this and were pleased; indeed, everything the king did pleased them.
So all the people and all Israel understood that day that it had not been from the king to put to death Abner the son of Ner.
And the king spoke to his servants: “Know you not that a prince and a great man has fallen this day in Israel?
I am weak today, though anointed king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too hard for me. May Yahweh repay the evildoer according to his evil!”{n}

notes.text: Amnon means “faithful.”
Called Daniel in 1 Chronicles 3:1. The meaning of Chileab is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “Dalouia” (reported).
Absalom means “my father is peace.” Maacah means “oppression” (uncertain); Talmai perhaps means “furrowed” (uncertain). Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
Adonijah means “my lord is Yahweh.” Haggith means “festal.”
Shephatiah means “Yahweh has judged.” The meaning of Abital is “my father is dew” (uncertain).
Ithream means “remainder of the people” (uncertain). The meaning of Eglah is “heifer.”
Rizpah means “glowing coal.” Aiah means “falcon.”
So some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint (Brenton, “Jebosthe the son of Saul”). The traditional Hebrew text lacks the name here.
Or “where he was.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Sirah means “thorn” (uncertain).
Or “fall.”
The Hebrew word covered various skin diseases.
Or “who holds a spindle,” that is, one who is unfit for war (uncertain).
The Septuagint reads “I am this day a mere kinsman of his, and as it were a subject” (Brenton, modernized). The Hebrew is difficult.

verses.text: When Saul’s son{a} heard that Abner had died in Hebron, his hands grew feeble, and all Israel was troubled.

Now Saul’s son had two men who were captains of raiding bands. The name of the one was Baanah, and the name of the other Rechab,{b} sons of Rimmon a man of Beeroth, of the sons of Benjamin (for Beeroth also is reckoned to Benjamin;
the Beerothites fled to Gittaim and have been sojourners there until this day).

Jonathan, Saul’s son, had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news about Saul and Jonathan came out of Jezreel, and his nurse took him up and fled. And as she made haste to flee, he fell and became lame. His name was Mephibosheth.{c}
Then Rechab and Baanah, sons of Rimmon of Beeroth, went off, and in the heat of the day they reached the house of Ish-bosheth, while he was lying down for his midday rest.
They came there into the middle of the house as though to fetch wheat, and they struck him in the belly. Then Rechab and Baanah his brother escaped.{d}
When they came into the house, as he lay on his bed in his bedchamber, they struck him and killed him and beheaded him. They took his head and went by the way of the Arabah all night.

They carried Ish-bosheth’s head to David in Hebron and said to the king, “Here is the head of Ish-bosheth son of Saul, your enemy, who sought to kill you. Yahweh has granted my lord the king revenge today on Saul and his line.”
But David answered Rechab and Baanah his brother, the sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, and said to them, “As Yahweh lives, who has redeemed my soul out of all adversity,
when a man told me, ‘Saul is dead,’ thinking he was bringing good news, I seized him and killed him at Ziklag. That was the reward I gave him for his news!
How much more, when wicked men have murdered an innocent man in his own house, on his own bed, will I demand his blood from your hands and remove you from the earth!”

David gave an order to his young men, and they killed them, cut off their hands and feet, and hung the bodies beside the pool at Hebron. But they took Ish-bosheth’s head and buried it in Abner’s tomb at Hebron.

notes.text: The Hebrew lacks the name here; the Septuagint reads “Memphibosthe” (reported), but most interpreters understand Ish-bosheth.
Baanah means “son of affliction” (uncertain). Rechab means “rider.” Rimmon means “pomegranate.” Beeroth means “wells.”
Mephibosheth means “from the mouth of shame.” He is called Merib-baal (“Baal contends” or “the lord is advocate”) in 1 Chronicles 8:34; see the note on Ish-bosheth at 2:8.

The Septuagint reads differently: “And behold, the porter of the house was winnowing wheat, and she slumbered and slept, and the brothers Rechab and Baanah slipped into the house” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: Then all the tribes of Israel came to David at Hebron and spoke, saying, “See, we are your bone and your flesh.

Even in time past, when Saul was king over us, it was you who led Israel out and brought Israel in. And Yahweh said to you, ‘You shall shepherd my people Israel, and you shall be prince over Israel.’”
When all the elders of Israel had come to the king at Hebron, King David made a covenant with them there in Yahweh’s presence, and they anointed David as king over Israel.
Thirty years old was David at his becoming king, and forty years he reigned.
In Hebron he reigned over Judah seven years and six months, and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years over all Israel and Judah.

The king and his men went to Jerusalem against the Jebusites, the people living in that land. They told David, “You will never get in here; even the blind and the lame can turn you back,” thinking, “David cannot enter.”
Nevertheless David captured the stronghold of Zion,{a} which is the City of David.

That day David said, “Anyone who wants to defeat the Jebusites should get up through the water shaft{b} to attack those ‘lame and blind’ whom David hates.” This is why people say, “The blind and the lame may not enter the house.”
David dwelt in the stronghold and called it the City of David. And David built round about from the Millo{c} inward.
And David went on and grew great, for Yahweh God of Armies was with him.
Hiram{d} king of Tyre sent messengers to David, and cedar trees, and carpenters and masons,{e} and they built David a house.
And David perceived that Yahweh had established him king over Israel, and that he had exalted his kingdom for the sake of his people Israel.
David took more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem after he came from Hebron, and more sons and daughters were born to David.
These are the names of those born to him in Jerusalem: Shammua, Shobab, Nathan, Solomon,{f}
Ibhar, Elishua, Nepheg, Japhia,
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet.{g}
When the Philistines heard that they had anointed David king over Israel, all the Philistines went up to seek David. David heard of it and went down to the stronghold.
The Philistines had come and spread out across the Valley of Rephaim.{h}
And David inquired of Yahweh, “Shall I go up against the Philistines? Will you give them into my hand?” Yahweh said to David, “Go up, for I will surely give the Philistines into your hand.”

So David came to Baal-perazim, and David struck them there. And he said, “Yahweh has broken through my enemies before me, like a breaking through of waters.” Therefore he called the name of that place Baal-perazim.{i}
They abandoned their idols there, and David and his men carried them away.{j}
Yet again the Philistines came up and spread themselves out in the Valley of Rephaim.
When David inquired of Yahweh, he said, “You shall not go up. Circle around behind them, and come upon them opposite the balsam trees.{k}
And when you hear the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, then bestir yourself, for then Yahweh has gone out before you to strike the camp of the Philistines.”
And David did so, as Yahweh had commanded him, and struck the Philistines from Geba{l} all the way to Gezer.

notes.text: Zion was the fortified hill of the Jebusite city, the southeastern ridge of Jerusalem. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
The Hebrew word tsinnor is uncertain; perhaps “water shaft” or “channel,” or a kind of hook or weapon (scholarly review). The Septuagint reads “let him attack with the dagger” (Brenton, modernized).
Millo means “filling,” probably a terraced earthwork.
Hiram means “my brother is exalted” (uncertain).
Hebrew “craftsmen of wood and craftsmen of stone for walls.”
Shammua means “heard.” Shobab perhaps means “returning” (uncertain). Nathan means “he has given.” Solomon is related to the word for “peace.”

Ibhar means “he chooses.” Elishua means “God is salvation.” Nepheg perhaps means “sprout” (uncertain). Japhia means “he shines forth.” Elishama means “God has heard.” Eliada means “God knows.” Eliphelet means “God is deliverance.”
Rephaim means “ghosts” or the name of an ancient people of great stature; the valley lay southwest of Jerusalem.
Baal-perazim means “lord of breaking through.”
First Chronicles 14:12 adds that they were burned.
Or “baka shrubs”; the exact kind of tree is uncertain. Likewise in verse 24.
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 14:16 read “Gibeon” (reported).

verses.text: David again gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand.

And David arose and went with all the people who were with him from Baale-judah,{a} to bring up from there the ark of God, which is called by the name, the name of Yahweh of Armies, who sits enthroned on the cherubim.
They placed the ark of God upon a new wagon and brought it out from Abinadab’s house on the hill; and Uzzah and Ahio,{b} Abinadab’s sons, drove the new wagon,
with the ark of God;{c} and Ahio went before the ark.
David and all the house of Israel were making merry before Yahweh with all kinds of instruments of fir wood,{d} with lyres and harps and tambourines and rattles and cymbals.
They came to the threshing floor of Nacon,{e} and because the oxen had stumbled, Uzzah put out his hand and took hold of the ark of God.
And the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Uzzah, and God struck him there for his error,{f} and he died there beside the ark of God.
David was angry because Yahweh had broken out against Uzzah. And he called that place Perez-uzzah,{g} as it is named to this day.
David was afraid of Yahweh that day, and he said, “How can the ark of Yahweh come to me?”
So David would not take the ark of Yahweh to himself into the City of David, but David turned it aside to the house of Obed-edom{h} the Gittite.
The ark of Yahweh remained in the house of Obed-edom the Gittite three months, and Yahweh blessed Obed-edom and all his household.

News came to King David: “Yahweh has blessed the household of Obed-edom, with all that he has, on account of the ark of God.” So David went and had the ark of God brought up from Obed-edom’s house into the City of David with joy.
When those who carried the ark of Yahweh had gone six paces, he sacrificed an ox and a fattened animal.
And David danced before Yahweh with all his might, and David was girded with a linen ephod.
So David and all the house of Israel brought up the ark of Yahweh with shouting and with the sound of the horn.
As the ark of Yahweh came into the City of David, Michal the daughter of Saul looked out through the window and saw King David leaping and whirling before Yahweh, and she despised him in her heart.
They brought in the ark of Yahweh and set it in its place, inside the tent that David had pitched for it. And David offered burnt offerings and peace offerings before Yahweh.
When David had made an end of offering the burnt offerings and the peace offerings, he blessed the people in the name of Yahweh of Armies.

And he apportioned to all the people, to the whole throng of Israel, to man and to woman, one loaf of bread apiece, a cake of dates,{i} and a cake of raisins. Then all the people departed, each to his house.

When David went home to bless his household, Saul’s daughter Michal came out to meet him. “How splendid the king of Israel looked today,” she said, “exposing himself before his servants’ slave girls, the way some vulgar person would expose himself!”
David said to Michal, “It was before Yahweh, who chose me above your father and above all his house, to appoint me prince over the people of Yahweh, over Israel; and I will make merry before Yahweh.
I will make myself yet more lightly esteemed than this, and I will be lowly in my own eyes.{j} But with the maids you speak of, with them I shall have honor.”
And Michal the daughter of Saul had no child to the day of her death.

notes.text: Baale-judah means “lords of Judah,” another name for Kiriath-jearim (1 Chronicles 13:6; Joshua 15:9). Some Hebrew manuscripts and other witnesses reportedly read “Baalah of Judah.”
Uzzah means “strength.” Ahio means “his brother” (uncertain); the Septuagint reads “his brothers” (reported).
The Hebrew repeats part of verse 3 here: “and they carried it out of the house of Abinadab, which was on the hill, with the ark of God.” The Septuagint has a shorter text (reported).

So the traditional Hebrew text, literally “with all woods of cypress.” The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 13:8 read “with all their might and with songs” (Brenton, “on well-tuned instruments mightily, and with songs,” modernized).
Nacon means “prepared” (uncertain). First Chronicles 13:9 reads “Chidon.” The Septuagint reads “Nachor” (Brenton).
The Hebrew word is uncertain. First Chronicles 13:10 reads “because he put out his hand to the ark.”
Perez-uzzah means “breaking out against Uzzah.”
Obed-edom means “servant of Edom” (uncertain).
The Hebrew word is uncertain; perhaps “a portion of meat.” The Septuagint reads “a joint of meat” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “in your eyes” (reported).

verses.text: Now it came to pass, when the king lived in his house and Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies round about,
that the king said to Nathan the prophet, “See now, I dwell in a house of cedar, but the ark of God dwells within curtains.”
And Nathan said to the king, “Go, do all that is in your heart, for Yahweh is with you.”
But that same night the word of Yahweh came to Nathan, saying,
“Go and tell my servant David, ‘Thus says Yahweh: Would you build me a house for me to dwell in?
For I have not dwelt in a house from the day I brought the sons of Israel up out of Egypt even until this day, but I have gone about in a tent and in a tabernacle.

In all places where I have walked with all the sons of Israel, did I speak a word with any of the tribes{a} of Israel, whom I commanded to shepherd my people Israel, saying, “Why have you not built me a house of cedar?”’
Now then, speak thus to my servant David: ‘So says Yahweh of Armies: From the sheepfold I took you, from behind the flock, that you should be prince over my people, over Israel.
I have been with you wherever you went and have cut off all your enemies from your presence. And I will make you a great name, like the name of the great ones who are on the earth.

And I will appoint a place for my people Israel and will plant them, that they may dwell in their own place and be troubled no more. And the sons of wickedness shall afflict them no more, as at the first,
from the day that I commanded judges to be over my people Israel. And I will give you rest from all your enemies. Moreover, Yahweh declares to you that Yahweh will make you a house.{b}
When your days are complete and you sleep with your fathers, I will raise up your seed after you, which shall proceed out of your bowels, and I will make his kingdom firm.
He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he does wrong, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of Adam,
but my steadfast love shall not depart from him, as I took it from Saul, whom I put away from before you.
Your house and your kingdom will be secure forever before you.{c} Your throne will last for all time.’”
According to all these words and according to all this vision, so Nathan spoke to David.
Then King David went in and sat before Yahweh and said, “Who am I, Lord Yahweh, and what is my house, that you have brought me thus far?
And yet this was a small thing in your eyes, Lord Yahweh. You have spoken also of your servant’s house for a great while to come, and this is the instruction for mankind,{d} Lord Yahweh!
And what more can David say to you? For you know your servant, Lord Yahweh!
Because of your word, and according to your own heart, you have done all this greatness, to make your servant know it.
Therefore you are great, Lord Yahweh. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

Is there another nation on earth like your people Israel, whom God went out to redeem for himself as a people, to win a name for himself, and to perform great and awesome acts for them,{e} by driving out nations and their gods ahead of your people, whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt?
And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever, and you, Yahweh, became their God.
And now, Yahweh God, the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house, confirm it forever, and do as you have spoken.
May your name be great forever, so that people say, ‘Yahweh of Armies is God over Israel,’ and may your servant David’s house be established in your presence.
For you, Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, have revealed to your servant, saying, ‘I will build you a house.’ Therefore your servant has found courage{f} to pray this prayer to you.
And now, Lord Yahweh, you are God, and your words are truth, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.
Please be pleased now to bless your servant’s house so that it continues in your presence forever. You, Lord Yahweh, have spoken, and by your blessing your servant’s house will be blessed forever.”

notes.text: So the Hebrew, shivte. First Chronicles 17:6 reads “judges” (shofte), a very similar word.
That is, a royal dynasty. The Septuagint reads “and the Lord will tell you that you shall build a house to him” (Brenton, modernized).
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint read “before me” (reported).
The Hebrew is obscure, literally “and this is the law of man.” First Chronicles 17:17 reads differently.

The Hebrew is difficult, literally “for you,” “for your land”; compare 1 Chronicles 17:21 and the Septuagint (Brenton, “to do mightily and nobly, so that you should cast out nations and their tabernacles,” modernized).
Literally “found his heart.”

verses.text: Some time later David defeated the Philistines and brought them under control, and he took Metheg-ammah{a} from Philistine hands.

He also defeated Moab. He made the people lie on the ground and measured them off with a cord: two cord-lengths of them to be put to death and one full length to be spared. So the Moabites became David’s subjects and paid him tribute.
David also defeated Hadadezer{b} son of Rehob, king of Zobah, when Hadadezer went to restore his control{c} along the Euphrates River.
David captured from him 1,700 horsemen{d} and 20,000 foot soldiers. He crippled all but a hundred of the chariot horses, keeping only enough for a hundred chariots.
When the Arameans{e} of Damascus came to help Hadadezer king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand men of the Arameans.
Then David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and the Arameans became David’s servants, bringing tribute. Yahweh gave David victory everywhere he went.
David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadadezer and brought them to Jerusalem.{f}
From Betah and Berothai,{g} cities belonging to Hadadezer, King David carried off a huge amount of bronze.{h}
When Toi{i} king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the army of Hadadezer,

Toi sent Joram{j} his son to King David to ask after his welfare and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadadezer and struck him; for Hadadezer had often been at war with Toi. And in his hand were vessels of silver and vessels of gold and vessels of bronze.
These also King David set apart to Yahweh, with the silver and the gold that he had set apart from every nation that he brought under,
from Aram,{k} from Moab, from the Ammonites, from the Philistines, from Amalek, and out of the plunder of Hadadezer son of Rehob, king of Zobah.
And David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down the Arameans{l} in the Valley of Salt, eighteen thousand men.
He stationed garrisons throughout Edom, and all the Edomites became David’s subjects. Yahweh gave David victory everywhere he went.
So David reigned over all Israel, and David executed justice and righteousness for all his people.
Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army, and Jehoshaphat{m} the son of Ahilud was recorder,
and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Ahimelech the son of Abiathar{n} were priests, and Seraiah{o} was secretary,
and Benaiah{p} the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites,{q} and David’s sons were priests.{r}

notes.text: Metheg-ammah means “bridle of the mother city” (uncertain); 1 Chronicles 18:1 reads “Gath and its villages.”
Hadadezer means “Hadad is help”; Hadad was the Aramean storm god.
Literally “his hand,” that is, his control or a monument (uncertain).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint and 1 Chronicles 18:4 read “a thousand chariots and seven thousand horsemen” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “Aram” and “Arameans” (Syrians). Likewise throughout.

Or “golden quivers” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “golden bracelets” and adds, “And Susakim king of Egypt took them, when he went up to Jerusalem in the days of Rehoboam son of Solomon” (Brenton, modernized).
Betah is called Tibhath in 1 Chronicles 18:8; the Septuagint reads “Metebac” (Brenton). Berothai means “my wells” (uncertain).
The Septuagint adds “with that Solomon made the bronze sea, and the pillars, and the basins, and all the furnishings” (Brenton, modernized; compare 1 Chronicles 18:8).
Called Tou in 1 Chronicles 18:9. The meaning of the name is uncertain.
Joram means “Yahweh is exalted.” First Chronicles 18:10 reads “Hadoram.”
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “out of Idumea”), and 1 Chronicles 18:11 read “Edom,” a word very similar in Hebrew.
So the Hebrew. Some Hebrew manuscripts and 1 Chronicles 18:12 read “Edomites”; the Septuagint reads “he smote Idumea” (Brenton). See verse 14.
Jehoshaphat means “Yahweh has judged.”
So the Hebrew. The Syriac reportedly reads “Abiathar son of Ahimelech” (compare 1 Samuel 22:20). Zadok means “righteous.”
Seraiah means “Yahweh has prevailed” (uncertain). He is called Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16.
Benaiah means “Yahweh has built.” Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.”
The Cherethites and Pelethites were royal guards, perhaps from Crete and Philistia.
Hebrew kohanim, the usual word for priests. First Chronicles 18:17 reads “chief officials at the king’s side”; the Septuagint reads “princes of the court” (Brenton).

verses.text: And David said, “Is there yet any who is left of the house of Saul, that I may show him kindness for Jonathan’s sake?”
There was a servant of Saul’s household named Ziba,{a} and he was summoned to David. “Are you Ziba?” the king asked. “At your service,” he answered.
The king asked, “Is there no one left of Saul’s house to whom I may show God’s kindness?” Ziba told the king, “A son of Jonathan is still alive; he is lame in both feet.”
The king said to him, “Where is he?” Ziba said to the king, “Look, he is in the house of Machir{b} the son of Ammiel, at Lo-debar.”{c}
Then King David sent and fetched him from the house of Machir the son of Ammiel, from Lo-debar.
Mephibosheth the son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came to David and fell on his face and did obeisance. David said, “Mephibosheth!” And he answered, “Here is your servant!”

David said to him, “Fear not, for I will surely show you kindness for Jonathan your father’s sake, and I will restore to you all the land of Saul your father, and you shall eat bread at my table continually.”
Mephibosheth bowed and said, “What is your servant, that you take notice of a dead dog like me?”
Then the king called to Ziba, Saul’s servant, and said to him, “All that belonged to Saul and to all his house I have given to your master’s son.

You are to farm the land for him, you and your sons and your servants, and bring in the produce, so that your master’s son will have food to eat. But Mephibosheth, your master’s son, will always eat at my table.” Ziba had fifteen sons and twenty servants.
Ziba told the king, “Your servant will do all that my lord the king commands.” “And Mephibosheth ate at my{d} table like one of the king’s sons.”
Mephibosheth had a young son whose name was Mica.{e} And all who dwelt in the house of Ziba were servants to Mephibosheth.
So Mephibosheth dwelt in Jerusalem, for he ate continually at the king’s table. And he was lame in both his feet.

notes.text: Ziba perhaps means “plant” or “strength” (uncertain).
Machir means “sold.” Ammiel means “my kinsman is God.”
Lo-debar means “no pasture” or “no thing” (uncertain), a town east of the Jordan.
So the Hebrew; the words may be the king’s. The Septuagint reads “at the table of David” (Brenton).
Mica means “who is like?” (short for “who is like Yahweh?”).

verses.text: Some time later the king of the Ammonites died, and his son Hanun{a} became king in his place.

David said, “I will be kind to Hanun son of Nahash, just as his father was kind to me.” So David sent a delegation of his servants to console him over his father. When David’s servants reached the land of the Ammonites,

But the Ammonite commanders told their lord Hanun, “Is David really honoring your father, in your opinion, by sending men to console you? Has David not rather sent his servants to you to explore the city, spy on it, and overthrow it?”
So Hanun seized David’s servants and shaved away one half of their beards, and he cut away their robes at the middle, up to their hips, and sent them off.
When they told it to David, he sent to meet them, for the men were greatly ashamed. And the king said, “Stay at Jericho until your beards have grown, and then return.”
When the Ammonites realized that they had become hateful to David, they hired 20,000 Aramean foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, 1,000 men from the king of Maacah, and 12,000 men from Tob.{b}
When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the host of the mighty men.
The Ammonites marched out and took up battle positions at the city gate, while the Arameans of Zobah and Rehob and the men of Tob and Maacah took up positions separately in the open country.
When Joab saw that the battle was set against him both in front and behind, he chose some of all the choice men of Israel and arrayed them against the Arameans.
He put the rest of the troops under his brother Abishai, who drew them up in formation against the Ammonites.
Joab said, “If the Arameans prove too strong for me, you are to come to my aid; and if the Ammonites prove too strong for you, I will come to yours.
Be strong, and let us play the man for our people and for the cities of our God. And may Yahweh do what is good in his eyes.”
So Joab and the people who were with him drew near to battle against the Arameans, and they fled before him.
When the Ammonites saw the Arameans flee, they too fled from Abishai and retreated into the city. Joab then left the battle with the Ammonites and returned to Jerusalem.
When the Arameans saw that they had been beaten before Israel, they gathered themselves together.
Hadadezer sent for the Arameans from across the River,{c} and they came to Helam,{d} led by Shobach, the commander of Hadadezer’s army.
David was told, so he mustered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and went to Helam. The Arameans lined up to meet David and fought against him.

And the Arameans fled before Israel, and David killed of the Arameans the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen,{e} and he struck Shobach the captain of their army, so that he died there.
When all the kings who served Hadadezer saw they had been defeated by Israel, they came to terms with Israel and served them. And the Arameans were afraid to give the Ammonites any more help.

notes.text: Hanun means “favored.”
Or “the men of Ish-tob.” Tob means “good.” The Septuagint reads “Istob” (Brenton) and “the king of Amalek” for “the king of Maacah.” Beth-rehob means “house of the broad place.”
That is, the Euphrates.
Helam was east of the Jordan; its location is uncertain.
First Chronicles 19:18 reads “seven thousand charioteers and forty thousand foot soldiers.” The Septuagint here agrees with the Hebrew (Brenton).

verses.text: Now it came to pass at the return of the year, at the time when kings go out to battle,{a} that David sent Joab and his servants with him and all Israel, and they ravaged the sons of Ammon and besieged Rabbah.{b} But David remained in Jerusalem.

It happened, at the time of evening, that David arose from his couch and walked about on the roof of the king’s house. And from the roof he saw a woman bathing, and the woman was very fair to look upon.
David sent and inquired about the woman. And one said, “Is not this Bathsheba,{c} the daughter of Eliam,{d} the wife of Uriah the Hittite?”{e}
So David sent messengers and took her, and she came in to him, and he lay with her. (She was cleansing herself from her impurity.) Then she went back to her house.
The woman conceived, and she sent and told David, and said, “I am with child.”
Then David sent to Joab, “Send me Uriah the Hittite.” And Joab sent Uriah to David.
When Uriah had come to him, David asked how Joab was faring and how the people fared and how the war went.
David told Uriah, “Go home and wash your feet.” Uriah left the palace, and a gift from the king followed him.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and did not go down to his house.
So they reported to David, “Uriah went not down to his house.” And David asked Uriah, “Is it not from a journey that you come? For what reason did you not go down to your house?”

Uriah said to David, “The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in booths, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are camped in the open field. Shall I then go into my house, to eat and to drink and to lie with my wife? By your life, and by the life of your soul, I will not do this thing.”
Then David said to Uriah, “Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will send you away.” So Uriah remained in Jerusalem that day and the next.
David invited him, and Uriah ate and drank in his presence, and David made him drunk. Yet that evening he went out and slept on his bed with his lord’s servants; he never went down to his own house.
In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah.
In it he wrote, “Put Uriah at the front, where the fighting is fiercest, then pull back from him so that he will be struck down and die.”
So as Joab was keeping watch on the city, he assigned Uriah to the place where he knew that valiant men were.
And the men of the city came out and fought with Joab, and some of the people of David’s servants fell. Uriah the Hittite died also.
Then Joab sent and told David all the things concerning the war.
And he charged the messenger, saying, “When you have finished telling all the matters of the war to the king,
then if the king’s anger flares up, and he says to you, ‘For what reason did you approach so close to the city to fight? Did you not know they would shoot from upon the wall?

Who killed Abimelech son of Jerubbesheth?{f} Did not a woman drop an upper millstone on him from the wall, so that he died at Thebez? Why did you venture near the wall?’ then you are to say, ‘Your servant Uriah the Hittite is also dead.’”
So the messenger departed, and he came and reported to David everything for which Joab had sent him.{g}
The messenger said to David, “The men prevailed against us and came out against us into the field, but we drove them back to the entrance of the gate.
Then the archers shot at your servants from the wall. Some of the king’s servants are dead, and your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead also.”
David told the messenger, “Tell Joab this: ‘Do not let this matter upset you, for the sword devours one person and then another. Press your attack on the city and destroy it.’ Give him courage.”
When the wife of Uriah heard that Uriah her husband was dead, she mourned for her husband.
And when the mourning was past, David sent and gathered her into his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. But the thing that David had done was evil in the eyes of Yahweh.

notes.text: Literally “at the return of the year,” that is, in the spring. So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “when the time of the year for kings going out to battle had come round”), and 1 Chronicles 20:1. The traditional Hebrew text reads “messengers” (malʾakhim) for “kings” (melakhim).
Rabbah means “great (city),” the Ammonite capital, modern Amman.
Bathsheba means “daughter of an oath” or “daughter of seven.” She is called Bath-shua in 1 Chronicles 3:5.
Eliam means “God is my kinsman.” He is called Ammiel in 1 Chronicles 3:5.
Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
That is, Jerubbaal, Gideon (Judges 6:32; 9:50–54); compare the note on Ish-bosheth at 2:8. The Septuagint reads “Jerobaal son of Ner” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds a longer form of David’s angry questions, repeating those of verses 20–21 (Brenton).

verses.text: And Yahweh sent Nathan to David. He came to him and said to him, “There were two men in one city, the one rich and the other poor.
The rich man had flocks and herds in great abundance;

but the poor man had nothing except one little ewe lamb, which he had bought and kept alive. And it grew up with him and with his children together. It would eat of his own morsel and drink from his own cup and lie in his bosom, and it was to him as a daughter.

Now a traveler arrived at the rich man’s house, and the rich man was unwilling to take an animal from his own flock or herd to cook a meal for the visitor who had come to him. He took the poor man’s lamb instead and prepared it for his guest.”
Then David’s anger was greatly kindled against the man, and he said to Nathan, “As Yahweh lives, the man who did this is a son of death!{a}
And he shall restore the lamb fourfold,{b} because he did this thing and because he had no pity.”
Nathan said to David, “You are the man! This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: ‘I anointed you king over Israel, and I rescued you from Saul’s hand.
I gave you your master’s house and your master’s wives into your bosom, and gave you the house of Israel and of Judah. And if that had been too little, I would have added to you as much again.
Why have you despised Yahweh’s word,{c} doing what is evil in his sight? You killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword and took his wife as your own; you murdered him with the sword of the Ammonites.
Now therefore the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife.’
This is what Yahweh says: ‘I will bring trouble on you from your own household. Before your eyes I will take your wives and give them to another man, and he will sleep with them in broad daylight.
For you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel and before the sun.’”
David said to Nathan, “I have sinned against Yahweh.” And Nathan said to David, “Yahweh also has put away your sin; you shall not die.
Nevertheless, because by this deed you have utterly scorned the enemies of Yahweh,{d} the child also who is born to you shall surely die.”
