Then Nathan went to his house. And Yahweh struck the child that Uriah’s wife bore to David, and it became very sick.
David therefore sought God for the child. And David fasted and went in and lay all night on the ground.
The elders of his house stood beside him to raise him up from the ground, but he was not willing, and he ate no bread with them.

On the seventh day the child died. David’s servants were afraid to tell him that the child was dead, for they said, “While the child was still alive, we spoke to him and he paid no attention to our voice. How can we tell him that the child is dead? He may do himself harm.”
But when David saw that his servants were whispering together, David perceived that the child was dead. And David said to his servants, “Is the child dead?” They said, “He is dead.”
David got up from the ground, washed, anointed himself, and changed his clothes. He went into Yahweh’s house and worshiped. Then he went home, asked for food, and they set it before him, and he ate.
His servants said to him, “What is this you are doing? You fasted and wept for the child while he was still living, yet when the child died you got up and ate food.”
He said, “While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept, for I said, ‘Who knows whether Yahweh will be gracious to me, that the child may live?’
But now he is dead. Why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he will not return to me.”
Then David comforted Bathsheba his wife, and went in to her and lay with her, and she bore a son, and he called his name Solomon.{e} And Yahweh loved him
and sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and he called his name Jedidiah,{f} because of Yahweh.
Now Joab fought against Rabbah of the sons of Ammon and took the royal city.
Joab sent messengers to David with the message, “I have fought against Rabbah and captured the water city.{g}
Now therefore gather the rest of the people together and encamp against the city and take it, lest I take the city and my name be called over it.”
So David gathered all the people together and went to Rabbah and fought against it and took it.

He took the crown of their king{h} from his head. Its weight was about seventy-five pounds{i} of gold, with a precious stone, and it was set on David’s head. And he brought out the spoil of the city, a very great amount.

And the people that were in it he brought forth and set them at saws and at sledges of iron and at axes of iron, and made them toil in the brickworks.{j} So he dealt with every city of the sons of Ammon. And David returned with all the people to Jerusalem.

notes.text: That is, deserves to die.
So the Hebrew (compare Exodus 22:1). The Septuagint reads “sevenfold” (reported).
Some Septuagint manuscripts read “despised Yahweh” (reported); compare verse 10.

The Hebrew includes “the enemies of,” probably as a scribal softening to avoid saying David scorned Yahweh himself. The Septuagint reads the same (Brenton, “given great occasion of provocation to the enemies of the Lord”).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “she called.”
Jedidiah means “beloved of Yahweh.” The Septuagint reads “Jeddedi” (Brenton).
That is, the part of the city that controlled the water supply.
Or “of Milcom,” the Ammonite god (1 Kings 11:5); the Hebrew malkam can be read either way. The Septuagint reads “Molchom their king” (Brenton).
Hebrew “a talent,” about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).

So the traditional reading (qere), describing forced labor. The written text (ketiv) reads “made them pass through Malkan,” perhaps a reference to Molech worship (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “put them under the saw … and made them pass through the brick kiln” (Brenton, modernized), which some understand as execution (scholarly review).

verses.text: Now after this it came to pass that Absalom the son of David had a fair sister whose name was Tamar.{a} And Amnon the son of David loved her.
Amnon became so tormented over his sister Tamar that he fell ill, for she was a virgin, and it seemed out of reach for Amnon to do anything to her.
But Amnon had a friend whose name was Jonadab,{b} the son of Shimeah, David’s brother. And Jonadab was a very shrewd man.
He said to him, “Why are you so lean from morning to morning, son of the king? Will you not tell me?” Amnon said to him, “I love Tamar, the sister of Absalom my brother.”

Jonadab said to him, “Lay yourself upon your bed and make yourself sick. When your father comes in to look on you, tell him, ‘Pray, let Tamar my sister come and feed me with bread, and let her make the dish before my eyes, so that I may watch and eat from her hand.’”

So Amnon lay down and feigned sickness. And the king came in to look on him, and Amnon said to the king, “Pray, let Tamar my sister come and make a couple of cakes before my eyes, that I may eat from her hand.”
Then David sent home to Tamar, saying, “Go now to your brother Amnon’s house and prepare food for him.”
So Tamar went to the house of Amnon her brother, and he was lying in bed. And she took dough and kneaded it and made cakes in his sight and baked the cakes.
And she took the pan and poured them out before him, but he refused to eat. And Amnon said, “Send everyone out from me.” So everyone went out from him.
Then Amnon said to Tamar, “Bring the food into the chamber, that I may eat from your hand.” And Tamar took the cakes she had made and brought them into the chamber to Amnon her brother.
But when she brought them near to him to eat, he took hold of her and said to her, “Come, lie with me, my sister.”
“No, my brother,” she answered, “do not force me, because such a thing is never done in Israel. Do not commit this disgrace.{c}
As for me, where would I take my disgrace? And you would be counted as one of the fools in Israel. Please, speak to the king; he will not refuse me to you.”
But he would not listen to her voice. Being stronger than she, he forced her and lay with her.
Then Amnon was seized by a hatred of her so intense that it was stronger than the love he had felt for her. “Get up and leave!” he told her.
But she said to him, “No, for this wrong in sending me away is greater than the other that you did to me.”{d} But he would not listen to her.
Then he summoned the lad who attended him and said, “Send this one away from me, out of doors, and fasten the door behind her.”
She had on her a long-sleeved tunic,{e} for in such robes the king’s daughters who were virgins were dressed. So his attendant put her outside and fastened the door behind her.
And Tamar put ashes on her head and rent the long-sleeved tunic that was on her. And she put her hand upon her head and went off, crying out as she walked.

Her brother Absalom said to her, “Has your brother Amnon{f} been with you? Keep quiet now, my sister; he is your brother. Do not let this weigh on your heart.” And Tamar stayed in her brother Absalom’s house, a desolate woman.
When King David heard of all these things, he was very angry.{g}
But Absalom spoke to Amnon neither good nor bad, for Absalom hated Amnon, because he had humbled his sister Tamar.
Two whole years later, Absalom held a sheep-shearing in Baal-hazor near Ephraim, and he called all the sons of the king.
Absalom came to the king and said, “See now, your servant has sheepshearers. Let the king, I pray, and his servants go with your servant.”
The king said to Absalom, “No, my son, let us not all go now, lest we be burdensome to you.” He pressed him, but he would not go, though he blessed him.
Then Absalom said, “If not, please let my brother Amnon go with us.” And the king said to him, “Why should he go with you?”
But Absalom kept urging him, until he let Amnon and all the king’s sons go with him.{h}

Then Absalom commanded his young men, saying, “Mark now, when Amnon’s heart is merry with wine, and I say to you, ‘Strike Amnon,’ then kill him. Do not fear. Have not I commanded you? Be courageous and be valiant.”
So the young men of Absalom did to Amnon as Absalom had commanded. Then all the king’s sons arose, and each man mounted his mule and fled.
While they were on the road, the tidings reached David: “Absalom has slain every one of the king’s sons, and there is not one of them left.”
Then the king arose and tore his garments and lay on the earth. And all his servants stood by with their clothes torn.

But Jonadab son of Shimeah, David’s brother, spoke up: “My lord should not think they have killed all the young princes; only Amnon is dead. This has been Absalom’s intention{i} ever since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.
Now therefore let not my lord the king take the thing to his heart, to think that all the king’s sons are dead; for Amnon alone is dead.”
But Absalom fled. And the young man who kept the watch lifted up his eyes and looked, and look, a great company was approaching on the road behind him{j} along the hillside.
Jonadab said to the king, “See, the king’s sons are coming. According to your servant’s word, so it has come to be.”
As soon as he had finished speaking, look, the king’s sons came and lifted up their voice and wept. And the king also and all his servants wept very bitterly.
But Absalom fled and went to Talmai the son of Ammihud,{k} king of Geshur. And David mourned for his son day after day.
So Absalom fled and went to Geshur, and was there three years.
King David’s spirit longed to go out{l} to Absalom, for he had been consoled about Amnon’s death.

notes.text: Tamar means “palm tree.”
Jonadab means “Yahweh is generous.” Shimeah is called Shammah in 1 Samuel 16:9 and Shimea in 1 Chronicles 2:13.
Hebrew nevalah, a word for gross folly or sacrilege; compare verse 13, “fools” (nevalim).
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Or “a robe reaching to the palms and soles” (uncertain); the same phrase describes Joseph’s robe (Genesis 37:3).
Hebrew “Aminon,” perhaps a diminutive or a scornful form.
The Septuagint adds a sentence saying that David did not grieve his son Amnon’s spirit, since he loved him as his firstborn (Brenton, modernized). 4QSam-a reportedly contains the same addition.
The Septuagint adds “and Absalom made a banquet like the banquet of the king” (Brenton, modernized).
Literally “mouth.”
So the Hebrew; the meaning is uncertain. The Septuagint adds “by the way of Horonaim” (Brenton, “by the way of Oronen,” modernized) and a report to the king.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “Ammihur.” The Septuagint adds “to the land of Chamaachad” (Brenton).

The Hebrew is uncertain, literally “and David the king was spent to go out to Absalom.” 4QSam-a reportedly reads “the spirit of the king.” The Septuagint reads “King David ceased to go out after Absalom” (Brenton).

verses.text: Now Joab the son of Zeruiah perceived that the king’s heart went out to Absalom.{a}

Joab sent someone to Tekoa{b} to bring a wise woman from that town, and he said to her, “Please act like a mourner: dress in mourning clothes, do not anoint yourself with oil, and be like a woman who has been grieving over the dead for a long time.
Then go to the king and speak these words to him.” And Joab told her what to say.
When the woman of Tekoa spoke{c} to the king, she fell on her face to the ground and did obeisance and said, “Save, O king!”
And the king said to her, “What troubles you?” She answered, “Truly I am a widow; my husband is dead.
And your handmaid had two sons, and they quarreled together in the field. There was no one to part them, and the one struck the other and killed him.

Now the whole clan has risen up against your servant. They say, ‘Surrender the one who struck down his brother, so that we may execute him for the life of the brother he killed.’ That would destroy the heir as well. They would put out the one ember I have left, and leave my husband without name or descendant on the earth.”
Then the king said to the woman, “Go to your house, and I will give orders concerning you.”
The woman of Tekoa said to the king, “Let the guilt be on me, my lord the king, and on my father’s house; the king and his throne are blameless.”
“Bring me anyone who speaks against you,” the king said, “and he will never touch you again.”

Then she said, “Please let the king remember Yahweh your God, that the avenger of blood may destroy no more, lest they destroy my son.” He said, “As Yahweh lives, not one hair of your son shall fall to the ground.”
Then the woman said, “Let your handmaid, I pray, speak a word to my lord the king.” He said, “Speak.”

And the woman said, “Why then have you devised such a thing against the people of God? For in speaking this word the king is as one who is guilty, in that the king does not bring home again his banished one.

For we must surely die, and are as water spilled on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. But God does not take away a life; he devises means so that the banished one is not cast out from him.
The reason I have come to say this to my lord the king is that the people have frightened me. So your servant thought, ‘Let me speak to the king; perhaps the king will grant his servant’s request.
For the king will listen, to rescue his handmaid out of the grasp of the man who seeks to cut off both me and my son together from God’s inheritance.’
Then your handmaid said, ‘Let the word of my lord the king be for rest,’ for as a messenger{d} of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and evil. And may Yahweh your God be with you!”
The king answered the woman, “Please do not conceal from me anything I ask you.” “Let my lord the king speak,” the woman said.

The king asked, “Is Joab’s hand behind all this?” The woman replied, “As you live, my lord the king, no one can turn right or left from anything my lord the king says. It was your servant Joab who instructed me, and he told me everything to say to your servant.
To change the face of the matter your servant Joab has done this thing. But my lord is wise, according to the wisdom of a messenger of God, to know all things that are in the earth.”
The king then said to Joab, “Very well, I will do this. Go and bring the young man Absalom back.”

Joab fell with his face to the ground, bowed low, and blessed the king. “Today your servant knows that I have found favor with you, my lord the king,” said Joab, “because the king has granted his servant’s request.”
So Joab arose and went to Geshur and brought Absalom to Jerusalem.
The king said, “Let him turn to his own house; but my face he shall not see.” So Absalom turned to his own house and did not see the king’s face.
Now in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty. From the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.

And when he polled his head (it was at every year’s end that he polled it, because it weighed heavily on him; therefore he polled it), he weighed the hair of his head, about five pounds{e} by the king’s weight.
There were born to Absalom three sons and one daughter, whose name was Tamar. She was a woman fair to look upon.{f}
Absalom lived in Jerusalem for two full years without once seeing the king’s face.
Then Absalom sent for Joab, to send him to the king, but he would not come to him. And he sent again a second time, but he would not come.
Therefore he said to his servants, “See, Joab’s field is next to mine, and he has barley there. Go and set it on fire.” So Absalom’s servants set the field on fire.{g}
Then Joab arose and came to Absalom at his house and said to him, “Why have your servants set my field on fire?”

Absalom told Joab, “I sent word to you, ‘Come here, so that I can send you to the king to ask, “Why did I come back from Geshur? I would be better off still there.”’ Now let me see the king’s face; and if there is any fault in me, let him have me killed.”
So Joab went to the king and told him. And he called for Absalom. He came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom.

notes.text: Or “was against Absalom.” The Hebrew can be read either way.
Tekoa was a town about 6 miles (10 kilometers) south of Bethlehem, later the home of the prophet Amos.
So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and other versions (reported). The traditional Hebrew text reads “said.”
Or “angel.” Likewise in verse 20.
Hebrew “200 shekels,” about 5 pounds (2.3 kilograms). The Septuagint likewise reads “two hundred shekels according to the royal shekel” (Brenton).

The Septuagint adds, “and she becomes the wife of Rehoboam son of Solomon, and she bears to him Abijah” (Brenton, modernized). Compare 1 Kings 15:2, where Abijah’s mother is called Maacah daughter of Abishalom.
The Septuagint, and 4QSam-a reportedly, add that Joab’s servants came to him with torn clothes and told him that Absalom’s servants had set the field on fire (Brenton, paraphrased).

verses.text: After this it came about that Absalom prepared for himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run before him.

Absalom would get up early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever any man with a lawsuit was on his way to the king for a decision, Absalom would call to him and ask, “What town are you from?” and when he answered, “Your servant is from one of the tribes of Israel,”
then Absalom would tell him, “Look, your matters are sound and just, but there is none from the king to give you a hearing.”
Absalom would say moreover, “O that I were made judge in the land! Then every man who had a dispute or a cause might come to me, and I would do him justice.”
And whenever a man came near to do him obeisance, he would stretch out his hand and seize him and kiss him.
In this manner Absalom did to all Israel who came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel.
At the end of forty years{a} Absalom said to the king, “Let me go, I pray, and pay my vow, which I have vowed to Yahweh, in Hebron.
While I was living at Geshur in Aram, your servant made a vow: ‘If Yahweh truly brings me back to Jerusalem, I will worship Yahweh.’”{b}
The king said to him, “Go in peace.” So he arose and went to Hebron.
Absalom sent secret messengers to all the tribes of Israel with this instruction: “As soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, say, ‘Absalom has become king in Hebron!’”
Now with Absalom went two hundred men out of Jerusalem, men who had been called, and they went in their simplicity and knew nothing at all.

And while he was offering the sacrifices, Absalom sent for Ahithophel{c} the Gilonite, David’s counselor, from his city, from Giloh. So the plot became mighty, for the people with Absalom grew ever more in number.
A messenger came to David, saying, “The hearts of the men of Israel have gone after Absalom.”

David told all his servants who were with him in Jerusalem, “Come, let us flee, or we will not escape from Absalom. Hurry and leave, in case he catches up with us quickly, brings disaster down on us, and puts the city to the sword.”
The king’s servants said to the king, “Look, your servants are ready to do whatever my lord the king shall choose.”
So the king went out, and all his household after him. And the king left ten concubines to keep the house.
And the king went out, and all the people after him, and they halted at the Far House.{d}

All his servants marched past at his side, together with all the Cherethites, all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men who had followed him from Gath, and they marched past the king.{e}
Then the king said to Ittai{f} the Gittite, “Why do you also go with us? Go back and stay with the king, for you are a foreigner and also an exile from your own place.

Yesterday was your coming, and today shall I make you go up and down with us, when I myself go wherever I can go? Return, and take back your brothers with you. Steadfast love and faithfulness be with you.”{g}
But Ittai answered the king, “As Yahweh lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether in death or in life, your servant will be there too.”
David said to Ittai, “Go on and cross over.” So Ittai of Gath went across, with all his men and all the children who were with him.
And the whole country was weeping with a great voice while all the people crossed over. And the king went over the brook Kidron,{h} and all the people passed on toward the way of the wilderness.

And look, Zadok also came, and all the Levites with him, carrying the ark of the covenant of God. And they set down the ark of God, and Abiathar went up,{i} until all the people had finished passing out of the city.
Then the king said to Zadok, “Carry back the ark of God into the city. If I find favor in the eyes of Yahweh, he will cause me to return and will show me it and the place where it dwells.
But if he says thus, ‘I have no delight in you,’ here I am; let him do to me as seems good to him.”
The king said also to Zadok the priest, “Are you a seer?{j} Return in peace to the city, you and your two sons with you, Ahimaaz your son and Jonathan son of Abiathar.
See, I will wait at the fords{k} of the wilderness until word comes from you to inform me.”
Zadok therefore and Abiathar returned the ark of God to Jerusalem, and there they stayed.

But David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up, with his head covered, and he went barefoot. And all the people who were with him covered every man his head, and they went up, weeping as they went.
David was told, “Ahithophel is one of the conspirators with Absalom.” So David prayed, “Yahweh, please turn Ahithophel’s advice into foolishness.”
When David came to the summit, where God was worshiped, look, Hushai{l} the Archite came to meet him with his coat torn and earth upon his head.
David said to him, “If you pass on with me, you will be a burden to me.

But if you return to the city and say to Absalom, ‘Your servant I will be, O king; I was your father’s servant formerly, and now I am yours,’ then you shall bring to nothing for me the advice of Ahithophel.
And are there not with you Zadok and Abiathar the priests? So it shall be that every word you hear out of the king’s house, you shall report it to Zadok and Abiathar the priests.
Look, they have there with them their two sons, Ahimaaz of Zadok and Jonathan of Abiathar; and by their hand you shall send me every word you hear.”
So Hushai, David’s friend, came into the city, just as Absalom was coming into Jerusalem.

notes.text: So the Hebrew and the Septuagint (Brenton, “after forty years”). Some Septuagint manuscripts, the Syriac, and Josephus reportedly read “four years,” which fits the context better (scholarly review).
Some Septuagint manuscripts reportedly add “in Hebron.”
Ahithophel means “brother of folly” (uncertain), perhaps a scribal alteration. Giloh was a town in the hill country of Judah. The Septuagint reads “the Theconite … from Gola” (Brenton).
Hebrew Beth-merhak, perhaps the last house of the city.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. The Septuagint has a longer text (Brenton).
Ittai means “with me” (uncertain).
So the Septuagint (reported). The Hebrew reads “take back your brothers with you, steadfast love and faithfulness.”
Kidron means “dark” or “turbid,” the valley east of Jerusalem.
Or “offered sacrifices.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew is uncertain; perhaps “Do you see?” The Septuagint reads “Behold, you shall return” (Brenton, modernized).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “the plains.”
Hushai means “quick” (uncertain).

verses.text: When David had gone a little past the summit, there was Ziba, Mephibosheth’s servant, waiting to meet him with a pair of saddled donkeys carrying two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred raisin cakes, a hundred bunches of summer fruit,{a} and a skin of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “What do you mean by these?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on, the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat, and the wine for any who grow faint in the wilderness.”
The king asked, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba answered the king, “He is staying in Jerusalem, because he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will give back to me my father’s kingdom.’”
Then the king said to Ziba, “Look, everything of Mephibosheth’s is yours.” And Ziba said, “I bow myself; may I find grace in your sight, my lord the king.”
As King David approached Bahurim,{b} a man from the family of Saul’s house came out from there, named Shimei{c} son of Gera. He cursed continually as he came out.
And he threw stones at David and at all the servants of King David, while all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.
And thus said Shimei as he cursed: “Go out, go out, man of bloodshed, base fellow!{d}

Yahweh has paid you back for all the bloodshed in the house of Saul, whose throne you took, and Yahweh has handed the kingdom over to your son Absalom. Look at you, ruined by your own wrongdoing, because you are a man of blood!”
Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over, I pray, and take off his head.”
But the king said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? If he is cursing because{e} Yahweh has said to him, ‘Curse David,’ who then shall say, ‘Why have you done so?’”
David said to Abishai and all his servants, “My own son, who came from my body, is trying to kill me; how much more this Benjamite! Leave him alone and let him curse, for Yahweh has told him to.
It may be that Yahweh will look on my affliction,{f} and that Yahweh will repay me with good for his cursing this day.”
So David and his men went along the road, and Shimei walked along the side of the hill alongside him, cursing as he walked, and he hurled stones over against him and threw dust.
The king and all the people with him arrived exhausted,{g} and there he rested.
Now Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, came to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this the kindness you show your companion? Why did you not go with your companion?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No, but whom Yahweh and this people and all the men of Israel have chosen, his will I be, and with him I will remain.
And again, whom should I serve? Should it not be his son? As I have served in your father’s presence, so will I be in your presence.”
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give your counsel. What shall we do?”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines, whom he has left to keep the house. All Israel will then hear that you have become a stench to your father, and the hands of all your supporters will grow strong.”
They spread for Absalom the tent upon the housetop, and Absalom went in unto his father’s concubines before the eyes of all Israel.
In those days the advice Ahithophel gave was regarded as if a man had consulted the word of God. That was how highly all of Ahithophel’s advice was valued by both David and Absalom.

notes.text: Probably cakes of summer fruit such as figs. The Septuagint reads “a hundred cakes of dates” (Brenton).
Bahurim means “young men,” a village east of Jerusalem near the Mount of Olives.
Shimei means “heard” (short for “Yahweh has heard”). Gera means “grain” (uncertain).
Hebrew “man of Belial.”
So the traditional reading (qere). The written text reads “If he curses, and if.”
So the Septuagint (Brenton, “look on my affliction”) and other ancient versions. The written Hebrew text reads “on my iniquity”; the traditional reading (qere) reads “on my eye,” perhaps “my tears.”
The Hebrew reads “arrived weary” without naming a place; perhaps a place name, ʿAyephim, has dropped out (compare 17:22, “the Jordan”).

verses.text: Moreover, Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Let me now choose twelve thousand men, and I will arise and pursue after David this night.
I will come upon him while he is weary and his hands are slack, and I will make him tremble, and all the people who are with him will flee. And I will strike the king alone.
And I will bring back all the people to you. The man whom you seek is as the return of all;{a} so all the people shall be at peace.”
And the saying pleased Absalom and all the elders of Israel.
Then Absalom said, “Call now Hushai the Archite also, and let us hear likewise what is in his mouth.”
When Hushai came to Absalom, Absalom spoke to him, saying, “Thus has Ahithophel spoken. Shall we do according to his word? If not, you speak.”
Then Hushai said to Absalom, “The counsel that Ahithophel has given this time is not good.”

Hushai added, “You know that your father and his men are warriors, and they are in a fierce mood, like a bear in the wild robbed of her cubs. Your father is also an experienced fighter, and he will not spend the night with the troops.

Look, he is hidden now in one of the pits or in some other place. And it will come to pass, when some of them fall at the first, that whoever hears it will say, ‘There has been a slaughter among the people who follow Absalom.’
Then even the valiant man, whose heart is as the heart of a lion, will utterly melt. For all Israel knows that your father is a mighty man, and those who are with him are valiant men.
Therefore I counsel that all Israel be gathered to you, from Dan even to Beersheba, as the sand that is by the sea for multitude, and that you go to battle in your own person.{b}

So shall we come upon him in some place where he shall be found, and we will light upon him as the dew falls on the ground. And of him and of all the men who are with him there shall not be left even one.
And if he gathers himself into a town, then all Israel will carry cords to that town, and we will haul it down into the ravine, until not even a pebble is found there.”

Absalom and all the men of Israel said, “The counsel of Hushai the Archite is better than the counsel of Ahithophel.” For Yahweh had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel, to the intent that Yahweh might bring evil upon Absalom.
Then Hushai said to Zadok and to Abiathar the priests, “Thus and thus did Ahithophel counsel Absalom and the elders of Israel, and thus and thus have I counseled.

Now therefore send quickly and tell David, saying, ‘Do not lodge this night at the fords of the wilderness, but by all means pass over, lest the king be swallowed up, and all the people who are with him.’”
Jonathan and Ahimaaz were staying beside En-rogel.{c} A servant girl used to go and bring them word, and they would go and tell King David, for they dared not be seen coming into the city.
But a lad saw them and told Absalom. So the two of them went away quickly and came to the house of a man in Bahurim, who had a well in his courtyard, and they went down into it.
The woman took a covering, spread it over the mouth of the well, and scattered grain over it, so that nothing was noticed.

When Absalom’s servants reached the woman at the house, they asked, “Where are Ahimaaz and Jonathan?” She said to them, “They went across the brook.”{d} They searched and found no one, so they returned to Jerusalem.
After they had left, the two climbed out of the well and went to inform King David. “Get up and cross the river quickly,” they told him, “for Ahithophel has advised this against you.”
Then David arose, and all the people who were with him, and they crossed the Jordan. By the morning light not one of them was lacking who had not crossed the Jordan.

When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey and arose and went home to his city. He set his house in order and hanged himself, and he died and was buried in the tomb of his father.
David arrived at Mahanaim, and Absalom crossed the Jordan with all the men of Israel.
Absalom set Amasa{e} over the army in place of Joab. Now Amasa was the son of a man named Ithra the Israelite,{f} who had gone in to Abigal the daughter of Nahash, sister of Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
And Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
When David came to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the sons of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lo-debar, and Barzillai{g} the Gileadite of Rogelim,
brought couches, bowls, and pottery vessels, also wheat and barley, meal and roasted grain, beans and lentils and roasted seeds,{h}
honey, curds, sheep, and cheese from cows, for David and his people to eat, for they said, “The people are hungry, tired, and thirsty out in the wilderness.”

notes.text: The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “as a bride returns to her husband: only you seek the life of one man” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “your face going into battle.” Some ancient versions reportedly read “in their midst.”
En-rogel means “spring of the fuller” (uncertain), just south of Jerusalem.
The meaning of the Hebrew word mikhal is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “gone a little way beyond the water” (Brenton).
Amasa means “burden” (uncertain).
So the Hebrew. First Chronicles 2:17 reads “Jether the Ishmaelite”; the Septuagint reads “Jether of Jezreel” (Brenton). Abigal is a form of Abigail.
Shobi perhaps means “captor” (uncertain). Barzillai means “man of iron.” Rogelim means “fullers.”
The Hebrew repeats “parched grain”; the Septuagint lacks the repetition (reported).

verses.text: Then David mustered the people who were with him and set over them captains of thousands and captains of hundreds.

And David sent out the people, a third under the hand of Joab, a third under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said to the people, “I will surely go out with you myself also.”

But the men said, “You must not go out. If we run away, nobody will worry about us, and if half of us are killed, nobody will worry either. But you are worth ten thousand of us.{a} So it is better that you send help to us from the city.”
“I will do whatever seems best to you,” the king told them. So the king stood beside the gate while all the troops marched out in units of hundreds and thousands.

And the king commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai, saying, “Deal gently for my sake with the young man, with Absalom.” And all the people heard when the king gave all the captains charge concerning Absalom.
So the people went out into the field against Israel, and the battle was in the forest of Ephraim.{b}
The people of Israel were beaten there before the servants of David, and there was a great slaughter there that day, twenty thousand men.
For the battle there was spread over the face of all the country, and the forest devoured more people that day than the sword devoured.

Absalom chanced upon the servants of David. Absalom was riding on his mule, and the mule passed beneath the tangled boughs of a great oak, and his head was caught fast in the oak, and he was hung up{c} between the heavens and the earth, and the mule beneath him passed on.
And a certain man saw it and told Joab, “Look, I saw Absalom hanging in an oak.”
Joab said to the man who told him, “And look, you saw him! Why then did you not strike him down there to the ground? It would have been on me to give you ten pieces of silver{d} and a belt.”

But the man replied to Joab, “Even if a thousand pieces of silver{e} were weighed into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the king’s son. We heard the king command you, Abishai, and Ittai, ‘Protect{f} the young man Absalom for me.’
Else, had I wrought treachery against his life{g}—and no matter is hid from the king—you yourself would have stood off from me.”
Then Joab said, “I may not linger thus with you.” And he took three darts{h} in his hand and thrust them into the heart of Absalom while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.
And ten young men who carried Joab’s armor surrounded Absalom and struck him and killed him.
Then Joab blew the horn, and the people returned from pursuing after Israel, for Joab held back the people.
They took Absalom and cast him into the great pit in the forest and raised over him a very great heap of stones. And all Israel fled, each man to his tent.

Now Absalom in his lifetime had taken and set up for himself the pillar which is in the King’s Valley, for he said, “I have no son to keep my name in remembrance.”{i} And he called the pillar after his own name, and it is called Absalom’s Monument to this day.
Then Ahimaaz the son of Zadok said, “Let me now run and carry the king tidings, how Yahweh has delivered him from the hand of his enemies.”
Joab said to him, “You shall not be the bearer of tidings this day; you shall bear tidings another day. But this day you shall bear no tidings, because the king’s son is dead.”
Then Joab said to the Cushite,{j} “Go, tell the king what you have seen.” The Cushite bowed himself to Joab and ran.
Ahimaaz son of Zadok again said to Joab, “Whatever happens, please let me run after the Cushite too.” Joab asked, “Why run, my son? You will get no reward for this news.”
“Whatever happens,” he said, “I want to run.” “Run, then,” Joab told him. So Ahimaaz ran by way of the plain{k} and passed the Cushite.
Now David was sitting between the two gates. The watchman went up to the roof over the gate by the wall, and he lifted up his eyes and looked, and there was a man running alone.
The watchman called out and told the king. The king said, “If he is alone, he has news to report.” The runner kept coming closer.
Then the watchman spotted another man running. He shouted to the gatekeeper, “Look, a man running alone again!” “That one is bringing news too,” said the king.
The watchman said, “I think the running of the foremost is like the running of Ahimaaz the son of Zadok.” And the king said, “He is a good man and comes with good tidings.”

Then Ahimaaz called out and said to the king, “All is well!”{l} And he bowed himself before the king with his face to the earth and said, “Blessed be Yahweh your God, who has delivered up the men who lifted up their hand against my lord the king!”
The king asked, “Is the young man Absalom safe?” Ahimaaz answered, “When Joab was sending off the king’s servant, and your servant as well, I saw a huge uproar, but I did not know what it was about.”
The king said, “Turn aside and stand here.” So he turned aside and stood still.
And look, the Cushite came, and the Cushite said, “Let my lord the king receive tidings! For Yahweh has judged for you today against the hand of all those rising against you.”

The king said to the Cushite, “Is it well with the young man Absalom?” The Cushite answered, “May the enemies of my lord the king, and all who rise up against you to do you harm, be as that young man is.”
The king was shaken. He went up to the room over the gateway and wept, and as he went he said, “My son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, Absalom, my son, my son!”{m}

notes.text: So two Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint (Brenton, “you are as ten thousand of us”), and the Vulgate (reported). The traditional Hebrew text reads “for now there are ten thousand like us.”
The forest of Ephraim was east of the Jordan, in Gilead, despite its name.
So the Septuagint and other ancient versions (reported). The Hebrew reads “he was set.”
Hebrew “ten of silver,” that is, ten shekels, about 4 ounces (115 grams).
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms). The Septuagint reads “a thousand shekels of silver” (Brenton).
So some Hebrew manuscripts and ancient versions (reported), reading “for me.” The traditional text reads “whoever you are.”
So the written Hebrew text (ketiv); the traditional reading (qere) is “my life.” Marked for scholarly review.
Hebrew “three sticks” or “three rods”; perhaps spears or javelins.
Compare 14:27, which says Absalom had three sons; perhaps they died young.
That is, a man from Cush, the region south of Egypt (Nubia).
That is, the plain of the Jordan Valley.
Hebrew “Peace!”
In Hebrew this verse is 19:1, and 19:1–43 in English is 19:2–44 in Hebrew. The Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering (Brenton).

verses.text: It was told Joab, “Look, the king weeps and mourns for Absalom.”{a}
So the victory that day was turned into mourning for all the people, for the people heard it said that day, “The king grieves for his son.”
And the people crept into the city on that day, the way a people creeps in that is put to shame by fleeing in the fight.
But the king covered his face, and the king cried with a loud voice, “O my son Absalom, O Absalom, my son, my son!”
Joab went into the house to the king and said, “Today you have humiliated all your servants, who today saved your life, and the lives of your sons and daughters, your wives, and your concubines,

in that you love your haters and hate your lovers. For you have made known today that princes and servants count for nothing with you. For this day I know that had Absalom lived and we all died this day, that would have been pleasing in your sight.

Now then, rise, go forth and speak kindly to your servants. For by Yahweh I swear, unless you go forth, not one man will stay the night with you; and that will be a greater evil to you than every evil that has come upon you from your youth until now.”

Then the king arose and sat in the gate. And they told all the people, saying, “Look, the king is sitting in the gate.” And all the people came before the king. Now Israel had fled, every man to his tent.

Throughout all the tribes of Israel the people were quarreling and saying, “The king delivered us from our enemies’ grip and rescued us from Philistine power, yet now he has had to flee the land because of Absalom.
But Absalom, whom we anointed over us, has died in the battle. So now, why are you silent about returning the king?”

King David sent word to the priests Zadok and Abiathar: “Tell the elders of Judah, ‘Why should you be the last to bring the king back to his palace, when what all Israel is saying has already reached the king at his house?{b}
You are my brothers; you are my bone and my flesh. Why then should you be the last to bring back the king?’
And say to Amasa, ‘Are you not my bone and my flesh? God do so to me and more also, if you shall not be commander of the army before me continually in the place of Joab.’”
So he swayed the heart of all the men of Judah as one man, and they sent word to the king, “Return, you and all your servants.”
So the king returned and came to the Jordan. And Judah came to Gilgal to go to meet the king, to bring the king over the Jordan.
Shimei the Benjamite, son of Gera, from Bahurim, hurried and went down with the men of Judah to meet King David.
And a thousand men of Benjamin were with him, and Ziba the servant of Saul’s house, and his fifteen sons and his twenty servants with him; and they rushed down to the Jordan before the king.
They crossed the ford{c} to carry the king’s household over and to do whatever he wished. As the king was about to cross the Jordan, Shimei son of Gera threw himself down before him

and he said to the king, “Let not my lord reckon iniquity to me, nor remember how your servant did perversely on the day my lord the king went out of Jerusalem, that the king should take it to his heart.
For your servant knows that I have sinned. Therefore, look, I have come today, the first of all the house of Joseph, to go down to meet my lord the king.”
But Abishai the son of Zeruiah answered and said, “Shall not Shimei be put to death for this, because he cursed the anointed of Yahweh?”

But David said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah, that you should this day become an adversary{d} to me? Shall any man be put to death in Israel today? Am I not sure that today I am king over Israel?”
The king told Shimei, “You will not die,” and gave him his oath.

Then Mephibosheth the son of Saul came down to meet the king. He had not dressed his feet nor trimmed his beard nor washed his clothes, from the day the king departed until the day he came again in peace.
And when he came from Jerusalem{e} to meet the king, the king asked him, “For what reason did you not go along with me, Mephibosheth?”
He answered, “My lord the king, my servant deceived me. Your servant had planned to say, ‘I will have a donkey saddled so that I can ride and go with the king,’ because your servant is lame.
And he has slandered your servant to my lord the king. But my lord the king is as an angel of God. Do therefore what is good in your eyes.

For all my father’s house were nothing but men of death before my lord the king, yet you placed your servant with those eating at your table. What right more have I, that I should still cry to the king?”
The king said to him, “Why say more about your affairs? I have decided: you and Ziba will divide the land.”
And Mephibosheth said to the king, “Indeed, let him take it all, since my lord the king has come safely to his own house.”
Now Barzillai the Gileadite had come down from Rogelim, and he crossed to the Jordan with the king, to send him on his way across the Jordan.
Barzillai was very old, eighty years of age. He had supplied the king with food during his stay at Mahanaim, for he was a man of great wealth.
And the king said to Barzillai, “Cross over with me, and I will provide for you with me in Jerusalem.”
But Barzillai said to the king, “How many are the days of the years of my life, that I should go up with the king to Jerusalem?

Today I am eighty years old. Can I distinguish good from bad? Can your servant savor what he eats or drinks? Can I still listen to the voices of male and female singers? So why should your servant add to my lord the king’s load?
Your servant would go just a little way over the Jordan with the king. And why should the king repay me with such a reward?

Let your servant go back, please, so that I can die in my hometown near the grave of my father and mother. But your servant Chimham{f} is here. Let him cross over with my lord the king, and do for him whatever you think good.”
And the king answered, “Chimham shall go over with me, and I will do to him whatever is good in your eyes; and all that you choose to ask of me, that will I do for you.”
Then all the people went over the Jordan, and the king went over. And the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him, and he returned to his own place.
When the king crossed over to Gilgal, Chimham crossed along with him. All the troops of Judah and half the troops of Israel brought the king across.

And look, all the men of Israel came to the king and said to the king, “Why have our brothers the men of Judah stolen you away and brought the king and his household over the Jordan, and all David’s men with him?”

The men of Judah answered the men of Israel, “It is because the king is a near relative of ours. Why does this make you angry? Have we eaten at the king’s expense? Have we taken any gift for ourselves?”

And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, “Ten parts in the king are ours, and in David too we have a greater claim than you.{g} Why then have you made light of us? Was not our word the first to bring back our king?” But the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

notes.text: English 19:1–43 is Hebrew 19:2–44; English 18:33 is Hebrew 19:1. The Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering.
The Hebrew places the clause “when the word of all Israel has come to the king” at the end of the verse; the Septuagint has it in the same place (Brenton).
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “And the ferry crossed over.”
Or “a satan,” that is, an accuser or opponent.
Or “came to Jerusalem.”
Chimham perhaps means “longing” (uncertain). He is apparently Barzillai’s son (compare 1 Kings 2:7).
The Septuagint reads “we are older than you” (Brenton); some scholars reportedly prefer “we are the firstborn rather than you.”

verses.text: A scoundrel{a} named Sheba{b} son of Bichri, a Benjamite, was there by chance. He blew a horn and proclaimed, “We have no part in David, no inheritance in Jesse’s son. Everyone to your tents, Israel!”
So all the men of Israel deserted David and followed Sheba son of Bichri, but the men of Judah stayed with their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

And David came to his house at Jerusalem. And the king took the ten women, his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and placed them in a house of ward and fed them, yet he went not in unto them. So they were shut up until the day of their death, living as in widowhood.
Then the king said to Amasa, “Summon me the men of Judah within three days, and you yourself be present here.”
Amasa went to summon Judah, but he took longer than the time he had been given.

And David said to Abishai, “Now Sheba the son of Bichri will do us more harm than Absalom. Take your lord’s servants and pursue after him, lest he find for himself fortified cities and escape out of our sight.”{c}
Joab’s men, the Cherethites, the Pelethites, and all the warriors marched out after Abishai. They left Jerusalem to pursue Sheba son of Bichri.

When they were at the great stone that is in Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them. Now Joab was girded in his soldier’s garment, and over it was a belt with a sword fastened upon his loins in its sheath; and as he went forward, it fell out.
And Joab said to Amasa, “Is it well with you, my brother?” And Joab took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him.

Amasa did not notice the sword in Joab’s hand, and Joab stabbed him in the stomach, spilling his intestines on the ground. He did not need to strike him again, and Amasa died. Then Joab and his brother Abishai went on in pursuit of Sheba son of Bichri.
And one of Joab’s young men stood over him and said, “He who delights in Joab, and he who is David’s, let him go after Joab.”

And Amasa lay wallowing in his blood in the middle of the highway. And when the man saw that all the people stood still, he carried Amasa out of the highway into the field and threw a garment over him, since he saw that everyone who came by him stood still.
When he was removed from the highway, every man went on after Joab to pursue Sheba the son of Bichri.
And Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel to Abel of Beth-maacah,{d} and all the Bichrites{e} gathered together and followed him in also.
They came and besieged him in Abel of Beth-maacah, building a siege ramp against the city that rose against its outer wall. Meanwhile all the troops with Joab were hammering the wall to make it fall.
Then a wise woman cried from the city, “Hear, hear! Say, I pray you, to Joab, ‘Come near here, that I may speak with you.’”
He came near to her, and the woman said, “Are you Joab?” He answered, “I am.” Then she said to him, “Hear the words of your maidservant.” And he said, “I am listening.”
Then she spoke, saying, “They used to speak in former times, saying, ‘Let them but ask counsel at Abel,’ and so they ended the matter.{f}
I am of those who are peaceable and faithful in Israel. You seek to destroy a city and a mother in Israel. Why will you swallow up the inheritance of Yahweh?”
Joab answered and said, “Far be it, far be it from me, that I should swallow up or destroy!

That is not the case. A man from the hill country of Ephraim, named Sheba son of Bichri, has raised his hand against the king, against David. Give him up alone, and I will leave the city.” “His head will be tossed to you over the wall,” the woman told Joab.

Then the woman went to all the people in her wisdom. And they cut off the head of Sheba the son of Bichri and threw it out to Joab. So he blew the horn, and they dispersed from the city, every man to his tents. And Joab returned to Jerusalem to the king.
Now Joab was over all the army of Israel, and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and over the Pelethites,
and Adoram{g} was in charge of the labor gangs, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud was recorder,
and Sheva was secretary, and Zadok and Abiathar were priests,
and also Ira the Jairite{h} was a priest to David.

notes.text: Hebrew “a man of belial.”
Sheba perhaps means “seven” or “oath” (uncertain). Bichri perhaps means “youthful” or “firstborn” (uncertain).
Hebrew uncertain; literally “and snatch away our eye.” The Septuagint reads “so he will blind our eyes” (Brenton, modernized).
Abel of Beth-maacah means “meadow of the house of Maacah,” in the far north.
So the Hebrew; some ancient versions reportedly read “Berites” or “all the choice men.”
The Septuagint reads a longer saying about asking in Abel and in Dan whether the faithful in Israel had failed (Brenton); some scholars reportedly think “and in Dan” is original.
Adoram is a shortened form of Adoniram (1 Kings 4:6), the reading of the Septuagint (Brenton).
The Septuagint reads “Iras the son of Iarin” (Brenton). Jairite refers to the clan of Jair, a Manassite (Numbers 32:41).

verses.text: Now there was a famine in the days of David for three years, year following year. And David sought the face of Yahweh. And Yahweh said, “It is on account of Saul and his house of blood, because he put the Gibeonites to death.”

The king summoned the Gibeonites and spoke to them. (The Gibeonites were not Israelites but a remnant of the Amorites; the Israelites had sworn an oath to them,{a} but in his zeal for Israel and Judah Saul had tried to wipe them out.)
And David said to the Gibeonites, “What shall I do for you? And with what shall I make atonement, that you may bless the inheritance of Yahweh?”

The Gibeonites answered him, “Between us and Saul or his house it is not a question of silver or gold, and we have no right to put anyone in Israel to death.” “Then what do you say?” he asked. “I will do it for you.”
They said to the king, “The man who consumed us and who planned against us, that we should be destroyed from remaining in any of the borders of Israel,
let seven men of his sons be given to us, and we will hang them up{b} to Yahweh at Gibeah of Saul, the chosen of Yahweh.”{c} And the king said, “I will give them.”
But the king spared Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan the son of Saul, because of the oath of Yahweh that was between them, between David and Jonathan the son of Saul.
The king took Rizpah daughter of Aiah’s two sons by Saul, Armoni and Mephibosheth, along with the five sons that Merab{d} daughter of Saul bore to Adriel son of Barzillai the Meholathite.

And he gave them into the hand of the Gibeonites, and they hanged them on the mountain before Yahweh, and the seven of them fell together. They were put to death in the days of harvest, in the first days, at the start of barley harvest.{e}

Then Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth and spread it for herself upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water poured upon them from the heavens. And she let neither the birds of the air settle on them by day nor the beasts of the field by night.
When it was told David what Rizpah the daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul, had done,

David went and collected the bones of Saul and his son Jonathan from the citizens of Jabesh-gilead, who had taken them secretly from the public square of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them the day they defeated Saul on Gilboa.
And he brought up from there the bones of Saul and the bones of Jonathan his son, and they gathered the bones of those who were hanged.

And they buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan his son in the land of Benjamin in Zela,{f} in the tomb of Kish his father. And they did all that the king commanded. And after that God was moved by entreaty for the land.
The Philistines had war again with Israel, and David went down, and his servants with him, and they fought against the Philistines. And David grew weary.
And Ishbi-benob,{g} who was one of the descendants of the giants,{h} whose spearhead weighed about 7½ pounds{i} of bronze, and who was girded with something new,{j} thought to kill David.

But Abishai son of Zeruiah helped him, and he struck down the Philistine and slew him. Then the men of David took an oath to him, saying, “Never again shall you go forth with us into battle, lest you put out the lamp of Israel.”
And it came to pass after this that there was once more war with the Philistines at Gob. At that time Sibbecai the Hushathite slew Saph, who was among the offspring of the giants.
And there was again a battle with the Philistines at Gob, and Elhanan son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, slew Goliath of Gath,{k} and the wood of his spear was like a weaver’s beam.
And there was again a battle at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, twenty-four in number; and he also was born to the giant.
And when he taunted Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimei,{l} David’s brother, struck him down.
These four were born to the giant in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

notes.text: See Joshua 9:3–27.
The exact form of execution is uncertain; perhaps “impale” or “expose.” So also verses 9 and 13.

So the Hebrew. Some scholars, following a reported reading, emend to “on the mountain of Yahweh” (compare verse 9). The Septuagint reads “in Gibeon of Saul, as chosen out for the Lord” (Brenton, modernized).

So two Hebrew manuscripts and some Septuagint manuscripts (reported); compare 1 Samuel 18:19. Most Hebrew manuscripts and Brenton’s Septuagint read “Michal.” Armoni perhaps means “of the palace” (uncertain).
Barley harvest fell in April–May.
Zela perhaps means “rib” or “side” (uncertain).
So the traditional reading (qere). Ishbi-benob perhaps means “his dwelling is in Nob” (uncertain).
Hebrew “the Rapha” or “the Raphah,” the ancestor of a race of giants (Deuteronomy 2:11); so also verses 18, 20, and 22.
Hebrew “three hundred shekels,” about 7½ pounds (3.4 kilograms). The Septuagint also reads “three hundred shekels of brass” (Brenton).
Hebrew “girded with a new [thing]”; the noun is missing. The Septuagint reads “girded with a club” (Brenton).

First Chronicles 20:5 says that Elhanan son of Jair killed Lahmi, brother of Goliath the Gittite. Compare 1 Samuel 17, where David kills Goliath. “Oregim” means “weavers” and may have been copied from the end of the verse. Marked for scholarly review.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “Shimei”; elsewhere he is called Shimeah (13:3) or Shammah (1 Samuel 16:9).

verses.text: And David spoke to Yahweh the words of this song on the day when Yahweh delivered him from the hand of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.{a}
He said: “Yahweh is my crag and my stronghold and my deliverer,
my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield and the horn{b} of my salvation, my high retreat and my place of flight, my savior; from violence you save me.
I call upon Yahweh, who is to be praised, and from my enemies I am saved.
“For the breakers of death encircled me; the torrents of worthlessness{c} terrified me;
the cords of Sheol{d} surrounded me; the snares of death came to meet me.
When I was hemmed in, I cried out to Yahweh; unto my God I cried. Out of his temple my voice was heard by him; my cry for help reached his ears.
“Then the earth heaved and rocked; the bases of the heavens quivered and tottered, for his anger burned.
Smoke rose from his nostrils, and consuming fire from his mouth; burning coals blazed out of him.
He bowed the heavens and came down, and thick darkness was under his feet.
He rode upon a cherub and flew; he was seen{e} upon the wings of the wind.
He made darkness around him his shelters, a gathering of waters, thick clouds of the skies.
From the brightness before him coals of fire were kindled.
Yahweh thundered from the heavens, and the Most High gave forth his voice.
He sent out arrows and scattered them, lightning, and routed them.
Then the channels of the sea appeared; the foundations of the world were laid bare at the rebuke of Yahweh, at the blast of the breath of his nostrils.
“He sent from on high; he took me; he drew me out of many waters.
He delivered me from my strong enemy, from those who hated me, for they were too strong for me.
They came upon me in the day of my calamity, but Yahweh was my support.
He led me forth into a wide space; he set me free, for he took pleasure in me.
“Yahweh dealt with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he repaid me.
For I have kept the ways of Yahweh, and have not done wickedly against my God.
For all his rulings were in front of me, and his decrees I did not put away from me.
I was blameless in his sight, and I guarded myself from wrongdoing.
And Yahweh has repaid me according to my righteousness, according to my cleanness before his eyes.
“To the faithful one you are faithful; to the mighty man of integrity you deal with integrity;
to the cleansed one you deal cleanly, but to the twisted one you deal shrewdly.
And the afflicted people you save, but your eyes are upon the haughty, to bring them low.
For you are my lamp, O Yahweh, and Yahweh lights up my darkness.
For with you I rush upon a raiding band; with my God I spring over a rampart.
As for God, his way is perfect; Yahweh’s word is proven true; he is a shield for all who shelter in him.
“For who is God, besides Yahweh? And who is a rock, besides our God?
This God is my strong fortress,{f} and he sets the blameless free in his way.{g}
He makes my feet like the feet of does, and sets me upon my high places.
He teaches my hands to make war, and my arms bend a bronze bow.
You have given me the shield of your salvation, and your answering{h} has made me great.
You widened my stride beneath me, and my ankles did not slip.
I chased my foes and wiped them out; I turned not back till I had made an end of them.
I consumed them; I shattered them, so that they did not rise; they fell beneath my feet.
You dressed me with strength for the battle; you made my attackers sink beneath me.
You gave me the necks of my foes; my haters—I put an end to them.
They looked, but there was none to save; they cried to Yahweh, but he did not answer them.
I beat them fine as the dust of the earth; I crushed them and stamped them like the mire of the streets.
“You delivered me from the strivings of my people;{i} you kept me as the head of the nations; a people whom I had not known served me.
Sons of a foreign land came cringing to me; at the hearing of the ear they hearkened to me.
Sons of a foreign land faded away and came quaking{j} from their strongholds.
“Yahweh lives! Blessed be my rock; exalted be God, the rock who saves me,
the God who gives me vengeance and brings down peoples under me,
who brings me out from my enemies. You lift me up above those who rise against me; you deliver me from the man of violence.
For this I will praise you, O Yahweh, among the nations, and sing praises to your name.
He gives great victories{k} to his king and shows faithful love to his anointed, to David and his descendants forever.”

notes.text: This song closely parallels Psalm 18, with many small differences in wording.
“Horn” is a figure for strength.
Hebrew “belial.”
Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.
So the Hebrew; Psalm 18:10 and some Hebrew manuscripts read “he soared” (reported). The Septuagint reads “was seen” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; Psalm 18:32 reads “who girds me with strength,” and the Septuagint here reads “who strengthens me with might” (Brenton).
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “and has made my way blameless” (compare Psalm 18:32), so the Septuagint (Brenton).
Or “your humility,” “your condescension”; Psalm 18:35 reads “your gentleness.” The Septuagint reads “your propitious dealing” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Psalm 18:43 read “the people” (reported).
So Psalm 18:45; the Hebrew here reads “girded themselves” (uncertain).
So the traditional reading (qere), as in Psalm 18:50 “great salvation”; the written text reads “He is a tower.” Marked for scholarly review.

verses.text: These are the last words of David: “David son of Jesse declares, the man raised up on high declares, the anointed of Jacob’s God, Israel’s sweet singer:{a}
“The Spirit of Yahweh speaks by me; his word is upon my tongue.
The God of Israel spoke; the Rock of Israel said to me: ‘One who rules people with justice, who rules in the fear of God,
is like the light of morning when the sun rises, a morning without clouds, when from brightness after rain the tender grass springs out of the earth.’
“Is my house not like this with God? He has made an everlasting covenant with me, arranged in every detail and made secure. Will he not make all my salvation and every desire grow?{b}
But worthless men{c} are all like thorns thrust away, for they cannot be taken with the hand;
and the man who touches them must be armed with iron and a spear’s wood, and they are utterly burned with fire in their place.”{d}

These are the names of the mighty men whom David had: Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite,{e} chief of the three.{f} He was Adino the Eznite; he wielded his spear{g} against eight hundred whom he slew at one time.
After him came Eleazar son of Dodo, son of Ahohi, among the three warriors with David when they challenged the Philistines assembled there for battle while the Israelites pulled back.
He rose up and struck the Philistines until his hand grew tired and stuck to his sword. Yahweh brought about a great victory that day, and the troops came back after him only to plunder the dead.
And next to him was Shammah son of Agee, a Hararite. When the Philistines had assembled at Lehi,{h} there was a portion of a field full of lentils there, and the people fled before the Philistines.
But he took his stand in the midst of the plot and defended it and struck the Philistines. And Yahweh wrought a great salvation.
And three of the thirty chief men went down and came at harvest time to David at the cave of Adullam, while a troop of Philistines was encamped in the valley of Rephaim.
David was then in the stronghold, and the garrison of the Philistines was then at Bethlehem.
David was longing for water and said, “If only someone would bring me a drink from the well by the gate at Bethlehem!”
So the three warriors broke through the Philistine camp, drew water from the well by the gate at Bethlehem, and carried it back to David. But he refused to drink any of it and poured it out to Yahweh

and said, “Far be it from me, O Yahweh, that I should do this. Is it not the blood of the men who went with their lives in their hands?” So he was not willing to drink it. These things the three mighty men did.
Now Abishai, the brother of Joab, the son of Zeruiah, was chief of the three.{i} And he wielded his spear against three hundred and slew them, and he had a name among the three.
Was he not the most honored of the three?{j} And he became their commander, but he did not attain to the three.

And Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was the son of a valiant man{k} of Kabzeel, great in deeds. He struck down the two sons of Ariel{l} of Moab. He also went down and struck a lion in the midst of a pit on a day of snow.
He also killed an Egyptian, an impressive man.{m} The Egyptian held a spear, but Benaiah went down against him with a club, wrenched the spear from his hand, and killed him with his own spear.
These things Benaiah the son of Jehoiada did, and he had a name among the three mighty men.
Among the thirty he was honored, yet to the three he did not come. And David appointed him over his bodyguard.{n}
Asahel the brother of Joab was one of the thirty; Elhanan the son of Dodo of Bethlehem,
Shammah of Harod, Elika of Harod,
Helez the Paltite, Ira the son of Ikkesh of Tekoa,
Abiezer of Anathoth, Mebunnai the Hushathite,
Zalmon the Ahohite, Maharai of Netophah,
Heleb son of Baanah from Netophah, and Ittai son of Ribai from Gibeah of the Benjamites,
Benaiah of Pirathon, Hiddai of the brooks of Gaash,
Abi-albon the Arbathite, Azmaveth of Bahurim,
Eliahba of Shaalbon, the sons of Jashen, Jonathan,{o}
Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,
Eliphelet son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maacathite; Eliam son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,
Hezro of Carmel, Paarai the Arbite,
Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite,
Zelek the Ammonite, and Naharai the Beerothite, the armor-bearer of Joab son of Zeruiah,
Ira the Ithrite, and also Gareb the Ithrite,
and Uriah the Hittite—thirty-seven in all.{p}

notes.text: Or “the favorite of the songs of Israel,” or “the delight of the Strong One of Israel” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “and beautiful are the psalms of Israel” (Brenton, modernized).
Or as a statement: “For he will cause to sprout all my salvation and all my desire.”
Hebrew “belial.”
Hebrew “in the sitting” (uncertain); perhaps “on the spot.”

Josheb-basshebeth means “one who sits in the seat” (uncertain). First Chronicles 11:11 reads “Jashobeam, a Hachmonite”; the Septuagint reads “Jebosthe the Chananite” (Brenton), which may reflect Ishbosheth or Ishbaal (compare 2:8). Marked for scholarly review.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “the captain” or “of the third ones.” Some Septuagint manuscripts reportedly read “of the three.”

So 1 Chronicles 11:11 and the Septuagint (Brenton, “he drew his sword against eight hundred”), in part. The Hebrew phrase “He was Adino the Eznite” is uncertain; Chronicles has instead “he wielded his spear,” and reads “three hundred.” Marked for scholarly review.
Or “at Lehi” (compare Judges 15:9); possibly “in a troop.” Lehi means “jawbone.”
So the Hebrew; two Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac reportedly read “of the thirty.”
Or “He was more honored than the three” (uncertain); compare 1 Chronicles 11:21.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text reads “a living man.”
Ariel perhaps means “lion of God” (uncertain); the Hebrew reads only “the two Ariel of Moab,” perhaps “two champions of Moab.” The Septuagint reads “the two sons of Ariel of Moab” (Brenton).
Hebrew “a man of appearance”; 1 Chronicles 11:23 reads “a man of great stature, five cubits tall” (about 7 feet 6 inches, 2.3 meters).
Hebrew “his bodyguard,” literally “those who listen”; perhaps a privy council.
Hebrew uncertain; 1 Chronicles 11:34 reads “the sons of Hashem the Gizonite, Jonathan son of Shagee.”
The list as it stands names fewer than thirty-seven; the total probably includes the leaders named in verses 8–23 and Joab (uncertain).

verses.text: Once more the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Israel, and he incited David against them, saying, “Go, number Israel and Judah.”{a}

So the king said to Joab, the commander of the army, who was with him, “Go now to and fro through all the tribes of Israel, from Dan to Beersheba, and muster the people, that I may know the number of the people.”

But Joab said to the king, “Now may Yahweh your God increase the people a hundredfold, however many they may be, and may the eyes of my lord the king behold it! But my lord the king, why does he take pleasure in this matter?”
Nevertheless the word of the king was stronger than Joab and the army’s commanders. So Joab went out, with the army’s commanders, from before the king to count the people of Israel.
They crossed the Jordan and encamped at Aroer, on the right side of the city that is in the middle of the valley of Gad, and on toward Jazer.
Then they came to Gilead and to the land of Tahtim-hodshi,{b} and they came to Dan-jaan and around to Sidon,
They came to the fortress of Tyre and all the cities of the Hivites and Canaanites, and they finished at the Negeb of Judah at Beersheba.
So when they had gone through all the land, they came to Jerusalem at the end of nine months and twenty days.
And Joab handed over the total of the census of the people to the king: Israel had eight hundred thousand men of valor drawing the sword, and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand men.{c}

But David’s heart struck him after he had numbered the people. And David said to Yahweh, “I have sinned greatly in what I have done. But now, O Yahweh, take away, I pray, the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”
And when David arose in the morning, the word of Yahweh came to the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying,
“Go and tell David, ‘This is what Yahweh says: I am offering you three options. Pick one of them, and that is what I will do to you.’”

So Gad came to David and told him and said to him, “Shall seven{d} years of famine come to you in your land? Or will you flee three months before your foes while they pursue you? Or shall there be three days’ pestilence in your land? Now consider and see what answer I shall return to him who sent me.”
David answered Gad, “I am very distressed. Let us fall into Yahweh’s hand, for his compassion is great, but do not let me fall into the hand of man.”
So Yahweh sent a plague upon Israel from morning to the time appointed.{e} And from Dan even to Beersheba seventy thousand men of the people died.

And when the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem to destroy it, Yahweh relented from the evil and said to the destroying angel among the people, “Enough! Now let your hand drop.” And the angel of Yahweh was by the threshing floor of Araunah{f} the Jebusite.

Then David spoke to Yahweh when he saw the angel who was striking the people, and said, “Look, it is I who have sinned, and I who have done wrong. But these sheep, what have they done? Let your hand turn, I beg you, upon me and upon the house of my father.”
And Gad came that day to David and said to him, “Go up, raise an altar to Yahweh on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite.”
So David went up according to the word of Gad, as Yahweh had commanded.
Araunah looked and saw the king and his servants approaching. He went out and bowed down before the king with his face to the ground.
And Araunah said, “Why has my lord the king come to his servant?” David said, “To buy the threshing floor from you, to build an altar to Yahweh, that the plague may be held back from the people.”
Araunah said to David, “May my lord the king take it and offer whatever he sees fit. Here are the oxen for the burnt offering, and the threshing sledges and the oxen’s yokes for fuel.
The whole of it, O king, Araunah hands over to the king.”{g} Araunah said also to the king, “May Yahweh your God take pleasure in you.”

But the king said to Araunah, “No, but I will surely buy it from you for a price. I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God that cost me nothing.” So David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for about 20 ounces of silver.{h}
David built an altar to Yahweh there and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings.{i} Then Yahweh answered the prayer for the land, and the plague on Israel was halted.

notes.text: Compare 1 Chronicles 21:1, where Satan incites David.

Hebrew uncertain; Tahtim-hodshi may mean “lowlands of Hodshi.” The Septuagint reads “the land of Thabason, which is Adasai” (Brenton); some scholars emend to “Kadesh in the land of the Hittites” (reported).
First Chronicles 21:5 gives 1,100,000 for Israel and 470,000 for Judah. The Septuagint here agrees with the Hebrew (Brenton).
So the Hebrew. The Septuagint (Brenton) and 1 Chronicles 21:12 read “three.”
Or “until the time of the assembly” (uncertain). The Septuagint reads “from morning till noon” and adds that it was the days of wheat harvest (Brenton).

So the traditional reading (qere); the written Hebrew text spells the name in several ways in this chapter (reported). First Chronicles 21:15 calls him Ornan; the Septuagint reads “Orna” (Brenton). The name may be Hurrian, perhaps a title meaning “lord” (uncertain).
Or “All this, O king, does Araunah give to the king.” Some interpreters reportedly read “Araunah the king,” suggesting a former Jebusite ruler.
Hebrew “fifty shekels,” about 20 ounces (575 grams). First Chronicles 21:25 reads “six hundred shekels of gold” (about 15 pounds, 6.9 kilograms) for the whole site.
The Septuagint adds “and Solomon made an addition to the altar afterwards, for it was little at first” (Brenton, modernized).

books.name: 1 Kings
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex. The Septuagint (Old Greek) of 1 Kings differs from the Hebrew in many places. It adds two collections of extra material about Solomon after 2:35 and 2:46 (numbered 2:35a–o and 2:46a–l, the so-called “miscellanies”), as well as a long alternative account of Jeroboam’s rise after 12:24 (12:24a–z) and other shorter additions. It also puts much of chapters 6–7 in a different order, and it reverses chapters 20 and 21, so that the story of Naboth’s vineyard comes before the wars with Ben-hadad. The major differences are given in the footnotes. Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (4:21–5:18 English = 5:1–32 Hebrew), this is noted. The regnal years and the synchronisms between the kings of Judah and Israel are translated as they stand, without harmonization. Measurements are given in modern US units, and calendar dates with their modern-month equivalents, with the originals and metric figures in the footnotes. Personal and place names whose meaning is known or likely have a note at their first appearance.

verses.text: Now King David was old and well along in years. They would cover him with clothes, yet he could not keep warm.
His servants told him, “Let a young woman, a virgin, be found for my lord the king to wait on him and look after him. She can lie in your arms, and my lord the king will stay warm.”
So they looked for a lovely girl in every part of the land of Israel, and they found Abishag{a} the Shunammite{b} and brought her to the king.
The young woman was very beautiful. She took care of the king and served him, but the king did not know her.
Then Adonijah{c} son of Haggith{d} began to exalt himself, saying, “I am the one who will be king.” He got chariots and horsemen ready for himself, with fifty men running ahead of him.
His father had never once rebuked him by saying, “Why have you done this?” He was also very handsome, and he was born next after Absalom.{e}
He conferred with Joab the son of Zeruiah and with Abiathar{f} the priest, and they followed Adonijah and helped him.
But Zadok{g} the priest, Benaiah{h} the son of Jehoiada, Nathan{i} the prophet, Shimei, Rei,{j} and David’s mighty men were not with Adonijah.
Adonijah slaughtered sheep, cattle, and fattened calves at the Stone of Zoheleth,{k} next to En-rogel.{l} He invited all his brothers, the king’s sons, and all the men of Judah who served the king,
Nathan the prophet, though, and Benaiah and the mighty men and his brother Solomon{m} he left uninvited.
Nathan then spoke to Bathsheba{n} the mother of Solomon. “Have you not heard,” he said, “that Haggith’s son Adonijah reigns now, and David our lord knows nothing of it?
So come now, let me counsel you, so that you can rescue your own life and your son Solomon’s life.
Go in at once to King David and say to him, ‘My lord the king, did you not promise your servant, “Your son Solomon is to reign after me and sit on my throne”? Then why is Adonijah king?’
While you are still speaking there with the king, I will come in after you and confirm your words.”
So Bathsheba went in to the king in his room. The king was very old, and Abishag the Shunammite was attending the king.
Bathsheba bowed down and paid homage to the king, and the king said, “What do you wish?”
She said to him, “My lord, you yourself swore to your servant by Yahweh your God, ‘Surely Solomon your son will reign after me, and he will sit on my throne.’
But now, look, Adonijah has become king, and you, my lord the king, do not know it.
