From there he went on to Mount Carmel, and from there he returned to Samaria.

notes.text: Gilgal means “circle (of stones).” This Gilgal was probably in the hills north of Bethel, not the one near Jericho.
Bethel means “house of God.”
Hebrew “from over your head,” that is, from being your master; likewise in verse 5.
Hebrew “a mouth of two,” the firstborn son’s portion of an inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17).
Hebrew ’aph-hu’, “he too.” Some take it with the preceding question: “Where is Yahweh, the God of Elijah, indeed?”
Hebrew “from opposite.”
Or “is barren.” Hebrew meshakkalet, “bereaving”; likewise in verse 21.
Hebrew ne‘arim qetannim, “small youths”; the term can cover boys or young men.

verses.text: In the eighteenth year of Jehoshaphat king of Judah, Jehoram son of Ahab began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twelve years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, though not to the extent of his father and mother, for he took away the sacred stone of Baal that his father had set up.
Yet he clung to the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he had made Israel sin; he did not turn from them.
Mesha{a} king of Moab raised sheep, and as tribute he delivered to Israel’s king a hundred thousand lambs and the wool of a hundred thousand rams.
But when Ahab died, the king of Moab rebelled against the king of Israel.
So King Jehoram marched out of Samaria at that time and mustered all Israel.

He also sent this message to Jehoshaphat, Judah’s king: “Moab’s king has revolted against me. Will you join me in war against Moab?” He replied, “I will go up. You and I are one; my people are yours, and my horses are yours.”
He asked, “By which road shall we go up?” Jehoram answered, “By the road through the wilderness of Edom.”{b}
So the king of Israel marched out together with the kings of Judah and Edom. After a winding route of seven days, the army and the animals that followed them had run out of water.
“What a disaster!” exclaimed the king of Israel. “Yahweh has summoned these three kings only to deliver us into Moab’s power.”

Jehoshaphat asked, “Isn’t there a prophet of Yahweh here, so that we can seek Yahweh’s will through him?” An officer of the king of Israel replied, “Elisha son of Shaphat is here; he used to pour water over Elijah’s hands.”
Jehoshaphat said, “The word of Yahweh is with him.” So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom went down to him.

Elisha said to the king of Israel, “What have I to do with you?{c} Take yourself to the prophets of your father and your mother.” The king of Israel replied, “Do not say that. Yahweh has called these three kings together to hand them over to Moab.”
Elisha said, “As Yahweh of hosts lives, before whom I stand, if I did not have regard for Jehoshaphat king of Judah, I would not look at you or even see you.
But now bring me a musician.” And while the musician played, the hand of Yahweh came on him.
He said, “This is what Yahweh says: ‘Make this wadi full of pools.’{d}
For this is what Yahweh says: ‘You will see no wind and you will see no rain, yet this wadi will be filled with water, and you will drink, you, your cattle, and your animals.’
This is only a small thing in the sight of Yahweh; he will also give Moab into your hand.
You will attack every walled city and every important town. You will cut down every good tree, block every spring, and spoil every good field by covering it with stones.”
The next morning, when the grain offering{e} was due, water suddenly flowed in from the direction of Edom, and the ground was covered with it.
When all the Moabites heard that the kings had come up to fight against them, everyone old enough to put on armor, and older, was called out and stationed at the border.
They got up at dawn, and as the sun rose over the water, the Moabites looked across and saw the water red like blood.
“Blood!” they said. “The kings must have turned their swords on each other{f} and slaughtered one another. On to the spoil, Moab!”
But when they came to the camp of Israel, the Israelites rose up and struck the Moabites, who fled before them. They pressed on into the land, striking Moab as they went.{g}

They tore down the towns. On every good field each man threw a stone, until it was covered. They stopped up every spring and felled every good tree, until only the stones of Kir-hareseth{h} were left, and the slingers surrounded it and attacked it.
When Moab’s king saw that the fighting was too strong for him, he took seven hundred men who could wield the sword and tried to break through toward the king of Edom, but they failed.

Then he took his firstborn son, who was to reign after him, and sacrificed him as a burnt offering on the wall. Great wrath{i} fell on Israel, and they pulled back from him and went home to their land.

notes.text: Mesha may mean “salvation.” His own inscription, the Moabite Stone (about 840 B.C.), tells of Moab’s revolt from the Moabite side.
Edom, “red,” the land south of the Dead Sea.
Hebrew “What to me and to you?”
Or “trenches.” Hebrew “Make this wadi pits, pits.”
Hebrew “at the going up of the minchah,” the morning grain offering.
Hebrew uncertain; perhaps “have surely put each other to the sword.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; some ancient witnesses read “they went on striking.”
Kir-hareseth means “city of potsherds” or “wall of potsherds.” It is probably modern Kerak in Jordan.
Hebrew qetseph, “wrath, fury.” Whose wrath is not stated.

verses.text: Now the wife of one of the sons of the prophets cried out to Elisha, “Your servant my husband is dead, and you know that your servant feared Yahweh. But now the creditor has come to take my two children as his slaves.”
Elisha said to her, “What can I do for you? Tell me, what do you have in the house?” She said, “Your servant has nothing in the house except a flask of oil.”
He said, “Go around to your neighbors and borrow jars from all of them, empty ones, as many as you can.
Then go in and shut the door behind you and your sons, and pour oil into all these vessels. As each is filled, set it aside.”
So she went from him and closed the door on herself and her sons. While they brought her the jars, she went on pouring.
When all the jars were full, she said to her son, “Bring me one more jar.” But he replied, “There isn’t another one.” And then the oil ceased.
She came and told the man of God, and he said, “Go, sell the oil and pay your debt, and you and your sons can live on the rest.”
One day Elisha passed through Shunem,{a} where a wealthy woman lived, and she urged him to eat a meal. After that, every time he came by, he stopped there for a meal.
She told her husband, “I can tell that the man who regularly comes by here is a holy man of God.
Let us make a small walled room on the roof and put a bed, a table, a chair, and a lamp there for him. Then whenever he comes to us, he can stay there.”
One day he arrived, went up into the roof room, and lay down to rest.
He said to his servant Gehazi,{b} “Call this Shunammite woman.” He called her, and she stood before him.

He said to Gehazi, “Say to her, ‘You have gone to all this trouble for us. What may we do in return? Would you like a word put in for you with the king or the army commander?’ ” She answered, “I live among my own people.”
He said, “What then can be done for her?” Gehazi answered, “Well, she has no son, and her husband is old.”
He said, “Call her.” When he had called her, she stood in the doorway.
He said, “At this season, when the time comes round, you will be holding a son in your arms.” She said, “No, my lord, man of God, do not deceive your servant.”
But the woman conceived and bore a son at that season, when the time came round, as Elisha had told her.
The child grew, and one day he went out to join his father, who was with the reapers.
He said to his father, “My head, my head!” His father said to a servant, “Carry him to his mother.”
The servant lifted him and carried him to his mother. The boy sat on her lap until noon, and then he died.
She went up, laid him on the bed of the man of God, shut the door on him, and went out.
Then she called to her husband and said, “Please send me one of the servants and one of the donkeys, so that I may hurry to the man of God and come back.”
He said, “Why are you going to him today? It is neither new moon nor Sabbath.” She said, “It is all right.”{c}
Then she saddled the donkey and said to her servant, “Drive on, go! Do not slow down for me unless I tell you.”
So she set out and came to the man of God at Mount Carmel. When the man of God caught sight of her far off, he told Gehazi his servant, “There is the Shunammite woman.
Run now to meet her and ask her, ‘Are you well? Is your husband well? Is the child well?’ ” She answered, “All is well.”

When she reached the man of God at the mountain, she grabbed his feet. Gehazi stepped forward to shove her aside, but the man of God said, “Let her be. She is deeply troubled, and Yahweh has kept the reason from me; he hasn’t told me.”
Then she said, “Was it I who asked my lord for a son? Did I not tell you, ‘Do not raise my hopes’?”{d}
He said to Gehazi, “Tuck up your robe, take my staff, and be off. Greet no one you meet, and answer no one who greets you. Lay my staff on the boy’s face.”
But the child’s mother said, “As Yahweh lives, and as you yourself live, I will not leave you.” So Elisha rose and went with her.
Gehazi hurried on ahead and set the staff on the boy’s face, yet there was no voice and no sign of life. So he turned back to meet Elisha and reported, “The child did not wake up.”
When Elisha came into the house, there was the boy, dead, lying on his bed.
He went in and closed the door behind the two of them, and he prayed to Yahweh.
Then he got up on the bed and lay on the child, putting his mouth on his mouth, his eyes on his eyes, and his hands on his hands. As he stretched himself over him, the child’s body grew warm.
Then he got down and paced to and fro in the house once, then went up and stretched himself over him again. Seven times the boy sneezed, and then his eyes opened.
Elisha summoned Gehazi and said, “Call the Shunammite.” Gehazi called her, and when she entered the room, Elisha said, “Pick up your son.”
She entered, dropped at his feet, and bowed low to the ground. Then she took her son and left the room.

Elisha returned to Gilgal while there was a famine in the land. As the sons of the prophets were sitting before him, he said to his servant, “Put the large pot on and boil a stew for the sons of the prophets.”

One man went out to the countryside to gather herbs. There he found a wild vine and filled the fold of his cloak with its wild gourds.{e} He returned and sliced them into the stew pot, though no one knew what they were.
They served it to the men, but when the men began to eat the stew, they shouted, “Man of God, death is in the pot!” They were unable to eat it.
Elisha said, “Bring me flour,” and he tossed it into the pot. “Pour it out for the people to eat,” he said. And there was nothing harmful in the pot.
A man from Baal-shalishah{f} arrived with twenty barley loaves made from the first harvest, and some fresh grain in his bag,{g} for the man of God. Elisha said, “Hand it out for the people to eat.”

His servant objected, “How am I supposed to serve this to a hundred men?” Elisha repeated, “Hand it out for the people to eat. This is what Yahweh says: ‘They will eat, and there will be food left over.’ ”
So he set it before them, and they ate and had some left over, according to the word of Yahweh.

notes.text: Shunem, in the Jezreel Valley, near modern Sulam; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
Gehazi may mean “valley of vision.”
Hebrew “Shalom,” “peace”; likewise in verse 26.
Or “Do not deceive me.”
Probably colocynth, a bitter and purgative wild gourd.
Baal-shalishah means “lord of Shalishah,” “the third.” It lay near Gilgal in the hill country of Ephraim.
The meaning of the Hebrew word translated “in his sack” is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “and cakes of figs.”

verses.text: Naaman,{a} commander of the army of the king of Aram, was a great man in his master’s eyes and highly regarded, because through him Yahweh had given victory to Aram. He was a mighty warrior, but he had a serious skin disease.{b}
Now the Arameans had gone out on raids and had taken captive a young girl from the land of Israel, and she served Naaman’s wife.
She told her mistress, “I wish my master could go to the prophet in Samaria. He would rid him of his skin disease.”
So Naaman went in and told his lord, “This is what the girl from the land of Israel said.”
The king of Aram said, “Go now, and I will send a letter to the king of Israel.” So he went, taking with him about 750 pounds of silver,{c} about 150 pounds of gold,{d} and ten sets of clothing.
The letter he delivered to Israel’s king said: “Along with this letter comes my servant Naaman, whom I have sent so that you may rid him of his skin disease.”

When the king of Israel read the letter, he tore his clothes and said, “Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man sends me word to cure someone of his skin disease? Just look and see how he is seeking a quarrel with me.”

When Elisha the man of God heard that the king of Israel had ripped his garments, he sent this message to the king: “Why did you rip your garments? Send the man to me, and he will find out that there is a prophet in Israel.”
So Naaman arrived with his horses and chariots and stopped at the entrance of Elisha’s house.
Elisha sent a messenger out to him, saying, “Go, bathe in the Jordan seven times. Then your flesh will become sound again, and you will be clean.”
But Naaman grew angry and went away, saying, “I thought that surely he would come out to me, stand and call on the name of Yahweh his God, wave his hand over the place, and cure the disease.
Are not Abana{e} and Pharpar, the rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? Could I not wash in them and be clean?” So he turned and went off in a rage.

But his servants came near and said to him, “My father,{f} had the prophet ordered some hard thing, you would have done it, would you not? All the more, then, since all he says is, ‘Bathe and be clean.’ ”
So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, just as the man of God had instructed. His skin became like the skin of a child, and he was clean.

He went back to the man of God with all his attendants and stood in front of him. “Now I know,” he said, “that nowhere on earth is there a God besides the God of Israel. So I ask you to take a present{g} from your servant.”
But he said, “As Yahweh lives, before whom I stand, I will accept nothing.” Naaman urged him to accept, but he refused.
Then Naaman said, “If not, then please let your servant have two mule-loads of soil,{h} because from now on your servant will offer burnt offering or sacrifice to no other god but Yahweh.

But in this one matter may Yahweh pardon your servant: when my master enters Rimmon’s{i} temple to worship there and leans on my arm, and so I bow down in Rimmon’s temple too, when I bow there, may Yahweh pardon your servant in this matter.”
He said to him, “Go in peace.” And when Naaman had gone some distance{j} from him,

Gehazi, the servant of Elisha the man of God, said to himself, “See how my master has spared Naaman, this Aramean, by not taking what he offered. As Yahweh lives, I will run after him and get something from him.”
So Gehazi hurried after Naaman. Naaman, seeing a man running to catch up with him, stepped down from his chariot to meet him. “Is all well?” he asked.

“All is well,” Gehazi said. “My master sent me with this message: ‘Two young men from the company of the prophets have just arrived from the hill country of Ephraim. Please provide them with about 75 pounds of silver{k} and two changes of clothes.’ ”
Naaman said, “Please, take about 150 pounds.”{l} He urged him and tied up the silver in two bags with two sets of clothing, and handed them to two of his own servants to carry ahead of Gehazi.
When he came to the hill,{m} he took them from their hands and stored them in the house. Then he sent the men away, and they left.
Gehazi went in and stood beside his master. Elisha asked him, “Where have you come from, Gehazi?” “Your servant didn’t go anywhere,” he answered.

But Elisha said, “Was my spirit not there with you when the man stepped down from his chariot to greet you? Is this the time to take money, or clothes, or olive groves and vineyards, sheep and cattle, male and female servants?
So Naaman’s skin disease will stick to you and to your descendants for all time.” Gehazi left Elisha’s presence with a skin disease as white as snow.

notes.text: Naaman means “pleasant.”
Hebrew metsora‘, from tsara‘at, traditionally translated “leprosy.” The term covered a range of skin conditions, not only Hansen’s disease; likewise throughout this chapter.
Hebrew “ten talents of silver.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so about 340 kilograms.
Hebrew “six thousand of gold,” probably shekels. A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so about 69 kilograms. The Septuagint reads “six thousand pieces of gold.”
So the Ketiv; the Qere reads Amanah. Abana may mean “stony”; Pharpar may mean “swift.”
Hebrew ’avi, “my father,” a respectful address. Some interpreters read the consonants instead as “if.”
Hebrew berakah, “blessing.”
Hebrew “a load of a pair of mules.” The Septuagint adds “of the red earth.”
Rimmon, the Aramean storm god Hadad-Rimmon. The name may mean “thunderer”; Hebrew rimmon also means “pomegranate.”
Hebrew “a stretch of land,” an uncertain distance.
Hebrew “a talent of silver.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms).
Hebrew “two talents,” about 68 kilograms.
Hebrew ‘ophel, “the hill” or “the citadel.” The Septuagint reads “a secret place.”

verses.text: The sons of the prophets said to Elisha, “Look, the place where we live under your charge is too cramped for us.
Let us go to the Jordan, where each of us can cut a beam, and let us build ourselves a place to live there.” He said, “Go.”
Then one of them said, “Please be willing to come with your servants.” He answered, “I will come.”
So he went with them. When they reached the Jordan, they began cutting down trees.
But as one of them was felling a beam, the iron ax head fell into the water. He cried out, “Oh no, my master! It was borrowed!”{a}
The man of God asked, “Where did it fall?” When he showed him the place, Elisha cut off a stick, threw it in there, and made the iron float.
“Lift it out,” he said. And the man stretched out his hand and grabbed it.
Once, while Aram’s king was fighting against Israel, he conferred with his officers and said, “My camp will be at such and such a place.”
But the man of God sent this warning to Israel’s king: “Be careful to avoid that place, because the Arameans are going down there.”
The king of Israel sent men to the place the man of God had told him about. Time and again he warned the king, so that he was on guard there, more than once or twice.
The mind of the king of Aram was greatly troubled over this. He summoned his officers and demanded, “Which one of us is siding with Israel’s king? Tell me!”
One of his servants said, “None of us, my lord the king. Elisha, the prophet in Israel, reports to Israel’s king even what you say in your bedroom.”
He said, “Go and find out where he is, so that I may send and seize him.” He was told, “He is in Dothan.”{b}
So he sent horses and chariots there and a strong force. They came by night and surrounded the city.
Early the next morning, the servant of the man of God got up and went outside. An army with horses and chariots encircled the city. “Oh, my master, what are we going to do?” the servant asked.
He answered, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.”
Then Elisha prayed, “Yahweh, please open his eyes so that he may see.” Yahweh opened the servant’s eyes, and he saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire all around Elisha.
When the Arameans came down against him, Elisha prayed to Yahweh, “Strike this people with blindness.”{c} And he struck them with blindness, as Elisha had asked.
Elisha told them, “You are on the wrong road, and this is the wrong city. Come after me, and I will lead you to the man you seek.” And he took them to Samaria.
As soon as they had entered Samaria, Elisha said, “Yahweh, open the eyes of these men so that they may see.” Yahweh opened their eyes, and they saw that they were inside Samaria.
When the king of Israel saw them, he said to Elisha, “Shall I strike them down, my father? Shall I strike them down?”

“Don’t kill them,” he answered. “Would you kill men you did not capture with your own sword and bow?{d} Set food and water in front of them so that they can eat and drink, and send them back to their master.”
So he prepared a great feast for them. When they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away, and they went to their master. And the Aramean raiding bands stopped coming into the land of Israel.
Some time later Ben-hadad king of Aram mustered his whole army, went up, and laid siege to Samaria.
There was a great famine in Samaria. The siege went on until a donkey’s head sold for about 2 pounds of silver,{e} and half a pint of dove’s dung{f} for about 2 ounces of silver.{g}
As the king of Israel was walking along the city wall, a woman called out to him, “Save me, my lord the king!”
He said, “If Yahweh will not save you, where am I to get help for you? From the threshing floor? From the winepress?”
The king then said to her, “What is troubling you?” She replied, “This woman told me, ‘Give up your son so that we can eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.’
So we cooked my son and ate him. On the following day I told her, ‘Now it is your son’s turn to be eaten,’ but she has hidden him away.”
When the king heard the woman’s words, he tore his clothes. As he was walking along the wall, the people looked, and there was sackcloth underneath, on his body.
He said, “May God deal with me, and even more severely, if Elisha son of Shaphat’s head remains on his shoulders by the end of today.”

Elisha was seated at home with the elders around him. The king had dispatched a man, but before the messenger got there, Elisha said to the elders, “Do you realize that this murderer’s son has sent a man to cut off my head? When the messenger arrives, close the door and press against it to keep him out. The sound of his master’s steps is right behind him, isn’t it?”
While he was still speaking with them, the messenger{h} came down to him and said, “This disaster is from Yahweh. Why should I wait for Yahweh any longer?”

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “and it was hidden.”
Dothan means “two wells.”
Hebrew sanwerim, a rare word for a dazzling or confusing blindness (compare Genesis 19:11).
Or “Do you strike down those you have taken captive with your sword and bow?” that is, even prisoners of war are not killed.
Hebrew “eighty of silver,” probably shekels. A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so about 920 grams. The Septuagint reads “fifty pieces of silver.”
Hebrew “a quarter of a kab.” A kab was about 1 1/4 quarts (1.2 liters), so about a third of a liter. “Dove’s dung” may be a popular name for a cheap food such as carob pods or wild bulbs.
Hebrew “five of silver,” probably shekels, about 57 grams.
So the Hebrew and the Septuagint. Many interpreters read “the king,” since the king seems to be speaking (compare 7:2, 17).

verses.text: Elisha said, “Hear the word of Yahweh. This is what Yahweh says: ‘About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, 7 quarts of fine flour will sell for about 2/5 ounce of silver, and 14 quarts of barley for 2/5 ounce.’ ”{a}

The officer on whose arm the king leaned answered the man of God, “Even if Yahweh were to make windows in the sky, could this happen?” Elisha said, “Your own eyes will see it happen, but not a bite of it will you eat.”
At the entrance to the city gate sat four men who had a serious skin disease.{b} They said to each other, “Why should we stay here until we die?

If we decide to go into the city, we will die there, since famine is inside. If we keep sitting here, we die all the same. So come, let us desert to the Aramean camp. Should they let us live, we live; and if they kill us, we will only die.”
So at dusk they got up and headed for the Arameans’ camp. Yet when they reached its outskirts, not a soul was to be found.

For the Lord{c} had caused the Aramean army to hear what sounded like chariots, horses, and a vast army, and they told each other, “Israel’s king must have paid the Hittite kings and the Egyptian{d} kings to come against us!”
So at dusk they had run off, leaving behind tents, horses, and donkeys, the whole camp as it stood, to save their lives.

When these men with the disease reached the far side of the camp, they went into a tent, ate and drank, and took silver, gold, and garments from it, and went off to hide them. Then they returned and entered a second tent, took things from it, and hid those as well.

But then they said to each other, “What we are doing is wrong. Today is a day for good news, yet we are saying nothing. If we wait until dawn, we will be punished. Let’s go now and report to the royal household.”

So they went and shouted up to the city’s gatekeepers, “We have been to the Arameans’ camp, and there was no one there, not a human voice, only the horses tied up, the donkeys tied up, and the tents just as they were.”
The gatekeepers called out, and the news was told inside the king’s household.

The king rose in the night and told his officers, “I will explain to you what the Arameans are up to. They are aware that we are starving. So they have slipped out of their camp and are hiding out in the fields, expecting that we will come out of the city, so that they can capture us alive and get inside.”

One of his servants replied, “Have men take five of the horses that are left in the city. They will be no worse off than the whole crowd of Israelites remaining here, or the whole crowd of Israelites who have already died.{e} Let’s send them out and find out.”
So they took two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army, saying, “Go and see.”
They followed them as far as the Jordan, and the whole road was littered with clothing and equipment that the Arameans had thrown away in their haste. The messengers returned and told the king.
Then the people went out and plundered the Aramean camp. So 7 quarts of fine flour sold for 2/5 ounce of silver, and 14 quarts of barley for 2/5 ounce, according to the word of Yahweh.

Now the king had appointed the officer whose arm he leaned on to take charge of the gate. The crowd trampled him there in the gate, and he died, as the man of God had said when the king came down to him.
For when the man of God had said to the king, “About this time tomorrow, at the gate of Samaria, 14 quarts of barley will sell for 2/5 ounce of silver, and 7 quarts of fine flour for 2/5 ounce,”

the officer had answered the man of God, “Even if Yahweh opened windows in heaven, could this come about?” And Elisha had told him, “Your own eyes will see it happen, but not a bite of it will you eat.”
That is just what happened to him: the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died.

notes.text: Hebrew “a seah of fine flour for a shekel, and two seahs of barley for a shekel.” A seah was about 7 quarts (about 7.3 liters); a shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams). These were low prices compared with 6:25. Likewise in verses 16 and 18.
Hebrew metsora‘im; see the note at 5:1.
Hebrew Adonai.
Some interpreters take Hebrew Mitsrayim, “Egypt,” as Musri, a land in Anatolia, alongside the Hittite kings of northern Syria.
The Hebrew of this verse is repetitive and somewhat uncertain.

verses.text: Elisha had told the woman whose son he had brought back to life, “Leave with your family and live as a foreigner wherever you are able, because Yahweh has summoned a famine that will come upon the land for seven years.”
The woman did what the man of God said. She left with her family and lived as a foreigner in Philistine territory for seven years.
When the seven years had passed, the woman came back from Philistine territory and went to make a plea to the king to get back her house and land.
The king was talking with Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, saying, “Tell me all the great things Elisha has done.”

Just as Gehazi was recounting to the king how Elisha had brought a dead boy back to life, in came the woman whose son it was, appealing to the king for her house and her field. Gehazi said, “My lord the king, this is the woman, and this is her son whom Elisha restored to life.”

When the king questioned the woman, she told him. So the king assigned an official to her, saying, “Give back everything that was hers, along with all the produce of the field from the day she left the land until now.”
Elisha came to Damascus at a time when Ben-hadad, Aram’s king, was sick. When the king heard, “The man of God has arrived here,”
he said to Hazael, “Take a gift with you and go to meet the man of God. Inquire of Yahweh through him, asking, ‘Will I recover from this illness?’ ”

Hazael went to meet Elisha with a present: forty camels loaded with every sort of fine product from Damascus. He arrived, stood in front of Elisha, and said, “Your son Ben-hadad king of Aram has sent me to ask, ‘Will I recover from this sickness?’ ”
Elisha said to him, “Go and say to him,{a} ‘You will certainly recover.’ But Yahweh has shown me that he will certainly die.”
He fixed his gaze on him and stared until he was ashamed.{b} Then the man of God wept.

“Why are you crying, my lord?” asked Hazael. Elisha replied, “Because I know what evil you will do to the people of Israel: you will burn down their strongholds, put their young men to the sword, smash their children, and cut open their pregnant women.”
Hazael said, “What is your servant, a mere dog, that he should do this great thing?” Elisha answered, “Yahweh has shown me that you will be king over Aram.”
Hazael left Elisha and went back to his master, who asked, “What did Elisha say to you?” “He said that you would surely get well,” Hazael replied.
But the next day Hazael took the bed cover, dipped it in water, and spread it over the king’s face, and he died. And Hazael reigned in his place.
In the fifth year of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah,{c} Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat king of Judah began to reign.
He was thirty-two years old when he became king, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.
He followed the path of Israel’s kings, just as Ahab’s house did, since he had married a daughter of Ahab. He did evil in Yahweh’s sight.
Yet Yahweh was unwilling to destroy Judah, for the sake of his servant David, because he had pledged to keep a lamp burning for David and his descendants forever.
In his days Edom revolted against Judah’s rule and set up a king of their own.
Then Joram crossed over to Zair{d} with all his chariots. He rose by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and his chariot commanders, but his army fled to their tents.{e}
So Edom has been in revolt against Judah’s rule to this day. At that same time Libnah{f} revolted too.
The rest of the acts of Joram and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
Joram slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in David’s city, and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
In the twelfth year of Joram son of Ahab king of Israel, Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah began to reign.
Ahaziah was twenty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah,{g} a granddaughter{h} of Omri king of Israel.
He walked in the way of Ahab’s house and did evil in Yahweh’s sight just as Ahab’s house had, for he was related by marriage to Ahab’s house.
He went with Joram son of Ahab to war against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead, and the Arameans wounded Joram.

King Joram went back to Jezreel to be healed of the wounds that the Arameans had given him at Ramah,{i} when he fought against Hazael king of Aram. And Ahaziah son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Joram son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was wounded.

notes.text: So the Qere and many ancient witnesses; the Ketiv reads “Go and say, ‘You will certainly not recover.’ ”
The subject is unclear. Either Elisha stared at Hazael until Hazael was embarrassed, or the reverse.
The clause “while Jehoshaphat was king of Judah” is in both the Hebrew and the Septuagint, but many interpreters regard it as an accidental repetition from the end of the verse.
The location of Zair is unknown; 2 Chronicles 21:9 lacks it.
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult, and the outcome of the battle is unclear.
Libnah means “whiteness.” It was a town in the Shephelah of Judah.
Athaliah may mean “Yahweh is exalted.”
Hebrew “daughter,” here in the sense of female descendant; she was Ahab’s daughter (verse 18).
That is, Ramoth-gilead.

verses.text: Elisha the prophet summoned one of the sons of the prophets and said to him, “Tuck up your robe, take this flask of oil in your hand, and go to Ramoth-gilead.
When you arrive, look for Jehu{a} son of Jehoshaphat son of Nimshi. Go in, get him to rise from among his companions, and take him into an inner room.
Then take the flask of oil, pour it on his head, and say, ‘This is what Yahweh says: I anoint you king over Israel.’ Then open the door and run. Do not linger.”
So the young man, the young prophet, went to Ramoth-gilead.
When he arrived, the army commanders were sitting together. He said, “I have a message for you, commander.” Jehu asked, “For which of us?” He replied, “For you, commander.”

Jehu rose and entered the house. The young prophet poured the oil over his head and declared, “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: I am anointing you king over the people of Yahweh, over Israel.
You are to wipe out the dynasty of your master Ahab. Thus I will exact vengeance from Jezebel for the blood of my servants the prophets, and for the blood of every servant of Yahweh.
The whole house of Ahab will perish. I will cut off from Ahab every male in Israel, whether bond or free.{b}
I will make the house of Ahab like the house of Jeroboam son of Nebat and like the house of Baasha son of Ahijah.
As for Jezebel, dogs will eat her in the plot of ground at Jezreel, with nobody to give her burial.” Then he opened the door and ran.
When Jehu came out to his master’s officers, one asked him, “Is all well? What did this madman want with you?” He answered, “You know the man and the way he talks.”
They said, “That is not true! Tell us.” So he said, “He told me such and such, and said, ‘This is what Yahweh says: I anoint you king over Israel.’ ”
At once every one of them took off his cloak and laid it beneath Jehu on the bare steps.{c} Then they sounded the ram’s horn and shouted, “Jehu has become king!”
That is how Jehu son of Jehoshaphat, the son of Nimshi, plotted against Joram. (Joram and all Israel had been defending Ramoth-gilead against King Hazael of Aram,

but King Joram had gone back to Jezreel to be healed of the wounds the Arameans had given him when he fought with Hazael king of Aram. Jehu said, “If this is your wish, let no one slip out of the city to go and report this in Jezreel.”
Then Jehu got into his chariot and drove to Jezreel, where Joram was recovering and where Ahaziah king of Judah had gone to visit him.
The lookout standing on the tower in Jezreel saw Jehu’s troops coming and said, “I see a body of troops.” Joram ordered, “Send a horseman out to them to ask, ‘Is it peace?’ ”

So the horseman rode out to meet him and said, “The king asks, ‘Is it peace?’ ” Jehu said, “What do you care about peace? Fall in behind me.” The lookout reported, “The messenger reached them, but he is not coming back.”
Then he sent a second horseman, who came to them and said, “The king asks, ‘Is it peace?’ ” Jehu answered, “What do you care about peace? Fall in behind me.”
Again the lookout reported, “He got to them, and he is not returning either. The chariot driver must be Jehu son of Nimshi, for he drives like a madman.”

Joram said, “Harness the chariot.” When it was harnessed, Joram king of Israel and Ahaziah king of Judah set out, each riding his own chariot, to confront Jehu, and they encountered him by the land that had belonged to Naboth the Jezreelite.
When Joram saw Jehu, he asked, “Is it peace, Jehu?” He answered, “How can there be peace, as long as the whoring and the many sorceries of your mother Jezebel go on?”
Joram turned his chariot around{d} and fled, shouting to Ahaziah, “Treachery, Ahaziah!”
Jehu drew his bow with all his strength and hit Joram between the shoulders. The arrow came out through his heart, and he slumped down in his chariot.

Jehu said to Bidkar his officer, “Pick him up and throw him onto the plot of the field of Naboth the Jezreelite. Remember how you and I were riding side by side behind Ahab his father, when Yahweh uttered this oracle{e} against him:

‘I swear that yesterday I saw the blood of Naboth and of his sons, declares Yahweh, and I will pay you back in this same field, declares Yahweh.’ So pick him up now and throw him into that field, in keeping with Yahweh’s word.”

When Ahaziah king of Judah saw this, he fled toward Beth-haggan.{f} Jehu chased him and shouted, “Shoot him too!” And they shot him{g} in his chariot on the ascent to Gur, near Ibleam. He fled to Megiddo and died there.
His servants carried him in a chariot to Jerusalem and buried him in his tomb with his ancestors in the city of David.
In the eleventh{h} year of Joram son of Ahab, Ahaziah had become king over Judah.
Jehu then entered Jezreel, and Jezebel heard about it. She put makeup on her eyes,{i} arranged her hair, and gazed down from a window.
As Jehu entered the gateway, she called out, “Have you come in peace, Zimri, you murderer of your master?”{j}
He looked up at the window and said, “Who is on my side? Who?” Two or three eunuchs looked down at him.
He said, “Throw her down!” So they threw her down, and some of her blood spattered on the wall and on the horses, and they trampled her.
Then he went in, ate and drank, and said, “See to this cursed woman and bury her, for she was a king’s daughter.”
But when they went to bury her, they found nothing of her except the skull, the feet, and the palms of her hands.

They came back and told him, and he said, “This is the word of Yahweh, which he spoke through his servant Elijah the Tishbite: ‘In the plot of ground at Jezreel the dogs will eat the flesh of Jezebel.
Jezebel’s corpse will be like dung on the open field in the plot of ground at Jezreel, so that nobody can say, This is Jezebel.’ ”

notes.text: Jehu means “Yahweh is he.”
Hebrew ‘atsur we‘azub; see the note at 1 Kings 14:10.
The meaning of Hebrew gerem ha-ma‘aloth, here “bare steps,” is uncertain; it may mean “the top of the stairs.”
Hebrew “turned his hands,” that is, wheeled the chariot by its reins.
Hebrew massa’, “burden,” a word used for a solemn prophetic pronouncement.
Beth-haggan means “house of the garden”; it is probably modern Jenin.
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Hebrew lacks “And they shot him.”
8:25 gives the twelfth year; the two figures reflect different ways of reckoning and are left unchanged.
Hebrew “set her eyes in antimony,” a dark eye paint.
Zimri killed his master King Elah and reigned only seven days (1 Kings 16:9–18).

verses.text: Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. So Jehu wrote letters and sent them to Samaria, to the officials of Jezreel,{a} to the elders, and to the guardians of Ahab’s sons. He wrote:
“You have your master’s sons with you, along with chariots, horses, a walled city, and weapons. So as soon as this letter arrives,
pick the best and most capable of your master’s sons, set him on his father’s throne, and fight for your master’s house.”
But they were terrified and said, “Two kings could not hold out against him. How can we?”

So the palace administrator, the governor of the city, the elders, and the guardians sent word to Jehu: “We are at your service and will carry out every order you give. We are not going to crown anyone. Act as you think best.”

Then he wrote them a second letter: “If you side with me and will heed my voice, bring the heads of your master’s sons with you and report to me in Jezreel about this time tomorrow.” The seventy princes were then being raised by the city’s prominent men.
When the letter reached them, they took the king’s sons and slaughtered all seventy. They put their heads in baskets and sent them to him at Jezreel.
When the messenger came and told him, “They have brought the heads of the king’s sons,” he said, “Pile them in two heaps at the entrance of the gate until morning.”
In the morning he went out, took his stand, and declared to all the people, “You are blameless. I am the one who plotted against my master and slew him. Yet who killed every one of these?
Know, then, that not one word of Yahweh that Yahweh spoke against the house of Ahab will fall to the ground. Yahweh has done what he said through his servant Elijah.”
So Jehu struck down all who were left of the house of Ahab in Jezreel, all his leading men, his close friends, and his priests, until he left him no survivor.
Then he set out and went toward Samaria. On the way, at Beth-eked of the Shepherds,{b}

Jehu came upon relatives of Ahaziah king of Judah. He asked, “Who are you?” They answered, “We are Ahaziah’s relatives, and we have come down to greet the sons of the king and the sons of the queen mother.”
He said, “Take them alive.” So they took them alive and slaughtered them at the pit of Beth-eked, forty-two men. He did not spare any of them.

Leaving there, he met Jehonadab{c} son of Rechab coming toward him. Jehu greeted him and asked, “Are you as faithful to me as I am to you?” “I am,” Jehonadab answered. Jehu said,{d} “Then give me your hand.” Jehonadab gave him his hand, and Jehu pulled him up beside him in the chariot.
He said, “Come with me and see my zeal for Yahweh.” So he had him ride in his chariot.
On reaching Samaria, he killed everyone left in Samaria from Ahab’s family until none remained, just as Yahweh had told Elijah.
Then Jehu gathered all the people and said to them, “Ahab served Baal a little. Jehu will serve him a great deal.

Now call together for me all of Baal’s prophets, all who serve him, and all his priests. Not one may be absent, because I am holding a great sacrifice for Baal. Whoever fails to come will die.” But Jehu was acting deceitfully in order to destroy those who served Baal.
Jehu ordered, “Proclaim a sacred assembly for Baal.” So they proclaimed it.
Jehu sent word throughout Israel, and all the worshipers of Baal came. Not one stayed away. They entered the house of Baal, and it was filled from one end to the other.
He said to the keeper of the wardrobe, “Bring out robes for all the worshipers of Baal.” So he brought out robes for them.

Then Jehu and Jehonadab son of Rechab entered Baal’s temple. Jehu told those who served Baal, “Look carefully and make sure that no servant of Yahweh is here with you; only those who serve Baal may be here.”

Then they went in to offer sacrifices and burnt offerings. Jehu had posted eighty men outside and said, “If any of the men I am handing over to you escapes, the one who lets him go will pay with his own life.”

As soon as Jehu had completed the burnt offering, he told the guards and officers, “Go in and strike them down; do not let anyone escape.” They killed them with swords and threw out the bodies. Then the guards and officers went into the inner room{e} of Baal’s temple.
They brought out the sacred pillar{f} of the house of Baal and burned it.
They demolished the pillar of Baal, tore down the house of Baal, and made it a latrine,{g} as it is to this day.
Thus Jehu wiped out Baal from Israel.
Even so, Jehu did not abandon the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had led Israel into: the golden calves in Bethel and Dan.

Yahweh said to Jehu, “Because you have done well in carrying out what is right in my eyes, and have done to the house of Ahab all that was in my heart, your sons will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.”
But Jehu was not careful to walk in the law of Yahweh the God of Israel wholeheartedly. He never departed from Jeroboam’s sins, by which he made Israel sin.
In those days Yahweh started to trim away pieces of Israel.{h} Hazael struck them down in every border region of Israel,
from the Jordan eastward, all the land of Gilead, the Gadites, the Reubenites, and the Manassites, from Aroer by the Wadi Arnon, that is, Gilead and Bashan.
The other events of Jehu’s reign, everything he did and all his power, are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.
Jehu slept with his ancestors, and they buried him in Samaria. And Jehoahaz{i} his son reigned in his place.
The time Jehu reigned over Israel in Samaria was twenty-eight years.

notes.text: So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “Samaria.” Some interpreters suggest “the city.”
Or “the shearing house of the shepherds.” Beth-eked means “house of binding,” perhaps a place where sheep were tied for shearing.
Jehonadab means “Yahweh is generous.” His descendants, the Rechabites, appear in Jeremiah 35.
So the Septuagint; the Hebrew lacks “Jehu said.”
Hebrew “to the city of the house of Baal”; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps the inner sanctuary or citadel.
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Hebrew reads the plural “pillars” with “burned it.”
So the Qere; the Ketiv reads a cruder word for the same thing.
Or “to reduce Israel.”
Jehoahaz means “Yahweh has grasped.”

verses.text: When Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she set out to destroy the entire royal family.

But Jehosheba,{a} King Joram’s daughter and Ahaziah’s sister, took Joash{b} son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were about to be murdered. She hid the boy and his nurse in a sleeping room, out of Athaliah’s reach, and he was not killed.
He stayed hidden with her in Yahweh’s house for six years, while Athaliah ruled over the land.

In the seventh year Jehoiada{c} sent for the commanders of hundreds of the Carites{d} and of the guards and brought them to him in Yahweh’s house. He made a covenant with them, put them under oath in Yahweh’s house, and showed them the king’s son.
He gave them these orders: “Here is your assignment. The third of you who begin your duty on the Sabbath will keep watch over the king’s palace,
one third will be at the Sur Gate, and one third at the gate behind the guards. You will keep watch over the palace in turns.{e}
Your two divisions that go off duty on the Sabbath will keep watch over Yahweh’s house for the king.
Surround the king, each of you with weapons in hand. Whoever comes near your lines must die. Keep close to the king as he comes and goes.”
The commanders of hundreds did just as Jehoiada the priest ordered. Each took his men, both the Sabbath shift coming on and the Sabbath shift going off, and came to Jehoiada the priest.
The priest handed out to the commanders the spears and small shields that once belonged to King David and were kept in Yahweh’s house.
The guards took up their positions, each with weapon in hand, from the south side of the house to the north side, around the altar and the house, all around the king.
Jehoiada led out the king’s son, set the crown on his head, and gave him the covenant document.{f} They proclaimed him king and anointed him; then they clapped and shouted, “May the king live!”
Athaliah heard the noise made by the guards and the crowd and went to the people gathered at Yahweh’s house.

She looked, and there was the king, stationed beside the pillar according to custom, the officers and trumpeters at his side, while the people of the land were all celebrating and sounding trumpets. Athaliah ripped her garments and shouted, “Conspiracy! Conspiracy!”

Jehoiada the priest commanded the officers in charge of the troops: “Bring her out through the ranks, and put to the sword anyone who follows her.” The priest had said, “She must not be killed at Yahweh’s house.”
So they seized her, and she went by the way of the horses’ entrance to the king’s palace, and there she was put to death.
Jehoiada made a covenant between Yahweh and the king and the people, that they would be Yahweh’s people, and also between the king and the people.

Then all the people of the land went to the house of Baal and tore it down. They smashed its altars and its images to pieces, and before the altars they slew Mattan, Baal’s priest. Then the priest stationed watchmen over Yahweh’s house.

He then led the commanders of hundreds, the Carites, the guards, and the whole populace, and together they escorted the king down from Yahweh’s house and went through the guards’ gate to the palace. He took his seat on the royal throne.
All the people of the land celebrated, and the city was calm, because Athaliah had been put to death by the sword at the royal palace.
Jehoash{g} was seven years old when he became king.

notes.text: Jehosheba means “Yahweh is an oath.” 2 Chronicles 22:11 calls her Jehoshabeath and adds that she was the wife of Jehoiada the priest.
Joash, also spelled Jehoash (verse 21), means “Yahweh has given.”
Jehoiada means “Yahweh knows.”
The Carites were probably foreign mercenaries, perhaps from Caria in Asia Minor.
The meaning of the Hebrew word rendered “in turns” is uncertain.
Hebrew ‘eduth, probably a written copy of the covenant law (compare Deuteronomy 17:18).
Hebrew 12:1. The Hebrew numbers in chapter 12 run one higher than the English.

verses.text: In the seventh year of Jehu, Jehoash began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah{a} of Beersheba.
Jehoash did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes all his days, because Jehoiada the priest instructed him.{b}
Yet the high places were not removed; the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places.

Jehoash said to the priests, “All the money brought as holy gifts into Yahweh’s house, the money each person is assessed,{c} the money from the valuation of persons, and all the money anyone freely chooses to bring into Yahweh’s house,
let the priests receive, each from his own contact,{d} and let them repair the house wherever damage is found.”
But by the twenty-third year of King Jehoash the priests still had not repaired the damage to the house.

So King Jehoash summoned Jehoiada the priest and the other priests and said to them, “Why are you not repairing the damage to the house? From now on take no more money from your contacts, but hand it over for repairing the house.”
The priests agreed not to collect any more money from the people, and also not to be the ones to repair the damage to the temple.

Then Jehoiada the priest took a chest, bored a hole in its lid, and set it beside the altar, on the right as one enters Yahweh’s house. The priests who guarded the threshold put into it all the money brought into Yahweh’s house.
Each time the chest was seen to be well filled with money, the royal secretary came up with the high priest, and they bagged{e} and counted the money found in Yahweh’s house.
They gave the money that had been weighed out to the men doing the work, those appointed over Yahweh’s house. These paid it out to the carpenters and builders who worked on Yahweh’s house,
to the masons and stonecutters, and for buying timber and dressed stone to repair the damage to Yahweh’s house, and for everything else spent on repairing the house.
But no silver basins, snuffers, sprinkling bowls, trumpets, or any vessels of gold or silver were made for Yahweh’s house from the money brought into Yahweh’s house.
It was given to the workmen, and with it they repaired Yahweh’s house.
They did not ask for an accounting from the men to whom they handed the money to pay the workers, for they dealt honestly.
The money from guilt offerings and sin offerings was not brought into Yahweh’s house; it belonged to the priests.
About that time Hazael king of Aram attacked Gath and took it. Then Hazael turned his attention to marching against Jerusalem.

Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred objects that his ancestors Jehoshaphat, Jehoram, and Ahaziah, kings of Judah, had dedicated, his own sacred gifts, and all the gold found in the treasuries of Yahweh’s house and of the king’s palace, and sent them to Hazael king of Aram. Then Hazael withdrew from Jerusalem.
The rest of the acts of Joash and all that he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
His servants rose up, formed a conspiracy, and struck down Joash at Beth-millo,{f} on the road that goes down to Silla.{g}
His servants Jozacar{h} son of Shimeath and Jehozabad son of Shomer attacked him, and he died. He was buried with his ancestors in the city of David, and his son Amaziah{i} became king after him.

notes.text: Zibiah means “gazelle.” Verse numbers in this chapter follow the English; the Hebrew numbers run one higher.
Or “did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes all the days that Jehoiada the priest instructed him.” Compare 2 Chronicles 24:2, 17–22.
The Hebrew phrase is obscure; it may refer to the census tax (Exodus 30:13) or to money “that passes” as current.
The meaning of Hebrew makkar, here “contact,” is uncertain; it may mean an acquaintance, a donor, or an assessor. The Septuagint reads “from his sale.” Likewise in verse 7.
Or “tied up,” that is, in bags; some interpreters read “melted down.”
Beth-millo means “house of the Millo,” probably a building on the earthwork terrace in Jerusalem (compare 1 Kings 9:15).
The location of Silla is unknown. The Septuagint reads “Sela.”
Jozacar means “Yahweh has remembered.” The Septuagint reads “Jezirchar.” 2 Chronicles 24:26 names the men Zabad and Jehozabad.
Amaziah means “Yahweh is strong.”

verses.text: In the twenty-third year of Joash son of Ahaziah king of Judah, Jehoahaz son of Jehu became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned seventeen years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight and followed the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin; he never turned from them.
So Yahweh’s anger burned against Israel, and he kept handing them over to Hazael king of Aram and to Ben-hadad son of Hazael throughout that time.
Then Jehoahaz pleaded with Yahweh, and Yahweh listened to him, for he saw how the king of Aram was oppressing Israel.
Yahweh gave Israel a deliverer,{a} and they escaped from Aram’s grip. So the Israelites lived in their homes{b} as they had before.
Yet they did not turn from the sins of the house of Jeroboam, by which he made Israel sin, but kept walking in them. The Asherah pole{c} also stood in Samaria.

Jehoahaz had no army left except fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers, because the king of Aram had wiped out the rest and left them like the dust trampled on a threshing floor.
The rest of the acts of Jehoahaz, all he did, and his might, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?
Jehoahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in Samaria. And Joash his son reigned in his place.
In the thirty-seventh year of Joash king of Judah, Jehoash son of Jehoahaz became king over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned sixteen years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight. He did not turn from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin, but walked in them.
The rest of the acts of Joash, all he did, and the might with which he fought against Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?
Joash slept with his fathers, and Jeroboam{d} sat on his throne. Joash was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel.
When Elisha had fallen ill with the illness from which he would die, Joash king of Israel went down to him and wept over him, crying, “My father, my father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen!”
Elisha said to him, “Take a bow and arrows,” and he took a bow and arrows.
Then he said to the king of Israel, “Grip the bow.” When he had gripped it, Elisha laid his own hands on the king’s hands.

“Open the east window,” Elisha said, and Joash opened it. “Shoot,” said Elisha, and he shot. Elisha declared, “Yahweh’s arrow of victory, the arrow of victory over Aram! At Aphek you will strike the Arameans down until they are finished.”
Elisha then said, “Pick up the arrows,” and the king picked them up. “Strike the ground,” Elisha told the king of Israel. He struck it three times, then stopped.
The man of God was angry with him and said, “You should have struck five or six times. Then you would have struck Aram until you had made an end of it. Now you will strike Aram only three times.”
Elisha died and they buried him. Now Moabite raiders used to come into the land each spring.{e}
Once, as some men were burying a man, they caught sight of a raiding band, so they threw the man into Elisha’s tomb. When the man touched Elisha’s bones, he came to life and stood up on his feet.
Hazael king of Aram oppressed Israel throughout the days of Jehoahaz.
Yet Yahweh showed them favor and pity and turned back to them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. He would not destroy them, and even now he has not thrown them out of his sight.
When Hazael king of Aram died, Ben-hadad his son reigned in his place.

Jehoash son of Jehoahaz then took back from Ben-hadad son of Hazael the towns that Hazael had seized in battle from his father Jehoahaz. Joash defeated Ben-hadad three times and regained the towns of Israel.

notes.text: The deliverer is not named; he may be Jeroboam II (14:27) or an Assyrian king who pressed Aram from the north.
Hebrew “in their tents.”
Hebrew ’asherah, a wooden pole or image of the goddess Asherah.
This is Jeroboam II (14:23–29). Jeroboam probably means “may the people increase.”
Hebrew “at the coming of the year,” that is, in spring, the season for campaigns (compare 1 Kings 20:22, 26).

verses.text: In the second year of Joash son of Joahaz king of Israel, Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddin{a} of Jerusalem.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, though not like his ancestor David. He acted in every way as his father Joash had acted.
Yet the high places were not removed; the people kept sacrificing and burning incense on them.
When he had a secure hold on the royal power, he put to death the officials who had assassinated his father the king.

But he did not kill the murderers’ children, in keeping with what is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, where Yahweh commanded, “Parents are not to die for their children, nor children for their parents; each is to die for his own sin.”{b}
He killed ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt and captured Sela{c} in battle, and he renamed it Joktheel,{d} the name it still has today.
Then Amaziah sent envoys to Jehoash son of Jehoahaz son of Jehu, king of Israel, with this challenge: “Come, let us face each other in battle.”

Jehoash king of Israel sent back this reply to Amaziah king of Judah: “A thornbush in Lebanon sent word to a cedar in Lebanon, ‘Give your daughter to my son as his wife.’ Then a wild animal of Lebanon passed by and trampled the thornbush.
You have indeed beaten Edom, and now your heart has carried you away. Enjoy your glory, and stay home! Why stir up trouble that will bring you down, and Judah along with you?”
But Amaziah would not listen. So Jehoash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah faced each other at Beth-shemesh,{e} which belongs to Judah.
Israel defeated Judah, and every man ran off home.{f}

At Beth-shemesh Jehoash king of Israel captured Amaziah king of Judah, son of Jehoash son of Ahaziah. Then he came to Jerusalem and broke down the wall of Jerusalem for about 600 feet,{g} from the Ephraim Gate to the Corner Gate.
He carried off all the gold and silver and all the vessels found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace, as well as hostages, and went back to Samaria.
The rest of the acts of Jehoash, what he did, his might, and how he fought with Amaziah king of Judah, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?
Jehoash slept with his fathers and was buried in Samaria with the kings of Israel. And Jeroboam his son reigned in his place.
Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah lived fifteen years after the death of Jehoash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel.
The rest of the acts of Amaziah, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
A conspiracy was formed against him in Jerusalem, and he fled to Lachish. But they sent men after him to Lachish, and they killed him there.
They carried him back on horses, and he was buried in Jerusalem with his fathers in the city of David.
Then all the people of Judah took Azariah,{h} who was sixteen years old, and made him king in place of his father Amaziah.
He rebuilt Elath{i} and restored it to Judah, after the king had slept with his fathers.
In the fifteenth year of Amaziah son of Joash king of Judah, Jeroboam son of Joash king of Israel began to reign in Samaria, and he reigned forty-one years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight. He did not turn from any of the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin.

It was he who won back Israel’s territory, from Lebo-hamath{j} down to the Sea of the Arabah,{k} as Yahweh the God of Israel had promised through his servant Jonah{l} son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.{m}
For Yahweh had seen how very bitter Israel’s suffering was. Neither bond nor free remained,{n} and Israel had nobody to help it.
Yahweh had not said that he would blot out Israel’s name from under heaven, so he saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Joash.

The other events of Jeroboam’s reign, including all he did, his strength, his battles, and how he won back Damascus and Hamath, which had once belonged to Judah,{o} are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.
Jeroboam slept with his fathers, the kings of Israel, and Zechariah{p} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: So the Ketiv; the Qere and 2 Chronicles 25:1 read “Jehoaddan.” The name may mean “Yahweh is delight.”
Deuteronomy 24:16.
Sela means “rock”; it was a stronghold of Edom.
Joktheel may mean “God destroys” or “God nourishes”; the meaning is uncertain.
Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.”
Hebrew “to his tent.”
Hebrew “four hundred cubits.” A cubit was about 18 inches (45 centimeters), so about 180 meters.
Azariah means “Yahweh has helped.” He is also called Uzziah (15:13; 2 Chronicles 26:1).
Elath, at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba, means “terebinths” or “palms.”
Or “the entrance of Hamath,” at the northern border.
That is, the Dead Sea.
Jonah means “dove.” This is the prophet of the book of Jonah.
Gath-hepher means “winepress of the well,” a town in Zebulun.
Hebrew ‘atsur we‘azub; see the note at 1 Kings 14:10.
The Hebrew of this clause, literally “to Judah in Israel,” is obscure.
Zechariah means “Yahweh has remembered.”

verses.text: In the twenty-seventh year of Jeroboam king of Israel, Azariah son of Amaziah king of Judah began to reign.
He was sixteen years old when he became king, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah{a} of Jerusalem.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, just as his father Amaziah had done in everything.
Yet the high places were not removed; the people kept sacrificing and burning incense on them.

Yahweh struck the king with a serious skin disease,{b} and it lasted until the day he died. He lived in a separate house,{c} and Jotham{d} the king’s son ran the palace and ruled the people of the land.
The rest of the acts of Azariah, all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
Azariah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the city of David. And Jotham his son reigned in his place.
In the thirty-eighth year of Azariah king of Judah, Zechariah son of Jeroboam reigned over Israel in Samaria for six months.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, as his fathers had done. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin.
Shallum son of Jabesh conspired against him, struck him down in front of the people,{e} killed him, and reigned in his place.
The rest of the acts of Zechariah are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.
So the word that Yahweh had spoken to Jehu came true: “Your sons will sit on the throne of Israel to the fourth generation.” And so it happened.
Shallum son of Jabesh began to reign in the thirty-ninth year of Uzziah{f} king of Judah, and he reigned one full month in Samaria.
Then Menahem{g} son of Gadi came up from Tirzah to Samaria, struck down Shallum son of Jabesh in Samaria, killed him, and reigned in his place.
The rest of the acts of Shallum and the conspiracy he formed are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.

At that time Menahem, setting out from Tirzah, attacked Tiphsah{h} and everyone in it and its territory, because they would not open their gates to him. He sacked it and ripped open all its pregnant women.
In the thirty-ninth year of Azariah king of Judah, Menahem son of Gadi began to reign over Israel, and he reigned ten years in Samaria.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight. Throughout his reign he did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin.
Pul{i} king of Assyria came against the land, and Menahem gave Pul about 37 tons of silver,{j} so that Pul would help him tighten his grip on the kingdom.

Menahem raised the money from Israel, from all the wealthy men, about 20 ounces of silver{k} from each, to give to the king of Assyria. So the king of Assyria turned back and did not stay in the land.
The rest of the acts of Menahem, all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel?
Menahem slept with his fathers, and Pekahiah{l} his son reigned in his place.
In the fiftieth year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekahiah son of Menahem began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned two years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin.

His officer Pekah{m} son of Remaliah conspired against him. With fifty men from Gilead, Pekah struck him down at Samaria, in the citadel of the royal palace, together with Argob and Arieh.{n} Pekah killed him and took his place as king.
The rest of the acts of Pekahiah, all he did, are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.
In the fifty-second year of Azariah king of Judah, Pekah son of Remaliah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned twenty years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight. He did not turn from the sins of Jeroboam son of Nebat, by which he made Israel sin.

In the days of Pekah king of Israel, Tiglath-pileser{o} king of Assyria came and captured Ijon, Abel-beth-maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, and Galilee, all the land of Naphtali, and he deported the people to Assyria.
Hoshea{p} son of Elah plotted against Pekah son of Remaliah, attacked and killed him, and became king in his place in the twentieth year of Jotham son of Uzziah.
The rest of the acts of Pekah, all he did, are written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Israel.
In the second year of Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel, Jotham son of Uzziah king of Judah began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerusha daughter of Zadok.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, just as his father Uzziah had done in everything.
Yet the high places were not removed; the people kept sacrificing and burning incense on them. He built the Upper Gate of Yahweh’s house.
The rest of the acts of Jotham, all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
It was in those days that Yahweh first sent Aram’s king Rezin{q} and Remaliah’s son Pekah to attack Judah.
Jotham slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David his ancestor. And Ahaz{r} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: Jecoliah means “Yahweh is able.”
Hebrew metsora‘; see the note at 5:1.
Hebrew beth ha-hophshith, perhaps “a house of freedom,” that is, free from royal duties; the exact sense is uncertain.
Jotham means “Yahweh is perfect.”
The Hebrew qabol-‘am, “before the people,” is unusual. The Septuagint reads “in Keblaam,” which some take as Ibleam (compare 9:27).
Uzziah is another name for Azariah; it means “Yahweh is my strength.”
Menahem means “comforter.”
So the Hebrew. Tiphsah was a town on the Euphrates, far from Israel; some ancient witnesses read “Tappuah,” and the Septuagint reads “Tirzah.”
Pul was the Babylonian throne name of Tiglath-pileser III (verse 29).
Hebrew “a thousand talents of silver.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so about 34,000 kilograms.
Hebrew “fifty shekels of silver.” A shekel weighed about 0.4 ounce (11.5 grams), so about 575 grams.
Pekahiah means “Yahweh has opened (the eyes).”
Pekah means “he has opened (the eyes).”
The Hebrew of “along with Argob and Arieh” is obscure; the words may be names of people killed with the king or of places, and may have been misplaced from verse 29.
Tiglath-pileser III reigned in Assyria about 745–727 BC.
Hoshea means “salvation.”
Rezin is probably Aramaic for “pleasing” or “prince.”
Ahaz means “he has grasped,” a short form of Jehoahaz.

verses.text: In the seventeenth year of Pekah son of Remaliah, Ahaz son of Jotham king of Judah began to reign.
Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. Unlike his ancestor David, he did not do what was right in the eyes of Yahweh his God.
He followed the path of Israel’s kings. He even made his own son go through fire,{a} imitating the disgusting customs of the nations that Yahweh had expelled ahead of the Israelites.
He sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every leafy tree.
Then Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah king of Israel came up to wage war against Jerusalem. They besieged Ahaz but could not conquer him.{b}
At that time Rezin king of Aram{c} recovered Elath for Aram and drove the Judeans out of Elath. Then Edomites{d} came to Elath and have lived there to this day.
Ahaz sent envoys to Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria to say, “I am your servant and your son. Come up and rescue me from the grasp of the king of Aram and the king of Israel, who are attacking me.”
Ahaz took the silver and gold found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace and sent it as a present{e} to the king of Assyria.
The king of Assyria agreed. He marched up against Damascus and captured it, deported its people to Kir,{f} and put Rezin to death.
King Ahaz traveled to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria. There he saw the altar and sent Uriah{g} the priest a sketch of the altar and detailed plans for its construction.
Uriah the priest built the altar exactly as King Ahaz had instructed from Damascus, finishing it before King Ahaz came back from Damascus.
When the king arrived from Damascus and saw the altar, he approached the altar and went up on it.
There he offered up his burnt offering and grain offering, made his drink offering, and dashed against the altar the blood from his fellowship sacrifices.
The bronze altar that stood before Yahweh he moved from the front of the house, from between the new altar and Yahweh’s house, and put it on the north side of his altar.

King Ahaz commanded Uriah the priest, “Offer the morning burnt offering and the evening grain offering on the large altar, together with the king’s burnt offering and grain offering, and the burnt offering of all the people of the land with their grain offerings and drink offerings. Sprinkle all the blood of the burnt offerings and the sacrifices on it. The bronze altar will be for me to use for seeking guidance.”{h}
Uriah the priest did all that King Ahaz commanded.
King Ahaz cut away the panels of the stands and took the basins off them. He lowered the Sea from the bronze oxen beneath it and placed it on a stone pavement.
Because of the king of Assyria, he removed from Yahweh’s house the covered Sabbath passage{i} that had been built in the house, and the king’s outer entrance.
The rest of the acts of Ahaz, all he did, are they not written in the Book of the Annals of the Kings of Judah?
Ahaz slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David. And Hezekiah{j} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: That is, he offered his son as a burnt sacrifice; compare 3:27 and Deuteronomy 18:10.
Compare Isaiah 7:1–9.
Many interpreters read “Rezin king of Aram” as a later addition and “Aram” as “Edom” in this verse, since the two words look alike in Hebrew.
So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “Arameans.”
Or “a bribe.”
Kir was the land the Arameans came from (Amos 9:7); its location is unknown.
Uriah means “Yahweh is my light.”
Or “for me to consider.” The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the Qere; the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “a base for the throne.”
Hezekiah means “Yahweh strengthens.”

verses.text: In the twelfth year of Ahaz king of Judah, Hoshea son of Elah began to reign over Israel in Samaria, and he reigned nine years.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, though not to the degree of the kings of Israel who came before him.
Shalmaneser{a} king of Assyria marched up against him, and Hoshea became his vassal and paid him tribute.

But the king of Assyria discovered that Hoshea was plotting against him. He had sent envoys to So{b} king of Egypt and had withheld the yearly tribute owed to Assyria’s king. So Assyria’s king seized him and locked him in prison.
Then the king of Assyria invaded the whole land. He went up to Samaria and besieged it for three years.
In Hoshea’s ninth year, the king of Assyria conquered Samaria and deported the Israelites to Assyria. He resettled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes.{c}
This happened because the Israelites had sinned against Yahweh their God, the one who led them out of Egypt, out from under the hand of Egypt’s king, Pharaoh. They revered other gods
and lived by the customs of the nations whom Yahweh had driven out before the Israelites, and by the customs that the kings of Israel had introduced.{d}
The Israelites did in secret{e} things that were not right against Yahweh their God. They built high places for themselves in all their towns, from watchtower to fortified city.
They set up for themselves sacred pillars and Asherah poles on every high hill and under every leafy tree.
There they burned incense on all the high places, as the nations had done whom Yahweh had carried away before them. They did wicked things that provoked Yahweh to anger.
They served idols,{f} although Yahweh had told them, “You must not do this.”

Yahweh had warned Israel and Judah by means of all his prophets and seers: “Turn from your wicked ways and obey my commands and decrees, following the entire law that I gave your ancestors and delivered to you through my servants the prophets.”
But they would not listen. They hardened their necks like their ancestors, who had no faith in Yahweh their God.

They spurned his statutes, the covenant he cut with their fathers, and the solemn warnings he gave them. They went after empty things and became empty themselves,{g} following the nations around them, though Yahweh had commanded them not to act as those nations did.
They abandoned all the commandments of Yahweh their God and made for themselves cast images, two calves. They made an Asherah pole, bowed down to all the host of heaven, and served Baal.
They made their sons and daughters pass through the fire. They practiced divination and sought omens, and they sold themselves to do evil in Yahweh’s sight, provoking him to anger.
So Yahweh was furious with Israel and put them out of his sight. No one remained except the tribe of Judah.
Even Judah did not keep the commandments of Yahweh their God but followed the customs Israel had introduced.
So Yahweh rejected all the descendants of Israel. He humbled them and handed them over to plunderers, until he had thrown them out of his sight.
When he tore Israel from the house of David, they made Jeroboam son of Nebat king. Jeroboam drove Israel away from following Yahweh and made them commit a great sin.
The Israelites kept on in every sin Jeroboam had committed and never turned from them,
until Yahweh removed Israel from his presence, just as he had said through all his servants the prophets. So Israel was exiled from their own land to Assyria, where they are to this day.

From Babylon, Cuthah, Avva, Hamath, and Sepharvaim{h} the Assyrian king brought people and settled them in Samaria’s towns where the Israelites had lived. These newcomers took over Samaria and made their homes in its towns.
When they first settled there, they did not revere Yahweh, so Yahweh sent lions among them, which killed some of them.

They told the king of Assyria, “The peoples you deported and resettled in the cities of Samaria do not know the rules{i} of the god of that land. He has sent lions among them, and the lions are killing them because they do not know what that god requires.”
The king of Assyria then commanded, “Send back one of the priests you carried away from there. Have him return, settle there, and instruct the people in what the god of that land requires.”
So one of the priests whom they had deported from Samaria came and lived in Bethel, and he taught them how they should revere Yahweh.
But each nation still made its own gods and set them up in the shrines of the high places that the people of Samaria had made, each nation in the towns where they lived.
Those from Babylon fashioned Succoth-benoth; those from Cuth, Nergal; those from Hamath, Ashima;
The Avvites made Nibhaz and Tartak, and the Sepharvites burned their children in the fire to Adrammelech and Anammelech, the gods of Sepharvaim.{j}
They also revered Yahweh, and they appointed from their own number all sorts of people as priests of the high places, who offered sacrifices for them in the shrines of the high places.
So they revered Yahweh but served their own gods, in the manner of the nations from which they had been deported.

To this day they keep their former practices. They do not truly revere Yahweh, nor do they follow the statutes, the rules, the law, or the commandment that Yahweh gave to the descendants of Jacob, whom he named Israel.{k}
Yahweh had made a covenant with them and charged them, “Do not revere other gods, bow down to them, serve them, or sacrifice to them.
Yahweh, who brought you up from the land of Egypt with great power and an outstretched arm, is the one you are to revere. Bow down to him and sacrifice to him.
The statutes, the rules, the law, and the commandment that he wrote for you, you must always be careful to do. Do not revere other gods.
Never forget the covenant I cut with you, and revere no other gods.
Instead, revere Yahweh your God, and he will rescue you from the hand of all your enemies.”
But they would not listen, and they kept on with their former practices.
