So these nations revered Yahweh and also served their carved images. Their children and grandchildren do as their ancestors did, to this day.

notes.text: Shalmaneser V reigned in Assyria about 727–722 BC.
So may be the name of a pharaoh, perhaps Osorkon IV, or a place name, Sais, in the Nile delta.
The Septuagint reads “the mountains of the Medes.”
The Hebrew of this clause is awkward; it may mean “and of the kings of Israel, which they practiced.”
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; it may mean “ascribed things falsely to.”
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Hebrew hebel, “vapor” or “breath,” a play on the idea of worthlessness.
These were cities in Mesopotamia and Syria.
Hebrew mishpat, here “custom” or “required rites.” Likewise in verses 27, 33, 34, and 40.
The names in verses 30–31 refer to deities whose identities are largely uncertain. Nergal was a Mesopotamian god of the underworld.
Verse 34 appears to contradict verses 32–33; it may mean that these people did not worship Yahweh in the way the law required. Jacob was renamed Israel in Genesis 32:28.

verses.text: In the third year of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Hezekiah son of Ahaz king of Judah began to reign.
He was twenty-five years old when he became king, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Abi{a} daughter of Zechariah.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes, just as his ancestor David had done in everything.

He removed the high places, smashed the sacred pillars, and cut down the Asherah pole. He broke into pieces the bronze serpent that Moses had made, for up to then the Israelites had kept offering incense to it. People called it Nehushtan.{b}
Hezekiah trusted in Yahweh the God of Israel. Among all the kings of Judah, none was like him, whether after him or before him.
He held fast to Yahweh and never stopped following him. He kept the commandments Yahweh had given Moses.
Yahweh was with him, and he succeeded in whatever he undertook. He rebelled against the king of Assyria and would not serve him.
He struck down the Philistines all the way to Gaza and its borders, from lookout tower to walled town.
In the fourth year of King Hezekiah, the seventh of Hoshea son of Elah king of Israel, Shalmaneser king of Assyria came up against Samaria and besieged it.
At the end of three years they captured it. In Hezekiah’s sixth year, which was the ninth year of Hoshea king of Israel, Samaria fell.
The king of Assyria took the Israelites away to Assyria. He resettled them in Halah, in Gozan by the Habor River, and in the cities of the Medes,
because they had not obeyed the voice of Yahweh their God but had broken his covenant, all that Moses the servant of Yahweh had commanded. They would neither listen nor obey.
In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib{c} king of Assyria came up against all the fortified towns of Judah and captured them.

Hezekiah king of Judah sent word to the king of Assyria at Lachish: “I have sinned. Pull back from me, and I will bear any burden you lay on me.” So Assyria’s king imposed on Hezekiah king of Judah about 11 tons of silver and about 1 ton of gold.{d}
Hezekiah gave him all the silver found in Yahweh’s house and in the treasuries of the king’s palace.
At that time Hezekiah stripped the gold from the doors of Yahweh’s temple and from the doorposts that he, Hezekiah king of Judah, had overlaid, and gave it to the king of Assyria.

From Lachish the Assyrian king sent his Tartan, Rab-saris, and Rabshakeh{e} with a large army to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem. They went up and came to Jerusalem. When they arrived, they took their stand by the channel of the upper pool, which is on the road to the Washer’s Field.
When they called for the king, out to meet them came Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, Shebnah the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder.
The Rabshakeh told them, “Tell Hezekiah that this is what the great king, the king of Assyria, says: What is the basis for your confidence?
You say you have strategy and strength for war, but these are empty words. On whom are you now relying, that you have rebelled against me?
Look, you are leaning on Egypt, a cracked reed for a walking stick, which will stab into the palm of whoever puts weight on it. Such is Egypt’s king Pharaoh to everyone who trusts him.

But if you tell me, “We are relying on Yahweh our God,” is he not the one whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, telling Judah and Jerusalem, “You must worship before this altar in Jerusalem”?
Now then, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you can put riders on them!
How could you possibly repel even one governor, the lowest-ranking of my master’s officials, when you are depending on Egypt for chariots and cavalry?
Besides, is it without Yahweh that I have come up against this place to destroy it? Yahweh himself told me, Go up against this land and destroy it.’ ”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, Shebnah, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, “Kindly use Aramaic with your servants, since we know that language. Do not address us in Hebrew{f} while the people on the wall can hear.”

But the Rabshakeh replied, “Was it to your master and you alone that my master sent me to say these things? Was it not to the men on the wall, who along with you will be eating their own excrement and drinking their own urine?”{g}
Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out loudly in Hebrew: “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Assyria!
The king says this: ‘Do not let Hezekiah fool you; he cannot save you from his hand.
Do not let Hezekiah convince you to trust in Yahweh when he says, ‘Yahweh will certainly save us; this city will not be handed over to the king of Assyria.’

Pay no attention to Hezekiah. This is what the king of Assyria says: ‘Make a peace agreement with me{h} and surrender to me. Then every one of you will eat the fruit of his own vine and fig tree and drink the water of his own well,

until I arrive and carry you off to a land just like yours, a land of grain and new wine, of bread and vineyards, of olive oil and honey, so that you will live and not die.’ Do not let Hezekiah mislead you by claiming, ‘Yahweh will save us.’
Has any of the gods of the nations ever rescued his land from the hand of the king of Assyria?
Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah? Did they rescue Samaria from my hand?
Which of the gods of any country has delivered it from my power? So how can Yahweh deliver Jerusalem from my power?”
But the people kept silent and did not answer him a word, for the king’s command was, “Do not answer him.”

Then Eliakim son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, Shebna the secretary, and Joah son of Asaph the recorder came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn and reported to him what the Rabshakeh had said.

notes.text: Abi is a short form of Abijah, “Yahweh is my father” (2 Chronicles 29:1).
Nehushtan sounds like Hebrew nehosheth, “bronze,” and nahash, “serpent.” Compare Numbers 21:8–9.
Sennacherib reigned in Assyria 705–681 BC; his campaign against Judah was in 701 BC.
Hebrew “three hundred talents of silver and thirty talents of gold.” A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so about 10,200 and 1,020 kilograms.
These are Assyrian titles: Tartan, “commander in chief”; Rab-saris, “chief officer”; Rabshakeh, “chief cupbearer” or field commander.
Hebrew “in Judean.”
So the Qere; the Ketiv uses cruder words.
Hebrew “Make a blessing with me.”

verses.text: When King Hezekiah heard this, he tore his clothes, covered himself with sackcloth, and went into Yahweh’s house.
Eliakim, who was over the household, Shebna the scribe, and the elders among the priests, dressed in sackcloth, were sent by him to the prophet Isaiah{a} son of Amoz.
They told him, “Hezekiah says this: ‘This day is one of anguish, reproof, and humiliation. The babies are at the mouth of the womb, and there is no strength to bring them out.

Perhaps Yahweh your God has heard all the words of the Rabshakeh, sent by his master the king of Assyria to insult the living God, and will rebuke him for the words Yahweh your God has heard. So pray for the remnant of our people who remain.’ ”
When King Hezekiah’s servants came to Isaiah,
Isaiah told them, “Say to your master, ‘Yahweh says this: Do not be frightened by what you have heard, the words with which the lackeys of the king of Assyria have insulted me.
I am about to put a spirit in him, so that he will hear a rumor and go back to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.’ ”
The Rabshakeh went back and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had moved on from Lachish.
Then Sennacherib received word about Tirhakah,{b} king of Cush:{c} “He has come out to fight you.” Once more he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying:
“Say this to Hezekiah king of Judah: ‘Your God, in whom you trust, is fooling you when he says Jerusalem will never fall into the Assyrian king’s grip. Do not listen.
You have surely heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all the lands, devoting them to destruction. Will you then be rescued?
Did the gods of the nations rescue those whom my predecessors destroyed: Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?
Where are the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, and the kings of Sepharvaim, Hena, and Ivvah?’ ”
Hezekiah received the letter from the messengers and read it. Then he went up to Yahweh’s house and spread it out before Yahweh.
And Hezekiah prayed before Yahweh: “Yahweh, God of Israel, you who sit above the cherubim, you and you only are God of every kingdom on earth. Heaven and earth are your making.
Turn your ear, Yahweh, and listen. Open your eyes, Yahweh, and look. Listen to the words that Sennacherib sent to mock the living God.
It is true, Yahweh, that the kings of Assyria have laid waste the nations and their lands.
They have cast their gods into the flames and wiped them out, since those were no gods at all, just wood and stone that people had shaped.
Now, Yahweh our God, save us, I pray, from his hand, so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you, Yahweh, alone are God.”
Isaiah son of Amoz then sent this message to Hezekiah: “This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: I have heard your prayer concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria.
This is the word Yahweh has spoken concerning him: “The virgin daughter Zion holds you in contempt and laughs you to scorn. Daughter Jerusalem tosses her head behind your back.
Whom have you taunted and reviled? Whom have you shouted at, looking down your nose so haughtily? It was Israel’s Holy One!

Through your messengers you have mocked the Lord,{d} boasting, ‘Riding at the head of my chariot host{e} I have climbed the heights of the mountains, the farthest reaches of Lebanon. I cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest junipers. I entered its most remote lodging place, its densest forest.{f}
I dug wells and drank foreign waters. Under my tramping feet every river of Egypt ran dry.’{g}
Have you not heard? Long ago I planned it. From days of old I shaped it, and now I have brought it about, that you should turn fortified cities into heaps of ruins,
while their inhabitants, drained of strength, were dismayed and put to shame. They became like plants in the field and tender green shoots, like grass on the rooftops, scorched before it grows up.{h}
I know where you stay, where you go, where you come from, and how you rage against me.
Because you have raged against me and your arrogance has reached my ears, a ring will go through your nostrils, a bridle between your lips, and I will lead you home again the way you arrived.”

“And here, Hezekiah, is your sign: for this year the food will be whatever sprouts on its own, and next year whatever comes up from that. But in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.
The survivors of the house of Judah who are left will again take root below and bear fruit above.
Out of Jerusalem a remnant will emerge, a band of escapees from Zion’s mountain. Yahweh’s{i} jealous passion will accomplish this.
Therefore this is what Yahweh says about the king of Assyria: Into this city he will not come; no arrow of his will fly over it. No shield of his will confront it, or heap up a siege ramp against it.
By the road he came, by that same road he will go back, and he will not enter this city, declares Yahweh.
I will shield this city to rescue it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.”
That very night the angel of Yahweh went out and struck down 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. When the survivors{j} got up early in the morning, there were all the dead bodies.
So Sennacherib king of Assyria broke camp and went home. He stayed in Nineveh.
As he bowed down in the house of Nisroch{k} his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his own sons, cut him down with swords and fled to Ararat country.{l} And Esarhaddon{m} his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: Isaiah means “Yahweh is salvation.”
Tirhakah (Taharqa) was a Cushite ruler of Egypt’s Twenty-fifth Dynasty, here probably still commander of the army.
That is, the upper Nile region (modern Sudan).
Hebrew Adonai.
So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “With the chariot of my chariots.”
Hebrew “the forest of its Carmel,” that is, its garden-land.
Hebrew Matsor, a poetic name for Egypt; it can also mean “siege.”
So the Hebrew; Isaiah 37:27 and some ancient witnesses read “like a terraced field.” The Hebrew phrase is uncertain.
The Septuagint reads “of Yahweh of hosts,” as in Isaiah 37:32.
Hebrew “they.”
Nisroch is otherwise unknown; it may be a corruption of Nusku or Marduk.
Ararat is Urartu, in the region of modern Armenia.
Esarhaddon reigned in Assyria 681–669 BC.

verses.text: Around that time Hezekiah fell ill and was close to dying. The prophet Isaiah son of Amoz came to him and said, “Yahweh says this: ‘Put your household in order, because you are going to die; you will not get well.’ ”
Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall and prayed to Yahweh:
“Yahweh, please call to mind that I have walked in your presence with loyalty and an undivided heart and have done what is right in your eyes.” And Hezekiah broke down in tears.
Before Isaiah had got out past the middle courtyard,{a} the word of Yahweh came to him:

“Go back and tell Hezekiah, the leader of my people, ‘This is what Yahweh, the God of your ancestor David, says: I have listened to your prayer and seen your tears. I am going to heal you. Two days from now you will go up to Yahweh’s house.
I am adding fifteen years to your life. From the hand of Assyria’s king I will deliver both you and this city, and I will defend this city for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David.’ ”
Then Isaiah said, “Bring a lump of pressed figs.” They brought it and put it on the boil, and he recovered.
Hezekiah had asked Isaiah, “What will be the sign that Yahweh is going to heal me and that I will go up to Yahweh’s house the day after tomorrow?”
Isaiah answered, “This is your sign from Yahweh that he will do what he has promised: Shall the shadow move forward ten steps{b} or go back ten steps?”
Hezekiah said, “It is easy for the shadow to lengthen by ten steps. No, let the shadow turn back ten steps.”
So the prophet Isaiah called out to Yahweh, and Yahweh brought the shadow back the ten steps it had already gone down on the stairway of Ahaz.
At that time the king of Babylon, Berodach-baladan{c} son of Baladan, sent Hezekiah letters and a present, having heard that Hezekiah was sick.

Hezekiah welcomed{d} the envoys and showed them his entire storehouse: the silver, the gold, the spices, the fine oil, his armory, and everything in his treasuries. There was nothing in his palace or anywhere in his realm that Hezekiah failed to show them.
Then the prophet Isaiah came to King Hezekiah and asked him, “What did those men say, and where did they come from to see you?” Hezekiah replied, “They came from a distant land, from Babylon.”
Isaiah asked, “What have they seen in your palace?” Hezekiah answered, “They saw everything in my palace. Nothing among my treasures did I keep from them.”
Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Listen to Yahweh’s word:
The days are surely coming when all that is in your palace, and all that your ancestors have accumulated until now, will be taken to Babylon. Nothing will remain, says Yahweh.
And some of your own descendants, born from you, will be taken away, and they will serve as eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.”
Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of Yahweh you have spoken is good.” For he was thinking, “Surely, then, my own days will be peaceful and secure.”

The rest of Hezekiah’s history, all his mighty deeds, and how he built the pool and the channel{e} and brought water into the city, are they not recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah?
Then Hezekiah lay down with his fathers, and Manasseh{f} his son became king after him.

notes.text: So the Qere and the Septuagint; the Ketiv reads “the middle city.”
Or “degrees”; Hebrew ma‘aloth, steps of a stairway used to mark time by the shadow.
Isaiah 39:1 and the Septuagint read “Merodach-baladan.” The name is Babylonian Marduk-apla-iddina, “Marduk has given an heir.”
Hebrew “listened to.” The Septuagint and Isaiah 39:2 read “rejoiced over.”
That is, the tunnel cut through rock to bring the Gihon spring’s water into the city, known today as Hezekiah’s Tunnel.
Manasseh means “causing to forget.”

verses.text: Manasseh was twelve when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem fifty-five years. His mother was named Hephzibah.{a}
He did what Yahweh considered evil, copying the detestable customs of the nations Yahweh had driven out ahead of the Israelites.

He rebuilt the shrines on the high places that his father Hezekiah had torn down. He put up altars to Baal and made an Asherah pole,{b} just as Ahab king of Israel had done, and he bowed down to the whole army of the sky and served them.
He built altars inside Yahweh’s house, the very place of which Yahweh had said, “In Jerusalem I will put my name.”
In both courtyards of Yahweh’s house he built altars for all the starry host.

He made his own son pass through the fire.{c} He practiced fortune-telling and omen reading and appointed people who consulted ghosts and familiar spirits. He did a great deal of evil in Yahweh’s eyes, provoking him to anger.

The carved image of Asherah that he had made he placed in the house about which Yahweh had told David and his son Solomon, “In this house and in Jerusalem, which I chose out of all the tribes of Israel, I will set my name forever.

I will never again make Israel’s feet wander from the land I gave their ancestors, provided only that they take care to do all that I have commanded them, the whole law my servant Moses laid on them.”
But they would not listen. Manasseh misled them into doing more evil than the nations Yahweh had wiped out before the Israelites.
So Yahweh spoke through his servants the prophets:
“Manasseh king of Judah has committed these detestable acts, worse than anything the Amorites before him did, and with his idols{d} he has led Judah into sin as well.
Therefore this is what Yahweh the God of Israel says: I am bringing such disaster on Jerusalem and Judah that both ears of everyone who hears of it will ring.

I will measure Jerusalem with the same line I used for Samaria and weigh it with the same plumb line I used for Ahab’s house.{e} I will wipe Jerusalem clean the way a dish is wiped, turned upside down after the wiping.
What is left of my own heritage I will abandon, giving them into the power of their enemies, to be pillaged and stripped by every foe they have,
because they have done what is evil in my eyes and have gone on angering me ever since the day their fathers left Egypt, right up to today.”
What is more, Manasseh poured out the blood of the innocent in such quantity that Jerusalem was soaked with it end to end, besides the sin he led Judah into by doing evil in Yahweh’s eyes.
The rest of Manasseh’s history, all he did and the sin he committed, is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, is it not?
Manasseh died and was buried in the garden of his own house, the garden of Uzza, and his son Amon{f} succeeded him as king.
Amon was twenty-two when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem two years. His mother was Meshullemeth,{g} daughter of Haruz, from Jotbah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, as his father Manasseh had done.
He followed his father’s path in every way, serving and bowing down to the idols his father had served.
He turned his back on Yahweh, his fathers’ God, and refused to go in Yahweh’s way.
Amon’s own servants formed a conspiracy and murdered the king inside his house.
Then the people of the land put to death everyone who had plotted against King Amon, and they crowned Josiah,{h} Amon’s son, to succeed him.
The rest of what Amon did is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, is it not?
He was buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and his son Josiah reigned after him.

notes.text: Hephzibah means “my delight is in her.”
A wooden cult object associated with the goddess Asherah.
Some ancient witnesses, including the Septuagint, read “his sons.” The rite probably refers to child sacrifice.
The Hebrew word gillulim is a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
Builders’ tools, used here as an image of judgment by the same standard applied to Samaria and Ahab’s dynasty.
Amon means “faithful” or “master builder.”
Meshullemeth means “one repaid” or “one at peace.”
Josiah means “Yahweh supports.”

verses.text: Josiah became king at the age of eight and reigned thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother was Jedidah,{a} the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath.
He did what was right in Yahweh’s eyes and followed every step of his ancestor David, never veering off to right or left.
In the eighteenth year of his reign,{b} King Josiah sent Shaphan{c} the secretary, son of Azaliah and grandson of Meshullam, to Yahweh’s house. He told him:
“Go up to Hilkiah{d} the high priest and have him count out the silver brought into Yahweh’s house, which the doorkeepers have gathered from the people.
It is to be handed to the men in charge of the work on Yahweh’s house, and they are to pay it to the laborers repairing the damage to the building:
the carpenters, the builders, and the stonemasons, and to buy timber and cut stone to restore the house.
But no accounting is to be required of them for the silver given to them, for they work honestly.”
Hilkiah the high priest told Shaphan the secretary, “I have found the scroll of the law in Yahweh’s house.” Hilkiah gave the scroll to Shaphan, who read it.

Then Shaphan the secretary went to the king and gave him a report: “Your servants have emptied out the silver that was found in the house and handed it over to the men in charge of the work on Yahweh’s house.”
Then Shaphan the secretary informed the king, “There is a scroll that Hilkiah the priest handed to me.” And Shaphan read it aloud in the king’s presence.
As soon as the king heard what was written in the scroll of the law, he tore his clothes.
He commanded Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam son of Shaphan, Achbor{e} son of Micaiah, Shaphan the secretary, and Asaiah the king’s servant:

“Go and ask Yahweh on my behalf, and on behalf of the people and all Judah, about what is written in this scroll that has been found. Yahweh’s rage is burning hot against us, since our fathers never heeded what this scroll says or did all that it lays down for us.”

Hilkiah the priest, Ahikam, Achbor, Shaphan, and Asaiah went to consult the prophetess Huldah,{f} the wife of Shallum son of Tikvah, son of Harhas, who was in charge of the wardrobe. She lived in the Second District{g} of Jerusalem, and they talked with her there.
and she said to them, “This is what Yahweh the God of Israel says: Tell the man who sent you to me,
‘Yahweh says this: I am about to bring disaster on this place and on those who live here, everything written in the scroll the king of Judah has read.
Because they have abandoned me and burned offerings to other gods, angering me with all the things their hands have made, my fury will blaze against this place and will not be put out.’
But to the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of Yahweh, say this: ‘Yahweh the God of Israel says this about the words you have heard:

Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before Yahweh when you heard what I spoke against this place and its inhabitants, that they would become a horror and a curse, and because you tore your clothes and wept before me, I in turn have heard you, declares Yahweh.

For this reason I will bring you to rest with your ancestors, and you will be buried in peace. You will not witness any of the disaster that I will bring on this place.’ ” They carried her reply back to the king.

notes.text: Jedidah means “beloved.”
That is, 622 BC. The Septuagint adds “in the eighth month.”
Shaphan means “rock badger.”
Hilkiah means “Yahweh is my portion.”
Achbor means “mouse.”
Huldah means “mole” or “weasel.”
Hebrew Mishneh, a newer district of Jerusalem, probably on the western hill.

verses.text: The king then summoned all of the elders of Judah and Jerusalem to meet with him.

He went up to Yahweh’s house with all the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, the priests, the prophets, and all the people, from the least to the greatest. He read aloud to them every word of the Book of the Covenant that had been found in Yahweh’s house.

The king stood by the pillar and made a covenant in Yahweh’s presence to follow Yahweh and to keep his commands, laws, and decrees wholeheartedly, with his entire soul, confirming the words of the covenant written in this book. All the people pledged themselves to the covenant.

The king ordered Hilkiah the high priest, the priests of the second rank, and the doorkeepers to remove from Yahweh’s temple every object made for Baal, for Asherah, and for all the host of the sky. He burned them outside Jerusalem in the fields of the Kidron and carried their ashes to Bethel.

He eliminated the pagan priests{a} whom the kings of Judah had appointed to make offerings of incense at the high places in the cities of Judah and around Jerusalem. He also removed those who burned incense to Baal, to the sun and moon, to the constellations,{b} and to the whole host of heaven.
He took the Asherah from Yahweh’s house out of Jerusalem to the Kidron Valley and burned it there. He ground it to dust and scattered the dust over the graves of the common people.
He tore down the quarters of the cult prostitutes{c} that were in Yahweh’s house, where the women wove coverings{d} for Asherah.

Josiah brought all the priests from the cities of Judah and made unclean the high places where they had burned incense, from Geba to Beersheba.{e} He demolished the gate shrines{f} at the entrance of the Gate of Joshua, the city governor, which was on a person’s left as he entered the city gate.
The priests of the high places did not go up to Yahweh’s altar in Jerusalem, but they ate unleavened bread among their fellow priests.
Topheth{g} in the Ben-hinnom Valley he made unclean, so that nobody might ever again hand over a son or daughter to Molech by fire.

He removed the horses that the kings of Judah had dedicated to the sun at the entrance to Yahweh’s house, next to the room of Nathan-melech the official, in the colonnade,{h} and he burned the chariots of the sun.

The altars that the kings of Judah had built on the roof by Ahaz’s upper room, and the altars Manasseh had built in the two courtyards of Yahweh’s house, the king pulled down. He smashed them there{i} and threw their rubble into the Kidron Valley.

The king made unclean the high places facing Jerusalem on the east, to the right of the Mount of Ruin,{j} which Solomon king of Israel had built for Ashtoreth the detestable goddess of the Sidonians, for Chemosh the detestable god of Moab, and for Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites.
He shattered the sacred pillars, cut down the Asherah poles, and filled their sites with human bones.

He also demolished the altar at Bethel, the high place that Jeroboam son of Nebat had made, the one who led Israel into sin. He burned down that high place, ground it into powder, and burned the Asherah pole.

As Josiah turned around, he saw the tombs there on the hillside. He sent men to take the bones out of the tombs and burned them on the altar, defiling it, in keeping with the word of Yahweh proclaimed by the man of God who had foretold these things.{k}
Then he asked, “What is this marker I see?” The men of the city answered, “It is the grave of the man of God who came from Judah and announced these very things you have done to the altar of Bethel.”
“Let it be,” he said. “Don’t let anyone move his bones.” So they left his bones alone, together with the bones of the prophet from Samaria.
Josiah also removed all the shrines of the high places in the towns of Samaria that Israel’s kings had built, angering Yahweh.{l} He did to them just what he had done at Bethel.
Every priest of those high places he put to death on their own altars, and on them he burned the bones of the dead. After that he went back to Jerusalem.
The king commanded all the people, “Celebrate the Passover to Yahweh your God, as it is written in this scroll of the covenant.”
No Passover like it had been kept since the days of the judges who led Israel, nor in all the days of the kings of Israel and the kings of Judah.
But in King Josiah’s eighteenth year this Passover was celebrated to Yahweh in Jerusalem.

In addition, Josiah swept away those who called up the dead or consulted spirits, the teraphim,{m} the idols, and every loathsome thing to be seen across Judah and Jerusalem, in order to fulfill the words of the law written in the scroll Hilkiah the priest had found in Yahweh’s house.
No earlier king could compare with him in turning back to Yahweh with all his heart, soul, and might in line with the whole law of Moses, and no later king ever rose to equal him.
Even so, Yahweh did not turn from the burning heat of his great anger, which blazed against Judah because of all that Manasseh had done to provoke him.
Yahweh said, “Judah too I will remove from my sight as I removed Israel. I will reject this city I chose, Jerusalem, and the house of which I said, ‘My name shall be there.’ ”
The rest of Josiah’s history and all he did are recorded in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, are they not?

In his days Pharaoh Neco{n} king of Egypt marched up to the king of Assyria{o} at the Euphrates River. King Josiah went out to confront him, and the moment Neco saw him at Megiddo, he put him to death.

His servants carried his body by chariot from Megiddo, brought him to Jerusalem, and buried him in his own tomb. Then the people of the land took Jehoahaz{p} son of Josiah, anointed him, and made him king in his father’s place.
Jehoahaz was twenty-three when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem three months. His mother was Hamutal, daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, just as his fathers had done.
Pharaoh Neco imprisoned him at Riblah in the land of Hamath so that he could not rule in Jerusalem,{q} and he placed on the land a fine of about 3¾ tons of silver and about 75 pounds of gold.{r}
Eliakim, Josiah’s son, was installed by Pharaoh Neco as king to succeed Josiah his father, and Neco gave him the new name Jehoiakim.{s} Jehoahaz he carried off to Egypt, where he died.

Jehoiakim paid the silver and gold to Pharaoh, but to meet Pharaoh’s demand he had to tax the land. He exacted the silver and gold from the people of the land, from each according to his assessment, to pay Pharaoh Neco.
Jehoiakim was twenty-five when he took the throne, and he ruled in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother was Zebidah, daughter of Pedaiah, from Rumah.
He did evil in Yahweh’s sight, just as his fathers had done.

notes.text: Hebrew kemarim, a term used only for priests of foreign or idolatrous cults.
Or “the signs of the zodiac”; the Hebrew mazzaloth is uncertain.
Hebrew qedeshim; the precise role of these cult functionaries is debated.
Hebrew “houses”; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps woven hangings or garments.
That is, from the northern to the southern edge of Judah.
The Hebrew is uncertain; with a small change it may read “the shrines of the goat-demons.”
Topheth probably means “fireplace” or “hearth,” deliberately vocalized like boshet, “shame.”
Hebrew parwarim, a word of uncertain meaning.
Or “He hurried from there”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew Mount of Mashchith, a wordplay on Mishchah, “Anointing,” the Mount of Olives.
The Septuagint adds “when Jeroboam stood by the altar at the festival. And he turned and lifted his eyes to the grave of the man of God,” as in 1 Kings 13.
So the Septuagint; the Hebrew lacks “Yahweh.”
Household gods or images.
Neco II reigned in Egypt 610–595 BC.
Or “against the king of Assyria.” Neco in fact marched to support Assyria against Babylon in 609 BC.
Jehoahaz means “Yahweh has grasped.” He is also called Shallum (Jeremiah 22:11).
So the Qere; the Ketiv reads “while he reigned in Jerusalem.”
Hebrew 100 talents of silver and a talent of gold, about 3,400 kg of silver and 34 kg of gold. The Septuagint reads “100 talents of gold.”
Jehoiakim means “Yahweh raises up.” Eliakim means “God raises up.”

verses.text: During Jehoiakim’s reign Nebuchadnezzar{a} king of Babylon came up against him, and Jehoiakim became his vassal for three years. Then he changed course and rebelled against him.

Yahweh sent raiding bands of Chaldeans, Arameans, Moabites, and Ammonites against Jehoiakim; he let them loose on Judah to destroy it, in keeping with the word Yahweh had spoken through his servants the prophets.
Surely this came on Judah at Yahweh’s command, to thrust them out of his sight because of Manasseh’s sins, everything he had done,
and also because of the innocent blood he had shed. He had flooded Jerusalem with innocent blood, and Yahweh was not willing to forgive.
The rest of Jehoiakim’s history and all he did are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, are they not?
Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin{b} his son became king after him.
The king of Egypt did not march out of his own country again, for the king of Babylon had seized everything that had belonged to him, from the Wadi of Egypt{c} to the Euphrates River.
Jehoiachin was eighteen when he came to the throne, and he reigned in Jerusalem three months. His mother was Nehushta,{d} daughter of Elnathan, from Jerusalem.
He did what was evil in the sight of Yahweh, in every way like his father before him.
It was then that the troops of Babylon’s king Nebuchadnezzar came up to Jerusalem and laid siege to the city.
Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came to the city while his servants were laying siege to it.

Jehoiachin king of Judah gave himself up to the king of Babylon, along with his mother, his servants, his officials, and his palace officers. In the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign,{e} the king of Babylon took Jehoiachin captive.

Just as Yahweh had warned, Nebuchadnezzar hauled off all the treasures of Yahweh’s house and the palace treasures, and he stripped away the gold from all the vessels Solomon king of Israel had made for Yahweh’s temple.
He exiled all Jerusalem: all the commanders and all the leading warriors, 10,000 captives, along with every craftsman and metalworker.{f} No one was left except the poorest people of the land.
He took Jehoiachin into exile to Babylon. The king’s mother, the king’s wives, his court officers, and the leading men of the land he also led away into exile from Jerusalem to Babylon.
The king of Babylon brought to Babylon as exiles all the men of valor, 7,000 of them, and 1,000 craftsmen and metalworkers, all of them strong men fit for war.
In Jehoiachin’s place the king of Babylon made his uncle{g} Mattaniah king and changed his name to Zedekiah.{h}
Zedekiah was twenty-one when he came to the throne, and he reigned in Jerusalem eleven years. His mother was Hamutal,{i} daughter of Jeremiah, from Libnah.
He did what was evil in the sight of Yahweh, in every way like Jehoiakim before him.
Indeed, because of Yahweh’s anger, it came to this in Jerusalem and Judah, until he flung them away from his presence. And Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon.

notes.text: The Babylonian name Nabu-kudurri-usur means “Nabu, protect the heir.” He reigned 605–562 BC.
Jehoiachin means “Yahweh establishes.” He is also called Jeconiah and Coniah.
That is, Wadi el-Arish, on Egypt’s border with Canaan.
Nehushta means “bronze.”
That is, 597 BC.
Or “smith”; the Hebrew masger is uncertain, perhaps “locksmith” or “fortification builder.”
Hebrew “his father’s brother.” The Septuagint reads “his son.”
Mattaniah means “gift of Yahweh”; Zedekiah means “Yahweh is righteousness.”
So the Qere; the Ketiv reads “Hamital.”

verses.text: So in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month (December–January),{a} Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon came against Jerusalem with his whole army. He camped outside it and built siege works all around it.
The city stayed under siege until King Zedekiah’s eleventh year.
By the ninth day of the fourth month (June–July){b} the famine inside the city had become so severe that the common people had nothing left to eat.

Then the city wall was breached, and all the fighting men fled{c} by night through the gate between the two walls near the king’s garden, though the Chaldeans were all around the city. The king{d} headed off toward the Arabah.{e}
But the Chaldean army chased after the king and caught up with him on the plains of Jericho, and all his troops deserted him and scattered.
They seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah, where sentence was passed on him.
Zedekiah’s sons were slaughtered while he watched. Then Zedekiah’s eyes were put out, and he was bound in bronze shackles and taken to Babylon.

On the seventh day of the fifth month (July–August){f} (that was the nineteenth year of King Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon), Nebuzaradan,{g} commander of the guard and a servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem.
He set fire to Yahweh’s house, the palace, and every house in Jerusalem; every great house he burned down.
The whole Chaldean army that was with the commander of the guard tore down the walls surrounding Jerusalem.
Nebuzaradan, commander of the guard, carried into exile the people who remained in the city, those who had defected to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the population.{h}
But the commander of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to tend the vineyards and work the fields.
The Chaldeans broke up the bronze pillars of Yahweh’s house, the movable stands, and the bronze Sea{i} that were in Yahweh’s house, and they carried the bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, shovels, snuffers, dishes, and all the bronze articles used in the temple service.
The commander of the guard took the firepans and the sprinkling bowls, whatever was of gold for its gold and whatever was of silver for its silver.
The bronze from the two pillars, the Sea, and the movable stands that Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house was too much to weigh.

Each pillar was 27 feet{j} high, with a bronze capital on top. The capital stood 4½ feet{k} high, and a latticework with pomegranates encircled the capital, all of bronze. The second pillar, with its latticework, was the same.
The commander of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three doorkeepers.

From the city he took one court official who had command of the fighting men, five members of the king’s inner circle{l} still found in the city, the secretary of the army commander,{m} who mustered the people of the land, and sixty men of the people of the land who were found in the city.
Nebuzaradan the commander of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
There at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, the king of Babylon had them struck down and put to death. So Judah went into exile, away from its land.
Over the people who remained in the land of Judah, those whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, he appointed Gedaliah{n} son of Ahikam, son of Shaphan, as governor.

The army officers and their men all heard that the king of Babylon had made Gedaliah governor, so they went to Gedaliah at Mizpah. They were Ishmael son of Nethaniah, Johanan son of Kareah, Seraiah son of Tanhumeth the Netophathite, and Jaazaniah son of a Maacathite, along with their men.
Gedaliah took an oath to reassure them and their men. “Don’t be afraid of serving the Chaldean officials,” he said. “Stay in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and all will go well for you.”

In the seventh month (September–October),{o} however, Ishmael son of Nethaniah, son of Elishama, a member of the royal family, arrived with ten men. They attacked and killed Gedaliah, as well as the Jews and Chaldeans who were with him at Mizpah.
At that, the whole population, small and great alike, and the commanders of the troops got up and left for Egypt, fearing what the Chaldeans would do.

In the thirty-seventh year after Jehoiachin king of Judah went into exile, in the year Evil-merodach{q} became king of Babylon, he freed{r} Jehoiachin from prison on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month (February–March).{p}
He spoke kindly to him and gave him a seat of honor above the seats of the other kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin changed out of his prison clothes and ate at the king’s table every day for the rest of his life.
And his upkeep was supplied without fail from the king, a fixed share day by day, for as long as he lived.

notes.text: Hebrew “the tenth month,” later called Tebeth, which fell in December–January; the exact modern dates varied with the lunar calendar. The year is 588 BC.
Hebrew lacks “fourth”; it is supplied from Jeremiah 52:6. The fourth month, later called Tammuz, fell in June–July. The year is 587 or 586 BC.
Hebrew lacks “fled”; compare Jeremiah 52:7.
Hebrew “he.”
That is, the Jordan Valley.
Hebrew “the fifth month,” later called Ab, which fell in July–August. Jeremiah 52:12 reads “the tenth day.”
Nebuzaradan is Babylonian Nabu-zer-iddin, “Nabu has given offspring.”
Or “the artisans,” reading ha’amon with a slight change (compare Jeremiah 52:15); the Hebrew reads hehamon, “the multitude.”
That is, the great basin of 1 Kings 7:23–26.
Hebrew 18 cubits, about 8.1 meters.
Hebrew 3 cubits, about 1.35 meters. 1 Kings 7:16 and Jeremiah 52:22 give the capital’s height as 5 cubits (7½ feet).
Hebrew “five men of those who saw the king’s face.” Jeremiah 52:25 reads “seven.”
Or “the secretary, the commander of the army.”
Gedaliah means “Yahweh is great.”
Hebrew “the seventh month,” later called Tishri (the older Ethanim of 1 Kings 8:2), which fell in September–October.
Hebrew “the twelfth month,” later called Adar, which fell in February–March. Jeremiah 52:31 reads “the twenty-fifth day.” The year is 561 BC.
Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk.” He reigned 562–560 BC.
Hebrew “lifted the head of.”

books.name: 1 Chronicles
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where Chronicles is called Paraleipomena, “things left out”), using Brenton’s public-domain English translation, and against the parallel passages in Genesis, Samuel, Kings, and the Psalms. Only a very small Dead Sea Scrolls fragment of Chronicles survives; it is mentioned only in general terms. Where Chronicles differs from its parallels in names, numbers, or wording, the footnotes say so. Each personal and place name receives a brief note on its meaning at its first mention in Chronicles; many such meanings are uncertain, and the notes say so. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which in places differs from the Hebrew; the footnotes give the Hebrew numbering where they differ. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes, and dates are given with their modern-month spans.

verses.text: Adam,{a} Seth, Enosh,
Kenan,{b} Mahalalel, Jared,
Enoch,{c} Methuselah, Lamech,
Noah,{d} Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
The sons of Japheth: Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras.{e}
The sons of Gomer: Ashkenaz, Diphath,{f} and Togarmah.
The sons of Javan: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Rodanim.{g}
The sons of Ham: Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan.{h}
The sons of Cush: Seba, Havilah, Sabta, Raama, and Sabteca. The sons of Raama: Sheba and Dedan.{i}
Cush became the father of Nimrod; he began to be a mighty one in the earth.{j}
Mizraim became the father of Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,{k}
Pathrusim, and Casluhim, from whom came the Philistines, and Caphtorim.{l}
Canaan became the father of Sidon his firstborn, and Heth,{m}
the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites;
the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites;
the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the people of Hamath.{n}
Shem had sons named Elam, Asshur, Arpachshad, Lud, and Aram, as well as Uz, Hul, Gether, and Meshech.{o}
Arpachshad became the father of Shelah, and Shelah became the father of Eber.{p}
To Eber were born two sons: the name of the one was Peleg, for in his days the earth was divided, and his brother’s name was Joktan.{q}
Joktan fathered Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and Jerah,{r}
along with Hadoram, Uzal, and Diklah,{s}
and also Ebal, Abimael, and Sheba,{t}
and Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab. All of these were Joktan’s sons.{u}
Shem, Arpachshad, Shelah,
Eber, Peleg, Reu,{v}
Serug, Nahor, Terah,{w}
Abram, that is, Abraham.{x}
The sons of Abraham: Isaac and Ishmael.{y}
Their family records show that Ishmael’s oldest son was Nebaioth, followed by Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam,{z}
and then Mishma, Dumah, Massa, Hadad, and Tema,{aa}
and Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah. Those were Ishmael’s sons.{ab}
The sons of Keturah, Abraham’s concubine: she bore Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The sons of Jokshan: Sheba and Dedan.{ac}
The sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the sons of Keturah.{ad}
Abraham became the father of Isaac. The sons of Isaac: Esau and Israel.{ae}
The sons of Esau: Eliphaz, Reuel, Jeush, Jalam, and Korah.{af}
The sons of Eliphaz: Teman, Omar, Zephi, Gatam, Kenaz, and of Timna, Amalek.{ag}
The sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah.{ah}
The sons of Seir: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah, Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan.{ai}
The sons of Lotan: Hori and Homam; and Lotan’s sister was Timna.{aj}
The sons of Shobal: Alian, Manahath, Ebal, Shephi, and Onam. The sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Anah.{ak}
The son{al} of Anah: Dishon. The sons of Dishon: Hamran, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.{am}
The sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan. The sons of Dishan:{an} Uz and Aran.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the Israelites: Bela son of Beor, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.{ao}
When Bela died, Jobab son of Zerah of Bozrah reigned in his place.{ap}
When Jobab died, Husham of the land of the Temanites reigned in his place.{aq}
After Husham died, Hadad son of Bedad took his place as king. He was the one who defeated Midian in the country of Moab, and his city was named Avith.{ar}
When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place.{as}
When Samlah died, Shaul from Rehoboth by the River became king in his place.{at}
When Shaul died, Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.{au}
After Baal-hanan died, Hadad took his place as king. His city was named Pai, and his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Me-zahab.{av}
And Hadad died. ¶The chiefs of Edom were: chief Timna, chief Aliah, chief Jetheth,{aw}
chief Oholibamah, chief Elah, chief Pinon,{ax}
chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mibzar,{ay}
chief Magdiel, chief Iram. These are the chiefs of Edom.{az}

notes.text: Names: Adam, “human being,” related to adamah, “ground”; Seth, “appointed” (Genesis 4:25); Enosh, “man, mortal.” Verses 1–4 follow Genesis 5.
Kenan, perhaps “smith” or “possession”; Mahalalel, “praise of God”; Jared, “descent.”
Enoch, “dedicated”; Methuselah, perhaps “man of the spear”; Lamech, meaning uncertain.
Noah, “rest” (Genesis 5:29); Shem, “name”; Ham, perhaps “hot”; Japheth, perhaps “may he enlarge” (Genesis 9:27).

These names, which follow Genesis 10, mostly stand for peoples and regions; their meanings are largely unknown. Madai is Media; Javan is Ionia (the Greeks); Tubal and Meshech were peoples of Asia Minor. Gomer, Magog, and Tiras are uncertain.
So the Hebrew; Genesis 10:3 and some Hebrew manuscripts here read “Riphath” (in Hebrew the letters d and r look alike). Ashkenaz and Togarmah were peoples to the north; meanings uncertain.

So the Hebrew; Genesis 10:4 reads “Dodanim.” Rodanim probably means the people of Rhodes, and Kittim those of Cyprus. Elishah and Tarshish are places in the west; meanings uncertain. The Septuagint (B text) reads “the Citians and Rhodians.”
Cush is the region south of Egypt (Nubia); Mizraim is Egypt; Put is probably Libya; Canaan perhaps means “low land” or “land of purple.”
Peoples and places of Arabia and Africa; meanings uncertain. Sheba, perhaps “oath” or “seven,” and Dedan were in Arabia.
Nimrod perhaps means “let us rebel.”
The Septuagint (B text) lacks verses 11–16 and 17b–23. Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, and Naphtuhim are peoples (the ending -im is plural); meanings uncertain. Lehabim may be Libyans.
Pathrusim are the people of Pathros (Upper Egypt); Caphtorim are probably the people of Crete. Casluhim, meaning uncertain. Compare Genesis 10:14, where the order differs slightly.
Sidon perhaps means “fishing place”; Heth is the ancestor of the Hittites.

These are peoples of Canaan and Syria. Arkites, Arvadites, and Hamathites are named for the cities Arka, Arvad, and Hamath (“fortress”); Sinites and Zemarites for nearby places; Jebusites for Jebus (Jerusalem). Amorites probably means “westerners.” Other meanings uncertain.

Genesis 10:23 lists Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash (here Meshech) as sons of Aram; Chronicles lists them with Shem’s sons. Names: Elam, “highland” (Persia); Asshur, Assyria; Arpachshad, Lud, Uz, Hul, and Gether, uncertain; Aram, perhaps “high,” the ancestor of the Arameans (Syrians).
Shelah, “sprout” or “sending”; Eber, “region beyond,” perhaps linked to the word “Hebrew.”
Peleg means “division”; Joktan, perhaps “small.”
Almodad, Sheleph, uncertain; Hazarmaveth, “court of death” (Hadramaut in southern Arabia); Jerah, “moon.”
Hadoram, perhaps “Hadad is exalted”; Uzal, uncertain; Diklah, “palm grove.”
So the Hebrew; Genesis 10:28 reads “Obal.” Ebal, uncertain; Abimael, “my father is God”; Sheba, see verse 9.
Ophir, a land famous for gold; Havilah, perhaps “sandy land”; Jobab, uncertain.
Reu, perhaps “friend.”
Serug, perhaps “branch”; Nahor, perhaps “snorting”; Terah, uncertain, perhaps related to a word for “moon.”
Abram means “exalted father,” and Abraham, by sound, “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5).
Isaac means “he laughs”; Ishmael, “God hears.”
Nebaioth, uncertain; Kedar, “dark”; Adbeel, uncertain; Mibsam, “sweet smell.” These names follow Genesis 25:13–15.
Mishma, “hearing”; Dumah, “silence”; Massa, “burden” or “oracle”; Hadad, the name of a storm god; Tema, “desert” (an Arabian oasis).
Jetur, uncertain (the Itureans); Naphish, uncertain; Kedemah, “eastward.”
Keturah means “incense.” Zimran, perhaps “wild goat” or “song”; Jokshan, uncertain; Medan and Midian, perhaps “strife”; Ishbak, uncertain; Shuah, perhaps “sinking”; Dedan, uncertain.
Ephah, “darkness”; Epher, “young deer”; Hanoch, “dedicated” (same as Enoch); Abida, “my father knows”; Eldaah, perhaps “God has called.”
Esau, perhaps “hairy” (Genesis 25:25); Israel, “he strives with God” or “God strives” (Genesis 32:28).
Eliphaz, perhaps “my God is fine gold”; Reuel, “friend of God”; Jeush, “he gathers” or “he helps”; Jalam, perhaps “hidden”; Korah, “bald.”

According to Genesis 36:11–12, Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz and the mother of Amalek; the Hebrew here lists Timna and Amalek with the sons. The translation “and of Timna, Amalek” follows some Septuagint manuscripts and Genesis; the Septuagint (B text) lists both as sons. Names: Teman, “south”; Omar, uncertain; Zephi (Genesis 36:11 Zepho), perhaps “watch”; Gatam, Kenaz, uncertain; Timna, perhaps “restrained”; Amalek, uncertain.
Nahath, “quietness”; Zerah, “dawning, rising”; Shammah, perhaps “desolation”; Mizzah, uncertain.
Seir means “hairy, shaggy” (a wooded hill country). Lotan, perhaps “covering”; Shobal, uncertain; Zibeon, “hyena”; Anah, perhaps “answer”; Dishon and Dishan, “mountain goat”; Ezer, “help.”
Hori, ancestor of the Horites (perhaps “cave-dwellers”); Homam (Genesis 36:22 Hemam), uncertain.
Alian (Genesis 36:23 Alvan), Manahath (“rest”), Ebal, Shephi (Genesis Shepho), and Onam (“vigorous”); Aiah means “falcon” or “kite.” Several of these meanings are uncertain.
Hebrew “sons.”
Hamran (Genesis 36:26 Hemdan, “pleasant”), Eshban, Ithran (“abundance”), and Cheran; meanings mostly uncertain.
Hebrew “Dishon”; Genesis 36:28 reads “Dishan.” Bilhan, perhaps “modest”; Zaavan, perhaps “disquieted”; Jaakan (Genesis 36:27 Akan), uncertain; Uz and Aran, uncertain.
Bela, “devouring”; Beor, perhaps “burning”; Dinhabah, uncertain. Verses 43–54 follow Genesis 36:31–43.
Jobab, uncertain; Zerah, see verse 37; Bozrah, “sheepfold” or “fortress.”
Husham, perhaps “haste”; the Temanites, “southerners.”
Hadad, a storm god’s name; Bedad, perhaps “alone”; Avith, perhaps “ruins.”
Samlah, “garment”; Masrekah, perhaps “vineyard.”
Shaul, “asked for”; Rehoboth, “broad places.” The River is probably the Euphrates, or a local river.
Baal-hanan means “the lord (or Baal) is gracious”; Achbor, “mouse.”
Genesis 36:39 reads “Hadar” and “Pau” and does not record his death (verse 51). Hadad, see verse 46; Pai, uncertain; Mehetabel, “God does good”; Matred, perhaps “pursuit”; Me-zahab, “waters of gold.”
Aliah (Genesis 36:40 Alvah), uncertain; Jetheth, uncertain. Timna, see verse 36.
Oholibamah, “tent of the high place”; Elah, “terebinth”; Pinon, uncertain.
Mibzar, “fortress”; Kenaz and Teman, see verse 36.
Magdiel, “gift (or excellence) of God”; Iram, perhaps “city” or “watchful.”

verses.text: The sons of Israel were Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun,{a}
along with Dan, Joseph, Benjamin, Naphtali, Gad, and Asher.{b}
The sons of Judah: Er, Onan, and Shelah; these three were born to him by Bath-shua the Canaanite. Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, and he put him to death.{c}
And Tamar his daughter-in-law bore Perez and Zerah to him. All the sons of Judah were five.{d}
The sons of Perez: Hezron and Hamul.{e}
The sons of Zerah: Zimri, Ethan, Heman, Calcol, and Dara,{f} five in all.
The son{g} of Carmi: Achar, who brought trouble on Israel, who acted unfaithfully regarding what was devoted to destruction.{h}
The son of Ethan: Azariah.{i}
The sons of Hezron who were born to him: Jerahmeel, Ram, and Chelubai.{j}
Ram became the father of Amminadab, and Amminadab became the father of Nahshon, chief of the people of Judah.{k}
Nahshon became the father of Salma, and Salma became the father of Boaz.{l}
Boaz became the father of Obed, and Obed became the father of Jesse.{m}
Jesse became the father of his firstborn Eliab, Abinadab the second, and Shimea the third,{n}
Nethanel the fourth, Raddai the fifth,{o}
Ozem the sixth, David the seventh.{p}
Their sisters were Zeruiah and Abigail. The sons of Zeruiah: Abishai, Joab, and Asahel, three.{q}
Abigail bore Amasa, and the father of Amasa was Jether the Ishmaelite.{r}
Caleb son of Hezron had children by his wife Azubah, and by Jerioth as well;{s} her sons were Jesher, Shobab, and Ardon.{t}
When Azubah died, Caleb took Ephrath, who bore him Hur.{u}
Hur became the father of Uri, and Uri became the father of Bezalel.{v}
Afterward Hezron went in to the daughter of Machir the father of Gilead, whom he married when he was sixty years old, and she bore him Segub.{w}
Segub became the father of Jair, who had twenty-three cities in the land of Gilead.{x}
Then Geshur and Aram captured Havvoth-jair from them, along with Kenath and the villages around it, sixty towns in all.{y} All of these were descendants of Machir, the father of Gilead.
After the death of Hezron in Caleb-ephrathah, Abijah, Hezron’s wife, bore him Ashhur the father of Tekoa.{z}
The sons of Jerahmeel, the firstborn of Hezron: Ram his firstborn, Bunah, Oren, Ozem, and Ahijah.{aa}
Jerahmeel also had another wife, whose name was Atarah; she was the mother of Onam.{ab}
The sons of Ram, the firstborn of Jerahmeel: Maaz, Jamin, and Eker.{ac}
The sons of Onam: Shammai and Jada. The sons of Shammai: Nadab and Abishur.{ad}
Abishur’s wife was named Abihail, and she gave birth to Ahban and Molid.{ae}
The sons of Nadab: Seled and Appaim; and Seled died without sons.{af}
The son of Appaim: Ishi. The son of Ishi: Sheshan. The son of Sheshan: Ahlai.{ag}
And the sons of Jada the brother of Shammai: Jether and Jonathan; Jether died with no sons.{ah}
The sons of Jonathan: Peleth and Zaza. These were the descendants of Jerahmeel.{ai}
Sheshan had no sons, but daughters. And Sheshan had a servant, an Egyptian, named Jarha.{aj}
So Sheshan married his daughter to his servant Jarha, and she gave birth to Attai.{ak}
Attai became the father of Nathan, and Nathan became the father of Zabad.{al}
Zabad became the father of Ephlal, and Ephlal became the father of Obed.{am}
Obed became the father of Jehu, and Jehu became the father of Azariah.{an}
Azariah became the father of Helez, and Helez became the father of Eleasah.{ao}
Eleasah became the father of Sismai, and Sismai became the father of Shallum.{ap}
Shallum became the father of Jekamiah, and Jekamiah became the father of Elishama.{aq}
The sons of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel: Mesha his firstborn, who was the father of Ziph; and the sons of Mareshah the father of Hebron.{ar}
The sons of Hebron: Korah, Tappuah, Rekem, and Shema.{as}
Shema became the father of Raham the father of Jorkeam, and Rekem became the father of Shammai.{at}
The son of Shammai: Maon; and Maon was the father of Beth-zur.{au}
Ephah also, Caleb’s concubine, bore Haran, Moza, and Gazez; and Haran became the father of Gazez.{av}
Jahdai’s sons were Regem, Jotham, Geshan, Pelet, Ephah, and Shaaph.{aw}
Maacah, Caleb’s concubine, bore Sheber and Tirhanah.{ax}
She also bore Shaaph the father of Madmannah, Sheva the father of Machbenah and the father of Gibea; and the daughter of Caleb was Achsah.{ay}
These were the sons of Caleb. The sons of Hur, Ephrathah’s firstborn: Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim,{az}
Salma the father of Bethlehem, and Hareph the father of Beth-gader.{ba}
Shobal the father of Kiriath-jearim had sons: Haroeh, half of the Menuhoth.{bb}
And the clans of Kiriath-jearim: the Ithrites, the Puthites, the Shumathites, and the Mishraites; from these came the Zorathites and the Eshtaolites.{bc}
The sons of Salma: Bethlehem, the Netophathites, Atroth-beth-joab, and half of the Manahathites, the Zorites.{bd}
The clans also of the scribes who lived at Jabez: the Tirathites, the Shimeathites, and the Sucathites. These are the Kenites who came from Hammath, the father of the house of Rechab.{be}

notes.text: Reuben, “look, a son”; Simeon, “hearing”; Levi, “attached”; Judah, “praised”; Issachar, “there is reward”; Zebulun, “honor” or “dwelling” (Genesis 29–30).
Dan, “judge”; Joseph, “may he add”; Benjamin, “son of the right hand”; Naphtali, “my wrestling”; Gad, “good fortune”; Asher, “happy.”
Er, “watchful”; Onan, “vigor”; Shelah, see 1:18; Bath-shua, “daughter of Shua” (Genesis 38:2). Compare Genesis 38:7.
Tamar, “palm tree”; Perez, “breach”; Zerah, “dawning.”
Hezron, perhaps “enclosure”; Hamul, “spared.”

So the Hebrew; some ancient witnesses and 1 Kings 4:31 read “Darda.” Zimri (Joshua 7:1 Zabdi), “my praise” or “my protection”; Ethan, “enduring”; Heman, “faithful”; Calcol, “sustenance”; Dara, uncertain.
Hebrew “sons.”
Achar means “trouble” and is a play on Hebrew ‘oker, “troubler”; Joshua 7:1 calls him Achan. Carmi means “my vineyard.”
Azariah means “Yahweh has helped.”
Jerahmeel, “may God have compassion”; Ram, “high”; Chelubai, another form of Caleb (verse 18), perhaps “dog.”
Amminadab, “my kinsman is noble”; Nahshon, perhaps “serpent” or “bronze.”
Salma, perhaps “garment” (Ruth 4:20–21, Salmah and Salmon); Boaz, uncertain, perhaps “in him is strength.”
Obed, “servant, worshiper”; Jesse, uncertain, perhaps “Yahweh exists” or “man.”
Eliab, “my God is father”; Abinadab, “my father is noble”; Shimea, “hearing” (1 Samuel 16:9 Shammah).
Nethanel, “God has given”; Raddai, perhaps “ruling.”
First Samuel 16:10–11 and 17:12 say Jesse had eight sons, with David the youngest; Chronicles names seven. Some ancient versions add Elihu (compare 27:18). Ozem, perhaps “strength”; David, “beloved.”
Zeruiah, perhaps “balm”; Abigail, “my father is joy”; Abishai, “my father is gift”; Joab, “Yahweh is father”; Asahel, “God has made.”
Second Samuel 17:25 calls him Ithra the Israelite. Amasa, “burden-bearer”; Jether, “abundance.”
Or “fathered Jerioth by Azubah his wife.” The Hebrew is unclear.
Caleb, “dog” (or “wholehearted”); Azubah, “forsaken”; Jerioth, “curtains”; Jesher, “uprightness”; Shobab, “returning”; Ardon, uncertain.
Ephrath, “fruitfulness”; Hur, perhaps “white linen” or “child.”
Uri, “my light”; Bezalel, “in the shadow (protection) of God” (Exodus 31:2).
Machir, “sold”; Gilead, perhaps “rugged”; Segub, “exalted.”
Jair, “he enlightens.”
Geshur, “bridge”; Aram, the Arameans (Syria); Havvoth-jair, “villages of Jair”; Kenath, “possession.”

So the Hebrew, which is difficult. The Septuagint reads “after the death of Hezron, Caleb came to Ephrathah”; many scholars suggest the text originally said Caleb took Hezron’s wife. Abijah, “Yahweh is my father”; Ashhur, perhaps “black”; Tekoa, “trumpet blast.”
Bunah, “understanding”; Oren, “pine tree”; Ozem, see verse 15; Ahijah, “brother of Yahweh.” The Hebrew may mean that Ahijah was a wife of Jerahmeel.
Atarah, “crown”; Onam, “vigorous.”
Maaz, “anger”; Jamin, “right hand”; Eker, “root, offspring.”
Shammai, perhaps “he heard”; Jada, “he knows”; Nadab, “generous”; Abishur, “my father is a wall.”
Abihail, “my father is strength”; Ahban, “brother of the wise”; Molid, “begetter.”
Seled, “exultation”; Appaim, “nostrils” or “face.”
Hebrew “sons” throughout this verse. Ishi, “my salvation”; Sheshan, uncertain, perhaps “lily”; Ahlai, “ah, would that.”
Jether, see verse 17; Jonathan, “Yahweh has given.”
Peleth, “swiftness”; Zaza, uncertain.
Jarha, uncertain.
Attai, “timely.”
Nathan, “he has given”; Zabad, “gift.”
Ephlal, “judgment”; Obed, see verse 12.
Jehu, “Yahweh is he”; Azariah, see verse 8.
Helez, “strength”; Eleasah, “God has made.”
Sismai, uncertain; Shallum, “recompense.”
Jekamiah, “may Yahweh raise up”; Elishama, “God has heard.”
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. Mesha, “salvation”; Ziph, perhaps “refining”; Mareshah, “summit”; Hebron, “alliance.” “Father” here may mean the founder or chief of a town.
Korah, see 1:35; Tappuah, “apple”; Rekem, “variegated”; Shema, “hearing.”
Raham, “compassion”; Jorkeam, perhaps “the people spread”; Shammai, see verse 28.
Maon, “dwelling”; Beth-zur, “house of rock.”
Ephah, see 1:33; Haran, “mountaineer”; Moza, “going forth”; Gazez, “shearer.”
Jahdai, perhaps “Yahweh leads”; Regem, “friend”; Jotham, “Yahweh is perfect”; Geshan, uncertain; Pelet, “escape”; Shaaph, uncertain.
Maacah, perhaps “oppression”; Sheber, “breaking”; Tirhanah, uncertain.
Madmannah, “dunghill”; Sheva, “vanity” or “Yahweh contends”; Machbenah, uncertain; Gibea, “hill”; Achsah, “anklet” (Joshua 15:16–17).
Ephrathah, see Ephrath, verse 19; Shobal, uncertain; Kiriath-jearim, “city of forests.”
Bethlehem, “house of bread”; Hareph, perhaps “plucking”; Beth-gader, “house of the wall.”
Or “Reaiah, half of the Manahathites” (compare 4:2 and verse 54). Haroeh, “the seer”; Menuhoth, “resting places.”
Ithrites, “of Jether”; Puthites, Shumathites, Mishraites, uncertain; Zorathites and Eshtaolites, from Zorah (“hornets”) and Eshtaol (perhaps “asking”).
Netophathites, from Netophah (“dropping”); Atroth-beth-joab, “crowns of the house of Joab”; Manahathites, see verse 52; Zorites, uncertain.

Or “Tirathites, Shimeathites, and Sucathites,” perhaps meaning “gatekeepers, those who hear, and those who dwell in booths”; the meaning is uncertain. Jabez, “he causes pain” (4:9); Kenites, perhaps “smiths”; Hammath, “hot spring”; Rechab, “rider” (Jeremiah 35).

verses.text: These were the sons of David born to him at Hebron: Amnon, the oldest, whose mother was Ahinoam of Jezreel; Daniel, the second, whose mother was Abigail of Carmel;{a}
the third Absalom, the son of Maacah daughter of Talmai king of Geshur; the fourth Adonijah, the son of Haggith;{b}
the fifth Shephatiah, by Abital; the sixth Ithream, by Eglah his wife.{c}
Six were born to him in Hebron, where he reigned seven years and six months; and in Jerusalem he reigned thirty-three years.{d}
These sons were born to him at Jerusalem: Shimea, Shobab, Nathan, and Solomon. These four were born to Bath-shua daughter of Ammiel;{e}
then Ibhar, Elishama, Eliphelet,{f}
Nogah, Nepheg, Japhia,{g}
Elishama, Eliada, and Eliphelet, nine.{h}
All these were David’s sons, apart from the sons of his concubines. Their sister was Tamar.{i}
Solomon’s son was Rehoboam; Abijah his son, Asa his son, Jehoshaphat his son,{j}
Joram his son, Ahaziah his son, Joash his son,{k}
Amaziah his son, Azariah his son, Jotham his son,{l}
Ahaz his son, Hezekiah his son, Manasseh his son,{m}
Amon his son, Josiah his son.{n}
The sons of Josiah: the firstborn Johanan, the second Jehoiakim, the third Zedekiah, the fourth Shallum.{o}
The sons of Jehoiakim: Jeconiah his son, Zedekiah his son.{p}
The sons of Jeconiah the captive:{q} Shealtiel his son,{r}
Malchiram, Pedaiah, Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Hoshama, and Nedabiah.{s}
The sons of Pedaiah: Zerubbabel and Shimei. The sons of Zerubbabel: Meshullam and Hananiah, and Shelomith was their sister;{t}
and Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, Hasadiah, and Jushab-hesed, five.{u}
The sons of Hananiah: Pelatiah and Jeshaiah; the sons of Rephaiah, the sons of Arnan, the sons of Obadiah, the sons of Shecaniah.{v}
The son{w} of Shecaniah: Shemaiah. And the sons of Shemaiah: Hattush, Igal, Bariah, Neariah, and Shaphat, six.{x}
The sons of Neariah: Elioenai, Hizkiah, and Azrikam, three.{y}
The sons of Elioenai: Hodaviah, Eliashib, Pelaiah, Akkub, Johanan, Delaiah, and Anani, seven.{z}

notes.text: Second Samuel 3:3 calls the second son Chileab. Amnon, “faithful”; Ahinoam, “my brother is pleasantness”; Jezreel, “God sows”; Daniel, “God is my judge”; Abigail, see 2:16; Carmel, “garden land.”
Absalom, “father of peace”; Maacah, see 2:48; Talmai, perhaps “furrowed”; Geshur, see 2:23; Adonijah, “my lord is Yahweh”; Haggith, “festal.”
Shephatiah, “Yahweh has judged”; Abital, “my father is dew”; Ithream, “remnant of the people”; Eglah, “heifer.”
Compare 2 Samuel 5:4–5.

Bath-shua, “daughter of Shua” or “daughter of wealth,” is Bathsheba, “daughter of an oath” (2 Samuel 11:3), and Ammiel, “my kinsman is God,” is Eliam, “my God is kinsman,” with the parts reversed. Shimea (2 Samuel 5:14 Shammua), see 2:13; Shobab, see 2:18; Nathan, see 2:36; Solomon, “peaceable.”

Ibhar, “he chooses”; Elishama, see 2:41 (here 2 Samuel 5:15 reads “Elishua,” “God is salvation”); Eliphelet, “God is deliverance.” This Eliphelet and Nogah (verse 7) are not in 2 Samuel 5:14–16; compare 14:5–6.
Nogah, “brightness”; Nepheg, “sprout”; Japhia, “he shines.”
Eliada, “God knows.” Compare 14:7, Beeliada.
Tamar, see 2:4 (2 Samuel 13).
Rehoboam, “the people are enlarged”; Abijah, see 2:24 (1 Kings 15:1 Abijam); Asa, perhaps “healer”; Jehoshaphat, “Yahweh has judged.”
Joram (or Jehoram), “Yahweh is exalted”; Ahaziah, “Yahweh has grasped”; Joash, perhaps “Yahweh has given.”
Amaziah, “Yahweh is mighty”; Azariah, see 2:8 (also called Uzziah, 2 Chronicles 26); Jotham, see 2:47.
Ahaz, “he has grasped”; Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens”; Manasseh, “causing to forget.”
Amon, “faithful” or “master craftsman”; Josiah, “Yahweh supports.”
Johanan, “Yahweh is gracious”; Jehoiakim, “Yahweh raises up”; Zedekiah, “Yahweh is righteousness”; Shallum, see 2:40 (Jehoahaz, 2 Kings 23:30–31; Jeremiah 22:11).
Jeconiah, “Yahweh establishes” (also Jehoiachin, Coniah). This Zedekiah was apparently a son of Jeconiah; 2 Kings 24:17 calls Zedekiah Jehoiachin’s uncle.
Or “Jeconiah: Assir.” The Hebrew word ’assir means “captive,” and it may be read as a name.
Shealtiel, “I asked of God.”

Malchiram, “my king is exalted”; Pedaiah, “Yahweh has ransomed”; Shenazzar, a Babylonian name, perhaps “may Sin protect”; Jekamiah, see 2:41; Hoshama, “Yahweh has heard”; Nedabiah, “Yahweh is generous.”

Elsewhere Zerubbabel is called the son of Shealtiel (Ezra 3:2; Haggai 1:1); here he is listed as the son of Pedaiah, perhaps Shealtiel’s brother. Zerubbabel, “seed (offspring) of Babylon”; Shimei, “famous”; Meshullam, “repaid” or “friend”; Hananiah, “Yahweh is gracious”; Shelomith, “peaceable.”
Hashubah, “esteemed”; Ohel, “tent”; Berechiah, “Yahweh blesses”; Hasadiah, “Yahweh is kind”; Jushab-hesed, “kindness is returned.”

The Hebrew is unclear. The Septuagint has “Rephaiah was his son, then Arnan, then Obadiah, then Shecaniah.” The names mean: Pelatiah, “Yahweh delivers”; Jeshaiah, “Yahweh saves”; Rephaiah, “Yahweh heals”; Arnan, perhaps “agile”; Obadiah, “servant of Yahweh”; Shecaniah, “Yahweh dwells.”
Hebrew “sons.”
Only five names are listed; one may have dropped out. Shemaiah, “Yahweh hears”; Hattush, uncertain; Igal, “he redeems”; Bariah, “fugitive”; Neariah, “youth of Yahweh”; Shaphat, “he judges.”
Elioenai, “toward Yahweh are my eyes”; Hizkiah, a form of Hezekiah; Azrikam, “my help has arisen.”
Hodaviah, “give thanks to Yahweh”; Eliashib, “God restores”; Pelaiah, “Yahweh is wonderful”; Akkub, “heel” or “protected”; Johanan, see verse 15; Delaiah, “Yahweh has drawn up”; Anani, “my cloud.”

verses.text: The sons of Judah: Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.{a}
Reaiah the son of Shobal became the father of Jahath, and Jahath became the father of Ahumai and Lahad. These were the clans of the Zorathites.{b}
These were the sons{c} of Etam: Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash; and the name of their sister was Hazzelelponi;{d}
and Penuel the father of Gedor, and Ezer the father of Hushah. These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah, the father of Bethlehem.{e}
Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.{f}
Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. These were the sons of Naarah.{g}
The sons of Helah: Zereth, Izhar,{h} and Ethnan.{i}
Koz became the father of Anub, Zobebah, and the clans of Aharhel the son of Harum.{j}
Jabez was more honored than his brothers; and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, “Because I bore him in pain.”{k}

Jabez called out to the God of Israel, “If only you would truly bless me and extend my territory! Let your hand be with me, and keep me from harm, so that I will not be in pain!” And God gave him what he asked for.
Chelub the brother of Shuhah became the father of Mehir, who was the father of Eshton.{l}
Eshton became the father of Beth-rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir-nahash. These are the men of Recah.{m}
The sons of Kenaz: Othniel and Seraiah. The sons of Othniel: Hathath{n} and Meonothai.{o}
Meonothai became the father of Ophrah; and Seraiah became the father of Joab the father of Ge-harashim,{p} for they were craftsmen.{q}
The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh: Iru, Elah, and Naam. The son{r} of Elah: Kenaz.{s}
The sons of Jehallelel: Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.{t}
The sons of Ezrah: Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon. And she{u} conceived Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa.{v}
And his Judahite wife bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Soco, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. These are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married.{w}
The sons of the wife of Hodiah, the sister of Naham: the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maacathite.{x}
The sons of Shimon: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-hanan, and Tilon. The sons of Ishi: Zoheth and Ben-zoheth.{y}
The sons of Shelah son of Judah were Er, the founder of Lecah; Laadah, the founder of Mareshah; and the families of the linen workers at Beth-ashbea;{z}
and Jokim, and the men of Cozeba, and Joash, and Saraph, who ruled in Moab and returned to Lehem.{aa} (The records are ancient.)
These were the potters and the inhabitants of Netaim and Gederah;{ab} they lived there with the king in his work.
The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul;{ac}
Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, Mishma his son.{ad}
The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son.{ae}
Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers did not have many children, and their whole clan did not multiply like the people of Judah.
They settled in Beersheba, Moladah, and Hazar-shual,{af}
and in Bilhah, Ezem, and Tolad,{ag}
and in Bethuel, Hormah, and Ziklag,{ah}
and in Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susim, Beth-biri, and Shaaraim. These were their towns until David became king.{ai}
And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities,{aj}
and all the villages around those towns as far as Baal. These were the places where they lived, and they kept records of their families.{ak}
Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah,{al}
Joel; Jehu son of Joshibiah, son of Seraiah, son of Asiel;{am}
and Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, and Benaiah;{an}
and Ziza son of Shiphi, son of Allon, son of Jedaiah, son of Shimri, son of Shemaiah{ao} —
these mentioned by name were chiefs in their clans, and their fathers’ houses increased greatly.
They went to the entrance of Gedor,{ap} to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks,
There they found fertile, good pasture, and the land was wide, calm, and undisturbed; the people who had lived there earlier were descendants of Ham.

These men, listed by name, arrived in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah. They attacked their tents and the Meunites{aq} who were there, destroyed them completely, as is still the case, and settled in their place, since there was pasture there for their flocks.
Five hundred of these Simeonites went to Mount Seir with Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, as their leaders.{ar}
They struck the rest of the Amalekites who had escaped, and have lived there until this day.

notes.text: Here “sons” means descendants over several generations. Names, see chapter 2; Carmi, see 2:7.
Reaiah, “Yahweh has seen”; Jahath, perhaps “he snatches up”; Ahumai, uncertain; Lahad, perhaps “oppression.” Zorathites, see 2:53.
So the Septuagint; Hebrew “father.”
Etam, “place of birds of prey”; Jezreel, see 3:1; Ishma, “desolation” or “he hears”; Idbash, “honeyed”; Hazzelelponi, perhaps “give shade, you who turn to me.”
Penuel, “face of God”; Gedor, “wall”; Ezer, see 1:38; Hushah, “haste.” Hur and Ephrathah, see 2:19, 50.
Ashhur and Tekoa, see 2:24; Helah, perhaps “ornament”; Naarah, “girl.”
Ahuzzam, “possession”; Hepher, “well”; Temeni, “southerner”; Haahashtari, “the Ahashtarite,” perhaps a clan name.
So the Hebrew margin (Qere), meaning “he shines”; the written text (Ketiv) reads “Zohar” (“whiteness”).
Zereth, uncertain; Ethnan, “gift” (perhaps “hire”).
Koz, “thorn”; Anub, perhaps “grape”; Zobebah, uncertain; Aharhel, uncertain; Harum, “exalted.”
Jabez (Hebrew ya‘bets) sounds like the Hebrew for “pain” (‘otseb), with two letters reversed. The Septuagint renders the end of verse 10 as “that you would make me know that you will not grieve me.”
Chelub, “basket” or a form of Caleb; Shuhah, “pit”; Mehir, “price”; Eshton, perhaps “restful.”

The Septuagint reads “the city of Naas, the brother of Eselom the Kenizzite” and “men of Rechab.” Beth-rapha, “house of a giant” or “of healing”; Paseah, “limping”; Tehinnah, “supplication”; Ir-nahash, “city of a serpent” (or “of bronze”); Recah, uncertain.
The Septuagint (B text) gives only Hathath; some Greek manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate add “and Meonothai,” and the start of verse 14 seems to assume it.
Kenaz, see 1:36; Othniel, perhaps “lion of God” or “my strength is God”; Seraiah, “Yahweh is prince”; Hathath, “terror”; Meonothai, “my dwellings.”
Ge-harashim means “valley of craftsmen” (Nehemiah 11:35).
Ophrah, “fawn”; Joab, see 2:16.
Hebrew “sons.”
Jephunneh, perhaps “he will be turned”; Iru, uncertain; Elah, see 1:52; Naam, “pleasantness.” The Hebrew of the end of the verse reads “and Kenaz”; the sense is uncertain.
Jehallelel, “he praises God”; Ziph, see 2:42; Ziphah, the feminine form; Tiria, uncertain; Asarel, uncertain, perhaps “God has bound.”
The subject is unclear; the second half of verse 18 (“These are the sons of Bithiah . . .”) seems to belong before this clause, making Bithiah the mother.

Ezrah, “help”; Jether, see 2:17; Mered, “rebellion”; Epher, see 1:33; Jalon, perhaps “lodging”; Miriam, uncertain, perhaps “beloved” or “bitterness”; Shammai, see 2:28; Ishbah, “he praises”; Eshtemoa, “obedience” or “I will make myself heard.”

Or “his wife Jehudijah.” Jered, see Jared, 1:2; Gedor, see verse 4; Heber, “companion”; Soco, “branches”; Jekuthiel, perhaps “God will nourish”; Zanoah, perhaps “rejected”; Bithiah, “daughter of Yahweh”; Pharaoh, the title of the king of Egypt, “great house.”
Hodiah, “majesty of Yahweh”; Naham, “consolation”; Keilah, perhaps “fortress”; Garmite, perhaps “bony”; Maacathite, of Maacah (see 2:48).
Shimon, uncertain; Amnon, see 3:1; Rinnah, “shout of joy”; Ben-hanan, “son of the gracious one”; Tilon, uncertain; Ishi, see 2:31; Zoheth, uncertain; Ben-zoheth, “son of Zoheth.”
Shelah, see 2:3; Er, see 2:3; Lecah, “walking”; Laadah, uncertain; Mareshah, see 2:42; Beth-ashbea, “house of Ashbea,” uncertain.

Or “who married into Moab and returned to Lehem”; the Hebrew is obscure. The Latin Vulgate takes the names as words. Jokim, “Yahweh raises up”; Cozeba, “deceiving”; Joash, see 3:11; Saraph, “burning”; Lehem, “bread” (perhaps Bethlehem). The Septuagint reads “and he changed their names to Abederin and Athukiim.”
Or “who lived among plantations and hedges.” Netaim means “plants” and Gederah “sheepfold” or “wall.”
Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15 read Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul. Nemuel, perhaps “day of God”; Jamin, see 2:27; Jarib, “he contends”; Zerah, see 1:37; Shaul, see 1:48.
Shallum, see 2:40; Mibsam and Mishma, see 1:29–30.
Hammuel, perhaps “God is my kinsman” or “heat of God”; Zaccur, “remembered”; Shimei, see 3:19.
These towns follow Joshua 19:2–8. Beersheba, “well of seven” or “of an oath”; Moladah, “birth”; Hazar-shual, “fox village.”
Bilhah (Joshua 19:3 Balah), “faltering”; Ezem, “bone”; Tolad (Joshua 19:4 Eltolad), “birth.”
Bethuel (Joshua 19:4 Bethul), perhaps “house of God”; Hormah, “devoted to destruction”; Ziklag, uncertain.
Beth-marcaboth, “house of chariots”; Hazar-susim, “village of horses”; Beth-biri (Joshua 19:6 Beth-lebaoth), perhaps “house of my creation”; Shaaraim (Joshua 19:6 Sharuhen), “two gates.”
Etam, see verse 3; Ain, “spring”; Rimmon, “pomegranate”; Tochen (Joshua 19:7 Ether), “measure”; Ashan, “smoke.”
Baal, “lord, master” (Joshua 19:8 Baalath-beer).
Meshobab, “restored”; Jamlech, “he makes king”; Joshah, “Yahweh’s gift”; Amaziah, see 3:12.
