When your days are fulfilled for you to go to be with your fathers, I will raise up your offspring after you, who shall be of your sons, and I will establish his kingdom.
He shall build me a house, and I will establish his throne forever.
I will be his father, and he shall be my son.{f} I will not take my steadfast love away from him, as I took it from him who was before you.
But I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom forever, and his throne shall be established forever.’”{g}
According to all these words, and according to all this vision, so Nathan spoke to David.
Then King David went in and sat before Yahweh and said, “Who am I, Yahweh God, and what is my house, that you have brought me this far?
Yet even this was too little in your sight, God. You have also spoken about the future of your servant’s house, and you have looked on me as a man of high rank,{h} Yahweh God.
What more can David say to you about the honor done to your servant? For you know your servant.
Yahweh, for your servant’s sake, and according to your own heart, you have worked all this greatness, to make known all these great things.{i}
Yahweh, there is no one like you, neither is there any God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears.

What one nation in the earth is like your people Israel, whom God went to redeem to be his own people, to make for yourself a name by great and awesome things, in driving out nations from before your people whom you redeemed out of Egypt?{j}
For you made your people Israel your own people forever; and you, Yahweh, became their God.
Now, Yahweh, let the word that you have spoken concerning your servant and concerning his house be established forever, and do as you have spoken.
Let your name be established and magnified forever, saying, ‘Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, is Israel’s God’; and the house of David your servant shall be established before you.
For you, my God, have revealed to your servant that you will build him a house. Therefore your servant has found courage to pray before you.
Now, Yahweh, you are God, and you have promised this good thing to your servant.
Now it has pleased you to bless the house of your servant, that it may continue forever before you. For you, Yahweh, have blessed, and it is blessed forever.”{k}

notes.text: Verses 1–27 parallel 2 Samuel 7:1–29. Chronicles omits “Yahweh had given him rest from all his enemies around him” (2 Samuel 7:1). Nathan, “he has given.”
Second Samuel 7:5 has a question: “Shall you build me a house to dwell in?”
Hebrew “from tent to tent and from tabernacle”; the words “to tabernacle” are supplied from the sense. Compare 2 Samuel 7:6.
Hebrew shophet, “judge”; 2 Samuel 7:7 reads shibte, “tribes,” probably a copying difference.
Second Samuel 7:11 reads “Yahweh will make you a house”; the house here is a dynasty.
Chronicles omits 2 Samuel 7:14b, “When he commits iniquity, I will chasten him with the rod of men.”
Second Samuel 7:16 reads “your house and your kingdom … before you … your throne.” Chronicles speaks of God’s house and kingdom.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; compare 2 Samuel 7:19, “and this is the law for man.”
Second Samuel 7:21 reads “For your word’s sake.”
Second Samuel 7:23 adds “from Egypt, the nations and their gods.”
Some witnesses read “and may it be blessed forever.”

verses.text: After this David struck the Philistines and subdued them, and he took Gath and its towns out of the hand of the Philistines.{a}
He struck Moab, and the Moabites became servants to David and brought tribute.{b}
David also struck Hadarezer king of Zobah, toward Hamath, as he went to establish his dominion at the river Euphrates.{c}
David seized a thousand of his chariots, seven thousand charioteers, and twenty thousand foot soldiers. David crippled all the chariot horses except enough for a hundred chariots.{d}
When the Syrians of Damascus came to help Hadarezer king of Zobah, David struck down twenty-two thousand men of the Syrians.{e}
Then David put garrisons in Syria of Damascus, and the Syrians became servants to David and brought tribute. Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went.
David took the shields of gold that were on the servants of Hadarezer and brought them to Jerusalem.
From Tibhath and from Cun, cities of Hadarezer, David took very much bronze, with which Solomon made the bronze sea, the pillars, and the vessels of bronze.{f}
When Tou king of Hamath heard that David had struck all the host of Hadarezer king of Zobah,{g}

he sent Hadoram his son to King David to greet him and to bless him, because he had fought against Hadarezer and struck him; for Hadarezer had been at war with Tou. And he sent all kinds of vessels of gold and silver and bronze.{h}

These also King David dedicated to Yahweh, with the silver and the gold which he carried away from all the nations, from Edom, and from Moab, and from the sons of Ammon, and from the Philistines, and from Amalek.
Moreover Abishai son of Zeruiah slew of the Edomites in the Valley of Salt eighteen thousand.{i}
He put garrisons in Edom, and all the Edomites became servants to David. And Yahweh gave victory to David wherever he went.
So David reigned over all Israel, and he executed justice and righteousness for all his people.
Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the army; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;{j}
and Zadok the son of Ahitub and Abimelech the son of Abiathar were priests; and Shavsha was secretary;{k}
and Benaiah the son of Jehoiada was over the Cherethites and the Pelethites; and the sons of David were chief officials in the service of the king.{l}

notes.text: Verses 1–17 parallel 2 Samuel 8:1–18. Second Samuel 8:1 reads “took Metheg-ammah,” perhaps “the bridle of the mother city.” Gath, “winepress.”
Chronicles omits the execution of two-thirds of the Moabite captives (2 Samuel 8:2).
Hadarezer, “Hadad is help” (2 Samuel 8:3 Hadadezer); Zobah, an Aramean kingdom; Euphrates, see 5:9.
Second Samuel 8:4 reads “a thousand seven hundred horsemen” and does not mention the chariots; the Septuagint of Samuel agrees with Chronicles.
Syrians, Hebrew “Aram”; Damascus, perhaps “well-watered.”
Second Samuel 8:8 reads “Betah and Berothai” and does not mention Solomon’s use of the bronze. Tibhath, “slaughter”; Cun, perhaps “established.” On the bronze sea, see 2 Chronicles 4:2–5.
Tou (2 Samuel 8:9 Toi), uncertain.
Hadoram, “Hadad is exalted” (2 Samuel 8:10 Joram, “Yahweh is exalted”).

Second Samuel 8:13 credits David himself (“when he returned from striking eighteen thousand Arameans,” perhaps a misreading of Edom); Psalm 60 heading credits Joab with twelve thousand. Edomites, of Edom (“red”).
Jehoshaphat, “Yahweh has judged”; Ahilud, “a brother is born.”

Second Samuel 8:17 reads “Ahimelech the son of Abiathar” (as do many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate here) and “Seraiah,” who is called Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25 and Shisha in 1 Kings 4:3. Ahitub, see 6:7; Abimelech, “my father is king”; Shavsha, uncertain.
Second Samuel 8:18 reads “and David’s sons were priests.” Cherethites and Pelethites, the king’s foreign guard, perhaps Cretans and Philistines.

verses.text: Some time later, Nahash king of the Ammonites died, and his son became king in his place.{a}

David said, “I will show kindness to Hanun the son of Nahash, because his father showed kindness to me.” So David sent messengers to comfort him concerning his father. And David’s servants came into the land of the sons of Ammon to Hanun to comfort him.{b}

But the Ammonite officials told Hanun, “Do you think David is honoring your father by sending men to console you? Haven’t his servants come to you to explore the country, overthrow it, and spy on it?”
So Hanun seized David’s servants, shaved them, cut their clothes off at the hips, and sent them away.

When David was told what had happened to the men, he sent messengers to meet them, since they were deeply humiliated. “Wait at Jericho until your beards grow back,” the king said, “and then come home.”{c}

When the sons of Ammon saw that they had made themselves odious to David, Hanun and the sons of Ammon sent about 37 tons of silver{d} to hire chariots and horsemen for themselves from Mesopotamia, from Aram-maacah, and from Zobah.{e}

So they hired thirty-two thousand chariots, and the king of Maacah with his people, who came and encamped before Medeba. The sons of Ammon gathered themselves together from their cities and came to battle.{f}
When David heard of it, he sent Joab and all the army of the mighty men.
The sons of Ammon came out and set the battle in array at the gate of the city, and the kings who had come were by themselves in the field.
Now when Joab saw that the battle was set against him before and behind, he chose out of all the choice men of Israel and set them in array against the Syrians.
He placed the rest of the army under his brother Abishai, and they lined up to face the Ammonites.
Joab said, “If the Arameans prove too strong for me, you are to come to my aid; and if the Ammonites prove too strong for you, I will come to yours.
Be of good courage, and let us be strong for our people and for the cities of our God. And may Yahweh do what seems good to him.”
So Joab and the people who were with him drew near before the Syrians to the battle, and they fled before him.
When the sons of Ammon saw that the Syrians had fled, they likewise fled before Abishai his brother and entered the city. Then Joab came to Jerusalem.

When the Syrians saw that they had been put to the worse before Israel, they sent messengers and brought out the Syrians who were beyond the River, with Shophach the captain of the host of Hadarezer at their head.{g}

It was told David, and he gathered all Israel together and crossed over the Jordan, and came upon them and set the battle in array against them. So when David had set the battle in array against the Syrians, they fought with him.
The Syrians fled before Israel, and David killed of the Syrians the men of seven thousand chariots and forty thousand footmen, and put to death Shophach the captain of the host.{h}
When the servants of Hadarezer saw that they were put to the worse before Israel, they made peace with David and served him. So the Syrians would not help the sons of Ammon any more.

notes.text: Verses 1–19 parallel 2 Samuel 10:1–19. Nahash, “serpent”; Ammon, “people.”
Hanun, “favored.”
Jericho, perhaps “moon city.”
Hebrew “a thousand talents”; about 34 metric tons. Not mentioned in 2 Samuel 10:6.
Hebrew Aram-naharaim, “Aram of the two rivers.” Second Samuel 10:6 names Beth-rehob, Zobah, Maacah, and Tob. Maacah, see 2:48.

Second Samuel 10:6 reads “twenty thousand foot soldiers … and twelve thousand men of Tob,” giving the same total of thirty-two thousand, but footmen rather than chariots. Medeba, perhaps “waters of quiet.”
Shophach (2 Samuel 10:16 Shobach), perhaps “pouring.” The River is the Euphrates.
Second Samuel 10:18 reads “the men of seven hundred chariots and forty thousand horsemen.”

verses.text: In the spring, when kings go out to war, Joab led out the army and ravaged the land of the Ammonites. He came to Rabbah and besieged it, but David stayed in Jerusalem. Joab attacked Rabbah and tore it down.{a}

David took the crown of their king from off his head,{b} and found it to weigh about 75 pounds of gold,{c} and there were precious stones in it; and it was set on David’s head. He brought out the spoil of the city in great abundance.
He brought out the city’s people and put them to work using saws, iron picks, and axes.{d} David did this to each Ammonite city. Then David and his whole army returned to Jerusalem.
It came to pass after this that there arose war with the Philistines at Gezer; at that time Sibbecai the Hushathite slew Sippai, of the sons of the giants;{e} and the Philistines were brought low.
There was again war with the Philistines, and Elhanan the son of Jair killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath the Gittite, the shaft of whose spear was like a weaver’s beam.{f}
There was again war at Gath, where there was a man of great stature, who had twenty-four fingers and toes, six on each hand and six on each foot; and he also was descended from the giants.{g}
When he defied Israel, Jonathan the son of Shimea, David’s brother, killed him.{h}
These were descended from the giants in Gath, and they fell by the hand of David and by the hand of his servants.

notes.text: Verses 1–3 parallel 2 Samuel 11:1; 12:26, 30–31. Chronicles omits the story of Bathsheba and Uriah (2 Samuel 11:2–12:25) and Joab’s summons to David (2 Samuel 12:27–29). Rabbah, “great (city).”
Or “the crown of Milcom,” the god of the Ammonites; the Hebrew consonants malkam can be read either way.
Hebrew “a talent”; about 34 kilograms.
So 2 Samuel 12:31; Hebrew “and he sawed them with the saw, with iron picks, and with saws.” The verb wayyasar (“and he sawed”) may be a copying error for wayyasem (“and he set them”).
Hebrew “of the Rephaim.” Second Samuel 21:18 reads “Saph” and “at Gob.” Sippai, perhaps “threshold.”

Second Samuel 21:19 reads “Elhanan the son of Jaare-oregim, the Bethlehemite, killed Goliath the Gittite.” Chronicles names Lahmi (from the last part of “the Bethlehemite”) as Goliath’s brother, reconciling the text with 1 Samuel 17. Jair, “he enlightens”; Lahmi, perhaps “my bread”; Goliath, uncertain.
Verses 6–8 parallel 2 Samuel 21:20–22.
Jonathan, see 2:32; Shimea, see 2:13.

verses.text: Satan stood up against Israel and moved David to number Israel.{a}
David said to Joab and to the princes of the people, “Go, count Israel from Beersheba even to Dan; and bring me word, that I may know their number.”{b}
Joab replied, “May Yahweh multiply his people a hundred times over! My lord the king, aren’t they all my lord’s servants? Why does my lord want this done? Why make Israel guilty?”
Nevertheless the king’s word prevailed against Joab. Therefore Joab departed and went throughout all Israel, and came to Jerusalem.

Joab gave the sum of the numbering of the people to David. All those of Israel were one million one hundred thousand men who drew the sword; and in Judah were four hundred and seventy thousand men who drew the sword.{c}
But he did not count Levi and Benjamin among them, for the king’s word was abhorrent to Joab.{d}
God was displeased with this thing, so he struck Israel.
David said to God, “I have sinned greatly in doing this thing. But now, please take away the iniquity of your servant, for I have acted very foolishly.”
Yahweh spoke to Gad, David’s seer, saying,{e}
“Go and speak to David, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh: I offer you three things. Choose one of them, that I may do it to you.’”
So Gad came to David and said to him, “Thus says Yahweh: ‘Take your choice:

three years of famine; or three months of fleeing from your enemies while their swords overtake you; or three days of Yahweh’s sword, a plague in the land, with Yahweh’s angel destroying across the whole territory of Israel.’ Now decide what reply I should carry to the one who sent me.”{f}
David said to Gad, “I am in great distress. Let me fall now into the hand of Yahweh, for very great are his mercies; and let me not fall into the hand of man.”
So Yahweh sent a pestilence on Israel, and there fell of Israel seventy thousand men.

And God sent an angel to Jerusalem to destroy it. As he was about to destroy, Yahweh looked, and he relented of the evil, and said to the destroying angel, “It is enough; now stay your hand.” The angel of Yahweh was standing by the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.{g}

David lifted up his eyes and saw the angel of Yahweh standing between earth and heaven, having a drawn sword in his hand stretched out over Jerusalem. Then David and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell on their faces.{h}

David said to God, “Was it not I who ordered the counting of the people? I am the one who has sinned and done terrible wrong. But what have these sheep done? Yahweh my God, let your hand strike me and my family instead, and spare your people from the plague.”
Then the angel of Yahweh commanded Gad to say to David that David should go up and set up an altar to Yahweh on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.
David went up at the saying of Gad, which he had spoken in Yahweh’s name.
Ornan turned back and saw the angel, and his four sons who were with him hid themselves. Now Ornan was threshing wheat.{i}
As David came to Ornan, Ornan looked and saw David, and went out of the threshing floor and bowed himself to David with his face to the ground.

Then David said to Ornan, “Give me the site of this threshing floor, that I may build on it an altar to Yahweh. You shall sell it to me for the full price, that the plague may be stopped from the people.”

Ornan said to David, “Take it for yourself, and let my lord the king do what is good in his eyes. Look, I give the oxen for burnt offerings, and the threshing sledges for wood, and the wheat for the grain offering; I give it all.”
King David answered Ornan, “No, I will buy it at its full price. I refuse to take what is yours and give it to Yahweh, or to present a burnt offering that cost me nothing.”
So David gave to Ornan for the place gold weighing about fifteen pounds.{j}
David built an altar to Yahweh there and presented burnt offerings and peace offerings. He called out to Yahweh, who answered him from heaven with fire on the altar for burnt offerings.{k}
Then Yahweh commanded the angel, and he put his sword back into its sheath.
At that time, when David saw that Yahweh had answered him on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite, he sacrificed there.
For the tabernacle of Yahweh, which Moses made in the wilderness, and the altar of burnt offering, were at that time in the high place at Gibeon.
But David could not go before it to inquire of God, for he was afraid because of the sword of the angel of Yahweh.

notes.text: Verses 1–27 parallel 2 Samuel 24:1–25. Second Samuel 24:1 says “The anger of Yahweh was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them.” Hebrew satan, without the article, may be read as the proper name Satan or as “an adversary.”
Beersheba, “well of seven” or “well of the oath”; Dan, “judge.” Chronicles omits the route of the census (2 Samuel 24:5–8).

Second Samuel 24:9 reads “in Israel eight hundred thousand valiant men … and the men of Judah were five hundred thousand.” The figures cannot be fully reconciled; Chronicles may include the standing army (27:1–15) or follow a different source.
This explanation is found only in Chronicles; compare Numbers 1:47–49.
Gad, “fortune.”
Second Samuel 24:13 reads “seven years of famine” (the Septuagint of Samuel reads “three years,” as here).
Ornan (2 Samuel 24:16 Araunah), perhaps a Hurrian name or title, “lord.”
This verse is not in the standard text of 2 Samuel, but a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel (4QSam-a) has a similar verse at 2 Samuel 24:16.
Second Samuel 24:20 says only that Araunah looked out and saw the king and his servants coming toward him.

Hebrew “six hundred shekels of gold by weight,” about 6.9 kilograms. Second Samuel 24:24 says David bought the threshing floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, about 1¼ pounds (575 grams). Chronicles speaks of the whole “place,” the future temple site.
See Leviticus 9:24; 1 Kings 18:38. The fire from heaven is not mentioned in 2 Samuel.

verses.text: Then David said, “This is the house of Yahweh God, and this is the altar of burnt offering for Israel.”{a}
David commanded to gather together the foreigners who were in the land of Israel, and he set stonecutters to cut dressed stones to build the house of God.
David prepared iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates and for the clamps, and bronze in abundance beyond weighing,
and cedar trees without number; for the Sidonians and the Tyrians brought cedar trees in abundance to David.{b}

David said, “Solomon my son is young and tender, and the house that is to be built for Yahweh must be exceedingly magnificent, of fame and of glory throughout all countries. I will therefore make preparation for it.” So David prepared abundantly before his death.
Then he called for Solomon his son and charged him to build a house for Yahweh, the God of Israel.
David said to Solomon, “My son, as for me, it was in my heart to build a house to the name of Yahweh my God.

But the word of Yahweh came to me, saying, ‘You have shed blood abundantly and have made great wars. You shall not build a house to my name, because you have shed much blood upon the earth in my sight.

Behold, a son shall be born to you, who shall be a man of rest. I will give him rest from all his enemies all around; for his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quietness to Israel in his days.{c}
He shall build a house for my name. He shall be my son, and I will be his father; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel forever.’
Now, my son, may Yahweh be with you, so that you may prosper and build the house of Yahweh your God, as he has spoken concerning you.
May Yahweh give you wisdom and understanding as he makes you ruler over Israel, so that you will keep the law of Yahweh your God.
Then you will prosper, if you are careful to do the statutes and the ordinances which Yahweh commanded Moses concerning Israel. Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid, nor be dismayed.

Now see, in my affliction I have prepared for the house of Yahweh about 3,750 tons of gold and 37,500 tons of silver,{d} and bronze and iron beyond weighing, for it is in abundance. I have also prepared timber and stone, and you may add to them.
There are also workmen with you in abundance, cutters and workers of stone and timber, and all kinds of men who are skillful in every kind of work.
There is no counting the gold, silver, bronze, and iron. Get up and begin the work, and may Yahweh be with you.”
David also commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son, saying,

“Is not Yahweh your God with you? And has he not given you rest on every side? For he has delivered the inhabitants of the land into my hand, and the land is subdued before Yahweh and before his people.

Now set your heart and your soul to seek Yahweh your God. Arise therefore and build the sanctuary of Yahweh God, to bring the ark of the covenant of Yahweh and the holy vessels of God into the house that is to be built for the name of Yahweh.”

notes.text: This verse identifies Ornan’s threshing floor as the site of the temple; compare 2 Chronicles 3:1.
Sidonians, of Sidon (“fishing”); Tyrians, of Tyre (14:1).
Solomon (Hebrew Shelomoh) sounds like shalom, “peace.”

Hebrew “a hundred thousand talents of gold and a million talents of silver”: about 3,750 tons (3,400 metric tons) of gold and 37,500 tons (34,000 metric tons) of silver. The figures are enormous, perhaps intentionally hyperbolic; compare 29:4, 7.

verses.text: When David was old and full of days, he made Solomon his son king over Israel.{a}
And he assembled all the princes of Israel, and the priests and the Levites.
The Levites were numbered from thirty years old and upward, and their number, counted head by head, was thirty-eight thousand men.{b}
“Of these,” David said, “twenty-four thousand shall oversee the work of the house of Yahweh, six thousand shall be officers and judges,
four thousand shall be gatekeepers, and four thousand shall praise Yahweh with the instruments that I made for praise.”{c}
David divided them into divisions corresponding to the sons of Levi: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari.
Of the Gershonites: Ladan and Shimei.{d}
The sons of Ladan: Jehiel the chief, and Zetham, and Joel, three.{e}
The sons of Shimei: Shelomoth, Haziel, and Haran, three. These were the heads of the fathers’ houses of Ladan.{f}
And the sons of Shimei: Jahath, Zina, Jeush, and Beriah. These four were the sons of Shimei.{g}
Jahath was the chief, and Zizah the second; Jeush and Beriah, however, had few sons, and therefore they were reckoned as one father’s house, one assignment.{h}
The sons of Kohath: Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel, four.

The sons of Amram: Aaron and Moses. And Aaron was separated, that he should sanctify the most holy things, he and his sons forever, to burn incense before Yahweh, to minister to him, and to bless in his name forever.
But as for Moses the man of God, his sons were named among the tribe of Levi.
The sons of Moses: Gershom and Eliezer.
The sons of Gershom: Shebuel the chief.{i}
The sons of Eliezer: Rehabiah the chief. Eliezer had no other sons, but the sons of Rehabiah were very many.{j}
The sons of Izhar: Shelomith the chief.{k}
The sons of Hebron: Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, and Jekameam the fourth.{l}
The sons of Uzziel: Micah the chief, and Isshiah the second.{m}
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Mahli: Eleazar and Kish.
Eleazar died having no sons, only daughters; and their kinsmen, the sons of Kish, married them.
The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jeremoth, three.{n}

These were the sons of Levi after their fathers’ houses, even the heads of the fathers’ houses of those who were enrolled, by the number of names counted head by head, who did the work for the service of the house of Yahweh, from twenty years old and upward.{o}
For David said, “Yahweh, the God of Israel, has given rest to his people, and he dwells in Jerusalem forever.
So the Levites will no longer need to carry the tabernacle or any of its vessels for its service.”
For by the last words of David the sons of Levi were numbered from twenty years old and upward.

Their office was to be at the side of the sons of Aaron for the service of the house of Yahweh, in the courts and in the chambers, in the cleansing of everything holy, and in any work for the service of the house of God;
also for the showbread, for the fine flour for a grain offering, for the unleavened wafers, for the baked offering, for the offering mixed with oil, and for all measures of quantity and size.
They were to stand every morning to thank and praise Yahweh, and likewise at evening,
and whenever burnt offerings were presented to Yahweh on Sabbaths, at new moons, and at the festivals, in the numbers prescribed for them, always before Yahweh.
So they took responsibility for the tent of meeting and the holy place, and for assisting their relatives, Aaron’s descendants, in serving Yahweh’s house.

notes.text: Compare 1 Kings 1:1–40, where Solomon is made king amid a struggle for succession; Chronicles does not narrate that struggle.

Numbers 4:3 sets the age at thirty; Numbers 8:24 at twenty-five. In verses 24 and 27 of this chapter the age is twenty, as in 2 Chronicles 31:17 and Ezra 3:8. Verse 27 explains the change as David’s last instruction.
Hebrew “that I made”; the Septuagint reads “that he made.”
Ladan (6:17 and Exodus 6:17 Libni), perhaps “for pleasure”; Shimei, see 4:26.
Jehiel, see 15:18; Zetham, “olive tree”; Joel, see 4:35.
Some think Shimei here should be Jehiel, as Shimei’s sons follow in verse 10. Shelomoth, “peaceful”; Haziel, “God sees”; Haran, perhaps “mountaineer.”
Jahath, see 4:2; Zina (verse 11 Zizah; the Septuagint reads Ziza here), uncertain; Jeush, see 1:35; Beriah, see 7:23.
Or “a single class for duty.”
Shebuel (24:20 Shubael), perhaps “return, O God.” Gershom, see 6:16.
Rehabiah, “Yahweh has enlarged”; Eliezer, see 15:24.
Shelomith (24:22 Shelomoth), “peaceful.”
Jeriah, “Yahweh sees”; Amariah, see 6:7; Jahaziel, see 12:4; Jekameam, “may the people rise.”
Micah, see 5:5; Isshiah, see 12:6.
Mahli, see 6:19; Eder, “flock”; Jeremoth, “heights.”
See note on verse 3.

verses.text: The divisions of the sons of Aaron were these. The sons of Aaron: Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.{a}
But Nadab and Abihu died before their father and had no children, so Eleazar and Ithamar served as priests.{b}
David, with Zadok of the sons of Eleazar and Ahimelech of the sons of Ithamar, divided them according to their offices in their service.{c}
More leaders were found among Eleazar’s descendants than among Ithamar’s, so they were organized this way: sixteen family heads from Eleazar’s descendants and eight from Ithamar’s, by their families.
They divided them by lot, the one sort with the other; for there were officers of the sanctuary and officers of God both of the sons of Eleazar and of the sons of Ithamar.

Shemaiah the son of Nethanel the scribe, one of the Levites, recorded them in the presence of the king, the princes, Zadok the priest, Ahimelech the son of Abiathar, and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the priests and of the Levites: one father’s house being drawn for Eleazar, and one drawn for Ithamar.{d}
The first lot came forth to Jehoiarib, the second to Jedaiah,{e}
the third to Harim, the fourth to Seorim,{f}
the fifth to Malchijah, the sixth to Mijamin,{g}
the seventh to Hakkoz, the eighth to Abijah,{h}
the ninth to Jeshua, the tenth to Shecaniah,{i}
the eleventh to Eliashib, the twelfth to Jakim,{j}
the thirteenth to Huppah, the fourteenth to Jeshebeab,{k}
the fifteenth to Bilgah, the sixteenth to Immer,{l}
the seventeenth to Hezir, the eighteenth to Happizzez,{m}
the nineteenth to Pethahiah, the twentieth to Jehezkel,{n}
the twenty-first to Jachin, the twenty-second to Gamul,{o}
the twenty-third to Delaiah, the twenty-fourth to Maaziah.{p}
This was the order of their service for entering Yahweh’s house, following the procedure set for them by their ancestor Aaron, just as Yahweh, the God of Israel, had commanded him.
And of the rest of the sons of Levi: of the sons of Amram, Shubael; of the sons of Shubael, Jehdeiah.{q}
Of Rehabiah: of the sons of Rehabiah, Isshiah the chief.
Of the Izharites, Shelomoth; of the sons of Shelomoth, Jahath.
The sons of Hebron:{r} Jeriah the chief, Amariah the second, Jahaziel the third, Jekameam the fourth.
The sons of Uzziel, Micah; of the sons of Micah, Shamir.{s}
The brother of Micah, Isshiah; of the sons of Isshiah, Zechariah.
The sons of Merari: Mahli and Mushi. The sons of Jaaziah: Beno.{t}
The sons of Merari: of Jaaziah, Beno, Shoham, Zaccur, and Ibri.{u}
Of Mahli: Eleazar, who had no sons.
Of Kish, the sons of Kish: Jerahmeel.{v}
The sons of Mushi: Mahli, Eder, and Jerimoth. These were the sons of the Levites by their fathers’ houses.

These likewise cast lots even as their brothers the sons of Aaron, in the presence of David the king, Zadok, Ahimelech, and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the priests and of the Levites, the head of each father’s house the same as his younger brother.

notes.text: Nadab, see 2:28; Abihu, “he is my father”; Eleazar, see 6:3; Ithamar, “island of palms.”
See Leviticus 10:1–2.
Ahimelech, “my brother is king.” Compare 18:16, where the Hebrew reads Abimelech.
Hebrew “one father’s house taken for Eleazar, and taken, taken for Ithamar”; the Septuagint reads “one to Eleazar, and one to Ithamar.” Shemaiah, see 3:22; Nethanel, see 2:14.
Jehoiarib (9:10 Jehoiarib), “Yahweh contends”; Jedaiah, see 4:37. The Maccabees were of the course of Jehoiarib (1 Maccabees 2:1).
Harim, “consecrated”; Seorim, “barley.”
Malchijah, “Yahweh is king”; Mijamin, “from the right hand.”
Hakkoz, “the thorn”; Abijah, “Yahweh is father.” Zechariah the father of John the Baptist belonged to the division of Abijah (Luke 1:5).
Jeshua, “Yahweh is salvation”; Shecaniah, “Yahweh has dwelt.”
Eliashib, see 3:24; Jakim, see 8:19.
Huppah, “canopy”; Jeshebeab, perhaps “father’s dwelling.”
Bilgah, “cheerfulness”; Immer, “lamb.”
Hezir, “swine”; Happizzez, “the shattering.”
Pethahiah, “Yahweh opens”; Jehezkel, “God strengthens” (the same name as Ezekiel).
Jachin, “he establishes”; Gamul, “weaned.”
Delaiah, see 3:24; Maaziah, “Yahweh is a refuge.”
Shubael, see 23:16; Jehdeiah, “Yahweh rejoices.”
“Of Hebron” and “the chief” are supplied from 23:19; the Hebrew reads “And my sons: Jeriah.”
So the Hebrew margin (Qere); the written text (Ketiv) reads Shamur. Shamir, “thorn.”
Jaaziah, “Yahweh strengthens”; Beno, “his son.” The Hebrew of verses 26–27 is uncertain; beno may mean “his son” rather than a name.
Shoham, “onyx”; Zaccur, see 4:26; Ibri, “Hebrew.”
Jerahmeel, see 2:9; Kish, see 23:21.

verses.text: David and the army commanders also set aside for service some of the descendants of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, who were to prophesy with the music of lyres, harps, and cymbals. The list of men who did this service was:{a}
Of the sons of Asaph: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah, and Asharelah, the sons of Asaph, under the hand of Asaph, who prophesied at the king’s order.{b}

Of Jeduthun, the sons of Jeduthun: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Shimei,{c} Hashabiah, and Mattithiah, six, under the direction of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with the lyre in giving thanks and praising Yahweh.{d}
Of Heman, the sons of Heman: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, and Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, and Romamti-ezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth.{e}
All these were sons of Heman, the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up his horn;{f} and God gave Heman fourteen sons and three daughters.

They were all under the direction of their father for song in the house of Yahweh with cymbals, harps, and lyres, for the service of the house of God. Asaph, Jeduthun, and Heman were under the direction of the king.
Their number, with their brothers who were trained in singing to Yahweh, all who were skilled, was two hundred and eighty-eight.
They cast lots for their duties, small and great alike, teacher as well as pupil.
The first lot fell for Asaph to Joseph;{g} the second to Gedaliah, he and his brothers and his sons, twelve;
the third to Zaccur, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the fourth to Izri, his sons and his brothers, twelve;{h}
the fifth to Nethaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the sixth to Bukkiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the seventh to Jesharelah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;{i}
the eighth to Jeshaiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the ninth to Mattaniah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the tenth to Shimei, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the eleventh to Azarel, his sons and his brothers, twelve;{j}
the twelfth to Hashabiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the thirteenth, Shubael, his sons and his brothers, twelve;{k}
the fourteenth, Mattithiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the fifteenth, to Jeremoth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;{l}
the sixteenth, to Hananiah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the seventeenth, to Joshbekashah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the eighteenth, to Hanani, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the nineteenth, to Mallothi, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the twentieth, to Eliathah, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the twenty-first, to Hothir, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the twenty-second, to Giddalti, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the twenty-third, to Mahazioth, his sons and his brothers, twelve;
the twenty-fourth, to Romamti-ezer, his sons and his brothers, twelve.{m}

notes.text: Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, see 6:33, 39; 16:41. Here their music is called prophecy (compare 2 Kings 3:15).
Zaccur, see 4:26; Joseph, “may he add”; Nethaniah, “Yahweh has given”; Asharelah (verse 14 Jesharelah), perhaps “upright toward God.”
Shimei is supplied from verse 17; the Hebrew and the Septuagint list five names but say “six.”
Gedaliah, “Yahweh is great”; Zeri (verse 11 Izri), perhaps “balm”; Jeshaiah, “Yahweh saves”; Hashabiah, see 6:45; Mattithiah, see 9:31.

Bukkiah, “flask of Yahweh”; Mattaniah, see 9:15; Uzziel, see 4:42; Shebuel (verse 20 Shubael), see 23:16; Jerimoth (verse 22 Jeremoth), see 7:7; Hananiah, “Yahweh is gracious”; Hanani, “gracious.” The remaining names, read together, form a short prayer: “Be gracious to me, Yah, be gracious to me; you are my God (Eliathah); I have magnified (Giddalti) and I have exalted (Romamti) help (ezer); sitting in hardship (Joshbekashah), I have spoken (Mallothi); he has given abundantly (Hothir) visions (Mahazioth).”
Hebrew “to lift up the horn,” an idiom for giving strength or honor.
The Hebrew gives no number for Joseph; the total of 288 (verse 7) implies twelve for each of the twenty-four lots.
Izri, see Zeri, verse 3.
Jesharelah, see verse 2 (Asharelah).
Azarel (verse 4 Uzziel), see 12:6.
Shubael, see verse 4 (Shebuel).
Jeremoth, see verse 4 (Jerimoth).
The twenty-four musical courses parallel the twenty-four priestly courses of chapter 24.

verses.text: As for the divisions of the gatekeepers: of the Korahites, Meshelemiah the son of Kore, of the sons of Asaph.{a}
Meshelemiah had sons: Zechariah the firstborn, Jediael the second, Zebadiah the third, Jathniel the fourth,{b}
Elam the fifth, Jehohanan the sixth, Eliehoenai the seventh.{c}
Obed-edom had sons: Shemaiah the firstborn, Jehozabad the second, Joah the third, Sachar the fourth, Nethanel the fifth,{d}
Ammiel the sixth, Issachar the seventh, Peullethai the eighth; for God blessed him.{e}
Also to Shemaiah his son were sons born who ruled over their fathers’ house, for they were mighty men of valor.
The sons of Shemaiah were Othni, and Rephael, and Obed, and Elzabad, whose brothers were strong men, Elihu, and Semachiah.{f}
All these were of the sons of Obed-edom; they and their sons and their brothers were able men with strength for the service, sixty-two of Obed-edom.
Meshelemiah had sons and brothers, able men, eighteen.
Hosah, of the sons of Merari, had sons: Shimri the chief (for though he was not the firstborn, his father made him chief),{g}
Hilkiah the second, Tebaliah the third, Zechariah the fourth. All the sons and brothers of Hosah were thirteen.{h}
Of these were the divisions of the gatekeepers, by their chief men, having charges like their brothers, to minister in the house of Yahweh.
They cast lots, small and great alike, by their fathers’ houses, for each gate.
Eastward the lot fell to Shelemiah. Then for Zechariah his son, a wise counselor, they cast lots, and his lot came out northward.{i}
To Obed-edom southward, and to his sons the storehouse.{j}
To Shuppim and Hosah westward, by the gate of Shallecheth, at the causeway going up, guard beside guard.{k}
Eastward were six Levites, northward four a day, southward four a day, and for the storehouse two and two.
For the Parbar westward, four at the causeway and two at the Parbar.{l}
These were the divisions of the doorkeepers, of the sons of the Korahites and of the sons of Merari.
Of the Levites, Ahijah was over the treasures of the house of God and over the treasures of the dedicated things.{m}
The sons of Ladan, the sons of the Gershonites belonging to Ladan, the heads of the fathers’ houses belonging to Ladan the Gershonite: Jehieli.{n}
The sons of Jehieli: Zetham, and Joel his brother, over the treasures of the house of Yahweh.
Of the Amramites, the Izharites, the Hebronites, and the Uzzielites:
Shebuel the son of Gershom, the son of Moses, was ruler over the treasures.
His brothers: from Eliezer came Rehabiah his son, and Jeshaiah his son, and Joram his son, and Zichri his son, and Shelomoth his son.{o}

This Shelomoth and his brothers were over all the treasures of the dedicated things which King David and the heads of the fathers’ houses, the officers of thousands and of hundreds, and the commanders of the army had dedicated.{p}
Out of the spoil taken in the wars they dedicated things to strengthen the house of Yahweh.
Also all that Samuel the seer, and Saul the son of Kish, and Abner the son of Ner, and Joab the son of Zeruiah had dedicated, everything dedicated was in the care of Shelomoth and his brothers.{q}
Of the Izharites, Chenaniah and his sons were appointed to outside duties over Israel, as officers and judges.{r}
From the Hebronites: Hashabiah and 1,700 of his relatives, capable men, were responsible for Israel west of the Jordan in all of Yahweh’s work and in the king’s service.{s}

Of the Hebronites, Jerijah was chief of the Hebronites, according to their generations by fathers’ houses. In the fortieth year of the reign of David they were sought out, and mighty men of valor were found among them at Jazer of Gilead.{t}

King David appointed him and his brothers, two thousand seven hundred able men, heads of fathers’ houses, over the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of the Manassites, for every matter pertaining to God and for the affairs of the king.

notes.text: Meshelemiah (verse 14 Shelemiah; 9:21), “Yahweh repays”; Kore, see 9:19. “Asaph” is perhaps a copying error for Ebiasaph (9:19).
Zechariah, see 9:21; Jediael, see 7:6; Zebadiah, see 8:15; Jathniel, “God gives.”
Elam, see 8:24; Jehohanan, “Yahweh is gracious”; Eliehoenai, “my eyes are toward Yahweh.”
Obed-edom, see 13:13; Shemaiah, see 3:22; Jehozabad, “Yahweh has given”; Joah, see 6:21; Sachar, see 11:35; Nethanel, see 2:14.
Ammiel, see 3:5; Issachar, see 12:32; Peullethai, “wage of Yahweh.” The blessing recalls 13:14.
Othni, perhaps “my strength”; Rephael, “God heals”; Obed, see 2:12; Elzabad, see 12:12; Elihu, see 12:20; Semachiah, “Yahweh sustains.”
Hosah, see 16:38; Shimri, see 4:37.
Hilkiah, see 6:13; Tebaliah, “Yahweh has immersed.”
Shelemiah, see verse 1.
Hebrew “the house of the gatherings,” a storehouse.
The Hebrew “Shuppim” may be a copying repetition of the last word of verse 15. Shallecheth, “casting out.”
Parbar, perhaps “colonnade” or “court”; the meaning is uncertain.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “their brothers.” Ahijah, see 2:25.
Jehieli, a family name from Jehiel (23:8).
Joram, “Yahweh is exalted”; Zichri, see 8:19.
Shelomoth (Hebrew written text Shelomith), see 23:9.
Abner, “father of light”; Ner, see 8:33. Samuel, “name of God” or “heard by God.”
Chenaniah, see 15:22.
Hashabiah, see 6:45. Hebrew “beyond the Jordan westward,” as seen from the east; that is, west of the Jordan.
Jerijah (23:19 Jeriah), “Yahweh sees”; Jazer, “he helps.”

verses.text: Here is the roster of the Israelites: the heads of families, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and their officers who served the king in everything about the divisions that were on duty month by month through the whole year. Each division had 24,000 men:{a}
Over the first division for the first month (in March–April) was Jashobeam the son of Zabdiel; in his division were twenty-four thousand.{b}
He was of the children of Perez, the head of all the captains of the host for the first month.
Over the division of the second month (in April–May) was Dodai the Ahohite, with his division, and Mikloth was the leader; in his division were twenty-four thousand.{c}
The third army commander, for the third month (May–June), was Benaiah son of Jehoiada the priest, the chief. His division had 24,000.{d}
This Benaiah was a warrior among the Thirty and was in command of the Thirty. His division was led by his son Ammizabad.{e}
The fourth commander, for the fourth month (June–July), was Joab’s brother Asahel, and after him his son Zebadiah. His division had 24,000.{f}
The fifth commander, for the fifth month (in July–August), was Shamhuth the Izrahite; in his division were twenty-four thousand.{g}
The sixth commander, for the sixth month (August–September), was Ira son of Ikkesh from Tekoa. His division had 24,000.
The seventh commander, for the seventh month (September–October), was Helez from Pelon, a descendant of Ephraim. His division had 24,000.
The eighth commander, for the eighth month (October–November), was Sibbecai from Hushah, a Zerahite. His division had 24,000.{h}
The ninth, for the ninth month (in November–December), was Abiezer the Anathothite, of the Benjaminites; in his division were twenty-four thousand.
The tenth, for the tenth month (in December–January), was Maharai the Netophathite, of the Zerahites; in his division were twenty-four thousand.
The eleventh commander, for the eleventh month (January–February), was Benaiah from Pirathon, a descendant of Ephraim. His division had 24,000.
The twelfth commander, for the twelfth month (February–March), was Heldai from Netophah, of the family of Othniel. His division had 24,000.{i}
Furthermore, over the tribes of Israel: of the Reubenites, Eliezer the son of Zichri was ruler; of the Simeonites, Shephatiah the son of Maacah;{j}
of Levi, Hashabiah the son of Kemuel; of Aaron, Zadok;{k}
of Judah, Elihu, of the brothers of David; of Issachar, Omri the son of Michael;{l}
of Zebulun, Ishmaiah the son of Obadiah; of Naphtali, Jerimoth the son of Azriel;{m}
of the sons of Ephraim, Hoshea the son of Azaziah; of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Joel the son of Pedaiah;{n}
of the half-tribe of Manasseh in Gilead, Iddo the son of Zechariah; of Benjamin, Jaasiel the son of Abner;{o}
of Dan, Azarel the son of Jeroham. These were the princes of the tribes of Israel.{p}
David did not count those who were twenty years old or younger, since Yahweh had promised to make Israel as numerous as the stars in the sky.
Joab the son of Zeruiah began to count them, but did not finish; and for this there came wrath on Israel; neither was the number put into the account of the chronicles of King David.{q}
Over the king’s treasuries was Azmaveth the son of Adiel; and over the storehouses in the country, in the cities, in the villages, and in the towers was Jonathan the son of Uzziah.{r}
Over those who did the work of the field, tilling the ground, was Ezri the son of Chelub.{s}
Shimei from Ramah was over the vineyards, and Zabdi from Shepham was in charge of the wine stored from the vineyards.{t}
Baal-hanan from Geder was in charge of the olive and sycamore-fig trees in the foothills, and Joash was in charge of the oil supplies.{u}
Over the herds that grazed in Sharon was Shitrai the Sharonite; and over the herds in the valleys was Shaphat the son of Adlai.{v}
Obil the Ishmaelite was in charge of the camels, and Jehdeiah from Meronoth was in charge of the donkeys.{w}
Jaziz the Hagrite was in charge of the flocks. All these were officials over King David’s property.{x}
Jonathan, David’s uncle, was a counselor, a man of understanding and a scribe; and Jehiel the son of Hachmoni attended the king’s sons.{y}
Ahithophel was the king’s counselor, and Hushai the Archite was the king’s friend.{z}
After Ahithophel came Jehoiada the son of Benaiah, and Abiathar; and Joab was commander of the king’s army.{aa}

notes.text: The months in this chapter are numbered from the spring new year (Nisan); because the calendar was lunar, each month spans parts of two of ours.
Jashobeam, see 11:11; Zabdiel, “gift of God.” Perez, see 2:4.
Hebrew “Dodai the Ahohite and his division, and Mikloth the leader”; perhaps read “Eleazar the son of Dodai” (11:12). Dodai, “beloved”; Mikloth, see 8:32.
Or “the son of Jehoiada, the chief priest.” Benaiah, see 11:22.
Ammizabad, “my people has given.”
Asahel was killed by Abner before David reigned over all Israel (2 Samuel 2:23), so this list may reflect a time when his son Zebadiah held the post in his name.
Shamhuth, perhaps “desolation” (11:27 Shammoth the Harorite); Izrahite, perhaps a Zerahite of Judah.
Zerahites, of Zerah (2:4).
Heldai (11:30 Heled), “mole” or “enduring”; Othniel, “lion of God” or “God is my strength.”
Eliezer, see 15:24; Zichri, see 8:19; Shephatiah, see 3:3; Maacah, see 2:48. Gad and Asher are not listed; Levi and Aaron are counted separately.
Kemuel, “God raises up.”
The Septuagint reads Eliab, David’s eldest brother (2:13). Elihu, see 12:20; Omri, see 7:8; Michael, see 5:13.
Ishmaiah, see 12:4; Obadiah, see 12:9; Jerimoth, see 7:7; Azriel, see 5:24.
Hoshea, “salvation”; Azaziah, see 15:21; Pedaiah, see 3:18.
Iddo, see 6:21; Jaasiel, see 11:47; Abner, see 26:28.
Azarel, see 12:6; Jeroham, see 6:27.
See chapter 21. “Chronicles” here is Hebrew “the account of the days.”
Adiel, see 4:36; Uzziah, “Yahweh is strength.”
Ezri, “my help”; Chelub, see 4:11.
Ramathite, of Ramah (“height”); Zabdi, see 8:19; Shiphmite, perhaps of Shepham (Numbers 34:10).
Shephelah, “lowland,” the foothills west of Judah. Baal-hanan, “the Lord is gracious”; Gederite, of Geder; Joash, see 12:3.
Sharon, “plain”; Shitrai, perhaps “officer”; Shaphat, see 3:22; Adlai, uncertain.
Obil, “camel driver”; Ishmaelite, of Ishmael (“God hears”); Jehdeiah, see 24:20; Meronothite, of Meronoth.
Jaziz, perhaps “he moves”; Hagrite, see 5:10.
Or “nephew”; Hebrew dod, “uncle” or “beloved.” Jonathan, see 2:32; Jehiel, see 15:18; Hachmoni, “wise.”
Ahithophel, “brother of folly”; Hushai, “quick”; Archite, of the Archites (Joshua 16:2). See 2 Samuel 15:12, 32–37.
Jehoiada, see 11:22; Abiathar, see 15:11; Joab, see 2:16.

verses.text: David summoned to Jerusalem all of Israel’s officials: the tribal leaders, the commanders of the divisions serving the king, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and those in charge of all the king’s and his sons’ property and livestock, as well as the palace officials, the warriors, and every brave fighter.

Then David the king stood up on his feet and said, “Hear me, my brothers and my people! As for me, it was in my heart to build a house of rest for the ark of the covenant of Yahweh, and for the footstool of our God, and I had made ready to build it.{a}
But God told me, ‘You will not build a house for my name, since you are a warrior and have shed blood.’

Yet Yahweh, the God of Israel, selected me from my whole family to be king over Israel for all time. He chose Judah as leader, and from Judah’s clan he chose my father’s family; and among my father’s sons, he was pleased to make me king over all of Israel.
And of all my sons (for Yahweh has given me many sons) he has chosen Solomon my son to sit on the throne of the kingdom of Yahweh over Israel.{b}
He said to me, ‘Solomon your son, he shall build my house and my courts; for I have chosen him to be my son, and I will be his father.
I will establish his kingdom forever, if he is constant to do my commandments and my ordinances, as at this day.’

Now therefore, in the sight of all Israel, the assembly of Yahweh, and in the hearing of our God, keep and seek out all the commandments of Yahweh your God, that you may possess this good land and leave it as an inheritance to your children after you forever.

“You, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and with a willing mind; for Yahweh searches all hearts and understands every purpose of the thoughts. If you seek him, he will be found of you; but if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever.
Take heed now, for Yahweh has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary. Be strong and do it.”
Then David gave his son Solomon the plans for the temple porch, its buildings, its storerooms, its upper rooms, its inner rooms, and the room for the atonement cover;{c}

and the pattern of all that he had in mind{d} for the courts of the house of Yahweh, for all the chambers around, for the treasuries of the house of God, and for the treasuries of the dedicated things;
also for the divisions of the priests and the Levites, for all the work of the service of the house of Yahweh, and for all the vessels of service in the house of Yahweh;
of gold by weight for all the vessels of gold for every kind of service, and of silver by weight for all the vessels of silver for every kind of service;

the weight of gold for the lampstands and their lamps of gold, by the weight of each lampstand and its lamps; and for the lampstands of silver, silver by weight for each lampstand and its lamps, according to the use of each lampstand;
and the weight of gold for each of the tables for the bread of the Presence, and silver for the silver tables;
and pure gold for the forks, the basins, and the cups; and for the golden bowls, gold by weight for each bowl; and for the silver bowls, silver by weight for each bowl;
and for the altar of incense, refined gold by weight; and gold for the pattern of the chariot, the cherubim that spread their wings and covered the ark of the covenant of Yahweh.{e}
“All this,” said David, “he made clear to me in writing from the hand of Yahweh, all the works of this pattern.”{f}

Then David said to Solomon his son, “Be strong and courageous, and do it. Do not be afraid or dismayed, for Yahweh God, my God, is with you. He will not leave you nor forsake you, until all the work for the service of the house of Yahweh is completed.

Behold, there are the divisions of the priests and the Levites for all the service of the house of God; and there shall be with you in all kinds of work every willing, skillful man, for any manner of service; also the captains and all the people will be entirely at your command.”

notes.text: The ark as God’s footstool: compare Psalms 99:5; 132:7.
The kingdom is called “the kingdom of Yahweh”; compare 17:14; 29:23.
Hebrew “the house of the covering” (kapporet), the gold lid of the ark (Exodus 25:17–22).
Hebrew “that was with him by the spirit,” or “that he had by the Spirit.”
The cherubim are pictured as God’s chariot throne; compare Ezekiel 1; 10.
Or “All this he made clear to me in writing, because the hand of Yahweh was upon me.” The Hebrew is difficult.

verses.text: King David said to all the assembly, “Solomon my son, whom alone God has chosen, is young and inexperienced, and the work is great; for the palace is not for man but for Yahweh God.{a}

With all my strength I have provided for the house of my God: gold for the gold objects, silver for the silver, bronze for the bronze, iron for the iron, and wood for the wooden objects; and also onyx, stones for setting, antimony and stones of many colors, every kind of precious stone, and large amounts of marble.{b}
Moreover, because I delight in the house of my God, I have a treasure of my own of gold and silver, and I give it to the house of my God, over and above all that I have provided for the holy house:
about 112 tons of gold, of the gold of Ophir, and about 262 tons of refined silver, for overlaying the walls of the houses,{c}
gold for gold objects and silver for silver objects, and for all the work the craftsmen will do. Now who is willing to give himself today to Yahweh by contributing?”{d}
Then the family heads, the tribal leaders of Israel, the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, and the officials in charge of the king’s work gave willingly.
They gave for the service of the house of God about 188 tons of gold and about 185 pounds in gold coins,{e} about 375 tons of silver, about 675 tons of bronze, and about 3,750 tons of iron.{f}
Anyone who owned precious stones gave them to the treasury of Yahweh’s house, under the care of Jehiel the Gershonite.{g}
Then the people rejoiced, for they offered willingly, because with a perfect heart they offered willingly to Yahweh. David the king also rejoiced with great joy.
Therefore David blessed Yahweh in the presence of all the assembly, and David said: “Blessed are you, Yahweh, the God of Israel our father, forever and ever.{h}

Yours, Yahweh, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty; for all that is in the heavens and in the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, Yahweh, and you are exalted as head over all.{i}
Riches and honor come from before you, and you are ruler over all. In your hand is power and might; it is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to everyone.
Now therefore, our God, we thank you, and praise your glorious name.
“But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and of your own we have given you.
We are foreigners and temporary residents in your sight, just as our ancestors all were. Our days on earth are like a shadow that passes, and nothing remains.{j}
Yahweh our God, all this store that we have prepared to build you a house for your holy name comes from your hand, and is all your own.

My God, I know that you examine the heart and take pleasure in honesty. In the honesty of my heart I have given all these things willingly, and now I have seen with joy your people here giving willingly to you.
Yahweh, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, our fathers, keep this forever in the inclinations of the thoughts of the heart of your people, and direct their heart toward you.
Give my son Solomon a wholehearted desire to keep your commands, your statutes, and your decrees, to carry out all of them, and to build the palace for which I have made these preparations.”
Then David said to all the assembly, “Now bless Yahweh your God.” And all the assembly blessed Yahweh, the God of their fathers, and bowed down and worshiped Yahweh and the king.{k}

On the next day they offered sacrifices to Yahweh and offered burnt offerings to Yahweh: a thousand bulls, a thousand rams, and a thousand lambs, with their drink offerings, and sacrifices in abundance for all Israel.
They ate and drank before Yahweh on that day with great gladness. And they made Solomon the son of David king a second time, and anointed him to Yahweh to be prince, and Zadok to be priest.{l}
Then Solomon sat on the throne of Yahweh as king in place of David his father; and he prospered, and all Israel obeyed him.
All the officials and the mighty men, and also all the sons of King David, pledged their allegiance to Solomon the king.{m}
Yahweh magnified Solomon exceedingly in the sight of all Israel, and bestowed on him such royal majesty as had not been on any king before him in Israel.
Thus David the son of Jesse reigned over all Israel.
The time that he reigned over Israel was forty years: he reigned seven years in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.{n}
He died at a good old age, full of days, riches, and honor; and Solomon his son reigned in his place.
Now the acts of King David, first and last, are written in the records of Samuel the seer, in the records of Nathan the prophet, and in the records of Gad the seer,{o}
with all his reign and his might, and the times that went over him, and over Israel, and over all the kingdoms of the lands.

notes.text: Hebrew birah, “citadel” or “palace,” a late word used here of the temple.
The identity of several of these stones is uncertain. “Antimony” (Hebrew pukh) was used as eye paint; others take it as a dark or inlay stone.

Hebrew “three thousand talents of gold … seven thousand talents of refined silver”: about 102 metric tons of gold and 238 metric tons of silver. Ophir, a land famous for gold, perhaps in southern Arabia or east Africa.
Hebrew “to fill his hand,” an idiom for consecration.

Hebrew “ten thousand darics,” about 84 kilograms. The daric (Hebrew ’adarkon) was a Persian gold coin of about 8.4 grams, first minted under Darius I (about 515 B.C.). Its mention here is an anachronism: the writer gives the value in the currency of his own day. Some take the word as drachmas.

Hebrew “five thousand talents … ten thousand talents of silver, eighteen thousand talents of bronze, and a hundred thousand talents of iron”: about 170 metric tons of gold, 340 metric tons of silver, 612 metric tons of bronze, and 3,400 metric tons of iron.
Jehiel, see 23:8.
Verses 10–13 are often called David’s prayer. The doxology added to the Lord’s Prayer in some late manuscripts of Matthew 6:13 echoes verse 11.
Or “and you are exalted over all as head.”
Or “and there is no hope.”
Bowing before the king is an act of honor, not of worship as given to God; the same Hebrew verb is used for both.
“A second time” refers back to 23:1. Compare 1 Kings 1:32–40, where Solomon is anointed by Zadok and Nathan.
Hebrew “gave a hand under Solomon.”
Compare 2 Samuel 5:4–5 and 1 Kings 2:11, where David reigned seven years and six months in Hebron.
Hebrew “in the words of Samuel the seer.” These sources may be the books of Samuel or other prophetic records.

books.name: 2 Chronicles
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where Chronicles is called Paraleipomena, “things left out”), using Brenton’s public-domain English translation, and against the parallel passages in Genesis, Samuel, Kings, and the Psalms. Only a very small Dead Sea Scrolls fragment of Chronicles survives; it is mentioned only in general terms. Where Chronicles differs from its parallels in names, numbers, or wording, the footnotes say so. Each personal and place name receives a brief note on its meaning at its first mention in Chronicles; many such meanings are uncertain, and the notes say so. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which in places differs from the Hebrew; the footnotes give the Hebrew numbering where they differ. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes, and dates are given with their modern-month spans.

verses.text: Solomon the son of David strengthened himself in his kingdom, and Yahweh his God was with him and made him exceedingly great.{a}
Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel, the heads of the fathers’ houses.
Solomon and the whole assembly with him went to the high place at Gibeon, because God’s tent of meeting was there, the one that Moses the servant of Yahweh had made in the desert.{b}
But the ark of God David had brought up from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.{c}
And the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was there before the tabernacle of Yahweh; and Solomon and the assembly sought it.{d}
Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before Yahweh, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
In that night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask what I shall give you.”
Solomon said to God, “You have shown great steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place.
Now, Yahweh God, may the promise you made to my father David come true, for you have made me king over a people as countless as the dust of the earth.
Give me now wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this great people of yours?”

God said to Solomon, “Since this was your desire, and you did not ask for riches, wealth, or honor, or for the death of those who hate you, or even for a long life, but asked for wisdom and knowledge to govern my people, over whom I have made you king,
Wisdom and knowledge are granted to you. On top of that, I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, more than any king before you has had or any king after you will have.”
So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem; and he reigned over Israel.{e}
Solomon collected chariots and horsemen. He had 1,400 chariots and 12,000 horsemen, which he kept in the chariot cities and near himself in Jerusalem.{f}
The king made silver and gold in Jerusalem as common as stones, and he made cedars as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah.{g}
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s traders bought them from Kue at a price.{h}
A chariot imported from Egypt cost about 15 pounds of silver, and a horse about 3¾ pounds. They were also sold on to all the kings of the Hittites and the kings of Aram.{i}

notes.text: Verses 1–13 parallel 1 Kings 3:4–15. Solomon, from shalom, “peace.” David, “beloved.”

Gibeon, “hill.” Chronicles explains why Solomon worshiped at Gibeon: the tent of meeting was there (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29). Moses, perhaps Egyptian “born,” associated in Exodus 2:10 with Hebrew “drawn out.”
Kiriath-jearim, “city of forests.” Jerusalem, perhaps “foundation of Shalem” or “city of peace.” See 1 Chronicles 13; 15.

Bezalel, “in the shadow of God”; Uri, “my light” or “fiery”; Hur, perhaps “white” or “noble.” The Hebrew vowels read “he had put” (sam) before the tabernacle; the Septuagint reads “was there” (sham), with the same consonants. “Sought it” may mean “sought him,” that is, Yahweh.
Hebrew “to the high place.” The Septuagint reads “from the high place,” as the context requires.
Verses 14–17 parallel 1 Kings 10:26–29; compare 2 Chronicles 9:25–28.
The Shephelah (“lowland”) is the foothill region west of Judah.
Egypt, Hebrew Mitsrayim. Kue is probably Cilicia in southeastern Asia Minor. Some interpreters read “Muzri,” a land in Asia Minor, for “Egypt” in these verses.

Hebrew “six hundred of silver … a hundred and fifty,” probably shekels: about 6.9 kilograms and 1.7 kilograms. Hittites, descendants of Heth; Aram, perhaps “highland,” here the Aramean kingdoms of Syria.

verses.text: Solomon purposed to build a house for the name of Yahweh, and a royal house for himself.{a}
Solomon counted out seventy thousand men to bear burdens, eighty thousand men to quarry stone in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them.{b}
Solomon sent this message to Huram king of Tyre: “Deal with me as you dealt with my father David, to whom you supplied cedar for building the house where he would live.{c}

Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of Yahweh my God, to dedicate it to him, to burn before him incense of sweet spices, for the continual showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and at the appointed feasts of Yahweh our God. This is for Israel forever.
The house that I build is great, for our God is greater than all gods.
Yet who can build a house for him, when the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot hold him? Who am I to build him a house, other than a place for burning incense in his presence?

Now therefore send me a man skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue, who knows how to engrave engravings, to be with the skilled men who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.{d}
Send me also cedar trees, cypress trees, and algum trees out of Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon; and behold, my servants will be with your servants,{e}
even to prepare me timber in plenty; for the house that I am about to build shall be great and wonderful.

Behold, to your servants, the woodcutters who cut the timber, I will give about 120,000 bushels of crushed wheat, about 120,000 bushels of barley, about 120,000 gallons of wine, and about 120,000 gallons of oil.”{f}
Huram king of Tyre wrote a letter in reply to Solomon: “It is because Yahweh loves his people that he has made you their king.”

Huram also said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth, who has given King David a wise son, endowed with discretion and understanding, who will build a house for Yahweh and a royal house for himself.
I am now sending you Huram-abi,{g} a skilled man with great understanding,

His mother belonged to the tribe of Dan, and his father was a Tyrian. He is trained to work in gold, silver, bronze, and iron, in stone and wood, and in purple, blue, and crimson thread and fine linen. He can do any kind of engraving and can carry out any design given to him, working with your craftsmen and those of my lord, your father David.{h}
Now let my lord send his servants the wheat, barley, olive oil, and wine that he promised.
We will cut as many trees from Lebanon as you need and float them in rafts down the sea to Joppa, and you can haul them up to Jerusalem.”{i}
Solomon took a count of all the foreigners living in Israel, following the census his father David had taken, and the total was 153,600.{j}
He made seventy thousand of them bearers of burdens, eighty thousand quarriers in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred overseers to make the people work.

notes.text: In Hebrew, 2:1 is 1:18, and 2:2–18 are 2:1–17. Verses 1–18 parallel 1 Kings 5:1–18 (Hebrew 5:15–32).
First Kings 5:16 gives three thousand three hundred overseers. Adding the chief officers (8:10 two hundred fifty; 1 Kings 9:23 five hundred fifty), both books reach a total of 3,850.
Huram, a form of Hiram (as in Kings), perhaps “my brother is exalted.” Tyre, “rock.”
Judah, associated with “praise” (Genesis 29:35).
Lebanon, “white,” from its snow-capped mountains. Algum is an unidentified fine wood; 1 Kings 10:11 has almug.

Hebrew gives 20,000 cors each of crushed wheat and barley, and 20,000 baths each of wine and oil. A cor is about 6 bushels (220 liters), and a bath about 6 gallons (22 liters), so the totals are about 4,400,000 liters each of wheat and barley, and 440,000 liters each of wine and oil. First Kings 5:11 lists twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of beaten oil (the Septuagint of Kings has twenty thousand baths).
Huram-abi, “Huram is my father,” or “Huram my master craftsman”; 1 Kings 7:13 calls him Hiram.
First Kings 7:14 says his mother was a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. She may have been of Danite descent living in Naphtali, or the traditions differ. Dan, “judge.”
Joppa, “beautiful,” the port of modern Jaffa.
Compare 1 Chronicles 22:2.

verses.text: Solomon began building Yahweh’s house in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, the place where Yahweh had shown himself to his father David. It was at the site David had prepared, the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.{a}
He began to build on the second day of the second month (in April–May), in the fourth year of his reign.{b}
These are the foundations that Solomon laid for building the house of God: the length, by the old standard of measure, was ninety feet, and the breadth thirty feet.{c}
The porch in front of the house was thirty feet long, matching the breadth of the house, and its height was a hundred and eighty feet; and he overlaid it inside with pure gold.{d}
The great house he paneled with cypress wood, overlaid it with fine gold, and carved palm trees and chains on it.{e}
He adorned the house with precious stones for beauty; and the gold was gold of Parvaim.{f}
He overlaid also the house, the beams, the thresholds, and its walls, and its doors, with gold; and engraved cherubim on the walls.
He built the Most Holy Place. It was 30 feet long, matching the width of the temple, and 30 feet wide. He covered it with about 22½ tons of fine gold.{g}
The weight of the nails was about a pound and a quarter of gold. He overlaid the upper rooms with gold.{h}
In the room of the most holy place he made two cherubim of sculptured work, and they overlaid them with gold.{i}

The wings of the cherubim together were thirty feet long: one wing of the first, seven and a half feet, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, seven and a half feet, touched the wing of the other cherub.{j}
And one wing of the other cherub, seven and a half feet, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, seven and a half feet, joined the wing of the first cherub.
The wings of these cherubim spread out thirty feet. They stood on their feet, facing the house.{k}
He made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, and worked cherubim on it.{l}
In front of the house he made two pillars about fifty-two feet high, and the capital on the top of each was seven and a half feet.{m}
He made chains in the inner sanctuary and put them on the tops of the pillars; and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains.{n}
He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right hand and the other on the left; and called the name of the one on the right hand Jachin, and the name of the one on the left Boaz.{o}

notes.text: Moriah, perhaps “Yahweh provides” or “seen by Yahweh”; only here and in Genesis 22:2 (“the land of Moriah”), linking the temple site with the place of Isaac’s offering. Ornan, see 1 Chronicles 21:15; Jebusite, of Jebus (“trodden place”), the old name of Jerusalem. Verses 1–17 parallel 1 Kings 6–7.

Hebrew “in the second month, on the second”; the second “on the second” is lacking in the Septuagint and may be a copying error. The second month is Ziv (1 Kings 6:1), later Iyyar, counting from the spring new year. First Kings 6:1 dates this to the 480th year after the exodus.

Hebrew “the length in cubits after the first measure was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits,” about 27 by 9 meters, taking a cubit as 18 inches (45 centimeters). “The first measure” was probably an older, longer cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters), which would give about 102 by 34 feet. Compare 1 Kings 6:2, which also gives a height of thirty cubits.
Hebrew “twenty cubits … a hundred and twenty,” about 9 and 54 meters. Some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac read “twenty cubits” for the height; 1 Kings 6:3 gives no height for the porch.
“Great house” is the main hall (the holy place).
Parvaim, an unidentified source of gold, perhaps in Arabia.
Hebrew “six hundred talents,” about 20 metric tons, taking a talent as about 75 pounds (34 kilograms). Each dimension here is twenty cubits (about 9 meters).
Hebrew “fifty shekels,” about 575 grams.
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “sculptured work” (tsa‘atsu‘im) is uncertain.
Hebrew “twenty cubits … five cubits”: about 9 meters, and 2.3 meters for each wing. Compare 1 Kings 6:23–28, where the cherubim are of olive wood, ten cubits high.
Or “toward the main hall.”
First Kings does not mention the veil at this point, but describes doors of olive wood (1 Kings 6:31–32).

Hebrew “thirty-five cubits … five cubits,” about 16 meters and 2.3 meters. First Kings 7:15, 2 Kings 25:17, and Jeremiah 52:21 give eighteen cubits (about 27 feet; 8.1 meters) for each pillar; thirty-five may be their combined length, or a different measure. First Kings 7:16 gives the capitals as five cubits; 2 Kings 25:17 gives three.
Hebrew “in the inner sanctuary” (baddevir); many scholars emend to “like a necklace” (karabid), since the chains were on the pillars outside.
Jachin, “he establishes”; Boaz, perhaps “in him is strength.”

verses.text: He made an altar of bronze, thirty feet long, thirty feet broad, and fifteen feet high.{a}
Then he made the Sea of cast metal, fifteen feet from brim to brim, round all about; its height was seven and a half feet, and a line of forty-five feet measured its circumference.{b}
Beneath it, all around, were figures of oxen encircling it, ten to every foot and a half, surrounding the Sea; the oxen were in two rows, cast together with it.{c}

It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east; and the Sea was set on them above, and all their hind parts were toward the center.
Its thickness was about three inches, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily; it could hold about eighteen thousand gallons.{d}
He also made ten basins for washing, and set five on the right and five on the left. In them they rinsed what was used for the burnt offering, but the Sea was for the priests to wash in.
He made the ten lampstands of gold as prescribed for them, and set them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.{e}
He made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left; and he made a hundred basins of gold.{f}
He made the court of the priests and the great court, and doors for the court, and overlaid their doors with bronze.
He set the Sea at the right side of the house, to the southeast.
Huram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Huram completed the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God:{g}
the two pillars, the two bowl-shaped tops on the pillars, and the two networks covering the bowls on top of the pillars;
and the 400 pomegranates for the two networks, with two rows of pomegranates on each network covering the bowl-shaped tops on the pillars.
He made the stands, and the basins on the stands;{h}
the one Sea, and the twelve oxen under it.
Huram-abi made the pots, shovels, forks, and all the related tools from polished bronze for King Solomon, for Yahweh’s house.{i}
In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.{j}
Solomon made all these utensils in very great quantity, for the weight of the bronze was not sought out.
Solomon made all the furnishings for God’s house: the gold altar, and the tables for the bread of the Presence,{k}
and the lampstands with their lamps of pure gold, to burn according to the ordinance in front of the inner sanctuary;
the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold, of the most perfect gold;

the snuffers, the basins, the dishes for incense, and the fire pans, of pure gold; and as for the entrance of the house, its inner doors to the most holy place and the doors of the house, the main hall, were of gold.{l}

notes.text: Hebrew “twenty cubits long, twenty cubits broad, and ten cubits high,” about 9 by 9 by 4.5 meters. This altar is not described in the standard text of 1 Kings 7, though 1 Kings 8:64 and 9:25 mention it. Verses 2–5 parallel 1 Kings 7:23–26.
Hebrew “ten cubits … five cubits … thirty cubits”: about 4.5 meters across, 2.3 meters high, and 13.5 meters around. The round figure thirty for the circumference is an approximation.
Hebrew “ten in a cubit.” First Kings 7:24 has “gourds” (peqa‘im) instead of “oxen” (beqarim); the two Hebrew words look alike.

Hebrew “a handbreadth” (about 7.5 centimeters) and “three thousand baths” (about 66,000 liters). First Kings 7:26 gives two thousand baths (about 12,000 gallons; 44,000 liters). Chronicles may include the capacity to the brim, or the figures reflect different measures.
Compare Exodus 25:31–40; 1 Kings 7:49 also has ten lampstands.
Or “bowls” for sprinkling.
Huram, see 2:3. Verses 11–22 parallel 1 Kings 7:40–50. Hebrew “Huram” here and “Huram-abi” in verse 16; Kings has Hiram.
Hebrew “he made the stands, and he made the basins”; compare 1 Kings 7:43.
Hebrew “Huram his father”; see 2:13.
Jordan, “descender.” Succoth, “booths.” Zeredah (1 Kings 7:46 Zarethan), perhaps “cooling.”
Hebrew “bread of the face”; see 1 Chronicles 9:32.
Or “the hinges of the doors”; compare 1 Kings 7:50.

verses.text: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of Yahweh was finished. And Solomon brought in the holy things of David his father, the silver, the gold, and all the vessels, and put them in the treasuries of the house of God.{a}
Then Solomon assembled in Jerusalem the elders of Israel and all the tribal heads, the family leaders of the Israelites, to bring up Yahweh’s covenant ark from the city of David, which is Zion.{b}
And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast in the seventh month (in September–October).{c}
All the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.{d}
They brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests, the Levites, brought them up.{e}
King Solomon and the entire community of Israel who had assembled with him stood in front of the ark and sacrificed so many sheep and cattle that no one could record or count them.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of Yahweh to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, the most holy place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles from above.
The poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the ark in front of the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside; and it is there to this day.{f}
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets Moses had placed there at Horeb, where Yahweh made a covenant with the Israelites after they came out of Egypt.{g}
Now when the priests came out of the holy place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without keeping to their divisions,{h}
