Nehemiah was not a priest; for a layman to enter the temple building was forbidden (Numbers 18:7).

Hebrew Elul, the sixth month, which fell in August–September; in 445 BC its twenty-fifth day fell about the beginning of October. Fifty-two days of work means the building began early in the fifth month, Av (July–August).

verses.text: When the wall was built and I had hung the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites were appointed,
I put Jerusalem in the charge of Hanani my brother and of Hananiah, the commander of the citadel, for he was a faithful man who feared God beyond many.

And I said{a} to them, “The gates of Jerusalem must stay closed until the sun is hot; while the gatekeepers stand at their posts, have them close the doors and fasten them. And set watches drawn from those who live in Jerusalem, every man at his station and every man in front of his house.”
Now the city was broad and large, with few people in it, and the houses had not been built.

And my God put it into my heart to bring together the nobles, the officials, and the people, to enroll them by their genealogy. I came upon the register of the genealogy of those who came up at the beginning, and I found in it this record:{b}
These are the people of the province who came back from captivity in exile, the ones King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had deported. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah,{c} Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:
the sons of Parosh, 2,172;
the sons of Shephatiah, 372;
the sons of Arah, 652;
the sons of Pahath-moab, of the sons of Jeshua and Joab, 2,818;
the sons of Elam, 1,254;
the sons of Zattu, 845;
the sons of Zaccai, 760;

The Levites: the descendants of Jeshua, that is, of Kadmiel through the line of Hodevah, 74.

The temple servants: the sons of Ziha, of Hasupha, of Tabbaoth,
the sons of Keros, of Sia, of Padon,
the sons of Lebana, of Hagaba, of Shalmai,
the sons of Hanan, of Giddel, of Gahar,

the sons of Bakbuk, of Hakupha, of Harhur,
the sons of Bazlith, of Mehida, of Harsha,
the sons of Barkos, of Sisera, of Temah,
the sons of Neziah, and of Hatipha.
Of Solomon’s servants: the sons of Sotai, of Sophereth, of Perida,
the sons of Jaala, of Darkon, of Giddel,
the sons of Shephatiah, of Hattil, of Pochereth-hazzebaim, and of Amon.
The temple servants together with the sons of Solomon’s servants totaled 392.
And these went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they were unable to show their fathers’ house and their lineage, whether they were of Israel:
the sons of Delaiah, of Tobiah, and of Nekoda, 642.
And from the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai (this man had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and taken their name).
These searched for their entry among those enrolled in the genealogies, but it was not found, and so they were barred from the priesthood as unclean.
The governor{e} told them that they were not to eat any of the most holy food until a priest should arise to consult the Urim and Thummim.
The whole assembly together was 42,360,
besides their male and female servants, who were 7,337. And they had 245 singing men and singing women.
Their horses were 736, their mules 245,{f}
their camels 435, and their donkeys 6,720.
Some of the family heads contributed to the work. The governor gave the treasury 1,000 gold darics (about 18½ pounds of gold),{g} 50 bowls, and 530 priestly garments.
Some of the family heads gave the treasury for the work 20,000 gold darics (about 370 pounds of gold){h} and about 1⅓ tons of silver.{i}
And what the rest of the people gave was 20,000 gold darics (about 370 pounds of gold), about 1¼ tons of silver,{j} and 67 priests’ garments.

The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all the rest of Israel settled in their own towns. When the seventh month (September–October){k} arrived, the Israelites were living in their towns.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and he said.”
Verses 6–73 repeat Ezra 2:1–70 with many small differences in names and numbers.
Ezra 2:2 has Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mispar, and Rehum for Azariah, Raamiah, Mispereth, and Nehum, and lacks Nahamani.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Nephushsim.
Hebrew Tirshatha, a Persian title, perhaps “His Excellency.” See Ezra 2:63.
This verse is lacking in most Hebrew manuscripts; it is supplied from some manuscripts and from Ezra 2:66. As a result, verses 69–73 in this translation are numbered 68–72 in the Hebrew.
Hebrew darkemonim, the Persian gold daric (or perhaps the Greek drachma). A daric weighed about 0.3 ounce (8.4 grams), so 1,000 darics weighed about 8.4 kilograms.
That is, about 168 kilograms.
Hebrew “2,200 minas of silver.” A mina was about 1¼ pounds (575 grams), so 2,200 minas is about 2,750 pounds (1,265 kilograms).
Hebrew “2,000 minas of silver,” about 2,500 pounds (1,150 kilograms).
Hebrew “the seventh month,” Tishri, which fell in September–October; here the autumn of 445 BC.

verses.text: All the people assembled together in the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which Yahweh had given to Israel.{a}
So on the first day of the seventh month (September–October),{b} Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly of men and women and everyone able to understand what they heard.

He read in it before the square in front of the Water Gate from first light until midday, before the men and women and all who could understand; and all the people listened closely to the Book of the Law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform{c} made for this purpose. Beside him on his right stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah; and on his left stood Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood.
And Ezra blessed Yahweh, the great God, and all the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped Yahweh with their faces to the ground.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah—the Levites—were explaining the Law to the people, as the people stood in their places.
They read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly,{d} and they gave the meaning, and made the reading understood.

Then Nehemiah the governor,{e} Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people told everyone, “This day is holy to Yahweh your God. Do not mourn or weep.” The people had all been weeping as they heard the words of the Law.
Nehemiah said, “Go and enjoy rich food and sweet drinks, and send some to anyone who has nothing ready, since this day is holy to our Lord.{f} Do not be sad, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
The Levites, too, were quieting all the people and saying, “Hush, for the day is holy; do not grieve.”
Then all the people went off to eat and drink, to send portions to others, and to celebrate with great joy, because they had grasped the words that were explained to them.
On the second day, the heads of families from among all the people, together with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law.
And they found it written in the Law that Yahweh had commanded by Moses that the sons of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month,{g}

and that they were to announce and spread the word through all their towns and in Jerusalem: “Go out to the hill country and fetch boughs of olive and of wild olive, of myrtle and palm and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.”

So the people went out and brought branches and built themselves booths, each on his own roof, in their courtyards, in the courtyards of God’s house, and in the squares by the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim.

So the whole assembly who had come back from the captivity made booths and dwelt in them; for since the days of Jeshua{h} son of Nun until that day the sons of Israel had not done it. And the joy was exceedingly great.
And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.

notes.text: Nehemiah 7:73b–8:12 is retold in the Greek book 1 Esdras (9:37–55), which ends with this scene.
Hebrew “the first day of the seventh month,” the day of trumpet blasts (Leviticus 23:24), which later became the Jewish New Year (Rosh Hashanah).
Hebrew “a tower of wood.”
Or “with interpretation,” perhaps meaning that the Hebrew was explained or translated into Aramaic, the everyday language of the time.
Hebrew Tirshatha, a Persian title; see Ezra 2:63.
Hebrew Adonai.
See Leviticus 23:33–43. The Feast of Booths (Sukkot, or Tabernacles) began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (September–October).
Jeshua is a later form of the name Joshua.

verses.text: On the twenty-fourth day of this month (in September–October){a} the sons of Israel gathered, fasting, wearing sackcloth, with dust upon them.
And the offspring of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.
And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of Yahweh their God for about three hours;{b} for another three hours they made confession and worshiped Yahweh their God.
On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and they called out loudly to Yahweh their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, “Stand up and bless Yahweh your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.

“You alone are Yahweh.{c} You made the heavens, even the highest heavens, with all their host; the earth and everything on it; the seas and everything in them. You give life to all of them, and the host of heaven bows down to you.
You are Yahweh God, who chose Abram, brought him out from Ur of the Chaldeans, and named him Abraham.{d}

You found his heart faithful toward you and cut a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites—to give it to his seed. And you have fulfilled your words, because you are righteous.
“And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea,{e}

You gave signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants, and against all the people of his land, for you knew how proudly they dealt with them; and you made yourself a name that remains to this day.
And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.
By a pillar of cloud you led them by day, and by a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should go.
You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them just rulings and true laws, and good decrees and commands.
You made your holy Sabbath known to them, and through your servant Moses you gave them commands, decrees, and a law.

When they were hungry you gave them bread from heaven, and when they were thirsty you brought them water from the rock. You told them to go in and take over the land you had promised with an oath to give them.
“But they, our fathers, behaved proudly; they hardened their necks and would not listen to your commandments.

They would not listen; they did not call to mind your wonders that you had done among them, but hardened their necks and in their rebellion set up a head to go back to their bondage.{f} But you are a God of pardons, gracious and compassionate, long-suffering and great in steadfast love,{g} and you did not abandon them.
Even when they cast for themselves an image of a calf and said, ‘This is your God, who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and committed terrible blasphemies,

you did not abandon them in the desert, because of your great compassion. By day the pillar of cloud did not leave them but guided them on their path, and by night the pillar of fire lit up the way they were to go.
You gave your good Spirit to teach them. You did not hold back your manna from their mouths, and you gave them water when they were thirsty.
For forty years you fed them in the wilderness; they wanted for nothing. Their garments did not wear out, and their feet did not swell.
You gave them kingdoms and peoples and parceled them out as a border.{h} They took the land of Sihon—that is,{i} the land of the king of Heshbon—and the land of Og king of Bashan as their own.
You made their sons as many as the stars of the sky, and you brought them into the land of which you had told their fathers that they would go in to possess it.

So their descendants entered and took possession of the land. You subdued the Canaanites who lived there and handed them over to your people, along with their kings and the peoples of the land, to deal with as they wished.

They took strong cities and fertile ground, and came to own houses filled with every good thing, cisterns dug out, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in plenty. They ate, were satisfied, grew fat, and reveled in your great goodness.
“Yet they disobeyed and rebelled against you; they threw your law behind their backs and killed your prophets, who testified against them to bring them back to you; and they committed great contempt.

So you handed them over to their foes, who oppressed them. In their time of distress they cried to you, and you heard from heaven, and in your great compassion you gave them saviors to save them out of the hand of their foes.

Yet as soon as they had relief, they went back to doing evil before you. So you abandoned them to their enemies, who ruled over them. Again they cried out to you, and from heaven you heard and delivered them, time after time, in your compassion.

You testified against them to bring them back to your law, but they acted proudly and would not listen to your commandments; they sinned against your ordinances, by which a man who does them shall live.{j} They turned away a defiant shoulder, hardened their necks, and would not listen.
For many years you put up with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets, but they would not pay attention. So you gave them into the hands of the peoples around them.
Yet in your abundant compassion you did not make a full end of them or abandon them, for you are a God gracious and compassionate.

“And now, our God, great, mighty, and awesome God, who keeps covenant and faithful love: do not let all the hardship that has come on us seem small to you, on our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors, and all your people, from the time of the kings of Assyria until today.
You are in the right in all that has come on us; you have acted in faithfulness, while we have done wickedly.
Our kings, our officials, our priests, and our fathers have not done your law, nor heeded your commandments and the testimonies with which you warned them.
In their kingdom, with the great goodness you gave them, and in the broad and fertile land you put before them, they did not serve you, nor did they turn back from their evil deeds.
Look—today we are slaves, slaves in the very land you gave our fathers to eat its fruit and its good things.
Its plentiful harvest belongs to the kings whom you set over us because of our sins; they have power over our bodies and our cattle at their pleasure, and we are in great distress.
“For all this we are making a sure agreement and writing it, and on the sealed copy are our officials, our Levites, and our priests.”{k}

notes.text: Hebrew “the twenty-fourth day of this month,” the seventh month, Tishri, two days after the close of the Feast of Booths.
Hebrew “a quarter of the day.” The daylight hours were about twelve, so a quarter was about three hours.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a shorter spelling of “you.” The Septuagint begins the verse “And Ezra said.”
Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham was understood as “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
So the traditional Hebrew text. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint read “in Egypt,” that is, “set up a head to return to their bondage in Egypt” (compare Numbers 14:4).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and steadfast love.”
Or “allotted them as a boundary.”
Or “and.”
See Leviticus 18:5.
In the Hebrew text this verse is 10:1, and 10:1–39 is numbered 10:2–40.

verses.text: On the seals were the names of{a} Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah,
Seraiah, Azariah, and Jeremiah,
Pashhur, Amariah, and Malchijah,
Hattush, Shebaniah, and Malluch,
Harim, Meremoth, and Obadiah,
Daniel, Ginnethon, and Baruch,
Meshullam, Abijah, and Mijamin,
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
And the Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;
and their relatives Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, and Hanan,
Mica, Rehob, and Hashabiah,
Zaccur, Sherebiah, and Shebaniah,
Hodiah, Bani, and Beninu.
The leaders of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, and Bani,
Bunni, Azgad, and Bebai,
Adonijah, Bigvai, and Adin,
Ater, Hezekiah, and Azzur,
Hodiah, Hashum, and Bezai,
Hariph, Anathoth, and Nebai,{b}
Magpiash, Meshullam, and Hezir,
Meshezabel, Zadok, and Jaddua,
Pelatiah, Hanan, and Anaiah,
Hoshea, Hananiah, and Hasshub,
Hallohesh, Pilha, and Shobek,
Rehum, Hashabnah, and Maaseiah,
Ahiah, Hanan, and Anan,
Malluch, Harim, and Baanah.

The rest of the people, including the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the surrounding peoples to follow the Law of God, along with their wives and all their sons and daughters who were old enough to understand,

they hold fast with their brothers, their nobles, and come under a curse and an oath to walk in the Law of God given through Moses, God’s servant, and to keep and perform every commandment of Yahweh our Lord,{c} with his ordinances and statutes.
We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.

If the peoples of the land bring wares or grain of any sort on the day of the Sabbath to sell, we will buy none of it from them on a Sabbath or holy day. We will also let the seventh year lie fallow and give up the claim on every debt.{d}
We also accept the responsibility of giving each year an eighth of an ounce of silver{e} toward the service of the house of our God:

for the bread of the Presence, for the continual grain offering and the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts, for the holy offerings and the sin offerings that make atonement for Israel, and for every task of the house of our God.

We have also cast lots among the priests, Levites, and people for the wood offering, to bring it to the house of our God at set times each year, by our family groups, to burn on the altar of Yahweh our God, as the Law prescribes.
We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of Yahweh;

also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks;

We will also bring the first batch of our dough{f} and our contributions, the fruit of every kind of tree, the new wine, and the oil to the priests, at the storerooms of the house of our God, and a tenth of our crops to the Levites, since the Levites collect the tithes in all the towns where we work the soil.

A priest, a descendant of Aaron, is to be with the Levites when they collect the tithes, and the Levites are to take a tenth of those tithes up to the house of our God, to the rooms of the storehouse.

For into the storerooms the sons of Israel and the sons of Levi are to bring the contribution of grain, new wine, and oil; there are the holy vessels, and the priests who serve, the gatekeepers, and the singers. We will not forsake the house of our God.

notes.text: Hebrew “Upon the sealed ones (were).”
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Nobai.
Hebrew Adonai, with the suffix “our.”
See Exodus 23:10–11; Deuteronomy 15:1–2.
Hebrew “a third of a shekel,” about ⅛ ounce (4 grams). Exodus 30:13 had required half a shekel.
Or “dough.”

verses.text: The leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one in ten would come to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city and nine in ten in the towns.
And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.

These are the heads of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah each lived on his own property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the sons of Solomon’s servants.{a}
Some of the people of Judah and Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. From Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, a descendant of Perez;
and Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.{b}
All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 valiant men.
And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah,
and after him Gabbai and Sallai,{c} 928.
Joel son of Zichri was overseer over them, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in charge over the city.
Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin,
Seraiah, son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the official in charge of God’s house,
and their brothers who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah,
with his brothers, heads of fathers’ houses, 242; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer,
and their brothers, valiant warriors, 128. Their overseer was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim.{d}
And of the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni;
Shabbethai and Jozabad, from the heads of the Levites, over the outer work for the house of God;

Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, the leader who started the thanksgiving prayer; Bakbukiah, who ranked second among his relatives; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.{e}
All the Levites in the holy city were 284.
The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were 172.
And the rest of Israel, and of the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, each in his inheritance.
But the temple servants lived on the Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants.

The chief officer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, from the descendants of Asaph, the singers responsible for the service of God’s house.
For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a settled provision for the singers, as each day required.
And Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah son of Judah, was at the king’s hand{f} in all matters concerning the people.
As for the villages with their fields, some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba{g} and its surrounding villages,{h} in Dibon and its villages, and in Jekabzeel and its villages,
and in Jeshua and in Moladah and Beth-pelet,
in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its villages,
in Ziklag, in Meconah and its villages,
in En-rimmon, in Zorah, in Jarmuth,
Zanoah, Adullam, and their villages; Lachish with its fields; and Azekah with its villages. They settled from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom.
The Benjaminites lived from Geba onward,{i} in Michmash, Aija, and Bethel with its villages,
Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah,
Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim,
Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat,
Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen.{j}
And certain divisions of the Levites that were in Judah were joined to Benjamin.

notes.text: The list in verses 3–19 has a close parallel in 1 Chronicles 9:2–17, with many differences.
Or “of the Shelanite,” a descendant of Shelah son of Judah (Numbers 26:20).
The Hebrew is uncertain; some read “and his brothers, valiant men.”
Or “son of the great ones,” that is, of a leading family.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Jedithun.
That is, the king’s agent or adviser for the affairs of the Jews.
The older name of Hebron (Genesis 23:2), “town of four” or “town of Arba.”
Hebrew “daughters.” Likewise in verses 27, 28, 30, and 31.
Or “The sons of Benjamin from Geba lived at Michmash….”
Hebrew Ge-harashim.

verses.text: These are the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, and Ezra,
Amariah, Malluch, and Hattush,
Shecaniah, Rehum, and Meremoth,
Iddo, Ginnethoi, and Abijah,
Mijamin, Maadiah, and Bilgah,
Shemaiah, Joiarib, and Jedaiah,
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their fellow priests in the time of Jeshua.
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah; he and his brothers had charge of the thanksgiving songs.
Bakbukiah and Unni,{a} their brothers, stood across from them by divisions.{b}
Jeshua fathered Joiakim; Joiakim fathered Eliashib; and Eliashib fathered Joiada;
Joiada fathered Jonathan; and Jonathan fathered Jaddua.{c}
And in the days of Joiakim were priests, heads of fathers’ houses: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah;
of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan;
of Melicu,{d} Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;
of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai;
of Iddo,{e} Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam;
of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin,{f} of Moadiah, Piltai;
of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jehonathan;
of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi;
of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber;
of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethanel.
As for the Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, heads of fathers’ houses were written down, and the priests as well, up to the reign of Darius the Persian.{g}
The family heads of the descendants of Levi were recorded in the Book of the Chronicles up to the time of Johanan son of Eliashib.

The leaders of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel, along with their fellow Levites, who stood opposite them to give praise and thanks, one group answering the other, as David the man of God had commanded.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates.
These were in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and of Ezra the priest, the scribe.

For the dedication of Jerusalem’s wall they searched out the Levites wherever they lived and brought them to Jerusalem to keep the dedication joyfully, with songs of thanks and with music on cymbals, harps, and lyres.
And the sons of the singers gathered together from the surrounding district around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites,
and from Beth-gilgal and the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, since the singers had made villages for themselves around Jerusalem.
And the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people and the gates and the wall.
I had the officials of Judah go up on top of the wall, and I set two large thanksgiving choirs in procession. One went along the top of the wall southward,{h} toward the Dung Gate;
And after them went Hoshaiah and half of the leaders of Judah,
and Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam,
Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah,
and some of the priests’ sons with trumpets: Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph;
and his brothers, Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God. And Ezra the scribe went before them.
At the Fountain Gate they climbed straight up the steps of the City of David, on the rising part of the wall above David’s palace, and went on to the Water Gate on the east.
The second thanksgiving choir went northward,{i} with me following and half the people, on top of the wall, beyond the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall,
over the Gate of Ephraim, past the Old Gate,{j} by the Fish Gate and Hananel’s Tower and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they took their stand at the Gate of the Guard.
So both choirs that gave thanks stood in the house of God, and I and half of the officials with me;
and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;
and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang aloud, with Jezrahiah as their leader.
On that day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, because God had given them great joy. The women and children rejoiced too, and the sound of Jerusalem’s celebration was heard far away.

On that day men were appointed over the storerooms for the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes. They were to gather into them, from the fields around the towns, the portions required by the Law for the priests and Levites, because the people of Judah were pleased with the priests and Levites who served.
They performed the charge of their God and the charge of cleansing, and so did the singers and gatekeepers, as David and Solomon his son had commanded.
For in David’s day, and Asaph’s, long before, there were chiefs{k} over the singers, and songs of praise and thanks to God.

And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah gave the portions for the singers and the gatekeepers, as each day required. And they set apart that which was for the Levites, and the Levites set apart that which was for the sons of Aaron.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Unno.
Or “by watches”; Hebrew “for watches.”

Jaddua was high priest about 330 BC, according to Josephus. The Jonathan of this verse is probably the Johanan of verses 22–23 (see the Elephantine papyri, which name a high priest Johanan about 410 BC).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Malluchi. Compare Malluch in verse 2.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Iddi.
A name seems to have dropped out of the Hebrew text here.
Probably Darius II, king of Persia 423–404 BC, though some think of Darius III (336–330 BC).
Hebrew “to the right,” that is, to the south for one facing east.
Hebrew “to the front,” perhaps “opposite”; the Septuagint and other ancient versions read “to the left,” that is, to the north.
Or “the Jeshanah Gate”; see 3:6.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has the singular, “a head.”

verses.text: On that day the Book of Moses was read aloud to the people, and in it they found it written that an Ammonite or a Moabite must never come into the assembly of God,
because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to curse them. Yet our God turned the curse into a blessing.{a}
When the people heard the Law, they set apart from Israel everyone of foreign mixture.
Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the chambers of the house of our God, and who was related to Tobiah,

had made ready for him a great room, where before they used to store the grain offering, the frankincense, and the vessels, with the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil commanded for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the contributions due the priests.
I was not in Jerusalem while all this was happening, because in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon{b} I had gone back to the king. Some time later I asked the king for leave
When I came to Jerusalem I learned of the wrong Eliashib had done for Tobiah in fitting out a room for him in the courts of God’s house.
It displeased me deeply, and I flung all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room.
At my command they purified the rooms, and I put back in them the vessels of God’s house along with the grain offering and the frankincense.
I also learned that the Levites had not been given their share, so that the Levites and singers who did the work had each gone back to his own farm.
I rebuked the officials and asked, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” Then I gathered the Levites and singers and restored them to their posts.
And all Judah brought in the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil to the storerooms.

Over the storerooms I put in charge Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah from the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, to help them, since they were counted trustworthy; it fell to them to hand out shares to their brothers.
Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God and for its services.

In those days I saw men in Judah treading the winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves and loading donkeys with them, and with wine, grapes, figs, and every sort of burden, bringing them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. And I testified against them on the day they sold provisions.
Tyrians who lived there also brought in fish and every kind of merchandise and sold it on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, even in Jerusalem.
Then I confronted the nobles of Judah and said to them, “What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?
Is this not what your fathers did, so that our God brought all this evil on us and on this city? And you add to the wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath!”

When the gates of Jerusalem grew shadowed before the Sabbath, I gave word and the doors were shut, and I ordered that they not be opened until the Sabbath was over. I set some of my young men over the gates so that no burden would come in on the Sabbath day.
The traders and the sellers of all sorts of wares then lodged outside Jerusalem, once and twice.
But I warned them and said to them, “Why are you lodging in front of the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on they did not come on the Sabbath.

And I told the Levites to purify themselves and come to keep the gates, so as to hallow the Sabbath day. For this, too, remember me, my God, and have pity on me as befits your abundant steadfast love.
In those days also I saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.{c}
Half of their children spoke Ashdodite, and none of them knew how to speak Judean,{d} only the tongue of one people or another.

I contended with them and cursed them; I struck some of the men and tore out their hair, and I put them under oath by God: “Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take any of their daughters for your sons or yourselves.

Didn’t Solomon king of Israel sin because of women like these? Among the many nations there was no king like him. He was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Yet even he was drawn into sin by foreign women.{e}
And must we hear of you doing all this great evil, being faithless to our God by marrying foreign women?”
One of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite, so I drove him away from me.
Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and the Levites.
So I purified them from everything foreign and set up the duties for the priests and the Levites, each man in his task,
and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.

notes.text: See Deuteronomy 23:3–5; Numbers 22–24.
That is, in 433–432 BC. The Persian king also bore the title king of Babylon.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) spells “Ashdodite” and “Ammonite” slightly differently.
Hebrew “Jewish” (yehudit), the language of Judah, that is, Hebrew; compare 2 Kings 18:26.
See 1 Kings 11:1–8.

books.name: Esther
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint in Brenton’s public-domain English translation. This is the Hebrew book of Esther, which does not name God. The Greek form of Esther adds six longer passages (the Additions to Esther), which will be given with the Apocrypha. Esther is the only book of the Hebrew Bible of which no fragment has been found among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Where the written Hebrew text (ketiv) and the traditional reading (qere) differ, the footnotes give the other reading. Persian names are explained in the footnotes. Weights, measures, and money are given in modern US units, and calendar dates with their modern-month equivalents, with the originals and metric figures in the footnotes. Dates BC are approximate.

verses.text: It happened in the days of Ahasuerus{a}—this is the Ahasuerus who reigned from India as far as Cush,{b} over 127 provinces—
in those days, as King Ahasuerus was seated upon the throne of his kingdom, which was in Susa the citadel,{c}
in the third year of his rule{d} he gave a banquet for all his officials and attendants. Persia’s and Media’s military leaders, the nobles,{e} and the provincial governors were in his presence,
when for many days—180 days{f}—he made a show of the wealth of his glorious kingdom and the precious splendor of his greatness.
When these days were completed, the king held for all the people who were found in Susa the citadel, from great to small, a feast of seven days in the court of the garden of the king’s palace.

There were hangings of white cotton and violet, held by cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble; couches of gold and silver stood on a pavement of porphyry, marble, mother-of-pearl, and costly stone.{g}
Drinks were served in vessels of gold, the vessels each different from the other, and royal wine was plentiful, as befitted the king’s bounty.{h}
And the drinking was by rule: no one was compelled, for so the king had ordered every officer of his household, to do as each man wished.
Queen Vashti{i} also held a feast for the women in the royal house that belonged to King Ahasuerus.

On the seventh day, when the king’s heart was merry with wine, he told Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha and Abagtha, Zethar and Carkas, the seven eunuchs{j} who served in the presence of King Ahasuerus,
to bring Queen Vashti before the king wearing the royal crown,{k} to show the peoples and the officials her beauty, for she was lovely to look at.
But Queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s word sent by the eunuchs. Then the king was very angry, and his wrath burned within him.
So the king spoke to the wise men who knew the times—for this was the king’s practice before all who knew law and judgment;
those closest to him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, who saw the king’s face and sat first in the kingdom—
“According to law, what must be done to Queen Vashti, since she did not carry out the order of King Ahasuerus brought by the eunuchs?”
Then Memucan{l} said before the king and the princes, “Not against the king alone has Queen Vashti done wrong, but against all the princes and all the peoples in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus.

For word of what the queen did will reach every woman, so that they will look with scorn on their husbands, saying, ‘King Ahasuerus ordered Queen Vashti brought into his presence, and she would not come.’
This very day the noble ladies of Persia and Media who have heard of the queen’s deed will speak of it to all the king’s princes, and there will be contempt and wrath enough.

If it pleases the king, let a royal word go out from him and be written among the laws of Persia and Media, so that it cannot pass away, that Vashti is not to come before King Ahasuerus again; and let the king give her royal position to a companion of hers who is better than she.
So when the king’s decree that he makes is heard throughout all his kingdom, vast as it is, all wives will give honor to their husbands, from great to small.”
The word pleased the king and the princes, and the king did as Memucan said.

And he dispatched letters to every one of the king’s provinces, each province in its writing and each people in its tongue, that every man should rule in his household and speak the tongue of his own people.{m}

notes.text: Ahasuerus is the Hebrew form of the Persian name Khshayarsha, known in Greek as Xerxes; this is Xerxes I, king of Persia 486–465 BC. The Hebrew book of Esther never names God; its story tells of providence without speaking of it. The Greek (Septuagint) form of Esther includes six longer passages, with prayers and letters, that are not in the Hebrew. This translation follows the Hebrew; those Greek Additions to Esther will be given with the Apocrypha.
That is, from the Indus valley to the upper Nile (ancient Nubia, modern Sudan).
Susa (Hebrew Shushan), the winter capital of the Persian kings, in what is now southwestern Iran. “The citadel” is the fortified royal quarter of the city.
That is, 483 BC.
Hebrew partemim, a Persian loanword for nobles or men of the first rank.
About six months.
The identification of several of these materials is uncertain. Hebrew karpas (“cotton”) is a Persian loanword.
Hebrew “according to the hand of the king.”
Vashti is probably a Persian name meaning “the desired” or “the best.” Greek historians name Xerxes’ queen as Amestris; the relation of the two is debated.
Or “officials.” Hebrew saris can mean a court officer in general, but in Persian courts it usually meant a eunuch. The names of the eunuchs and princes in this book are Persian.
Hebrew keter, a turban-like crown, a Persian word found in the Bible only in Esther.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Momucan.
The meaning of the last clause is uncertain; perhaps that the husband’s language was to be spoken in a household of mixed peoples.

verses.text: Some time later, once King Ahasuerus’s fury had cooled, he thought of Vashti, of what she had done, and of the decision made about her.
Then the king’s young men who attended him said, “Let young virgins of fair appearance be sought for the king.

Let the king also name officials throughout his empire to collect every attractive young virgin into the harem at the citadel of Susa, under the supervision of Hegai,{a} the king’s eunuch who guards the women; and let them be given beauty treatments.
And the girl who is good in the king’s eyes, let her be queen in place of Vashti.” The word was good in the king’s eyes, and he did so.
There was a Jewish man in Susa the citadel whose name was Mordecai,{b} son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,
who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the exiles taken with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away.{c}

He was raising Hadassah,{d} that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter, because she had lost both parents. The young woman had a lovely figure and a beautiful face, and Mordecai took her in as his own daughter after her father and mother died.

So when the king’s word and his decree were heard, and when many young women were gathered to Susa the citadel into the custody of Hegai, Esther also was taken into the king’s house, into the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women.

The girl was good in his eyes and won his favor, and he quickly provided her cosmetics and her portions, and seven chosen young women from the king’s house, and he moved her and her young women to the best place in the house of the women.
Esther had not revealed her people or her birth, because Mordecai had instructed her that she must not reveal it.
Day by day Mordecai would walk up and down before the court of the women’s house to find out how Esther fared and what was being done with her.

Now when each girl’s turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus, after she had been treated under the regulations for the women for twelve months—for so the days of their beautifying were completed: six months with oil of myrrh and six months with spices and the women’s cosmetics—
then in this way the girl went in to the king: whatever she asked for was given her to take with her from the house of the women to the king’s house.

She went in at evening, and at dawn she came back to a different women’s quarters under the care of Shaashgaz,{e} the king’s eunuch who guarded the concubines. She could not return to the king unless he had taken delight in her and called her by name.

Now when it came the turn of Esther—daughter of Abihail, Mordecai’s uncle, whom Mordecai had taken as a daughter—to go in to the king, she requested nothing beyond what Hegai, the king’s eunuch who kept the women, told her. And Esther found favor in the sight of everyone who looked at her.
So Esther was taken to King Ahasuerus, into his royal house, in the tenth month, which is the month of Tevet (December–January),{f} in the seventh year of his reign.
And the king loved Esther more than all the women, and she won grace and favor before him more than all the virgins, so that he set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.

Then the king gave a huge banquet for all his officials and attendants in honor of Esther. He also proclaimed a tax holiday{g} for the provinces and handed out gifts in keeping with a king’s generosity.
When the virgins were assembled a second time, Mordecai sat in the gate of the king.{h}
Esther had not made known her kindred or her people, just as Mordecai had commanded her, for Esther did what Mordecai said, just as when she was brought up by him.
During those days, as Mordecai sat in the gate of the king, two of the king’s eunuchs who guarded the threshold, Bigthan and Teresh, grew angry and plotted to strike at King Ahasuerus.
Mordecai learned of it and informed Queen Esther, and Esther reported it to the king, giving Mordecai’s name as her source.
When the matter was investigated and found to be so, the two of them were hanged on a pole.{i} And it was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence.

notes.text: Hegai is a Persian name; in verse 8 it is spelled Hege.
Mordecai is a Babylonian name, related to that of the god Marduk. A Persian official named Marduka appears in tablets from Persepolis of this period.
That is, in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:10–17). The one carried away may be Kish, Mordecai’s great-grandfather, rather than Mordecai himself.
Hadassah is Hebrew for “myrtle.” Esther is probably from the Persian for “star,” though some connect it with the Babylonian goddess Ishtar.
A Persian name.
That is, at the turn of 479 to 478 BC, four years after Vashti was put aside (1:3).
Perhaps a remission of taxes, or a holiday.
That is, he held an office at the royal court; the gate complex was the seat of government business.
Hebrew “on a tree” or “on wood”; probably impaled or displayed on a stake, the Persian manner of execution. Likewise throughout the book.

verses.text: After these things King Ahasuerus promoted Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite,{a} and lifted him up, and set his seat above all the princes who were with him.
And all the king’s servants who were at the king’s gate would bow down and do homage to Haman, for the king had so commanded concerning him. But Mordecai would not bow down or do homage.
And the king’s servants in the king’s gate asked Mordecai, “Why are you disobeying the order of the king?”
When they had said this{b} to him every day, and he paid them no heed, they reported it to Haman, to find out whether Mordecai’s claims would hold, for he had let them know he was a Jew.
When Haman noticed that Mordecai would not kneel or bow to him, he was seething with rage.

Yet he scorned to lay a hand on Mordecai by himself, since they had made known to him Mordecai’s people; and Haman set out to wipe out all the Jews, Mordecai’s people, in the entire realm of Ahasuerus.

In the first month, which is the month of Nisan (March–April), in the twelfth year of King Ahasuerus,{c} they cast Pur{d}—that is, the lot—before Haman, from day to day and from month to month, to the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar (February–March).{e}

Then Haman said to King Ahasuerus, “There is a certain people scattered and dispersed among the peoples in all the provinces of your kingdom. Their laws differ from those of every people, and they do not keep the king’s laws, so it is not worth the king’s while to let them be.
If the king approves, let an order be written to destroy them, and I will pay about 375 tons of silver{f} to the officials in charge, to be deposited in the royal treasury.”
So the king took his signet ring from his hand and gave it to Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, the adversary of the Jews.
And the king said to Haman, “The silver is given to you, the people also, to do with them as is good in your eyes.”

The king’s secretaries were summoned on the thirteenth day of the first month,{g} and an order was written exactly as Haman instructed, addressed to the king’s satraps, to the governors of every province, and to the officials of every people, in each province’s own writing and each people’s own language. It was drafted in King Ahasuerus’s name and stamped with the king’s signet ring.

Letters were sent by the hands of couriers to all the king’s provinces, to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all the Jews, from young to old, children and women, on one day, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar (February–March),{h} and to plunder their goods.
A copy of the text was to be proclaimed as law in each province and displayed to every people, so that they would be prepared for that day.
The couriers went out in haste by the king’s word, and the law was given out in Susa the citadel. And the king and Haman sat down to drink, but the city of Susa was in confusion.

notes.text: Haman and Hammedatha are probably Persian names. “Agagite” recalls Agag king of Amalek, the foe of Saul son of Kish (1 Samuel 15); Mordecai is of the line of Kish (2:5).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a slightly different form of the same verb.
That is, 474 BC.
Pur is a Babylonian (Akkadian) word, puru, “lot.” Its plural, Purim, gives the festival its name (9:24–26).
The Hebrew is brief; the Septuagint adds that the lot fell on the thirteenth day of Adar (see verse 13).
Hebrew “10,000 talents,” about 340 metric tons; a talent was about 75 pounds (34 kilograms). Herodotus reckons the yearly revenue of the whole Persian empire at about 15,000 talents.
The thirteenth of Nisan, in March–April, the day before Passover (Leviticus 23:5).
That is, eleven months later, in 473 BC.

verses.text: Mordecai knew everything that had been done. He tore his garments, clothed himself in sackcloth and ashes, and went out through the city, crying a great and bitter cry.
He came only as far as before the gate of the king, since none might come within the gate of the king dressed in sackcloth.
And in every province, wherever the king’s word and his law reached, there was great mourning among the Jews, with fasting and weeping and lamenting; many lay in sackcloth and ashes.
Esther’s maids and eunuchs came and reported it to her, and the queen was in deep distress. She sent clothes for Mordecai to wear in place of his sackcloth, but he refused them.
So Esther summoned Hathach,{a} one of the king’s eunuchs who had been assigned to serve her, and sent him to Mordecai to find out what was wrong and why.
Hathach went out to Mordecai, to the city square before the gate of the king.
And Mordecai told him all that had happened to him, and the exact sum of silver that Haman had promised to weigh out into the king’s treasuries for the Jews,{b} to destroy them.

He also gave him a copy of the written law that had been given out in Susa for their destruction, to show it to Esther and explain it to her, and to charge her to go in to the king to plead with him and make request before him for her people.
Hathach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai.
Then Esther spoke to Hathach and gave him a message for Mordecai:

“Every royal official and every person in the provinces knows that anyone, man or woman, who approaches the king in the inner court without an invitation faces a single penalty: death, unless the king extends his golden scepter to spare that person’s life. And I have not been invited into the king’s presence for thirty days.”
And they told Mordecai Esther’s words.
Then Mordecai said to reply to Esther, “Do not imagine in your soul that in the king’s house you will escape, more than all the Jews.

If you hold your peace at such a time as this, relief and rescue will rise up for the Jews from some other place,{c} while you and your father’s family will be lost. And who knows if you have not reached the throne for just such a time?”
Then Esther said to reply to Mordecai,

“Go and assemble all the Jews to be found in Susa, and fast on my behalf; neither eat nor drink for three days, night and day. My maids and I will fast in the same way. Then I will go in to the king, which is not by the law. And if I am lost, I am lost.”
So Mordecai went away and did everything Esther had commanded him.

notes.text: A Persian name.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) spells “the Jews” with an extra letter (hayyehudiyyim). The same difference occurs at 8:1, 8:7, 8:13, 9:15, and 9:18.
Many interpreters, Jewish and Christian, have seen in “another place” a veiled reference to God, whom the book never names.

verses.text: On the third day Esther put on her royal robes and stood in the inner court of the king’s house, opposite the king’s house, while the king was sitting on his royal throne in the royal house, opposite the entrance of the house.

And when the king saw Queen Esther standing in the court, she won favor in his eyes, and the king held out to Esther the golden scepter that was in his hand. Then Esther drew near and touched the tip of the scepter.
The king asked her, “What is troubling you, Queen Esther? What do you want? Even if it is half my kingdom, you will have it.”
Esther said, “If it pleases the king, let the king and Haman come today to the feast that I have prepared for him.”
Then the king said, “Bring Haman quickly, to do as Esther has said.” So the king and Haman came to the feast that Esther had prepared.
While they were drinking wine, the king asked Esther again, “What is your wish? You will have it. What do you want? Even half the kingdom will be granted.”
Then Esther answered and said, “My petition and my request is this:

if the king looks on me with favor, and if it pleases him to grant my wish and fulfill my request, may the king and Haman come to a banquet that I will arrange for them; tomorrow I will tell the king what I want.”
That day Haman left in high spirits, cheerful of heart. But when he saw Mordecai at the palace gate, neither standing up nor flinching in his presence, Haman was seething with anger at Mordecai.
Yet Haman held himself in check and went home, and he sent and brought his friends and Zeresh{a} his wife.
And Haman recounted to them the glory of his riches, the number of his sons, and all the ways the king had promoted him, and how he had lifted him up above the princes and the servants of the king.
And Haman went on, “Even Queen Esther brought nobody else besides me with the king to the feast she had made; and tomorrow, too, I am called to her with the king.
But none of this satisfies me, as long as I keep seeing Mordecai the Jew seated in the gate of the king.”

Then Zeresh his wife and all his friends said to him, “Let a pole be made, 75 feet{b} high, and in the morning speak to the king, and let them hang Mordecai on it. Then go in merrily with the king to the feast.” The word pleased Haman, and he had the pole made.

notes.text: A Persian name.
Hebrew “fifty cubits,” about 23 meters.

verses.text: On that night the king’s sleep fled, and he ordered the book of memorable deeds, the chronicles, to be brought, and they were read before the king.
There it was found written that Mordecai had reported on Bigthana and Teresh, two eunuchs of the king who guarded the threshold, who had plotted to strike at King Ahasuerus.
The king asked, “What reward or recognition did Mordecai receive for this?” The king’s attendants answered, “Nothing has been done for him.”
The king said, “Who is out in the courtyard?” At that moment Haman was walking into the palace’s outer courtyard to ask the king whether Mordecai could be hanged on the stake he had set up for him.
And the king’s young men said to him, “Look, Haman is standing in the court.” And the king said, “Let him come in.”

So Haman entered, and the king put this question to him: “What is the right treatment for a man whom the king wishes to honor?” Haman reasoned privately, “Surely he means me. Whom would the king wish to honor more?”
And Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king delights to honor,
let royal garments be brought in which the king has been clothed, and a horse on which the king has ridden, with a royal crown set on its head.{a}

Then give the robe and horse into the care of one of the king’s noblest officials, and have him dress the man the king wishes to honor and parade him on the horse through the city square, shouting before him, ‘So the king rewards the man he delights to honor!’”
Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry, take the clothing and the horse, as you have said, and do so to Mordecai the Jew who sits at the king’s gate. Let nothing fall short of all that you have spoken.”
So Haman took the robe and the horse, dressed Mordecai, and led him on the horse through the city square, shouting before him, “So the king rewards the man he delights to honor!”
Then Mordecai returned to the king’s gate. But Haman hurried to his house, mourning, with his head covered.

Haman told his wife Zeresh and all his friends everything that had happened to him. His advisers and his wife Zeresh said to him, “If Mordecai, in front of whom your fall has begun, is of Jewish descent, you cannot defeat him; you are certain to be ruined before him.”
They were still talking with him when the king’s eunuchs came and hastily brought Haman to Esther’s feast.

notes.text: Persian reliefs show royal horses with a crested headdress. Or “and on whose head a royal crown has been set,” referring to the man.

verses.text: So the king and Haman came in to drink with Queen Esther.
On that second day, over their wine, the king once more asked Esther, “What is your wish, Queen Esther? You will have it. What do you want? Even half the kingdom will be granted.”
Queen Esther replied, “If I have won your favor, my king, and if it seems good to you, spare my life; that is my wish, and spare my people; that is my request.

For I and my people have been sold off for destruction, for slaughter, and for annihilation. If we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I would have kept still; such distress would not be worth the king’s trouble.”{a}
Then King Ahasuerus spoke and said to Queen Esther, “Who is he, and where is he, whose heart has filled him to do this?”
And Esther said, “An adversary and an enemy—this evil Haman!” Then Haman was terrified before the king and the queen.

And the king rose in his wrath from the wine feast and went into the palace garden, but Haman stayed to beg Queen Esther for his life, for he saw that evil had been determined against him by the king.

When the king came back from the palace garden to the room where they had been drinking, Haman had thrown himself onto the couch where Esther lay. The king exclaimed, “Would he even attack the queen while I am in the house?” The moment the words left the king’s lips, they covered Haman’s face.

Then Harbonah, one of the eunuchs attending the king, said, “There is also the stake Haman built for Mordecai, the man who spoke up to help the king; it is standing beside Haman’s house, 75 feet{b} tall.” The king ordered, “Hang him on it.”
So they hanged Haman on the stake he had built for Mordecai, and the king’s fury subsided.

notes.text: Or “for the enemy could not make good the king’s loss.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew “fifty cubits,” about 23 meters.

verses.text: That same day King Ahasuerus presented Queen Esther with the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews.{a} Mordecai was brought before the king, since Esther had revealed how he was related to her.
And the king took off his signet ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it to Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
And once more Esther spoke before the king; she threw herself at his feet, weeping, and implored him to undo the evil of Haman the Agagite and the scheme he had laid against the Jews.
The king stretched the golden scepter toward Esther, and she got up and stood in the king’s presence.

She said, “If it seems good to the king, and I have found favor with him, and the proposal strikes the king as proper and he is pleased with me, let an order be written to cancel the dispatches Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, composed to wipe out the Jews throughout the king’s provinces.
For how can I bear to look on the evil that will befall my people? And how can I bear to look on the destruction of my kindred?”

Then King Ahasuerus said to Queen Esther and to Mordecai the Jew, “Look, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and they have hanged him on the pole because he stretched out his hand against the Jews.

You yourselves may now write what you think best about the Jews, in the king’s name, and stamp it with the king’s signet ring, because a decree issued in the king’s name and marked with his ring cannot be reversed.”

Then the king’s scribes were summoned, at that time, in the third month—the month of Sivan (May–June)—on the twenty-third day.{b} And everything Mordecai ordered was written to the Jews, and to the satraps, governors, and provincial officials from India to Cush, 127 provinces, each province in its writing and each people in its tongue, and to the Jews in their own writing and tongue.
He wrote in the name of King Ahasuerus and sealed it with the king’s ring, and he sent letters by the hands of couriers on horseback, riding swift royal steeds bred from the stud.{c}

In them the king granted the Jews in each city the right to assemble and defend their lives, to destroy, slay, and wipe out any armed band of a people or province that should attack them, children and women,{d} and to take their goods as spoil,
on one day throughout all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, on the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month of Adar (February–March).
A copy of the text was to be proclaimed as law in each province and displayed to every people, so that the Jews would be prepared{e} on that day to repay their enemies.
So the couriers, mounted on the swift royal steeds, went out hurried and pressed by the king’s word. And the law was given out in Susa the citadel.
And Mordecai went out from the king’s presence in royal garments of violet and white, wearing a great crown of gold and a robe of fine linen and purple; and the city of Susa cried out with joy.
For the Jews there was light and gladness and joy and honor.

In each and every province and city to which the king’s word and his law came, the Jews had gladness and joy, feasting, and a good day. And many of the peoples of the land became Jews,{f} because dread of the Jews had come on them.

notes.text: For the spelling of “Jews” here and in verses 7 and 13, see the note on 4:7.
That is, about two months after Haman’s decree (3:12), in 474 BC.
The terms for the horses are Persian loanwords whose exact meaning is uncertain.
The phrase echoes Haman’s decree (3:13). Some take “children and women” as the objects of the attack against the Jews rather than of their defense.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a variant spelling.
Or “pretended to be Jews”; the Hebrew verb occurs only here.

verses.text: In the twelfth month—the month of Adar (February–March)—on the thirteenth day,{a} when the king’s command and law were due to be done, the day the foes of the Jews had hoped to overpower them, the reverse happened: the Jews themselves overpowered their haters.
In their cities in every province of King Ahasuerus the Jews assembled to strike at those who sought to harm them. Nobody stood against them, since dread of them had come on every people.
All the officials of the provinces and the satraps and the governors and the king’s administrators{b} supported the Jews, for the fear of Mordecai had fallen on them.
For Mordecai was great in the king’s house, and his fame went out through all the provinces; for the man Mordecai grew greater and greater.
The Jews struck down all their foes with the sword, slaughtering and destroying, and dealt as they willed with their haters.
In Susa the citadel the Jews killed and destroyed 500 men,
and Parshandatha and Dalphon and Aspatha{c}
and Poratha and Adalia and Aridatha
and Parmashta and Arisai and Aridai and Vaizatha,
the ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the adversary of the Jews. They killed them, but they did not lay their hands on the plunder.
On the same day the count of the slain in Susa the citadel came before the king.

The king said to Queen Esther, “In the citadel of Susa alone the Jews have killed and destroyed five hundred men, as well as Haman’s ten sons. What have they done in the rest of the royal provinces! Now what is your wish? It will be granted. What more do you ask? It will be done.”
And Esther said, “If it pleases the king, let it be granted to the Jews who are in Susa to do tomorrow also according to today’s law, and let the ten sons of Haman be hanged on the pole.”{d}
So the king commanded that it be done. A law was given out in Susa, and they hanged the ten sons of Haman.
And the Jews{e} in Susa assembled on the fourteenth of Adar as well and slew 300 men in Susa; but on the spoil they laid no hand.
The other Jews in the king’s provinces assembled and defended their lives and had rest from their foes; they slew 75,000{f} of their haters, but on the spoil they laid no hand.
This was on the thirteenth day of the month of Adar; and on its fourteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.
But the Jews who were in Susa gathered on its thirteenth day and on its fourteenth, and on its fifteenth day they rested and made it a day of feasting and gladness.

That is why the Jews of the villages, who live in the rural towns,{g} keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar as a day of gladness and feasting, a holiday, and a day of sending portions to one another.
And Mordecai wrote these things down and sent letters to all the Jews who were in all the provinces of King Ahasuerus, near and far,
to establish among them that they should keep the fourteenth day of the month of Adar and its fifteenth day,{h} year by year,

as the days when the Jews found relief from their enemies, and as the month when their grief was turned to joy and their mourning to a holiday; they were to observe them as days of banqueting and joy, exchanging gifts of food and giving presents to the needy.
So the Jews accepted what they had begun to do and what Mordecai had written to them.
For Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, who persecuted all the Jews, had planned to destroy the Jews and had thrown the Pur, that is, the lot, to crush{i} and destroy them.

But when it{j} came before the king, he commanded by letter that his evil plot which he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the pole.
Therefore they called these days Purim, after the name of Pur.{k} Therefore, because of all the words of this letter, and of what they had seen concerning this and what had come upon them,

the Jews established and took on themselves{l} and on their offspring and on all who joined them, so that it should not pass away, that they would keep these two days according to what was written and at their appointed time, year by year;

and that these days should be remembered and kept in every generation, by every family, every province, and every city, and that these days of Purim should not pass away from among the Jews, nor the memory of them cease from their offspring.
And Queen Esther, Abihail’s daughter, with Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority to make this second Purim letter binding.
And letters were sent to all the Jews, to the 127 provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, words of peace and truth,

to make these days of Purim binding at their set times, as Mordecai the Jew and Queen Esther had made them binding on them, and as they had bound themselves and their descendants concerning their fasts and their cry of lament.{m}
The command of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim, and it was written in the book.

notes.text: In 473 BC.
Hebrew “those who do the work that belongs to the king.”

The names of the ten sons of Haman in verses 7–9 are Persian. In Hebrew scrolls of Esther they are traditionally written in a column, each name on its own line, and they are read in one breath at the Purim reading.
That is, their bodies were to be displayed publicly.
For the spelling of “Jews” here and in verse 18, see the note on 4:7.
The Septuagint has 15,000.

So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a variant form of the word. To this day, Purim is kept on the 14th of Adar, but on the 15th (“Shushan Purim”) in Jerusalem and other anciently walled cities.
In the modern calendar these days fall in February or March.
Or “to throw them into panic.”
Or “she,” that is, Esther.
Purim means “lots,” the plural of pur (see 3:7). The festival falls on 14–15 Adar, in February or March.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has the singular, “and he took on himself.”
The fast of Esther is kept on 13 Adar, the day before Purim.

verses.text: King Ahasuerus{a} laid tribute on the land and on the coastlands of the sea.

And all the acts of his power and his might, and the full account of the greatness of Mordecai, to which the king raised him, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia?
For Mordecai the Jew was second to King Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and pleasing to the multitude of his brothers. He sought the good of his people and spoke peace to all his offspring.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) spells the name without one of its letters.

books.name: Job
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and against the Aramaic Targum of Job found at Qumran (11QtgJob, which preserves parts of chapters 17–42, and a small fragment from Cave 4, 4QtgJob). Job is mostly poetry, printed here line by line; its Hebrew contains more rare words and words found only once in the Bible (hapax legomena) than any other book, and many lines are uncertain; the footnotes say so. The Old Greek (Septuagint) Job was about one-sixth shorter than the Hebrew; the missing lines were later filled in from the Greek version of Theodotion and are not marked in Brenton’s English, so footnotes describe these gaps in general terms. The Septuagint also adds a longer speech by Job’s wife (2:9) and a longer ending (42:17). Every Septuagint reading cited was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation (quoted in modernized wording). Readings of 11QtgJob are stated in general terms (“is reported to read”) until they can be checked against the critical edition. Identifications of animals, plants, and precious stones are often uncertain and are footnoted. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (41:1–34), a footnote says so. The Hebrew name of God, YHWH, is written “Yahweh”; Shaddai is kept as a name (see the note at 5:17).

verses.text: In the land of Uz{a} there lived a man named Job.{b} He was blameless and upright, a man who revered God and kept away from evil.
There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.

His livestock was seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, and a very great body of servants; so that this man was greater than all the sons of the east.{c}
It was the custom of his sons to go and make a feast, each at his own house on his own day; and they would send and call their three sisters to eat and drink along with them.

When each round of feasting ended, Job would send for his children and set them apart. Early in the morning he would offer burnt offerings for every one of them, for Job thought, “Perhaps my children have sinned and cursed{d} God in their hearts.” This was Job’s regular practice.
Now there was a day when the sons of God{e} came to present themselves before Yahweh, and the Adversary{f} also came among them.
Yahweh said to the Adversary, “From where do you come?” Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “From roaming through the earth and from walking to and fro in it.”
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Have you set your heart upon my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man blameless and upright, one who fears God and turns aside from evil?”
Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “Is it for nothing that Job fears God?
Have you not hedged him about, and his house, and all that he has, on every side? The work of his hands you have blessed, and his livestock has burst out in the land.
But stretch out your hand now and touch all that he has, and surely he will bless{g} you to your face.”
Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Very well: all that he has is under your control. But you must not harm Job himself.” So the Adversary left Yahweh’s presence.
Now there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,
and a messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazing beside them,
and Sabeans{h} fell upon them and took them, and the servants they struck with the edge of the sword; and I alone, only I, have escaped to tell you.”
He was still speaking when another messenger arrived and reported, “Fire from God{i} dropped out of the sky, burning the sheep and servants and consuming them. Only I got away to bring you the news.”

He was still speaking when another came and reported, “Chaldean raiders in three bands charged the camels and took them. They struck down the servants with their swords. Only I got away to bring you the news.”
While he was yet speaking, another came and said, “Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,
A mighty wind blew in from across the desert and hit all four corners of the house. It collapsed on the young people, and they are dead. I am the only one who escaped to tell you.”
Then Job got up, tore his robe, and shaved his head. He threw himself on the ground and worshiped.
Through all of this Job sinned not, nor did he lay anything unseemly{k} to God’s charge.

notes.text: The location of Uz is uncertain; it was probably east or southeast of Israel, in or near Edom (compare Lamentations 4:21). The Septuagint’s ending (see the note at 42:17) places it “on the borders of Idumea and Arabia” (Brenton).
The meaning of the name Job (Hebrew ʾIyyov) is uncertain; proposals include “Where is the father?” and “one who is hostile.”
That is, the peoples east of Israel, in the Syrian and Arabian desert.
Hebrew “blessed,” used here and in 1:11, 2:5, and 2:9 as a euphemism for “cursed”; scribes apparently avoided writing “curse God.”
Hebrew bene ha-ʾelohim, heavenly beings of the divine court; so also 2:1 and 38:7. The Septuagint reads “the angels of God” (Brenton).

Hebrew ha-satan, “the satan,” that is, “the adversary” or “the accuser.” With the article it is a title or role in the heavenly court, not yet a personal name; so throughout chapters 1–2. The Septuagint reads “the devil” (Brenton).
Hebrew “bless”; see the note at 1:5.
The Sabeans were probably raiders from Sheba in southern Arabia; the Septuagint reads “the spoilers” (Brenton).
Or “a terrible fire,” probably lightning.
That is, to the earth, pictured as the mother of all (compare Psalm 139:15), or to the grave.
Or “nor did he charge God with wrongdoing”; Hebrew tiflah, “unseemliness.”

verses.text: Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before Yahweh, and the Adversary also came among them to present himself before Yahweh.
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “From where do you come?” Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “From roaming through the earth and from walking to and fro in it.”

Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Have you set your heart upon my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man blameless and upright, one who fears God and turns aside from evil? And he still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to swallow him up for no cause.”
Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “Skin for skin!{a} All that a man has he will give for his life.
But stretch out your hand now and touch his bone and his flesh, and surely he will bless{b} you to your face.”
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Look, he is in your hand; only spare his life.”
So the Adversary went out from the presence of Yahweh and struck Job with grievous sores{c} from the sole of his foot to his crown.
And he took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, while he sat in the midst of the ashes.{d}
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still hold fast your integrity? Bless{e} God, and die.”{f}
But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. Shall we indeed receive the good from God, and the evil we shall not receive?” In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

When Job’s three friends heard about all the trouble that had come on him, each one set out from his own home: Eliphaz from Teman, Bildad from Shuah, and Zophar from Naamah.{g} They agreed together to go and offer him sympathy and comfort.
And when they lifted up their eyes from afar and did not recognize him, they lifted up their voices and wept; and they tore each his robe and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward the heavens.
And they sat with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.

notes.text: Probably a proverb from barter: a man will give up one hide to save another, or any possession to save his own skin. The exact sense is uncertain.
Hebrew “bless”; see the note at 1:5.
Hebrew shekhin raʿ; perhaps boils or a skin disease; the exact illness cannot be identified.
The Septuagint reads “and sat upon a dung-heap outside the city” (Brenton, modernized).
