A house and riches come down from one’s ancestors;
a wife with insight is Yahweh’s gift.

Laziness casts into a deep sleep,
and an idle person will go hungry.

Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life;
whoever is careless of his ways will die.

Whoever is kind to the poor lends to Yahweh,
and he will repay him for his deed.

Train your son while hope remains;
do not lift your soul toward putting him to death.{b}

A man of great wrath will pay the penalty;
if you rescue him, you will have to do it again.

Hear counsel, take correction,
and in the end you will be wise.

Many are the plans in a man’s heart,
but it is Yahweh’s purpose that will stand.

What is desired in a person is loyal love,{c}
and a poor man is better than a liar.

The fear of Yahweh leads to life;
one has it and rests content, untouched by harm.

The lazy man plunges his hand into the bowl
and is too tired to lift it back to his lips.

Strike a mocker, and the naive will learn shrewdness;
correct a discerning person, and he will gain knowledge.

Whoever robs his father and drives out his mother
is a son who brings shame and disgrace.

Stop listening to discipline, my son,
and you will stray from words of knowledge.

A worthless witness mocks at justice,
and the mouth of the wicked swallows iniquity.

Judgments are ready for mockers,
and beatings for the backs of fools.

notes.text: The third line is uncertain; it may be a fragment of a lost saying. The Septuagint has a longer text here.
Or “do not set your heart on causing him to die,” that is, do not discipline in rage; or “do not let your heart be set on ruining him” by neglect.
Or “A person’s greed is his shame.”

verses.text:
Wine is a scoffer, strong drink a brawler;
no one led astray by it is wise.

A king’s fury is like the growl of a young lion;
whoever angers him forfeits his life.

It is to a man’s credit to keep clear of strife,
but every fool bares his teeth.

The lazy man does not plow when autumn comes;
at harvest he looks for a crop and there is none.

The purpose in a person’s heart is deep water,
but a discerning person will draw it up.

Plenty of people advertise their own devotion,
but who can locate someone truly trustworthy?

The righteous walks on in his integrity;
happy are his children after him!

A king seated on the throne of judgment
sifts out all evil with his eyes.

Who can say, “I have made my heart clean;
I am pure from my sin”?{a}

Two kinds of weights and two kinds of measures{b}—
Yahweh detests both of them.

Even a child makes himself known by his acts,
whether his conduct is pure and upright.

A listening ear, a seeing eye—
Yahweh is the maker of the pair.

Do not love sleep, or you will be poor;
keep your eyes open and you will have your fill of bread.

“Bad, bad,” says the buyer,
but when he goes off, then he boasts.{c}

There is gold and plenty of coral,
but lips with knowledge are the rarest jewel.

Take the garment of one who stands surety for a stranger;
hold it as a pledge when he guarantees a foreign woman.{d}

Food got by cheating tastes sweet at first,
but later the mouth is crammed with grit.

Plans are made firm by taking counsel;
wage war with sound guidance.

A gossip goes around revealing secrets,
so do not mix with someone whose lips are always open.

Whoever curses his father or his mother,
his lamp will go out in deepest darkness.

An inheritance seized in haste at the start
will not be blessed in the end.

Do not say, “I will pay back evil”;
wait for Yahweh, and he will rescue you.

Two kinds of weights are detestable to Yahweh,
and false scales are not good.

A man’s steps are from Yahweh;
how then can a person understand his own way?

It is a snare to blurt out, “Holy!”
and only afterward to think over one’s vows.

A wise king winnows the wicked
and drives the threshing wheel over them.

The human spirit is the lamp of Yahweh,
searching all the inner rooms of the belly.

Loyal love and faithfulness guard a king,
and by loyal love he holds up his throne.

The glory of young men is their strength,
and the splendor of the old is gray hair.

Blows that wound scour away evil,
and beatings reach the inner rooms of the belly.

notes.text: In the Septuagint verses 20–22 follow here, and verses 14–19 are absent.
Literally “a stone and a stone, an ephah and an ephah,” that is, one set of weights and measures for buying and another for selling. The ephah was a dry measure of about 3/5 bushel (22 liters).
The Septuagint lacks verses 14–19.
Or “a foreigner,” following another reading of the Hebrew; compare 27:13.

verses.text:
A king’s heart is a stream of water in Yahweh’s hand;
he turns it wherever he pleases.

Every way a man takes is right in his own eyes,
but Yahweh weighs hearts.

Doing righteousness and justice
pleases Yahweh better than sacrifice.

Haughty eyes and a proud heart—
the lamp of the wicked is sin.{a}

The plans of the diligent lead only to profit,
but everyone who is hasty comes only to want.{b}

Treasures gained by a lying tongue
are a vanishing vapor, snares of death.{c}

The violence of the wicked will sweep them away,
because they refuse to do what is just.

The way of a guilty man is crooked,
but the conduct of the pure is upright.

Better a spot on a corner of the rooftop
than a whole house with a contentious woman.

The soul of the wicked craves evil;
his neighbor finds no mercy in his eyes.

When a mocker is punished, the naive becomes wise;
when the wise is instructed, he gains knowledge.

The Righteous One{d} takes note of the wicked man’s house
and hurls the wicked into disaster.

Whoever closes his ears to a poor person’s plea
will call out himself and receive no reply.

A gift in secret soothes anger,
and a bribe in the cloak, strong wrath.

Justice carried out delights the righteous
and terrifies those who do wrong.

A person who strays off the road of insight
will end up resting among the company of the shades.

Whoever loves pleasure will be a poor man;
whoever loves wine and oil will not grow rich.

The wicked is a ransom for the righteous,
and the treacherous for the upright.

Better to live in a desert land
than with a quarrelsome and fretful wife.

Precious treasure and oil are in the dwelling of the wise,
but a foolish man swallows them up.

Whoever pursues righteousness and loyal love
finds life, righteousness, and honor.

A wise man goes up against a city of warriors
and brings down the stronghold they trusted.

Keep watch on mouth and tongue,
and you keep your soul out of distress.

“Mocker” is the name of the proud and arrogant man
who acts with insolent pride.

The craving of the sluggard kills him,
for his hands refuse to work.

He spends the whole day longing for more;
the righteous man gives without stinting.

The sacrifice of the wicked is detestable,
how much more when he brings it with evil intent!

A lying witness will perish,
but a man who listens will speak to the end.{e}

The wicked man hardens his face;
the upright man makes his ways sure.{f}

There is no wisdom, no understanding,
no counsel against Yahweh.

They harness the horse for the day of war,
yet the victory is Yahweh’s.

notes.text: Or “the tillage of the wicked”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Septuagint lacks this verse.
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Hebrew reads “for those who seek death.”
Or “A righteous man”; the subject of the second line suggests God.
Or “will speak successfully”; the meaning is uncertain.
So the Masoretic marginal reading; the written text has “understands his ways.”

verses.text:
A good name is to be chosen over great riches;
favor is better than silver and gold.

Rich and poor meet together;
Yahweh is the Maker of them all.

The shrewd sees trouble and hides,
but the naive go on and pay for it.

The reward of humility and the fear of Yahweh
is riches and honor and life.

Thorns and snares lie in the way of the crooked;
whoever guards his life keeps far from them.

Train a child in keeping with his way;
even when he is old he will not turn from it.{a}

The rich rules over the poor,
and the borrower is slave to the lender.

Whoever sows injustice will reap trouble,
and the rod of his fury will fail.{b}

The generous will be blessed,
for he shares his bread with the poor.{c}

Drive out the mocker and strife goes out;
quarreling and insult will stop.

One who loves a pure heart and has grace on his lips
will win the king’s friendship.

The eyes of Yahweh watch over knowledge,
but he overturns the words of the treacherous.

The sluggard says, “There is a lion outside!
I will be killed in the streets!”

The mouth of foreign women is a deep pit;
the one under Yahweh’s anger will fall into it.{d}

Folly is bound up in the heart of a boy;
the rod of discipline will drive it far from him.

Grinding down the poor to enrich oneself,
giving presents to the rich—both end in want.

Incline your ear and listen to the sayings of the wise,{e}
and apply your mind to what I know,

for it is pleasant if you keep them within you,
if all of them are ready on your lips.

so that you may rely on Yahweh,
I am teaching you these things today, you in particular.

See, I have written down for you thirty{f}
of counsel and knowledge,

to teach you what is right and true, words that can be relied on,
so that you can bring back a true answer to those who sent you?

Do not plunder a poor man just because he is poor,
and do not trample the lowly in the gate,

for Yahweh will plead their case
and rob of life those who rob them.

Do not befriend a hot-tempered man,
or go around with a man of rage,

or you will learn his ways
and get yourself caught in a snare.

Do not be one of those who strike hands in pledge,
who stand as security for debts.

If you have nothing to pay with,
why should your bed be taken from under you?

Do not move the ancient boundary stone
that your fathers set up.

You see a man who is quick and expert at his trade?
Before kings he will take his place,
not before men of no account.

notes.text: Or “according to the way he should go.” The Septuagint lacks this verse.
The Septuagint adds “God loves a cheerful and generous man, but he will bring the emptiness of his works to an end”; compare 2 Corinthians 9:7.
The Septuagint adds “Whoever gives freely wins victory and honor, but he takes away the life of those who possess them.”
The Septuagint adds “Evil ways lie before a man, and he does not like to turn from them, but he must turn aside from a twisted and evil way.”
A new collection begins here (22:17–24:22), with close parallels in the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, which is divided into thirty chapters.

So the Masoretic marginal reading, as many interpreters understand it; the written text reads shilshom, “formerly,” and the marginal reading shalishim is also taken as “excellent things.” The Septuagint reads “record them for yourself three times.”

verses.text:
When you take your seat to eat with someone in power,
pay close attention to what{a} is in front of you,

and put a knife to your throat
if you have a large appetite.

Have no longing for his dainties,
since that bread is a lie.

Do not wear yourself out getting rich;
have the sense to stop.

Let your eyes light on it, and it is gone,
for it will surely sprout wings
and fly off into the sky like an eagle.

Do not eat the bread of a stingy man{b}
or crave his delicacies,

You will bring up the little you have eaten
and ruin your pleasant conversation.

Waste no words on a fool’s ears;
he will look down on your sensible speech.

Do not move the ancient boundary stone
or go into the fields of the fatherless,

for their Redeemer{d} is strong;
he will plead their case against you.

Apply your mind to instruction,
your ear to the sayings of knowledge.

Do not hold back discipline from a boy;
if you strike him with the rod, he will not die.

Strike him with the rod yourself,
and you will rescue his life from Sheol.

My son, if your heart is wise,
my own heart too will be glad;

my very kidneys{e} will cheer
at the upright things your lips say.

Do not let your heart be jealous of sinners,
but stay in the fear of Yahweh all day.

There is surely a future,
and your hope will not be cut off.

Hear, my son; grow wise;
steer your heart down the road.

Do not be among those who guzzle wine
or those who gorge themselves on meat,

for the drunkard and the glutton will come to poverty,
and drowsiness will dress them in rags.

Listen to your father, who gave you life,
and do not despise your mother when she is old.

Buy truth and do not sell it—
wisdom, discipline, and understanding.

The father of a righteous son will shout for joy;
whoever fathers a wise son will be glad in him.

Let your father and your mother be glad;
let her who bore you rejoice.

My son, give me your heart,
and let your eyes take pleasure in{f} my ways.

For a prostitute is a deep pit,
and a foreign woman a narrow well.

She lies in wait like a robber
and adds to the number of the treacherous among men.

Who has woe? Who has sorrow?
Who has quarrels? Who has complaints?
Who has wounds for no reason?
Who has bloodshot eyes?

Those who linger late over wine,
who go in search of mixed wine.

Do not stare at wine when it is red,
when it sparkles in the cup
and goes down smoothly.

In the end it bites like a snake
and stings like a viper.

Your eyes will see strange sights,
and your heart will speak twisted things.

You will be like someone lying down in the middle of the sea,
like someone lying on top of a mast.{g}

“I was hit,” you say, “and it did not hurt me;
I was thrashed, and I never noticed.
How long till I am awake?
I will go after it again.”

notes.text: Or “who.”
Literally “of one evil of eye.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain; or “as he calculates in his soul, so is he.”
Hebrew go’el, the next of kin who defends a family member’s rights; here God himself.
Hebrew “kidneys,” thought of as the seat of the deepest feelings.
So the written Hebrew text; the Masoretic marginal reading has “keep.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.

verses.text:
Do not envy evil men
or long to be in their company,

for their hearts plot violence
and their lips talk of trouble.

By wisdom a house is built,
and by understanding it is made firm;

by knowledge its rooms are filled
with all kinds of precious and pleasant riches.

A wise man is strong,{a}
and a man of knowledge adds to his power,

for with guidance you will wage your war,
and with many counselors there is victory.

Wisdom is out of a fool’s reach;
at the city gate he has nothing to say.

Whoever plans to do evil
will be called a master schemer.

The scheming of folly is sin,
and the mocker is detestable to people.

If you lose heart in the day of trouble,
your strength is small.

Rescue those being taken away to death;
hold back those stumbling toward the slaughter.

If you say, “See, we did not know this,”
does not the one who weighs hearts perceive it?
Does not the one who guards your life know it?
Will he not repay a person according to his work?

Eat honey, my son, for it is good,
and the honeycomb is sweet to your taste.

Do not lie in wait, wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous;
do not destroy his resting place,

for seven times the righteous man may fall and get up again,
but the wicked are tripped up by disaster.

When your enemy goes down, do not celebrate;
when he trips, keep your heart from gloating,

lest Yahweh look on with disapproval
and withdraw his anger from that man.

Do not fret because of evildoers
or envy the wicked,

for there is no tomorrow for the evildoer;
the light of the wicked will go out.

My son, fear Yahweh and the king;
do not mix with those who change sides,{b}

for disaster from them will rise suddenly,
and who knows the ruin both of them can bring?{c}

These also are sayings of the wise:{d}
To show partiality in judgment is not good.

Anyone who tells a guilty man, “You are in the right,”
will be cursed by peoples and damned by nations,

but those who convict the guilty will find delight,
and a rich blessing will come upon them.

He kisses the lips
who gives an honest answer.

Do not testify against your neighbor for no reason;
would you mislead with your lips?

Do not say, “I will treat him the way he treated me;
I will repay him for his deed.”

I went past a lazy man’s field,
past the vineyard of a senseless man,

I looked and took it to heart;
I saw and received instruction:

a little sleep, a little slumber,
a little folding of the hands to rest,

and poverty will come on you like a prowler,
and want like an armed man.{e}

notes.text: So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Hebrew reads “A wise man is in strength.”
Or “with those of high rank”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Septuagint adds a long passage here (verses 22a–e in some editions) on the son who keeps the commandment and on the king’s tongue as a sword. In the Septuagint, 30:1–14 also follows here.
A short collection begins here (24:23–34).
In the Septuagint, 30:15–33 and 31:1–9 follow this verse; chapters 25–29 come next, and then 31:10–31.

verses.text: These too are proverbs of Solomon, which the men of Hezekiah{a} king of Judah copied out.

It is God’s glory to keep a thing hidden
and the glory of kings to search a matter through.

As the heavens for height and the earth for depth,
so the heart of kings is past searching out.

Clear the dross away from the silver,
and a vessel comes out for the smith;

clear the wicked away from the king’s presence,
and his throne will be made firm by righteousness.

Do not put yourself forward in the king’s presence
or take your stand in the place of the great,

Do not rush out to bring a quarrel to court,
for what will you do at the end
when your neighbor puts you to shame?

Argue your case with your neighbor himself,
and do not give away another’s secret,

or whoever hears will reproach you,
and your bad name will never go away.{c}

Apples of gold in settings of silver—
so is a word spoken at the right time.{d}

A gold ring, an ornament of fine gold—
so is a wise man’s rebuke to a listening ear.

Clouds and wind but no rain—
so is a man who boasts of a gift he never gives.

With patience a ruler may be won over,
and a soft tongue can break a bone.

Found honey? Eat just what you need,
or you will have too much and vomit it up.

Let your foot be seldom in your neighbor’s house,
or he will have his fill of you and hate you.

A war club, a sword, a sharpened arrow—
so is a man who testifies falsely against his neighbor.

A bad tooth, a slipping foot—
so is trust in a traitor on a day of trouble.

Like taking off a cloak on a cold day, like vinegar poured on soda,{e}
so is one who sings songs to a heavy heart.{f}

If the one who hates you is hungry, give him bread to eat;
if he is thirsty, give him water to drink,

So you will be piling live coals on his head,{g}
and Yahweh will reward you.

The north wind brings forth rain,
and a secretive tongue, angry looks.{h}

Better a spot on a corner of the rooftop
than a whole house with a contentious woman.

Cold water for a parched throat—
such is good news from a distant land.

Like a muddied spring or a polluted well
is a righteous man who gives way before the wicked.

To eat much honey is not good,
nor to search out one’s own glory.{i}

Like a city breached, left without walls,
is a man who has no control of his spirit.

notes.text: Hezekiah means “Yahweh strengthens.” He was king of Judah about 715–686 BC (2 Kings 18–20).
The last line may belong with verse 8.
The Septuagint adds “Favor and friendship set a person free; keep them for yourself, so that you do not become a target of reproach, but guard your ways peaceably.”
The meaning of the Hebrew for “settings” is uncertain; or “carvings.”
Hebrew nether, natron, a natural soda that fizzes when vinegar is poured on it.
The Septuagint adds “Like a moth in a garment and a worm in wood, so a man’s grief harms the heart.”
An image of making him burn with shame, or perhaps drawn from an Egyptian rite of penitence; quoted in Romans 12:20.
In Israel rain comes mostly from the west; “north” may mean “northwest,” or the saying may come from elsewhere.
The second line is uncertain; or “but to search out difficult things is glory.”

verses.text:
Like snow in summer or rain at harvest,
honor does not fit a fool.

Like a flitting sparrow, like a darting swallow,
a curse without cause does not land.{a}

A whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey,
and a rod for the backs of fools.

Do not answer a fool by his own folly,
or you will become like him yourself.

Answer a fool by his own folly,
or he will think himself wise.{b}

Whoever sends a message by a fool
cuts off his own feet and drinks down violence.

Like legs dangling uselessly from a lame man
is a proverb in the mouth of fools.

Like tying a stone into a sling
is giving honor to a fool.

A thorn that springs up in a drunkard’s grip—
such is a proverb in the mouths of fools.

An archer piercing all comers—
such is the man who hires a fool, or hires whoever happens along.{c}

Like a dog that goes back to its vomit
is a fool who repeats his folly.{d}

Do you see a man wise in his own eyes?
There is more hope for a fool than for him.

The sluggard says, “There is a lion in the road!
A lion loose in the squares!”

The door turns on its hinge,
and the sluggard on his bed.

The sluggard buries his hand in the dish;
he is too weary to bring it back to his mouth.

The sluggard is wiser in his own eyes
than seven people who answer sensibly.

Whoever seizes a passing dog by its ears
is like one who meddles in someone else’s quarrel.

Like a madman shooting
firebrands, arrows, and death

is the man who deceives his neighbor
and says, “I was only joking!”

Where there is no wood, the fire goes out;
where there is no whisperer, quarreling dies down.

Charcoal to embers and wood to fire—
so is a quarrelsome man for kindling strife.

The words of a whisperer are like tasty morsels;
they go down into the inner rooms of the belly.

Like a glaze of silver dross over clay
are burning lips with an evil heart.{e}

A man full of hate puts on a mask with his talk,
but inside he lays up treachery.

When he speaks graciously, do not believe him,
for seven abominations are in his heart.

Though his hatred is covered with guile,
his evil will be exposed in the assembly.

Dig a pit and you will drop into it;
roll a stone and it will come rolling back on you.

A tongue that lies hates its victims;
a smooth mouth brings about a downfall.

notes.text: So the Masoretic marginal reading; the written text has “does not come to it,” perhaps “does not come to him,” the one who utters it.
Verses 4 and 5 are set side by side on purpose: whether to answer a fool depends on the case.
The Hebrew of this verse is very obscure. Other proposals include “A master craftsman makes everything, but one who hires a fool is like one who hires passers-by.”
Quoted in 2 Peter 2:22. The Septuagint adds “There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace.”
Or, with a slight change of the Hebrew, “like glaze over clay”; a Ugaritic word suggests “silver dross” should be read as “glaze.”

verses.text:
Do not brag about tomorrow;
you have no idea what today will give birth to.

Let another praise you, not your own mouth;
a stranger, and not your own lips.

A stone is heavy and sand a burden,
but a fool’s provocation weighs more than both.

Fury is savage, anger an overflowing flood,
but jealousy—who can hold out against it?

Better an open rebuke
than love kept hidden.

Faithful are the wounds of a friend,
but the kisses of an enemy are profuse.{a}

A full stomach tramples on honey,
but to a hungry stomach everything bitter is sweet.

A bird wandering far from its nest,
a man wandering far from his place—they are alike.

Oil and incense gladden the heart,
and the sweetness of a friend comes from heartfelt counsel.{b}

Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart,
so that I can answer anyone who taunts me.

The shrewd sees trouble and hides;
the naive go on and pay for it.

Take the garment of one who stands surety for a stranger;
hold it as a pledge when he guarantees a foreign woman.

Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning,
it will be counted to him as a curse.

A steady dripping on a rainy day
and a quarrelsome wife are alike;

whoever would hold her back holds back the wind,
and his right hand meets only oil.{c}

Iron sharpens iron,
and one person sharpens the face of another.{d}

The keeper of a fig tree eats its figs;
the one who guards his master gets respect.

As water reflects face to face,
so the heart of a person reflects the person.

Sheol and Abaddon can never get enough,
nor can the eyes of humankind.{e}

The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold,
and a person is tested by the praise he receives.{f}

Though you pound a fool in a mortar,
in among the grain with a pestle,
his folly will not depart from him.

Know well the condition of your flocks;
set your heart on your herds,

for wealth does not last for all time,
and a crown is not passed down age after age.

When the hay is gone and the new growth appears
and the grass of the hills is gathered in,

lambs will supply your garments,
and goats will pay for a field,

and you will have goats’ milk in plenty to eat,
to feed your whole household,
and to keep your servant girls alive.

notes.text: Or “deceitful,” from a different understanding of the Hebrew.
The second line is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “but the soul is torn by calamities.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Or “so one person sharpens another.”
The Septuagint adds “Whoever fixes his eye is detestable to the Lord, and the uninstructed do not restrain their tongue.”
The Septuagint adds “The heart of the lawless seeks out mischief, but an upright heart seeks knowledge.”

verses.text:
The wicked run off with no one chasing them,
but the righteous are as bold as a young lion.

When a land rebels, its rulers are many,
but with a man of understanding and knowledge, order lasts.{a}

A poor man who grinds down the poor
is a driving rain that leaves no bread.

Those who abandon instruction{b} praise the wicked;
those who keep instruction fight against them.

Evil men have no grasp of justice;
those who seek Yahweh grasp it fully.

A poor man walking in his integrity is better off
than a rich man crooked in his two ways.

A son with understanding keeps the instruction,
but one who keeps company with gluttons shames his father.

One who swells his wealth by interest and profiteering
gathers it for someone who will be kind to the poor.

If one turns his ear from hearing instruction,
even his prayer is detestable.

Whoever leads the upright astray onto an evil road
will drop into his own pit,
but the blameless will inherit good.

A rich man is wise in his own sight,
but a poor man with discernment sees right through him.

When the righteous triumph, there is great splendor,
but when the wicked rise, people go into hiding.

Whoever covers up his wrongs will not prosper,
but whoever confesses and leaves them will find mercy.

Happy is the one who is always in awe,
but whoever hardens his heart tumbles into trouble.

A roaring lion, a charging bear—
such is a wicked ruler over a helpless people.

A prince who lacks understanding is a great oppressor,
but one who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.

A man burdened with another’s lifeblood
will flee to the pit; let no one hold him back.{c}

One who walks blamelessly will be kept safe,
but one crooked in his two ways will fall all at once.{d}

Whoever works his land will be filled with bread;
whoever chases empty things will be filled with poverty.

A trustworthy man has blessings in abundance;
a man racing to wealth will not stay innocent.

Favoritism is not good,
yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread.

The stingy man{e} hurries after wealth
and does not know that want will come to him.

Whoever rebukes a man will in the end find more favor
than one who flatters with his tongue.

Whoever robs his father or mother and says, “It is no crime,”
is partner to a destroyer.

The greedy stirs up strife,
but whoever trusts in Yahweh will grow fat.

Whoever trusts in his own heart is a fool,
but whoever walks in wisdom will escape.

One who gives to the poor will never lack,
but one who shuts his eyes will get many curses.

When the wicked rise, people hide;
when they perish, the righteous multiply.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult.
Hebrew torah, here probably the teaching of the wise as well as the law of God; so also in verses 7 and 9.
The Septuagint adds “Discipline your son, and he will love you and bring honor to your soul; he will not obey a lawless nation.”
Or “will fall into a pit,” reading one letter differently.
Literally “the man evil of eye,” as in 23:6.

verses.text:
Someone corrected again and again who keeps a stiff neck
will be shattered in a moment, past all mending.

When the righteous increase, the people rejoice,
but when a wicked man rules, the people groan.

A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father,
but one who keeps company with prostitutes squanders his wealth.

By justice a king gives a land stability,
but a man of levies{a} tears it down.

A man who flatters his neighbor
spreads a net for his feet.

In the offense of an evil man there is a snare,
but the righteous sings and rejoices.

The righteous knows the rights of the poor;
the wicked has no such understanding.

Mockers set a city ablaze,
but the wise turn anger away.

When a wise man goes to law with a fool,
the fool rages and laughs, and there is no rest.

Men of blood hate the blameless,
and as for the upright, they seek his life.{b}

A fool lets out all his temper,
but a wise man holds it back and calms it.

When a ruler pays heed to lies,
every one of his servants turns wicked.

The poor man and the oppressor meet together;
Yahweh gives light to the eyes of both.

A king who judges the poor faithfully
will have his throne made firm forever.

The rod and rebuke give wisdom,
but a boy left to himself shames his mother.

As the wicked multiply, so does transgression,
and the righteous will look on at their fall.

Discipline your son, and he will give you rest;
he will bring delight to your soul.

Where there is no vision,{c} the people run wild,
but happy is the one who keeps the instruction.

A servant cannot be corrected by words alone;
he understands, but he does not respond.

Do you see a man hasty with his words?
There is more hope for a fool than for him.

Whoever pampers his servant from youth
will find him a weakling{d} in the end.

An angry man stirs up strife,
and a hot-tempered man is full of offenses.

A man’s pride will bring him low,
but the lowly in spirit will take hold of honor.

To go shares with a thief is to hate yourself;
you hear the oath and say nothing.{e}

Fear of people sets a snare,
but whoever trusts in Yahweh is set high and safe.

Many seek a ruler’s face,
but a man’s justice comes from Yahweh.

The righteous loathe the man of injustice;
the wicked loathe the man of the straight road.

notes.text: Hebrew terumot, contributions, perhaps forced gifts or heavy taxes.
Or “but the upright care for his life.”
Hebrew hazon, prophetic revelation.
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain; or “an heir,” or “a cause of grief.”
A public curse was pronounced on any witness who withheld testimony (Leviticus 5:1).

verses.text:
The words of Agur{a} son of Jakeh, the oracle.{b}
This man’s utterance to Ithiel, to Ithiel and Ucal:{c}

I am more brute than man;
I lack a human’s understanding.

I have not learned wisdom,
nor do I have knowledge of the Holy One.

Who has gone up to the heavens and come down?
Who has gathered the wind in the hollow of his hands?
Who has wrapped up the waters in a cloak?
Who has fixed all the ends of the earth?
What is his name, and what is his son’s name?
Surely you know!

Every word of God has been through the fire;
he is a shield to those who take refuge in him.

Do not tack anything onto what he says,
lest he call you to account and you stand exposed as false.

Two things I request from you;
do not hold them back from me as long as I live:

or I may have too much and deny you
and say, “Who is Yahweh?”
or I may be poor and steal
and do violence to the name of my God.

Never run down a slave to his owner,
lest he call down a curse on you and you be held guilty.

There is a breed of people who curse their fathers
and give no blessing to their mothers,

a generation pure in its own eyes
yet not washed of its filth,

a generation—how lofty its eyes,
how raised its eyelids!—

a generation whose teeth are swords,
whose jaws are knives,
to devour the poor from the earth
and the needy from among humankind.

The leech{d} has a pair of daughters,
“Give!” and “Give!”
Three there are that are never full,
four that never cry, “Plenty!”:

Sheol, the barren womb,
earth that never has its fill of water,
and fire that never says, “Enough!”

An eye that sneers at a father
and makes light of a mother’s word
will be picked out by the valley ravens
and eaten by the young vultures.

Three things are beyond me,
four I cannot fathom:

how a vulture finds its way through the air,
how a snake finds its way over rock,
how a ship finds its way in the heart of the sea,
and how a man finds his way with a young woman.{e}

This is the way of an adulterous woman:
she eats and wipes her mouth
and says, “I have done nothing wrong.”

Three things make the earth shudder,
four it cannot endure:

under a slave when he becomes king,
and a godless fool when he is filled with food,

a despised woman who finally marries,
and a maidservant who replaces her mistress.

Four things on earth are small,
but they are exceedingly wise:

the ants are a people without strength,
yet they store up their food in summer;

the hyraxes,{f} a folk with no might,
who set up house among the cliffs;

the locusts have no king,
yet all of them march out in ranks;

the gecko{g} you can catch in your hand,
yet it is found in kings’ palaces.

Three there are with a splendid gait,
four that move with a splendid step:

the lion, mightiest among beasts,
who turns back from nothing;

the strutting rooster{h} or the he-goat,
and a king with his army around him.{i}

If you have been a fool, exalting yourself,
or if you have been plotting evil,
put your hand over your mouth.

notes.text: Agur may mean “gatherer” or “hired”; Jakeh perhaps “pious” or “obedient.” Nothing more is known of either. The Septuagint does not read these as names; it reads “My son, revere my words, receive them, and repent. These things the man says to those who trust in God, and I cease.” In the Septuagint, 30:1–14 stands after 24:22.
Hebrew hamassa’, “the oracle”; or “of Massa,” a north Arabian people descended from Ishmael (Genesis 25:14); compare 31:1.
Ithiel means “God is with me,” and Ucal perhaps “I am able.” With a different division of the Hebrew consonants the line reads “I am weary, O God; I am weary, O God, and exhausted.”
Hebrew ‘aluqah, perhaps a bloodsucking leech or a mythical vampire-like creature.
Or “a girl”; Hebrew ‘almah, a young woman of marriageable age.
Hebrew shephanim, the rock hyrax, a small animal that lives among rocks.
Or “lizard” or “spider”; the meaning of the Hebrew semamit is uncertain.
Hebrew zarzir motnayim, literally “girded of loins”; the animal is uncertain. The Septuagint has “a rooster strutting boldly among the hens”; others suggest a greyhound or a war horse.
The meaning of the Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
The verse plays on Hebrew ’aph, which means both “nose” and “anger.”

verses.text: The words of Lemuel,{a} king, an oracle{b} that his mother taught him:

What, my son? What, son of my womb?
What, son of my vows?

Do not hand over your vigor to women
or your ways to the destroyers of kings.

Kings, Lemuel, should not drink wine—
kings should not,
and rulers should not long for liquor,

lest they drink and lose sight of what is laid down
and pervert the cause of every oppressed person.

Let strong drink go to the man who is dying,
wine to those whose souls are bitter;

let them drink it down, forget how poor they are,
and think no more of their trouble.

Open your mouth for the one who cannot speak,
for the rights of all who are passing away.{c}

Open your mouth, judge rightly,
and defend the rights of the poor and needy.

A woman of valor{d}—who can find her?
Her worth is far beyond corals.

Her husband’s heart trusts in her,
and he will never lack for gain.

She does him good and not harm
all the days of her life.

She looks out for wool and flax
and works them with eager hands.

She is like the merchant ships;
she brings her food from far away.

While it is yet dark she is up,
setting out food for her house
and a share for her young women.

She looks a field over and acquires it;
with what her hands have earned she puts in a vineyard.

She wraps her waist in strength
and makes her arms strong.

She can taste that her dealings turn a profit;
all night her lamp stays lit.

She puts her hands to the distaff,
and her palms grasp the spindle.

Her palm is spread out to the poor;
her hands stretch toward the needy.

She has no fear of snow for her household,
for all her household are clothed in scarlet.{e}

She weaves bed coverings for herself;
she is dressed in fine linen and purple.

Her husband is known in the gates
when he takes his seat among the elders of the land.

She makes linen garments and sells them
and supplies sashes to the merchant.

She is clothed in strength and dignity,
and she smiles at the future.

She opens her mouth with wisdom,
and the teaching of loyal love{f} is on her tongue.

She keeps watch over the doings of her household
and does not eat the bread of idleness.

Her sons stand up and bless her;
her husband joins in her praise:

“Many daughters have done valiantly,
but you surpass them all.”

Charm is deceptive and beauty is a breath,{g}
but a woman who fears Yahweh—she shall be praised.

Give her the fruit of her hands,
and let her works praise her in the gates.

notes.text: Lemuel means “belonging to God.” He is otherwise unknown; the Septuagint does not read a name here (see the next note).

Hebrew massa’; or “king of Massa,” the north Arabian people mentioned at 30:1. The Septuagint reads “My words have been spoken by God, the oracular answer of a king, whom his mother instructed,” and places 31:1–9 after 30:33 within chapter 24.
Or “who are left desolate”; literally “children of passing away.”

Hebrew ’eshet chayil, a woman of strength, ability, and worth, the phrase used of Ruth (Ruth 3:11) and at 12:4. Verses 10–31 are an alphabetic acrostic: each verse begins with the next of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, from aleph in verse 10 through bet (11), gimel (12), dalet (13), he (14), vav (15), zayin (16), het (17), tet (18), yod (19), kaf (20), lamed (21), mem (22), nun (23), samekh (24), ayin (25), pe (26), tsade (27), qof (28), resh (29), and shin (30), to tav in verse 31. In the Septuagint this poem follows chapter 29.
Or, with the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses, “in double garments.”
Hebrew torat chesed; or “kindly instruction.”
Hebrew hevel, “vapor, breath,” the key word of Ecclesiastes.

books.name: Ecclesiastes
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (Old Greek), whose very literal Ecclesiastes is close to the Hebrew, and against the oldest manuscript of the book, 4QQoh-a (4Q109) from Qumran Cave 4, copied about 175–150 BC. That scroll preserves parts of 5:14–18 (Hebrew 5:13–17), 6:1, 3–8, and 12, and 7:1–10 and 19–20; its differences from the Masoretic Text are small (spelling, word order, and a few words), and the significant ones are footnoted. Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. The speaker’s title, Qoheleth (traditionally “the Preacher” or “the Teacher”), is kept untranslated; see the note at 1:1. The key word hevel, traditionally “vanity,” is rendered consistently as “a breath”; see the note at 1:2. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:17, so Hebrew 5:1–19 is English 5:2–20.

verses.text: The words of Qoheleth,{a} son of David,{b} king in Jerusalem.

A breath of breaths,{c} says Qoheleth,
a breath of breaths! Everything is a breath.

What does a person gain from all the toil
he labors at under the sun?

One generation leaves and another arrives,
yet the earth stays put forever.

The sun comes up and the sun goes down;
it pants back to its place, where it rises again.

Blowing toward the south,
then swinging round toward the north,
round and round goes the wind,
and on its rounds the wind comes back.

All the streams flow into the sea,
yet the sea is never full.
To the place where the streams flow,
there they keep on flowing.

All things are wearisome,
more than anyone can say.
The eye never has its fill of seeing,
nor is the ear filled up with hearing.

Is there a thing of which someone says,
“Look, this is new”?
It already existed in the ages
that were before our time.

No one remembers those who came first,
and those yet to come
will not be remembered either
by the ones who come after them.
I, Qoheleth, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.
I set my mind to seek and to explore by wisdom everything that is done under the heavens. It is a grim task that God has given human beings to keep them busy.
I have observed everything done under the sun, and it is all vapor, like trying to catch the wind.{d}

What is bent no one can straighten,
and what is missing no one can number.
I said to myself, “Look, I have grown great and gathered more wisdom than all who ruled Jerusalem before me; my mind has taken in a wealth of wisdom and knowledge.”
So I set my mind to understand wisdom, and to understand madness and folly.{e} I came to see that this too is a chasing after wind.

For with much wisdom comes much grief,
and whoever adds to knowledge adds to pain.

notes.text: Hebrew Qoheleth, a feminine participle from qahal, “assembly”: one who gathers or addresses an assembly, or perhaps one who gathers sayings (12:9). It is traditionally rendered “the Preacher” or “the Teacher”; the Greek title Ekklesiastes means “member of an assembly” or “speaker in an assembly.” It is kept untranslated here as the speaker’s title or pen name; in 12:8 it takes the article (“the Qoheleth”).
David means “beloved.”

Hebrew hevel habalim. Hevel means “breath” or “vapor,” something real but brief and impossible to grasp, and so “fleeting,” “futile,” or “absurd” depending on context; it is traditionally rendered “vanity” (Septuagint mataiotes). It is rendered “a breath” throughout this book so that its 38 occurrences can be traced and readers can weigh its sense in each place. “A breath of breaths” is a Hebrew superlative: “the most fleeting of breaths.”
Or “a feeding on wind” or “a striving after wind”; the Hebrew re‘ut ruach is uncertain. The same phrase occurs in 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6; 6:9.
The Septuagint reads “parables and understanding” for “madness and folly.”

verses.text: I said to myself, “Come on, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good.” But that too turned out to be a breath.
Of laughter I said, “It is mad,” and of pleasure, “What does it accomplish?”

I searched with my mind for a way to cheer my body with wine, while my mind still guided me with wisdom, and a way to grasp folly, until I could discover what is worth doing for people during their short lives under heaven.
I undertook great works: houses I built for myself, vineyards I planted for myself.
I made myself gardens and parks{a} and planted every kind of fruit tree in them.
I made myself pools of water to irrigate a forest of growing trees.
I acquired male and female slaves, and I had slaves born in my household. I also owned more herds and flocks than all who were before me in Jerusalem.
I piled up silver and gold for myself, the treasure of kings and provinces. I got myself male and female singers and the delights of mortals: many concubines.{b}
So I became great, surpassing all who were before me in Jerusalem, and my wisdom stayed with me.
Whatever my eyes asked for, I did not withhold from them. I kept no joy from my heart, for my heart found joy in all my labor, and that was my portion from all my labor.
Then I turned to survey all the works my hands had made and the labor I had put into making them, and see, it was all a breath and a chasing after wind. There was no gain under the sun.
So I turned to consider wisdom, madness, and folly. For what can the one who comes after the king do? Only what has already been done.{c}
I saw that wisdom has the advantage over folly, as light has the advantage over darkness.

The wise have eyes in their heads,
but the fool walks in the dark.
Yet I also came to know that one fate befalls them both.
So I said to myself, “The fool’s fate will be mine as well. Why then have I been so very wise?” And I told myself that this too is a breath.
For the wise, like the fool, will not be remembered for long; in the days to come both will long since be forgotten. How the wise die just like fools!
So I came to hate life, since what is done under the sun weighed on me as evil. For everything is a breath and a chasing after wind.
I hated all the toil I had toiled at under the sun, because I must leave it to whoever comes after me.
And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? Yet he will be master of everything I worked for and used my wisdom to gain under the sun. This too is a breath.
So I turned and let my heart sink into despair over all the toil I had labored at under the sun.
For here is someone whose labor was done with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must hand over his portion to someone who did not labor for it. This too is a breath and a great evil.
What do people get for all their toil and the striving of their hearts with which they labor under the sun?
All their days are pain, and their work is vexation; even at night their minds find no rest. This too is a breath.
There is nothing better for a person than to eat and drink and to find good in his toil. This too, I saw, is from the hand of God.
For who can eat or who can enjoy anything apart from him?{d}

To the one who pleases him God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy, but to the sinner he assigns the business of collecting and heaping up, so that it may be passed on to whoever is good in God’s sight. This too is a breath and a chasing after wind.

notes.text: Hebrew pardesim, a Persian loanword for walled parks or orchards, the source of the English word “paradise.”
Hebrew shiddah wesiddoth, an obscure phrase found only here; it is often taken as “many concubines,” but the Septuagint reads “a butler and female cupbearers.”
The Hebrew of the second half is difficult; literally “What is the man who will come after the king? That which they have already done.”
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Masoretic Text reads “apart from me.” “Enjoy” may also mean “worry” or “have sensation.”

verses.text:
For everything there is an appointed time,
and a season for every matter under the heavens:

a time to be born and a time to die,
a time to plant and a time to pull up what was planted;

a time to kill and a time to heal,
a time to tear down and a time to build up;

a time to weep and a time to laugh,
a time to mourn and a time to dance;

a time to throw stones and a time to gather stones,{a}
a time to embrace and a time to hold back from embracing;

a time to seek and a time to let go,
a time to hold on and a time to discard;

a time to rip and a time to stitch,
a time to keep silent and a time to speak;

a time to love and a time to hate,
a time for war and a time for peace.
What does the worker gain from his toil?
I have seen the task God has given human beings to keep them occupied.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity{b} in their hearts, yet in such a way that they cannot grasp what God has done from beginning to end.
I know that there is nothing better for them than to rejoice and to do good{c} as long as they live.
And also, that everyone should eat and drink and find good in all his toil: this is God’s gift.
I know that whatever God does lasts forever. Nothing can be added to it and nothing taken from it. God has done this so that people will stand in awe of him.
I also noticed something under the sun: where justice should be, there was wickedness, and where righteousness should be, there was wickedness.
I told myself, “God will judge both the righteous and the wicked, for there is a season for every affair and every action.”{e}
I told myself concerning humans, “God is testing them so they will see that they are no more than animals.”
For the fate of humans and the fate of beasts is one fate. The death of one is like the death of the other; one breath{f} is in them all. Humans have no edge over beasts, for everything is a breath.
All go to one place. All come from the dust, and to dust all return.
Who can say whether a human spirit goes up while an animal’s spirit goes down to the earth?{g}
So I saw that there is nothing better than for a person to rejoice in his work, for that is his lot. For who can bring him to see what will happen after him?

notes.text: The meaning of this pair is uncertain: perhaps clearing a field and building a wall, or a sexual euphemism, as the next line may suggest.
Hebrew ha‘olam; or “a sense of the ages” or, with a different vowel, “ignorance.”
Or “to enjoy themselves.”
Or “what has passed”; literally “what is pursued.”
The Hebrew “there” is unexpected; some read “he has appointed” with a slight change of vowels.
Hebrew ruach, “breath” or “spirit,” a different word from hevel.
So the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses; the Masoretic vowels read “Who knows the spirit of humans that rises upward…?”

verses.text: Once more I surveyed all the oppression practiced under the sun. Here are the oppressed in tears, and nobody to console them! Their oppressors had force on their side, and nobody to console the victims.
So I counted the dead, who died long ago, more fortunate than the living, who are still alive.
But better off than both is the one who has never yet been, who has not seen the evil deeds done under the sun.
And I saw that all toil and all skillful work come from one person’s rivalry with another. This too is a breath and a chasing after wind.

The fool folds his hands
and devours his own flesh.

Better one handful with quiet
than two fistfuls with toil and a chasing after wind.
Again I saw a breath under the sun:

There is someone all alone, with no companion, neither son nor brother, yet his toil never ends, and his eyes never have enough of wealth. “For whom am I toiling,” he asks, “and depriving myself of good things?” This too is a breath, a miserable business.

Two are better than one,
because together they earn a good return for their toil.

If they fall, one can lift up his partner.
But pity the one who falls with no one to help him up!

Again, when two sleep side by side, they have warmth,
but one by himself, how can he get warm?

Where one may be overpowered, two can make a stand,
and a cord of three strands is not quickly snapped.
Better a poor but wise youth than an old and foolish king who no longer knows how to take advice.
For the youth went from prison to the throne, though he had been born poor in that kingdom.{a}
I saw all the living who move about under the sun throng to the youth, the second one, who would rise up in the king’s place.
There was no end to all the people he led,{b} yet those who come later will not be pleased with him. This too is a breath and a chasing after wind.

notes.text: The Hebrew of verses 13–16 is allusive, and it is not always clear which figure is meant by “he.”
Or “all who went before them”; literally “all who were before them.”

verses.text: Watch your step{a} when you go to the house of God. To draw near and listen is better than for fools to offer a sacrifice, for they do not know that they are doing wrong.{b}

Don’t be hasty with your mouth,
or quick to speak a word in front of God.
God is in heaven and you are on earth,
so keep your words few.

For a dream comes with much busyness,
and a fool’s voice with many words.
When you vow a vow to God, do not put off paying it, for he takes no pleasure in fools. Pay what you vow.
Not vowing is better than vowing and not paying.
Do not let your speech lead your body{c} into sin, and do not tell the temple messenger{d} it was an accident. Why make God furious with your words and destroy what you have worked for?
For with many dreams come breaths and a flood of words.{e} Rather, fear God.
If you see the poor oppressed and justice and right violated in a province, do not be astonished at the matter. For one official is watched by a higher one, and still higher ones are over them.
But the gain from the land is for all; a king is served by the cultivated field.{f}

Whoever loves silver is never satisfied with silver,
nor whoever loves wealth with its income.
This too is a breath.

When goods increase,
so do those who consume them.
And what does their owner gain
except the sight of them with his eyes?

Sweet is the worker’s sleep,
whether he eats little or much,
but the rich man’s plenty
will not let him sleep.
There is a sickening evil I have seen under the sun: riches hoarded by their owner to his own harm.
Those riches are lost in a bad venture, and when he fathers a son, nothing is left in his hand.{g}
As he came out of his mother’s womb, naked he will go back, just as he came. He will take nothing for his toil that he can carry away in his hand.
This too is a sickening evil: exactly as he came, so he will go. What does he gain from toiling for the wind?
All his days he also eats in darkness, with much vexation, sickness, and anger.{h}

Here is what I have seen to be good: it is fitting for a person to eat and drink and enjoy good in all the toil he labors at beneath the sun for the number of days God grants him to live, for that is his lot.
Also, everyone to whom God has given riches and possessions, and the power to enjoy them, to accept his lot and rejoice in his toil, this is a gift of God.
For he will not dwell much on the days of his life, because God keeps him occupied with the joy of his heart.

notes.text: In Hebrew this verse is 4:17, and verses 2–20 are 5:1–19. The Ketiv reads “your feet.”
Or “for they do not know how to do anything but wrong.”
Hebrew “flesh.”
Probably a temple official or priest; the Septuagint reads “before God.”
Or “For in many dreams and many words there are breaths.” The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this verse is obscure.
Hebrew 5:13–17 (English 5:14–18) is partly preserved in 4QQoh-a, the oldest known manuscript of Ecclesiastes (about 175–150 BC).
The Septuagint reads “and mourning” for “he eats,” a similar-looking Hebrew word.

verses.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun, and it weighs heavily on humankind:

someone to whom God gives riches, possessions, and honor, so that he lacks nothing he could wish for, yet God does not give him the power to enjoy them; a stranger enjoys them instead. This is a breath and a sickening evil.

Suppose someone has a hundred children and lives for many years, however long his life may last, but he never enjoys his prosperity{a} and is not even buried properly; I say a stillborn baby is better off than he.
For it comes in a breath and departs in darkness, and in darkness its name is covered.{b}
It has not seen the sun or known anything, yet it has more rest than he does.
Even if he lived a thousand years twice over but did not enjoy good,{c} do not all go to one place?

All the toil of humankind is for the mouth,
yet the appetite is never filled.

For what advantage have the wise over fools?
What does the poor man gain by knowing how to conduct himself before the living?

Better what the eyes can see
than the roving of desire.
This too is a breath and a chasing after wind.
Whatever came into existence was named long ago, and what humanity is has been understood: no one is able to argue a case with someone stronger.
The more words, the more breath. What advantage is that to anyone?
Who knows what is good for a human being in life, during the few days of a fleeting life,{d} which passes like a shadow? Who can say what will happen on earth after he is gone?

notes.text: In 4QQoh-a (about 175–150 BC) the words of the opening clauses of this verse appear in a different order, without change in meaning.
In 4QQoh-a the original scribe wrote “and in darkness his name is covered,” referring to the man; a later scribe corrected it to agree with the Masoretic Text.
4QQoh-a uses some different words in this verse, with the same meaning.
Literally “the days of the life of his breath.”

verses.text:
A good name is better than fine perfume,{a}
and the day of death than the day of birth.

Better to go to a house of mourning
than to a house of feasting,
for that is the end of everyone,
and the living should take it to heart.

Grief is better than laughter,
for a sad face may mean a glad heart.

The heart of the wise is in the house of mourning,
but the heart of fools is in the house of pleasure.

Better to heed the rebuke of the wise
than to listen to the song of fools.

Surely extortion turns the wise into fools,
and a bribe corrupts the heart.{c}

The end of a thing is better than its start;
patience of spirit is better than pride of spirit.

Do not be quick in spirit to take offense,
for resentment lodges in the bosom of fools.

Do not ask, “How is it that former days were better than these?”
For it is not wisdom that prompts this question.

Wisdom is good together with an inheritance,
a benefit to those who see the sun.

For wisdom is a shelter as money is a shelter,
and the benefit of knowing is that wisdom keeps its owner alive.

Consider the work of God:
who can straighten what he has bent?

In a good day, enjoy the good,
and in a bad day, reflect:
God made this day as well as that,
so that no one can find out anything that will come after him.
In my fleeting days{d} I have seen both: a righteous person perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked person living long in his wickedness.
Do not be too righteous, and do not make yourself overly wise. Why destroy yourself?
Do not be too wicked, and do not play the fool. Why should you die before your time?
It is good to hold on to the one and not let go of the other, for whoever fears God will come through both.{e}

Wisdom makes the wise stronger{f}
than ten rulers in a city.

Surely there is no one on earth so righteous
that he does good and never sins.
Also, do not pay attention to everything that is said, or you may overhear your servant cursing you.
For your own heart knows how often you too have cursed others.
All this I tested by wisdom. I said, “I will be wise,” but it was far from me.
Whatever has come to be is distant and deep, deep indeed; who can fathom it?
I set my mind to know, to investigate, and to look for wisdom and the explanation of things,{g} and to recognize the stupidity of wickedness and the madness of folly.
And I find more bitter than death the woman who is a snare, whose heart is nets and whose hands are chains. Whoever pleases God escapes her, but the sinner is caught by her.
“See, this is what I found,” says Qoheleth,{h} “adding one thing to another to find the sum,
which I keep searching for but have not found: I found one upright man in a thousand, but among all of them I found not one upright woman.
Only see, this I did find: God made human beings upright, but they have sought out many schemes.”

notes.text: The Hebrew has a wordplay: shem, “name,” and shemen, “oil” or “perfume.”
Another wordplay: sirim, “thorns,” under the sir, “pot.”
Hebrew mattanah, “gift,” here in the sense of a bribe. 4QQoh-a may have a different verb in the first line.
Hebrew “days of my breath.”
Or “will avoid both extremes.”
So the Masoretic Text, “makes strong”; 4QQoh-a and the Septuagint read “helps.”
Hebrew heshbon, “account” or “reckoning,” also in verse 27.
The Hebrew has the verb in the feminine, “she says, Qoheleth”; dividing the letters differently gives “says the Qoheleth,” as in 12:8, a reading supported by the Septuagint.

verses.text:
Who is like the wise?
Who knows how to explain a matter?
Wisdom lights up a person’s face
and softens its hardness.{a}
I say:{b} obey the king’s command, because of the oath you swore before God.
Do not hurry to leave his presence, and do not persist in a bad cause, for he does whatever he likes.
Since the king’s word is supreme, who can say to him, “What are you doing?”
Whoever keeps the command will come to no harm, and a wise heart knows the proper time and procedure.
For every matter has its time and procedure, though human trouble lies heavy on a person.
No one knows what is to come; who can tell anyone how it will turn out?
No one has power over the wind{c} to restrain it, nor power over the day of death. There is no discharge in wartime, and wickedness will not rescue those who practice it.
All this I observed as I applied my mind to everything done under the sun, at a time when one person rules over another to his harm.
I also saw the wicked given burial; they had come and gone from the holy place, and people forgot{d} them in the very city where they had acted that way. This too is vapor.
Because the sentence against an evil deed is not carried out quickly, people’s hearts are fully set on doing evil.
A sinner may do evil a hundred times and still live long, yet I know that it will go well with those who fear God, because they stand in awe before him.
But things will not go well for the wicked, and his days will not stretch out like an evening shadow, because he does not fear God.

There is a breath that occurs on earth: there are righteous people who get what the deeds of the wicked deserve, and wicked people who get what the deeds of the righteous deserve. I said that this too is a breath.

So I recommend enjoyment, because nothing is better for people under the sun than eating, drinking, and having a good time. That will stay with them in their work during the days of life God gives them under the sun.
When I set my heart to know wisdom and to watch the business that goes on upon the earth, even going without sleep day and night,

then I saw all the work of God: no one can fathom the work that is done under the sun. However much people strive in searching, they will not find it out. Even if a wise person claims to know, he cannot discover it.

notes.text: Literally “and the strength of his face is changed”; the Septuagint reads “but a man of shameless face will be hated.”
The Hebrew “I” stands alone at the start of the verse; something may have dropped out.
Or “the spirit” or “the breath of life.”
So the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “praised,” which differs by one Hebrew letter.

verses.text: I took all this to heart and tested it: that the righteous and the wise, and all their deeds, are in God’s hands. Whether love or hatred lies in store, nobody knows; it all lies before them.

Everything is the same for everyone:{a} one fate for the righteous and the wicked, the good, the clean and the unclean, the one who sacrifices and the one who does not. As with the good person, so with the sinner; as with the one who swears an oath, so with the one who shrinks from swearing.

This is an evil in all that is done under the sun: that one fate comes to all. Moreover, human hearts are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and afterward they go to the dead.
But whoever is joined{b} to all the living has hope, for a live dog is better off than a dead lion.
For the living know that they will die, but the dead know nothing. They have no more reward, for even the memory of them is forgotten.{c}
Their love, their hate, and their jealousy have already vanished, and they will never again have a share in anything done under the sun.
Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a cheerful heart, for God has already approved what you do.
At all times wear white garments, and never let oil be missing from your head.

Enjoy life with the wife you love throughout your fleeting life that God has granted you under the sun, all your fleeting days,{d} since that is your reward in life and for the labor you do beneath the sun.
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your strength, for there is no work or planning or knowledge or wisdom in Sheol,{e} where you are going.

Again I saw under the sun that the swift do not win the race, the mighty do not win the battle, the wise do not always have bread, the intelligent are not always rich, and the knowledgeable are not always favored; time and chance meet them all.
Indeed, no one knows his time. As fish are seized in an evil net and birds are gripped in a snare, so human beings are trapped at an evil time, when it drops on them without warning.
This also I saw as wisdom under the sun, and it struck me as great:
There was a small city with few men in it, and a great king came against it, surrounded it, and built great siegeworks against it.
Now in it lived a man, poor but wise, and by his wisdom he rescued the city. But no one gave a thought to that poor man.
So I said, “Wisdom is better than might,” but the poor man’s wisdom is despised, and his words go unheeded.

Words of the wise heard in calm
are worth more than a fool-ruler’s shouting.

Wisdom is better than weapons of war,
but one sinner destroys much good.

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “Vanity is in all” at the beginning of this verse, joining the last word of verse 1 to it and reading hevel, “a breath,” for hakkol, “everything.”
So the Qere; the Ketiv reads “chosen.”
A wordplay in Hebrew: sakar, “reward,” and zeker, “memory.”
Literally “all the days of the life of your breath… all the days of your breath.” The Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses lack the repeated phrase.
The realm of the dead; the Septuagint has “Hades.”

verses.text:
Dead flies make a perfumer’s oil stink and ferment;
a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor.

The heart of the wise leans to the right hand,
the heart of the fool to the left.{a}

Even as the fool walks along the road, his sense fails him,
and he shows everyone that he is a fool.

If the ruler’s anger rises against you, do not leave your post,
for calmness lays great offenses to rest.
There is an evil I have seen under the sun, an error of the kind that comes from one in power:
folly is set in many high places, while the rich sit in lowly ones.
I have seen slaves on horseback and princes going on foot like slaves.

Whoever digs a pit may fall into it,
and whoever breaks through a wall may be bitten by a snake.

One who cuts stone may be injured by it,
and one who chops wood may be endangered by it.

If the snake bites before it is charmed,
there is no profit for the charmer.{b}

Words from a wise mouth win favor,
but a fool’s lips swallow him up.

What his mouth says starts out as folly,
and what it ends with is wicked madness.
The fool multiplies words, though no one knows what is to come; who can tell anyone what will happen after him?

A fool’s toil wears him out,
for he does not even know the way to town.

Woe to you, O land, when your king is a lad{c}
and your officials banquet at dawn!

Fortunate are you, land, whose king is from a noble family
and whose officials eat at the right time,
for strength and not for drunkenness!

Through laziness the rafters sag,
and through idle hands the house leaks.

Feasts are made for laughter,
and wine cheers the living,
and money answers for everything.

notes.text: The right hand stood for strength and favor, the left for weakness or misfortune.
Literally “master of the tongue.”
Or “a servant.” The Septuagint addresses a city here.
Or “in your bed”; the Hebrew madda‘ may mean “knowledge” or, with a different reading, “bed.”

verses.text:
Send your bread out on the surface of the waters,
for after many days you will find it again.

Share a portion with seven, or even with eight,
for you cannot know what disaster may come on the earth.

When clouds are full,
they empty rain on the earth;
and whether a tree falls south or north,
wherever it falls, there it lies.

Whoever keeps watching the wind will never sow,
and whoever keeps studying the clouds will never reap.

As you cannot tell the way the wind{a} goes
or how the bones form in the womb of a woman with child,
so you cannot grasp what God is doing,
he who makes it all.

Sow your seed in the morning,
and in the evening do not rest your hand,
for you do not know which will thrive, this or that,
or whether both alike will turn out well.

Sweet is the light,
and it is good for the eyes to look at the sun.
However many years a person lives, he should take joy in each of them, while remembering that the dark days will be many. Everything still to come is a breath.

Drive grief out of your heart
and keep harm away from your flesh,
for youth and its dark hair{c} are a breath.

notes.text: Or “the spirit” or “the life-breath,” entering the unborn child.
The Septuagint reads “walk in the ways of your heart blameless, but not in the sight of your eyes.”
Hebrew shacharuth, probably “the black hair” of youth, or “the dawn.”

verses.text:
Remember your Creator{a} in the days of your youth,
before the bad days come
and the years approach of which you will say,
“I have no pleasure in them”;

on the day when the keepers of the house shake,
and the men of strength stoop,
and the grinders cease since they are few,
and the ones who gaze through the windows are darkened;{b}

when the street doors are closed
and the grinding sound grows faint,
when people wake at the sound of a bird,
and all the singing girls are silenced;

before the silver cord is snapped{e}
and the bowl of gold is cracked,
and the pitcher smashed beside the spring,
and the wheel crushed at the cistern,

and the dust goes back to the ground it came from,
and the life breath{f} goes back to God who gave it.

“A breath of breaths,” says the Qoheleth;
“everything is a breath.”
Besides being wise, Qoheleth also taught the people knowledge, weighing, studying, and arranging many proverbs.
Qoheleth sought to find pleasing words and to write words of truth correctly.
The words of the wise are like goads, and the masters of collections are like nails driven firmly in; one Shepherd has given them.
And besides these, my son, take warning: to the making of many books there is no end, and much poring over them exhausts the flesh.
The end of the matter, now that all has been heard: fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole of being human.{g}
For God will bring every deed into judgment, including everything hidden, whether good or evil.

notes.text: The Hebrew form is plural, probably a plural of majesty. Some interpreters hear a play on bor, “pit” (the grave), or be’er, “well” (one’s wife, as in Proverbs 5:15–18).
Verses 3–5 are often read as a picture of old age: trembling arms, bent legs, few teeth, failing eyes; or as a household in mourning.
Its white blossoms are often taken as an image of white hair.
Probably the caper plant, whose buds were thought to stir the appetite.
So the Qere; the Ketiv reads “removed.”
Or “spirit,” Hebrew ruach.
Literally “for this is all of humanity” or “this is every person’s duty.”

books.name: Song of Songs
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (Old Greek) through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Fragments of four Song of Songs manuscripts were found at Qumran (4QCant-a, -b, -c and 6QCant); where the variants cited are not verified individually they are described as “some ancient witnesses.” The Hebrew text has no speaker labels, but its grammar (masculine and feminine forms, singular and plural) usually shows who is speaking; the speakers are identified only in the footnotes (“She,” “He,” “The friends,” the “daughters of Jerusalem”), and no headings have been added. Plants, spices, and places are explained at their first appearance. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; English 6:13 is Hebrew 7:1, so Hebrew 7:2–14 is English 7:1–13.

verses.text: The Song of Songs,{a} which is Solomon’s.{b}

Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth,{c}
for your love{d} is better than wine.

Draw me after you; let us run!
The king has brought me into his chambers.
We will rejoice and delight in you;{e}
we will praise your love more than wine.
How right they are to love you!

Black am I, and lovely,
you daughters of Jerusalem,
dark as the tents of Kedar,{f}
as the hangings of Solomon.

Do not look down on me for being dark,
for the sun has burned me.
My brothers were furious with me;
they put me in charge of the vineyards,
but my own vineyard I neglected.

Tell me, my beloved,
where you pasture your flock,
where you rest them at noon?
Why should I wander like a veiled woman{g}
among your friends’ flocks?

If you do not know, loveliest of women,
go out in the footprints of the sheep
and feed your kids
near the tents of the shepherds.{h}

To a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots
I compare you, my darling.{i}

Lovely are your cheeks between the earrings,
your neck among the beads.

Earrings of gold we will make for you,
dotted with silver.{j}

While the king lay on his couch,
my nard{k} spread out its scent.

My beloved is to me a sachet of myrrh{l}
that lies all night between my breasts.

My beloved is to me a cluster of henna blossoms{m}
in the vineyards of En-gedi.{n}

Look at you, my darling, so beautiful,
so beautiful! Your eyes are doves.{o}

How handsome you are, my beloved, how delightful!{p}
Our couch is green and leafy;

the beams of our house are cedars,
our rafters are junipers.{q}

notes.text: A Hebrew way of saying “the finest song.”
Or “for Solomon” or “about Solomon.” The name Shelomoh is connected with shalom, “peace.”
She speaks in verses 2–4, turning from “him” to “you.” The Hebrew has no speaker labels; here and below they are inferred from the grammar.
Hebrew dodim, “lovemaking” or “caresses”; also in verse 4. The Septuagint, reading the same letters differently, has “your breasts.”
The plural “we” may be the young women of verse 3 or the friends; “you” is masculine.
Kedar, a tribe of the Syrian–Arabian desert, whose name may mean “dark”; their tents were woven of black goat hair.
Perhaps veiled as a prostitute (compare Genesis 38:14–15); some ancient witnesses read “one who wanders.”
He replies in verse 8, or perhaps the friends.
He speaks in verses 9–11. Hebrew ra‘yati, “my companion,” his usual word for her in the Song. A mare loosed among chariot stallions was a famous image of distraction.
The “we” here may be his companions or the friends.
She speaks in verses 12–14. Nard, or spikenard, a costly perfume from a plant of the Himalayas.
Myrrh, a fragrant resin from trees of Arabia and East Africa, worn in a small pouch.
Henna, a shrub with fragrant clusters of white flowers, also used for dye.
En-gedi, “spring of the young goat,” an oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea.
He speaks.
She speaks in verses 16–17; some divide verse 17 between them.
Or “firs” or “cypresses”; the exact tree is uncertain.

verses.text:
I am a crocus{a} of Sharon,{b}
a lily of the valleys.

As a lily among the brambles,
so is my darling among the girls.{c}

Like an apple tree{d} among the trees of the forest,
so is my beloved among the young men.{e}
In his shade I delight to sit,
and his fruit is sweet to my taste.

He has brought me to the house of wine,
and his banner over me is love.

Revive me with raisin cakes,
refresh me with apples,
for I am faint with love.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles, by the wild does:
do not rouse, do not wake love
until it wishes!{f}

Hark! My beloved!
See, he is coming,
springing across the mountains,
bounding over the hills.

My beloved is like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer.
There he is, standing outside our wall,
looking in at the windows,
glancing through the latticework.

My beloved answers me and says,
“Up, my darling,
my beautiful one, come away,

for look, the winter is past;
the rain has ended and gone.

Blossoms appear in the land,
the season of singing{g} has come,
and the cooing of the turtledove
is heard in our land.

The fig tree ripens its early figs,
and the vines in bloom give off fragrance.
Arise, my darling,
my beautiful one, and come away.

My dove in the clefts of the rock,
in the hiding places of the cliff,
show me your form,
let your voice be heard,
for sweet is the sound of you
and lovely the sight of you.”

Seize the foxes for us,{h}
those little foxes
that spoil the vineyards
now that our vines are blossoming.

My beloved is mine and I am his;
he grazes among the lilies.

Until the day breathes
and the shadows slip away,
come back, my beloved, like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer
on the cleft mountains.{i}

notes.text: She speaks. The flower is uncertain: crocus, narcissus, or some other meadow flower; the Septuagint has “a flower of the plain.”
Sharon, the coastal plain south of Mount Carmel, known for its pastures and wildflowers; the name means “plain.”
He speaks.
Hebrew tappuach, perhaps the apple, apricot, or quince.
She speaks in verses 3–17.

A wordplay: tsevaoth, “gazelles,” and ’ayloth hassadeh, “does of the field,” sound like the divine titles “Yahweh of hosts” and “God Almighty” (El Shaddai), as though she swears by them in a veiled way. The Septuagint reads “by the powers and by the virtues of the field.” The refrain returns in 3:5 and 8:4.
Or “pruning,” as in the Septuagint; Hebrew zamir can mean either.
The speaker of verse 15 is uncertain; perhaps she quotes a song, or her brothers speak (compare 1:6).
Or “the mountains of Bether,” an unknown place, or “the mountains of spices” (compare 8:14). The Septuagint has “the mountains of the ravines.”

verses.text:
“I will rise now and go around the city,
through the streets and the squares;
I will seek the one my soul loves.”
I sought him but did not find him.

The watchmen came upon me,
those who patrol the city.
“The one my soul loves: have you seen him?”

I had barely left them
when I met the man I love.
I grabbed him and refused to release him
until I brought him to my mother’s home,
to the chamber of the woman who bore me.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem,
by the gazelles, by the wild does:
do not rouse, do not wake love
until it wishes!

all of them gripping swords,
trained in battle,
each with his sword at his thigh
against the terrors of the night.

King Solomon made himself a carriage{d}
of wood from Lebanon.{e}

Its posts he made of silver,
its back of gold,
its seat of purple wool,
its interior inlaid with love{f}
by the daughters of Jerusalem.

Come out, women of Zion,
and look at King Solomon
in the crown his mother set on him
at his wedding,
on the day his heart was glad.

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–5. Literally “in the nights.”
The speaker of verses 6–11 is unstated: perhaps the friends or a narrator. “Who is this” is feminine in Hebrew, referring to the litter or to the bride.
Frankincense, a white resin from trees of southern Arabia and Somalia, burned as incense.
Hebrew ’appiryon, found only here, perhaps a loanword from Persian or Greek for a palanquin or sedan chair.
Lebanon, “white,” from its snowcapped peaks, famous for its cedars.
