Or “inlaid with leather,” by a related Semitic word; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Your teeth are like a flock of shorn ewes
come up from the washing,
every one of them bearing twins,
and none among them bereaved.

A scarlet ribbon, those lips of yours,
and lovely is your mouth.
Like a half of pomegranate
is your temple behind your veil.

Your neck is like the tower of David,
built in courses,{c}
with a thousand shields hung on it,
all the round shields of warriors.

Your breasts are two fawns,
a gazelle’s twins,
grazing among the lilies.

Until the day breathes
and the shadows slip away,
I will go to the mountain of myrrh
and to the hill of frankincense.

You are beautiful through and through, my darling;
there is no flaw in you.

How fine is your love, my sister, my bride!
How much better your love than wine,
and the scent of your oils than any spice!

A garden locked up is my sister, my bride,
a spring{g} locked up, a fountain sealed.

Your shoots are an orchard{h} of pomegranates
with choicest fruits,
henna with nard,

You are a fountain in the gardens,
a well of living water,
streams flowing down from Lebanon.

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–15.
Gilead, the hill country east of the Jordan, known for its pastures; the name may mean “heap of witness” (compare Genesis 31:47–48).
Hebrew talpiyyoth, found only here; the meaning is uncertain: perhaps “in courses of stone,” “for weapons,” or “as a landmark.”
The Septuagint reads “Come from Lebanon, my bride.” The Hebrew “with me” may be read with a slight change of vowels as “come.”
Amana, a peak in the Anti-Lebanon range; Senir, the Amorite name for Hermon (Deuteronomy 3:9), or a nearby peak. Hermon, the highest mountain of the region, about 9,200 feet (2,814 meters).
“Sister” was a term of endearment for a beloved or bride in ancient Near Eastern love poetry; it does not imply kinship.
Hebrew gal, perhaps “pool” or “spring”; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read gan, “garden,” repeating the first line.
Hebrew pardes, “park” or “orchard” (compare Ecclesiastes 2:5).
Saffron, the dried stigmas of the crocus, used as a spice and dye.
Calamus, a fragrant reed or cane imported from the east (compare Exodus 30:23).
Aloes here means eaglewood, a fragrant Asian wood, not the medicinal aloe plant.
She speaks in verse 16.

verses.text:
My beloved thrust his hand through the opening,{d}
and my insides stirred for him.

I got up to open to my beloved,
and my hands dripped with myrrh,
my fingers with liquid myrrh,
on the handles of the bolt.

I put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem:
if you find my beloved,
what will you tell him?
That I am faint with love!

What makes your beloved better than any other,{f}
most beautiful of women?
What makes your beloved better than any other,
that you put us under oath like this?

My beloved is dazzling and ruddy,{g}
one who stands out among ten thousand.

His eyes are doves
by the water brooks,
washed in milk,
sitting in their settings.{i}

His cheeks are like beds of spice,
towers of perfumes.{j}
His lips are lilies
dripping liquid myrrh.

His legs are marble columns
resting on golden bases.
He looks as majestic as Lebanon,
as stately as cedar trees.

His mouth is utter sweetness;
he is wholly desirable.
Such is my lover, such is my friend,
women of Jerusalem.

notes.text: He speaks in the first four lines.
Or “drink deep of love.” The speaker of these two lines is uncertain: the friends, a narrator, or he himself.
She speaks in verses 2–8, recounting a dream-like night; he speaks in verse 2 and she answers in verse 3.
Literally “through the hole,” probably the keyhole or latch opening of the door.
Or “when he turned away”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The daughters of Jerusalem speak in verse 9.
She answers in verses 10–16. Hebrew tsach, “radiant” or “shining.”
Hebrew taltallim, found only here, perhaps “like palm fronds” or “curly.”
Or “sitting by brimming pools”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “pouring out perfumes,” with a change of vowels.
Tarshish, a distant port, perhaps in Spain; here probably a gemstone named for it, such as beryl or topaz.
Literally “sapphires”; the ancient stone of that name was probably lapis lazuli.

verses.text:
Where did your beloved go,{a}
loveliest among women?
In what direction did your beloved turn,
that we may seek him along with you?

My beloved has gone down to his garden,{b}
to the beds of spice,
to graze in the gardens
and to gather lilies.

I am my beloved’s and my beloved is mine;
he grazes among the lilies.

Turn your eyes away from me,
for they overwhelm me.
Your hair is a flock of goats
streaming down from Gilead.

Your teeth are a flock of ewes
come up from the washing,
every one of them bearing twins,
and none among them bereaved.

Like a half of pomegranate
is your temple behind your veil.

There may be sixty queens
and eighty concubines,
and young women past counting,

but my dove, my flawless one, is matchless,
her mother’s only daughter,
the pride of the woman who bore her.
Young women saw her and declared her happy;
queens and concubines sang her praise:

“Who is she, gazing out like the morning,
lovely as the moon,{e}
radiant as the sun,
formidable as an army with banners?”

I went down to the nut grove{f}
to see the new growth of the valley,
to see whether the vine had budded
and the pomegranates were in bloom.

Before I knew it, my desire set me
among the chariots of my noble people.{g}

notes.text: The daughters of Jerusalem speak in verse 1.
She speaks in verses 2–3.
He speaks in verses 4–10. Tirzah, “she is pleasing,” was a beautiful city and early royal capital of the northern kingdom (1 Kings 14:17; 16:23); the Septuagint translates the name as “Pleasure.”
Or “as the starry hosts”; the Hebrew nidgaloth is uncertain. Also in verse 10.
The poetic words here are levanah, “the white one,” for the moon, and chammah, “the hot one,” for the sun.
The speaker of verses 11–12 is uncertain, probably she, possibly he.
Or “among the chariots of Amminadib,” as a name, “my kinsman is noble”; the Septuagint has “the chariots of Aminadab.” The Hebrew of this verse is among the most obscure in the book.

In Hebrew this verse is 7:1, and 7:1–13 below are Hebrew 7:2–14. The friends call to her in the first two lines; she, or he, answers in the last two. Shulammite may mean “woman of Shulem” (perhaps Shunem, as in the Septuagint), or be a feminine form linked with Solomon and shalom, “the peaceful one.”
Or “the dance of Mahanaim,” a town east of the Jordan whose name means “two camps” (Genesis 32:2).

verses.text:
Your navel is a round goblet
that never runs short of spiced wine.
Your waist is a mound of wheat
hedged about with lilies.

Your two breasts are like two fawns,
twins of a gazelle.

How lovely you are, how delightful,
love, among all delights!{g}

This stature of yours is like a palm tree,
and your breasts are its clusters.

I said, “I will climb the palm tree;
I will take hold of its fruit stalks.”
May your breasts be like clusters of the vine,
the scent of your breath like apples,

I am my beloved’s,
and his desire is for me.

Let us go early to the vineyards
to see whether the vine has budded,
whether its blossoms have opened
and the pomegranates are in flower.
There I will give you my love.

The mandrakes{k} breathe out their scent,
and at our doors are all the finest fruits,
fresh ones and stored ones,
that I have laid up for you, my beloved.

notes.text: He speaks in verses 1–9a, or the friends in verses 1–5. English 7:1–13 is Hebrew 7:2–14.
Literally “daughter of a noble” or “prince’s daughter.”
Heshbon, “reckoning,” a city east of the Jordan, in what is now Jordan, known for its reservoirs.
Bath-rabbim, “daughter of many,” probably the name of a city gate.
Carmel, “garden land” or “orchard,” the wooded ridge rising above the Mediterranean near modern Haifa.
Purple dye, from the murex shell, was the costliest color in the ancient world.
Or “O loved one, daughter of delights,” following some ancient witnesses with a different division of the Hebrew letters.
She takes up his words in the last two lines and speaks in verses 10–13.
So the Masoretic Text; the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses read “over my lips and teeth.”
Or “in the villages”; Hebrew kefarim can mean either.
Mandrakes, a plant with a fragrant yellow fruit, thought to stir love and fertility (compare Genesis 30:14–16).

verses.text:
Oh, that you were like my own brother,{a}
one suckled at my mother’s breast!
Then if I met you outside, I could kiss you,
and no one would think less of me.

I would guide you and bring you
to my mother’s home, where she would instruct me.{b}
I would give you spiced wine to drink,
the nectar of my pomegranates.

His left hand is under my head,
and his right hand embraces me.

Many waters cannot put out love,
and rivers will not sweep it away.
If someone offered all the wealth of his house for love,
he would be utterly scorned.

We have a little sister,{h}
and she has no breasts yet.
What shall we do for our sister
on the day she is spoken for?

If she is a wall,
we will build on her a parapet of silver;
but if she is a door,
we will board her up with planks of cedar.

My vineyard, my very own, is mine to give.
The twenty-five pounds are yours, Solomon,
and five pounds{m} for those who tend its fruit.

Hurry away, my beloved,{o}
and be like a gazelle
or a fawn of the deer
on the mountains of spices.

notes.text: She speaks in verses 1–4.
Or, with the Septuagint and some other ancient witnesses, “into the room of the one who conceived me” (compare 3:4).
The refrain of 2:7 and 3:5, here without the oath by gazelles and does, and phrased as a question.
The friends speak in the first two lines.
She speaks in verses 5b–7. In the Hebrew, “you” in this verse is masculine. The Septuagint begins this verse “Who is this that comes up all white.”
Or “jealousy,” Hebrew qin’ah, the intense ardor of love.

Hebrew shalhevetyah. The ending -yah may be the short form of the divine name, “a flame of Yahweh,” or it may simply intensify the word, “a mighty flame,” as Hebrew sometimes uses divine names for a superlative. This is the only possible mention of God in the Song.
Her brothers speak in verses 8–9 (compare 1:6).
She speaks in verses 10–12.
Hebrew shalom, perhaps a wordplay on Solomon (Shelomoh) and the Shulammite (6:13).
Baal-hamon, “owner of abundance” or “lord of a multitude,” an unknown place; the name may be symbolic.
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 11.5 kilograms.
Hebrew “two hundred,” that is, two hundred shekels of silver, about 2.3 kilograms.
He speaks in verse 13; “you” is feminine.
She speaks in verse 14 (compare 2:17).

books.name: Isaiah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text), checked against the Great Isaiah Scroll from Qumran Cave 1 (1QIsa-a), copied about 125 BC and preserving the whole book, against the second, fragmentary Isaiah scroll from the same cave (1QIsa-b, 1Q8), whose text stands very close to the Masoretic Text, and against the Septuagint (Old Greek). Scroll readings were checked against Martin Abegg’s transcriptions (as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset); readings that could not be confirmed there are marked “reported.” Septuagint readings were checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Significant differences are footnoted; the scrolls’ many differences of spelling are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is rendered “Yahweh of Armies”; see the note at 1:9. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; English 9:1 is Hebrew 8:23, so English 9:2–21 is Hebrew 9:1–20, and English 64:1 is Hebrew 63:19b, so English 64:2–12 is Hebrew 64:1–11.

verses.text: The vision of Isaiah the son of Amoz, which he saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.{a}

Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth,
for Yahweh has spoken:
“I have nourished and brought up children,
and they have rebelled against me.

The ox knows his owner,
and the donkey the manger of its lord;
Israel has not known,
my people have not understood.”

Ah, sinful nation,
a people heavy with iniquity,
offspring of evildoers,
children who deal corruptly!
They have forsaken Yahweh,
they have despised the Holy One of Israel,
they have turned away backward.{b}

Why will you still be struck,
that you revolt more and more?
The whole head is sick,
and the whole heart faint.

From the sole of the foot even to the head
there is no soundness in it,
but wounds and bruises and fresh sores;
they have not been pressed out, nor bound up,
nor softened with oil.

“What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” says Yahweh.
“I have had my fill of burnt offerings of rams
and the fat of fed beasts;
and I take no delight in the blood of bulls,
or of lambs, or of he-goats.

When you come to stand in front of me,
who asked this of you,
this trampling of my courts?

Bring no more vain offerings;
incense is an abomination to me.
New moon and sabbath, the calling of assemblies—
I cannot endure iniquity along with the solemn meeting.

If you consent and listen,
the best of the land you shall eat;

How the faithful city has become a harlot!
She that was full of justice!
Righteousness lodged in her,
but now murderers.

Your silver has become dross,
your wine mixed with water.

Your rulers are rebels
and partners of thieves.
Every one of them loves bribes
and chases after payoffs.
They do not defend the orphan,
and the widow’s case never reaches them.

Therefore says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
the Mighty One of Israel:{j}
“Ah, I will ease myself of my adversaries,
and avenge myself on my enemies.

I will bring back your judges as they were at first,
and your advisers as they were in the beginning.
After that you will be called the City of Righteousness,
the Faithful City.”

Zion shall be redeemed with justice,
and her returning ones with righteousness.{l}

But the crushing of transgressors and sinners shall be together,
and those who forsake Yahweh shall be consumed.

You will be ashamed of the oak trees you wanted,
and embarrassed by the gardens you chose.{m}

For you shall be as an oak whose leaf withers,
and as a garden that has no water.

notes.text: Isaiah, Hebrew Yesha‘yahu, “Yahweh is salvation”; Amoz, “strong” (not the prophet Amos, a different name in Hebrew). Uzziah, “my strength is Yahweh”; Jotham, “Yahweh is perfect”; Ahaz, “he has grasped”; Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens.” Their reigns span about 790–686 BC; Uzziah died about 740 BC (6:1). Judah, perhaps “praised”; Jerusalem, perhaps “foundation of Shalem (peace).”
The Holy One of Israel, Isaiah’s characteristic title for God (about twenty-five times in the book). Israel, “God strives” or “he strives with God.”
Hebrew “as the overthrow of strangers”; some propose “as the overthrow of Sodom” (sedom for zarim), compare verses 9–10. The Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) adds “upon it.”
Zion, the hill of Jerusalem, meaning uncertain (perhaps “fortress”); “daughter of Zion” personifies the city. The cucumber field’s lodge was a watchman’s hut.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” Tseva’ot means “armies” or “hosts,” whether the armies of Israel, the stars, or the heavenly beings; the title presents Yahweh as commander of every power in heaven and earth. Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities destroyed in Genesis 19; meanings uncertain. Compare Romans 9:29.
Or “instruction” (torah), here prophetic teaching.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “your fingers with iniquity” (compare 59:3).
Or “correct the ruthless”; the Septuagint reads “deliver him that is suffering wrong.” The Hebrew hamots is uncertain.
Or “Though your sins are as scarlet, shall they be white as snow?” The Hebrew may be read as a question.
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord” (the master). “Mighty One of Israel,” Hebrew ’avir yisra’el; compare Genesis 49:24 (“Mighty One of Jacob”).
Or “purge away … as with potash.” Alloy, or “tin” or “lead,” the base metals separated in refining.
Or “her repentant ones.”
The oaks (or terebinths) and gardens were sites of the fertility cults.
Or “the strong man”; or, with a change of vowels, “your strength” (so the Great Isaiah Scroll, “your strength … your work”).

verses.text: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem.

And many peoples shall go and say,
“Come, and let us go up to the mountain of Yahweh,
to the house of the God of Jacob;
and he will teach us from his ways,
and we will walk in his paths.”
For the law shall go out from Zion,
and the word of Yahweh from Jerusalem.{b}

House of Jacob, come,
let us walk in Yahweh’s light.

For you have forsaken your people, the house of Jacob,
because they are filled with customs from the east,
and are soothsayers like the Philistines,
and they strike hands with the children of foreigners.{c}

Their land also is full of silver and gold,
and there is no end of their treasures;
their land also is full of horses,
and there is no end of their chariots.

The lofty looks of man shall be brought low,
and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down,
and Yahweh alone shall be exalted in that day.

and against all the high mountains,
and against all the hills that are lifted up;

and against every lofty tower,
and against every wall made strong;

and against all the ships of Tarshish,
and against all the pleasant craft.{h}
And the idols shall utterly pass away.

And men shall go into the caves of the rocks,
and into the holes of the earth,
from before the terror of Yahweh,
and from the splendor of his majesty,
when he arises to shake the earth with terror.

In that day men shall cast away their idols of silver
and their idols of gold,
which they made for themselves to worship,
to the moles and to the bats;{i}

to go into the clefts of the rocks,
and into the crevices of the crags,
from before the terror of Yahweh,
and from the splendor of his majesty,
when he arises to shake the earth with terror.

Stop trusting in man, who has but breath in his nostrils;
for at what is he to be valued?{j}

notes.text: Verses 2–4 appear also, with small differences, at Micah 4:1–3.
Jacob, “he grasps the heel” or “he supplants,” here the people descended from him. Or “instruction.”

Hebrew “they are filled from the east”; perhaps “filled with diviners from the east” (one word may have dropped out). Philistines, the people of the southern coastal plain. “Strike hands,” that is, make pacts or bargains.
Hebrew ’elilim, a scornful word for idols, sounding like ’elohim (“God”) and meaning “nothings” or “worthless things.”
Or “and you cannot raise them up.” The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this last line (“and do not forgive them”) and all of verse 10; the Septuagint has both.
Compare Revelation 6:15–16.
Lebanon, “white,” the snow-capped mountain range north of Israel; Bashan, the fertile highlands east of the Sea of Galilee.

Tarshish, a distant port in the west, perhaps Tartessus in Spain; “ships of Tarshish” were large seagoing ships. “Pleasant craft,” a rare Hebrew word, perhaps “beautiful vessels”; the Septuagint reads “every ship of the sea, and … every display of fine ships.”
Hebrew “to the dig-rats” (lahpor peroth), a word or words of uncertain meaning, probably moles or shrews; the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it as one word.
The Septuagint lacks this verse; the Great Isaiah Scroll has it.

verses.text:
For behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
takes away from Jerusalem and from Judah
support and supply,
all the support of bread,
and all the support of water;{a}

the warrior and the man of battle,
judge and prophet,
diviner and elder,

the commander of fifty and the man held in honor,
the counselor and the one wise in crafts,
and the one skilled in enchantment.

And I will give boys to be their princes,
and capricious ones shall rule over them.{b}

And the people shall oppress one another,
man against man, and each against his neighbor;
the youth shall behave himself proudly against the old man,
and the base against the honorable.

A man will seize his brother in his father’s house, saying,
“You have a coat; you be our leader,
and take charge of this heap of ruins”—

Their very expressions accuse them,
and they announce their sin like Sodom;
they do not conceal it.
How terrible for them!
They have done harm to themselves.

Say of the righteous that it shall be well with him,
for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.

Woe to the wicked man! Evil is his lot;
for the dealing of his own hands shall be rendered to him.{d}

My people are oppressed by children,
and women rule over them.
My people, your guides lead you astray
and confuse the path you walk.{e}

Yahweh stands up to plead,
and stands to judge the peoples.{f}

Yahweh will enter into judgment
with the elders of his people and their princes:
“It is you who have eaten up the vineyard;
the spoil of the poor is in your houses.

How dare you crush my people
and grind down the faces of the poor?”
says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.

Moreover Yahweh said:
“Because the daughters of Zion are proud,
and go about with necks stretched out
and glancing eyes,
tripping along as they walk,
and jingling with their feet;
In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, and the headbands, and the crescents;{h}
the pendants, and the bracelets, and the veils;
the headdresses, and the ankle chains, and the sashes, and the perfume boxes, and the amulets;
the rings, and the nose jewels;
the festal robes, and the mantles, and the shawls, and the purses;
the mirrors, and the fine linen, and the turbans, and the veils.

Your men shall fall by the sword,
and your mighty ones in the war.

And her gates shall lament and mourn;
and she, emptied, shall sit upon the ground.

notes.text: Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.” “Support and supply,” Hebrew mash‘en umash‘enah, masculine and feminine forms of one word: “every kind of support.”
Or “infants” or “wanton tyranny.” The Hebrew ta‘alulim is uncertain.
Or “to rebel against his glorious presence.”
Hebrew “the dealing of his hands”; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “shall return to him.”
The Septuagint reads “your exactors strip you, and extortioners rule over you,” perhaps taking the Hebrew as nosim (“creditors”) instead of nashim (“women”). “Swallow up,” or “confuse.”
The Septuagint reads “his people”; Hebrew “peoples.”
Or “their foreheads”; the Hebrew poth is uncertain. In verses 17–18 the Great Isaiah Scroll interchanges ’Adonai (“Lord”) and Yahweh, with scribal corrections above the line.
Many of the items in verses 18–23 are rare words whose exact sense is uncertain.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds a word: “for instead of beauty, shame.” “Branding” (ki) may refer to the branding of slaves; some take it as the conjunction “for.”

verses.text:
In that day the sprout of Yahweh shall be for beauty and for glory,
and the fruit of the land for pride and for splendor to the escaped of Israel.{a}
And it shall come to pass that he who is left in Zion and he who remains in Jerusalem shall be called holy, every one who is written for life in Jerusalem,
when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion, and shall have purged the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by the spirit of judgment and by the spirit of burning.{b}

And Yahweh will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud and smoke by day, and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there shall be a canopy.{c}
And there shall be a booth for a shade in the daytime from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from storm and from rain.

notes.text: Or “the sprout of Yahweh”; compare 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8. The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and Judah” after “Israel.”
Or “of destruction.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “of storm” (sa‘ar for ba‘er).
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the words from “and smoke” in verse 5 through “a shade in the daytime” in verse 6, probably by a copyist’s eye skipping from one similar word to another.

verses.text:
Now I will sing to my well-beloved
a song of my beloved about his vineyard:
My well-beloved had a vineyard
on a very fruitful hill.{a}

“And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah,
judge, I pray you, between me and my vineyard.

What more was there to do for my vineyard,
that I have not done in it?
Why, when I looked for it to yield grapes,
did it yield wild grapes?

Now let me tell you
what I am going to do to my vineyard:
I will remove its hedge, and it will be eaten up;
I will tear down its wall, and it will be trampled.

Woe to those who join house to house,
who add field to field,
until there is no room,
and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land!

For ten acres of vineyard shall yield about six gallons,
and six bushels of seed shall yield about half a bushel.”{e}

Woe to those who rise up early in the morning,
that they may follow strong drink;
who tarry late into the night,
till wine inflames them!

And man is bowed down, and each one is brought low,
and the eyes of the lofty are brought low.

But Yahweh of Armies is exalted in justice,
and God the Holy One shows himself holy in righteousness.

Then the lambs shall graze as in their pasture,
and strangers shall eat among the ruins of the fat ones.{g}

Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood,
and sin as with cart ropes;

who say, “Let him make speed, let him hasten his work,
that we may see it;
and let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near and come,
that we may know it!”

Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes,
and prudent in their own sight!

Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine,
and valiant men at mixing strong drink;

who justify the wicked for a bribe,
and take away the righteousness of the righteous from him!

Therefore, as flames lick up stubble
and dry grass shrivels in the fire,
so their roots will decay,
and their blossoms will drift off like dust.
They have rejected the teaching of Yahweh of Armies
and despised the word of Israel’s Holy One.{h}

whose arrows are sharp,
and all their bows bent;
their horses’ hoofs are counted like flint,
and their wheels like a whirlwind.

Their roaring shall be like a lioness,
they shall roar like young lions;
they shall growl and lay hold of the prey,
and carry it off, and none shall deliver.

notes.text: Or “the song of my beloved.” Hebrew “on a horn, a son of oil,” that is, a fertile hillside.
Hebrew be’ushim, “stinking things,” that is, rotten or worthless grapes.
A wordplay: “justice” (mishpat) but “bloodshed” (mispah); “righteousness” (tsedaqah) but “a cry” (tse‘aqah), the outcry of the oppressed.
Hebrew “In my ears, Yahweh of Armies”; “has sworn” is supplied (compare 22:14). The Septuagint reads “these things have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.”

Hebrew “ten yokes of vineyard,” the land ten teams of oxen could plow in a day, “shall yield one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield an ephah.” A bath was about 6 gallons (22 liters); a homer about 6 bushels (220 liters); an ephah about 3/5 bushel (22 liters), a tenth of the seed sown.
Sheol, the realm of the dead; the Septuagint reads Hades.
“The fat ones,” that is, the rich. For gerim, “strangers,” some read gedayim, “kids.” The Septuagint reads “lambs shall feed on the waste places of them that are taken away.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and flaming fire” for “and dry grass in the flame.”
This refrain recurs at 9:12, 17, 21; 10:4.

verses.text: In the year that King Uzziah died I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up, and his train filled the temple.{a}
Above him stood the seraphim. Each one had six wings: with two he covered his face, and with two he covered his feet, and with two he flew.{b}
And the foundations of the thresholds shook at the voice of him who called, and the house was filled with smoke.
Then I said, “Woe is me, for I am undone! For I am a man unclean of lips, and in the midst of a people unclean of lips I dwell; and the King, Yahweh of Armies, my eyes have seen!”{d}
Then one of the seraphim flew to me. In his hand was a glowing coal that he had taken from the altar with tongs.
And he touched my mouth with it and said, “Behold, this has touched your lips; and your iniquity is taken away, and your sin is atoned for.”
Then I heard the Lord’s voice say, “Whom shall I send? And who will go for us?” And I said, “Here I am! Send me.”

Make fat the heart of this people,
make heavy their ears,
and smear over their eyes;
so that they may not see with their eyes,
nor hear with their ears,
nor their heart understand,
and they turn and be healed.”{e}

Then I said, “Lord, how long?” And he answered:
“Until cities lie waste without inhabitant,
and houses without man,
and the land is utterly desolate,

and Yahweh has removed men far away,
and the forsaken places are many in the midst of the land.

If a tenth is still left in it,
that too will be burned,
like a terebinth or an oak
that leaves a stump after it is felled.
The holy seed is the stump.”{f}

notes.text: About 740 BC. “The Lord,” Hebrew ’Adonai. “Train,” the skirts of his robe. Compare John 12:41.
Seraphim, “burning ones,” heavenly beings; the word is also used of serpents (14:29; 30:6; Numbers 21:6). “Feet” may be a modest term for the lower body.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Holy, holy” (twice). Compare Revelation 4:8.
Or “I am silenced” or “I am ruined.”

Verses 9–10 are quoted in Matthew 13:14–15; Mark 4:12; John 12:40; Acts 28:26–27, largely following the Septuagint, which reads “For the heart of this people has become fat.” In verse 10 the Great Isaiah Scroll reads hashem for hashmen (“make fat”), perhaps a shortened spelling, or “appall,” as some have proposed.

Or “at its felling.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads mushleket, “cast down,” for beshalleket, “at its felling,” and bamah for bam (“in them”); the sense is uncertain. The Septuagint lacks the last line.

verses.text: And it came to pass in the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, that Rezin the king of Syria and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to make war against it, but could not prevail against it.{a}
And it was told the house of David, saying, “Syria has settled upon Ephraim.” And his heart and the heart of his people shook as the trees of the forest shake before the wind.{b}
Then Yahweh said to Isaiah, “Go out now to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway to the washers’ field;{c}
and say to him, ‘Be careful and keep still; have no fear, neither let your heart be faint because of these two stubs of smoldering firebrands, at the hot anger of Rezin and Syria and Remaliah’s son.
Aram has hatched an evil plan against you—and so have Ephraim and Remaliah’s son—saying,
“Let’s invade Judah, terrify it, split it open for ourselves, and make the son of Tabeel king over it,”{d}

For the head of Syria is Damascus,
and the head of Damascus is Rezin.
And within sixty-five years
Ephraim shall be shattered from being a people.{f}

And Samaria is the head of Ephraim,
and Remaliah’s son is the head of Samaria.
If you will not hold firm in trust,
surely you will not be held firm.”’”{g}
And Yahweh spoke again to Ahaz, saying,
“Ask a sign of Yahweh your God; ask it either in the depth below or in the height above.”{h}
But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, neither will I put Yahweh to the test.”
And he said, “Listen, house of David! Is it too little for you to tire men out, that you will tire out my God as well?

Butter and honey shall he eat,
when he knows to refuse the evil and choose the good.{j}
For before the child knows to refuse the evil and choose the good, the land whose two kings you dread shall be forsaken.

Yahweh will bring on you and on your people and on the house of your father such days
as have not come from the day when Ephraim broke away from Judah—the king of Assyria.”{k}
On that day Yahweh will whistle for the flies at the far ends of Egypt’s rivers, and for the bees in the land of Assyria.
And they shall come and shall rest, all of them, in the steep ravines, and in the clefts of the rocks, and upon all thornbushes, and upon all watering places.{l}
In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired beyond the River—with the king of Assyria—the head and the hair of the feet; and it shall also sweep away the beard.{m}
And it shall come to pass in that day that a man shall keep alive a young cow and two sheep;
and it shall come to pass, for the abundance of milk that they give, he shall eat butter; for butter and honey shall every one eat who is left in the midst of the land.
And it shall come to pass in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines, worth about twenty-five pounds of silver, shall become briers and thorns.{n}
With arrows and with bow shall one come there, because all the land shall become briers and thorns.
And as for all the hills that were dug with the hoe, you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns; but it shall be a place for sending out oxen and for the treading of sheep.

notes.text: Ahaz reigned about 735–715 BC. Rezin, perhaps “delight,” the last king of Aram (Syria) at Damascus; Pekah, “opened (eyes)”; Remaliah, perhaps “Yahweh has adorned.” This is the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734 BC; compare 2 Kings 16:5.
Hebrew Aram, the Aramean kingdom of Damascus. Ephraim, “doubly fruitful,” here the northern kingdom of Israel. “Settled upon,” or “is allied with.” David, “beloved.”
Shear-jashub, “a remnant shall return” (compare 10:21–22). Or “the fuller’s field.” Compare 36:2.
Tabeel, “God is good,” here with a pun on “good for nothing” (tav’al); perhaps an Aramean candidate for the throne.
Hebrew ’Adonai YHWH.

Damascus, the capital of Aram. Samaria (verse 9), the capital of the northern kingdom, fell to Assyria in 722 BC; the sixty-five years may reckon to the resettlement of the land (compare 2 Kings 17:24; Ezra 4:2).
A wordplay: “If you will not be firm (ta’aminu), you shall not be made firm (te’amenu).”
Or “make it deep as Sheol,” reading she’alah as she’olah.

Hebrew ha‘almah, “the young woman,” a girl of marriageable age, unmarried or newly married; it is not the usual Hebrew word for a virgin (betulah), and it does not of itself say whether she is a virgin. Or “is with child and is about to bear a son.” The Septuagint, made about two centuries before Christ, renders the word parthenos, ordinarily “virgin,” and Matthew 1:23 quotes the Septuagint (“Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel”) of the birth of Jesus. The second-century Jewish Greek translations of Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion are reported by early Christian writers to have read neanis, “young woman.” Immanuel, ‘immanu ’el, “God is with us” (compare 8:8, 10). “Shall call,” or “you shall call”; the Septuagint reads “you shall call,” and the Great Isaiah Scroll “he shall call” (or “one shall call”). The Great Isaiah Scroll also reads Yahweh for ’Adonai (“the Lord”).
Or “curds and honey,” the food of a land returned to pasture (verse 22). “When he knows,” or “so that he may know.”
Assyria, the great power of upper Mesopotamia, with its capital at Nineveh.
Or “all the pastures.”
The River, the Euphrates. “The hair of the feet,” the body hair; shaving was a mark of humiliation (2 Samuel 10:4).
Hebrew “a thousand of silver,” that is, a thousand shekels, about 25 pounds (11.5 kilograms).

verses.text: Yahweh said to me, “Take a large tablet and write on it in ordinary letters, ‘Belonging to Maher-shalal-hash-baz.’{a}
And I will take for myself faithful witnesses to testify, Uriah the priest and Zechariah the son of Jeberechiah.”{b}
And I went to the prophetess, and she conceived and bore a son. Then Yahweh said to me, “Call his name Maher-shalal-hash-baz;{c}
for before the child knows how to cry ‘My father’ and ‘My mother,’ the riches of Damascus and the spoil of Samaria shall be carried away before the king of Assyria.”
And Yahweh spoke to me yet again, saying,
For thus Yahweh spoke to me with a strong hand, and warned me not to walk in the way of this people, saying,{h}

And many shall stumble on it,
and fall and be broken,
and be snared and be taken.”

Bind up the testimony;
seal the law among my disciples.{k}

And I will wait for Yahweh,
who hides his face from the house of Jacob,
and I will look for him.
Behold, I and the children whom Yahweh has given me are for signs and for wonders in Israel from Yahweh of Armies, who dwells on Mount Zion.{l}
And when they say to you, “Seek the mediums and the spiritists who chirp and mutter,” is it not to its God that a people should inquire? On behalf of the living, should they inquire of the dead?{m}
To the law and to the testimony! Surely those who do not speak according to this word have no dawn.{n}

And they shall pass through it, hard pressed and hungry; and it shall come to pass that when they are hungry they shall fret themselves, and curse their king and their God, and turn their faces upward;
and they shall look to the earth, and behold, distress and darkness, the gloom of anguish; and into thick darkness they shall be thrust.{o}

notes.text: Hebrew “with the stylus of a man,” that is, in ordinary script. Maher-shalal-hash-baz, “the spoil speeds, the prey hastens,” foretelling the plundering of Damascus and Samaria (verse 4).

Uriah, “Yahweh is my light,” the priest of 2 Kings 16:10–16; Zechariah, “Yahweh remembers”; Jeberechiah, “Yahweh blesses.” “I will take,” so the Hebrew; the Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read imperatives (“take for me” / “make … witnesses”).
The prophetess, probably Isaiah’s wife.
Shiloah, “sent,” the gentle stream from the Gihon spring (compare Siloam, John 9:7), a symbol of the quiet rule of the house of David. “Rejoices in,” the sense of the Hebrew is uncertain.
Immanuel, “God is with us”; see 7:14.
The Septuagint reads “Know, O nations”; some read “Be joined together” for “Be broken.” The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the last line.
Hebrew ‘immanu ’el, “God is with us,” the name of 7:14.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and he turned me aside from walking” for “and warned me.”
Or “what they reverence.” Compare 1 Peter 3:14–15.
Compare Romans 9:33; 1 Peter 2:8.
Or “instruction” (torah), here Isaiah’s teaching.
Compare Hebrews 2:13.
Hebrew ’ovot and yidd‘onim, those who consulted ghosts and the spirits of the dead; compare Leviticus 19:31; 1 Samuel 28.
Or “surely they shall speak according to this word, for which there is no dawn.” The Hebrew is difficult.
In the Hebrew text 8:23 begins with the first line of English 9:1.

verses.text: Yet the gloom will lift from the land that was in anguish. At first he brought shame on the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, but afterward he has made glorious the road by the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the nations.{a}

For the yoke of his burden,
and the bar across his shoulder,
the rod of his taskmaster,
you have broken as on the day of Midian.{d}

For every boot of the warrior that tramped in the tumult,
and every cloak rolled in blood,
shall be for burning, food for the fire.

Of the increase of his rule and of peace
there shall be no end,
upon the throne of David and over his kingdom,
to establish it and to uphold it
with justice and with righteousness
from now on and forever.
The zeal of Yahweh of Armies will do this.{f}

A word the Lord sent into Jacob,
and it has fallen upon Israel;{g}

and all the people shall know it,
Ephraim and the inhabitant of Samaria,
who say in pride and in arrogance of heart:

So Yahweh raises the foes of Rezin against him,
and spurs on his enemies,

Yet the people have not turned to him who struck them,
nor have they sought Yahweh of Armies.

So Yahweh cuts off from Israel head and tail,
palm branch and reed, in one day—

the elder and the man of rank, he is the head;
and the prophet who teaches lies, he is the tail.

For those who lead this people lead them astray,
and those who are led by them are swallowed up.{j}

Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh,
and together they turn on Judah.
Despite all this, his anger has not turned away,
and his hand is still raised.{n}

notes.text: This verse is 8:23 in the Hebrew, and English 9:2–21 are Hebrew 9:1–20. Zebulun, “honor” or “dwelling”; Naphtali, “my wrestling”; Galilee, “circle” or “district,” here the region of the nations around Israel’s north. Or “Galilee of the Gentiles.” Verses 1–2 are quoted in Matthew 4:15–16 of the ministry of Jesus in Galilee.
Or “deep darkness.”

The Hebrew written text (ketiv) reads “you have not made great its joy”; the text as traditionally read aloud (qere) has “to it” (lo) for “not” (lo’), as here. The Great Isaiah Scroll has the written form, “not.”
Midian, “strife”; the day of Gideon’s victory over Midian (Judges 7). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Madim.”

Hebrew pele’ yo‘ets, ’el gibbor, ’avi‘ad, sar shalom; or “a Wonder of a Counselor,” “God the Warrior” (compare 10:21, where ’el gibbor is God himself), “Father forever.” Some, following medieval Jewish interpretation, take the long name as a sentence describing God who gives the child (“the Wonderful Counselor, the Mighty God, the Everlasting Father, calls him Prince of Peace”). The Septuagint reads “and his name is called the Messenger of great counsel, for I will bring peace upon the princes.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Prince of the peace” and “and he called.” In the Hebrew this is 9:5.

In the traditional Hebrew text the first word (lemarbeh, “of the increase”) is written with a final form of the letter mem in the middle of the word, a feature long discussed by interpreters; the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it normally. David, “beloved.”
The Septuagint reads “The Lord has sent death” (dever, “pestilence,” for davar, “word”).
Or “sycamore figs,” a common, cheap timber.
Hebrew Aram from the front and the Philistines from behind, that is, east and west. The Septuagint reads “Syria from the rising of the sun, and the Greeks from the setting of the sun.” Compare 5:25.
Or “confused.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “does not spare” (yahmol for yismah).
Or “is shaken” or “burned up”; the Hebrew ne‘tam is uncertain.
Or, with some, “the flesh of his neighbor” (re‘o for zero‘o). Manasseh, “causing to forget”; Ephraim, “doubly fruitful,” the two great tribes of the northern kingdom.

verses.text:
Woe to those who decree unjust decrees,
and the writers who keep writing oppression,

to turn aside the needy from justice,
and to rob the poor of my people of their right,
so that widows become their spoil,
and they plunder the fatherless!

What will you do on the day of punishment,
and in the ruin that comes from afar?
To whom will you flee for help,
and where will you leave your wealth?{a}

Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners,
or to fall among the slain.
For all this his anger has not turned back,
and his hand is stretched out still.{b}

Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger!
The staff in their hand is my fury.{c}

I send him against an ungodly nation,
I order him against a people who anger me,
to seize loot and take plunder
and to stomp on them like mud in the streets.

But this is not what he means,
nor is it what his heart devises;
but to destroy is in his heart,
and to cut off many nations.

For he says:
“Are my princes not every one of them kings?

As my hand has reached the kingdoms of the idols,
whose carved images were more than those of Jerusalem and of Samaria,

shall I not do to Jerusalem and her images
as I have done to Samaria and her idols?”
But when the Lord completes everything he is doing against Mount Zion and Jerusalem, I will punish the king of Assyria for the fruit of his proud heart and for his arrogant, haughty eyes.{e}

Does the axe brag against the one who chops with it?
Does the saw boast over the one who saws with it?
It would be like a rod swinging the person who lifts it,
or a staff raising someone who is not made of wood!{g}

And the Light of Israel shall become a fire,
and his Holy One a flame;
and it shall burn and devour
his thorns and his briers in one day.

And the rest of the trees of his forest shall be few,
so that a child could write them down.

And it shall come to pass in that day that the remnant of Israel, and the survivors of the house of Jacob, shall no more lean upon him who struck them, but shall lean upon Yahweh, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.

A remnant shall return, the remnant of Jacob,
to the Mighty God.{j}

For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea,
only a remnant of them shall return.
Destruction is decreed,
overflowing with righteousness.{k}

For the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, will bring about destruction, just as determined,
throughout the whole land.{l}
Therefore this is what the Lord, Yahweh of Armies, says: “My people who live in Zion, do not fear Assyria, though he hits you with a rod and raises his staff against you, as Egypt did.{m}
For in a very little while the indignation will come to an end, and my anger will turn to their destruction.
Yahweh of Armies will lash him with a whip, like the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb; he will lift his staff over the sea as he did in Egypt.{n}
And it shall come to pass in that day that his burden shall depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke shall be broken because of fatness.”{o}

Madmenah is in flight;
the inhabitants of Gebim flee for refuge.{s}

Behold, the Lord, Yahweh of Armies,
will lop the boughs with terrifying power;
and the tall of stature shall be hewn down,
and the lofty shall be brought low.

And he will cut down the thickets of the forest with iron,
and Lebanon shall fall by a Mighty One.{u}

notes.text: Hebrew “your glory.”
Or “Without me they shall crouch.” The Hebrew is uncertain. See 5:25.
Or “Ah, Assyria.” Assyria’s king is the tool of God’s judgment (verses 5–19).
Calno (Calneh), Carchemish (on the Euphrates), Hamath, and Arpad were cities of Syria and northern Mesopotamia taken by Assyria about 740–717 BC.
The Lord, here ’Adonai.
Or “like a bull.” “Treasures,” or “stores”; the Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this word.
Or “as if a rod should wave him who lifts it.”
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.”
Or “as when a standard-bearer faints”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Hebrew she’ar yashuv, the name of Isaiah’s son (7:3). Hebrew ’el gibbor, as in 9:6.
Verses 22–23 are quoted in Romans 9:27–28 from the Septuagint (“a remnant of them shall be saved”).
Or “in the midst of all the earth.”
Egypt, Hebrew Mitsrayim, the land of Israel’s first bondage.
Oreb, “raven,” the Midianite prince killed at the rock that bore his name (Judges 7:25).

Hebrew “from before oil” or “from before fatness,” perhaps meaning the ox has grown too fat for its yoke; many emend to “he has gone up from Samaria” or “from Rimmon.” The verse division is uncertain; the last words may begin verse 28.
Verses 28–32 trace an army’s advance on Jerusalem from the north. Aiath, probably Ai, “ruin”; Migron, perhaps “precipice”; Michmash, “hidden place.”
Geba and Gibeah, both “hill”; Ramah, “height.” Saul, “asked for,” Israel’s first king.
Gallim, “heaps”; Laishah, “lion”; Anathoth, the priestly town of Jeremiah. “Answer her,” reading ‘aniha; Hebrew ‘aniyyah, “poor.”
Madmenah, “dung heap”; Gebim, “cisterns” or “trenches.”
Nob, the priests’ town (1 Samuel 21–22), within sight of Jerusalem. Hebrew ketiv “the house of the daughter of Zion”; the Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “house.”
Or “by the Mighty One,” or “by a majestic one” (’addir). Lebanon here stands for the Assyrian army, as the forest image continues.

verses.text:
And a shoot shall come out from the stock of Jesse,
and a branch out of his roots shall be fruitful.{a}

And the Spirit of Yahweh shall rest upon him,
the Spirit of wisdom and understanding,
the Spirit of counsel and might,
the Spirit of knowledge and of the fear of Yahweh.{b}

And righteousness shall be the sash about his waist,
and faithfulness the sash about his hips.

Cows and bears will feed together,
their young will rest side by side,
and lions will eat straw like oxen.

And the suckling child shall play by the cobra’s hole,
and on the viper’s nest the weaned child shall lay his hand.
And it shall come to pass in that day that the root of Jesse, who stands for a banner of the peoples—to him the nations shall seek, and his place of rest shall be glorious.{e}

And it shall come to pass in that day that the Lord will set his hand a second time to recover the remnant of his people that remains, from Assyria and from Egypt, from Pathros and from Cush, from Elam and from Shinar, from Hamath and from the coastlands of the sea.{f}

And he will raise a banner for the nations,
and will gather the outcasts of Israel,
and assemble the scattered of Judah
from the four corners of the earth.

And the jealousy of Ephraim shall depart,
and the adversaries of Judah shall be cut off;
Ephraim shall not envy Judah,
and Judah shall not harass Ephraim.

And there shall be a highway for the remnant of his people
that remains from Assyria,
as there was for Israel
on the day when they came up from the land of Egypt.

notes.text: Jesse, David’s father (1 Samuel 16); the name’s meaning is uncertain, perhaps “Yahweh exists” or “gift.” “Branch,” Hebrew netser; compare Matthew 2:23. The Septuagint reads “a rod … and a blossom shall come up from his root.”
The Septuagint adds “godliness” after “knowledge” and puts “the fear of God” in verse 3, giving the seven gifts of later Christian tradition.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and by the breath of his lips the wicked shall be put to death.” Compare 2 Thessalonians 2:8.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read “shall graze” for “and the fatling”; compare 65:25.
Quoted in Romans 15:12 from the Septuagint (“he who rises to rule the nations; in him shall the nations hope”).
Pathros, Upper (southern) Egypt; Cush, the Nile lands south of Egypt (Nubia); Elam, southwest Iran; Shinar, Babylonia; Hamath, in Syria. The Lord, here ’Adonai.
Edom, “red,” south and east of the Dead Sea; Moab, east of the Dead Sea; Ammon, east of the Jordan, around modern Amman.
Or “will dry up” (some read hehrib for heherim). The River, the Euphrates. “Scorching,” the Hebrew word is uncertain.

verses.text:
And with joy you shall draw water
from the springs of salvation.

Sing to Yahweh, for he has done excellent things;
let it be known through all the earth.{c}

Cry out and shout, you who dwell in Zion,
for the Holy One of Israel is great among you.”{d}

notes.text: “You” is singular here; in verse 4 it is plural. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and turned away.”
Yah, a short form of the divine name; compare Exodus 15:2; Psalm 118:14. The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “God, God (’el ’el) is my salvation.”
Following the qere (muda‘at); the ketiv has another passive form of the same verb. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the word rendered “let it be known.”
Or “O inhabitress of Zion,” a feminine form for the city’s people.

verses.text: The oracle concerning Babylon, which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw.{a}

The noise of a multitude on the mountains,
like that of a great people!
The noise of the uproar of kingdoms,
of nations gathered together!
Yahweh of Armies is mustering
an army for battle.

Wail, for the day of Yahweh is near!
As destruction from the Almighty it shall come.{d}

Therefore all hands shall go limp,
and every man’s heart shall melt,

Behold, the day of Yahweh comes,
cruel, with fury and burning anger,
to make the land a desolation,
and to destroy its sinners from it.

I will punish the world for its evil,
the wicked for their wrongdoing.
I will end the pride of the haughty
and humble the arrogance of the ruthless.

I will make a mortal scarcer than pure gold,
even a man than the fine gold of Ophir.{f}

Therefore I will make the heavens tremble,
and the earth shall be shaken out of its place,
at the wrath of Yahweh of Armies
in the day of his burning anger.

And like a hunted gazelle,
and like sheep that no one gathers,
they shall each turn to his own people,
and each flee to his own land.

Every one who is found shall be thrust through,
and every one who is caught shall fall by the sword.

It shall never be inhabited,
nor lived in from generation to generation;
no Arab shall pitch his tent there,
nor shall shepherds make their flocks lie down there.

notes.text: Hebrew massa’, “burden,” “utterance,” a title for the oracles against the nations in chapters 13–23. Babylon (Hebrew Bavel), the great city on the Euphrates; Genesis 11:9 links the name with balal, “confuse.”
Or “those who exult in my majesty.”
Or “the whole earth.”
Hebrew Shaddai, traditionally “the Almighty,” with a wordplay: “as shod (destruction) from Shadday.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “shall not shine” (a different verb). Compare Matthew 24:29; Mark 13:24–25.
Ophir, a distant land famed for gold (1 Kings 9:28), perhaps in southern Arabia or East Africa.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the last line.
The Medes, a people of northwest Iran, who joined with the Persians to take Babylon in 539 BC.
The Chaldeans, the people of southern Babylonia whose dynasty ruled Babylon in the 7th–6th centuries BC. Sodom and Gomorrah, see 1:9.
The identity of several of the animals in verses 21–22 is uncertain. “Wild goats,” Hebrew se‘irim, also “goat-demons” (compare Leviticus 17:7).
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “again” (“shall not be prolonged again”).

verses.text: For Yahweh will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel, and settle them in their own soil; and the sojourner shall join himself to them, and they shall cleave to the house of Jacob.{a}

And peoples shall take them and bring them to their place; and the house of Israel shall possess them in the land of Yahweh as male and female servants; and they shall take captive those who took them captive, and rule over those who oppressed them.{b}
And it shall come to pass in the day that Yahweh gives you rest from your pain and turmoil, and from the hard service with which you were made to serve,

Yahweh has broken the staff of the wicked,
the scepter of rulers,

that struck the peoples in wrath
with an unceasing stroke,
that ruled the nations in anger
with a persecution none restrained.

The whole earth is at rest and is quiet;
they break forth into singing.

Even the cypresses rejoice over you,
the cedars of Lebanon:
‘Since you lay down,
no feller has come up against us.’

All of them shall answer
and say to you:
‘You too have become weak as we are!
You have become like us!’

Your splendor has been brought down to Sheol,
along with the music of your harps;
maggots are your bed beneath you,
and worms are your blanket.

How you are fallen from heaven,
O shining one, son of the dawn!
How you are cut down to the ground,
you who laid low the nations!{e}

I will ascend above the heights of the clouds;
I will make myself like the Most High.’{g}

Yet you shall be brought down to Sheol,
to the far reaches of the pit.

They that see you shall gaze at you,
they shall consider you:
‘Is this the man who made the earth to quake,
that made kingdoms shake,

that made the world as a wilderness,
and tore down its cities,
that would not open the house of his prisoners?’

but you are flung out of your tomb
as a detested shoot,
covered with the slain, run through with the sword,
who descend to the stones of the pit,
as a carcass trampled under foot.{h}

With them you shall have no share in burial,
for your land you have ruined,
your people you have killed.
The seed of evildoers
shall not be named forever.
“And I will rise up against them,” says Yahweh of Armies, “and cut off from Babylon name and remnant, offspring and descendant,” says Yahweh.{j}
“I will make it a home for hedgehogs and a place of marshes; I will sweep it with the broom of destruction,” declares Yahweh of Armies.{k}

Yahweh of Armies has sworn, saying:
“Surely as I have planned,
so shall it be;
and as I have purposed,
so shall it stand:

This is the plan decided for the whole earth,
and this is the hand stretched out over all the nations.

For Yahweh of Armies has purposed,
and who shall annul it?
And his hand is stretched out,
and who shall turn it back?
In the year that King Ahaz died this oracle came:{m}

Wail, gate! Cry out, city!
Panic, all you Philistines!
For a cloud of smoke is coming from the north,
and no one lags behind in his ranks.{p}

What then shall one answer the messengers of the nation?
“Yahweh has founded Zion,
and in her the afflicted of his people shall find refuge.”

notes.text: Or “the stranger,” the foreigner living among Israel.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “many” (“many peoples”) and reads “to their land and to their place.”

Hebrew madhebah, a word otherwise unknown (traditionally “the golden city”). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads marhebah, “insolence” or “onslaught” (compare rahav, “arrogance,” 3:5), a reading long proposed by scholars and supported by the ancient versions; the Septuagint reads “the taskmaster.”
Sheol, the realm of the dead. Hebrew repha’im, the dead, the “shades.” Hebrew “the he-goats of the earth,” that is, the leaders.

Hebrew helel ben shahar, “shining one, son of dawn,” probably the morning star (the planet Venus), here a taunt against the king of Babylon, using imagery known from Canaanite myth, in which a bright deity aspires to a higher throne and is cast down. The Septuagint renders heosphoros, “light-bringer,” “the morning star,” and the Latin Vulgate lucifer, “light-bearer,” the Latin name of the morning star; from the Latin comes the name Lucifer, which later Christian interpretation applied to Satan (compare Luke 10:18; Revelation 12:7–9). The Great Isaiah Scroll writes the word with an extra letter (heylil) but has no difference of sense. Or “you who weakened the nations.”
Hebrew Tsaphon, “the north,” also the name of a mountain (Mount Zaphon, Jebel Aqra in Syria) regarded in Canaanite religion as the home of the gods. Or “the mount of meeting.”
Hebrew ‘Elyon, “the Most High.”
Or “like a rejected shoot”; some read “like a loathsome miscarriage” (nephel for netser).
Or “with ruins” (some read ‘iyyim for ‘arim).
Hebrew “name and remnant, offspring (nin) and descendant (neked).”
Or “the owl” or “the bittern”; the animal is uncertain.
Assyria, compare 10:5–19; 37:36–38.
Ahaz died about 715 BC (some date it 727). Hebrew massa’, “oracle”; see 13:1.
Philistia, the land of the Philistines; compare 2:6. Hebrew saraph me‘opheph, “a flying seraph,” perhaps a winged serpent; compare 6:2; 30:6; Numbers 21:6.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and I will slay your remnant.” Some read “the firstborn of the poor shall feed in my pastures” (bekhari for bekhore).
Or “there is no one alone at his appointed place.” The Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text:
Dimon’s waters are full of blood,
and I will bring even more on Dimon:
a lion for those who escape from Moab
and for those left in the land.{h}

notes.text: Moab, the kingdom east of the Dead Sea; Genesis 19:37 links the name with “from father.” Ar and Kir, principal cities of Moab; Kir, “wall” or “city.” “Undone,” or “silenced.”
Or “to Bayith (the house).” Dibon, Nebo, and Medeba, towns of Moab; Nebo also a mountain and the name of a god. Shaving the head and beard were rites of mourning.
Heshbon, Elealeh, and Jahaz, towns of northern Moab. The Septuagint reads “the loins of Moab cry out.”

Zoar, “small,” at the south end of the Dead Sea (Genesis 19:22); Eglath-shelishiyah, perhaps “the third Eglath”; Luhith and Horonaim (“two caves”) are mentioned also on the Moabite Stone. Or “her nobles.”
Nimrim, “leopards,” a stream in southern Moab.
Or “the Brook of the Poplars” (or “of the Arabah”), probably the Zered, Moab’s southern border.
Eglaim, “two pools”; Beer-elim, “well of the mighty ones” or “well of the terebinths.”

Dimon, probably a wordplay on Dibon (verse 2) with dam, “blood.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Dibon” (as the Latin Vulgate), while 1QIsa-b agrees with the traditional Hebrew text (“Dimon”); the Septuagint also has Dimon.

verses.text:
And like fluttering birds,
like a scattered nest,
so shall the daughters of Moab be
at the fords of the Arnon.{b}

then a throne shall be established in steadfast love,
and one shall sit on it in faithfulness
in the tent of David,
judging and seeking justice,
and swift to do righteousness.{d}

So my bowels moan like a harp for Moab,
and my inward being for Kir-heres.{i}
And it shall come to pass, when Moab appears, when he wearies himself on the high place, and comes to his sanctuary to pray, that he shall not prevail.
This is the word that Yahweh spoke concerning Moab in time past.

But now Yahweh has spoken, saying, “Within three years, as the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab shall be brought into contempt, with all his great multitude; and the remnant shall be very small and feeble.”{j}

notes.text: Sela, “rock,” a stronghold of Edom (perhaps near later Petra), where the fugitives of Moab have fled. The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; Moab is apparently urged to send tribute to Jerusalem, as Moab’s king once sent lambs to Israel (2 Kings 3:4).
The Arnon, the great gorge of central Moab, running into the Dead Sea.
“The oppressor,” Hebrew hammets, uncertain; perhaps “the extortioner.”
Hebrew hesed, “steadfast love,” “loyal kindness,” the covenant faithfulness of God. David, “beloved.”
Compare Jeremiah 48:29–30.
Or “the foundations” (perhaps “men,” compare Jeremiah 48:31). Kir-hareseth, “city of potsherds,” the chief city of Moab (2 Kings 3:25), probably modern Kerak; compare verse 11, Kir-heres.

Sibmah and Jazer, towns of northern Moab famous for their vines. The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the words from “the lords of the nations” in verse 8 through “for the vine of Sibmah” in verse 9, probably by a copyist’s eye skipping between the two occurrences of “the vine of Sibmah”; 1QIsa-b has them, with the traditional Hebrew text. “The sea,” probably the Dead Sea.
“Shout,” Hebrew heydad, the cry of grape treaders, here turned to the battle shout of the enemy (compare Jeremiah 48:33).
Hebrew “my bowels,” the seat of the emotions. Kir-heres, “city of the sun”(?) or another form of Kir-hareseth (verse 7).
That is, counting the years exactly, as a hired worker counts the time of his service.

verses.text:
And it shall come to pass in that day
that the glory of Jacob shall be brought low,
and the fatness of his flesh shall grow lean.

Some gleanings will remain,
as when an olive tree is beaten:
two or three olives
high up at the very top,
four or five
on the branches of the fruit tree,
declares Yahweh, the God of Israel.

In that day man shall look to his Maker,
and his eyes shall have regard for the Holy One of Israel;

and he shall not look to the altars,
the work of his hands,
nor have regard for what his fingers have made,
either the Asherim or the incense altars.{e}

in the day of your planting you make them grow,
and in the morning you make your seed blossom;
yet the harvest flees away
in a day of sickness and incurable pain.

Listen, a roar from many peoples!
They roar like the roar of the seas.
And the thundering of nations!
They thunder like the thundering of great waters.

Nations make a roar like the roar of many waters,
but he rebukes them, and they run far off,
blown along like chaff in the hills,
like tumbleweed in a whirlwind.

In the evening, look, terror!
Before dawn, they are gone.
This is the share of those who strip us bare,
the fate of those who rob us.

notes.text: Damascus, the capital of Aram (Syria), taken by Assyria in 732 BC.
Aroer, “juniper”(?); here perhaps towns east of the Jordan. The Septuagint reads “forsaken for ever.”
Ephraim, the northern kingdom, allied with Damascus (7:1–9).
The Valley of Rephaim, southwest of Jerusalem, a fertile grain valley.
Asherim, sacred poles or trees associated with the goddess Asherah.
The Septuagint reads “the Amorites and the Hivites” for “the wooded heights and the hilltops” (hahoresh vehaamir), which many follow: “like the deserted cities of the Hivites and the Amorites.”
Or “plants of Naaman” (“pleasant one”), perhaps a title of the god Adonis, whose gardens were quickly forced into bloom. “A foreign god,” or “a stranger.”

verses.text:
Ah, land of whirring wings,
which is beyond the rivers of Cush,{a}

which sends ambassadors by sea,
in papyrus boats over the water!
Go, fast messengers,
to a nation tall and smooth-skinned,
to a people feared far and wide,
a mighty nation that tramples everything,
whose land is cut by rivers.{b}

All you inhabitants of the world,
and you who dwell on the earth,
when a banner is lifted up on the mountains, look!
and when a trumpet is blown, hear!

For this is what Yahweh told me:
“I will stay calm and watch from my dwelling,
like shimmering heat in the sunshine,
like a cloud of dew in the heat of the harvest.”{c}

For before the harvest, once the blossoming ends
and the flower turns into a ripening grape,
he will trim off the shoots with pruning knives,
and cut down and remove the spreading branches.

They shall be left together for the birds of prey of the mountains,
and for the beasts of the earth;
and the birds of prey shall summer on them,
and all the beasts of the earth shall winter on them.

notes.text: Cush, the land south of Egypt along the Nile (ancient Nubia, modern Sudan), whose rulers controlled Egypt about 715–663 BC. “Whirring wings,” perhaps insects, or the sails of ships; the Septuagint reads “you wings of the land of ships.”

Or “tall and smooth,” that is, of great height and glossy skin, or clean-shaven. Or “feared near and far.” Hebrew qav-qav, “line-line,” perhaps “mighty” or “of strange speech” (compare 28:10). The Hebrew is uncertain.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “I will be quiet.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “from a people” (as does the Septuagint) for “a people,” and lacks the first “of Armies.”

verses.text:
“I will stir up Egypt against itself:
brother will fight brother,
neighbor will fight neighbor,
city will fight city, kingdom will fight kingdom.

And the waters shall fail from the sea,
and the river shall be parched and dry;

And the fishermen shall mourn,
and all who cast a hook into the Nile shall lament,
and those who spread nets upon the waters shall languish.

And the workers in combed flax shall be ashamed,
and the weavers of white cloth.{f}

And her pillars shall be crushed,
and all who work for wages shall be grieved in soul.{g}

Where then are your wise men?
Let them tell you now, and let them know
what Yahweh of Armies has purposed against Egypt.

Yahweh has mingled within her
a spirit of distortion;
and they have caused Egypt to go astray in every work of hers,
as a drunken man staggers in his vomit.

Nothing will be accomplished in Egypt
by head or tail, palm branch or reed.{j}
In that day Egypt shall be like women, and shall tremble and fear before the shaking of the hand of Yahweh of Armies, which he shakes over it.
And the land of Judah shall become a terror to Egypt; every one to whom it is mentioned shall be afraid, because of the purpose of Yahweh of Armies that he purposes against it.
In that day there shall be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to Yahweh of Armies. One shall be called the City of Destruction.{k}
In that day there shall be an altar to Yahweh in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to Yahweh at its border.{l}

It will serve as a sign and a witness to Yahweh of Armies in the land of Egypt; when they cry out to Yahweh because of their oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and he will rescue them.{m}
And Yahweh shall make himself known to Egypt, and the Egyptians shall know Yahweh in that day, and shall worship with sacrifice and offering, and shall vow vows to Yahweh and pay them.
And Yahweh will strike Egypt, striking and healing; and they shall return to Yahweh, and he shall be entreated by them and heal them.
On that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria. Assyrians will come into Egypt and Egyptians into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship together with the Assyrians.{n}
In that day Israel shall be the third with Egypt and with Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth,
whom Yahweh of Armies has blessed, saying, “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.”{o}

notes.text: Egypt, Hebrew Mitsrayim.
Hebrew ’ittim, perhaps “ghosts” or “whisperers”; compare 8:19.
Hebrew ha’adon, “the Lord.” The “harsh master” may be an Assyrian or a Cushite ruler.
Hebrew “the rivers,” the Nile channels and canals of the delta; “streams of Egypt,” Hebrew ye’ore matsor, “Nile streams of Matsor,” a name for Egypt.
Hebrew ye’or, the Nile. Or “the reeds by the Nile.”
Or “shall be pale.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and they shall be ashamed.”
Or “her weavers,” reading shatoteyha (“her foundations,” MT) as a word for weavers. The Hebrew is uncertain.
Zoan, Greek Tanis, a royal city in the northeast delta. Pharaoh, Egyptian “great house,” the title of the king of Egypt.
Hebrew Noph, Memphis, the ancient capital near modern Cairo.

Hebrew ‘ir haheres, “city of destruction,” perhaps a wordplay. The Great Isaiah Scroll, some Hebrew manuscripts, and the Latin Vulgate read ‘ir haheres (with a different letter), “City of the Sun,” that is, Heliopolis (On, Genesis 41:45), the center of sun worship near Memphis. The Septuagint reads “city of Asedek” (“righteousness”). Canaan, the land west of the Jordan; its language, Hebrew.
A pillar, Hebrew matsevah, a standing stone marking a sacred place.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “and he will come down” for “and a champion.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks the second “Egypt” (“and into Assyria”).
Or “my possession.”

verses.text: In the year the Tartan, the commander in chief, came to Ashdod, sent by Sargon king of Assyria, and attacked Ashdod and captured it,{a}
at that time Yahweh spoke by Isaiah son of Amoz with these words: “Go, loosen the sackcloth from your hips and take your sandals off.” He did this, walking around stripped and barefoot.{b}
And Yahweh said, “As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and against Cush,{c}
so the king of Assyria will lead away Egypt’s prisoners and Cush’s exiles, young and old, naked and barefoot, with their buttocks bare, to Egypt’s shame.
And they shall be terrified and put to shame on account of Cush, to which they looked, and Egypt, in which they gloried.{d}
And the inhabitant of this coastland shall say in that day, ‘Behold, such is our hope, to which we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria; and we, how shall we escape?’”{e}

notes.text: Tartan, Assyrian turtanu, the title of the commander-in-chief. Ashdod, a Philistine city; its rebellion was crushed in 711 BC. Sargon II, king of Assyria 722–705 BC; Akkadian Sharru-kin, “the true king.”
“Naked,” perhaps stripped to a loincloth, as a captive.
Cush, see 18:1.
Or “their expectation.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “on which we relied” for “to which we fled.” “This coastland,” probably Philistia and the Mediterranean coast.

verses.text:
A message about the desert by the sea.
Like windstorms that sweep through the Negev,
it comes from the desert,
from a fearsome land.{a}

A hard vision has been told to me:
the treacherous deal treacherously,
and the spoiler spoils.
Go up, Elam! Lay siege, Media!
I have made all her groaning cease.{b}

They set the table,
spread out the cushions,
and eat and drink.
Get up, you officers,
and oil the shields!{d}

And if he sees a troop,
horsemen two by two,
a troop of donkeys,
a troop of camels,
he shall heed it closely,
with great heed.”{e}

Look, here come men in a chariot,
and riders in pairs!”
Then he answered,
“Babylon has fallen, has fallen!
All the carved images of her gods
lie smashed on the ground.”{g}

The oracle concerning Dumah.
One calls to me from Seir,
“Watchman, what of the night?
Watchman, what of the night?”{i}

The watchman says:
“Morning comes, and also the night.
If you will inquire, inquire;
come back again.”
For thus the Lord has said to me: “Within a year, as the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar shall come to an end;{l}
and the remainder of the number of the archers, the mighty men of the children of Kedar, shall be few; for Yahweh, the God of Israel, has spoken.”

notes.text: The wilderness of the sea, probably southern Babylonia by the Persian Gulf (“the Sealand”). The Negev, the dry south of Judah.
Elam and Media, peoples of Iran who joined the attack on Babylon (539 BC; compare 13:17).
Or “my mind reels.”
That is, oil the leather shields for battle.
Or “chariots,” as in verse 9; the Hebrew rekhev means a team or riders as well as a chariot.

Hebrew “And he cried out, a lion.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads haro’eh, “the seer” (or “the watchman”), for ’aryeh, “a lion,” the same letters rearranged: “Then the seer cried out.” The Septuagint has neither, reading “and call Urias.”
Compare Revelation 14:8; 18:2.
That is, Israel, beaten out like grain on the threshing floor.
Dumah, “silence,” perhaps an oasis in north Arabia (Genesis 25:14), here with a play on its meaning; the Septuagint reads Idumea (Edom). Seir, the hill country of Edom.
Dedan, an Arabian trading people (Genesis 10:7; Ezekiel 27:20).
Tema, an oasis in northwest Arabia (modern Tayma).
Kedar, “dark,” a tribe of north Arabian nomads (Genesis 25:13). The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Within three years” (compare 16:14) and Yahweh for ’Adonai (“the Lord”).

verses.text:
you who are full of uproar,
a tumultuous city, an exultant town?
Your slain are not slain with the sword,
nor are they dead in battle.

Your best valleys were filled with chariots,
and horsemen took up positions at the gate.

And the breaches of David’s city you beheld, how many they were;
and you gathered in the waters of the lower pool;

and you counted the houses of Jerusalem,
and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall;

and a basin you made between the two walls
for the waters of the old pool.
But to him who did it you did not look,
nor did you have regard for him who formed it long ago.{f}

But instead there was joy and celebration,
cattle being killed and sheep slaughtered,
meat being eaten and wine being drunk:
“Let’s eat and drink,
because tomorrow we will be dead.”{g}

Yahweh of Armies revealed this in my hearing:
“This sin will never be forgiven you until you die,”
says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies.
Thus says the Lord, Yahweh of Armies: “Go, get yourself to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the house, and say:{h}

‘What business do you have here, and who is there for you here,
that you have dug a tomb for yourself here,
cutting your burial place high up
and carving out a resting place in the rock?

Behold, Yahweh will hurl you away violently, O man,
and will grasp you firmly,

and will surely wind you round and round,
like a ball into a land broad on both hands;
there you shall die,
and there the chariots of your glory shall be,
you disgrace of your lord’s house.

And I will thrust you from your office,
and from your station he will pull you down.’
And it shall come to pass in that day that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah;{i}

I will dress him in your robe,
fasten your sash on him,
and entrust your authority to him;
he will act as a father to the people of Jerusalem
and to the house of Judah.

And I will fasten him as a peg in a sure place;
and he shall become a throne of honor to his father’s house.{k}
And they shall hang upon him all the weight of his father’s house, the offspring and the issue, every small vessel, from the bowls to all the jars.

In that day, says Yahweh of Armies, the peg that was fastened in a sure place shall give way; and it shall be cut down and fall, and the load that was upon it shall be cut off; for Yahweh has spoken.”

notes.text: The valley of vision, apparently Jerusalem itself, perhaps the Hinnom or Kidron valley, where prophetic visions were given.
Or “without a bow (being drawn).”

The Great Isaiah Scroll reads differently in the last two lines, perhaps “tearing down his holy place upon the mountain” (qodsho ‘al hahar for qir veshoa‘ ’el hahar). The Hebrew is uncertain; there is wordplay (meqarqar qir).
Elam, see 21:2; Kir, a land of uncertain location, compare 2 Kings 16:9; Amos 9:7.
The House of the Forest of Lebanon, Solomon’s armory hall (1 Kings 7:2; 10:17).
Compare 2 Kings 20:20; 2 Chronicles 32:3–5, 30, describing Hezekiah’s water works; “the old pool” may be the Siloam pool.
Quoted in 1 Corinthians 15:32.
Shebna, a royal official under Hezekiah, later secretary (36:3). His name may be a shortened form of Shebaniah, “Yahweh has returned”(?). “Steward,” Hebrew soken.
Eliakim, “God raises up”; Hilkiah, “my portion is Yahweh.” Compare 36:3.
Compare Revelation 3:7.
Or “a nail,” a tent peg or a wall peg for hanging things.

verses.text:
The oracle concerning Tyre.
Wail, O ships of Tarshish,
for it is laid waste, without house, without harbor!
From the land of Kittim it is revealed to them.{a}

Be silent, O inhabitants of the coast,
O merchants of Sidon,
whose messengers passed over the sea,
whom they filled.{b}

Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken,
the stronghold of the sea, saying:
“I have not labored nor given birth,
I have not reared young men,
nor brought up young women.”

When the report comes to Egypt,
they shall be in anguish at the report about Tyre.

Pass over to Tarshish;
howl, you who dwell on the coast!

Is this your joyful city,
whose beginning is of ancient days,
whose own feet bore her far away to dwell abroad?

Who has counseled this against Tyre,
the one who gave crowns,
whose dealers were princes,
whose merchants the honorable of the land?

Yahweh of Armies has purposed it,
to defile the pride of all glory,
to bring into contempt all the honored of the earth.

Wail, O ships of Tarshish,
for your stronghold is laid waste.
And it shall come to pass in that day that Tyre shall be forgotten seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years it shall be with Tyre as in the song of the harlot:{h}

“Pick up a harp,
walk around the city,
you forgotten prostitute;
play sweetly,
sing song after song,
so that people will remember you.”

And it shall come to pass at the end of seventy years that Yahweh will visit Tyre, and she shall return to her hire, and shall play the harlot with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth.

And her merchandise and her hire shall be holy to Yahweh; it shall not be stored or hoarded; for her merchandise shall be for those who dwell before Yahweh, for abundant food and for fine clothing.{i}

notes.text: Tyre, Hebrew Tsor, “rock,” the great Phoenician port city on an island off the coast of Lebanon. Tarshish, see 2:16. Kittim, Cyprus (from its city Kition), and later the western lands generally. Or “without house, without entering in.”
Sidon, “fishery,” the other great Phoenician city, north of Tyre. Or, with the Great Isaiah Scroll, “your messengers passed over the sea”; Hebrew “passing over the sea, they filled you.”
Shihor, a branch of the Nile in the eastern delta (compare Jeremiah 2:18). The grain trade of Egypt passed through Phoenician hands.
Or “like the Nile,” perhaps “overflow your land.” Or “there is no harbor (or shipyard) any more.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Work your land” (‘ivdi for ‘ivri).
Canaan, here Phoenicia; Phoenicians called themselves Canaanites.
“Virgin daughter of Sidon,” a personification of the city.
The verse is difficult; some read “the land of the Kittim” (Cyprus) or take it as a gloss pointing to the fall of Babylon. Hebrew ketiv “his siege towers.”
