not one grasps her hand.

So hear this now, you afflicted one,
drunken, yet not from wine:

This is what your Lord Yahweh says,
your God, who pleads the case of his people:
Look, I have taken from your hand the cup that made you stagger,
the bowl of my wrath; you will never drink from it again;{r}

notes.text: Abraham and Sarah (verse 2) are the rock and the quarry from which Israel came.
Compare Genesis 12:1–3; Ezekiel 33:24.
Eden, Hebrew ‘eden, “delight” (Genesis 2:8). The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “sorrow and sighing shall flee away,” as in verse 11.
Or “law,” Hebrew torah. Compare 2:3; 42:4.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his arm shall judge the peoples; the coastlands wait for him, and for his arm they hope.”
Hebrew kemo-ken, perhaps “like gnats” (compare ken, “gnat”) or “in like manner.” Compare Psalm 102:25–26; Hebrews 1:10–12; 2 Peter 3:10.
Compare 50:9.

Rahab, Hebrew rahav, “boisterous one,” “arrogance,” a mythic sea monster and a poetic name for Egypt (30:7; Psalm 87:4; 89:10); not the same name as Rahab of Jericho (Hebrew rahav with a different h). “Sea monster,” Hebrew tannin (27:1).
The Red Sea crossing (Exodus 14:21–22).
Repeated from 35:10.
Compare 40:6–8.
Or “He who is bound,” Hebrew tso‘eh, “one bent over,” perhaps a prisoner in fetters.
Compare Jeremiah 31:35.
Some propose “to stretch out” (lintot) for “to plant” (linto‘a).
Compare Jeremiah 25:15–29; Revelation 14:10; 16:19.
The Great Isaiah Scroll and the Septuagint read “who shall comfort you?”
Hebrew te’o, a wild ox or antelope, perhaps the oryx (Deuteronomy 14:5).
Hebrew Adonayikh Yahweh, “your Lord Yahweh.”
Or “Lie down, that we may walk over you.” The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and your oppressors” after “tormentors.”

verses.text: For thus says Yahweh: “For nothing you were sold, and not with silver shall you be redeemed.”
For thus says the Lord Yahweh: “My people went down into Egypt at the first to sojourn there, and Assyria oppressed them for no cause.{b}

And now, what have I here?” declares Yahweh, “seeing that my people are taken away for nothing? Those who rule over them howl,” declares Yahweh, “and continually, all the day long, my name is scorned.{c}
So my people will know my name; on that day they will know that I am the one who is speaking: here I am.”

How lovely upon the mountains
are the feet of the herald of good news,
who makes peace heard, who brings tidings of good,
who makes salvation heard,
who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”{d}

Yahweh has bared his holy arm
before the eyes of all the nations,
and all the ends of the earth shall see
the salvation of our God.

notes.text: “Take your seat”: Hebrew shevi, “sit (enthroned)”; with different vowels, “O captive.” “Loose” follows the read form of the Hebrew; the written form, which the Great Isaiah Scroll shares, has “they have loosed.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Thus says Yahweh,” without “Lord.”
Or “wail,” or “boast.” The Septuagint has “on account of you my name is continually blasphemed among the Gentiles,” which Paul quotes in Romans 2:24.
Romans 10:15 quotes the first two lines; compare Nahum 1:15 (2:1 in Hebrew) and 40:9.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “in compassion” (“when Yahweh returns to Zion in compassion”); compare the Septuagint, “when the Lord shall have mercy upon Zion.”
Paul applies the verse to the church in 2 Corinthians 6:17.
After “the God of Israel” the Great Isaiah Scroll adds “he shall be called the God of all the earth” (compare 54:5).
The fourth “Servant Song” runs from 52:13 to 53:12. Hebrew yaskil, “act with insight,” and so “prosper”; the Septuagint has “shall understand.”
Compare 6:1 and 57:15, where the same pair of words, “lifted up and exalted,” describes Yahweh himself. The Septuagint has “and be glorified exceedingly”; compare Acts 3:13.
So the Masoretic Text and the Great Isaiah Scroll; some ancient versions are reported to read “at him.” In 1QIsa-b the word is lost.

Hebrew mishhat, “disfigurement,” and 1QIsa-b agrees. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes the word with a final yod (mshhty), which some scholars read as mashahti, “I anointed”: “so I anointed his appearance beyond any man.” The Septuagint has “so shall your face be without glory from men.”

Hebrew yazzeh, the verb used of sprinkling blood and water in rites of cleansing (Leviticus 4:6; 16:14; Numbers 19:18). The Septuagint has “so shall many nations wonder at him,” and some render “startle.”
Romans 15:21 quotes the last two lines from the Septuagint.

verses.text:
Who has believed what we have heard?{a}
And the arm of Yahweh, to whom has it been revealed?{b}

notes.text: Or “our report,” “our message.” John 12:38 and Romans 10:16 quote this line.
For “the arm of Yahweh,” compare 51:9; 52:10.
Hebrew yoneq, “a suckling,” used of a shoot from a root; compare 11:1. The Septuagint has “we brought a report as of a child before him.”
Or “rejected by men”; Hebrew hadal ishim, perhaps “lacking men,” that is, deserted, or “least of men.”
Hebrew holi, “sickness” (also verse 4), and makh’ovot, “pains.”
Matthew 8:17 quotes the first two lines of Jesus’ healings. The Septuagint has “he bears our sins, and is pained for us.” First Peter 2:24 draws on verses 4–5 and 12.
Hebrew meholal, “pierced” or “wounded”; the Septuagint has “wounded.”
Hebrew musar shelomenu, “the discipline of our peace.”
Hebrew havurah, “stripe,” “welt.” Quoted in 1 Peter 2:24.
Hebrew hifgia‘, “caused to strike,” “caused to meet”; the same verb is rendered “intercedes” in verse 12. Compare 1 Peter 2:25.
Or “and he was afflicted.”
Acts 8:32–33 quotes verses 7–8 from the Septuagint: this is the passage the Ethiopian official was reading when Philip met him. Compare Jeremiah 11:19; Matthew 26:63; 1 Peter 2:23.

Hebrew me‘otser umimmishpat, “from detention and from judgment”; or “without restraint and without justice.” The Septuagint has “in his humiliation his judgment was taken away,” as quoted in Acts 8:33.
Or “who could tell of his descendants?” or “who gave thought to his fate?” The Septuagint has “who shall declare his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth.”

Hebrew nega‘ lamo, “a blow to them” (or “to him”). For “my people” the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his people” (‘ammo), and 1QIsa-b appears to read the same, though the final letter there is uncertain. The Septuagint has “because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death.”
Hebrew “he gave,” that is, “one made”; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “they gave.” The Septuagint has “I will give the wicked for his burial.”

Hebrew bemotav, “in his deaths,” a plural perhaps of intensity. The Great Isaiah Scroll writes bwmtw, which some scholars take as “his burial mound” or “his high place.” Compare Matthew 27:57–60, where Joseph of Arimathea, “a rich man,” buries Jesus.
First Peter 2:22 quotes the last two lines, with “sin” for “violence.”

Hebrew hehli, “he made sick.” The Great Isaiah Scroll reads wayhalleluhu, which has been taken as “and he pierced him” (compare meholal, verse 5). The Septuagint has “the Lord also is pleased to purge him from his stroke.”
Or “if you make his soul a guilt offering”; the Hebrew verb can be “you make” or “she (his soul) makes.” Hebrew asham, the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14–6:7.

“Light” follows the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsa-a) and 1QIsa-b, both of which read yir’eh ’or, “he shall see light,” and the Septuagint, “to show him light.” A third Qumran copy, 4QIsa-d, is reported to read “light” as well. The Masoretic Text lacks the word: “he shall see, he shall be satisfied.”
Or “by knowledge of him,” or “by his humiliation.”
So the Masoretic Text and, as far as legible, 1QIsa-b; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “his servant.” The Septuagint has “to justify the just one who serves many well.”
Or “with the great.” The Septuagint has “he shall inherit many.”
Or “and he shall divide the mighty as spoil.”
Jesus quotes this line of himself in Luke 22:37; some manuscripts of Mark 15:28 apply it to the crucifixion between two criminals.

Hebrew yafgia‘, “he makes intercession” (see the note on verse 6). The Great Isaiah Scroll and 1QIsa-b read “for their transgressions”; the Septuagint has “and was delivered because of their iniquities.”

verses.text:
For to the right hand and to the left you shall break out,
and your offspring shall dispossess nations
and make desolate cities to be inhabited.

For as a wife forsaken and grieved in spirit Yahweh has called you,
and as a wife of youth when she is rejected,” says your God.

“For a little moment I abandoned you,
yet in great mercies I will gather you in.

In a surge of anger{c} I hid my face from you for a moment,
but with everlasting loyal love I will have mercy on you,”
says Yahweh, your Redeemer.

“This is like the days of Noah to me:{d}
just as I promised that the waters of Noah
would never again flood the earth,
so I promise that I will not be angry with you
or scold you.

Though mountains may move
and hills be shaken,
my loyal love will never leave you,
and the covenant of peace I made will stand,”
says Yahweh, who has mercy on you.

All your sons shall be taught by Yahweh,{h}
and great shall be the peace of your sons.{i}

Should any assail you, it is not my doing;{j}
whoever assails you shall fall on your account.

Look, I am the one who made the blacksmith
who fans the charcoal fire
and forges a weapon for his purpose;
I also made the destroyer who ruins.

No weapon formed against you shall succeed,
and every tongue that rises against you in judgment you shall condemn.{k}
This is the inheritance of the servants of Yahweh,
and their vindication from me,” declares Yahweh.
the Septuagint has “strangers shall come to you by me.”

notes.text: Paul quotes the verse in Galatians 4:27.
Hebrew bo‘alayikh, “your husband,” plural in form (a plural of majesty), like “your Maker.”
Hebrew shetsef qetsef, a play on sound, “a gush of fury.”
Or, with the Hebrew letters divided differently (kime for ki me), “as the days of Noah”; the Great Isaiah Scroll appears to read so, though the letters are uncertain.
Hebrew pukh, the black paint used for the eyes, here a dark mortar that sets off the stones. The Septuagint has “carbuncle.”
Or “lapis lazuli.” Compare Revelation 21:18–21.
The identity of these stones (Hebrew kadkod and eqdah) is uncertain.
Jesus quotes this line in John 6:45.
For the second “your sons” (banayikh) the Great Isaiah Scroll has a waw added above the line, giving bonayikh, “your builders”; compare 49:17.
Hebrew gur yagur, “stir up strife,” “attack,” or “sojourn”;
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this line.

verses.text:
Why do you weigh out silver for what is not bread,
and your labor for that which never satisfies?
Hear me attentively, and eat that which is good,
and let your soul delight itself in fatness.

See, I made him a witness to the peoples,
a prince and commander for the peoples.

You will summon a nation you have never known,
and a nation that never knew you will hurry to you,
because of Yahweh your God, the Holy One of Israel,
who has made you glorious.

Seek Yahweh while he lets himself be found;
call upon him while he is near.

Let the wicked forsake his way,
and the man of iniquity his thoughts;
and let him return to Yahweh, that he may have compassion on him,
and to our God, for he will abundantly pardon.

For my thoughts are not your thoughts,
neither are your ways my ways, declares Yahweh.

For as the heavens are higher than the earth,
so my ways are higher than your ways,
and my thoughts than your thoughts.

For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven
and return not there, but water the earth
and make it bring forth and sprout,
and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater,{c}

so shall my word be that goes forth from my mouth;
it shall not return to me empty,
but it shall do what I desire,
and succeed in that for which I sent it.

For in joy you shall go out,
and in peace you shall be led forth;
the mountains and the hills shall break out before you into song,
and all the trees of the field shall clap their hands.

notes.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “and eat; come, buy,” probably because the copyist’s eye skipped from one “buy” to the next.
Hebrew hasde dawid hanne’emanim, “the sure acts of loyal love promised to David”; compare 2 Samuel 7:15–16. Acts 13:34 quotes the line from the Septuagint, “the holy and sure things of David.”
Compare 2 Corinthians 9:10.
Hebrew leshem, “for renown.”

verses.text:
Blessed is the man who does this,
and the son of man who holds fast to it,
who keeps the Sabbath so as not to profane it,
and keeps his hand from doing any evil.”

Let no foreigner who has joined himself to Yahweh say,
“Yahweh will surely keep me apart from his people”;
and let no eunuch say,
“Look, I am only a dry tree.”

For thus says Yahweh:
“To the eunuchs who keep my Sabbaths,
who choose the things in which I delight
and hold fast my covenant,

“As for the foreigners who attach themselves to Yahweh,
to serve him, to love Yahweh’s name
and to be his servants,
all who keep the Sabbath without desecrating it
and hold firmly to my covenant,

The Lord Yahweh declares,
who gathers the outcasts of Israel,
“I will yet gather others to him
besides those already gathered.”{e}

All you beasts of the field, come to devour,
all you beasts in the forest.

notes.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll begins the chapter with “For.”
Hebrew yad vashem, literally “a hand and a name.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “shall go up,” that is, “shall go up for acceptance on my altar.”
Jesus quotes the last two lines when he clears the temple (Mark 11:17; compare Matthew 21:13; Luke 19:46).
Compare John 10:16.
The written form of the Hebrew has “His watchman.”
Hebrew hozim, perhaps “panting” or “raving”; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “they are seers” (hozim, spelled differently), a bitter play on the prophets. The Septuagint has “dreaming of rest.”
Or “are strong of appetite.”
So the Masoretic Text; the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “let us take wine.”

verses.text:
The righteous man perishes,
and no one takes it to heart;
devout men are gathered away,
while none understands
that from the face of evil
the righteous man is gathered away.

At whom do you make sport?
Against whom do you open wide the mouth
and thrust out the tongue?
Are you not a brood of rebellion,
offspring of deceit,

you who burn with lust among the oaks,{c}
under every green tree,
who slay the children in the valleys,
under the clefts of the crags?

Upon a high and lofty mountain
you have set your bed;
there also you went up
to offer sacrifice.

You went down to the king{g} with oil,
and made your ointments many;
you dispatched your messengers to distant parts,
and debased yourself as far as Sheol.

You were tired out by your long journey,
but you never said, ‘There is no use’;
you found renewed strength,
so you did not give out.

“Whom did you dread and fear,
that you lied,
and did not remember me,
nor lay it to your heart?
Have I not kept silent, and that from of old,{h}
and so you fear me not?

I will declare your righteousness and your deeds,
but they shall not profit you.{i}

When you cry for help,
let your gathered hoard rescue you!
But the wind shall lift them all away;
a breath shall take them away.
But he who takes refuge in me shall possess the land
and inherit my holy mountain.”

And one shall say,
“Build up, build up, clear the way;{j}
lift every stumbling block
out of the way of my people.”

For this is what the lofty and exalted One says,
who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy:
“I live in a high and sacred place,
yet I am also with those who are crushed and humble in spirit,
revitalizing the humble spirit
and reviving the crushed heart.
“There is no peace,” says my God, “for the wicked.”{o}

notes.text: Or “each who walks in his uprightness.”
Hebrew “and she plays the harlot.”
Or “who inflame yourselves among the terebinths” or “among the gods.”
There is a play on words in the Hebrew: helqe nahal, “smooth stones of the valley,” and helqekh, “your portion.”
Probably a pagan symbol in place of the reminder of the law commanded in Deuteronomy 6:9.
“A hand” may be a euphemism for the male member.
Hebrew melekh, or perhaps Molech (compare Leviticus 18:21).
Or, with a slight change of the Hebrew, “and hidden my eyes.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “your collection,” anticipating verse 13.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “the highway.” Compare 40:3; 62:10.
Hebrew neshamot, “breaths,” the breath of life.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “I will lead him” and reads “I will repay him with consolations.”
The written form of the Hebrew has nov, the read form niv; both mean “fruit” of the lips, that is, praise. The Great Isaiah Scroll has “peace” once.
Paul echoes this line in Ephesians 2:17.
Compare 48:22.

verses.text:
Still they look for me every day
and take delight in learning my ways,
like a nation that has done right
and has not abandoned its God’s justice;
they ask me for fair rulings
and take pleasure in coming close to God.

‘Why have we fasted,’ they say, ‘and you do not see?
Why have we humbled our souls, and you take no notice?’
See, in the day of your fast you pursue your own business,
and drive hard all your workers.{b}

See, you fast for quarrel and strife,
and to hit out with the fist of wickedness.
You do not fast as on this day
to have your voice heard on high.

Is that the sort of fast I choose,
a day when someone humbles himself?
Is it hanging your head like a reed
and spreading out sackcloth and ashes to lie on?
Do you really call this a fast,
a day Yahweh will accept?

“Is not this the fast that I choose:
to loosen the fetters of wickedness,
to untie the cords of the yoke,
to send away the crushed as free,{c}
and that you break every yoke?

Then you will call, and Yahweh will answer;
you will cry for help, and he will say, ‘Here I am.’
If you remove the yoke from among you,
the pointing finger and the malicious talk,

if you spend yourselves for the hungry
and satisfy the need of the afflicted,
your light will shine in the dark,
and your night will turn into noon.

And Yahweh will guide you always
and satisfy your soul in scorched places
and make your bones strong;
and you shall be like a watered garden,
like a spring of water
whose waters never fail.

Your people will rebuild the old ruins
and raise up foundations from past generations;
you will be known as the one who repairs gaps in walls
and restores streets to live on.

“If you turn back your foot from the Sabbath,
from doing your pleasure on my holy day,
and call the Sabbath a delight,
the holy day of Yahweh honorable,
and honor it, not going your own ways,
nor seeking your own pleasure, nor speaking idle words,

then you shall take delight in Yahweh,
and I will set you riding on the high places of the land,
and nourish you with the inheritance of Jacob your father,
for the mouth of Yahweh has spoken.”

notes.text: Hebrew shofar.
Or “and exact all your debts.”
Luke 4:18 includes this line in Jesus’ reading in Nazareth, from the Septuagint, “to set at liberty those who are oppressed.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “with a garment.”
Or “shall be your rear guard”; compare 52:12.

verses.text:
Look, Yahweh’s arm is not too short to save,
and his ear is not too deaf to hear;

but your iniquities have made a division
between you and your God,
and your sins have hidden his face from you,
so that he does not hear.

Their threads shall not become a garment,
nor shall they clothe themselves with their handiwork.
Their doings are doings of iniquity,
and the work of violence is in their palms.

We roar, all of us, like bears,
and like doves we keep mourning;
we look for judgment, and there is none,
for deliverance, and it stays far off from us.

transgressing, and denying Yahweh,
and turning back from following our God,
speaking oppression and revolt,
conceiving and uttering from the heart words of falsehood.

Truth is gone,
and whoever turns from evil becomes a target.
Yahweh saw it, and it displeased him
that there was no justice.

He saw that there was no man,
and was astonished that none stepped in;
so his arm wrought deliverance for him,
and his own righteousness sustained him.

He put on righteousness like body armor,
and placed a helmet of salvation on his head;{d}
he put on clothes of vengeance
and wrapped himself in zeal like a cloak.

“And to Zion a Redeemer shall come,
and to them that turn from rebellion in Jacob,” declares Yahweh.{f}

“And as for me, this is my covenant with them,” says Yahweh: “My Spirit that is upon you, and my words that I have put in your mouth, shall not depart out of your mouth, nor out of the mouth of your offspring, nor out of the mouth of your offspring’s offspring,” says Yahweh,{g} “from this time forth and forevermore.”

notes.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this line; 1QIsa-b has it.
Paul quotes verses 7–8 in Romans 3:15–17.
The meaning of Hebrew ashmannim, “among the vigorous,” is uncertain.
Compare Ephesians 6:14, 17; 1 Thessalonians 5:8.
Or “when the enemy comes like a river, the Spirit of Yahweh lifts a banner against him.”
Paul quotes verses 20–21 in Romans 11:26–27 in a form close to the Septuagint, “the deliverer shall come for Zion’s sake, and shall turn away ungodliness from Jacob”; Paul has “from Zion.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks this second “says Yahweh”; 1QIsa-b has it.

verses.text:
Get up, shine, for your light has arrived,
and Yahweh’s glory has dawned on you.

For see, darkness shall cover the earth,
and deep gloom the peoples;
but upon you Yahweh will rise,
and his glory shall be seen upon you.

And nations shall walk to your light,
and kings to the brightness of your dawning.

Then you will look and glow with joy;
your heart will pound and swell,
because the riches of the sea will be brought to you
and the wealth of nations will come to you.

Who are these that fly along as a cloud,
as doves to their lattices?

The coastlands are waiting for me,
with the ships of Tarshish in the lead,
bringing your children from far away,
together with their silver and gold,
to honor the name of Yahweh your God,
the Holy One of Israel,
for he has made you glorious.

Foreigners will rebuild your walls,
and their kings will serve you;
though in anger I struck you down,
in kindness I have shown you mercy.

The splendor of Lebanon will come to you,
its cypress, plane and pine trees together,
to adorn my sanctuary;
and I will honor the place where I rest my feet.

The sons of your oppressors
shall come to you bowed low,
and all that scorned you shall fall down at the soles of your feet;{e}
they shall call you the City of Yahweh,
the Zion of the Holy One of Israel.

Instead of your being abandoned and hated,
so that none went through you,
I will make you an eternal pride,
the joy of generation after generation.

You will drink the milk of nations
and nurse at the breasts of kings;
then you will know that I, Yahweh, am your Savior
and Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob.

Violence will no longer be heard of in your country,
or devastation and destruction inside your borders;
you will name your walls Salvation
and your gates Praise.

And your people, every one of them righteous,
shall inherit the land for all time,
the shoot of my planting, the work of my hands,
that I may be glorified.{h}

notes.text: Hebrew “nursed upon the side.”
Compare Matthew 2:11.
So the Great Isaiah Scroll (“and they shall go up for acceptance”); the Masoretic Text has “they shall go up on acceptance, my altar.”
Or “with their kings leading them”; compare Revelation 21:25–26.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “all” before “the sons” and an erased word after it.

The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “by night”: “nor for brightness by night shall the moon give you light”; compare the Septuagint, “nor shall the rising of the moon lighten your night.” 1QIsa-b agrees with the Masoretic Text in lacking “by night.”
Or “your glory.” Compare Revelation 21:23; 22:5. 1QIsa-b is reported to end the verse at “everlasting light,” without this last line.
The written form of the Hebrew has “his planting.”

verses.text:
Strangers shall stand and shepherd your flocks;
foreigners shall be your plowmen and your vinedressers;

Their offspring shall be known among the nations,
and their descendants in the midst of the peoples;
all who see them shall acknowledge them,
that they are an offspring Yahweh has blessed.

For as the earth brings forth its growth,
and as a garden makes what is sown in it spring up,
so the Lord Yahweh will make righteousness and praise
spring up before all the nations.{j}

notes.text: The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “The Spirit of Yahweh,” without “Lord”; 1QIsa-b reads “The Spirit of Yahweh God” (Yahweh Elohim). The Septuagint has “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach good tidings to the poor.” Jesus reads verses 1–2a in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18–19) in a form close to the Septuagint, and declares, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.” For the anointed one (Hebrew mashiah), compare 11:2; 42:1; 45:1.

Hebrew peqah-qoah, “opening, opening,” perhaps “release” from the dark of prison (compare 42:7); the Great Isaiah Scroll writes it as one word. The Septuagint has “and recovery of sight to the blind,” which Luke 4:18 includes.
Jesus’ reading in Luke 4:19 stops before this line. Compare 34:8; 63:4.
There is a play on sound in the Hebrew: pe’er, “garland,” for efer, “ashes.”
Compare Exodus 19:6; 1 Peter 2:9; Revelation 1:6.
Or “and to their glory you shall succeed.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll has the second person, “instead of disgrace you shall rejoice in your portion … you shall possess a double portion; everlasting joy shall be yours.”
Or, with different vowels, “robbery with burnt offering.” The Septuagint has “robberies of injustice.”
Hebrew yekhahen pe’er, “acts as priest with a turban.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “Yahweh God” for “the Lord Yahweh.”

verses.text:
Because of Zion I will not hold my peace,
and because of Jerusalem I will not rest,
till her righteousness shines out like the dawn,
and her salvation like a blazing torch.

You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of Yahweh,
and a royal turban in the palm of your God.{b}

For as a youth weds a maiden,
your sons shall wed you;{g}
and with the joy of a bridegroom over his bride
your God shall rejoice over you.

I have posted guards on your walls,
Jerusalem;
they will never be quiet,
day or night.
You who remind Yahweh,
do not give yourselves any rest,

Yahweh has taken an oath by his right hand
and by the arm of his strength:
“I will not again give your grain
to be food for your enemies,
and the sons of foreigners shall not drink your new wine
for which you have toiled;

but those who gather it in shall eat it
and praise Yahweh,
and those who collect it shall drink it
in the courts of my sanctuary.”{i}

Look, Yahweh has announced
to the ends of the earth:
Tell Zion’s daughter,
“Look, your savior is coming;{k}
his reward comes with him,
and his payment goes before him.”

And they shall call them The Holy People,
The Redeemed of Yahweh;
and you shall be called Sought Out,
A City Not Forsaken.

notes.text: Compare 65:15; Revelation 2:17; 3:12.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “and a turban.”
Hebrew Azuvah.
Hebrew Shemamah.
Hephzibah means “My Delight Is in Her”; it was also the name of King Manasseh’s mother (2 Kings 21:1).
Beulah means “Married.”
Or, with different vowels, “so shall your Builder marry you” (bonayikh for banayikh); compare 49:17; 54:13.
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “and until he sets up.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “says your God” at the end.
For the last line the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “clear away the stone of stumbling; say among the peoples.” 1QIsa-b agrees with the Masoretic Text.
Compare 40:10. Matthew 21:5 combines “Say to the daughter of Zion” with Zechariah 9:9.

verses.text:
Why is there red upon your clothing,
and your garments as of one treading the vat?

For a day of vengeance was in my heart,
and the year of my redeemed ones had arrived.

I will tell of Yahweh’s faithful acts of love
and his praiseworthy deeds,
all that Yahweh has done for us,
and the great kindness toward the house of Israel
that he showed them out of his mercy
and his abundant love.

But they rebelled
and grieved his Holy Spirit;{g}
so he turned to be their enemy,
and he himself fought against them.

who sent his glorious arm
to march at Moses’ right hand,
who divided the water in front of them
to make an everlasting name for himself,

who led them through the depths?
Like a horse in the open country,
they did not stumble.

Like livestock that go down into the valley,
the Spirit of Yahweh gave them rest.
So you led your people,
to make for yourself a glorious name.

Gaze down from heaven and behold,
from your dwelling of holiness and splendor.
Where is your zeal, and where your might?
The stirring of your inward parts and your compassion
are held back from me.

O Yahweh, why do you make us stray from your ways,
and make our heart hard against fearing you?
Turn back for your servants’ sake,
for the tribes that are your heritage.

For a little while your holy people possessed it;{k}
our adversaries have trampled down your sanctuary.

We have become like those over whom you have never ruled,
like those who were not called by your name.{l}

notes.text: Edom, “red”; compare Genesis 25:30. The figure of the bloodied warrior is taken up in Revelation 19:13–15.
Bozrah, a chief city of Edom; the name sounds like batsir, “grape harvest.”
Hebrew tso‘eh, “bending,” perhaps “striding”; with a slight change, “marching.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “I trod them in my anger … on my garments,” probably because the copyist’s eye skipped between similar words; 1QIsa-b has the lines. Compare Revelation 14:19–20; 19:15.
Many Hebrew manuscripts and the Targum are reported to read “I shattered them” (ashabberem) for “I made them drunk” (ashakkerem).

The written form of the Hebrew has “not” (lo’), the read form “to him” (lo); the written form may be taken “In all their distress he did not afflict” or, joined to the next line with the Septuagint, “not an envoy nor an angel, but his own presence saved them.” The Great Isaiah Scroll has neither word. The Septuagint reads “not an ambassador, nor a messenger, but himself saved them.”
Compare Ephesians 4:30.
Or “Then his people remembered the days of old, of Moses.”
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint has “the shepherd of the sheep.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “he” (“our Redeemer from of old, he is your name”).
Or “possessed your sanctuary.”
In the Hebrew text this verse continues with the line that English Bibles number 64:1.

verses.text:
If only you would rend the heavens and descend,
so that the mountains shook before you,{a}

as when fire sets brushwood ablaze
and fire makes the water boil,
to make your name known to your adversaries,
that the nations might tremble at your presence!

When you did fearful deeds we had not hoped for,
you descended; the mountains shook before you.{b}

Since ages past no one has heard,
no ear has caught it,
nor has eye beheld any God but you
who works on behalf of him who waits for him.{c}

We have all become like one who is unclean,
and all our righteous deeds are like a stained garment.{e}
We all wither like a leaf,
and our iniquities, like the wind, carry us away.

Be not angry beyond measure, O Yahweh,
nor remember iniquity forever.
See, look, we pray, we are all your people.

The house of our holiness and our splendor,
in which our fathers gave you praise,
is burned up with fire,
and every precious thing of ours is a ruin.

After all this, Yahweh, will you hold back?
Will you stay silent and punish us without limit?

notes.text: 64:1 is 63:19b in the Hebrew text, and Hebrew 64:1–11 is numbered 64:2–12 in English Bibles.
The Great Isaiah Scroll lacks “that we did not look for” (literally “we did not wait for”), reading “awesome things we waited for.”
Paul echoes this verse in 1 Corinthians 2:9.
The Hebrew of the last line is obscure. The Septuagint has “therefore we have erred.”
Hebrew beged ‘iddim, “a garment of menstruation,” that is, ritually unclean (Leviticus 15:19–24).
Hebrew wattemugenu, “and made us melt”; the Septuagint and other ancient versions are reported to read “and delivered us.”
Compare 29:16; 45:9; Jeremiah 18:6; Romans 9:20–21.

verses.text:
All day long I have held out my hands
to a rebellious people,
who walk a path that is not good,
following their own plans;{b}

a people who provoke me
to my face continually,
sacrificing in the gardens
and burning incense upon the bricks;{c}

who say, ‘Stand back by yourself,
draw not near to me, for I am holier than you.’{e}
Such men are smoke in my nose,
a fire burning all day long.

This is what Yahweh says:
“When juice is still found in a cluster of grapes,
and someone says, ‘Do not spoil it,
because there is something good in it,’
I will do the same for the sake of my servants
and not destroy everyone.

I will bring forth offspring from Jacob,
and from Judah heirs of my mountains;
my chosen ones shall inherit it,
and my servants shall dwell there.

“But you who forsake Yahweh,
who forget my holy mountain,
who set a table for Gad,
and fill bowls of mixed wine for Meni,{g}

see, my servants shall shout from a glad heart,
and you shall cry out from a sore heart,
and howl from a shattered spirit.

so that whoever asks for a blessing in the land
will ask the God of truth{h} for it,
and whoever takes an oath in the land
will swear by the God of truth;
for the earlier troubles will be forgotten
and hidden from my sight.

“For see, I create new heavens
and a new earth,{i}
and the former things shall not be remembered,
nor come into mind.

They shall build houses and dwell in them;
they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

Before they call I will answer;
while they are yet speaking I will hear.

notes.text: Paul quotes verses 1–2 from the Septuagint in Romans 10:20–21, applying verse 1 to the Gentiles and verse 2 to Israel.
Or “their own thoughts.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads obscurely “and they suck (?) hands upon the stones.”
Or “among the rock tombs.”
Hebrew “for I am holy to you,” or, with different vowels, “for I would make you holy,” that is, pass holiness on to you.
Achor, “trouble”; compare Joshua 7:24–26; Hosea 2:15.
Gad and Meni are pagan gods of luck, “Fortune” and “Destiny”; meni puns on manah, “destine,” in verse 12. The Septuagint has “a table for the devil … a drink offering to Fortune.”
Hebrew Elohe amen, “the God of truth,” “the faithful God.” Compare 2 Corinthians 1:20; Revelation 3:14.
Compare 66:22; 2 Peter 3:13; Revelation 21:1.
Compare Revelation 21:4.
Or “the youth shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner shall be accursed at a hundred years old”; either way, a life of a hundred years shall be thought short.
Compare 11:6–9; Genesis 3:14.

verses.text:
My hand made all these things,
and that is how they all came into being,
declares Yahweh.
But this is the person I will look at:
the one who is humble, broken in spirit,
and trembles at my word.

Hear the word of Yahweh,
you who tremble at his word:
“Your kinsmen that hate you,
that thrust you away because of my name,
have said, ‘Let Yahweh show his glory,
that we may see your joy’;
yet they themselves shall be ashamed.

Hark, a tumult from the city!
Hark, from the temple!
It is the voice of Yahweh,
rendering recompense to his enemies!

Who has heard such a thing?
Who has seen such things?
Shall a land be born in one day?
Shall a nation be brought forth in a moment?
For as soon as Zion was in labor
she brought forth her sons.

Would I bring a baby to the moment of birth and not deliver it?”
says Yahweh;
“would I, the one who delivers, close the womb?”
says your God.

For thus says Yahweh:
“Behold, I will make peace flow to her as a river,
and the riches of the nations as a stream in flood;
and you shall be nursed, and borne upon the side,
and dandled upon the knees.

“Look, Yahweh is coming with fire,
and his chariots are like a whirlwind,
to repay his anger with fury
and his rebuke with blazing flames.

“People who consecrate and cleanse themselves to enter the gardens,
following someone in the middle,{f}
and who eat pork, detestable creatures and mice,
will all meet their end together, declares Yahweh.

They will bring all your relatives from every nation
as an offering to Yahweh,
on horses, in chariots and wagons,
on mules and on camels,
to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says Yahweh,
as the Israelites bring grain offerings
in clean containers to Yahweh’s house.

And of them too I will take some
to be priests, to be Levites, says Yahweh.{i}

“As the new heavens and the new earth
that I am making
will stand before me, declares Yahweh,
so your descendants and your name will stand.

And it shall be that month by month at the new moon,
and week by week on the Sabbath,
all flesh shall come to bow down before me,
declares Yahweh.

notes.text: Stephen quotes verses 1–2a in Acts 7:49–50; compare 1 Kings 8:27.
Or “like one who worships wickedness” (aven, “trouble,” “idolatry”).
Compare Revelation 12:5.
Or “from the abundance of her glory”; the meaning of Hebrew ziz is uncertain.
The Great Isaiah Scroll reads “For with fire Yahweh shall come to judge … all flesh,” lacking the second “Yahweh.”

So the read form of the Hebrew, “one (feminine),” perhaps a priestess or goddess; the written form has the masculine. The Septuagint has “and eat swine’s flesh in the porches.” For “shall come to an end together, declares Yahweh,” the Great Isaiah Scroll reads “together, says Yahweh.”
The Hebrew is abrupt, “And I, their works and their thoughts …”; “knowing” is supplied.
Hebrew “who draw the bow.” For “Pul” the Septuagint has “Phud” (Put), and in place of “who draw the bow” it has “Meshech.”
The Great Isaiah Scroll adds “to me” (“for priests, for Levites to me”).

Jesus applies the last lines to Gehenna in Mark 9:48. In synagogue reading verse 23 is repeated after verse 24, so that the book does not end on a note of judgment; the Great Isaiah Scroll and 1QIsa-b end with verse 24 as in the Masoretic Text.

books.name: Jeremiah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text, MT), checked against the Septuagint (LXX) through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Jeremiah survives in two editions. The Old Greek is about one-eighth shorter than the Hebrew (commonly estimated at some 2,700 fewer words), and it arranges the book differently: the oracles against the nations (Hebrew chapters 46–51) stand in the middle of the book, after 25:13, as Greek chapters 25:14–31:44 (often cited as LXX chs. 26–51), in a different order of nations (Elam, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab), and the rest of the book is renumbered. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, two Cave 4 manuscripts (4QJer-b and 4QJer-d) are reported to agree with the shorter, LXX-type text, while 4QJer-a and 4QJer-c support the longer Masoretic edition; so both editions existed in Hebrew, and many scholars regard the shorter one as the earlier. This translation follows the Hebrew, in its order and verse numbering. Whole verses that Brenton’s Septuagint lacks are footnoted where they occur (for example 10:6–8, 10; 17:1–4; 33:14–26; 39:4–13; 52:28–30); smaller Greek minuses (repeated titles such as “says Yahweh,” “of Armies,” and doublets) are too many to list and are described in general terms. Where the Greek order differs, the note gives the Greek location as numbered in Brenton. Qumran readings are stated in general terms (“is reported to”) until checked against the critical edition. Much of Jeremiah is poetry and is printed line by line; prose narrative and sermons are printed as paragraphs. Calendar months are given with their modern equivalents and footnoted. The Hebrew name of God, YHWH, is written “Yahweh”; “Yahweh of Armies” renders YHWH Sabaoth (see the note at 2:19).

verses.text: The words of Jeremiah{a} the son of Hilkiah,{b} of the priests who were in Anathoth{c} in the land of Benjamin,
to whom the word of Yahweh came in the days of Josiah{d} the son of Amon, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.{e}

It came also in the days of Jehoiakim{f} the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah{g} the son of Josiah, king of Judah, until the carrying away of Jerusalem into exile in the fifth month (in July–August).{h}
Now the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,

Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh!{i} See, I do not know how to speak,
for I am a youth.”

Be not afraid of their faces,
for with you am I to deliver you,” declares Yahweh.

Then Yahweh put forth his hand and touched my mouth, and Yahweh said to me,
“See, I have put my words in your mouth.

See, I have set you this day over the nations and over the kingdoms,
to pluck up and to pull down,
to destroy and to overthrow,
to build and to plant.”
The word of Yahweh came to me: “What are you looking at, Jeremiah?” I answered, “I see a branch of an almond tree.”{j}
Then Yahweh said to me, “You have seen well, for I am watching{k} over my word to perform it.”
And the word of Yahweh came to me a second time, saying, “What do you see?” And I said, “A boiling pot I see, and its face is turned away from the north.”{l}
Then Yahweh said to me, “Out of the north disaster shall break loose upon all the inhabitants of the land.

For look, I am summoning all the families of the northern kingdoms,” declares Yahweh. “They will come, and each ruler will set up his throne at the entrance of Jerusalem’s gates, facing all its surrounding walls and all the towns of Judah.
And I will speak my judgments against them for all their evil, in that they have forsaken me and have burned incense{m} to other gods and bowed down to the works of their own hands.
But you, gird up your loins; arise and speak to them all that I command you. Be not dismayed before them, lest I dismay you before them.

And I—see, I have made you this day a fortified city, and a pillar of iron, and walls of bronze against the whole land, against the kings of Judah, against its princes, against its priests, and against the people of the land.
And they will fight against you, but they shall not prevail against you, for with you am I,” declares Yahweh, “to deliver you.”

notes.text: Jeremiah (Hebrew Yirmeyahu) probably means “Yahweh exalts” or “Yahweh founds”; the meaning is uncertain.
Hilkiah means “My portion is Yahweh.”
Anathoth, a priestly town about 3 miles (5 kilometers) northeast of Jerusalem (Joshua 21:18); Abiathar the priest was banished there (1 Kings 2:26).
Josiah probably means “Yahweh supports” or “Yahweh heals”; uncertain.
That is, about 627 B.C.
Jehoiakim means “Yahweh raises up.”
Zedekiah means “Yahweh is righteousness.”
Hebrew “the fifth month,” Av, counted from the spring new year; that is, in 586 B.C. (see 52:12). The modern equivalent is approximate, since the Hebrew year was lunar.
Hebrew Adonai Yahweh. The Septuagint reads “O Lord, you that are supreme Lord” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew shaqed, “almond tree,” sounds like shoqed, “watching” (verse 12). The almond was called “the watcher” or “the wakeful tree” because it blossoms first in the year.
Hebrew shoqed; see the note at verse 11. The Septuagint reads “I have watched over my words to perform them” (Brenton).
Or “tilted away from the north,” that is, about to pour out toward the south.
Or “made offerings go up in smoke.”

verses.text: And the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,{a}

“Go and cry in the ears of Jerusalem, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh:
I remember for you the devotion{b} of your youth,
the love of your bridal days,
your going after me in the wilderness,
in a land not sown.

Listen to Yahweh’s word, house of Jacob,
and all the families of the house of Israel.

Thus has Yahweh spoken:
“What fault did your forefathers detect in me,
that far from me they strayed,
pursued what is vapor,{c} and turned to vapor?

They did not ask, ‘Where is Yahweh,
the one who rescued us from Egypt
and guided us across the wilderness,
across a land of deserts and pits,
a land of dry heat and pitch dark,
a land where nobody travels
and nobody makes a home?’

“So I will bring charges against you again,” declares Yahweh,
“and I will bring charges against your grandchildren.

For cross over to the coasts of Kittim{g} and see,
and send to Kedar{h} and consider diligently,
and see if there has been such a thing as this.

Has a nation exchanged its gods,
even though they are no gods?
Yet my people have exchanged their glory{i}
for that which does not profit.

Be appalled, O heavens, at this;
shudder, be utterly desolate,” declares Yahweh,

“for two evils my people have committed:
me they have forsaken,
the fountain of living waters,
to hew out for themselves cisterns,
broken cisterns, which cannot hold water.

“Is Israel a bondman? Or one born in the household?
Why then has he become spoil?

Also the men of Noph{j} and Tahpanhes{k}
have grazed{l} the crown of your head.

Is not this your own doing,
in abandoning Yahweh your God
when he guided you on the road?

Your own wickedness will punish you,
and your unfaithfulness will condemn you.
Understand, then, and recognize how bad and bitter it is
for you to abandon Yahweh your God
and to have no fear of me,”
declares the Lord Yahweh of Armies.{o}

“For long ago you broke your yoke
and tore off your bonds,
and you said, ‘I will not serve.’
For on every high hill
and under every green tree
you sprawled as a harlot.

Yet I had planted you a choice vine,
wholly of true seed.
How then have you turned yourself into
the degenerate shoots of a foreign vine before me?

For though you wash with lye
and use for yourself much soap,
the stain of your iniquity is before me,”
declares the Lord Yahweh.

a wild donkey used to the wilderness,
in the lust of her soul sniffing the wind!
In her heat who can turn her back?
All who seek her need not weary themselves;
in her month they will find her.

Keep your feet from going bare
and your throat from going dry.
But you answered, ‘It’s no use!
I love foreign gods,
and I will chase after them.’

“As a thief is ashamed when caught,
so the house of Israel is ashamed—
the people, their kings, their officials,
their priests and their prophets—

They say to a tree, ‘You are my father,’
and to a rock, ‘You are the one who bore me.’
They have faced away from me and shown me their backs;
but when they are in trouble they cry,
‘Come and save us!’

“Why do you contend with me?
All of you have transgressed against me,” declares Yahweh.

“To no purpose I smote your sons;
correction they would not receive.
Your sword consumed your prophets
like a ravaging lion.

Can a virgin forget her ornaments,
or a bride her sash?
Yet my people have forgotten me
days without number.

“How skillfully you pursue love!
Even wicked women
have learned from your example.

you say, ‘I am innocent;
certainly his anger has turned away from me.’
But look, I will put you on trial
for saying, ‘I have not sinned.’

How lightly you go about,
changing your way!
By Egypt also you shall be put to shame,
as you were put to shame by Assyria.

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks verse 1 and the opening words of verse 2, reading simply “And he said, Thus says the Lord” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew ḥesed, loyal love or covenant faithfulness.
Hebrew hevel, “vapor” or “breath,” often used of idols; the verb that follows plays on it.
Hebrew “a land of the Carmel,” that is, a garden land.
That is, the rulers.
Baal, “lord” or “master,” the Canaanite storm god.
Kittim, originally Kition on Cyprus; here the western islands and coastlands generally.
Kedar, a tribe of the Arabian desert to the east; so the verse means “search from west to east.”
An ancient Jewish tradition counts this as one of the “corrections of the scribes,” the original reading being “my glory.”
Noph is Memphis, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt.
Tahpanhes, an Egyptian frontier fortress in the eastern Nile Delta; see 43:7–9.
Or “have shaved” or “have broken”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Shihor, a branch of the Nile, or the Nile itself; the Septuagint has “Geon” (Brenton).
That is, the Euphrates.

Hebrew Adonai YHWH Tsevaʾot. “Yahweh of Armies” (traditionally “the LORD of hosts”) presents God as commander of the heavenly armies and of Israel’s forces. This title occurs more than 80 times in the Hebrew of Jeremiah; the Septuagint very often lacks “of Armies,” and here reads “says the Lord your God” (Brenton, modernized).
Probably the Valley of Ben-hinnom (see 7:31); the Septuagint reads “the burial-ground” (Brenton).
The Septuagint adds, “and according to the number of the streets of Jerusalem they sacrificed to Baal” (Brenton); compare 11:13.
Or “a land of deep gloom,” Hebrew maʾpelyah, found only here.
That is, they were not burglars caught in the act, whom it would have been lawful to kill (Exodus 22:2).
A gesture of grief and shame (2 Samuel 13:19).

verses.text:
“If a husband divorces his wife,{a}
and she goes away from him
to become another man’s wife,
may the first husband take her back?
Would the land not be thoroughly defiled by that?
You, however, have prostituted yourself with many lovers;
and now you want to return to me?” declares Yahweh.

“Look up at the barren hills{b} and see:
where have you not been ravished?
You waited for lovers beside the roads
like a nomad{c} in the desert,
and you defiled the land
with your prostitution and your evil.

So the showers were held back,
and the late rains{d} did not come.
Yet you had the brazen look of a prostitute;
you refused to feel shame.

Have you not just now cried to me,
‘My father, the companion of my youth are you!

Will he keep his anger forever?
Will he guard it to the end?’
See, so you have spoken,
yet you have done all the evil that you could.”
And Yahweh said to me in the days of Josiah the king, “Have you seen what she did, faithless Israel?{e} She went up on every high mountain and under every green tree, and there played the harlot.
And I said, after she had done all these things, ‘To me she will return’; but she did not return. And her treacherous sister Judah saw it.

And I saw that, because faithless Israel had committed adultery, I had dismissed her and handed her a writ of divorce; yet Judah her treacherous sister felt no fear, but went off and played the harlot as well.
And through the lightness of her harlotry she polluted the land, committing adultery with stone and with tree.
Even so, her unfaithful sister Judah did not come back to me wholeheartedly, but only in pretense,” declares Yahweh.
Then Yahweh said to me, “Faithless Israel has shown herself more righteous than treacherous Judah.

Only acknowledge your iniquity,
that against Yahweh your God you have transgressed,
and have scattered your ways to strangers
under every green tree,
and my voice you have not obeyed,’ declares Yahweh.
Return, O faithless children,” declares Yahweh, “for I am your husband;{f} and I will take you, one from a city and two from a clan, and I will bring you to Zion.
And I will grant you shepherds suited to my heart, who will pasture you with knowledge and insight.

And when you have increased and borne fruit in the land, in those days,” declares Yahweh, “men will speak no more of ‘the ark of Yahweh’s covenant.’ It will not rise in the mind; they will neither recall it nor miss it, nor will another be made.

At that time they shall call Jerusalem ‘The Throne of Yahweh,’ and all the nations shall be gathered to it, to the name of Yahweh, to Jerusalem; and they shall walk no more after the stubbornness of their evil heart.
In those days Judah’s house shall walk alongside Israel’s house, and together they shall come out of the northern land into the land that I bestowed on your fathers as a possession.

“And I had thought,
‘How gladly would I place you with my sons,
and grant you a delightful land,
the loveliest inheritance among the nations!’
And I thought you would call me ‘My Father,’
and never turn back from following me.

Surely, as a wife treacherously leaves her companion,
so have you dealt treacherously with me, O house of Israel,” declares Yahweh.

On the bare heights a cry is heard,
Israel’s sons weeping and entreating,
for they have twisted their way;
Yahweh their God they have forgotten.

“Return, O faithless sons;
I will heal your faithlessness.”
“See, we have come to you,
for you are Yahweh our God.

Truly, a delusion are the hills,
the tumult on the mountains;
truly in Yahweh our God
is the salvation of Israel.

But the shameful thing{g} has devoured
the labor of our fathers from our youth,
their flocks and their herds,
their sons and their daughters.

notes.text: Hebrew begins “Saying,” perhaps a fragment of a lost introduction. The law of Deuteronomy 24:1–4 forbids a man to take back a divorced wife who has married another.
Hebrew shefayim, bare hills, places of pagan worship; also in verse 21.
That is, a desert nomad lying in wait to rob travelers.
Hebrew malqosh, the spring rain of March–April that ripens the grain.
Hebrew meshuvah yisraʾel, literally “turning-away Israel,” the northern kingdom, exiled by Assyria in 722 B.C. Jeremiah plays repeatedly on shuv, “turn, return” (verses 12, 14, 22).
Or “I am your master”; Hebrew baʿalti, a play on Baal.
Hebrew habbosheth, “the Shame,” a contemptuous substitute for Baal (compare 11:13).

verses.text:
“If you return, O Israel,” declares Yahweh,
“to me you should return.
If you put away your abominations from before me,
and do not waver,

and if you swear, ‘As surely as Yahweh lives,’
sincerely, justly and rightly,
then the nations will invoke blessings by him,
and will boast in him.”

For thus says Yahweh to the men of Judah and to Jerusalem:
“Break up your fallow ground,
and do not sow among thorns.

Dedicate yourselves to Yahweh;
cut away the foreskins of your hearts,
people of Judah and residents of Jerusalem,
or my anger will blaze out like fire
and burn so that no one can put it out,
because of your evil actions.”

Announce this in Judah and proclaim it in Jerusalem:
“Sound the ram’s horn throughout the land;
shout out loud and say,
‘Gather together, and let us flee
to the fortified cities!’

For this gird on sackcloth;
lament and wail,
for the fierce anger of Yahweh
has not turned back from us.”
“And it shall come to pass in that day,” declares Yahweh, “that the heart of the king shall fail, and the heart of the princes; the priests shall be appalled, and the prophets astounded.”
Then I said, “Oh, Lord Yahweh! You have completely tricked this people and Jerusalem by promising, ‘You will have peace,’ while the sword is at our throats.”{a}

At that time it shall be said to this people and to Jerusalem,
“A scorching wind from the bare heights in the wilderness
comes toward the daughter of my people,
not to winnow nor to cleanse,

a wind too strong for these comes at my bidding.
Now I also will speak judgments against them.”

See, like clouds he comes up,
and like the whirlwind his chariots;
swifter than eagles are his horses.
Woe to us, for we are ruined!

Wash the evil out of your heart, Jerusalem,
so that you can be saved.
How long will your harmful thoughts
stay inside you?

For hark, one tells it from Dan,
and announces evil from the hills of Ephraim:{b}

“Warn the nations, see!
Proclaim against Jerusalem:
besiegers{c} come from a distant land;
they lift their voice against the cities of Judah.

Like keepers of a field they are against her round about,
because against me she has rebelled,” declares Yahweh.

“Your way and your deeds
have brought these things upon you.
This is your evil; how bitter it is!
How it reaches to your heart!”

One disaster follows another,
for the whole land is ruined.
In an instant my tents are destroyed,
my tent curtains in a moment.

How long must I see the signal
and hear the sound of the ram’s horn?

“For my people are foolish;
me they do not know.
Senseless children are they,
and they have no understanding.
Wise are they to do evil,
but to do good they know not.”

I looked on the earth, and see, it was formless and void;{e}
and to the heavens, and their light was gone.

I looked on the mountains, and see, they were quaking,
and all the hills moved to and fro.

I looked, and see, there was no man,
and all the birds of the heavens had fled.

I looked, and see, the garden land{f} was a wilderness,
and all its cities were broken down
before Yahweh, before his fierce anger.

And you, devastated one, what are you doing?
You dress in scarlet,
put on gold jewelry,
and paint your eyes with makeup,{g}
but you beautify yourself for nothing.
Your lovers reject you;
they are trying to kill you.

For I hear a cry as of one in travail,
distress as of one bringing forth her firstborn,
the cry of Zion’s daughter, panting,
spreading her hands:
“Ah me! My life is failing
before the slayers.”

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “And I said, O sovereign Lord, truly you have greatly deceived this people” (Brenton, modernized); some ancient witnesses read “And they shall say,” making the words those of the priests and prophets.
Dan is at the far north of the land; the hill country of Ephraim lies just north of Jerusalem: the invader draws nearer.
Hebrew notsrim, “watchers” or “besiegers”; a slight change of vowels gives “enemies.”
Hebrew “My inward parts,” regarded as the seat of the emotions.
Hebrew tohu wavohu, the words of Genesis 1:2.
Hebrew “the Carmel,” the fruitful land.
Hebrew puk, a black eye-paint made of antimony or galena.

verses.text:
Run to and fro through Jerusalem’s streets,
and look, I pray, and take note;
search through her open squares,
whether you can find a man,
whether there is one who does justice,
who seeks faithfulness,
that I may pardon her.

Though they say, “As Yahweh lives,”
yet falsely do they swear.

“How can I forgive you for this?
Your children have abandoned me
and sworn by gods that are not gods.
I fed them until they were full, yet they committed adultery
and crowded into the houses of prostitutes.

Well-fed stallions, lusty,{a} they have become;
each neighs after his neighbor’s wife.

“Go up among her terraced vines and ruin them,
yet do not finish her off;
lop away her tendrils,
for they belong not to Yahweh.

For utterly faithless to me have they been,
the house of Israel and the house of Judah,” declares Yahweh.

They have lied about Yahweh
and said, “It is not he;{b}
no harm shall come upon us,
nor shall we see sword or famine.

Therefore this is what Yahweh, the God of Armies, says:
“Because you have said this,
look, I am turning my words in your mouth into fire,
and this people into wood that it will burn up.

Look, I am bringing a nation against you from far away, house of Israel,” declares Yahweh.
“It is a lasting nation,
an ancient nation,
whose language you do not know,
and you cannot understand what they say.

Their quiver is a gaping tomb;
warriors, every one of them.{c}
“Yet even in those days,” declares Yahweh, “I will not make a full end of you.

And when they ask, ‘Why has Yahweh our God treated us like this?’ answer them, ‘You abandoned me and served foreign gods in your own land, so you will serve strangers in a land that does not belong to you.’

“Announce this among Jacob’s house;
make it heard in Judah, and say:

‘Hear now this, O foolish and heartless people,
who have eyes, yet see not,
who have ears, yet hear not.

Do you not fear me?’ declares Yahweh.
‘Will you not tremble in my presence?
I made the sand the boundary for the sea,
an eternal limit it cannot cross;

But this people has a heart both obstinate and defiant;
they have veered off and departed.

Never do they say within themselves,
“Come, let us fear Yahweh our God,
who sends rain at its proper time,
the early and the later showers,{d}
who guards for our sake
the fixed weeks of reaping.”

Your iniquities have turned these away,
and your sins have withheld the good from you.

“A horrible and appalling thing
has come to pass in the land:

the prophets prophesy falsely,
and the priests rule at their direction;{f}
and my people love it so.
But what will you do at its end?”

notes.text: Hebrew meshakim, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “well-equipped” or “lusty.”
Or “He will do nothing.”
The Septuagint lacks “Their quiver is like an open grave,” reading only “They are all mighty men” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew yoreh, the autumn rain (October–November), and malqosh, the spring rain (March–April).
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Or “rule by their own authority”; Hebrew “by their hands.”

verses.text:
“Flee for safety, O sons of Benjamin,
out of the midst of Jerusalem!
In Tekoa{a} blow the ram’s horn,
and over Beth-haccherem{b} raise a signal,
for disaster looms out of the north,
and great destruction.

The comely and delicate one,
the daughter of Zion, I will destroy.{c}

‘Consecrate war against her!{d}
Arise, and let us go up at noon!
Woe to us, for the day declines,
for the shadows of evening stretch out!

Arise, and let us go up by night
and destroy her palaces!’”

For this is what Yahweh of Armies says:
“Chop down her trees
and heap up a siege ramp to attack Jerusalem.
This city is due for punishment;
every part of it is full of oppression.

Be warned, O Jerusalem,
lest my soul be torn from you,
lest I make you a desolation,
a land uninhabited.”

This is what Yahweh of Armies says:
“They will pick the remnant of Israel
clean as a vine is picked;
like a grape harvester, run your hand
once more over the branches.”

To whom shall I speak and give warning,
that they may hear?
See, their ear is uncircumcised,
and they cannot hearken.
See, the word of Yahweh has become to them a reproach;
they take no delight in it.

Their houses shall pass over to others,
fields and wives together,
for I will stretch out my hand
against the inhabitants of the land,” declares Yahweh.

“From the smallest to the biggest,
they are all greedy for dishonest profit;
prophets and priests alike
all practice deceit.

The fracture of my people they have patched up carelessly,
declaring, ‘All is well, all is well,’
when nothing is well.

Thus has Yahweh spoken:
“Halt at the crossroads and look about;
inquire about the age-old tracks,
which is the good road, and travel on it,
and you will find repose for your souls.
But they replied, ‘We refuse to travel it.’

I set watchmen over you, saying,
‘Hearken to the sound of the ram’s horn!’
But they said, ‘We will not hearken.’

Therefore hear, O nations,
and know, O congregation, what is among them.{e}

Hear, O earth:
see, I am bringing disaster upon this people,
the fruit of their schemes,
because to my words they have not hearkened,
and my law—they have rejected it.

What use to me is incense arriving from Sheba,
or fragrant cane{f} from a far country?
Your whole offerings win no favor,
and your sacrifices give me no pleasure.”

Therefore thus says Yahweh:
“See, I am laying before this people stumbling blocks,
and fathers and sons together shall stumble on them;
neighbor and friend shall perish.”

We have heard news of them,
and our hands have gone weak;
anguish has gripped us,
like the pain of a woman giving birth.

Daughter of my people, wrap yourself in sackcloth
and wallow in the ashes;
mourn as one mourns an only son,
a wailing most bitter,
for in an instant the ravager
will fall upon us.

“I have made you a tester of metals,{h} one who examines my people,
so that you can learn and test how they live.

Rejected silver they are called,
for Yahweh has rejected them.”

notes.text: Tekoa, a town about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Jerusalem; its name sounds like the verb “blow” (tiqʿu).
Beth-haccherem, “house of the vineyard,” probably Ramat Rahel, between Jerusalem and Bethlehem.
Or “The daughter of Zion is like a lovely pasture”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Warfare was begun with religious rites.
The Hebrew of this line is obscure.
Hebrew qaneh, an aromatic reed, perhaps calamus.
Hebrew magor missaviv, a favorite phrase of Jeremiah (20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29).
Or “a fortress”; Hebrew mivtsar, perhaps a scribal note. The image is of refining silver from ore, using lead to carry off impurities.
So the Hebrew consonants read as “by fire the lead is consumed” (qere); the written text (ketiv) may be read “by their fire.”

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh, saying:{a}
“Stand at the gate of Yahweh’s house and announce this message there: ‘Listen to Yahweh’s word, all you people of Judah who go through these gates to worship Yahweh.
This is what Yahweh of Armies, Israel’s God, says: Reform your conduct and your actions, and I will let you dwell{b} in this place.
Put not your trust in lying words, saying, “The temple of Yahweh, the temple of Yahweh, the temple of Yahweh are these!”{c}
For only if you thoroughly reform your conduct and your actions, if you deal out true justice between one man and another,
if the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow you do not oppress, and innocent blood you do not shed in this place, and after other gods you do not walk to your own harm,
then I will let you dwell in this place, in the land that I gave to your fathers from of old even for evermore.
“‘See, you are trusting in lying words that cannot profit.
Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, burn incense to Baal, and walk after other gods whom you have not known,
and then come and stand in front of me in this house that bears my name, and say, “We are safe!”—only to carry on with all these detestable practices?
Has this house, which is called by my name, become a den of robbers in your eyes? I too, see, I have seen it,’ declares Yahweh.
“‘Go now to my place at Shiloh,{d} where I first gave my name a home, and see what I did to it because of my people Israel’s evil.
And now, because you have done all these deeds,’ declares Yahweh, ‘and I spoke to you, rising early and speaking, yet you did not hear, and I called you, yet you did not answer,
then I will do to the house that bears my name, the house you rely on, and to the place I gave to you and your ancestors, what I did to Shiloh.
And I will cast you out from my sight, as I cast out all your brothers, the whole offspring of Ephraim.’
“As for you, do not pray for this people, nor lift up a cry or a prayer for them, nor intercede with me, for I will not hear you.
Do you not see what they are doing in the cities of Judah and in the streets of Jerusalem?
Sons collect sticks, fathers light the fire, and wives work the dough, to bake cakes for the Queen of Heaven;{e} and they pour libations to other gods to stir up my anger.
Is it I whom they provoke?” declares Yahweh. “Is it not themselves, to the shame of their own faces?”

Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: “Look, my anger and fury will be poured out on this place, on humans and animals alike, on the field’s trees and the land’s crops; it will burn and will not be put out.”
Thus says Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel: “Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices, and eat flesh.{f}
For I did not speak to your fathers, nor command them, in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices.
But this thing I commanded them: ‘Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and you shall be my people; and walk in all the way that I command you, that it may be well with you.’
But they did not obey or incline their ear, but walked in their own counsels, in the stubbornness of their evil heart, and went backward and not forward.
From the day that your fathers came out of the land of Egypt until this day, I have sent to you all my servants the prophets, daily rising early and sending them.
Still they paid me no heed and bent no ear, but hardened their necks; they behaved worse than their ancestors.
“You will tell them all these words, but they will not listen to you; you will call out to them, but they will not answer you.{g}
And you shall say to them, ‘This is the nation that did not obey the voice of Yahweh its God and did not accept correction; faithfulness has perished; it is cut off from their mouth.’

“Shear off your hair{h} and cast it away;
raise a lament on the bare heights,
for Yahweh has rejected and forsaken
the generation of his wrath.”
“For Judah’s sons have done what is evil before me,” declares Yahweh. “Their loathsome idols they have placed in the house that bears my name, and so defiled it.
And they have built the high places of Topheth,{i} which is in the Valley of Ben-hinnom,{j} to burn their sons and their daughters in the fire, which I did not command, nor did it come into my mind.

Therefore, mark this: days are approaching,” declares Yahweh, “when it will no longer be named Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Killing; for they will bury in Topheth till no space is left.
And the corpses of this people will be food for the birds of the heavens and for the beasts of the earth, and none will frighten them away.

And I will make to cease from the cities of Judah and from the streets of Jerusalem the voice of mirth and the voice of gladness, the voice of the bridegroom and the voice of the bride, for the land shall become a ruin.

notes.text: The Septuagint lacks verse 1 and the first half of verse 2; its text begins, “Hear the word of the Lord, all Judea” (Brenton). The same sermon is summarized in chapter 26.
Or, with a change of vowels, “and I will dwell with you”; so also in verse 7.
The Septuagint has the phrase twice: “It is the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord” (Brenton).
Shiloh, where the tabernacle stood in the days of Eli (1 Samuel 1–4), was evidently destroyed after the Philistines captured the ark.
Probably Ishtar (Astarte), the Mesopotamian goddess of love and war, worshiped as “Queen of Heaven”; see also 44:17–25. The Septuagint reads “to make cakes to the host of heaven” (Brenton).
That is, eat even the burnt offerings, which were wholly burned; Yahweh no longer values them.
The Septuagint lacks this verse except for its opening words: “Therefore you shall speak this word to them” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “your crown” (nezer), as a sign of mourning; the word is addressed to Jerusalem as a woman.
Topheth, the place in the valley where children were burned as offerings; the name may mean “fireplace,” with its vowels perhaps changed to suggest boshet, “shame.”
Ben-hinnom, “son of Hinnom,” the valley south and west of Jerusalem; its later name Gehinnom gave rise to “Gehenna.”

verses.text: “At that time,” declares Yahweh, “people will take the bones of Judah’s kings, officials, priests, prophets and Jerusalem’s residents out of their graves

and spread them out under the sun, moon and all the stars of the sky, which they loved, served, followed, consulted and worshiped. Nobody will collect or bury them; they will lie like manure on the ground.
And death shall be chosen rather than life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family, in all the places where I have driven them,” declares Yahweh of Armies.

“Tell them this also, ‘This is what Yahweh says:
Does a man who falls not get up?
Does one who strays not come back?

Why then has this people turned away,
Jerusalem, in a perpetual turning away?
They hold fast to deceit;
they refuse to return.

I listened and heard,
but they do not speak what is right;
no man repents of his evil,
saying, “What have I done?”
Each one turns to his own course,
like a horse plunging into battle.

Even the stork in the heavens
knows her appointed seasons,
and the turtledove, the swift,{a} and the crane
keep the time of their coming;
but my people know not
the judgment of Yahweh.

“‘How can you say, “We are wise,
and the law of Yahweh is with us”?
But see, the lying pen of the scribes
has made it into a lie.

Were they ashamed of their detestable acts?
Not at all; they felt no shame,
and did not even know how to blush.
So they will fall along with the fallen;
when I punish them they will stumble,’ says Yahweh.

We looked for peace, but no good came;
for a time of healing, but see, terror.

The snorting of his horses is heard from Dan;
at the noise of his chargers’ neighing
all the land trembles.
They arrive and eat up the land and everything in it,
the town and its people.

“For look, I am letting loose snakes among you,
vipers against which no charm avails,
and they will bite you,” declares Yahweh.

Past all cure is my sorrow;{f}
faint within me is my heart.

Listen to my people crying
from a distant land:
“Is Yahweh no longer in Zion?
Is her King no longer there?”
“Why did they make me angry with their carved idols
and their worthless foreign gods?”

“The harvest is past, the summer is ended,
and we are not saved.”

For the wound of the daughter of my people I am wounded;
I mourn; dismay has taken hold of me.

Is there no balm{g} in Gilead?
Is there no physician there?
Why then has the healing of the daughter of my people
not gone up?{h}

notes.text: The identification of these birds is uncertain; Hebrew sus or sis may be the swift or the swallow.
The Septuagint lacks verses 11–12 (Brenton), which repeat 6:14–15.
Or “I will make an end of them”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this line is obscure; the Septuagint lacks it (Brenton).
Hebrew “water of rosh,” a poisonous plant, perhaps hemlock or poppy.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Hebrew tsori, an aromatic resin used as medicine, for which Gilead, east of the Jordan, was famous (Genesis 37:25). The plant is uncertain; suggestions include mastic and the balsam tree.
That is, the new flesh has not grown over the wound. In Hebrew, 9:1 is numbered 8:23.

verses.text:
Oh that my head were waters,
and my eyes a fountain of tears,
that I might weep day and night
for the slain of the daughter of my people!{a}

Oh that I had in the wilderness
a lodging place for wayfarers,
that I might leave my people
and go away from them!
For they are all adulterers,
a company of traitors.

Your dwelling is in the midst of deceit;
through deceit they refuse to know me, declares Yahweh.

Therefore thus says Yahweh of Armies:
“See, I will refine them and test them,
for what else can I do, because of the daughter of my people?

Shall I not punish them for these things?” declares Yahweh,
“and on a nation such as this
shall my soul not take vengeance?”

“Jerusalem I will turn into rubble heaps,
a haunt of jackals,
and Judah’s towns into a waste
where no one lives.”
What man is wise enough to grasp this? To whom has Yahweh’s mouth spoken, so that he can explain it? For what cause has the land perished, scorched like the desert, with none passing through?
And Yahweh said, “Because they have forsaken my law that I set before them, and have not obeyed my voice or walked in it,
but have walked after the stubbornness of their own hearts and after the Baals, as their fathers taught them.
Therefore thus says Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel: See, I will feed this people with wormwood, and give them poisoned water to drink.
I will scatter them among the nations whom neither they nor their fathers have known, and I will send the sword after them, until I have consumed them.”

For a sound of wailing is heard from Zion:
‘How we are ruined!
We are utterly ashamed,
because we have left the land,
because they have cast down our dwellings.’”

Hear, O women, the word of Yahweh,
and let your ear receive the word of his mouth;
teach your daughters a lament,
and each her neighbor a dirge.

For death has climbed in through our windows;
it has come into our strongholds,
cutting down the little ones in the street
and the youths in the public squares.

Say this: “So declares Yahweh:
‘Human corpses will lie
like manure across the open field,
like swaths of grain behind the harvester,
with no one to gather them up.’”

This is what Yahweh says:
“The sage must not glory in his wisdom,
nor the strong man glory in his strength,
nor the wealthy man glory in his wealth;

rather, if anyone would glory, let him glory in this:
that he has insight and knows me,
that I am Yahweh, who acts with steadfast love,
with justice and with righteousness on the earth.
For in these I take pleasure,” declares Yahweh.
“See, days are coming,” declares Yahweh, “when I will punish all those who are circumcised merely in the flesh:

Egypt, Judah, Edom, the sons of Ammon, Moab, and all who clip the corners of their hair,{c} who dwell in the wilderness; for all these nations are uncircumcised, and all the house of Israel is uncircumcised in heart.”

notes.text: In Hebrew, verse 1 is numbered 8:23, and verses 2–26 are numbered 9:1–25.
Hebrew ʿaqov yaʿqov, “supplanting he supplants,” a play on the name Jacob (Genesis 27:36).
Or “who dwell in the desert with clipped temples,” a custom of certain Arab tribes; compare Leviticus 19:27.

verses.text: Hear the word that Yahweh speaks to you, O house of Israel.

This is what Yahweh says:
“Do not copy the ways of the nations
or be terrified by signs in the sky,
though the nations are terrified by them;

for the practices of the peoples are mere vapor.
Someone fells a tree in the woods,
and a carver shapes it with his chisel.

There is none like you, O Yahweh;{b}
you are great, and your name is great in might.

Who could fail to fear you, King of the nations?
For to you it rightly belongs;
for among all the sages of the nations
and throughout their realms
none can compare with you.

They are altogether stupid and foolish;
the instruction of idols is but wood.

But Yahweh is God in truth;
he is the living God, the King for all ages.
When he is angry the earth shakes,
and the nations cannot withstand his fury.
This is what you are to tell them:{d} “The gods that never made heaven and earth will vanish from the earth and from beneath these skies.”

At the sound of his voice the waters in the skies roar,
and he lifts the clouds from the far edges of the earth.
He fashions lightning to go with the rain,
and draws the wind out of his treasuries.

They are vapor, a work of mockery;
in the time of their punishment they shall perish.

Pick up your pack from the ground,
you who live under siege!

For this is what Yahweh says:
“Look, I am about to hurl away the people of the land
this time,
and I will bring trouble on them
so that they will find out.”{f}

How I suffer from my injury!
My wound is severe.
Yet I said, “This is my sickness,
and I must put up with it.”

For the shepherds are stupid
and do not inquire of Yahweh;
therefore they have not prospered,
and all their flock is scattered.

Listen, a rumor! See, it comes—
a great commotion out of the north country,
to make the cities of Judah a desolation,
a lair of jackals.

I know, O Yahweh, that the way of man is not in himself;
it is not in man who walks to direct his steps.

Discipline me, Yahweh, but fairly;
not in anger, or you will reduce me to nothing.

Empty your fury on the nations that do not acknowledge you,
and on the clans that never invoke your name,
for they have eaten up Jacob;
they have eaten him and finished him off,
and made his pasture a waste.

notes.text: The Septuagint arranges verses 5 and 9 differently, placing the substance of verse 9 within verse 5.
The Septuagint lacks verses 6–8 and 10 (Brenton). A Hebrew manuscript from Qumran (4QJer-b) is reported to share this shorter form of the chapter.
Uphaz, an unknown place; some ancient witnesses read Ophir.
Verse 11 is in Aramaic, the only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah, and it contains a wordplay: the gods who did not “make” (ʿavadu) the heavens shall “perish” (yevadu).
That is, Yahweh, the one who belongs to Jacob as his share.
Or “that they may be found”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text: This is the word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh:
“Hear the terms of this covenant, and speak them to Judah’s men and to Jerusalem’s residents.
Tell them, ‘This is what Yahweh, Israel’s God, says: Cursed is the man who does not heed the terms of this covenant,
