The entire vale of carcasses and ashes{k} and every terrace down to the Kidron gorge, as far as the Horse Gate’s corner on the east, shall be holiness to Yahweh. Never again will it be plucked up or thrown down.”

notes.text: The Hebrew of verse 2 is difficult; it may refer to the exodus generation. The Septuagint reads “I found him warm in the wilderness with them that were slain with the sword” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “to him” (Brenton: “The Lord appeared to him from far”).
Rachel, “ewe.” The wife of Jacob and mother of Joseph and Benjamin, buried near Ramah (compare 1 Samuel 10:2); here she mourns her descendants carried away. Matthew 2:18 cites this verse.

The meaning of “a female surrounds a man” is uncertain and much debated. The Septuagint reads very differently: “for the Lord has created safety for a new plantation: men shall go about in safety” (Brenton). Item for scholarly review.
Perhaps the prophet’s words on waking from a revelatory dream.

Hebrew “cut a covenant,” the idiom for making a covenant, perhaps from the ritual of cutting animals (compare 34:18). The Septuagint reads “make a new covenant” (Brenton). Hebrews 8:8–12 cites verses 31–34 from the Greek.
Hebrew baʿalti, “I was husband (or master)”; the Septuagint reads “and I disregarded them” (Brenton), as in Hebrews 8:9.
Hebrew torah, “instruction, law.”
The Septuagint places verse 37 before verses 35–36 (Brenton 38:35–37).
The written Hebrew text has only “Look, days”; “coming” is supplied by the Hebrew margin (the Qere) and the ancient versions.
Hebrew “valley of the corpses and the fat ashes,” probably the Valley of Ben-hinnom (compare 7:31–32).

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh in the tenth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, which was the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar.{a}
At that time the army of Babylon’s king was besieging Jerusalem, and Jeremiah the prophet was shut up in the court of the guard, which was in the palace of Judah’s king.
For Zedekiah king of Judah had confined him, saying, “Why do you prophesy, ‘So says Yahweh: Look, I am handing this city over to the king of Babylon, and he will capture it;
Zedekiah king of Judah will not escape from the Chaldeans’ grip but will certainly be handed over to Babylon’s king, and will speak with him mouth to mouth and see him eye to eye;
to Babylon he will lead Zedekiah, and there he will remain until I attend to him, declares Yahweh; though you fight the Chaldeans, you will not succeed’?”{b}
Jeremiah said, “Yahweh’s word came to me:
‘Look, Hanamel son of Shallum your uncle is coming to you to say, “Buy for yourself my field in Anathoth, for yours is the right of redemption to buy it.”’

Then Hanamel my cousin came to me, as Yahweh had said, in the court of the guard, and said to me, ‘Buy my field in Anathoth, in the land of Benjamin, for the right of possession and of redemption is yours; buy it for yourself.’ Then I knew that this was Yahweh’s word.
“The Anathoth field I therefore purchased from Hanamel, my uncle’s son, and for it I weighed him out roughly seven ounces{c} of silver.
I signed the deed, sealed it, called in witnesses, and weighed the silver on scales.
Next I took the purchase document—the copy sealed up, holding the stipulations and terms, along with the copy left unsealed—

and handed this document over to Baruch{d} son of Neriah son of Mahseiah while Hanamel my uncle’s son looked on, together with the witnesses whose names were on the document and every Judean seated within the guard’s courtyard.
And before their eyes I charged Baruch:
‘So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: These documents—the sealed bill of sale and the unsealed one—take them and place them inside a clay jar,{e} that they may endure for a long time.
For this is what Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: People will once more buy houses, fields and vineyards in this land.’
“After I had given the deed of purchase to Baruch son of Neriah, I prayed to Yahweh:
‘Ah, Lord Yahweh! Look, it is you who made the heavens and the earth by your great power and by your outstretched arm; nothing is too wondrous for you.
You show steadfast love to thousands, yet repay the guilt of fathers into the lap of their children after them, O great and mighty God, whose name is Yahweh of Armies,
great in counsel and mighty in deed, whose eyes are open to all the ways of mankind, to give each according to his ways and according to the fruit of his deeds.
Signs and marvels you worked in Egypt’s land, and still today, both in Israel and across humankind, and won for yourself renown, as is plain today.
You brought your people Israel out of the land of Egypt with signs and wonders, with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, and with great terror.
And you gave them this land, which you swore to their fathers to give them, a land flowing with milk and honey.

Enter they did, and seize it they did, yet to your voice they paid no heed and in your instruction they did not walk; of everything you ordered them to do, not one thing they did. So you have caused all this disaster to meet them.

Look, siege ramps have been built up to the city to capture it, and because of sword, famine and plague the city has been handed over to the Chaldeans who attack it. What you said has happened, and you see it for yourself.
And yet you, Lord Yahweh, told me, “Buy the field with silver and have witnesses present,” though the Chaldeans are about to take the city.’”
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah:
“Look, I am Yahweh, the God of all flesh. Is anything too wondrous for me?
Therefore so says Yahweh: Look, I am handing this city to the Chaldeans and to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, and he will take it.

The Chaldeans who fight against this city will come and set this city on fire and burn it, with the houses on whose roofs they burned incense to Baal and poured out drink offerings to other gods, to provoke me.
For from their youth onward Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons have been doing only what is wrong in my eyes; Israel’s sons have only been vexing me with what their hands have made, declares Yahweh.{f}
From the day it was built until today this city has stirred up my anger and fury, so I am going to remove it from my presence,
on account of every wrong done by Israel’s sons and Judah’s sons to vex me—they and their kings, officials, priests, and prophets, Judah’s men and Jerusalem’s residents alike.
They turned to me the back and not the face; though I taught them early and persistently, they did not listen to accept correction.
They set up their detestable idols inside the house that bears my name and made it unclean.

Baal’s shrines they erected in the Ben-hinnom ravine, making sons and daughters of theirs cross through fire for Molech,{g} something I never ordered, which never once came into my thoughts—that they should commit this abhorrent act and so lead Judah into sin.
“So now this is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says about this city, which you say ‘has been handed over to the king of Babylon through sword, famine and plague’:
Look, I will gather them from every country where I scattered them in my anger, rage and great fury; I will return them to this place and make them live securely.
They shall be my people, and I will be their God.
One heart and one path I will grant them, so that they revere me always, to their benefit and the benefit of their descendants following them.
An everlasting covenant I will cut with them: never will I turn aside from doing them good, and reverence for me I will place within their hearts, so they do not depart from me.
It will be my joy to do good to them, and I will plant them in this land faithfully, with all my heart and soul.
For this is what Yahweh says: Just as I brought all this great disaster on this people, so I will bring on them all the good I am promising.
Fields will be bought in this land, which you say ‘is a wasteland, with no people or animals, and has been handed over to the Chaldeans.’

People will buy fields with silver and sign, seal and witness deeds, in the territory of Benjamin, in the area around Jerusalem, in the towns of Judah, in the hill country, in the foothills and in the Negev; for I will restore their fortunes, declares Yahweh.”

notes.text: That is, 588–587 B.C., during the final siege of Jerusalem.
The Septuagint ends the verse “and Zedekiah shall go into Babylon, and dwell there” (Brenton 39:5), lacking the rest.
Hebrew “seventeen shekels,” about 195 grams.

Baruch, “blessed.” Neriah, “Yahweh is my lamp.” Mahseiah, “Yahweh is a refuge.” Baruch was Jeremiah’s scribe and companion (chapters 36, 43, 45). A clay seal impression reading “Berekyahu son of Neriyahu the scribe” has been reported, but its authenticity is disputed. Item for scholarly review.
Hebrew “a vessel of clay,” the kind of jar in which documents were kept.
The Septuagint lacks the second half of verse 30 (Brenton 39:30).
Or “to the king.” Hebrew molekh, a deity or rite of child sacrifice; the Septuagint reads “to king Moloch” (Brenton).

verses.text: A second time Yahweh’s word reached Jeremiah, while he remained shut in within the guard’s courtyard:
“So says Yahweh, who makes it,{a} Yahweh who shapes it to set it firm—Yahweh is his name:
Call to me, and I will answer you and tell you great things, things fenced off,{b} that you have not known.
For so says Yahweh, God of Israel, about the houses of this city and the houses of Judah’s kings that are pulled down to make a defense against the siege ramps and the sword:

They are coming to fight the Chaldeans and fill the houses{c} with the dead bodies of people I struck down in my anger and fury, for I have turned my face away from this city because of all their wickedness.
Look, I will bring to it new flesh and healing; I will heal them and uncover for them a wealth of peace and faithfulness.
I will turn back the captivity of Judah and the captivity of Israel and build them up as at the first.
I will purify them from all the guilt by which they sinned against me, and pardon all the guilt by which they sinned and rebelled against me.

And this city shall be to me a name of joy, a praise and a glory before all the nations of the earth who hear of all the good I do for them; they will tremble and quake over all the good and all the peace I provide for it.

“So says Yahweh: Yet again there will sound out in this place—of which you keep saying, ‘Wasteland, bare of human and animal’—in Judah’s towns and along Jerusalem’s deserted lanes, void of human, of resident, of animal—

the sound of gladness and the sound of joy, the voice of bridegroom and the voice of bride, the voice of those who say,
‘Give thanks to Yahweh of Armies,
for Yahweh is good,
for his steadfast love endures forever!’
as they bring thank offerings into Yahweh’s house. For I will turn back the captivity of the land as at the first, says Yahweh.
“This is what Yahweh of Armies says: In this place, now a wasteland with no people or animals, and in all its towns, shepherds will once again let their flocks rest in pastures.

In the towns of the hill country, of the lowland, and of the Negev, in the land of Benjamin, around Jerusalem, and in Judah’s towns, flocks will again pass under the hands of the one who counts them, says Yahweh.
“Look, days are coming, declares Yahweh,{d} when I will fulfill the good word I spoke to the house of Israel and the house of Judah.
In those days and at that time I will make sprout for David a righteous Branch,{e} and he will execute justice and righteousness in the land.
In those days Judah will be saved and Jerusalem will dwell securely, and this is what she will be called: ‘Yahweh Our Righteousness.’{f}
For so says Yahweh: David shall never lack a man sitting on the throne of the house of Israel,
nor shall the Levite priests ever be short of a man in my presence, presenting whole burnt offerings, sending up grain offerings in smoke, and preparing sacrifices every day.”
Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah:
“So says Yahweh: Were you able to annul my covenant of the daytime and my covenant of the night, so that daytime and night no longer arrive in their season,
then my covenant with my servant David could also be broken, so that he would have no son to rule on his throne, and my covenant with the Levitical priests who serve me.
The stars of the sky cannot be counted, nor can the sand on the seashore be measured; in the same way I will increase the descendants of my servant David and the Levites who serve me.”
Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah:
“Have you not observed what this people have said: ‘The two clans{g} that Yahweh chose, he has rejected them’? So they despise my people, as though they were no longer a nation in their sight.
So says Yahweh: Unless I fixed my covenant of daytime and night, and appointed the statutes governing heaven and earth,

then I would also reject the descendants of Jacob and my servant David, and would not choose rulers from his line to rule Abraham’s, Isaac’s and Jacob’s descendants. But I will restore their fortunes and have compassion on them.”

notes.text: So the Hebrew, “who makes it” (that is, who brings his plan to pass). The Septuagint reads “who made the earth and formed it” (Brenton).
Hebrew betsuroth, “fortified, inaccessible”; some Hebrew manuscripts read netsuroth, “hidden.”
Hebrew “them,” probably the houses. The text of verses 4–5 is difficult.
Verses 14–26 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton). They expand the promise of 23:5–6 and are among the longest passages in the Hebrew text with no Greek counterpart. Item for scholarly review.
Compare 23:5, where the same promise appears in slightly different words.
Hebrew Yahweh Tsidqenu. At 23:6 the name is given to the king; here it is given to the city.
Probably Israel and Judah, though some take it as Judah and the house of David, or the royal and priestly lines of verses 17–22.

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, with his whole army, every kingdom of the earth under his rule, and all the peoples, were fighting against Jerusalem and against all its towns:
“So says Yahweh, God of Israel: Go and speak to Zedekiah king of Judah; tell him, ‘So says Yahweh: Look, I am delivering this city into the grip of Babylon’s king, and he will burn it with fire.

And you yourself will not slip from his grip; you will surely be seized and handed over to him. Your eyes will look into the eyes of Babylon’s king, his mouth will speak to your mouth, and to Babylon you will go.
Yet hear Yahweh’s word, O Zedekiah king of Judah: So says Yahweh concerning you: You will not die by the sword.

In peace you will die. And as spices were burned for your fathers, the former kings who were before you, so they will burn spices for you and lament for you, “Alas, lord!” For I myself have spoken the word, declares Yahweh.’”
Then Jeremiah the prophet spoke all these words to Zedekiah king of Judah in Jerusalem,

while the army of Babylon’s king was fighting against Jerusalem and against all the towns of Judah still holding out, Lachish and Azekah;{a} for these alone among Judah’s towns remained as fortified cities.
The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh after King Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people in Jerusalem to proclaim release{b} to them:
that each should set free his Hebrew slave, male or female, so that no one should hold a fellow Judean in bondage.
And all the officials and all the people who had entered into the covenant obeyed: each would set free his male and female slave and no longer hold them in bondage. They obeyed and let them go.
Later, though, they reversed course, fetched back the menservants and maidservants they had freed, and subdued them again into servitude.{c}
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh:
“So says Yahweh, God of Israel: I myself cut a covenant with your fathers on the day I brought them out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slaves, saying,

‘When seven years end{d} you shall each release your Hebrew kinsman who was sold to you; six years he serves you, and then you must dismiss him from you a free man.’ Your ancestors, though, paid me no heed and turned no ear.
You yourselves turned back today and did what was right in my eyes, proclaiming release each to his neighbor, and you cut a covenant before me in the house that bears my name.
But then you turned and profaned my name: each took back his male and female slave whom you had sent away free at their own desire, and you forced them to be your male and female slaves.

Therefore so says Yahweh: You have not obeyed me by proclaiming release each to his brother and to his neighbor. Look, I proclaim to you a release, declares Yahweh—to the sword, to plague, and to famine;{e} and I will make you a horror to all the kingdoms of the earth.
The men who overstepped my covenant, not upholding the covenant’s words that they cut in my presence, I will render like{f} the calf they sliced in two, between whose halves they walked—
the officials of Judah, the officials of Jerusalem, the court officials, the priests, and all the people of the land who passed between the parts of the calf.
I will give them into the hand of their enemies and of those who seek their life; their corpses shall be food for the birds of the heavens and the beasts of the earth.
And Zedekiah king of Judah and his officials I will give into the hand of their enemies, of those who seek their life, of the army of Babylon’s king that has withdrawn from you.{g}

Look, I am giving command, declares Yahweh, and I will bring them back to this city. They will fight against it, take it, and burn it with fire; and the towns of Judah I will make a desolation without inhabitant.”

notes.text: Lachish and Azekah were fortress towns in the Judean lowland southwest of Jerusalem. Ostraca found at Lachish (the “Lachish letters”) are reported to mention watching for the signals of Azekah, probably from this period.
Hebrew deror, “release, liberty,” the term used for the Jubilee in Leviticus 25:10.
The Septuagint shortens verses 10–11 (Brenton 41:10–11).
So the Hebrew, counting inclusively (compare Deuteronomy 15:1, 12). The Septuagint reads “When six years are accomplished” (Brenton).
The Hebrew plays on deror, “release”: those who would not release their slaves are released to disaster.
Hebrew lacks “like”; the comparison is implied. The rite of passing between the halves of an animal (compare Genesis 15:9–17) called down its fate on any party who broke the covenant.
The Babylonian army had temporarily lifted the siege when an Egyptian force approached (37:5).

verses.text: The word that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:
“Go to the house of the Rechabites,{a} speak with them, and bring them into Yahweh’s house, into one of the chambers, and give them wine to drink.”
So I brought Jaazaniah{b} son of Jeremiah, the son of Habazziniah, together with his brothers, all his sons and the entire Rechabite family,

and I brought them into Yahweh’s house, into the chamber of the sons of Hanan son of Igdaliah, the man of God, which was beside the officials’ chamber, above the chamber of Maaseiah son of Shallum, keeper of the threshold.
Then I set before the men of the Rechabite house bowls brimming with wine, and cups, and said to them, “Drink wine.”
But they answered, “We drink no wine, for Jonadab{c} son of Rechab, our father, commanded us: ‘You shall drink no wine, neither you nor your sons, for all time.

No house shall you build, no seed shall you sow, no vineyard shall you plant or own; but in tents you shall dwell all your days, so that you may live many days on the face of the land where you sojourn.’
We have obeyed the voice of Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, in all he charged us: to drink no wine all our days, we, our wives, our sons, and our daughters,
and to build no houses to dwell in. Vineyard, field, and seed we have none.
We have lived in tents and have obeyed everything our ancestor Jonadab ordered us to do.
But when Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon came up against the land, we said, ‘Come, let us go into Jerusalem before the army of the Chaldeans and the army of Aram.’ So we are living in Jerusalem.”
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah:
“So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Go and say to the men of Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem, Will you not take correction and listen to my words? declares Yahweh.

The words of Jonadab son of Rechab, which he commanded his sons, not to drink wine, have been kept; to this day they drink none, for they obey their father’s command. But I have spoken to you early and persistently, and you have not listened to me.

Every one of my servants the prophets I dispatched to you, rising early to send them, with the message: ‘Come back, each of you, from your wicked course; make your conduct good; stop chasing other gods to worship them; then you will remain on the soil I granted you and your ancestors.’ Yet you lent no ear and heeded me not.
The sons of Jonadab son of Rechab have kept the command their father gave them, but this people has not listened to me.

Therefore so says Yahweh, God of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am bringing on Judah and on all the inhabitants of Jerusalem all the calamity I have pronounced against them, because I spoke to them and they did not listen, I called to them and they did not answer.”

Then Jeremiah told the Rechabite family, “This is what Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: You have obeyed your ancestor Jonadab’s order, followed all his instructions and done everything he told you,
so this is what Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Jonadab son of Rechab will always have a descendant to serve me.”{d}

notes.text: The Rechabites were a clan descended from Jonadab son of Rechab (verse 6), who kept a semi-nomadic life of abstinence; they are linked with the Kenites in 1 Chronicles 2:55. Rechab may mean “rider” or “charioteer.” The Septuagint calls them “the Archabin” (Brenton).
Jaazaniah, “Yahweh listens.” The Septuagint calls him “Jechonias the son of Jeremin” (Brenton).
Jonadab (also Jehonadab), “Yahweh is generous.” He took part in Jehu’s purge of Baal worship (2 Kings 10:15–23), about 840 B.C., some two and a half centuries before this episode.
To “stand before” Yahweh is the language of service. The Septuagint adds “before my face while the earth remains” (Brenton).

verses.text: In the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,{a} this word came to Jeremiah from Yahweh:

“Take for yourself a scroll{b} and write on it every word I have spoken to you against Israel and against Judah and against all the nations, from the day I first spoke to you, in the days of Josiah, until this day.
Perhaps the house of Judah will hear of all the calamity I intend to do to them, so that each will turn from his evil way, and I may forgive their guilt and their sin.”
Jeremiah therefore summoned Baruch son of Neriah, and from Jeremiah’s lips{c} Baruch inscribed on a scroll every word that Yahweh had spoken to him.
Then Jeremiah charged Baruch: “I am restricted;{d} I cannot enter Yahweh’s house.

So you go, and on a day of fasting read aloud from the scroll that you wrote as I dictated, so that the people in Yahweh’s house hear Yahweh’s words; also read them to all the people of Judah who come in from their towns.
Perhaps their plea will fall before Yahweh, and each will turn from his evil way; for great is the anger and the wrath that Yahweh has pronounced against this people.”
And Baruch son of Neriah did all that Jeremiah the prophet commanded him, reading from the book the words of Yahweh in Yahweh’s house.

In the fifth year{e} of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah, in the ninth month (November–December),{f} the whole population of Jerusalem and everyone who had come from Judah’s towns to Jerusalem announced a fast before Yahweh.

Then Baruch read out Jeremiah’s words from the scroll, with all the people listening, in Yahweh’s house. He stood in the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan the scribe, up in the higher courtyard by the New Gate entrance of Yahweh’s house.
Micaiah son of Gemariah son of Shaphan, on hearing out of the book every one of Yahweh’s words,

he went down into the royal palace, to the secretary’s chamber. The officials were all seated there: Elishama the secretary, Delaiah son of Shemaiah, Elnathan son of Achbor, Gemariah son of Shaphan, Zedekiah son of Hananiah, and the rest of the officials.
And Micaiah told them all the words he had heard when Baruch read the book in the hearing of the people.

Then all the officials sent Jehudi son of Nethaniah son of Shelemiah son of Cushi to Baruch, saying, “The scroll that you read in the hearing of the people—take it in your hand and come.” So Baruch son of Neriah took the scroll in his hand and came to them.
They said to him, “Sit down and read it in our hearing.” So Baruch read it in their hearing.
When they heard all the words, they turned in alarm to one another and said to Baruch, “We must certainly report all these words to the king.”
Baruch they then questioned: “Explain to us—these words, how did you come to write them all? Was it from his lips?”
Baruch answered them, “From his own mouth he recited all these words to me, while I wrote them in ink on the scroll.”
Then the officials told Baruch, “Go and hide, you and Jeremiah, and don’t let anyone know where you are.”
So they went in to the king in the court, having deposited the scroll in the chamber of Elishama the scribe, and reported all the words in the king’s hearing.
Then the king sent Jehudi to get the scroll, and he took it from the chamber of Elishama the scribe. Jehudi read it in the hearing of the king and of all the officials standing beside the king.
The king was sitting in the winter house in the ninth month (in November–December),{g} with a fire burning in the brazier before him.
Each time Jehudi had read out three or four columns,{h} the king sliced them away with a penknife and tossed them onto the brazier’s flames, till the scroll was burned up whole on the brazier fire.
Neither king nor courtier, though hearing all these words, felt any dread; no one ripped his clothes.
Elnathan, Delaiah and Gemariah even begged the king not to burn the scroll, but he refused to listen to them.{i}
The king ordered Jerahmeel, a prince, along with Seraiah son of Azriel and Shelemiah son of Abdeel, to arrest Baruch the scribe and the prophet Jeremiah. But Yahweh concealed them.
Now after the king had burned the scroll with the words Baruch wrote at Jeremiah’s dictation, Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah:
“Take a new scroll and copy onto it all the earlier words that stood on the first scroll, the one Jehoiakim king of Judah burned.

And concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah you shall say, ‘So says Yahweh: You have burned this scroll, saying, “Why have you written on it that the king of Babylon will certainly come and destroy this land and cut off from it man and beast?”
Therefore so says Yahweh concerning Jehoiakim king of Judah: He shall have no one to sit on the throne of David, and his dead body shall be cast out to the heat by day and the frost by night.

I will punish him and his offspring and his servants for their guilt; I will bring on them, on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and on the men of Judah all the calamity I pronounced against them, but they would not listen.’”

Then Jeremiah took another scroll and gave it to Baruch son of Neriah the scribe, who wrote on it at Jeremiah’s dictation all the words of the book that Jehoiakim king of Judah had burned in the fire. And many similar words were added to them.

notes.text: That is, 605–604 B.C., the year of the battle of Carchemish (46:2).
Hebrew “a scroll of a book,” a roll of papyrus or leather.
Hebrew “from the mouth of Jeremiah”; so also “at my (his) dictation” in verses 6, 17, 27, 32.
Hebrew ʿatsur, “restrained, hindered”; the reason is not stated. The Septuagint reads “I am in prison” (Brenton), though 36:19, 26 suggest he was not under arrest.
That is, 604–603 B.C. The Septuagint reads “in the eighth year” (Brenton).
Hebrew “the ninth month,” Kislev. A fast may have been called because of the Babylonian advance; 604 B.C. saw Nebuchadnezzar’s campaign against Ashkelon.
Hebrew “the ninth month,” Kislev, the cold, rainy season.
Hebrew delathoth, “doors,” that is, columns of writing on the scroll.
The Septuagint reverses the sense: “But Elnathan and Godolias suggested to the king that he should burn the roll” (Brenton).

verses.text: Zedekiah son of Josiah reigned as king in place of Coniah son of Jehoiakim, having been made king over the land of Judah by Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon.
But neither he nor his servants nor the people of the land listened to the words of Yahweh that he spoke through Jeremiah the prophet.
King Zedekiah sent Jehucal{a} son of Shelemiah and the priest Zephaniah son of Maaseiah to the prophet Jeremiah to say, “Please pray to Yahweh our God for us.”
Jeremiah at that point still moved freely in and out among the populace; nobody had yet locked him up.
In the meantime Pharaoh’s army had marched out of Egypt, and when the Chaldeans who were besieging Jerusalem heard the news about them, they pulled back from Jerusalem.{b}
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet:
“This is what Yahweh, the God of Israel, says: To the king of Judah, who sent you to consult me, say this: Look, Pharaoh’s army, which set out to help you, is going home to Egypt.
And the Chaldeans will come back and fight against this city; they will capture it and burn it with fire.
So says Yahweh: Do not fool your own souls by telling yourselves, ‘Off from us the Chaldeans are sure to march.’ Depart they will not.

Even if you were to strike down the whole army of the Chaldeans fighting against you, and there remained among them only wounded men, each in his tent, they would rise up and burn this city with fire.”
Now when, on account of Pharaoh’s forces, the Chaldean host had pulled back from Jerusalem,
Jeremiah set out from Jerusalem to go to the land of Benjamin to take his share{c} there among the people.
But at the Benjamin Gate the sentry in command, whose name was Irijah son of Shelemiah, the son of Hananiah, grabbed the prophet Jeremiah and said, “You are going over to the Chaldeans!”
“False!” Jeremiah replied. “To the Chaldeans I am not defecting.” Irijah, though, refused to hear him; he laid hold of Jeremiah and led him off to the officials.
The officials were enraged at Jeremiah; they beat him and put him in confinement in the house of Jonathan the scribe, for they had made it into a prison.
So Jeremiah went into the cistern house,{d} into the vaulted cells, and remained there many days.

Then King Zedekiah sent and had him brought, and the king questioned him secretly in his house: “Is there any word from Yahweh?” Jeremiah said, “There is.” And he said, “Into the hand of Babylon’s king you will be given.”
Jeremiah further asked King Zedekiah, “In what have I sinned against you, your courtiers, or this people, that you have locked me up in a jail?
Where are your prophets now, the ones who told you, ‘The king of Babylon will not attack you or this land’?
So now, my lord king, kindly hear me: may my petition come before your face. Do not return me to Jonathan the secretary’s house, or there I shall perish.”

King Zedekiah then gave the order. Jeremiah was entrusted to the guard’s courtyard, and each day a round loaf from the Street of the Bakers was handed him, till the city’s bread ran out entirely. Thus Jeremiah stayed on in the guard’s courtyard.

notes.text: Jehucal, “Yahweh is able.” He is called Jucal at 38:1. A clay seal impression reading “Yehukal son of Shelemyahu” has been reported from excavations in Jerusalem. Item for scholarly review.
This lifting of the siege is the setting of 34:21–22 as well.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; perhaps to receive a share of a family inheritance (compare 32:6–15). The Septuagint reads “to buy thence a property in the midst of the people” (Brenton).
Hebrew “the house of the cistern,” an underground dungeon.

verses.text: Word of what Jeremiah was proclaiming to the whole populace reached the ears of Shephatiah, Mattan’s son; of Gedaliah, Pashhur’s son; of Jucal, Shelemiah’s son; and of Pashhur, Malchiah’s son:
“So says Yahweh: Whoever remains in this city will die by sword, by famine, and by plague; but whoever goes out to the Chaldeans will live; he will have his life as a prize of war{a} and live.
So says Yahweh: This city will surely be given into the hand of the army of Babylon’s king, and he will capture it.”

The officials then told the king, “This fellow must be executed. He is slackening the hands of the fighting men still left in the city, and of all the people too, with words like these. This fellow seeks not the good of this people but its ruin.”
“There—he is in your power,” King Zedekiah replied, “for against you the king is helpless.”

Jeremiah they took and flung into Malchiah the king’s son’s cistern within the guard’s courtyard, lowering him on cords. Water there was none in the pit, only sludge, and down into the sludge Jeremiah sank.
Ebed-melech,{b} a Cushite and an official in the royal household, heard that they had lowered Jeremiah into the cistern. At that time the king was seated in the Benjamin Gate.
Ebed-melech left the palace and said to the king:
“My lord the king, these men have done evil in all they have done to Jeremiah the prophet, casting him into the cistern; he will die of hunger where he is, for there is no more bread in the city.”
Then the king commanded Ebed-melech the Cushite, “Take thirty men{c} with you from here and draw Jeremiah the prophet up out of the cistern before he dies.”

So Ebed-melech took the men with him and went into the king’s house, to a place beneath the storehouse, and took from there worn-out rags and old clothes, and let them down by ropes to Jeremiah in the cistern.
Ebed-melech the Cushite said to Jeremiah, “Put the worn-out rags and clothes under your armpits, beneath the ropes.” Jeremiah did so.
Then they pulled Jeremiah up with the ropes and drew him out of the cistern. And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard.
King Zedekiah summoned Jeremiah the prophet, bringing him to himself at the third entryway of Yahweh’s house. “A question I shall put to you,” the king told Jeremiah. “Keep nothing back from me.”
Jeremiah answered Zedekiah, “If I answer you, you will certainly have me killed. And if I advise you, you will not listen to me.”
Then King Zedekiah swore secretly to Jeremiah, “As Yahweh lives, who made this life for us, I will not put you to death or give you into the hand of these men who seek your life.”

Then Jeremiah said to Zedekiah, “So says Yahweh, God of Armies, God of Israel: If you will indeed go out to the officers of Babylon’s king, your life will be spared, and this city will not be burned with fire; you and your household will live.
But if you do not surrender to the officers of the king of Babylon, then this city will be handed over to the Chaldeans, who will set it on fire, and you will not escape from them.”
“It is the Judeans gone over to the Chaldeans that I dread,” King Zedekiah told Jeremiah, “that I may be surrendered into their hands and they make sport of me.”
Jeremiah said, “You will not be handed over. Obey, I beg you, the voice of Yahweh in what I am telling you, and it will go well with you, and your life will be spared.
But if you refuse to go out, this is what Yahweh has shown me:

Look, all the women left in the house of Judah’s king will be led out to the officers of Babylon’s king, and they will say,
‘They misled you and overcame you,
those trusted friends of yours;{d}
now that your feet are sunk in the mire,
they have turned away from you.’

Every wife and son of yours will be marched out to the Chaldeans. Neither shall you escape their grip; in the grip of Babylon’s king you will be caught, and this city will be burned{e} to the ground.”
Then Zedekiah said to Jeremiah, “Let no one know of these words, and you will not die.
If the officials hear that I have talked with you, and they approach you and ask, ‘Tell us what you said to the king and what he said to you; keep nothing back from us and we will not kill you,’
then you shall say to them, ‘I was presenting my plea before the king, that he would not send me back to the house of Jonathan to die there.’”

Sure enough, the officials all came to Jeremiah and interrogated him, and he gave them answer exactly in the terms the king had ordered. Then they left off questioning him, since nobody had overheard the matter.
And Jeremiah remained in the court of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.{f}

notes.text: Hebrew “his life shall be to him as spoil,” that is, he will escape with his life and nothing more.
Ebed-melech, “servant of the king.” A Cushite, that is, from the upper Nile region (Nubia). He is promised deliverance in 39:15–18.
So the Hebrew, followed by the Septuagint (Brenton). One Hebrew manuscript is reported to read “three men,” which some prefer as more likely for the task.
Hebrew “the men of your peace.” The lines echo Obadiah 7.
So the ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “and you will burn this city,” that is, you will be the cause of its burning.
The last clause of the Hebrew, “and it came to pass when Jerusalem was taken,” introduces 39:1 in many translations.

verses.text: In the ninth year of Zedekiah king of Judah, in the tenth month (in December–January),{a} Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon and his whole army came against Jerusalem and laid siege to it.
In Zedekiah’s eleventh year, in the fourth month (in June–July),{b} on the ninth day of the month, the city wall was breached.

Then all the officials of Babylon’s king came in and took their seats in the Middle Gate: Nergal-sharezer, Samgar-nebo, Sarsechim the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag,{c} and all the rest of the officials of Babylon’s king.

On seeing them,{d} Zedekiah king of Judah and every fighting man took flight; under cover of night they slipped out of the city along the royal garden path, by the gateway between the double walls, and he headed off in the direction of the Arabah.

But the Chaldean army pursued them and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho. They seized him and brought him up to Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he passed sentence on him.
The king of Babylon slaughtered Zedekiah’s sons at Riblah before his eyes; all the nobles of Judah, too, the king of Babylon slaughtered.
Zedekiah’s eyes he put out, and bound him in bronze fetters to take him to Babylon.
The Chaldeans burned the king’s house and the houses of the people with fire, and tore down the walls of Jerusalem.
Then Nebuzaradan{e} the captain of the guard took the people who were still in the city, those who had defected to him and the rest of the population, into exile in Babylon.
Some of the destitute, though, who possessed nothing at all, Nebuzaradan the guard commander let remain in Judah’s land, and handed over to them vineyards and plowland that day.
Regarding Jeremiah, Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon issued orders by way of Nebuzaradan the guard commander:
“Fetch him; keep your eyes on his welfare; harm him in nothing. Rather, whatever he asks of you, so treat him.”
So Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, Nebushazban the Rab-saris, Nergal-sharezer the Rab-mag, and all the chief officers of Babylon’s king sent
and took Jeremiah from the court of the guard and entrusted him to Gedaliah{f} son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, to bring him home. So he stayed among the people.
Yahweh’s word had come to Jeremiah while he was shut up in the court of the guard:

“Go and say to Ebed-melech the Cushite, ‘So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am bringing my words upon this city for calamity and not for good, and they will come to pass before you on that day.
But I will rescue you on that day, declares Yahweh; you will not be handed over to the men you fear.
For rescue you I most certainly will; by the sword you shall not fall. Your life shall be your booty, since in me you put your trust, declares Yahweh.’”

notes.text: Hebrew “the tenth month,” Tevet; that is, January 588 B.C. (compare 52:4; 2 Kings 25:1). The Septuagint reads only “in the ninth month of Zedekiah” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “the fourth month,” Tammuz; that is, July 587 or 586 B.C. The exact year is debated. Item for scholarly review.

Rab-saris and Rab-mag are Babylonian titles, perhaps “chief official” and “chief magus” or “high officer.” The division of the names is uncertain; Samgar-nebo and Sarsechim may be a single name or a title and a name. Nergal-sharezer may be Neriglissar, a later king of Babylon (560–556 B.C.). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 4–13 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton). Verses 4–10 closely parallel 52:7–16 and 2 Kings 25:4–12.
Nebuzaradan, Akkadian Nabu-zer-iddin, “Nabu has given offspring.” His title, rab-ṭabbaḥim, is literally “chief of the butchers” or “chief cook,” a high military office.
Gedaliah, “Yahweh is great.” Son of Ahikam, who had protected Jeremiah (26:24). He was appointed governor of Judah after the fall of Jerusalem (40:5).

verses.text: This is the message that came to Jeremiah from Yahweh after Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard let him go at Ramah. Nebuzaradan had found him bound in chains among the prisoners of Jerusalem and Judah who were being deported to Babylon.{a}
The captain of the guard took Jeremiah and said to him, “Yahweh your God pronounced this calamity against this place.
Yahweh has brought it about and done as he said, because you sinned against Yahweh and did not obey his voice. So this thing has happened to you.

So now, look: today I am loosing the fetters from your wrists. Should coming along with me to Babylon please you, come, and I will keep an eye on you; should it displease you, stay. Look—all the land lies open before you; wherever you judge it good and fitting to go, go there.”

When Jeremiah still had not turned back,{b} he said, “Go back, then, to Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan, whom the king of Babylon has appointed over the towns of Judah, and stay with him among the people, or go wherever it seems right to you to go.” So the captain of the guard gave him provisions and a present, and let him go.
Jeremiah went off, then, to Mizpah{c} to Gedaliah son of Ahikam and lived with him in the midst of those still left in the land.

The army officers and their troops who were still out in the open country heard that the king of Babylon had appointed Gedaliah son of Ahikam as governor of the land and had placed under his care the men, women and children, the poorest of the land, who had not been deported to Babylon.

to Mizpah they came to Gedaliah—Ishmael{d} son of Nethaniah; Kareah’s sons Johanan{e} and Jonathan; Seraiah son of Tanhumeth; the sons of Ephai from Netophah; and Jezaniah, son of a Maacathite—each with his men.

Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, gave them and their men his oath: “Do not be afraid to serve the Chaldeans. Stay in the land, serve the king of Babylon, and everything will be fine for you.

As for me, look, I will stay at Mizpah to stand before the Chaldeans who come to us; but you, gather wine, summer fruit, and oil, store them in your vessels, and settle in your towns that you have taken over.”

Likewise, when all the Judeans in Moab, among the Ammonites, in Edom, and in all the other lands heard that the king of Babylon had left a remnant in Judah and had appointed over them Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan,
they all came back from every place where they had been scattered and arrived in the land of Judah, at Mizpah, to Gedaliah; and they harvested a huge amount of wine and summer fruit.
Johanan son of Kareah next came to Mizpah to Gedaliah, along with every captain of the troops out in the countryside,
and said to him, “Do you know that Baalis{f} king of the Ammonites has sent Ishmael son of Nethaniah to take your life?” But Gedaliah son of Ahikam would not believe them.

Then Johanan son of Kareah spoke secretly to Gedaliah at Mizpah: “Let me go and strike down Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and no one will know. Why should he take your life, so that all the Judeans gathered around you are scattered and the remnant of Judah perishes?”
But Gedaliah son of Ahikam said to Johanan son of Kareah, “You shall not do this thing, for you are speaking a lie about Ishmael.”

notes.text: The introduction “The word that came to Jeremiah” is not followed by a prophetic oracle until 42:7; the chapters that follow narrate events after the fall of Jerusalem. Ramah lay about 5 miles (8 km) north of Jerusalem and was apparently a staging point for deportation.
The Hebrew is difficult; perhaps “before he could answer.”
Mizpah, “watchtower,” a town in Benjamin, often identified with Tell en-Nasbeh, north of Jerusalem.
Ishmael, “God hears.” He was of royal descent (41:1).
Johanan, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Baalis, perhaps “son of delight.” A seal impression reported to name “Baʿalyishaʿ king of the Ammonites” may refer to him. Item for scholarly review.

verses.text: It was the seventh month (in September–October){a} when Ishmael son of Nethaniah son of Elishama—of the royal line, and among the king’s high officers—arrived with ten men at Mizpah to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. While they shared bread together there in Mizpah,

up sprang Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and the ten men accompanying him, and cut down Gedaliah son of Ahikam son of Shaphan by the sword; thus he killed the one Babylon’s king had put in charge of the land.
Every Judean with Gedaliah in Mizpah Ishmael likewise cut down, and the Chaldean fighting men found on the spot.
On the day after Gedaliah’s murder, before anyone knew of it,
eighty men arrived from Shechem, Shiloh,{b} and Samaria, their beards shaved, their clothes torn, their bodies gashed, carrying grain offerings and incense to bring to Yahweh’s house.{c}
Out from Mizpah to intercept them went Ishmael son of Nethaniah, sobbing all the way. Upon reaching them he urged, “Come along to Gedaliah son of Ahikam.”
Once they were inside the town, though, Ishmael son of Nethaniah butchered them, he and his companions, and pitched them into a cistern.
But ten men among them said to Ishmael, “Do not kill us, for we have stores hidden in the field—wheat, barley, oil, and honey.” So he held back and did not kill them along with their companions.

Now the cistern into which Ishmael threw all the corpses of the men he had struck down because of Gedaliah{d} was the one King Asa had made against Baasha king of Israel. Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled it with the slain.

Then Ishmael led away into captivity all who were left in Mizpah: the princesses of the royal house and the townsfolk remaining there, those Nebuzaradan the guard commander had entrusted to Gedaliah son of Ahikam. With these prisoners Ishmael son of Nethaniah set off, aiming to pass over to Ammon’s territory.
But when Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him heard of all the evil Ishmael son of Nethaniah had done,
they took all their men and went to fight Ishmael son of Nethaniah, and they found him at the great pool in Gibeon.
When all the people with Ishmael saw Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him, they rejoiced.
All the captives Ishmael had taken from Mizpah turned around, came back and joined Johanan son of Kareah.
But Ishmael son of Nethaniah escaped from Johanan with eight men and went to the Ammonites.

Johanan son of Kareah and all the army officers with him took all the survivors from Mizpah whom he had rescued from Ishmael son of Nethaniah, after Ishmael had killed Gedaliah son of Ahikam—soldiers, women, children and court officials, whom Johanan had brought back from Gibeon.
Off they went and halted at Geruth Chimham{e} close by Bethlehem, meaning to proceed into Egypt
to escape the Chaldeans, whom they feared because Ishmael son of Nethaniah had murdered Gedaliah son of Ahikam, whom the king of Babylon had appointed governor of the land.

notes.text: Hebrew “the seventh month,” Tishri; the year is not stated (perhaps 587 or 586 B.C., or later). Jewish tradition later observed a fast in the seventh month in memory of Gedaliah (compare Zechariah 7:5; 8:19).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “Salem” (Brenton).
The marks of mourning suggest pilgrims grieving over the destroyed temple, bringing offerings to its site.
Hebrew “by the hand of Gedaliah,” perhaps “alongside Gedaliah.” The Septuagint reads “is the great pit” (Brenton), which may reflect a different reading of similar Hebrew letters.
Or “the lodging place of Chimham”; compare 2 Samuel 19:37–40. The Septuagint reads “Gaberoch-amaa” (Brenton).

verses.text: Then all the commanders of the forces, with Johanan son of Kareah and Jezaniah{a} son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least to the greatest, came near
and said to Jeremiah the prophet, “Let our plea fall before you, and pray for us to Yahweh your God, for all this remnant—for we are left as a few out of many, as your own eyes see us—
so that Yahweh your God may show us which road to walk and what course to take.”
Jeremiah the prophet said to them, “I have heard you. Look, I will pray to Yahweh your God as you ask, and whatever Yahweh answers you I will tell you; I will hold back nothing from you.”
And they said to Jeremiah, “May Yahweh be a true and faithful witness against us if we do not act according to every word that Yahweh your God sends you to tell us.
Whether it is good or bad, the voice of Yahweh our God, to whom we send you, we will obey, so that it may go well with us when we obey the voice of Yahweh our God.”
At the end of ten days Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah.
He called Johanan son of Kareah and all the commanders of the forces with him, and all the people from the least to the greatest,
and said to them, “So says Yahweh, God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your plea before him:
If you will indeed remain in this land, then I will build you up and not pull you down; I will plant you and not uproot you; for I relent of the calamity I have done to you.{b}
Do not fear the king of Babylon, whom you now fear; do not fear him, declares Yahweh, for I am with you to save you and to rescue you from his hand.
I will grant you mercy, so that he will have mercy on you and let you return to your own soil.
But should you declare, ‘In this land we refuse to remain,’ and so turn a deaf ear to Yahweh your God’s voice,
insisting, ‘Not so! Egypt’s land is where we shall go, where no warfare will meet our eyes, no ram’s horn our ears, no craving for food our bellies; there we will settle,’
then hear now Yahweh’s word, O remnant of Judah: So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: If you are firmly set on going to Egypt and go to sojourn there,
the sword you fear will overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine you dread will cling to you there in Egypt, and there you will die.
Everyone who is determined to go to Egypt and live there will die by sword, famine or plague; none will survive or get away from the disaster I will bring on them.

This is what Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: Just as my anger and fury poured out on the people living in Jerusalem, so my fury will pour out on you when you enter Egypt. You will become a curse, an object of horror, a cursing word and a disgrace, and you will never see this place again.
Yahweh has spoken to you, O remnant of Judah: Do not go to Egypt. Know for certain that I have warned you today

that you have erred to your own peril.{c} You yourselves dispatched me to Yahweh your God with the words, ‘Intercede for us with Yahweh our God; all that Yahweh our God declares, report to us, and we will carry it out.’
I have declared it to you today, but you have not obeyed the voice of Yahweh your God in anything he sent me to tell you.
So understand clearly that you will die by sword, famine or plague in the place you want to go to live.”

notes.text: The Septuagint reads “Azarias the son of Maasæas” (Brenton); compare 43:2, where the Hebrew has Azariah son of Hoshaiah.
Or “for I grieve over the calamity.” Hebrew niḥamti expresses a change of heart; it is often rendered “repent” or “regret.”
Or “you have deceived yourselves”; the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text: When Jeremiah had finished telling all the people everything Yahweh their God had sent him to say,

Azariah son of Hoshaiah and Johanan son of Kareah, with every arrogant man among them, retorted to Jeremiah, “Falsehood is what you are telling! Yahweh our God never sent you with the words, ‘Do not enter Egypt to live as aliens there.’
No—it is Baruch son of Neriah stirring you up against us, so as to put us in Chaldean hands, to be killed or deported to Babylon.”
So Johanan son of Kareah, all the commanders of the forces, and all the people did not obey the voice of Yahweh to stay in the land of Judah.
Rather, Johanan son of Kareah, along with every troop captain, gathered up all Judah’s remnant—those who had come home from every nation where they had been scattered to dwell in Judah’s land—

the men, women and children, the king’s daughters, and everyone Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard had left with Gedaliah son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, and also the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch son of Neriah.
and they came into the land of Egypt, for they did not obey the voice of Yahweh. And they came as far as Tahpanhes.{a}
Then Yahweh’s word came to Jeremiah in Tahpanhes:
“Take in your hand some large stones and hide them in the mortar{b} in the brick terrace at the entrance to Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes, in the sight of the men of Judah,

and say to them, ‘So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am sending for Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, my servant,{c} and I will set his throne above these stones that I have hidden, and he will spread his royal canopy over them.
He will come and attack Egypt: death for those marked for death, captivity for those marked for captivity, and the sword for those marked for the sword.

I{d} will set fire to the temples of the gods of Egypt, and he will burn their idols and carry off their gods. As a shepherd picks the lice from his cloak, so he will pick Egypt clean, and he will depart from there unharmed.
He will shatter the obelisks{e} of Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt, and the temples of Egypt’s gods he will burn with fire.’”

notes.text: Tahpanhes, a fortress city in the eastern Nile Delta, commonly identified with Tell Defenneh (Greek Daphnae).

Hebrew malet, found only here; the meaning is uncertain (“mortar,” “clay,” or “pavement”). The Septuagint reads only “hide them in the entrance, at the gate of the house of Pharaoh” (Brenton, modernized).
The Septuagint lacks “my servant” (Brenton).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and other ancient versions read “He will kindle” (Brenton: “he shall kindle”).

Hebrew matstsevoth, “standing stones, pillars.” Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun,” is Heliopolis (Egyptian On), the city of the sun god; the Septuagint reads “the pillars of Heliopolis that are in On” (Brenton).

verses.text: The message that came to Jeremiah about all the Jews living in Egypt, in Migdol, Tahpanhes, Memphis{a} and the region of Pathros:{b}
“So says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: You yourselves have seen all the calamity I brought on Jerusalem and on every town of Judah. Look, today they lie in ruins, with no one living in them,
because of the wickedness they committed to provoke me, going off to burn incense and serve other gods whom they had not known—neither they, nor you, nor your fathers.
Yet I sent to you all my servants the prophets, rising early and sending, to say, ‘Oh, do not do this detestable thing that I hate!’
But they did not listen or turn their ear, to turn from their wickedness and stop burning incense to other gods.
So my wrath and my anger poured forth and blazed in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, and they became a ruin and a desolation, as they are this day.

“And now so says Yahweh, God of Armies, God of Israel: Why are you doing great harm to your own souls, cutting off from yourselves man and woman, child and infant, from the midst of Judah, so as to leave yourselves no remnant?
Why do you provoke me by your handiwork, offering incense to other gods in Egypt, the place you moved to, so that you will be destroyed and become a curse and a disgrace among all earth’s nations?
Have you forgotten the crimes of your ancestors, of the Judean kings and queens,{c} and your own crimes and those of your wives, committed in Judah and in Jerusalem’s streets?
To this day they have not humbled themselves or shown reverence or lived by my law and decrees that I gave to you and your ancestors.
“Therefore so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel: Look, I am setting my face against you for calamity, to cut off all Judah.

I will take the remnant of Judah who set their faces to go to the land of Egypt to sojourn there, and in the land of Egypt they will all come to an end: by sword they will fall, by famine they will be consumed, from the least to the greatest; by sword and by famine they will die, and they will become an oath, a horror, a curse, and a reproach.
I will punish those who live in the land of Egypt as I punished Jerusalem, with sword, famine, and plague,

so that of the remnant of Judah who came to sojourn in the land of Egypt none will escape or survive to return to the land of Judah, to which they long to return and dwell; for they will not return, except some fugitives.”{d}
Every man aware that his wife was offering incense to other gods, every woman present—a vast gathering—and the whole populace dwelling in Egypt’s land, in Pathros, made reply to Jeremiah:
“As for the word you have spoken to us in Yahweh’s name, we will not listen to you.

Rather, we will certainly do everything we have vowed: burn incense to the Queen of Heaven{e} and pour out drink offerings to her, as we did, we and our fathers, our kings and our officials, in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem. Then we had plenty of food, and we were well off and saw no calamity.
But since we stopped burning incense to the Queen of Heaven and pouring out drink offerings to her, we have lacked everything and have been consumed by sword and by famine.”

The women added,{f} “And when we were offering incense to Heaven’s Queen and pouring libations to her—was it apart from our husbands that we baked her cakes stamped with her likeness{g} and poured libations to her?”
To the whole people—men, women, every one of them who had replied in this way—Jeremiah then spoke:

“The incense that you burned in the towns of Judah and the streets of Jerusalem, you and your fathers, your kings and your officials, and the people of the land—did not Yahweh remember it? Did it not come into his mind?
Yahweh could no longer tolerate your evil deeds and the detestable things you did. So your land became a wasteland, a horror and a curse, empty of people, as you see today.

Because you burned incense and sinned against Yahweh and did not obey the voice of Yahweh or walk in his law, his statutes, and his testimonies, therefore this calamity has come upon you, as at this day.”
Jeremiah said further to all the people and all the women, “Hear Yahweh’s word, all Judah who are in the land of Egypt:

This is what Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, says: You and your wives have declared with your mouths and carried out with your hands what you said: ‘We will keep the vows we made, to burn incense to the Queen of Heaven and pour out drink offerings to her.’ Go ahead, then, keep your vows and fulfill them!

But hear Yahweh’s word, all you people of Judah who live in Egypt: Look, I swear by my great name, says Yahweh, that no one from Judah anywhere in Egypt will ever again invoke my name by saying, ‘As the Lord Yahweh lives.’
Look, I am watching over them for calamity and not for good. All the men of Judah in the land of Egypt will come to an end by sword and by famine until they are wholly gone.
Those who escape the sword will come back from Egypt to Judah, only a few, and all the survivors of Judah who went to Egypt to live will find out whose word stands, mine or theirs.
And this will be the sign for you, declares Yahweh, that I will punish you in this place, so that you may know that my words will surely stand against you for calamity:

So says Yahweh: Look, I am giving Pharaoh Hophra{h} king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies and of those who seek his life, as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, who sought his life.”

notes.text: Hebrew Noph, Memphis, the old capital of Lower Egypt near modern Cairo.
Pathros, Upper (southern) Egypt.
Hebrew “his wives”; the Septuagint reads “of your princes” (Brenton). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 1–14 are a sermon after the pattern of 7:1–15 and 11:1–17.

Probably the goddess Ishtar or Astarte (compare 7:18). The Hebrew vowels read melekheth, “work” or “handiwork,” perhaps a scribal attempt to avoid the title; many Hebrew manuscripts read malkath, “queen.”
The Hebrew lacks this clause; it is supplied because the speakers are the women (“our husbands”). Some ancient witnesses are reported to include it; Brenton does not.
Or “to portray her,” perhaps cakes in the shape of the goddess or stamped with her image.
Hophra, Egyptian Wahibre (Greek Apries), Pharaoh 589–570 B.C. He was overthrown in a revolt and later killed. The Septuagint calls him “Uaphres” (Brenton).

verses.text: This is the message the prophet Jeremiah gave to Baruch son of Neriah, when Baruch wrote these words in a scroll as Jeremiah dictated, in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:{a}
“So says Yahweh, God of Israel, concerning you, Baruch:
You said, ‘Woe is me! For Yahweh has added sorrow to my pain; I am worn out with my groaning, and rest I do not find.’
Thus you shall say to him: ‘So says Yahweh: Look, what I have built I am tearing down, and what I have planted I am uprooting—that is, the whole land.{b}
And you—great things you are hunting for yourself? Hunt them not. For look, upon all flesh I am bringing disaster, declares Yahweh; but your life I will hand you as booty wherever you may go.’”

notes.text: That is, 605–604 B.C., the year of chapter 36; this short word to Baruch is placed out of chronological order. In the Septuagint it stands at the end of the material corresponding to chapter 44 (Brenton 51:31–35).
The Septuagint lacks “that is, the whole land” (Brenton 51:34).

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the nations.{a}

About Egypt. This concerns the army of Pharaoh Neco{b} king of Egypt, which was camped at Carchemish{c} on the Euphrates River, and which Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon defeated in the fourth year of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah:

“Make ready buckler and shield,
and advance to battle!

Let not the swift flee,
nor the warrior escape;
in the north, by the river Euphrates,
they have stumbled and fallen.

“Who is this, swelling like the Nile,
like streams with heaving waters?

Egypt swells like the Nile,
like streams with heaving waters.
‘Up I will surge,’ he said; ‘the earth I will flood;
towns and their townsfolk I will wipe out.’

That day belongs to the Lord Yahweh of Armies,
a day of revenge, when he takes vengeance on his enemies.
The sword will eat until it is full
and drink until it is satisfied with their blood;
for the Lord Yahweh of Armies will hold a slaughter
in the northern land by the Euphrates River.

Go up to Gilead and get balm,
O virgin daughter of Egypt!
In vain you have multiplied remedies;
there is no new skin for you.
The word that Yahweh spoke to Jeremiah the prophet about the coming of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon to strike the land of Egypt:

Why has your mighty one been swept away?{f}
He did not stand, because Yahweh thrust him down.

There they cried out, ‘Pharaoh king of Egypt is but a noise;
he has let the appointed time go by.’{g}

As I live, declares the King,
whose name is Yahweh of Armies,
like Tabor among the mountains,
like Carmel by the sea, one will come.

Pack your bags for exile,
you who dwell there, daughter of Egypt!
For Memphis will become a waste,
a ruin without inhabitant.

“Egypt is a lovely young cow,
but a horsefly from the north has landed on her—yes, landed!

They will cut down her forest, declares Yahweh,
impenetrable though it is,
for they are more than locusts;
they are without number.

The daughter of Egypt is put to shame;
she is given into the hand of a people from the north.”
Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel, says: “Look, I am bringing punishment on Amon of No,{i} and on Pharaoh, and on Egypt with her gods and her kings, on Pharaoh and on those who trust in him.
I will deliver them to those seeking their lives, to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and his officers. Later, though, people will live in Egypt as in former times, declares Yahweh.{j}

Do not be afraid, Jacob my servant, declares Yahweh,
for I am with you.
I will completely destroy all the nations
where I have scattered you,
but I will not completely destroy you.
I will discipline you fairly,
but I will certainly not let you go unpunished.”{k}

notes.text: Verse 1 heads the oracles against the nations (chapters 46–51). It is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton), which places these oracles after 25:13, in a different order (Elam, Egypt, Babylon, Philistia, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab), in Brenton’s numbering 25:14 through chapter 31 (see the introduction to Jeremiah).
Neco II, Pharaoh 610–595 B.C. (compare 2 Kings 23:29–35).
Carchemish, on the upper Euphrates, where Nebuchadnezzar defeated the Egyptian army in 605 B.C. The Septuagint reads “Charmis” (Brenton).
Hebrew magor missaviv; compare 6:25; 20:3, 10.
Cush is the upper Nile region; Put probably Libya; the Ludim perhaps Lydians or an African people.

The Hebrew word division is uncertain. The Septuagint divides the letters differently and reads “Why has Apis fled from you? Your choice calf has not remained” (Brenton, modernized), a reference to the sacred bull of Memphis. Item for scholarly review.
Hebrew shaʾon heʿevir hammoʿed, a pun on Pharaoh’s name or title. The Septuagint transliterates: “Saon esbeie moed” (Brenton).
Hebrew “her voice goes like the serpent,” perhaps the hiss of a snake fleeing the woodcutters.
Amon was the chief god of No (Thebes) in Upper Egypt. The Septuagint reads “Ammon her son” (Brenton).
Verse 26 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Verses 27–28 nearly repeat 30:10–11. Here the Septuagint has them (Brenton 26:27–28).

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning the Philistines, before Pharaoh struck Gaza:{a}

This is what Yahweh says:
“Look, water is rising in the north,
turning into a flooding river;
it will flood the land and everything in it,
the city and its residents.
People will cry out,
and every resident of the land will wail

at the noise of the stamping hoofs of his stallions,
at the rattle of his chariots, the rumble of their wheels.
Fathers do not turn back for their children,
so limp are their hands,

because of the day that is coming
to destroy all the Philistines,
to cut off from Tyre and Sidon
every helper who remains.
For Yahweh is destroying the Philistines,
the remnant of the coastland of Caphtor.{b}

Ah, sword of Yahweh,
how long till you are quiet?
Put yourself back into your sheath;
rest and be still!

How can it rest,{d}
when Yahweh has given it orders?
He has assigned it to Ashkelon
and the coast.”

notes.text: The occasion is uncertain; perhaps Neco’s campaign about 609 B.C. The Septuagint lacks “that came to Jeremiah the prophet” and “before Pharaoh struck Gaza,” reading only “Thus says the Lord against the Philistines” (Brenton, modernized).

Caphtor, probably Crete or the Aegean region, from which the Philistines were said to have come (Amos 9:7). The Septuagint does not name Caphtor, reading “the remaining inhabitants of the islands” (Brenton 29:4).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “the remnant of the Enakim” (Brenton), that is, the Anakim. Item for scholarly review.
So the Septuagint and other ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “How can you be quiet.”

verses.text:
Hark! A cry from Horonaim:
‘Devastation and great ruin!’

Moab is broken;
her little ones have made their cry heard.

For up the ascent of Luhith
they go weeping, weeping as they climb;
for on the descent of Horonaim
they have heard the anguished cry of ruin.

Flee! Save your lives!
Be like a juniper in the wilderness.{d}

For because you trusted in your works and your treasures,
you also will be captured;
and Chemosh{e} will go out into exile,
his priests and his officials together.

A destroyer will enter every town,
and not one will get away;
the valley will be ruined and the plateau devastated,
just as Yahweh has said.

Cursed is he who does Yahweh’s work with slackness,
and cursed is he who holds back his sword from blood.

Then Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh,
as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, their confidence.{h}

“How can you say, ‘We are warriors,
mighty men for battle’?

The destroyer of Moab and her towns has come up,
and the pick of his young men have gone down to the slaughter,
declares the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

The calamity of Moab is near at hand,
and his disaster hastens swiftly.

Mourn him, every neighbor of his,
every one acquainted with his fame;
cry, ‘Alas, snapped is the sturdy rod,
the splendid staff!’

Come down from your glory
and sit on the parched ground,
O inhabitant, daughter of Dibon!
For the destroyer of Moab has come up against you;
he has ruined your fortresses.

Stand beside the road and watch,
you who live in Aroer!
Question the man who is running away and the woman who is escaping;
ask, ‘What happened?’

Moab is put to shame, for it is broken;
wail and cry out!
Tell it by the Arnon
that Moab is laid waste.
“Judgment has come upon the plateau, upon Holon, Jahzah, and Mephaath,
upon Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim,
upon Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, and Beth-meon,
upon Kerioth and Bozrah, and upon all the towns of the land of Moab, far and near.

The horn of Moab is cut off,
and his arm is broken, declares Yahweh.

Was Israel not an object of ridicule to you?
Was he found among thieves,
so that each time you mentioned him
you shook your head?

Quit the towns; make your home among the cliffs,
you dwellers of Moab!
Become like a dove that builds
on the far walls of a ravine’s mouth.

We have heard of the pride of Moab—
very proud is he—
of his loftiness, his pride, his arrogance,
and the haughtiness of his heart.

Heshbon cries, and to Elealeh,
to Jahaz, their voices carry,
from Zoar to Horonaim and to Eglath-shelishiyah;
for Nimrim’s waters too
are turned to wasteland.

And I will bring to an end in Moab, declares Yahweh,
him who offers on the high place
and burns incense to his god.

Yes, shorn is every head,
trimmed short is every beard;
cuts on every hand,
on every waist sackcloth.

On all of Moab’s rooftops and in its public squares
there is only mourning;
for I have smashed Moab
like a jar nobody wants, declares Yahweh.

Shattered—how they howl!
Moab—how he turns tail in disgrace!
A mockery Moab has turned into,
a terror to all his neighbors.”

Kerioth{l} is captured,
and the strongholds are seized.
The heart of Moab’s warriors on that day
will be like the heart of a woman in labor.

Moab will be destroyed from being a people,
because he magnified himself against Yahweh.

The one fleeing from terror
tumbles into the pit;
the one clambering up out of the pit
is caught fast by the trap.
For this I will bring on Moab—
their year of reckoning, declares Yahweh.

Yet I will restore the fortunes of Moab
in the latter days, declares Yahweh.”
Thus far the judgment on Moab.

notes.text: Moab lay east of the Dead Sea. Much of this oracle parallels Isaiah 15–16, and verses 45–46 parallel Numbers 21:28–29; 24:17.
Or “Misgab,” a place-name.
Hebrew beḥeshbon ḥashevu, a play on the name Heshbon (“reckoning”) and the verb “plot.” “Madmen” (a town) likewise plays on tiddommi, “you will be silenced.”
Or “like Aroer”; the Septuagint reads “as a wild donkey in the desert” (Brenton, modernized).
Chemosh, the national god of Moab. The Septuagint spells it “Chamos” (Brenton).
Hebrew tsits, usually “flower” or “wing”; the meaning is uncertain (perhaps “salt” or “a gravestone”). The Septuagint reads “Set marks upon Moab” (Brenton).
The image is of wine settled on its lees, now poured off by “tilters” who tip the jars.
Bethel may be the town of the northern sanctuary or the name of a deity known from other ancient sources.
Kir-heres, “wall of potsherds,” probably the Moabite capital Kir-hareseth (Isaiah 16:7, 11).
Some Hebrew manuscripts and Isaiah 16:8 lack “sea of”; the text is uncertain.
The Septuagint lacks the eagle image here and the second half of verse 41 (Brenton 31:40–41); compare 49:22.
Or “The towns.” Kerioth may be a place-name or the plural “towns.”
Hebrew paḥad wapaḥath wapaḥ, a sound play. Compare Isaiah 24:17–18.
Verses 45–47 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).

verses.text:
About the Ammonites.{a}
This is what Yahweh says:
“Does Israel have no children?
No one to inherit?
Then why has Milcom{b} taken over Gad,
and his people moved into its towns?

For this reason, look, the time is coming, declares Yahweh,
when I will sound the war cry
against Rabbah of the Ammonites;
it will become a ruined heap,
and its surrounding villages will be set ablaze;
then Israel will take the land from those who took it from him,
says Yahweh.

Howl, Heshbon—Ai lies ravaged!
Shriek, you daughters of Rabbah!
Wrap on sackcloth, keen,
dart back and forth among the walled pens!
For off to captivity Milcom marches,
his priests with his chiefs alongside.

Why do you boast of your valleys,
your valley flowing,{c} O faithless daughter,
who trusted in her treasures, saying,
‘Who will come against me?’

Look, I am bringing terror upon you,
declares Lord Yahweh of Armies,
from all who are around you;
you will be driven out, each straight ahead,
with none to gather the fugitives.

Yet later the lot of Ammon’s people I will turn back again,
is Yahweh’s utterance.”{d}

Concerning Edom.{e}
So says Yahweh of Armies:
“Is wisdom no more in Teman?
Has counsel perished from the prudent?
Has their wisdom gone stale?

Flee, turn back, dwell in the depths,
O inhabitants of Dedan!
For I will bring the calamity of Esau upon him,
the time when I punish him.

If grape pickers came to you,
wouldn’t they leave some grapes behind?
If thieves came at night,
they would take only as much as they wanted.{f}

But I have stripped Esau bare;
I have exposed his hiding places,
so that he cannot hide.
His descendants, relatives and neighbors are wiped out,
and he is gone.

Abandon your fatherless; I myself will preserve them;
on me let your bereaved wives rely.”

This is what Yahweh says: “Look, those who did not deserve to drink the cup will have to drink it; and will you be the one to escape without any punishment? You will not escape; you will certainly drink.
For by myself I have sworn, declares Yahweh, that Bozrah{g} will become a horror, a reproach, a waste, and a curse, and all her towns will be perpetual wastes.”

I have heard a message from Yahweh,
and a messenger has been sent to the nations:
“Assemble and march against her,
and get ready for battle!”

“For look, I will make you small among the nations,
despised among mankind.

The fear you cause has fooled you,
along with your proud heart,
you who live in the rock crevices,{h}
who occupy the mountaintop.
Even if you build your nest as high as an eagle’s,
I will pull you down from there,
declares Yahweh.

See, as a lion climbs out of Jordan’s jungle
toward an ever-green grazing ground,
in a moment I will chase him off it,
and whoever I pick I will set in charge of it.
Who compares with me? Who will call me to court?
Which shepherd can hold his ground before my face?”

So hear the plan Yahweh has devised against Edom
and the intentions he has toward the people of Teman:
the youngest of the flock will certainly be dragged off;
their pasture will certainly be horrified at their fate.

At the sound of their fall the earth shakes;
the cry—at the Red Sea{i} its sound is heard.

Mark it: as an eagle mounts and plunges,
so one spreads wide his feathers above Bozrah;
the hearts of Edom’s champions in that hour
will flutter like a woman’s in childbirth.

Damascus has grown feeble; she turns to flee,
and panic has seized her;
anguish and pangs have taken hold of her,
like a woman in labor.

How is the city of praise not forsaken,{k}
the town of my joy?

Because of this her young men will fall in her public squares,
and all her warriors will be quiet on that day,
declares Yahweh of Armies.

And I will kindle a fire in the wall of Damascus,
and it will consume the strongholds of Ben-hadad.”{l}

Concerning Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor,{m} which Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon struck down.
So says Yahweh:
“Rise up, go up against Kedar!
Destroy the people of the east!

Tents and flocks will be seized from them,
their tent hangings and every article;
camels they will lead off as their own,
shouting over them, ‘Dread all around!’

Run! Roam far away! Make your homes deep down,
dwellers of Hazor, is Yahweh’s utterance!
For Babylon’s king Nebuchadrezzar has devised a scheme against you,
contrived a design against you.

Arise, march against a nation lounging at ease,
untroubled in its living, is Yahweh’s utterance,
a people without door or bolt,
encamped apart from all.

Plunder their camels will be,
their droves of cattle booty.
To every wind I will fling the ones with trimmed temples,{n}
and from all quarters I will fetch their ruin, declares Yahweh.

Hazor will become a lair for jackals,
a permanent wasteland;
nobody will live there,
no person will stay in it.”
The word of Yahweh that came to Jeremiah the prophet concerning Elam,{o} at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah king of Judah:

So says Yahweh of Armies:
“Look, I am breaking the bow of Elam,
the chief of their might.

Yet when the final days come
Elam’s captivity I will turn around,
is Yahweh’s utterance.”

notes.text: Ammon lay northeast of Moab, with its capital at Rabbah (modern Amman). In the Septuagint the Ammon oracle follows those on Edom (Brenton 30:17–22).
Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5). The Hebrew vowels read malkam, “their king”; the Septuagint has “Melchol” (Brenton).
Or “your ebbing valley”; the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “the plains of the Enakim” (Brenton).
Verse 6 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Edom, south of the Dead Sea, descended from Esau. Verses 9–10 and 14–16 closely parallel Obadiah 1–6.
Or “would they not destroy only what was enough for them?”
Bozrah, a chief city of Edom.
Hebrew sela, perhaps also a play on the city Sela (2 Kings 14:7).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
Or “there is anxiety like the sea.”
Or “How the city of praise has been forsaken!” Some versions lack “not.”
Ben-hadad, “son of Hadad,” a name borne by several Aramean kings of Damascus.
Kedar, an Arabian tribe; Hazor here is probably a region of village settlements (Hebrew ḥatser), not the city in Galilee. The Septuagint reads “Kedar the Queen of the Palace” (Brenton).
Or “who shave their temples.” Compare 9:26; 25:23.
