Elam, east of Babylonia. In the Septuagint this oracle comes first among the oracles against the nations, after 25:13 (Brenton 25:14–20), with the date at its end.

verses.text: The word that Yahweh spoke concerning Babylon, concerning the land of the Chaldeans, by the hand of Jeremiah the prophet:{a}

“In those days and at that time, declares Yahweh,
the people of Israel will come,
they and the people of Judah together,
weeping as they come,
and Yahweh their God they will seek.

They will ask the way to Zion,
with their faces turned toward it, saying,
‘Come, let us join ourselves to Yahweh
in an everlasting covenant that will never be forgotten.’

All who found them devoured them,
and their foes said, ‘We are not guilty,
because they sinned against Yahweh, the pasture of righteousness,
Yahweh, the hope of their fathers.’

“Flee from the midst of Babylon,
go out from the land of the Chaldeans,
and be like male goats before the flock.

Chaldea will be loot;
her looters will all eat their fill, declares Yahweh.

“Exult you may, celebrate you may,
you pillagers of my inheritance;
skip you may like a calf on the threshing ground,
whinny you may like warhorses,

your mother will be deeply ashamed;
the one who gave birth to you will be humiliated.
Look, she will be the least of the nations,
an empty, parched wilderness.

Because of Yahweh’s wrath she will not be inhabited
but will be wholly desolate;
everyone who passes by Babylon will be appalled
and hiss because of all her wounds.

Array yourselves against Babylon all around,
all you who bend the bow;
shoot at her; spare no arrows,
for she has sinned against Yahweh.

“Israel is a scattered sheep,
driven away by lions.
First the king of Assyria devoured him,
and now at last Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon has gnawed his bones.

Therefore so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel:
Look, I am punishing the king of Babylon and his land,
as I punished the king of Assyria.

I will return Israel to his own grazing land,
and he will feed on Carmel and Bashan,
and his hunger will be satisfied
on the hills of Ephraim and in Gilead.

In those days and at that time, declares Yahweh,
iniquity will be sought in Israel, and there will be none,
and sins in Judah, and none will be found;
for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.

The sound of battle is in the land,
and great destruction!

Ah, the sledge that pounded all the world—
hacked off, splintered!
Ah, Babylon—a thing of horror
in the eyes of the peoples!

A trap I laid for you, Babylon, and you were snared
before you were aware;
discovered you were, and gripped,
since against Yahweh you picked a fight.

Yahweh has opened his storehouse
and taken out the weapons of his fury,
for the Lord Yahweh of Armies has a task
in the land of the Chaldeans.

Kill all her bulls;
let them go down to the slaughter.
Woe to them, for their day has come,
the time of their punishment.

“Hark! Fugitives and escapees from the land of Babylon,
to declare in Zion
the vengeance of Yahweh our God,
vengeance for his temple.{h}

So her young men will fall in her public squares,
and all her warriors will be silenced on that day, declares Yahweh.

The arrogant one will trip and fall,
and no one will lift him up;
I will set his towns on fire,
and it will burn up everything around him.

But their Redeemer is strong;
his name is Yahweh of Armies.
He will certainly take up their case,
bringing rest to the earth
but turmoil to the people of Babylon.

Sword upon the Chaldeans, declares Yahweh,
upon those who live in Babylon,
upon her princes and upon her sages!

Sword upon the babblers,{j} so that they turn foolish!
Sword upon her heroes, so that they shatter with fear!

A sword against her horses and her chariots,
and against all the mixed peoples in her midst,
that they may become like women!
A sword against her treasures, that they may be plundered!

Parching{k} upon her waters, so that they dry up!
For hers is a country of carved figures,
and over monstrous idols they rave.

As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbors, declares Yahweh,
no one will dwell there,
no human being will sojourn in her.

The king of Babylon heard the report of them,
and his hands fell limp;
anguish seized him,
pain like a woman in labor.

“See, as a lion climbs from the jungle of the Jordan
toward an ever-green grazing ground,{n}
in a moment I will chase them off it,
and whoever I pick I will set in charge of it.
Who compares with me? Who will call me to court?
Which shepherd can hold his ground before my face?

Therefore hear the plan that Yahweh has made against Babylon
and the purposes he has formed against the land of the Chaldeans:
surely the little ones of the flock will be dragged away;
surely their pasture will be appalled at them.

At the sound of the capture of Babylon the earth shakes,
and a cry is heard among the nations.”

notes.text: The Septuagint begins simply “The word of the Lord which he spoke against Babylon” (Brenton, modernized). Chapters 50–51 form the longest oracle in the book; in the Septuagint they are chapters 27–28 (Brenton).

Bel (“lord”) and Merodach (Babylonian Marduk) are titles of the chief god of Babylon. The Septuagint reads “Belus is confounded; the fearless, the luxurious Maerodach is delivered up” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous term, perhaps “dung pellets.”
So many manuscripts and ancient versions; other Hebrew manuscripts read “a bereaving.”
That is, surrendered.
Or “the sword of the dove.” The Septuagint reads “the Grecian sword” (Brenton), taking hayyonah as Yawan, “Greece.”

Merathaim (“double rebellion”) and Pekod (“punishment”) are wordplays on Babylonian place-names, Mat Marratim (the marsh region of southern Babylonia) and the Puqudu people. The Septuagint lacks both names, reading “Go up against it roughly” (Brenton).
The Septuagint lacks “vengeance for his temple” (compare Brenton 27:28).
Hebrew zadon, personified.
Hebrew baddim, “empty talkers,” that is, oracle priests.
Hebrew ḥorev, a sound play on ḥerev, “sword,” in verses 35–37. Some read “sword” here too.
Compare Isaiah 13:20–22; 34:13–15.
Verses 41–43 adapt 6:22–24, once spoken against Zion, now against Babylon.
Verses 44–46 adapt 49:19–21, once spoken against Edom.

verses.text:
This is what Yahweh says:
“Look, I am rousing a destroying spirit
against Babylon
and the people of Leb-kamai.{a}

And I will send to Babylon winnowers,
and they will winnow her
and empty her land,
for they will be against her on every side
in the day of disaster.

They will fall slain in the land of the Chaldeans,
pierced through in her streets.

For Israel and Judah have not been widowed
by their God, by Yahweh of Armies,
though their land is full of guilt
against the Holy One of Israel.

We tried to heal Babylon,
but she could not be healed.
Leave her, and let each of us go
back to his own country,
for her sentence reaches the sky
and rises as high as the clouds.

O you who dwell by many waters,
rich in treasures,
your end has come,
the measure of your unjust gain.{e}

Yahweh of Armies has sworn by himself:
‘Surely I will fill you with men, as with locusts,
and they will raise the shout of victory over you.’

At the sound of his thunder the waters overhead clamor,
and vapors climb at his bidding from earth’s far rim.
Lightning flashes he fashions to go with the rain,
and from his treasure chambers he releases the gale.

Hollow puffs they are, a laughable craft;
when their reckoning comes they will vanish.

Unlike these is Jacob’s Share,
since it is he who shaped everything,
and Israel is the clan he claims as his own;{g}
Yahweh of Armies—that is his name.

with you I shatter the horse and its rider;
with you I shatter the chariot and its driver;

Yet Babylon and every resident of Chaldea I will pay back
for every wicked act of theirs committed in Zion—
with your own eyes watching, declares Yahweh.

“See, I stand against you, mountain of ruin, declares Yahweh,
you that ruin all the world;
my hand I will reach out at you,
tumble you off the cliffs,
and turn you into a mountain of cinders.

No stone will be taken from you for a corner,
nor any stone for a foundation,
but you will be a perpetual desolation, declares Yahweh.

Consecrate nations against her,
the kings of the Medes,
their governors and all their commanders,
and every land under their dominion.

The land quakes and writhes,
for Yahweh’s purposes against Babylon stand,
to make the land of Babylon a desolation
with no inhabitant.

Runner runs to meet runner,
and messenger to meet messenger,
to tell the king of Babylon
that his city is captured from end to end;

the fords have been seized,
the reed marshes{j} burned with fire,
and the soldiers are terrified.

For so says Yahweh of Armies, God of Israel:
The daughter of Babylon is like a threshing floor
at the time it is trodden;
yet a little while
and the time of her harvest will come.

‘May the violence done to me and my body fall on Babylon,’
let the people of Zion say.
‘May my blood fall on those who live in Chaldea,’
let Jerusalem say.

Therefore so says Yahweh:
Look, I will plead your cause
and take vengeance for you.
I will dry up her sea
and make her fountain dry,

and Babylon will become a heap of ruins,
a haunt of jackals,
a horror and a hissing,
without inhabitant.{l}

Together they roar like lions;
they growl like lions’ cubs.

While they are heated I will set out their feast
and make them drunk, that they may revel,
then sleep a perpetual sleep
and not wake, declares Yahweh.

I will bring them down like lambs to the slaughter,
like rams and male goats.

“How Sheshach{m} is captured,
the praise of the whole earth seized!
How Babylon has become a horror
among the nations!

The sea has come up over Babylon;
she is covered by its roaring waves.

Her cities are turned to ruin,
a parched country, a steppe,
a country where nobody lives,
which no human being crosses.

Bel I will punish in Babylon,
and make him spit up what he gulped.
No longer will peoples flow to him like a river;
yes, Babylon’s wall is down.

Let your courage not sink,
nor be frightened by rumors heard around the land,
when one rumor arrives this year,
and next year yet another rumor,
with brutality throughout the land,
one ruler set against another.

For this reason, see, the days approach
when Babylon’s carved gods I will call to account;
her entire country will be disgraced,
and all her fallen will lie inside her.

Then sky and earth with everything in them
will sing aloud over Babylon,
since from the north her ravagers will arrive,
declares Yahweh.

For Israel’s slain Babylon herself must topple,
as by Babylon’s doing the slain of all the earth toppled.

“You who have escaped the sword,
go, do not stand still!
Remember Yahweh from far away,
and let Jerusalem come into your mind:

‘We are put to shame, for we have heard reproach;
disgrace has covered our faces,
for foreigners have entered
the holy places of the house of Yahweh.’

Therefore look, days are coming, declares Yahweh,
when I will punish her images,
and through all her land the wounded will groan.

Though Babylon should mount up to heaven,
and though she should fortify her lofty stronghold,
from me destroyers would come upon her,
declares Yahweh.

“Hark! A cry from Babylon!
Great destruction from the land of the Chaldeans!

I will make her officials and wise men drunk,
her governors, deputies and warriors;
they will sleep a never-ending sleep and not get up,
declares the King, whose name is Yahweh of Armies.

“Yahweh of Armies declares this:
Babylon’s wide rampart
will be razed flat,
and her towering gates
set ablaze.
So peoples toil in vain,
and nations wear themselves out just to feed the flames.”{o}

This is the message the prophet Jeremiah gave to Seraiah{p} son of Neriah, the son of Mahseiah, when Seraiah went to Babylon with Zedekiah king of Judah in the fourth year of Zedekiah’s reign. Seraiah was the officer in charge of arranging camp.{q}
Jeremiah wrote in one scroll all the disaster that would come upon Babylon, all these words that are written concerning Babylon.
Jeremiah told Seraiah, “When you get to Babylon, make sure you read all these words aloud,
and say, ‘O Yahweh, you have spoken concerning this place, to cut it off, so that nothing will dwell in it, neither man nor beast, and it will be a perpetual desolation.’
Once you have read the scroll to the end, fasten a stone to it and fling it into the Euphrates’ midstream,

then say, ‘In this way Babylon will go under, never to surface again, because of the ruin I am bringing on her; and they will be worn out.’”{r}
To this point the words of Jeremiah extend.

notes.text: Leb-kamai, literally “the heart of those who rise against me,” is an atbash cipher for Kasdim, “Chaldeans” (each letter replaced by its mirror in the alphabet, as with Sheshach; see 25:26). The Septuagint reads simply “against the Chaldeans dwelling therein” (Brenton, modernized). Item for scholarly review.
So the Hebrew consonants, which repeat “bend”; the Hebrew vowels and some ancient versions read instead “Let not the archer bend his bow, nor rise up in his armor.” The text is difficult.
Or “Take up the shields.”
The Medes, from northwestern Iran, joined in the overthrow of Assyria and later formed part of the Persian empire that took Babylon in 539 B.C.
Hebrew “the cubit (ammah) of your cutting off,” an idiom for the measure of a life or gain; the sense is uncertain.
Verses 15–19 repeat 10:12–16.
So many Hebrew manuscripts and 10:16; the Hebrew here lacks “Israel is.”
Hebrew mappets, “shatterer.” The speaker addresses Babylon (or possibly Cyrus); the verb “shatter” (napats) is repeated nine times.
Ararat (Urartu, near Lake Van), Minni (the Mannaeans), and Ashkenaz (the Scythians) were peoples to the north. The Septuagint reads “by me, and that for the people of Achanaz” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew agammim, “pools” or “reed thickets.”
So the Qere; the Kethib reads “us” throughout this verse. Zion speaks here.
Verse 37 is shortened in the Septuagint: “And Babylon shall be a desolation, and shall not be inhabited” (Brenton).

Sheshach is an atbash cipher for Babel (Babylon); see 25:26. The Septuagint lacks the name here, reading “How has the boast of all the earth been taken” (Brenton, modernized). Item for scholarly review.
Verses 45–48 are absent from the Septuagint, and verse 49 there begins “and in Babylon the slain men of all the earth shall fall” (Brenton).
Compare Habakkuk 2:13. The Septuagint reverses the sense: “and the peoples shall not labor in vain, nor the nations fail in their rule” (Brenton, modernized).

Seraiah, “Yahweh is prince,” was the brother of Baruch (compare 32:12). The Septuagint reads “when he went from Zedekiah” (Brenton, modernized), suggesting an embassy sent by the king rather than the king himself making the journey.

Hebrew sar menuḥah, “officer of the resting place,” that is, in charge of the king’s lodgings on the march. The Septuagint reads “over the bounties” (Brenton), taking it as minḥah, “gift” or “tribute.”

The Septuagint lacks “and they will be worn out” and the closing line about the words of Jeremiah (Brenton 28:64). The words “they will be worn out” repeat the end of verse 58 and may have marked the end of the oracle before chapter 52, a historical appendix, was added.

verses.text: Zedekiah was twenty-one years old when he became king, and he reigned eleven years in Jerusalem.{a} His mother’s name was Hamutal daughter of Jeremiah of Libnah.
He did what was evil in the eyes of Yahweh, just as Jehoiakim had done.{b}
Yahweh’s anger was the reason this happened to Jerusalem and Judah, until he threw them out of his sight. Zedekiah then rebelled against the king of Babylon.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, on the tenth day of the tenth month (December–January),{c} Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon marched against Jerusalem with his whole army; they set up camp around it and built siege works on every side.
The siege of the city lasted right up to King Zedekiah’s eleventh year.
In the fourth month (in June–July),{d} on the ninth day of the month, the famine became severe in the city, and there was no food for the people of the land.

Then the city was breached, and all the soldiers fled; they went out of the city by night by way of the gate between the two walls, by the king’s garden, while the Chaldeans were all around the city; and they went toward the Arabah.{e}
But the army of the Chaldeans pursued the king and overtook Zedekiah in the plains of Jericho, and all his army scattered from him.
They seized the king and brought him up to the king of Babylon at Riblah in the land of Hamath, and he pronounced sentence upon him.
The king of Babylon slaughtered the sons of Zedekiah before his eyes; he also slaughtered all the officials of Judah at Riblah.
Then he blinded the eyes of Zedekiah, bound him in bronze shackles, and the king of Babylon brought him to Babylon and put him in the house of custody{f} until the day of his death.

On the tenth day of the fifth month (July–August),{g} in the nineteenth year of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard, an officer serving the king of Babylon, entered Jerusalem.
He set fire to Yahweh’s house, the royal palace and all the houses of Jerusalem; he burned down every large building.
And all the army of the Chaldeans who were with the captain of the guard broke down all the walls around Jerusalem.

Some of the poorest of the people, and the rest of the people who were left in the city, and the deserters who had gone over to the king of Babylon, and the rest of the craftsmen, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile.{h}
But Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard left some of the poorest of the land to be vinedressers and plowmen.
The Chaldeans smashed the bronze pillars of Yahweh’s house, along with the stands and the bronze basin called the Sea in Yahweh’s house, and carried all the bronze to Babylon.
They also took away the pots, the shovels, the snuffers, the basins, the ladles, and all the bronze vessels used in the temple service.
The captain of the guard also took the bowls, fire pans, basins, pots, lampstands, ladles and drink-offering bowls—everything made of gold or silver.
The bronze of the two pillars, the Sea, the twelve bronze bulls under it,{i} and the stands that King Solomon had made for Yahweh’s house was too heavy to weigh.
As for the pillars, the height of each pillar was twenty-seven feet,{j} and a cord of eighteen feet would go around it; its thickness was about three inches; it was hollow.
A bronze capital stood on top, seven and a half feet high,{k} with a network and pomegranates around the capital, all bronze; the second pillar was the same, with its pomegranates.
There were ninety-six pomegranates on the sides;{l} all the pomegranates on the latticework all around numbered one hundred.
The captain of the guard took Seraiah the chief priest, Zephaniah the second priest, and the three keepers of the threshold;

From the city, too, he removed a eunuch who had charge over the fighting men, seven of those admitted to the king’s presence{m} who turned up in the city, the army commander’s scribe who enlisted the populace for war, and sixty of the common people discovered inside the city.
Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard took them and brought them to the king of Babylon at Riblah.
And the king of Babylon struck them down and put them to death at Riblah in the land of Hamath. So Judah went into exile from its land.
This is the number of the people whom Nebuchadrezzar carried into exile:{n} in the seventh year, 3,023 Judeans;
in the eighteenth year of Nebuchadrezzar, 832 persons from Jerusalem;
in the twenty-third year of Nebuchadrezzar, Nebuzaradan the captain of the guard carried into exile 745 Judeans; all the persons were 4,600.

In the thirty-seventh year of the exile of Jehoiachin king of Judah, in the twelfth month (in February–March),{o} on the twenty-fifth day of the month, Evil-merodach{p} king of Babylon, in the year he became king, lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of prison.
He spoke kindly to him and set his seat above the seats of the kings who were with him in Babylon.
So Jehoiachin put off his prison garments, and he ate bread regularly in the king’s presence all the days of his life.
His upkeep, a steady ration, was supplied him by Babylon’s king, each day’s share on its day, till he died—every day he lived.{q}

notes.text: About 597–586 B.C. Chapter 52 closely parallels 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, with differences noted below; it serves as a historical appendix showing the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s words.
Verses 2–3 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
Hebrew Tevet; January 588 B.C. The Septuagint reads “in the ninth month” (Brenton).
Hebrew Tammuz; July 586 B.C. (some date it to 587). The Septuagint lacks “in the fourth month” (Brenton). See the note at 39:2.
Arabah, the rift valley of the Jordan.
Or “the house of punishment”; the Septuagint reads “the grinding-house” (Brenton). 2 Kings 25:7 lacks the last clause.
Hebrew Av; August 586 B.C. 2 Kings 25:8 has “the seventh day.” The Septuagint lacks the clause about the nineteenth year (Brenton).
Verse 15 is absent from the Septuagint (Brenton).
2 Kings 25:16 lacks “the twelve bronze bulls”; the Septuagint here has “the twelve brazen oxen under the sea” (Brenton).
Hebrew “eighteen cubits” (about 8.1 m); the cord was “twelve cubits” (about 5.4 m); the thickness “four fingers” (about 7.5 cm). The Septuagint reads “thirty-five cubits” for the height (Brenton).
Hebrew “five cubits,” about 2.25 m. 2 Kings 25:17 has “three cubits.”
Or “facing the winds” (toward the four directions); the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew “seven men who saw the king’s face”; 2 Kings 25:19 has five.

Verses 28–30 are absent from the Septuagint (Brenton) and from 2 Kings 25. The figures (597, 586, and 582 B.C.) appear to follow a different reckoning, counting Nebuchadrezzar’s years from his accession, which explains why the “eighteenth year” here corresponds to the “nineteenth year” of verse 12.
Hebrew Adar; March 561 B.C. 2 Kings 25:27 has “the twenty-seventh day”; the Septuagint here reads “the four and twentieth day” (Brenton).
Evil-merodach, Babylonian Amel-Marduk, “man of Marduk,” son of Nebuchadrezzar (562–560 B.C.). The Septuagint spells it “Ulaemadachar” and adds that he “shaved him” (Brenton).

The book closes with Jehoiachin alive and honored in exile, a quiet sign of hope for the line of David. The Septuagint ends with “until the day when he died” (Brenton), lacking “all the days of his life”; compare 2 Kings 25:30.

books.name: Lamentations
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text), checked against the Septuagint through Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Lamentations is untitled in Hebrew beyond its first word, ʾekah, “How!”; the Septuagint calls it Threnoi, “Laments,” and opens with a sentence not found in the Hebrew, setting the book after Israel’s captivity and naming Jeremiah as the mourner (Brenton). Hebrew tradition likewise links it with Jeremiah (compare 2 Chronicles 35:25), though the book itself names no author. The five poems lament the fall of Jerusalem in 586 B.C. Chapters 1–4 are alphabetic acrostics: each stanza begins with the next of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet, and the footnotes name each letter. Chapters 1, 2, and 4 have one verse for each letter; chapter 3 is a triple acrostic, in which all three lines of each stanza begin with the same letter (66 verses). In chapter 1 the letter ayin comes before peh, as in the standard order, but in chapters 2, 3, and 4 peh precedes ayin; some ancient alphabet inscriptions are reported to show the same peh–ayin order, and a Qumran manuscript of Lamentations (4QLam) is reported to have it in chapter 1 as well. Chapter 5 is not an acrostic, but it keeps the alphabet’s twenty-two lines, a prayer rather than a dirge. Much of chapters 1–4 is in the so-called qinah or lament meter, a long line followed by a shorter, “limping” one. English versification is used; Adonai alone is rendered “the Lord,” and the divine name YHWH “Yahweh.” This is a CJT draft; items marked for scholarly review are listed in the project review file.

verses.text:
From{h} the daughter of Zion has departed
all her splendor.
Her princes have become like stags
that find no pasture;
they went without strength
before the pursuer.

Jerusalem calls to mind,{i} in her days of misery and homelessness,
all her treasured things
that she owned in ages past.
As her people dropped into the enemy’s grip,
with no one coming to her aid,
her adversaries stared at her;
they laughed at her collapse.{j}

All{p} her people groan
as they search for bread;
they give their treasures for food
to bring back life.
“See, O Yahweh, and look,
how worthless I have become!”

I called{ab} to my lovers,
but they deceived me;
my priests and my elders
perished in the city
while they sought food for themselves
to bring back their life.

verses.text:
Their mothers{q} they keep asking,
“Where is bread, where is wine?”
while swooning like men struck down
in the town’s open places,
while their breath ebbs away
in their mothers’ laps.

What witness{r} can I offer you? What likeness find for you,
daughter Jerusalem?
What match can I set beside you, to console you,
maiden daughter Zion?
For wide as the ocean is your shattering;
who could mend you?

Your prophets’{s} visions for you
were emptiness and plaster;{t}
they did not lay bare your guilt
so as to reverse your captivity,
but the oracles they saw for you
were empty and led you astray.

They clap{u} their hands at you,
all who pass along the way;
they hiss and wag their heads
at daughter Jerusalem:
“Is this the city that was called
the perfection of beauty, the joy of all the earth?”

“Look,{ad} Yahweh, and notice
who it is you have treated like this:
should women devour their own fruit,
infants they have nursed?
Should priest and prophet be murdered
in the Lord’s holy place?

verses.text: I{a}—a man who has looked on misery beneath the staff of his fury.{b}
Me he has driven off and made to walk in darkness and not light.
Yes, at me alone he swings his hand, over and over, the whole day long.
He{c} has worn away my flesh and my skin; he has broken my bones.
He has built siege works against me and ringed me with bitterness and hardship.{d}
In dark places he has made me dwell, like those long dead.
He has walled{e} me in, and I cannot get out; he has made my chains heavy.
Even when I cry and call for help, he shuts out my prayer.
He has walled up my ways with hewn stone; my paths he has made crooked.
A bear{f} lying in wait he is to me, a lion in hiding.
My ways he has turned aside; he has torn me to pieces; he has made me desolate.
He bent his bow and set me as a target for the arrow.
He has driven{g} into my kidneys the shafts of his quiver.{h}
I have become a laughingstock to all my people,{i} their taunt song all the day.
He has filled me with bitter herbs; he has sated me with wormwood.
He has made{j} my teeth crunch on grit; in the ashes he has pressed me down.
My soul is cast off from peace; I have forgotten what good is.
So I said, “Gone is my endurance, and my hope from Yahweh.”
Remember{k} my affliction and my wandering, the wormwood and the poison!
My soul remembers it well and is bowed down within me.{l}
Yet this I bring back to my heart; for this reason I wait in hope:
The steadfast love{m} of Yahweh never ceases;{n} his mercies do not come to an end;
they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
“Yahweh is my portion,” says my soul; “therefore I will hope in him.”
Good{o} is Yahweh to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.
Good it is that one should wait in silence for the salvation of Yahweh.
Good it is for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
Let him sit{p} alone and keep silent, when He has laid it on him;
let him put his mouth in the dust—perhaps there may be hope;{q}
let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and be filled with reproach.
For{r} the Lord will not cast off forever;
though he causes sorrow, he shows mercy, so great is his steadfast love;
for not willingly does he humble or sadden human beings.
To crush{s} underfoot all the prisoners of the earth,
to deny a man justice before the face of the Most High,
to subvert a person in his lawsuit—does the Lord not see?{t}
Who{u} can speak a thing into being, if the Lord did not decree it?
Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that both evil and good go forth?
What grievance has a living mortal—any man—over the penalty for his sins?
Let us search{v} and examine our ways and return to Yahweh!
Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to God in heaven:
“It is we who sinned and defied you; and you—you did not pardon.
You have wrapped{w} yourself in anger and pursued us; you have slain without pity;
you have wrapped yourself with a cloud, so that no prayer can pass through;
you have made us offscouring and refuse in the midst of the peoples.
They have opened{x} their mouths against us, all our enemies;{y}
panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction;{z}
streams of water pour from my eye over the ruin of my people’s daughter.
My eye{aa} flows on and does not cease, without respite,
until Yahweh looks down and sees from heaven;
my eye torments my soul because of all the daughters of my city.
Hunted{ab} me like a bird have my enemies without cause;
they silenced my life in the pit and cast stones on me;
waters flowed over my head; I said, “I am cut off.”
I called{ac} on your name, O Yahweh, from the depths of the pit;
you heard my plea: “Do not shut your ear to my cry for help!”{ad}
You drew near on the day I called to you; you said, “Do not be afraid!”
You have pleaded,{ae} O Lord, the causes of my soul; you have redeemed my life.
You have seen, O Yahweh, the wrong done to me; judge my case!
You have seen all their vengeance, all their schemes against me.
You have heard{af} their taunts, O Yahweh, all their schemes against me,
the lips of my assailants and their muttering against me all the day.
See their sitting and their rising: I am their taunt song.
You will repay{ag} them, O Yahweh, according to the work of their hands.
Hardness of heart you will hand them; on them be your curse!{ah}
You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under the heavens of Yahweh.”

verses.text:
How{a} the gold has grown dim,
the finest gold changed!
The holy stones lie scattered
at the head of every street.

Zion’s{b} treasured sons,
worth their weight in pure gold—
ah, now counted as clay jugs,
things a potter’s hands turn out!

The tongue{e} of the nursing infant cleaves
to the roof of its mouth for thirst;
little children beg for bread,
but no one breaks it for them.

Those who ate{f} dainties
are desolate in the streets;
those reared in scarlet
embrace dunghills.

For greater{g} was the iniquity of the daughter of my people
than the sin of Sodom,{h}
which was overthrown in a moment,
with no hands laid upon her.

Better off{l} were those slain by the sword
than those slain by hunger,
who pine away, pierced,
for lack of the fruits of the field.

The hands{m} of compassionate women
have boiled their own children;
they became their food
in the ruin of the daughter of my people.

Never{o} would earth’s kings have credited it,
nor any who live in the world,
that adversary or assailant would march
through Jerusalem’s gates.

It was{p} for the sins of her prophets,
the iniquities of her priests,
who shed in her midst
the blood of the righteous.

They staggered{q} through the streets like the blind,
soaked in so much blood
that no one dared touch
their clothing.

The breath{y} of our nostrils, the anointed of Yahweh,{z}
was caught in their pits,
he of whom we said, “Under his shadow
we shall live among the nations.”

verses.text:
Remember, Yahweh, what has happened to us;{a}
look and see how we are disgraced!

Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers,
our houses to foreigners.

Orphans we are, without a father;
our mothers are as women bereaved.

Our own water we drink for silver;
our wood comes to us for a price.

With a yoke on our necks{b} we are driven hard;
we are weary; no rest is given us.

To Egypt we have held out the hand,
and to Assyria, to get enough bread.

It was our fathers who sinned—they are gone—
yet the load of their guilt is ours to carry.

Slaves rule over us;
there is none to tear us from their hand.

At the peril of our lives we get our bread,
because of the sword in the wilderness.

Our skin is hot as an oven
from the burning heat of famine.

Women in Zion are ravished,
young women in the towns of Judah.

By their hands officials are strung up;
elders’ faces get no regard.

Young men carry the millstone,{c}
and boys stagger under loads of wood.

Gone from the gate are the old men,
gone from their songs the youths.

Our hearts’ gladness is at an end;
our dancing is changed to grief.

The crown has fallen from our head;
woe to us, for we have sinned!

Because of this our hearts are faint;
because of all this our eyes are clouded,

for Mount Zion, which lies desolate;
foxes{d} prowl over it.

Yet you, Yahweh, sit enthroned for all time;
your seat of rule stands age after age.

Why will you forget us forever,
forsake us for so many days?

Turn us back to yourself, O Yahweh, and we shall turn;
renew our days as of old—

—or have you cast us off completely,
raging against us beyond measure?{e}

notes.text: Chapter 5 is not an acrostic, but it has twenty-two verses, matching the letters of the alphabet, and its lines are mostly balanced couplets rather than the lament meter of chapters 1–4. Some Latin manuscripts are reported to title it “A Prayer of Jeremiah the Prophet.”
So a slight emendation; the Hebrew reads “Upon our necks we are pursued.”
The Septuagint reads “The chosen men lifted up the voice in weeping” (Brenton).
Or “jackals.”

The Hebrew of verse 22 (ki ʾim) is difficult; it may also be read “unless you have utterly rejected us.” In synagogue reading, verse 21 is repeated after verse 22 so that the book does not end on a note of rejection. The Septuagint reads “For you have indeed rejected us” (Brenton, modernized).

books.name: Ezekiel
books.sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, with the Greek Septuagint (Brenton’s public-domain edition) compared throughout. The Septuagint of Ezekiel is noticeably shorter than the Hebrew (it lacks, for example, 1:14, 10:14, and 40:30), and footnotes flag significant differences. Papyrus 967, a very early Greek manuscript of Ezekiel, is reported in scholarly literature to lack 36:23c–38 and to place chapter 37 after chapters 38–39; these reports are cited as reported and have not been checked against the papyrus itself. Ezekiel dates many of his oracles; each date is given in the text with its modern month span (from the spring new year), with the original month in a footnote. In the temple vision (chapters 40–48) measurements use Ezekiel’s “long cubit” (a standard cubit plus a handbreadth, about 21 inches or 53 cm) and his measuring reed of six long cubits (about 10.5 feet or 3.2 m); figures in the text are converted to US units, with the original units and metric figures in footnotes. “Son of man” (Hebrew ben adam) is kept as Yahweh’s address to the prophet because of its New Testament echoes; it means “human one, mortal.” Verse numbers follow the standard English versification. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: In the thirtieth year,{a} on the fifth day of the fourth month (in June–July),{b} while I was among the exiles beside the Chebar canal,{c} the heavens opened and I saw visions of God.
It was the fifth day of the month, in the fifth year after King Jehoiachin was taken into exile{d}—
the word of Yahweh came directly to the priest Ezekiel{e} son of Buzi,{f} in Chaldean territory beside the Chebar canal; and the hand of Yahweh was upon him there.

As I watched, a storm wind was sweeping in from the north: an immense cloud with fire flashing back and forth, a radiance surrounding it, and at its center something that gleamed like glowing metal{g} in the heart of the fire.
Within it was the form of four living creatures, and this was how they looked: they had a human shape,
but each one had four faces, and each had four wings.
Their legs were straight, and their feet were shaped like a calf’s hoof; they glittered like burnished bronze.
Human hands were under their wings on all four sides. And the faces and wings of the four of them looked like this:
their wings touched one another. They did not turn as they moved; each went straight ahead.
The form of their faces was this: each of the four had a human face in front, a lion’s face on the right, an ox’s face on the left, and an eagle’s face as well.
Those were their faces. Their wings were stretched upward; two wings of each creature touched the wings of the creature beside it, and two wings covered its body.
Each moved directly forward. Where the spirit{h} was to go, there they went; they never turned in their going.

As for the likeness of the living creatures, their appearance was like burning coals of fire, like torches. Fire moved to and fro among the creatures; the fire was bright, and lightning shot out of it.
And the living creatures darted back and forth like flashes of lightning.{i}
While I gazed at the living creatures, I noticed one wheel on the ground next to each creature, by all four of them.
The wheels and their construction looked like the sparkle of chrysolite;{j} all four had the same form, and they were built as though one wheel were set inside another.
In moving they went toward any one of their four sides and did not swing around while going.
Their rims were tall and fearsome, and the rims of all four were covered with eyes all around.
When the living creatures moved, the wheels moved beside them; when the creatures rose from the ground, the wheels rose too.
Where the spirit was to go, there they went, and the wheels lifted up together with them, because the spirit of the living creature{k} was in the wheels.

Whenever the creatures went, the wheels went; whenever they halted, the wheels halted; and whenever they were lifted off the ground, the wheels were lifted alongside them, because the spirit of the living creature was in the wheels.
Over the heads of the living creatures was the likeness of a vault,{l} gleaming like awe-inspiring crystal, stretched out above their heads.
Beneath the vault their wings were stretched straight out, one toward another; each creature also had two wings covering its body on one side and two on the other.
When they moved, I heard the sound of their wings like the roar of vast waters, like the voice of Shaddai,{m} a tumult like the noise of an army. When they stood still, they let their wings drop.
Then a voice came from above the vault over their heads; whenever they stood still, they lowered their wings.
Above the vault that was over their heads there was the likeness of a throne, like lapis lazuli in appearance,{n} and seated above on that likeness of a throne was a likeness with a human appearance.

From what looked like his waist upward I saw something like gleaming metal, with what seemed to be fire enclosing it all around; and from what looked like his waist downward I saw what seemed to be fire, with brightness surrounding him.

Like the look of the rainbow that shows in the clouds on a rainy day, such was the radiance all around him. That was how the likeness of the glory of Yahweh appeared. As soon as I saw it, I threw myself on my face, and I heard a voice speaking.

notes.text: The reference point of “the thirtieth year” is uncertain. It may be Ezekiel’s age (the age at which priests began service, Num 4:3), or it may be counted from some other event, such as Josiah’s reform.

Hebrew: “in the fourth month, on the fifth of the month.” Months are counted from the spring new year; the fourth month (later called Tammuz) fell in June–July. On the date given in v. 2 this was 593 BC.
Or “river.” The Chebar was a canal of the Euphrates near Nippur in Babylonia.
That is, 593 BC. Jehoiachin was deported to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:10–15); Ezekiel counts his dates from this exile.
Ezekiel means “God strengthens” or “may God strengthen.” The Greek has “Jezekiel.”
Buzi may mean “my contempt”; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew hashmal, a rare word of uncertain meaning; the Greek has “amber” (electrum). Also in v. 27.
Or “wind”; also in v. 20.
Verse 14 is not found in the Greek (Septuagint).
Hebrew tarshish, a precious stone of uncertain identity, perhaps beryl or topaz.
Or “the spirit of life”; “living creature” here is singular, perhaps referring to the creatures as a whole.
Or “platform,” “expanse”; the same word as in Gen 1:6.
Shaddai is a divine name, traditionally “the Almighty”; its original meaning is uncertain. The Greek lacks “like the voice of Shaddai.”
Hebrew sappir, probably lapis lazuli rather than the modern sapphire.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man,{a} get to your feet, and I will speak to you.”
While he was speaking with me, the Spirit came into me and stood me upright, and I listened to the one who addressed me.
He said to me, “Son of man, I am sending you to the people of Israel, to rebellious nations that have rebelled against me. They and their ancestors have revolted against me to this very day.
The descendants are hard-faced and stubborn-hearted. I am sending you to them, and you will say to them, ‘This is what the Lord Yahweh says.’
Whether they hear or hold back—since they are a house of rebels—they will come to know that a prophet has lived among them.

As for you, son of man, do not be afraid of them or of their words. Even though briars and thorns surround you and you sit among scorpions, do not fear their words or be shaken by their looks, for they are a rebellious house.
You are to speak my words to them whether they listen or refuse, for they are rebellious.
“But you, son of man, listen to what I am telling you. Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house. Open your mouth and eat what I am giving you.”
Then I looked, and a hand was stretched out to me, and in it was a written scroll.
He spread it open in front of me; it was inscribed inside and out, and on it were written laments, mourning, and woe.

notes.text: Hebrew ben adam, “son of a human being,” an idiom meaning “human one” or “mortal.” It stresses the prophet’s frailty before God and is used about ninety times in Ezekiel. The traditional rendering is kept because of the related expression in Dan 7:13 and Jesus’ use of “the Son of Man” in the Gospels.

verses.text: He said to me, “Son of man, eat what is in front of you. Eat this scroll, then go and speak to the house of Israel.”
So I opened my mouth, and he fed me the scroll.
He said to me, “Son of man, let your stomach take in this scroll I give you, and fill your insides with it.” So I ate, and in my mouth it tasted sweet as honey.
Then he said to me, “Son of man, go now to the house of Israel and speak my words to them.
It is not to a nation of strange lips and heavy tongue that you are sent, but to the house of Israel—
not to many peoples of unintelligible speech and hard language whose words you could not understand. Surely, if I had sent you to them, they would listen to you.
But the Israelites will not be willing to hear you, since they are not willing to hear me; the whole nation is hard-headed and hard-hearted.
Look, I am making your face firm to match their faces, and your brow firm to match their brows.
I have made your forehead like a diamond,{a} harder than flint. Do not fear them or be dismayed by their looks, for they are a rebellious house.”
He said to me, “Son of man, take to heart all my words that I speak to you, and listen closely.
Go now to the exiles, to your own people. Speak to them and tell them, ‘This is what the Lord Yahweh says,’ whether they listen or refuse.”
Then the Spirit raised me up, and I heard behind me the sound of a great earthquake: “May the glory of Yahweh be praised from where he dwells!”{b}
What I heard was the wings of the living creatures beating against each other and the rumbling of the wheels next to them, a great roaring noise.
The Spirit lifted me and took me away, and I went in bitterness, in the heat of my spirit, with the hand of Yahweh pressing hard on me.
I came to the exiles at Tel-abib,{c} the ones living beside the Chebar canal. I sat where they were sitting, and I remained there among them seven days, overwhelmed.
At the end of seven days the word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, I have set you as a lookout for Israel’s house. Whenever a word comes from my mouth, you are to warn them for me.

If I tell a wicked man, ‘You will surely die,’ and you give him no warning—if you say nothing to warn him away from his wicked course so as to save his life—that wicked man will die in his guilt, but I will require his blood from your hand.
But if you do warn the wicked, and he does not turn back from his wickedness and his evil course, he will die in his guilt, but you will have rescued your own life.

Again, when a righteous person turns from his righteousness and does wrong, and I put a stumbling block before him, he will die. Because you did not warn him, he will die for his sin; the righteous deeds he did will not be remembered, but I will hold you responsible for his blood.
But if you do warn the righteous person to avoid sin and he avoids it, he will certainly live, because he heeded the warning, and you will have rescued yourself.”
There the hand of Yahweh came upon me, and he said to me, “Get up and go out to the valley,{d} and there I will speak with you.”
So I rose and went out into the valley, and the glory of Yahweh was standing there, just like the glory I had seen beside the Chebar canal; and I threw myself on my face.
Then the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet. He spoke with me and said, “Go, shut yourself inside your house.
As for you, son of man, ropes will be put on you, and you will be bound with them so that you cannot go out among them.
I will make your tongue stick to the roof of your mouth so that you will be mute and unable to rebuke them, for they are a rebellious house.

But when I speak with you, I will open your mouth, and you will say to them, ‘This is what the Lord Yahweh says.’ Whoever will listen, let him listen; whoever will refuse, let him refuse; for they are a rebellious house.”

notes.text: Hebrew shamir, a very hard stone, perhaps emery or diamond.
With a slight change of one letter, the Hebrew could read “as the glory of Yahweh rose from its place,” which many scholars prefer.
In Hebrew Tel-abib suggests “mound of ripe grain”; it is probably a Hebrew form of a Babylonian name meaning “mound of the flood,” that is, an ancient ruin mound.
Or “plain.”

verses.text: “Now you, son of man, take a clay brick, set it before you, and engrave on it a city, Jerusalem.
Lay siege to it: build siege works against it, heap up a ramp against it, set up camps against it, and position battering rams against it all around.

Next take an iron baking plate and stand it up as a wall of iron separating you from the city. Set your face against it, so that it is under siege and you are its besieger. This will be a sign to the house of Israel.
“Next, lie down on your left side and place on it the guilt of the house of Israel. As many days as you lie on that side, you will carry their guilt.
I have assigned you a number of days matching the years of their guilt: three hundred ninety days.{a} So you will bear the guilt of the house of Israel.
When you have completed these, lie down a second time, on your right side, and bear the guilt of the house of Judah forty days—a day for each year; I have assigned it to you.
Fix your gaze on besieged Jerusalem, bare your arm, and prophesy against the city.
Look, I am tying you with cords, and you will not roll from one side to the other until you finish the days of your siege.

“Now take wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt; put them together in a single jar and bake your bread from them. All the days you are lying on your side—three hundred ninety days—you will eat it.
The food you eat will be weighed out: about eight ounces{b} a day. You will eat it at set times.
You will also drink water by measure, about two-thirds of a quart{c} a day; drink it at set times.
Eat it as you would a barley cake, baking it in their sight over human dung.”
Yahweh said, “This is how the Israelites will eat their food, defiled, among the nations where I am about to banish them.”
Then I said, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! I have never been made unclean. Since boyhood I have not eaten the flesh of an animal that died naturally or was mauled, and no foul meat has passed my lips.”
He answered me, “All right. I will allow you cow manure in place of human excrement, and you may bake your bread on it.”
Then he said to me, “Son of man, I am going to break the food supply in Jerusalem. They will eat their food by weight, anxiously, and drink their water by measure, in horror,
so that they will lack bread and water, stare at one another in horror, and waste away in their guilt.

notes.text: The Greek has “one hundred ninety days” here and in v. 9, and “one hundred fifty days” in v. 4.
Hebrew: “twenty shekels” (about 230 grams).
Hebrew: “a sixth of a hin” (about 0.6 liter).

verses.text: “Now you, son of man, take a sharp sword and use it like a barber’s razor, running it over your head and beard. Then take balances and divide up the hair you cut off.

A third you are to burn with fire in the middle of the city when the siege days are over. A third you are to take and cut up with the sword around the city. A third you are to scatter to the wind, and I will draw a sword to pursue them.
Take from them a few strands and tuck them into the folds of your garment.
Then take some more of them, cast them into the fire, and let them burn. Out of that fire a blaze will go forth against the whole house of Israel.
“This is what the Lord Yahweh says: This is Jerusalem. I placed her at the center of the nations, with countries all around her.
She has defied my laws with more evil than the other nations have, and my decrees more than the lands around her; she has rejected my laws and has refused to follow my decrees.

“Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: Because you have been more turbulent than the nations around you, have not walked in my statutes or carried out my judgments, and have not even acted by the standards of the nations around you,{a}
therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: I, I myself, am against you. I will carry out judgments in your midst in the sight of the nations.
For all your abominations I will deal with you in a way I have not dealt before and in a way I will never deal again.
So in your midst fathers will eat their sons, and sons will eat their fathers. I will carry out punishments against you, and I will scatter whatever is left of you in every direction.

Therefore, as I live, declares the Lord Yahweh, because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your detestable things and all your abominations, I myself will withdraw;{b} my eye will not spare, and I will have no pity.

A third of your people will die by plague or perish of hunger inside your walls; a third will be cut down by the sword outside them; and the last third I will scatter in all directions, drawing a sword to pursue them.
“Then my anger will be spent, and I will satisfy my fury on them and be appeased. And they will know that I, Yahweh, have spoken in my zeal, when I have spent my fury on them.
I will turn you into a wasteland and an object of scorn among the surrounding nations, before the eyes of everyone who travels past.

You will become a disgrace and a thing of mockery, an object lesson and a horror to the nations about you, when I bring judgments upon you with anger, fury, and furious punishments. I, Yahweh, have spoken.
When I shoot at them the deadly arrows of famine, arrows meant to destroy, which I will send to destroy you, I will increase the famine on you and break your supply of bread.

I will send against you famine and savage beasts that will rob you of your children. Pestilence and blood will pass through your streets, and I will bring a sword down on you. I, Yahweh, have spoken.”

notes.text: Some ancient witnesses lack “not,” reading “but have acted by the standards of the nations” (compare 11:12).
Or “I will cut you down”; the Hebrew verb is uncertain.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, set your face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy against them.

Say, ‘Mountains of Israel, hear the word of the Lord Yahweh! This is what the Lord Yahweh says to the mountains and the hills, to the ravines and the valleys: Look, I will bring a sword against you, and I will destroy your high places.{a}
Your altars will be laid waste and your incense stands broken; and the slain among you I will throw down before your idols.{b}
I will lay the corpses of the people of Israel before their idols and scatter your bones around your altars.

In all the places where you live, your cities will lie in ruins and your high places will be devastated, so that your altars are broken down and left in ruins, your idols are shattered and finished, your incense altars are chopped down, and everything you made is erased.
The slain will fall among you, and you will know that I am Yahweh.
“‘Yet I will leave a remnant: some of you will escape the sword among the nations when you are scattered through the countries.

Then those of you who escape will remember me among the nations where they are held captive—how I was crushed by their unfaithful hearts that turned away from me, and by their eyes that went lusting after their idols. They will loathe themselves for the evils they have done, for all their abominations.
And they will know that I am Yahweh; I did not threaten in vain to bring this disaster on them.’

“This is what the Lord Yahweh says: Strike your hands together, stamp your foot, and cry out, ‘How terrible!’ because of all the vile practices of the house of Israel, for they will die by the sword, by hunger and by disease.
Whoever is far away will die of plague; whoever is near will fall by the sword; and whoever remains and is spared will die of famine. So I will spend my fury on them.

And you will know that I am Yahweh when their slain lie among their idols around their altars, on every high hill, on all the mountaintops, under every green tree and every leafy oak—wherever they offered soothing aromas to all their idols.
I will stretch out my hand against them and make the land a desolate waste, from the wilderness to Diblah,{c} in all their settlements. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”

notes.text: Local hilltop shrines used for worship, often of other gods.
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous word for idols, perhaps “dung-gods”; it occurs some forty times in Ezekiel.
The location of Diblah is unknown. Many scholars read Riblah, a town in Syria, since the Hebrew letters d and r look very similar.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to me:
“You, son of man—this is what the Lord Yahweh says to the land of Israel:{a} An end! The end has come upon the four corners of the land.
The end is here for you now. I will let loose my anger on you, I will judge you by how you have lived, and I will repay you for all your vile practices.
My eye will not spare you, and I will have no pity. I will repay you for your ways, and your abominations will remain in your midst. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.
“This is what the Lord Yahweh says: Disaster! A unique disaster—look, it is coming!
An end has come; the end has come. It has roused itself against you—look, it is coming!
Your doom{b} has come to you, inhabitant of the land. The time has come; the day is near—a day of panic, not of joyful shouting on the mountains.
Soon I will pour my wrath upon you; I will bring my anger to its full against you. I will judge you according to your ways and hold all your abominations against you.
My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity. I will repay you for your ways, and your abominations will remain in your midst. Then you will know that it is I, Yahweh, who strike.
“Look, the day! Look, it is coming! Your doom has gone out; the rod has blossomed, arrogance has budded.
Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness. None of them will be left—none of their crowd, none of their wealth, nothing of distinction among them.{c}
The time has come; the day has arrived. Let the buyer not rejoice or the seller mourn, for wrath is upon all its throng.

The seller will not return to what was sold as long as both of them live, for the vision concerns all its throng; it will not be revoked. Because of their guilt, not one of them will preserve his life.{d}
“The trumpet has sounded and everything is prepared, yet nobody marches out to fight, because my fury is against their whole crowd.
The sword is outside; plague and famine are inside. Whoever is in the field will die by the sword, and whoever is in the city will be devoured by famine and plague.
Even if their survivors escape, they will be on the mountains like doves of the valleys, all of them moaning, each for his guilt.
Every hand will hang limp, and every knee will run with water.{e}
They will put on sackcloth, and horror will cover them. Shame will be on every face and baldness on every head.

They will throw their silver into the streets, and their gold will become a thing unclean. Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them on the day of Yahweh’s fury. They will not fill their appetites or their bellies with it, for it was the stumbling block of their guilt.
Their beautiful ornaments they turned to pride, and from them they made the images of their abominations and their detestable things. That is why I am making it unclean to them.
I will hand it over as loot to foreigners and as spoil to the earth’s most wicked people, and they will defile it.
I will avert my face from them as they profane my treasured place. Robbers will come into it and profane it.
“Forge a chain,{f} for the land is full of bloody crimes and the city is full of violence.
I will bring in the most evil of the nations, and they will seize their houses. I will end the pride of the mighty, and their sanctuaries will be profaned.
Anguish is coming! They will look for peace, and there will be no peace.
Calamity will follow calamity and rumor will follow rumor. They will seek a vision from a prophet, but instruction will perish from the priest and counsel from the elders.

The king will mourn, and the prince will be clothed in desolation; the hands of the common people will shake. I will treat them as their ways deserve and judge them by their own judgments. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”

notes.text: The Greek arranges vv. 3–9 in a different order and in a shorter form.
Hebrew tsephirah, a word of uncertain meaning; also in v. 10. Others render “turn” or “crown.”
The Hebrew of v. 11 is obscure.
The Hebrew of v. 13 is difficult; “will preserve his life” may also be rendered “will strengthen himself.”
That is, they will wet themselves with fear.
The meaning of this phrase is uncertain; the Greek lacks it.

verses.text: In the sixth year, on the fifth day of the sixth month (in August–September),{a} I was sitting in my house, and the elders of Judah were seated in front of me, when the hand of the Lord Yahweh fell on me there.
I looked, and there was a figure that appeared to be fire;{b} from what looked like his waist downward he was fire, and from his waist upward he had a dazzling glow, like gleaming metal.

He reached out something shaped like a hand and grabbed me by the hair of my head. The Spirit raised me up between earth and sky and brought me to Jerusalem in visions from God, to the doorway of the north-facing inner gate, where the idol that arouses jealousy stood.
And there was the glory of the God of Israel, like the vision I had seen in the valley.
Then he said to me, “Son of man, raise your eyes northward.” So I raised my eyes northward, and there it was: north of the gate of the altar, at its entrance, stood this idol of jealousy.

He said to me, “Son of man, do you see what they are doing? Do you see the terrible vile practices the house of Israel carries on here, which drive me away from my sanctuary? You will see even worse vile practices.”
Next he led me to the doorway of the court, and as I looked I saw a hole in the wall.
“Son of man,” he said, “break through the wall.” I broke through the wall, and I found a door.
He said to me, “Go in and see the evil abominations they are committing here.”
I entered and looked: engraved over the whole wall were figures of every sort of crawling creature and detestable animal, together with all the idols of the house of Israel.

In front of them stood seventy of the elders of the house of Israel, and Jaazaniah{c} son of Shaphan{d} stood in their midst. Every man held a censer in his hand, and a fragrant cloud of incense was going up.

He said to me, “Son of man, do you see what the elders of the house of Israel do in darkness, every one of them in his chamber of carved images? They are saying, ‘Yahweh does not see us; Yahweh has abandoned the land.’”
He said to me further, “You will yet see them committing abominations greater still.”
Then he took me to the doorway of the gate of Yahweh’s house on the north side, and women were sitting there weeping for Tammuz.{e}
He said to me, “Have you seen this, son of man? You will see still greater abominations than these.”

Then he brought me into the inner court of the house of Yahweh, and there at the entrance of the temple of Yahweh, between the porch and the altar, were about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple of Yahweh and their faces toward the east. They were bowing down eastward to the sun.

He said to me, “Have you seen this, son of man? Is it not enough for the house of Judah to commit the abominations they are committing here, that they must also fill the land with violence and provoke me again and again? Look, they are putting the branch to their nose!{f}
Therefore I will act in fury. My eye will not spare, and I will have no pity. Though they cry in my ears with a loud voice, I will not listen to them.”

notes.text: Hebrew: “in the sixth month, on the fifth of the month,” counting from the spring new year; this was the month later called Elul, in 592 BC. The Greek has “the fifth month” (July–August).
Hebrew esh, “fire”; the Greek reads ish, “a man,” which many scholars prefer (compare 1:27).
Jaazaniah means “Yahweh listens.”
Shaphan means “rock badger” (hyrax). He was probably the royal secretary under Josiah (2 Kgs 22:3), whose family supported Jeremiah.
Tammuz (Sumerian Dumuzi) was a Mesopotamian god of fertility whose death was mourned each summer; the fourth month of the later Jewish calendar (June–July) is named after him.
The meaning of this expression is uncertain; it apparently describes a pagan ritual gesture or an insult. Jewish tradition reads “to my nose,” one of the “corrections of the scribes.”

verses.text: Then he called out in my hearing with a loud voice, “Bring near those appointed to punish the city, each with his weapon of destruction in his hand.”

Then six men came by way of the upper gate that looks northward, each gripping his weapon of destruction. Among them was a man in linen clothing, with a scribe’s writing kit at his side. They entered and stood next to the bronze altar.

The glory of the God of Israel rose up from the cherub{a} where it had rested and moved to the doorway of the temple. Then Yahweh called to the man who was wearing linen and had a scribe’s inkwell at his waist,
and Yahweh told him, “Pass through the city, all through Jerusalem, and mark{b} the foreheads of the people who sigh and groan over all the abominations done within it.”
While I listened, he said to the others, “Follow him through the city and kill. Show no mercy and spare no one.

Old man, youth, and maiden, little ones and women—slay them all, to utter destruction. But do not come near anyone who bears the mark. Start at my sanctuary.” So they started with the elders standing in front of the temple.
He told them, “Make the temple unclean and fill its courtyards with corpses. Go!” So they went out and killed throughout the city.
While they struck the people down and I was left by myself, I threw myself facedown and cried, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Will you wipe out the whole remnant of Israel in pouring out your fury on Jerusalem?”

He answered me, “The wrongdoing of Israel and Judah is enormous. The land is filled with murder, and the city is filled with injustice, because they say, ‘Yahweh has forsaken the land, and Yahweh cannot see.’
As for me, my eye will not spare, and I will have no pity; I will bring their conduct down on their own heads.”
Then the man in linen clothing, the writing kit at his side, brought his report: “I have done just as you ordered me.”

notes.text: Cherubim were winged heavenly beings, often guardians of holy places (Gen 3:24); here, probably the cherubim of the ark in the Most Holy Place.
Hebrew taw, the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in the script of the time was written like an X or a cross.

verses.text: Then I looked, and above the vault over the heads of the cherubim there appeared something like lapis lazuli, in form like a throne.

He said to the man dressed in linen, “Go in among the whirling wheels{a} beneath the cherubim. Take a double handful of the fiery coals from between the cherubim and throw them across the city.” I watched him go in.
The cherubim were standing on the south side of the house when the man went in, and the cloud filled the inner court.
Then the glory of Yahweh rose up from the cherub and moved to the doorway of the temple. The cloud filled the temple, and the radiance of the glory of Yahweh filled the courtyard.
The noise of the wings of the cherubim carried all the way to the outer court, like the voice of El Shaddai{b} speaking.
When he commanded the man dressed in linen, “Take fire from among the whirling wheels, from among the cherubim,” the man went in and stood beside a wheel.
One of the cherubim reached out his hand from between the cherubim to the fire that was among them, took some, and put it into the hands of the man clothed in linen, who took it and went out.
Something shaped like a human hand could be seen beneath the wings of the cherubim.
I looked, and there were four wheels beside the cherubim, one wheel beside each cherub; the wheels looked like the gleam of a chrysolite stone.
As for their appearance, all four had the same form, as if one wheel were inside another.
As they moved, they could travel in any of their four directions; they did not turn as they moved, but followed the direction the head faced, without turning.
Their whole bodies—backs, hands, and wings—and the wheels too were covered with eyes all around; the four of them had their wheels.
As for the wheels, I heard them called “the whirling wheels.”{c}
Each of them had four faces: the first face was that of a cherub, the second was that of a man, the third was that of a lion, and the fourth was that of an eagle.{d}
Then the cherubim rose up. They were the same living creatures I had seen at the Chebar canal.
As the cherubim went, the wheels went at their side; and as the cherubim lifted their wings to mount up from the earth, the wheels too stayed with them and did not turn away.
When the cherubim stood still, the wheels stood still; when they rose, the wheels rose with them, for the spirit of the living creature was in them.
Then the glory of Yahweh departed from the doorway of the temple and halted over the cherubim.

As I watched, the cherubim lifted their wings and rose up from the earth, and the wheels went out alongside them. They halted at the entry of the east gate of Yahweh’s house, and above them was the glory of the God of Israel.
They were the same living creatures I had seen under the God of Israel at the Chebar canal; and I recognized that they were cherubim.
Every one had four faces and four wings, and something like human hands was under their wings.
Their faces looked just like the faces I had seen beside the Chebar canal. Each of them moved straight forward.

notes.text: Or “whirling wheels” (Hebrew galgal); also in vv. 6 and 13.
El Shaddai is traditionally “God Almighty”; the original meaning of Shaddai is uncertain.
Hebrew galgal, a word suggesting whirling or rolling.
Verse 14 is not found in the Greek. Compare 1:10, where the face of an ox stands in place of “the face of the cherub.”

verses.text: The Spirit then raised me and brought me to the east-facing gate of Yahweh’s house. At the gate’s entrance were twenty-five men, and I saw among them two leaders of the people, Jaazaniah son of Azzur{a} and Pelatiah{b} son of Benaiah.{c}
He said to me, “Son of man, these are the men who plot evil and give bad advice in this city.
They say, ‘Is not the time near to build houses? This city is the pot, and we are the meat.’{d}
Therefore prophesy against them; prophesy, son of man.”
Then the Spirit of Yahweh fell upon me, and he told me, “Say, ‘This is what Yahweh says: That is what you are saying, house of Israel; I know the thoughts that rise in your mind.
You have multiplied your slain in this city and filled its streets with the dead.
Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: The bodies you have laid in its midst are the meat, and this city is the pot; but you I will bring out of it.
You have feared the sword, and the sword is what I will bring upon you, declares the Lord Yahweh.
I will drag you out of the city and deliver you into the hands of outsiders, and I will carry out my sentences against you.
You will fall by the sword; I will judge you at the border of Israel. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.
This city will not serve as your cooking pot, nor will you be the meat inside it; at the frontier of Israel I will judge you.
Then you will know that I am Yahweh, whose statutes you have not walked in and whose judgments you have not carried out; instead, you have acted by the standards of the nations around you.’”{e}
While I was prophesying, Pelatiah son of Benaiah died. Then I fell facedown and cried out with a loud voice, “Ah, Lord Yahweh! Will you put a complete end to the remnant of Israel?”
The word of Yahweh came to me:

“Son of man, your brothers—your own brothers, your relatives,{f} and the whole house of Israel, all of them—are the ones of whom the inhabitants of Jerusalem have said, ‘Keep far from Yahweh; this land was given to us as our possession.’

“Therefore say, ‘This is what the Lord Yahweh says: Although I removed them far away among the nations and dispersed them across the countries, I have been a small sanctuary{g} for them in the countries where they have gone.’
“Therefore say, ‘The Lord Yahweh declares: I will collect you from the nations, bring you together from the countries where you were dispersed, and give you the land of Israel.’
They will come there and clear out of it all its vile things and all its abominations.
I will give them a single heart{h} and place a new spirit inside them. I will remove the stony heart from their bodies and give them a heart of flesh,
so that they may walk in my statutes, keep my judgments, and carry them out. Then they will be my people, and I will be their God.
But those whose hearts follow the desire of their vile things and abominations—I will repay their deeds on their own heads, declares the Lord Yahweh.”
Then the cherubim lifted their wings, with the wheels beside them, and the glory of the God of Israel was above them.
The glory of Yahweh went up from the midst of the city and stopped over the mountain east of the city.{i}
The Spirit lifted me up and brought me in the vision, by the Spirit of God, to the exiles in Chaldea. Then the vision I had seen left me,
and I told the exiles everything Yahweh had shown me.

notes.text: Azzur means “helper”; this Jaazaniah is a different man from the one in 8:11.
Pelatiah means “Yahweh rescues,” which gives point to the question in v. 13.
Benaiah means “Yahweh has built.”
Or “The time is not near to build houses.” The image of the pot suggests the leaders saw themselves as the choice meat, safe inside the city.
Verses 11–12 are not found in the Greek.
Hebrew: “the men of your redemption,” that is, relatives with the right and duty to redeem family property (Lev 25:25). The Greek has “the men of your captivity.”
Or “I have been to them a sanctuary in small measure.”
Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek have “another heart”; others render “an undivided heart.”
That is, the Mount of Olives.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, you live among a rebellious house, people who have eyes for seeing yet see nothing and ears for hearing yet hear nothing, because they are a house of rebels.

“Now you, son of man, get your belongings ready for exile, and in daylight, with them watching, set out for exile. From where you live, move to another place while they look on; perhaps they will see it, even though they are a rebellious house.
Bring out your baggage by day as they watch, like baggage for exile; then in the evening go out yourself as they watch, like those who go into exile.
While they watch, dig through the wall and carry the baggage out through it.
With them watching, hoist it onto your shoulder and take it out at dusk. Hide your face so that you do not look at the land, because I have made you an omen to the house of Israel.”

I did just as I was commanded. By day I brought out my baggage as though for exile, and in the evening I dug through the wall with my hands. I carried it out in the darkness, lifting it onto my shoulder as they watched.
In the morning the word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, did not the Israelites, that rebellious house, ask you, ‘What are you doing?’
Tell them, ‘The Lord Yahweh says this: This message{a} is about the prince in Jerusalem and all the Israelites living there.’
Say, ‘I am a sign to you. What I have done will be done to them; they will go away into exile and captivity.’
The prince among them will hoist his baggage onto his shoulder at dusk and leave; they will break through the wall to get him out. He will hide his face so that his eyes do not see the land.
I will spread my net over him, and he will be caught in my snare. I will bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, yet he will not see it, and there he will die.{b}
All who surround him—his attendants and all his soldiers—I will scatter in every direction, and I will draw a sword and chase after them.
Then they will know that I am Yahweh, when I disperse them among the nations and scatter them through the countries.
But I will spare a few of them from the sword, from famine, and from plague, so that among the nations where they go they may recount all their abominations. Then they will know that I am Yahweh.”
The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, eat your bread with trembling, and drink your water with shuddering and anxiety.

Then tell the people of the land, ‘The Lord Yahweh says this about those living in Jerusalem, in the land of Israel: They will eat their food in fear and drink their water in horror, because their land will be emptied of everything in it, on account of the violence of everyone who lives there.
The inhabited towns will be laid waste, and the land will become a desolation. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.’”
The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, what is this proverb you have in the land of Israel: ‘The days drag on, and every vision comes to nothing’?

So tell them, ‘The Lord Yahweh says this: I will end this saying, and it will never again be heard on the lips of Israel.’ Instead tell them, ‘The days are at hand, and with them the substance of every vision.
No more will there be empty visions or smooth-tongued divination among the people of Israel.

For I am Yahweh. I will speak whatever word I speak, and it will be carried out without further delay. In your days, rebellious house, I will speak the word and carry it out, declares the Lord Yahweh.’”
The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, the house of Israel is saying, ‘The vision he sees is for many days from now; he prophesies about distant times.’
So tell them, ‘The Lord Yahweh says this: Not one of my words will be postponed again. The word I speak will be done, declares the Lord Yahweh.’”

notes.text: Hebrew massa, “burden” or “oracle,” a play on the baggage (also something carried) and on the “prince” (nasi, “one lifted up”).
Zedekiah was blinded before he was taken to Babylon (2 Kgs 25:7).

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to me:
“Son of man, prophesy against the prophets of Israel who are prophesying. Say to those who prophesy out of their own imagination, ‘Hear the word of Yahweh!
This is what the Lord Yahweh says: Woe to the foolish prophets who follow their own spirit and have seen nothing!
Your prophets, Israel, have been like jackals among ruins.
You did not climb up to the gaps or rebuild the wall for the house of Israel so that it could hold in battle on the day of Yahweh.
Their visions are empty and their divining a lie. “Yahweh’s declaration,” they announce, though Yahweh never sent them; and still they wait for him to make their word come true.
Have you not seen a false vision and spoken a lying divination when you say, “Yahweh declares,” though I have not spoken?
“‘Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: Because you have spoken falsehood and seen lies, I am against you, declares the Lord Yahweh.

My hand will come down on the prophets whose visions are empty and whose divinations are lies. In the circle of my people they will have no seat; in the roll of Israel’s house they will not be written; into Israel’s land they will not come. And you will know that I am the Lord Yahweh.
“‘Because—yes, because—they have led my people astray, saying, “Peace,” when there is no peace, and when someone builds a flimsy wall, they coat it with whitewash,
tell those who plaster it with whitewash that it is going to collapse. A flooding rain will come, and you, mighty hailstones, will fall, and a stormy wind will break loose.
When the wall has collapsed, will anyone not ask you, “Where did the plaster go that you smeared on it?”
“‘Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh says: In my fury I will make a storm wind burst out; in my anger there will be torrential rain, and in my fury hailstones to destroy.
I will tear down the wall you coated with whitewash and level it to the ground, so that its foundation is laid bare. When it falls, you will perish within it. Then you will know that I am Yahweh.
So I will exhaust my anger on the wall and on those who plastered it with whitewash. And I will tell you, “The wall no longer exists, and neither do those who plastered it—
those prophets of Israel who prophesied to Jerusalem and beheld for her visions of peace, though peace there was none, declares the Lord Yahweh.”’
“As for you, son of man, set your face against the daughters of your people who prophesy out of their own imagination. Prophesy against them

and say, ‘The Lord Yahweh says this: Woe to you women who stitch magic bands{a} on every wrist and fashion veils for heads of every size, to trap souls! Will you trap the souls of my people and preserve souls for yourselves?
