Those who act wickedly against the covenant he will corrupt with smooth words, but the people who know their God will stand firm and take action.
The wise among the people{u} will give understanding to many, though for some days they will fall by sword and flame, by captivity and plunder.
As they fall, a little help will come to them,{v} and many will attach themselves to them with flattery.
Some of the wise will fall, so that refining, purifying, and cleansing may be done among them until the time of the end, for it is still to come at the appointed time.

“The king will do whatever he pleases. He will lift himself up and make himself greater than any god, and he will say astonishing things against the God of gods. He will do well until the time of wrath ends, because what has been decided will take place.
He will ignore the gods of his ancestors and the one women desire,{w} and he will ignore every other god, because he will make himself greater than all of them.
Instead, he will honor the god of fortresses—a god his fathers did not know he will honor with gold and silver, with precious stones and costly things.{x}

He will attack the most heavily defended strongholds with the aid of a foreign god. He will shower honor on those who recognize him, put them in authority over many, and distribute land in return for payment.

“At the time of the end the king of the south will clash with him, and the king of the north will storm against him with chariots and horsemen and many ships. He will enter countries and overflow and pass through.{y}
He will enter the Beautiful Land, and many{z} will stumble; but these will be rescued from his hand: Edom, Moab, and the chief part of the Ammonites.
He will stretch out his hand against countries, and the land of Egypt will not escape.
He will gain control of the treasures of gold and silver and of all the precious things of Egypt, and the Libyans and Cushites{aa} will follow in his train.
But news from the east and the north will terrify him, and in a great rage he will set out to destroy and to devote many to destruction.
He will pitch his royal tents between the sea and the beautiful holy mountain. Yet his end will come, and no one will help him.

notes.text: The Hebrew is abrupt; “him” is probably Michael (10:21). The Old Greek and Theodotion read “in the first year of Cyrus.” Chapter 11 surveys, in the form of prophecy and without naming names, the history of the Persian kings, Alexander the Great, and the wars between the Ptolemies of Egypt (“the king of the south”) and the Seleucids of Syria (“the king of the north”), culminating in Antiochus IV Epiphanes (verses 21–45). The identifications given in these notes are those commonly proposed.
The fourth king is probably Xerxes I (486–465 BC), who invaded Greece in 480 BC.
Alexander the Great.
Ptolemy I of Egypt and his former general Seleucus I, founder of the Seleucid kingdom.

So the ancient versions; the Hebrew reads “the one who fathered her.” Berenice, daughter of Ptolemy II, married Antiochus II (about 252 BC); she, her son, and her attendants were murdered after his death.
Ptolemy III, Berenice’s brother, who invaded the Seleucid kingdom in 246 BC.
The sons of Seleucus II: Seleucus III and Antiochus III “the Great.”
The battle of Raphia (217 BC), where Ptolemy IV defeated Antiochus III.
Hebrew “at the end of the times, years.”
Probably the capture of Sidon by Antiochus III in about 199 BC.
Hebrew “the daughter of women.” Antiochus III gave his daughter Cleopatra I in marriage to Ptolemy V in 194/193 BC.
Or “to destroy him”; the Hebrew is literally “to destroy her.”
The Roman consul Lucius Scipio defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BC. The Hebrew of the last clause is difficult.
Seleucus IV (187–175 BC), whose minister Heliodorus tried to seize the temple treasury (2 Maccabees 3); “the glory of the kingdom” is probably Jerusalem or its temple.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC), who took the throne in place of the legitimate heir, his nephew Demetrius.
Probably the high priest Onias III, deposed in 175 BC and murdered in 171 BC (compare 9:26).
Antiochus IV’s first invasion of Egypt (170–169 BC) against Ptolemy VI.
In 169 BC Antiochus plundered the temple in Jerusalem (1 Maccabees 1:20–24).
Kittim originally meant Cyprus, then the western lands generally; here the Romans, whose envoy Popillius Laenas forced Antiochus to leave Egypt in 168 BC. The Old Greek reads “Romans.”
Hebrew hashshiqquṣ meshomem. See the note at 9:27, and compare 8:13; 12:11; 1 Maccabees 1:54; Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14.
Hebrew maskilim, “those who have insight” or “who make others wise”; likewise in verse 35 and at 12:3, 10.
Often taken as a reference to the Maccabean revolt, which began in 167 BC.
Probably the god Tammuz-Adonis (compare Ezekiel 8:14).
Probably Olympian Zeus, whose cult Antiochus promoted, or Jupiter Capitolinus of Rome.

Verses 40–45 do not correspond to any known events of Antiochus’s last years; he died in Persia in 164 BC, not between the sea and Jerusalem (verse 45). Many scholars therefore think that the author’s historical survey ends at verse 39 and that what follows is genuine prediction; others apply these verses to a figure of the last days.
Or, with a slight change of vowels, “tens of thousands.”
That is, the people of the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia).

verses.text:
“At that time Michael will arise,
the great prince who stands guard over your people.
There will be a time of distress
such as has not been since there was a nation
until that time.
But at that time your people will be delivered,
everyone who is found written in the book.

The wise will be radiant
like the shining of the firmament,{b}
and those who bring many to righteousness
will be as the stars, forever and ever.
But you, Daniel, keep the words secret and seal the book until the time of the end. Many will run to and fro, and knowledge will increase.”{c}
Then I, Daniel, looked, and two more figures were standing there, one on this side of the river and the other on the opposite side.
One of them asked the man dressed in linen, who was above the water of the river, “How long will it be before these amazing events end?”

I heard the man dressed in linen, who was above the water of the river, raise both his right and left hands to heaven and swear by the one who lives forever that it would be a time, times and half a time;{d} and when the breaking of the holy people’s power is complete, all these things will be finished.
I heard, but I did not understand. So I said, “My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?”
He said, “Go your way, Daniel, for the words are kept secret and sealed until the time of the end.
Many will purify themselves, make themselves white, and be refined, but the wicked will act wickedly. None of the wicked will understand, but the wise will understand.
From the time the daily burnt offering is stopped and the abomination that causes devastation{e} is set up, there will be 1,290 days.
Blessed is the one who waits and reaches 1,335 days.
But you, go your way until the end. You will rest, and you will rise to your allotted place at the end of the days.”{f}

notes.text: This is the clearest statement in the Old Testament of a resurrection of the dead to judgment (compare Isaiah 26:19). Hebrew deraʾon, “contempt, abhorrence,” occurs elsewhere only in Isaiah 66:24.
Hebrew raqiaʿ, the “expanse” or “firmament” of Genesis 1:6–8.
The Old Greek reads “until many go mad and the earth is filled with wrongdoing.”
See the note at 7:25.

See the notes at 9:27 and 11:31. The figures of 1,290 days here and 1,335 days in verse 12 both slightly exceed three and a half years (compare 7:25; 8:14); they may be successive recalculations of the expected end.

Here the Hebrew-Aramaic book of Daniel ends. The Greek versions add the stories of Susanna (placed before chapter 1 in Theodotion) and of Bel and the Dragon (after chapter 12); see the note at 3:23 and the source note.

books.name: Hosea
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition). Hosea’s Hebrew is among the most difficult in the Old Testament, perhaps reflecting a northern dialect as well as damage in transmission, and many lines are uncertain; significant difficulties are footnoted. The Septuagint (Old Greek) has been consulted throughout. Hosea is the first of the Twelve Prophets (the “Minor Prophets”), which were copied together on a single scroll in antiquity. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, the Hebrew manuscripts of the Twelve from Qumran (including 4QXII-a, one of the oldest, and 4QXII-c, d, and g, which preserve parts of Hosea) and the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr), a Jewish revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew, generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers follow the standard English numbering, which differs from the Hebrew in three places: English 1:10–11 is Hebrew 2:1–2, so English 2:1–23 is Hebrew 2:3–25; English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, so English 12:1–14 is Hebrew 12:2–15; and English 13:16 is Hebrew 14:1, so English 14:1–9 is Hebrew 14:2–10.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Hosea{a} son of Beeri in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash,{b} king of Israel.

When Yahweh first spoke through Hosea, he told him, “Go and marry a promiscuous woman, and have children who share her unfaithfulness,{c} because the land is guilty of terrible unfaithfulness in abandoning Yahweh.”
So he went and took Gomer daughter of Diblaim, and she conceived and bore him a son.
Yahweh said to him, “Name him Jezreel,{d} because a little while more and I will avenge the blood of Jezreel upon the house of Jehu, and I will bring the kingdom of the house of Israel to an end.
On that day I will break the bow of Israel in the Valley of Jezreel.”
She conceived again and bore a daughter, and he said to him, “Call her name Lo-ruhamah,{e} for I will no longer show compassion to the house of Israel, that I should in any way forgive them.
But to the house of Judah I will show compassion, and I will save them by Yahweh their God; I will not save them by bow or sword or warfare, by horses or horsemen.”
When she had weaned Lo-ruhamah, she conceived and bore a son.
And he said, “Call his name Lo-ammi,{f} for you are not my people, and I am not your I AM.”{g}

Yet the number of the children of Israel{h} shall be like sand by the sea, which no one can measure or count; and in the very place where they were told, “You are not my people,” they shall be called, “Children of the living God.”{i}
The people of Judah and the people of Israel will be united again; they will name one leader for themselves and go up out of the land, because Jezreel’s day will be a mighty one.

notes.text: The name means “salvation” or “he has saved,” from the same root as Joshua and Isaiah.
Hebrew Yoʾash, a variant spelling of Jehoash. Jeroboam II reigned about 786–746 BC; Hosea’s ministry began in his last years and continued after the fall of his dynasty (compare 1:4).

Hebrew zenunim, “promiscuity, fornication,” used throughout Hosea as a figure for Israel’s worship of other gods (especially Baal) and for its political alliances. Whether Gomer was unfaithful before the marriage or only afterward (looking back from its outcome) is debated.

The name means “God sows.” Jezreel was the town and valley where Jehu wiped out the house of Ahab (2 Kings 9–10). Jehu’s dynasty ended when his great-great-grandson Zechariah, son of Jeroboam II, was assassinated in about 746 BC (2 Kings 15:8–12). In 2:22–23 the name is turned to promise: God will “sow” Israel in the land.
The name means “not pitied” or “shown no compassion.”
The name means “not my people.”
Hebrew loʾ-ʾehyeh lakem, “I am not ‘I AM’ to you,” echoing the divine name revealed in Exodus 3:14 (“I AM WHO I AM”). Most translations render “I am not your God,” following the sense.
Verses 10–11 are 2:1–2 in the Hebrew text.
Quoted in Romans 9:26.

verses.text: Say to your brothers, “Ammi,”{a} and to your sisters, “Ruhamah.”

“Contend with your mother, contend—
for she is no wife of mine,
and I am no husband of hers—
and let her remove her harlotry from her face,
her adulteries from between her breasts,

lest I strip her bare
and set her out as on the day of her birth,
make her like the wilderness,
leave her like a land of drought,
and let her die of thirst.

Upon her children also I will have no compassion,
because they are children of whoredom.

For their mother has been unfaithful;
the one who bore them has behaved shamefully.
She said, ‘I will chase after my lovers,
who supply my food and drink,
my wool and linen, my oil and my wine.’

Therefore I am going to hedge up her{b} way with thorns,
and I will build a wall against her,
so that she cannot find her paths.

She will pursue her lovers but not overtake them;
she will search for them but not find them.
Then she will say, ‘Let me go back to my first husband,
for it was better with me then than it is now.’

She never realized that I was the one who gave her
grain, new wine, and oil,
and piled up silver for her,
and the gold they used for Baal.{c}

So I will repossess my grain at harvest
and my new wine in its season;
I will rip away my wool and linen,
which were meant to hide her nakedness.

Now I will uncover her shame{d} in the sight of her lovers,
and no one will rescue her out of my hand.

I will make all her merriment cease,
her feasts, her new moons, and her Sabbaths,
every one of her appointed times.

I will devastate her vines and fig trees,
about which she said, ‘These are my pay
from my lovers.’
I will turn them into a jungle,
and wild animals will eat them.

I will call her to account for the days of the Baals,
when she offered incense to them,
decked herself with her ring and her necklace,
and went after her lovers,
but forgot me,” declares Yahweh.

“Therefore, look, I am going to allure her
and lead her into the wilderness,
and speak to her heart.

From there I will give back her vineyards to her,
and make the Valley of Achor{e} a doorway of hope.
And there she shall respond as in the days of her youth,
as in the day when she came up out of the land of Egypt.

For I will remove the names of the Baals from her mouth,
and they will be remembered by name no more.

On that day I will make a treaty for them
with the wild animals, the birds of the sky,
and the crawling creatures.
I will shatter bow, sword, and warfare and remove them from the land,
and I will let everyone rest in safety.

I will betroth you to me in faithfulness,
and you will know Yahweh.

the earth will answer the grain, the new wine, and the oil,
and they will answer Jezreel.{g}

notes.text: That is, “my people” and “pitied.” Verses 1–23 are 2:3–25 in the Hebrew text.
Hebrew “your”; the Septuagint and Syriac read “her.”
Or “that they used for Baal.” Baal was the Canaanite storm god, believed to give rain and fertility.
Hebrew naḇluth, a rare word, perhaps “lewdness” or “genitals.”
The name means “trouble,” recalling the sin of Achan (Joshua 7:24–26).
Hebrew ʾishi, “my man, my husband,” and baʿli, “my master, my husband,” a word identical with the name of the god Baal.
Here the name keeps its meaning, “God sows.”
Quoted in Romans 9:25 and echoed in 1 Peter 2:10.

verses.text: Yahweh said to me, “Go once more and love a woman, loved by a lover{a} and committing adultery, even as Yahweh loves the children of Israel, though they look to other gods and love raisin cakes.”{b}
So I bought her for myself for fifteen pieces of silver and about nine bushels of barley.{c}
I said to her, “For many days you will live with me as mine. You will not be a prostitute or belong to any other man, and I will be the same toward you.”{d}
For many days the children of Israel shall remain with no king and no prince, with no sacrifice and no pillar, with no ephod and no household gods.{e}
Afterward the people of Israel will return and seek Yahweh their God and David their king, and they will come trembling to Yahweh and to his goodness in the latter days.

notes.text: Or “loved by a husband” or “loves a companion.” Most take the woman to be Gomer; some think she is another woman.
Probably offerings used in pagan worship (compare Jeremiah 7:18; 44:19).

Hebrew “a homer of barley and a lethech of barley,” a homer and a half-homer (about 330 liters). The silver was probably fifteen shekels (about 6 ounces or 170 grams). The Septuagint has “a homer of barley and a skin of wine.”
The Hebrew is terse; it may mean “so will I also be to you” or “and I too will not come to you.”
Hebrew teraphim. The pillar (matsseḇah) was a standing stone used in worship; the ephod was a priestly garment used to seek oracles.

verses.text:
Hear the word of Yahweh, children of Israel,
for Yahweh has a dispute{a} with those who live in the land:
no truth is there, no steadfast love,
no knowledge of God in the land.

Swearing and deceiving, killing and theft and adultery—they burst all bounds,
and blood touches blood.

That is why the land mourns,
and all its residents are wasting away,
together with the creatures of the wild and the flying birds;
even the ocean’s fish are vanishing.

By day you shall stumble,
and by night the prophet shall stumble beside you,
and I will make your mother perish.

My people perish for want of knowledge.
Since you have spurned knowledge,
I spurn you from serving me as priest;
since you forgot your God’s instruction,
your sons I too will forget.

The more they increased, the more they sinned against me;
I will change their glory into disgrace.{c}

On my people’s sin they feed,
and to their iniquity they lift up their appetite.

And it will be: like people, like priest.
I will punish them for their ways
and repay them for their deeds.

to whoredom.
Wine and new wine take away the understanding.{d}

On the tops of the mountains they sacrifice,
and on the hills they burn offerings,
under oak, poplar, and terebinth,
because their shade is good.
Therefore your daughters play the whore,
and your daughters-in-law commit adultery.

For like a stubborn heifer,
Israel is stubborn;
can Yahweh now pasture them
like a lamb in a broad meadow?

Ephraim is joined to idols;
leave him alone.

When their drinking is over,{g} they give themselves to whoring;
her rulers dearly love shame.

A wind has bundled them{h} in its wings,
and their sacrifices will bring them shame.

notes.text: Hebrew riḇ, a legal dispute or lawsuit.
The Hebrew is difficult; literally “and your people are like those who contend with a priest.”
An ancient scribal tradition (one of the “corrections of the scribes”) says the original read “they exchanged my glory for disgrace.”
Hebrew “the heart,” the seat of thought.
Hebrew qedeshot, “consecrated women,” probably women attached to a shrine; the exact nature of their role is debated.
Beth-aven, “house of wickedness,” is a mocking name for Bethel, “house of God” (compare 5:8; 10:5; Amos 5:5).
Or “Their liquor is gone” or “Their drink has turned sour.” The Hebrew of verse 18 is very uncertain.
Hebrew “her.”

verses.text:
Rebels have gone deep into slaughter,{a}
but I am a rebuke to them all.

Their actions will not let them
turn back to their God;
a spirit of prostitution lives inside them,
and they do not know Yahweh.

Blow the horn in Gibeah,
the trumpet in Ramah!
Raise the cry at Beth-aven:
“Behind you, Benjamin!”{d}

Ephraim will become a wasteland
on the day of punishment;
I announce to Israel’s tribes
what is certain.

Ephraim is crushed and oppressed, broken by judgment,
for he willingly walked after filth.{e}

So I am like a moth to Ephraim,
and like rot to the house of Judah.

When Ephraim noticed his illness,
and Judah his injury,
Ephraim turned to Assyria
and appealed to the great king.{f}
But he cannot cure you
or heal your injury.

For I will be like a lion to Ephraim,
and like a young lion to the house of Judah.
I, even I, will tear and go away;
I will carry off, and none shall rescue.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this line is obscure; some, with a change of letters, read “they have made deep the pit of Shittim.”
Ephraim, the largest tribe of the north, is Hosea’s usual name for the northern kingdom of Israel.
Or “a month shall devour them with their portions.” The meaning is uncertain.
Verses 8–14 probably reflect the Syro-Ephraimite war of about 734–732 BC (2 Kings 16:5–9; Isaiah 7).
Hebrew tsaw, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “a command” or a mocking word for idols. The Septuagint reads “vanities.”
Hebrew melek yareḇ, traditionally “King Jareb.” With a different division of the letters, malki raḇ, it is the Assyrian royal title “the great king.” Likewise at 10:6.

verses.text:
Ephraim, what am I to do with you?
Judah, what am I to do with you?
Your loyalty is like mist at morning,
like dew that vanishes early.

For I delight in steadfast love{c} and not sacrifice,
in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

But they, like Adam,{d} broke the covenant;
there they betrayed me.

Gilead is a town of evildoers,
tracked with blood.

In the house of Israel I have seen a horrible thing;
Ephraim’s harlotry is there; Israel is defiled.

For you also, Judah, a harvest is appointed,
when I restore the fortunes of my people.

notes.text: A poetic way of saying “very soon.” Early Christian writers saw here a foreshadowing of the resurrection of Christ on the third day (compare 1 Corinthians 15:4).
So the Septuagint and Syriac, by a different division of the letters; the Hebrew reads “and your judgments are light that goes out.”
Hebrew ḥeseḏ, loyal, covenant love. The Septuagint has “mercy”; Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7.
Or “like mortals” or (with a change of one letter) “at Adam,” a town in the Jordan valley (Joshua 3:16), which would suit “there.”

verses.text:
Yet it never occurs to them
that I keep in mind all their evil.
Their own deeds now hem them in;
they stand right in front of me.

By their evil they cheer the king,
and by their lies, the officials.

They are all adulterers;
they are like an oven heated by the baker,
who ceases to stir the fire
from the kneading of the dough until it is leavened.

On the day of our king the princes made themselves sick with the heat of wine;
he stretched out his hand with scoffers.

Ephraim mixes himself among the peoples;
Ephraim is a flat cake not turned.

Strangers devour his strength,
and he does not know it;
gray hairs are sprinkled upon him,
and he does not know it.

Woe to them, for they have wandered away from me!
Ruin upon them, for they have revolted against me!
I would ransom them,
yet they tell lies about me.

Though I trained and strengthened their arms,
yet against me they devise evil.

They turn, but not toward heaven;{e}
they are like a warped bow.
Their officials will die by the sword
for their insolent speech.
This will make them a laughingstock in Egypt.

notes.text: So the Syriac and Targum; the Hebrew reads “their baker.”
Hebrew “their judges.” In the last years of the northern kingdom four of its six kings were assassinated (2 Kings 15).
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
So some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint; most manuscripts read “they gather themselves together.” Gashing the body was a rite of Baal worship (1 Kings 18:28).
Hebrew loʾ ʿal, “not up,” obscure; perhaps “not to the Most High” or “to what does not profit.”

verses.text:
Set the horn to your mouth!
Like a vulture{a} one comes upon Yahweh’s house,
since they have broken my covenant
and defied my instruction.

To me they cry,
“My God, we—Israel—know you.”

Israel has spurned what is good;
the enemy shall pursue him.

They have crowned kings, but not by my will;
they have appointed princes, but without my knowledge.
Of their silver and gold they have fashioned idols
to their own cutting off.

For this thing too is out of Israel;
a workman fashioned it,
and it is not God.
Samaria’s calf
will be smashed to pieces.

Though they hire them among the nations,
now I will gather them up.
And they shall soon writhe
under the burden of the king of princes.{c}

Ephraim made many altars to take away sin,
but they became altars for committing sin.

Though I write for him my laws by the ten thousand,
they are regarded as a strange thing.

For Israel has forgotten his Maker
and built palaces,
and Judah has multiplied fortified cities;
but I will send a fire upon his cities,
and it shall devour her strongholds.

notes.text: Or “eagle.” “The house of Yahweh” here may mean the land or people of Israel.
The golden calf set up by Jeroboam I at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28–30). The Hebrew may also be read as a command: “Reject your calf, Samaria.”
Probably the Assyrian king. The Septuagint reads “they shall cease for a little while from anointing a king and princes.”

verses.text:
Do not celebrate, Israel,
do not rejoice as other peoples do;
you have been faithless to your God.
You have loved a prostitute’s fee
on every threshing floor where grain is beaten.

Threshing floor and winepress shall not feed them,
and the new wine shall fail her.

What will you do on the solemn day,
the day of Yahweh’s festival?

The days of reckoning have come,
the days of payment are here;
let Israel know it!
“The prophet is a fool,
the man of the spirit is out of his mind!”—
so great is your iniquity,
so great your hostility.

I found Israel
like grapes in the desert;
like the early fruit on a fig tree
at its first bearing
I looked on your ancestors.
But they went to Baal-peor{c}
and dedicated themselves to the Shameful Thing,
and they became as loathsome as the thing they loved.

Like a bird Ephraim’s glory will fly off—
no childbirth, no womb, no conceiving!

Though they raise sons,
I will rob them of them until not one remains.
Woe to them indeed
when I turn away from them!

Ephraim, as I have seen, was like Tyre,{d} planted in a meadow;
but Ephraim must lead out his children to slaughter.

Give them, Yahweh—
what will you give?
Give them a miscarrying womb
and dry breasts.

notes.text: Hebrew Moph, the ancient capital of Lower Egypt, near modern Cairo, famous for its necropolis.
See Judges 19–21.
See Numbers 25:1–5. “The Shameful Thing” (Hebrew bosheth) is a common substitute for the name Baal.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Gilgal was a major sanctuary (4:15; 12:11; Amos 4:4) and the place where Saul was made king (1 Samuel 11:15).

verses.text:
Their heart is false;{b}
now they must bear their guilt.
He himself will break down their altars
and wreck their pillars.

For soon they will say,
“We have no king,
because we did not fear Yahweh;
and a king—what could he do for us?”

For the calf{c} of Beth-aven
the people of Samaria tremble.
Its people mourn over it,
and its idol-priests{d} writhe over it,
over its glory, because it has departed from them into exile.

The thing itself will be carried to Assyria
as tribute to the great king.{e}
Ephraim will be put to shame,
and Israel will be disgraced for his counsel.

Samaria and her king are swept off{f}
like a chip on the face of the waters.

The high places of Aven,{g} the sin of Israel,
will be wiped out.
Thorn and thistle will climb over their altars,
and they will say to the mountains, “Cover us,”
and to the hills, “Fall on us.”{h}

the din of war shall rise against your people,
and every fortress of yours shall be ruined,
as Shalman{n} ruined Beth-arbel in the day of battle,
when the mother was dashed to pieces upon her children.

So it shall be done to you, Bethel,
because of your utter wickedness.
At daybreak the king of Israel
will be cut off completely.

notes.text: Or “a luxuriant vine”; the Hebrew boqeq can also mean “empty” or “ravaged.”
Or “divided” or “slippery.”
So the Septuagint; the Hebrew has the feminine plural, “calves,” perhaps in mockery.
Hebrew kemarim, a word used only of priests of false gods (2 Kings 23:5; Zephaniah 1:4).
See the note at 5:13.
Or “Samaria’s king is destroyed.”
That is, Beth-aven (Bethel); aven means “wickedness.”
Quoted in Luke 23:30 and echoed in Revelation 6:16.
The Hebrew of this line is obscure.
So a Hebrew reading (Qere); the written text (Kethiv) may mean “their two springs” or “their two eyes.”
Hebrew “I passed over the goodness of her neck.” Threshing was light work, and the ox was free to eat while it worked (Deuteronomy 25:4).
Or “teaches you righteousness”; the Hebrew verb yarah can mean both “to rain” and “to teach.” The Septuagint reads “until the fruits of righteousness come to you.”
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint reads “in your chariots.”
Perhaps Shalmaneser V of Assyria (727–722 BC) or Salamanu, a king of Moab mentioned in Assyrian records. Neither the event nor the location of Beth-arbel is otherwise known.

verses.text:
When Israel was a youth, I loved him,
and from Egypt I summoned my son.{a}

The more they{b} called them,
the farther they went from them;{c}
they kept sacrificing to the Baals
and burning offerings to carved images.

notes.text: Israel as God’s son recalls Exodus 4:22–23. The Septuagint reads “I called his children.” Matthew 2:15 quotes the line, following the Hebrew, of the return of the child Jesus from Egypt, seeing in Jesus the one who sums up and fulfills Israel’s history.
The Septuagint reads “I.”
The Septuagint reads “from me.”
So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate; the Hebrew reads “his.”
Or, with different vowels, “as those who lift an infant to their cheeks.”
Or, joining the word to verse 4, “to him. They will return…”
Or “their boasters” or “their oracle-priests”; Hebrew baddim.
Or “they are called to the yoke”; the Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Two cities destroyed together with Sodom and Gomorrah (Deuteronomy 29:23).
Or “I will not come into the city.”
Verse 12 is 12:1 in the Hebrew text.
Or “roams unruly against God.” The Hebrew verb is uncertain.
Or “holy ones.”

verses.text:
In the womb he grabbed his brother’s heel,{b}
and in his manhood he strove with God.

Yahweh, the God of Armies,{e}
Yahweh is his name!{f}

A trader, with false scales in his hand,
he loves to defraud.{g}

By a prophet Yahweh brought Israel up from Egypt,
and by a prophet he was kept.{k}

notes.text: Verses 1–14 are 12:2–15 in the Hebrew text.
The name Jacob sounds like the Hebrew word for “heel” (Genesis 25:26). For the struggle with God, see Genesis 32:22–32; the name Israel was explained as “he strives with God.”
Or “He found him at Bethel” (Genesis 28:10–22; 35:1–15).
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Syriac read “with him.”
Hebrew YHWH ʾelohe hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “the LORD God of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Hebrew zikro, “his memorial,” the name by which he is to be remembered (Exodus 3:15).
Hebrew kenaʿan, “Canaan,” which also means “merchant.”
Probably the Feast of Booths, when Israel lived in temporary shelters (Leviticus 23:42–43).
There are wordplays in Hebrew between Gilead, Gilgal, and gallim, “heaps.”
See Genesis 28:5; 29:1–30.
That is, Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15; 34:10).

verses.text:
Therefore they will be like the morning mist,
like dew that soon passes away,
like chaff swirled from the threshing floor,
like smoke from a window.{b}

It was I who knew you{d} in the wilderness,
in the land of burning drought.

So to them I am become a lion;
I will watch by the way like a leopard.

It is your destruction, Israel,
that you are against me, against your help.{f}

Where is your king now, to rescue you in every town?
Where are your rulers,{g}
the ones you asked for:
“Give me a king and officials”?

I keep giving you a king in my anger
and taking him away in my fury.

The iniquity of Ephraim is tied up in a bundle;
his sin is stored away.

Labor pains are coming upon him,
yet he is a son without wisdom,
for at the right time he does not come forth
to the place where children are born.

Though he flourishes among his brothers,{j}
an east wind will come,
the wind of Yahweh rising from the desert,
and his spring will dry up,
his fountain run dry;
it will plunder his treasury
of every precious thing.

notes.text: Or “They say to them, ‘Sacrifice!’ Men kiss calves.” The Hebrew is uncertain; kissing an idol was an act of homage (1 Kings 19:18).
That is, from an opening in the roof or wall through which smoke escaped.
The Septuagint here adds a long passage on God as creator of heaven and earth.
The Septuagint and Syriac read “who fed you,” a difference of one letter.
Hebrew “the enclosure of their heart.”
The Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint and Syriac read “I will destroy you, Israel; who will help you?”
Hebrew “your judges.” For the request, see 1 Samuel 8:5–6.
The realm of the dead. The first two lines may also be read as statements: “I will ransom them … I will redeem them.”
Paul quotes these lines, following the Septuagint, in 1 Corinthians 15:55: “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?”
There is a wordplay between yaphriʾ, “flourishes,” and the name Ephraim.
Verse 16 is 14:1 in the Hebrew text. Samaria fell to the Assyrians in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:5–6).

verses.text:
Return, Israel, to Yahweh your God,{a}
for your iniquity has made you stumble.

Bring words with you
as you return to Yahweh.
Say to him:
“Take every iniquity away,
receive us graciously,
and we will offer the fruit of our lips.{b}

Who is wise? Let him grasp these things.
Who is discerning? Let him know them.
For straight are the ways of Yahweh;
the righteous walk in them,
but in them transgressors stumble.

notes.text: Verses 1–9 are 14:2–10 in the Hebrew text.
So the Septuagint and Syriac; the Hebrew reads “we will pay bulls, our lips,” meaning that praise will take the place of sacrifices (compare Hebrews 13:15).
Hebrew “like Lebanon”; likewise in verses 6 and 7.
Or “they will revive like grain.”
Or “Ephraim will say, ‘What more have I to do with idols?’ ”

books.name: Joel
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. The date of Joel is uncertain; the book names no king, and proposals range from the ninth century to the fourth century BC, with many scholars favoring the Persian period. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, parts of Joel survive in the Qumran manuscripts of the Twelve Prophets (4QXII-c and others) and in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll of the Twelve (Mur 88); the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr) is not reported to preserve Joel. These witnesses generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers follow the standard English numbering. The Hebrew text divides the book into four chapters: English 2:28–32 is Hebrew 3:1–5, and English 3:1–21 is Hebrew 4:1–21.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Joel{a} son of Pethuel.

Listen to this, you elders;
hear me, everyone in the land!
Has anything like it occurred in your lifetime,
or in your ancestors’ time?

Recount it to your children,
and let your children recount it to theirs,
and their children to the generation after.

Wake up, you drunkards, and weep;
wail, all you who drink wine,
over the sweet wine,
for it is snatched from your mouth.

For a nation has come up against my land,
mighty and past counting;
its teeth are a lion’s teeth,
and it has the fangs of a lioness.

Mourn like a young bride{c} in sackcloth
weeping for the husband of her youth.

No grain gift or wine offering
reaches the house of Yahweh.
The priests are in mourning,
Yahweh’s servants.

Gird on sackcloth and beat your breasts, you priests;
howl, you servants of the altar.
Come, lie all night in sackcloth,
you who serve my God!
For grain offering and drink offering
are kept back from your God’s house.

Declare a fast;
proclaim a sacred gathering.
Assemble the elders
and every resident of the land
at the house of Yahweh your God,
and call to Yahweh for help.

Is not the food cut off
before our very eyes,
joy and gladness
from the house of our God?

To you, Yahweh, I call,
for fire has consumed
the pastures of the wilderness,
and flame has scorched
all the trees of the field.

Even the wild beasts pant for you,
for the streams of water have dried up,
and fire has consumed
the pastures of the wilderness.

notes.text: The name means “Yahweh is God.”

Four Hebrew words for locusts (gazam, ʾarbeh, yeleq, ḥasil), perhaps different species or stages of growth, perhaps simply poetic synonyms; the renderings here follow their probable root meanings. Compare 2:25.
Hebrew bethulah, often “virgin,” here probably a young bride whose husband has died before or soon after the marriage.
Hebrew tappuaḥ, perhaps the apricot or quince.
There is a wordplay in Hebrew: keshod mishshadday, “like destruction (shod) from Shaddai.” Compare Isaiah 13:6.
The Hebrew of this line contains three words found nowhere else, and its meaning is uncertain.
Or “bear the guilt.” The Septuagint reads “have perished.”

verses.text:
Blow the horn in Zion;
sound the alarm on my holy mountain!
Let all who live in the land tremble,
for the day of Yahweh is coming; it is near—

a day of darkness and deep gloom,
a day of cloud and heavy darkness!
Like the dawn spread upon the mountains
a people comes, vast and strong;
there has never been anything like it from ancient times,
nor will there be again after it
for years, from generation to generation.

Ahead of them fire consumes,
behind them flames burn.
Before them the land is a paradise like Eden,
behind them a barren desert;
nothing gets away.

They look like horses,{a}
and they gallop like steeds of war.

With a noise like chariots
they leap on the mountaintops,
like the crackle of a flame of fire
consuming stubble,
like a mighty people
drawn up for battle.

Before them peoples writhe in anguish;
every face grows pale.{b}

None crowds his neighbor;
each goes in his own path.
Through the weapons{c} they burst
and do not break off.

The earth quakes before them;
the heavens shake.
Sun and moon grow dark,
and the stars withdraw their shining.

“Yet even now,” declares Yahweh,
“turn back to me with your whole heart,
with fasting, with weeping, and with mourning.”

Who knows whether he will turn and relent
and leave a blessing behind him,
a grain offering and a drink offering
for Yahweh your God?

gather the people.
Make the assembly holy;
bring together the elders;
gather the little ones,
even babies who nurse at the breast.
Let the bridegroom come out of his chamber,
and the bride from her canopy.

Between the porch and the altar{e}
let the priests who serve Yahweh weep
and say, “Have pity on your people, Yahweh,
and do not give your inheritance over to reproach,
for the nations to mock.
Why should they say among the peoples,
‘Where is their God?’ ”

Then Yahweh was zealous for his land
and had compassion on his people.

Yahweh answered and said to his people,
“Look, I am sending you
grain, new wine, and oil,
and you will be filled with them;
and I will no more make you
a reproach among the nations.

The northerner I will drive far from you,
banish him into a land dry and desolate,
his front ranks into the eastern sea,
his hindmost into the western sea.{f}
His stink will go up,
his reek will rise,
for he has done great things.

Be glad, children of Zion,
and rejoice in Yahweh your God,
for he has given you the early rain in righteousness;{g}
he has poured down showers for you,
the early and the latter rain, as before.

The threshing floors will be full of grain,
and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.

I will repay you for the years
that the swarmer has eaten,
the hopper, the stripper, and the cutter,{h}
my great army, which I sent among you.

You will eat your fill and be satisfied,
and praise the name of Yahweh your God,
who has dealt wondrously with you.
And my people will never again be put to shame.

You will realize that I am present in Israel,
that I am Yahweh your God, and no other exists.
My people will never again be disgraced.

Even upon servants, men and women,
I will pour out my Spirit in those days.

I will show wonders in the heavens and on the earth:
blood and fire and columns of smoke.

The sun will be turned to darkness
and the moon to blood,
before the day of Yahweh comes,
the great and fearsome day.

Everyone who invokes Yahweh’s name
will be rescued.{j}
On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem
some will escape,
just as Yahweh promised,
and among the survivors
will be those Yahweh summons.”

notes.text: The head of a locust resembles that of a horse; compare Revelation 9:7–9. Whether chapter 2 describes a second locust plague, an invading army pictured as locusts, or the apocalyptic army of the day of Yahweh is debated.
Or “gathers a glow”; the Hebrew is uncertain (compare Nahum 2:10).
Or “through the water channels.”
Compare Exodus 34:6–7; Jonah 4:2.
That is, in the court of the priests, between the entrance porch of the temple and the altar of burnt offering.
The eastern sea is the Dead Sea; the western sea is the Mediterranean.

Or “the teacher of righteousness.” The Hebrew hammoreh can mean either “the early rain” or “the teacher”; the second sense was taken up at Qumran, whose leader was called “the Teacher of Righteousness.” The early rain falls in October–November; the latter rain in March–April.
See the note at 1:4.

Verses 28–32 are 3:1–5 in the Hebrew text. Peter quotes them at Pentecost (Acts 2:17–21), following the Septuagint with some changes (“in the last days,” and “my servants … my maidservants” in verse 29). Compare also Numbers 11:29.
Quoted in Romans 10:13, where Paul applies “the name of the Lord” to Jesus.

verses.text:
“For look, in those days and at that time,
when I restore the fortunes of Judah and Jerusalem,{a}

They gambled for my people,
gave a boy in exchange for a prostitute,
and sold a girl for wine to drink.
“What do you want with me, Tyre and Sidon, and all the districts of Philistia? Are you taking revenge on me? If so, I will quickly and swiftly return your actions upon your own heads.
For you took my silver and my gold and carried my rich treasures into your temples.{c}
The people of Judah and of Jerusalem you have sold off to the Greeks,{d} to remove them far from their own borders.
I am going to stir them up from where you sold them, and bring your actions back upon your own heads.
I will sell your sons and daughters to the people of Judah, who will trade them to the Sabeans,{e} a faraway nation; Yahweh has spoken.”

Come quickly, all you surrounding nations,
assemble in that place.
Yahweh, bring down your warriors!

Let the nations rouse themselves
and come up to the Valley of Jehoshaphat;
for there I will sit to judge
all the nations round about.

Put in the sickle,
for the harvest is ripe.
Come, tread,
for the winepress is full.
The vats overflow,
for their wickedness is great.{h}

Multitudes, multitudes
in the valley of decision!
For the day of Yahweh is near
in the valley of decision.

Sun and moon grow dark,
and the stars withdraw their shining.

Yahweh roars from Zion
and utters his voice from Jerusalem,
and the heavens and the earth shake.
But Yahweh is a refuge for his people,
a stronghold for the children of Israel.

“So you will know that I am Yahweh your God,
dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain.
Jerusalem will be holy,
and strangers will never again pass through it.

“On that day
the mountains will drip new wine,
the hills will run with milk,
and all the dry riverbeds of Judah
will carry water.
A spring will rise from Yahweh’s house
and irrigate the Valley of Shittim.{i}

Egypt will be made a desolation,
Edom a wasted wilderness,
because of the violence against Judah’s people,
whose innocent blood they shed in their land.

But Judah will be inhabited forever,
and Jerusalem from generation to generation.

notes.text: Chapter 3 is chapter 4 in the Hebrew text.

The name means “Yahweh judges” (compare “the valley of decision” in verse 14). Since at least the fourth century AD it has been identified with the Kidron Valley east of Jerusalem, but the name may be symbolic.
Or “palaces.”
Hebrew “the sons of the Yevanim,” the Ionians (compare Daniel 8:21).
The people of Sheba in southwest Arabia, traders on the incense routes.
Hebrew “Sanctify war,” since battle was begun with religious rites.
The reverse of Isaiah 2:4 and Micah 4:3.
Compare Revelation 14:14–20.
The name means “acacias.” Perhaps the dry wadi running from Jerusalem toward the Dead Sea (compare Ezekiel 47:1–12; Zechariah 14:8).
Or “I will declare innocent their blood that I had not declared innocent.” The Septuagint and Syriac read “I will avenge their blood and will not leave it unpunished.”

books.name: Amos
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Amos prophesied in the northern kingdom of Israel in the reign of Jeroboam II (about 786–746 BC), probably around 760 BC. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, as reported in the published editions, portions of Amos are preserved in the Qumran manuscripts of the Twelve Prophets (4QXII-c, 4QXII-g, and others), in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll (Mur 88), and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. The combination ʾAdonay YHWH, frequent in Amos, is rendered “the Lord Yahweh.” Verse numbers in Amos are the same in English and Hebrew.

verses.text: The words of Amos, one of the sheep breeders{a} of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.{b}

He said:
“Yahweh roars from Zion
and from Jerusalem lifts his voice;
the shepherds’ pastures mourn,
and the summit of Carmel withers.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Damascus,
yes, for four,{c} I will not turn it back;
because with sledges of iron
they threshed Gilead.

So I will hurl a fire at Hazael’s dynasty,
and it will devour Ben-hadad’s strongholds.{d}

I will smash Damascus’s gate bolt,
and remove the king{e} who sits in the Valley of Aven
and the scepter-bearer in Beth-eden;
and Aram’s population will be deported to Kir,”
says Yahweh.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Gaza,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they carried off whole communities{f} as captives
to hand them over to Edom.

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Gaza,
and it will consume her fortresses.

I will remove the king of Ashdod,
and the scepter-bearer of Ashkelon;
I will strike Ekron with my hand,
and the Philistines who remain will die,”
says the Lord Yahweh.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Tyre,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they delivered up whole communities to Edom
and did not remember the covenant of brothers.

So I will send a fire upon the wall of Tyre,
and it will consume her fortresses.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Edom,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because he hunted his brother{g} with the sword
and stifled all compassion;
his anger tore without ceasing,
and he kept his fury forever.

So I will send a fire upon Teman,
and it will consume the fortresses of Bozrah.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of the Ammonites,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead
to widen their own border.

So I will set Rabbah’s{h} wall ablaze,
and the fire will devour her strongholds,
amid war cries on the day of combat,
amid a gale on the day of the tempest.

Into exile their king{i} shall go,
he and his princes with him,”
says Yahweh.

notes.text: Hebrew noqedim, used also of Mesha king of Moab (2 Kings 3:4); perhaps an owner or manager of flocks rather than a simple herdsman (compare 7:14). Tekoa was a village about 10 miles (16 kilometers) south of Jerusalem.
A major earthquake remembered long afterward (Zechariah 14:5); archaeological evidence at several sites, including Hazor, suggests a date of about 760 BC.
A numerical saying meaning “for sin upon sin,” building to a climax (compare Proverbs 30:15–31). “It” is probably the punishment.
Hazael and his son Ben-hadad were kings of Aram (Syria) in the ninth century BC (2 Kings 8:7–15; 13:3, 24).

Or “the inhabitants.” Aven (“wickedness”) and Beth-eden (“house of delight”) may be mocking names. Kir was the original homeland of the Arameans (9:7); they were exiled there by Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kings 16:9).
Hebrew “a complete exile,” sparing no one; likewise in verse 9.
Edom descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob (Genesis 25:19–34; 36:1).
The capital of Ammon, the site of modern Amman in Jordan.
Or “Milcom,” the god of the Ammonites (so some Greek manuscripts; compare Jeremiah 49:3).

verses.text:
So I will send a fire upon Moab,
and it will consume the fortresses of Kerioth;{b}
Moab will die amid tumult,
with shouting and the blast of the horn.

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Judah,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they have rejected the law of Yahweh
and have not kept his statutes,
and their lies{d} have led them astray,
the lies after which their fathers walked.

So I will send a fire upon Judah,
and it will consume the fortresses of Jerusalem.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“For three transgressions of Israel,
yes, for four, I will not turn it back;
because they sell the righteous for silver,
and the needy for a pair of sandals—

they stretch out beside every altar
on garments taken in pledge,{f}
and in the house of their God they drink
the wine of those who have been fined.

“Yet I was the one who wiped out the Amorites ahead of them,
though they stood as tall as cedars
and were as sturdy as oak trees;
I wiped out their fruit on top
and their roots below.

And it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt
and led you forty years in the wilderness,
to take possession of the land of the Amorite.

I raised up prophets from among your sons,
and Nazirites from among your young men.{g}
Is that not so, people of Israel?”
declares Yahweh.

“But you gave the Nazirites wine to drink,
and you ordered the prophets,
‘You shall not prophesy.’

The stoutest-hearted among the mighty
shall run away naked in that day,”
declares Yahweh.

notes.text: A desecration of the dead, denying the king rest in his grave.
A city of Moab, mentioned also on the Mesha Stone (about 840 BC).
That is, the king or chief ruler.
That is, their false gods.
Or “who pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor,” that is, who covet even the dust the poor put on their heads in mourning.
The law required that a cloak taken in pledge be returned by nightfall (Exodus 22:26–27; Deuteronomy 24:12–13).
People under a vow of separation to God, who abstained from wine (Numbers 6:1–21; Judges 13:4–5).
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “I will make you totter” or “I will split the ground beneath you.”

verses.text: Listen to this message Yahweh has announced against you, Israelites, against the entire clan I led out of Egypt:

Do two walk together
unless they have arranged to meet?

Does a lion roar in the forest
when he has no prey?
Does a young lion cry out from his den
unless he has caught something?

Does a bird fall into a snare on the ground
when there is no bait{b} for it?
Does a trap spring up from the ground
when it has taken nothing?

Is a horn blown in a city
and the people not tremble?
Does disaster come to a city
unless Yahweh has done it?

Announce to the strongholds of Ashdod{d}
and to the strongholds of Egypt,
“Gather on Samaria’s hills
and witness the great panic inside her
and the cruelty within her.”

“They do not know how to do right,” declares Yahweh,
“those who store up violence and robbery in their fortresses.”

Therefore this is what the Lord Yahweh declares:
“An enemy will encircle the country;
he will pull down your defenses,
and your strongholds will be looted.”

This is what Yahweh says:
“As a shepherd snatches out of the lion’s mouth
a pair of legs or a piece of an ear,{e}
so will the children of Israel be snatched away, those who sit in Samaria
on the edge of a couch
and on the cushions{f} of a bed.”

“Hear and testify against the house of Jacob,”
declares the Lord Yahweh, the God of Armies,{g}

“For in the day I call Israel to account for his crimes,
I will also deal with the altars of Bethel;
the altar’s horns{h} will be lopped off
and drop to the ground.

I will strike the winter house along with the summer house,
and the houses of ivory{i} will perish,
and the great houses will come to an end,”
declares Yahweh.

notes.text: That is, chosen and cared for (compare Genesis 18:19).
Or “no trap.”
Hebrew sod, the confidential deliberation of a council (compare Jeremiah 23:18, 22).
The Septuagint reads “Assyria.”
A shepherd brought such remains to prove that an animal had been killed by a wild beast and not stolen (Exodus 22:13).
The meaning of the Hebrew word (demesheq) is uncertain; traditionally “Damascus,” perhaps “damask” or “the leg.”
Hebrew ʾelohe hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “God of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
The projections at the four corners of the altar, which a fugitive might grasp for sanctuary (1 Kings 1:50).
Houses with ivory inlay; many carved ivories of this period have been excavated at Samaria.

verses.text:
Hear this word, you cows of Bashan{a}
who are on the mountain of Samaria,
who oppress the poor, who crush the needy,
who say to your lords,{b} “Bring, and let us drink!”

The Lord Yahweh has sworn by his holiness
that the days are surely coming upon you
when they will take you away with hooks,
the last of you with fishhooks.

And you will go out through the breaches,
each straight ahead,
and you will be cast out toward Harmon,”{c}
declares Yahweh.

burn leavened bread as a thank offering,
and announce your freewill offerings, make them known;
for that is what you love, people of Israel!”
declares the Lord Yahweh.

“I gave you cleanness of teeth{e} in all your cities,
and lack of bread in all your places;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

Two or three towns staggered to another town
to drink water and could not get enough;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

“I overthrew some of you,
as God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah,
and you were like a burning stick snatched from the fire;
but you have not come back to me,”
declares Yahweh.

For look—the one who shapes the mountains and creates the wind,
who tells mankind what he is thinking,{f}
who turns dawn to darkness
and strides upon the high places of the earth—
Yahweh, the God of Armies, is his name!

notes.text: Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee, was famous for its rich pastures and well-fed cattle (Deuteronomy 32:14; Psalm 22:12). The phrase is addressed to the wealthy women of Samaria.
Hebrew ʾadonehem, “their lords,” that is, their husbands (compare Genesis 18:12).
The meaning is uncertain; perhaps a place name, or (with a slight change) “Mount Hermon.”
The law required tithes yearly or every three years (Deuteronomy 14:22–29); Amos mocks their zeal.
That is, nothing to eat.
Or “what his own (God’s) thought is.” Verse 13 is the first of three hymn fragments in Amos (compare 5:8–9; 9:5–6).

verses.text: Hear this word, which I lift up over you as a lament, house of Israel:

“Fallen, no more to rise,
is the young woman Israel;{a}
forsaken on her own soil,
with no one to raise her up.”

For this is what the Lord Yahweh says:
“The city that marched out a thousand strong
will have a hundred left,
and the one that marched out a hundred strong
will have ten left, for the house of Israel.”

For this is what Yahweh says to the house of Israel:
“Seek me and live;

Look for Yahweh, and you will live,
or he will sweep through Joseph’s house like a blaze,
and it will burn with nobody able to put it out at Bethel—

you who turn justice into wormwood{d}
and fling righteousness to the ground!

He who made the Pleiades and Orion,{e}
who turns deep darkness into morning
and darkens day into night,
who calls for the waters of the sea
and pours them out on the face of the earth—
Yahweh is his name—

who flashes destruction upon the strong,
so that destruction comes upon the fortress.

They hate the one who reproves in the gate,{f}
and they loathe the one who speaks with integrity.

Because you stamp on the poor
and extract grain taxes from them,
you have built mansions of carved stone,
yet you will never live in them;
you have set out lovely vineyards,
yet you will never drink the wine.

For I am aware of your many rebellions
and your enormous sins—
you oppress the innocent, accept payoffs,
and push the poor aside in court.

So the wise keep quiet at such a time,
because the times are wicked.

Seek good and not evil,
that you may live;
and so Yahweh, the God of Armies, will be with you,
as you have said.

Hate evil and love good,
and establish justice in the gate;
it may be that Yahweh, the God of Armies,
will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.

So this is what Yahweh, the God of Armies, the Lord, says:
“Wailing will fill every plaza,
and in every street they will cry, ‘Oh no! Oh no!’
Farmers will be summoned to grieve,
and professional mourners{g} to wail;

and in all vineyards there will be wailing,
for I will pass through your midst,”
says Yahweh.

Disaster for you who yearn for Yahweh’s day!
What will Yahweh’s day mean for you?
It will be dark, not bright—

as when a man escapes a lion
only to be met by a bear,
or goes indoors, rests a hand on the wall,
and is bitten by a snake.

Is not the day of Yahweh darkness, not light,
gloom with no brightness in it?

“I hate, I reject your festivals,
and I take no delight in your solemn assemblies.{h}

Though you bring me whole burnt offerings and your gifts of grain,
they will not please me;
the fat beasts of your peace offerings
I will not regard.

Remove from my presence the clamor of your songs;
I will not hear the music of your lyres.

Instead, let justice surge like the waters,
and righteousness like a stream that never fails.{i}

“Was it sacrifices and grain offerings that you brought me
those forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?

therefore I will send you into exile beyond Damascus,”
says Yahweh, whose name is the God of Armies.

notes.text: Hebrew “the virgin Israel,” a poetic personification of the nation. Verse 2 is in the limping rhythm of the Hebrew funeral lament (qinah).
A wordplay in Hebrew: haggilgal galoh yigleh.
Hebrew “will become aven (wickedness, nothingness),” alluding to the name Beth-aven (see the note at Hosea 4:15).
A bitter-tasting plant, used figuratively for what is poisonous (compare 6:12).
Hebrew kimah and kesil, two constellations, probably the Pleiades and Orion (compare Job 9:9; 38:31).
The open area at the city gate where the elders sat to hear legal cases; likewise in verses 12 and 15.
Professional mourners, often women (Jeremiah 9:17–20).
Hebrew “I will not smell,” alluding to the pleasing aroma of sacrifice (Leviticus 26:31).
Hebrew naḥal ʾethan, a wadi that does not dry up in summer.

Sakkuth and Kaiwan are Mesopotamian names for the planet Saturn, worshiped as a god. The Hebrew vowels (Sikkuth, Kiyyun) may be a deliberate distortion modeled on shiqquts, “detestable thing.” The Septuagint reads “the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan,” and is quoted in Acts 7:42–43. The verse may also be read as past: “You carried Sakkuth…”

verses.text:
Disaster for those lounging comfortably in Zion
and those feeling safe on Samaria’s mountain,
the famous leaders of the foremost nation,
the ones Israel’s people turn to!

You who put off the day of disaster
bring near the seat of violence.

They lie on beds of ivory
and sprawl on their couches;
they eat lambs from the flock
and calves from the stall.

They improvise{b} to the sound of the harp;
like David they devise for themselves instruments of song.

They drink wine from bowls
and anoint themselves with the finest oils,
but they do not grieve over the ruin of Joseph.

So now they shall go into exile at the head of the exiles,
and the feasting of the loungers shall be gone.{c}

The Lord Yahweh has sworn by himself, declares Yahweh, the God of Armies:
“I abhor the pride of Jacob
and hate his fortresses;
and I will hand over the city and everything in it.”
If ten men remain in one house, they will die.

And when a relative,{d} the one who burns the dead, picks up the body to carry it out of the house, he will say to whoever is in the innermost parts of the house, “Is anyone else with you?” and he will say, “No.” Then he will say, “Hush! We must not mention the name of Yahweh.”

For look, Yahweh commands,
and the great house will be struck into fragments,
and the small house into splinters.

Do horses run on rocks?
Does one plow the sea with oxen?{e}
But you have turned justice into poison
and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood—

“For look, I am raising up against you a nation, house of Israel,”
declares Yahweh, the God of Armies,
“and they will oppress you from Lebo-hamath{g}
to the Brook of the Arabah.”

notes.text: Calneh and Hamath, cities in northern Syria, and Gath, a Philistine city, were all conquered in the eighth century BC. Some reverse the last line: “Is your territory greater than theirs?”
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “strum” or “babble.”
Hebrew marzeaḥ, a feast or banqueting association, often connected with funerary rites (compare Jeremiah 16:5).

Hebrew dod, “uncle” or “kinsman.” The phrase that follows (meśarepho) is usually understood as “the one who burns him,” whether in cremation (unusual in Israel) or burning spices in his honor; the Hebrew of the verse is difficult.
So by a different division of the Hebrew letters (babbaqar yam); the Hebrew text reads “Does one plow there with oxen?”
Lo-debar means “nothing,” and Karnaim means “a pair of horns,” a symbol of strength; both were towns in Gilead, apparently recaptured by Jeroboam II (2 Kings 14:25).
Hebrew “the entrance of Hamath,” the ideal northern border of Israel. The Brook of the Arabah was probably at the southern end of the Dead Sea. Compare 2 Kings 14:25.

verses.text: This is what the Lord Yahweh showed me: he was forming locusts when the late crop{a} was beginning to sprout, the late crop after the king’s mowing.
When the locusts had eaten every green thing in the country, I cried, “Lord Yahweh, please pardon! How will Jacob survive? He is so tiny.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “It shall not be,” said Yahweh.
The Lord Yahweh showed me this: he was summoning a judgment of fire, and it consumed the vast deep{b} and began to consume the land.
Then I said, “Lord Yahweh, please stop! How can Jacob stand? He is so small.”
Yahweh relented concerning this. “This also shall not be,” said the Lord Yahweh.
He showed me this: there stood the Lord by a wall made true by a plumb line,{c} and a plumb line was in his hand.
Yahweh asked me, “What are you looking at, Amos?” I answered, “A plumb line.” Then the Lord said, “Look, I am placing a plumb line among my people Israel; I will no longer overlook them.

The high places of Isaac will be laid waste,
and the sanctuaries of Israel will be ruined,
and I will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword.”
Then Amaziah, priest of Bethel, sent this message to Jeroboam, Israel’s king: “Amos is plotting against you right in the heart of Israel. The country cannot endure everything he says.
For this is what Amos has said: ‘Jeroboam will die by the sword, and Israel will surely go into exile away from its land.’ ”
And Amaziah said to Amos, “Seer, go, run off to the land of Judah, and earn your bread there, and prophesy there;
but never again prophesy at Bethel, for it is the king’s sanctuary and a royal house.”
Amos answered Amaziah, “I am no prophet, nor a prophet’s son;{d} I am a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs.{e}
But Yahweh took me from following the flock, and Yahweh said to me, ‘Go, prophesy to my people Israel.’
Now hear the word of Yahweh. You are saying, ‘Prophesy no more against Israel; stop dripping words{f} against Isaac’s house.’

Therefore Yahweh says: ‘Your wife will become a prostitute in town; your children will be killed by the sword; your land will be surveyed and divided; you yourself will die in a foreign, unclean country,{g} and Israel will certainly be taken from its homeland into exile.’ ”

notes.text: The crop that grew after the spring rains, in about March–April. The king apparently took the first cutting as a tax.
Hebrew tehom, the subterranean waters thought to feed springs and rivers (Genesis 7:11).

Hebrew ʾanak, a word occurring only here (four times). Traditionally “plumb line,” but it is the Akkadian word for “tin,” and some interpret “a wall of tin” as a symbol of weakness or of military defense; the meaning remains debated.
Or “I was no prophet, nor a prophet’s son.” The Hebrew has no verb. “A prophet’s son” means a member of a prophetic guild (compare 2 Kings 2:3–7).
The fruit of the sycamore fig had to be slit or pinched to ripen; it grew in the lowlands, not at Tekoa itself.
Hebrew “drip,” that is, let words fall.
That is, a foreign land.

verses.text: The Lord Yahweh showed me this: a basket of ripe fruit.
He asked, “What are you looking at, Amos?” I answered, “A basket of ripe fruit.” Then Yahweh told me, “The end{a} has arrived for my people Israel; I will no longer overlook them.
The songs of the temple{b} will become wailings on that day,” declares the Lord Yahweh. “The dead bodies will be many, thrown out everywhere. Hush!”

Hear this, you who trample the needy
and would bring the poor of the land to an end,

who say, “When will the new moon pass,
so we can sell our grain?
When will the Sabbath be done,
so we can set out our wheat,
shrinking the measure and inflating the price,{c}
and tipping deceitful balances,

buying the poor with silver
and the destitute for a pair of sandals,
and selling even the wheat sweepings?”

Yahweh has sworn by the pride of Jacob:{d}
“Surely I will never forget any of their deeds.

Will not the land quake because of this,
and all its inhabitants mourn?
Will it not all rise up like the Nile,
heave, and subside like the river of Egypt?”

“Look, the days are coming,” declares the Lord Yahweh,
“when I will send a famine on the land—
not a famine of bread, nor a thirst for water,
but of hearing the words of Yahweh.

They will wander from sea to sea,
and from north to east they will run about
seeking the word of Yahweh,
but they will not find it.

On that day the lovely young women and the young men
will faint for thirst.

Those who swear by the guilt of Samaria,{f}
and say, ‘As your god lives, Dan,’
and, ‘As the way of Beersheba lives,’
will fall and never rise again.”

notes.text: A wordplay in Hebrew between qayits, “summer fruit,” and qets, “end.” The fruit was gathered in August–September.
Or “palace.”

Hebrew “making the ephah small and the shekel great,” that is, giving short measure (the ephah was a dry measure of about two-thirds of a bushel, or 22 liters) and weighing the buyer’s silver with an overweight shekel (normally about two-fifths of an ounce, or 11.5 grams).
Perhaps a title of God himself (compare 1 Samuel 15:29), or spoken in irony of Israel’s arrogance (6:8).
A total eclipse of the sun was visible in the region on June 15, 763 BC, and is recorded in Assyrian sources.
Or “by Ashimah of Samaria,” a goddess (compare 2 Kings 17:30). Dan and Beersheba were sanctuaries at the northern and southern ends of the land.

verses.text:
Though they burrow into Sheol,
my hand will take them from there;
though they mount to the heavens,
I will pull them down from there.

Though they hide on Carmel’s peak,
I will hunt them out and seize them there;
though they hide from my eyes on the floor of the sea,
I will command the serpent there to bite them.

And if they go into captivity before their enemies,
there I will command the sword, and it will kill them;
I will fix my eyes upon them
for harm and not for good.”

He constructs his upper chambers in the sky
and sets his dome{c} over the earth;
he summons the sea’s waters
and pours them over the land’s surface—
Yahweh is his name.

“Are you not like the Cushites{d} to me,
people of Israel?” declares Yahweh.
“Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt,
and the Philistines from Caphtor,{e}
and the Arameans from Kir?

Look, the eyes of the Lord Yahweh are upon the sinful kingdom,
and I will destroy it from the face of the ground,
except that I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,”
declares Yahweh.

“For I am giving the command,
and I will sift Israel’s house among all the nations,
as grain is sifted in a sieve,
and not one pebble will drop to the ground.

All the sinners of my people will die by the sword,
who say, ‘Disaster will not overtake or meet us.’

“On that day I will lift up
David’s collapsed shelter,{f}
mend its cracks,
restore its ruins,
and rebuild it as it was long ago,

I will plant them on their land,
and they will never again be uprooted
from the land that I have given them,”
says Yahweh your God.

notes.text: Or “upon.” The altar is probably that of Bethel.
Hebrew YHWH hatstseḇaʾoth, traditionally “the LORD of hosts,” the God who commands the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Or “his band” or “his bundle”; the meaning of the Hebrew ʾaguddah is uncertain here.
The people of the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia).
Probably Crete.
Hebrew sukkah, a hut or shelter, here a figure for the dynasty or kingdom of David in its weakened state.

Hebrew “over whom my name is called,” marking them as his possession. The Septuagint, reading ʾadam (“humankind”) for ʾedom and yidreshu (“seek”) for yirshu (“possess”), has “so that the remnant of humankind, and all the nations upon whom my name is called, may seek me.” James quotes the verses in this Greek form at the Jerusalem council (Acts 15:16–17) to support the inclusion of the Gentiles.
Hebrew “will melt.”
Or “restore the fortunes.”

books.name: Obadiah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Obadiah, the shortest book of the Old Testament, is a single chapter of twenty-one verses directed against Edom; it most likely reflects Edom’s conduct when Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587/586 BC (compare Psalm 137:7). Verses 1–9 closely parallel Jeremiah 49:7–22. Among the ancient manuscripts, as reported in the published editions, parts of Obadiah survive in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll of the Twelve (Mur 88) and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. Verse numbers are the same in English and Hebrew.

verses.text:
The vision of Obadiah.{a}
This is what the Lord Yahweh says about Edom—
a report we have heard from Yahweh,
and a messenger is sent out among the nations:
“Up! Let us go to war against her!”—

“Look, I am making you small among the nations;
you will be utterly despised.

The arrogance of your heart has deceived you,
you who dwell in the clefts of the rock,{b}
whose dwelling is on the heights,
who say in your heart,
‘Who can bring me down to the ground?’

Though you fly high as the eagle,
though you place your nest among the stars,
even from there I will pull you down,”
declares Yahweh.

“Had thieves come to you,
or robbers in the night—
how you are ruined!—
would they not have stolen just enough for themselves?
Had grape pickers come to you,
would they not have left some gleanings?

How Esau has been ransacked,
his hidden treasures sought out!

“Because of the violence done to your brother Jacob,
shame will cover you,
and you will be cut off forever.

In the day you stood by, at a distance,
in the day aliens took away his riches,
when foreigners passed through his gates
and threw lots over Jerusalem,
you as well were one of them.

But you should not have stared in glee{f} on your brother’s day,
on the day of his disaster;
you should not have exulted over Judah’s people
in the day of their destruction,
nor opened wide your mouth
in the day of trouble.

You should never have waited at the fork in the road{h}
to kill his escaping refugees,
or surrendered his survivors
on the day of disaster.

“For the day of Yahweh is near
upon all the nations.
As you have done, it will be done to you;
your deeds will return on your own head.

Jacob’s family will become a blaze,
Joseph’s family a flame,
and Esau’s family dry straw;
they will ignite it and burn it up,
and no one in Esau’s family will survive.
Yahweh has said so.

“The people of the Negev{k} shall take the mount of Esau as their own,
and those of the Shephelah{l} the Philistines’ land;
Ephraim’s fields and Samaria’s fields they shall possess,
and Benjamin shall have Gilead.

Deliverers{o} will go up on Mount Zion
to rule the mount of Esau,
and the kingdom will be Yahweh’s.

notes.text: The name means “servant of Yahweh.” Nothing else is known of the prophet; he is not to be identified with the Obadiah of 1 Kings 18.
Hebrew selaʿ, “rock,” perhaps also alluding to Sela, an Edomite stronghold (2 Kings 14:7). Edom’s mountain strongholds, south and east of the Dead Sea, were hard to reach.
The meaning of the Hebrew mazor is uncertain; perhaps “a net” or “a wound.” The Hebrew text reads “your bread”; some, with a small addition, read “those who eat your bread.”
Edom was proverbial for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7; compare Job 2:11, where Eliphaz is from Teman).
A region or chief city of Edom.
Hebrew “do not gloat.” The eight prohibitions in verses 12–14 have the force of a reproach for what Edom has already done.
Hebrew ʾed, “calamity,” here three times, sounds like the name Edom.
The meaning of the Hebrew pereq is uncertain; perhaps “the breach” or “the mountain pass.”
“You” is plural here, perhaps addressing Judah, which drank the cup of God’s wrath (compare Jeremiah 25:15–29), or Edom, which caroused on Mount Zion after its fall.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Vulgate, with different vowels, read “will dispossess those who dispossessed them.”
The dry southern region of Judah.
The low hills between the Judean highlands and the coastal plain.
A Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon (1 Kings 17:9). The Hebrew of the first two lines is difficult.
Probably Sardis in Asia Minor. In later Jewish usage the name was applied to Spain, hence “Sephardic” Jews.
Or “Those who have been delivered,” following the Septuagint and Syriac.

books.name: Jonah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Jonah son of Amittai is the prophet named in 2 Kings 14:25, in the reign of Jeroboam II (about 786–746 BC); the book itself is a narrative about him rather than a collection of his oracles, and its date of composition is debated. Among the ancient manuscripts, as reported in the published editions, portions of Jonah are preserved in the Qumran scrolls of the Twelve (4QXII-a, 4QXII-f, 4QXII-g), in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll (Mur 88), and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally agree with the Masoretic Text. Versification: English 1:17 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–10 is Hebrew 2:2–11; this translation follows the English numbering.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh came to Jonah{a} son of Amittai:
“Up! Go to Nineveh,{b} the great city, and denounce it, for their evil has risen up before my face.”

But Jonah got up to run away to Tarshish,{c} away from the presence of Yahweh. He went down to Joppa{d} and found a ship bound for Tarshish. He paid its fare and went down into it, to go with them to Tarshish, away from Yahweh’s presence.
Yahweh, however, hurled a great wind onto the sea, and so mighty a storm arose on the sea that the ship was about to break apart.{e}

The sailors were terrified, and each man cried out to his own god. They hurled the cargo on board into the sea to lighten the ship for themselves. Jonah, though, had gone down into the hold of the vessel, lain down, and fallen fast asleep.
The captain came to him and said, “How can you be sleeping? Get up, call on your god! Perhaps that god will give a thought to us, and we will not perish.”
The sailors said to one another, “Let’s cast lots to determine who is responsible for this calamity.” The lot was cast, and it landed on Jonah.
“Explain,” they demanded, “who is responsible for this calamity? What work do you do? Where is your home? What land are you from, and who are your people?”
He told them, “I am a Hebrew, and I fear Yahweh, the God of heaven, who made the sea and the dry land.”
At this the men were seized with a great fear, and said to him, “What is this that you have done?” For the men knew he was fleeing from Yahweh’s presence, because he had told them.
So they said to him, “What must we do with you to make the sea grow quiet around us?” For the sea kept getting rougher.
He told them, “Lift me up and hurl me into the sea; then the sea will quiet down around you. I know that it is my fault this mighty storm has struck you.”
Still the men rowed hard{f} to get back to land, but they could not, for the sea was raging against them more and more.
So they cried out to Yahweh: “Please, Yahweh, do not let us perish for this man’s life, and do not lay innocent blood on us; for you, Yahweh, have done just as you pleased.”
Then they picked Jonah up and hurled him into the sea, and the sea stopped its raging.
And the men feared Yahweh with a great fear; they offered a sacrifice to Yahweh and made vows.
Yahweh appointed{g} a great fish{h} to swallow Jonah, and Jonah was in the belly of the fish three days and three nights.{i}

notes.text: The name means “dove.” He is the prophet of 2 Kings 14:25, from Gath-hepher in Galilee.
The capital of Assyria, on the east bank of the Tigris opposite modern Mosul, Iraq. Assyria was Israel’s most feared enemy; it destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC.
A distant port in the far west, probably Tartessus in southern Spain—the opposite direction from Nineveh.
Modern Jaffa, part of Tel Aviv, on the Mediterranean coast.
Hebrew “the ship thought to be broken.” The verb “hurl” recurs in verses 5, 12, and 15.
Hebrew “dug,” a vivid word for straining at the oars.
Hebrew manah, “appoint, assign.” God likewise “appoints” the plant, the worm, and the east wind in chapter 4.

Hebrew dag gadol, “a great fish.” The Hebrew does not say “whale”; the Septuagint has kētos, “sea creature,” the word used in Matthew 12:40, which older English versions rendered “whale.” Jesus cites Jonah’s three days and nights in the fish as “the sign of Jonah” (Matthew 12:39–41; Luke 11:29–32).
English 1:17 is Hebrew 2:1.

verses.text: Then Jonah prayed to Yahweh his God from the belly of the fish.{a}

You flung me into the depths,
into the heart of the seas,
and the current swirled around me;
all your breakers and your billows
swept over me.

As my life was ebbing away,
I remembered Yahweh,
and my prayer came to you,
into your holy temple.

Those who cling to empty idols{e}
abandon their loyalty.{f}

But I will offer sacrifice to you
with a song of thanks;
the vow I made I will fulfill.
Deliverance belongs to Yahweh!”
Then Yahweh spoke to the fish, and it vomited Jonah out onto the dry land.

notes.text: English 2:1–10 is Hebrew 2:2–11. In 2:1 the Hebrew uses the feminine form dagah for “fish,” elsewhere the masculine dag; the difference is probably only stylistic.
The realm of the dead.
So the Hebrew; with a slight change, “how shall I look again,” as in Theodotion’s Greek.
