Or “threatened my life.” Hebrew nefesh can mean both “throat” and “life.”
Hebrew “worthless vanities.”
Or “forsake the one who is loyal to them,” that is, God; Hebrew ḥesed.

verses.text: A second time the word of Yahweh came to Jonah:
“Up! Go to Nineveh, the great city, and announce to it the word I am giving you.”
So Jonah got up and went to Nineveh, as Yahweh had said. Now Nineveh was a city great even to God,{a} a walk of three days across.{b}
Jonah began going into the city, one day’s walk, and he called out, “Forty days more, and Nineveh will be overturned!”{c}
The people of Nineveh believed God. They called a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest of them to the least.
The news reached Nineveh’s king, who stood up from his throne, removed his royal robe, wrapped himself in sackcloth, and sat in the dust.
And he had a proclamation cried through Nineveh: “By decree of the king and his nobles: Let neither human nor beast, herd nor flock, taste anything. Let them not graze or drink water.
Let human and beast alike be covered with sackcloth, and let them call to God with all their strength. Let each one turn from his evil ways and from the violence that is in his hands.
Who can tell? Perhaps God will turn back and relent,{d} and turn away from the heat of his anger, and we will not perish.”
God saw their deeds—that they had turned back from their wicked conduct—and God relented of the harm he had threatened to do to them, and did not do it.

notes.text: Hebrew “a great city to God,” possibly an idiom for “an exceedingly great city.”

Hebrew “a journey of three days,” about 60 miles (100 kilometers); perhaps the circuit of greater Nineveh and its districts, or the time needed to visit it all. The walls of ancient Nineveh enclosed about 1,850 acres (750 hectares).
Hebrew haphak, the word used of the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19:25), but which can also mean “turned around, changed.”
Or “change his mind.” Compare Joel 2:14.

verses.text: But to Jonah this seemed a great evil, and he was furious.{a}

He prayed to Yahweh and said, “Ah, Yahweh, is this not just what I said when I was still back home? That is why I made haste to run off to Tarshish. For I knew you were a God gracious and merciful, long-suffering and rich in steadfast love,{b} who relents over calamity.
So now, Yahweh, please take my life from me, for I am better off dead than alive.”
And Yahweh said, “Is it right for you to be so angry?”
Jonah went out of the city and settled on its east side. There he made himself a shelter and sat in its shade to watch what would happen to the city.
Then Yahweh God appointed a plant{c} and made it grow up over Jonah, to be shade over his head, to rescue him from his misery.{d} Jonah was very glad because of the plant.
At daybreak the next day God sent a worm that gnawed the plant, and it dried up.
When the sun rose, God sent a sweltering east wind, and the sun beat on Jonah’s head until he nearly fainted. He wished he were dead and said, “Death is better for me than life.”
God asked Jonah, “Is your anger over the plant justified?” “It is,” he replied. “I am so angry I could die.”
Then Yahweh said, “You took pity on the plant, though you did not labor over it or make it grow. It came up in a night and perished in a night.
And may I not pity Nineveh, the great city, where there live over a hundred and twenty thousand human beings who cannot tell their right hand from their left,{e} and a great many beasts besides?”{f}

notes.text: Hebrew “it was evil to Jonah, a great evil, and it burned to him.” The word “evil” echoes 3:8 and 3:10.
Hebrew ḥesed. This confession echoes Exodus 34:6–7; compare Joel 2:13.
Hebrew qiqayon, perhaps the castor-oil plant, which grows quickly and has broad leaves; older versions have “gourd.”
Hebrew raʿah, “evil,” the same word as in 4:1.
Perhaps meaning small children, or people without moral or religious understanding.
The book ends with God’s question unanswered.

books.name: Micah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew Masoretic Text as given in the Westminster Leningrad Codex (Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible edition), with the Septuagint (Old Greek) consulted. Micah of Moresheth prophesied in the reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah of Judah (about 740–690 BC), before and after the fall of Samaria in 722 BC; Jeremiah 26:18 quotes Micah 3:12. Among the ancient manuscripts, as reported in the published editions, portions of Micah survive in the Qumran scrolls of the Twelve (4QXII-a, 4QXII-f, 4QXII-g), in a commentary from Qumran (1QpMic), in the Wadi Murabbaʿat scroll (Mur 88), and in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr); these generally support the Masoretic Text. Versification: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14, and English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this translation follows the English numbering.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Micah{a} of Moresheth{b} in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah,{c} which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.

For look: Yahweh is coming out from his place;
he will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.

The mountains will melt beneath him,
and the valleys split open,
like wax in front of the fire,
like water poured down a slope.

All this is for Jacob’s rebellion,
for the sins of the house of Israel.
What is Jacob’s rebellion?
Is it not Samaria?
And what are Judah’s high places?{d}
Are they not Jerusalem?

“So I will make Samaria a rubble heap in the open country,
a place for planting vines;
I will tumble her stones down into the valley
and lay bare her foundations.

For the inhabitants of Maroth{k} writhe, waiting for good,
because disaster has come down from Yahweh
to the gate of Jerusalem.

Hitch the horses to the chariot,
you residents of Lachish!{l}
She was where Daughter Zion’s sin began,
for Israel’s rebellions were found in you.

Make yourself bald, shear your hair,
for the children you delight in;
widen your baldness like the vulture’s,
since they are carried away from you as captives.

notes.text: The name is a short form of Micaiah, “Who is like Yahweh?” Compare 7:18.
Moresheth-gath (1:14), a town in the Shephelah about 22 miles (35 kilometers) southwest of Jerusalem.
Jotham reigned about 750–735 BC, Ahaz about 735–715 BC, and Hezekiah about 715–686 BC.
So the Hebrew; the Septuagint and Targum read “what is the sin of the house of Judah?”
Hebrew “hire,” the wage of a prostitute, a figure for the wealth gained through idolatrous worship.
An echo of David’s lament in 2 Samuel 1:20. In verses 10–15 each town’s name is the basis for a play on words, most of which cannot be carried into English.
“House of dust.”
“Beautiful town.”
Sounds like the Hebrew for “come out.”
The meaning of the last line is uncertain.
Sounds like the Hebrew for “bitterness.”
Lachish sounds like the Hebrew rekesh, “steeds.” It was Judah’s second city, besieged and taken by the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC.
Or “a dowry,” as for a bride leaving home.
Achzib sounds like ʾakzab, “deceptive,” a stream that dries up.
Hebrew yoresh, “one who takes possession,” a play on Mareshah.
The cave where David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 22:1); Israel’s leaders will be fugitives again.

verses.text:
Woe to those who plan iniquity
and work out evil upon their beds!
When morning dawns they carry it out,
because it is in the power of their hand.

They covet fields and seize them,
and houses, and take them away;
they defraud a man and his household,
a man and his inheritance.

So this is what Yahweh says:
“See, I am devising evil against this clan,
and you will not slip your necks out from under it,
nor stride along with heads held high;
it will be a time of calamity.

In that day they will take up a taunt against you
and wail a bitter lament, saying,
‘We are utterly ruined;
he exchanges the portion of my people.
How he takes it away from me!
To traitors he divides our fields.’

Therefore you will have no one to cast the measuring line by lot{a}
in the assembly of Yahweh.

Is this what you say, house of Jacob?
“Has Yahweh’s Spirit run out of patience?
Is this how he acts?”
Do my words not benefit
the person who lives honestly?

But lately my people have risen up as an enemy.
You strip the robe off the cloak
from those who pass by trustingly,
like men returning from war.

The women of my people you drive out
from their pleasant houses;
from their young children you take away
my splendor forever.

Get up and go,
for this is no place of rest;
because of uncleanness it will destroy,
with a grievous destruction.

If a man walking in wind and falsehood should lie, saying,
“I will preach to you of wine and beer,”
he would be the preacher for this people!

The one who breaks open the way goes up ahead of them;
they burst out, they go through the gate
and leave by it.
Their king goes on in front of them,
Yahweh at their head.”

notes.text: That is, no share when the land is divided again.
Hebrew naṭaph, “drip,” used of prophetic speech, as in Amos 7:16. The Hebrew of verses 6–11 is difficult in places.
Hebrew Bozrah, here probably “an enclosure,” though Bozrah was also a city of Edom famous for its sheep.

verses.text:
Then I said:
Hear me, you chiefs of Jacob,
you governors of Israel’s house!
Shouldn’t you understand justice?

you devour my people’s flesh,
skin them alive,
smash their bones,
and carve them up like cuts for the pot,
like meat for a kettle.

Then they will cry to Yahweh,
but he will not answer them;
he will hide his face from them at that time,
because they have made their deeds evil.

This is what Yahweh says concerning the prophets
who lead my people astray,
who, when they have something to chew,
cry “Peace!”
but declare holy war against anyone
who puts nothing in their mouths:

But as for me, I am filled with power,
with the Spirit of Yahweh,
with justice and with might,
to declare to Jacob his rebellion
and to Israel his sin.

Hear this, heads of the house of Jacob
and rulers of the house of Israel,
who abhor justice
and twist all that is straight,

who build Zion with bloodshed
and Jerusalem with wrong.

Her heads give judgment for a bribe,
her priests teach for a fee,
her prophets divine for money;
yet they lean on Yahweh and say,
“Is not Yahweh in our midst?
No disaster will come upon us.”

So on your account
Zion will be plowed like a field,
Jerusalem made a mound of rubble,
and the mountain of the house a forest height.{c}

notes.text: Hebrew “from them.”
Hebrew “mustache,” a gesture of mourning or shame (Leviticus 13:45).
This verse is quoted in Jeremiah 26:18, about a century later, where the elders recall that Hezekiah heeded it and sought Yahweh’s favor.

verses.text:
In the days to come{a}
the mountain of Yahweh’s house
shall stand firm as the highest of the mountains,
lifted up above the hills,
and peoples shall stream to it.

Many nations will come, saying,
“Come, let’s go up Yahweh’s mountain,
to the temple of Jacob’s God,
that he may teach us his ways
and we may follow his paths.”
Teaching{b} will come out of Zion,
and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.

Everyone will sit under their own grapevine and fig tree,
unafraid,
for Yahweh of Armies{c} has promised it.

Though every people marches
in the name of its own god,
we will march in the name of Yahweh our God
for all time.

“In that day,” declares Yahweh,
“I will gather the lame
and assemble the scattered,
those whom I have afflicted.

The lame I will make a remnant,
and the outcast a mighty nation;
and Yahweh will reign over them on Mount Zion
from now on and forever.

And you, tower of the flock,{d}
hill{e} of Daughter Zion,
to you it will come—
the former dominion will return,
the kingdom of Daughter Jerusalem.”

Why do you cry out now?
Have you no king?
Has your adviser died,
that agony seizes you like a woman giving birth?

Now many nations
have assembled against you,
saying, “Let her be desecrated,
and let us feast our eyes on Zion.”

But they do not know
the thoughts of Yahweh;
they do not grasp his purpose,
how he has bundled them like sheaves for the threshing floor.

notes.text: Verses 1–3 are nearly identical to Isaiah 2:2–4; Micah and Isaiah were contemporaries.
Hebrew torah.
Hebrew YHWH tsebaʾot, traditionally “the Lord of hosts”: Yahweh as commander of the armies of heaven and of Israel.
Hebrew Migdal-eder, perhaps a watchtower over Jerusalem; compare Genesis 35:21.
Hebrew Ophel, the fortified hill south of the temple mount.
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; perhaps “push.”
Hebrew “devote to destruction” (ḥerem), here meaning to dedicate the plunder wholly to God.

verses.text:
Therefore he will give them up until the time
when she who is in labor has given birth;
then the rest of his brothers will return
to the people of Israel.

He will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of Yahweh,
in the majesty of the name of Yahweh his God.
And they will dwell secure, for now he will be great
to the ends of the earth.

They will shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword,
the land of Nimrod{f} at its gates;{g}
he will deliver us from Assyria
when it comes into our land
and treads within our borders.

Then the remnant of Jacob will be
among many peoples
like dew from Yahweh,
like showers on the grass,
which wait for no one
and do not linger for mortals.

And the remnant of Jacob will be among the nations,
in the midst of many peoples,
like a lion among the animals of the woods,
like a young lion among the sheepfolds,
which, when it goes through, treads down and mauls,
and none can deliver.

Let your hand be lifted over your foes,
and may all your enemies be cut off!

I will cut off the cities of your land
and tear down all your strongholds;

I will cut off the sorceries in your hand,
and soothsayers you will have no more;

I will cut off your carved images
and your sacred pillars from among you,
and never again will you bow
before what your own hands have made;

I will tear out your Asherah poles{h} from your midst
and demolish your towns.{i}

In anger and fury I will take revenge
on the nations that did not listen.”

notes.text: English 5:1 is Hebrew 4:14. The meaning of the first line is uncertain; perhaps “gash yourself, daughter of raiders.”

English 5:2–15 is Hebrew 5:1–14; this verse is Hebrew 5:1. Ephrathah is the clan district around Bethlehem, the hometown of David (Ruth 4:11; 1 Samuel 17:12), about 6 miles (9 kilometers) south of Jerusalem. Matthew 2:6 quotes this verse, in a free form, as fulfilled in the birth of Jesus at Bethlehem; compare John 7:42.
Or “from days of eternity.” The phrase may refer to the ancient line of David or, as Christian interpreters have understood it, to the ruler’s origin before time.
Or “This one will be peace,” or “This will be our peace.”
“Seven… eight” is a Hebrew idiom for “more than enough.”
The legendary founder of Mesopotamian cities (Genesis 10:8–12).
So the Hebrew; with a slight change, “with the drawn sword.”
Wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah.
Or, with a slight change, “your idols.”

verses.text:
Hear now what Yahweh is saying:
“Rise, plead your case before the mountains,
and let the hills hear your voice.”

“My people, what have I done to you?
How have I worn you out? Answer me!

I brought you out of Egypt
and freed you from the land of slavery;
I sent Moses ahead of you,
with Aaron and Miriam.

With what shall I come before Yahweh
and bow down to God on high?
Shall I come before him with burnt offerings,
with calves a year old?

Is Yahweh delighted by rams in their thousands,
by oil flowing in ten thousand streams?
Shall I give my firstborn for my rebellion,
the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

Can I forget{j} the treasures gained by wickedness
in the house of the wicked,
and the short measure{k} that is accursed?

Shall I acquit the one with crooked scales,
with a bag of false weights?

So I in turn have begun to strike you,{l}
to lay you waste because of your sins.

You will eat but not be satisfied,
and hunger{m} will remain within you;
you will put things aside but not save them,
and what you save I will give to the sword.

notes.text: Hebrew rib, a formal legal complaint; the mountains and the foundations of the earth are summoned as witnesses (compare Deuteronomy 32:1; Isaiah 1:2).
See Numbers 22–24.
Shittim was Israel’s last camp east of the Jordan (Numbers 25:1; Joshua 3:1); Gilgal its first camp west of it (Joshua 4:19).
Or “saving acts.”
Hebrew ʾadam, “human being.”
Hebrew ḥesed, loyal and steadfast love.
Or “carefully, attentively.”
So the Septuagint, reading the Hebrew with different vowels; the Masoretic Text reads “sees.”
The meaning of the Hebrew of this line is uncertain; perhaps “Hear, tribe and assembly of the city.”
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Hebrew “the lean ephah.” The ephah was a dry measure of about two-thirds of a bushel (22 liters); merchants used undersized measures to cheat buyers.
Or, following the Septuagint, “I have made you sick by striking you.”
The meaning of the Hebrew word is uncertain.
Omri and his son Ahab, kings of Israel in the ninth century BC, were remembered for Baal worship and injustice (1 Kings 16–21).
Hebrew “her.”

verses.text:
Woe is me! For I have become
like one at the gathering of summer fruit,
like the gleaning after the grape harvest:
no cluster to eat,
no early fig that I crave.

Their hands are skilled at evil;
the official asks for gifts,
the judge for a bribe,
and the great man speaks out what his greed desires—
so they weave it together.

The best of them is like a briar,
the most upright worse than a thorn hedge.
The day of your watchmen,{a} your punishment, has come;
now will be their confusion.

Rejoice not over me, you my foe!
I have fallen, yet I will get up;
I sit in the dark,
yet Yahweh is a light to me.

I will bear Yahweh’s anger,
because I have sinned against him,
until he takes up my case
and brings about justice for me.
He will lead me out to the light;
I will see his saving righteousness.

Then my enemy will see it,
and disgrace will cover her,
the one who taunted me,
“Where is Yahweh your God?”
My eyes will gloat over her;
she will be trampled
like street mud.

A day to rebuild your walls!
On that day your borders will be pushed far outward.{c}

Yet the land will lie waste
on account of those who dwell in it,
the outcome of their doings.

Shepherd your people with your staff,
the flock that is your inheritance,
who live alone in a forest
in the midst of a fruitful land;{f}
let them graze in Bashan and Gilead
as in days long ago.

As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt,
I will show them{g} marvelous things.

Who is a God like you,{h}
pardoning iniquity
and passing over the rebellion
of the remnant of his inheritance?
He does not cling to his wrath for all time,
for faithful love is his delight.

He will once more show us mercy;
he will trample down our guilt.
You will hurl all our{i} sins
into the ocean’s depths.

You will show faithfulness to Jacob,
steadfast love to Abraham,
as you swore to our ancestors
from the days of old.

notes.text: That is, the day the prophets warned of.
Jesus quotes this verse in Matthew 10:35–36; compare Luke 12:53.
Or “the decree will be far removed.” The meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew matsor, “Egypt” or “fortress,” a play on words.
The Euphrates.
Hebrew Carmel, “garden land,” perhaps also the mountain of that name.
Hebrew “him.”
A play on Micah’s name, “Who is like Yahweh?” (1:1).
So the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate; Hebrew “their.”

books.name: Nahum
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, especially 4QXII-g) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Nahum also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: English 1:15 is Hebrew 2:1, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14.

verses.text: An oracle concerning Nineveh. The book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.{a}

Yahweh is a jealous God and an avenger;{b}
Yahweh avenges, and is a master of wrath.
Yahweh takes vengeance on his adversaries,
and he keeps wrath for his enemies.

Yahweh is patient and mighty,
but he never lets the guilty go unpunished.
He travels in the whirlwind and the tempest,
and the clouds are the dust kicked up by his feet.

He rebukes the sea and dries it,
and all the rivers he makes dry.
Bashan languishes, and Carmel,
and the flower of Lebanon fades.

The mountains quake because of him,
and the hills melt away.
The earth heaves at his presence,
the world and all who dwell in it.

Who can stand before his indignation?
And who can rise up in the heat of his anger?
His wrath is poured out like fire,
and the rocks are torn apart by him.

Thus says Yahweh:
“Though they are at full strength and many as well,
even so they shall be cut down and pass away.
Though I have afflicted you,
I will afflict you no more.

And now I will break his yoke from off you,
and I will tear your bonds apart.”

And Yahweh has given command concerning you:
“No more of your name shall be sown;
out of the house of your gods I will cut off
the graven image and the molten image.
I will prepare your grave, for you are vile.”

notes.text: “Oracle”: Hebrew massa’, which can also mean “burden.” The name Nahum means “comfort” or “comforter.” Where Elkosh was is not known.

Hebrew El qanno’. The poem in verses 2–8 seems partly to follow the order of the Hebrew alphabet (an acrostic), though the pattern is incomplete. In the next line, “a master of wrath” is literally “a lord (ba‘al) of wrath,” meaning one full of wrath.

“Her place” refers to Nineveh. The Septuagint has “those that rise up against him,” reading the Hebrew letters differently. The next line can also be translated “and he will pursue his enemies into darkness.”
The Hebrew of this verse is obscure, and the translation is uncertain.
Hebrew beliyya‘al, “worthlessness, wickedness.” The same word is translated “the worthless one” in verse 15.
Compare Isaiah 52:7, which Romans 10:15 quotes. In Hebrew this verse is 2:1, so English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:2–14.

verses.text:
For Yahweh is restoring the majesty of Jacob
like the majesty of Israel,
for the emptiers have emptied them out
and destroyed their vine branches.

The gates of the rivers are opened,
and the palace melts away.

Nineveh has been like a pool of water all her days,{d}
and now they flee.
“Stand! Stand!” they cry,
but no one turns back.

Take the spoil of silver, take the spoil of gold!
For the store has no end,
wealth of every precious thing.

Emptiness, desolation, and ruin!
Hearts melt and knees give way;
anguish is in all loins,
and all their faces grow pale.

Where now is that lions’ lair,
the place where young lions fed,
where lion and lioness walked,
and cubs played unafraid?

The lion ripped up plenty for his young
and choked the kill for his mates;
he stocked his caves with victims
and his lairs with mangled meat.

notes.text: Hebrew 2:2. “One who scatters” can also be translated “a shatterer.” The Septuagint differs: “one who has been delivered from affliction has come up panting into your presence.”

Literally “and the cypresses are made to quiver.” The Septuagint has “and the horsemen shall be thrown into confusion,” reading parashim (“horsemen”) for beroshim (“cypresses”). The Hebrew word translated “steel” (peladot) is rare, and its meaning is uncertain; some take it to mean “torches.”
The Hebrew word translated “It is decided” (hutstsav) is obscure. Some older translations treat it as a name (“Huzzab”); others take it to mean the queen or a goddess’s image.
The Hebrew phrase translated “all her days” is difficult. The Septuagint has “her waters shall be as a pool of water.”

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is given as “Yahweh of Armies” throughout. In Hebrew this verse is 2:14.
Hebrew “her chariots.” The Septuagint has “your multitude.”

verses.text:
The crack of the whip and the rumble of the wheel,
the galloping horse and the bounding chariot!

Horsemen charging, the flashing sword and the glittering spear,
a multitude of slain, a mass of corpses,
dead bodies without end;
they stumble over their dead.

All for the countless harlotries of the harlot,
graceful and charming, a mistress of sorceries,
who sells nations by her harlotries
and peoples by her sorceries.

“I am your enemy,” announces Yahweh of Armies,
“and I will pull your skirts up over your face,
show the nations your nakedness
and the kingdoms your disgrace.

I will cast filth upon you
and disgrace you,
and set you up as a gazingstock.

Cush was her strength, and Egypt, without limit;
Put and the Libyans were your helpers.{d}

Your shepherds slumber, O king of Assyria;
your nobles lie still.
Your people are scattered on the mountains,
with no one to gather them.

Nothing can ease your injury;
your wound is fatal.
Everyone who learns of you
applauds your fall.
For who has escaped your endless cruelty?

notes.text: “Comforters” (menahamim) plays on the name Nahum (“comfort”).
No-amon, “city of Amon,” is Thebes in Upper Egypt. The Assyrians sacked it about 663 BC.
Here “the sea” (yam) means the broad waters of the Nile. “And water her wall” is literally “from the sea her wall.” The Septuagint has “and whose walls are water.”

Cush is the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia). Put was probably in Libya, though some place it on the African coast of the Red Sea. The Hebrew has “your helpers,” but the Septuagint has “her helpers.”
The Hebrew uses several words for locusts (yeleq, ’arbeh, and gov in verse 17). The kinds or stages of locust they refer to are uncertain.
The words translated “guardsmen” (minzarim) and “officials” (tifsarim) are rare. The second may be a loanword from Akkadian, and the precise meaning of both is uncertain.

books.name: Habakkuk
books.sourceNote:
Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against several other witnesses:
- The Habakkuk Commentary (Pesher Habakkuk, 1QpHab) from Qumran Cave 1, copied in the late 1st century BC. It quotes Habakkuk 1–2 phrase by phrase and differs from the Masoretic Text at several points.
- The Hebrew Minor Prophets scroll from Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD).
- The Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation.
The scroll readings come from Martin Abegg’s transcriptions, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. Portions of Habakkuk also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly and are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 2:13). Poetry is printed line by line.

verses.text: The oracle that Habakkuk the prophet saw.{a}

Yahweh, how long must I plead for help
while you refuse to listen?
I shout to you, “Violence!”
yet you do not rescue.

Why do you make me see iniquity,
and why do you look upon trouble?
Ruin and violence are before me;
there is strife, and contention arises.

“Look among the nations, and see;{b}
be astonished and amazed!
For I am doing a work in your days
that you would not believe if it were told.

For behold, I am raising up the Chaldeans,{c}
that bitter and impetuous nation,
which marches through the breadth of the earth
to seize dwellings that are not its own.

It is dreadful and fearsome;
its justice and its dignity go forth from itself.

At kings they scoff,
and rulers are a laughingstock to them.
They laugh at every fortress,
for they heap up earth and capture it.

Then they sweep on like the wind and pass by,
and become guilty, they whose own strength is their god.”{e}

Your eyes are too pure to look upon evil,
and you cannot gaze upon wrong.
Why then do you look on the treacherous{g}
and keep silent when the wicked swallows up
one more righteous than he?

You make mankind like the fish of the sea,
like creeping things that have no ruler.

Therefore he sacrifices to his net
and burns incense to his dragnet;
for by them his portion is rich
and his food is plentiful.

Shall he therefore keep emptying his net,{h}
and slaying nations continually without pity?

notes.text: “Oracle”: Hebrew massa’, which can also mean “burden.” The meaning of the name Habakkuk is uncertain. It may come from a Hebrew root meaning “embrace,” or it may be related to the Akkadian name of a garden plant (hambaququ).

The Septuagint has “Behold, you despisers,” apparently reading bogedim (“traitors, the treacherous”) for baggoyim (“among the nations”). Acts 13:41 quotes the verse in that form. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran (1QpHab) quotes the line as “among the nations,” as the Masoretic Text has it. Its commentary, however, applies the passage to “the traitors.”
The Chaldeans were the Neo-Babylonian dynasty and its people. They overthrew Assyria and conquered Judah, taking Jerusalem in 597 and 586 BC.
The Hebrew phrase translated “the set of their faces” is obscure.
Literally “and he shall be guilty, he whose strength is his god.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “and he makes his strength his god” (wayyasem instead of we’ashem).

According to an ancient Jewish tradition, this is one of the places where the scribes altered the wording out of reverence, and the original was “You shall not die.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran and the Septuagint both read “we.”
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran has a plural, “Why do you look on, you treacherous ones?”
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “Therefore he keeps drawing his sword” (harbo, instead of hermo, “his net”).

verses.text:
Shall not all these take up a taunt against him,
with mocking riddles about him, and say,
“Woe to him who multiplies what does not belong to him—
how long?—
and makes himself heavy with pledges!”

Shall not those who bite you rise up in a moment,
and those wake who shake you violently?
And you shall become plunder to them.

Because you plundered so many nations,
the rest of the peoples will plunder you,
for human bloodshed and violence to the land,
to cities and everyone who lives in them.

Woe to him who gets evil gain for his house,
to set his nest on high,
to be delivered from the grasp of evil!

For out of the wall the stone shall cry,
and out of the timber the rafter shall answer it.

Doom to the man who constructs a town by murder
and establishes a city on injustice!

You will be sated with shame instead of glory.
Drink, you also, and be exposed as uncircumcised!{j}
The cup in Yahweh’s right hand will come around to you,
and utter disgrace will be upon your glory.

What profit is an idol
when its maker has carved it,
a molten image and a teacher of falsehood,
that the one who shapes it should trust in what he has shaped,
making idols that cannot speak?

Woe to him who says to a piece of wood, “Wake up!”
or to a mute stone, “Arise!”
Can this teach?
Behold, it is plated with gold and silver,
and there is no breath at all within it.

But Yahweh is in his holy temple;
let all the earth keep silence before him.

notes.text: Or “concerning my reproof.”
Or “so that a herald may run with it.”
Hebrews 10:37 quotes verses 3–4 in their Septuagint form. Compare “the end” here with 2 Peter 3:9.

Or “by his faith.” Hebrew be’emunato: ’emunah is steadfastness, faithfulness, and trust. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran quotes the line as it stands in the Masoretic Text, and its commentary applies it to those whom God will deliver “because of their toil and their faith in the Teacher of Righteousness.” The Septuagint reads “by my faith” (or “by my faithfulness,” meaning God’s). Some Septuagint manuscripts read “my righteous one shall live by faith,” the form that Hebrews 10:38 follows. The Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever is reported to read “by his faith,” agreeing with the Hebrew. Paul quotes the line, without a pronoun, in Romans 1:17 and Galatians 3:11.
The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “wealth (hon) is treacherous” instead of “wine (hayyayin).” The Septuagint has “the arrogant man and the scorner.”
Sheol is the realm of the dead, the grave.
Compare Isaiah 11:9.
Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel.

The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads “to look upon their festivals” (mo‘adehem instead of me‘orehem, “their nakedness”). Its commentary applies the verse to an attack by “the Wicked Priest” on the Teacher of Righteousness on the Day of Atonement.

The Hebrew he‘arel means “show your foreskin, be exposed as uncircumcised.” The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran reads hera‘el, “and stagger,” with two letters reversed. The Septuagint (“shake… and quake”) and other ancient versions point the same way, and many translations follow that reading.
“Will terrify you” follows the Septuagint. The Masoretic Text has a form usually read as “will terrify them,” and the Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran has another spelling of the word.

verses.text: A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, according to Shigionoth.{a}

God came from Teman,
the Holy One from Mount Paran. Selah{c}
His glory blanketed the skies,
and the earth overflowed with his praise.

Pestilence went before his face,
and plague went out at his feet.{e}

Under affliction I saw the tents of Cushan;{g}
the curtains of Midian’s land were shaking.

Was Yahweh angry with the rivers?
Was your anger against the rivers,
or your fury against the sea,
when you rode upon your horses,
your chariots of salvation?

Sun and moon stood still in their dwelling
at the light of your arrows as they flew,
at the gleam of your flashing spear.

In fury you strode over the earth;
in wrath you threshed the nations.

You went forth for the salvation of your people,
for the salvation of your anointed.
You crushed the head of the house of the wicked,
laying bare the foundation to the neck. Selah

You trampled the sea with your horses,
the heaving of many waters.

yet I will rejoice in Yahweh;
I will exult in the God of my salvation.

notes.text: Shigionoth is probably a musical or liturgical term. Its meaning is unknown; compare the title of Psalm 7. The Habakkuk Commentary from Qumran comments only on chapters 1–2.
The Septuagint has a very different text here, beginning “You shall be known between the two living creatures.”

Teman (in Edom) and Mount Paran (in the Sinai peninsula) lie to the south of Judah. Compare Deuteronomy 33:2 and Judges 5:4. Selah is a term of uncertain meaning, probably musical or liturgical; it occurs here and in verses 9 and 13.
Hebrew qarnayim, literally “horns,” used here of rays of light.
Hebrew dever (“pestilence”) and reshef (“plague, burning fever”). Reshef is also the name of a Canaanite god of plague, and here it may picture plague as one of God’s attendants.
Or “and shook the earth.”
Cushan appears only here. It may be a poetic name for Cush, or the name of a tribe connected with Midian (compare Numbers 12:1).
The Hebrew of this line is notoriously obscure. Literally it is “sworn were the rods (or tribes) of the word.”
The Wadi Murabba‘at Minor Prophets scroll reads “the clouds poured out water,” as in Psalm 77:17. The Masoretic Text has “the torrent of waters swept by.”
The Hebrew of verse 14 is difficult, and the translation is uncertain.
Hebrew YHWH Adonai. “My high places” are the heights.
This note is addressed to the leader of the temple music, like the titles of many psalms.

books.name: Zephaniah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, 4QXII-b, -c, and -g) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Zephaniah also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 2:9). Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: in Zephaniah, English and Hebrew verse numbers are the same.

verses.text: The word of Yahweh that came to Zephaniah the son of Cushi, the son of Gedaliah, the son of Amariah, the son of Hezekiah, in the days of Josiah the son of Amon, king of Judah.{a}

“I will utterly sweep away everything
from upon the face of the ground,” declares Yahweh.

“I will remove people and livestock;
I will remove the birds that fly in the sky
and the fish of the ocean,
and the idols{b} along with the wicked.
I will eliminate humanity
from the face of the earth,” declares Yahweh.

those who have turned back from following Yahweh,
who have not sought Yahweh nor inquired of him.”

Hush in the presence of the Lord Yahweh!
The day of Yahweh is close;
Yahweh has made ready a slaughter
and set apart those he has invited.

“And it shall come to pass on the day of Yahweh’s sacrifice
that I will punish the princes and the sons of the king,
and all who are clothed in foreign clothing.

On that day I will punish
all who leap across the threshold,{e}
and those who load their lords’ houses
with violent loot and lies.

“On that day,” declares Yahweh,
“there shall be the sound of a cry from the Fish Gate,
a wail from the Second Quarter,{f}
and a great crash from the hills.

At that time I will search Jerusalem with lamps,
and I will punish the men
who are thickening on their dregs,{h}
who say in their heart,
‘Yahweh will not do good,
nor will he do evil.’

Their wealth shall become plunder
and their houses a waste.
Though they build houses, they shall not dwell in them;
though they plant vineyards, they shall not drink their wine.”

The great day of Yahweh is near,
it is near and hurries greatly.
Hark, the day of Yahweh! It is bitter;
the mighty man cries aloud there.

That day will be a day of rage,{i}
a time of anguish and misery,
a time of wreckage and waste,
a time of darkness and dimness,
a time of storm clouds and blackness,

a day of the ram’s horn and of the war cry
against the walled cities
and against the high corner towers.

“I will bring distress upon mankind,
and they shall walk like the blind,
because they have sinned against Yahweh;
their blood shall be poured out like dust,
and their flesh like dung.”

Neither their silver nor their gold
will have power to save them
on the day of Yahweh’s fury.
His blazing jealousy will consume
the whole earth,
for he will bring a sudden, terrifying end
to everyone living on the planet.

notes.text: Zephaniah means “Yahweh has hidden” or “Yahweh has treasured up”; Cushi means “Cushite”; Gedaliah, “Yahweh is great”; Amariah, “Yahweh has spoken”; and Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens.” This Hezekiah may be the king of that name (reigned about 715–686 BC), though the text does not say so. Josiah reigned about 640–609 BC.
The Hebrew phrase “and the stumbling blocks” (perhaps meaning idols) is obscure, and the Septuagint lacks it.
Hebrew kemarim, a word used for priests of foreign gods (compare 2 Kings 23:5 and Hosea 10:5). The Septuagint has “the names of the priests.”
Malcam means “their king.” It probably refers to Milcom, the god of the Ammonites (1 Kings 11:5), and some ancient versions read “Milcom.” The Septuagint has “their king.”
This may refer to a pagan custom (compare 1 Samuel 5:5), or to palace servants rushing in to seize the goods of others.
The Fish Gate and the Second Quarter (Hebrew Mishneh) were in the northern part of Jerusalem.
Hebrew Makhtesh, “mortar” or “hollow,” probably a district of Jerusalem. “The people of Canaan” may also be translated “the merchants.”
That is, like wine left too long on its sediment: complacent and stagnant (compare Jeremiah 48:11).
In the Latin Vulgate, the opening words of this verse are Dies irae, dies illa (“A day of wrath, that day”). They gave the medieval hymn Dies irae its name.

verses.text:
Gather yourselves together and gather,{a}
O nation without shame,

before the decree brings forth—
like chaff the day passes by—
before the fierce anger of Yahweh
comes upon you,
before there comes upon you
the day of the anger of Yahweh.

Disaster for those living along the coast,
you nation of Cretans!{d}
Yahweh’s message is aimed at you,
Canaan, land of the Philistines:
I will wipe you out, leaving no one living there.

And the land by the sea shall become pastures,
caves for shepherds, and pens for sheep.{e}

“I have listened to Moab’s insults
and the abuse of the Ammonites,
who have mocked my people
and boasted over their borders.

Therefore, as surely as I live,” announces Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel,{f}
“Moab will end up like Sodom,
and Ammon like Gomorrah,
overgrown with weeds, pits of salt,
and permanent ruin.
The rest of my people will loot them;
those of my nation who are left will take their land.”

This is what they get for their arrogance,
for scorning and boasting
against the people of Yahweh of Armies.

Yahweh will terrify them,
for he will wither all the earth’s gods;{g}
and every distant shore of the nations
will worship him, each in its own place.

You also, O Cushites,{h}
shall be slain by my sword.

And he will stretch out his hand against the north
and destroy Assyria,
and he will make Nineveh a desolation,
dry as the wilderness.

Flocks will bed down in her center,
every kind of creature;{i}
the desert owl and the porcupine
will roost on her capitals;
hooting will sound from the windows,
rubble will fill the doorways,
because he has stripped her cedar paneling bare.

This is the exultant city
that dwelt securely,
that said in her heart,
“I am, and there is none else.”
How she has become a desolation,
a lair for wild beasts!
Everyone who passes by her
hisses and shakes his fist.

notes.text: The Hebrew of verses 1–2 is difficult. The verb in verse 1 may mean “gather like stubble,” and the phrase translated “before the decree takes effect” is literally “before the decree gives birth.”
“Hidden” (Hebrew sathar) may echo the name Zephaniah (“Yahweh has hidden”), though the verb is different.
The verse plays on the Hebrew names: Gaza (‘Azzah) will be forsaken (‘azuvah), and Ekron (‘Eqron) will be uprooted (te‘aqer).
The Cherethites were a people of the coast, closely linked with the Philistines and probably from Crete (Kaphtor).
The Hebrew word translated “meadows” (keroth) is uncertain. It may refer to wells or to shepherds’ huts, and it may echo “Cherethites” in verse 5.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is translated “Yahweh of Armies” throughout.
Or “he will make lean,” that is, cut off the offerings by which the gods were thought to be fed.
Cush is the upper Nile region (ancient Nubia). Egypt was ruled by a Cushite dynasty until 656 BC.

“Nation” may refer to any kind of creature (“every kind of beast”). The birds and animals named in this verse cannot be identified with certainty. The Septuagint differs in several places, for example “ravens in her porches.”

verses.text:
Woe to her who is rebellious and defiled,
the oppressing city!{a}

I said, ‘Surely you will fear me;
you will accept correction.’
Then her dwelling would not be cut off,
for all that I appointed against her.
But they rose early and made all their deeds corrupt.

“Therefore wait for me,” declares Yahweh,
“until the day that I rise up for the prey.{b}
For my judgment is to gather the nations,
that I may assemble the kingdoms,
to pour my indignation on them,
even all my fierce anger;
for all the earth shall be devoured
by the fire of my zeal.

In that day you will not be ashamed
for any of your doings
in which you transgressed against me;
for then I will take away from among you
those who exult in their pride,
and you shall no longer be haughty
on my holy mountain.

Instead I will leave among you
a poor and humble people,
who will find shelter in Yahweh’s name.

Shout for joy, daughter of Zion;
sing out, Israel!
Rejoice and celebrate with your whole heart,
daughter of Jerusalem!

Behold, at that time I will deal with all who afflict you,
and I will rescue the limping
and gather those who were driven away,
and I will make them a praise and a name
in every land where they were put to shame.{h}

At that time I will lead you home,
and at that time I will assemble you;
I will make you famous and honored
among every people on earth,
when I reverse your misfortunes before your very eyes,” says Yahweh.

notes.text: Hebrew mor’ah, “rebellious,” may play on mar’ah, “seen,” or on Moriah, the temple mount. The city is Jerusalem.
Hebrew la‘ad, “for the prey.” The Septuagint has “for a witness,” reading the same letters as le‘ed.
Literally “I will turn to the peoples a pure lip.” The Wadi Murabba‘at Minor Prophets scroll reads “upon the peoples.”
That is, “side by side, with one accord.”
The Hebrew of the second line is difficult. Some take “the daughter of Putsai” as a place name. The Septuagint has “I will receive my dispersed ones; they shall offer sacrifices to me.”
Literally “he will be silent in his love,” perhaps meaning that he will no longer speak of their sins. The Septuagint has “and shall renew you in his love,” reading yehaddesh for yaharish.
The Hebrew of this verse is obscure, and the translation is uncertain. The Septuagint has “And I will gather your afflicted ones. Alas! who has taken up a reproach against her?”
Literally “in all the earth, their shame.”

books.name: Haggai
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, 4QXII-b and -e) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Haggai also survive (reportedly) in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 1:2). Dates are given with their approximate modern months; the notes give the original month and, where it is commonly reckoned, the exact date. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: in Haggai, English and Hebrew verse numbers are the same.

verses.text: On the first day of the sixth month of King Darius’s second year (in August–September),{a} a message from Yahweh came through the prophet Haggai{b} for Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who governed Judah, and for the high priest Joshua son of Jehozadak:{c}
“Thus says Yahweh of Armies:{d} This people says, ‘The time has not come, the time for the house of Yahweh to be rebuilt.’”
Then Yahweh’s message came through the prophet Haggai:
“Is it a time for you yourselves to dwell in your paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins?{e}
Now therefore, thus says Yahweh of Armies: Set your heart on your ways.

You have sown much and brought in little; you eat, but never to fullness; you drink, but never to drunkenness; you clothe yourselves, but no one is warm. And he who earns wages earns them for a bag pierced with holes.
“Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Set your heart on your ways.
Go up into the hills, bring timber, and rebuild the house, so I can enjoy it and be honored there, says Yahweh.

You expected a large harvest, but it turned out small; whatever you brought home, I blew away. Why? announces Yahweh of Armies. Because my house remains a ruin, while every one of you hurries off to his own house.
Therefore over you the heavens have held back the dew, and the earth has held back its produce.
I have summoned a drought{f} over the land and the hills, over the grain, the new wine, the oil, whatever the soil produces, over people and livestock, and over everything they work for.”

Then Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of Yahweh their God and the words of Haggai the prophet, as Yahweh their God had sent him. And the people feared before Yahweh.
Then Haggai, the messenger of Yahweh, spoke to the people with Yahweh’s message,{g} saying, “I am with you, declares Yahweh.”

And Yahweh stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and the spirit of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and the spirit of all the remnant of the people. And they came and did work on the house of Yahweh of Armies, their God,
on the twenty-fourth day of the month, in the sixth month (in August–September), in the second year of Darius the king.{h}

notes.text: Hebrew “in the sixth month,” that is, Elul, in the calendar whose year begins in the spring. The second year of Darius I (who reigned 522–486 BC) is 520 BC. As the dates are commonly reckoned, this day was about August 29, 520 BC. Because the Hebrew months were lunar, each corresponds to parts of two modern months.
Haggai probably means “festal” (from hag, “feast”). The Septuagint has “Speak to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, of the tribe of Judah.”

Zerubbabel probably means “seed of Babylon”; Shealtiel, “I have asked God”; Joshua, “Yahweh saves” (in Greek, Iēsous, “Jesus”); Jehozadak, “Yahweh is righteous.” Joshua is called Jeshua in Ezra and Nehemiah.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is translated “Yahweh of Armies” throughout.
Hebrew harev, “in ruins.” The same word appears in verse 9.
Hebrew horev, “drought,” plays on harev, “in ruins” (verses 4 and 9): because the house lies in ruins (harev), Yahweh calls a drought (horev).
Or “with Yahweh’s commission.” The word “messenger” (mal’akh) is the same word as in Malachi (“my messenger”).
About September 21, 520 BC. Some scholars attach the date to the beginning of 2:1.

verses.text: On the twenty-first day of the seventh month (in September–October),{a} Yahweh’s message came through the prophet Haggai:{b}
“Speak now to Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, governor of Judah, and to Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest, and to the remnant of the people, saying,
‘Who is left among you who saw this house in its former glory? And how do you see it now? Is it not as nothing in your eyes?

Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, declares Yahweh. Be strong, O Joshua son of Jehozadak, the high priest. Be strong, all you people of the land, declares Yahweh. Work, for I am with you, declares Yahweh of Armies,
This is the promise I made you when you left Egypt.{c} My Spirit remains among you. Do not be afraid.
“‘For thus says Yahweh of Armies: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land.{d}
And I will make all nations tremble, and the desirable things of every nation shall come,{e} and I will fill this house with glory, says Yahweh of Armies.
The silver is mine, and the gold is mine, declares Yahweh of Armies.
The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former, says Yahweh of Armies. And in this place I will give peace, declares Yahweh of Armies.’”{f}
On the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (in November–December) of Darius’s second year,{g} Yahweh’s message came to the prophet Haggai:
“Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Ask the priests for a ruling:{h}
‘If a man carries holy meat in the fold of his garment, and with his fold touches bread or pottage or wine or oil or any food, will it be made holy?’” And the priests answered, “No.”
Then Haggai said, “If someone defiled by a corpse touches any of these, will it be defiled?” And the priests answered, “It will be defiled.”
Then Haggai answered and said, “So is this people, and so is this nation before me, declares Yahweh, and so is every work of their hands; and what they offer there is unclean.{i}
“And now, set your heart on it from this day onward.{j} Before stone was laid upon stone in the temple of Yahweh,
how did you fare? When one came to a heap of twenty measures, there were but ten; when one came to the wine vat to draw fifty measures, there were but twenty.{k}
I struck you with blight and with mildew and with hail in all the work of your hands, yet you did not turn to me,{l} declares Yahweh.
Set your heart from this day onward, from the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month (in November–December), from the day that the foundation of the temple of Yahweh was laid—set your heart on it:
Is the seed yet in the barn? As for the vine, the fig tree, the pomegranate, and the olive tree, they have borne nothing. From this day on I will bless you.”
And the word of Yahweh came a second time to Haggai on the twenty-fourth day of the month, saying,
“Tell Zerubbabel, governor of Judah: I am about to shake the sky and the earth,
and I will topple royal thrones and break the power of the foreign kingdoms. I will overturn chariots and their drivers; horses and riders will fall, each killed by his comrade’s sword.

On that day, declares Yahweh of Armies, I will take you, O Zerubbabel my servant, the son of Shealtiel, declares Yahweh, and I will make you like a signet ring,{m} for I have chosen you, declares Yahweh of Armies.”

notes.text: Tishri, the seventh month. The twenty-first day was the last day of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:34–36). As commonly reckoned, it was about October 17, 520 BC.
The Wadi Murabba‘at Minor Prophets scroll reads “came to Haggai.”
The Septuagint lacks the first clause, “according to the word that I covenanted with you when you came out of Egypt.”
Quoted in Hebrews 12:26–27. The Septuagint has “Yet once I will shake the heaven, and the earth.”

Or “the desire of all nations shall come.” The Hebrew noun is singular (“desire,” “what is desired”), but the verb is plural, which suggests valued things. The Latin Vulgate’s “the desired one of all nations will come” gave rise to a messianic reading. The Septuagint has “the choice portions of all the nations.”
The Septuagint adds “even peace of soul for a possession to everyone who builds, to raise up this temple.”
About December 18, 520 BC. Kislev is the ninth month.
Hebrew torah, “instruction” or “law.”

The Septuagint adds “and whoever approaches them shall be defiled because of their early burdens; they shall be pained because of their toils; and you have hated him who reproved in the gates” (compare Amos 5:10).
Hebrew “upward,” meaning either “from this day forward” or “backward from this day.” The same expression appears in verse 18.
The measures are not named in the Hebrew. The Septuagint has “twenty measures of barley.” In the second clause, the Hebrew “fifty” is literally “fifty of the winepress” (purah).
Compare Amos 4:9. The Hebrew is literally “yet there was not you to me.” The Septuagint has “yet you did not return to me.”
A signet ring was a royal seal, a sign of authority. This reverses the word against Zerubbabel’s grandfather Jehoiachin (Coniah) in Jeremiah 22:24.

books.name: Zechariah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex (the Masoretic Text). It was checked against the Hebrew Minor Prophets scrolls from Qumran (4QXII, 4QXII-a, -e, and -g) and Wadi Murabba‘at (MurXII, early 2nd century AD), whose text is very close to the Masoretic Text. The transcriptions used are Martin Abegg’s, as published in the ETCBC Dead Sea Scrolls dataset. It was also checked against the Septuagint, using Brenton’s public-domain English translation. Portions of Zechariah also survive in the Greek Minor Prophets Scroll from Nahal Hever (8HevXIIgr, about the turn of the era), which is a revision of the Septuagint toward the Hebrew. Its readings could not be checked directly, so any that are cited are marked “reported.” Significant differences are footnoted; differences of spelling and damage to the scrolls are not. The divine title YHWH Tseva’ot is translated “Yahweh of Armies” (see the note at 1:3). Dates are given with their approximate modern months; the notes give the original month and, where it is commonly reckoned, the exact date. Poetry is printed line by line. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible: English 1:18–21 is Hebrew 2:1–4, and English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:5–17.

verses.text: In the eighth month (October–November) of Darius’s second year,{a} Yahweh’s word came to the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,{b}
“Yahweh was very angry with your fathers.
Therefore say to them, Thus says Yahweh of Armies:{c} Return to me, declares Yahweh of Armies, and I will return to you, says Yahweh of Armies.

Do not be like your ancestors, whom the earlier prophets called out to: ‘This is what Yahweh of Armies says: Turn away at once from your wicked paths and your wicked actions.’ But they would not listen or give me any notice, says Yahweh.
Your fathers—where are they? And the prophets—do they live forever?

But the warnings and decrees I commissioned my servants the prophets to deliver, did they not overtake your ancestors? They repented and said, ‘Yahweh of Armies has done to us exactly what he planned for our paths and actions.’”
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, the month of Shebat (January–February), in Darius’s second year,{d} Yahweh’s word came to the prophet Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,
In the night I had a vision: a man riding a red horse, who halted among the myrtle trees in the glen;{e} behind him were red, chestnut, and white horses.{f}
Then I said, “What are these, my lord?” And the angel who talked with me said to me, “I will show you what these are.”
The man standing among the myrtles replied, “These are the ones Yahweh has sent to patrol the earth.”
They reported to Yahweh’s angel, who stood among the myrtles, “We have patrolled the earth, and look, the whole earth is calm and quiet.”
Then the angel of Yahweh answered, “O Yahweh of Armies, until when will you withhold compassion from Jerusalem and from the cities of Judah, with which you have been indignant now seventy years?”{g}
And Yahweh answered the angel who talked with me with good words, words of comfort.
So the angel who talked with me said to me, “Cry out, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies: I am jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion with a great jealousy.
And with great anger I am angry with the nations at ease; for I was only a little angry, but they furthered the evil.
Therefore this is Yahweh’s word: I have come back to Jerusalem in mercy; my house will be rebuilt there, declares Yahweh of Armies, and the surveyor’s cord will be stretched across Jerusalem.’
Proclaim once more: ‘This is what Yahweh of Armies says: My towns will again brim with prosperity, and Yahweh will again console Zion and once more select Jerusalem.’”{h}
And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns!{i}
And I said to the angel who talked with me, “What are these?” And he said to me, “These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem.”
Then Yahweh showed me four craftsmen.

I asked, “What have these come to do?” He replied, “These are the horns that dispersed Judah so that nobody could lift up his head. But these craftsmen have come to frighten them and to hurl down the horns of the nations that raised a horn against Judah’s land in order to scatter its people.”

notes.text: Hebrew “in the eighth month,” that is, Marcheshvan (later Heshvan), in the calendar whose year begins in the spring, in 520 BC. No day is given. Because the Hebrew months were lunar, each corresponds to parts of two modern months.
Zechariah means “Yahweh remembers”; Berechiah, “Yahweh blesses”; Iddo perhaps “timely.” Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 call Zechariah “the son of Iddo,” that is, his grandson or descendant. Compare Matthew 23:35.

Hebrew YHWH Tseva’ot, traditionally “the LORD of hosts.” The “armies” are the forces of heaven (the angels and the stars) and sometimes the armies of Israel. The title is translated “Yahweh of Armies” throughout.
Shebat (Shevat) is the eleventh month. As commonly reckoned, this was about February 15, 519 BC.
Or “in the deep place.” The Septuagint has “between the shady mountains” (also in verses 10–11), reading harim, “mountains,” for hadassim, “myrtles.”
The color of the second group (Hebrew seruqqim) is uncertain: perhaps “sorrel,” “bay,” or “speckled.” The Septuagint has four colors: “red, and grey, and piebald, and white.”
Compare Jeremiah 25:11–12 and 29:10. From the destruction of the temple in 586 BC to this vision is about seventy years (counted inclusively).
Hebrew tov, “good,” also “prosperity.”
English 1:18–21 is Hebrew 2:1–4.

verses.text: And I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand!{a}
I asked, “Where are you headed?” He told me, “To measure Jerusalem, to find out its width and its length.”
And behold, the angel who talked with me went out, and another angel went out to meet him
and he said to him, “Run, speak to this young man, saying, ‘Jerusalem will be settled like unwalled villages, because of the great number of men and cattle in her midst.
And I myself will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares Yahweh, and I will be the glory in her midst.’”
Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, declares Yahweh, for I have spread you out like the four winds of the heavens, declares Yahweh.{b}
Up, O Zion! Escape, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.
For this is what Yahweh of Armies says: after glory he sent me{c} against the nations that plundered you—for whoever touches you touches the apple of his eye:{d}
“For see, I am swinging my hand over them, and they shall be spoil to their own servants; and you will know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me.
Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come, and I will dwell in your midst, declares Yahweh.
And many nations shall join themselves to Yahweh in that day and shall be my people. And I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that Yahweh of Armies has sent me to you.
And Yahweh will take possession of Judah as his portion in the holy land,{e} and will again choose Jerusalem.
Be silent, all flesh, before Yahweh, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling.”

notes.text: English 2:1–13 is Hebrew 2:5–17.
The Septuagint has “for I will gather you from the four winds of heaven.”
The Hebrew of this phrase is obscure. It may mean “after the glory (that is, the vision) he sent me,” or “with glory he sent me,” or “for his glory’s sake.”

Hebrew “his eye.” Jewish tradition lists this as one of the “corrections of the scribes” (tiqqune sopherim), and it reports that the original reading was “my eye.” The word translated “pupil” (bavah) is literally “gate” or “little one” of the eye.
This is the only place in the Hebrew Bible where the land is called “the holy land.”

verses.text: Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of Yahweh, and the Accuser{a} standing at his right hand to accuse him.
And Yahweh said to the Accuser, “Yahweh rebuke you, O Accuser!{b} Yahweh who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?”
Now Joshua was clothed in filthy garments, and he was standing before the angel.

And he spoke up and said to those standing in front of him, “Take the filthy clothes off him.” And to him he said, “See, I have made your iniquity pass away from you, and I will clothe you in fine robes.”
And I said, “Let them put a clean turban on his head.” So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of Yahweh was standing by.
And the angel of Yahweh solemnly charged Joshua, saying,

“This is what Yahweh of Armies says: If you follow my paths and observe my requirements, then you will govern my house and guard my courtyards, and I will grant you free passage among these attendants.
Listen, Joshua the high priest, you and your colleagues seated before you, for they are men who serve as a sign: I am about to bring my servant, the Branch.{c}

For behold, the stone that I have set before Joshua: on one stone are seven eyes.{d} Behold, I will engrave its inscription, declares Yahweh of Armies, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.
In that day, declares Yahweh of Armies, you shall call each man to his neighbor, beneath the vine and beneath the fig tree.”

notes.text: Hebrew hassatan, “the adversary” or “the accuser.” With the article, it is a title (compare Job 1–2), not yet a personal name. The verb “to accuse him” (lesitno) comes from the same root. The Septuagint has “the Devil.”
Compare Jude 9. The Septuagint has “The Lord rebuke you, O Devil.”
Hebrew tsemah, “sprout” or “shoot,” a title of the coming king from David’s line (Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15). See also 6:12.
Or “seven facets.” The verb translated “engrave” is used for cutting gems; the Septuagint has “I am digging a trench.”

verses.text: Then the angel who had spoken to me before came back and woke me, like someone woken from sleep.

And he said to me, “What do you see?” And I said, “I have looked, and there is a lampstand entirely of gold, and its bowl upon its top, and its seven lamps upon it, seven and seven pipes for the lamps that are upon its top.{a}
And there are two olive trees by it, one on the right of the bowl and the other on its left.”
And I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, “What are these, my lord?”
Then the angel who talked with me answered and said to me, “Do you not know what these are?” I said, “No, my lord.”
Then he answered and said to me, “This is the word of Yahweh to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says Yahweh of Armies.
What are you, great mountain? In front of Zerubbabel you will become level ground. He will bring out the capstone to shouts of ‘Blessing, blessing on it!’”{b}
Moreover, the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,
“Zerubbabel’s hands have laid this house’s foundation; his hands will also finish it. Then you will recognize that Yahweh of Armies sent me to you.

For who has despised the day of small things? For these seven shall rejoice and shall see the plumb stone in the hand of Zerubbabel.{c} These are the eyes of Yahweh, which range through the whole earth.”
Then I answered and said to him, “What are these two olive trees on the right and the left of the lampstand?”
A second time I asked him, “What are the two olive branches next to the two golden spouts that empty out the golden oil?”{d}
He answered me, “Do you not know what these things are?” And I said, “No, my lord.”
Then he said, “These are the two sons of oil{e} who stand by the Lord of all the earth.”{f}

notes.text: That is, perhaps seven pipes to each lamp (forty-nine in all), or fourteen in all. The Septuagint has “and seven oil funnels to the lamps.”
Or “Beauty, beauty to it!” (Hebrew hen hen). The Septuagint differs: “I will bring out the stone of the inheritance, the grace of it the equal of my grace.”

Hebrew “the stone, the tin” (ha’even habbedil), probably a plumb weight or a separating stone. The Septuagint has “the plummet of tin.” In the Hebrew, “these seven” are the eyes of Yahweh (compare 3:9).
The Hebrew of this verse is difficult. The word translated “pipes” is unique, and the last phrase is literally “that empty the gold out of themselves.”
Hebrew bene hayyitshar, “sons of fresh oil,” that is, the anointed ones. They are probably Zerubbabel and Joshua. Compare Revelation 11:4.
Hebrew adon, “lord,” not the divine title Adonai. This title also appears at 6:5.

verses.text: Again I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, a flying scroll!{a}
And he said to me, “What do you see?” I answered, “I see a flying scroll. Its length is thirty feet, and its breadth fifteen feet.”{b}

He told me, “This is the curse sweeping over the surface of the whole land. Everyone who steals will be removed, as the one side of the scroll declares, and everyone who swears falsely will be removed, as the other side declares.{c}

I will send it out, declares Yahweh of Armies, and it shall enter the house of the thief and the house of him who swears falsely by my name. And it shall lodge in the midst of his house and consume it, both its timber and its stones.”
Then the angel who was speaking with me stepped forward and told me, “Look up and notice what is appearing.”
And I said, “What is it?” He said, “This is the measuring basket that is going out.”{d} And he said, “This is their eye in all the land.”{e}
And behold, a round cover of lead was lifted,{f} and this was a woman sitting in the basket!
And he said, “This is Wickedness.” And he cast her down into the middle of the basket, and cast the lead weight upon its opening.
Then I raised my eyes and looked, and there came out two women, with wind in their wings; and they had wings like a stork’s wings, and they raised the basket up between the earth and the heavens.
Then I said to the angel who talked with me, “Where are they taking the basket?”
He said to me, “To build a house for it in the land of Shinar.{g} And when it is prepared, it will be set down there on its base.”

notes.text: The Septuagint has “a flying sickle,” reading maggal for megillah.
Hebrew “twenty cubits … ten cubits,” about 9 by 4.5 meters. A cubit is about 18 inches (45 centimeters).
Or “shall be cleaned out” or “shall go unpunished.” The Hebrew word (niqqah) is ambiguous. Each side of the scroll apparently bore one of the two curses.

Hebrew ephah, a dry measure of about 3/5 bushel (22 liters). Here it is the container that held that amount, a basket or barrel; so also in verses 7–11. It could not normally hold a person, which marks this as a vision.
Hebrew “their eye.” The Septuagint has “their iniquity,” reading ‘awonam for ‘enam, a difference of one letter. Many translators follow it.
Hebrew kikkar, “round thing,” the same word used for a talent, a weight of about 75 pounds (34 kilograms). Literally “a talent of lead”; the Septuagint has the same.
Shinar is Babylonia (Genesis 10:10 and 11:2, the land of the tower of Babel). The Septuagint has “the land of Babylon.”

verses.text: And again I lifted up my eyes and saw, and behold, four chariots coming out from between two mountains! And the mountains were mountains of bronze.
With the first chariot were red horses, and with the second chariot black horses,
in the third chariot white horses, and in the fourth chariot spotted, strong horses.{a}
Then I answered and said to the angel who talked with me, “What are these, my lord?”
The angel replied, “These are heading out to the four winds of heaven, after standing in the presence of the Lord of the whole earth.{b}
The one with the black horses is going out to the land of the north, and the white have gone out after them,{c} and the dappled have gone out to the land of the south.”
And the strong ones went out and sought to go and walk to and fro through the earth. And he said, “Go, walk to and fro through the earth.” So they walked to and fro through the earth.
Then he called to me and said, “Look, those heading to the northern land have settled my Spirit in the northern land.”{d}
And the word of Yahweh came to me, saying,
“Take from the captivity, from Heldai, from Tobijah, and from Jedaiah, and come yourself on that same day; come to the house of Josiah son of Zephaniah, where they have arrived from Babylon.{e}
Take from them silver and gold, and make crowns,{f} and set it on the head of Joshua the son of Jehozadak, the high priest.
And speak to him, saying, ‘Thus says Yahweh of Armies: See, a man whose name is Branch! From his place he shall sprout up,{g} and he shall build the temple of Yahweh.
He is the one who will construct Yahweh’s temple and wear majesty, and sit and govern from his throne. There will also be a priest at his throne,{h} and the two will share a peaceful understanding.’
And the crown shall be for Helem and for Tobijah and for Jedaiah and for Hen son of Zephaniah, as a memorial in the temple of Yahweh.{i}
People from far away will come and help build Yahweh’s temple. Then you will recognize that Yahweh of Armies sent me to you. All this will happen if you faithfully listen to Yahweh your God.”

notes.text: The colors are uncertain. The Hebrew of the fourth group has two words (“dappled” and “strong”); the Septuagint has “piebald and ash-coloured.” In verse 7, “strong” (amutstsim) may be another color.
Or “These are the four spirits of heaven.” The Hebrew ruhot means both “winds” and “spirits.”
Or “toward the west” (literally “behind them”). The Hebrew does not mention a group going east.
Or “have set my anger at rest.” The Hebrew is literally “have caused my spirit to rest.” The Septuagint has “my anger.”

Heldai means “mole” or “enduring”; Tobijah, “Yahweh is good”; Jedaiah, “Yahweh knows”; Josiah, “Yahweh supports.” The Septuagint translates the names as common nouns: “from the chief men, and from the useful men of it, and from them that have understood it.”
Hebrew ‘atarot is plural (“crowns”), but the verb “set” and the verb in verse 14 are singular. It may mean a single elaborate crown.
Hebrew yitsmah, “he shall sprout,” a play on Tsemah, “Branch.” Compare 3:8.
The Septuagint has “and there shall be a priest on his right hand.”

Helem is probably Heldai (verse 10), and Hen (“grace”) is probably Josiah. Hen may also be translated “as a kindness to the son of Zephaniah.” The Septuagint has “to them that wait patiently … and for the favour of the son of Sophonias, and for a psalm in the house of the Lord.”

verses.text: In King Darius’s fourth year, Yahweh’s word came to Zechariah on the fourth day of the ninth month, Kislev (November–December).{a}
Now Bethel had sent Sharezer and Regem-melech and their men to entreat the favor of Yahweh,{b}
saying to the priests of the house of Yahweh of Armies and to the prophets, “Shall I weep in the fifth month (in July–August), abstaining as I have done these many years?”{c}
Then the word of Yahweh of Armies came to me, saying,

“Speak to everyone in the land and to the priests: In the fifth and seventh months (September–October) of these seventy years, when you fasted and mourned, was it really for me that you fasted, for me?{d}
And when you eat and when you drink, is it not you who eat and you who drink?
Were not these the words that Yahweh proclaimed by the former prophets, when Jerusalem was inhabited and at ease, with her cities around her, and the Negev and the lowland were inhabited?”{e}
And the word of Yahweh came to Zechariah, saying,
“Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Judge with true justice; show steadfast love and compassion, each to his brother;
do not exploit the widow, the orphan, the foreigner, or the poor; and let none of you plan harm against a fellow Israelite in your heart.”
But they would not pay attention; they turned a stubborn back and dulled their ears so they could not listen.
They made their hearts like adamant so as not to hear the law and the words that Yahweh of Armies had sent by his Spirit through the former prophets. Therefore great wrath came from Yahweh of Armies.
“And it came to pass that as he called and they would not hear, so they called and I would not hear,” says Yahweh of Armies,

“and I scattered them with a storm wind among all the nations that they had not known. Thus the land was left desolate behind them, so that no one went to and fro, and they made the pleasant land a desolation.”

notes.text: Kislev (Chislev) is the ninth month. As commonly reckoned, this was about December 7, 518 BC, nearly two years after the visions of 1:7–6:15.

Or “Now Bethel-sharezer had sent Regem-melech and his men.” Sharezer means “protect the king”; Regem-melech perhaps “friend of the king.” The Septuagint has “And Sarasar and Arbeseer the king and his men sent to Bethel.”

Hebrew “in the fifth month,” that is, Ab. The fast in this month mourned the burning of the temple in 586 BC (2 Kings 25:8–9). The Septuagint has “The holy offering has come in here in the fifth month.”
Hebrew “in the fifth and in the seventh,” that is, Ab and Tishri. The fast in the seventh month mourned the murder of Gedaliah (2 Kings 25:25).
Hebrew Negev, “the dry country,” the south of Judah; and the Shephelah, “the lowland,” the low hills toward the coast.

verses.text: And the word of Yahweh of Armies came, saying,
“Thus says Yahweh of Armies: I am jealous for Zion with great jealousy, and I am jealous for her with great wrath.
Thus says Yahweh: I have returned to Zion and will dwell in the midst of Jerusalem, and Jerusalem shall be called the City of Faithfulness, and the mountain of Yahweh of Armies, the Holy Mountain.
Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Old men and old women will yet dwell in the broad places of Jerusalem, each man with his staff in his hand for very age.
And the streets of the city shall be full of boys and girls playing in its streets.
Thus says Yahweh of Armies: If it is too wonderful in the eyes of the remnant of this people in those days, should it also be too wonderful in my eyes? declares Yahweh of Armies.
Thus says Yahweh of Armies: Behold, I will save my people from the land of the sunrise and from the land of the sunset,{a}
and I will bring them to dwell in the midst of Jerusalem. And they shall be my people, and I will be their God, in faithfulness and in righteousness.”

Thus says Yahweh of Armies: “Let your hands be strong, you who hear in these days these words from the mouth of the prophets, which were spoken in the day the house of Yahweh of Armies was founded, that the temple might be built.
For before those days there were no wages for people or for animals; and nobody who traveled was safe from the enemy; I set everyone against his own neighbor.
But now I will not deal with the remnant of this people as in the former days, declares Yahweh of Armies.
For peace will be sown: the vine will yield its fruit, the soil will give its harvest, and the skies will release their dew. I will let the remnant of this people inherit all of this.{b}
And as you have been a curse among the nations, O house of Judah and house of Israel, so will I save you, and you shall be a blessing. Do not fear, but let your hands be strong.”
