Uzziah then said to her, “My daughter, the Most High God has blessed you beyond every woman upon the earth;{c} and blessed be the Lord God, maker of heaven and earth, who directed you to wound the head of the chief of our enemies.
Never shall the hope you showed{d} fade from the hearts of people as they remember God’s might, for all ages.

God grant that this be an everlasting glory to you, and may he visit you with blessings, since you did not hold back your own life when our people were humbled, but went out to meet our fall, walking a straight road before our God.” And all the people said, “Amen! Amen!”{e}

notes.text: Short sword: Greek akinakēs, the Persian short sword or dagger, another Persian-period detail.
The hand of a woman: compare Judges 4:9, 21 (Jael and Sisera) and 9:53–54 (Abimelech). The phrase answers Judith’s prayer at 9:10.
Above all the women on earth: compare the blessing on Jael in Judges 5:24, and on Mary in Luke 1:42.
Your hope: some manuscripts read “your praise.”
Amen! Amen!: Greek genoito, genoito, “so be it, so be it,” the usual Greek rendering of Hebrew amen.

verses.text: Then Judith told them, “Brothers, hear me. Take this head and fasten it up on the battlements of your wall.

When dawn lights the sky and the sun comes up over the land, each of you is to take his gear of war, and every strong man is to march out of the town. Put a leader at their head, as though you meant to go down into the plain upon the Assyrian outpost; only do not go down.

Then they will seize their arms and hurry to their camp and rouse the officers of the Assyrian army. These will rush to the tent of Holofernes and will not find him. Panic will fall on them, and they will flee before you.
Then you, and everyone who dwells anywhere in Israel’s territory, must follow on their heels and strike them down along their roads.
But first, before any of this, call Achior the Ammonite to me, that he may look on and know the man who held Israel’s house in contempt and packed him off to us as though to die.”
They therefore sent for Achior from Uzziah’s house. When he arrived and beheld Holofernes’ head in a man’s hand amid the gathered people, he fell forward on his face and his senses left him.
Once they had lifted him up, he dropped at Judith’s feet and bowed down before her, saying, “May you be blessed in all Judah’s dwellings, and among all nations! Whoever hears your name will tremble.
So now, relate to me everything you have done during these days.” Judith then recounted to him before all the people everything she had done from the day she left until the hour she spoke with them.
When she finished speaking, the people raised a great shout, and their town rang with joyful noise.
When Achior saw all that the God of Israel had done, he believed in God firmly. He was circumcised, and was joined to the house of Israel, remaining so to this day.{a}
As soon as day broke, they hung the head of Holofernes from the wall. Every man took up his weapons, and they went out by companies to the passes in the mountains.
When the Assyrians saw them, they sent a message to their commanders, who went to the generals, the captains over thousands, and every other officer.
They came to Holofernes’ tent and said to the steward of all his household, “Wake our lord, for the slaves have dared to come down against us to give battle, to their own utter destruction.”
So Bagoas went in and knocked at the entrance of the tent,{b} for he supposed that Holofernes was sleeping with Judith.
When no one answered, he opened it and went into the bedchamber and found him sprawled dead on the platform,{c} with his head cut off and gone.
He cried out with a loud voice, weeping and groaning and shouting, and tore his clothes.
Then he went into the tent where Judith had been lodging; finding her gone, he leaped out among the troops and cried,
“The slaves have broken faith! A single Hebrew woman has put shame on King Nebuchadnezzar’s house. See: Holofernes on the ground, and no head on him!”
On hearing these words the Assyrian army’s chiefs ripped their tunics, their spirits were thrown into turmoil, and a mighty cry and clamor went up in the midst of the camp.

notes.text: To this day: Deuteronomy 23:3 forbade Ammonites to enter the assembly of the LORD. Achior’s full acceptance into Israel by circumcision is one of the book’s striking features; later rabbinic discussion debated how such a rule applied (reported). Scholarly review recommended.
The entrance of the tent: literally “the curtain of the tent,” perhaps clapping his hands before it, since one could not knock on a curtain.
Platform: Greek chelōnis, literally “tortoise,” apparently the low step or footboard of a couch. The sense is uncertain.

verses.text: When those still in their tents heard it, they were dumbfounded at what had happened.
Fear and trembling fell upon them; no man held his place beside his comrade any longer, but streaming out all together they fled along every track across the plain and through the hill country.
Those who had camped in the hills around Bethulia were routed as well. Then the Israelites, every fighting man among them, poured out against them.

Uzziah sent messengers to Betomasthaim, Bebai, Choba and Kola,{a} and throughout Israel’s territory, to report what had been accomplished and to urge all of them to pour out upon the enemy and destroy them.

On hearing this, the Israelites with one accord fell upon them and cut them down as far as Choba. Men came also from Jerusalem and from all the hill country, for word had reached them of what had befallen the enemy’s camp. Those in Gilead and in Galilee outflanked them and inflicted heavy losses, until they had passed Damascus and its borders.
The remaining people of Bethulia swept down on the Assyrian camp, plundered it, and became very rich.

The Israelites, returning from the slaughter, took possession of what was left; and the villages and farmsteads of the hill country and the plain seized a great deal of booty, for there was an immense quantity of it.

Then the high priest Joakim, together with the council of elders of Israel resident in Jerusalem, arrived to view the benefits the Lord had wrought for Israel, to see Judith with their own eyes, and to wish her peace.
When they came to her, they all blessed her with one voice and said to her, “You are Jerusalem’s pride, Israel’s great glory, the great boast of our race!
“All this your hand has achieved; you have wrought blessing for Israel, and God has been pleased with them. May the Lord Almighty bless you for ever and ever!” And all the people said, “Amen!”

For thirty days the whole people stripped the camp of spoil. To Judith they presented Holofernes’ tent, every piece of his silver plate, his couches and drinking bowls, and all his gear. She accepted these, packed her mule, yoked her wagons, and piled everything onto them.
Every woman in Israel hurried to see her; they called down blessings on her, and a band of them formed a dance for her. In her hands she took leafy wands,{b} and passed them to the women about her;

and she and her companions wore wreaths of olive leaves. She walked in front of everyone in the dance, leading all the women, while all Israel’s men followed, armed and garlanded, singing as they went.
Judith began this song of thanksgiving before all Israel, and all the people loudly sang this hymn of praise after her.{c}

notes.text: Kola: Betomasthaim is probably the Betomesthaim of 4:6. Bebai, Choba (compare 4:4) and Kola are unidentified.
Leafy wands: Greek thyrsoi, the leafy staffs carried in processions in honor of Dionysus. Here they are simply festive emblems (compare 2 Maccabees 10:7).
After her: this verse is 16:1 in the Latin-based numbering of the KJV Apocrypha, where chapter 15 has 13 verses and chapter 16 has 26. This translation follows the Greek numbering (14 and 25 verses).

verses.text:
Out of the northern hills Asshur came marching,
tens of thousands strong in his might;
their host stopped up the torrent beds,
and their horsemen blanketed the hills.

He vowed to set my borders ablaze,
to slay my young men with the sword,
to dash my nursing infants to the ground,
to seize my little ones as plunder
and make my maidens his spoil.

The Lord Almighty has thwarted them
by a woman’s hand.

For their champion did not fall by young men’s blows,
nor did sons of Titans{b} strike him down,
nor towering giants attack him;
but Judith, Merari’s daughter,
undid him by the beauty of her face.

She stripped off her widow’s robe
for the lifting up of Israel’s sufferers.
With fragrant oil she smoothed her face,

bound up her hair with a headband,
and put on a linen gown to lead him astray.

Her sandal ravished his eye,
her beauty took his soul captive,
and the sword went through his neck!

Persians shuddered at her daring,
and Medes were dismayed at her boldness.{c}

To my God I will raise a fresh hymn:
Lord, great are you, and full of glory,
wonderful in strength, unconquerable.

Let all your creation serve you,
for you spoke, and they came to be.
You sent out your spirit, and it built them;
there is none who can withstand your voice.

For the mountains will be shaken to their foundations, and the waters with them;
before your face the rocks will melt like wax.
But to those who fear you
you will still show mercy.

Woe to the nations that rise up against my race!
On judgment day the Lord Almighty will repay them,
giving their bodies over to fire and worm,
and they will weep in pain forever.{e}
When they got to Jerusalem, they worshiped God. Once the people were cleansed, they presented their burnt offerings, their voluntary offerings, and their gifts.

Every article of Holofernes that the people had bestowed on her Judith consecrated to God; the canopy too, which she had carried off for herself from his sleeping quarters, she presented to God as a dedicated gift.
For three months the people continued feasting in Jerusalem before the sanctuary, and Judith stayed with them.
After this they all returned home, each to his own inheritance. Judith went back to Bethulia and lived on her estate, and in her time she was honored throughout the whole country.
Many longed to wed her, yet from the day her husband Manasseh died and was joined to his people, she never lay with a man as long as she lived.

Her fame went on increasing, and she grew old in the house of her husband until she was a hundred and five. Her maid she released into freedom. At Bethulia she died, and they laid her in the tomb-cave of Manasseh her husband.
For seven days Israel’s house lamented her. While still living she had shared out her goods among all the near kin of Manasseh her husband and among her own closest relations.
In Judith’s lifetime, and for many days after she died, there was no one to make the Israelites afraid again.{f}

notes.text: A God who crushes wars: so Exodus 15:3 in the Greek, “the Lord who shatters wars.” The song draws on the Song of the Sea (Exodus 15) and the Song of Deborah (Judges 5).
Titans: in Greek myth the Titans were the older race of gods; in the Greek Bible the word can render Hebrew Rephaim, the legendary giants (as in 2 Samuel 5:18, 22 in some Greek manuscripts).
Boldness: the mention of Persians and Medes, rather than Assyrians, is one of the book’s anachronisms (see the note at 1:1).
Cowered: the subjects of the verbs in this verse are ambiguous in the Greek; the translation supplies “the enemy” where the sense seems to require it. Scholarly review recommended.
Weep in pain forever: compare Isaiah 66:24; Sirach 7:17. This is one of the earliest expressions of eternal punishment for the wicked.
Long time after her death: the Vulgate adds that the day of Judith’s victory was celebrated as a festival among the Jews; this is not in the Greek.

books.name: Additions to Esther
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of Esther in A. Rahlfs, *Septuaginta* (1935), checked against H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint* (1891–94; public domain). The Greek book of Esther contains six passages, about 107 verses, that are not in the Hebrew. Only these six Additions are given here; the rest of Esther appears with the Hebrew canon. Additions B and E, the two royal letters, were composed in Greek; A, C, D and F may go back to a Semitic original (reported). The colophon at F11 dates the Greek translation to the reign of a Ptolemy and a Cleopatra, probably in the late 2nd or early 1st century BC. Two numbering systems are in use. Jerome placed the Additions together at the end of Esther in the Latin Vulgate, and the King James Apocrypha follows that order as Esther 10:4–16:24. As a result, the dream’s interpretation (10:4–13) comes before the dream itself (11:2–12:6). Modern editions instead put each Addition back in its place in the Greek story and label them A to F. This translation presents them in the story’s order, as chapters 1–6 = Additions A–F. Verses are numbered within each Addition (A1–17, B1–7, C1–30, D1–16, E1–24, F1–11), following the KJV verse divisions. Each chapter heading gives both the Rahlfs reference (for example, Esther 1:1a–r) and the KJV reference (for example, 11:2–12:6): A = 11:2–12:6; B = 13:1–7; C = 13:8–14:19; D = 15:1–16; E = 16:1–24; F = 10:4–11:1. The Additions supply what the Hebrew book lacks: the name of God, prayer, and an explicit account of divine help. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord.” Months are given with their approximate modern equivalents. The Additions are received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches (in the Catholic Bible as part of Esther); Protestant churches place them among the Apocrypha.

chapters.heading: Addition A: Mordecai’s Dream and the Eunuchs’ Plot
chapters.title: Greek Esther 1:1a–r (KJV Apocrypha 11:2–12:6). In the Greek book this stands before Esther 1:1.

verses.text: It was the second regnal year of Artaxerxes the Great,{a} on the first day of Nisan (March–April),{b} that Mordecai{c} son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of Benjamin’s tribe, beheld a dream.
A Jew by birth, he made his home in the city of Susa,{d} a man of standing who waited on the king within his court.
He was one of that captive company whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried off out of Jerusalem along with Jeconiah king of Judea.{e} And this was his dream:
Behold, voices and din, thunderclaps and quaking, turmoil upon the earth!
And behold, two huge dragons{f} came out, the pair of them primed to wrestle, and from them there rose a mighty roar.
At that roar every nation got itself ready for war, to wage battle on a nation of righteous ones.
And behold, a day of murk and gloom, of pressure and narrow straits, of ill-usage and vast turmoil upon the earth!
The whole righteous nation was thrown into confusion; dreading the evils laid up for them, they braced themselves to perish, and they raised a cry to God.
And out of their cry, as if out of a small spring, there came to be a great river, waters in plenty.
Light, and the sun came up; the humble were raised on high and swallowed up the illustrious.
Mordecai, the one who had seen this dream and what God had purposed to do, awoke; he held it fast in his heart and longed to grasp it in its every word, until night came.
Now Mordecai was taking his ease in the court with Gabatha and Tharra,{g} two of the king’s eunuchs who kept watch over the court.
He caught their reckonings and searched out their worries, and he learned that they were making ready to lay hands on King Artaxerxes; so he informed the king about them.
The king put the two eunuchs to examination; they owned the deed and were led away.{h}
The king wrote these matters down for a record, and Mordecai likewise put into writing an account of them.
Then the king charged Mordecai to serve in the court and bestowed gifts on him in return for these things.
But Haman son of Hammedatha, the Bougaean,{i} enjoyed great honor in the king’s sight, and he looked for a way to do harm to Mordecai and to his people because of the king’s two eunuchs.{j}

notes.text: Artaxerxes: the Greek Esther calls the king Artaxerxes (Old Persian Artakhshaça, “whose rule is through truth,” reported); the Hebrew book calls him Ahasuerus (Ahashverosh), who is generally identified with Xerxes I (486–465 BC). On that identification the second year is about 485/484 BC. Josephus likewise calls him Artaxerxes (reported).
Nisan: the first month of the Jewish year, of Babylonian origin; it began at the new moon of March–April.

Mordecai: Greek Mardochaios, Hebrew Mordekhai, probably a name formed from that of the Babylonian god Marduk. Jair means “he gives light,” Shimei “heard,” and Kish perhaps “gift” (reported); Shimei and Kish are names connected with the family of Saul (2 Samuel 16:5; 1 Samuel 9:1). Benjamin means “son of the right hand.”

Susa: Hebrew Shushan, a royal residence of the Persian kings in Elam, in southwest Iran. Greek “Susa the city” may mean the city as distinct from the fortified citadel (compare Esther 1:2 Hebrew), but the distinction is not certain.

Jeconiah: Greek Iechonias, also called Jehoiachin (“Yahweh establishes”), deported in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15). Read strictly, this would make Mordecai well over a hundred years old under Xerxes. The same difficulty arises in Hebrew Esther 2:6, where the clause may instead refer to his great-grandfather Kish.
Dragons: Greek drakontes, great serpents or dragons. Mordecai explains them in Addition F (F4) as himself and Haman.

Gabatha and Tharra: these are Bigthan (or Bigthana) and Teresh in Hebrew Esther 2:21. The KJV Apocrypha begins chapter 12 with this verse (A12 = KJV 12:1). The plot reported here doubles the one told in Esther 2:21–23, which the Hebrew places in the seventh year or later.
Were led away: a common Greek euphemism for being taken off to execution. KJV has “strangled.” In Hebrew Esther 2:23 the two are hanged (or impaled) on a stake.

Haman: Greek Aman; the meaning of the name is uncertain (perhaps Persian or Elamite, reported). Hammedatha (Greek Amadathos) is a Persian name, perhaps “given by the moon” or “given by Haoma” (reported). “Bougaean” (Greek Bougaios) is obscure; it seems to stand where the Hebrew calls him an “Agagite” (Esther 3:1), linking him with Agag the Amalekite (1 Samuel 15:8). In Addition E (E10) he is called a Macedonian. Review.

Because of the king’s two eunuchs: here Haman’s enmity comes from the fate of the eunuchs, whereas in Esther 3:2–6 it comes from Mordecai’s refusal to bow to him. The two motives stand side by side in the Greek book.

chapters.heading: Addition B: The King’s Letter against the Jews
chapters.title: Greek Esther 3:13a–g (KJV Apocrypha 13:1–7). In the Greek book this follows Esther 3:13.

verses.text: And of the letter this is the copy: “The Great King Artaxerxes writes thus to the governors of the hundred and twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia,{a} and to the district officials set beneath them:

“Having become ruler over many nations and gained mastery over the whole inhabited world, I have willed, never buoyed up by the brashness of my power but ever handling affairs with fairness and mildness, to establish for my subjects lives free of every billow, to furnish a kingdom tamed and open to travel as far as its outermost limits, and to bring back that peace for which every person yearns.

When I put the question to my counselors how this end might be attained, Haman—one excelling among us in good sense, shown to be unwavering in his loyalty and firm in his faithfulness, and holding as his prize the second dignity of the realm—

made plain to us that, mingled among all the tribes over the world, there is a certain hostile people whose laws set it against every nation, a people who forever brush aside the edicts of the kings, so that the joint rule{b} which we steer without fault cannot be settled firm.

Since we have therefore perceived that this nation, unique among all, lies continually athwart every human being, following an alien code of living by its laws, and bearing ill will to our affairs, bringing the foulest evils to pass, so that the kingdom fails to win stability,

we have accordingly given orders that the persons pointed out to you in the writings of Haman—who has charge of our affairs and is a second father to us{c}—be wholly uprooted, women and children with them, by their enemies’ swords, with no compassion and no sparing, on the fourteenth of the twelfth month, Adar (February–March), of this current year,{d}

to the end that those who were of old, and are now, ill-disposed may in a single day go down by force to Hades,{e} and for the time hereafter leave our affairs to us steady and untroubled to the last.”

notes.text: India to Ethiopia: the limits of the Persian empire as given in Esther 1:1. “India” is the Indus valley region; “Ethiopia” (Hebrew Cush) is the Nile land south of Egypt. Additions B and E were composed in Greek, in the ornate style of Hellenistic royal correspondence; the KJV Apocrypha prints B as 13:1–7.
Joint rule: Greek synarchia, a rare word for a shared or unified government; the sense is uncertain.
Second father: an honorary title for the king’s chief minister; compare Genesis 45:8 and Addition E (E11).

Fourteenth … Adar: the Greek text of Esther 3:7 likewise has the fourteenth, but Hebrew Esther 3:13 and Addition E (E20) have the thirteenth. Adar is the twelfth month, beginning at the new moon of February–March.
Hades: Greek Hadēs, the realm of the dead, corresponding to Hebrew Sheol.

chapters.heading: Addition C: The Prayers of Mordecai and Esther
chapters.title: Greek Esther 4:17a–z (KJV Apocrypha 13:8–14:19). In the Greek book this follows Esther 4:17.

verses.text: Then Mordecai besought the Lord, recalling to mind every work of the Lord, and spoke:{a}
“Lord, Lord, King holding sway over all things, since the whole universe rests in your authority, and none can stand opposed to you when your will is to save Israel—
for it was you who made the heaven and the earth and everything to be wondered at under heaven,
and Lord of all are you; nor is there one who shall array himself against you, who are the Lord.
All things are known to you. You know, Lord, that it was not in insolence, nor in haughtiness, nor in a craving for glory that I did this, the not bowing low before the haughty Haman;{b}
for I would have been well content to kiss the very soles of his feet to keep Israel safe.
Rather, I acted so, lest I set a mortal’s glory higher than God’s glory; and to none will I bow low except to you, my Lord, and I will not do these things in haughtiness.
And now, Lord God, the King, God of Abraham,{c} have pity on your people, for they are watching us to bring us to ruin, and they have set their hearts on destroying your inheritance from the first.
Do not look past your portion, which you ransomed out of the land of Egypt for your own.
Give ear to my plea; show mercy to your allotted share, and change our mourning into feasting, so that living we may hymn your name, Lord; and do not blot out the mouth of those who give you praise.”
And all Israel shouted aloud with their whole strength, for their death stood before their eyes.
Esther the queen too, gripped by mortal anguish, fled for refuge to the Lord.{d}

Putting off the robes of her glory, she wrapped herself in robes of hardship and lament. Instead of costly fragrances she heaped her head with ash and filth; she brought her body very low, and every spot that her joyful adornment had graced she covered with locks of her twisted hair.
And she made her plea to the Lord God of Israel, saying: “My Lord, our King, you alone are he; come to my aid, who am alone and have no helper apart from you,
since my danger lies in my hand.{e}

I have heard from my birth, in the tribe of my father’s house, that you, Lord, chose out Israel from among all the nations, and our fathers from all who went before them, as a possession forever, and that you performed for them whatever you had spoken.
But now we have done wrong before your face, and you have given us up into our enemies’ grasp,
in return for our giving glory to their gods. Just are you, Lord!
And now they have not had their fill of the bitterness of our bondage; they have laid their hands on the hands of their idols,{f}
to cancel what your mouth decreed, to wipe out your inheritance, to block up the mouth of those who praise you, and to snuff out the glory of your house and of your altar;
to open the mouth of the nations to extol the virtues of vain things, and to have a king of flesh held in wonder forever.

Do not, Lord, hand over your scepter to things that have no being;{g} do not let them jeer at our fall, but turn their counsel back upon themselves, and make a public example of the one who began this against us.
Remember, Lord; reveal yourself in the hour of our distress, and put courage into me, King of the gods and Master over every power.
Set fitting and well-measured speech in my mouth before the lion,{h} and turn his heart to loathing of him who makes war on us, to make an end of him and those who are of one mind with him.
But us, deliver by your hand, and help me, who am alone and have none but you, Lord.
Knowledge of everything is yours, and you know that I have hated the glory of the lawless and loathe the bed of the uncircumcised and of every foreigner.{i}

You know my constraint: that I loathe the emblem of my proud station that rests on my head on the days I am on display; I loathe it like a cloth of a woman’s impurity,{j} and on my days of quiet I do not put it on.
Your slave woman has not eaten at the table of Haman, nor have I honored a banquet of the king, nor drunk wine of drink offerings.{k}
Since the day of my change of fortune until now your slave woman has found no gladness except in you, Lord God of Abraham.
O God, mighty over all, hear the voice of those who have lost hope; save us from the hand of the wicked, and save me from my fear.”

notes.text: The Lord: Greek kyrios, used throughout these prayers, where the Hebrew book of Esther never names God at all. The KJV Apocrypha prints Mordecai’s prayer as 13:8–18 (C1 = 13:8). Review.
Bowing low: Greek proskynein, the bow or prostration paid to Persian kings and high officials. Mordecai explains here a refusal that the Hebrew book leaves unexplained (Esther 3:2–4).
Abraham: “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5).

Esther: Greek Esthēr, Hebrew Ester, perhaps from Persian stāra, “star,” or from the name of the goddess Ishtar (reported); her Hebrew name was Hadassah, “myrtle” (Esther 2:7). The KJV Apocrypha begins chapter 14 here (C12 = 14:1).
My danger lies in my hand: that is, “I am taking my life in my hands”; compare Judges 12:3 and 1 Samuel 19:5.
Laid their hands on the hands of their idols: that is, they have made a solemn pledge before their gods.
Things that have no being: the idols, or the false gods they represent.
The lion: the king.
Bed of the uncircumcised: the prayer presents Esther’s marriage to the Persian king as something forced on her, answering a question the Hebrew book does not raise.
A cloth of a woman’s impurity: Greek rhakos katamēniōn, a menstrual cloth (compare Leviticus 15:19–24; Isaiah 64:6). The “emblem” is her royal headdress.
Wine of drink offerings: wine poured out to pagan gods (compare Deuteronomy 32:38). Compare Daniel 1:8, and contrast Hebrew Esther, which says nothing about Esther keeping food laws.

chapters.heading: Addition D: Esther Goes In to the King
chapters.title: Greek Esther 5:1, 1a–f, 2, 2a–b (KJV Apocrypha 15:1–16). In the Greek book this takes the place of Hebrew Esther 5:1–2.

verses.text: On the third day, when she left off praying, she laid aside the garments of her worship{a} and arrayed herself in her splendor.
Then, made radiant, she invoked God, overseer and savior of all, and took along her two maids;
on the one she leaned, as a woman given to delicate ways,{b}
while the other came after, bearing up her gown.
She herself was rosy in the full bloom of her loveliness, her face glad as though it were loving, but her heart was pinched tight with fear.

Having passed through all the doors, she came to stand face to face with the king. He was sitting upon the throne of his kingdom, robed in all the attire of his majesty, the whole of it gold and precious stones, and he was exceedingly fearsome.
Lifting his face, ablaze with glory, he looked upon her in the full heat of wrath; the queen dropped, her color turned as she swooned, and she sank forward over the head of the maid going before her.

Then God turned the king’s spirit to mildness;{c} in anxious haste he leapt up off his throne and gathered her into his arms till she recovered, and he soothed her with peaceable words, saying to her:
“Esther, what troubles you? Your brother am I.{d} Be of good courage;
by no means shall you die, for our ordinance is a common one. Come forward.”{e}
And lifting the golden staff he laid it upon her neck,
kissed her, and said, “Talk with me.”
Her answer to him was: “My lord, you appeared to me like an angel of God, and at the dread of your glory my heart was shaken.{f}
For you are a marvel, my lord, and your face is brimful of graces.”
But as she was conversing with him, she fell down from faintness;
and the king was in turmoil, and his whole retinue set about reviving her.

notes.text: The garments of her worship: Greek therapeia, which can mean either worship or servitude; the garments are her mourning clothes of C13.
Given to delicate ways: or “as one daintily bred.” The Greek pictures a lady of the court leaning on an attendant.
God turned the king’s spirit: this sentence states what the Hebrew book only implies; God’s action is the turning point of the Greek story.
Brother: an affectionate form of address; compare Song of Songs 4:9, “my sister, my bride.”
Our ordinance is a common one: Greek koinon to prostagma hēmōn. The sense is uncertain: perhaps “the order applies to ordinary subjects, not to you,” or “our command is shared between us.” Review.
My lord: here Greek kyrios addresses the king, not God.

chapters.heading: Addition E: The King’s Letter on Behalf of the Jews
chapters.title: Greek Esther 8:12a–x (KJV Apocrypha 16:1–24). In the Greek book this follows Esther 8:12.

verses.text: Set down below is a transcript of the letter: “Artaxerxes, the Great King, to the district rulers of the hundred and twenty-seven satrapies stretching from India to Ethiopia, and to all who are of one mind with our government: greeting.{a}
“Many who are honored over and over by the boundless generosity of their benefactors grow the more swollen in mind;
and not only do they seek to do mischief to our subjects, but, unable to carry their glut of good things, they take in hand to scheme against their very benefactors.

Not only do they root out thankfulness from among people, but, carried away by the bragging of those who have never tasted goodness, they imagine they will slip past the justice of God, who sees all things always, the justice that hates evil.
Often, too, the coaxing of friends who were trusted to manage affairs has made many of those set in high office share the guilt of innocent blood and wrapped them in disasters past remedy,
when such men, through the lying sophistry of their malice, beguiled the guileless good faith of the rulers.

And one may see this not so much from the more ancient histories that we have handed down, as by looking into what has been wickedly carried out close at hand through the plague of those who hold power undeservingly.
We must take thought for the days to come, that we may furnish the kingdom undisturbed and at peace for all humankind,
making use of changes and always deciding matters that come into view with a more reasonable response.
For Haman son of Hammedatha, a Macedonian,{b} truly a stranger to Persian blood and far removed from our kind nature, was hosted among us

and met with the goodwill that we bear toward every nation, so far that he came to be proclaimed our father and continued to be honored with prostration by everyone, as the figure next after the royal throne.
But he did not bear his high station; he set to work to strip us of our dominion and of our breath,
and with tangled tricks of deceit he begged for the ruin of Mordecai, our savior and benefactor at all times, and of Esther, the faultless partner of our royal rule, together with their whole nation.
For by these means he thought to find us bereft and to carry over the sovereignty of the Persians to the Macedonians.
We, however, find that the Jews, handed over to obliteration by this thrice-accursed wretch,{c} are no malefactors, but live as citizens under the most just of laws,
being sons of the Most High, the most great and living God, who keeps the kingdom on its course for us and for our ancestors in the finest condition.
You will therefore do well to make no use of the documents dispatched by Haman son of Hammedatha,
because the very man who devised these things has been hung up{d} at the gates of Susa with all his house, God, who rules over everything, having swiftly paid him back the judgment he merited.
Set out the copy of this letter openly in every place, and let the Jews follow their own customs,
and lend them aid, so that they may ward off those who assail them in their time of trouble on the thirteenth of the twelfth month, Adar (February–March), on that same day.{e}
For God, who wields all power, has made this day for them a joy, in place of ruin for the chosen race.
And you too, among your named festivals, keep it as a day of note with every kind of feasting,
so that now and in later times it may be salvation for us and for the Persians who wish us well, but for those who plot against us a remembrance of their destruction.

Any city or land whatever that does not act in keeping with these orders shall be devoured in fury by spear and fire; it shall be rendered not only untrodden by people but most odious to beasts and birds for all time.”

notes.text: Greeting: Greek chairein, the usual opening of a Hellenistic letter. Like Addition B, this letter was composed in Greek in an elaborate rhetorical style. The KJV Apocrypha prints it as 16:1–24 (E1 = 16:1).

A Macedonian: in Addition A (A17) Haman is a “Bougaean.” Calling the Persian king’s enemy a Macedonian reflects the Hellenistic setting of the additions, after Alexander’s conquest of Persia (331 BC). Some witnesses read differently (reported).
Thrice-accursed: Greek trisalitērios, a strong term of abuse.
Hung up: Greek estaurōsthai, which can mean impaled, crucified or hanged. In Hebrew Esther 7:10 Haman alone is hanged, and his ten sons are killed and hung up afterward (9:7–14).
Thirteenth … Adar: compare Hebrew Esther 8:12 and 9:1. Addition B (B6) has the fourteenth. Adar began at the new moon of February–March.

chapters.heading: Addition F: The Dream Explained, and the Colophon
chapters.title: Greek Esther 10:3a–l (KJV Apocrypha 10:4–11:1). In the Greek book this closes the book, after Esther 10:3.

verses.text: And Mordecai said, “From God these things have come.{a}
For I have called to mind the dream I saw about these matters; not one word of it has gone unfulfilled.
The little spring that turned into a river—there was light and sun and plentiful water—the river is Esther, whom the king wedded and made queen.
The two dragons are myself and Haman.
The nations are those that banded together to destroy the name of the Jews.

And my nation, this is Israel, who cried aloud to God and were saved. Yes, the Lord saved his people; the Lord delivered us out of all these evils; and God worked the signs and the great portents such as have not occurred among the nations.
On this account he appointed two lots,{b} the one for God’s people and the other for every nation;
and these two lots came to the hour and the season and the day of judgment in God’s presence and among all the nations.
And God remembered his people and gave judgment in favor of his inheritance.

So these days shall be theirs in the month of Adar (February–March), on the fourteenth and fifteenth of that month, with gathering and joy and gladness in God’s presence, age after age without end, among Israel his people.”

Dated the fourth year that Ptolemy and Cleopatra reigned:{c} Dositheus,{d} who claimed to be a priest and Levite, together with Ptolemy his son, delivered the foregoing letter of Purim,{e} affirming that it was genuine and that Lysimachus son of Ptolemy, one of the residents of Jerusalem, had translated it.

notes.text: From God: the KJV Apocrypha prints F1–10 as 10:4–13 and the colophon (F11) as 11:1; its chapter 11 then continues with Addition A (11:2). This is why the Vulgate numbering places the dream after its interpretation.
Two lots: an explanation of the name Purim, from Akkadian puru, “lot” (Esther 3:7; 9:24–26). Here the lots become symbols of God’s judgment between Israel and the nations.

Ptolemy and Cleopatra: several Ptolemaic kings ruled with a queen named Cleopatra, so the date is uncertain. The proposals most often made are 114/113 BC (Ptolemy IX), 78/77 BC (Ptolemy XII) and 49/48 BC (Ptolemy XIII), reported. Ptolemy means “warlike.” Review.
Dositheus: “gift of God.” Lysimachus means “loosing of battle.” This note, a colophon, vouches for the Greek translation of the book as it was brought to Egypt.
Letter of Purim: the Greek has “the letter of Phrourai,” apparently a form of Purim; it may refer to the whole book or to the Purim letter of Esther 9:20–32.

books.name: Wisdom of Solomon
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of the Wisdom of Solomon as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 2 (1891; public domain), which follows Codex Vaticanus (B) and records the readings of Sinaiticus (ℵ), Alexandrinus (A) and others. The book was composed in Greek, probably in Alexandria in the first century BC or early first century AD; it has no Hebrew original. It belongs to the Septuagint and is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Verse numbering follows standard English (NRSV) usage. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes. Variant readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844) was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text:
for he lets himself be found by those who do not test him,
and reveals himself to those who do not doubt him.

For crooked reasonings separate people from God,
and his power, when it is tested, exposes the foolish;

because wisdom will not enter a soul that devises evil,
nor dwell in a body held in pledge to sin.

For a holy spirit of discipline{b} will flee from deceit,
and will withdraw from senseless reasonings,
and will be put to shame when wrongdoing comes in.

Because the spirit of the Lord has filled the inhabited world,
and that which holds all things together has knowledge of every voice.

Therefore no one who utters unjust things will escape notice,
nor will Justice,{e} when she convicts, pass him by.

because a jealous ear hears all things,
and the murmur of grumbling is not hidden.

Do not court death by the error of your life,
nor draw destruction on yourselves by the works of your hands;

because God did not make death,
and he takes no delight in the destruction of the living.

He made everything so that it could exist,
the creatures{g} of the world are health-giving,
there is no deadly poison in them,
and Hades has no dominion{h} on earth.
For justice is immortal.{i}

But the ungodly invited death with their hands and words;{j}
they thought of it as a friend and pined away,
and they struck a pact with it,
since they deserve to be among its possessions.

notes.text: Greek kyrios, “Lord,” the Septuagint’s usual rendering of the divine name YHWH; this translation keeps “Lord” in the Greek books. The opening address “you who judge the earth” echoes Ps 2:10.
Or “of instruction”; Greek paideia, training or correction. Some manuscripts (as reported, Sinaiticus) read “of wisdom.”
Greek “from his lips.”
Greek “his kidneys,” thought of as the seat of the emotions.
Greek dikē, justice personified as an avenging power.
Or “goes unpunished”; Greek “will not go empty.”
Or “the creatures,” “the things that come into being”; Greek geneseis.
Or “palace,” “dominion”; Greek basileion.
The Latin tradition adds a further line, “but injustice is the acquisition of death,” which is not in the Greek manuscripts used here.
That is, death.

verses.text:
For, reckoning wrongly, they said to themselves,
“Brief and full of grief is this life of ours,
and for a mortal’s end there is no cure,
nor is anyone known who has come back{a} out of Hades.

when it is put out, the body will turn to ashes,
and the spirit will be scattered like thin air.

In time our name will be forgotten,
and nobody will recall what we did;
our lives will vanish like the remnants of a cloud,
and disperse like fog
driven off by the sun’s beams
and pressed down by its warmth.

For our allotted time is the passing of a shadow,
and there is no going back from our end,
because it is sealed up and no one turns it back.

“Come, then, let us enjoy the good things that are present,
and make use of the creation{b} eagerly, as in youth.

With wine of great price and with perfumes let us be filled,
and let no blossom of spring{c} get by us.
Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither.

But let our strength be our law of justice,
for what is weak proves itself useless.

“Let us lie in wait for the just man, because he is inconvenient to us,
and he opposes our deeds;
he reproaches us for sins against the law,
and charges us with sins against our training.

He claims to possess knowledge of God,
and names himself a son{d} of the Lord.

He has become to us a reproof of our thoughts;
he is a burden to us even to look at,

because his life is unlike that of others,
and his paths are of another kind.

We are counted by him as something counterfeit,
and he keeps away from our ways as from uncleanness;
he calls the last end of the just happy,
and boasts that God is his father.

Let us find out whether what he says is true,
and make trial of how things go with him when he departs.

For if the just man is God’s son, he will help him,
and will rescue him from the hand of his adversaries.

Let us examine him with insult and torture,
so that we may know his gentleness,
and put his forbearance to the proof.

Let us condemn him to a shameful death,
for, according to his words, he will be watched over.”{e}

Thus they reasoned, and they were led astray,
for their wickedness blinded them,

for God created humankind for incorruption,
and made it the image of his own eternity;{g}

but death entered the world through the devil’s{h} jealousy,
and those on his side experience it.

notes.text: Or “to release anyone.”
Or “of created things.”
Some manuscripts read “flower of the air”; others “flower of life.”
Or “servant”; Greek pais can mean either.
Literally “for there will be a visitation of him according to his words.”
Greek mystēria, “mysteries.”
Some manuscripts read “of his own nature” (Greek idiotētos for aidiotētos), as reported.
Greek diabolos, “slanderer,” here commonly understood of the serpent of Gen 3.

verses.text:
But the souls of the just are in the hand of God,
and no torment will ever{a} touch them.

In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died,
and their departure was reckoned an affliction,

and their going from us a ruin;
but they are at peace.

For though in the sight of people they were punished,
their hope is full of immortality.

After a small correction they will receive great blessings,
for God tried them and judged them fit for himself;

like gold in the furnace he tried them,
and like a whole burnt offering{b} he accepted them.

In the time of their visitation they will shine out,
and they will run like sparks through stubble.

Nations they shall judge, over peoples they shall hold sway,
and over them the Lord shall be king to the ages.

But the ungodly will receive punishment as their reasonings deserve,
those who disregarded the just{d} and rebelled against the Lord;

Their wives are foolish, and their children evil;
cursed is their offspring.

Blessed too the eunuch who has worked no lawless thing with his hand
nor plotted evil things against the Lord;
to him a chosen gift shall be given for his fidelity,
and in the Lord’s sanctuary a portion all the more delightful.

For good toil yields a fruit of glory,
and the root of good sense never gives way.

But the children of adulterers will never mature,
and the offspring of an illicit union will disappear.

Even if they live long, they will be counted as nothing,
and at the last their old age will be without honor.

Should they die quickly, hope is not theirs,
nor any comfort in the day when the verdict is given.{e}
For hard is the end of an unrighteous generation.

notes.text: The Greek uses an emphatic double negative.
Greek holokarpōma, a sacrifice wholly consumed on the altar.
Some manuscripts add “and he watches over his holy ones,” as at 4:15.
Or “what is just.”
Greek “of decision,” that is, of the verdict.

verses.text:
Though for a season they may sprout in branches,
yet, set unsteadily, they will be rocked by the wind
and torn up by the roots under the gales’ force.

Their shoots will be snapped off unfinished,
their fruit worthless,
unripe for food, fit for nothing at all.

For children born of unlawful unions{b}
are witnesses of wickedness against their parents when they are examined.
But the just, though he come to his end early, will be at rest.

For honorable old age is not that of long time,
nor is it measured by number of years;

but understanding is gray hair for human beings,
and a spotless life is ripe old age.

Being pleasing to God, he was loved,
and while living among sinners he was taken up.{c}

He was snatched away so that evil might not alter his understanding
or guile deceive his soul.

For the bewitching of trivial things obscures what is good,
and the roving of desire perverts an innocent mind.
Made complete in a brief span, he filled out lengthy times;

for his soul was pleasing to the Lord;
therefore he hurried him{d} out of the midst of wickedness.
But the peoples saw and did not understand,
nor did they take such a thing to heart,

that grace and mercy are with his chosen ones,
and he watches over his holy ones.

A righteous person who has died will judge the living ungodly,
and a youth swiftly made complete will judge the long old age of the unrighteous.

They will look on the wise man’s death
without grasping what the Lord intended for him
or why he set him in safety.

They will look on and sneer,
but the Lord will mock them.

Cowering, they will come to the counting of their sins,
and their own lawless acts will stand opposite and accuse them.

notes.text: Greek “of it.”
Greek “of lawless sleep.”
Greek metetethē, the word used of Enoch in Gen 5:24 (Septuagint).
Or “it hurried”; the subject may be the soul.

verses.text:
Then the righteous one will take his stand with much boldness
facing those who afflicted him
and who set his toils at nothing.

At the sight they will be thrown into turmoil by a terrible fear
and stand astonished at a deliverance beyond all expectation.

Repenting, they will say to one another,
and groan through distress of spirit:

“This is the man we used to laugh at,
whom we made a proverb of scorn — senseless that we were!
His way of life we counted lunacy,
and his death a dishonor.

How has he been numbered among the children{a} of God,
and his lot is among the holy ones?

What did our arrogance profit us?
And what good has wealth, with our boasting, brought us?

“All those things have passed away like a shadow,
and like a rumor that runs by;

or as with a bird darting through the air:
no mark of its course is to be found,
but the slight breeze, whipped by the stroke of its feathers
and split by its whirring force,
is crossed by its beating wings,
and afterward nothing in it shows that it went that way;

or as, when an arrow is shot at a target,
the air, cut through, at once closes up again,
so that no one knows its pathway.

So it is with us: no sooner were we born than we ceased to exist,
and we had no mark of virtue to display,
but were used up in our wickedness.”

For the hope of the ungodly is like chaff{b} carried by the wind,
and like fine frost{c} driven away by a storm;
it is scattered like smoke before the wind,
and it passes like the memory of a guest who stays a single day.

But the righteous live to the age,
in the Lord is their recompense,
and the Most High takes thought for them.

Therefore they will receive a majestic kingdom
and a beautiful crown from the Lord’s hand,
for he will cover them with his right hand
and protect them with his arm.

He will take his zeal as his full armor,
and will arm creation to repel his enemies;

he will put on justice as a breastplate,
and wear impartial judgment as a helmet;
he will take holiness as an invincible shield,

he will whet unbending anger into a blade,
and the world{d} will go to war at his side against those who have lost their senses.

Well-aimed shafts of lightning will fly,
and as from a well-drawn bow of clouds they will leap to the target,

a blast of might{e} will stand up against them
and scatter them like a whirlwind winnowing grain.
So lawlessness will turn the whole earth to desert,
and ill-doing will topple the seats of the powerful.

notes.text: Greek “sons”; the “holy ones” may be angels.
Greek chnous, fine down or dust.
Some manuscripts read “spider’s web” (Greek arachnē for pachnē), as reported.
Greek kosmos, “the world.”
Or “a spirit of power.”

verses.text:
Listen, therefore, you kings, and understand;
learn, you judges of the ends of the earth.

Give ear, you who rule over multitudes,
and who take pride in throngs of nations.

For your authority came to you from the Lord,
and your rule from the Most High,
who will examine what you do and scrutinize your plans.

For though you were ministers of his reign, you gave no upright judgment,
you did not guard the law,
and you did not walk by God’s design.

Fearfully and fast he will stand over you,
since on those who stand high a sharp judgment comes.

The least may be forgiven out of pity,
but the strong will be strongly examined.

For the Master of all does not back away before anyone,
and is not impressed by rank,
since he made small and great alike,
and cares for them all equally.
For the mighty a stern scrutiny lies ahead.

To you, then, O sovereigns, my words are addressed,
so that you may learn wisdom and not fall away.

For those who keep holy things in holiness will be made holy,
and those who have been taught them will find a defense.

Therefore set your desire on my words;
long for them, and you will be instructed.

Wisdom is bright and never fades,
readily noticed by those who love her,
and discovered by those who look for her.
She is quick to be recognized by those who long for her, coming to meet them first.

Whoever rises early to seek her will not grow weary,
for he will find her sitting at his gates.

To think upon her is the perfection of understanding,
and whoever keeps vigil for her sake will soon be free from care,

Her starting point is the truest longing for discipline;
and care for discipline is love;

and love of her is the keeping of her laws,
and attention to her laws is assurance of incorruption,
and incorruption brings one near to God;
Thus the longing for wisdom raises one up to royal rule.{a}

If, then, you delight in thrones and scepters, O sovereigns of peoples,
honor wisdom, so that you may reign for ever.

What wisdom is and how she came to be I will declare,
and I will not hide secret things from you,
but I will trace her out from the beginning of creation,
and bring the knowledge of her into the open,
and I will not pass by the truth;

nor will I travel in company with wasting envy,
for envy has no fellowship with wisdom.

A host of the wise keeps the world safe,
and a prudent king is the steadiness of a people.
Therefore be instructed by my words, and you will profit.

notes.text: Verses 17–20 form a chain argument (sorites), each clause taking up the last word of the one before.

verses.text:
within a period of ten months,{b} curdled in blood
from a man’s seed and the pleasure that comes with sleep.
I was nursed in swaddling clothes and with cares.
For no king has had any other beginning of existence;
there is for all one entrance into life, and a like departure.

Therefore I prayed, and understanding was granted me;
I called upon God, and a spirit of wisdom came to me.

I preferred her before scepters and thrones,
and wealth I held as nothing beside her.

Beyond health and good looks I loved her,
and I chose to have her rather than light,
because the radiance that comes from her never sleeps.

Together with her all good things came to me,
and in her hands wealth past counting.

Over all of them I was glad, since wisdom goes at their head,
though I was unaware that she was the one who bore{c} them.

Without guile I learned, and without grudging I share;
I do not hide away her riches;

For in his hand are both we ourselves and our sayings,
and all good sense and the know-how of the crafts.

He himself gave me true knowledge of the things that are:
to know how the universe is put together and how its elements act;

the beginning and end and middle of times,
the shifts of the solstices{e} and the changes of the seasons,
the cycles of years and the positions of the stars,

whatever is hidden and whatever is manifest I learned,
for wisdom, the artisan of all things, taught me.

For there is in her a spirit, thinking and holy,
only-begotten, many-sided, fine,
quick to move, distinct, unsoiled,
plain, unharmed, fond of the good, sharp,

unhindered, beneficent, humane,
steadfast, sure, free from care,
all-powerful, overseeing all,
and passing through all spirits
that are intelligent, pure, and most subtle.{g}

For wisdom is more mobile than any motion;
because of her purity she pervades and penetrates all things.

For she is a reflected radiance of everlasting light,
a spotless mirror of the working of God,
and an image of his goodness.
For God loves nothing except the one who lives together with wisdom.

for night succeeds to it,
but against wisdom evil does not prevail.

notes.text: That is, Adam.
Ten lunar months, about nine calendar months.
Greek genesin, “origin” or “begetter”; some manuscripts read genetin, “mother.”
Or “to speak with judgment.”
Greek tropōn, “turnings,” the turning points of the sun’s course.
Or “winds.”
Verses 22–23 list twenty-one attributes (3 × 7), a number of perfection.
Greek pantokratōr, “ruler of all.”

verses.text:
From end to end she stretches out in strength,
and she manages the whole well.

She proclaims her noble birth by living with God,
and the Master of all loved her.

For she is an initiate in the knowledge of God,
and one who chooses among his works.

If riches are a possession to be desired in life,
what is richer than wisdom, who works all things?

And if understanding is at work,
who more than she is the artisan of what exists?

So I resolved to bring her home to live with me,
knowing she would advise me well
and comfort me in worry and sorrow.

Through her I will gain fame among crowds
and respect from the elders, young as I am.

Sharp I shall be found in giving judgment,
and before the powerful I shall be a marvel.

When I am quiet they will wait on me,
and when I speak they will pay attention,
and if I go on talking, they will put hands over their mouths.

Through her I shall possess deathlessness,
and I shall leave to those who come after me a memory that lasts for ever.

I shall order the affairs of peoples,
and nations shall be made subject to me.

Fearsome tyrants will be afraid when they hear of me;
I will prove kind toward the people, and brave in battle.

Turning these things over within myself,
and weighing them in my heart,
that deathlessness lies in being akin to wisdom,

and good delight in her friendship,
and in the toils of her hands riches that do not run out,
and good sense in practice at her side,
and fair fame in taking part in her words,
I went all around searching how I might take her for my own.

I was a child of good nature,
and a good soul fell to my lot;
or rather, being good, I entered an undefiled body.{b}

But perceiving that I would not otherwise gain possession of her unless God gave her —
and it was a mark of understanding to know whose gift she was —
I appealed to the Lord and implored him,
and with my whole heart I said:

notes.text: The four cardinal virtues of Greek philosophy.
The verse reflects the Greek idea of the soul’s existence before the body; verse 19 states it the other way.

verses.text:
“God of the fathers and Lord of mercy,
who made all things by your word,

and by your wisdom formed humankind
to have dominion over the creatures that came into being by you,

and to govern the world in holiness and justice,
and to pronounce judgment in uprightness of soul,

grant me the wisdom that shares the seat of your thrones,
and do not reject me from among your children.{a}

for even if one is perfect among the children of men,
yet without the wisdom that comes from you he will be counted as nothing.

It was you who picked me as king of your people
and as judge of your sons and your daughters.

You ordered me to build a sanctuary on your holy mountain,
and an altar in the city where you make your dwelling,
a replica of the sacred tent you prepared long ago.

Wisdom is with you; she knows what you do
and was there when you created the world,
she grasps what pleases you
and what accords with your commands.

Send her forth from the holy heavens,
and from the throne of your glory dispatch her,
that she may be with me and labor with me,
and that I may learn what is pleasing to you.

For she knows all things and has insight into them,
and in what I do she will lead me with good sense
and keep watch over me by her glory.

“For what human being can learn the counsel of God?
Or who can conceive what the Lord wills?

For the reasonings of mortals are timid,
and our designs are likely to fail;

for a perishable body weighs down the soul,
and this earthly tent burdens the mind that ponders many things.

Who has learned your counsel, unless you gave wisdom
and sent your holy spirit from on high?

So it was that the ways of earth’s dwellers were made straight,
and human beings learned the things that please you,
and through wisdom they were brought to safety.”

notes.text: Or “servants”; Greek paides.
Greek “thrones,” a plural of majesty.

verses.text:
She it was who guarded the father of the world, the first to be shaped,
when he had been created alone,
and drew him out of his own fall,
and gave him strength to rule over all things.

But when one who was unjust{a} turned from her in his anger,
he was destroyed together with the brother-killing rage he gave way to.

And when because of him the earth was drowned, wisdom saved it once more,
piloting the righteous one{b} on a cheap timber.

She rescued a just man{e} when the ungodly were perishing;
he fled from the fire that came down on the Five Cities.

To their evil there still bears witness
a smoking land left waste,
and plants that bear fruit not brought to its time,
and, standing as a memorial of a soul without faith, a pillar of salt.

For they walked past wisdom
and so were not merely harmed by not knowing what is good,
but also left to the living a monument to their senselessness,
that what they stumbled in might not escape notice.
Wisdom rescued from troubles those who served her.

She guided a righteous one{f} along straight paths
when he fled from the anger of his brother;
she let him see God’s kingdom,
she gave him the knowledge of holy things,
she made him thrive in his hard work
and multiplied what his labors produced.

In the greed of those who overpowered him she stood at his side
and gave him wealth.

When a just man{h} was sold, she did not abandon him,
but rescued him from sin.

She descended with him into the pit,
and did not abandon him in his chains,
until she delivered to him a royal scepter
and power over those who had oppressed him;
she exposed his accusers as liars,
and granted him lasting glory.

A holy people and a blameless offspring
she delivered from a nation of oppressors.

Into the soul of the Lord’s attendant{i} she went,
and she stood up to fearsome kings with portents and signs.

To the holy ones she paid out the reward of their toil;
she led them on a wonderful road,
and she was for them a covering in the day
and a blaze of stars all night.

She brought them over the Red Sea,
and led them through deep waters;

but their enemies she drowned,
and cast them up from the depth of the abyss.

for wisdom opened the mouths of the mute,
and made the tongues of infants speak clearly.

notes.text: Cain (Gen 4). Throughout chapters 10–19 the biblical figures are not named.
Noah (Gen 6–9).
At Babel (Gen 11).
Abraham (Gen 12–22; for the child, Gen 22).
Lot (Gen 19). The “Five Cities” (Greek Pentapolis) are those of Gen 14:2.
Jacob (Gen 27–31).
Jacob’s wrestling at the Jabbok (Gen 32).
Joseph (Gen 37–41).
Moses.

verses.text: She prospered their works by the hand of a holy prophet.

Through a desert where no one lived they made their way,
and in places with no path they set up their tents.
They took a stand against those at war with them and beat back their enemies.

They were thirsty and called on you,
and from a sheer cliff water was given them,
and from hard rock relief from thirst.

For by the very means through which their foes were chastised,
by these, when they were at a loss, they received benefit.{a}

In place of a river’s ever-running spring
churned with gore and filth{b}

as a reproof of the order to murder the babies,
you gave them plenty of water when they had no hope of it,

making plain by the thirst they then felt
in what manner you chastised their opponents.

For when they were put to the test, though they were being corrected with mercy,
they learned how the ungodly suffered when judged with anger.

For you tested them as a father does in warning,
but you examined the others as a stern king does in condemnation.
Whether absent or present, they were equally distressed,

for double sorrow gripped them,
and they moaned as they remembered the past.

For when they heard that through their own punishments
the others had been benefited, they perceived the Lord.

For the one whom long before they had cast out and exposed{c}
and then rejected with scorn,
him they admired at the end of the events,
having thirsted in a way unlike the just.
so they would know that the instruments of someone’s sin are the instruments of his punishment.

For your almighty hand,
which fashioned the world from shapeless matter,
had no shortage of ways to send a horde of bears or fierce lions against them,

or newly created unknown beasts full of rage,
either breathing out fiery breath,
or belching thick smoke,
or flashing terrible sparks from their eyes;

not only could their harm destroy them utterly,
but even the very sight of them could kill by fright.

Even without these, they could have been felled by one breath,
hunted down by justice
and blown away by your mighty spirit.
But you have ordered everything by measure, number, and weight.

For great might is ever at your side,
and the strength of your arm, who shall stand against it?

The whole universe before you is like the small weight that turns a balance,{e}
and like a dewdrop at dawn coming down to the ground.

But you are merciful to all, because you can do everything,
and you pass over human sins so that people may repent.

How would anything remain if you did not wish it?
Or what you had not called, how would it be kept?
You spare all things, because they are yours, O Master, lover of souls.{f}

notes.text: The theme of chapters 11–19: the same elements that punished Egypt benefited Israel.
The first plague (Exod 7:14–24).
Moses as an infant (Exod 1:22–2:3).
Egyptian animal worship.
Compare Isa 40:15.
Or “lover of life.”

verses.text: For your incorruptible spirit is in all things.

So those who slip you reprove bit by bit,
and in the things where they go wrong you remind and admonish them,
that they may be set free from evil and put their trust, Lord, in you.
For the ancient dwellers in your holy land{a}

you hated, because they practiced hateful deeds,
acts of witchcraft and impious rites,

and parents who slaughtered souls that had no helper,
you resolved to wipe out by our fathers’ hands,

so that the land most precious of all in your sight
might receive a worthy colony of God’s children.{c}

not that you could not hand the ungodly over to the righteous in a battle line,
or rub them out all together through terrible beasts or a harsh word;

But by judging them gradually you gave them time to repent,
though you knew well that their origin was wicked,
their evil was inborn,
and their thinking would never change.

For their seed was cursed from the start,{e}
nor was it out of fear of anyone that you granted impunity for what they did wrong.

For who shall say, “What did you do?”
Or who shall stand up against your sentence?
Who shall charge you over nations destroyed that you yourself had made?
Or who shall come and stand against you as pleader for unrighteous men?

There is no god but you, who cares for all,
that you should show him your verdicts were not unjust;

nor shall king or tyrant be able to look you in the face
on behalf of those you have punished.

Being righteous, you order all things righteously,
and you judge it foreign to your might
to pass sentence on one who ought not to be chastised.

For your strength is the source of justice,
and your sovereignty over all causes you to spare all.

For you display strength when someone doubts that your power is complete,
and among those who do know it you put boldness to shame.

By such deeds you taught your people
that the righteous man must be a lover of humankind,
and you made your sons to be of good hope,
that for sins you grant a change of mind.

For if the enemies of your children, who were owed death,
you punished with such heed and such pardon,
giving them times and room in which to be rid of evil,

with what exactness you have judged your own sons,
to whose fathers you gave oaths and covenants of good pledges!

So while you discipline us, you strike our enemies ten thousand times harder,
so that we think of your goodness when we judge,
and expect mercy when we ourselves are judged.

So those who lived unjustly and foolishly
you tormented with their own abominations.

For they wandered very far along the roads of going astray,
taking for gods the most worthless and dishonored of animals,
fooled the way infants are who have no sense.

And so, as on children without reason,
you sent a judgment that made sport of them.

But those not set right by playful rebukes of correction
shall find a judgment worthy of God.

For in the very things that made them suffer and chafe,
in the things they counted gods and by which they were punished,
they saw and acknowledged as true God him whom they had refused to know before;
and so the utmost sentence came down on them.

notes.text: The Canaanites.
The Greek of verses 5–6 is difficult and the text may be corrupt.
Or “servants.”
Or “hornets” (Exod 23:28; Deut 7:20).
Compare the curse of Canaan, Gen 9:25.

verses.text:
but either fire or wind or swift air,
or the circle of the stars or rushing water
or the lights of heaven, governors of the world, they took for gods.

and if they were struck with wonder at their power and working,
let them perceive from these how much more powerful is the one who formed them.

For from the greatness and beauty of created things
their Maker is seen by analogy.{b}

for, living among his works, they search,
and they are won over by the sight, because what they see is beautiful.
But again, not even they are to be pardoned;

But wretched, with their hopes in dead things, are those
who called the works of human hands gods,
gold and silver, worked with skill, and likenesses of living things,
or a useless stone, the work of an ancient hand.

Suppose a woodcutter saws down a tree easy to handle,
skillfully strips off all its bark,
and, shaping it handsomely,
makes a useful vessel for the service of life,

and burns the leftovers of his work
to cook his food and eat his fill;

and the leftover from these, good for nothing,
a crooked stick grown full of knots,
he takes and carves with the care of his idle hours,
and shapes it with the experience of his leisure;{d}
he forms it into the image of a man,

then, making for it a dwelling worthy of it,
he sets it in the wall and fastens it with iron.

So he takes thought for it that it may not fall,
knowing that it cannot help itself,
for it is an image and needs help.

and for getting and working and good fortune in the use of his hands
he begs strong handiness of the thing most helpless in its hands.

notes.text: Greek ton onta, “the one who is,” echoing the Septuagint of Exod 3:14.
Greek analogōs, “correspondingly.”
Greek aiōn, here perhaps “the universe.”
Some manuscripts read “with the skill of understanding.” Compare Isa 44:9–20.

verses.text:
Again, someone preparing to sail and about to cross the wild waves
calls upon a piece of wood more rotten than the vessel that carries him.

For that boat was thought up by the craving for profit,
and wisdom as craftswoman put it together;

but it is your providence, Father, that steers it,
because you have given it a way even in the sea
and a safe path among the waves,

showing that you can save from every danger,
so that even one without skill may go aboard.
For blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes;{b}

but the handmade thing is accursed, both it and the one who made it —
he, because he worked it, and the perishable thing, because it was named a god.
For hated alike by God are the impious and his impiety;
For the deed done shall be chastised along with its doer.

So on the idols of the nations too there shall come a visitation,
since among the things God made they turned into a loathsome thing,
traps for human souls
and a noose for the feet of fools.

For the devising of idols was the beginning of fornication,{c}
and their invention the corruption of life;

For they were not there at the start,
and they shall not remain to the age;

For through the empty conceit of human beings they entered the world,
and therefore a speedy end has been planned for them.

For a father, consumed with untimely grief
for a child suddenly taken from him,
made an image of him,
and now honored as a god one who was once a dead human being,
and handed on to those under him mysteries and initiations.

Then, strengthened by time, the impious habit was guarded as if it were law,
and by order of tyrants the carved figures received worship.

When people could not honor kings face to face, since they lived far away,
they imagined the king’s likeness from a distance
and made a visible statue of the king they revered,
so that in their eagerness they could flatter the absent king as if he were there.

And to heighten the cult even among those who did not know him,
the craftsman’s love of distinction pushed them on.

For he, wishing perhaps to gratify the man in power,
used his art to force the likeness into something finer;

and the crowd, drawn in by the charm of the workmanship,
now reckoned as an object of reverence the one they had a little earlier honored as a man.

Then it was not enough for them to go wrong about knowing God,
but living in a great war of ignorance,
they label such terrible evils peace.

For whether they practice child-slaying rites or secret mysteries,
or hold frenzied revels with strange laws,

and all is a confusion of blood and murder, theft and deceit,
corruption, faithlessness, tumult, perjury,

For worshiping idols that must not even be named{f}
is the start, source, and end of all evil.

For they either rave in their merriment, or prophesy lies,
or live unjustly, or readily commit perjury;

for since they trust in lifeless idols,
they swear wickedly and expect to suffer no harm.

But on both counts what is just will come after them:
that they thought badly of God, attaching themselves to idols,
and that they swore unjustly and with guile, holding holiness in contempt.

For it is not the power of what people swear by,
but the righteous penalty for sinners,
that always catches up with the wrongdoing of the unjust.

notes.text: Gen 6:1–4. The “raft” is Noah’s ark.
Later Christian writers applied this line to the cross; in its setting it refers to the ark.
Here, as often in the prophets, a figure for unfaithfulness to God.
Greek “for living.”
Greek geneseōs enallagē, “exchange of origin”; the sense is disputed, perhaps “perversion of nature.”
Or “nameless idols.”

verses.text:
But you, our God, are kind and truthful,
long-suffering, governing everything with mercy.

For even if we sin, we are yours, aware of your might;
but we will not sin, knowing that you count us as yours.

For to be acquainted with you is righteousness made whole,
and to recognize your might is the taproot of deathlessness.

We have not been led astray by what human craft has wickedly devised,
nor by the barren toil of those who paint shadow-pictures,
a shape smeared with assorted colors,

the sight of which comes to fools as a reproach,{a}
and one longs for the breathless form of a dead likeness.

Lovers of evil things and worthy of such hopes
are those who make them and those who desire them and those who worship them.

And with evil labor he molds a vain god from the same clay,
he who a little while ago came into being out of earth
and in a little while goes back to that from which he was taken,
when the debt of the soul lent him is called in.

Yet his care is not that he must labor and die,
nor that his span of life is short;
rather he vies with goldsmiths and silversmiths
and copies the bronze-workers,
and holds it a glory to shape false things.

His heart is ashes, his hope cheaper than dirt,
and his life of less worth than clay,

He reckoned our life to be a plaything,
and existence a fair for making profit,
for one must make money, he says, from any source, even from evil.

For this one knows beyond all others that he is sinning,
when out of earthly stuff he makes brittle wares and graven images.

But most foolish of all, and more miserable than an infant’s soul,
are the enemies of your people who oppressed them.{b}

For they counted even every idol of the nations as gods,
which have no eyes to use for seeing,
no nostrils for drawing in air,
no ears for hearing,
no fingers on their hands for touching,
and feet that are idle for walking.

Moreover, they worship even the most hateful animals,
which, compared for stupidity, are worse than all others;

Nor do they even happen to be fair to look at, as animals go, so as to be wanted,
but they have fled both from God’s praise and from his blessing.{c}

notes.text: Or, with a slight change, “stirs desire in fools.”
The Egyptians.
Compare Gen 1:31; 3:14.

verses.text:
So by creatures of that same sort they paid a fitting penalty,
tortured by swarms of vermin.

For on those tyrants a want that could not be avoided had to come,
but to these it had only to be shown how their foes were being tortured.

for a short time they were thrown into alarm for their correction,
having a token of rescue to bring the command of your law to mind.

For the one who turned was kept safe not by the thing he looked at,
but on account of you, who rescue all.

And in this too you persuaded our foes
that you are he who sets free from every harm.

but your sons not even the fangs of venom-spitting serpents overcame,
for your mercy came alongside and cured them.

For to call your sayings to mind they were stung,
and swiftly brought through safely,
so that they might not fall into deep forgetting
and be cut off from your good deeds.

For it was neither herb nor plaster that made them well,
but your word, Lord, which makes all things whole.

For you hold authority over life and over death,
and you bring down to the gates and bring up.

A man may kill through his evil,
but the spirit, once gone out, he does not bring back,
nor does he free the soul that has been taken.
To escape from your hand is impossible;

For the ungodly, who denied that they knew you,
were whipped by the might of your arm,
chased by strange rains and hailstorms and downpours that would not be begged off,
and eaten up by fire.{d}

For—the most amazing thing—in water, which puts out everything,
the fire burned even more strongly,
since the universe fights for the righteous.

For at one time the flame was tamed,
so as not to burn up the animals sent against the ungodly,
but that they themselves, on seeing it, might grasp
that God’s judgment was driving them;

and at another time, even in the midst of water, it blazed beyond fire’s own power,
to ruin the yield of an unrighteous land.

For your food{f} showed your kindness toward your children,
and, suiting the appetite of whoever ate it,
it turned into whatever each one desired.

Snow and ice{g} held out against fire and did not melt,
that they might know that it was fire that ruined the enemies’ harvests,
fire flaming in the hail
and lightning-flashing in the rains;

and this same fire, again, so that the righteous might be fed,
had forgotten even its own power.

For the creation that serves you, its maker,
is stretched tight to chastise the unrighteous,
and slackens to do good to those who rely on you.

So then too, being changed into everything,
it was in service to your gift that nourishes all,
according to the wish of those in want,

For what was not ruined by fire
melted simply when it was warmed by a brief sunbeam,

so that people would know they must get up before sunrise to thank you,
and must address you as daylight begins;

For the ungrateful man’s hope will thaw like winter’s hoarfrost
and run off like water that serves no purpose.

notes.text: The frogs and other plagues (Exod 8).
The plague of hail and lightning (Exod 9:13–35).
The manna (Exod 16; Ps 78:25). Jewish tradition held that the manna tasted as each person wished.
Or “sustenance”; Greek hypostasis.
“Snow and ice” here describe the manna (Num 11:7; Exod 16:14, 21).
Compare Deut 8:3.

verses.text:
Great are your judgments and hard to recount;
therefore souls without instruction went astray.

For when lawless men had supposed that they held a holy nation in their power,
they lay prisoners of darkness and captives of a long night,
shut in under their roofs,
exiles from the everlasting providence.{a}

For thinking to go unseen in their secret sins,
they were scattered under a dark curtain of forgetfulness,
horribly dismayed and thrown into panic by apparitions.

For not even the inner chamber that held them kept them free of fear,
but noises crashed around them and terrified them,
and gloomy phantoms with unsmiling faces appeared.

No force of fire had strength to give light,
nor did the bright flames of the stars endure to lighten that hateful night.

Only a self-kindled blaze showed through to them, full of fear,
and, terrified at the sight they could not see,
they thought the things they did see worse still.

The tricks of the magic art lay humbled,
and its boast of wisdom was put to a shameful test.

For those who promised to drive away terrors and disorders from a sick soul
