in the fifth year, on the seventh day of the month,{b} when the Chaldeans captured Jerusalem and set it ablaze.
And Baruch read out the words of this book in the ears of Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah,{c} and in the ears of all the people who came to the book,

and in the ears of the men of power and of the king’s sons, and in the ears of the elders, and in the ears of all the people from the least to the greatest, of all who lived in Babylon by the river Sud.{d}
And they wept and fasted and prayed before the Lord;
and they collected silver, each according to what his hand could give,

and this they dispatched to Jerusalem, to Jehoiakim the priest,{e} whose father was Hilkiah and whose grandfather was Shallum, and to the priests and every one of the people present with him at Jerusalem,

at the time when he received the vessels of the Lord’s house, carried off out of the temple, to bring them back to Judah’s land, on the tenth of Sivan{f} — vessels of silver made by Zedekiah son of Josiah, Judah’s king,
after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried off Jeconiah and the rulers and the captives and the men of power and the people of the land from Jerusalem, and brought them to Babylon.
And they said: See, we send you silver; with it purchase whole burnt offerings, sin offerings, and incense; make ready a grain offering, and present them on the altar of the Lord our God;
and pray for the life of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and for the life of Belshazzar his son,{g} that their days may be like the days of heaven above the earth.

And the Lord will give us strength and will give light to our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and under the shadow of Belshazzar his son, and we shall serve them many days and find favor before them.
And make prayer for us to the Lord our God, because against the Lord our God we have sinned, and to this day the Lord’s fury and his anger have not turned from us.
And you shall read out this book that we have sent to you, to make confession in the house of the Lord on the day of the feast and on the days of the appointed season.
Then say: Righteousness belongs to the Lord our God,{h} while shame covers our faces, as it does today, every person of Judah and all who live in Jerusalem,
our kings as well, and our rulers, our priests, our prophets, and our fathers,
because we have sinned before the Lord
and disobeyed him, and we did not heed the voice of the Lord our God, to walk in the ordinances of the Lord that he set before our face.
From the day when the Lord brought our fathers out of the land of Egypt until this day we have been disobedient to the Lord our God, and we were careless in not heeding his voice.

And the evils have fastened on us, and the curse that the Lord ordained by Moses his servant on the day he led our fathers out of Egypt’s land, to give us a land flowing with milk and honey, as it is this day.{i}
And we did not heed the voice of the Lord our God, in all the words of the prophets whom he sent to us;
but we went off each one in the intent of his own evil heart, to serve other gods and to do what is evil in the eyes of the Lord our God.

notes.text: Jeremiah’s secretary (Jer 32:12; 36:4–32; 45:1). The Greek spells the names Nērias, Maasaias, Sedekias, Asadias and Chelkias.
The month is not named. If counted from the fall of Jerusalem (587/586 BC), the fifth year is about 582 BC.
Jeconiah (Jehoiachin) was taken to Babylon in 597 BC (2 Kgs 24:8–17; 25:27–30).
The river Sud is otherwise unknown.
Not the high priest of 2 Kgs 25:18 (Seraiah); this Jehoiakim is otherwise unknown.
Sivan is the third month, May–June. Most take “he” as Baruch.
Compare Jer 29:7. Belshazzar was in fact the son of Nabonidus (compare Dan 5:2).
Verses 1:15–2:19 closely follow the prayer of Dan 9:4–19.

verses.text: So the Lord made good on the warning he had spoken against us, against the judges who ruled Israel, against our kings and our leaders, and against everyone in Israel and Judah,
to bring upon us great evils, such as had not been done under the whole of heaven as he did in Jerusalem, according to what is written in the law of Moses,
that a man among us would eat his son’s flesh, and another his daughter’s flesh.{a}
He put them under the power of all the kingdoms around us, to become an object of scorn and ruin among all the surrounding nations where the Lord had dispersed them.
And they were laid low and not lifted up, because against the Lord our God we sinned, not heeding his voice.
To the Lord our God belongs righteousness, but to us and to our fathers shame of face, as it is this day.
All that the Lord spoke against us, all these evils have come upon us.
Yet we have not entreated the face of the Lord, that each might turn back from the intents of his evil heart.
And the Lord kept watch over the evils, and the Lord brought them upon us; for the Lord is righteous in all his works that he commanded us.
And we did not heed his voice, to walk in the ordinances of the Lord that he set before our face.

And now, Lord God of Israel, who brought your people out of the land of Egypt with a strong hand and with signs and with wonders and with great power and with a lifted-up arm, and made yourself a name, as it is this day:
we have sinned, we have done impiety, we have done wrong, Lord our God, against all your just decrees.
Let your fury turn away from us, for we are left few among the nations where you scattered us.
Hear, Lord, our prayer and our petition, and deliver us for your own sake, and grant us favor in the eyes of those who led us away captive,
so that the whole earth may know that you are the Lord our God, for Israel and his race are called by your name.
Lord, look down from your holy house and take thought for us; bend your ear, Lord, and hear;
open your eyes, Lord, and look; it is not the dead in Hades, whose life breath has left their bodies, who will give the Lord glory and vindication;{b}
but the soul that is grieved beyond measure, that goes about bowed and feeble, and the eyes that fail, and the soul that hungers, will give you glory and justice, Lord.
For it is not on the just deeds of our fathers and our kings that we lay down our plea for mercy before your face, Lord our God.{c}
For you have sent your fury and your wrath upon us, as you spoke by the hand of your servants the prophets, saying:
This is what the Lord says: Bow your shoulders to serve the king of Babylon, and you will stay on the soil I gave to your ancestors.{d}
But if you do not heed the voice of the Lord to serve the king of Babylon,

I will silence in the cities of Judah and in the outskirts of Jerusalem the sound of mirth and the sound of gladness, the bridegroom’s sound and the bride’s sound, and all the land will be a waste with no one dwelling in it.{e}

But we did not obey your voice by serving the king of Babylon; and you fulfilled the warnings you gave through your servants the prophets, that our kings’ bones and our ancestors’ bones would be dug up from where they lay.{f}
And see, they lie cast out to the day’s heat and the night’s frost; and in cruel pains they died, by famine and by sword and by pestilence.{g}
And the house that bears your name you have reduced to what it is now, because of the evil done by Israel’s house and Judah’s house.
Yet you have dealt with us, Lord our God, according to all your gentleness and according to all your great compassion,
just as you declared through your servant Moses on the day you ordered him to write your law in front of the Israelites:
If you will not heed my voice, this great and teeming throng will surely be turned into a little band among the nations where I will scatter them.{h}
For I know that they will not heed me, because it is a stiff-necked people. But in the land of their exile they will turn back to their heart,{i}
and they will know that I am the Lord their God. And I will give them a heart and ears that hear,
and in the land of their exile they shall praise me, and my name they shall remember,
and they will turn back from their stiff back and from their wicked deeds, for they will remember the way of their fathers, who sinned before the Lord.
I will return them to the land I promised with an oath to their forefathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and they will be its masters; I will make them numerous, and they will not dwindle.
And I will set up for them a covenant of the age, that I may be their God and they may be my people; and I will no longer remove my people Israel from the land that I have given them.{j}

notes.text: Greek apostolē, “a sending,” probably for Hebrew deber, “pestilence” (compare Jer 32:36).

verses.text: Lord Almighty, God of Israel, a soul in anguish and a wearied spirit cries out to you.
Hear, Lord, and have mercy, for we have sinned before you.
For you sit enthroned to the age, and we are perishing to the age.

Lord Almighty, God of Israel, hear now the prayer of Israel’s dead{a} and of the sons of those who sinned before you, who would not listen to the Lord their God’s voice; and so the evils have fastened on us.
Do not remember the wrongdoings of our fathers, but remember your hand and your name at this time.
For you are the Lord our God, and we will praise you, Lord.

For this reason you have set the fear of you in our hearts, that we might call upon your name; and in our exile we shall praise you, since we have put away from our heart all the wrongdoing of our fathers who sinned before you.
Look, today we are in exile where you dispersed us, an object of scorn, a curse, and a punishment for everything our ancestors did wrong in turning away from the Lord our God.

Hear, Israel, the commandments of life;{b}
give ear to know understanding.

Why, Israel, why is it that you are in your enemies’ land,
grown old in a country not your own,

that you have been defiled together with the dead,
that you are counted among those in Hades?
You have forsaken the spring of wisdom.

If you had walked in the way of God,
you would be dwelling in peace to the age.

Find out where understanding is,
where power is, where insight is,
and so learn at once
where long life and survival are,
where to find light for the eyes, and peace.

Who has discovered where she dwells?
Who has gone in to her treasure-houses?

Where now are the nations’ rulers,
and those who were lords over the earth’s beasts,

those who made sport with the birds of heaven,
and those who heaped up silver and gold,
in which human beings trust,
and of whose getting there is no end?

For those who worked silver with such anxious care —
there is no finding out their works.{c}

They have disappeared and descended to Hades,
and others have taken their places.

No news of her reached Canaan,
and she was never seen in Teman;{d}

nor the sons of Hagar, who seek understanding on the earth,
the traders of Merran{e} and Teman,
the tellers of tales and the seekers of understanding —
the way of wisdom they have not known,
nor have they remembered her paths.

O Israel, how great is the house of God,
and how vast the place of his possession!{f}

It is great and has no end;
it is lofty and without measure.

There the giants were born, the renowned of old,{g}
great in stature, skilled in war.

Not these did God choose,
nor to these did he grant the way of knowledge;

and they perished because they had no insight;
they perished through their folly.

Who has climbed into heaven and seized her
and fetched her down from the clouds?{h}

Who has crossed over the sea and found her,
and will bring her back for choice gold?

There is no one who knows her way,
nor anyone who ponders her path.

the One who sends out the light, and it goes;
he called it, and it obeyed him with trembling.

This is our God;
no other shall be reckoned beside him.

He found out the whole way of knowledge
and gave her to Jacob his servant
and to Israel, the one he loved.

After this she appeared on earth
and lived her life among human beings.{i}

notes.text: Greek “dead.” Probably the Hebrew methe, “men of,” was read as methe, “dead of”; NRSV renders “people.”
The poem of 3:9–4:4 draws on Job 28 and Deut 30:11–20, and, like Sir 24:23, identifies Wisdom with the Law (4:1).
The Greek of this verse is obscure.
Teman in Edom was famed for wisdom (Jer 49:7; Obad 8–9).
Merran is unknown; perhaps Midian (compare Gen 37:28).
The whole creation is meant.
Gen 6:4.
Deut 30:12–13; compare Rom 10:6–7.
Compare Prov 8:31; Sir 24:8–12. Many Christian writers from the 2nd century AD on read this verse of the incarnation; some scholars think it a later addition.

verses.text:
She is the book of the commandments of God
and the law that endures to the age.
All who hold her fast are bound for life,
but those who forsake her will die.

Turn back, Jacob, and take hold of her;
walk toward her shining, in the face of her light.

Do not give your glory to another,
or the things that profit you to a foreign nation.

Blessed are we, Israel,
for what is pleasing to God is known to us.

Take courage, my people,
you who keep Israel’s name in memory.

You were sold to the nations,
not for destruction;
but because you provoked God to anger
you were handed over to your adversaries.

You angered your Maker
by offering sacrifices to demons rather than to God.{a}

You forgot the everlasting God, who nursed you,
and you grieved Jerusalem, who reared you.

For she saw the wrath from God coming upon you,
and said:
Hear, you who dwell near Zion;
God has laid great mourning upon me,

for I have seen the captivity of my sons and daughters,
which the Everlasting brought upon them.{b}

For with gladness I nursed them,
but with weeping and mourning I sent them away.

Let no one rejoice over me, a widow
forsaken by many;
I have been made desolate for the sins of my children,
because they turned aside from the law of God

They did not recognize his decrees,
nor follow the paths of his commandments,
nor walk the way of instruction in his righteousness.

Let the neighbors of Zion come
and remember the captivity of my sons and daughters,
which the Everlasting brought upon them.

For he summoned a nation against them from far away,
a ruthless nation with a foreign language,
that showed no respect for the elderly
and no compassion for the young.{c}

And they led away the widow’s dear sons
and left her who was alone bereft of her daughters.
But I — how can I help you?

For the One who brought these evils upon you
will deliver you from the hand of your enemies.

Go, children, go on your way,
for I am left desolate.

Take courage, children, cry out to God,
and he will deliver you from tyranny,
from the hand of enemies.

My hope is fixed on the Eternal One that he will rescue you,
and delight has come to me from the Holy One
because of the compassion that will quickly reach you
from your eternal Savior.

For with mourning and weeping I sent you away,
but God will restore you to me
with joy and gladness to the age.

For as the neighbors of Zion have now seen your captivity,
so they will soon see your salvation from God,
which will come upon you with great glory
and with the splendor of the Everlasting.

Children, endure patiently
the anger God has brought on you.
Your enemy has chased you down,
but soon you will watch him be destroyed
and tread on his neck.

My tender ones have walked rough roads;
they were taken off like a flock carried away by enemies.
Be brave, children, and call on God, for the one who sent this upon you will keep you in mind.

For as your mind was set on straying from God,
so turn back now with ten times the zeal to seek him.

For the One who brought these evils upon you
will bring you everlasting joy along with your salvation.

Take heart, Jerusalem:
he who named you will give you comfort.

Wretched are those who did you harm
and rejoiced at your fall.

Wretched are the cities that your children served as slaves;
wretched is she who received your sons.{d}

For as she rejoiced at your fall
and was glad over your ruin,
so she will be grieved at her own desolation.

And I will take away her delight in her crowds,
and her proud boasting will be turned into mourning.

Fire will fall on her from the Eternal One for many days,
and for a long while demons will make their home in her.{e}

Turn your eyes eastward, Jerusalem,
and behold the joy that comes to you from God.

Look, your sons are on their way, whom you sent off;
they are coming home, assembled from east and west
by the command of the Holy One,
celebrating God’s glory.

notes.text: “The Everlasting” (ho aiōnios) is used as a title of God throughout 4:5–5:9.
Babylon.

verses.text:
Take off, Jerusalem, the robe of your mourning and your affliction,
and put on to the age the comeliness of the glory from God.{a}

Wrap around yourself the double cloak of the righteousness that is from God;
set on your head the diadem of the glory of the Everlasting.

For God will show your brightness
to every place under heaven.

For your name will be called by God to the age:
“Peace of Righteousness” and “Glory of Godliness.”

Rise up, Jerusalem, and stand on the summit;
face east
and watch your children gather from sunset to sunrise
by the command of the Holy One,
rejoicing that God has not forgotten them.

They left you on foot,
driven off by their enemies;
but God is bringing them back to you,
lifted up in glory like a royal throne.

For God has commanded that every lofty mountain
and the hills of the age be brought low,
and the ravines filled up to make the ground level,
so that in God’s glory Israel may go securely.{b}

The forests too, and every sweet-smelling tree,
have given Israel shade by God’s command.

For with joy God will lead Israel
by the light of his glory,
with his own mercy and righteousness.

notes.text: Verses 5:1–9 are close in wording to the Psalms of Solomon 11 (1st century BC); compare Isa 52:1; 60–62.

books.name: Letter of Jeremiah
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of the Letter of Jeremiah (Epistle of Jeremiah) as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which follows Codex Vaticanus (B) with the readings of Alexandrinus (A) and others. In the Greek manuscripts it stands as a separate piece after Lamentations (or after Baruch); in the Latin Vulgate and the King James Version it is printed as Baruch chapter 6, and verse numbers here (1–73) match Baruch 6:1–73 in those Bibles. It is a sermon against idolatry in the form of a letter of Jeremiah to the exiles (compare Jer 10:1–16; 29:1–23; Isa 44:9–20), built on the refrain “they are not gods; do not fear them.” Many scholars hold that it was written in Hebrew or Aramaic, perhaps in the 4th–2nd century BC; no Semitic text survives. A small Greek papyrus fragment from Qumran Cave 7, 7QpapEpJer gr (7Q2), copied about 100 BC, preserves parts of verses 43–44, as reported, and shows that the work was known in Greek by then; 2 Macc 2:1–3 may allude to it. It is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes; dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844) was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: A copy of a letter Jeremiah sent to the people about to be deported to Babylon by the king of the Babylonians, informing them of what God had commanded him.{a}
Because of the sins you have committed against God, Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Babylonians, will deport you to Babylon.
So when you come into Babylon, you will stay there many years and a long time, up to seven generations;{b} and after this I will bring you out from there in peace.
But now you will see in Babylon gods of silver and gold and wood carried on shoulders,{c} which put fear into the nations.
Be on your guard, then, that you yourselves do not become altogether like the foreigners, and that fear of them does not seize you
when you see the crowd before and behind them worshiping them. But say in your mind: “It is you, Master, whom we must worship.”
For my angel is with you, and he himself is watching over your lives.{d}
Their tongues are polished smooth by a craftsman, and they themselves are covered with gold and silver; yet they are fakes and cannot talk.
And taking gold, as for a girl who loves finery, they make crowns for the heads of their gods.
And sometimes the priests even filch gold and silver from their gods and spend it on themselves,
and they will give some of it even to the prostitutes on the roof.{e} And they deck them out with clothing like human beings — the gods of silver and gold and wood.
Yet these cannot save themselves from tarnish and moths, though they are wrapped in purple clothing.
People wipe their faces because of the dust from the temple, which lies thick upon them.
And one holds a scepter like a man who judges a land, yet he cannot put to death the one who offends against him.
Another has a dagger in his right hand, and an ax, yet he cannot deliver himself from war and from robbers.
From this it is known that they are not gods; so do not fear them.
Just as a vessel someone uses is worthless once it is smashed, so are their gods once they are installed in their temples. Their eyes are full of dust kicked up by the feet of visitors.

And as the courtyards are shut up all around a man who has wronged a king and is being taken off to die, so their priests secure their temples with doors, with locks and with bars, lest they be plundered by robbers.
They light lamps for them, more than for themselves, though the gods cannot see a single one of them.
They are just like a beam of the temple, and men say their hearts are eaten out, while creatures that creep from the ground devour both them and their clothing, and they do not notice.
Their faces are blackened by the smoke from the temple.
Upon their bodies and upon their heads light bats, swallows, and birds, and cats as well.{f}
By this you may know that they are no gods; so have no fear of them.
For as for the gold they wear for beauty, unless someone wipes off the tarnish, they will not shine; for not even when they were being cast did they feel it.
They are bought at any price, though there is no breath in them.
Having no feet, they are carried on shoulders, showing their own dishonor to human beings; and those who serve them are put to shame,

because if one of them falls to the ground, it is raised up by them; and if someone sets it upright, it will not move by itself; and if it is tilted, it cannot straighten itself; but offerings are set before them as before the dead.
And the sacrifices made to them their priests sell and make use of; and likewise their wives preserve some of it with salt, but to the poor and helpless they give nothing.
A woman in her monthly impurity or in childbed touches their sacrifices.{g} Knowing, then, from these things that they are not gods, do not fear them.
For how can they be called gods? For women serve meals to gods of silver and gold and wood.
And the priests sit in their houses of worship with garments rent, heads and beards shorn, bareheaded;
they bellow and cry aloud before their gods, like mourners at the meal for one who has died.
The priests take some of their clothing and dress their own wives and children with it.
Whether they suffer evil from anyone or good, they cannot repay it. They can neither set up a king nor remove one.
Likewise they can give neither wealth nor a copper coin;{h} if someone makes a vow to them and does not pay it, they will not call him to account.
From death they can save no one, nor snatch the feeble from the mighty.
They cannot bring a blind man back to sight; they cannot rescue a man who is in distress.
They will not take pity on a widow or do good to an orphan.
Like quarried stones from the hillside are these wooden things, plated over with gold and silver, and all who serve them will be shamed.
How, then, can anyone imagine them gods or call them so? Even the Chaldeans themselves show them no respect;
for when they meet someone who is mute and cannot talk, they bring him to Bel{i} and ask that he speak, as if Bel could grasp it.
Yet they themselves cannot perceive this and forsake them, for they have no sense.

And the women, with cords around them, sit along the roads, burning bran for incense; and when one of them is drawn aside by some passerby and lies with him, she taunts the woman beside her, because she was not thought as worthy as herself and her cord was not broken.{j}
All that is done for them is false. How then can anyone think or call them gods?
They are made by carpenters and goldsmiths; they can be nothing other than what the craftsmen wish them to be.
And those who make them will not themselves last long; how then can the things made by them be gods?
For they have left lies and a reproach to those who come after.
For when war or evils come upon them, the priests consult together where they may hide themselves with them.
How then can one not perceive that they are not gods, who cannot save themselves from war or from evils?
For since they are of wood and overlaid with gold and silver, it will be known afterward that they are false.
It will be plain to all the nations and the kings that they are not gods but works of human hands, and that there is no work of God in them.
Who then does not know that they are not gods?
For they cannot set up a king over a land, or give rain to human beings.
They are powerless to settle their own case or to rescue a person who has been wronged; they are like crows flying between sky and earth.{k}
For when fire falls upon a house of gods of wood or overlaid with gold or silver, their priests will flee and be saved, but they themselves will be burned up like beams in the middle.
And they cannot withstand a king or enemies. How then can anyone suppose or admit that they are gods?
Gods of wood and overlaid with silver and gold cannot save themselves from thieves and robbers;
the strong will strip off their gold and silver and the clothing that wraps them and go off with it, and they cannot help themselves.

So it is better to be a king who displays his own courage, or a household jar that serves its owner’s needs, than these false gods; or a door in a house that protects what lies inside, than these false gods; or a wooden column in a palace, than these false gods.
For sun and moon and stars, being bright and sent out for some use, are obedient.
So also the lightning, when it flashes, is fair to see; and in the same way the wind blows in every land.
And when the clouds are ordered by God to pass over the whole inhabited world, they carry out the order.
And when fire is sent from above to burn up mountains and forests, it carries out its orders. These idols cannot compare to them in appearance or in power.
Therefore one must neither think nor call them gods, since they are not able either to judge a cause or to do good to human beings.
Knowing, then, that they are not gods, do not fear them.
For they can neither curse nor bless kings;
They cannot give signs in the sky for the nations, or shine like the sun, or light up the night like the moon.
Better than they are the beasts of the field, for these can run into a covert and help themselves.
So in no way is it plain to us that they are gods; therefore do not fear them.
For as a scarecrow in a patch of cucumbers{l} keeps no watch over anything, so are their wooden gods with their gold and silver plating.
In the same way their wooden gods, overlaid with gold and silver, resemble a thornbush in a garden where birds of every kind settle, or a corpse tossed out in the dark.
By the purple and the fine linen{m} rotting on them you can tell that they are not gods; and they themselves will finally be devoured and become a disgrace across the land.
Far better is an upright person who owns no idols, for he will be free of disgrace.

notes.text: In the Latin Vulgate and the King James Version this letter is Baruch 6, and its verses are numbered Baruch 6:1–73. Compare the letter of Jer 29:1–23.
Jer 25:11–12 and 29:10 speak of seventy years; “seven generations” lengthens the exile, perhaps to suit a later author’s own time.
The processions of the Babylonian gods, as at the New Year festival; compare Isa 46:1–7.
“He himself” is God’s angel or God; the Greek is abrupt.
Literally “on the housetop”; the Greek is obscure, and some render “in the brothel.”
This is the only mention of cats in the Bible.
Greek chalkos, a small bronze coin.
Bel (“lord”) is a title of Marduk, the chief god of Babylon; compare Bel and the Dragon. In the Greek, verse 40 runs on into verse 41 without a break.
Compare the custom described by Herodotus (1.199). The Qumran papyrus 7QpapEpJer gr (7Q2), about 100 BC, preserves parts of verses 43–44 in Greek, as reported.
The image is obscure: perhaps crows that flit about to no purpose.
The Greek reads “marble” (marmaros), probably a corruption; “fine linen” (or “sheen”) follows a widely accepted correction, as reported.

books.name: Additions to Daniel: Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of Daniel 3:24–90 in the version of Theodotion, as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which gives on facing pages the Old Greek (Septuagint proper, preserved in full only in the Chigi manuscript 88 and the Syro-Hexapla, with Papyrus 967 reported in later editions) and the Theodotion text that replaced it in church use. Differences of substance in the Old Greek are given in the notes. These verses are part of the Greek and Latin book of Daniel, standing between Dan 3:23 and 3:24 of the Hebrew-Aramaic text; in the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles they are numbered Daniel 3:24–90, and the verse numbers here (1–68) follow NRSV and do not correspond one-for-one with those. They include the Prayer of Azariah (vv. 1–22), a prose narrative (vv. 23–27), and the Song of the Three (vv. 28–68), whose second part (vv. 35–68, the Benedicite) has long been sung in Christian worship. No Semitic text survives; many scholars hold that the prayer and song were composed in Hebrew, perhaps in the 2nd century BC. Azariah, Hananiah and Mishael are the Hebrew names of Abednego, Shadrach and Meshach (Dan 1:6–7). These additions are received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place them among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes; dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844), which translates the Old Greek, was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: And they walked about in the midst of the flame, singing hymns to God and blessing the Lord.{a}
And Azariah stood up and prayed thus, and opening his mouth in the midst of the fire he said:

Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers,
and praiseworthy, and your name is glorified to the ages.

For you are righteous in all that you have done to us,
and all your works are true, and your ways are straight,
and all your judgments are truth.

You have carried out true judgments
in everything you have brought down upon us
and upon our ancestors’ holy city, Jerusalem;
for with truth and justice you brought all this
upon us because of our sins.

nor did we keep them or do as you commanded us,
so that it might go well with us.

And all that you brought upon us,
and everything that you did to us,
you did in true judgment.

Do not hand us over to the end, for your name’s sake,
and do not annul your covenant,

and do not take your mercy away from us,
for the sake of Abraham, the one beloved by you,
and for the sake of Isaac your servant
and Israel your holy one,

For, Master, we have been made fewer than every nation
and are brought low today in all the earth because of our sins.
But with a crushed soul and a humbled spirit may we be received,{e}

And now we follow you with all our heart,
we revere you and look for your face.
Do not let us be disgraced,

but treat us with your kindness
and with your overflowing compassion.

And rescue us according to your wonders,
and give glory to your name, Lord.

and let them know that you alone are Lord God,
and glorious over the whole inhabited world.
And the king’s servants who had thrown them in did not stop heating the furnace with naphtha and pitch and tow and brushwood.
And the flame poured out above the furnace to about seventy-three feet;{g}
and it spread out and burned up those of the Chaldeans whom it found around the furnace.
But the angel of the Lord came down together with those around Azariah into the furnace and shook the flame of the fire out of the furnace,
and made the middle of the furnace as if a wind of dew were whistling through it; and the fire did not touch them at all, nor give them pain, nor trouble them.
Then the three, as from one mouth, sang a hymn and glorified and blessed God in the furnace, saying:

Blessed are you, Lord, God of our fathers,
and praiseworthy and exalted above all to the ages;

and blessed is the holy name of your glory,
and greatly praised and exalted above all to all the ages.

Blessed are you in the temple of your holy glory,
and hymned above all and glorified above all to the ages.{h}

Blessed are you who look upon the abysses,
seated on the cherubim,
and praiseworthy and exalted above all to the ages.

Blessed are you on the throne of your kingship,
and hymned above all and exalted above all to the ages.

Blessed are you in the firmament of heaven,
and hymned and glorified to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all you works of the Lord;{i}
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you heavens;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you angels of the Lord;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all you waters above the heaven;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all you powers;{j}
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, sun and moon;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you stars of heaven;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, every shower and dew;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all you winds;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, fire and burning heat;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, chill and scorching;{k}
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, dews and snowfalls;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, nights and days;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, light and darkness;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, frost and cold;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, hoarfrosts and snows;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, lightnings and clouds;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Let the earth bless the Lord;
let it hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, mountains and hills;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all things that spring up on the earth;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you springs;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, seas and rivers;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you sea monsters{l} and all things that move in the waters;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, all you birds of heaven;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you wild beasts and all you cattle;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you sons of human beings;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, Israel;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you priests of the Lord;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you slaves of the Lord;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you spirits and souls of the righteous;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Bless the Lord, you who are holy and lowly in heart;
hymn him and exalt him above all to the ages.

Give thanks to the Lord, for he is kind,
for his mercy is to the ages.{n}

notes.text: Inserted after Dan 3:23. The Old Greek opens instead: “So Hananiah and Azariah and Mishael prayed and sang hymns to the Lord when the king commanded that they be thrown into the furnace.”
Nebuchadnezzar, or, in the author’s own day, perhaps Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175–164 BC).
Compare Hos 3:4. The line fits the time when the temple worship was halted (167–164 BC; 1 Macc 1:41–64), as many hold.

The Greek line “and be fully accomplished behind you” (ekteleisai opisthen sou) is obscure; the Old Greek, as reported, reads differently here, and some correct the text to “and may we wholly follow you.”
Greek “forty-nine cubits,” about 22 m; a cubit is about 18 inches (45 cm).
The order of verses 31–34 differs somewhat between Theodotion and the Old Greek, as reported.
Verses 35–68 are the canticle known from its Latin opening as the Benedicite. The refrain renders hymneite kai hyperypsoute auton eis tous aiōnas.
The heavenly hosts.
The sequence of the elements named in verses 42–51 differs between Theodotion and the Old Greek, as reported.
Greek kētē, the great creatures of the sea, including whales.
Dan 1:6–7: Shadrach, Abednego and Meshach.
The Greek and Latin text of Daniel continues at 3:24 of the Hebrew-Aramaic (“Then King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished…”), numbered Dan 3:91 in the Vulgate.

books.name: Additions to Daniel: Susanna
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of Susanna in the version of Theodotion, as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which also prints the Old Greek (Septuagint proper, preserved in full in the Chigi manuscript 88 and the Syro-Hexapla) on the facing page; differences of substance in the Old Greek are given in the notes. In Theodotion’s manuscripts Susanna stands at the head of the book of Daniel, introducing Daniel as a youth; in the Old Greek and in the Latin Vulgate it follows Dan 12, and in the Vulgate and Catholic Bibles it is numbered Daniel 13 (verses 1–64 here match Dan 13:1–64). The Old Greek is shorter (it has nothing corresponding to verses 1–5a or the bath scene of 15–18 in the same form, and ends differently). The puns on tree names in verses 54–59 suggested to early readers (Julius Africanus, about AD 240, as reported) that the story was composed in Greek; others hold that an original Hebrew or Aramaic story was retold with new puns. Susanna is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844), which translates the Old Greek, was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: There was a man living in Babylon, and his name was Joakim.{a}
And he took a wife whose name was Susanna,{b} daughter of Hilkiah, very beautiful and one who feared the Lord.
Her parents, too, were just people, and they had instructed their daughter in keeping with Moses’ law.
Joakim was extremely wealthy, and next to his house he had a garden; the Jews regularly visited him, since he was the most respected of all of them.
And two elders from the people were appointed judges in that year, about whom the Master had spoken: “Lawlessness came out of Babylon, from elders who were judges, who seemed to guide the people.”{c}
These men spent much time in Joakim’s house, and all who had cases to be judged would come to them there.
And when the people went away at midday, Susanna would go in and walk about in her husband’s garden.
And the two elders watched her every day going in and walking about, and they came to be in lust for her.
And they twisted their own minds and turned their eyes away so as not to look to heaven or remember just judgments.
And both were pierced with desire for her, yet they did not disclose their pain to each other,
for they were ashamed to disclose their lust, that they wished to lie with her.
And they watched eagerly every day to see her.
They said to each other, “Let’s go home; it is time for lunch.” So they left and separated.

And turning back they came to the same place, and when they questioned each other about the reason, they owned up to their lust. And then together they fixed a time when they would be able to find her alone.

And it happened, while they were watching for a fit day, that she went in as on the day before and the day before that, with only two maidservants, and she wished to bathe in the garden, for it was hot.{d}
And there was no one there except the two elders, who had hidden and were watching her.
And she said to the maids, “Bring me olive oil and soap, and shut the doors of the garden, so that I may bathe.”
And they did just as she told them: they closed the garden doors, then slipped out through the side doors to fetch what she had asked for; and the elders they never saw, since these were in hiding.
And it happened, when the maids had gone out, that the two elders got up and ran to her and said,
“Look, the doors of the garden are shut, and no one sees us, and we are in desire for you; so agree with us and be with us.
But if not, we will testify against you that a young man was with you and that this is why you sent the maids away from you.”
Susanna groaned and said, “I am trapped on all sides. If I do this, it means my death; if I refuse, I will not get away from you.
Better that I refrain and fall into your hands than that I sin in the Lord’s sight.”
Then Susanna shouted aloud, and the pair of elders shouted out against her as well.
And one of them ran and opened the doors of the garden.
And when those in the house heard the outcry in the garden, they rushed in by the side door to see what had happened to her.
And when the elders told their tale, the slaves were deeply ashamed, for never had such a word been spoken about Susanna.
And it happened on the next day, when the people gathered to her husband Joakim, that the two elders came, full of their lawless intent against Susanna, to have her put to death.
And they said before the people, “Send for Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, who is Joakim’s wife.” And they sent.
And she came, and her parents and her children and all her relatives.
Now Susanna was exceedingly delicate and beautiful in appearance.
And the lawless men ordered her to be unveiled, for she was veiled, so that they might take their fill of her beauty.
And those with her and all who saw her were weeping.
Then the pair of elders rose in the middle of the people and placed their hands on her head.{e}
But she, in tears, gazed up heavenward, because her heart had put its trust in the Lord.
And the elders said, “While we were walking about in the garden by ourselves, this woman came in with two maids, and she shut the doors of the garden and sent the maids away.
Then a youth, who was lying hidden there, approached her and lay with her.
And we were in a corner of the garden, and seeing the lawlessness we ran to them;
and though we saw the two of them together, we could not hold him, since he was stronger than we were; he opened the doors and sprang out.
But we seized this woman and questioned her as to who the young man was,
and she refused to tell us. This is our testimony.” Because they were elders and judges of the people, the assembly believed them and sentenced her to death.
And Susanna cried out with a loud voice and said, “God of the age, who knows hidden things, who knows all things before they come to be,
you know that they have testified falsely against me. And see, I am dying, though I have done none of the things that these men have wickedly made up against me.”
And the Lord heard her voice.
And as she was being led away to be destroyed, God stirred up the holy spirit of a young boy whose name was Daniel,{f}
and he shouted with a loud voice, “I am clean of the blood of this woman!”
Then the whole people swung round toward him and said, “What is this you have just said?”
And he, standing in their midst, said, “Are you such fools, sons of Israel? Without examining and without learning the plain truth, have you condemned a daughter of Israel?
Go back to the place of judgment, for these men have testified falsely against her.”
So the whole people hurried back. And the elders said to him, “Come, take your seat in our midst and make it known to us, since God has granted you the rank of an elder.”
Daniel said to them, “Set the two a good distance apart, one from the other, and I will put them to the question.”
And when they had been separated one from the other, he called one of them and said to him, “You who have grown old in days of evil, now your sins have come home, which you committed before,
judging unjust judgments, condemning the innocent and letting the guilty go free, though the Lord says, ‘The innocent and the righteous you shall not kill.’{g}
Now then, if you really saw her, tell me: under what tree did you see them having intercourse with each other?” And he said, “Under a mastic tree.”{h}
And Daniel said, “Well have you lied against your own head; for already the angel of God has received the sentence from God and will split you in two.”
And putting him aside, he ordered them to bring the other, and said to him, “Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you, and desire has twisted your heart.
This is how you were dealing with the daughters of Israel, and they were having intercourse with you out of fear; but a daughter of Judah would not endure your lawlessness.
Now tell me: beneath which tree did you see them having sex?” He answered, “Under an evergreen oak.”{i}
And Daniel said to him, “Well have you too lied against your own head; for the angel of God is waiting with the sword to saw you in two, so as to destroy you both.”
And the whole assembly cried out with a loud voice and blessed God, who saves those who hope in him.

And they rose up against the two elders, because Daniel had convicted them out of their own mouth of having testified falsely, and they did to them just as they had wickedly planned to do to their neighbor;
acting according to the law of Moses,{j} they killed them. And innocent blood was saved on that day.
And Hilkiah and his wife gave praise for their daughter, with Joakim her husband and all her relatives, because nothing shameful was found in her.
And Daniel became great before the people from that day onward.{k}

notes.text: In the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles this book is Daniel 13. Verses 1–5a are lacking in the Old Greek, which begins abruptly with the elders.
Hebrew shoshannah, “lily.”
The saying is not found in the Old Testament; some compare Jer 29:20–23, where two false prophets in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, are condemned for adultery.
Verses 15–18 have no counterpart in the Old Greek, which tells the story without the bath.
The Old Greek, as reported, reads instead that “an angel of the Lord gave a spirit of understanding to a young man,” Daniel.
Exod 23:7.

Greek schinos, the mastic or lentisk, a small evergreen shrub. Daniel answers with a pun: schinos / schisei, “will split.” An English imitation would be “under a clove tree … the angel will cleave you.”
Greek prinos, the holm oak (Quercus ilex). The pun is prinos / prisai, “to saw.” An English imitation would be “under a yew … to hew you.”
Deut 19:16–21. The Old Greek, as reported, says that they gagged them, led them out, and threw them into a ravine, and that the angel of the Lord cast fire between them.
The Old Greek ends instead with praise of the young: “For this reason the young are beloved of Jacob for their simplicity…,” as reported.

books.name: Additions to Daniel: Bel and the Dragon
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of Bel and the Dragon in the version of Theodotion, as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which also prints the Old Greek (Septuagint proper, preserved in the Chigi manuscript 88 and the Syro-Hexapla) on the facing page; differences of substance in the Old Greek are given in the notes. In the Greek manuscripts the two stories close the book of Daniel; in the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles they are numbered Daniel 14 (verses 1–42 here match Dan 14:1–42). The Old Greek is titled as a work of the prophet Habakkuk, a Levite and the son of Joshua, and it calls Daniel a priest, son of Abal. Both stories mock idol worship (compare Isa 44:9–20; Jer 10; Jer 51:44, where God promises to punish Bel in Babylon and force him to give back what he has swallowed). The language behind the Greek, and the date (often put in the 2nd century BC), are uncertain. Bel and the Dragon is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Measures are given in US units with the original and metric values in the notes; dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton’s English (1844), which translates the Old Greek, was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: King Astyages was gathered to his fathers, and Cyrus the Persian received his kingdom.{a}
And Daniel lived as a companion of the king and was honored above all his Friends.{b}
And the Babylonians had an idol whose name was Bel,{c} and there were spent on it each day twelve artabas of fine flour and forty sheep and six measures of wine.
And the king revered it and would go each day to bow down to it, but Daniel bowed down to his own God.

And the king said to him, “Why do you not bow down to Bel?” And he said, “Because I do not revere idols made by hand, but the living God, who created the heaven and the earth and has lordship over all flesh.”
The king asked him, “Don’t you agree that Bel is a living god? Can’t you see how much he consumes every day?”
Daniel laughed and said, “Let no one mislead you, O king: this thing is clay within and bronze without, and never has it eaten or drunk a thing.”
The king was furious and summoned his priests. He told them, “Unless you tell me who is consuming these supplies, you will die.
But if you can prove that Bel consumes them, Daniel will die, because he has insulted Bel.” Daniel told the king, “Let it be as you say.”
Now the priests of Bel were seventy, besides their wives and children. And the king went with Daniel into the house of Bel.
And the priests of Bel said, “See, we are going outside; and you, O king, set out the food and mix the wine and put it out, and shut the door and seal it with your signet ring.
Come in at dawn tomorrow, and if you do not find that Bel has eaten everything, we will die—otherwise Daniel, who is lying about us, will.”
But they were unconcerned, for they had made a hidden entrance under the table, and through it they would go in continually and consume the things.

And it happened, when they had gone out, that the king set out the food for Bel. And Daniel ordered his servants, and they brought ashes and sifted them through the whole temple in the presence of the king alone. And they went out and shut the door and sealed it with the king’s signet ring and departed.
And the priests came in the night, as was their habit, with their wives and children, and they ate and drank everything up.
And the king rose early in the morning, and Daniel with him.
And he said, “Are the seals unbroken, Daniel?” And he said, “They are unbroken, O king.”
And it happened, as soon as the doors were opened, that the king looked at the table and cried out with a loud voice, “Great are you, Bel, and with you there is no deceit, not even one!”
And Daniel laughed and held back the king from going in, and said, “Look now at the floor and take note whose footprints these are.”
The king said, “I see the tracks of men, of women, and of children.”
The king was furious; he arrested the priests along with their wives and children, and they pointed out the secret doors by which they entered to eat what was set on the table.
And the king killed them and handed Bel over to Daniel, and he overturned it and its temple.{d}
And there was a great dragon,{e} and the Babylonians revered it.
And the king said to Daniel, “You will not say that this one too is bronze! See, it lives and eats and drinks; you cannot say that this is not a living god. So bow down to it.”
And Daniel said, “I will bow down to the Lord my God, for he is a living God.
But you, O king, give me authority, and I will kill the dragon without sword or rod.” And the king said, “I give it to you.”
And Daniel took pitch and fat and hair, and boiled them together and made cakes and put them into the dragon’s mouth; and the dragon ate and burst open. And he said, “See the things you revere!”

And it happened, when the Babylonians heard it, that they were greatly indignant and gathered against the king and said, “The king has become a Jew! He has torn down Bel and killed the dragon and slaughtered the priests.”
And they came to the king and said, “Hand Daniel over to us; otherwise we will kill you and your household.”
And the king saw that they pressed him hard, and being forced, he handed Daniel over to them.
And they threw him into the lions’ pit, and he was there six days.{f}
And in the pit there were seven lions, and they had been given every day two bodies and two sheep; but at that time they were not given them, so that they would devour Daniel.
Now the prophet Habakkuk was in Judea;{g} he had cooked a stew, crumbled bread into a bowl, and was heading to the field to bring it to the harvesters.
And the angel of the Lord said to Habakkuk, “Take the meal that you have to Babylon, to Daniel, into the lions’ pit.”
Habakkuk said, “Lord, Babylon I have never laid eyes on, and the pit I do not know.”
And the angel of the Lord took hold of the crown of his head, and carrying him by the hair of his head, set him down in Babylon above the pit, in the rush of his spirit.{h}
And Habakkuk shouted, saying, “Daniel, Daniel, take the meal that God has sent you!”
And Daniel said, “For you have remembered me, O God, and you have not forsaken those who love you.”
And Daniel got up and ate; and the angel of God at once returned Habakkuk to his own place.
And on the seventh day the king came to mourn Daniel, and he came to the pit and looked in, and there sat Daniel.
Then the king shouted, “You are great, Lord, God of Daniel, and there is no god but you!”
And he drew him out, and the ones who had been the cause of his ruin he threw into the pit, and they were devoured instantly before his face.{i}

notes.text: In the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles this book is Daniel 14. Astyages, the last king of the Medes, was overthrown by Cyrus about 550 BC; Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC. The Old Greek has no such opening. After its title, it begins by introducing a priest named Daniel, son of Abal, who was a companion of the king of Babylon.
“Friends” was a court title.
Bel (“lord”) is Marduk, the god of Babylon. Twelve artabas are about 19 bushels (about 670 liters); six metrētai are about 60 gallons (about 230 liters), as these measures are usually reckoned.
The Old Greek, as reported, says that the king handed Bel over to Daniel and that Daniel destroyed it.
Greek drakōn, a great serpent. The cult of a living serpent is otherwise unattested at Babylon; compare the mušḫuššu dragon of Marduk on the Ishtar Gate.
Compare Dan 6:16–24, where Daniel spends one night with the lions under Darius.
The prophet of the book of Habakkuk, of the late 7th century BC.
Compare Ezek 8:3. “His spirit” may be the angel’s or God’s.
Compare Dan 6:24. The Old Greek, as reported, ends with the king’s praise of “the Lord God” and adds no further notice.

books.name: 1 Maccabees
books.sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of 1 Maccabees in H. B. Swete’s edition of the Septuagint (Cambridge, 1909; public domain), with Brenton’s public-domain English version consulted as a check. The book survives only in Greek, though it was almost certainly written in Hebrew in the late second century BC. Dates are given in the book by the Seleucid era (“the kingdom of the Greeks”); each is converted in the text to its year BC, with the modern month span for any named month, and the original reckoning is in a footnote. 1 Maccabees appears to count most years from spring 311 BC, but some dates seem to follow the autumn 312 BC reckoning, so converted years may be off by one. Weights and sums of money are given in approximate modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes; ancient standards varied. Greek kyrios is translated “Lord” and theos “God”; the book usually avoids naming God and speaks of “Heaven.” Verse numbers follow the standard English versification. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: After Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian,{a} who had come out of the land of the Kittim,{b} had defeated Darius, king of the Persians and the Medes, he became king in his place, having first ruled over Greece.{c}
He fought many wars, seized fortresses, and put kings to death.
He pushed on to the far ends of the earth and plundered a host of nations. When the earth fell silent before him, he grew proud, and his heart swelled with arrogance.
He built up a very powerful army and ruled over lands, nations and princes, who paid him tribute.
After this he took to his bed and knew that he was dying.
So he called in his officers, the nobles who had grown up with him from boyhood, and while he was still alive he split his kingdom among them.
Alexander had reigned twelve years when he died.{d}
Then his officers took control, each in his own territory.
When he died, they all put on royal crowns, as did their sons for many years after them, and they brought great suffering to the earth.
From them sprang a sinful shoot: Antiochus Epiphanes,{e} King Antiochus’s son, who had once been held hostage at Rome. He took the throne in the year 137 of the kingdom of the Greeks (175 BC).{f}

In those days some renegades came out of Israel and persuaded many, saying, “Come, let us make a treaty with the nations around us, for ever since we kept ourselves apart from them, many troubles have overtaken us.”
The proposal pleased them,
and a number of the people were quick to go to the king, who gave them permission to adopt the customs of the Gentiles.
So they built a gymnasium{g} in Jerusalem in keeping with Gentile custom,
disguised their circumcision,{h} and abandoned the holy covenant. They joined themselves to the Gentiles and sold themselves to do evil.
When Antiochus saw that his rule was secure, he set his mind on becoming king of the land of Egypt as well, so that he might rule over both kingdoms.
He invaded Egypt with a massive force, with chariots, elephants, cavalry, and a large fleet.
He waged war against Ptolemy king of Egypt,{i} and Ptolemy turned back before him and fled, and many fell wounded.
They captured the fortified cities in the land of Egypt, and he carried off the plunder of the land.
After his conquest of Egypt, Antiochus turned back in the year 143 (169 BC).{j} He marched against Israel, coming up to Jerusalem with a massive force.
In his pride he entered the sanctuary and carried off the golden altar,{k} the lampstand that gave light, and all its equipment,
the table for the bread of the Presence,{l} the libation cups and bowls, the gold censers, the curtain, and the crowns; and he peeled away all the gilded decoration from the temple’s facade.
He took the silver and the gold and the precious vessels, and he took whatever hidden treasures he found.
Gathering everything up, he went back to his own land. He had committed murder and had spoken with great arrogance.
Deep grief came over Israel in every place where they lived.
Leaders and elders groaned; girls and youths lost their strength; the women’s beauty faded.
Every bridegroom took up a lament, and the bride sitting in her chamber went into mourning.
The land quaked for those who lived in it, and the whole house of Jacob was clothed in shame.
Two years later the king sent a chief tax collector{m} to the cities of Judah, and he came to Jerusalem with a massive force.
He spoke to them with peaceful words, but deceitfully, and they believed him. Then he fell on the city without warning, dealt it a heavy blow, and killed many people of Israel.
He looted the city and burned it, and he demolished its houses and the walls that surrounded it.
Women and children they carried away as captives, and the cattle they took for themselves.
Next they walled the City of David with a strong, high wall and powerful towers, and they used it as their fortress.{n}
They stationed a sinful people there, lawless men, and these entrenched themselves in it.
They stocked it with weapons and provisions, and they collected the spoils of Jerusalem and stored them there. It became a dangerous snare,
an ambush against the sanctuary, an evil adversary{o} to Israel at all times.
Around the sanctuary they shed innocent blood, and they defiled the sanctuary.
Because of them the people of Jerusalem fled. The city became a home for foreigners; it became foreign to its own offspring, and its children abandoned it.
Her sanctuary lay as barren as a desert; her festivals were turned to mourning, her sabbaths to disgrace, and her honor to scorn.
Her disgrace became as great as her glory had been, and her exaltation was turned into mourning.
Then the king wrote to his whole kingdom that all should be one people
and that each should give up their own customs. All the nations accepted the king’s command.
Many Israelites, too, were content with his cult: they offered sacrifices to idols and desecrated the sabbath.
The king also sent letters by messengers to Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, ordering them to follow customs foreign to the land:
to end the whole burnt offerings, sacrifices and drink offerings in the sanctuary, and to defile the sabbaths and festivals,
to defile the sanctuary and those who were holy,
to build altars, sacred precincts, and idol shrines, to sacrifice pigs and other unclean animals,
and to leave their sons uncircumcised. They were to make themselves abhorrent with every kind of impurity and profanation,
so that they would forget the law and change all its ordinances.
Whoever did not obey the king’s command was to die.
In words like these he wrote to his whole kingdom. He appointed inspectors over all the people and ordered the cities of Judah to offer sacrifice, city by city.
Many of the people flocked to them, all who were deserting the law, and they wrought evil in the land.
They drove Israel into hiding in every place where they could take refuge.

On the fifteenth day of Kislev (in November–December), in the year 145 (167 BC),{p} they set up a desolating abomination{q} on the altar of burnt offering, and they built altars in the towns all around Judah.
They burned incense at the doors of houses and in the streets.
Any books of the law they found, they tore up and burned.
Anyone found possessing a book of the covenant, and anyone who kept to the law, was put to death by the king’s decree.
Month after month they used their power against the Israelites who were found in the towns.
On the twenty-fifth day of each month they offered sacrifices on the pagan altar that had been placed on top of the altar of burnt offering.{r}
As the decree required, they executed women who had circumcised their children,
and they hung the infants from their mothers’ necks; they also killed their families and those who had circumcised them.
Yet many in Israel held firm and made up their minds that they would not eat anything unclean.
They chose to die rather than be defiled by food or profane the holy covenant, and they died.
Very great wrath came upon Israel.{s}

notes.text: Alexander the Great (356–323 BC), son of Philip II of Macedon. The name Alexander means “defender of men.”
Greek Chettiim. The Kittim were originally the people of Kition in Cyprus; the name came to be used for the peoples of the west across the sea, here the Macedonians and Greeks.
Or “he became king in his place, the first to rule over Greece.” The sense of the Greek is uncertain; Alexander ruled Greece before defeating Darius III of Persia (331 BC).
Alexander reigned 336–323 BC.
Antiochus IV (reigned 175–164 BC). Epiphanes means “manifest,” a title claiming that a god was made visible in him.

Greek: in the 137th year of the kingdom of the Greeks, that is, the Seleucid era, which began with Seleucus I. 1 Maccabees generally counts its years from the spring of 311 BC, so year 137 ran from spring 175 to spring 174 BC. Some of its dates appear to use the reckoning from autumn 312 BC, and dates converted here may be a year off.
A Greek athletic and educational center, where men exercised naked.
Literally “made foreskins for themselves,” that is, they underwent a procedure to hide their circumcision.
Ptolemy VI Philometor (reigned 180–145 BC).
Greek: in the 143rd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
The altar of incense, overlaid with gold (Exodus 30:1–10).
Literally “the table of the setting out,” the table for the sacred loaves (Exodus 25:23–30).
Literally “a ruler of tribute.” 2 Maccabees 5:24 names him Apollonius, the commander of the Mysians.
Greek akra. The Akra was a fortress near the temple held by Seleucid troops until Simon captured it in 141 BC (13:49–51). Its exact location is debated.
Greek diabolos, “slanderer” or “adversary.”

Greek: the fifteenth day of Chaseleu (the Hebrew month Kislev, the ninth month), in the 145th year of the Seleucid era (see note on 1:10). The year ran from spring 167 to spring 166 BC, so this was December 167 BC.

Greek bdelygma erēmōseōs, the “abomination of desolation” of Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11 (compare Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14). It was probably a pagan altar or sacred object set on top of the altar of burnt offering (see 1:59; 6:7). 2 Maccabees 6:2 says the temple was rededicated to Olympian Zeus. The Hebrew phrase in Daniel (shiqquts shomem) may be a mocking wordplay on Baal Shamem, “lord of heaven.”
That is, on the twenty-fifth of Kislev, December 167 BC. Exactly three years later the temple was rededicated on the same day (4:52–54).
Or “Very great wrath was upon Israel.” The wrath may be God’s or the persecutor’s.

verses.text: At that time Mattathias{a} son of John, son of Simeon, a priest descended from Joarib,{b} left Jerusalem and made his home at Modein.{c}
He had five sons: John, called Gaddi;
Simon, called Thassi;
Judas, called Maccabeus;{d}
Eleazar, called Avaran; and Jonathan, called Apphus.{e}
He saw the blasphemous things being done in Judah and in Jerusalem,
and he said, “What a tragedy! Why was I born to see my people and the holy city ruined, and to sit by while the city is delivered to its enemies and the sanctuary to outsiders?
Her temple has become like a man disgraced;{f}
the vessels that were her glory have been carried off as captives. Her infants have been killed in her streets, her young men by the enemy’s sword.
What nation has not taken a share of her royal possessions{g} and not seized her plunder?
All her ornaments have been stripped away; she was free, and now she is a slave.
Look at it! Our holy place, our beauty and our glory lie in ruins, and the Gentiles have defiled them.
Why should we go on living?”
Mattathias and his sons then tore their garments, wrapped themselves in sackcloth, and wept bitterly.
The king’s officers who were forcing the people to abandon their religion came to the town of Modein to make them offer sacrifice.
Many from Israel went over to them, but Mattathias and his sons gathered together.
Then the king’s officers spoke to Mattathias and said, “You are a leader in this town, honored and great, and supported by sons and brothers.

So come forward now and carry out the king’s order, as all the nations have, along with the leading men of Judah and those still left in Jerusalem. You and your household will then be counted as Friends of the King,{h} and silver, gold and many gifts will be your reward, yours and your sons’.”
But Mattathias answered in a loud voice, “Even if all the nations within the king’s realm obey him, each of them forsaking the worship of their ancestors and choosing to follow his commands,
still I, my sons, and my brothers will walk in our ancestors’ covenant.
Heaven forbid that we should abandon the law and its ordinances!
The king’s words we will not heed, nor will we swerve from our worship to the right or to the left.”
As soon as he had said this, a Jew stepped forward in full view of everyone to offer a sacrifice on the altar at Modein, as the king had ordered.
Mattathias saw it and was fired with zeal; he trembled to his depths{i} and let his rightful anger rise. Running forward, he cut the man down on the altar.
He also killed the royal officer who was forcing people to sacrifice, then and there, and he pulled the altar down.
So he showed his zeal for the law, as Phinehas had done to Zimri son of Salu.{j}
Then Mattathias cried out in the town with a loud voice, “Everyone who is zealous for the law and upholds the covenant, come out and follow me!”
He and his sons fled to the hills, leaving behind everything they owned in the town.
Then many who sought righteousness and justice went down into the desert to make their homes there,
they and their sons, their wives, and their livestock, because hardships pressed hard on them.
Word came to the king’s officers and to the soldiers in Jerusalem, the City of David, that men who had disobeyed the king’s command had gone to hide in the wilderness.
Many hurried after them, overtook them, and camped opposite them. They prepared to attack them on the sabbath day.
“Enough!” they told them. “Come out, obey the king’s word, and live.”
“We will not come out,” they replied, “and we will not obey the king’s word and desecrate the sabbath day.”
Then the enemy quickly attacked them.
But they did not answer them; they did not hurl a stone at them or block up their hiding places.
They said, “Let us all die with clean hands. Heaven and earth are our witnesses that you are killing us unjustly.”
So the enemy attacked them on the sabbath, and about a thousand of them died, along with their wives, children and livestock.
When Mattathias and his friends learned of it, they grieved deeply for them.
They said to each other, “If we all follow the example of our brothers and will not fight the Gentiles for our lives and our laws, they will quickly erase us from the earth.”
So that day they resolved, “If anyone comes to attack us on the sabbath day, let us fight against him, so that we do not all die as our brothers died in their hiding places.”
Then a band of Hasideans{k} joined them, strong fighters from Israel, every one of them devoted to the law of his own free will.
Everyone who had fled from the troubles joined them and strengthened them.
They raised an army and, in their anger, cut down sinners and, in their fury, those who broke the law; the survivors escaped to the Gentiles to be safe.
Mattathias and his sons went around and tore down the altars,
and every uncircumcised boy they came upon inside Israel’s territory they circumcised by force.
They pursued the proud, and the work went well under their hands.
They rescued the law from the power of the Gentiles and of kings, and they did not let the sinner triumph.{l}
As the days of Mattathias’s death drew near, he told his sons, “Now arrogance and rebuke have taken firm hold; it is a season of overthrow and blazing wrath.
Now, my children, be zealous for the law, and give your lives for the covenant of our ancestors.
Remember the deeds our ancestors did in their generations, and you will win great honor and an everlasting name.
Was not Abraham found faithful when he was tested, and it was credited to him as righteousness?{m}
Joseph kept the commandment in his time of distress and became lord of Egypt.
Phinehas our forefather, for his burning zeal, was granted the covenant of an everlasting priesthood.{n}
Joshua,{o} because he carried out the command, became a judge in Israel.
Caleb, for testifying before the congregation, was given land as his heritage.
David, for his mercy, inherited a royal throne forever.
Elijah, because of his great zeal for the law, was taken up into heaven.
Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael believed and were saved from the flame.{p}
Daniel, because of his innocence, was rescued from the mouth of the lions.
So consider this, generation after generation: none who hope in him will lack strength.
Do not fear the words of a sinner, for his glory will end in dung and worms.
He is honored today, but tomorrow he will be nowhere to be found; he has gone back to dust, and his plans have come to nothing.
My children, be strong and courageous for the law, for by it you will gain glory.
“Here is your brother Simeon.{q} I know he is a man of good counsel; always listen to him. He will be a father to you.
Judas Maccabeus, strong and mighty since boyhood, shall lead your army and wage the war against the peoples.{r}
Gather around you all who observe the law, and avenge the wrongs done to your people.
Pay back the Gentiles in full, and hold fast to the commands of the law.”
Then he blessed them and was gathered to his ancestors.
He died in the year 146 (166 BC),{s} and his sons buried him in his ancestors’ tomb at Modein. All Israel mourned him deeply.

notes.text: Mattathias (Hebrew Mattithyahu) means “gift of Yahweh.” His family is known as the Hasmoneans, after an ancestor named Hasmon (Josephus, Antiquities 12.265).
Joarib is the priestly family of Jehoiarib (1 Chronicles 24:7), the first of the twenty-four priestly divisions. Joarib means “Yahweh contends.”
Modein was a village about 17 miles (27 km) northwest of Jerusalem.

Maccabeus is usually explained as “the hammer” (from Hebrew or Aramaic maqqabah), but the meaning is uncertain; other proposals include “designated by Yahweh.” The meanings of the other sons’ nicknames (Gaddi, Thassi, Avaran, Apphus) are unknown. The sons’ names: John means “Yahweh is gracious,” Simon “he has heard,” Judas (Judah) “praised,” Eleazar “God has helped,” Jonathan “Yahweh has given.”
Avaran may mean “the piercer,” and Apphus “the wary one,” but these meanings are uncertain.
The Greek text reads “like a man of honor,” which does not fit the context; many editors read “like a man without honor” (adoxos for endoxos), followed here.
Or “her palaces”; the Greek basileia can mean either.
A formal rank at the Seleucid court, bestowing honors and privileges.
Literally “his kidneys trembled,” the kidneys being thought the seat of deep emotion.
Numbers 25:6–15. Salu (Greek Salom) was Zimri’s father.
Greek Asidaioi, from Hebrew hasidim, “the devout” or “the loyal ones,” a group devoted to strict observance of the law.
Literally “did not give a horn to the sinner.” The horn is a symbol of strength.
Numbers 25:13.
Greek Iēsous, the Greek form of Joshua. Joshua means “Yahweh saves.”
Daniel 3, where they are known by their Babylonian names Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.
That is, Simon (2:3); Simeon is the fuller form of the name.
Or “fight the people’s battle.” The Greek is ambiguous.
Greek: in the 146th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10), from spring 166 to spring 165 BC.

verses.text: Then his son Judas, who was called Maccabeus, rose up to take his place.
All his brothers stood by him, as did all who had attached themselves to his father, and they fought Israel’s battle gladly.
He spread his people’s glory far and wide. Like a giant he put on his breastplate; he strapped on his weapons of war and fought battle after battle, guarding the camp with his sword.
In his exploits he was like a lion, like a lion’s whelp roaring over its prey.
He tracked down the lawless and hunted them out, and he gave to the flames those who troubled his people.
The lawless shrank back in fear of him, all who practiced lawlessness were thrown into confusion, and deliverance prospered by his hand.
He made many kings bitter, but he made Jacob glad by his deeds, and his memory will be a blessing forever.
He went through the towns of Judah and wiped out the ungodly from the land,{a} and so he turned wrath away from Israel.
His reputation spread to the ends of the earth, and he gathered in those who were dying.
Apollonius{b} then mustered Gentiles, along with a large force from Samaria, to make war on Israel.
When Judas learned of it, he went out to meet him, defeated him, and killed him. Many fell slain, and the remainder ran away.
Then they stripped the dead. Judas kept Apollonius’s sword for himself, and he fought with it all his days.
Seron, commander of the Syrian army, heard that Judas had gathered a large band around him, an assembly of faithful men who were ready for war.
He said, “I will make myself a name and gain glory in the kingdom by fighting Judas and those with him, who treat the king’s command with contempt.”
A strong army of the ungodly once more marched up with him to help him take vengeance on the Israelites.
As he neared the pass that climbs to Beth-horon,{c} Judas came out against him with a handful of men.
But when they saw the army coming against them, they asked Judas, “How can so few of us fight against so great a horde? We are worn out, having had nothing to eat all day.”
Judas answered, “It is easy for many to be delivered into the hands of a few. In the sight of Heaven{d} it makes no difference whether it saves by many or by few.
Victory in battle does not depend on the size of an army; strength comes from Heaven.
These men are coming at us full of insolence and lawlessness, to wipe out us, our wives, and our children, and to plunder us.
But we are fighting for our lives and our laws.
He himself will crush them before our eyes. As for you, have no fear of them.”
When he stopped speaking, he charged at them suddenly, and Seron and his army were crushed before him.
They pursued them down the slope of Beth-horon to the plain. Some eight hundred of the enemy fell, while the rest escaped into Philistine country.
Then Judas and his brothers began to be dreaded, and alarm fell on the nations around them.
His fame reached the king, and every nation talked of the battles Judas fought.
When King Antiochus heard these reports, he was enraged. He sent orders and assembled all the forces of his kingdom, a very powerful army.
He opened his treasury and paid his troops for a year, ordering them to be prepared for any need.

Then he found that the money in his treasury had run short and that the revenues from the province were small, because of the strife and disaster he had brought on the land by abolishing the laws that had been in force from ancient times.
He was afraid that he would not have enough, as had happened more than once, for the expenses and the gifts that he used to hand out lavishly, more freely than the kings before him.{e}
