So Swete’s Greek text; compare v. 34 and 10:30, 38, where the three districts are themselves taken from Samaria.
Greek: three hundred talents, about 22,500 lb (10,200 kg). Weight standards varied.
“Father” was a court title of honor.
Aphairema (Ephraim, John 11:54), Lydda (Lod, Acts 9:32), and Rathamin (perhaps Ramathaim, 1 Samuel 1:1).
Trypho, “luxury,” was the nickname of Diodotus, a general.
So Swete’s Greek text; some ancient witnesses read “Imalkue.”
Antiochus VI Epiphanes Dionysus, about four years old.
The three districts of v. 34 and perhaps the region around Akrabattene or Perea; uncertain.
The Ladder of Tyre, a headland on the coast north of Ptolemais.
Kedesh in Galilee, northwest of Lake Huleh (Joshua 20:7).
The Sea of Galilee.
Swete’s Greek reads “Nasor,” probably for Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verses.text: Seeing that the time was working in his favor, Jonathan chose men and sent them to Rome to confirm and renew the friendship with the Romans.
To the Spartans{a} and to other places too he sent letters to the same effect.
So they journeyed to Rome, entered the Senate chamber, and said, “Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish nation have sent us to renew for them the friendship and alliance as it stood before.”
The Romans gave them letters to the authorities in each place, asking them to send the envoys on their way to the land of Judah in peace.
Here is a copy of what Jonathan wrote to the Spartans:
“Jonathan the high priest, the council of elders of the nation, the priests, and all the remaining Jewish people send greetings to the Spartans, their brothers.
A letter was sent long ago to the high priest Onias by Arius,{b} who was king among you at the time, saying that you are our brothers, as the attached copy shows.
Onias received the envoy with honor and accepted the letter, in which alliance and friendship were plainly declared.
Now we, though we stand in no need of these, since we take encouragement from the holy books in our hands,
have ventured to send envoys to renew our brotherhood and friendship, lest we grow strangers to you; for many years have passed since your message came to us.
For our part, we always remember you without fail, at our festivals and on the other proper days, in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers, as is right and fitting when remembering brothers.
And we rejoice in your renown.
But as for us, many troubles and many wars have hemmed us in, and the kings around us have fought against us.
We did not wish to trouble you, nor our other friends and allies, over these wars,
for we have the help that comes from heaven to aid us, and we have been rescued from our enemies, and our enemies have been brought low.
So we have chosen Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, and have sent them to the Romans to renew our former friendship and alliance with them.
We have instructed them to go to you also, to greet you, and to deliver to you this letter of ours concerning the renewal of our brotherhood.
And now you will do well to send us a reply to this.”
This is a copy of the letter that was sent to Onias:
“Arius king of the Spartans to Onias the high priest, greetings.
A writing has come to light about the Spartans and the Jews, showing that the two are brothers, of Abraham’s stock.{c}
Now that this is known to us, you will do well to write us of how you fare.
We on our side write to you that your livestock and your property are ours, and ours are yours. We therefore command that our envoys report to you accordingly.”
Now Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius had come back with a larger army than before to make war on him.
He marched out of Jerusalem and confronted them in the region of Hamath,{d} giving them no opportunity to set foot in his own country.
He sent spies into their camp, who came back and reported that the enemy were drawn up to fall upon the Jews by night.
So when the sun had set, Jonathan ordered his men to stay awake and under arms, ready for battle all night long, and he posted sentries around the camp.
When the enemy heard that Jonathan and his men were ready for battle, they became afraid, their courage failed, and they lit fires in their camp.{e}
Jonathan and his men, seeing the fires still alight, knew nothing of it till dawn.
Then Jonathan gave chase, but could not catch them, since they were already across the river Eleutherus.
So Jonathan turned aside against the Arabs called Zabadeans,{f} struck them down, and took their spoil.
Then he broke camp, came to Damascus, and marched through all that region.
Simon too set out and marched as far as Askalon and the nearby strongholds. He turned to Joppa and seized it before the enemy could,
for he had heard that its people were about to hand the stronghold over to the supporters of Demetrius. He stationed a garrison there to guard it.
When Jonathan came back, he called the elders of the people together and made plans with them to build strongholds in Judea,
to build the walls of Jerusalem higher, and to raise a tall wall between citadel and city, cutting the citadel off so that it would stand alone and its garrison could neither buy nor sell.
So they came together to build. A section of the wall along the eastern ravine had collapsed, and he repaired the part known as Chaphenatha.{g}
And Simon built Adida{h} in the Shephelah,{i} fortifying it and fitting it with gates and bars.
Then Trypho sought to become king of Asia, to put on the crown, and to lay hands on King Antiochus.
But he was afraid that Jonathan would not allow him and would make war on him. So he sought a way to seize and kill him, and he set out and came to Beth-shan.{j}
Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand picked men in battle array, and he too came to Beth-shan.
When Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, he was afraid to raise a hand against him.
Instead he welcomed him with honor, commended him to all his Friends, and gave him gifts. He ordered his Friends and his troops to obey Jonathan as they would himself.
Then he said to Jonathan, “Why have you put all these people to so much trouble, when there is no war between us?

Send them home now, and pick a few men to stay with you. Come with me to Ptolemais, and I will turn it over to you, together with the other strongholds, the remaining troops and all the officials. Then I will turn around and go home; that is the reason I came.”
Jonathan believed him and did what he said. He sent his troops away, and they returned to the land of Judah.
He kept with him three thousand men, of whom he left two thousand in Galilee, while a thousand went with him.
But as soon as Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the townspeople barred the gates and took him prisoner, and every man who had come in with him they put to the sword.
Trypho then sent troops and cavalry into Galilee and the Great Plain{k} to destroy all Jonathan’s men.
These, believing that Jonathan had been seized and had perished along with his companions, encouraged one another and marched in close order, ready for battle.
Their pursuers, seeing that these men would sell their lives dearly, gave up the chase.
So all of them reached the land of Judah safely. They mourned for Jonathan and those with him, and they were in great fear; all Israel mourned deeply.
And all the surrounding nations tried to destroy them, saying, “They have no leader or helper. Let us attack them now and erase their memory from among human beings.”

notes.text: The Spartans, citizens of Sparta (Lacedaemon) in southern Greece.
Arius (Areus) I, king of Sparta 309–265 BC; Onias I was high priest about 320–290 BC.
The tradition of kinship between Spartans and Jews is also found in 2 Maccabees 5:9 and Josephus (Antiquities 12.226).
The region around Hamath on the Orontes, in Syria.
The fires were meant to make it look as if the camp was still occupied while the enemy withdrew (vv. 29–30); some ancient witnesses add “and withdrew.”
An Arab tribe, perhaps near Zabdani northwest of Damascus.
The meaning of Chaphenatha is uncertain; perhaps Aramaic for “the double one.”
Adida, Hebrew Hadid (Ezra 2:33), near Lydda.
The Shephelah, “lowland,” the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain.
Greek: Bethsan, Hebrew Beth-shan, “house of quiet” (Greek name Scythopolis).
The Great Plain, the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon).

verses.text: Simon heard that Trypho had raised a large army to invade the land of Judah and lay it waste.
He saw how terrified the people were, so he went up to Jerusalem and called them together.
He encouraged them, saying, “You yourselves know what great things I and my brothers and my father’s house have done for the laws and the sanctuary, and what wars and hardships we have seen.
For this cause all my brothers have perished for Israel’s sake, and I alone am left.
And now, I would never spare my own life in any time of trouble, for I am no better than my brothers.
Rather I will avenge my nation and the sanctuary and our wives and children, for all the nations have gathered out of hatred to crush us.”
Hearing these words, the people took fresh heart,
and they answered with a loud shout, “You are our leader in place of Judas and Jonathan your brother.
Fight our battles, and whatever you tell us, we will do.”
So he assembled all the fighting men and hurried to finish the walls of Jerusalem, and he fortified it on every side.
He sent Jonathan son of Absalom to Joppa with a sizable force; he drove out its inhabitants and remained there.
Then Trypho marched out of Ptolemais at the head of a great force to enter Judah’s land, and Jonathan was with him as a prisoner.
Simon encamped at Adida, facing the plain.
When Trypho learned that Simon had taken his brother Jonathan’s place and intended to fight him, he sent messengers to Simon with this message:
“We are holding your brother Jonathan because of silver he owed to the king’s treasury for the posts he had.
Send now about four tons of silver{a} and two of his sons as hostages, so that when he is released he will not revolt against us, and we will release him.”
Simon knew that they were speaking to him deceitfully, but he sent for the money and the boys, lest he bring great hostility on himself from the people,
lest they say, “Jonathan died because Simon would not send the silver and the boys.”
So he sent the boys and the silver, but Trypho broke his word and did not release Jonathan.
After this, Trypho came to invade the land and ruin it. He took the road around by Adora,{b} but wherever he went, Simon and his army kept pace alongside him.
The citadel garrison, for their part, sent messenger after messenger to Trypho, pressing him to reach them through the wilderness and get food to them.
So Trypho made ready all his cavalry to go, but that night there was a very heavy snowfall, and because of the snow he did not go. He set out and went into Gilead.
When he drew near Baskama,{c} he killed Jonathan, and he was buried there.
Then Trypho turned back and went to his own land.
Simon sent for the bones of his brother Jonathan and buried him at Modein, the town of their ancestors.
All Israel lamented him with great lamentation and mourned for him many days.
Over the tomb of his father and his brothers Simon built a monument, high enough to be seen, with polished stone at back and front.
He erected seven pyramids, one opposite another, for his father and mother and four brothers.

For the pyramids he designed an elaborate arrangement: he put up tall columns around them, and on the columns he set suits of armor as an eternal memorial, and next to the armor he carved ships, so that everyone sailing the sea could see them.
This tomb that he built at Modein remains to this day.
Trypho dealt treacherously with the young King Antiochus; he killed him
and reigned in his place. He put on the crown of Asia and brought great disaster on the land.
But Simon built up the strongholds of Judea, girding them with high towers and great walls, with gates and bars, and he stored food in the strongholds.
Simon also chose men and sent them to King Demetrius, asking him to grant the land relief, for all that Trypho did was plunder.
King Demetrius answered him in line with this request, writing him the following letter:
“King Demetrius to Simon, high priest and Friend of kings, and to the elders and nation of the Jews, greetings.
We have received the golden crown, and also the palm branch{d} that you sent. We are prepared to establish a lasting peace with you, and to instruct our officials to give you tax exemptions.
All the agreements we have made with you stand, and the strongholds that you have built shall be yours.
We pardon any errors and offenses committed up to this day, and we cancel the crown tax that you owed; and whatever other tax was collected in Jerusalem shall be collected no longer.
Any of you who are qualified to join our bodyguard, let them be enrolled, and let there be peace between us.”
In the year 170 (142 BC){e} the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel,
and the people started writing in their documents and contracts, “In the first year of Simon, great high priest, commander, and leader of the Jews.”
In those days Simon{f} camped against Gaza{g} and surrounded it with troops. He built a siege tower, brought it up to the city, battered one of the towers, and captured it.
The men in the siege tower leaped out into the city, and a great uproar arose in the city.
The townspeople, wives and children with them, climbed onto the wall, rending their garments, and shouted aloud, begging Simon to make peace with them.
“Do not treat us as our wicked deeds deserve,” they said, “but as your mercy allows.”
So Simon made terms with them and did not attack them. He drove them out of the city and purified the houses that held idols, and then he entered it singing hymns of praise.
He cast out all uncleanness from it and settled in it men who observe the law. He strengthened its fortifications and built a residence there for himself.
The garrison of the citadel in Jerusalem, cut off from going out to the countryside to buy and sell, suffered severe hunger, and many of them died of starvation.
They begged Simon for peace, and he agreed. He drove them out from there and cleansed the fortress of its defilement.

On the twenty-third day of the second month (in April–May) in the year 171 (141 BC),{h} the Jews went into it with praise and palm branches, with harps, cymbals and lyres, with hymns and songs, because a great enemy had been defeated and removed from Israel.
He made it a law that this day be kept with gladness year by year. The temple mount beside the citadel he made still stronger, and there he made his home, he and his men.
When Simon saw that his son John{i} had grown to manhood, he appointed him commander of all the forces, and John lived at Gazara.

notes.text: Greek: one hundred talents, about 7,500 lb (3,400 kg). Weight standards varied.
Adora (Adoraim, 2 Chronicles 11:9), southwest of Hebron.
Location unknown; probably northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
Greek baïn, a palm branch, perhaps of gold, given as a token of homage.
Greek: in the 170th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Greek: he; Simon is meant.
So Swete’s Greek text; many editors read Gazara (Gezer), following v. 53, 14:7, and Josephus, since Gaza lay outside Simon’s territory.
Greek: the twenty-third of the second month of the 171st year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). The second month is Iyyar (April–May).
John Hyrcanus, ruler of Judea 134–104 BC.

verses.text: In the year 172 (140 BC){a} King Demetrius assembled his forces and marched into Media to gain reinforcements for his war against Trypho.
Arsaces,{b} king of Persia and Media, learned that Demetrius had entered his territory, and he dispatched one of his commanders to take Demetrius alive.
The commander went out, defeated Demetrius’s army, took him prisoner, and brought him to Arsaces, who had him placed under guard.

As the crown of all his honors, he captured Joppa as a harbor
and made a gateway to the islands of the sea.

He enlarged the frontiers of his people
and held the land firmly in his grip.

He gathered in a host of captives;
he became master of Gazara, Beth-zur, and the citadel,
and removed its uncleanness from it,
and there was none to withstand him.

Old men sat in the streets,
all talking together of good things,
and the young men put on splendid garments and the dress of war.

He supplied the towns with food
and furnished them with means of defense,
until the fame of his glory was spoken of to the ends of the earth.

He established peace in the land,
and Israel rejoiced with great joy.

Each sat under his own vine and his own fig tree,{c}
and there was none to make them afraid.

None remained in the land to wage war on them;
in those days kings were broken.

He brought splendor to the holy place
and increased its sacred furnishings.
News of Jonathan’s death reached Rome and even Sparta, and there was deep sorrow.
But once they learned that Simon his brother had taken his place as high priest and was ruling over the country and the towns in it,
they wrote to him on bronze tablets, to renew the friendship and alliance that they had made with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
And these were read before the assembly in Jerusalem.

This is a copy of the letter sent by the Spartans:
“From the rulers and the city of the Spartans, greetings to Simon the high priest, to the elders and priests, and to the rest of the Jewish people, our brothers.
The envoys sent to our people have told us of your glory and honor, and we were glad at their coming.

Their report we have entered among the people’s resolutions, in these words: ‘Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, Jewish envoys, have come before us to renew their friendship with us.

Our people resolved to welcome these men with honor and to lay up a copy of their words in the public records, as a memorial for the Spartan people.’ And they have written a copy of this to Simon the high priest.”
After this Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a great golden shield weighing about 1,250 pounds,{d} to confirm the alliance with the Romans.
Hearing of these events, the people asked, “What thanks can we give to Simon and his sons?

For he and his brothers and his father’s house have stood firm; they have fought and driven off Israel’s enemies and secured its freedom.” So they inscribed this on bronze tablets and set them on a pillar on Mount Zion.

What follows is a copy of the inscription:
“In the year 172 (140 BC),{e} on the eighteenth day of Elul (in August–September), the third year of Simon the great high priest,
at Asaramel,{f} in the great assembly of the priests and the people, the nation’s rulers, and the elders of the land, this was made known to us:

‘Since wars have often arisen in the country, Simon son of Mattathias, a priest of the line of Joarib,{g} together with his brothers, put themselves in peril and stood against their nation’s foes, to keep their sanctuary and the law standing; and they won high renown for their people.
Jonathan rallied the nation and became their high priest, and then he was gathered to his people.
When their enemies resolved to invade their country and lay it waste, and to lay hands on their sanctuary,
then Simon rose up and fought for his nation. He spent much of his own wealth; he armed the soldiers of his nation and paid their wages.
Judea’s towns he fortified, and Beth-zur too, on Judea’s frontier, which had once been the enemy’s arsenal, and there he posted Jews as a garrison.

He fortified Joppa by the sea, and Gazara on the borders of Azotus, where the enemy had formerly lived. There he planted Jewish settlers and furnished the towns with all they required for their rebuilding.

The people saw how faithful Simon was and what glory he meant to bring his nation, and they chose him as their leader and high priest for all that he had done, and for the uprightness and good faith he had kept toward his people. He sought in every way to exalt his people.

In his days things prospered in his hands, so that the Gentiles were driven out of the country, and likewise the men in the City of David at Jerusalem, who had made a citadel for themselves and would go out from it to pollute the area around the sanctuary, doing great damage to its purity.
He settled Jews in it and fortified it to protect the country and the city, and he made the walls of Jerusalem higher.
For these reasons King Demetrius confirmed his high priesthood,
made him one of his Friends, and paid him high honors.
For he had heard that the Romans called the Jews friends, allies and brothers, and that they had given Simon’s envoys an honorable welcome.
The Jews and the priests have been pleased to have Simon as their leader and high priest for all time, till a prophet worthy of trust should appear,{h}
and that he should be commander over them and take charge of the sanctuary, appointing officials over its tasks and over the country, the weapons, and the strongholds;
that he should take charge of the sanctuary, and be obeyed by all; that all contracts in the country should be written in his name; and that he should be clothed in purple and wear gold.

No one among the people or the priests will be allowed to overturn any of these decisions, to contradict what he says, to call a gathering in the country without him, or to dress in purple or wear a gold clasp.
Anyone who goes against these terms or sets any of them aside shall be held guilty.’
The whole people consented to let Simon act on these terms.
So Simon accepted, and agreed to serve as high priest and as general and ethnarch{i} of the Jews and the priests, and to stand at the head of all.”
They gave orders that this inscription be placed on bronze tablets and set up in the precincts of the sanctuary in a prominent place,
and that copies of it be deposited in the treasury, so that Simon and his sons might have them.

notes.text: Greek: in the 172nd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Arsaces, the royal title of the Parthian kings; here Mithradates I (about 171–138 BC).
Compare Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25.
Greek: a thousand minas, about 1,250 lb (570 kg); the mina was one sixtieth of a talent, and standards varied.
Greek: the eighteenth of Elul, of the 172nd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). Elul is the sixth month (August–September).
So Swete’s Greek text (Saramel in some ancient witnesses). The meaning is uncertain; perhaps Hebrew for “court of the people of God,” or a title, “prince of the people of God.”
Joarib (Jehoiarib), the first of the priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24:7).
Compare 4:46.
Ethnarch, “ruler of the nation.”

verses.text: A letter from Antiochus, the son of King Demetrius,{a} was sent from the islands of the sea to Simon, who was priest and ethnarch of the Jews, and to the whole nation.

Its contents were as follows:
“King Antiochus to Simon the great priest and ethnarch, and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.

Whereas certain pestilent men have made themselves masters of my fathers’ kingdom, and it is my purpose to reclaim that kingdom and set it back as it once stood, I have recruited a host of troops and fitted out warships.
I mean to land in the country so that I may go after those who have ruined our country and laid waste many towns in my kingdom.
So now I confirm for you all the tax cancellations granted by the kings before me, and any other exemptions they gave you.
You may strike coins of your own, to be the currency of your land.{b}
Jerusalem and the sanctuary shall be free. All the weapons you have made and the strongholds you have built and now hold shall remain yours.
Every debt you owe to the royal treasury, and any royal dues that may arise hereafter, are canceled for you from now on and for all time.
And when we have regained our kingdom, we will bestow great honor on you, your nation, and the temple, so that your glory will be made plain in all the earth.”
In the year 174 (138 BC){c} Antiochus marched into the land of his ancestors. The troops came over to him in a body, until only a few remained on Trypho’s side.
With King Antiochus in pursuit, Trypho fled and reached Dor{d} on the seacoast;
for he knew that troubles had piled up against him and that his troops had deserted him.
Antiochus pitched camp against Dor with a hundred twenty thousand fighting men and eight thousand horsemen.
He encircled the town, and the ships closed in from the sea. So he pressed the town hard by land and sea and let no one go out or come in.
Then Numenius and his companions arrived from Rome, bringing letters to the kings and countries, in which was written the following:
“Lucius,{e} consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy,{f} greetings.
The Jewish envoys have come to us as our friends and allies to renew the old friendship and alliance. Simon the high priest and the Jewish people sent them,
and they have brought a gold shield weighing about 6,250 pounds.{g}
We have therefore decided to write to the kings and countries, so that they will not try to harm the Jews, attack them or their towns or their land, or aid anyone who fights against them.
It is our decision to receive the shield at their hands.
So if any troublemakers have fled from their land and found shelter with you, hand them over to Simon the high priest, so that he can punish them under their own law.”
Letters to the same effect went to King Demetrius,{h} to Attalus,{i} Ariarathes,{j} and Arsaces,

and to all the countries: to Sampsames,{k} to the Spartans, and to Delos, Myndos, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Cos, Side, Arados, Rhodes, Phaselis, Gortyn, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.{l}
And a copy of the whole was written out for Simon the high priest.
King Antiochus besieged Dor in its outskirts,{m} continually throwing his forces against it and building siege engines; and he shut Trypho in, so that no one could go out or in.
Simon sent him two thousand picked men to fight on his side, along with silver and gold and a good deal of equipment.
But Antiochus would not accept them. He broke every agreement he had made with Simon before and turned against him.
He sent Athenobius, one of his Friends, to confer with him, saying, “You hold Joppa and Gazara and the citadel in Jerusalem, which are towns of my kingdom.
You have laid waste their territory, done great harm to the land, and made yourselves masters of many places in my kingdom.
Now then, hand over the towns you have seized, and the tribute of the places you have taken outside the borders of Judea;

or else give me in their place about nineteen tons of silver,{n} and for the destruction you have caused and for the tribute of the towns, another nineteen tons. Otherwise we will come and make war on you.”

So Athenobius, the king’s Friend, came to Jerusalem. When he saw the splendor of Simon, his sideboard laden with gold and silver vessels, and his great retinue, he was astounded. He gave him the king’s message.
Simon answered him, “We have neither taken foreign land nor seized anything that belongs to others, but only the inheritance of our ancestors, which our enemies at one time unjustly took.
Now that we have the opportunity, we are holding firmly to the inheritance of our ancestors.

As for Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, those towns were doing great harm among our people and in our land; for them we will give about four tons of silver.”{o} Athenobius did not answer him a word,
but returned in a rage to the king and reported to him these words, the splendor of Simon, and all he had seen. And the king was furious.
Meanwhile Trypho boarded a ship and fled to Orthosia.{p}
Then the king made Cendebeus commander-in-chief of the coastal region and gave him troops of infantry and cavalry.
He ordered him to encamp facing Judea, to rebuild Kedron{q} and strengthen the towns,{r} and to wage war on the people, while the king pursued Trypho.
So Cendebeus came to Jamnia and began to provoke the people, invading Judea, taking the people captive, and killing them.
At Kedron, which he rebuilt, he stationed cavalry and soldiers to go out and patrol the roads of Judea, as the king had commanded him.

notes.text: Antiochus VII Sidetes (reigned 138–129 BC), younger brother of Demetrius II.
No coins of Simon are known; the first Hasmonean coins were struck later, perhaps under John Hyrcanus.
Greek: in the 174th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Dor, a coastal town south of Mount Carmel.
Perhaps Lucius Caecilius Metellus, consul in 142 BC, or Lucius Calpurnius Piso, consul in 139 BC; uncertain.
Ptolemy VIII Euergetes II of Egypt.
Greek: five thousand minas, about 6,250 lb (2,850 kg); compare 14:24, which gives a thousand minas.
Demetrius II, then a captive in Parthia (14:3).
Attalus II of Pergamum.
Ariarathes V of Cappadocia.
Sampsames, perhaps Samsun on the Black Sea; uncertain.
Cities and regions of Greece, Asia Minor, the islands, and North Africa.
Greek: in the second; the meaning is uncertain. It may mean “on the second day” or “a second time.”
Greek: five hundred talents of silver, about 37,500 lb (17,000 kg); likewise in the next clause. Weight standards varied.
Greek: one hundred talents, about 7,500 lb (3,400 kg).
Orthosia, a port on the Phoenician coast north of Tripolis.
Kedron, probably modern Qatra, near Jamnia.
So Swete’s Greek text; some ancient witnesses read “its gates.”

verses.text: Coming up from Gazara, John reported to Simon his father all that Cendebeus was about.

Simon summoned his two eldest sons, Judas and John, and said to them, “From our youth until this day, I and my brothers and my father’s house have fought Israel’s wars, and time and again we have succeeded in rescuing Israel.
But now I have grown old, while you, by Heaven’s mercy, are of full age. Stand in my place and my brother’s; march out and do battle on behalf of our people, and may aid from heaven go with you.”
So John chose from the country twenty thousand fighting men and horsemen, and they marched against Cendebeus and spent the night at Modein.
Rising early, they advanced into the plain, where a great host of foot and horse came marching against them, with a stream between the two armies.
John and his men took up position facing the enemy. Seeing that his men were afraid to cross the stream, he crossed over first; and when the men saw him, they crossed after him.
He divided his army, placing the horsemen in the midst of the foot soldiers, for the enemy’s cavalry was very numerous.
They blew the trumpets, and Cendebeus and his army fled. Many of them fell wounded, and the rest ran to the fortress.
It was then that John’s brother Judas was wounded; but John pursued the enemy until he came to Kedron, which Cendebeus had built.
They fled to the towers in the fields of Azotus, and John burned it{a} with fire. About a thousand of them fell, and he returned to Judea in safety.
Now Ptolemy son of Abubus had been made governor of the plain of Jericho, and he possessed a great deal of silver and gold,
for he was the high priest’s son-in-law.
His heart grew proud, and he resolved to make himself master of the country; so he plotted treachery against Simon and his sons, to do away with them.

Simon was traveling through the towns of the country, seeing to their needs. In the year 177 (134 BC), in the eleventh month (in January–February), the month of Shebat,{b} he went down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas.
The son of Abubus received them with guile in the small fort he had built, named Dok.{c} There he held a great drinking feast for them, having hidden men in the place.

When Simon and his sons were drunk, Ptolemy and his men sprang up, grabbed their weapons, and burst in on Simon in the banquet hall; they murdered him, along with his two sons and some of his servants.
So he committed a great act of treachery and repaid good with evil.
Then Ptolemy put these things in writing and dispatched it to the king, urging him to send forces to his support and to hand over to him their country and towns.
He sent other men to Gazara to do away with John, and he sent letters to the officers of the thousands, inviting them to come to him so that he might give them silver, gold, and gifts.
Still others he sent to take possession of Jerusalem and the temple hill.
But a messenger outran them and told John at Gazara that his father and brothers were dead, and said, “He has sent men to kill you too.”
When John heard this, he was deeply shaken. He seized the men who had been sent to kill him and executed them, because he had learned that they were trying to kill him.
The rest of John’s story, his wars and the brave deeds he performed, the walls he built, and his other accomplishments,
are recorded in the annals of his high priesthood, from the time he succeeded his father as high priest.{d}

notes.text: “It” probably refers to Azotus; some take it to mean the town of Kedron. Swete’s Greek reads “about a thousand” of the enemy fell; some ancient witnesses read “two thousand.”
Greek: in the 177th year, in the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). Shebat (Shevat) is January–February.
Dok, a small fortress on a hill above Jericho.
John Hyrcanus ruled 134–104 BC. No such annals are known to survive.

books.name: 2 Maccabees
books.sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of 2 Maccabees in H. B. Swete’s edition of the Septuagint (Cambridge, 1909; public domain), with Brenton’s public-domain English version consulted as a check. The book was composed in Greek; after two prefaced letters to the Jews of Egypt (1:1–2:18), it presents itself as an abridgment of a five-volume history by Jason of Cyrene. Dates are given by the Seleucid era; each is converted in the text to its year BC, with the modern month span for any named month, and the original reckoning is in a footnote. Converted years may be off by one, since the era was reckoned from autumn 312 BC in some sources and from spring 311 BC in others. Weights and sums of money are given in approximate modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes; ancient standards varied. Greek kyrios is translated “Lord” and theos “God.” Verse numbers follow the standard English versification. This is a draft awaiting scholarly review.

verses.text: To their kindred, the Jews throughout Egypt, greetings from their kindred, the Jews in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea: true peace.
May God do you good, and may he remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give all of you a heart to worship him and to carry out his will with a great heart and a willing spirit.
May he open your hearts to his law and commandments, and may he give you peace.
May he listen to your prayers and be reconciled with you, and never abandon you in a time of trouble.
Here and now we are praying for you.

In the reign of Demetrius, in the year 143 BC,{a} we Jews wrote to you: “During the suffering and crisis that fell on us in those years, after Jason and his supporters betrayed the holy land and the kingdom,{b}
they set fire to the gateway and shed innocent blood. Then we pleaded with the Lord and were heard; we offered sacrifice and fine flour, we lit the lamps, and we set out the loaves.”
And now see that you keep the days of Booths in the month of Chislev (in November–December).{c}

Written in the year 124 BC.{d} From those in Jerusalem and Judea, the senate, and Judas, to Aristobulus, who is of the stock of the anointed priests and tutor to King Ptolemy, and to the Jews of Egypt: greeting, and health.{e}
Having been rescued by God from grave dangers, we give him great thanks, as men who stood in battle array against a king.
For it was he who hurled out those who drew up for battle against the holy city.
When the leader reached Persia with an army that seemed irresistible, they were cut to pieces in the temple of Nanea through a trick employed by Nanea’s priests.{f}
On the pretext of marrying the goddess, Antiochus came to the place with his Friends, meaning to take its great riches as a dowry.
The priests of Nanea had laid out the treasures, and Antiochus went inside the walls of the sacred area with a small escort; as soon as he was in, they locked the temple.
Opening a secret door in the paneled ceiling, they hurled stones and struck down the leader as if with thunderbolts; then they cut the bodies in pieces and threw the heads to those outside.
Our God be praised in all things, he who gave up the impious to judgment!

We are about to keep the cleansing of the sanctuary on the twenty-fifth of Chislev (in November–December), and so we judged it needful to make this known to you, that you also may observe a feast of Booths and of the fire which appeared when Nehemiah, the builder of the sanctuary and altar, brought up sacrifices.{g}

For when our ancestors were being led away to Persia, devout priests of that time secretly took some of the fire from the altar and hid it in the hollow of a dry cistern, where they made it secure, so that the place was unknown to anyone.
After many years had passed, when it pleased God, Nehemiah, sent by the king of Persia, dispatched the descendants of the priests who had hidden the fire to recover it.

They told us they had found no fire, only a thick liquid. He ordered them to scoop some up and bring it. After the materials for the sacrifices had been laid on the altar, Nehemiah commanded the priests to splash the liquid over the wood and everything on it.
When this was done and some time had passed, and the sun, which had been behind clouds, shone out, a great blaze flared up, so that everyone marveled.
And as the offering burned, the priests made prayer, both priests and all the rest, Jonathan beginning and the others answering, as Nehemiah did.
The prayer went like this: “O Lord, Lord God, Creator of all things, awe-inspiring and strong, just and merciful, you alone are King and kind,
you alone are bountiful, you alone are just, almighty, and eternal. You rescue Israel from every evil; you made our ancestors your chosen ones and consecrated them.
Receive the offering for the whole of Israel your people; keep safe your inheritance and sanctify it.
Bring our dispersion together again; free those in bondage among the Gentiles; regard the scorned and abhorred; and so let the Gentiles learn that you are our God.
Punish those who oppress us and insolently abuse us in their arrogance.
Plant your people in your holy place, as Moses said.”
Then the priests sang the hymns.
Once the sacrifice was burned up, Nehemiah gave orders to pour what remained of the liquid upon some large stones.
When this was done, a flame blazed up, but it was consumed by the light that shone back from the altar.{h}

Once the affair came to light, the Persian king was told that where the priests carried into exile had concealed the fire, liquid had been found, and that Nehemiah’s company had used it to purify the offerings.
The king fenced off the place and made it sacred, after investigating the matter.
And to those on whom the king bestowed favor, he gave a share of the many gifts he received.{i}
Nehemiah’s company gave this the name nephthar, interpreted as “cleansing”; but among most it goes by the name naphtha.{j}

notes.text: Greek: in the 169th year (Seleucid era). The Seleucid era is the reckoning used in the books of Maccabees, counted from the founding of the Seleucid kingdom in autumn 312 BC or spring 311 BC; converted years may be off by one. Demetrius is Demetrius II.
Jason the high priest; see 4:7–26 and 5:5–10.

Literally “the days of Booths of the month of Chislev,” that is, the festival of the temple’s rededication (Hanukkah), kept for eight days in the manner of Booths; see 10:6. Chislev is the ninth month, November–December.
Greek: in the 188th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:7). Many interpreters attach this date to the first letter; others take it as the opening of the second letter.
Aristobulus was a Jewish philosopher of Alexandria; the king is probably Ptolemy VI Philometor. The second letter (1:10–2:18) claims to come from Judas Maccabeus and so would date from about 164 BC.

Nanea (Nanaia) was a goddess worshiped in Persia and Mesopotamia. This account of the death of Antiochus differs from 1 Macc 6:1–16 and 2 Macc 9; it may reflect the death of Antiochus III in 187 BC, who died plundering a temple in Elymais.
Chislev is the ninth month, November–December. The traditional reconstruction of the temple was by Zerubbabel and Joshua (Ezra 3–6); this tradition credits Nehemiah.
The sense of this verse is uncertain.
Or “the king took many gifts and gave a share to them”; the Greek is obscure.
Nephthar is of uncertain origin and meaning; the explanation “purification” is the author’s. Naphtha is a flammable petroleum liquid.

verses.text: The records show that the prophet Jeremiah instructed those being taken into exile to take some of the fire with them, as already described,

and that the prophet, having handed them the law, charged the deportees not to forget the Lord’s ordinances, nor to be led astray in their thoughts on seeing images of gold and silver and their finery.
With other such words he exhorted them never to let the law depart from their hearts.
The writing also told how the prophet, warned by an oracle, ordered the tent and the ark to go along with him, and how he went out to the mountain that Moses had climbed to view God’s inheritance.{a}
Arriving there, Jeremiah found a cave-like dwelling, and into it he carried the tent, the ark, and the altar of incense; then he blocked up the entrance.
Some of his companions came up afterward meaning to mark the way, but they could not find it.
When Jeremiah learned of this, he rebuked them: “Unknown that place will be, until God brings his people together in one assembly and mercy comes.

Then the Lord will reveal where they are, and the Lord’s glory and the cloud will appear, just as they were displayed in the days of Moses, and when Solomon prayed that the place would be wonderfully consecrated.”
It was also made clear how Solomon, being endowed with wisdom, offered a sacrifice for the dedication and completion of the sanctuary.
Just as Moses prayed to the Lord and fire came down from heaven and devoured the sacrifices, so too Solomon prayed, and the fire descended and consumed the whole burnt offerings.
And Moses said, “Because the sin offering had not been eaten, it was consumed.”{b}
Likewise Solomon too kept the eight days.{c}

The same things are also recorded in the archives and in Nehemiah’s memoirs, which add that he founded a library and gathered the books about the kings and the prophets, the writings of David, and the kings’ letters about gifts dedicated to God.{d}
In the same way Judas also gathered up all the books that had been scattered because of the war that befell us, and we have them in our possession.
So if you need any of them, send people to fetch them for you.
Since, then, we are about to celebrate the purification, we write to you. You will do well, therefore, to keep these days.
It is God who has saved all his people and has given back to all the inheritance, the kingship, the priesthood, and the consecration,

as he pledged in the law. Our hope rests on God, that he will be quick to pity us and to gather us from everywhere under heaven into the holy place; for out of great evils he delivered us, and he cleansed the place.
The story of Judas Maccabeus and his brothers,{e} the purification of the great temple, and the dedication of the altar,
and further the wars against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator,{f}

and the manifestations from heaven granted to those who strove valiantly, with honor, on behalf of Judaism,{g} so that, few as they were, they overran the whole land and chased off the barbarian multitudes,

and won back the temple renowned throughout the inhabited world, and set the city free, and reestablished the laws then on the verge of being overthrown, the Lord in all his gentleness being merciful toward them,
all this, made known by Jason the Cyrenian in five books, we will try to shorten into one composition.
For we saw the flood of figures, and the difficulty that the sheer mass of material poses for anyone wishing to plunge into the narratives of the history,
and we have aimed to bring delight to those who wish to read, ease to those inclined to commit things to memory, and benefit to all who come upon the work.
For us who have taken on the toil of abridging, the task is no easy one; it is a matter of sweat and sleepless nights,
just as it is no light thing for one preparing a banquet who seeks the enjoyment of others. Even so, for the sake of the gratitude of many, we shall gladly endure the toil,
leaving to the original author the precise treatment of every detail, while we exert ourselves to follow the outlines of an abridgment.

For as the master builder of a new house must concern himself with the entire structure, while the one who undertakes to paint and decorate it must look into what is suitable for adornment, so I judge it to be in our case.
To enter into the subject, to range over it in discussion, and to busy oneself with particulars is the task of the first compiler of the history;
but the one who recasts it must be allowed to aim at brevity of expression and to forgo exhaustive treatment.
So at this point let us begin the narrative, adding only this much to what has been said; it would be foolish to go on at length in the preface and then shorten the history itself.

notes.text: Mount Nebo; see Deut 32:49; 34:1–4.
See Lev 10:16–20.
“Votive offerings”: gifts dedicated to the temple.
Maccabeus, the surname of Judas, perhaps means “hammer” (Aramaic maqqaba), but the meaning is uncertain.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes (“God manifest”) and his son Antiochus V Eupator (“of a noble father”).
This is the earliest known use of the Greek word “Judaism,” the name for the Jewish way of life; compare 8:1; 14:38.

verses.text: The holy city lived in complete peace and the laws were observed with great faithfulness, thanks to the devotion of Onias the high priest and his loathing of evil,{a}
and so the kings themselves honored the place and enhanced the temple with magnificent gifts,
so that even Seleucus, king of Asia, met from his own revenues all the costs connected with the service of the sacrifices.{b}
But a certain Simon, of the tribe of Benjamin,{c} who had been appointed captain of the temple, fell into a dispute with the high priest about the regulation of the city market.
Unable to prevail over Onias, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia,{d}

and informed him that the treasury in Jerusalem was overflowing with immense amounts of money, too much to count, and that it had nothing to do with the sacrificial accounts but could come under the king’s control.
When Apollonius met the king, he told him of the money that had been disclosed to him. The king chose Heliodorus, his chief minister, and sent him with orders to carry off the reported wealth.{e}
Heliodorus at once took the road, in appearance to visit the towns of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, but in reality to accomplish what the king intended.

On arriving at Jerusalem and being kindly welcomed by the high priest of the city, he laid before him the information that had been given and made plain why he had come, and he asked whether these things were really so.
The high priest explained that there were deposits belonging to widows and orphans,

and that some belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, a man holding a very eminent place. So far was it from what Simon, that ungodly man, alleged. The whole came to fifteen tons of silver and seven and a half tons of gold.{f}
It was completely unthinkable to wrong people who had trusted in the holiness of the place and in the sacredness and inviolability of a temple honored all over the world.
But Heliodorus insisted, because of the king’s orders, that the money had to be seized for the royal treasury in any case.
Fixing a day, he went in to manage the examination of these funds, and anguish of no small degree gripped the entire city.

The priests flung themselves down before the altar in their priestly robes and cried out to Heaven, to the one who had laid down the law concerning deposits, asking him to preserve these intact for those who had placed them there.
Whoever looked on the high priest’s countenance was pierced in mind, for his appearance and his altered complexion revealed the agony within his soul.
Fear and a shuddering of the body had spread over him, and by these the grief settled in his heart was made evident to the onlookers.
Crowds of people also ran out of their houses to join in a public plea, because the holy place was about to be disgraced.

The women, with sackcloth bound beneath their breasts, filled the roadways in great numbers; and of the virgins kept in seclusion, some ran to the gateways, some to the walls, and some leaned out to look through the windows.
And all of them, stretching out their hands toward heaven, made their entreaty.
It was pitiable to see the multitude prostrate in a mixed throng, and the anxious expectation of the high priest in his great anguish.
While they were calling upon the almighty Lord to keep the things entrusted safe and secure for those who had entrusted them,
Heliodorus went on with what had been decided.

But when he was already present at the treasury with his guards, the Ruler over spirits and every power made a great appearing, so that all who had dared to come along were struck with dismay at God’s might and gave way to weakness and fear.

For a horse appeared to them, carrying a terrifying rider and decked with the most beautiful harness; charging violently, it lashed at Heliodorus with its forefeet, and the one mounted on it seemed to wear a full suit of golden armor.
Two other young men also appeared to him, remarkably strong, splendid in beauty, and gorgeously dressed; they stood on either side of him and flogged him without pause, inflicting many blows on him.
When he had suddenly fallen to the ground and was enveloped in deep darkness, they picked him up, put him on a stretcher,
and carried away the man who had just entered that treasury with a great retinue and all his bodyguard, now helpless; and they plainly recognized the sovereign power of God.
So he, by God’s working, lay cast down, voiceless and bereft of every hope of rescue,

while they blessed the Lord who had wondrously glorified his own place; and the sanctuary, so lately brimming with dread and confusion, was now full of joy and rejoicing, since the almighty Lord had shown himself.
Soon certain of Heliodorus’s intimates asked Onias to call on the Most High and grant life to the man who lay at his very last gasp.
The high priest, fearing that the king might suspect that some foul play had been done to Heliodorus by the Jews, offered a sacrifice for the man’s recovery.

As the high priest was offering the sacrifice of atonement, those same youths, clad in the same garments, once more appeared to Heliodorus. Standing there, they said, “Owe Onias the high priest much thanks; on his account the Lord has granted you life.
As for you, scourged from heaven, proclaim to everyone God’s mighty strength.” When they had said this, they were seen no more.
Heliodorus then offered a sacrifice to the Lord and made extravagant vows to the one who had spared his life; he said goodbye to Onias and marched his troops back to the king.
He bore testimony to everyone of the deeds of the supreme God that he had seen with his own eyes.
The king asked Heliodorus who might be a fit man to dispatch once again to Jerusalem, and he answered:

“Should you have some foe or someone scheming against the state, dispatch him there, and you will receive him back well scourged, if indeed he comes through alive; for truly a power of God surrounds that place.
The one whose abode is in heaven is himself its overseer and helper, and those who arrive there to do it harm he smites and destroys.”
This was the outcome of the affair of Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury.

notes.text: Onias III, high priest about 196–175 BC.
Seleucus IV Philopator, king 187–175 BC.
Some ancient witnesses read “of Bilgah,” a priestly family (Neh 12:5, 18).
Coelesyria (“Hollow Syria”) was the region between the Lebanon ranges, extending in official usage to Palestine.
Literally “the one in charge of affairs.”
Greek: four hundred talents of silver and two hundred talents of gold. A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg).

verses.text: But the aforesaid Simon, who had turned informer against the funds and against his own homeland, went about slandering Onias, as if it were Onias who had stirred Heliodorus up and had been the author of these evils.
He dared to call the city’s benefactor, the protector of his fellow countrymen and zealous upholder of the laws, a conspirator against the state.
When the enmity advanced so far that even murders were carried out by one of Simon’s trusted agents,
Onias saw how dangerous the rivalry was, and that Apollonius son of Menestheus, governor of Coelesyria and Phoenicia, was fanning Simon’s malice.{a}
So he betook himself to the king, not as an accuser of his fellow citizens but with an eye to the welfare, both public and private, of all the people.
For he saw that without the king’s attention it was impossible for public affairs to find peace, and that Simon would not cease from his folly.
When Seleucus died and Antiochus, known as Epiphanes, took the throne, Jason, the brother of Onias, got the high priesthood through bribery,{b}
promising the king in a petition about thirteen and a half tons of silver, and from some other revenue about three tons more.{c}

Besides this he engaged to pay in writing about five and a half tons further, if leave were given him by the king’s authority to found a gymnasium and a training corps of youths, and to register the people of Jerusalem as citizens of Antioch.{d}
The king agreed; and as soon as Jason held the office, he immediately moved his countrymen over to the Greek way of life.

He set aside the royal privileges granted to the Jews, obtained through John the father of Eupolemus, who had gone on the embassy to the Romans for friendship and alliance;{e} and abolishing the lawful ways of life, he brought in new customs contrary to the law.
With relish he founded a gymnasium right below the citadel, and he made the noblest of the young men submit to wearing the broad-brimmed hat.{f}
Thus Hellenism reached its height and the adoption of alien customs advanced, through the boundless profanity of Jason, an impious man and in no way a high priest,

that the priests were no longer eager for the services of the altar. Despising the sanctuary and neglecting the sacrifices, they hastened, once the gong summoned for the discus, to take part in the unlawful exercises provided in the wrestling school.{g}
Counting their ancestral honors as nothing, they prized Greek distinctions above all.
For this reason a grievous calamity overtook them, and the very people whose ways they envied and wished to resemble in every respect became their enemies and punishers.
For to act impiously against the divine laws is no light matter, as the period that follows will show.
When the games held every fifth year were being celebrated at Tyre, and the king was present,{h}

the polluted Jason sent official delegates, purporting to be Antiochenes from Jerusalem, conveying nearly three pounds of silver for the sacrifice to Heracles.{i} But the bearers themselves thought it unfitting to spend it on a sacrifice,
and so, on account of those bringing it, it went to the construction of warships.{j}

Apollonius son of Menestheus was dispatched to Egypt for the enthronement of King Philometor,{k} and Antiochus, discovering that Philometor had turned unfriendly toward his interests, looked to his own safety. So he went to Joppa and from there came down to Jerusalem.
He was received in grand style by Jason and the city and was ushered in with torchlight and shouting. After that he marched his army into Phoenicia.
After three years, Jason sent Menelaus, brother of the Simon mentioned above, to deliver the money to the king and to finish the records on urgent business.{l}
But Menelaus, once presented to the king, flattered him with the bearing of a man of power and so drew the high priesthood to himself, outbidding Jason by about eleven tons of silver.{m}
After receiving the king’s commission he returned, bringing nothing worthy of the high priesthood but having the passions of a cruel tyrant and the rage of a savage beast.
So Jason, who had undermined his own brother, was undermined in turn by another and was driven as a fugitive into the land of Ammon.
Menelaus kept firm hold of the office, but of the money promised to the king he paid nothing in due order.
Sostratus, the citadel’s commandant, pressed for payment, for the collecting of the dues belonged to him; and on this account both men were called before the king.
Menelaus left his own brother Lysimachus as his deputy in the high priesthood, and Sostratus left Crates, the commander of the Cypriots, in his place.{n}
Matters standing thus, the citizens of Tarsus and Mallus rose in revolt, since their towns had been handed over as a gift to Antiochis, a concubine of the king.
So the king went off in haste to settle matters, leaving as his deputy Andronicus, a man of high rank.

Menelaus, supposing a favorable moment had come, purloined certain golden vessels belonging to the sanctuary and made a present of them to Andronicus; others he had already sold off in Tyre and the neighboring towns.
When Onias had clear knowledge of this, he exposed him publicly, having withdrawn to a place of sanctuary at Daphne near Antioch.{o}

Therefore Menelaus, taking Andronicus aside, urged him to kill Onias. Andronicus went to Onias, and resorting to treachery, gave him his right hand with oaths. Though still suspected, he persuaded Onias to come out from the sanctuary, and at once he shut him away and killed him, with no regard for justice.{p}
For this reason not only Jews but many people of other nations too were indignant and displeased at the unjust murder of the man.
On the king’s return from the districts of Cilicia, the city’s Jews appealed to him, joined by Greeks who shared their loathing of wrongdoing, concerning the senseless slaying of Onias.
Antiochus was grieved at heart and moved to pity, and he wept because of the moderation and great good conduct of the deceased.

Blazing with anger, he immediately took off Andronicus’s purple robe and ripped his clothes off, then led him through the whole city to the very spot where he had committed the crime against Onias; there he killed the murderer, as the Lord paid him back with the punishment he deserved.

When many sacrileges had been committed in the city by Lysimachus with the connivance of Menelaus, and the report had spread abroad, the populace gathered against Lysimachus, for many of the gold vessels had already been carried off.

As the crowds were rising and becoming filled with rage, Lysimachus armed about three thousand men and began unjust violence, with a certain Auranus leading, a man advanced in years and no less in folly.

When the people saw the attack of Lysimachus, some seized stones, some thick pieces of wood, and others grabbed handfuls of the ashes lying near, and they hurled them in wild confusion at Lysimachus and his men.
As a result they wounded many of them, struck down some, and put all of them to flight; and the temple robber himself they killed beside the treasury.
A charge was brought against Menelaus over these matters.
When the king came to Tyre, the three men sent by the council of elders presented the case before him.
But Menelaus, already losing, offered Ptolemy son of Dorymenes a substantial sum if he would bring the king round.
So Ptolemy, taking the king aside into a colonnade as if for fresh air, induced him to change his mind.
Menelaus, the cause of all the evil, he acquitted of the charges, while the unfortunate men, who would have been freed as innocent even if they had pleaded before Scythians, he sentenced to death.{q}
So those who had pleaded on behalf of the city, the country districts, and the sacred vessels swiftly underwent that undeserved punishment.
For this cause Tyrians too, out of abhorrence of the wickedness, bore the cost of their funeral with great generosity.
Yet Menelaus kept his office through the covetousness of the powerful, ever thriving in wickedness, set up as the great traitor to his fellow citizens.

notes.text: In 3:5 the governor is called Apollonius son of Thraseas; the relation of the two names is uncertain.
Antiochus IV Epiphanes became king in 175 BC.
Greek: three hundred sixty talents of silver, and eighty talents. A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg).
Greek: one hundred fifty talents (see note on 4:8). Or “to register the Antiochenes in Jerusalem”; the Greek may refer to a citizen body of Antioch formed within Jerusalem.
See 1 Macc 8:17.
The petasos, a broad-brimmed hat associated with Hermes, patron of athletics, was worn by youths in the gymnasium.
Or “after the signal for the discus”; the Greek is uncertain.
Games in honor of Heracles (Melqart) held at Tyre every four years (counted inclusively as the fifth).

Greek: three hundred drachmas. The drachma, a silver coin, weighed about 0.15 ounce (4.3 g). Heracles was identified with Melqart, god of Tyre. Some ancient witnesses read “three thousand three hundred.”
Literally “on account of those present”; the sense is uncertain.
Greek protoklisia, apparently the enthronement of Ptolemy VI Philometor, about 172 BC.
About 172 BC.
Greek: three hundred talents (see note on 4:8).
Mercenaries from Cyprus.
Daphne, a suburb of Antioch, had a famous sanctuary of Apollo and Artemis with right of asylum.
Onias III was killed about 170 BC.
The Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, were proverbial for barbarity.

verses.text: About this time Antiochus made his second expedition into Egypt.{a}
And it came about that over the whole city, for nearly forty days, there appeared horsemen racing through the air, clad in garments woven with gold, armed with lances in companies,

swords drawn, troops of cavalry drawn up in order, charges and countercharges on either side, shields brandished, a forest of spears, missiles flying, the flash of golden ornaments, and armor of every kind.
So everyone prayed that the apparition might prove a good omen.

When a false rumor arose that Antiochus had departed this life, Jason took no fewer than a thousand men and made a sudden assault on the city. The defenders on the wall were driven back, and when at last the city was being taken, Menelaus fled for refuge into the citadel.

But Jason went on slaughtering his own fellow citizens without mercy, not perceiving that success against one’s own kindred is the greatest failure, but imagining that he was setting up trophies over enemies and not over his own nation.
He did not win the office; in the end he gained only shame from his plot and passed again as a fugitive into the land of Ammon.

In the end he came to a miserable death. Imprisoned by Aretas, the ruler of the Arabs,{b} he ran from city to city, hunted by everyone, hated as a lawbreaker, and despised as the butcher of his own country and people, and he was cast up on the shore in Egypt.
He who had driven many from their own land into exile died in exile, having sailed off to the Lacedaemonians in hope of finding shelter there on account of kinship.{c}
He who had thrown out multitudes to lie unburied went unmourned himself, and had no funeral of any kind, nor any place in an ancestral tomb.
When news of what had happened reached the king, he concluded that Judea was in revolt. So, setting out from Egypt raging like a wild beast, he took the city by storm.
He commanded his soldiers to cut down without mercy those they met, and to slay those who went up onto the housetops.
Young and old were killed; boys, women and children were destroyed; unmarried girls and infants were slaughtered.
Within the space of three days eighty thousand were lost, forty thousand in hand-to-hand fighting, and as many again were sold as slaves as were slain.
Not satisfied with this, he made bold to go into the sanctuary holiest on all the earth, with Menelaus as his guide, that betrayer of the laws and of his native land.
With polluted hands he seized the holy vessels, and with profane hands he swept away the offerings that other kings had set up to enhance the glory and honor of the place.
Antiochus grew haughty in mind, failing to see that the Master’s anger had been roused briefly over the sins of the city’s inhabitants, and that this accounted for his neglect of the place.

But had they not happened to be entangled in many sins, this man too, like Heliodorus whom King Seleucus sent to inspect the treasury, would have been flogged as soon as he came forward and turned back from his rash act.
Yet it was not for the place’s sake that the Lord chose the people; rather, he chose the place for the people’s sake.

So the place itself, having partaken in the calamities that came upon the people, later had its part in their blessings; abandoned when the Almighty was angry, it was set up again with all splendor once the great Master was reconciled.

So Antiochus took away about sixty-eight tons from the sanctuary{d} and hastened off to Antioch, supposing in his pride that he could sail upon dry land and march across the open sea, such was the loftiness of his heart.
He left governors to afflict the people: at Jerusalem, Philip, by race a Phrygian and in character more barbarous than the man who appointed him;
and Andronicus at Gerizim; and in addition Menelaus, who ruled over his fellow citizens more harshly than the others did, and who held a hateful attitude toward the Jewish citizens.{e}
He sent Apollonius, the Mysian commander,{f} at the head of an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering him to kill every adult man and to sell the women and the young.
When Apollonius reached Jerusalem, he pretended to come in peace and waited until the holy sabbath day; then, finding the Jews resting, he ordered his troops to march in formation under arms.
All who came out to watch he put to the sword, and rushing into the city with his armed men he killed great numbers.

But Judas Maccabeus, with about nine others, withdrew into the wilderness and lived like wild animals in the mountains with his companions; they continued to eat what grew wild, so as not to share in the defilement.{g}

notes.text: About 168 BC. Some historians count this as the king’s second campaign, others as his third.
Aretas I, king of the Nabateans. Greek tyrannos here means “ruler,” not necessarily “tyrant.”
The Spartans claimed kinship with the Jews; see 1 Macc 12:6–23.
A talent was about 75 pounds (34 kg).
Or “having a hostile disposition toward the citizens, being Jews”; the Greek is uncertain.
Greek mysarchēs, perhaps “commander of the Mysians” (mercenaries from Asia Minor), or a pun meaning “chief of the abominable”; compare 1 Macc 1:29.
Literally “being himself about the tenth.” See 1 Macc 2:28.

verses.text: Not long afterward the king sent out an old Athenian{a} to force the Jews to abandon their ancestral laws and to cease living by the laws of God,

and also to defile the sanctuary in Jerusalem and name it after Olympian Zeus, and the one at Gerizim after Zeus the Protector of Strangers, in keeping with the character of those who dwelt in that place.{b}
Harsh and hard for everyone to bear was the onset of this evil.

For the sanctuary was filled with debauchery and reveling by Gentiles who idled with prostitutes and had intercourse with women within the sacred courts, and who moreover carried in things that were forbidden.
The altar was heaped with abominable offerings, prohibited by the laws.
One could neither keep the sabbath nor observe the ancestral feasts, nor so much as confess oneself to be a Jew.

On the king’s birthday each month they were led, under bitter compulsion, to partake of the sacrificial entrails;{c} and when the festival of Dionysus came round, they were compelled to walk in the procession for Dionysus wearing wreaths of ivy.
By a motion of Ptolemy,{d} an edict was published to the Greek towns round about, directing them to treat the Jews in the same fashion and make them eat of the sacrifices,
and should put to death those who did not choose to go over to Greek ways. So one could see the misery that had come.

For instance, two women were brought in for having circumcised their children. They hung the babies at their mothers’ breasts, paraded the women publicly about the city, and flung them headlong from the wall.

Others, who had gathered nearby in caves in order to keep the seventh day in secret, were betrayed to Philip and were all burned together, because their reverence for that most holy day kept them from defending themselves.
Now I urge those who come upon this book not to lose heart because of these calamities, but to consider that these punishments were meant not for the destruction of our race but for its discipline.
Indeed, not to let the ungodly alone for long, but to bring retribution on them swiftly, is a sign of great kindness.
With other nations, the Lord patiently waits to punish them until their sins have reached their full measure; but he chose not to treat us in that way,
lest he should take vengeance on us afterward, when our sins have come to their full height.
Therefore he never withdraws his mercy from us. Though he disciplines with calamity, he does not abandon his own people.
But let this much be said by way of reminder; after these few words we must come back to the narrative.
Eleazar, one of the foremost scribes, a man already advanced in age and of most noble bearing, was being forced to open his mouth to eat swine’s flesh.
But he, preferring death with honor to life with defilement, spat it out{e} and went of his own accord to the rack,
as men ought to come forward who have the courage to refuse what it is not lawful to taste, even out of love of life.

The overseers of that lawless feast of sacrifice, since they had known the man from long ago, drew him aside in private and pressed him to have meat brought that he himself had prepared and that he was allowed to eat, and to make a show of eating the portions of sacrificial flesh commanded by the king,
so that by doing this he might be released from death and, for the sake of his old friendship with them, be treated kindly.

But he formed a lofty judgment, one that befitted his age, the eminence of his advanced years, the gray hair he had won to his honor, his blameless manner of life from boyhood, and still more the holy legislation established by God; and he made answer accordingly, bidding them dispatch him to Hades without delay.{f}
“It does not befit our time of life to pretend,” he said, “lest many of the young suppose that Eleazar at ninety years has gone over to an alien religion,
and through my pretense, for the sake of a brief moment of life, they be led astray because of me, while I bring defilement and disgrace upon my old age.
Even if I escape human punishment for now, I will not escape the hands of the Almighty, whether I live or die.
So by giving up my life bravely now, I will prove myself worthy of my old age,
bequeathing to the young a noble pattern, so that they may meet a good death eagerly and gallantly on behalf of the sacred and holy laws.” When he had said so much, he went straightway to the rack.
Those who led him, who a little before had been kindly disposed toward him, now turned hostile, because the words he had just spoken were in their opinion sheer madness.

As he was about to die from the blows, he groaned and said, “The Lord, whose knowledge is holy, can see that I could have escaped death, yet I am suffering terrible pain in my body from this beating; but in my soul I gladly endure it, because I fear him.”
Such was the manner of his death; and to the young, and to most of his people as well, he left behind his dying as a pattern of high courage and a remembrance of virtue.

notes.text: Or “Geron the Athenian”; Greek gerōn means “old man” and may also be a proper name. Some ancient witnesses read “an Antiochian.”

Zeus Xenios, protector of strangers. The phrase “in keeping with the character of those who dwelt in that place” may refer to the Samaritans’ hospitality or, ironically, to their being of foreign origin; the Greek is uncertain.
Or “to the monthly sacrifice” on the king’s birthday.
Probably Ptolemy son of Dorymenes (4:45); compare 8:8.
Or “led himself to it”; the Greek of vv. 19–20 is compressed.
Hades, the abode of the dead.

verses.text: It happened also that seven brothers were arrested along with their mother, and the king tried to compel them, by torturing them with whips and thongs, to touch the forbidden pig’s flesh.
One of them, acting as spokesman, said, “What do you intend to ask us and learn from us? We stand ready to die sooner than transgress the laws of our fathers.”
In a fury the king commanded pans and caldrons to be heated red-hot.

As soon as they were heated, he ordered the tongue of their spokesman to be cut out, the skin of his head to be torn away in the Scythian manner, and his hands and feet to be lopped off, while his remaining brothers and his mother looked on.

After he was left totally helpless, the king ordered him brought to the fire while still breathing and fried in a pan. As the smoke from the pan drifted far and wide, the brothers and their mother kept encouraging each other to die bravely, saying:

“The Lord God is watching over us and truly feels compassion for us, as Moses made clear in the song that testifies against the people to their faces, when he said, ‘He will have compassion on his servants.’”{a}

When the first had died in this way, they brought forward the second to be made sport of. They tore off the skin of his head along with the hair and asked him, “Will you eat, before your body is punished limb by limb?”
He answered in the language of his ancestors{b} and told them, “No.” So he too underwent the tortures in turn, as the first had done.
And at his final gasp he said, “Fiend that you are, you set us free from life here and now; but since we die on behalf of his laws, the King of the world will raise us to an eternal return to life.”
After him the third was made a mockery. When they demanded his tongue, he quickly thrust it out, and he courageously stretched forth his hands,
and nobly said, “From Heaven I received these, and for the sake of his laws I count them as nothing, and from him I hope to receive them back again.”
so that the king and his company were amazed at the youth’s courage, since he treated the pains as of no account.
When this one too had died, they mistreated and tortured the fourth in the same way.

Close to death, he spoke these words: “Better it is for those who pass away at human hands to look for the hopes that come from God, that they will be raised by him once more. For you, though, there will be no rising again to life.”
Next they led forward the fifth and abused him.
Looking at the king, he said, “You hold authority among mortals, though you yourself are perishable, and you do what you please. But do not imagine that God has forsaken our race.
Only wait, and you will behold his mighty power, how he will torment you and your descendants.”

After him they brought the sixth. On the point of dying, he said, “Do not be led astray to no purpose. We suffer these things on our own account, for we sinned against our own God; that is why such marvels have come about.
But you, do not think you will go unpunished, now that you have undertaken to fight against God.”
The mother was the most remarkable of all, and deserves to be remembered with honor. She watched her seven sons die in a single day, yet she bore it bravely because of her hope in the Lord.
In the language of her ancestors she encouraged each of them, filled with a noble spirit; rousing her woman’s reasoning with a man’s courage, she said to them,
“How you appeared within my womb I cannot tell. Not I bestowed on you spirit and life; not I arranged in order the elements that compose each one of you.

It is the world’s Creator, then, who formed humanity at its birth and found out how all things come to be, who will give spirit and life back to you again in mercy, since now you hold yourselves of no account on behalf of his laws.”

Antiochus felt he was being mocked, and suspected that her words were an insult. The youngest son was still alive, and the king not only appealed to him with words but also gave him his sworn word that he would make him rich and fortunate if he would abandon his ancestors’ ways, and that he would make him his Friend and give him a high position.
Because the young man paid no attention at all, the king summoned the mother and urged her to advise the boy to save himself.
After he had urged her at length, she undertook to persuade her son.

But she leaned close to him, scorned the cruel tyrant, and said in her ancestral language: “My son, take pity on me. For nine months I carried you in my womb, and for three years I nursed you; I raised you and brought you up to this age, and I have cared for you.

Child, I ask you to lift your eyes to the sky and the earth, to look at all that is in them, and to understand that God made them from what did not exist.{c} So it is too that the human race comes to be.
Do not fear this butcher, but prove worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that in God’s mercy I may receive you back along with your brothers.”
She was still speaking when the young man said, “For whom are you waiting? To the king’s decree I do not listen; I heed the decree of the law given through Moses to our fathers.
But you, who have devised every kind of evil against the Hebrews, will not escape God’s hands.
For we are suffering because of our own sins.
And if, for the sake of rebuke and discipline, our living Lord is angry with us for a little while, he will be reconciled again with his own servants.
But you, impious man, foulest of all mortals, do not soar up idly, swelling with hopes that have no ground, as you lift your hand against Heaven’s children.
You have not yet escaped the judgment of the all-seeing, almighty God.
For our brothers, after enduring brief pain, have now fallen under God’s covenant of ever-flowing life;{d} but you, by the judgment of God, will bear the just penalty for your arrogance.

Like my brothers, I surrender body and soul for our ancestral laws, and I call upon God to be quickly gracious to the nation, and through afflictions and scourges to bring you to acknowledge that he and he alone is God,
and that in me and my brothers the Almighty’s anger, rightly kindled against all our race, may be stayed.”
Enraged, the king treated this one more savagely than the rest, taking the mockery bitterly.
So he too died in purity, putting his whole trust in the Lord.
Last of all, after her sons, the mother died.
Concerning the sacrificial meals and the surpassing cruelties, then, so much has been shown.

notes.text: Deut 32:36; the “song” is the Song of Moses, Deut 32:1–43 (see Deut 31:19–21).
That is, probably Aramaic, or Hebrew.
Or “out of things that were not”; this is often cited as an early statement of creation from nothing.
