Salt is fine. But if it goes flat, how can you restore its flavor? Keep salt among yourselves, and live in peace with each other.”

notes.text: His appearance was changed: Greek *metamorphōthē*, traditionally “transfigured.”
Bleacher: Greek *gnapheus*, a fuller, who cleaned and whitened cloth.
Elijah … Moses: representing the Prophets and the Law. *Moses* is explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out.”
Rabbi: Hebrew, “my great one,” “my master,” a respectful title for a teacher.
Ps 2:7; Deut 18:15; compare Isa 42:1.
Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew).
Compare Isa 53:3; Ps 22:6–7.
‘If you are able’!: Jesus repeats the father’s words. Many later manuscripts read “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes.”
Through prayer: many manuscripts add “and fasting”; the Westcott–Hort text, with the first hand of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks the words.
Who believe: many manuscripts add “in me.”
A great millstone: literally “a donkey’s millstone,” the large upper stone of a mill turned by a donkey.

Gehenna: Greek form of Hebrew *Ge-Hinnom*, “Valley of Hinnom,” a ravine south of Jerusalem once used for child sacrifice (Jer 7:31) and later a symbol of the place of final judgment. In verse 45 many manuscripts add “into the fire nothing can put out.”

Verse 44 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others). Many later manuscripts add, “where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched,” repeated from verse 48.
Verse 46 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts. Many later manuscripts repeat verse 48 here as well (“where their worm does not die and the fire is not quenched”).
Many manuscripts add “and every sacrifice will be salted with salt” (compare Lev 2:13); Codex Bezae has this clause instead of the other. The Westcott–Hort text has the shorter reading.

verses.text: Setting out from there, Jesus went into the territory of Judea and beyond the Jordan.{a} Again crowds gathered to him, and as was his habit, he taught them once more.
Some Pharisees{b} came up and, to test him, asked whether a man is permitted to divorce his wife.
He answered by asking, “What instruction did Moses give you?”
They said, “Moses allowed a man to write out a certificate of divorce and send her away.”{c}
Jesus told them, “It was because your hearts were hard that he wrote you this command.
But from the start of creation, ‘male and female he made them.’{d}
‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother,{e}
and the two will become one flesh.’ So they are two no longer, but a single flesh.
What God has yoked together, then, no human being should split apart.”
Once they were indoors again, the disciples asked him about it.
He said to them, “Any man who divorces his wife and weds another woman commits adultery against her;
and if she divorces her husband and weds another man, she commits adultery.”
People kept bringing little children to Jesus for him to touch, but the disciples scolded them.
When Jesus saw this, he was indignant. “Let the little children come to me,” he told them. “Do not hold them back, for God’s kingdom belongs to such as these.
Amen, I tell you, anyone who will not receive God’s kingdom as a little child receives it will never get into it.”
And he gathered them into his arms and blessed them, laying his hands on them.
As Jesus was starting out on his way, a man ran up, knelt in front of him, and asked, “Good Teacher, what must I do to inherit everlasting life?”
“Why call me good?” Jesus replied. “Nobody is good except one—God.
You know the commands: ‘You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not give false evidence; you shall not defraud; respect your father and mother.’ ”{f}
“Teacher,” he said, “I have kept all of these since I was young.”
Jesus fixed his eyes on him and loved him. “One thing you still lack,” he told him. “Go, sell whatever you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven. Then come, follow me.”
At these words the man’s face fell, and he went off grieving, for he owned great estates.
Jesus looked around and said to his disciples, “How hard it will be for the wealthy to enter God’s kingdom!”
The disciples were startled at his words. But Jesus said to them again, “Children, how hard it is to enter God’s kingdom!{g}
A camel can squeeze through the eye of a needle more easily than a wealthy person can enter the kingdom of God.”
They were astonished beyond measure and said to one another, “Then who can be saved?”
Jesus gazed at them and said, “For mortals this cannot be done, but not for God; everything is possible for God.”{h}
Peter started to say to him, “Consider that we have left everything behind and have followed you.”
Jesus said, “Amen, I tell you, there is no one who has left house or brothers or sisters or mother or father or children or fields for my sake and for the gospel
will receive a hundredfold now, in this very age—houses, brothers and sisters, mothers and children, and farms, though with persecutions—and, in the age to come, life without end.
But many who are first will be last, and the last will be first.”

They were traveling the road up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was in front. The disciples were amazed, and those trailing behind were fearful. Again he took the Twelve apart from the others and began to explain what would happen to him.
“Listen,” he said, “we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes. They will condemn him to death and hand him over to the Gentiles,
They will mock him, spit on him, flog him and kill him, and after three days he will rise.”
Then James and John, Zebedee’s sons, approached him. “Teacher,” they said, “we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you.”
“What do you want me to do for you?” he asked them.
They replied, “Allow us to sit with you in your glory, one at your right hand and one at your left.”
Jesus said to them, “You have no idea what you are asking. Can you drink the cup I am drinking, or be baptized with the baptism I am being baptized with?”{i}
“We are able,” they answered. Then Jesus told them, “You will drink the cup that I drink, and you will undergo the baptism that I undergo;
but who sits at my right or my left is not for me to grant; those places belong to the ones for whom they are prepared.”
When the ten heard about it, they began to be indignant with James and John.
Jesus called them together and said to them, “You know that those regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise power over them.
It is not to be that way among you. Instead, anyone who wants to become great among you must be your servant,
and whoever would hold first place among you is to be everybody’s slave.
For the Son of Man himself did not come to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom{j} for many.”
They came to Jericho.{k} As Jesus was leaving Jericho with his disciples and a sizable crowd, the son of Timaeus, Bartimaeus,{l} a blind beggar, was sitting beside the road.
Hearing that it was Jesus of Nazareth,{m} he began to shout, “Son of David,{n} Jesus, have mercy on me!”
Many rebuked him, telling him to keep quiet, but he only cried out more loudly, “Son of David, take pity on me!”
Jesus stopped and said, “Call him.” So they called the blind man, saying, “Cheer up! Get up—he is calling you.”
He threw off his cloak, jumped to his feet, and went to Jesus.
Jesus asked him, “What do you want me to do for you?” The blind man said, “Rabbouni,{o} let me see again.”
Jesus told him, “Go; your faith has made you well.” Instantly he could see, and he followed Jesus along the road.

notes.text: Beyond the Jordan: that is, Perea, east of the river. Many manuscripts read “by way of the far side of the Jordan.”
Some Pharisees: the words are bracketed by Westcott–Hort; Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts lack them, giving “people asked him.”
Gen 2:24. Many manuscripts add “and be united to his wife”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks the words.
Exod 20:12–16; Deut 5:16–20. *Do not cheat* may reflect Deut 24:14 or Exod 20:17.
Many manuscripts read “how hard it is for those who trust in riches to enter God’s kingdom”; the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks the phrase.
Compare Gen 18:14; Job 42:2.
The cup … the baptism: images for suffering and death (compare 14:36; Ps 75:8; Isa 51:17).
Ransom: Greek *lytron*, the price paid to free a slave or captive. Compare Isa 53:10–12.
Jericho: Hebrew *Yericho*, perhaps “moon city” or “fragrant place,” about 15 miles (24 km) northeast of Jerusalem.
Bartimaeus: Aramaic *bar Timai*, “son of Timaeus,” as Mark explains. *Timaeus* may come from Greek *timē*, “honor,” or from Aramaic, “unclean,” “defiled.”
Jesus of Nazareth: literally “the Nazarene.”
Son of David: a messianic title (2 Sam 7:12–16; Isa 11:1).
Rabbouni: Aramaic, “my master,” “my teacher,” a more emphatic form of Rabbi.

verses.text: As they drew close to Jerusalem, near Bethphage{a} and Bethany{b} at the Mount of Olives,{c} Jesus sent off two of his disciples
telling them, “Go to the village opposite you. Just as you go in, you will come upon a young donkey tethered there, one nobody has yet sat on. Untie it and lead it here.
If anybody asks you, ‘Why are you doing that?’ say, ‘The Lord{d} needs it, and he will send it back here without delay.’ ”
Off they went, and they came upon a colt tethered by a doorway out on the street, and they set it loose.
Some of the bystanders said to them, “What do you mean by untying that colt?”
They answered as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go.
Then they led the colt to Jesus, laid their cloaks over it, and Jesus mounted it.
Many people laid their coats along the road, and others strewed branches cut from the fields.

Blessed is the coming kingdom of our father David!
Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
Entering Jerusalem, he went to the temple and surveyed everything there; then, because the hour was late, he went back out with the Twelve to Bethany.
On the following day, when they had left Bethany, he felt hungry.
Seeing in the distance a fig tree in leaf, he went to check whether it had any fruit. When he reached it he found only foliage, for the season for figs had not yet come.{g}
He said to the tree, “Let no one eat your fruit ever again.” His disciples were listening.

They reached Jerusalem, and Jesus entered the temple precincts and started to expel the sellers and buyers who were doing business there. He knocked over the tables of the money changers{h} and the benches of the dove sellers,
and he would not allow anyone to carry goods through the temple courts.
He taught them: “Does Scripture not say, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer for every nation’?{i} Yet you have made it a robbers’ den.”{j}
The chief priests and scribes learned of this and searched for some means of doing away with him. They were afraid of him, for the entire crowd was astonished at his teaching.
And each evening they{k} would leave the city.
Early in the morning, as they passed by, they saw the fig tree withered from the roots up.
Peter remembered and said to him, “Rabbi, look! The fig tree you cursed has withered.”
Jesus answered them, “Have faith in God.{l}
Amen, I tell you, should anyone say to this mountain, ‘Rise up and hurl yourself into the sea,’ and have no doubt in his heart, but trust that what he says is happening, it will be so for him.
For this reason I say to you: whatever you ask for in prayer, believe that you have already received it, and it will be yours.
And whenever you stand up to pray, forgive whatever grievance you have against someone, so that your Father in heaven may also forgive your wrongdoings.”
Once more they arrived in Jerusalem. While Jesus was strolling in the temple precincts, the chief priests, scribes, and elders approached him
They asked him, “On what authority do you do these things? Or who authorized you to do them?”
Jesus said to them, “I will ask you one question. Answer me, and I will tell you on what authority I act in this way.
John’s baptism—was it from heaven or from human beings? Answer me.”
They argued among themselves, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say, ‘Then why did you not believe him?’
But should we say, ‘From human beings’?”—they were afraid of the people, for everyone held that John had truly been a prophet.
So their answer to Jesus was, “We cannot say.” Jesus replied, “Then I will not tell you either on what authority I am doing these things.”

notes.text: Bethphage: Aramaic, “house of unripe figs,” a village on the Mount of Olives.
Bethany: perhaps “house of the poor” or “house of Ananiah,” a village about 2 miles (3 km) east of Jerusalem.
Mount of Olives: the ridge east of Jerusalem across the Kidron Valley (compare Zech 14:4).
The Lord: or “its master.” The Greek *kyrios* can mean “Lord” or “owner.”
Hosanna: Hebrew *hoshi’ah na*, “save, please!” (Ps 118:25), which had become a shout of praise.
Ps 118:26. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Compare Jer 8:13; Hos 9:10; Mic 7:1.
Money changers: they exchanged foreign coins for the Tyrian silver coins required for paying the temple tax.
Isa 56:7. *All the nations*: or “all the Gentiles.”
Jer 7:11. *Hideout for robbers*: literally “a cave of bandits.”
They: Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and some others, followed by Westcott–Hort, read “they”; Sinaiticus and many manuscripts read “he.”
Have faith in God: or “Have the faith that comes from God.” Sinaiticus, Bezae and a few others read “If you have faith in God.”

Verse 26 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and in the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others). Many later manuscripts add, “But if you do not forgive, neither will your Father in heaven forgive your wrongdoings” (compare Matt 6:15).

verses.text: Then he began to speak to them in parables: “A man planted a vineyard, put a wall around it, dug a pit for the winepress, and built a watchtower.{a} He leased it to tenant farmers and went abroad.
At harvest time he dispatched a slave to the farmers to receive his share of the grapes from them.
But they grabbed him, beat him, and sent him off with nothing.
Again he sent them another slave. This one they struck on the head and treated shamefully.
He sent still another, and that one they murdered. He sent many more; some they beat and some they killed.
He still had one left to send, a son he dearly loved. Last of all he sent him to them, thinking, ‘They will have regard for my son.’
But those tenants said to one another, ‘Here is the heir! Come on, we will kill him, and the inheritance will belong to us.’
So they seized him and killed him, and flung him outside the vineyard.
What then will the vineyard’s owner do? He will come and destroy those tenants, and hand the vineyard over to others.

Have you never read this scripture:
‘The stone the builders rejected as worthless
has turned out to be the chief cornerstone.

This came about from the Lord,{b}
and it is a marvel in our eyes’?”{c}
They were looking for a way to lay hands on him, for they knew the parable had been told against them; yet they feared the crowd. So they let him be and departed.
Next they sent to him some of the Pharisees and Herodians,{d} to catch him out in something he said.

They came to him and said, “Teacher, we know you are truthful and do not bow to anyone, since you pay no attention to a person’s status but teach God’s way truthfully. Does the Law permit paying the census tax{e} to Caesar, or not? Are we to pay or not to pay?”
Seeing through their pretense, he replied, “Why are you testing me? Fetch me a silver coin{f} and let me have a look.”
They brought one, and he asked them, “Whose likeness is this, and whose inscription?” “Caesar’s,” they told him.
Jesus said to them, “What belongs to Caesar, give back to Caesar, and what belongs to God, give to God.” And they were utterly amazed at him.
Then some Sadducees{g} came to him—the people who say there is no resurrection—and put a question to him.
“Teacher,” they said, “Moses laid down for us in writing: should a man die childless, leaving a widow, his brother is to marry her and produce descendants for the dead man.{h}
Now there were seven brothers. The first took a wife and died without leaving any children.
The second took her, and he too died leaving no children; the third likewise.
Not one of the seven had children by her. Finally the woman herself died.
In the resurrection, when they rise, whose wife will she be? The seven of them all had her as wife.”
Jesus told them, “Surely this is why you are wrong: you are ignorant both of the scriptures and of the power of God.
For when people rise from among the dead, men do not marry and women are not given in marriage; they are like the angels in heaven.

And as for the dead being raised, have you not read in the book of Moses, in the passage about the bush,{i} how God spoke to him, saying, ‘I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’?{j}
He is not God of corpses but of the living. You are badly mistaken.”
One of the scribes came up and heard them debating. Seeing that Jesus had answered them well, he asked him, “Which commandment ranks first of all?”
Jesus answered, “The first is this: ‘Hear, Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one.{k}
love the Lord{l} your God with your whole heart, your whole soul, your whole mind and your whole strength.’{m}
The second is this: ‘You shall love your neighbor as you love yourself.’{n} No other commandment is greater than these.”
The scribe said to him, “Teacher, you have spoken well. You are right that God is one and there is no other besides him,
And to love him with one’s whole heart, whole understanding, and whole strength, and to love one’s neighbor as oneself, outweighs all the whole burnt offerings and sacrifices.”{o}
When Jesus saw how thoughtfully he had replied, he said to him, “You are not far from God’s kingdom.” And after that nobody dared to question him any more.
While teaching in the temple, Jesus took up the matter and asked, “How can the scribes claim that the Messiah is David’s son?

It was David himself who said, moved by the Holy Spirit:
‘The Lord said to my lord,
“Take your seat at my right hand
until I put your enemies beneath your feet.” ’{p}
David himself calls him ‘lord’; so how can he be his son?” And the great crowd listened to him with delight.
In his teaching he said, “Be on your guard against the scribes, who like to parade about in long robes and to be greeted with deference in the marketplaces,
and who want the chief seats in the synagogues and the places of honor at banquets.
They swallow up widows’ houses and, for show, pray at great length. These will receive the heavier sentence.”
He sat down across from the treasury{q} and watched how the crowd dropped money into the offering chests. Many rich people were putting in large sums.
Then a poor widow came and dropped in two tiny copper coins, together worth only a sixty-fourth of a day’s wage.{r}
He called the disciples over and told them, “Amen, I say to you: more has gone into the treasury from this destitute widow than from all the rest.
For they all gave out of their surplus, but she, out of her want, put in everything she possessed—all she had to live on.”

notes.text: Vineyard … lookout tower: the description echoes Isa 5:1–2.
The Lord: Greek *kyrios*; in Ps 118:23 the Hebrew has the divine name, Yahweh.
Herodians: supporters of the dynasty of Herod, here allied with the Pharisees as in 3:6.
Poll tax: Greek *kēnsos* (Latin *census*), the head tax paid directly to Rome.
Silver coin: Greek *dēnarion*, the Roman denarius, a day’s wage for a laborer, bearing the emperor’s image.
Sadducees: a priestly party that accepted only the written law as binding and denied the resurrection; the name is probably derived from Zadok, the priest of David and Solomon (2 Sam 8:17).
Deut 25:5–6 (levirate marriage); compare Gen 38:8.
The bush: Exod 3:1–6, the burning bush.
Deut 6:4, the *Shema* (from its first word, “Hear”). Both occurrences of “Lord” stand for the divine name, Yahweh, in the Hebrew. *Israel* means “he strives with God” (Gen 32:28).
The Lord: in Deut 6:5 the Hebrew has Yahweh.
Deut 6:5. Mark lists four faculties (heart, soul, mind, strength) where the Hebrew has three.
Compare 1 Sam 15:22; Hos 6:6.
Ps 110:1. The first “Lord” stands for the divine name, Yahweh, in the Hebrew; the second (“my lord”) translates *adoni*, a title of honor.
Treasury: the thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests in the Court of the Women.

Two tiny copper coins: Greek *lepta duo*, “two lepta,” the smallest copper coins in circulation; Mark adds, “which make a *kodrantēs*” (Latin *quadrans*), one sixty-fourth of a denarius, the denarius being a laborer’s day’s wage.

verses.text: As he was leaving the temple, one of his disciples said to him, “Teacher, look! What enormous stones, what splendid buildings!”
Jesus answered him, “You see these great structures? Not a single stone will be left here upon another; every one will be pulled down.”
Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately as he was sitting on the Mount of Olives opposite the temple:
“Tell us, when is this to happen? And what will be the signal that all these things are about to reach their completion?”
Jesus began to tell them, “Take care that nobody leads you astray.
Many will come using my name, claiming, ‘I am he,’{a} and they will lead many astray.
When you hear the noise of battles and rumors of wars, do not be alarmed. These things have to happen, but that is not yet the finish.
One nation will rise against another, and one kingdom against another. There will be earthquakes in many places, and famines. These things are just the beginning of the labor pains.
“As for you, be on your guard. They will hand you over to councils,{b} and you will be flogged in synagogues; you will stand before governors and kings on my account, to bear witness to them.
And first the good news must be proclaimed among all the nations.
Whenever they arrest you and bring you to trial, do not fret beforehand about what you will say; just say whatever is given you at that moment, for it is not you who speak but the Holy Spirit.
Brothers will betray brothers to death, and fathers their children; children will rise against parents and have them put to death.
Everyone will hate you because of my name. But whoever holds out to the end will be saved.
“When you see the desolating abomination{c} standing where he ought not to be—let the reader take note—then those in Judea must escape to the hills.
Anyone on the rooftop must not go down or go inside to fetch anything out of the house;
anyone out in the field must not turn back to pick up a cloak.
How hard it will be in those days for women expecting a child and for mothers with babies at the breast!
Pray that it does not happen in winter.
For those days will bring distress such as has never been from the beginning of the creation God made until now, and never will be again.
Had the Lord not cut short those days, no living being would survive; but for the sake of the chosen, whom he has chosen for himself, he has cut the days short.
And at that time, if anyone says to you, ‘Look, the Messiah is here!’ or ‘Look, he is there!’ do not believe it.
For pretended messiahs and pretended prophets will arise and work signs and marvels, aiming to deceive even the chosen, were that possible.
So keep watch; I have forewarned you of everything.

the stars will be falling out of the sky,
and the powers in the heavens will be shaken.’{d}
Then they will see the Son of Man coming in clouds{e} with great power and glory.
And then he will send out the angels and gather [his] chosen ones from the four winds, from the farthest edge of the earth to the farthest edge of the sky.
“Learn the lesson from the fig tree. As soon as its branch turns tender and puts out leaves, you know summer is close.
So it is with you: when you see these things taking place, know that he{f} is near, right at the doors.
Amen, I tell you, this generation will not pass away before all these things have happened.
Sky and earth will pass away, but my words will never pass away.
“But that day or hour nobody knows—not the angels in heaven, nor the Son,{g} but only the Father.
Be on the lookout and keep alert, since the appointed moment is unknown to you.{h}
It is like a man away on a journey, who leaves his house and puts his slaves in charge, each with his own task, and orders the doorkeeper to keep awake.
Stay awake, then, because the master of the house may return at any time unknown to you—late in the evening, at midnight, at cockcrow, or early in the morning.{i}
Otherwise he may come without warning and find you sleeping.
What I say to you I say to everyone: Keep awake!”

notes.text: I am he: literally “I am,” perhaps echoing the divine self-designation (Exod 3:14; Isa 43:10).
Councils: Greek *synedria*, local Jewish courts.
Desolating abomination: literally “the abomination of desolation,” Dan 9:27; 11:31; 12:11; compare 1 Macc 1:54. The participle “standing” is masculine, suggesting a person.
Isa 13:10; 34:4; compare Joel 2:10.
Coming in clouds: Dan 7:13.
He: or “it.”
Nor the Son: these words, present in all the major manuscripts of Mark, are omitted in some late manuscripts of Matt 24:36.

The appointed moment is unknown to you: literally “you do not know when the time is”; Westcott–Hort bracket “is” (*estin*). Many manuscripts add “and pray” after “keep alert” (Sinaiticus and others); Vaticanus and Bezae lack it.
Late in the evening … early in the morning: the four Roman watches of the night, roughly six to nine in the evening, nine to midnight, midnight to three, and three to six in the morning.

verses.text: Two days remained until the Passover and the feast of Unleavened Bread.{a} Meanwhile the chief priests and scribes were seeking a way to seize Jesus by a trick and put him to death.
For they said, “Not at the feast, in case there is an uproar among the people.”

He was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper,{b} sitting at the table, when a woman arrived with an alabaster jar of very expensive perfume, pure nard.{c} She broke the jar open and poured the perfume on his head.
Some of those present grumbled indignantly to one another, “What was the point of squandering the ointment like this?
It could have been sold for over three hundred days’ wages{d} and the money given to the poor.” And they spoke sharply to her.
But Jesus said, “Leave her alone. Why are you making trouble for her? She has done a beautiful thing for me.
The poor you always have among you, and you can do good to them [always] whenever you wish; but me you will not always have.
She has done what lay in her power: she has anointed my body ahead of time for its burial.
Amen, I tell you, in every part of the world where the good news is preached, her deed too will be spoken of, so that she is remembered.”
Judas Iscariot,{e} who was one of the Twelve, went to the chief priests in order to hand Jesus over to them.
They were delighted to hear it and promised to pay him in silver. So he kept looking for a convenient opportunity to hand him over.

On the first day of the Unleavened Bread, the day the Passover lambs were slaughtered, his disciples said to him, “Where would you like us to go and get things ready for you to eat the Passover meal?”
He sent two of his disciples with these instructions: “Go into the city, and a man carrying a clay jar of water will meet you. Follow him,
and whatever house he enters, tell its master, ‘The Teacher says: Where is the room set aside for me, so that I can eat the Passover there with my disciples?’
He himself will point out to you a spacious room upstairs, already furnished with couches. Get things ready for us there.”
The disciples set out, came into the city, and found everything just as he had told them; and they prepared the Passover.
When evening came, he arrived with the Twelve.
And as they reclined at the meal, Jesus said, “Amen, I tell you, one of you will betray me—one who is eating with me.”{f}
Grief came over them, and one after another they began asking him, “Surely not I?”
He told them, “It is one of the Twelve, one who is dipping his bread with me into the [one] bowl.
The Son of Man will go as the Scriptures say about him; but how terrible for the one by whom the Son of Man is handed over! It would have been better for that man never to have been born.”
While they were eating, he took a loaf, said the blessing, broke it, and gave it to them with the words, “Take it; this is my body.”{g}
Then he took a cup, gave thanks, and handed it to them, and they all drank from it.
And he told them, “This is my blood of the covenant,{h} poured out on behalf of many.
Amen, I tell you, never again will I drink of the fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in God’s kingdom.”
After singing the hymn,{i} they went out to the Mount of Olives.
But once I am raised, I will lead the way before you into Galilee.”
Peter declared, “Everyone else may fall away, but not I.”
Jesus said to him, “Amen, I tell you: this very night, before a rooster crows twice, you will deny me three times.”
But Peter kept protesting all the more forcefully, “Even if it means dying alongside you, I will not disown you!” And all of them were saying the same.
They went to a place named Gethsemane,{k} and he said to his disciples, “Stay here while I pray.”
Taking with him Peter, James, and John, he began to be filled with alarm and anguish.
“My soul is crushed with grief, even to death,”{l} he told them. “Wait here and stay awake.”
Going on a little farther, he fell to the ground and prayed that, if it were possible, the hour might pass him by.
“Abba,{m} Father,” he said, “for you all things are possible. Take this cup away from me. Yet let it be not what I want, but what you want.”
He came back and found them asleep. “Simon,” he said to Peter, “are you sleeping? Had you not the strength to stay awake a single hour?
Keep awake and pray, so that you do not come into the time of testing.{n} The spirit is eager, but human nature is frail.”
Once more he went away and prayed, [saying the same words.]
And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were weighed down; and they had no idea what to say to him.
Coming back a third time, he said to them, “Still asleep? Still taking your rest?{o} It is enough; the hour is here. See, the Son of Man is being betrayed into sinners’ hands.
Get up, let us go. Look, the one betraying me is close at hand.”
And just then, as he was speaking, up came Judas, one of the Twelve, with a mob carrying swords and cudgels, dispatched by the chief priests, scribes, and elders.
His betrayer had given them a prearranged sign: “The man I kiss—he is the one. Take hold of him and lead him off securely.”
As soon as he arrived, he went straight up to Jesus, said, “Rabbi!” and kissed him warmly.
Then they laid hands on him and arrested him.
One of those standing nearby drew a sword and slashed at the high priest’s slave, slicing off his ear.
Jesus responded, “Have you come out with swords and cudgels to capture me as though I were a bandit?
Every day I was among you in the temple teaching, and you never arrested me. But this is happening so that the Scriptures will be fulfilled.”
Then they all deserted him and ran away.
A young man was following him, wearing only a linen cloth over his naked body. They seized him,
but he left the linen cloth behind and fled naked.{p}
They took Jesus away to the high priest,{q} and all the chief priests, elders, and scribes assembled.
Peter trailed behind at a distance, as far as the inside of the high priest’s courtyard, and he was sitting among the attendants, keeping warm by the blaze.
Meanwhile the chief priests and the entire Council{r} kept searching for evidence against Jesus that would justify putting him to death, yet they could find none.
Many gave false evidence against him, but their statements did not agree.
Some men then rose and testified falsely against him, saying,
“We ourselves heard him say, ‘I will pull down this temple made with hands, and within three days I will build another, not made with hands.’ ”
But even so, their accounts were inconsistent.
Then the high priest stood up in their midst and questioned Jesus: “Have you no answer to make? What is this testimony these men bring against you?”
He kept silent and said nothing in reply. Once more the high priest put a question to him: “Are you the Christ, the Son of the Blessed?”{s}
“I am,” said Jesus, “and you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of the Power{t} and coming with the clouds of heaven.”{u}
At that the high priest ripped his garments. “What further need have we of witnesses?” he said.
“You heard him blaspheme. How does it seem to you?” And all of them judged him worthy of death.
Then some started spitting at him; they covered his face, punched him, and taunted him, “Prophesy!” And the attendants took him and slapped him.
Peter was down in the courtyard when one of the high priest’s maidservants came along.
Noticing Peter warming himself, she looked closely at him and said, “You too were with the Nazarene, this Jesus.”
But he denied it: “I have no idea what you mean—I don’t understand it.” And he went outside into the entryway.{v}
The servant girl saw him there and began telling the bystanders once more, “This fellow is one of them.”
Again he denied it. A little while afterward the bystanders said to Peter again, “You certainly are one of them, for you are a Galilean.”{w}
Then he began to put himself under a curse and to swear, “I have no knowledge of this man you speak of.”

And right then the rooster crowed for the second time, and Peter recalled the word Jesus had spoken to him: “Twice the rooster will crow, and before that you will have disowned me three times.” And he broke down and wept.{x}

notes.text: Passover … Unleavened Bread: the Passover meal on the evening beginning 15 Nisan, followed by the seven-day festival of Unleavened Bread (Exod 12:1–20; Lev 23:5–8).
Simon the leper: presumably a man Jesus had healed. *Simon* means “he has heard.”
Pure nard: Greek *nardou pistikēs*, spikenard, an aromatic oil imported from the Himalayas; *pistikēs* probably means “genuine.”
More than three hundred days’ wages: literally “more than three hundred denarii,” a denarius being a laborer’s day’s wage.
Iscariot: probably Hebrew *ish Qeriyot*, “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea (Josh 15:25).
Eating with me: compare Ps 41:9.
This is my body: Westcott–Hort and the earliest manuscripts lack “eat” after “take it,” which many later manuscripts add (compare Matt 26:26).
Blood of the covenant: Exod 24:8; compare Zech 9:11. Many manuscripts read “the new covenant” (compare Luke 22:20; 1 Cor 11:25); Westcott–Hort, following Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack “new.”
The hymn: probably the second half of the Hallel (Pss 115–118), sung at the close of the Passover meal.
Zech 13:7.
Gethsemane: Aramaic *gat shemanim*, “oil press.”
Abba: Aramaic for “father,” the intimate address of a child to a parent; compare Rom 8:15; Gal 4:6.
Time of testing: or “temptation.”

Still asleep? Still taking your rest?: or, as a command, “Sleep on now and take your rest.” *It is enough*: Greek *apechei*, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “the account is settled,” “he (the betrayer) has received payment,” or “it is far off.” Bezae and some others add “the end.”
Fled naked: this episode is found only in Mark. Some have suggested the young man was Mark himself, but this is conjecture.
The high priest: Caiaphas (Matt 26:57), high priest AD 18–36.
Council: Greek *synedrion*, the Sanhedrin, the supreme Jewish court in Jerusalem, presided over by the high priest.
The Blessed: a reverent Jewish substitute for the name of God.
The Power: another reverent substitute for the name of God. The words echo Ps 110:1.
Entryway: or “forecourt.” Many manuscripts add “and a rooster crowed” (Alexandrinus, Bezae and others); Westcott–Hort, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack it.
Galilean: many later manuscripts add “and your speech gives you away” (compare Matt 26:73).
He broke down and wept: the meaning of the Greek *epibalōn* is uncertain; perhaps “he thought of it,” “he threw himself down,” or “he covered his head.”

verses.text: Early in the morning, the chief priests conferred with the elders, the scribes and the entire Council. Then they tied up Jesus, took him away, and handed him over to Pilate.{a}
Pilate questioned him: “You are the king of the Jews?” “You say so,”{b} he answered.
The chief priests kept bringing many charges against him.
So Pilate questioned him once more: “Have you nothing to say in reply? Listen to how many accusations they are making against you!”
But Jesus gave no further answer at all, which left Pilate astonished.
At each festival Pilate used to set free for them one prisoner, whomever they requested.
There was a man called Barabbas{c} held in prison with the rebels who had committed murder during the uprising.
So the crowd went up and started demanding that he follow his usual practice for them.
Pilate replied, “Is it your wish that I set free the king of the Jews for you?”
For he was aware that it was out of envy that the chief priests had handed Jesus over.
The chief priests, however, incited the crowd to ask that he free Barabbas for them in place of Jesus.
Pilate spoke to them again: “Then what am I to do with the one you call the king of the Jews?”
They shouted back, “Crucify him!”
“Why? What crime has he committed?” Pilate asked. But they only shouted louder, “Crucify him!”
Pilate, intent on pleasing the crowd, released Barabbas to them; and he had Jesus scourged{d} and then gave him up for crucifixion.
The soldiers marched him off inside the palace courtyard (the governor’s residence){e} and summoned the whole company of troops.{f}
They dressed him in purple, twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on his head.
Then they began to salute him: “Hail, king of the Jews!”
They kept hitting him on the head with a reed and spitting on him, and bending their knees, they paid him mock homage.
When their mockery was over, they pulled the purple robe off him, dressed him in his own garments, and took him out for crucifixion.
A passerby, Simon of Cyrene,{g} the father of Alexander and Rufus,{h} was coming in from the country, and they forced him to carry Jesus’ cross.
They brought Jesus to the place called Golgotha, which translated means “Place of a Skull.”{i}
They held out to him wine laced with myrrh,{j} but he would not take it.
And they crucified him and divided up his clothes, throwing dice for them to see what each would take.{k}
It was nine o’clock in the morning{l} when they crucified him.
The notice of the charge against him was inscribed: THE KING OF THE JEWS.
Two bandits{m} were crucified along with him, the one at his right, the other at his left.
People going by hurled insults at him, shaking their heads{o} and saying, “Ha! You who would tear down the temple and rebuild it in three days,
save yourself and come down from the cross!”
In the same way the chief priests, along with the scribes, mocked him among themselves: “He saved others, but he cannot save himself!
This Messiah, this king of Israel—let him climb down from the cross this minute, so we can see it and believe!” Even the men crucified beside him reviled him.
When noon came, darkness fell over the whole land{p} until three in the afternoon.{q}
At three o’clock Jesus cried out in a loud voice, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani?”{r} which translated means, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Some of the bystanders who heard it said, “Listen, he is calling Elijah.”
Someone ran and filled a sponge with sour wine,{s} fixed it to a reed, and held it up for him to drink, saying, “Leave him alone! Let us see if Elijah comes to take him down.”
Then Jesus gave a great cry and breathed out his life.
And the curtain of the temple{t} was torn in two from top to bottom.
When the centurion{u} who stood facing him saw that he had died in this way,{v} he said, “Truly this man was God’s Son!”{w}
Some women were also looking on from far away, among them Mary Magdalene,{x} Mary the mother of James the younger and of Joses, and Salome.{y}
While he was in Galilee they used to follow him and provide for him; and many other women were there as well, who had traveled up to Jerusalem with him.
It was already evening, and because it was Preparation Day—the day before a Sabbath—
Joseph of Arimathea{z} came, a prominent Council member who was also looking for God’s kingdom. He ventured boldly into Pilate’s presence and requested Jesus’ body.
Pilate was astonished that he had already died. He called the centurion and asked whether Jesus had been dead for long.{aa}
Once the centurion had confirmed it, Pilate gave Joseph the body.
Joseph bought a linen cloth, took Jesus down, wrapped him in it, and laid him in a tomb that had been cut into the rock. He then rolled a stone across the tomb’s entrance.
Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses saw the place where they put him.

notes.text: Pilate: Pontius Pilate, Roman prefect (governor) of Judea AD 26–36.
You say so: an evasive or affirmative answer, meaning “That is your word for it” or “It is as you say.”
Barabbas: Aramaic *bar Abba*, “son of the father.” Some manuscripts of Matthew (27:16–17) give his name as “Jesus Barabbas.”
Scourged: Greek *phragellōsas*, from Latin *flagellum*, a scourge of leather thongs weighted with bone or metal, the brutal preliminary to crucifixion.
Governor’s residence: Greek *praitōrion* (Latin *praetorium*), the official residence of the Roman governor in Jerusalem.
Whole company of troops: literally “the whole cohort,” Greek *speira*, a unit of a Roman legion, nominally 600 soldiers, though the term was used of smaller detachments.
Cyrene: a Greek city on the coast of North Africa (modern Libya), with a large Jewish community. *Simon* means “he has heard.”
Alexander and Rufus: *Alexander* is Greek, “defender of men”; *Rufus* is Latin, “red.” They were apparently known to Mark’s readers (compare Rom 16:13).
Golgotha: Aramaic *gulgulta*, “skull.” The Latin equivalent, *calvaria*, gives the traditional name “Calvary.”
Wine laced with myrrh: a drink perhaps meant to dull the pain (compare Prov 31:6).
Ps 22:18. *Throwing dice*: literally “casting lots.”
Nine in the morning: literally “the third hour,” counting from sunrise at about six o’clock.
Bandits: or “rebels” (Greek *lēstai*), the term Josephus uses for insurgents.

Verse 28 is lacking in the Westcott–Hort text and in the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, Bezae and others). Many later manuscripts add, “And the scripture was fulfilled that says, ‘He was counted among the lawless’ ” (Isa 53:12; compare Luke 22:37).
Shaking their heads: compare Ps 22:7; 109:25; Lam 2:15.
Land: or “earth.” Compare Amos 8:9.
Noon … three in the afternoon: literally “the sixth hour … the ninth hour.”

Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani: Ps 22:1, in Aramaic, transliterated in Greek. *Eloi* is Aramaic for “my God” (the Westcott–Hort reading here); some manuscripts have the Hebrew form *Eli* (compare Matt 27:46). *Three o’clock*: literally “the ninth hour.” Westcott–Hort bracket the second “my God” in Mark’s translation.
Sour wine: Greek *oxos*, a cheap wine vinegar drunk by soldiers and laborers. Compare Ps 69:21.
Curtain of the temple: probably the curtain separating the Most Holy Place from the Holy Place (Exod 26:31–33).
Centurion: a Roman officer commanding about a hundred soldiers.
Died in this way: literally “breathed out thus.” Many manuscripts read “cried out and breathed his last in this way.”
God’s Son: or “a son of God.” The Greek lacks the article; the phrase may express a Roman soldier’s recognition of a divine man or the full Christian confession (compare 1:1, 11; 9:7).
Mary Magdalene: that is, Mary of Magdala, a town on the western shore of the lake; *Magdala* comes from Aramaic *migdal*, “tower.”
Salome: from Hebrew *shalom*, “peace.” She may be the mother of James and John (compare Matt 27:56).
Arimathea: probably Ramathaim (Ramah), the birthplace of Samuel (1 Sam 1:1), northwest of Jerusalem; the name means “heights.” *Joseph* means “may he add” (Gen 30:24).
Had been dead for some time: Vaticanus, Bezae and some others, followed by Westcott–Hort in the margin, read “was already dead.”

verses.text: Once the Sabbath had ended, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome purchased fragrant spices, intending to go and anoint him.
Very early on the first day of the week, just after sunrise, they made their way to the tomb.
They were saying to one another, “Who is going to roll the stone back from the tomb’s entrance for us?”
But when they looked up, they saw that the stone—an exceedingly large one—had already been rolled away.
Going into the tomb, they saw a young man dressed in a white robe sitting on the right-hand side, and they were struck with amazement.
“Do not be so amazed,” he said to them. “You are looking for Jesus the Nazarene, the one who was crucified. He has been raised; he is not here. See the spot where they laid him.
Now go and tell his disciples, and Peter, ‘He is going on ahead of you into Galilee. There you will see him, just as he told you.’ ”
They came out and fled from the tomb, seized with trembling and bewilderment; and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.{a}
[[After he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had driven out seven demons.
She went and told those who had been with him, as they mourned and wept.
But when they heard that he was alive and that she had seen him, they would not believe it.
After this he showed himself in another form to two of them as they were walking along on their way into the country.
They went back and told the others, but these did not believe them either.

Later he showed himself to the eleven themselves as they reclined at table, and he rebuked them for their unbelief and stubbornness of heart, because they had not believed those who had seen him after he was raised.{b}
He said to them, “Go out into all the world and announce the good news to the whole creation.
Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever refuses to believe will be condemned.
Those who believe will be attended by these signs: they will cast out demons by my name; they will speak in new tongues;{c}
they will pick up snakes [with their hands],{d} and if they drink any deadly poison it will do them no harm; they will lay their hands on the sick, and these will recover.”
So then, after speaking with them, the Lord [Jesus] was taken up into heaven and sat down at God’s right hand.{e}
Then the disciples set out and proclaimed the message far and wide, the Lord working alongside them and confirming the word through the accompanying signs.]]{f}

notes.text: For they were afraid: here the earliest manuscripts, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, end the Gospel of Mark, as do the Sinaitic Syriac, about a hundred Armenian manuscripts, and the two oldest Georgian manuscripts; Eusebius and Jerome report that almost all Greek copies known to them ended here. Westcott–Hort print 16:9–20 and the shorter ending within double brackets as early additions, not part of Mark’s original text. Whether Mark intended to end at 16:8, or a lost ending once followed, remains debated. See the note at 16:20 for the endings found in other manuscripts.
Raised: Westcott–Hort bracket “from the dead.”
New tongues: Vaticanus lacks “new”; Westcott–Hort retain it.
With their hands: Westcott–Hort bracket these words, which Alexandrinus and many others lack.
God’s right hand: compare Ps 110:1. *Jesus* is bracketed by Westcott–Hort.

The endings of Mark. (1) The *longer ending* (16:9–20, printed here in double brackets) appears in Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, Bezae, Washingtonianus and the great majority of later manuscripts, and Irenaeus (late 2nd century) knew of it. Its vocabulary and style differ markedly from the rest of Mark, and it draws on the resurrection accounts of the other Gospels and Acts. (2) The *shorter ending*, which Westcott–Hort also print in double brackets, comes after 16:8 in a few manuscripts (alone in Codex Bobiensis and the Old Latin k; in several Greek manuscripts it is followed by the longer ending). In summary, it says the women briefly passed on their instructions to Peter’s companions, and that afterward Jesus himself sent out through them, from east to west, the holy and unfading message of eternal salvation. [Amen.] (3) The *Freer Logion*, found only in Codex Washingtonianus (W, 4th–5th century) after 16:14, includes in part a reply from the disciples that this age of lawlessness and unbelief lies under Satan, who prevents God’s truth and power from overcoming the unclean powers of the spirits, and so they ask Christ to reveal his righteousness at once. Christ answers that the span of years of Satan’s authority is complete, but that other terrible things are near, even for those sinners for whom he was handed over to death, so that they might turn to the truth, sin no more, and inherit the spiritual and imperishable glory of righteousness in heaven. Jerome mentions a form of this saying (*Against the Pelagians* 2.15). None of the early papyri of Mark (P45, P88, P137) preserves this chapter.

books.name: Luke
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The earliest manuscripts of Luke are the papyri P75 (about AD 200–225), which preserves most of chapters 3–18 and 22–24, P4 (about AD 200) and P45 (3rd century); where they are cited in the notes, their readings are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Westcott and Hort printed in double brackets a number of short passages near the end of the Gospel that are missing only from Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses (the so-called “Western non-interpolations,” including 22:19b–20; 24:3, 6, 12, 36, 40, 51–52), judging them additions; most modern editions, supported by P75, accept them as original. They are printed here in double brackets with a note. Passages found in later manuscripts but absent from the earliest witnesses (17:36; 23:17) keep their traditional verse numbers, and their text is given in the notes. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from the Greek of Luke, with the source given in a note. Money, measures and times of day are given in modern terms in the text (for example, a denarius as “a day’s wage”), with the original term in a note. The Gospel is anonymous; from the second century it has been attributed to Luke, the physician and companion of Paul (Col 4:14; Phlm 24; 2 Tim 4:11), who also wrote the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 1:1). Most scholars date it about AD 80–90; others date it in the early 60s.

verses.text: Seeing that many have undertaken to set in order an account of the events that have been brought to fulfillment among us,
in keeping with what was handed down to us by the people who were eyewitnesses from the outset and who became servants of the message,
it seemed right to me as well, after investigating everything carefully from the beginning, to write an orderly account for you, most excellent Theophilus,{a}
in order that you might come to recognize how reliable are the matters in which you were instructed.{b}

In the time of Herod, king of Judea,{c} a certain priest by the name of Zechariah belonged to the priestly division of Abijah.{d} His wife, Elizabeth by name, was herself one of Aaron’s descendants.{e}
Both of them were upright before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and requirements of the Lord.{f}
Yet they were childless, for Elizabeth could not conceive, and both of them were well on in years.
It came about that, as he was carrying out his priestly duties before God while his division was on duty,
according to the custom of the priesthood, the lot fell to him to go into the sanctuary of the Lord and burn incense.{g}
And all the throng of the people was outside, praying at the time of the incense offering.
There appeared to him an angel of the Lord, standing to the right of the incense altar.
Zechariah was shaken when he saw him, and fear fell upon him.
But the angel said to him, “Do not be afraid, Zechariah, for your prayer has been answered. Your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you are to name him John.{h}
He will bring you joy and gladness, and many will be happy because of his birth,
For in the Lord’s sight he will be great. Wine and strong drink he must never drink,{i} and he will be full of the Holy Spirit while still in his mother’s womb.
Many of Israel’s sons he will turn back to the Lord their God.

And he will go ahead of him in Elijah’s spirit and power, to turn fathers’ hearts toward their children,{j} and those who disobey toward the wisdom of the just, to have a people ready and prepared for the Lord.”
Zechariah said to the angel, “How shall I know this? For I am an old man, and my wife is advanced in her days.”
In reply the angel said, “I am Gabriel.{k} I stand before God, and I have been sent to talk with you and to announce this good news to you.
Look, you will be silent, unable to say a word, until the day when these things happen, since you did not trust my words, which will come true at their proper time.”
Meanwhile the people were waiting for Zechariah, and they wondered why he was taking so long in the sanctuary.
On coming out he was unable to speak to them, and they understood that he had seen a vision in the sanctuary. He went on making signs to them and stayed speechless.
When his days of service were completed, he went back to his home.
Some time afterward Elizabeth his wife became pregnant, and for five months she kept out of sight, saying,
“The Lord has done this for me. In these days he has looked on me with favor, to remove my shame before others.”
In the sixth month the angel Gabriel was sent from God to a town of Galilee named Nazareth,{l}
to a virgin promised in marriage to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary.{m}
He came in to where she was and said, “Greetings, you who have been shown favor! The Lord is with you.”{n}
But she was deeply troubled at his words, and she kept wondering what sort of greeting this might be.
Then the angel told her, “Mary, have no fear; you have found grace in God’s sight.
Listen: you will conceive and bear a son, and Jesus is the name you are to give him.{o}
He will be great and will be called the Son of the Most High, and the Lord God will give him the throne of his ancestor David.
and over Jacob’s house he will reign for all ages; his kingdom will never come to an end.”
But Mary asked the angel, “How can this be, when I have no relations with a man?”
In reply the angel told her, “The Holy Spirit will come over you, and the Most High’s power will cast its shadow over you. That is why the child to be born will be called holy, Son of God.{p}
And look, Elizabeth your relative has also conceived a son in her old age, and this is the sixth month for her who was called barren.
For no word from God will be without power.”{q}
Mary said, “Here I am, the Lord’s slave woman.{r} Let it happen to me as you have said.” And the angel departed from her.
In those days Mary set out and went in haste into the hill country, to a town of Judah.
She went into Zechariah’s house and gave Elizabeth her greeting.
And as Elizabeth heard Mary greet her, the child jumped in her womb, and Elizabeth became full of the Holy Spirit.
With a great cry she called out, “Among women you are blessed, and blessed is the fruit your womb bears!
And how has this happened to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
The moment the sound of your greeting came to my ears, look, the child within me jumped for joy.
Blessed is the woman who believed that the things the Lord has told her would be fulfilled.”

And Mary said,{s}
“My soul magnifies the Lord,
and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior,

because he has looked upon the lowliness of his slave woman.
For look, from now on all generations will call me blessed,

for great things have been done for me by the Mighty One,
and his name is holy.

His mercy is for generation after generation
to those who fear him.

He has worked might with his arm;
he has scattered those who are proud in the thinking of their hearts.

He has pulled down the powerful from their thrones
and raised the humble high.

The hungry he has filled with good things,
and the rich he has sent away empty.

He has come to the help of Israel his servant,
remembering mercy,

as he spoke to our fathers,
to Abraham and to his offspring forever.”{t}
Mary remained with her some three months, and then went back home.
Elizabeth’s time to deliver arrived, and she gave birth to a son.
When her neighbors and family heard how the Lord had magnified his mercy toward her, they shared her joy.
On the eighth day they came for the child’s circumcision, and they wanted to call him Zechariah, his father’s name.
But his mother spoke up: “No; he is to be called John.”
They told her, “None of your kin bears this name.”
Then they gestured to his father, asking what name he wished to give him.
Asking for a tablet, he wrote the words, “John is his name.” And all of them marveled.
Instantly his mouth was opened, and his tongue too, and he began speaking and praising God.
Fear came on all who lived around them, and throughout the whole hill country of Judea all these things were talked about.
Everyone who heard of it kept it in mind and said, “What will this child be, then?” For the Lord’s hand was indeed with him.
Then Zechariah his father was filled with the Holy Spirit and prophesied, saying,{u}

“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel,
because he has visited his people and brought about their redemption.

He has raised up a horn of salvation{v} for us
in the house of David his servant,
as he spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old:

salvation from our enemies
and from the hand of all who hate us,

to show mercy to our fathers
and to remember his holy covenant,

the oath that he swore to Abraham our father,
to grant us

that, rescued from the hand of our enemies,
we might serve him without fear,
in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.

And you, child, will be called a prophet of the Most High;
for you will walk ahead of the Lord to make his ways ready,{w}

to grant his people the knowledge of salvation
by the forgiving of their sins,

because of the tender mercy of our God,
by which the dawn from on high will visit us,{x}

to give light to those sitting in darkness and in death’s shadow,
to direct our feet into the path of peace.”
And the child kept growing and gaining strength in spirit, and he lived in the desert places until the day of his public appearance to Israel.

notes.text: Theophilus: a Greek name meaning “friend of God” or “loved by God.” *Most excellent* was a title of respect used for persons of rank (compare Acts 23:26; 24:3; 26:25). He may have been Luke’s patron.
Taught: Greek *katēchēthēs*, “informed” or “instructed.”
Herod the Great, king of Judea under Roman authority from 37 to 4 BC. *Judea* here means the whole Jewish homeland.

Zechariah … Abijah: *Zechariah* means “Yahweh remembers.” The priests were divided into twenty-four divisions that served in the temple in turn; Abijah’s was the eighth (1 Chr 24:10). *Abijah* means “Yahweh is my father.”
Elizabeth: Greek *Elisabet*, Hebrew *Elisheba* (Exod 6:23, the name of Aaron’s wife), probably “my God is an oath.” The meaning of *Aaron* is uncertain.
The Lord: in Old Testament phrasing like this, *kyrios* stands for Yahweh, as throughout Luke 1–2 where it refers to God (for example 1:9, 11, 15, 16, 17, 25, 28, 38, 45, 46, 58, 66, 68, 76).
Each morning and evening a priest burned incense on the golden altar in the holy place of the temple (Exod 30:7–8); a priest might receive this honor only once in his life.
John: Greek *Iōannēs*, from Hebrew *Yohanan*, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Compare Num 6:3; Judg 13:4; 1 Sam 1:11. *Strong drink* (Greek *sikera*) is fermented drink other than wine, such as beer.
Mal 4:5–6 (3:23–24 in Hebrew). *Elijah* means “my God is Yahweh.”
Gabriel: “God is my mighty one” or “man of God” (compare Dan 8:16; 9:21).
Nazareth: a small village in Galilee, not mentioned in the Old Testament; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
Joseph … Mary: *Joseph* means “may he add” (Gen 30:24). *Mary* (Greek *Mariam*) is the Hebrew name *Miriam*; its meaning is uncertain.

Greetings: Greek *chaire*, literally “rejoice,” the ordinary greeting. *Favored one* translates *kecharitōmenē*, “one who has been shown grace.” Many later manuscripts add “Blessed are you among women” (from 1:42); the earliest witnesses do not have it.
Jesus: the Greek form of the Hebrew *Yeshua* (*Yehoshua*, Joshua), “Yahweh saves.”
Or “the holy one to be born will be called the Son of God.” Some manuscripts add “of you” after “to be born.”
Or “For nothing will be impossible with God.” Compare Gen 18:14.
Slave woman: Greek *doulē*, the feminine of *doulos*, “slave” or “bond-servant” (also in 1:48).

Mary’s song (traditionally called the *Magnificat*, from its first word in Latin) echoes Hannah’s song (1 Sam 2:1–10) and many psalms. A few Old Latin manuscripts and some early writers attribute the song to Elizabeth.
Compare Gen 17:7; 22:17–18; Mic 7:20. *Abraham* is explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
Zechariah’s song is traditionally called the *Benedictus*, from its first word in Latin.
Horn of salvation: the horn is a figure of strength (1 Sam 2:10; Ps 18:2; 132:17).
Compare Isa 40:3; Mal 3:1. In the Hebrew text, the Lord is Yahweh.

Will visit us: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus; many manuscripts read “has visited us.” *The dawn from on high* (Greek *anatolē*, “rising,” also used in the Greek Old Testament for the messianic “Branch,” Jer 23:5; Zech 3:8) may refer to the rising sun or star (compare Num 24:17; Mal 4:2).

verses.text: At that time an edict was issued by Caesar Augustus{a} for a registration of the entire inhabited world.
This was the first registration, made when Quirinius was governing Syria.{b}
So all were on their way to register, every one to his home town.
Joseph too went up out of Galilee, out of Nazareth town, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem,{c} since he belonged to David’s house and lineage,
to be registered with Mary, who was promised to him in marriage and was pregnant.
While they were in Bethlehem, the time came for her to deliver her child,
There she bore her son, her firstborn. She swaddled him and put him to lie in a feeding trough, since the guest room had no space for them.{d}
Nearby, in the open country, shepherds were spending the night guarding their flocks.
An angel of the Lord stood before them, and the glory of the Lord shone all around them, and they were overcome with fear.{e}
The angel said to them, “Have no fear. See, I am announcing to you good news of a great joy, which is for the whole people.
For today, in the city of David, a Savior has been born for you, who is the Messiah, the Lord.{f}
This is to be your sign: a newborn baby, swaddled and lying in a feeding trough, is what you will find.”
And all at once there appeared with the angel a multitude of the army of heaven, praising God and saying,

“Glory to God in the highest heavens,
and on earth peace among people of his good pleasure!”{g}
After the angels had left them and gone into heaven, the shepherds said to each other, “Come, let us go over to Bethlehem and look at what has taken place, this thing the Lord has told us of.”
They went in haste and found Mary and Joseph, and the baby lying in the feeding trough.
Having seen him, they reported the word that had been spoken to them concerning this child.
And all who heard were astonished at what the shepherds told them.
But Mary kept all these things, pondering them in her heart.
Then the shepherds returned, giving glory and praise to God for everything they had heard and seen, all of it as they had been told.
When eight days had passed and it was time to circumcise him, he was given the name Jesus, the name given by the angel before he was conceived in the womb.
When the days of purification required by the law of Moses{h} had passed, Joseph and Mary brought him to Jerusalem to present him to the Lord
(as it is written in the law of the Lord, “Every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord”),{i}
and to offer a sacrifice according to what is said in the law of the Lord, “a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.”{j}
Now there was a man in Jerusalem whose name was Simeon.{k} This man was upright and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel, and the Holy Spirit was upon him.
The Holy Spirit had disclosed to him that he would not see death until he had seen the Lord’s Messiah.{l}
Led by the Spirit, he came into the temple; and when the parents brought in the child Jesus to do for him what was customary under the law,
Simeon took him into his arms and blessed God, saying,

“Now, Master, you are letting your slave depart
in peace, according to your word,{m}
for my eyes have seen your salvation,
which you made ready before the face of all peoples,

a light for revelation to the nations
and for glory to your people Israel.”{n}
His father and mother were marveling at what was said about him.
Simeon blessed them and said to Mary his mother, “Look, this child is destined for the fall and the rising of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be spoken against
(and a sword will pierce through your own soul too), so that the thoughts of many hearts may be laid bare.”
There was also a prophetess, Anna{o} the daughter of Phanuel,{p} of the tribe of Asher.{q} She was far advanced in years. After her girlhood she had lived with her husband seven years,
and after that was a widow up to the age of eighty-four.{r} She never went away from the temple, but served God night and day with fasting and prayer.
Coming up at that very moment, she gave thanks to God and spoke of the child to everyone who was looking for Jerusalem’s redemption.
Once they had carried out all that the law of the Lord required, they went back into Galilee, to Nazareth, their town.
The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom, and the grace of God was upon him.
Each year his parents would go to Jerusalem for the Passover feast.
When he was twelve years old, they went up as the custom of the festival required.
After the days were over, as they were returning, the boy Jesus stayed behind in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it.
Thinking he was in the traveling party, they went a day’s journey and then began searching for him among their relatives and acquaintances.
Not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem to look for him.
Three days later they found him in the temple, seated in the midst of the teachers, both listening to them and putting questions to them.
Everyone who heard him was amazed by his insight and by the answers he gave.
His parents were astonished to see him, and his mother said, “Child, why have you treated us so? Here your father and I have been anxiously seeking you.”
“Why did you look for me?” he said to them. “Didn’t you know I had to be in my Father’s house?”{s}
But they did not understand the saying he spoke to them.
And he went down with them to Nazareth and was subject to them. His mother kept all these words in her heart.
And Jesus kept advancing in wisdom and in stature,{t} and in favor with God and people.

notes.text: Caesar Augustus: Octavian, the first Roman emperor (31 BC–AD 14). *Augustus*, “revered,” was a title given him by the Roman Senate in 27 BC.

Quirinius: Publius Sulpicius Quirinius, Roman legate of Syria from AD 6, when he conducted a census of Judea (compare Acts 5:37). How this registration relates to the reign of Herod (1:5) is a long-debated historical question; some render “this registration took place before Quirinius was governing Syria.” Scholarly review recommended.
Bethlehem: “house of bread,” David’s hometown (1 Sam 16:1; Mic 5:2).

Guest room: Greek *katalyma*, a lodging place or guest room (used of the upper room in 22:11), not necessarily an inn. The *feeding trough* (traditionally “manger”) suggests the part of the house or shelter where animals were kept.
An angel of the Lord … the glory of the Lord: in Old Testament phrasing, the angel and glory of Yahweh.
The Messiah, the Lord: Greek *christos kyrios*, “anointed Lord.” A few witnesses read “the Lord’s Messiah,” as in 2:26.

People of his good pleasure: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, first hands, and Codex Bezae), which read *eudokias*, “of good pleasure,” meaning people on whom God’s favor rests. Most later manuscripts read *eudokia*, giving “peace on earth, good will toward people.”
The purification of a mother after childbirth (Lev 12:1–8) and the redemption of a firstborn son (Exod 13:2, 12–15; Num 18:15–16). *Moses* is explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out.”
Exod 13:2, 12. In the Hebrew text, the Lord is Yahweh; the phrase *the law of the Lord* likewise means the law of Yahweh (also 2:24, 39).
Lev 12:8, the offering allowed to those who could not afford a lamb.
Simeon: Hebrew *Shimon*, linked with “hear” (Gen 29:33).
The Lord’s Messiah: literally “the Lord’s anointed,” an Old Testament phrase for the king chosen by Yahweh (1 Sam 24:6; Ps 2:2).
Simeon’s song is traditionally called the *Nunc Dimittis*, from its first words in Latin. *Master* is Greek *despotēs*.
Anna: Hebrew *Hannah*, “grace” or “favor” (1 Sam 1:2).
Phanuel: a form of *Penuel*, “face of God” (Gen 32:30–31).
Asher: “happy” or “blessed” (Gen 30:13). The tribe belonged to the northern kingdom of Israel.
Or “had been a widow for eighty-four years.”
Or “about my Father’s affairs”; literally “in the things of my Father.”
Or “in age.” Compare 1 Sam 2:26.

verses.text: It was the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar.{a} Pontius Pilate was the governor of Judea;{b} Herod was the tetrarch of Galilee,{c} his brother Philip the tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias the tetrarch of Abilene.{d}
during the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas,{e} the word of God came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness.
And he came into the whole area around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance that leads to forgiveness of sins,
and all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’”{g}
John said to the crowds that came out to be baptized by him, “You brood of snakes! Who told you that you could escape the wrath that is coming?
Produce fruit that shows you have repented. And do not start telling yourselves, ‘Abraham is our father.’ I tell you, God can make children for Abraham out of these stones.
The ax is already at the root of the trees, and every tree that fails to bear good fruit will be chopped down and thrown into the fire.”
The crowds kept asking him, “What then should we do?”
He answered them, “Whoever has two tunics{h} should share with the one who has none, and whoever has food should do the same.”
Tax collectors{i} also came to be baptized, and they said to him, “Teacher, what should we do?”
He answered them, “Exact nothing beyond the amount you are directed to collect.”
Soldiers also kept asking him, “And we, what should we do?” He told them, “Do not take money from anyone by force or by false accusation, and be content with your pay.”
The people were filled with expectation, and everyone wondered in their hearts whether John might be the Messiah.
John answered them all, “I baptize you with water; but one is coming who is mightier than I, the strap of whose sandals I am not worthy to untie. He will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.
He holds his winnowing fork{j} in his hand, ready to clear his threshing floor and store the wheat in his barn; but the chaff he will burn with a fire that cannot be put out.”
So with many other words of exhortation he proclaimed the good news to the people.
But Herod the tetrarch, who had been rebuked by him on account of Herodias, his brother’s wife,{k} and on account of all the evil things Herod had done,
added this to them all: he shut John up in prison.
Now when all the people were baptized, and Jesus also had been baptized and was praying, heaven was opened,
and the Holy Spirit descended on him in a physical form, as a dove. And a voice spoke from heaven: “You are my Son, whom I love; you make me very glad.”{l}
Jesus himself was about thirty years old when he began. He was the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, the son of Heli,{m}
the son of Matthat, the son of Levi, the son of Melchi, the son of Jannai, the son of Joseph,
the son of Mattathias, the son of Amos, the son of Nahum, the son of Esli, the son of Naggai,
the son of Maath, the son of Mattathias, the son of Semein, the son of Josech, the son of Joda,
the son of Joanan, the son of Rhesa, the son of Zerubbabel, the son of Shealtiel, the son of Neri,
the son of Melchi, the son of Addi, the son of Cosam, the son of Elmadam, the son of Er,
the son of Jesus,{n} the son of Eliezer, the son of Jorim, the son of Matthat, the son of Levi,
the son of Simeon, the son of Judah, the son of Joseph, the son of Jonam, the son of Eliakim,
the son of Melea, the son of Menna, the son of Mattatha, the son of Nathan, the son of David,
the son of Jesse, the son of Obed,{o} the son of Boaz, the son of Sala, the son of Nahshon,
the son of Admin, the son of Arni,{p} the son of Hezron, the son of Perez, the son of Judah,
the son of Jacob, the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, the son of Terah, the son of Nahor,
the son of Serug, the son of Reu, the son of Peleg, the son of Eber, the son of Shelah,
the son of Cainan,{q} the son of Arphaxad, the son of Shem, the son of Noah, the son of Lamech,
the son of Methuselah, the son of Enoch, the son of Jared, the son of Mahalaleel, the son of Cainan,
the son of Enosh, the son of Seth, the son of Adam, the son of God.{r}

notes.text: Tiberius Caesar: Roman emperor AD 14–37. His fifteenth year was probably AD 28–29, depending on how the years were reckoned.
Pontius Pilate: Roman prefect of Judea AD 26–36.
Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, ruler of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC to AD 39. A *tetrarch* (“ruler of a fourth”) was a minor ruler under Roman authority.
Philip, another son of Herod the Great, ruled the territories northeast of the Sea of Galilee. Lysanias ruled Abilene, northwest of Damascus; he is otherwise known from an inscription.
Annas was high priest AD 6–15 and remained influential; Caiaphas, his son-in-law, was high priest AD 18–36 (John 18:13). *Caiaphas* is a family name of uncertain meaning.
Isaiah: “Yahweh is salvation.”
Isa 40:3–5, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Tunics: the *chitōn* was a garment worn next to the skin, under the outer cloak.
Tax collectors: men who collected tolls and taxes for the Romans or for Herod, often despised as collaborators and extortioners.
Winnowing shovel: a wooden fork or shovel used to toss threshed grain into the wind, which blew the chaff away.
Herodias was the wife of Herod Antipas’s half-brother (Mark 6:17 calls him Philip); Antipas married her after divorcing his first wife.
Compare Ps 2:7; Isa 42:1. Codex Bezae and some Old Latin witnesses read, from Ps 2:7, “You are my Son; today I have fathered you.”

Luke’s genealogy runs from Jesus back to Adam and differs from Matthew’s (Matt 1:1–16) between David and Joseph. The difference has been explained in various ways (for example, as Mary’s line, or by levirate marriage); none is certain. The Old Testament names are given in their Old Testament forms where they can be identified.
Jesus: here the name of an ancestor; it is the Greek form of *Joshua*.
Obed: the Westcott–Hort text reads *Iōbēl*, with Sinaiticus (first hand) and Vaticanus; most manuscripts read *Iōbēd*, the Obed of Ruth 4:21–22. The same person is meant.

Admin … Arni: so the Westcott–Hort text, with some early manuscripts; the names do not appear in the Old Testament list (Ruth 4:19; 1 Chr 2:9–10, “Ram”). Many manuscripts read “the son of Amminadab, the son of Aram” (compare Matt 1:3–4). The manuscripts vary widely here.
Cainan: this name appears in the Greek Old Testament (Gen 11:12) but not in the Hebrew text.
The son of God: Adam had no human father; compare Gen 1:26–27; 5:1–3. *Adam* means “human being” or “humankind.”

verses.text: Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the wilderness
where for forty days he was put to the test by the devil.{a} Through those days he ate nothing, and at their end he felt hunger.
The devil said to him, “If you are the Son of God, tell this stone to turn into bread.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘A person shall not live on bread alone.’”{b}
Then the devil led him up and showed him all the kingdoms of the inhabited world in an instant of time.
“All this authority, and the glory of these kingdoms, I will give to you,” the devil told him, “for it has been given into my hands, and I give it to whomever I choose.
If you, then, will bow down in worship before me, it will all be yours.”
Jesus answered him, “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.’”{c}
Then he brought him to Jerusalem and set him on the pinnacle{d} of the temple and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down from here,

for it is written,
‘He will give his angels orders concerning you, to guard you closely,’

and,
‘They will lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot on a stone.’”{e}
In answer Jesus told him, “It is said, ‘Do not test the Lord your God.’”{f}
Having completed every kind of testing, the devil went away from him until a fitting time.
And Jesus went back into Galilee in the Spirit’s power, and word of him spread throughout the whole countryside.
He taught in their synagogues, and everyone gave him praise.
He went to Nazareth, where he had grown up, and on the sabbath he entered the synagogue as he usually did and stood to read.
The scroll of the prophet Isaiah was handed to him. He unrolled the scroll and found the place where it was written,

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me,
because he has anointed me
to bring good news to the poor.
He has sent me to proclaim release to captives
and recovery of sight to the blind,
to send away the crushed in freedom,
to proclaim the year of the Lord’s favor.”{g}
He rolled the scroll up, returned it to the attendant, and took his seat. Everyone in the synagogue kept looking at him.
He began by saying to them, “Today this scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
Everyone bore witness to him and wondered at the words of grace coming from his lips, and they kept saying, “Isn’t this Joseph’s son?”
He said to them, “No doubt you will quote me this proverb: ‘Doctor, cure yourself!’ What we heard had happened in Capernaum,{h} do here also in your own hometown.”
