He said, “The Jews have arranged to ask you to bring Paul down to the Sanhedrin tomorrow, as if intending to look into his case with more care.

Do not give in to them, then; for upward of forty of them lie in wait for him, men who have cursed themselves not to eat or drink until they have done away with him; even now they stand ready, only awaiting your promise.”
So the tribune sent the youth away with a warning: “Breathe to nobody that you have made this known to me.”
Then, calling over a pair of his centurions, he said, “By nine o’clock tonight{e} have two hundred soldiers in readiness to march to Caesarea, along with seventy cavalry and two hundred spearmen;{f}
and have beasts on hand to mount Paul and convey him safe to Felix{g} the governor.”
And he wrote a letter in these terms:{h}
“Claudius Lysias to the most excellent Governor Felix: greeting.
The Jews had laid hold of this man and were on the point of killing him, when I intervened with my troops and took him from them, having found out that he is a Roman.
Wishing to ascertain the ground of their charges against him, [I brought him down to their Sanhedrin.]
I discovered that the charges concerned disputes over their Law, and that there was nothing against him worthy of death or of bonds.
Information then reached me of a plot to be carried out against the man, and I have forthwith dispatched him to you, directing his accusers as well to lay their case against him before you.”{i}
So the soldiers, as ordered, took charge of Paul and conducted him by night as far as Antipatris.{j}
On the morrow they went back to the barracks, leaving the cavalry to continue with him.
These, on entering Caesarea, handed the letter to the governor and presented Paul as well before him.
He read it and asked from which province Paul came; and learning it was Cilicia,
he said, “I will hear your case in full whenever your accusers also are here,” and he ordered him kept under guard in Herod’s praetorium.{k}

notes.text: Ananias: high priest about AD 47–59; the name is Hebrew Hananiah, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Exod 22:28.
Many later manuscripts add, “Let us not fight against God.”
Put themselves under a curse: Greek *anathematizō*.
Nine o’clock tonight: literally “from the third hour of the night.”
Spearmen: the meaning of the rare Greek *dexiolabous* is uncertain; perhaps “bowmen,” “slingers,” or “led horses.”
Felix: Antonius Felix, procurator of Judea about AD 52–59; the name is Latin, “fortunate, happy.”

In these terms: or “of this kind.” Codex Bezae and some Latin manuscripts add, “for he was afraid that the Jews might seize Paul and kill him, and that he would afterward be accused of having taken a bribe.”
Many later manuscripts add “Farewell.”
Antipatris: a town about 37 miles (60 km) northwest of Jerusalem and 25 miles (40 km) south of Caesarea.
Praetorium: the governor’s residence, built as a palace by Herod the Great.

verses.text: Five days afterward the high priest Ananias came down, bringing certain elders and a pleader, one Tertullus,{a} and these laid their information against Paul before the governor.
When [he] had been called in, Tertullus opened the accusation thus: “Through you we enjoy great peace, and by your forethought reforms are coming about for this nation;
at every turn and in every place, most excellent Felix, we welcome it with the fullest gratitude.
But that I may not detain you longer, I entreat you of your forbearance to give us a brief hearing.
For we have found this fellow a very plague, a stirrer-up of riots among all the Jews throughout the world, and a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes.{b}
He even attempted to profane the temple; and so we took hold of him.{c}
From him, should you question him in person, you may ascertain the truth of everything of which we charge him.”
The Jews too joined in the attack, asserting that so these things stood.
The governor then gestured for Paul to speak, and Paul answered: “I know you have judged this nation for a good many years, and so I am glad to defend myself before you.
You are able to verify that not more than twelve days are past since I went up to worship at Jerusalem;
and neither in the temple did they find me arguing with anyone or gathering a crowd, nor in the synagogues, nor about the city.
Nor can they make good to you the charges they now bring against me.
This much I do confess to you: after the Way, which they call a sect, so do I serve the God of my fathers, believing all that accords with the Law and all that is written in the Prophets,
holding a hope toward God, which these men themselves also look for, that there is to be a resurrection of both righteous and unrighteous.
Therefore I too exercise myself to keep at all times a conscience void of offense toward God and toward men.
Now after several years I came to bring alms to my nation, and offerings;
in the midst of which they found me purified in the temple, with no crowd and no tumult. But some Jews from Asia —
these ought to be present before you to accuse me, if they had anything against me.
Or else let these men here say what wrongdoing they found when I stood before the Sanhedrin,
unless it be this one cry which I uttered standing among them: ‘Over the resurrection of the dead I am under judgment before you this day.’”
Felix, though, being rather well informed concerning the Way, adjourned the hearing: “Once Lysias the tribune is down here,” said he, “I shall determine your matter.”
He directed the centurion to hold him under guard, yet with a measure of freedom, forbidding none of his friends to wait on him.
Some days later Felix arrived with Drusilla{e} his wife, who was a Jewess, and he sent for Paul and listened to him on faith in Christ Jesus.
But as he discoursed of righteousness and self-mastery and the judgment to come, Felix took fright and answered, “Go your way for the present; when I find a convenient season I will send for you.”
At the same time he was hoping too that money would be given [him] by Paul; on which account he sent for him all the oftener and conversed with him.
But when two years had run their course, Felix was succeeded by Porcius Festus;{f} and wishing to do the Jews a favor, Felix left Paul in bonds.

notes.text: Tertullus: a Latin name, a diminutive of Tertius, “third.” He was a professional advocate (Greek *rhētōr*, “orator”).
Nazarenes: the earliest Jewish name for the followers of Jesus, after Nazareth.
Took hold of him: the Westcott–Hort text ends the sentence here and continues directly with verse 8, so that “him” in verse 8 refers to Paul.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 7 (with the end of verse 6 and the beginning of verse 8); the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some later manuscripts, and the printed editions from Erasmus, include additional words saying that the speakers would have judged him by their own Law, but that Lysias the tribune intervened, took him from their hands by force, and ordered his accusers to appear before the governor. In that reading, “him” in verse 8 refers to Lysias.

Drusilla: a Latin name, a diminutive of Drusus (meaning uncertain). She was the youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I (12:1), who had left her first husband to marry Felix. Some Western witnesses add that it was she who wished to see Paul.
Festus: Porcius Festus, procurator of Judea about AD 59–62; the name is Latin, “festive, joyful.” Felix was recalled about AD 59.

verses.text: Festus, then, three days after setting foot in his province, went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
And the chief priests and the principal men of the Jews laid information before him against Paul, and they kept urging him,
begging as a favor to themselves, to his hurt, that he would summon him to Jerusalem — laying an ambush to make away with him on the road.
Festus answered, however, that Paul was being held at Caesarea, and that he himself would shortly be setting out thither.
“So let those among you who are men of standing,” said he, “go down with me, and if there is anything amiss in the man, let them accuse him.”
After staying among them no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea; and on the next day he took his seat on the tribunal and commanded Paul to be brought.
When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood round him, bringing many and grave charges which they could not prove,
while Paul pleaded in his defense, “Neither against the Law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I committed any offense.”
But Festus, wishing to put the Jews under obligation, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and there be judged on these matters before me?”
Said Paul, “At Caesar’s tribunal I stand, where I ought to be judged. To the Jews I have done no wrong, as you too know very well.

If I am guilty and have done anything deserving death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth in the charges these men bring against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
Then Festus, after conferring with his council, replied, “To Caesar you have appealed; to Caesar you shall go.”
When some days had passed, Agrippa the king and Bernice{a} arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to Festus.
As they were staying there a good many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a man left a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews brought information, asking for sentence against him.
I told them that Romans have no custom of handing over anyone as a favor, before the accused has faced the accusers in person and had a chance to answer the charges.
When therefore they had assembled here, I lost no time; the day following I sat down upon the judgment seat and gave orders for the man to be fetched.
When the accusers stood up around him, they brought no charge of such evil deeds as I was supposing;
rather they had certain questions against him about their own religion{b} and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
Being at a loss how to inquire into these things, I asked whether he would go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning them.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of His Majesty the Emperor,{c} I ordered him held until I could send him on to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I would like to hear this man myself.” Festus replied, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”

Accordingly, on the morrow, there came Agrippa and Bernice amid much display, and they went into the hall of hearing with the tribunes and the city’s leading men; and Festus gave the word, and Paul was led in.

And Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all you men here present with us, you behold this man concerning whom the whole multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both in Jerusalem and here, crying out that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found that he had done nothing deserving of death; and as he himself appealed to His Majesty, I determined to send him.

Yet I have nothing definite to write to my lord{d} about him. Therefore I have brought him out before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination has been held I may have something to write.
For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to signify as well the charges against him.”

notes.text: Agrippa and Bernice: Herod Agrippa II, son of Agrippa I (12:1), king of territories north and east of Galilee; the name is Latin, of uncertain meaning. Bernice, his sister, is the Macedonian form of Greek Pherenike, “bringer of victory.”
Religion: or “superstition” (Greek *deisidaimonia*); compare 17:22.
His Majesty the Emperor: Greek *ho Sebastos*, “the Revered One,” the Greek equivalent of the title Augustus; here Nero.
My lord: Greek *kyrios*, used of the emperor.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Paul, “Leave is given you to speak on your own behalf.” Then Paul stretched forth his hand and made his defense:
“Touching all the things whereof I am accused by Jews, King Agrippa, I count myself fortunate that it is before you I am to answer for myself today,
the more so because you are expert in all the customs and controversies among Jews. I pray you, therefore, hear me out with patience.
“My manner of life from youth, spent from the beginning among my own nation and at Jerusalem, all Jews know,
having known me a long while, if only they would bear witness, that after the strictest party of our religion I lived a Pharisee.
And now for the hope of the promise made by God to our fathers I stand here on trial,
a promise our twelve tribes, earnestly serving night and day, hope to attain. For this hope, O king, I am accused by Jews!
Why is it judged a thing past belief among you, if God raises the dead?
“I myself, indeed, once thought it my duty to do many things in opposition to the name of Jesus of Nazareth.
And this I did in Jerusalem: many of the saints I shut up in prisons, having received authority from the chief priests, and when they were put to death I cast my vote{a} against them.
In all the synagogues I often had them punished and tried to make them blaspheme. I was so furiously angry at them that I even chased them to cities in foreign lands.
“On such an errand I was journeying to Damascus with authority and commission from the chief priests,
when at midday, O king, I saw on the road a light out of heaven, brighter than the brilliance of the sun, shining round about me and those who journeyed with me.
And when we had all fallen to the earth, I heard a voice saying to me in the Hebrew language,{b} ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? It is hard for you to kick against the goads.’{c}
I asked, ‘Lord, who are you?’ The Lord replied, ‘Jesus am I, whom you persecute.

But rise and stand upon your feet; for to this end have I appeared to you, to appoint you a servant and a witness both of the things in which you have seen me{d} and of those in which I will appear to you,
rescuing you from the people and from the Gentiles, to whom I send you,

I am sending you to open their eyes, so that they will turn from the dark to the light, and from Satan’s control to God. Then they will receive forgiveness of sins and a share with those who have been made holy by trusting in me.’
Hence, King Agrippa, to that vision from heaven I was not disobedient,
but to them of Damascus first, and at Jerusalem, and over all the region of Judea, and to the Gentiles, I proclaimed that they must repent and turn to God, performing deeds worthy of repentance.
On this account Jews seized me in the temple and tried to make an end of me.
Having therefore obtained the help that is from God, I stand to this day bearing witness to small and great alike, saying nothing beyond what the prophets and Moses said should come to pass:
that the Messiah was to suffer, and that he, first of the resurrection from the dead, would proclaim light both to the people and to the Gentiles.”
And as he was so making his defense, Festus said with a loud voice, “You are mad, Paul! Your great learning is turning you to madness.”
But Paul said, “I am not mad, most excellent Festus, but am uttering words of truth and soberness.
For the king knows of these matters, and to him I speak with boldness; for I am persuaded that none of these things escapes his notice, since this was not done in a corner.
King Agrippa, do you believe the prophets? I know that you believe.”
And Agrippa said to Paul, “In a little you would persuade me to play the Christian!”{e}
And Paul said, “I would pray to God that, whether in little or in much, not only you but also all who hear me this day might become such as I am — save for these chains.”
Then the king rose, and the governor and Bernice, and those who sat with them;
and when they had withdrawn, they spoke to one another, saying, “This man does nothing deserving death or imprisonment.”
And Agrippa said to Festus, “This man could have been set at liberty, had he not appealed to Caesar.”

notes.text: Cast my vote: literally “brought down a pebble,” the voting stone; whether Paul had a formal vote in the Sanhedrin is uncertain, and the phrase may simply mean “I gave my approval.”
The Hebrew language: probably Aramaic.
Kick against the goads: a Greek proverb for useless resistance, from an ox kicking against the pointed stick of its driver.
Seen me: some manuscripts read “have seen.”

In a little you would persuade me to play the Christian: the Greek is difficult. It may mean “In a short time,” or “With so little,” and the verb may mean “persuade me to become” or “persuade me to act as.” Many later manuscripts read “You almost persuade me to become a Christian.”

verses.text: Now when it was resolved that we should sail away for Italy, they handed over Paul and certain other prisoners to a centurion named Julius,{a} of the Augustan Cohort.{b}
Embarking in a ship of Adramyttium,{c} which was about to sail to the ports along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, there being with us Aristarchus, a Macedonian of Thessalonica.
The next day we landed at Sidon. Julius treated Paul with kindness and allowed him to visit his friends so they could provide for his needs.
Putting out from thence, we sailed under the lee of Cyprus, because the winds were against us.
And when we had sailed across the open sea off Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came down to Myra in Lycia.{d}
There the centurion found a ship of Alexandria sailing for Italy, and put us aboard her.
Many a day we crept along slowly and with much ado got abreast of Cnidus; then, the wind forbidding our approach, we slipped under the lee of Crete by Salmone.
Coasting along it with difficulty, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the town of Lasea.
Much time having now been spent, and the voyage being already perilous because even the Fast{e} was already gone by, Paul gave them warning,
saying to them, “Sirs, I perceive that this voyage will be with injury and heavy loss, not only of the cargo and the ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion paid more heed to the pilot and to the owner of the ship than to the things spoken by Paul.

And because the harbor was ill suited to winter in, the majority advised putting out from there, in hope that they might somehow reach Phoenix, a harbor of Crete looking toward the southwest and northwest,{f} and winter there.
When a south wind blew softly, supposing they had gained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed along Crete, hugging the shore.
But not long after, there rushed down from it a tempestuous wind, the one called Euraquilo.{g}
And when the ship was caught and could not face the wind, we gave way to it and were driven along.
Darting in to the shelter of a small island named Cauda,{h} we barely managed to secure the skiff.
After hoisting it up, they used helps, undergirding the ship; and fearing lest they should run aground on the Syrtis,{i} they lowered the gear,{j} and so were driven along.
As we were exceedingly storm-tossed, the next day they began to throw cargo overboard;
and the third day they flung out the ship’s furniture with their own hands.
And when neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small tempest lay upon us, all hope of our being saved was at last being taken away.
When they had long gone without food, Paul stood up in their midst and said, “Sirs, you ought to have hearkened to me and not have set sail from Crete, and so have been spared this injury and loss.
Yet now I counsel you to take heart; for there shall be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For there stood by me this night an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve,
and he told me, ‘Paul, have no fear. You are going to stand before Caesar. And God has granted you the lives of all who are sailing with you.’
So take heart, sirs; for I have faith in God that it shall be even as I have been told.
But we must run aground on a certain island.”
On the fourteenth night, as we were drifting across the Adriatic Sea,{k} around midnight the sailors sensed that land was near.
And taking soundings they found a hundred and twenty feet; a little farther on they sounded again and found ninety feet.{l}
And fearing lest we should be cast upon rocky places, they let go four anchors from the stern and longed for day to come.
And as the sailors were seeking to flee from the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea under color of laying out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men abide in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let her fall off.
While day was coming on, Paul besought them all to partake of food, saying, “This is the fourteenth day you have continued in suspense and without food, having taken nothing.
Therefore I urge you to take some food, for it is for your preservation; for not a hair shall perish from the head of any of you.”
And having said this, he took bread, gave thanks to God in the presence of all, and broke it and began to eat.
Then they were all encouraged and themselves also took food.
(We were in all about seventy-six persons{m} in the ship.)
And when they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, casting out the wheat into the sea.
When daylight came, they did not recognize the coast, but they saw a bay with a sandy beach, and they decided to try to run the ship aground there.
So casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time loosing the lashings of the steering oars; and hoisting the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
But striking a place where two seas met,{n} they beached the vessel; the prow stuck and stayed fast, unmoved, while the stern began to go to pieces under the violence of the surf.
The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim off and escape.
But the centurion, wishing to bring Paul safely through, kept them from their purpose, and ordered that those who could swim should cast themselves overboard first and get to land,
and the rest, some on planks and some on pieces of the ship. And so it came to pass that all were brought safe to land.

notes.text: Julius: a Roman family name, perhaps from Iulus, legendary son of Aeneas; the meaning is uncertain.
Augustan Cohort: or “Imperial Cohort.”
Adramyttium: a port in Mysia, on the northwest coast of Asia Minor.
Myra in Lycia: some Western witnesses add that the crossing took fifteen days.
The Fast: the Day of Atonement, on the tenth of Tishri, in late September or early October, after which sailing on the Mediterranean was considered dangerous.
Southwest and northwest: literally “toward Lips and toward Chorus,” the names of the southwest and northwest winds; the exact sense is uncertain.
Euraquilo: a hybrid of Greek *euros*, “east wind,” and Latin *aquilo*, “north wind”: a northeaster. Many later manuscripts read *Euroclydōn*.
Cauda: many manuscripts read “Clauda.” The island is modern Gavdos, south of Crete.
Syrtis: the gulf of shoals and quicksands off the coast of Libya.
Lowered the gear: perhaps “let down the sea anchor” or “lowered the mainsail”; the Greek is uncertain.
Adriatic Sea: in ancient usage the central Mediterranean between Greece, Italy, and Africa, not only the modern Adriatic.
A hundred and twenty feet … ninety feet: literally “twenty fathoms … fifteen fathoms”; about 37 and 27 meters.

Seventy-six persons: so Codex Vaticanus, followed by the Westcott–Hort text. Most manuscripts read “two hundred seventy-six,” and some “two hundred seventy-five.” In Greek numerals the difference may arise from a single letter.
A place where two seas met: or “a sandbar,” “a reef.”

verses.text: Once safe ashore, we learned then that the island was called Malta.{a}
The islanders{b} showed us unusual kindness. Because it had begun to rain and was cold, they built a fire and welcomed all of us.
But when Paul had gathered a bundle of sticks and laid them on the fire, a viper came out by reason of the heat and fastened on his hand.
When the natives saw the creature hanging from his hand, they said one to another, “No doubt this man is a murderer, whom, though he has escaped the sea, Justice{c} has not suffered to live.”
But he flung the beast off into the flames and took no hurt.
But they were expecting him to swell up or suddenly fall down dead; and after they had waited a long while and saw nothing amiss come to him, they changed their minds and said that he was a god.
Now in the neighborhood of that place were lands belonging to the chief man of the island, named Publius,{d} who received us and entertained us courteously three days.
And it fell out that the father of Publius lay sick of fever and dysentery; to whom Paul went in, and having prayed and laid his hands on him, he healed him.
When this had taken place, the rest [also] on the island who had diseases came and were cured.
They also honored us with many honors, and when we were setting sail they put on board such things as we needed.
After three months we sailed in a ship from Alexandria that had spent the winter at the island. It carried the Twin Brothers{e} as its figurehead.
Putting in at Syracuse, we stayed there three days.
And thence we made a circuit{f} and arrived at Rhegium; and after one day a south wind sprang up, and on the second day we came to Puteoli.
There we found brothers and were entreated to stay with them seven days. And so we came to Rome.
The brothers there, having had word of us, came out from the city to meet us at Appius’ Market and the Three Inns;{g} and at the sight of them Paul gave God thanks and was heartened.
On our entry into Rome,{h} leave was granted Paul to lodge on his own, along with the soldier set to guard him.

It came to pass after three days that he called together the leading men of the Jews; and when they had come together, he said to them, “Brothers, though I had done nothing against the people or the customs of our fathers, yet I was delivered a prisoner from Jerusalem into the hands of the Romans,
who, when they had examined me, were minded to release me, because there was no cause for death in me.
But when the Jews objected, I had no choice but to appeal to Caesar, even though I had nothing to accuse my own nation of.
On this account, then, I invited you here, to see you face to face and talk with you; for it is for Israel’s hope that I wear this chain.”
They told him, “For our part, no letters about you have reached us out of Judea, nor has any brother arrived to report or tell anything evil about you.
But we think it fitting to hear from you what your views are; for as concerning this sect, it is known to us that everywhere it is spoken against.”

And when they had appointed him a day, they came to him at his lodging in greater numbers. To them he expounded the matter from morning till evening, testifying to the kingdom of God and seeking to persuade them concerning Jesus from both the Law of Moses and the Prophets.
And some were persuaded by what was spoken, while others disbelieved.
And being at variance among themselves, they departed, after Paul had spoken one word: “Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah the prophet to your fathers,

saying,
‘Go to this people, and say,
By hearing you will hear, and shall in no wise understand;
and seeing you will see, and shall in no wise perceive.

For the heart of this people has grown gross,
and with their ears they have heard heavily,
and their eyes they have closed;
lest at any time they should see with their eyes,
and hear with their ears,
and understand with their heart,
and turn again, and I should heal them.’{i}
Know, then, that to the Gentiles this saving work of God is sent; and they, for their part, will listen.”
And he abode two whole years in his own hired dwelling,{k} and welcomed all who came in to him,
proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching the things concerning the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, unhindered.

notes.text: Malta: Greek *Melitē*; the Westcott–Hort text, following Codex Vaticanus, reads *Melitēnē*. The name is perhaps from Phoenician, “refuge,” but the meaning is uncertain.
Natives: Greek *barbaroi*, people who did not speak Greek; the Maltese spoke a Punic dialect.
Justice: Greek *Dikē*, the goddess of justice and retribution.
Publius: a Latin first name, perhaps related to *populus*, “people”; the meaning is uncertain. His title, “chief man” (Greek *prōtos*), is attested on Maltese inscriptions.
The Twin Brothers: Greek *Dioskouroi*, Castor and Pollux, sons of Zeus and patrons of sailors.
Made a circuit: some manuscripts read “cast off.”
Appius’ Market and the Three Inns: Latin Forum Appii and Tres Tabernae, stations on the Appian Way, about 43 and 33 miles (69 and 53 km) south of Rome.

Entry into Rome: many manuscripts, mainly Western and Byzantine, add “the centurion delivered the prisoners to the commander of the camp,” and continue “but Paul was allowed to live by himself outside the camp.”
Isa 6:9–10, following the Greek translation of the Old Testament.

The Westcott–Hort text and the earliest manuscripts do not include verse 29; the number is kept here only to preserve the traditional verse numbering. Some later manuscripts add a sentence saying that after Paul spoke, the Jews left, arguing vigorously among themselves.
Hired dwelling: or “at his own expense.”

books.name: Romans
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The earliest substantial manuscript of Paul’s letters is P46 (Chester Beatty papyrus, usually dated about AD 200), which contains most of Romans 5–16; its readings, like those of other manuscripts, are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. The letter’s ending circulated in several forms: the closing doxology (16:25–27) stands at the end of chapter 16 in the earliest manuscripts, after 14:23 in most later ones, after 15:33 in P46, in both places in some, and nowhere in others; some evidence suggests a fourteen-chapter or fifteen-chapter form of the letter (see the notes at 14:23, 15:33, 16:24 and 16:25). A verse absent from the earliest manuscripts (16:24) keeps its traditional number, with its text given in a note. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from Paul’s Greek, with the source given in a note. Greek *Christos* is usually rendered “Christ,” as part of Jesus’ name, and “Messiah” where it is clearly a title (9:5). Greek *adelphoi*, “brothers,” addresses the whole congregation, women and men. The letter is undisputedly Paul’s, written through Tertius (16:22), probably from Corinth about AD 56–57, before his final journey to Jerusalem (15:25).

verses.text: From Paul,{a} slave{b} of Christ Jesus,{c} an apostle by calling, set apart for God’s gospel{d}
the gospel God promised beforehand through his prophets in holy writings,
concerning his Son, who as to the flesh was born from the seed of David,
and who was installed as Son of God with power, by the Spirit of holiness,{e} when he rose from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord.
Through him we were given grace and a commission as apostle, to bring about faithful obedience{f} among every non-Jewish nation for the sake of his name;
and among them are you also, called to belong to Jesus Christ.
To all who are in Rome,{g} beloved of God, called to be saints:{h} grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because the report of your faith is spreading through the whole world.
For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the gospel of his Son, is my witness how without ceasing I make mention of you,
always asking in my prayers that somehow, at last, by God’s will I may succeed in coming to you.
For I long to see you, to share with you some spiritual gift so that you may be made firm;
or rather, that we may be encouraged together among you, each by the other’s faith, both yours and mine.

Brothers,{i} I want you to know that many a time I have planned to come to you, though up to now I have been hindered, in order to gather some fruit among you as well, just as among the other Gentiles.
To Greeks and to barbarians,{j} to the wise and to the foolish, I am a debtor;
so, for my part, I am eager to preach the gospel to you also who are in Rome.
I am not ashamed of the gospel,{k} for it is the power of God bringing salvation to all who believe, the Jew first{l} and the Greek as well.
For God’s righteousness{m} is unveiled in it, starting from faith and aiming at faith; as scripture says, “The righteous person will live by faith.”{n}
For God’s wrath is being revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and wickedness of people who by their wickedness hold down the truth.
because what may be known of God lies open before them; God himself has shown it to them.
From the world’s creation onward, the unseen things of God, his everlasting power and godhead, are discerned and grasped through what he has made, leaving them without defense.
For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for a likeness in the shape of mortal man and of birds and four-footed beasts and creeping things.
That is why God handed them over, in their hearts’ desires, to uncleanness, so that their bodies were degraded among them.
They traded God’s truth for a falsehood, and revered and served what was made instead of the Maker, who is praised forever. Amen.
For this reason God gave them up to dishonorable passions. Their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature;

and in the same way the men abandoned natural intimacy with women and burned with desire for one another, men doing shameful things with men and receiving in themselves the fitting penalty for their straying.
And since they did not see fit to keep God in their knowledge, God gave them up to an unfit mind,{o} to do what ought not to be done.
They have been filled with every kind of wickedness, evil, greed, malice; they are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, spite. They are gossips,
gossips, God-haters,{p} bullies, haughty, braggarts, devisers of wrongdoing, defiant toward parents,
senseless, faithless,{q} heartless, ruthless.{r}
They know well God’s decree that people who do such things are worthy of death; yet they do them, and what is more, they approve of others who do them.

notes.text: Paul: Latin *Paulus*, “small”; his Jewish name was Saul (Acts 13:9).
Slave: Greek *doulos*, a slave or bondservant; also used of God’s servants such as Moses and the prophets.

Christ Jesus: *Christ* (Greek *Christos*) means “Anointed One,” the equivalent of Hebrew *Mashiach*, “Messiah.” In Paul’s letters it usually functions as part of Jesus’ name. Some manuscripts read “Jesus Christ.”
Gospel: Greek *euangelion*, “good news.”
Spirit of holiness: probably the Holy Spirit, though some understand Jesus’ own holy spirit.
The obedience of faith: either “the obedience that consists in faith” or “the obedience that comes from faith.”
In Rome: a few witnesses, including Codex Boernerianus (G) and some early writers (as reported), lack “in Rome” here and in 1:15, perhaps because the letter circulated more generally.
Saints: Greek *hagioi*, “holy ones,” those set apart for God; Paul’s usual term for believers.
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, used by Paul of fellow believers, women and men alike.
Barbarians: non-Greek-speaking peoples.
The gospel: many later manuscripts read “the gospel of Christ.”
First: bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; Vaticanus and Codex Boernerianus (as reported) lack it.
The righteousness of God: either God’s own righteousness (his saving justice and faithfulness) or the righteous standing that God gives.
Hab 2:4. Or “The righteous will live by faith.” The Hebrew text reads “by his faithfulness.”
An unfit mind: Greek *adokimon noun*, a wordplay with *edokimasan*, “they did not see fit.”
Haters of God: or “hateful to God.”
Faithless: or “covenant-breakers,” “untrustworthy.”
Ruthless: many later manuscripts add “implacable.”

verses.text: So you have no defense, whoever you are, O man, who sit in judgment. In judging the other person you pass sentence on yourself, since you who judge are doing those same things.
We know that the judgment of God falls in accordance with truth on those who practice such things.
O man, judging people who do such things while doing them yourself, do you really think you will escape God’s judgment?
Or do you think lightly of his rich goodness, his patience and long-suffering, unaware that the goodness of God is leading you toward repentance?
With your hard and unrepentant heart you are heaping up wrath against yourself for the day of wrath, the day God’s just judgment is unveiled.
He “will give back to every person as his deeds deserve”:{a}
to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;
but to those who are self-seeking{b} and disobey the truth but obey wickedness, wrath and fury.
Trouble and anguish will come upon every human soul that works evil, upon the Jew first and the Greek as well;
but glory, honor and peace upon everyone who works what is good, upon the Jew first and the Greek as well.
For God shows no partiality.
All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified.
Whenever Gentiles, who lack the law, do by nature what the law contains, these people, though they lack the law, are their own law.
They display the law’s work inscribed on their hearts; their conscience adds its testimony, and their thoughts in turn accuse them or perhaps defend them,
on the day when God, as my gospel declares, judges people’s hidden things through Christ Jesus.{c}
Now you bear the name of Jew; you lean on the law; you make your boast in God;
you know his will and can tell what really matters,{d} being taught out of the law;
and if you are confident that you are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, possessing in the law the very shape of knowledge and truth.
Well then, you who teach another, will you not teach yourself? You who proclaim, “Do not steal,” are you a thief?
You who forbid adultery, do you commit it yourself? You who detest idols, do you plunder their temples?{e}
You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?
For, as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”{f}
Circumcision does have worth if you keep the law; but if you break the law, your circumcision turns into uncircumcision.
If, then, an uncircumcised man observes the law’s just demands, will his lack of circumcision not be reckoned to him as circumcision?
Then the one who is physically uncircumcised but fulfills the law will judge you, who with the written code and circumcision are a breaker of the law.
For a Jew is not one outwardly, nor is circumcision something outward in the flesh.
No, the true Jew is one in secret, and true circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit, not in the letter. Such a person’s praise{g} comes from God, not from people.

notes.text: Self-seeking: Greek *eritheia*, selfish ambition or rivalry.
Christ Jesus: some manuscripts read “Jesus Christ.” Verses 14–15 may be a parenthesis, with v. 16 continuing v. 13.
Tell what really matters: or “approve what is excellent.”
Rob temples: perhaps plundering pagan temples, or more broadly committing sacrilege.
Isa 52:5, following the Greek Old Testament; compare Ezek 36:20.
Praise: a wordplay on *Jew* (from *Judah*), which means “praised” (Gen 29:35; 49:8).

verses.text: What advantage, then, does the Jew have? Or what good is there in circumcision?
Much, in every respect. To begin with, it was to them that God’s oracles were committed.
What then if some proved unfaithful? Will their faithlessness cancel out God’s faithfulness?
Far from it! Let God be found true, though every human being be a liar, as it stands written, “So that you may be shown in the right in your words, and win when you are put on trial.”{a}
But if our wrongdoing brings out God’s righteousness, what are we to say? That God does wrong in bringing his wrath upon us? (I am speaking in human terms.)
Far from it! For then how could God judge the world?
Yet if my lie makes God’s truth overflow all the more to his glory, why should I, of all people, still be judged a sinner?
And why not say, as we are slanderously charged with saying, and as some assert that we say, “Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is deserved.
What follows? Do we have the upper hand?{b} By no means. We have already brought the charge that Jews and Greeks alike all lie under sin,
as it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;
there is no one who understands; there is no one who seeks out God.
Every one has swerved away; all alike have gone bad. Not one does what is kind, no, not a single one.{c}
Their throat is a grave thrown open; with their tongues they keep deceiving.{d} The venom of asps is under their lips.{e}
Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.{f}
Swift are their feet to shed blood;
ruin and misery lie along their paths,
and the way of peace they have not known.{g}
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”{h}
Now we understand that everything the law declares is addressed to those under the law, so that no one has anything to say and the entire world is held accountable to God.
For by works of the law no flesh will be justified{i} before him;{j} for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.
But now, apart from the law, God’s righteousness has been disclosed, attested by the Law and the Prophets:
a righteousness of God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ{k} to all who believe. No distinction is made,
all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
and are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
He is the one God set forth publicly as a mercy seat,{l} through faith, by means of his blood, to show forth his righteousness, since in his patience God had let earlier sins go unpunished;
it was to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be righteous and also the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus.
Where, then, is boasting? It has been shut out. By what kind of law? A law of works? No, but by a law of faith.
For we reckon that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,
if indeed God is one;{m} he will declare the circumcised righteous out of faith, and the uncircumcised by means of the very same faith.
Do we then nullify the law through faith? Far from it! Instead, we uphold the law.

notes.text: Ps 51:4 (50:6 Greek), following the Greek Old Testament.
Do we have the upper hand?: the meaning of Greek *proechometha* is disputed; it may mean “Are we at a disadvantage?” or “Are we making excuses?”
Ps 14:1–3 (13:1–3 Greek); 53:1–3; compare Eccl 7:20.
Isa 59:7–8; compare Prov 1:16.
Justified: Greek *dikaioō*, “declare righteous, acquit, put in the right”; related to *dikaiosynē*, “righteousness,” and *dikaios*, “righteous.”
Compare Ps 143:2.

Faith in Jesus Christ: or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.” The Greek genitive can be read either way; the same question arises in 3:26 and Gal 2:16, 20; 3:22; Phil 3:9. “Jesus” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text and absent from Vaticanus (as reported).

Mercy seat: Greek *hilastērion*, the word used in the Greek Old Testament for the gold cover of the ark of the covenant, where atoning blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Lev 16:14–15); or more generally “a means of atonement,” “a sacrifice of atonement,” “propitiation.”
God is one: echoing the Shema (Deut 6:4).

verses.text: What then shall we say of Abraham,{a} our forefather according to the flesh?{b}
For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”{c}
Now to the one who works, his wages are not credited as a gift but as what is owed.
But to the one who does not work, yet trusts in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.
Just so David also speaks of the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works:
“How happy are they whose lawbreaking is pardoned, whose sins are hidden from view!
How happy the man against whom the Lord will by no means reckon sin!”{d}
This blessedness, then: does it come upon the circumcised, or upon the uncircumcised too? For we say, “Faith was credited to Abraham as righteousness.”
Under what circumstances, then, was it credited? Was he circumcised at the time, or not? He was not yet circumcised; he was uncircumcised.

And he was given circumcision as a sign, a seal of the righteousness by faith that was his in uncircumcision. So he is father to all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness is credited to them as well,
and the father of the circumcised, to those who are not only circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps of the faith our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.
For the promise to Abraham and his offspring, that he would inherit the world, did not arrive by way of the law but by the righteousness that comes from faith.
For if it is the adherents of the law who are heirs, faith has been emptied of meaning and the promise made void.
For the law produces wrath; but where no law exists, there is no violation either.

For this reason it comes from faith, in order to be by grace, so that the promise stands firm for every descendant, not only the one belonging to the law, but also the one belonging to Abraham’s faith. He is father of us all,

just as Scripture says, “I have appointed you father of many nations.”{e} He stands so before God, in whom he put his faith, the God who makes the dead alive and summons what does not exist as though it did.
Past all hope, he believed in hope, that he would be made father of many nations, in keeping with the word, “So shall your descendants be.”{f}
Without wavering in faith he took full account of{g} his body, already{h} as good as dead at about a hundred years of age, and of the deadness of Sarah’s{i} womb.
He did not waver in distrust at God’s promise; instead he grew strong in faith and gave glory to God,
being fully assured that what God had promised he could also perform.
So it was that “it was credited to him as righteousness.”
But the phrase “it was credited to him” was not recorded for his benefit alone,
but for ours also. It will be credited to us who believe in him who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,
who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

notes.text: What then shall we say of Abraham: so the Westcott–Hort text with Vaticanus (as reported). Most manuscripts include the verb “found,” giving a question like “What, then, are we to say that Abraham, our forefather, discovered by natural means?” (with differences in word order). *Abraham* is explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
According to the flesh: that is, by physical descent.
Ps 32:1–2 (31:1–2 Greek). In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Took full account of: so the Westcott–Hort text with the earliest manuscripts; most later manuscripts insert “not,” giving “Not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body.”
Already: Greek *ēdē*, bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text and lacking in some manuscripts.
Sarah: Hebrew, “princess” (Gen 17:15).

verses.text: Having been justified, then, by faith, let us have{a} peace toward God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Through him we have also been granted entry by faith{b} into this grace where we now stand, and we boast in our hope of sharing God’s glory.
More than that, we exult even in our afflictions, knowing that affliction works out endurance,
and endurance, tested character, and tested character, hope;
and this hope does not disappoint, since God’s love has flooded our hearts by the Holy Spirit he has given us.
For while we were still helpless, at the appointed time Christ died on behalf of the ungodly.
It is rare for anyone to die for a just person, though for a truly good person someone might possibly find the courage to die.
But God proves how he loves us: Christ died for us when we were yet sinners.
How much more, then, now that we have been justified by his blood, shall we be saved through him from the wrath.
For if we were reconciled to God through his Son’s death while still enemies, how much more certain is it that, now reconciled, we will be saved through his life.
And not only that, but we also exult in God through our Lord Jesus Christ,{c} through whom we have now received the reconciliation.
Therefore, just as through one man sin made its entrance into the world, and through sin death, so death spread to all people, inasmuch as all sinned.{d}
Sin was already present in the world until the law came, though no account of sin is kept where law is absent.
Still, death reigned from Adam{e} until Moses, even over people whose sins were not like Adam’s offense; Adam is a pattern of the one who was coming.

But the gift does not match the offense. For if the many died through one person’s offense, how much more has God’s grace, and the gift that came by the grace of one person, Jesus Christ, overflowed to the many.
Again, the gift does not resemble the outcome of the one man’s sin. For judgment followed one trespass and led to condemnation, but the free gift followed many trespasses and led to acquittal.

For if, by the trespass of the one, death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.
So then, as one trespass led to condemnation for all people, so too one righteous act{f} leads to acquittal and life for all people.
For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.
The law slipped in so that the offense would multiply; but where sin multiplied, grace multiplied far more,
so that, as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.

notes.text: Let us have: Greek *echōmen*, the reading of the Westcott–Hort text, supported by many early witnesses, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (original hands), Alexandrinus, Ephraemi, and Bezae (as reported). Other witnesses, including correctors of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, read *echomen*, “we have,” printed in NA28 and SBLGNT. The two forms were pronounced alike in later Greek, and many scholars judge “we have” to suit the context of vv. 1–11 better.
By faith: bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; lacking in Vaticanus, Bezae, and some others (as reported).
Jesus Christ: “Christ” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Inasmuch as all sinned: or “because all sinned”; Greek *eph’ hō*. The Latin rendering “in whom” (that is, in Adam) shaped later Western doctrine.
Adam: Hebrew, “man, humankind,” related to *adamah*, “ground” (Gen 2:7).
One righteous act: or “the righteous requirement of one.”

verses.text: What then shall we say? Should we persist in sin so that grace may multiply?
Absolutely not! We have died to sin; how can we still continue in it?
Or are you unaware that all of us who were baptized{a} into Christ Jesus{b} were baptized into his death?
So we were buried with him through baptism into death, in order that, as Christ was raised from the dead through the Father’s glory, we too may live a new kind of life.
For if we have grown together with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also share in the likeness of his resurrection.
This we know: our old humanity was crucified along with him, to put out of action the sin-ruled body, so that we would be slaves of sin no more.
For the one who has died has been set free{c} from sin.
But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him,
knowing that Christ, now raised from the dead, will never die again; death no longer lords it over him.
In dying, he died to sin a single time for all; in living, he lives to God.
You too, then, must count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.{d}
So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its cravings.
Do not keep offering the parts of your body to sin as tools{e} of wickedness, but offer yourselves to God as people brought from death to life, and your body’s parts to God as tools of righteousness.
Sin will not rule over you, because you live not under law but under grace.
What then? Shall we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Never!

Surely you know that if you present yourselves to anyone as slaves for obedience, you are that master’s slaves whom you obey, slaves either of sin, ending in death, or of obedience, ending in righteousness.
But thanks be to God that you, once slaves of sin, have obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over;
and, set free from sin, you have been enslaved to righteousness.

I speak in human fashion on account of your fleshly weakness. As you once put your limbs and faculties in bondage to uncleanness and lawlessness, for lawless ends,{f} so now put them in bondage to righteousness, for holiness.
While you were sin’s slaves, righteousness had no claim on you.
And what harvest did you have back then? Things that now make you ashamed, for those things end in death.
But now that you have been freed from sin and have become slaves of God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness, and its end is eternal life.
For the wages that sin pays are death, but God’s free gift is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.text: Baptized: Greek *baptizō*, “dip, immerse, wash.”
Christ Jesus: “Jesus” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Set free: Greek *dedikaiōtai*, literally “has been justified,” here in the sense “acquitted” or “released.”
In Christ Jesus: many later manuscripts add “our Lord.”
Tools: or “weapons”; Greek *hopla*.
For lawless ends: Greek “to lawlessness,” bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.

verses.text: Or do you not realize, brothers (for I am speaking to people acquainted with law), that the law has authority over a person only as long as that person lives?
Take the married woman: the law binds her to her living husband, but should the husband die, she is discharged from the law concerning the husband.

So she will be labeled an adulteress if she takes up with another man while her husband is alive. But if her husband dies, the law no longer binds her, and she commits no adultery by marrying someone else.

In the same way, my brothers, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so as to belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sin, aroused through the law, were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
Now, however, having died to what once held us fast, we have been discharged from the law, so as to be slaves in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.

What are we to conclude? That the law is sinful? Certainly not! But I would never have recognized sin without the law. I would not have known about greed unless the law had said, “You must not covet.”{a}
Sin, seizing the opening given by the commandment, worked in me every kind of covetous desire. For apart from the law, sin lies dead.
Once, without law, I was living; but with the commandment’s arrival sin revived, and I died.
The very commandment that was meant for life turned out for me to bring death.
For sin, seizing the opening given by the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
The law, then, is holy; holy too is the commandment, and just, and good.

Did what is good, then, become death to me? Never! It was sin, so that it might be exposed as sin, that brought about my death through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful past all measure.
For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am made of flesh,{b} sold as a slave under sin.
I do not grasp what I am doing. For I do not carry out what I desire; instead I do the very thing I loathe.
But when I do the thing I do not will, I am agreeing that the law is fine.
So now it is no longer I who carry it out, but sin that dwells in me.
For I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh. The wanting is there in me, but the carrying out of what is good is not.
For the good I want, I fail to do; but the evil I do not want, that is what I keep doing.
And if what I am doing is what I do not will, then the doer is no longer I, but the sin that has its home in me.
This, then, is the law I find: when I want to do good, evil lies close at hand.
For in my inner being I delight in the law of God,
but I see another law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.
What a miserable man I am! Who will deliver me out of this body that is bound for death?
Thanks be{c} to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.

notes.text: Exod 20:17; Deut 5:21.
Made of flesh: Greek *sarkinos*; many later manuscripts read *sarkikos*, “fleshly.”
Thanks be: so the Westcott–Hort text (*charis* [*de*]). Many manuscripts read “I thank God”; others read “the grace of God” or “the grace of the Lord.”

verses.text: There is therefore at present no sentence of condemnation against those in Christ Jesus.{a}
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you{b} free from the law of sin and of death.

The law was powerless because of the flesh’s weakness, but God did what it could not: he sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, as a sin offering,{c} and passed sentence on sin within the flesh,
so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.
For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.
The mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace,
for the flesh-minded outlook is at enmity with God; to God’s law it does not submit; indeed it is unable to.
Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
You, however, are not in flesh but in Spirit, provided that God’s Spirit makes his home in you. If someone lacks Christ’s Spirit, that person is not his.
Yet if Christ is within you, the body is a dead thing on account of sin, but the Spirit is life on account of righteousness.

If the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead lives in you, then the one who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also bring your mortal bodies to life, by means of his Spirit residing in you.{d}
So then, brothers, we are debtors, but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.
For if you live by the flesh, you will die; but if you use the Spirit to kill the practices of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.
The spirit you received was not one of slavery, plunging you back into fear; what you received was the Spirit of sonship,{e} in whom we call out, “Abba!{f} Father!”
The Spirit himself bears witness together with our spirit that we are children of God,
and if we are children, we are heirs as well: God’s heirs, and Christ’s co-heirs, if we share his suffering in order to share his glory too.
In my reckoning, what we suffer in the present age does not deserve to be set beside the glory about to be unveiled for us.
For the creation waits with eager longing for the unveiling of the sons of God.
For creation was placed under futility, not of its own will, but on account of the one who placed it there, in hope{g}
that creation itself will be freed from enslavement to corruption into the glorious freedom of God’s children.
For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering birth pains together until now.
Not that alone: we too, holding the Spirit as firstfruits, groan within ourselves while we eagerly await adoption,{h} the redeeming of our body.
It was in hope that we were saved. But a hope that is seen is no hope. Who hopes for what is in plain sight?{i}
If our hope is for what we do not see, we wait eagerly for it with perseverance.
Likewise the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what we should pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with groanings too deep for words.
And the one who examines our hearts knows the Spirit’s intention, since the Spirit pleads on behalf of God’s holy people in line with God’s will.
We know that God works all things together{j} for the good of those who love him, who are called in keeping with his purpose.
For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers.
Whom he predestined, these he called as well; whom he called, these he justified as well; whom he justified, these he glorified as well.
What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who can be against us?
He spared not even his own Son but handed him over on behalf of us all. How then shall he fail to give us everything along with him, as a gift?
Who will bring a charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies.
Who is there to condemn? It is Christ Jesus{k} who died, or rather was raised,{l} who sits at God’s right hand, who also pleads for us!
Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?{m} Shall affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?
As Scripture says, “On your account we face death all day long; we are counted as sheep for slaughter.”{n}
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
I am persuaded that not death, not life, not angels, not principalities, not the present, not the future, not powers,
not height, not depth, nor any other created thing will have power to part us from God’s love in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.text: In Christ Jesus: many later manuscripts add “who walk not according to the flesh,” and some add further “but according to the Spirit” (compare v. 4).
You: so the Westcott–Hort text with Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts read “me,” others “us.”
As an offering for sin: or simply “concerning sin”; the Greek phrase *peri hamartias* often renders “sin offering” in the Greek Old Testament.
Through his Spirit dwelling in you: so the Westcott–Hort text (genitive); many manuscripts read “because of his Spirit dwelling in you” (accusative). “Also” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Sonship: Greek *huiothesia*, a legal term for adoption granting full rights of inheritance.
Abba: Aramaic, “father.”
In hope: or, joining to v. 21, “in hope, because the creation itself...”
Adoption: a few witnesses, including P46 and Bezae (as reported), lack “adoption.” “We” (*hēmeis*) after “firstfruits” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Who hopes for what is in plain sight?: some manuscripts read “why does anyone still hope for what he sees?”; others “why does anyone still wait for what he sees?”

All things work together: so the Westcott–Hort text in its main reading; “God” is printed in brackets after it, from P46, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, and a few others (as reported), giving “God works all things together for good” or “in all things God works for good.” Grammatically, “all things” may also be the object, with the Spirit (v. 27) as subject: “he works all things together for good.”
Christ Jesus: “Jesus” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Raised: “from the dead” is added in brackets in the Westcott–Hort text, following Sinaiticus (original hand) and others (as reported).
Of Christ: Sinaiticus reads “of God”; Vaticanus reads “of God in Christ Jesus” (as reported).

verses.text: I am speaking the truth in Christ; I am not lying, as my conscience confirms by the Holy Spirit:
I carry a great sorrow and an unceasing anguish in my heart.
I could pray to be accursed{a} myself, severed from Christ, on behalf of my brothers, my own flesh-and-blood kin.
They are Israelites;{b} theirs are the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises;
theirs are the patriarchs, and from them, by physical descent, comes the Messiah, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen.{c}
But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are descended from Israel are Israel,
nor are they all Abraham’s children because they are his offspring; rather, “Through Isaac{d} your offspring will be named.”{e}
That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are God’s children, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.
For this was the wording of the promise: “At this season I will return, and Sarah will have a son.”{f}
And not only so, but Rebekah too conceived children by one man, our forefather Isaac.
For before they were born, before they had done anything either good or worthless, in order that God’s electing purpose might remain in force, resting not on deeds but on the one who calls,
it was said to her, “The elder shall be slave to the younger.”{g}
As it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”{h}
What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Never!
For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.”{i}
So then it does not depend on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy.
For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, to display my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”{j}
So, then, he shows mercy to whom he chooses, and to whom he chooses he gives a hard heart.
You will say to me then, “Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?”
But rather, O man, who are you to answer God back? Shall the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me this way?”{k}
Has the potter not the authority over his clay to make from a single lump this pot for an honored purpose and that one for an ordinary purpose?
What if God, wanting to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction,
and did so to make the wealth of his glory known upon vessels of mercy, prepared in advance for glory:
namely us, whom he also called, not only from among the Jews but also from among the Gentiles?
So he says in Hosea{l} also, “The people not mine I will name ‘My people,’ and the one not loved I will name ‘Loved.’{m}
And in the very place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”{n}
And Isaiah{o} proclaims about Israel: “Even if Israel’s people are as many as the sand by the sea, only a remnant will be rescued;
for the Lord will execute his word upon the earth, bringing it to an end and cutting it short.”{p}
And as Isaiah foretold, “Had not the Lord of Hosts left us a seed, we would have fared as Sodom did, and resembled Gomorrah.”{q}
What should we say, then? That non-Jews, who were not chasing after righteousness, have grasped righteousness, the righteousness that comes through faith;
but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not attain to that law.
Why? Because they did not pursue it from faith, but as though it were from works.{r} They stumbled over the stone of stumbling,
just as Scripture says, “Look, I place in Zion a stone that makes people stumble, a rock that trips them up; and the one who trusts in him will not be disgraced.”{s}

notes.text: Accursed: Greek *anathema*, devoted to destruction.
Israelites: *Israel*, the name given to Jacob, is explained in Gen 32:28 as “he strives with God.”

The Messiah, who is God over all, blessed forever. Amen: the punctuation is disputed, and early manuscripts lack punctuation. The Westcott–Hort text prints a comma after “descent,” as rendered here; its margin offers a full stop there, so that the next sentence becomes a separate doxology: “God, who is over all, be blessed forever. Amen.” Other possible punctuations make “who is over all” describe the Messiah, with a separate sentence praising God, or make “God” a further title of the Messiah in the same sentence.
Isaac: Hebrew, “he laughs” (Gen 17:17–19; 21:6).
Exod 33:19.
Exod 9:16.
Hosea: Hebrew, “salvation.”
Isaiah: Hebrew, “Yahweh is salvation.”

Isa 10:22–23, following the Greek Old Testament; compare Hos 1:10. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is “the Lord Yahweh of Hosts.” Many later manuscripts expand v. 28: “for he will finish the matter and cut it short in righteousness, because the Lord will make a short work upon the earth.”
Isa 1:9. Greek *Kyrios Sabaōth*, for Hebrew *Yahweh Tseva’ot*, Yahweh of the armies (of heaven). Sodom and Gomorrah: Gen 19:24–25.
From works: many later manuscripts add “of the law.”
Isa 28:16 combined with Isa 8:14.

verses.text: Brothers, my heart’s goodwill and my plea to God on their behalf is for their salvation.
I can testify for them that they have zeal for God, though not a zeal guided by knowledge.
Not recognizing the righteousness that comes from God, and seeking to set up their own, they did not yield to God’s righteousness.
For Christ is the goal{a} of the law, bringing righteousness to everyone who believes.
For Moses describes law-based righteousness this way: “Whoever does these things shall live by them.”{b}
But the righteousness based on faith speaks this way: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will climb up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down),
“or, ‘Who will go down into the abyss?’” (that is, to bring Christ up from among the dead).
But what does it say? “The word is close to you, on your lips and in your heart”{c} (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim):
that if with your mouth you confess Jesus as Lord, and in your heart believe that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
For one believes with the heart and so is made righteous, and one confesses with the mouth and so is saved.
For the Scripture says, “No one who puts his trust in him will be put to shame.”{d}
There is no difference between Jew and Greek; the same Lord is Lord of all, and pours out his riches on all who call upon him.
For “everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.”{e}
But how can people call upon him without first believing in him? And how believe in him if they never heard of him? And how hear of him with no one proclaiming?
And how are people to herald unless they are sent? As it is written, “How lovely are the feet of those who announce good news!”{f}
But not everyone has obeyed the good news. For Isaiah asks, “Lord, who has trusted our message?”{g}
Faith, then, arises from hearing the message, and the message comes by the word of Christ.{h}
But, I ask, is it that they never heard? Of course they heard: “Their sound went forth into every land, and their sayings to the far reaches of the world.”{i}
But I ask, did Israel not understand? First Moses says, “I will provoke you to jealousy by what is no nation; by a senseless nation I will rouse you to anger.”{j}
And Isaiah grows bold and says, “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I became plain to see for those who were not asking for me.”{k}
But of Israel he says, “All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”{l}

notes.text: Goal: Greek *telos*, “end, goal, culmination”; often understood as “end” in the sense of termination.
Joel 2:32 (3:5 Hebrew). In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh; Paul applies the verse to Jesus as Lord (vv. 9, 12).
Isa 52:7; compare Nah 1:15. Many later manuscripts expand the quotation: “...of those who announce the gospel of peace, who announce good news of good things.”
Isa 53:1, following the Greek Old Testament; “Lord” is not in the Hebrew text.
Of Christ: many later manuscripts read “of God.”
Deut 32:21.

verses.text: I ask, then, has God rejected his people? Never! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.{a}
No, God has not cast off his people whom he knew in advance. Do you not know what Scripture says in the story of Elijah,{b} when he appeals to God against Israel?
“Lord, your prophets they have put to death, your altars they have demolished; I am the only one remaining, and now they want my life.”{c}
But what is the divine answer to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.”{d}
Just so, in this present time too, a remnant exists, selected by grace.
But if by grace, then not from works, or grace would cease to be grace.{e}
What then? What Israel is seeking, it has not obtained. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened,
just as Scripture says, “God has given them a numbed spirit, eyes for not seeing and ears for not hearing, up to this present day.”{f}
David also says, “May their table turn into a net and a snare, a cause of stumbling and a payback to them;
may their eyes grow dark, unable to see, and may you keep their backs bowed forever.”{g}
So I ask, did they stumble in order to fall? Never! Rather, through their trespass salvation has come to the Gentiles, to provoke Israel to jealousy.
If their false step is wealth for the world, and their loss is wealth for the Gentiles, what will their fullness be?
Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I make much of my ministry
in the hope that I may somehow provoke my own people{h} to jealousy and save some of them.
If casting them away brings the world’s reconciliation, what will receiving them back bring, if not life out of death?
If the portion of dough offered as firstfruits is holy, so is the whole batch; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
Now if certain branches were snapped off, and you, being wild olive, were grafted in among the rest and became a sharer in the rich sap of the olive’s root,
do not look down on the branches. If you do, remember that you do not hold up the root; the root holds up you.
“But,” you will say, “branches were snapped off to make room for me to be grafted in.”
Quite so: they were snapped off for unbelief, while you hold your place through faith. So do not think proud thoughts; fear instead.
If God did not spare the branches that grew there by nature, he will not spare you either.{i}
Consider, then, God’s kindness and his severity: severity toward those who fell, but toward you God’s kindness, provided you continue in that kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off.
And they too, if they do not remain in unbelief, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.

You were cut out of an olive that grows wild by nature and grafted, contrary to nature, into a garden olive; how much more readily will these natural branches be grafted back into the tree that is their own!

For I would not have you uninformed, brothers, about this mystery, so that you do not think yourselves wise: a partial hardening has befallen Israel until the Gentiles in their full number have come in;
and so all Israel will be saved, just as Scripture says, “Out of Zion will come the Rescuer, and he will banish ungodliness from Jacob.{j}
and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”{k}
With respect to the gospel, they are opposed to God for your benefit; but with respect to election, they are loved because of their ancestors.
For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
Just as you once defied God but have now been shown mercy through their defiance,
so they too have now been disobedient, so that by the mercy shown to you they also may now{l} receive mercy.
For God has shut up all people together in disobedience, so that he may have mercy on all.
Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!
“For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”{m}
“Or who has given him a gift first, so that he must be repaid?”{n}
For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.

notes.text: Benjamin: Hebrew, “son of the right hand” (Gen 35:18).
Elijah: Hebrew, “my God is Yahweh.”
1 Kgs 19:10, 14. “Lord” is not in the Hebrew text.
Grace would cease to be grace: many later manuscripts add, “But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.”
My own people: literally “my flesh.”
He will not spare you either: many manuscripts read “perhaps he will not spare you either.”
Jacob: Hebrew, “he grasps the heel” (Gen 25:26), hence “he supplants.”
Now: lacking in P46 and many other manuscripts (as reported); some read “later.”
Isa 40:13, following the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Job 41:11 (41:3 Hebrew).

verses.text: So I urge you, brothers and sisters, by God’s mercies, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, set apart and pleasing to God; this is your rational{a} worship.
Stop being molded by the pattern of this age, and be changed by a renewed mind, so that you can test and recognize God’s will: what is good, acceptable, and complete.
Through the grace granted me I say to every one of you: do not rate yourself above what is fitting, but rate yourself soberly, in keeping with the measure of faith God has allotted each.
For just as in one body we have many parts, and the parts do not all have the same function,
so we, many as we are, are one body in Christ, and individually we are parts of one another.
We have gifts that differ according to the grace given us. If prophecy, let it be in proportion to our faith;
if service, in serving; the one who teaches, in teaching;
whoever exhorts, by exhorting; whoever gives, generously;{b} whoever governs, diligently; whoever shows compassion, cheerfully.
Let love be free of pretense. Loathe what is evil; cling to what is good.
In brotherly love be warmly devoted to one another; in showing honor, go ahead of one another.
Do not lag in zeal; be aglow with the Spirit;{c} serve the Lord.{d}
Rejoice in hope, hold firm in affliction, persist in prayer.
Contribute to the needs of the saints; pursue hospitality.
Bless those who persecute you;{e} bless and do not curse.
Rejoice with people who rejoice; weep with people who weep.
Be of one mind toward one another. Do not set your mind on lofty things, but associate with the lowly.{f} Do not be wise in your own estimation.
Pay back no one evil for evil. Give thought to what is honorable in the sight of all people.
As far as possible, and as far as it rests with you, live peaceably with all.
