Fortunatus, and Achaicus: *Fortunatus* is Latin, “fortunate”; *Achaicus* is Greek, “the Achaean,” perhaps a name for a freedman.
Asia: the Roman province in western Asia Minor, whose capital was Ephesus.

Aquila and Prisca: *Aquila* is Latin, “eagle”; *Prisca* (diminutive *Priscilla*, Acts 18:2) is Latin, “ancient, venerable.” Many later manuscripts read “Priscilla.” They had lived in Corinth (Acts 18:1–3).
A curse: Greek *anathema*, “let him be accursed.”
*Marana tha*: Aramaic, “Our Lord, come!” The Greek letters can also be divided *maran atha*, “Our Lord has come” (or “is coming”). Compare Rev 22:20.
The Lord Jesus: many later manuscripts read “our Lord Jesus Christ.”
In Christ Jesus: many manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: 2 Corinthians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), in the public-domain electronic edition of Maurice A. Robinson, with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The earliest substantial manuscript of the letter is P46 (Chester Beatty papyrus, usually dated about AD 200); its readings, like those of other manuscripts, are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from Paul’s Greek, with the source given in a note. Greek *Christos* is rendered “Christ,” as part of Jesus’ name. Greek *adelphoi*, “brothers,” addresses the whole congregation, women and men. The letter is undisputedly Paul’s, sent in the name of Paul and Timothy (1:1) from Macedonia (2:13; 7:5; 9:2), probably about AD 55–56, after 1 Corinthians and before Romans. Its integrity is much debated. Every manuscript presents the letter as it stands here, with no trace of another arrangement; but many scholars think it was assembled from two or more of Paul’s letters to Corinth. The main proposals are these: (1) chapters 10–13, with their abrupt change to sharp self-defense and rebuke, belong to a different letter from chapters 1–9, either the earlier “tearful letter” mentioned in 2:3–4 and 7:8 or a later letter written after fresh trouble; (2) 6:14–7:1, which interrupts the appeal of 6:13 and 7:2 and has unusual vocabulary, is an insertion, whether Paul’s own (perhaps a fragment of the earlier letter mentioned in 1 Cor 5:9) or not; (3) chapters 8 and 9, each of which introduces the collection for Jerusalem as if afresh, were originally separate notes; and (4) 2:14–7:4 is a separate defense of Paul’s ministry set into an account of his travels (2:13 resumes at 7:5). Others defend the unity of the letter as it stands, explaining its shifts by pauses in dictation, fresh news, or a deliberate rhetorical strategy that saves the hardest words for the end. The “tearful letter” itself may be lost, may survive in chapters 10–13, or (in an older view) may be 1 Corinthians. This translation follows the canonical order without rearrangement.

verses.text: From Paul, by God’s will an apostle of Christ Jesus, and from Timothy{a} our brother, to God’s church at Corinth,{b} together with all the saints throughout Achaia:{c}
grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and the God who gives every comfort,{d}
who comforts us in all our trouble, so that we in turn can comfort those in any trouble through the comfort with which God himself comforts us.
For just as Christ’s sufferings overflow into our lives, so too through Christ our comfort overflows.
If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation; if we are comforted, it is for your comfort, which takes effect when you patiently bear the same sufferings that we also suffer.
Our hope for you is unshaken; we know that as partners in the sufferings you are partners in the comfort too.
We would not have you unaware, brothers, of the trouble that came upon us in Asia.{e} We were weighed down far past our strength, so much so that we gave up hope even of staying alive.
In our own minds we had heard our death sentence pronounced. That happened to make us trust not in ourselves but in the God who brings the dead back to life.
He rescued us from so deadly a peril, and he will rescue us; on him we have fixed our hope that he will go on rescuing us,
as you too join in helping us by your prayers, so that thanks may be given on our behalf by many people for the favor granted to us through the prayers of many.

Here is our boast: our conscience testifies that we have behaved in the world, and most of all with you, with purity{f} and sincerity that come from God, relying not on human cleverness but on God’s grace.
Nothing we write to you is beyond what you can read and take in, and I hope you will take it in completely,
just as you have partly understood us, that we are a reason for you to be proud, as you are for us, when our Lord Jesus comes.{g}
It was in this confidence that I intended to come first to you, so that you might have a second joy,{h}
My plan was to visit you on the way to Macedonia, then to return to you after Macedonia, and to be sent on by you toward Judea.
When I planned this, was I being fickle? Or do I make my plans in a worldly way, ready to say “Yes, yes” and “No, no” in the same breath?
God is faithful, and as surely as he is, our message to you was never “Yes” that was also “No.”
For the Son of God, Jesus Christ, whom Silvanus,{i} Timothy, and I announced to you, was not “Yes and No”; in him it has always been a firm “Yes.”
For however many are God’s promises, in him they find their “Yes.” That is why it is through him also that we say the “Amen” to God, for his glory.
Now it is God who makes both us and you secure in Christ, and who has anointed us;
He has stamped us with his seal, and has put his Spirit in our hearts as the first installment of what is to come.{j}
With my life at stake I call God to bear witness: I stayed away from Corinth in order to spare you.
Not that we lord it over your faith; we are working with you for your joy, for it is by faith that you stand firm.

notes.text: Timothy: Greek, “one who honors God.”
Corinth: capital of the Roman province of Achaia.
Achaia: the Roman province of southern Greece.
Every comfort: Greek *paraklēsis*, which can mean comfort, encouragement, or appeal; the related verb occurs throughout vv. 3–7.
Asia: the Roman province in western Asia Minor, whose capital was Ephesus.
Holiness: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts read “simplicity” or “frankness.”
Our Lord Jesus: many manuscripts add “Christ.”

Second joy: so the Westcott–Hort text, with the corrected Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and a few others (as reported); most manuscripts read *charin*, “favor” or “benefit” (“a second benefit”), and the two words differ by one letter in Greek.
Silvanus: Latin form of *Silas* (Acts 15:22), probably from Aramaic *sheila*, “asked for”; associated in Latin with *silva*, “forest.”
The first installment of what is to come: Greek *arrabōn*, a first installment that guarantees the rest.

verses.text: So I made up my mind not to pay you another painful visit.
For if I cause you pain, who is left to cheer me except the very one I have pained?
And I wrote just as I did{a} so that when I came I would not be pained by those who ought to make me glad, for I am confident about all of you that my joy is the joy of you all.
Out of deep affliction and heartache I wrote to you, shedding many tears,{b} not to grieve you but so that you would know how overflowing my love for you is.
Whoever has given grief has grieved not me alone but, to a degree (I do not want to press the point too hard), every one of you.
For such a person this punishment by the majority is enough,
so that now, instead, you should rather forgive and comfort him, or he may be overwhelmed by excessive grief.
So I urge you to confirm your love for him.
For this was my purpose in writing too: to test you and find out whether you are obedient in everything.
Whomever you pardon, I pardon too. And what I have pardoned, if there was anything for me to pardon, I have pardoned for your sake before Christ,
so that Satan may not gain the advantage over us; for we are not ignorant of his designs.
When I came to Troas{c} for the gospel of Christ, though a door was opened for me in the Lord,
I had no peace of mind, since my brother Titus{d} was nowhere to be found; so I took leave of them and set out for Macedonia.
But thanks to God, who constantly leads us in victory as prisoners in Christ’s parade{e} and uses us to spread the aroma of knowing him everywhere.
We are Christ’s sweet scent offered up to God, both among people on the way to salvation and among people on the way to ruin:
to the one, a smell of death leading to death; to the other, a fragrance of life leading to life. And who is equal to such a task?
For we are not like so many,{f} peddling the word of God for profit; we speak in Christ with sincerity, as men sent from God, in God’s presence.

notes.text: I wrote just as I did: this and v. 4 refer to a letter written “with many tears” between 1 Corinthians and this letter, often called the “tearful letter.” See the introduction.
Shedding many tears: see the note on v. 3.
Troas: Alexandria Troas, a port in northwestern Asia Minor.
Titus: a Latin name, of uncertain meaning; a Gentile co-worker of Paul (Gal 2:1–3).
Triumphal procession: the Roman victory parade, in which captives were led along; the image may be of God leading his apostles either as captives or as fellow victors.
So many: many manuscripts read “the rest.”

verses.text: Is this the start of more self-commendation? Or must we, as certain others do, present letters of reference to you, or ask you for them?
Our letter is you yourselves, inscribed on our hearts,{a} recognized and read by all the world.
It is clear that you are Christ’s letter, delivered by us, inscribed not in ink but by the living God’s Spirit, not on stone tablets but on the tablets of human hearts.{b}
That is the kind of trust we place in God, through Christ.
Not that we are competent by ourselves to reckon anything as coming from us; our competence comes from God,
who has made us competent as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

The ministry that brought death was engraved in letters on stones, and yet it came in glory, so much so that the sons of Israel were unable to fix their eyes on Moses’ face because of the glory shining there, glory that was fading.{c}
Then surely the Spirit’s ministry will have still greater glory!
If the ministry that brought condemnation was glorious, far richer in glory is the ministry that brings righteousness.
In fact, set beside this surpassing glory, the thing that was once glorified has lost its glory altogether.
For if what was fading away came with glory, much more does what lasts remain in glory.
Possessing a hope like this, we speak out with complete frankness.
We are not like Moses, who would cover his face with a veil to stop the sons of Israel from staring at the end of a glory that was being abolished.{d}
But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when the old covenant is read, that same veil remains unlifted, because only in Christ is it done away with.
To this present day a veil covers their hearts whenever Moses is read aloud;
but whenever someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.{e}
Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.

And all of us, with unveiled faces reflecting{f} as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another, as it comes from the Lord, the Spirit.{g}

notes.text: Our hearts: a few manuscripts, including Sinaiticus (as reported), read “your hearts.”
Tablets of human hearts: literally “tablets that are hearts of flesh,” echoing Exod 24:12; 31:18 and Ezek 11:19; 36:26; compare Jer 31:33.
Fading: compare Exod 34:29–35.
The end of a glory that was being abolished: or “the outcome of what was being abolished,” or “the goal of what was fading.”
Taken away: echoing Exod 34:34, where “the Lord” is Yahweh; the subject (“someone,” or “Moses,” or “their heart”) is unexpressed in Greek.
Reflecting: or “beholding.”
The Lord, the Spirit: or “the Spirit of the Lord,” or “the Lord who is the Spirit.”

verses.text: Because we hold this ministry by God’s mercy, we never give up.

We have renounced shameful, underhanded ways; we do not practice cunning or tamper with God’s word; but by openly declaring the truth we commend ourselves to everyone’s conscience in the sight of God.
And even if our gospel is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing.
The god of this present age has blinded the unbelieving minds of these people, so that the light of the gospel, which displays the glory of Christ, God’s image, does not dawn on them.
It is not ourselves that we proclaim; we proclaim Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants{a} on account of Jesus.
For the God who commanded, “Let light shine from the darkness,”{b} has made light shine in our hearts so that we can illuminate the knowledge of God’s glory shining from the face of Christ.{c}
But we hold this treasure in clay jars,{d} to show that the surpassing power belongs to God and does not come from us.
We are hard pressed on every side, but not hemmed in; at a loss, but not at our wits’ end;
hunted down, but not abandoned; knocked to the ground, but not destroyed;
always carrying about in our body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.
While we live, we are continually being surrendered to death because of Jesus, so that Jesus’ life may be displayed in our mortal flesh as well.
Death, then, is busy in us, and life is busy in you.
We have the same spirit of trust that the Scripture describes: “I believed, therefore I spoke.”{e} We also believe and therefore speak,
for we know that the one who raised the Lord Jesus{f} will raise us as well with Jesus and place us, together with you, in his presence.
All this is for your benefit, so that as grace spreads to more and more people it may make thanksgiving abound all the more, and God may be glorified.
That is why we never give up. Though our outward person is decaying, our inward person is renewed from one day to the next.
The light trouble of this passing moment is working out for us a glory that is eternal and weighty, past all comparison,
for our gaze is fixed not on what is visible but on what is invisible. What is visible lasts for a time; what is invisible lasts for ever.

notes.text: Servants: literally “slaves.”
Gen 1:3; compare Isa 9:2.
Face of Christ: many manuscripts read “Jesus Christ,” and some “Christ Jesus.”
Clay jars: or “earthenware vessels,” cheap and fragile pottery.
Ps 116:10 (115:1 Greek), following the Greek Old Testament.
The Lord Jesus: “Lord” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.

verses.text: We know that if the tent that is our earthly house is taken down, we have a building from God, a house not built by human hands, everlasting in the heavens.
Meanwhile we groan in this tent, longing to put on over it our dwelling from heaven,
assuming that, once we have put it on,{a} we will not be found naked.
For while we remain in this tent we groan under our burden, not because we wish to be unclothed, but because we wish to be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.
God is the one who prepared us for exactly this, and who gave us the Spirit as a down payment guaranteeing what is coming.
So we are always full of courage. We know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord,
for our life is guided by faith, not by sight.
We are confident, I repeat, and would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.
Whether we are in our home or away from it, then, our one ambition is to be pleasing to him.
Every one of us must be exposed to view before Christ’s tribunal, so that each person may receive his due for the deeds done through the body, good or evil.
Since we know the fear of the Lord, we seek to win people over. God sees us as we are, and I trust that your consciences see us so as well.
We are not recommending ourselves to you once more; rather, we are giving you a reason to be proud of us, so that you can respond to those who boast about outward show rather than inner reality.
If we have lost our senses, that is God’s concern; if we are sober-minded, that is for your benefit.
For Christ’s love holds us fast, since we have reached this conclusion: one man died for all, and therefore all have died.
His death was for all, so that the living should stop living to please themselves and live instead for the one who died and rose again on their behalf.
So from now on we regard no one from a merely human point of view. Even if we once regarded Christ in that way, we no longer do.
So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation.{b} The old things have gone; look, new things have come into being!{c}
Everything is God’s doing. He has reconciled us to himself by means of Christ, and has assigned to us the service of reconciling others:
God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,{d} no longer charging people with their offenses, and he has placed in our hands the message of reconciliation.
We are envoys, then, representing Christ, and God is appealing to you through our words. On Christ’s behalf we plead with you: be reconciled to God.
The one who knew no sin God made to be sin{e} for our sake, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

notes.text: Once we have put it on: so the Westcott–Hort text and most manuscripts (as reported), *endysamenoi*; the original hand of Claromontanus and a few others read *ekdysamenoi*, “once we have taken it off,” which some editors prefer as less obvious.
There is a new creation: or “he is a new creature.”
New things have come into being: many later manuscripts read “all things have become new.”
God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself: or “in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself.”
Sin: or “a sin offering,” a sense the Hebrew word for “sin” can bear (for example Lev 4:24).

verses.text: As God’s fellow workers, then, we also appeal to you not to let the grace of God you have received go for nothing.
For he says, “At the moment of my favor I heard you, and on the day of rescue I helped you.”{a} Listen, now is the time of favor; now is the day of rescue!
We give nobody any cause for offense in anything, so that our service may not be discredited.
Instead, as God’s servants we commend ourselves in every way: by great endurance, in afflictions, in hardships, in distresses,
in floggings, in imprisonments, in riots, in labors, in sleepless nights, in hunger;
in integrity, in understanding, in forbearance, in goodness, in the Holy Spirit, in love without pretense,
in the message of truth, in God’s power; armed with righteousness in right hand and left;
through honor and dishonor, through slander and praise; treated as impostors, and yet true;
as unknown, and yet well known; as dying, and look, we live on; as punished, and yet not put to death;
as grieving, yet always rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, yet possessing everything.
We have been completely open with you, Corinthians; we have welcomed you with an open heart.
It is not on our side that you are cramped; you are cramped in your own affections.
In return (I speak as to my children), open wide your hearts as well.
Do not be yoked unequally with unbelievers.{b} For what partnership can righteousness have with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?
What harmony is there between Christ and Beliar?{c} What does a believer share with an unbeliever?

What common ground can God’s temple share with idols? For we{d} are the sanctuary of the living God; as God declared: “I will dwell among them and walk with them, and I will be their God, and they will be my people.”{e}
So “Leave their company and keep yourselves apart, says the Lord, and lay no hand on what is unclean;{f} then I will receive you,{g}
I will be a Father to you, and to me you will be sons and daughters, declares the Lord Almighty.”{h}

notes.text: Isa 49:8, following the Greek Old Testament. In the Hebrew text the speaker is Yahweh.
Yoked unequally with unbelievers: compare Deut 22:10; Lev 19:19.
Beliar: a form of *Belial* (Hebrew, “worthlessness”), used in Jewish writings of the period as a name for Satan.
We: many manuscripts read “you.”
Lev 26:11–12; compare Ezek 37:27.
Isa 52:11. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.
Ezek 20:34, following the Greek Old Testament.
2 Sam 7:14, 8; compare Isa 43:6. “The Lord Almighty” renders the Greek Old Testament’s *kyrios pantokratōr*, which translates the Hebrew “Yahweh of hosts.”

verses.text: These, dear friends, are the promises we hold; so let us purify ourselves of everything that pollutes flesh or spirit, and in reverence for God bring our holiness to completion.
Open your hearts to us. Not one person have we wronged, corrupted, or exploited.
I am not saying this to condemn you; I have told you before that you are in our hearts, to die together and to live together.
My frankness with you is great, and great is my pride in you. I am full to the brim with encouragement; through all our troubles my joy overflows.
For even when we came into Macedonia, our flesh had no relief; we were afflicted at every turn: conflicts outside, fears within.
Yet God, the comforter of the lowly, gave us comfort when Titus arrived,
and not only by his arrival but also by the comfort he had received from you, as he told us of your longing, your sorrow, your zeal for me, so that I rejoiced still more.
Granted that my letter grieved you, I have no regrets about it. I did regret it at the time (for I see that the letter pained you, if only briefly),{a}
but now I am glad, not that you were pained, but that the pain brought you to repentance. Your sorrow was of God’s kind, so that we did you no damage in any respect.
For grief as God intends it produces a repentance that leads to salvation and leaves no regret, but the world’s grief produces death.

Look at what this godly sorrow has brought about in you: such diligence, such eagerness to be cleared, such outrage, such dread, such yearning, such ardor, such determination to set things right! In every way you have proved yourselves blameless in this affair.
So my letter was written not for the sake of the offender or for the sake of the injured party, but so that before God you yourselves might see clearly how devoted you are to us.{b}
This is what has brought us comfort. And on top of our comfort, we were made gladder still by Titus’ gladness, because all of you have refreshed his spirit.
Whatever I bragged about you to him, you have not embarrassed me; just as everything we told you was true, so what we boasted to Titus about you turned out to be accurate as well.
His heart goes out to you even more as he recalls how all of you obeyed, and how you welcomed him in awe and trembling.
I rejoice that in everything I can have confidence in you.

notes.text: If only briefly: the punctuation of vv. 8–9 is uncertain; the sentence may instead run “even if I regretted it, I see that the letter pained you, if only briefly; now I am glad…”
How devoted you are to us: literally “your earnestness on our behalf”; many later manuscripts read “our earnestness on your behalf.”

verses.text: Brothers, we want you to know about the grace God has bestowed on the churches of Macedonia.
In the midst of a severe ordeal of affliction, their overflowing joy and their deep poverty have welled up in a wealth of generosity.
I can vouch that they gave what they could afford, and even more than that, entirely on their own initiative,
begging us with much entreaty for the privilege of taking part in this service to the saints.
And they did not do merely what we had hoped; they gave themselves first to the Lord and then, by God’s will, to us.
So we have urged Titus that, as he had made a beginning, he should also bring this act of grace to completion among you.
You excel in everything: in faith, in speech, in knowledge, in every kind of eagerness, and in the love from us that lives in you.{a} See that you excel in this act of grace as well.
I am not saying this as an order; I am testing the genuineness of your love by the eagerness of others.
You are familiar with the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ:{b} he was rich, yet for your sakes he made himself poor, so that by his poverty you might be made rich.
And in this matter I am giving you my advice. It is to your advantage, since a year ago you were the first not only to act but even to want to act.
So now finish the task, so that the eagerness of your intention may be matched by its accomplishment, as your means allow.
For if the willingness is there, a gift is acceptable in proportion to what a person has, not what he does not have.
The aim is not that others should have relief while you are hard pressed, but that there should be equality.
At the present time your surplus can meet their need, so that their surplus may in turn meet your need, and so there may be equality.
As Scripture says, “The one who collected a lot did not have too much, and the one who collected a little did not have too little.”{c}
But thanks be to God, who puts into Titus’ heart the same eager concern for you that I have.
For he not only welcomed our appeal; being very eager himself, he is going to you of his own accord.
Along with him we are sending the brother whose service in the gospel has won him praise in every church.
More than that, he has been appointed by the churches to travel with us as we administer this act of grace, for the glory of the Lord himself and to show our goodwill.
We are taking this precaution so that no one may blame us about the way we are administering this generous gift.
Our purpose is to do what is right not just before the Lord but before human eyes as well.{d}
With them we are also sending our brother, whom we have repeatedly put to the test in numerous matters and found keen, and who is now far keener because of his great trust in you.
As for Titus, he is my partner and fellow worker in your service; as for our brothers, they are envoys{e} of the churches, a glory to Christ.
Show them, then, in front of the churches, how real your love is and why we take pride in you.

notes.text: The love from us that lives in you: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P46 and Vaticanus (as reported); many manuscripts read “your love for us.”
Our Lord Jesus Christ: “Christ” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Exod 16:18.
Prov 3:4, following the Greek Old Testament.
Envoys: Greek *apostoloi*, “apostles,” here in the general sense of messengers sent by the churches.

verses.text: It is quite unnecessary for me to write to you about this service to the saints,
I am well aware how willing you are; I keep boasting of you to the Macedonians that Achaia has been prepared since a year ago, and your enthusiasm has stirred up most of them.
Still, I am sending the brothers, so that our boast of you on this point may not be proved hollow, and so that you will be prepared, just as I kept saying.
Otherwise, if any Macedonians come with me and find you unprepared, we (to say nothing of you) would be humiliated for having been so confident.{a}
I therefore judged it needful to ask the brothers to go to you ahead of me and get your promised gift ready beforehand, so that it may be on hand as a free gift, not one extracted from you.{b}
Remember this: whoever sows sparingly will reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will reap generously.
Each one should give as he has made up his mind, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for “God loves a cheerful giver.”{c}
God has the power to cause all kinds of grace to abound toward you, so that in every circumstance you always have all you need and have plenty left for every good deed.
As it is written, “He has scattered his gifts, he has given to the poor; his righteousness endures for ever.”{d}
He who supplies seed to the sower and bread for food{e} will supply and multiply your seed and increase the harvest of your righteousness.
In every way you will be made rich enough for every kind of generosity, and your generosity, passed on by us, will lead to thanksgiving to God.
For the carrying out of this public service is not only filling up what the saints lack; it also spills over into abundant thanks to God.
Through the proof that this service provides, they will glorify God for the obedience of your confession of the gospel of Christ and for the generosity of your sharing with them and with all,
and their longing for you and their prayers for you will reflect God’s grace, which surpasses all bounds in you.
Thanks be to God for his indescribable gift!

notes.text: So confident: many later manuscripts add “in this boasting.”
Extracted from you: literally “as greed,” that is, as an extortion.
Prov 22:8, in the Greek Old Testament only.
Bread for food: Isa 55:10.

verses.text: It is I myself, Paul, who plead with you by the meekness and kindness of Christ, I who am “lowly” in your presence but “daring” toward you from a distance.
I beg you that when I am present I may not have to show the boldness I count on displaying against certain people who reckon that we behave by worldly standards.
For though we live in the flesh, we do not wage war by the flesh.
The weapons we fight with are not of the flesh, but powerful through God for tearing down strongholds. We demolish arguments
and every lofty barrier raised up against the knowledge of God, and we take every thought prisoner to make it obey Christ,
and we stand ready to punish every disobedience, once your obedience is complete.
Look at what is right before your eyes.{a} If anyone is sure that he belongs to Christ, let him think again and consider that, as he is Christ’s, so are we.
Even if I boast rather freely about our authority, which the Lord gave for building you up and not for pulling you down, I will not be put to shame.
I do not want to seem to be frightening you with my letters.
For “His letters,” they say, “are weighty and forceful, but his bodily presence is feeble and his speaking amounts to nothing.”
Let such a person understand that what we are in word by letter when absent, we are also in action when present.

We would not venture to rank ourselves or measure ourselves against certain of those who write their own testimonials. They gauge themselves by each other and rate themselves against each other, and they have no sense.{b}
We, however, will not boast beyond limits, but will keep to the limits of the field{c} God has assigned to us as our measure, a field that reaches even as far as you.
We are not stretching beyond our bounds, as if we had never reached you; in fact we came as far as you, the first to bring the gospel of Christ.
We do not boast beyond limits in other people’s labors. Our hope is that as your faith grows, our field among you may be greatly enlarged,
so that we may carry the gospel to regions past you, and not take credit for ground another has already worked.
“Whoever boasts must make his boast in the Lord.”{d}
Approval comes not to the person who recommends himself, but to the person the Lord recommends.

notes.text: Look at what is right before your eyes: or, as a question, “Are you looking at things as they appear on the surface?” or, as a command, “Look at the facts.”

They have no sense: some Western witnesses (as reported) lack these words and the first words of v. 13, so that the sentence runs: “…but we gauge ourselves by ourselves and rate ourselves against ourselves, and will not boast beyond limits…”
Field: Greek *kanōn*, a measuring rule, and so a measured area or sphere of work.
Jer 9:24; compare 1 Cor 1:31. In the Hebrew text, “the Lord” is Yahweh.

verses.text: I wish you would bear with a little foolishness from me! Do bear with me.
I feel for you a jealousy that is God’s own, for I promised you in marriage to one husband, to present you to Christ as a pure virgin.
My fear is that, just as the snake tricked Eve{a} with its craftiness, your thoughts may be corrupted and drawn away from single-minded and pure{b} loyalty to Christ.

Someone arrives proclaiming a Jesus other than the Jesus we proclaimed, or you take in a spirit unlike the Spirit you took in before, or a gospel unlike the gospel you welcomed, and you tolerate it beautifully!
Yet in my estimation I fall short of these superlative apostles in nothing.
I may lack training as a speaker, but I do not lack knowledge; we have made that clear to you in every way and in every respect.
Was it a sin, then, that I lowered myself to lift you up, proclaiming God’s good news to you without charging you anything?
Other churches I plundered, taking pay from them so as to minister to you.

While I was with you and ran short, I was a drain on nobody; my needs were met by the brothers who arrived from Macedonia. I have kept myself from weighing on you in any way, and I will keep on doing so.
By the truth of Christ that is in me, nobody throughout Achaia shall stop me from making this boast.
And why? Because I do not love you? God knows I do!
I will continue as I am doing, so as to deny any opening to those who are looking for one, so that in their boasting they may be found to work on the same terms as we do.
Men like that are sham apostles, dishonest laborers, masquerading as Christ’s apostles.
And no wonder, for Satan himself disguises himself as an angel of light.
It is hardly surprising, then, if his ministers masquerade as ministers of righteousness. They will end as their works deserve.
Again I say, nobody should think me a fool. Or if you must, then welcome me even as a fool, so that I may boast a little myself.
What I am saying in this boastful confidence I am saying not as the Lord would, but as in foolishness.
Since many boast according to the flesh, I too will boast.
Wise as you are, you are glad to tolerate fools.
You tolerate a man who makes slaves of you, who eats you up, who snatches what is yours, who lords it over you, who slaps your face.
I admit, to our discredit, that we have been weak in comparison! Still, whatever anyone ventures to boast about (this is fool’s talk), I will venture it too.
Are they Hebrews? So am I. Are they Israelites? So am I. Are they descendants of Abraham? So am I.
Are they ministers of Christ? (Now I am raving.) I am a better one: in labors more abundantly, in prisons more often, in beatings beyond counting, and many times facing death.
From the Jews I received thirty-nine lashes{c} on five occasions.
Three times I was beaten with rods; once I was stoned; three times I was shipwrecked; a night and a day I spent adrift at sea;

I have been constantly on the road, at risk from flooded rivers, at risk from robbers, at risk from my countrymen, at risk from the nations, at risk in towns, at risk in open country, at risk on the sea, at risk among sham brothers;
I have known labor and weariness, many nights without sleep, hunger and thirst, frequent fasting, cold and lack of clothing.
Besides everything else, I carry the pressure of care for all the churches, bearing down on me each day.
When someone is weak, am I not weak as well? When someone is tripped up, am I not on fire?
If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness.
The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, he who is blessed for ever, knows that I am not lying.
In Damascus the governor{d} under King Aretas{e} was guarding the city of the Damascenes in order to seize me,
but I was let down in a basket through a window in the wall and escaped his hands.

notes.text: Eve: Hebrew *Chavvah*, associated with *chai*, “living” (Gen 3:20).
Single-minded and pure: “and pure” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text; many manuscripts lack it, and others put the two words in reverse order.
Thirty-nine lashes: literally “forty less one,” keeping within the limit of forty set in Deut 25:3.
The governor: Greek *ethnarchēs*, a ruler or representative of a people.
Aretas: Aretas IV, king of the Nabateans (about 9 BC–AD 40), whose capital was Petra. Compare Acts 9:23–25.

verses.text: Boast I must.{a} Nothing is gained by it, but I will move on to visions and revelations granted by the Lord.
I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven; I do not know whether it happened in the body or outside the body; God knows.
And I know that this man (whether in the body or apart from the body I cannot say; God knows)
was snatched up into paradise{b} and heard words too sacred for speech, which no human being is permitted to utter.
About such a man I will boast, but about myself I will not boast, except of my weaknesses.
Even if I should choose to boast, I would be no fool, for I would be telling the truth. But I hold back, so that nobody may credit me with more than he sees in me or hears from me,

even given the surpassing greatness of what was revealed.{c} So, to keep me from becoming overly elated, I was handed a thorn in the flesh, Satan’s messenger, to beat me about, so that I would not become overly elated.
Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, asking that it might leave me.

His word to me was, “My grace suffices for you, for my power reaches its completion in weakness.” Gladly, then, I will rather boast of my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest upon me like a tent.
That is why, for Christ’s sake, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and pressures; for when I am weak, then it is that I am strong.
I have turned into a fool; you drove me to it. I ought to have had your commendation, for I came behind those superlative apostles in nothing, even though I am nothing.
The marks of a true apostle were produced among you with all perseverance, by signs, wonders, and mighty works.
How were you put at a disadvantage compared with the rest of the churches, apart from this: I personally laid no burden on you? Pardon me for this injustice!

See, I am ready to come to you for this third time, and I will not be a drain on you. It is not your possessions I am after but you. Children are not obliged to save up for their parents; parents save up for their children.
For my part, I will most gladly spend and be spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?
Very well, then: I did not burden you myself. Yet, crafty as I am, I caught you by trickery, did I?
Of those I dispatched to you, was there one through whom I took advantage of you?
I asked Titus to visit you and sent the brother along. Did Titus take advantage of you? Were we not guided by one Spirit, and did we not tread in the same tracks?
Have you been supposing all this time that we are defending ourselves before you? We are speaking before God in Christ, and all of it, dear friends, is for your upbuilding.

My fear is that on my arrival I may find you otherwise than I want, and you may find me otherwise than you want; that there may be strife, envy, fits of temper, factions, backbiting, whispering, conceit, and turmoil.

I am afraid that on my return my God may bring me low in front of you, and that I may grieve for many who were sinning before and have not turned away from the uncleanness, fornication, and sensuality they indulged in.

notes.text: Boast I must: many manuscripts read “If I must boast,” and some “I must boast, though it is not profitable.”
Paradise: from a Persian word for a walled garden; in the Greek Old Testament, the garden of Eden, and in Jewish writings, the abode of the righteous with God.

What was revealed: the punctuation is disputed. These words may instead close v. 6 (“…more than he sees in me or hears from me, even given the extraordinary revelations”) or begin a new sentence with v. 7, as here. Many manuscripts lack “For that reason.”

verses.text: This will be the third time I am coming to you. “Every charge must be established on the evidence of two or three witnesses.”{a}
I warned those who sinned before and all the rest, and I warn them now, absent now as I was present on my second visit: if I come again, I will not spare them,
because you are looking for evidence that it is Christ who speaks in me. Toward you he is not feeble; he is mighty in your midst.
For he was crucified in weakness, but he lives by God’s power. We too are weak in him, but we shall live with him by God’s power in dealing with you.{b}
Put yourselves under scrutiny to see whether you are living in the faith; test yourselves. Can you not recognize that Jesus Christ is in you? Unless, that is, you fail the test.
I hope you will come to recognize that we have not failed it.
Our prayer to God is that you will do no wrong; not that we may be seen to stand approved, but that you may do good while we may look like failures.
We have no power to act against the truth, only for the truth.
We are glad when we are weak and you are strong. And this is what we pray for: your complete restoration.
This is why I am writing from a distance: so that when I arrive I will not need to be severe in exercising the authority the Lord gave me for building you up, not for demolishing you.
Finally, brothers, farewell.{c} Set yourselves right, take my appeal to heart, agree with one another, live in peace; and the God of love and peace will be with you.
Greet one another with a holy kiss.
All the saints send you greetings.{d}
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ,{e} the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit{f} be with you all.{g}

notes.text: Deut 19:15.
In dealing with you: Greek *eis hymas*, bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Farewell: or “rejoice.”
Greetings: in the Greek text, and in some translations, vv. 12–13 are numbered as v. 12, and v. 14 as v. 13.
The Lord Jesus Christ: “Christ” is bracketed in the Westcott–Hort text.
Fellowship of the Holy Spirit: or “sharing in the Holy Spirit.”
With you all: many manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Galatians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The oldest substantial manuscript of Galatians is the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), with Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century); where papyrus readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from Paul’s Greek, with the source given in a note. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name, as it usually does in Paul’s letters. Galatians is one of the seven letters whose authorship by Paul is accepted by nearly all scholars. Whether it was sent to the ethnic Galatians of north-central Asia Minor or to the churches of the Roman province of Galatia founded on Paul’s first journey (Acts 13–14) is debated, and dates proposed range from about AD 48 to the mid-50s.

verses.text: From Paul,{a} an apostle{b} commissioned neither by people nor through any human agent, but by Jesus Christ{c} and God the Father, who raised him from the dead,
and all the brothers{d} who are with me, to the churches of Galatia:{e}
May grace and peace be yours from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ,{f}
who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,
to whom be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.
I am astonished that you are deserting so quickly the one who summoned you by the grace of Christ, and defecting to a different message,{g}
which is not another gospel at all. It is only that there are some people who are unsettling you and want to twist the gospel of Christ.
But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should proclaim to you a gospel contrary to the one we proclaimed to you, let him be accursed.{h}
As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone is proclaiming to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.
Am I now looking for human approval, or for God’s? Is it people I am trying to please? Were I still courting people’s favor, I could not be Christ’s servant.{i}
For I want you to know, brothers, that the gospel I proclaimed is not of human origin.
No human being handed it to me, and no one taught it to me; it came by a revelation from Jesus Christ.{j}
You have heard how I once lived as a follower of Judaism: how violently I hunted down God’s church and set out to ravage it.
I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, and I was far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.
But then God, who chose me while I was still in my mother’s womb{k} and called me through his grace, decided
to disclose his Son within me, so that I would announce him among the nations.{l} At once, without talking it over with any mortal,{m}
nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me. Instead I went away into Arabia,{n} and then returned to Damascus.
Three years later I did go up to Jerusalem, to become acquainted with Cephas,{o} and I spent fifteen days in his company.
Of the other apostles I saw no one, apart from James, the brother of the Lord.{p}
As for the things I write to you, look: before God, I am telling no lie.
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.{q}
The churches in Judea that are in Christ still did not know my face.
All they had heard was this: “The one who used to persecute us now proclaims as good news the faith that he once set out to ravage.”
And they glorified God because of me.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one who is sent,” a messenger with authority from the one who sends him.

*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.” In Paul’s letters it usually functions as part of Jesus’ name and is rendered “Christ.”
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women; so throughout the letter.
Galatia: a region and Roman province in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey), named after the Gauls (Celts) who settled there in the third century BC.

From God our Father and from the Lord: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus. Many other manuscripts, reportedly including P46 and Vaticanus, read “from God the Father and our Lord.”
Gospel: Greek *euangelion*, “good news”; so throughout.
Accursed: Greek *anathema*, something handed over to God for destruction, the Greek Old Testament’s word for Hebrew *ḥerem* (Josh 6:17).
Slave: Greek *doulos*, a slave or bond-servant, one wholly owned by a master.
A revelation of Jesus Christ: either a revelation that came from Jesus Christ, or one in which Jesus Christ was revealed (compare verse 16).
Before I was born: literally “from my mother’s womb,” echoing the calls of the prophets (Isa 49:1; Jer 1:5).
Gentiles: Greek *ethnē*, “nations,” the non-Jewish peoples.
Any human being: literally “flesh and blood.”
Arabia: probably the Nabatean kingdom, which lay south and east of Damascus and extended into the Sinai (compare 4:25).
*Cephas*: Aramaic *Kepha*, “rock,” the name Jesus gave to Simon; its Greek equivalent is *Peter* (John 1:42).

*James*: the English form of Greek *Iakōbos*, that is, *Jacob* (“heel-grabber” or “he supplants,” Gen 25:26). This James led the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18). The Greek can also be read, “I saw no other apostle, only James.”
Cilicia: the region on the southeast coast of Asia Minor, whose chief city was Tarsus, Paul’s birthplace (Acts 22:3).

verses.text: Then after fourteen years{a} I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas,{b} taking Titus{c} along also.

I went up because of a revelation, and I laid before them the gospel that I proclaim among the Gentiles. I did so privately before those who were held in high esteem, for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.
Yet Titus, my companion, though a Greek, was not forced to undergo circumcision.
The pressure came from false brothers who had been smuggled in, men who crept in to spy out the freedom that is ours in Christ Jesus, intending to enslave us.{d}
We did not give in to them by submitting even for a moment,{e} so that the truth of the gospel might remain with you.
And from those who were held in esteem (whatever they once were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality){f} — those esteemed men added nothing to my message.
Quite the reverse: they saw that the gospel for the uncircumcised had been put into my hands, as the gospel for the circumcised had been put into Peter’s.{g}
For God, who empowered Peter for his mission as apostle to the circumcised, empowered me as well for mine to the Gentiles.

James, Cephas, and John,{h} who were reputed to be pillars, acknowledged the grace granted to me, and they gave Barnabas and me their right hands in partnership: we were to go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised.
Their one request was that we keep the poor in mind, and that was the very thing I had made it my concern to do.
But when Cephas came to Antioch,{i} I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.
Until certain people arrived from James, he had been eating with Gentiles; but once they came he started to withdraw and hold himself aloof, fearing the advocates of circumcision.
The rest of the Jews joined him in this pretense,{j} so that even Barnabas was carried away by their pretense.

I saw that they were not walking straight with the truth of the gospel, and I said to Cephas before everyone, “You are a Jew, yet you live in Gentile fashion and not in Jewish fashion. How then can you force the Gentiles to adopt Jewish ways?”
We are Jews by nature, not sinners of Gentile stock,

but we know that no one is put right with God{k} by works of the law, only through faith in Jesus Christ.{l} And so we ourselves came to believe in Christ Jesus, so as to be put right by faith in Christ and not by works of the law; for by works of the law no human being{m} will be put right.
But if, while we seek to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are also found to be sinners, does that make Christ a servant of sin? Certainly not!
For if I rebuild what I once tore down, I prove that I am a lawbreaker.
Through the law I have died to the law, in order to live to God. With Christ I have been crucified.{n}
I no longer live; Christ lives in me. The life I live now in this body,{o} I live through trusting the Son of God, who loved me and surrendered himself for my sake.
I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness came through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

notes.text: After fourteen years: counted either from his conversion or from the visit of 1:18.
*Barnabas*: interpreted in Acts 4:36 as “son of encouragement”; the derivation is uncertain.
*Titus*: a Latin name of uncertain meaning; he was a Gentile coworker of Paul (2 Cor 8:23; Titus 1:4).
The Greek sentence of verses 4–5 is broken off and does not complete its grammar; the opening words have been supplied to make the sense clear.

A moment: literally “an hour,” an idiom for a brief time. A few Western witnesses lack “to them, not even,” which reverses the sense (“we gave in for a moment”); the earliest manuscripts, including P46, have the negative.
Shows no partiality: literally “does not receive the face of a person,” a Hebrew idiom for judging by appearances.
*Peter*: Greek *Petros*, “rock,” the Greek equivalent of *Cephas* (1:18).
*John*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yohanan*, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Antioch: Antioch in Syria, on the Orontes River, the third city of the Roman Empire and a center of the early Gentile mission (Acts 11:19–26).
Pretense: Greek *hypokrisis*, “play-acting,” traditionally “hypocrisy.”
Put right with God: traditionally “justified”; Greek *dikaioō*, to declare or put in the right before God; related to *dikaiosynē*, “righteousness.”
Faith in Jesus Christ: Greek *pistis Iēsou Christou*, which may also be translated “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ”; so also later in the verse, in 2:20 and 3:22. Scholars are divided.
No human being: literally “all flesh shall not,” echoing Ps 143:2 (142:2 in the Greek Old Testament).
In the Greek text, “I have been crucified with Christ” begins verse 20.
In the body: literally “in the flesh.”

verses.text: Senseless Galatians! Who has put you under a spell, you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly displayed on the cross?{a}
I only want to find out one thing from you: was it by keeping the law that you received the Spirit, or by believing what you heard?{b}
Can you be that senseless? You started out with the Spirit; are you now completing it through human effort?{c}
Have you experienced so much to no purpose? If it really was to no purpose.{d}
When God gives you the Spirit and works deeds of power among you, is it because you do works of the law, or because you heard and believed?
It was the same with Abraham: “He believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”{e}
You see, then, that the people of faith are the real children{f} of Abraham.
The Scripture saw ahead that God would put the nations right through faith, and announced the good news to Abraham in advance: “All nations will be blessed through you.”{g}
Accordingly the people of faith share the blessing with Abraham, who had faith.
All who depend on works of the law live under a curse, for it stands written, “A curse is on everyone who does not abide by all that is written in the book of the law, to do it.”{h}
That no one is put right with God by the law is clear, because “By faith the righteous one will live.”{i}
But the law does not rest on faith; on the contrary, “The one who does them will live by them.”{j}
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.”{k}
This was so that the blessing of Abraham might reach the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, and that through faith we might receive the Spirit who was promised.
Friends, I will use an everyday illustration:{l} even a person’s will, once it is validated, cannot be canceled or amended by anyone else.
The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. Scripture does not say “offsprings,” referring to many, but speaks of one: “and to your offspring,”{m} that is, Christ.
My point is this: a covenant that God had already ratified is not annulled by the law, which came into being four hundred and thirty years afterward,{n} so as to make the promise void.
If the inheritance depended on the law, it would no longer depend on a promise; yet it was by a promise that God freely granted it to Abraham.
What, then, was the law for? It was added to deal with offenses,{o} until the descendant to whom the promise was made would arrive; it was ordained through angels, by means of an intermediary.{p}
A go-between does not act for one party alone; but God is one.{q}
Does this set the law against the promises of God? By no means! If a law had been given that was able to make alive, righteousness would truly have been by the law.
But Scripture has locked up everything under the power of sin, so that what was promised might be given, by faith in Jesus Christ, to those who believe.
Until faith came, we were kept under guard by the law, confined until the coming faith should be revealed.
So the law became our guardian{r} until Christ came, so that we might be justified by faith.
But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.
For in Christ Jesus you are all children of God through faith.
All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ like a garment.
Gone are the distinctions of Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female;{s} all of you are one in Christ Jesus.
If you are Christ’s, you are Abraham’s offspring, and heirs as the promise said.

notes.text: Publicly displayed: Greek *prographō*, to placard or post a public notice. Later manuscripts add “that you should not obey the truth” and “among you.”
Hearing with faith: or “the message of faith”; Greek *akoē* means both “hearing” and “what is heard”; also in verse 5.
The flesh: Greek *sarx*, here human nature apart from God, and perhaps also a pointed allusion to circumcision.
Experienced: or “suffered”; the Greek verb *paschō* can be used of good experiences as well as of suffering.
Gen 15:6, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament. *Abraham* means “father of a multitude” (Gen 17:5).
Children: literally “sons”; so also in 3:26 and 4:6–7, where it carries the legal sense of heirs.
Gen 12:3, combined with Gen 18:18. *Nations* and *Gentiles* translate the same Greek word, *ethnē*.
Deut 27:26, quoted freely from the Greek Old Testament, with wording drawn from Deut 28:58.
Hab 2:4. The Hebrew reads “by his faithfulness”; the Greek Old Testament reads “by my faithfulness.” The Greek can also be read “The one who is righteous by faith will live.”
Lev 18:5. In the Hebrew text it is introduced by “I am Yahweh.”
Deut 21:23, quoted freely. *Tree*: Greek *xylon*, “wood,” also used of the cross (Acts 5:30).
Literally “I speak according to man.”
Offspring: literally “seed,” a collective noun in Hebrew and Greek. The promise is found in Gen 12:7; 13:15; 17:8; 24:7.

Four hundred and thirty years: compare Exod 12:40, where the Greek Old Testament and the Samaritan Pentateuch count this period as including the time in Canaan as well as Egypt; the Hebrew counts it for Egypt alone.
Because of transgressions: either to restrain them, or to expose them and define them as such (compare Rom 4:15; 5:20).
Through angels: a Jewish tradition held that angels took part in giving the law at Sinai (Deut 33:2 in the Greek Old Testament; Acts 7:53; Heb 2:2). *Mediator*: Moses.

This verse is notoriously difficult and has been interpreted in hundreds of ways. Its point may be that the law came indirectly, through intermediaries, while the promise came directly from the one God.
Guardian: Greek *paidagōgos*, a household slave who escorted a boy to school and supervised his conduct until he came of age; not a teacher.
Male and female: the wording echoes Gen 1:27 in the Greek Old Testament; note the change from “nor” to “and.”

verses.text: I mean this: so long as the heir is under age, he is no better off than a slave, even though all the property is his.
Guardians and stewards have charge of him until the time his father has fixed.
So with us also: when we were minors, we were enslaved under the elemental forces of the world.{a}
But when the full time had arrived, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born subject to the law,
so that he might buy freedom for those subject to the law, and that we might be adopted as children.{b}
And because you are children, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba! Father!”{c}
You are therefore no longer a slave but a son, and since you are a son, God has also made you an heir.{d}
In the past, not knowing God, you served as slaves those who by nature are not gods.
But now you know God, or rather God knows you. How can you go back again to those feeble and beggarly elemental forces, and long to be their slaves once more?
You are observing special days and months and seasons and years!
I fear for you, that I may have labored over you in vain.
Brothers, I beg you, become as I am, because I also have become as you are. You did me no wrong.
As you know, it was an illness of the body{e} that first gave me the occasion to preach the gospel to you,
and although my condition put you to the test,{f} you neither scorned nor spurned me;{g} instead you made me welcome as though I were an angel of God, even as though I were Christ Jesus.
Where then is your sense of blessing? For I can testify that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.
Have I then become your enemy by telling you the truth?
Those people are eager to win you over, but with bad intentions. They would like to isolate you, so that you will be eager to follow them.
It is good to be courted for a good purpose at all times, and not only when I am present with you.
My little children, I am once again in labor pains for you, until Christ takes shape in you.
I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am at a loss about you.
Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?
For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.{h}
But the son of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, and the son of the free woman through the promise.
This is an allegory:{i} the two women stand for two covenants. One comes from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery; that is Hagar.{j}
Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia;{k} she matches the Jerusalem of today, which is enslaved along with her children.
The Jerusalem that is above, though, is free, and that city is our mother.
Now you, brothers, like Isaac, are children of the promise.{m}
Yet just as then the child born by natural descent harassed the child born through the Spirit, so it is today.
But what does Scripture say? “Drive out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall never share the inheritance with the son of the free woman.”{n}
So, brothers, we are not the slave woman’s children but the free woman’s.

notes.text: Elemental forces: Greek *stoicheia*, “basic elements,” meaning either the elementary principles of religion, or the physical elements and the spiritual powers thought to rule them; also in verse 9.
Adopted as children: Greek *huiothesia*, the legal adoption of a son, which gave him full rights as heir.
*Abba*: Aramaic for “father,” the word Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36); Paul gives the Greek translation after it.
God has also made you an heir: literally “an heir through God”; later manuscripts read “an heir of God through Christ.”
An illness of the body: literally “a weakness of the flesh.” Its nature is unknown; verse 15 has suggested to some an eye disease.
My condition put you to the test: literally “your trial in my flesh,” so the earliest manuscripts; later ones read “my trial that was in my flesh.”
Spurned: literally “spit out,” perhaps alluding to the ancient practice of spitting to ward off evil from someone sick.
Gen 16:15; 21:2. The slave woman is Hagar, the free woman Sarah.
Taken figuratively: Greek *allēgoroumena*, “spoken as an allegory.”
*Hagar*: perhaps related to Arabic *hajara*, “to flee” or “to emigrate”; the meaning is uncertain.

Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia: literally “Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia,” so the Westcott–Hort text. Some manuscripts, including Sinaiticus, read “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia.” Paul may be playing on an Arabic word for rock or mountain that sounded like *Hagar*; this is uncertain.
Isa 54:1, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament.
*Isaac*: Hebrew *Yitsḥaq*, “he laughs” (Gen 21:6). Some manuscripts read “we … are.”
Gen 21:10, where Sarah says “with my son Isaac.”

verses.text: Christ freed us so that we might be free. So stand your ground, and do not let yourselves be held once more under a slave’s yoke.
Take note: I, Paul, say to you plainly that Christ will be of no use to you at all if you let yourselves be circumcised.
I declare again to every man who accepts circumcision that he is bound to carry out the entire law.
You who look to the law to put you right with God have been severed from Christ; you have dropped out of grace.
But we, by the Spirit and through faith, wait eagerly for the righteousness we hope for.
For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is faith working through love.
You were running a good race. Who blocked your way and kept you from obeying the truth?
Such persuading does not come from him who calls you.
It takes only a little yeast to work through all the dough.
I am confident in the Lord about you that you will take no other view. But the one who is unsettling you will bear the penalty, whoever he may be.
But if I, brothers, am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been removed.
I wish those who are disturbing you would go so far as to castrate themselves!{a}
Brothers, you were called to be free. But do not let freedom become a foothold for the flesh; instead, be slaves to one another through love.
For the whole law is summed up in a single command: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”{b}
If you go on biting and tearing at one another, watch out, or you will be eaten up by one another.
This is what I say: let the Spirit direct your steps, and you will never satisfy the cravings of the flesh.
What the flesh craves is contrary to the Spirit, and what the Spirit desires is contrary to the flesh; the two are at war with each other, to keep you from doing whatever you wish.
But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law.
Now the works of the flesh are plain: sexual immorality, impurity, indecency,
idolatry, sorcery,{c} hatreds, strife, jealousy, fits of rage, selfish rivalries, divisions, factions,
jealousy,{d} drinking parties, orgies, and similar things. I warn you, as I warned you earlier, that those who practice such things will not inherit God’s kingdom.
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no law.
And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
Since the Spirit gives us life, let the Spirit also order our steps.
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another and envying one another.

notes.text: Castrate themselves: Greek *apokoptō*, “cut off,” a bitter play on circumcision, perhaps alluding to the self-castration practiced by priests of the goddess Cybele in Galatia.
Sorcery: Greek *pharmakeia*, the use of drugs and potions in magic.
Envy: later manuscripts add “murders.”

verses.text: Brothers, if someone is caught in any wrongdoing, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness. Watch yourself, so that you also are not tempted.
Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way fulfill the law of Christ.{a}
Anyone who imagines he is something, when he is nothing, is fooling himself.
Let each one examine his own work, and then his reason for pride will be in himself alone, and not in comparison with someone else.
For each will carry his own load.{b}
Whoever is being instructed in the word should share every good thing with his instructor.
Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. Whatever a person sows, that he will also reap.
Sow to please your own flesh, and from the flesh you will reap ruin; sow to please the Spirit, and from the Spirit you will reap eternal life.
We must not tire of doing what is right, for when the time comes we shall reap, if we do not lose heart.
Therefore, whenever we get the chance, let us work for the good of all, above all for those in the family of believers.
Notice how large the letters are as I now write to you in my own hand!{c}
Those who want to make a good showing in the flesh are the ones who are trying to compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.
Even those who are circumcised do not keep the law themselves; they want you circumcised so that they can boast of your flesh.
But as for me, may I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which{d} the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; what matters is a new creation.
And for all who will follow this rule, peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.{e}
For the rest, let no one make trouble for me, because I carry the marks of Jesus branded on my body.{f}
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.

notes.text: Fulfill: the Westcott–Hort text has the command; other manuscripts, among them Vaticanus as reported, read “you will fulfill.”
Load: Greek *phortion*, a person’s own pack, distinct from the heavy “burdens” (*barē*) of verse 2.
In my own hand: Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe (Rom 16:22) and added a closing in his own handwriting (1 Cor 16:21; 2 Thess 3:17).
Through which: or “through whom.”

And upon the Israel of God: or “that is, upon the Israel of God.” The phrase may refer to the church of Jews and Gentiles together, or to Jewish believers, or to the Jewish people as a whole. Compare the Jewish benediction “Peace be upon Israel” (Ps 125:5; 128:6).
Marks: Greek *stigmata*, brands such as were put on slaves to show who owned them; here the scars of Paul’s sufferings for Jesus (2 Cor 11:23–25).

books.name: Ephesians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The oldest manuscript of Ephesians is the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), with Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century); where their readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. Old Testament quotations are translated afresh from the Greek of the letter, with the source given in a note. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: the letter names Paul as its author (1:1; 3:1) and was received as his from the second century. Many modern scholars, noting its style, its long sentences, its developed view of the church, and its close dependence on Colossians, hold that it was written in Paul’s name by a follower after his death, perhaps about AD 80–90; others defend Paul’s authorship, dating it to his imprisonment about AD 60–62. The question remains open. Because the words “in Ephesus” are absent from the earliest manuscripts (see the note on 1:1) and the letter has no personal greetings, many think it was a circular letter to several churches in Asia.

verses.text: Paul,{a} an apostle{b} of Christ Jesus{c} by God’s will, to the holy ones who are in Ephesus,{d} who are also faithful in Christ Jesus:
grace be yours, and peace, from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in Christ has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms.{e}
For he chose us in him before the world was founded, that we should be holy and without blemish in his presence. In love{f}
he marked us out beforehand to be adopted as his children through Jesus Christ, in keeping with the good pleasure of his will,
so that the glory of his grace might be praised, the grace he has freely given us in the one he loves.{g}
In him, through his blood, we have redemption, the forgiveness of our wrongdoings, as rich as his grace is rich,
that grace he has poured out on us in full measure, with all wisdom and insight.
He has made known to us the secret of his will,{h} according to the good purpose that he set forth in Christ,
a plan for the fullness of the times:{i} to bring all things together under one head in Christ, the things in heaven and the things on earth.
In him we also were made God’s portion,{j} having been marked out beforehand by the purpose of the one who works out everything as his will determines,
in order that we, who were first to place our hope in Christ, might bring praise to his glory.
In him you also, after hearing the true message, the gospel{k} that saves you, and believing in him, received the promised Holy Spirit as your seal.{l}
The Spirit is the down payment{m} on our inheritance, until God redeems those who are his own possession, to the praise of his glory.
That is why I too, since I heard of your faith in the Lord Jesus and your regard for all the holy ones,{n}
never stop giving thanks for you as I mention you in my prayers.
My prayer is that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the glorious Father, will give you a spirit of wisdom and insight as you get to know him,
the eyes of your heart having been filled with light, so that you may know what hope his calling holds, what wealth of glory is in his inheritance among the holy ones,
and how surpassingly great his power is toward us who believe. It is the same mighty strength at work
that he put to work in Christ when he raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand{o} in the heavenly realms,
far above all rule, authority, power, and lordship,{p} and every title that can be given, not only in the present age but in the coming one.
God has placed everything beneath his feet,{q} and made him head over everything for the sake of the church.
The church is his body, the fullness of him who fills all in all.{r}

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one who is sent,” a messenger with the authority of the sender.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”

In Ephesus: these words are absent from the earliest manuscripts, P46 (about AD 200) and the original hands of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (4th century), and from the text known to Origen; Westcott and Hort print them in brackets. Without them the Greek reads awkwardly, “to the holy ones who are, and faithful in Christ Jesus,” and the letter may have been a circular with a space for the name of each church. In the second century Marcion knew it as the letter “to the Laodiceans” (compare Col 4:16). *Ephesus*, a port on the west coast of Asia Minor, was the capital of the Roman province of Asia, where Paul worked for over two years (Acts 19:1–20).
In the heavenly realms: Greek *en tois epouraniois*, “among the heavenly things,” a phrase found only in this letter (also 1:20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). Verses 3–14 are a single sentence in Greek.
In love: these words may go either with what precedes (“without blemish before him in love”) or, as here, with verse 5.
The one he loves: literally “the Beloved,” a title for Christ.
Secret: Greek *mystērion*, traditionally “mystery,” not a puzzle but God’s purpose once hidden and now disclosed; so throughout the letter.
Plan: Greek *oikonomia*, “household management,” the arrangement by which God carries out his purpose; also in 3:2, 9.
Were made God’s portion: or “obtained an inheritance.” The Greek verb *klēroō* means to be chosen by lot or allotted, as Israel was the Lord’s allotted portion (Deut 32:9).
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
Sealed: a seal marked ownership and guaranteed that something was genuine and protected.
Down payment: Greek *arrabōn*, a deposit or first installment that guarantees the full amount will follow.

Your regard for: literally simply “your [faith] toward”; the Westcott–Hort text, with P46, the original hands of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus, lacks the word “love,” which most later manuscripts include (“your love toward all the holy ones”), probably from Col 1:4.
At his right hand: an echo of Ps 110:1 (109:1 in the Greek Old Testament), the place of highest honor and authority.
Ruler … dominion: terms for ranks of spiritual powers, as in Col 1:16.
Ps 8:6 (8:7 in Hebrew).
Who fills all in all: or “who is being filled, all in all.” The Greek participle can be middle or passive, and the meaning of the whole phrase is much discussed.

verses.text: As for you, you were dead through your wrongdoings and sins,
in which you once lived your lives,{a} following the course of this world, following the ruler of the domain of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the children of disobedience.{b}
Among them all of us also once lived, in the cravings of our flesh, doing what the flesh and its impulses willed, and we were by nature children of wrath, as the rest of humankind were.
But God is rich in mercy, and because of the great love he had for us,
even when we were dead through our wrongdoings, made us alive together with Christ (it is by grace you have been saved),
and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus,
so that in the ages to come he might display the overflowing riches of his grace in his kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.
It is by grace that you are saved, through faith. Nor does this come from you: it is God’s gift,{c}
and not earned by works, so that no one may boast.
We are his handiwork,{d} created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance as the path for our lives.
Keep in mind, then, that you were once Gentiles by birth,{e} people whom those calling themselves “the circumcision” (a circumcision done in the flesh by hand) called “the uncircumcision.”
Remember that at that time you were without Christ, cut off from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, with no hope and without God in the world.
But now, in Christ Jesus, you who were once far away have come near through Christ’s blood.
For he is our peace. He made the two groups one and broke down the dividing wall that kept them apart,{f}
the hostility, by setting aside in his flesh the law with its commandments and regulations, so that in himself he might create one new humanity{g} out of the two, so making peace,
and that through the cross he might reconcile both of them to God in a single body, killing the hostility by it.{h}
And he came and proclaimed peace to you who were far off and peace to those who were near,{i}
for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.
Consequently you are no longer strangers and outsiders; you are fellow citizens with God’s people and belong to God’s household,
You stand built upon the foundation laid by the apostles and prophets, and its cornerstone is Christ Jesus himself.{j}
In him the whole building is joined together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord.
and in him you too are being built up together to become a place where God lives by the Spirit.

notes.text: Lived your lives: literally “walked,” a Hebrew idiom for one’s conduct; so throughout the letter.
