Children of disobedience: literally “sons of disobedience,” a Hebrew idiom for people marked by disobedience; also in 5:6.
This … God’s gift: the Greek pronoun “this” is neuter and refers to the whole event of salvation by grace through faith, not to “faith” alone (a feminine noun).
Handiwork: Greek *poiēma*, “something made,” a work of craftsmanship or art.
Gentiles: Greek *ethnē*, “nations,” the non-Jewish peoples; so throughout.
Dividing wall: perhaps an allusion to the barrier in the Jerusalem temple that kept Gentiles out of the inner courts on pain of death, a stone warning from which survives.
Humanity: literally “man” (Greek *anthrōpos*, “human being”); also in 4:13, 22, 24.
By it: that is, by the cross; or “in himself.”
Isa 57:19; compare Isa 52:7.
Cornerstone: Greek *akrogōniaios*, the stone that sets the line of a building (Isa 28:16 in the Greek Old Testament); some understand it as the capstone at the top of an arch.

verses.text: This is why I, Paul, am a prisoner of Christ Jesus on behalf of you Gentiles{a} —
assuming that you have heard how God entrusted me with the stewardship{b} of his grace for your benefit:
the secret was disclosed to me by a revelation, as I wrote in brief a little earlier.{c}
When you read this, you will be able to perceive my understanding of the secret of Christ.
This was not disclosed to people{d} in earlier ages as it has now been uncovered by the Spirit to his holy apostles and prophets:
through the gospel the Gentiles are co-heirs with Israel, parts of one body, and partners in the promise in Christ Jesus.
I was made a minister{e} of this gospel through the gift of God’s grace, which was granted to me by the exercise of his power.
Though I am less than the least of all God’s people, I was given this privilege: to announce to the nations the boundless wealth of Christ,
and to bring to light what the plan of the secret is,{f} which for ages past was hidden in God who created all things,
so that through the church the manifold wisdom of God might now be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms.
This was according to the eternal purpose{g} that he carried out in Christ Jesus our Lord,
in whom we have boldness and confident access to God through faith in him.{h}
I ask you, therefore, not to be discouraged by my afflictions on your behalf, for they are your glory.
For this reason I kneel before the Father,{i}
from whom every family{j} in heaven and on earth takes its name.
I pray that from the wealth of his glory he may give you strength, and make you mighty through his Spirit in the inner person,
so that Christ may make his home in your hearts through faith; and that you, rooted and founded firmly in love,
will be strong enough to comprehend, along with all God’s people, how wide, how long, how high, and how deep{k}
is the love of Christ that surpasses understanding, and so be filled with all the fullness of God.
To the one who can accomplish immeasurably more than anything we ask or think, through the power operating within us,
to him be glory in the church and in Christ Jesus through every generation, forever and ever. Amen.

notes.text: Paul breaks off his sentence here and takes it up again in verse 14.
Stewardship: the same Greek word, *oikonomia*, as “plan” in 1:10 and 3:9.
A little earlier: probably referring to 1:9–10 and 2:11–22.
Humankind: literally “the sons of men.”
Servant: Greek *diakonos*, “servant” or “minister,” one who serves on another’s behalf.
To bring to light: many manuscripts add “for all people” (“to make all people see”); the Westcott–Hort text, with the original hand of Sinaiticus and with Alexandrinus, lacks it.
Eternal purpose: literally “purpose of the ages.”
Faith in him: or “his faithfulness.”
The Father: later manuscripts add “of our Lord Jesus Christ.”
Family: Greek *patria*, a family or clan descended from one father, a wordplay on *patēr*, “father.”
Breadth … depth: the object is not stated; probably the love of Christ (verse 19), or the whole scope of God’s purpose.

verses.text: As a prisoner for the Lord, then, I appeal to you to lead a life that is worthy of the call you have received,
Be humble in every way and gentle; be patient, putting up with one another in love,
doing all you can to preserve the unity that the Spirit gives, through the peace that ties you together.
There is one body and one Spirit, as there is one hope to which you were called;
one Lord, one faith, one baptism;
one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.
But to each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift.

That is why it says, “When he went up on high he led captives away,
and he gave gifts to people.”{a}
(Now what does “he went up” mean, except that he had also gone down into the lower regions, the earth?{b}
The one who went down is the same one who also went up far above all the heavens, so that he might fill all things.)
And he is the one who gave certain people to be apostles, others prophets, others evangelists, and others pastors and teachers,{c}
to equip the holy ones for the work of service, for the building up of the body of Christ,
until all of us arrive at the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, at mature adulthood, at the measure of the stature{d} of the fullness of Christ.
Then we will no longer be infants, tossed about by the waves and swept around by every wind of teaching, by human trickery, by craftiness in deceitful scheming.{e}
Rather, as we speak the truth in love, we are to grow in all respects into Christ, who is the head.
from whom the whole body, joined and knit together by every supporting ligament, grows as each part does its work, and builds itself up in love.
This then I tell you, and I insist on it in the Lord: do not go on living like the Gentiles, whose minds are set on empty things.
Their understanding is darkened, and they are estranged from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because their hearts have grown hard.
They have become callous and have given themselves over to indecency, to practice every kind of impurity with greed.
But you did not learn Christ that way —
if indeed you have heard of him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus:
that you were to put away your former way of life, the old self{f} that is being ruined by its deceitful desires,
and to be made new in the spirit of your minds,
and to clothe yourselves with the new self, which has been created after God’s likeness{g} in righteousness and holiness that come from the truth.
So, putting away falsehood, let each of you speak the truth with his neighbor,{h} for we are members of one another.
“Be angry, yet do not sin.”{i} Let the sun not set while you are still angry,
and do not give the devil{j} a foothold.
The thief must no longer steal; rather he must work hard, doing what is good with his own hands, so that he may have something to share with anyone in need.
Let no foul language leave your lips, only what is useful for building others up as the occasion demands, so that your words will bring grace to those who listen.
And do not bring grief to God’s Holy Spirit, with whom you have been sealed for the day when you will be redeemed.{k}
Let all bitterness and rage and anger and shouting and slander be removed from you, along with all malice.
Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, just as God in Christ forgave you.{l}

notes.text: Ps 68:18 (68:19 in Hebrew; 67:19 in the Greek Old Testament), where the Hebrew and the Greek read “you received gifts among people.” The reading “gave” agrees with an interpretation also found in the Aramaic Targum of the Psalms, which applies the verse to Moses giving the law.

The lower regions, the earth: or “the regions lower than the earth,” that is, the realm of the dead. The Greek may mean either the earth itself (the incarnation) or the underworld. Later manuscripts add “first” after “gone down.”
Pastors: Greek *poimenes*, “shepherds.” The Greek groups “pastors and teachers” together, perhaps as one ministry.
Stature: or “age”; Greek *hēlikia* can mean either.
Trickery: Greek *kybeia*, “dice-playing,” cheating.
Self: literally “man” (Greek *anthrōpos*); also in verse 24.
After God’s likeness: literally “according to God.”
Zech 8:16.
Ps 4:4 (4:5 in Hebrew), in the wording of the Greek Old Testament.
Devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer.”
Compare Isa 63:10.
You: some manuscripts read “us.”

verses.text: So be imitators of God, as dearly loved children,
and live in love, just as Christ loved you{a} and gave himself up for you as an offering and a sacrifice to God, a fragrant aroma.{b}
As is fitting among holy people, sexual immorality, any kind of impurity, or greed should not so much as be mentioned among you.
Shameful conduct, silly talk, and coarse jesting are not fitting either; let there be thanksgiving instead.
Of this you may be quite certain: no one who is sexually immoral, impure, or greedy (for greed is idolatry) has a share in the kingdom of Christ and of God.
Let no one deceive you with empty words, for because of these things the wrath of God comes on the children of disobedience.
So do not become partners with them.
There was a time when you were darkness; now, in the Lord, you are light. Conduct yourselves as children of the light,
since what the light produces{c} is every kind of goodness, righteousness, and truth.
Test and discover what pleases the Lord.
Take no part in the fruitless works of darkness; instead, expose them.
For it is shameful even to speak of the things they do in secret.
But everything exposed by the light becomes visible,
Take great care, then, how you conduct yourselves, as wise people and not as fools,
making the most of the time,{e} because the days are evil.
So do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is.
Do not be drunk on wine, for that is the way of ruin;{f} let the Spirit fill you instead,
speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making music to the Lord with your heart,
giving thanks at all times and for all things to God the Father, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ;
and be subject to one another in the fear of Christ.{g}
Wives, submit to your own husbands as to the Lord.{h}
For the husband is head of the wife as Christ also is head of the church; he himself is the Savior of the body.
Just as the church is subject to Christ, wives should also be subject to their husbands in all things.
Husbands, love your wives in the way that Christ loved the church and offered himself on her behalf,
so that he might make her holy, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word,
so that he might present the church to himself glorious, with no stain or wrinkle or any such flaw, holy and without blemish.
So husbands too are bound to love their wives as they love their own bodies; to love one’s wife is to love oneself.
For no one ever hated his own body,{i} but he nourishes it and cares for it, just as Christ does the church,
because we are members of his body.{j}
“For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.”{k}
There is a great secret here, and I take it to refer to Christ and the church.
However, each one of you must also love his wife as himself, and the wife must see that she respects her husband.{l}

notes.text: You: some manuscripts read “us,” here and later in the verse.
A fragrant aroma: literally “an odor of fragrance,” the Greek Old Testament phrase for a sacrifice acceptable to God (Gen 8:21; Exod 29:18).
The light: later manuscripts read “the Spirit,” from Gal 5:22.

Not a quotation of any known Old Testament text; probably an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, drawing on Isa 26:19; 60:1. In the Greek text the first half of verse 14 (“for everything … is light”) completes verse 13.
Making the most of the time: literally “buying up the opportunity.”
The way of ruin: Greek *asōtia*, dissipation, a wasted and unrestrained life (compare Luke 15:13).
Verse 21 completes the sentence that begins in verse 18, and at the same time heads the instructions to the household that follow (5:22–6:9).

Wives, submit: the Greek of the earliest manuscript, P46, and of Vaticanus has no verb here and takes it from verse 21 (“submitting … wives to your husbands”). Other manuscripts supply “let them submit” or “submit.”
Body: literally “flesh.”
Later manuscripts add “of his flesh and of his bones,” from Gen 2:23; the Westcott–Hort text, with P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lacks it.
Gen 2:24, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament.
Respects: literally “fears,” in the sense of reverence or respect.

verses.text: Children, obey your parents in the Lord,{a} for this is right.
“Honor your father and your mother” (this is the first commandment with a promise),
“so that it may go well with you and you may live long on the earth.”{b}
Fathers, do not provoke your children to anger, but bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord.
Slaves,{c} obey those who are your masters in this life,{d} with fear and trembling, with an undivided heart, as though you were obeying Christ;
not only while you are watched, as people-pleasers,{e} but as slaves of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart,
rendering service with goodwill, as to the Lord and not to human beings,
for you know that the Lord will repay each one for whatever good he has done, whether slave or free.
And masters, do the same toward them, and stop threatening them, knowing that both their Master and yours is in heaven, and that with him there is no favoritism.{f}
Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the might of his strength.
Clothe yourselves in God’s full armor,{g} so that you may hold your ground against the devil’s tactics.
We are not wrestling{h} with flesh and blood; we are fighting the rulers, the authorities, the world powers of this present darkness, the spiritual hosts of wickedness in the heavenly realms.
That is why you must take up God’s full armor, so that when the evil day comes you can withstand it, and after you have done all you can, remain standing.
Stand, then, with the belt of truth fastened around your waist,{i} and with righteousness as your breastplate,
and with your feet fitted with readiness{j} for the good news of peace.
Above all, lift the shield of faith,{k} by which you can extinguish all the burning arrows shot by the evil one.
And take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.
Pray at every time in the Spirit, with every prayer and request. To that end stay alert, with all perseverance and petition for all the holy ones,
and also for me, that when I open my mouth, words may be given to me so that I may boldly make known the secret of the good news,{l}
for which I am an ambassador in chains, so that I may declare it boldly, as I ought to speak.
Tychicus,{m} our dear brother and a faithful servant in the Lord, will give you all the news, so that you too may know about my affairs and how I am getting on.
That is exactly why I am sending him to you: to let you know how things stand with us, and to encourage you.
Peace be to the brothers,{n} and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with a love that does not die.{o}

notes.text: In the Lord: the Westcott–Hort text brackets these words, which are absent from Vaticanus and some Western witnesses.

Exod 20:12; Deut 5:16, in the wording of the Greek Old Testament of Deuteronomy. The commandment continues “in the land that Yahweh your God is giving you”; the letter omits these words. *On the earth* can also be translated “in the land.”
Slaves: Greek *douloi*, slaves or bond-servants, as in verses 6 and 8. Slavery was widespread in the Roman world, and many members of the early churches were slaves.
Masters: Greek *kyrioi*, “lords,” the same word as “Lord.” Here “in this life” is literally “according to the flesh.”
Only while you are watched: literally “according to eye-service.”
Favoritism: Greek *prosōpolēmpsia*, literally “receiving of faces,” a Hebrew idiom for partiality.
Full armor: Greek *panoplia*, the complete equipment of a heavily armed soldier. The imagery of verses 14–17 draws on Isa 11:5; 52:7; 59:17.
Wrestling: Greek *palē*, a wrestling match, a struggle.
Waist: literally “loins.”
Readiness: or “firm footing”; Greek *hetoimasia* can mean either.
Shield: Greek *thyreos*, the large, door-shaped shield of a Roman soldier, which could be soaked in water to put out burning arrows.
Of the good news: the Westcott–Hort text brackets these words, which are absent from Vaticanus and some other witnesses.
*Tychicus*: from Greek *tychē*, “fortune,” “fortunate.” He was from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4; Col 4:7; 2 Tim 4:12).
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women.
With a love that does not die: literally “in incorruption,” “in immortality.” The phrase may also go with “grace” or with “our Lord Jesus Christ.” Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Philippians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The oldest manuscripts of Philippians are the papyri P46 (about AD 200) and P16 (3rd–4th century), with Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century); where their readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. The hymn in 2:6–11 is set as poetry. Philippians is one of the seven letters whose authorship by Paul is accepted by nearly all scholars. It was written from prison, most often thought to be in Rome (about AD 60–62), though Ephesus (about AD 54–55) and Caesarea have also been proposed. Some scholars hold that the present letter combines two or three shorter letters (noting the sharp change of tone at 3:2); others defend its unity.

verses.text: From Paul{a} and Timothy,{b} slaves{c} of Christ Jesus,{d} to all God’s holy people{e} in Christ Jesus who live in Philippi,{f} together with the overseers and helpers:{g}
grace and peace to you from God our Father and from the Lord Jesus Christ.
Each time I call you to mind, I thank my God.
In every prayer I offer for you all, my prayer is a joyful one,
because of your partnership in spreading the good news{h} from the very first day until now.
I am confident of this very thing, that the one who began a good work in you will carry it through to its finish, right up to the day of Christ Jesus.

And it is fitting that I should think this of you all, because you are in my heart.{i} All of you are partners with me in grace,{j} in my chains as well as in my defense and confirmation of the good news.
God is my witness how I long for all of you with the deep affection{k} of Christ Jesus.
And I pray this: that your love may grow richer and richer still in knowledge and in every kind of insight,
so that you can approve the things that really matter,{l} and be pure and free from fault on the day of Christ,
filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ, to the glory and praise of God.
Brothers,{m} I want you to understand that what has happened to me has actually served to move the good news forward.
The result is that the whole imperial guard{n} and all the rest have come to see that it is for Christ that I wear these chains.
And most of the brothers, gaining confidence in the Lord from my imprisonment, are daring all the more to speak the word of God without fear.{o}
Some indeed preach Christ because they are envious and quarrelsome; but some do it from good will.
These do it from love, knowing that I am placed here to defend the good news.
The others announce Christ from selfish ambition, not with pure motives, supposing that they will make my chains harder to bear.{p}
What does it matter? Only that in every way, whether for show or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in that I rejoice. Yes, and I will go on rejoicing,
I know that this will turn out for my deliverance,{q} through your prayers and the support of the Spirit of Jesus Christ,
This is my eager expectation and hope: that I will never be put to shame, but that, boldly now as always, Christ will be magnified through my body, whether by my life or by my death.
For me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain.
If I am to go on living in the body, that means fruitful work for me, and I do not know which I prefer.{r}
I am caught between two desires: I long to depart and be with Christ, which would be far better,
but for your sake it is more necessary that I remain in the body.{s}
Convinced of this, I know that I will stay, and stay on with you all, for your progress and joy in the faith,
so that when I come to you once more, your pride in Christ Jesus may abound on my account.

Only, live as citizens{t} worthy of Christ’s good news, so that whether I come and see you or am away and hear about you, I may learn that you are standing firm in a single spirit, contending together as one soul for the faith that the good news brings,
not frightened in any way by your opponents. To them this is a sign of their destruction, but of your salvation, and this comes from God.
For it has been granted to you, for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him,
for you have the same contest on your hands as you once saw me fight, and as you now hear I am fighting still.{u}

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God,” Paul’s coworker, who had helped found the church at Philippi (Acts 16:1–12).
Slaves: Greek *douloi*, slaves or bond-servants, wholly owned by their master.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
God’s holy people: Greek *hagioi*, “holy ones,” traditionally “saints”; the believers as set apart for God.

Philippi: a Roman colony in Macedonia (northern Greece), named after Philip II, father of Alexander the Great. Paul founded the church there about AD 49–50 (Acts 16:11–40); it was his first in Europe.
Overseers and helpers: Greek *episkopoi* and *diakonoi*, traditionally “bishops and deacons,” here probably local leaders and those who served the congregation.
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
Because you are in my heart: or “because you hold me in your heart”; the Greek can be read either way.
Partners with me in grace: or “sharers in my grace,” perhaps meaning the privilege of suffering for Christ (1:29).
Deep affection: Greek *splanchna*, literally “inward parts,” the seat of the emotions; also in 2:1.
Approve the things that really matter: or “test the things that differ.”
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women; so throughout.
Imperial guard: Greek *praitōrion*, either the Praetorian Guard, the emperor’s bodyguard in Rome, or the governor’s headquarters in a provincial capital (as in Acts 23:35).
Of God: some manuscripts lack these words; others read “of the Lord.”
Later manuscripts reverse the order of verses 16 and 17.
This will turn out for my deliverance: the exact wording of Job 13:16 in the Greek Old Testament. *Deliverance* (Greek *sōtēria*) can also mean “salvation,” or vindication before God.
The Greek of this verse is broken and can be punctuated in several ways.
In the body: literally “in the flesh,” as also in verse 22.
Live as citizens: Greek *politeuesthe*, a striking word in a letter to a Roman colony whose people prized their citizenship (compare 3:20).
Compare Acts 16:19–24; 1 Thess 2:2.

verses.text: If, then, Christ gives you any encouragement, if love brings you any consolation, if you have any fellowship in the Spirit,{a} if you know any tenderness and pity,
then complete my joy by thinking alike, having the same love, being one in soul and one in mind.
Do nothing out of rivalry or empty conceit; instead, in humility count others as better than yourselves.
Each of you should keep an eye not just on what concerns yourself, but on what concerns others as well.
Let this mind be in you that was also in Christ Jesus:{b}

but he emptied himself,{e}
taking the form of a slave,
being made in human likeness.
And when he was found in human shape,

he humbled himself
and became obedient as far as death,
even death on a cross.

For this reason God raised him to the very highest
and graciously gave him that name
which is above all names,

so that at Jesus’ name
every knee may bow,
of those in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth,
So, my dear friends, just as you have always obeyed, not only when I was present but much more now that I am absent, work out your own salvation with fear and trembling,
God is the one working in you, both the willing and the doing, for the sake of what pleases him.
Do everything without grumbling or arguing,
so that you may be faultless and pure, God’s children without defect among a warped and crooked generation,{g} in which you shine like stars in the universe,{h}
holding fast{i} the word of life, so that I may have reason to boast on the day of Christ that I did not run in vain or toil in vain.{j}
Even if my life is being poured out like a drink offering{k} on the sacrifice and service that come from your faith, I am glad and I celebrate with every one of you.
You also should be glad, and celebrate with me.
I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I also may be cheered by news of you.
I have no one else like him, who will care with genuine concern for your welfare.
Everyone else is seeking what is his own, not what is Jesus Christ’s.
You know how he has proved himself: like a child alongside his father, he has slaved with me for the good news.
So he is the one I hope to send, the moment I can see what will happen to me.
and I trust in the Lord that I myself will also come soon.
I have thought it necessary, though, to send back to you Epaphroditus,{l} my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, whom you sent as your messenger{m} to minister to my needs.
He has been homesick for you all, and upset that word of his sickness reached you.
He really was sick, almost dying. But God showed mercy to him, and not only to him but to me, so that I would be spared one sorrow after another.
I am the more eager to send him, therefore, so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious.
So welcome him in the Lord with all joy, and hold people like him in honor,
for he nearly died for Christ’s work,{n} gambling with his life to complete the service you yourselves could not give me.

notes.text: Fellowship in the Spirit: or “fellowship with the Spirit,” “a share in the Spirit.”

Let this mind be in you …: or “Think among yourselves in the way that is fitting for those who are in Christ Jesus.” The Greek is compressed and can be read either way. Verses 6–11 are widely thought to be an early Christian hymn, either composed by Paul or quoted by him.
Form: Greek *morphē*, the outward shape that expresses what something truly is; also in verse 7.
Something to be grasped: Greek *harpagmos*, a rare word meaning either something seized or something to be clung to or exploited for one’s own advantage. Scholars are divided.
Emptied himself: Greek *ekenōsen*, “made himself empty” or “poured himself out”; the following phrases explain how.

Verses 10–11: Isa 45:23, where in the Hebrew it is Yahweh who says, “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.” Here the homage due to Yahweh is given to Jesus, and the name above every name (verse 9) is probably *Lord* (*kyrios*), the Greek Old Testament’s rendering of the divine name. *Under the earth*: the realm of the dead.
A crooked and twisted generation: from Deut 32:5 in the Greek Old Testament, where the phrase describes Israel in the wilderness, whose grumbling (verse 14) is a theme of the Exodus story.
Stars: Greek *phōstēres*, “lights,” “luminaries,” the word used of the sun, moon and stars in Gen 1:14–16 and of the wise in Dan 12:3 in the Greek Old Testament.
Holding fast: or “holding out”; Greek *epechō* can mean either.
Compare Isa 49:4; 65:23.
Poured out as a drink offering: Greek *spendomai*, used of wine poured out over or beside a sacrifice (Num 28:7); Paul speaks of his possible death.
*Epaphroditus*: Greek, “charming” or “belonging to Aphrodite,” a common name. He is probably not the same person as Epaphras of Colossae (Col 1:7).
Messenger: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent,” here an envoy of the church, not an apostle in the narrower sense.
Christ’s work: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Vaticanus; other manuscripts read “of the Lord,” and some have neither.

verses.text: Finally, my brothers, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble for me, and for you it is a safeguard.
Beware the dogs! Beware the workers of evil! Beware the cutters!{a}
We are the true circumcision, we who serve by God’s Spirit,{b} take pride in Christ Jesus, and place no trust in human credentials,
I could put confidence in the flesh myself, if I chose. Does someone else imagine he has reason to rely on the flesh? I have more:
I was circumcised when eight days old; I am an Israelite by race, a Benjaminite by tribe,{c} a Hebrew of Hebrew parents; regarding the law I was a Pharisee;
regarding zeal, I persecuted the church; regarding the righteousness that the law requires, I was faultless.
Yet all that was profit to me, I have reckoned as loss for Christ’s sake.
Indeed, I reckon everything a loss, compared with the supreme value of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For him I have lost everything, and I think of it all as garbage,{d} if only I may gain Christ
and be found in him, without any righteousness of my own based on the law, but having the righteousness that is through faith in Christ,{e} a righteousness from God, resting on faith.
I want to know him and the power of his resurrection and the sharing of his sufferings, being shaped to share his death,
in hope that I may somehow arrive at the resurrection from among the dead.
I am not claiming that I have already obtained this or have already been made perfect; but I press on, hoping to grasp the purpose for which Christ Jesus grasped me.
Brothers, I do not reckon that I have yet laid hold of it. Only this: I forget what is behind, I stretch out toward what is in front,
I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.{f}
All of us who are mature should take this view; and if on any point you see things differently, God will make that clear to you as well.
Only let us keep in line with what we have already attained.{g}
Brothers, join together in imitating me, and keep your eyes on those who live by the example you have in us.
For many, as I have often told you before and now tell you weeping, walk as enemies of Christ’s cross.
Destruction is where they will end. Their stomach is their god; they glory in what should shame them; earthly things fill their thoughts.
But our citizenship{h} is in heaven, and from there we are eagerly awaiting a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ.
By the power with which he can make all things subject to himself, he will change the body of our humiliation and conform it to the body of his glory.

notes.text: Dogs … cutters: harsh terms for those who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised. *Dogs* was an insult some Jews used of Gentiles, here turned back on them; *cutters* (Greek *katatomē*, “mutilation,” “cutting up”) is a bitter play on *peritomē*, “circumcision” (verse 3).
By the Spirit of God: some manuscripts, including P46 as reported, read “worship God in the Spirit.”

*Benjamin*: Hebrew, “son of the right hand” (Gen 35:18), the tribe of King Saul, after whom Paul was named. *Pharisee*: probably “separated one,” a member of the lay movement devoted to strict observance of the Law and its traditions.
Garbage: Greek *skybala*, refuse or dung.
Faith in Christ: or “the faithfulness of Christ.”
Prize: Greek *brabeion*, the award given to the winner in the athletic games. *Upward call*: or “heavenly call.”
Later manuscripts add “Let us be of the same mind” and similar words.
Citizenship: Greek *politeuma*, the commonwealth or state to which one belongs; compare 1:27.

verses.text: So then, my brothers, beloved and longed for, you who are my joy and my crown,{a} stand firm like this in the Lord, dear friends.
I appeal to Euodia and I appeal to Syntyche{b} to agree with each other in the Lord.

Yes, and I ask you too, my true companion,{c} help these women, for they have contended side by side with me in the work of the good news, together with Clement{d} and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the book of life.
Rejoice in the Lord always. Again I will say it: rejoice.
Make your gentleness known to all people. The Lord is close at hand.{e}
Stop worrying about anything; in every situation, through prayer and requests with thanksgiving, bring your needs to God.
And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.
Finally, brothers, whatever things are true, worthy of respect, right, pure, lovable, well spoken of — if there is any virtue, any praise — let your thoughts dwell on these.
Put into practice the things you learned from me and received, the things you heard from me and saw in me; and the God of peace will be with you.
It gave me great joy in the Lord that your care for me has blossomed again at last. You were caring all along, of course, but you lacked the chance.
I do not say this out of want; I have learned to be self-sufficient,{f} whatever my situation.

I know what it is to be brought low, and I know what it is to have more than enough. In each and every case I have been initiated into the secret of being full and of being hungry, of abundance and of want.
I can do all things through him who gives me strength.{g}
Yet you did well to share in my distress.
And you Philippians know yourselves that in the early days of the good news, when I set out from Macedonia, no church shared with me in the matter of giving and receiving except you alone.
for even when I was in Thessalonica{h} you sent me something for my need, once and then again.
Not that I seek the gift, but I seek the profit that increases to your credit.{i}
I now have everything, and more than enough. I am amply provided for, having received from Epaphroditus what you sent: a fragrant aroma,{j} a sacrifice that God accepts and finds pleasing.
And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.
To our God and Father be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Greet every holy one in Christ Jesus. The brothers who are with me greet you.
All the holy ones greet you, especially those of Caesar’s household.{k}
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.{l}

notes.text: Crown: Greek *stephanos*, the wreath given to a victor in the games or to an honored guest at a feast.
*Euodia*: Greek, “a good journey” or “fragrance.” *Syntyche*: Greek, “good fortune” or “companion.” Both were women who had worked with Paul (verse 3).
True companion: Greek *gnēsie syzyge*, “genuine yokefellow.” Some take *Syzygus* as a personal name, which would then mean “true to your name.”
*Clement*: Latin *Clemens*, “merciful,” “gentle.”

The Lord is close at hand: or “the Lord is near,” perhaps an echo of Ps 145:18 (144:18 in the Greek Old Testament), where “the Lord” is Yahweh in the Hebrew. The words may refer to the Lord’s nearness in place or to his coming in time.
Self-sufficient: Greek *autarkēs*, “content,” “self-sufficient,” a key term of Stoic philosophy; Paul’s sufficiency comes from the one who strengthens him (verse 13).
Him: later manuscripts read “Christ.”
Thessalonica: the capital of the province of Macedonia, about 90 miles (150 km) west of Philippi (Acts 17:1–9).
Profit … to your credit: the language of bookkeeping, used throughout verses 15–18.
A fragrant aroma: literally “an odor of fragrance,” the Greek Old Testament phrase for a sacrifice acceptable to God (Gen 8:21; Exod 29:18).
Caesar’s household: the slaves and freedmen in the service of the emperor, who worked in Rome and throughout the empire.
Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Colossians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The oldest manuscript of Colossians is the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), with Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century); where their readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord.” *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: the letter names Paul and Timothy as its senders (1:1) and closes with Paul’s own signature (4:18). Its personal greetings closely match those of Philemon. Many modern scholars, pointing to differences of vocabulary, style and thought from the undisputed letters, think it was written by a disciple or coworker of Paul, perhaps Timothy, either late in Paul’s life or soon after his death; others hold that Paul wrote it during his imprisonment, about AD 55–62. The question remains open. Colossae was a small town in the Lycus valley of Phrygia (in modern Turkey), near Laodicea and Hierapolis; the church there was founded not by Paul but by Epaphras (1:7; 2:1).

verses.text: From Paul,{a} an apostle{b} of Christ Jesus{c} through God’s will, and from Timothy{d} our brother,
to the holy and faithful brothers{e} in Christ at Colossae: grace to you and peace from God our Father.{f}
Whenever we pray for you, we give thanks to God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,
since word has reached us of your faith in Christ Jesus and of the love you hold for all God’s holy people.{g}
This springs from the hope stored up for you in heaven. You heard of it before, in the message of truth, the good news{h}
that has come to you. All over the world that good news is bearing fruit and spreading, just as it has done among you since the day you heard it and came to know God’s grace as it truly is.
You learned it from Epaphras,{i} our dear fellow slave, who serves Christ faithfully on our behalf.{j}
It was he who told us of your love in the Spirit.
For this reason, from the day we heard, we have not ceased praying for you. We ask that you may be filled with the knowledge of what God wills, with all the wisdom and understanding the Spirit gives,
so that you may walk worthily of the Lord, pleasing him in all respects, fruitful in good work of every kind, and growing in your knowledge of God;
made strong with all strength, as his glorious might supplies, so that you may endure everything and be patient, with joy;
and thanking the Father, who has made you fit{k} to share the lot of the holy ones in the light.{l}
He rescued us from the dominion of darkness and moved us into the kingdom of the Son he loves.{m}
It is in him that we are redeemed and our sins are forgiven.{n}
He is the image of the invisible God, firstborn before all creation,{o}

since in him all things were created, in the heavens and on the earth, what can be seen and what cannot, whether thrones or lordships or rulers or authorities.{p} Everything has been created through him and for him.
He exists before everything, and in him everything holds together.
He is also the head of the body, the church. He is the beginning, firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things he himself might come to hold first place.
For in him all the fullness was pleased to dwell,{q}
and through him to bring everything back into harmony with himself, establishing peace by the blood shed on his cross{r} — everything on earth and everything in heaven.
You were once estranged from God and his enemies in your thinking, as shown by the wicked things you did;
he has now reconciled{s} in his body of flesh through his death, so as to bring you into his presence holy, spotless and free from any charge,

provided you continue in the faith, grounded and steady and not shifted from the hope held out in the good news you heard. That good news has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and I, Paul, became its servant.{t}
I am glad now to suffer for you. In my own flesh I am completing what remains of Christ’s afflictions,{u} for the sake of his body, the church.
I became the church’s servant by the commission{v} God gave me for your benefit: to bring God’s word to its full completion,
the secret{w} that was kept hidden through ages and generations but has now been revealed to his holy ones.
To them God chose to make known how rich and glorious this secret is among the Gentiles:{x} it is Christ in you, the hope of glory.
He is the one we announce. We warn and instruct everyone, with all the wisdom we have, so that we may present{y} each one mature in Christ.
To this end I toil and strive, with all the energy he so powerfully works in me.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one who is sent,” a messenger with the authority of the sender.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.”
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women; so throughout.
God our Father: later manuscripts add “and the Lord Jesus Christ.”
God’s holy people: Greek *hagioi*, “holy ones,” traditionally “saints”; so throughout.
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
*Epaphras*: a short form of *Epaphroditus*, “charming.” He was a native of Colossae (4:12) who evidently founded the church there; he was later in prison with Paul (Phlm 23).
On our behalf: so the Westcott–Hort text, with P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus as reported; many manuscripts read “on your behalf.”
You: some manuscripts read “us.”
The lot: Greek *klēros*, a portion assigned by lot, as Canaan was shared out among the tribes of Israel (Josh 14:1–2).
The Son he loves: literally “the Son of his love.”
Later manuscripts add “through his blood,” from Eph 1:7.
Firstborn: Greek *prōtotokos*, a title of rank and preeminence as well as of priority in time (compare Ps 89:27). Verses 15–20 are widely thought to be an early Christian hymn.
Thrones … authorities: ranks of spiritual powers, as in Eph 1:21.
All the fullness was pleased: or “God was pleased that all the fullness should dwell”; compare 2:9.
Of his cross: the Westcott–Hort text adds “through him” in brackets.
He has now reconciled: Vaticanus and P46 as reported read “you have now been reconciled.”
Servant: Greek *diakonos*, “servant” or “minister”; also in verse 25.

What remains of Christ’s afflictions: literally “what is lacking of the afflictions of Christ”; not a deficiency in Christ’s saving death, but probably the sufferings that Christ’s people must bear, in which Christ shares (compare Acts 9:4), or the trials expected before the end.
Commission: Greek *oikonomia*, “stewardship,” the task given to a household manager.
Secret: Greek *mystērion*, traditionally “mystery,” not a puzzle but God’s purpose once hidden and now disclosed; so throughout.
Gentiles: Greek *ethnē*, “nations,” the non-Jewish peoples.
Present: that is, present before God.

verses.text: I want you to know how hard I struggle for you, for those at Laodicea,{a} and for everyone who has not seen me face to face.{b}
My goal is that their hearts will be comforted and held together in love, and that they will gain the full wealth of confident understanding and recognize God’s mystery, which is Christ.{c}
In him lie hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
I say this so that no one may mislead you with persuasive talk.
For though I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, and I am delighted to see how orderly you are and how firm your faith in Christ is.{d}
Therefore, as you received Christ Jesus the Lord, so go on living in him,{e}
rooted in him and built up in him, made firm in the faith as you were taught, and brimming over with thanksgiving.
See to it that no one carries you off as plunder by means of philosophy, by hollow deception that follows the traditions of men and the elemental forces of the world,{f} and does not follow Christ.
For in him the whole fullness of deity lives in bodily form,
and it is in him, the head of every ruler and power, that you have been made full.
In him you were also circumcised, with a circumcision not done by hands, by stripping off the body of the flesh,{g} in the circumcision of Christ.
You were buried with him in baptism, and with him you were also raised through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead.
And when you were dead in your wrongdoings and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, God made you alive together with him. He forgave us all our wrongdoings,{h}
He wiped out the bond that was written against us, with its decrees that opposed us.{i} He has taken it out of the way, fastening it with nails to the cross.
He stripped the rulers and authorities,{j} put them on open display, and led them along in his triumphal procession by means of the cross.
So do not let anyone pass judgment on you over food or drink, or in the matter of a festival or new moon or sabbath.
They are only a shadow of things that were coming; the body that casts it is Christ’s.{k}
Let no one disqualify you,{l} insisting on self-abasement and the worship of angels,{m} going on about what he has seen,{n} puffed up without reason by his fleshly mind,
and not holding fast to the head. From him the whole body, supported and held together by its joints and ligaments, grows with a growth that comes from God.
If with Christ you died to the elemental forces of the world, why do you submit to regulations as though you still lived in the world:
“Hands off! Taste nothing! Touch nothing!”
All these things perish as they are used. They are based on human commands and teachings.{o}
These rules do appear wise, with their invented religion, their humility, their harsh handling of the body; but they are worth nothing at all in checking the indulgence of the flesh.{p}

notes.text: Laodicea: a prosperous city about 10 miles (16 km) west of Colossae (compare Rev 3:14–22).
Face to face: literally “my face in the flesh.”

God’s secret, which is Christ: so the Westcott–Hort text (literally “the secret of God, Christ”), reported for P46 and Vaticanus. Few passages have so many variant readings; others include “of God,” “of Christ,” “of God, which is Christ,” “of God the Father of Christ,” and “of God and of the Father and of Christ.” The many forms probably arose as scribes tried to clarify the short reading.
Orderly … firm: military terms, *taxis* (“ranks,” “order”) and *stereōma* (“solid front”).
Living: literally “walking,” a Hebrew idiom for one’s conduct; so throughout.
Elemental forces: Greek *stoicheia*, the basic elements or principles; also in verse 20 (see the note on Gal 4:3).
Later manuscripts add “of sins.”
Us: some manuscripts read “you.”
Bond: Greek *cheirographon*, a handwritten certificate of debt signed by the debtor.
Stripped: or “disarmed.” *Triumphal procession*: as a victorious Roman general paraded his captives through the city. *By means of the cross*: literally “in it”; or “in him.”
The body that casts it: literally “the body,” the reality in contrast to the shadow.
Disqualify: Greek *katabrabeuō*, to rule against someone, as an umpire might deny an athlete the prize.
Worship of angels: either worship offered to angels, or the worship angels offer, which some claimed to share in visions.
Going on about what he has seen: the Greek is obscure. *Embateuō* may mean “enter into,” perhaps a term from initiation rites. Later manuscripts read “what he has not seen.”
Compare Isa 29:13.
The Greek of this verse is difficult, and its last clause can also be understood as “they serve only to indulge the flesh.”

verses.text: Since, then, you were raised together with Christ, aim for what is above, where Christ sits at God’s right hand.{a}
Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.
For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.
When Christ appears, he who is our life,{b} you too will appear with him, in glory.
So put to death whatever in you belongs to the earth:{c} sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed, which is idolatry.
Because of these things the wrath of God is coming.{d}
You too once followed these ways, when you lived among them.
But now you must put all of them away: anger, rage, malice, slander, and foul language from your mouths.
Stop lying to each other. You have taken off the old self{e} and its ways of acting,
and clothed yourselves with the new, which is constantly made new, so as to know God fully, after the likeness of the one who created it.{f}
In this new life it makes no difference whether one is Greek or Jew, circumcised or not, barbarian or Scythian,{g} slave or free. Christ is everything, and he is in everyone.
So then, since God has chosen you, made you holy, and loved you, put on heartfelt compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience as your clothing.
Put up with each other; and if one of you has reason to blame another, be gracious and forgive. The Lord{h} has forgiven you; you must do likewise.
Over all these clothe yourselves with love, the bond that holds all perfection together.{i}
Let the peace of Christ rule{j} in your hearts, since you were called to it as members of one body. And be thankful.
Let Christ’s message live among you in all its fullness. Teach and counsel each other with all wisdom, and with thankful hearts sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs to God.
And whatever you do, in word or deed, do it all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
Wives, be subject to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord.
Husbands, love your wives, and never treat them bitterly.
Children, obey your parents in all things, for in the Lord this is pleasing.
Fathers, do not exasperate your children, so that they do not become discouraged.
Slaves,{k} obey your earthly masters{l} in everything, not only when they are watching, as people-pleasers, but with sincerity of heart, fearing the Lord.
Whatever you do, work at it wholeheartedly, as for the Lord and not for people,
since you know that you will receive the inheritance from the Lord as your reward. You are serving the Lord Christ.
Whoever does wrong will get back the wrong he did, and no partiality will be shown.{m}

notes.text: Sits at God’s right hand: an echo of Ps 110:1 (109:1 in the Greek Old Testament).
Our: some manuscripts read “your.”
Whatever in you belongs to the earth: literally “the members that are on the earth.”
Many manuscripts add “on the children of disobedience,” from Eph 5:6; the Westcott–Hort text, with P46 and Vaticanus as reported, lacks it.
Self: literally “man” (Greek *anthrōpos*, “human being”).
Compare Gen 1:26–27.
Barbarian: one who did not speak Greek. *Scythian*: a people north of the Black Sea, regarded by Greeks as the most uncivilized of barbarians.
The Lord: some manuscripts read “Christ,” others “God.”
The bond that holds all perfection together: literally “the bond of perfection,” or “of completeness.”
Rule: Greek *brabeuō*, to act as umpire.
Slaves: Greek *douloi*, slaves or bond-servants. Slavery was widespread in the Roman world, and many members of the early churches were slaves; compare Philemon.
Masters: Greek *kyrioi*, “lords,” the same word as “Lord” throughout verses 22–24; *earthly* is literally “according to the flesh.”
Partiality: literally “receiving of faces,” a Hebrew idiom for partiality.

verses.text: Masters, give your slaves what is right and fair; remember that you also have a Master in heaven.
Keep at prayer, staying alert in it with thanksgiving.
And pray for us at the same time, asking God to open up a door for the word, that we may speak of Christ’s secret, the reason I am bound,
and that I may make it clear, as I ought to speak.
Walk in wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the time.{a}
Your words should always be full of grace and flavored with salt, so that you will know what answer to give to each one.
Tychicus{b} will tell you all about my affairs. He is a dear brother, a faithful servant and a fellow slave in the Lord.
That is the very reason I have sent him to you: to let you know our situation,{c} and to bring comfort to your hearts.
He comes with Onesimus,{d} our faithful and dear brother, who is one of you. They will tell you about everything here.
Greetings from Aristarchus,{e} who is in prison with me, and from Mark, Barnabas’s cousin.{f} You have had orders concerning Mark: make him welcome if he comes to you.
Greetings, too, from Jesus called Justus.{g} Of the circumcised, these three alone are working with me for God’s kingdom, and they have proved a great comfort to me.
Epaphras, who is one of you, a slave of Christ Jesus, sends greetings. He is always wrestling in his prayers on your behalf, that you may stand mature and fully assured in all the will of God.
For I testify that he has worked hard for you and for those in Laodicea and in Hierapolis.{h}
Luke,{i} the beloved physician, greets you, and so does Demas.{j}
Greet the brothers at Laodicea, and also Nympha, with the church that meets in her house.{k}
And when this letter has been read among you, see that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea.{l}
And tell Archippus,{m} “See that you complete the ministry you have received in the Lord.”
I, Paul, write this greeting with my own hand.{n} Remember my chains. Grace be with you.{o}

notes.text: Making the most of the time: literally “buying up the opportunity.”
*Tychicus*: from Greek *tychē*, “fortune,” “fortunate.” He was from the province of Asia (Acts 20:4; Eph 6:21–22).
Our situation: literally “the things concerning us”; so the Westcott–Hort text; many manuscripts read “that he may know your situation.”
*Onesimus*: Greek, “useful,” a common name for slaves. He is the runaway slave of the letter to Philemon (Phlm 10).
*Aristarchus*: Greek, “best ruler.” He was from Thessalonica and traveled with Paul (Acts 19:29; 20:4; 27:2).
*Mark*: Latin *Marcus*, a common Roman name; the John Mark of Acts 12:12, 25; 15:37–39. *Barnabas*: interpreted in Acts 4:36 as “son of encouragement.”
*Jesus*: a common Jewish name, the Greek form of Joshua. *Justus*: Latin, “just,” “righteous,” a name often taken by Jews.
Hierapolis: a city about 6 miles (10 km) north of Laodicea, famous for its hot springs.
*Luke*: Latin *Lucas*, perhaps short for *Lucanus* or *Lucius*. By tradition he is the author of the Gospel of Luke and Acts.
*Demas*: probably a short form of *Demetrius*, “belonging to Demeter.” He later deserted Paul (2 Tim 4:10).
*Nympha*: Greek, “bride,” a woman’s name. Some manuscripts read the man’s name *Nymphas* and “his house”; others read “their house.”
The letter from Laodicea: a letter otherwise unknown, unless it is the letter now called Ephesians (see the note on Eph 1:1) or Philemon. A later forged “Letter to the Laodiceans” survives in Latin.
*Archippus*: Greek, “master of horses.” He is also greeted in Phlm 2.
Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe and added a closing in his own handwriting (2 Thess 3:17).
Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: 1 Thessalonians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early manuscripts are Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century), with portions in the papyri P46 (about AD 200), P30 and P65 (3rd century); where their readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Verse divisions at 2:6–7 and 2:11–12 differ slightly among editions. First Thessalonians is accepted as Paul’s by nearly all scholars and is probably the earliest surviving Christian writing, sent from Corinth about AD 50, a few months after Paul, Silvanus and Timothy had founded the church in Thessalonica (Acts 17:1–10; 18:5).

verses.text: Paul,{a} Silvanus{b} and Timothy,{c} to the church of the Thessalonians{d} in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:{e} grace to you, and peace.{f}
At all times we thank God for every one of you, and mention you in our prayers.
Without ceasing we call to mind, before our God and Father, how your faith is at work, how your love labors, and how your hope in our Lord Jesus Christ holds steady.{g}
For we know, brothers{h} whom God loves, that he has chosen you,
for our gospel message{i} reached you not merely as words but with power, with the Holy Spirit, and with full assurance. You remember how we conducted ourselves among you, for your benefit.
And you became imitators of us and of the Lord; in spite of great affliction you welcomed the message with the joy the Holy Spirit gives.
As a result you became an example to every believer in Macedonia and Achaia.{j}
The Lord’s word has sounded forth from you like a trumpet, and not in Macedonia and Achaia only; in every place the news of your faith toward God has spread abroad, so we need say nothing about it.
People themselves report what kind of welcome we had among you, and how you turned to God from idols, to serve a God who is living and true,
and to wait for his Son from heaven, Jesus, whom he raised from the dead, who rescues us from the wrath that is coming.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
*Silvanus*: Latin, “of the forest,” the Roman form of the name *Silas* (Acts 15:40; 17:4), probably from Aramaic *She’ila*, “asked for.”
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.”
Thessalonians: the people of Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia, a major port on the Egnatian Way, the road that crossed northern Greece.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
Later manuscripts add “from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”
Holds steady: literally “the endurance of hope.”
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women; so throughout.
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
Macedonia … Achaia: the two Roman provinces of northern and southern Greece.

verses.text: You yourselves know, brothers, that our visit to you was not in vain.
As you know, we had already suffered and been shamefully treated at Philippi,{a} yet with our God’s help we found the courage to tell you God’s good news in the face of great opposition.
For our appeal did not spring from error or impure motives, nor did it use trickery.
Rather, just as God has tested us and entrusted us with the good news, so we speak, not to please human beings, but to please God, who tests our hearts.
As you know, we never came with flattering words, nor with a pretext for greed — God is our witness —
We did not look for praise from people, whether from you or anyone else, though as apostles{b} of Christ we might have insisted on our importance.{c}
Instead we became like little children among you.{d} As a nurse cherishes her own children,
In the same way, because we cared so much for you, we were delighted to give you not just God’s gospel but our own selves, since you had grown so precious to us.
You remember, brothers and sisters, our hard work and exhaustion: we labored night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you while we announced God’s gospel to you.
You can testify, and so can God, how holy, upright and beyond reproach our conduct was among you who believe.
You know how, like a father with his own children, we treated each one of you, encouraging and comforting you
and pleading with you to walk{e} in a manner that befits the God who is calling you to his own kingdom and glory.

This is another reason we give thanks to God unceasingly: when the word of God reached you through our preaching, you took it in, not as the word of mere humans, but as what it really is, God’s word, now active in you who believe.
For you, brothers, have followed the pattern of the churches of God in Judea that are in Christ Jesus. You have suffered from your own fellow citizens just as they did from the Judeans,{f}
who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets, and drove us out. They displease God and oppose all people,
who try to stop us speaking to the Gentiles{g} for their salvation. In this way they are always filling up their sins to the brim. But the wrath has overtaken them at last.{h}
But we, brothers, when we were torn away from you for a short time,{i} in person but not in heart, longed all the more eagerly to see you face to face.
We wanted to visit you — I, Paul, again and again{j} — but Satan{k} stood in our way.
For who is our hope, our joy, the crown we will boast of in the presence of our Lord Jesus when he comes?{l} Who, if not you?
Yes, you are our glory and our joy.

notes.text: Philippi: see Acts 16:19–40.
Apostles: Greek *apostoloi*, “those who are sent,” messengers with the authority of the sender.
Made our weight felt: or “been a burden to you” (compare 2:9); the Greek *en barei* can mean either weight of authority or financial burden. In some editions these words begin verse 7.

Like little children: Greek *nēpioi*, “infants,” the reading of the Westcott–Hort text and of the earliest manuscripts, including P65, the original hand of Sinaiticus, and Vaticanus as reported. Many manuscripts read *ēpioi*, “gentle,” which differs by a single letter; the preceding word ends in *n*, so either could have arisen from the other by a slip of the eye. Many modern translations prefer “gentle” as better suited to the context.
Walk: a Hebrew idiom for one’s conduct; so throughout.
The Judeans: Greek *Ioudaioi*, here probably the people of Judea who opposed the churches there, not the Jewish people as a whole; Paul himself and the Judean churches were Jewish.
Gentiles: Greek *ethnē*, “nations,” the non-Jewish peoples.

At last: or “completely,” “to the end.” Because of the harshness of verses 14–16 and the apparent reference to a past disaster, some scholars think they were added after the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70; no manuscript lacks them, and most scholars regard them as Paul’s.
A short time: literally “a season of an hour,” an idiom for a brief time.
More than once: literally “both once and twice,” an idiom.
Satan: Hebrew, “adversary,” “accuser.”
When he comes: literally “at his coming,” Greek *parousia*, “presence,” “arrival,” used of the visit of a ruler; so throughout. *Crown*: the victor’s wreath.

verses.text: So, since we could stand it no longer, we thought it best to stay behind in Athens{a} by ourselves,
and we sent Timothy, our brother and God’s servant{b} in the good news of Christ, to make you firm and to encourage you for the sake of your faith,
so that none of you would be unsettled by these troubles. You know well that we are appointed for them.
In fact, when we were with you, we kept telling you beforehand that we were going to suffer affliction, and so it has turned out, as you know.
So I too, unable to stand it any longer, sent to learn how your faith was holding up. I feared that the tempter might somehow have tempted you, and that all our work would come to nothing.

Timothy, however, has come back to us from you just now, bringing good news of your faith and your love. He tells us that your memories of us are always warm, and that you long to see us, as we long to see you.
That is why, brothers, your faith has comforted us concerning you, in the midst of all our hardship and trouble.
For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord.
What thanks can we ever give back to God for you, for all the joy with which we rejoice over you in our God’s presence?
Night and day we beg him, with the utmost urgency, to let us see your faces and make good whatever your faith still lacks.
Now may our God and Father himself, and our Lord Jesus, direct our way to you.
And as for you, may the Lord cause your love to grow and overflow, toward each other and toward everyone, just as ours does toward you,
so that he may strengthen your hearts to be blameless in holiness before our God and Father at the coming of our Lord Jesus with all his holy ones.{c}

notes.text: Athens: see Acts 17:15–34.

God’s servant: so the Westcott–Hort text, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus as reported. Some manuscripts, reportedly including Vaticanus, read “God’s coworker”; others read “our coworker,” and many combine the two.
With all his holy ones: echoing Zech 14:5, “Yahweh my God will come, and all the holy ones with him.” The holy ones may be angels or God’s people, or both. Some manuscripts add “Amen.”

verses.text: Finally, brothers and sisters, we beg and encourage you in the Lord Jesus: you received instruction from us about the way you must live to please God (and you do live that way); now excel even more.
For you know what instructions we gave you through the Lord Jesus.
For this is the will of God, your sanctification:{a} that you abstain from sexual immorality;
that each of you learn to master his own body{b} in a holy and respectful way,
not with lustful passion as the Gentiles have, who know nothing of God;
and that no one transgress against and wrong his brother in this matter, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things,{c} as we told you before and solemnly warned you.
God called us not for uncleanness but to be holy.
So whoever rejects this rejects not a human being but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you.{d}
As for love among believers, there is no need for anyone to write to you, since you have been taught by God himself to love each other.
And you are in fact doing so toward all the brothers in the whole of Macedonia. Still, brothers, we urge you to excel in it even more,
and to aim at a quiet life, attending to your own business and earning your living by the work of your own hands, just as we told you,
so that your conduct will win the respect of outsiders and you will lack nothing.
Friends, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who have fallen asleep in death,{e} so that you will not grieve like everyone else, who has no hope.
For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, so too through Jesus God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep.{f}
For this we declare to you by a word of the Lord: we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go ahead of those who have fallen asleep.
The Lord himself will descend from heaven with a shout of command, with an archangel’s voice, and with God’s trumpet, and those who died in Christ will rise first.{g}
Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord.{h}
So encourage one another with these words.

notes.text: Sanctification: Greek *hagiasmos*, being made holy; also in verses 4 and 7.
Gain control over his own body: literally “acquire his own vessel.” *Vessel* may mean one’s own body, or, as some interpret it, a wife (“take a wife for himself”).
The Lord is an avenger: an echo of Ps 94:1 (93:1 in the Greek Old Testament), “God of vengeance, Yahweh,” and of Deut 32:35. Here *Lord* probably refers to Jesus as judge.
Gives his Holy Spirit to you: an echo of Ezek 36:27; 37:14 in the Greek Old Testament.
Asleep in death: literally “sleeping,” a common euphemism for death; so also “fallen asleep” in verses 14–15.
Through Jesus: these words may go with “fallen asleep” (“those who have fallen asleep through Jesus,” that is, as believers) or, as here, with “bring.”
Trumpet: in the Old Testament the trumpet announces the coming of God and the gathering of his people (Exod 19:16; Isa 27:13; Joel 2:1; Zech 9:14).
To meet: Greek *eis apantēsin*, used of a delegation going out from a city to welcome an arriving dignitary and escort him back.

verses.text: Now concerning the times and the seasons, brothers, you have no need for anything to be written to you.
You know perfectly well yourselves that the day of the Lord{a} is coming the way a thief comes by night.
When they are saying, “All is peaceful and secure,”{b} ruin will come on them all at once, like birth pains on a woman with child, and there will be no escape for them.
You, though, brothers, are not living in the dark, so that the day should catch you unawares as daylight catches thieves.{c}
Every one of you is a child of light and a child of the day.{d} We are not of the night, nor of the darkness.
So we must not sleep like everyone else, but stay alert and keep our heads clear.
Sleepers sleep by night, and drinkers get drunk by night.
But because we belong to the day, let us keep clear heads, protected by the breastplate of faith and love and wearing the hope of salvation as a helmet.{e}
God did not appoint us to suffer wrath; he appointed us to win salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ.
He died for us so that, awake or asleep, we may live together with him.
So comfort each other and strengthen each other, as indeed you already do.
We ask you, brothers, to respect those who labor among you, who lead you in the Lord and admonish you,
and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace among yourselves.
We appeal to you, brothers: warn those who are out of line,{f} cheer up the discouraged, hold on to the weak, and be patient toward everyone.
See to it that no one returns harm for harm; rather, always aim at what is good, for one another and for all.
Rejoice always,
pray without ceasing,
whatever happens, give thanks; this is what God wills for you in Christ Jesus.
Do not quench the Spirit.
Do not despise prophecies,
but test everything; hold fast what is good.
Abstain from every form of evil.
Now may the God of peace himself sanctify you completely, and may your spirit and soul and body be kept whole and blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
The one calling you can be trusted, and he will do it.
Brothers, pray for us also.
Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss.
By the Lord I charge you to have this letter read aloud to every brother and sister.{g}
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.{h}

notes.text: The day of the Lord: in the Old Testament, the day of Yahweh, when God comes to judge and to save (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31; Zeph 1:14–18); here applied to the coming of the Lord Jesus.
All is peaceful and secure: literally “peace and security,” perhaps a slogan of Roman imperial propaganda (Latin *pax et securitas*); compare also Jer 6:14.
As daylight catches thieves: literally “like thieves,” the reading of the Westcott–Hort text, with Alexandrinus and Vaticanus as reported. Many manuscripts read “like a thief,” as in verse 2.
Child: literally “son,” a Hebrew idiom for one marked by something.
Compare Isa 59:17.
Out of line: Greek *ataktoi*, “disorderly,” traditionally “idle,” perhaps those who had stopped working (compare 4:11; 2 Thess 3:6–12).
Every brother and sister: literally “all the brothers”; later manuscripts read “all the holy brothers.”
Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: 2 Thessalonians
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early manuscripts are Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus (4th century), with portions in the papyrus P92 (3rd–4th century); where their readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation or phrase, a note says so. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: the letter names Paul, Silvanus and Timothy as its senders (1:1) and closes with Paul’s signature (3:17). Many scholars accept it as Paul’s, written from Corinth soon after 1 Thessalonians, about AD 50–51. Many others think it was written later in Paul’s name, pointing to its close imitation of the wording of 1 Thessalonians alongside a different teaching about the timing of the end (compare 2:1–12 with 1 Thess 5:1–3), and to the warning about letters falsely claiming to come from Paul (2:2; 3:17). The question remains open.

verses.text: Paul,{a} Silvanus{b} and Timothy,{c} to the Thessalonians’ church,{d} which is in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ:{e}
grace and peace be yours from God the Father{f} and the Lord Jesus Christ.
We are bound to thank God for you at all times, brothers,{g} and rightly so, because your faith is growing beyond measure, and the love that every one of you has for one another keeps on increasing.
So we ourselves boast about you among God’s churches, telling of your endurance and faith through all the persecutions and troubles you are bearing.
This is evidence of God’s just judgment, and its purpose is that you should be counted worthy of God’s kingdom, for which you are indeed suffering.
For it is surely just in God’s eyes to repay with trouble those who are troubling you,
and to grant rest to you who are afflicted, and to us too, at the revealing of the Lord Jesus from heaven with his powerful angels
in a blaze of fire,{h} dealing out vengeance to those who have no knowledge of God and to those who will not heed the good news{i} of our Lord Jesus.
These will pay the penalty of everlasting ruin, shut out from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might,{j}
on that day when he comes to be glorified in his holy ones and to be marveled at among all who have believed; and you are among them, because you believed our testimony.{k}

With this in view we pray for you constantly, asking our God to make you worthy of his calling and by his power to bring to completion every desire you have for goodness and every work that faith produces,
so that our Lord Jesus’ name will be honored through you, and you through him, according to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus Christ.{l}

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
*Silvanus*: Latin, “of the forest,” the Roman form of the name *Silas* (Acts 15:40; 17:4).
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.”
Thessalonians: the people of Thessalonica, the capital of the Roman province of Macedonia (see 1 Thess 1:1).
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
God the Father: some manuscripts read “God our Father.”
Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women; so throughout.
In a blaze of fire: literally “in a fire of flame,” echoing Isa 66:15 and Exod 3:2. Some manuscripts read “in flaming fire.”
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.

From the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might: words from Isa 2:10, 19, 21 in the Greek Old Testament, where the Hebrew has “from before the terror of Yahweh and from the splendor of his majesty.”
Glorified in his holy ones … that day: echoing Ps 89:7 (88:8 in the Greek Old Testament) and Isa 2:11, 17, where the glory and the day belong to Yahweh.

So that the name … may be glorified: echoing Isa 66:5 in the Greek Old Testament. *Our God and the Lord Jesus Christ*: or “our God and Lord, Jesus Christ.” Because “Lord” lacks the article in Greek, a few interpreters take both titles to refer to Jesus (compare Titus 2:13); but “Lord Jesus Christ” often occurs without the article, and most take the phrase to name God and Jesus separately.

verses.text: Now, brothers, concerning the coming{a} of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we ask you
not to be quickly shaken in your thinking or alarmed, whether by a spirit, or by a spoken word, or by a letter supposed to be from us, claiming that the day of the Lord has already arrived.{b}
Do not let anyone lead you astray in any way. That day will not come unless the rebellion{c} happens first, and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the one destined for destruction.{d}
He is the adversary who lifts himself up over everything that people call a god or venerate, until he goes so far as to sit down in God’s temple and display himself as being God.{e}
Do you not remember that I kept telling you these things when I was still with you?
And you know what is holding him back now, so that he will be revealed at his proper time.
For the secret{f} of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now holds it back will do so until he is taken out of the way.{g}
Then the lawless one will be exposed, and the Lord{h} will destroy him by the breath from his mouth and put an end to him at the brightness of his arrival.{i}
The coming of the lawless one is by the working of Satan,{j} with all power and with signs and wonders that serve the lie,
and with every kind of unrighteous trickery aimed at the perishing, who would not welcome a love for the truth that would have saved them.
For this reason God sends them a power that leads them astray, so that they believe what is false,
in order that all who have not believed the truth but have delighted in wickedness may be condemned.
