But we are bound to thank God for you always, brothers loved by the Lord, because God chose you from the beginning{k} to be saved, through the Spirit’s work of making you holy and through your faith in the truth.
To this he called you through our good news, so that you might obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.
So then, brothers, stand firm and hold on to the traditions that you were taught by us, whether by word of mouth or by our letter.
Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and by grace gave us eternal encouragement and good hope,
encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.

notes.text: Coming: Greek *parousia*, “presence,” “arrival,” used of the visit of a ruler; also in verses 8 and 9.

The day of the Lord: in the Old Testament, the day of Yahweh, when God comes to judge and to save (Amos 5:18–20; Joel 2:31); here applied to the coming of the Lord Jesus. Later manuscripts read “the day of Christ.” *By a spirit*: that is, by a prophetic utterance.
Rebellion: Greek *apostasia*, “revolt,” “falling away.”
Man of lawlessness: many manuscripts read “man of sin.” *The one destined for destruction*: literally “the son of destruction,” a Hebrew idiom.
Compare Dan 11:36; Ezek 28:2.
Secret: Greek *mystērion*, traditionally “mystery,” here the hidden working of lawlessness.

The one who now holds it back: Greek *ho katechōn* (masculine), following *to katechon* (neuter), “what is holding him back,” in verse 6. Paul’s readers knew what he meant (verse 5), but it is unknown today. Suggestions include the Roman empire and its emperor, the preaching of the good news and Paul himself, an angel, or God’s own restraint.
The Lord: the Westcott–Hort text adds “Jesus” in brackets, with Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus as reported.

Slay with the breath of his mouth: from Isa 11:4, where the shoot of Jesse “will kill the wicked with the breath of his lips.” Some manuscripts read “consume” for “slay.” *Splendor*: Greek *epiphaneia*, “appearing,” “manifestation.”
Satan: Hebrew, “adversary,” “accuser.”
From the beginning: some manuscripts, reportedly including Vaticanus, read *aparchēn*, “as firstfruits,” instead of *ap’ archēs*, “from the beginning.”

verses.text: Finally, brothers, pray for us, that the word of the Lord may spread swiftly and be honored, as it was among you,{a}
and that we will be delivered from twisted and wicked people, since not everyone has faith.
Yet the Lord keeps faith: he will make you firm and protect you from the evil one.{b}
Our trust in the Lord concerning you is that you are carrying out our instructions now and will keep carrying them out.
May the Lord direct your hearts to the love of God and to the endurance of Christ.
We command you, brothers and sisters, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, to stay away from any believer who lives in idleness{c} and not by the teaching they received from us.{d}
You know well enough how to follow our example: there was nothing idle in our conduct while we lived among you.
We did not take free meals from anybody; we toiled and labored, working night and day, so that we would be a burden to none of you.
Not that we lack the right to support; we wanted to make ourselves a pattern for you to copy.
Even while we were with you, we gave you this rule: anyone unwilling to work should not eat.
For we hear that some among you are living in idleness, not busy at work but busybodies.{e}
Such people we instruct and appeal to in the Lord Jesus Christ: let them settle down to their work quietly and eat bread they have earned.{f}
But you, brothers, must never tire of doing what is right.
Should anyone refuse to heed our word in this letter, mark him out and keep apart from him, so that he will feel shame.
Yet do not treat him as a foe; admonish him as you would a brother.
Now may the Lord of peace himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with you all.
This greeting is in my own handwriting: Paul. It is the sign of genuineness in all my letters; this is my hand.{g}
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all.{h}

notes.text: Spread swiftly: literally “run”; compare Ps 147:15 (147:4 in the Greek Old Testament).
The evil one: or “evil.”
In idleness: Greek *ataktōs*, “in a disorderly way,” “out of line”; also in verses 7 and 11. The context shows that the disorder was a refusal to work.
They received: some manuscripts read “you received.”
Not busy … busybodies: a wordplay in Greek, *mēden ergazomenous alla periergazomenous*.
Eat bread they have earned: literally “eat their own bread.”
Paul usually dictated his letters to a scribe and added a closing in his own handwriting (1 Cor 16:21; Gal 6:11; Col 4:18).
Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: 1 Timothy
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early manuscripts are Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi (4th–5th century); Codex Vaticanus lacks this letter. Where manuscript readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation, a note says so. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus, often called the Pastoral Letters, name Paul as their author. The traditional view holds that Paul wrote them near the end of his life, perhaps after a release from the imprisonment described in Acts 28. Many modern scholars think they were written by a follower of Paul in his name, perhaps around AD 80–110, pointing to differences from the undisputed letters in vocabulary, style, church organization and the settings they describe. Others hold that Paul wrote them, perhaps through a secretary who shaped their wording. The question remains open.

verses.text: Paul,{a} apostle{b} of Christ Jesus under orders from God our Savior and from Christ Jesus, who is our hope,{c}
to Timothy,{d} his true son in the faith: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
As I was leaving for Macedonia,{e} I asked you to remain in Ephesus{f} so you could instruct certain individuals to quit teaching a different doctrine
and to stop occupying themselves with myths and with genealogies that go on without end. These breed speculation rather than God’s ordering of things,{g} which is known by faith.
The aim of that charge is love, springing from a clean heart, a good conscience and faith without pretense.
Some have missed the mark here and wandered off into empty talk.
They want to be teachers of the law, yet they have no understanding either of the words they use or of the matters they insist on so confidently.
Now we know that the law is a fine thing, provided it is used lawfully,

with this understanding: law is not laid down for an upright person but for those who flout law and will not be ruled, for the godless and sinful, for the unholy and profane, for those who strike their fathers or mothers, for murderers,
the sexually immoral, men who lie with males,{h} kidnappers,{i} liars, perjurers, and whatever else stands opposed to healthy teaching,
in keeping with the glorious good news{j} of the blessed God, which was entrusted to me.
I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who has empowered me, because he considered me faithful and placed me in his service,
though in time past I was a blasphemer, a persecutor and a man of violence. But I was shown mercy, because I acted in ignorance, in unbelief,
and the grace of our Lord overflowed beyond measure, together with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus.
Here is a saying to be trusted and worthy of complete acceptance:{k} Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners. And of these I am the foremost.

Yet this is exactly why mercy was shown me: Christ Jesus meant to make me, the chief of sinners, the first showcase of all his patience, a pattern for those who would later put their trust in him and gain life everlasting.
To the eternal King, the immortal, unseen, only God,{l} be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.
This charge I commit to you, Timothy my son, in line with the prophecies once spoken about you, so that by their help you may fight the good fight,{m}
holding on to faith and a good conscience. By thrusting conscience aside, some have made shipwreck of their faith.
Hymenaeus and Alexander{n} are among them, and I have turned them over to Satan{o} so that discipline will teach them not to slander God.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent,” a messenger or envoy.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.”
Macedonia: the Roman province in northern Greece.
Ephesus: the chief city of the Roman province of Asia, on the western coast of modern Turkey.
God’s ordering of things: Greek *oikonomia theou*, “God’s household management,” that is, his plan or arrangement; some manuscripts read *oikodomēn*, “God’s building up.”

Men who lie with males: Greek *arsenokoitai*, a rare compound of “male” and “bed,” apparently drawn from Lev 18:22 and 20:13 in the Greek Old Testament; compare 1 Cor 6:9. Its precise range of meaning is debated.
Kidnappers: or “slave traders,” those who seize people to sell them.
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
A saying to be trusted: literally “faithful is the word,” a formula found in these letters (3:1; 4:9; 2 Tim 2:11; Titus 3:8) to introduce or confirm a saying.
The only God: later manuscripts read “the only wise God.”
Fight the good fight: literally “wage the good warfare.”
*Hymenaeus*: Greek, named after Hymen, the god of weddings; compare 2 Tim 2:17. *Alexander*: Greek, “defender of men”; perhaps the man of 2 Tim 4:14.
Satan: Hebrew, “adversary,” “accuser.” *Handed over to Satan*: compare 1 Cor 5:5; probably exclusion from the church’s fellowship.

verses.text: My first request, then, is this: let petitions, prayers, pleas and thanksgivings be made for everyone,
for kings and all who hold high positions, so that we may lead a peaceful and quiet life in all godliness and dignity.
This is good, and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,
whose will is that all people be saved and come to know the truth.

For there is one God,
and one mediator also between God and humankind,
the man Christ Jesus,

who offered himself as a ransom on behalf of all,
the witness borne at the right moment.{a}
For this I was appointed a herald and an apostle (I speak the truth, I am not lying),{b} a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth.
So I want the men everywhere to pray, raising holy hands, without anger or quarreling.
Likewise the women should adorn themselves in fitting dress, with modesty and good sense, not with braided hair and gold or pearls{c} or costly clothes,
but with what suits women who profess reverence for God, namely good works.
A woman should learn in quietness, in full submission.
I do not permit a woman to teach or to domineer over a man;{d} she is to remain quiet.
For Adam was formed first, and Eve after him.{e}
And Adam was not the one deceived; the woman was deceived and became a transgressor.{f}
Yet she will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith and love and holiness, with good sense.{g}

notes.text: The testimony given at the proper time: literally “the testimony in its own times.” Verses 5–6 may quote an early confession; the setting as verse here is editorial.
I speak the truth: later manuscripts add “in Christ.”
Pearls: in the ancient world among the costliest of gems.

Domineer over: Greek *authentein*, found only here in the New Testament. Its sense is debated: “have authority over,” “assume authority over,” or “dominate.” *A woman … a man*: or “a wife … her husband”; the same Greek words serve for both.
*Adam*: Hebrew, “human being,” related to *adamah*, “ground” (Gen 2:7). *Eve*: Hebrew *Chawwah*, “living” (Gen 3:20).
Compare Gen 3:13.

Saved through childbearing: the meaning is much debated. Proposals include being kept safe in childbirth; being saved through the birth of the Messiah (compare Gen 3:15); or being saved while fulfilling an ordinary role as wife and mother. *They*: probably women generally, or the women and their children.

verses.text: Here is a trustworthy saying:{a} whoever sets his heart on being an overseer{b} is longing for a fine task.
An overseer, then, must be above reproach, the husband of one wife,{c} clear-headed, self-controlled, orderly, hospitable, able to teach,
not a heavy drinker,{d} not a brawler but gentle, not quarrelsome, free from the love of money.
He should govern his own home well and have children who obey him with all proper respect.
If someone cannot govern his own home, how can he look after the church of God?
He should not be newly converted,{e} in case pride goes to his head and he falls into the condemnation that came on the devil.{f}
He must also be well thought of by outsiders, so that he does not fall into disgrace and into the devil’s trap.
Deacons{g} likewise must be worthy of respect, not double-tongued, not addicted to much wine, not out for shameful gain.
They must hold the secret{h} of the faith with a clear conscience.
And they too should first be tested; then, if no charge can be brought against them, let them serve as deacons.
Women, likewise,{i} must be worthy of respect, not slanderers, clear-headed, faithful in everything.
Each deacon is to be the husband of one wife and to govern his children and his home well.
Those who serve well in this office win for themselves an honorable rank and much confidence in the faith that rests in Christ Jesus.
Though I expect to be with you soon, I am sending you these instructions
so that, should I be held up, you may know what conduct befits those in God’s house, the church of the living God, which upholds the truth as a pillar and a base.

And beyond all question great is the secret of our godliness:
He who was made visible in the flesh,{j}
was vindicated in the Spirit,{k}
was seen by angels,
was proclaimed among the nations,
was believed in throughout the world,
was taken up in glory.

notes.text: A trustworthy saying: some manuscripts read “a human saying,” perhaps meaning “a common saying.”
Overseer: Greek *episkopos*, “one who watches over,” traditionally “bishop.” In these letters the overseers appear to be the same as the elders (compare Titus 1:5–7).

The husband of one wife: literally “a man of one woman.” This may forbid polygamy, remarriage after divorce or after a spouse’s death, or unfaithfulness; the precise sense is debated. So also in verse 12.
Not a heavy drinker: literally “not given to wine.”
Newly converted: Greek *neophytos*, “newly planted.”
The devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer”; so also in verse 7. *The condemnation that came on the devil*: or “the condemnation the devil brings.”
Deacons: Greek *diakonoi*, “servants,” “ministers”; here church officers.
Secret: Greek *mystērion*, traditionally “mystery”; so also in verse 16.
Women: or “wives,” that is, the deacons’ wives; or women who serve as deacons (compare Rom 16:1).

He who: so the earliest manuscripts, reportedly including Sinaiticus before correction, Alexandrinus and Ephraemi before correction (Greek *hos*). Some manuscripts read “which” (*ho*), agreeing with “secret.” Later manuscripts read “God” (*theos*), a change easily made in Greek manuscripts, where *hos* (ΟΣ) and the abbreviation for *theos* (ΘΣ) differ by two small strokes. The lines that follow are widely thought to quote an early hymn; the setting as verse is editorial.
Vindicated in the Spirit: or “justified by the Spirit,” or “shown to be righteous in spirit.”

verses.text: Now the Spirit says in plain words that in later times some will desert the faith, giving heed to spirits that lead astray and to teachings that come from demons,
through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences have been seared as with a branding iron.
They prohibit marrying and insist that people keep away from foods, which God made to be shared with thanks by those who have faith and have come to know the truth.
For all that God made is good, and nothing should be refused when it is accepted with thanks,
since God’s word and prayer consecrate it.
By pointing out these things to the believers,{a} you will be an excellent servant of Christ Jesus, fed on the message of the faith and the sound teaching you have followed closely.
But have nothing to do with profane myths fit only for old women. Train yourself for godliness instead.{b}
Bodily training has some little value; godliness has value in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the life to come.
This saying is to be trusted and worthy of complete acceptance.
That is why we toil and struggle,{c} because we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all people, especially of those who believe.
Give these instructions and teach them.
Do not let anyone think little of you because you are young.{d} Instead, be a pattern for the faithful in what you say and how you live, in love, faith and purity.
Till I arrive, give your attention to reading Scripture aloud,{e} to exhorting and to teaching.
Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy when the council of elders{f} laid their hands on you.
Make these things your care and your whole occupation, so that your advance is evident to everyone.
Keep a close watch on yourself and on your teaching; persist in these things, for by doing so you will save both yourself and those who listen to you.

notes.text: Brothers: Greek *adelphoi*, the usual term for fellow believers, including both men and women.
Train: Greek *gymnaze*, from the word for athletic exercise; so also “training” in verse 8.
Struggle: some manuscripts read “suffer reproach.”
Young: in Greek usage the term for youth could cover adults up to about forty.
Reading Scripture aloud: literally “the reading,” that is, reading aloud in the assembly.
Council of elders: Greek *presbyterion*, the body of elders (*presbyteroi*).

verses.text: Never harshly criticize an older man, but urge him as though he were your father. Treat younger men like brothers,
elderly women as you would mothers, and young women as sisters, with complete purity.
Honor widows who are truly in need.{a}
But if a widow has children or grandchildren, they should first learn to practice their religion at home and to repay their parents, since this pleases God.{b}
A real widow, one left on her own, has put her hope in God and continues day and night in petitions and prayers.
But a widow who gives herself to luxury is dead though she is alive.
Give these instructions too, so that they may be beyond reproach.
Anyone who does not provide for his own relatives, and especially for members of his household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.
Let a widow be put on the list only if she is not under sixty years of age and has been the wife of one husband,{c}

and is known for good works: if she has brought up children, if she has shown hospitality, if she has washed the feet of God’s people,{d} if she has helped the afflicted, if she has devoted herself to every kind of good work.
But refuse to enroll younger widows, for when their desires draw them away from Christ, they want to marry,
and so they incur condemnation for having set aside their first pledge.{e}
They also pick up the habit of being idle and wandering from house to house; and they become not merely idle but also gossips and meddlers, who say things they should not.
So I would have younger widows marry, bear children, manage their homes, and give the adversary no opening for abuse.
For some have already turned aside to follow Satan.
If any believing woman has widows in her family,{f} she should assist them, and the church should not be burdened, so that it can assist those who are truly widows in need.
Elders who lead well should be considered worthy of a double honor,{g} especially those who labor in preaching and teaching.
Scripture says, “Do not muzzle an ox as it threshes,”{h} and, “The laborer has earned his pay.”{i}
Do not entertain a charge brought against an elder unless two or three witnesses bear it out.{j}
Any who keep on sinning you should reprove publicly, so that the others will be afraid.
I solemnly charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the chosen angels to keep these rules without prejudging anyone, doing nothing out of partiality.
Do not rush to ordain anyone,{k} and do not take part in the sins of others. Keep yourself pure.
Stop drinking water alone; use a little wine because of your stomach and the illnesses you so often have.
Some people’s sins are plain to see, going ahead of them to judgment, but the sins of others follow after them.
So too good works are plain to see, and those that are not cannot remain hidden.

notes.text: Honor: the word may include financial support; so also “honor” in verse 17.
Pleasing: later manuscripts read “good and pleasing.”
The wife of one husband: literally “a woman of one man”; compare 3:2.
God’s people: literally “the holy ones,” traditionally “the saints.” Washing the feet of guests was a menial act of hospitality (John 13:14).
First pledge: literally “first faith,” probably a pledge to remain unmarried in the service of Christ.
Believing woman: later manuscripts read “believing man or woman.”
Elders: Greek *presbyteroi*, the leaders of the congregation; in verse 1 the same word means simply “older man.” *Double honor*: probably including payment; compare verse 18.
Do not muzzle an ox as it threshes: Deut 25:4; compare 1 Cor 9:9. Oxen were driven over the harvested grain to loosen the kernels.
The laborer has earned his pay: a saying of Jesus, found in Luke 10:7 and in a slightly different form in Matt 10:10. Here it is cited alongside Scripture.
Compare Deut 19:15.
Laying hands on: that is, appointing someone to office (4:14), or possibly restoring someone who has sinned.

verses.text: Let all who are under the yoke as slaves regard their own masters as deserving all honor, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be spoken against.

Those who have believing masters must not think less of them because they are brothers; rather, they should serve them all the better, since those who benefit from their good service are believers and dear to God.{a} Teach and urge these things.
If anyone teaches a different doctrine and does not hold to the healthy words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with godliness,
he is swollen with conceit and understands nothing. He has a sick craving for controversies and quarrels about words, from which come envy, strife, slander, evil suspicions,
and constant friction among people who are corrupted in mind and robbed of the truth, who imagine that godliness is a means of gain.{b}
There is indeed great gain in godliness combined with contentment.
For we brought nothing into the world, and so we can take nothing out of it.{c}
Having food and clothing,{d} we will be satisfied with that.
People who want to be rich, however, tumble into temptation and a snare, and into many foolish and hurtful cravings that drag them down into ruin and destruction.
For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil,{e} and some, in reaching for it, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves through with many pangs.
But you, man of God, flee from these things. Pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, endurance, gentleness.
Fight the good fight{f} of the faith; take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession in the presence of many witnesses.
I charge you in the sight of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in his testimony before Pontius Pilate,{g}
to keep the commandment spotless and blameless until the appearing{h} of our Lord Jesus Christ,
This he will make manifest in his own good time, he the blessed and sole Ruler, the King of kings and Lord of lords,{i}
who alone is immortal, living in light no one can approach, whom no human eye has ever seen or is able to see. His be the honor and the everlasting power. Amen.

Those who are rich in this present world you must instruct not to think too highly of themselves and not to pin their hopes on wealth, which is so uncertain, but on God, who gives us all things in abundance for our enjoyment.
Tell them to do good, to grow rich in fine deeds, to give freely and share with others,
and so lay up treasure for themselves as a sound foundation for what is to come, in order to grasp the life that is real life.
Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Turn away from godless chatter and the contradictions of what is falsely called knowledge,{j}
which some have professed and so have missed the mark concerning the faith. Grace be with you all.{k}

notes.text: Those who benefit from their good service: or “those who devote themselves to good service,” referring to the masters. *Dear to God*: literally “beloved.”
Later manuscripts add “From such people withdraw.”
And so: the Greek is awkward, literally “that.” Later manuscripts read “and it is clear that.” Compare Job 1:21; Eccl 5:15.
Clothing: or “shelter”; the Greek word means “coverings.”
A root of all kinds of evil: or “the root of all evils.”
Fight the good fight: literally “contend in the good contest,” an image from athletic competition.
*Pontius Pilate*: the Roman governor of Judea, AD 26–36, under whom Jesus was crucified. *Pilate*: Latin *Pilatus*, perhaps “armed with a javelin.”
Appearing: Greek *epiphaneia*, “appearance,” “manifestation.”
King of kings and Lord of lords: literally “the King of those who reign and Lord of those who rule”; compare Deut 10:17; Rev 17:14; 19:16.
Knowledge: Greek *gnōsis*. Later groups claiming special knowledge were called “Gnostics,” but whether such teaching is in view here is uncertain.
With you all: the “you” is plural. Later manuscripts read “with you” (singular) and add “Amen.”

books.name: 2 Timothy
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early manuscripts are Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi (4th–5th century); Codex Vaticanus lacks this letter. Where manuscript readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord”; where it stands for the divine name in an Old Testament quotation, a note says so. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: the letter presents itself as Paul’s last words, written from prison in Rome as he faced death (1:8, 17; 4:6–8). As with 1 Timothy and Titus, the traditional view holds that Paul wrote it; many modern scholars think it was written by a follower of Paul in his name, perhaps around AD 80–110. Some who doubt Paul’s authorship of 1 Timothy and Titus think this letter is his, or that it preserves genuine personal notes from him (as in 4:9–21). The question remains open.

verses.text: Paul,{a} by God’s will an apostle{b} of Christ Jesus, sent to make known the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus,{c}
to Timothy,{d} my dearly loved son: grace, mercy, peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
I give thanks to God, whom I serve with a clean conscience as my forebears did, as I keep you in mind without ceasing in my prayers by night and by day.
I remember the tears you shed, and I yearn to see you again, so that my joy may be complete.
I am reminded of the unfeigned faith that is in you, a faith that lived first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice,{e} and that I am convinced lives in you as well.
For this reason I urge you to rekindle the gift of God that came to you when I placed my hands on you.
For the spirit God gave us is not one of cowardice; it is a spirit of power, of love and of self-discipline.{f}
So never be ashamed of bearing witness to our Lord, nor of me his prisoner. Instead, take your share of hardship for the good news,{g} relying on the power of God,
who rescued us and called us with a holy calling, not on the basis of anything we had done, but because of his own purpose and the grace he bestowed on us in Christ Jesus before time began,{h}
and now it has been made plain by the appearing{i} of Christ Jesus our Savior, who has put an end to death’s power and, by the good news, shed light on life and immortality.
for which I have been appointed herald, apostle and teacher.{j}
That is why I endure these sufferings. But I feel no shame, because I know whom I have trusted, and I am persuaded that what I have placed in his keeping he can guard until that day.{k}
Hold to the wholesome words you heard from me as a model, living in the faith and love that are ours in Christ Jesus.
Through the Holy Spirit, who dwells in us, keep safe the fine treasure committed to your care.
You know that all the believers in Asia{l} have abandoned me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes.{m}
May the Lord show mercy to the household of Onesiphorus,{n} for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains.
On the contrary, when he arrived in Rome, he searched hard for me and found me.
The Lord grant that he finds mercy with the Lord on that day! How much he did for me in Ephesus you already know better than anyone.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent,” a messenger or envoy.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.”
*Lois*: Greek, perhaps “more desirable.” *Eunice*: Greek *Eunikē*, “good victory.” Compare Acts 16:1.
The spirit God gave us: or “God did not give us a spirit of cowardice, but of power …”; the reference may be to the Holy Spirit or to a disposition he imparts. *Self-discipline*: or “sound judgment.”
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel”; so throughout.
Before time began: literally “before eternal times.”
Appearing: Greek *epiphaneia*, “appearance,” “manifestation”; also in 4:1 and 4:8.
Teacher: later manuscripts add “of the Gentiles.”
What I have placed in his keeping: or “what he has placed in my keeping”; literally “my deposit.” Compare verse 14.
Asia: the Roman province in the west of modern Turkey, with Ephesus its chief city.
*Phygelus*: Greek, perhaps “fugitive.” *Hermogenes*: Greek, “born of Hermes.”
*Onesiphorus*: Greek, “bringer of benefit.”

verses.text: You, then, my son, draw your strength from the grace that is in Christ Jesus.
What you heard from me in the presence of many witnesses, pass on to reliable people who will be competent to teach others as well.
Take your share of hardship{a} like a good soldier of Christ Jesus.
No soldier on active duty gets entangled in the business of civilian life; his aim is to please the officer who enlisted him.
Likewise an athlete is not crowned unless he competes by the rules.
The farmer who toils should be the first to eat from the harvest.
Think about what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into everything.
Keep in mind Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, a descendant of David,{b} as proclaimed in my good news,
It is for this good news that I suffer hardship, even to the point of wearing chains like a wrongdoer. Yet the word of God is not in chains.
That is why I endure all things for the sake of God’s chosen ones, so that they also may gain the salvation found in Christ Jesus, along with eternal glory.

Here is a saying to be trusted:{c}
If we have died with him, we shall also live with him;

if we endure, we shall also reign with him;
if we deny him, he also will deny us;

if we are faithless, he remains faithful,
for he cannot deny himself.
Keep reminding them of these things, and charge them in the sight of God{d} not to wrangle over words, which does no good and only brings ruin on those who listen.
Do your utmost to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker with no cause for shame, cutting a straight path with the word of truth.{e}
But steer clear of godless chatter, for those who indulge in it will advance further and further into ungodliness,
and their talk will eat its way like gangrene. Hymenaeus and Philetus{f} are among them;
they have strayed from the truth, claiming that the resurrection has already happened, and they are overturning the faith of some.
Nevertheless God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: “The Lord knows those who are his,”{g} and, “Let everyone who names the name of the Lord turn away from wickedness.”{h}
In a great house there are utensils of gold and silver, and also of wood and clay, some meant for special occasions and others for ordinary use.
Anyone, then, who keeps himself clean of these will be a vessel for noble use, consecrated, of service to the owner, fit for any good task.
Flee the passions of youth, and pursue righteousness, faith, love and peace, together with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
Refuse to be drawn into stupid and uninstructed debates; you know that they give birth to fights.
And a servant{i} of the Lord must not be quarrelsome but kind toward all, able to teach, patient when wronged,
gently instructing those who resist him. It may be that God will give them a change of heart, so that they come to know the truth,
and they may come to their senses and escape the devil’s snare, having been held captive by him to do his will.{j}

notes.text: Take your share of hardship: later manuscripts read “so endure hardship.”
A descendant of David: literally “from the seed of David.” *David*: Hebrew, “beloved.”
A saying to be trusted: literally “faithful is the word”; compare 1 Tim 1:15. The lines that follow are widely thought to quote an early hymn or confession; the setting as verse is editorial.
In the sight of God: some manuscripts read “in the sight of the Lord.”
Cutting a straight path with: Greek *orthotomounta*, literally “cutting straight,” perhaps an image from road-building or plowing; that is, handling the word rightly.
*Hymenaeus*: Greek, named after Hymen, the god of weddings; compare 1 Tim 1:20. *Philetus*: Greek, “beloved.”
The Lord knows those who are his: from Num 16:5 in the Greek Old Testament, where “the Lord” renders the divine name, Yahweh.
Names the name of the Lord: echoing Isa 26:13 and the call to separate from the wicked in Num 16:26; in these passages “the Lord” stands for Yahweh.
Servant: Greek *doulos*, “slave.”
The devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer.” *Held captive by him to do his will*: or “held captive by the devil, so as to do God’s will”; the Greek pronouns are ambiguous.

verses.text: Understand this: in the last days hard times will come.
For people will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy,
heartless, unforgiving, slanderers, without self-control, brutal, haters of what is good,
traitors, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
keeping up an outward form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such people.
Some of these slip into people’s homes and make captives of foolish women who are loaded down with sins and driven by various passions,
women who are forever learning yet can never reach a real understanding of the truth.
Just as Jannes and Jambres{a} opposed Moses, so these people oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified in regard to the faith.
But they will not get much further, for their folly will be plain to everyone, as the folly of those two also became plain.
But you have closely followed what I taught, how I lived, what I aimed at, my faith, my patience, my love, my endurance,
my persecutions and sufferings, the things that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium and at Lystra,{b} the persecutions I endured. Yet from all of them the Lord rescued me.
Indeed, everyone who sets out to live a devout life in Christ Jesus will meet persecution,
and evil people and swindlers will advance into worse and worse, leading others astray and being led astray themselves.
But as for you, hold on to what you have learned and become convinced of, knowing from whom you learned it,{c}
and that from childhood you have known the sacred writings, which can make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
All Scripture is breathed out by God and useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction and for training in righteousness,{d}
so that the person who belongs to God may be complete, equipped for every good work.

notes.text: *Jannes and Jambres*: names given in Jewish tradition to Pharaoh’s magicians who opposed Moses (Exod 7:11, 22). *Moses*: Hebrew *Mosheh*, explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out.”

*Antioch* … *Iconium* … *Lystra*: cities in southern Asia Minor where Paul was persecuted (Acts 13:50; 14:5–6, 19). This Antioch, named after the Seleucid king Antiochus, lay near Pisidia; Lystra was Timothy’s home town (Acts 16:1).
From whom: the Greek is plural, “from which people,” perhaps including Timothy’s mother and grandmother (1:5). Later manuscripts read the singular.
All Scripture is breathed out by God and useful: or “Every scripture breathed out by God is also useful.” *Breathed out by God*: Greek *theopneustos*, “God-breathed,” traditionally “inspired by God.”

verses.text: I give you this solemn charge before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom:
proclaim the word; be ready in season and out of season; convince, rebuke and encourage, with unfailing patience and teaching.
For a time is coming when people will not put up with healthy teaching, but, with ears itching for something new, they will heap up teachers for themselves to suit their own desires,
they will stop listening to the truth and turn aside to fables instead.
But you, keep your head in all circumstances, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist,{a} carry out your ministry to the full.
For my part, my life is already being poured out like a drink offering,{b} and the moment of my departure is at hand.
I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
From now on a crown of righteousness is waiting for me, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will give me on that day, and not to me alone but to everyone who has longed for his appearing.
Do your best to come to me soon.
Demas has abandoned me; he loved the present age, and he has gone off to Thessalonica. Crescens is away in Galatia,{c} Titus in Dalmatia.{d}
Only Luke is with me. Fetch Mark and bring him along, because he is very useful to me for the work.{e}
Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.{f}
Bring with you, when you come, the cloak I left in Troas at the house of Carpus,{g} and the books too, especially the parchments.{h}
That coppersmith Alexander treated me very badly; the Lord will requite him as his deeds deserve.{i}
You too should be on guard against him, for he strongly opposed our message.
When I first defended myself, nobody came to my support; all abandoned me. May it not be held against them!
But the Lord stood beside me and made me strong, so that through me the message would be preached in full and all the nations would hear it. So I was snatched from the lion’s mouth.{j}
The Lord will deliver me from every wicked scheme and bring me safely to his heavenly kingdom. Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.
Greet Prisca and Aquila,{k} and the household of Onesiphorus.
Erastus stayed in Corinth, and Trophimus I left ill at Miletus.{l}
Do your best to come before winter.{m} Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia and all the brothers.{n}
The Lord be with your spirit.{o} Grace be with you all.{p}

notes.text: Evangelist: Greek *euangelistēs*, “one who brings good news.”
Drink offering: wine poured out as a sacrifice (Num 15:1–10; 28:7); compare Phil 2:17.
*Demas*: Greek, probably short for *Demetrios*, “belonging to Demeter”; compare Col 4:14; Phlm 24. *Crescens*: Latin, “growing.” *Galatia*: some manuscripts read “Gaul.”
*Titus*: Latin, of uncertain meaning. *Dalmatia*: a region on the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, in modern Croatia and its neighbors.
*Luke*: Greek *Loukas*, probably from Latin *Lucius*, “light.” *Mark*: Latin *Marcus*, perhaps from Mars, the Roman god of war; compare Acts 15:37–39; Col 4:10.
*Tychicus*: Greek, “fortunate.”
*Carpus*: Greek, “fruit.” *Troas*: a port in northwestern Asia Minor near ancient Troy.
Books … parchments: the books were probably papyrus scrolls; the parchments, writings on prepared animal skin, perhaps notebooks or copies of Scripture.

*Alexander*: Greek, “defender of men”; compare 1 Tim 1:20. *The Lord will requite him as his deeds deserve*: echoing Ps 62:12 (61:13 in the Greek Old Testament) and Prov 24:12, where it is God, Yahweh, who repays each according to his deeds. Later manuscripts read “may the Lord requite him.”
The lion’s mouth: a figure for deadly danger, echoing Ps 22:21 (21:22 in the Greek Old Testament); compare Dan 6:20–22.
*Prisca*: Latin, “ancient,” “venerable”; called *Priscilla* in Acts 18:2. *Aquila*: Latin, “eagle.”
*Erastus*: Greek, “beloved”; compare Acts 19:22; Rom 16:23. *Trophimus*: Greek, “nourishing”; compare Acts 20:4; 21:29. *Miletus*: a port on the coast of Asia, south of Ephesus.
Before winter: sea travel on the Mediterranean largely stopped from about mid-November to March.

*Eubulus*: Greek, “well-advised.” *Pudens*: Latin, “modest.” *Linus*: Greek, the name of a legendary singer; later tradition names a Linus as an early leader of the church in Rome. *Claudia*: Latin, feminine of *Claudius*. *Brothers*: Greek *adelphoi*, fellow believers, including both men and women. *All*: the Westcott–Hort text has “all” in brackets.
The Lord: later manuscripts read “The Lord Jesus Christ.”
With you all: the “you” is plural. Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Titus
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early manuscripts are Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Alexandrinus and Codex Ephraemi (4th–5th century), with a small fragment in the papyrus P32 (about AD 200); Codex Vaticanus lacks this letter. Where manuscript readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Authorship: the letter names Paul as its author, writing to his coworker Titus, whom he had left on the island of Crete. As with 1 and 2 Timothy, the traditional view holds that Paul wrote it, perhaps after a release from the imprisonment described in Acts 28; many modern scholars think it was written by a follower of Paul in his name, perhaps around AD 80–110. The question remains open.

verses.text: Paul,{a} a servant{b} of God and an apostle{c} of Jesus Christ, sent to further the faith of God’s chosen ones and their grasp of the truth that leads to godliness,{d}
resting on the hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, pledged before time began,{e}
and at the right moment he made his message visible in the preaching entrusted to me by command of God our Savior,
to Titus,{f} my genuine child in our shared faith: grace and peace{g} from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Savior.
The reason I left you behind in Crete{h} was so that you would set in order what still needed doing and appoint elders{i} in each town, as I instructed you.
An elder must be blameless, the husband of one wife,{j} with children who are believers{k} and are not open to the charge of wild living or disobedience.
For an overseer,{l} as God’s steward, has to be beyond reproach: not headstrong, not hot-tempered, not a drunkard, not violent, not grasping for gain,
but hospitable, a lover of goodness, sensible, just, devout and self-controlled.
He must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as it was taught, so that he can both encourage others with healthy teaching and refute those who speak against it.
For there are many who will not submit to authority, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party.{m}
They have to be silenced, for they are turning whole families upside down by teaching for the sake of dishonest profit what they have no business teaching.
One of them, a prophet of their own, has said, “Cretans are liars forever, savage beasts, idle bellies.”{n}
That testimony is true. So reprove them sharply, so that they may be healthy in the faith,
paying no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of people who reject the truth.
To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; their very minds and consciences are defiled.
They profess to know God, yet their conduct disowns him; they are abhorrent and rebellious, and worthless for anything good.

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
Servant: Greek *doulos*, “slave.”
Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent,” a messenger or envoy.
*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”
Before time began: literally “before eternal times.”
*Titus*: Latin, of uncertain meaning. Titus was a Greek convert who worked closely with Paul (Gal 2:1–3; 2 Cor 8:23).
Grace and peace: later manuscripts read “grace, mercy and peace.”
Crete: the large island south of Greece in the Mediterranean Sea.
Elders: Greek *presbyteroi*, the leaders of a congregation; in verse 7 the same people are called “overseers.”
The husband of one wife: literally “a man of one woman”; compare 1 Tim 3:2. The precise sense is debated.
Who are believers: or “who are faithful,” that is, trustworthy.
Overseer: Greek *episkopos*, “one who watches over,” traditionally “bishop.”
Those of the circumcision party: literally “those of the circumcision,” probably Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the law.

Cretans are liars forever …: a line traditionally attributed to the Cretan poet and seer Epimenides (about 600 BC). The first words, “Cretans always lie,” also appear in a hymn of Callimachus (3rd century BC).

verses.text: But as for you, speak what fits healthy teaching.
Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, sensible, sound in faith, in love and in endurance.
In the same way, the older women should behave as befits the holy, not spreading slander and not in bondage to drink. They should be teachers of what is right,
and so train the young women to love their husbands and their children,
to be sensible, chaste, good managers of their homes,{a} kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God may not be maligned.
Urge the younger men, too, to be sensible.
In every respect show yourself a model of good works; in your teaching show integrity and seriousness,
and sound words beyond criticism, so that whoever stands against us may be put to shame for lack of anything evil to say of us.{b}
Slaves are to be submissive to their own masters in everything, to give satisfaction, not talking back,
not pilfering, but showing complete and genuine reliability, so that in every way they may adorn the teaching about God our Savior.
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to all people,
It schools us to say no to impiety and to the cravings of this world, and to live with self-control, justice and devotion in the age that now is,
as we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, Christ Jesus.{c}
He gave himself for us to set us free from all lawlessness and to cleanse for himself a people who would be his own treasure, eager to do good works.{d}
Speak about these things; urge and correct with full authority. Let no one disregard you.

notes.text: Good managers of their homes: Greek *oikourgous*, “workers at home”; later manuscripts read *oikourous*, “keepers at home.”
Us: later manuscripts read “you.”

Our great God and Savior, Christ Jesus: or “the great God and our Savior Christ Jesus.” In Greek a single article governs both nouns (“the great God and Savior of us”), and by the rule known as Granville Sharp’s (after the English scholar who described it in 1798), two singular personal nouns joined by “and” under one article refer to the same person. On that reading Jesus is here called “God.” Others take the phrase to name two persons, God and Jesus, or render “the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior, which is Christ Jesus.” *Appearing*: Greek *epiphaneia*, “appearance,” “manifestation.”
To set us free … his own treasure: echoing Ps 130:8 and Ezek 37:23, and the phrase “a people for his own possession” in Exod 19:5 and Deut 7:6; 14:2 in the Greek Old Testament.

verses.text: Remind them to be subject to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work,
to slander no one, to avoid quarrels, to be gentle, and to show every courtesy to all people.
For we too were once foolish, disobedient and led astray, slaves to all sorts of passions and pleasures, spending our days in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.
But when the kindness and the love for humankind{a} of God our Savior appeared,
he rescued us, not on the basis of any righteous acts we had performed, but because of his own compassion, by means of the bath of new birth and the renewing work of the Holy Spirit,{b}
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior,
so that, made righteous by his grace, we might become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

Here is a trustworthy saying.{c} On these matters I want you to speak with confidence, so that those who have put their trust in God may be intent on devoting themselves to good works.{d} These things are excellent and of benefit to everyone.
But avoid foolish controversies and genealogies, dissensions and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and futile.
Give one warning, then a second, to anyone who stirs up division,{e} and after that have no more to do with him;
you may be sure that a man like that has turned aside and goes on sinning, condemned by his own verdict.
As soon as I send Artemas to you, or Tychicus,{f} make every effort to join me at Nicopolis,{g} since that is where I have resolved to pass the winter.
Do all you can to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way, and see that they lack nothing.{h}
Our people must also learn to commit themselves to doing good, so as to supply urgent needs and not be unproductive.
All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.{i}

notes.text: Love for humankind: Greek *philanthrōpia*, from which English “philanthropy” comes.
Rebirth: Greek *palingenesia*, “new beginning,” “regeneration.” *Washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit*: or “the washing of rebirth, and renewal by the Holy Spirit.”
Here is a trustworthy saying: literally “faithful is the word”; compare 1 Tim 1:15. It probably refers to verses 4–7.
Devoting themselves to good works: or “taking the lead in honest occupations”; so also in verse 14.
Stirs up division: Greek *hairetikos*, “factious,” from which English “heretic” comes.
*Artemas*: Greek, short for *Artemidoros*, “gift of Artemis.” *Tychicus*: Greek, “fortunate”; compare 2 Tim 4:12.
Nicopolis: Greek, “city of victory”; probably the city of that name in Epirus, on the western coast of Greece.

*Zenas*: Greek, short for *Zenodoros*, “gift of Zeus.” *Lawyer*: either an expert in the Jewish law or a Roman jurist. *Apollos*: Greek, short for *Apollonios*, “belonging to Apollo”; compare Acts 18:24; 1 Cor 3:6.
With you all: the “you” is plural. Later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Philemon
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. Philemon is preserved in Codex Sinaiticus and other early manuscripts; the third-century papyrus P87 contains parts of verses 13–15 and 24–25, as reported in the standard editions. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord.” *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name, as it usually does in Paul’s letters. Philemon is one of the seven letters whose authorship by Paul is accepted by nearly all scholars. It was written from prison (verses 1, 9–10, 13), probably in Rome (about AD 60–62) or Ephesus (about AD 53–55); the place is debated. It is closely linked with Colossians, which names the same companions (Col 4:7–17).

verses.text: Paul,{a} a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy{b} our brother, to Philemon,{c} our dear friend and fellow worker,
and to Apphia{d} our sister, and to Archippus{e} our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets in your house.
Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
I always give thanks to my God when I remember you in my prayers,
because I keep hearing about your love and the faithfulness you show toward the Lord Jesus and all God’s holy people.{f}
My prayer is that the sharing that springs from your faith may prove active and powerful, through a full knowledge of all the good that is ours in Christ.{g}
For I have had much joy and encouragement from your love, because the hearts{h} of the holy people have been refreshed through you, brother.
For this reason, though in Christ I have every right to be bold and to order you to do what is fitting,
yet for love’s sake I prefer to make a request. Being who I am, Paul, an old man,{i} and at present a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well,
appeal to you for my child, whom I fathered in my chains: Onesimus.{j}
Once he was useless to you, but now he is truly useful,{k} both to you and to me.
I am sending him back to you, and in sending him I am sending my very heart.
I wanted to keep him here with me, so that he might serve me on your behalf while I am in chains for the good news.{l}
But I chose to do nothing without your agreement, so that your goodness would not come from compulsion but from your own free will.
Maybe this is why he was away from you for a time,{m} so that you might receive him back for good,
no longer merely as a slave but as something better than a slave, a beloved brother. He is especially precious to me, and still more to you, both as a person{n} and in the Lord.
So if you count me as your partner, welcome him as you would welcome me.
And if he has done you any wrong, or is in debt to you at all, put it down to me.
I, Paul, am writing this with my own hand: I will repay it. I need not mention to you that you owe me your very self.
Yes, brother, let me have some benefit{o} from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ.
I am writing to you confident of your obedience, knowing that you will do even more than I say.
And one more thing: prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be given back to you.{p}
Epaphras,{q} my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings,
and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers.{r}
The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.{s}

notes.text: *Paul*: Latin *Paulus*, “small.” Paul also had the Jewish name *Saul* (Acts 13:9), after the first king of Israel (“asked for”).
*Timothy*: Greek *Timotheos*, “one who honors God.” He was Paul’s long-time coworker (Acts 16:1–3).
*Philemon*: Greek, “affectionate” or “one who loves.” He was evidently a believer of some means in Colossae (compare Col 4:9, 17), in whose house the church met.
*Apphia*: a name known from inscriptions in Phrygia; its meaning is uncertain. She is often thought to be Philemon’s wife, but the letter does not say so.
*Archippus*: Greek, “master of horses” (compare Col 4:17).
God’s holy people: Greek *hagioi*, “holy ones,” traditionally “saints,” the believers as set apart for God; also in verse 7.

The Greek of this verse is compressed and has been understood in several ways. *Fellowship* (*koinōnia*) may mean the sharing that comes from faith, or Philemon’s generous sharing with others. *Ours*: literally “in us”; some manuscripts read “in you.” *In Christ*: literally “into Christ,” which may mean “for the sake of Christ,” “bringing us closer to Christ,” or “to the glory of Christ.”
Hearts: Greek *splanchna*, literally “inward parts,” the seat of the affections; also in verses 12 and 20.
An old man: Greek *presbytēs*. Some scholars suggest emending it to *presbeutēs*, “ambassador” (compare Eph 6:20), but no manuscript is known to read this, and the text is kept.
*Onesimus*: Greek, “useful” or “profitable,” a name common among slaves. Paul plays on its meaning in verse 11 and again in verse 20. *Fathered*: that is, Paul led him to faith while in prison.
Useless … useful: Greek *achrēstos* … *euchrēstos*, a play on the name *Onesimus*. The words may also echo *Christos*, which was pronounced much like *chrēstos*, “useful” or “kind.”
Good news: Greek *euangelion*, traditionally “gospel.”
A short time: literally “for an hour,” an idiom for a brief period, not a clock time.
As a man: literally “in the flesh,” that is, in ordinary human relationships, including his place in Philemon’s household.
Have some benefit: Greek *onaimēn*, from the same root as *Onesimus*, another play on the name.
Your prayers … to you: here “you” is plural, addressing the whole church, as also in verses 3 and 25.

*Epaphras*: a shortened form of *Epaphroditus*, “charming” or “belonging to Aphrodite.” He was from Colossae and founded the church there (Col 1:7; 4:12). He is probably a different person from the Epaphroditus of Philippians.

*Mark*: Latin *Marcus*, probably “of Mars”; he is John Mark (Acts 12:12; Col 4:10). *Aristarchus*: Greek, “best ruler,” from Thessalonica (Acts 19:29; 27:2). *Demas*: probably short for *Demetrius*, “belonging to Demeter” (compare 2 Tim 4:10). *Luke*: Greek *Loukas*, a Latin name probably meaning “from Lucania” (Col 4:14).
Some later manuscripts add “Amen.”

books.name: Hebrews
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek text of B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort, *The New Testament in the Original Greek* (1881; public domain), with Tischendorf’s eighth edition (1869–72; public domain) consulted. Variant readings were also compared with the SBL Greek New Testament, the Nestle–Aland *Novum Testamentum Graece*, and the Byzantine text of Robinson and Pierpont, which were consulted for variants only. The chief early witnesses are the papyrus P46 (about AD 200), which places Hebrews among Paul’s letters directly after Romans, the papyrus P13 (3rd–4th century), and Codices Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus (4th–5th century); Vaticanus breaks off at 9:14. Where manuscript readings are cited in the notes, they are reported from the standard editions and have not been verified against the manuscripts. *Christos* is rendered “Christ” where it functions as part of Jesus’ name. Old Testament quotations generally follow the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint); where they quote a passage that has the divine name in Hebrew, “Lord” renders Greek *kyrios* and a note gives *Yahweh*. Authorship: the work names no author. Eastern churches from the late 2nd century linked it with Paul, while Tertullian named Barnabas, and Origen remarked that “who wrote the letter, God truly knows.” Other proposals include Apollos, Luke, Silvanus and Priscilla. The writer knew Timothy (13:23) and had heard the message from those who heard the Lord (2:3). Its date is uncertain, though many place it before AD 96, when 1 Clement appears to use it. The question of authorship remains open.

verses.text: In many portions and in many ways God spoke long ago to our ancestors through the prophets,{a}
but in these final days he has addressed us through a Son, whom he designated heir of everything and through whom he also created the universe.{b}

He is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact imprint of his very being, and he bears up all things by his mighty word. After he had made purification for sins, he took his seat at the right hand of the Majesty on high,{c}
So he has come to rank as far above the angels as the name he has received as his inheritance surpasses theirs.

And when, again, he leads the firstborn into the inhabited world, he declares,
“All the angels of God must bow down before him.”{f}

These will come to ruin, but you continue;
like clothing, every one of them will grow old.

You will fold them up like a robe,
and like clothing they will be replaced.
But you remain the same,
and your years will never run out.”{j}
Are they not all spirits in holy service, sent out to serve for the sake of those who are going to inherit salvation?{l}

notes.text: Our ancestors: literally “the fathers.”
In these last days: literally “at the end of these days.” *The ages*: or “the universe,” “the worlds.”

Radiance: or “reflection.” *Exact imprint*: Greek *charaktēr*, the mark stamped on a coin or seal. *Purification for sins*: later manuscripts read “purification for our sins by himself.” *Took his seat … at the right hand*: echoing Ps 110:1.
Ps 2:7. *I have become your Father*: literally “I have begotten you.”
Deut 32:43 in the Greek Old Testament (not in the standard Hebrew text, but compare a Hebrew copy among the Dead Sea Scrolls); compare Ps 97:7. *Again, when he brings*: or “when he again brings.”
Ps 104:4 in the Greek Old Testament. *Winds*: or “spirits”; the same Greek word means both.

Ps 45:6–7. *Your throne, O God, is*: or “God is your throne.” *Forever and ever*: Westcott and Hort bracket “and ever.” *His kingdom*: so the Westcott–Hort text, following P46, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus as reported; most manuscripts read “your kingdom.”
Ps 102:25–27 in the Greek Old Testament. *Lord*: the Greek Old Testament adds this word; in the Hebrew psalm the one addressed is Yahweh (verses 12, 19).
Like a garment: these words are not in the psalm; P46, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus as reported include them here, while later manuscripts omit them.
Spirits in holy service: literally “ministering spirits.”

verses.text: For this reason it is all the more necessary for us to hold on to the things we have heard, or we may be carried off course.
For if the message spoken through angels proved valid, and every violation and disobedience received its just penalty,{a}
how can we avoid punishment if we ignore such a great salvation? The Lord first announced it, and those who listened to him confirmed it for us,
while God corroborated it with signs, wonders, and a variety of miracles, and by distributing gifts of the Holy Spirit according to his will.
It was not to angels, after all, that he made subject the coming world we are speaking about.

For a brief time you ranked him beneath the angels;
you wreathed him with glory and honor;{c}

all things you have placed beneath his feet.”
In subjecting all things to him, he has left nothing outside his rule. Yet at present we do not see all things made subject to him.

What we do see is Jesus, made for a short time lower than the angels, and now, on account of the death he suffered, wearing a crown of glory and honor, so that by God’s grace he might taste death on behalf of every one.{d}
It was right that God, the one for whose sake and by whose agency everything exists, should bring the founder of their salvation to completion through sufferings, as he leads many sons into glory.{e}
For the one who makes holy and those who are made holy all have one origin. That is why he is not ashamed to call them brothers,{f}
Because the children share flesh and blood, he likewise shared in these, so that by dying he might destroy the one who has the power of death, namely the devil,{j}
and set free all those who through fear of death were held in slavery all their lives.
For surely it is not angels he takes hold of to help, but he takes hold of the descendants of Abraham.{k}
So it was necessary for him to become like his brothers in all things, in order to be a high priest merciful and faithful in what concerns God, making atonement for the people’s sins.{l}
Because he himself suffered when he was tested, he is able to help those who are being tested.{m}

notes.text: The message spoken through angels: Jewish tradition held that angels took part in the giving of the law at Sinai; compare Deut 33:2 in the Greek Old Testament; Acts 7:53; Gal 3:19.
Ps 8:4–6 in the Greek Old Testament. *Man … son of man*: a human being, humankind. In verses 8–9 the writer applies the psalm to Jesus.

For a little while: or “a little.” The Hebrew of Ps 8:5 reads “a little lower than God” (or “than divine beings”). *Honor*: later manuscripts add “and set him over the works of your hands”; Westcott and Hort bracket these words.

*Jesus*: the Greek form of Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.” *By the grace of God*: so nearly all manuscripts. A few manuscripts, and some writers known to Origen in the 3rd century, read *chōris theou*, “apart from God,” instead of *chariti theou*, “by the grace of God.” The rarer reading is defended by some scholars as the harder one; most editors follow the reading in the text.
Sons: including daughters; the Greek uses the masculine plural for a mixed group. *Founder*: Greek *archēgos*, “leader,” “pioneer,” “trailblazer.” *Bring … to completion*: or “make perfect.”
One origin: literally “are all from one,” that is, from one Father, or from one family. *Brothers*: Greek *adelphoi*, which includes sisters when used of a group; so throughout.
Ps 22:22. *Assembly*: Greek *ekklēsia*, the word usually rendered “church.”
Isa 8:17 in the Greek Old Testament; compare 2 Sam 22:3.
The devil: Greek *diabolos*, “slanderer.”
Takes hold of: or “gives help to.” *Descendants*: literally “seed.” *Abraham*: Hebrew, explained in Gen 17:5 as “father of a multitude.”
Making atonement for: or “making propitiation for,” “wipe away.”
Tested: or “tempted”; the same Greek word covers both.

verses.text: So then, holy brothers, who share in a heavenly calling, fix your thoughts on Jesus, the apostle and high priest of the faith we confess.{a}
He has been faithful to the one who appointed him, as Moses too was faithful in all his house.{b}
But Jesus has been counted worthy of greater glory than Moses, in the way that the one who builds a house is held in higher honor than the house.
Every house has its builder, and the one who built all things is God.
Moses indeed was faithful in all God’s house, as an attendant, bearing witness to the things that were going to be spoken,{c}
but Christ is faithful as a Son set over God’s house; and that house is ourselves, provided we keep firm hold of our boldness and of the hope that is our boast.{d}

Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says,
“Today, if you hear his voice,

do not make your hearts hard as they did at the Provocation,
at the time of the Testing in the desert,{e}

where your ancestors put me to the test by trying me,
though they saw my works for forty years.

So in my wrath I swore an oath:
‘Into my rest they shall not come.’ ”{f}
Take care, brothers, that none of you has an evil, unbelieving heart that turns away from the living God.
Rather, keep urging one another on, day by day, for as long as there is a “today,” so that sin’s deceit may harden none of you.
For we have come to share in Christ, provided that we keep the confidence we had at the start unshaken to the last.{g}

In the words of Scripture,
“Today, if you should hear his voice,
do not make your hearts hard as they did at the Provocation.”
Who were they who heard and yet rebelled? Was it not all those who came out of Egypt led by Moses?
And with whom was God angry for forty years? Was it not with those who sinned, whose bodies fell in the wilderness?{h}
To whom did he swear that they would never come into his rest? Was it not to those who refused to obey?
And we see that unbelief kept them from coming in.

notes.text: Apostle: Greek *apostolos*, “one sent.” *Jesus*: later manuscripts read “Christ Jesus.” *Christ*: Greek *Christos*, “Anointed One,” equivalent to Hebrew *mashiach*, “Messiah.”

*Moses*: Hebrew *Mosheh*, explained in Exod 2:10 as “drawn out”; it may come from an Egyptian word for “son.” *In all God’s house*: Num 12:7 in the Greek Old Testament; literally “in all his house.” Westcott and Hort bracket “all”; P13, P46 and Vaticanus as reported omit it.
Attendant: Greek *therapōn*, an attendant, from Num 12:7.
*Hope that is our boast*: later manuscripts add “firm to the end”; Westcott and Hort bracket these words, which P13, P46 and Vaticanus as reported omit (compare verse 14).
Ps 95:7–11 in the Greek Old Testament. *The rebellion … testing*: in Hebrew these are the place names *Meribah*, “quarreling,” and *Massah*, “testing” (Exod 17:7; Num 20:13).
They shall not come: literally “if they shall enter,” a Hebrew form of oath meaning “they shall not enter.”
Come to share in Christ: or “become partners of Christ.” *Confidence*: Greek *hypostasis*, “assurance,” “resolve”; compare 1:3; 11:1.
Whose bodies fell: compare Num 14:29, 32.

verses.text: Since, then, the promise of entering his rest still stands, let us be wary that none of you should seem to have fallen short of it.
For good news has been brought to us as well as to them. Yet the word they heard was of no benefit to them, because they were not joined in faith with those who truly listened.{a}

For we who trust do enter that rest, as he said,
“So I vowed in my anger,
‘They will never come into my rest,’ ”
even though his work was done from the creation of the world.{b}
For in one place he speaks of the seventh day like this: “God rested from all his works on the seventh day.”{c}
And again in this passage he says, “They shall never enter my rest.”
It still remains, then, that some are to come into it, and since those to whom the good news came first did not come in, because they would not obey,
Had Joshua given them rest, God would not afterward have spoken of a further day.{e}
So then, a sabbath rest remains for the people of God;{f}
for anyone who has come into God’s rest has ceased from his labors, just as God ceased from his own.
So let us be earnest to come into that rest, so that none of us falls through the same kind of disobedience they showed.

For God’s word is alive and powerful, cutting more sharply than any double-edged sword, slicing through to the place where soul and spirit, joints and marrow meet, and able to assess the heart’s thoughts and motives.
No creature is hidden from his sight, but all things are bare and laid open to the eyes of the one to whom we must give account.{g}
Since, then, we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast the faith we confess.
Ours is not a high priest who cannot feel for us in our frailties; he has been put to the test in all things just as we are, yet without sinning.
Let us then approach the throne of grace boldly, to receive mercy and discover grace that helps when we need it.

notes.text: Because they were not united in faith with those who listened: so the Westcott–Hort text, with most early manuscripts as reported. Some manuscripts read “because it was not combined with faith in those who heard it.”
Gen 2:2.
*David*: Hebrew, probably “beloved.” The Greek Old Testament gives Psalm 95 a heading naming David.
*Joshua*: Hebrew *Yehoshua*, “Yahweh saves”; the Greek name is *Iēsous*, the same as “Jesus.”
Sabbath rest: Greek *sabbatismos*, “sabbath-keeping”; *sabbath* is Hebrew for “ceasing,” “rest.”
Laid open: literally “with the neck bent back,” exposed. *To whom we must give account*: or “with whom we have to do.”

verses.text: Every high priest is chosen from among men and appointed to act on their behalf in matters relating to God, to offer gifts and sacrifices for sins.
He is able to deal gently with the ignorant and the wayward, since he himself is beset by weakness.
and for that reason he has to bring an offering for sins on his own account as well as on behalf of the people.
And no one takes this honor on himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was.{a}

During his life in the flesh he offered prayers and earnest requests, with a loud outcry and with tears, to the one who had power to rescue him from death, and he was heard because of his devotion.{d}
Son though he was, he learned obedience from the things he suffered.{e}
And once made complete, he became for all who obey him the cause of salvation that lasts forever,
since God designated him a high priest in the order of Melchizedek.
On this subject we have a great deal to say, and it is difficult to make clear, because you have grown dull of hearing.
By now you should be teaching others, yet you need someone to teach you once more the basic rudiments of the sayings of God. You have come to need milk rather than solid food.{f}
For everyone who lives on milk is unacquainted with the message of righteousness, being still an infant.
But solid food belongs to the mature, to those whose faculties have been trained by practice to tell good from evil.

notes.text: *Aaron*: Hebrew, of uncertain meaning; Moses’ brother and the first high priest (Exod 28:1).

Ps 110:4. *Melchizedek*: Hebrew, “my king is righteousness” or “king of righteousness” (7:2); the king and priest of Salem who blessed Abraham (Gen 14:18–20). *In the order of*: or “after the manner of.”
Because of his devotion: or “because of his reverent fear”; others render “and was delivered from his fear.”
He learned … he suffered: Greek *emathen … epathen*, a play on words.
Basic rudiments: or “first principles,” literally “the elements of the beginning.”

verses.text: So let us leave behind the elementary teaching about Christ and press on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God,{a}
teaching about washings and the laying on of hands, about the raising of the dead and the judgment that lasts forever.{b}
And this we will do, if God permits.
There is no way, when people have once received the light, have tasted the gift from heaven, have come to share in the Holy Spirit,
who have experienced how good God’s word is, and the powers of the coming age,
and then have fallen away, to bring them back to repentance again; for they are crucifying the Son of God afresh to their own ruin, and making a public mockery of him.{c}
Ground that soaks up the rain falling on it time after time, and brings forth plants of use to those for whom it is worked, has a share in God’s blessing.
But land that yields thorns and thistles is worthless and close to a curse, and in the end it is burned.{d}
Even though we speak this way, dear friends, we are confident of better things in your case, things that go with salvation.
For God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you showed for his name in serving the saints, as you still serve them.{e}
And we long for each one of you to show the same eagerness for the full assurance of hope until the end,
so that you may not become sluggish, but imitate those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.
When God gave his promise to Abraham, he swore by himself, because there was no one greater for him to swear by,
saying, “Surely I will bless you and multiply you.”{f}
And so Abraham, having waited with patience, received what was promised.
People swear by someone greater than themselves, and for them an oath serves as confirmation and puts an end to every dispute.
In the same way, God, wanting to show the heirs of the promise even more plainly that his purpose could not change, guaranteed it with an oath,
so that through two things that cannot change, in which God cannot possibly lie, we who have taken refuge might be strongly encouraged to lay hold of the hope that lies before us.
This hope we hold as the soul’s anchor, firm and secure, and it goes in to the inner place beyond the curtain,{g}
where Jesus has entered for us as a forerunner, having become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.

notes.text: The elementary teaching about Christ: literally “the word of the beginning of the Christ.” *Maturity*: or “perfection,” “completion.”

Teaching about washings: so the Westcott–Hort text, following Vaticanus as reported (“a foundation … teaching”); most manuscripts read “of teaching about washings.” *Washings*: Greek *baptismoi*, “baptisms,” “ritual washings.”
For they are crucifying: or “while they are crucifying.” *Afresh*: or “for themselves”; the Greek *anastaurountas* can mean either.
Thorns and thistles: compare Gen 3:17–18.
Saints: literally “holy ones,” that is, God’s people.
Gen 22:17. *Surely I will bless you and multiply you*: literally “blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you.”
The inner place beyond the curtain: the inmost room of the sanctuary, the Most Holy Place (Lev 16:2, 12).

verses.text: For this Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High, went out to meet Abraham when he came back from the slaughter of the kings, and he blessed him;{a}
and Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. His name means first “king of righteousness,” and then he is also king of Salem, that is, “king of peace.”
He is without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life; but, made like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.{b}
Notice how great this man was, to whom the patriarch Abraham gave one tenth of the plunder.
The descendants of Levi who receive the priesthood are ordered by the law to collect a tenth from the people, from their own relatives, although they too are Abraham’s descendants.{c}
But this man, whose ancestry is not traced from them, took tithes from Abraham and gave a blessing to the man who held the promises.
Beyond any dispute, the lesser is blessed by the greater.
In the first case, tenths are collected by mortals; in the second, by someone who is declared to be alive.
