One is larger: perhaps the Great Bear (the Big Dipper), which never sets at northern latitudes; compare “the Bear” in Job 9:9; 38:32.

verses.text: At the ends of the earth I saw twelve gates open toward all the quarters, from which the winds come out and blow over the earth.
Three of them open on the face of the sky, three toward the west, three on the right of the sky, and three on the left.{a}
The first three are those of the east, then three of the north, then three of the south, and three of the west.

Through four of them come winds of blessing and well-being, and from the other eight come harmful winds. When these are sent, they bring destruction on the whole earth, on the water on it, on all who live on it, and on everything in the water and on the land.
The first wind from those gates, called the east wind, comes out through the first gate in the east, the one leaning toward the south. From it come desolation, drought, heat, and ruin.
Through the second gate, in the middle, comes what is right: from it come rain, fruitfulness, well-being, and dew. Through the third gate, toward the north, come cold and drought.
After these come the south winds, through three gates. Through the first of them, leaning toward the east, a hot wind comes out.
Through the middle gate next to it come sweet smells, dew and rain, well-being and health.
Through the third gate, toward the west, come dew and rain, locusts and desolation.
After these come the north winds. From the seventh gate, on the east side, come dew and rain, locusts and desolation.
From the middle gate come, straight on, health and rain, dew and well-being. Through the third gate, on the west side, come mist and frost, snow and rain, dew and locusts.
After these four come the west winds. Through the first gate, next to the north, come dew and frost, cold, snow, and ice.
From the middle gate come dew and rain, well-being and blessing. Through the last gate, next to the south, come drought and desolation, burning and ruin.
So the twelve gates of the four quarters of heaven are finished. All their laws, all their plagues, and all their benefits I have shown you, my son Methuselah.{b}

notes.text: The face of the sky: the east. In Semitic orientation one faces east, so “right” is south and “left” is north.
*Methuselah*: Hebrew *Metushelaḥ*, perhaps “man of the javelin” or “man of Shelah.” Enoch’s son (Gen 5:21–27), to whom the Astronomical Book and the Epistle are addressed.

verses.text: The east is named as the first quarter, since it comes first.{a} The second is called the south, because the Most High will come down there; there especially the one who is blessed forever will come down.
The west quarter is called “the waning,” because there all the lights of heaven wane and go down.

The fourth quarter, called the north, is divided into three: the first part is for human habitation; the second holds seas of water, the deeps, forests, rivers, darkness, and mist; and the third part holds the garden of righteousness.
I saw seven high mountains, higher than all the mountains on the earth; from there frost comes out, and days, seasons, and years pass away.
I saw seven rivers on the earth, larger than all other rivers. One of them comes from the west and pours its waters into the Great Sea.{b}
Two flow down from the north and empty into the Red Sea in the east.
The other four come out on the north side to their own sea: two of them to the Red Sea, and two into the Great Sea, where they empty; some say, into the desert.
I saw seven great islands in the sea and on the land: two on the land and five in the Great Sea.{c}

notes.text: The quarter names are wordplays in Aramaic or Hebrew: east, *qedem*, also means “first, before”; south, *darom*, is explained as *dar rum*, “the Exalted One dwells,” here “the Most High will descend there”; west, *maʿarav*, is linked with *ʿarav*, “to go down, wane”; north, *tsafon*, with *tsafun*, “hidden.”

The Great Sea: the Mediterranean. *The Red Sea*: the *Erythraean Sea*, the waters south and east of Arabia (see the note at 32:2). The rivers may be the Nile, Tigris, Euphrates, and others known to ancient geographers.
Charles counts this as 77:8; some editions number it 77:9.

verses.text: These are the names of the sun: the first Oryares, and the second Tomas.{a}
The moon has four names: the first is Asonya, the second Ebla, the third Benase, and the fourth Erae.
These are the two great lights. Their circle is like the circle of heaven, and the two circles are the same size.
In the circle of the sun there are seven portions of light more than in the moon, and these are passed on in fixed amounts until the seventh portion of the sun is used up.
They set and go into the western gates, make their circuit by way of the north, and come out through the eastern gates on the face of the sky.
When the moon rises, a fourteenth part appears in the sky, and on the fourteenth day it completes its light.
Fifteen parts of light are passed to it until the fifteenth day, when its light is completed according to the sign of the year; it becomes fifteen parts, and the moon grows by fourteenths.

As it wanes it loses one part a day: fourteen parts remain after day one, thirteen after day two, then twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, and two by day thirteen; by day fourteen only half a seventh is left, and by day fifteen the last of its light is gone.
Some months last twenty-nine days, and one lasts twenty-eight.
Uriel showed me another law: when light is passed to the moon, and from which side the sun passes it.
All the time the moon is growing in its light, it is drawing it to itself while facing the sun, for fourteen days, until it is lit all over and its light is complete in the sky.
Its first day bears the name new moon, since light first dawns on it then.
It becomes full exactly on the day the sun sets in the west; it rises from the east at night and shines all night long until the sun rises opposite it, and the moon is seen opposite the sun.
On the side from which the moon’s light comes, it wanes again there until all the light is gone and all the days of the month are finished, and its disk is empty, without light.
It makes three months of thirty days, and at its time it makes three months of twenty-nine days each, in which it completes its waning in the first period, in the first gate, for 177 days.{b}
As it goes out, it shows itself through three thirty-day months and three twenty-nine-day months.
At night it looks like a man for twenty days each time,{c} and by day it looks like the sky, for there is nothing else in it but its light.

notes.text: The names of the sun and moon are of uncertain origin. *Oryares* may come from Hebrew *ʾor ḥeres*, “light of the sun”; *Tomas* perhaps from Hebrew *ḥammah*, “heat,” or Aramaic. Of the moon’s names, *Asonya*, *Ebla*, *Benase*, and *Erae* may reflect Hebrew *ʾishon*, “pupil (of the eye),” *levanah*, “white one,” *ben ḥese*, “son of the full moon,” and *yareaḥ*, “moon.” All are guesses.
177 days: 3 × 30 + 3 × 29 = 177, half of a lunar year of 354 days.
Like a man: perhaps the “man in the moon”; the text is uncertain.

verses.text: Now, my son, I have shown you everything, and the law of all the stars of heaven is complete.
He showed me all their laws for every day, for every season of rule, for every year and its going out, and for the order set for it every month and every week;
and the waning of the moon that takes place in the sixth gate, for in this sixth gate its light is completed, and after that the waning begins;
and the waning that takes place in the first gate in its season, until 177 days are completed, which, counted in weeks, are twenty-five weeks and two days.{a}
It falls behind the sun and the order of the stars by exactly five days in the course of one period,{b} when this place that you see has been passed through.
This is the picture and outline of every light, which Uriel the archangel, their leader, showed me.

notes.text: One period: half a year; 182 − 177 = 5. Compare 74:10–16.

verses.text: At that time Uriel the angel spoke to me in reply: “Look, Enoch, I have shown you everything. I have revealed everything to you, so that you may behold the sun and the moon, the guides of heaven’s stars, and all who turn them, their tasks, their times, and their departures.

In those times the fruit of the earth will be late
and will not grow at its proper time,
and the fruit of the trees will be held back in its season.

The moon will change its order
and will not appear at its time.

In those days the sun will be seen, and it will travel in the evening at the edge of the great chariot in the west,
and will shine more brightly than the order of light allows.

Many chiefs of the stars will break the order,
will change their circuits and their tasks,
and will not appear at the times set for them.

The whole order of the stars will be hidden from the sinners,
and the thoughts of those on the earth will go wrong about them;
they will turn away from all their ways,
they will err and take them for gods.

Evil will multiply upon them,
and punishment will come on them
to destroy them all.”

He said to me,
“Look, Enoch, at these heavenly tablets;{a}
read what is written on them,
and take note of every single thing.”
I looked at the heavenly tablets and read everything written there and understood it all. I read the book of all human deeds and of all mortals who will be on the earth to the farthest generations.

At once I blessed the great Lord, the King of glory forever, for having made all the works of the world.
I praised the Lord for his patience,
and blessed him on account of the children of humankind.

After that I said,
“Happy is the one who dies in righteousness and goodness,
about whom no book of wrongdoing has been written
and against whom no day of judgment will be found.”

Those seven holy ones{b} brought me and set me on the earth in front of the door of my house, and said to me, “Tell everything to your son Methuselah, and show all your children that no human being is righteous before the Lord, for he is the one who made them.

We will leave you with your son for one year, until you give your instructions, so that you may teach your children, write things down for them, and bear witness to all your children. In the second year they will take you from among them.{c}

Let your heart be strong,
for the good will announce righteousness to the good;
the righteous will rejoice with the righteous
and congratulate one another.

But sinners will die with sinners,
and the apostate will go down with the apostate.

Those who do right will die because of human deeds
and be gathered in because of the deeds of the wicked.”
Then they stopped speaking with me, and I went back among my people, praising the Lord of the world.

notes.text: The heavenly tablets: a heavenly record of all that will happen and of God’s laws, prominent also in Jubilees (for example 3:10; 5:13). Compare Ps 139:16; Dan 10:21.
Those seven holy ones: the seven archangels of 20:1–8.
Compare 82:1 and chapters 91 and 106–107, where Enoch instructs Methuselah.

verses.text: Now, my son Methuselah, I am telling you all these things and writing them down for you. I have revealed everything to you and given you books about all of them. So keep safe, my son Methuselah, the books from your father’s hand, and pass them on to the generations of the world.

I have given wisdom to you and your children,
and to the children you will have,
so that they in turn hand it on to their own children through the generations,
a wisdom past their understanding.

Those who understand it will not sleep,
but will keep their ears open to learn this wisdom,
and it will please those who eat it more than fine food.

Happy are all the righteous! Happy are all who walk in the way of righteousness and do not sin as the sinners do in counting all their days, the days in which the sun crosses the sky, going in and out of each gate for thirty days alongside the chiefs of thousands who order the stars, and with the four extra days that split the year into quarters, which guide them and go in with them on those four days.
Because of these, people will go wrong and will not count them in the full reckoning of the year; they will go wrong and not recognize them accurately.
They are part of the year’s count and stand written truly forever: in gates one, three, four, and six, one day apiece, so that the year is filled out at 364 days.

Its account is accurate and its recorded reckoning exact, for Uriel showed me and revealed to me the lights, the months, the festivals, the years, and the days—Uriel, to whom the Lord of all the creation of the world has subjected the host of heaven.
He has authority over night and day in heaven, to make the light shine on human beings: sun, moon, and stars, and all the powers of heaven that turn in their circling chariots.
Here are the ranks of the stars that go down each in its place, its season, its festival, and its month.
Here also are the names of their guides, who see to it that each comes in on time, by rank and season and month, in its term of rule and its station.

First come in the four leaders who split the year into quarters; next the twelve rank-leaders who apportion the months; then, for the 360 days, chiefs of thousands who apportion the days; and for the four extra days, leaders who mark off the quarters.
These chiefs of thousands are slotted in between one leader and the next, each following a station, while the leaders themselves do the dividing.
These are the names of the leaders who divide the four appointed parts of the year: Milkiel, Helemmelek, Meleyal, and Narel.{a}

Their guides are named Adnarel, Iyasusael, and Elomeel. These three come after the rank-leaders, and one more comes after those three, who in turn come after the station-leaders that mark off the quarters of the year.
At the beginning of the year Melkeyal rises first and rules; he is called Tamaini and “sun.” All the days of his rule while he governs are ninety-one days.{b}

These are the signs of the days to be seen on earth in the days of his rule: sweat, heat, and calm. All the trees bear fruit and put out leaves; the wheat is harvested; the roses bloom, and all the flowers that come up in the field; but the trees of winter wither.{c}
These are the names of the leaders under them: Berkael, Zelebsel, and another chief of a thousand who is added, called Hiluyaseph. And the days of this one’s rule are ended.
The next leader after him is Helemmelek, whom they call “the shining sun.” All the days of his light are ninety-one days.{d}

These are the signs of his days on the earth: scorching heat and dryness. The trees ripen their fruit and bring all their fruit to ripeness and readiness; the sheep mate and conceive; all the fruit of the earth is gathered in, and everything in the fields, and the winepress. These things happen in the days of his rule.

These are the names, the orders, and the leaders of those chiefs of thousands: Gidaiyal, Keel, and Heel, and the name of the chief of a thousand added to them is Asfael. And the days of his rule are ended.{e}

notes.text: *Milkiel*: “my king is God.” *Helemmelek*: perhaps “the king’s companion” or “the king is strong.” *Meleyal*: “fullness of God.” *Narel*: “light of God” or “fire of God.” The names of the lesser leaders are of uncertain meaning.
Ninety-one days: one quarter of the 364-day year. Beginning at the spring equinox, this first quarter runs roughly from late March to late June.
The wheat harvest in the land of Israel falls in May–June.
The second quarter, roughly late June to late September.
The book breaks off here; the leaders of the third and fourth quarters are not given.

verses.text: Now, my son Methuselah, I will show you all the visions I have seen, telling them to you one by one.{a}

I saw two visions before I married, and they were quite unlike each other. The first came while I was learning to write; the second, before I married your mother, was a fearful vision. About them I prayed to the Lord.
I had lain down to sleep at my grandfather Mahalalel’s house{b} and in a vision I watched the sky give way, torn loose and falling onto the earth.

As it fell on the earth, I saw the earth swallowed in a vast abyss. Mountains hung upon mountains, hills sank down onto hills, and tall trees were ripped from their trunks, flung down, and sunk in the abyss.
Then a word came into my mouth, and I raised my voice and cried out, “The earth is destroyed!”
My grandfather Mahalalel, who was lying near me, woke me and asked, “Why are you crying out like this, my son? Why such wailing?”

I told him the whole vision I had seen, and he said to me, “You have seen something terrible, my son. Your dream vision is grave; it concerns the secrets of all the earth’s sin. The earth must sink into the abyss and be utterly destroyed.
Now, my son, get up and plead with the Lord of glory, since you are a man of faith, that a remnant may be left on the earth and that he may not wipe out the whole earth.
My son, all this will come down on the earth from heaven, and there will be vast destruction on the earth.”
After that I got up and prayed, pleaded, and begged, and I wrote down my prayer for the generations of the world. I will show it all to you, my son Methuselah.

When I had gone outside and seen the sky, the sun coming up in the east, the moon going down in the west, a scattering of stars, the whole earth, and all things just as he had known them from the start, I blessed the Lord of judgment and praised him, because he had made the sun come out of the windows of the east, so that it climbed and rose over the face of the sky and set out and went on along the path appointed for it.

notes.text: The Book of Dreams (chapters 83–90) contains two dream visions. Aramaic fragments of it are reported from Qumran (4QEn c–f), and it is usually dated to about 165–160 BC, during the Maccabean revolt, because the Animal Apocalypse (chapters 85–90) ends its review of history around that time.
*Mahalalel*: Hebrew *Mahalalʾel*, “praise of God.” Enoch’s great-grandfather in Gen 5:12–18 (Mahalalel, Jared, Enoch); the Ethiopic here calls him grandfather.

verses.text: Lifting my hands in righteousness, I blessed the Holy and Great One. I spoke using my mouth’s breath and the fleshly tongue that God made for human beings to speak with; he gave them breath, a tongue, and a mouth to speak with:

“Blessed are you, Lord, King,
great and mighty in your greatness,
Lord of all the creation of heaven,
King of kings and God of the whole world!
Your power, your kingship, and your greatness last forever and ever,
and your rule through all generations.
All the heavens are your throne forever,
and the whole earth your footstool forever and ever.{a}

For you made all things and you rule all things;
nothing is too hard for you.
Wisdom never leaves the place of your throne
or turns away from your presence.
You know, see, and hear everything,
and nothing is hidden from you, for you see everything.

Now the angels of your heavens have done wrong,
and your anger rests on human flesh
until the great day of judgment.

Now, God and Lord and great King,
I beg and plead with you to grant my prayer:
leave me descendants on the earth;
do not destroy all human flesh
and empty the earth of people,
making the destruction permanent.

Now, my Lord, remove from the earth the flesh that has roused your anger,
but establish the flesh of righteousness and uprightness
as a plant of eternal seed.{b}
Do not hide your face from your servant’s prayer, Lord.”

notes.text: Compare Isa 66:1.
A plant of eternal seed: compare “the plant of righteousness” at 10:16 and 93:2, 5, 10, an image for the faithful remnant of Israel.

verses.text: Later I had a second dream, and I will tell you all of it, my son.
Enoch raised his voice and spoke to his son Methuselah: “I will speak to you, my son. Hear my words, and turn your ear to your father’s dream vision.{a}

Before I married your mother Edna,{b} I saw in a vision on my bed: there was a bull coming out of the earth, and that bull was white.{c} After it came a young cow, and with her came two bulls, one black and the other red.
The black bull gored the red one and chased him across the earth, and after that I could no longer see the red bull.
But the black bull grew, and that young cow went with him. I saw many cattle come from him, looking like him and following him.
That cow, the first one, left the first bull to look for the red one, but did not find him. She mourned bitterly over him and kept searching.
I watched until the first bull came to her and calmed her, and from then on she cried no more.
Next she gave birth to a second white bull,{d} and then to many bulls and black cows.
In my sleep I saw that white bull also grow and become a great white bull, and many white bulls came from him that looked like him.
They began to father many white bulls like themselves, one after another, a great many.

notes.text: Chapters 85–90 are known as the Animal Apocalypse. They retell history from Adam to the end time in symbols: the patriarchs before Jacob are bulls (white for the righteous line, black for the wicked); fallen angels are stars; Israel are sheep; the nations are wild beasts and birds of prey; and angels appear as men. The notes identify each figure as most scholars read it.
*Edna*: perhaps “delight” (Hebrew *ʿednah*). Enoch’s wife, not named in Genesis; Jubilees 4:20 also calls her Edna.
The white bull is Adam; the heifer is Eve; the black and red bulls are Cain and Abel.
Another white bull: Seth (Gen 4:25).

verses.text: Again, as I slept, I looked with my eyes and saw the sky above, and there a star fell from heaven,{a} and it got up, ate, and grazed among those cattle.
After that I saw the large black cattle, and they all changed their stalls, their pastures, and their herds, and began to live together.{b}
Again I looked in the vision toward the sky, and I saw many stars come down and throw themselves from heaven to that first star. They became bulls among those cattle and grazed with them.{c}
I looked at them and saw that they all exposed their organs like stallions and began to mount the cows of the cattle. They all became pregnant and gave birth to elephants, camels, and donkeys.{d}
All the cattle were afraid of them and terrified, and began to bite with their teeth, to devour, and to gore with their horns.
They even began to devour those cattle, and all the children of the earth began to shake and tremble before them and run away from them.

notes.text: A star: the first fallen angel, probably Asael (Azazel), compare 88:1 and 10:4.
The line of Seth (white) and the line of Cain (black) mingle.
The Watchers come down (chapter 6; Gen 6:1–4).
The giants, in three kinds, compare 7:2 and the note there.

verses.text: Again I saw how they began to gore one another and devour one another, and the earth began to cry out.
I raised my eyes to heaven again and saw in the vision beings coming out of heaven who looked like white men.{a} Four came out from that place, and three with them.

The three who came out last took me by the hand and carried me off, far from the earth’s generations, up to a lofty place. They showed me a tower rising high above the earth, with all the hills lower than it.
One of them said to me, “Stay here until you see everything that happens to those elephants, camels, and donkeys, and to the stars and the cattle, all of them.”

notes.text: Like white men: angels. The four are the archangels of chapter 10 (Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, and Sariel or Phanuel); the three with them are other angels who take Enoch up.

verses.text: I saw one of the four who had come out first seize that first star which had fallen from heaven. He tied it hand and foot and threw it into an abyss; that abyss was narrow and deep, dreadful and dark.{a}
Another of them unsheathed a sword and handed it to the elephants, camels, and donkeys, and they began to strike one another, and the whole earth shook because of them.{b}

As I watched in the vision, one of the four who had come out threw stones down from heaven, gathered and took all the great stars whose organs were like stallions’, tied them all hand and foot, and threw them into an abyss of the earth.

notes.text: Compare 10:4–5, where Raphael binds Asael and casts him into darkness.
Compare 10:9–12.

verses.text: One of those four went to that white bull{a} and taught him a secret, without his being afraid. He had been born a bull and became a man. He built himself a great vessel and lived on it, and three bulls lived with him in that vessel, and they were shut in.
Again I raised my eyes toward heaven and saw a high roof with seven streams of water on it, and those streams poured a great deal of water into an enclosure.
I looked again, and springs opened on the floor of that great enclosure, and the water began to swell and rise over the floor. I watched that enclosure until its whole floor was covered with water.
Water, darkness, and mist grew over it. When I looked at how high the water was, it had risen above the height of the enclosure and was pouring over it, and it stood on the earth.
All the cattle of that enclosure were herded together until I saw them sink, swallowed up, and die in that water.

But the vessel floated on the water, while all the cattle, elephants, camels, and donkeys sank to the bottom with all the animals. I could no longer see them; they could not get away, but died and sank into the depths.
Again I watched in the vision until those streams were taken away from that high roof, the chasms of the earth were leveled, and other abysses were opened.
Then the water began to drain into these until the earth could be seen. The vessel came to rest on the earth, the darkness withdrew, and light appeared.

That white bull who had become a man came out of the vessel, and the three bulls with him. One of the three was white like that bull, one was red as blood, and one was black. And that white bull left them.{b}

They began to produce wild animals and birds, so that there came to be different kinds: lions, leopards, wolves, dogs, hyenas, wild boars, foxes, badgers, pigs, falcons, vultures, kites, eagles, and ravens. Among them a white bull was born.{c}
They began to bite one another. But the white bull born among them fathered a wild donkey and a white bull with it, and the wild donkeys multiplied.{d}
The bull born from him fathered a black wild boar and a white sheep. The boar fathered many boars, but the sheep fathered twelve sheep.{e}
When those twelve sheep had grown, they handed one of them over to the donkeys, and the donkeys in turn handed that sheep over to the wolves, and that sheep grew up among the wolves.{f}
The Lord brought the other eleven to share its home and pasture among the wolves, and they increased into many flocks.

The wolves began to fear them and oppressed them, even destroying their little ones; they threw their young into a river full of water.{g} But the sheep began to cry out over their little ones and to complain to their Lord.

A sheep that had been rescued from the wolves fled and escaped to the wild donkeys.{h} I saw the sheep mourning and crying out, pleading with their Lord with all their strength, until the Lord of the sheep came down from a lofty dwelling at the sheep’s cry and came to them and shepherded them.
He called the sheep that had escaped the wolves and spoke with it about the wolves, that it should warn them not to touch the sheep.

The sheep went to the wolves as the Lord had said, and another sheep met it and went with it.{i} The two went together into the gathering of those wolves and spoke with them, warning them not to touch the sheep from then on.
After that I saw the wolves oppress the sheep harshly with all their might, and the sheep cried out.
The Lord came to the sheep, and they began to strike those wolves.{j} The wolves began to wail, but the sheep grew quiet and at once stopped crying out.
I watched the sheep until they left the wolves behind. But the wolves’ eyes were blinded, and they set out after the sheep with all their might.
The Lord of the sheep led the way, with his whole flock behind him. His face was dazzling, glorious, and fearful to look at.
But the wolves began to chase those sheep until they reached a sea of water.
That sea was split, and the water stood on one side and the other in front of them. Their Lord went at their head and stood between the flock and the wolves.{k}
Since the wolves did not yet see the sheep, they went into the middle of that sea; the wolves followed the sheep and ran after them into the sea.
When they saw the Lord of the sheep, they turned to run from his face, but the sea came back together and became as it had been made; the water swelled and rose until it covered those wolves.
I watched until all the wolves chasing those sheep had died and drowned.

The sheep, however, came safely out of the water into a desert without water or pasture, and there their eyes started to open so that they could see.{l} I saw the Lord of the sheep shepherding them, providing water and pasture, while that sheep went ahead as their guide.
That sheep went up to the top of that high rock,{m} and the Lord of the sheep sent it to them.
After that I saw the Lord of the sheep standing in front of them. His appearance was great, fearful, and majestic; all those sheep saw him and were afraid before his face.
They were all afraid and trembled because of him, and they cried out to the sheep that was with them, “We cannot stand before our Lord or look at him.”{n}
The sheep that led them went up again to the top of that rock. Meanwhile the flock grew blind and strayed from the path it had shown them, and that sheep did not know it.{o}
The Lord of the sheep was very angry with them. That sheep found out, came down from the top of the rock, came to the sheep, and found most of them blinded and gone astray.
When they saw it, they were afraid and trembled before it, and wanted to go back to their folds.

That sheep took other sheep with it, came to the sheep that had strayed, and began to kill them,{p} and the sheep were afraid of it. So that sheep brought back the strayed sheep, and they returned to their folds.
In this vision I kept watching until that sheep turned into a man, constructed a house for the Lord of the sheep, and settled the whole flock in it.{q}

I watched until the sheep that had met the sheep who led them fell asleep.{r} I watched until all the great sheep died and young ones took their place; these reached a pasture and drew near a stream.{s}
Then that sheep, their leader who had become a man, parted from them and fell asleep, and all the sheep looked for it and wept over it bitterly.{t}
I watched until they stopped weeping for that sheep and crossed that stream of water. Then two sheep arose as leaders in place of those who had led them and fallen asleep.{u}
I watched until the sheep came to a good place, a pleasant and glorious land, and I watched until those sheep were satisfied; and that house stood among them in the pleasant land.
Sometimes their eyes were opened and sometimes blinded, until another sheep rose up to lead them and turned them all back, and their eyes came open.{v}
The dogs, foxes, and wild boars began to devour those sheep, until the Lord of the sheep raised up a ram from among them to lead them.{w}
That ram began to butt those dogs, foxes, and wild boars on every side, until he had destroyed them all.
That sheep whose eyes were opened saw that ram among the sheep, until it abandoned its glory and began to butt those sheep, trample them, and behave disgracefully.
The Lord of the sheep sent the lamb to another lamb, to make it a ram and leader of the sheep in place of the ram that had abandoned its glory.{x}
It went to it, spoke with it privately, and made it a ram, prince and leader of the sheep; but through all this those dogs were oppressing the sheep.
The first ram chased that second ram, and the second ram got up and fled from it. I watched until those dogs brought down the first ram.{y}
The second ram then took the lead of the young sheep.

The flock increased greatly, while every dog, foxes, and wild boars were afraid and fled from it. The ram gored the wild beasts to death, and they had no more power among the sheep and robbed them of nothing. This ram had many offspring and then died, and a young sheep took its place as ram and became prince and leader of those sheep.{z}

That house became large and wide, and it was built for those sheep. On the house rose a great high tower for the Lord of the sheep.{aa} The house was low, but the tower was raised high, and the Lord of the sheep took his stand upon it, and a full table was laid before him.

Again I saw those sheep going astray and walking in many paths and abandoning that house of theirs. The Lord of the sheep summoned some of the flock and sent them to the rest, who set about killing them.{ab}

One of them was saved and not killed. It hurried away and cried out over the sheep, and they tried to kill it, but the Lord of the sheep rescued it from them, lifted it up to where I was, and settled it there.{ac}
He sent many other sheep to those sheep to testify to them and lament over them.

After that I saw that when they abandoned the house of the Lord and his tower, they fell away completely and their eyes were blinded. I saw the Lord of the sheep carry out great slaughter among them in their flocks, until those sheep brought on that slaughter themselves and betrayed his place.
He handed them over to the lions and leopards, the wolves and hyenas, the foxes, and all the wild beasts, and those wild beasts began to tear those sheep apart.
I saw that he abandoned that house of theirs and their tower and gave them all over to the lions to tear and devour them, to all the wild beasts.
I began to cry out with all my strength and appeal to the Lord of the sheep, pleading with him about the sheep, that they were being devoured by all the wild beasts.
But he stayed silent, though he saw it, and was glad that they were devoured, swallowed, and robbed, and left them to be devoured by all the beasts.

He called seventy shepherds{ad} and threw those sheep to them to pasture them. He said to the shepherds and their companions, “From now on, each of you is to pasture the sheep, and do everything I command you.
I will hand them over to you counted, and tell you which of them are to be destroyed; destroy those.” And he handed those sheep over to them.
He called another and said to him, “Watch and note everything the shepherds do to these sheep, for they will kill more of them than my orders allow.{ae}
Write down every excess and destruction the shepherds carry out: how many they destroy at my command and how many on their own whim. Record against each shepherd all the destruction he causes.

Read me the tally of those they kill and those they give up to be killed, so that it may stand as evidence against them and I may know all the shepherds’ actions and judge their conduct, whether they keep the command I gave them.
But they must not know it. Do not tell them or warn them, but simply record against each one all the destruction the shepherds cause, each in his time, and bring it all up to me.”
I watched until those shepherds pastured in their season, and they began to kill and destroy more than they had been told, and they handed those sheep over to the lions.
The lions and leopards ate and devoured most of those sheep, with the wild boars sharing the meal; and they burned that tower and tore down that house.{af}
I grieved deeply over that tower, because the house of the sheep had been torn down, and afterward I could not see whether those sheep went into that house.

The shepherds and their companions handed those sheep over to all the wild beasts to devour them, and each of them received a set number in his time. The other wrote in a book how many of them each one destroyed.
Each one killed and destroyed far more than was allotted, and I began to weep and mourn over those sheep.

So in the vision I saw the one who wrote: how he wrote down each one destroyed by those shepherds, day by day, and carried the whole book up, laid it down, and showed it to the Lord of the sheep—everything they had done, all that each of them had done away with, and all they had handed over to destruction.
It was read aloud to the Lord of the sheep; then he took it from the writer, read it himself, sealed it, and set it aside.

Right away I saw the shepherds pasture for twelve hours.{ag} Three of those sheep turned back, came and went in, and began to rebuild everything of that house that had fallen down;{ah} the wild boars tried to stop them but could not.{ai}

They began to build again as before, and they raised up that tower, and it was called the high tower. Once more they laid a table in front of the tower, yet every loaf on it was polluted and unclean.{aj}
Through all this the flock’s eyes were sightless, and so were their shepherds’. Great numbers were handed to the shepherds to be destroyed, who stamped on them and ate them up.
The Lord of the sheep stayed silent until all the sheep were scattered over the field and mixed with the beasts, and the shepherds did not rescue them from the beasts.

The one who wrote the book carried it up, showed it, and read it before the Lord of the sheep. He pleaded with him on their behalf and begged him for them as he showed him all the shepherds’ deeds, and he testified before him against all the shepherds.
He took the book itself, laid it down beside him, and left.

notes.text: That white bull: Noah. He is born a bull but becomes a man, perhaps meaning he is taught by angels or set apart; Moses likewise becomes a man in verse 36. The three bulls are Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
Shem is white (the chosen line); Ham and Japheth are red and black, though which is which is uncertain.

The wild animals and birds are the nations. Lions, leopards, and others appear later as Israel’s oppressors: Egyptians are wolves; Philistines dogs; Edomites wild boars; Ammonites and Moabites foxes; Assyrians lions; Babylonians leopards (or tigers); Greeks eagles and other birds of prey; Seleucid Syrians ravens. *A white bull*: Abraham.
A wild donkey: Ishmael, called “a wild donkey of a man” in Gen 16:12. *A white bull*: Isaac. The wild donkeys are the Arabs or Midianites.
The black wild boar: Esau, ancestor of Edom. *The white sheep*: Jacob, whose twelve sons are the twelve sheep. From here on Israel is pictured as sheep.
Joseph, sold to the Ishmaelites/Midianites and taken to Egypt (Gen 37:25–36).
Moses, who fled to Midian (Exod 2:15).
Another sheep: Aaron (Exod 4:27).
The plagues of Egypt (Exod 7–12).
Opening and blinding of the eyes is the vision’s image for Israel’s faithfulness and apostasy.
Mount Sinai (Exod 19).
The golden calf (Exod 32).
The Levites’ slaughter in Exod 32:26–28.
The house: here the tabernacle (Exod 25–40); later it stands for Jerusalem, with the “tower” as the temple.
Fell asleep: died. Aaron’s death (Num 20:28).
The Jordan.
The death of Moses (Deut 34).
Two sheep: perhaps Joshua and Caleb, or Joshua and Eleazar.
The period of the judges; the other sheep is probably Samuel.
A ram: Saul, the first king. The dogs are the Philistines; the foxes Ammon and Moab; the boars Edom/Amalek.
The lamb sent is Samuel; the other lamb is David (1 Sam 16).
Saul pursues David and dies fighting the Philistines (1 Sam 18–31).
The last sentence (Charles’s 48b) tells of David’s death and Solomon’s succession; some manuscripts place it after verse 48.
The tower: Solomon’s temple. The house is now Jerusalem.
The prophets, compare 1 Kgs 19:10; Neh 9:26.
Elijah, taken up to heaven (2 Kgs 2:11), now dwelling with Enoch.

Seventy shepherds: angelic rulers set over Israel from the exile to the end time, each for a fixed period. The number recalls the seventy years of Jer 25:11–12 and the seventy weeks of years of Dan 9:24, and the seventy nations of Gen 10. Their periods fall into four groups of 12, 23, 23, and 12 (89:72; 90:1, 5).
Another: a recording angel, perhaps Michael (compare 90:14, 17).
The Babylonian destruction of Jerusalem and the temple in 587/586 BC, with Edom joining in (Obad 10–14; Ps 137:7).
Twelve hours: the periods of twelve shepherds, the Persian era. Each shepherd’s term is called an hour.
Three sheep: probably Zerubbabel, Jeshua the high priest, and Ezra or Nehemiah (Ezra 3–6; Neh 2–6).
The wild boars: here the Samaritans and neighboring peoples who opposed the rebuilding (Ezra 4).
The author judges the worship of the second temple to be impure, perhaps over calendar or priestly disputes; compare Mal 1:7.

verses.text: I watched until thirty-five shepherds had taken up the pasturing in this way,{a} each completing his term as the first ones had; and others took them in hand to pasture them for their term, each shepherd in his own term.

Next in my vision every bird of the air came flocking: eagles, vultures, kites, and ravens, with the eagles at the head of them all,{b} and they set upon the sheep, pecking out their eyes and feeding on their flesh.
The sheep cried out because the birds were eating their flesh. As for me, I looked on and mourned in my sleep over that shepherd who was pasturing the sheep.

I watched until those sheep were devoured by the dogs, eagles, and kites, and they left them no flesh, skin, or sinew, until only their bones were standing; then their bones too fell to the ground, and the sheep became few.
I watched until twenty-three had taken up the pasturing and completed, in their terms, fifty-eight periods.{c}
But look: lambs were born to those white sheep,{d} and they began to open their eyes and see, and to cry out to the sheep.
They cried out to them, but the sheep did not listen to what they said; they were completely deaf, and their eyes were utterly blinded.
I saw in the vision the ravens swoop on those lambs and seize one of them,{e} and tear the sheep to pieces and devour them.
I watched until horns grew on those lambs, and the ravens knocked their horns down. Then I watched until a great horn sprouted on one of those sheep,{f} and their eyes were opened.
It looked at them, and it cried out to the sheep, and the rams caught sight of it and came running to it together.
Still, through all this, those eagles, vultures, ravens, and kites kept tearing the sheep, swooping on them and devouring them. The sheep stayed silent, but the rams mourned and cried out.
The ravens fought hard against it, striving to topple its horn, yet they could not prevail.

I watched until the shepherds, eagles, vultures, and kites came and called to the ravens to break the horn of that ram. They fought and battled with it, and it fought with them and cried out for its help to come.{g}
I kept watching until the man who listed the shepherds’ names and took them up to the Lord of the sheep arrived to aid it and revealed all things to it; he had descended to assist that ram.{h}
I watched until the Lord of the sheep came to them in anger, and everyone who saw him ran, and all of them collapsed into his shadow away from his presence.
All the eagles, vultures, ravens, and kites gathered together, and all the sheep of the field came with them; they all came together and helped one another to break that ram’s horn.{i}

I watched that man who wrote the book at the Lord’s command, until he opened the book about the destruction that the last twelve shepherds had done, and showed before the Lord of the sheep that they had destroyed far more than those before them.

I watched until the Lord of the sheep came to them, took in his hand the staff of his anger, and struck the earth. The earth split open, and all the beasts and all the birds of the sky fell away from those sheep and were swallowed up in the earth, and it closed over them.
I kept watching until the sheep were handed a mighty sword and marched out against all the beasts of the field to kill them, and all the beasts and birds of the sky fled from before them.
I watched until a throne was set up in the pleasant land,{j} and the Lord of the sheep sat on it, and the other took the sealed books and opened them before the Lord of the sheep.{k}

The Lord called those men, the first seven white ones,{l} and ordered them to bring before him all the stars whose organs were like stallions’, starting with the first star that led the way; and they brought them all before him.

He said to the man who wrote before him, who was one of those seven white ones, “Take those seventy shepherds to whom I handed over the sheep, and who on their own authority took them and killed more than I commanded.”
And look, I saw them all bound, and they all stood before him.
Judgment was held first on the stars. Tried and convicted, they were sent off to the place of sentence; they were thrown into an abyss full of fire and flame and full of pillars of fire.{m}
The seventy shepherds were then tried, convicted, and hurled into that abyss of fire.

At that time I saw a similar abyss opened in the middle of the earth, full of fire. The blinded sheep were led in, every one tried and convicted, and cast into this blazing pit, where they burned. It lay on the right-hand side of the house.{n}
I watched the sheep burn, bones and all.

I stood up to look, until they folded up that old house. They carried off all its pillars, and all the beams and decorations of the house were folded up with it, and they carried it away and put it in a place in the south of the land.

I kept watching until the Lord of the sheep brought in a fresh house, bigger and loftier than before, and raised it where the folded-up one had stood. Every pillar in it was new, and its adornments were new too, and grander than those of the old house he had removed. All the sheep were inside it.{o}
I saw every remaining sheep, with every beast of the earth and every bird of the air, bowing down and paying homage to those sheep, pleading with them and obeying them in everything.{p}

After that, those three who were dressed in white, who had taken me by the hand and brought me up before, took me up with the hand of that ram also holding me, and set me down among those sheep before the judgment took place.{q}
Every one of those sheep was white, with fleece thick and clean.

All that had been destroyed and scattered, along with every wild beast and every bird of the air, assembled in the house, and the Lord of the sheep was full of joy because they were all good and had come back to his house.

I watched until they laid down that sword that had been given to the sheep; they brought it back into the house, and it was sealed in the Lord’s presence. All the sheep were invited into that house, but it could not hold them.
Every one of them had open eyes and beheld what was good, and there was not one among them who did not see.
I saw that the house was large and wide and very full.
Then I saw a white bull born, big-horned,{r} and every wild beast and every bird of the air stood in awe of him and made constant petition to him.

I watched until all their kinds were transformed and they all became white bulls. The first among them became a lamb,{s} which grew into a mighty creature with huge black horns on its head; and the Lord of the sheep took delight in it and in the whole herd.
I slept among them, and I woke up having seen everything.
This is the vision I saw while I slept. I woke up and blessed the Lord of righteousness and gave him glory.

Then I wept bitterly, and my tears would not stop until I could bear it no longer. When I looked, they ran down because of what I had seen, for everything will come and be fulfilled, and all human deeds in their order were shown to me.
On that same night the earlier dream came back to me, and it made me weep and left me shaken, for I had seen that vision.”

notes.text: Thirty-five shepherds: 12 of the Persian period plus 23 more, carrying the story into the Greek period after Alexander the Great (332 BC).
The eagles: the Macedonians/Greeks, probably the Ptolemies of Egypt, who ruled Judea about 301–200 BC. The ravens are the Seleucids of Syria.
Fifty-eight periods: 12 + 23 + 23 shepherds, leaving the last 12 for the final age (90:17).
The lambs: a reform movement among pious Jews in the early second century BC, perhaps the group behind this book or the Hasidim of 1 Macc 2:42.
One of those lambs: probably the high priest Onias III, murdered about 171 BC (2 Macc 4:33–35; compare Dan 9:26).

A great horn: Judas Maccabeus, leader of the Jewish revolt against the Seleucid king Antiochus IV from 166 BC (1 Macc 3–9). The vision’s history ends with his struggles, which dates it to about 164–160 BC.
Verses 13–15 and 16–18 seem to be two versions of the same scene; Charles rearranged them (13, 16, 19 then 14, 15, 17, 18). This translation keeps the manuscript order.
That man: the recording angel of 89:61, often taken as Michael, who in 2 Macc 11:6–8 sends a heavenly rider to aid Judas.
The sheep of the field: probably wild sheep, that is, the Hellenizing Jews who sided with the Seleucids.
The pleasant land: the land of Israel (compare Dan 8:9; 11:16).
Compare Dan 7:9–10.
The first seven white ones: the seven archangels (20:1–8; compare 87:2).
To the right: south of Jerusalem, the Valley of Hinnom (Gehenna); compare 27:1–3.
The new house: a new Jerusalem built by God himself; compare Isa 54:11–12; Ezek 40–48; Rev 21:2. Notably no tower (temple) is mentioned.
Compare Isa 49:23; 60:14.
Before the judgment: the order is odd; some read “before the judgment” as “after.” The ram may be Elijah, here pictured as a ram, who returns before the end (Mal 4:5); compare 89:52.
A white bull: a messianic figure. Humanity returns to the condition of Adam (the first white bull, 85:3), and all the nations become white bulls.

A lamb: the Ethiopic word *nagar* (“word,” or a corruption) is unclear; Charles emended to “wild ox” (Hebrew *reʾem*), others keep “lamb.” This translation follows the common reading “lamb,” noting the uncertainty.

verses.text: Then Methuselah went and called all his brothers to him and gathered his relatives.

He spoke to all the children of righteousness and said,
“Hear, you sons of Enoch, all your father’s words,
and listen well to the voice of my mouth.
I urge you and tell you, beloved:
love uprightness and walk in it.

Do not come near uprightness with a divided heart,
and do not keep company with the double-hearted,
but walk in righteousness, my sons.
It will guide you on good paths,
and righteousness will go with you.

Wrongdoing will again reach its full measure on the earth,
and all deeds of wrongdoing, violence,
and transgression will prevail twice over.

When sin, wrongdoing, blasphemy,
and violence in every kind of deed increase,
and apostasy, transgression, and impurity increase,
a great punishment will come from heaven on all these,
and the holy Lord will come out in anger and punishment
to carry out judgment on the earth.

In those days violence will be cut off at its roots,
and the roots of wrongdoing together with deceit,
and they will be destroyed from under heaven.

All the idols of the nations will be given up,
their temples burned with fire,
and they will be removed from the whole earth.
The nations will be thrown into the judgment of fire
and perish in anger and in harsh judgment forever.

The righteous will rise from their sleep,
and wisdom will rise and be given to them.

After that the roots of wrongdoing will be cut off, and the sinners will be destroyed by the sword … will be severed from the blasphemers everywhere; schemers of violence and speakers of blasphemy alike will fall by the sword.{c}

After that there will be another week, the eighth, the week of righteousness,{d}
and a sword will be given to it,
so that righteous judgment may be carried out on the oppressors,
and sinners will be handed over to the righteous.

At its end they will gain houses through their righteousness,
and a house will be built for the Great King in glory forever.{e}

After that, in the ninth week,
righteous judgment will be revealed to the whole world;
all the works of the wicked will vanish from the whole earth,
the world will be written down for destruction,
and all humankind will look to the path of uprightness.

After this, in the tenth week, in its seventh part,
there will be the great eternal judgment,
in which he will take vengeance among the angels.

After that there will be many weeks without number, forever,
in goodness and righteousness,
and sin will never again be mentioned.

So now, my sons, I am telling you and pointing out to you
which roads lead to righteousness and which to violence.
I will show them to you again,
so that you may know what will happen.

Listen to me now, my sons:
keep to the roads of righteousness
and keep off the roads of violence;
for everyone who travels the roads of wrongdoing will perish forever.”

notes.text: Chapters 91–108 make up the final section of 1 Enoch: Enoch’s instruction to his children (91), the Apocalypse of Weeks (93:1–10 with 91:11–17), and the Epistle proper (92; 94–105), followed by the Birth of Noah (106–107) and a closing appendix (108). The Aramaic fragments (4QEn g) and the Greek Chester Beatty papyrus (for 97:6–107:3) are reported to support most of it; it is usually dated to the second century BC. In the Ethiopic manuscripts the order is disturbed: the last three “weeks” (91:12–17) stand before the first seven (93:3–10). The Aramaic is reported to have them in sequence, and many translations rearrange them; this translation keeps the Ethiopic order and numbering, and the notes point to the sequence.
The first end: the flood.
The text of this verse is damaged; the gap is marked by an ellipsis.

The eighth week: in the sequence of the Apocalypse of Weeks this follows 93:10. Each “week” is an age of world history; the author probably lived in the seventh, the time of the “apostate generation” (93:9) in the early second century BC.
A house … for the Great King: a new temple. *The Great King*: God (compare Ps 48:2; Matt 5:35).
Compare Isa 65:17; 66:22; 2 Pet 3:13; Rev 21:1.

verses.text: The book written by Enoch—Enoch wrote this complete teaching of wisdom, praised by everyone and judge of the whole earth—for every child of mine who will dwell on the earth, and for the generations to come who will practice uprightness and peace.{a}

Do not let your spirit be troubled because of the times,
for the Holy and Great One has set days for everything.

He will be gracious to the righteous one and give him lasting uprightness,
and give him power, so that he will have goodness and righteousness
and walk in eternal light.

Sin will perish in darkness forever
and will not be seen again from that day on, forever.

notes.text: This verse is the heading of the Epistle of Enoch proper; the bracketed words in Charles (“Enoch indeed wrote … all the earth”) may be a scribe’s addition.

verses.text: Afterward Enoch handed on the books and began to tell from them.

Enoch said,
“About the children of righteousness,
about the chosen of the world,
and about the plant of uprightness,{a} I will speak these things;
I, Enoch, will declare them to you, my sons,
according to what appeared to me in the heavenly vision,
what I learned from the word of the holy angels,
and what I came to understand from the heavenly tablets.”

After me, in the second week, great wickedness will arise,
and deceit will have sprung up.
In it will be the first end,{c}
and in it a man will be saved.
After it is over, wrongdoing will grow,
and a law will be made for the sinners.

After that, at the end of the fifth week,
the house of glory and dominion will be built forever.{f}

After that, in the sixth week, all who live in it will be blinded,
and the hearts of all of them will godlessly abandon wisdom.
In it a man will go up,{g}
and at its end the house of dominion will be burned with fire,
and the whole race of the chosen root will be scattered.
For who is there among all humankind who can hear the voice of the Holy One without being shaken? Who can think his thoughts? Who is there who can look on all the works of heaven?{i}
How could anyone look at heaven? Who could grasp heavenly things, or see a soul or spirit and report on it, or go up and see all their ends and grasp them or act like them?
Who among all people could know how wide and how long the earth is, and to whom has the measure of all of them been shown?
Or is there anyone who could tell the length of heaven, how great its height is, what it rests on, how many stars there are, and where all the lights rest?

notes.text: The plant of uprightness (or righteousness): Israel, or the faithful within it; compare 10:16; 84:6; Isa 60:21; 61:3.
The seventh: Enoch is the seventh from Adam (Gen 5; Jude 14).
The first end: the flood. *A man*: Noah. *A law … for the sinners*: the laws given after the flood (Gen 9:1–7).
A man: Abraham. His descendants, Israel, are “the plant of righteousness.”
The law of Sinai and the tabernacle (or the land of Israel as an “enclosure”).
The temple of Solomon.
A man: Elijah (2 Kgs 2:11). *The house of dominion … burned*: the destruction of the temple in 587/586 BC and the exile.
The sequence continues at 91:11–17 (weeks eight to ten).
Verses 11–14 are a separate wisdom poem on the limits of human knowledge, compare Job 38; Isa 40:12–14; Sir 1:2–3. Its rhetorical questions contrast with Enoch, who has been shown these things.

verses.text:
To certain people of a generation the paths of violence and of death will be revealed,
and they will keep far from them
and not follow them.

Now I tell you, the righteous:
do not walk in the path of evil or in the paths of death,
and do not come near them, so that you are not destroyed.

But seek and choose for yourselves righteousness and a chosen life,
and walk in the paths of peace,
and you will live and prosper.

Woe to those who build their houses with sin;
for they will be overthrown from all their foundations
and fall by the sword.
Those who get gold and silver in judgment will suddenly perish.

You have committed blasphemy and wrongdoing
and have made yourselves ready for the day of slaughter,
the day of darkness and the day of the great judgment.

So I tell you and declare to you:
the one who created you will overthrow you,
and there will be no pity at your fall,
and your Creator will rejoice at your destruction.

In those days your righteous ones will be
a rebuke to the sinners and the wicked.

notes.text: The woes (94:6–100:9; 103:5–8) attack wealthy oppressors and apostates, in the style of the prophets (Isa 5:8–23; Amos 6:1–7) and of Luke 6:24–26.

verses.text:
If only my eyes were a cloud of water,
so that I might weep over you
and pour down my tears like rain from a cloud,
and so find rest from my heart’s distress!

Who has allowed you to practice insult and wickedness?
Judgment will catch up with you, sinners.

Woe to you who pronounce curses that cannot be undone;
healing will be far from you because of your sins.

Woe to you who repay your neighbor with evil;
for you will be repaid according to your deeds.

Woe to you, lying witnesses,
and those who weigh out injustice,
for you will suddenly perish.

Take hope, you righteous! For the sinners will suddenly perish before you,
and you will rule over them as you wish.

Woe to you, sinners, for your riches make you look like the righteous,
yet your own hearts expose you as sinners,
and that will testify against you, a reminder of your evil deeds.

Woe to you, the mighty,
who use your might to oppress the righteous;
for your day of ruin is on its way.
Then many good days will come to the righteous, on the day of your judgment.

notes.text: Rock badgers: the hyrax, a small animal that shelters in rocks (Ps 104:18; Prov 30:26). *The sirens*: the Ethiopic borrows the Greek *seirēnes*, which the Greek Bible uses for desert creatures (perhaps ostriches or jackals) in Isa 13:21. The verse is obscure and some think it is out of place.
Compare Amos 6:6.
Compare Jer 2:13.

verses.text:
Believe, you righteous, that the sinners will be put to shame
and perish on the day of wrongdoing.

Know, you sinners, that the Most High has your destruction in mind,
and the angels of heaven rejoice over your destruction.

What will you do, you sinners,
and where will you run on that day of judgment,
when you hear the sound of the prayer of the righteous?

You will fare like those
against whom this word will stand as evidence:
“You have been companions of sinners.”

At that time the righteous will pray and be heard by the Lord,
and your time of judgment will arrive.

Woe to you, sinners, who live in the middle of the sea and on the dry land;
the memory of you is evil against you.

Woe to you who get silver and gold unjustly and say,
“We have grown rich and have possessions,
and have gotten everything we wanted.

Your lies will flow away like water,
for your wealth will not last
but will quickly fly up from you;
because you got it all unjustly,
you will be handed over to a great curse.

notes.text: From 97:6 to 107:3 a Greek text survives in the Chester Beatty–Michigan papyrus (fourth century AD). Where it differs from the Ethiopic in meaning, the notes say so.
Compare Luke 12:16–21.

verses.text:
Now I swear to you, the wise and the foolish,
that you will see many things on the earth.

You men will put on more finery than a woman
and more colors than a young girl;
in royalty, grandeur, and power,
in silver, gold, and purple,
in splendor and in food you will be poured out like water.

So they will lack teaching and wisdom,
and through this they will perish along with their possessions;
with all their glory and splendor,
in shame, slaughter, and great poverty,
their spirits will be thrown into the furnace of fire.

Barrenness was not given to woman;
because of the deeds of her own hands she dies childless.{b}

By the Holy Great One I swear to you, sinners,
that every evil thing you do lies open in heaven,
and none of your oppressive deeds are covered or hidden.
Do not think in your spirit or say in your heart that you do not know and do not see that every sin is recorded every day in heaven before the Most High.
From now on you know that all the oppression you inflict is written down every day until the day of your judgment.
Woe to you, fools, for you will perish through your folly. You sin against the wise, and so good fortune will not be your share.

Now know that you are ready for the day of destruction. Do not hope to live, sinners; you will go away and die, for you know no ransom. You are made ready for the day of the great judgment, for the day of distress and great shame for your spirits.

Woe to you, stubborn of heart, who do evil and eat blood!{c} Where do you get good things to eat and drink and be full? From all the good things the Lord Most High has placed in abundance on the earth. So you will have no peace.

Woe to you who love deeds of wrongdoing! Why do you hope for good fortune for yourselves? Know that you will be handed over to the righteous, and they will cut off your necks and kill you and show you no mercy.
Woe to you who rejoice at the distress of the righteous, for no grave will be dug for you.
Woe to you who treat the words of the righteous as nothing, for you will have no hope of life.
Woe to you who write down lying and wicked words; for they write down their lies so that people will hear them and act wickedly toward their neighbor.{d}
So they will have no peace but will die a sudden death.

notes.text: Sin was not sent: the Epistle insists on human responsibility for sin, in tension with the Book of the Watchers, which traces evil to the fallen angels (chapters 6–16).
The meaning is uncertain; the sense may be that suffering comes from human deeds, not from God’s decree.
Eat blood: forbidden in Gen 9:4; Lev 17:10–14.
Perhaps aimed at rival teachers or writings; compare 104:10–11.

verses.text:
Woe to those who twist the words of uprightness
and break the eternal law,
and make themselves into what they were not, into sinners;
they will be trampled on the earth.

In those days, you righteous, get ready to raise your prayers as a reminder
and set them as evidence before the angels,
so that they may set the sin of the sinners as a reminder before the Most High.

In those days the nations will be stirred up,
and the families of the nations will rise on the day of destruction.

In those days the destitute will go out and carry off their children
and abandon them, so that their children perish because of them;
they will abandon their nursing infants and not return to them,
and will have no pity on their loved ones.
Again I swear to you, sinners, that sin is made ready for a day of unending bloodshed.

Those who worship stones, and carved images of gold, silver, wood, stone, and clay, and those who worship unclean spirits and demons and all kinds of idols in ignorance, will get no help at all from them.

They will become wicked through the folly of their hearts,
and their eyes will be blinded by the fear of their hearts
and by visions in their dreams.

Through these they will become wicked and afraid,
for they will have done all their work in a lie
and worshiped a stone;
so in an instant they will perish.

But in those days, happy is everyone who takes wisdom’s words to heart and grasps them,
who keeps to the Most High’s ways and follows his righteous road,
and do not become wicked with the wicked;
for they will be saved.

Woe to you who spread evil to your neighbors;
for you will be killed in Sheol.{a}

Woe to those who do wrong and help oppression,
and kill their neighbors, until the day of the great judgment.

For he will throw down your glory,
bring affliction on your hearts,
rouse his fierce anger,
and put every one of you to the sword;
and the holy and righteous, all of them, will recall your sins.

notes.text: *Sheol*: Hebrew *sheʾol*, the realm of the dead; compare 22:1–14.

verses.text:
In those days fathers will be struck down together with their sons in one place,
and brothers will fall dead one with another,
until the streams run with their blood.

The horse will wade up to its chest in the blood of sinners,
and the chariot will sink to its top.{a}

In those days the angels will come down into the hidden places
and gather in one place all who brought down sin,
and the Most High will rise on that day of judgment
to carry out great judgment among sinners.

Then the children of the earth will see the wise in safety
and grasp everything this book says,
and realize that wealth cannot save them
when their sins bring them down.

Woe to you, stubborn of heart,
who stay awake to plan wickedness;
fear will come on you,
and there will be no one to help you.
Now know that he will ask the angels in heaven about your deeds, and the sun, the moon, and the stars about your sins, because on the earth you pass judgment on the righteous.
He will call every cloud, mist, dew, and rain to testify against you; for they will all be held back because of you from coming down on you, and they will remember your sins.
Now go ahead and give gifts to the rain so that it will not be held back from coming down on you, or to the dew, if it has accepted gold and silver from you to come down!{c}
When frost and snow with their cold, and all the snowstorms with all their plagues, fall on you, in those days you will not be able to stand before them.

notes.text: Compare Rev 14:20.
Like the pupil of an eye: traditionally “the apple of the eye”; compare Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8.
Irony: the rich cannot bribe the weather. The Greek is reported to differ here.

verses.text: Look at the sky, you children of heaven, and at every work of the Most High; fear him and do no evil in his presence.
If he shuts the windows of heaven and holds back the rain and the dew from falling on the earth because of you, what will you do then?
If he sends his anger on you because of your deeds, you cannot plead with him, for you spoke proud and arrogant words against his righteousness. So you will have no peace.
Do you not see the sailors on ships, how their vessels are tossed about by the waves and shaken by the winds, and are in great danger?
They are afraid because all their valuable goods go out on the sea with them, and their hearts dread that the sea will swallow them and they will die in it.
Are not the whole sea and all its waters and all its motion the work of the Most High? Has he not set limits to what it does and hemmed it in on every side with sand?{a}
When he rebukes it, it takes fright and dries up, and every fish in it perishes, together with all that it holds. Yet you sinners who live on the land have no fear of him.
Is it not he who formed heaven and earth and whatever fills them? Who gave insight and wisdom to every creature that moves over the land and through the sea?
Do not the sailors fear the sea? Yet sinners do not fear the Most High.

notes.text: Compare Job 38:8–11; Jer 5:22.

verses.text:
In those days, when he brings a terrible fire on you,
where will you run, and where will you find rescue?
When he hurls his word against you,
will you not be shaken and afraid?

All the lights will be shaken with great fear,
and all the earth will be shaken and tremble in alarm.

All the angels will carry out their orders
and try to hide from the presence of the Great Glory,
and the children of the earth will tremble and shake.
You sinners will be cursed forever,
and you will have no peace.

Do not be afraid, you souls of the righteous;
take hope, you who have died in righteousness.

Do not grieve if your soul has gone down to Sheol in grief,
and your body did not fare in life as your goodness deserved;
but wait for the day of the sinners’ judgment,
the day of cursing and punishment.

Yet when you die, the sinners say over you,
“As we die, so the righteous die,
and what good have they gained from their deeds?
I tell you, sinners: you are content to eat and drink, to rob and sin, to strip people naked, to get wealth and see good days.
Have you seen how the righteous end, that no violence of any kind is found in them until they die?
“Still, they perished and became as though they had never been, and their spirits went down to Sheol in distress.”

notes.text: The sinners’ argument recalls Eccl 2:14–16; 3:19–21; Wis 2:1–5.

verses.text: And now I make this vow to you, the righteous, by the splendor of the Great One, the Honored and Powerful, who rules, and by his majesty I vow it to you:

I know a mystery;
I have read the heavenly tablets
and seen the holy books,
and I have found written and engraved in them about them:

every blessing, joy and glory has been made ready for them
and recorded for the spirits of those who have died in righteousness;
your reward for your hard work will be a rich share of good things,
and your portion is far better than the portion of those still alive.

The spirits of you who have died in righteousness will live and rejoice;
their spirits will not perish, nor their memory before the face of the Great One,
for all the generations of the world.
So do not fear their scorn any longer.

Woe to you, sinners, when you have died,
if you die in the wealth of your sins,
and those like you say of you,
“Happy are the sinners! They have seen all their days.

Now they have died in prosperity and wealth,
and have seen no distress or killing in their life;
they have died in honor,
and no judgment was carried out on them while they lived.”

Know that their souls will be brought down to Sheol,
and they will be wretched in their great distress.

Do not say of the righteous and good who are alive,
“In our troubled days we have worked hard and known every trouble;
we have met much evil and been worn out,
and have become few and small in spirit.

We were ruined, and nobody came to our aid, not even with a word;
we were tormented and crushed, and we gave up expecting to see another day of life.

Those who hated us and struck us have ruled over us,
and we bowed our necks to those who hated us,
but they had no pity on us.

We wanted to get away from them, to escape and rest,
but found no place to run to and be safe from them.

We complained to the rulers in our distress
and cried out against those who devoured us,
but they paid no attention to our cries
and would not listen to our voice.

They helped those who robbed us, devoured us, and made us few. They hid their oppression and did not remove from us the yoke of those who devoured us, scattered us, and murdered us. They hid their murders and did not remember that they had raised their hands against us.”{b}

notes.text: Compare Deut 28:13, 44.
Verses 9–15 voice the complaint of the righteous; the answer follows in chapter 104.

verses.text: I vow to you that the angels in heaven keep you in mind for good in the presence of the Great One’s glory, and that your names are inscribed there before him.{a}

Take hope! For before, you were put to shame through evil and affliction, but now you will shine like the lights of heaven; you will shine and be seen, and the gates of heaven will be opened to you.{b}
When you cry out, let your cry be for justice, and justice will show itself to you; for all you have suffered will be avenged upon the rulers and upon everyone who aided your plunderers.
Take hope, and do not throw away your hope; for you will have great joy like the angels of heaven.

What will you have to do? You will not have to hide on the day of the great judgment, you will not be found as sinners, and the eternal judgment will be far from you for all the generations of the world.

Now do not be afraid, you righteous, when you see the sinners growing strong and prospering in their ways. Do not keep company with them, but keep far from their violence; for you will become companions of the hosts of heaven.
Though you sinners say, “None of our sins will be searched out and written down,” still they will write down all your sins every day.
Now I tell you that light and darkness, day and night, both look upon all your sins.

Do not be wicked in your hearts; do not lie or alter the words of uprightness, or call the words of the Holy Great One lies, or pay attention to your idols; for all your lying and all your wickedness lead not to righteousness but to great sin.
Now I know this mystery: sinners will alter and twist the words of righteousness in many ways; they will speak wicked words, lie, practice great deceptions, and write books about their own words.
But if they copy out my words faithfully into their own languages, neither altering them nor cutting anything away, but setting down faithfully everything that I first declared about them,{c}
then I know another mystery: books will be given to the righteous and the wise, to be a source of joy, uprightness, and much wisdom.
The books will be given to them, and they will believe them and rejoice over them; and then all the righteous who have learned from them all the paths of uprightness will be rewarded.

notes.text: Compare Dan 12:1; Luke 10:20.
Compare Dan 12:3.
This passage, with its concern for faithful copying and translation “in their languages,” is notable in a work that itself survives mainly in translation. Compare Rev 22:18–19.

verses.text: In those days, says the Lord, they will call to the children of the earth and testify about their wisdom: “Show it to them, for you are their guides, and rewards over the whole earth.
For I and my son will be joined with them forever in the paths of uprightness in their lives. You will have peace. Rejoice, you children of uprightness!” Amen.{a}

notes.text: I and my son: the phrase is unusual; it may refer to God and the righteous (or Israel) as his son, or be a Christian touch. The Greek papyrus is reported to lack this chapter.

verses.text: Some days later my son Methuselah chose a wife for his son Lamech, and she conceived and bore him a son.{a}

The child’s body was as white as snow and as ruddy as a rose in blossom; the hair on his head and his long locks were white like wool, and his eyes were lovely. When he opened his eyes, the whole house filled with light, as if the sun were shining in it.
Then he stood up in the hands of the midwife, opened his mouth, and spoke with the Lord of righteousness.
Lamech, his father, was terrified of him and ran away to his own father, Methuselah.

He said to him, “I have fathered a strange son, different from and unlike a human being, resembling the children of the God of heaven. His nature is different; he is not like us. His eyes are like the rays of the sun, and his face is glorious.
I think he cannot have come from me, but from the angels, and I fear that something extraordinary will happen on earth in his time.
Now, my father, I am here to plead with you and beg you to go to Enoch, our father, and learn the truth from him, for he lives among the angels.”

When Methuselah heard what his son said, he traveled to the ends of the earth to find me, for he had been told that I was there. He called out, and I heard his voice and went to him. I said to him, “I am here, my son. Why have you come to me?”
He answered, “I have come to you because of something that worries me greatly, a troubling sight.

Now, my father, hear me. A son has been born to my son Lamech, unlike anyone else. His nature is not like a human nature. The color of his body is whiter than snow and redder than a rose in bloom, the hair of his head is whiter than white wool, his eyes are like the rays of the sun, and when he opened his eyes he lit up the whole house.
He rose up from the midwife’s hands, opened his mouth, and praised the Lord of heaven.

His father Lamech became afraid and fled to me. He does not believe that the boy is his, but that he is in the likeness of the angels of heaven. So I have come to you so that you may tell me the truth.”

I, Enoch, replied, “The Lord is going to do something new on earth. I have seen it before in a vision, and I am telling you now: in the days of my father Jared, certain angels of heaven disobeyed the Lord’s command.{b}
They sin and break the law; they have joined themselves to women and sin with them, have married some of them, and have fathered children by them.
A great destruction will come over the whole earth; there will be a flood and great destruction for one year.{c}
This son who has been born to you will be left on the earth, and his three children will be saved with him; when all humankind on the earth dies, he and his sons will be saved.
They will produce giants on the earth, not of spirit but of flesh, and there will be great punishment on the earth, and the earth will be cleansed of all impurity.{d}

Now tell your son Lamech that the one who has been born is truly his son. Name him Noah, for he will be left to you, and he and his sons will be saved from the destruction that will come on the earth because of all the sin and all the wrongdoing that will reach its full measure on the earth in his days.{e}

After that, injustice will grow greater still than the injustice that had at first reached its full measure on earth. For I know the mysteries of the holy ones: the Lord himself has revealed them to me and explained them, and I have read them on the heavenly tablets.

notes.text: Chapters 106–107 tell of Noah’s miraculous birth, a story also found in the Genesis Apocryphon from Qumran (1QapGen 2–5). *Lamech*: Hebrew *Lemekh*, of uncertain meaning (Gen 5:25–31).
*Jared*: Hebrew *Yered*, “descent,” explained in 6:6 as the time when the Watchers came down.
For one year: the flood lasts a year and ten days in Gen 7:11; 8:14 (or a full year by the 364-day calendar).
