When the sinner grew arrogant, he knocked down fortified walls with a battering ram,
and you did not stop him.

Foreign nations went up to your altar;
they trampled it arrogantly, with their sandals on,

because the sons of Jerusalem had made the Lord’s sacred things unclean;
they had desecrated the offerings made to God by their lawless acts.

For this reason he said, “Throw them far away from me.”
The beauty of his glory was of no benefit to them.{b}

It was despised before God;
it was utterly dishonored.

Sons and daughters went into a wretched captivity;
their necks were sealed, and they were marked out among the nations.

He treated them according to their sins,
because he abandoned them into the hands of the powerful.

For he turned his face away from pitying them,
young and old and their children alike.

For they had done evil all together,
so as not to listen.

The heaven was angry,
and the earth detested them,

because no one on earth had ever done
what they did.
So the earth will recognize all your judgments, God, as just.

They made fun of their lawless acts, as they themselves used to do;
they put their wrongdoing on public display in the face of the sun.

Because these women defiled themselves in a confusion of mixed unions,
my belly and my inward parts ache over this.

I will declare you righteous, God, with an upright heart,
for your righteousness lies in your judgments, God.

For you paid sinners back according to their deeds,
and according to their sins, which were very wicked.
You uncovered their sins so that your judgment would be seen;

you wiped out their memory from the earth.
God is a just judge, and no one’s appearance impresses him.{d}

For the nations reproached Jerusalem by trampling her down;
her beauty was dragged down from the throne of glory.

She put on sackcloth in place of her fine robe,
a rope around her head in place of a crown.

She was stripped of the turban of glory
which God had put on her;
in dishonor her beauty was thrown to the ground.

And I looked, and pleaded before the face of the Lord, and said:
“Enough, Lord, of your hand weighing heavily on Israel,
by bringing the nations against it.

For they have mocked and have shown no mercy,
in anger and rage and bitter fury,

and they will make an end of us,
unless you, Lord, rebuke them in your anger.

For they have not acted out of zeal,
but out of the desire of their soul,
to pour out their anger on us in plunder.

His body was carried to and fro on the waves in great disgrace,
and there was no one to bury him.

He said, “I shall be master of land and sea,”
and he did not realize that God is great,
powerful in his enormous might.

He himself is king over the heavens,
and judges kings and rulers.

It is he who raises me to glory,
and who puts the proud to sleep in everlasting destruction and dishonor,
because they did not know him.

And now, you magnates of the earth, behold the Lord’s judgment:
he is a mighty and righteous king,
who judges all that lies under the sky.

to separate the righteous from the sinner,
and to repay sinners forever according to their deeds,

and to have mercy on the righteous, away from the humiliation by the sinner,
and to repay the sinner for what he did to the righteous.

For the Lord is good to those who call on him with patience,
to act according to his mercy toward his devout ones,
and to let them stand before him continually in strength.
Blessed be the Lord forever in the presence of his servants.

notes.text: Jerusalem is probably “foundation of Shalem” or “city of peace,” but the origin of the name is uncertain.
“His glory” here is probably the glory of God dwelling in the temple.
Greek *pornai*, “prostitutes.” Verses 13–14 are obscure; the idea seems to be that the Gentile soldiers treated the city’s people as they would treat prostitutes, openly, in daylight.
That is, he shows no partiality (compare Deut 10:17).

The Greek of this verse is hard and probably damaged, and a few manuscripts read differently. “The dragon” is the foreign conqueror of verse 1, whom most scholars identify with the Roman general Pompey (who took Jerusalem in 63 BC); compare Jer 51:34 and Ezek 29:3. His death is described in verses 30–31.
Pompey was murdered on the Egyptian shore in 48 BC after his defeat by Julius Caesar; his body was left on the beach and cremated by a freedman. The psalm does not name him.

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon, about the righteous.

verses.text: Why are you sleeping, my soul, and not blessing the Lord?

The righteous always remember the Lord,
in confession and in declaring the Lord’s judgments to be right.

The righteous do not make light of the Lord’s discipline,
and their good will is always before the Lord.

The righteous stumble and they declare the Lord just;
they fall and look to see what God will do for them;
they look out from where their rescue will come.

The confidence of the righteous is from God their savior.
Sin upon sin does not lodge in the house of a righteous man.

The righteous constantly looks over his house,
to remove any wrong done by his own transgression.
He makes atonement for sins of ignorance by fasting and humbling his soul,
and the Lord cleanses every devout man and his household.

The sinner stumbles and curses his life,
the day he was born and the pains of his mother’s labor.
He adds sins to sins as long as he lives.

He falls, for his fall is evil, and he will not get up;
the destruction of the sinner is forever,
and he will not be remembered when God visits the righteous.
This is the portion of sinners forever.

But those who fear the Lord will rise up to eternal life,
and their life will be in the Lord’s light, which will never come to an end.

notes.text: “Watch” translates Greek *egrēgorsis*, “wakefulness”; it may refer to the night watches, or to the stations at which singers and watchmen served in the temple.

chapters.title: Solomon’s dialogue with the people-pleasers.{a}

verses.text:
Excessive in words, excessive in outward display beyond everyone,
he is harsh in his speech when he condemns sinners in judgment.

His hand is the first against them, as though in zeal,
and yet he is himself guilty in many kinds of sin and in lack of self-control.

His eyes are on every woman, without distinction;
his tongue lies when he makes a contract with an oath.

At night and in secret places he sins as though no one sees him;
with his eyes he talks to every woman in an appointment for wickedness.
He is quick to enter every house with a cheerful face, as though he were innocent.

May God remove those who live in hypocrisy among the devout,
in the ruin of his flesh and with a life of poverty.

May God uncover the works of the people-pleasers,
and may his works become a laughingstock and a mockery.

May the devout declare the judgment of their God to be just,
when sinners are removed from the face of the righteous,
the people-pleaser who speaks only with deceit.

And their eyes are on a man’s house in its security, like a snake,
to break up each other’s wisdom with the words of lawless men.

His words are deceptions,
aiming at the fulfillment of unjust desire.

He does not stop until he has succeeded in scattering them as orphans,
and he has made a house desolate for the sake of lawless desire.
He deceived them with words, saying that there is no one who sees and judges;

Lord, may his portion be dishonor in your presence;
may he leave with groans and arrive to curses.

May his life be in pains and poverty and helplessness, Lord;
may his sleep be in sorrows and his waking in distress.

May sleep be taken from his temples at night;
may he fail in every work of his hands, in dishonor.

May his house be empty,
lacking everything that would fill his soul,
and may his old age be spent in the loneliness of childlessness, until he is taken away.

May the flesh of the people-pleasers be torn apart by wild animals,
and the bones of the lawless lie in the sun, in dishonor.
May crows pull out the eyes of those who put on a show,
because they have laid waste many people’s houses in dishonor and scattered them in their greed.

They did not remember God,
and they did not fear God in any of this.

They provoked God and made him angry, so that he would remove them from the earth,
because they pretended to be on the side of innocent souls, deceiving them.
Blessed are those who fear the Lord in their innocence.

The Lord will rescue them from deceitful men and sinners,
and he will rescue us from every trap of the lawless.

May God remove those who in arrogance do every kind of wrong,
for the Lord our God is a great and mighty judge in righteousness.
Lord, may your mercy be on all who love you.

notes.text: Greek *anthrōparesko*, “those who please men”; compare Col 3:22 and Eph 6:6. The psalm attacks hypocrites, probably the religious and political leaders of the Hasmonean period, who put on a show of devotion.
Hades (Greek *hadēs*) is the realm of the dead, the Hebrew Sheol, which is never full (Prov 27:20; Hab 2:5).

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon.

verses.text:
Lord God, I will praise your name with joy
among those who know your righteous judgments.

For you are kind and merciful,
a refuge for the poor,
so when I cry out to you, do not be silent toward me.
For no one can take plunder away from a powerful man,
and who can take anything from all that you have made, unless you give it?

For a man and his portion are weighed out by you;
he will not add to it, to have more than your judgment allows, God.

When we are afflicted we will call on you for help,
and you will not turn away our plea,
for you are our God.

Do not lay your hand heavily on us,
lest in our need we sin.

Even if you do not turn us back, we will not hold back,
but we will come to you.

For if I am hungry I will cry out to you, God,
and you will give to me.

You feed the birds and the fish,
when you send rain in the deserts so that the green grass can spring up,

and so prepare fodder in the wilderness for every living creature;
and if they are hungry, they lift their faces to you.

You feed kings and rulers and peoples, God,
and what hope has the poor and needy man, if not you, Lord?

And you will listen. For who is so kind and gentle but you?
You cheer the humble soul by opening your hand with mercy.

A man’s kindness is given sparingly, and it is for a day;
and if he repeats it without grumbling, even that is a marvel.

But your gift is great, with kindness, and rich,
and the one whose hope is in you will not be held back from your gift.
Your mercy is over all the earth, Lord, in kindness.
Blessed is the one whom God remembers with a fair measure of sufficiency.
If a man has too much, he sins;

enough in moderation is sufficient, together with righteousness,
and in that is the Lord’s blessing: to have enough, with righteousness.

Those who fear the Lord rejoiced in good things,
and your kindness is upon Israel in your kingdom.{a}
May the Lord’s glory be blessed, for he is our king.

notes.text: Israel (“God strives” or “he who strives with God,” Gen 32:28) is the name given to Jacob and then to his descendants.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: in hope.

verses.text: Happy is the man who is prepared in heart to invoke the Lord’s name.
When he remembers the name of the Lord, he will be saved;

the Lord sets his paths straight,
and the Lord his God keeps the work of his hands safe.

Because of the dreams of the night his soul is not troubled;
when he crosses rivers or in storms at sea, he will not be afraid.

He gets up from sleep and blesses the name of the Lord;
when his heart is calm, he sings to the name of his God.

And he prays to the Lord for his whole house,
and the Lord listens to the prayer of everyone who fears God.

Whatever he asks for, he will receive from the Lord;
the Lord will answer every request of a man who is hoping in God.
Blessed be the Lord, who shows mercy to those who love him in sincerity.
Blessed is the Lord forever.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: of turning back.{a}

verses.text:
Do not take your dwelling far from us, God,
lest those who hate us without cause attack us.

For you have rejected them, God;
do not let their feet trample on your holy inheritance.

Discipline us yourself, as you wish,
but do not hand us over to the nations.

For if you send death, you yourself command it for us;
you will have mercy on us.
While your name dwells among us, we will find mercy,
and the nation will have no power against us.

For you are our protector,
and we will call on you, and you will listen to us.
For you will have pity on the house of Israel forever, and you will not reject it.

We are under your yoke forever, and under the rod of your discipline.
You will set us straight in the time of your visit.

notes.text: Greek *epistrophēs*; in the Psalms of Solomon the word suggests “repentance” or “being brought back” to God.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: for victory.{a}

verses.text:
The sound of distress and the cry of war has reached my ear,
the sound of a trumpet blaring slaughter and destruction.

The noise of a great crowd, like a very strong wind,
like a storm of fire raging through the desert.
And I said in my heart, “Where, then, will God judge it?”
I heard a sound from Jerusalem, the holy city.

My loins were shattered at the news,
my knees gave way;

my heart was terrified,
and my bones trembled like flax stalks.

God uncovered their sins in the face of the sun;
the whole earth knew the righteous judgments of God.
Their lawless acts were in hidden underground rooms, to provoke him:
son with mother and father with daughter were mixed together;

each committed adultery with his neighbor’s wife;
they made agreements with each other with oaths about these things.

They plundered the holy things of God,
as though there were no heir to redeem them.

They trampled the altar of the Lord, in every uncleanness,
and with menstrual blood they defiled the sacrifices as if they were common meat.

There was no sin they left undone;
they surpassed the nations.

For this reason God mixed a spirit of confusion for them,
and made them drink a cup of unmixed wine to drunkenness.
He brought one from the end of the earth, one who strikes with power;
he decided on war against Jerusalem and its land.

He entered like a father into the house of his sons, in peace;
he set his feet down with great security.
He captured her fortified towers and the wall of Jerusalem,
and God led him in safety while they went astray.{b}

He destroyed their rulers and every wise counselor;
he spilled the blood of Jerusalem’s residents as if it were dirty water.

He led away their sons and daughters,
whom they had fathered in defilement.
They did according to their uncleanness, as their fathers had done.
They defiled Jerusalem and the things that were consecrated to God’s name.
God was shown to be righteous in his judgments among the nations of the earth,
and the devout of God were like lambs in their innocence in the midst of them.
Praised be the Lord, who judges all the earth in his righteousness.
See now, God, you have shown us your judgment in your righteousness;
our eyes have seen your judgments, God.

We have declared your honored name righteous forever,
for you are the God of righteousness, who judges Israel with discipline.
Turn your mercy toward us, God, and have pity on us;
bring together Israel’s scattered people with compassion and goodness.

For your faithfulness is with us,
and though we stiffened our necks, you are our discipliner.

Do not overlook us, our God,
lest the nations swallow us up as though there were no one to redeem us.

You have been our God from the beginning,
and our hope is in you, Lord.

We will not turn away from you,
for your judgments toward us are kind.

The favor is ours and our children’s forever.
Lord, our savior, we will never be shaken again, for all time.

Praised be the Lord in his judgments through the mouth of the devout,
and may Israel be blessed by the Lord forever.

notes.text: The Greek *eis nikos* may stand for Hebrew *lamnatseach* (“for the leader”), a heading found in many biblical psalms, as in Ps 4–6.

The verses refer to Pompey’s entry into Jerusalem in 63 BC, apparently by agreement with one of the rival Hasmonean brothers (Hyrcanus II), followed by the siege and storming of the temple hill by his troops.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: for reproof.

verses.text:
When Israel was led away in exile to a foreign land,
when they had turned away from the Lord who had redeemed them,

they were thrown out of the inheritance that the Lord had given them.
Israel is dispersed among every nation, according to the word of God,

so that you, God, may be shown to be righteous in your righteousness,
by our lawless acts.
For you are a just judge over all the peoples on earth.
No one who does wrong can be hidden from your knowledge,

and the righteous deeds of your devout are before you, Lord;
and where could a person hide from your knowledge, God?

Our deeds are by our own choice and by the authority of our own soul,
to practice justice or injustice in what our hands do.
And in your righteousness you visit the sons of men.

The one who does righteousness stores up life for himself with the Lord,
and the one who does wrong is himself to blame for the ruin of his soul.
For the Lord’s judgments are in righteousness, for each man and household.
To whom will you be kind, God, if not to those who call on the Lord?
He will cleanse a soul from sins in confession, in open acknowledgment,
for shame is ours, and on our faces, because of everything.
And whose sins will he pardon, if not those of sinners?

You will bless the righteous, and will not call them to account for what they have sinned,
and your kindness is for sinners when they repent.

And now, you are God, and we are your people, whom you have loved.
Look, and have pity, God of Israel, for we are yours.
Do not take your mercy away from us, lest they set upon us.

You made a covenant with our fathers about us,
and we put our hope in you as our soul turns back.
The Lord’s mercy is on the house of Israel forever and ever.

notes.text: Abraham (“father of a multitude,” Gen 17:5) is named here as the ancestor to whom the covenant promise was first given.

chapters.title: Among the hymns, of Solomon.

verses.text:
How fortunate is the one the Lord keeps in mind by reproving him,
and who is hemmed in from the way of evil by the whip,
to be cleansed from sin, that it may not multiply.

The one who prepares his back for the lashes will be cleansed,
for the Lord is kind to those who endure discipline.

For he will make the ways of the righteous straight,
and will not bend them in his discipline.

The Lord’s compassion rests on those who love him sincerely,
and the Lord will not forget his servants but treat them mercifully.

For the testimony lies in the Law, an everlasting covenant;
the Lord’s testimony oversees what people do with their lives.

Our Lord is righteous and devout in his judgments forever,
and Israel will praise the name of the Lord with gladness.

And the devout will confess him in the people’s gathering,
and God will pity the poor, to the joy of Israel.

For God is kind and merciful forever,
and the assemblies of Israel will glorify the name of the Lord.
The salvation of the Lord is on the house of Israel, for everlasting gladness.{a}

notes.text: Swete’s Greek text reads *sōphrosynē* (“sound mind, self-control”), but editors commonly read *euphrosynē* (“gladness”), as in verses 6 and 7. “Gladness” is used here. This is a point to check against the manuscripts.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: for expectation.

verses.text: Blow the trumpet in Zion, the trumpet that calls the holy ones.{a}

Announce in Jerusalem the voice of the one who brings good news,
for God has had mercy on Israel by visiting them.

Stand on a height, Jerusalem, and look at your children,
gathered from east and west, all together, by the Lord.

From the north they come with the joy of their God;
from far-off islands God has gathered them.
He lowered high mountains to make level ground for them.

The hills fled at their coming;
the forests gave them shade as they passed.

God made every fragrant tree spring up for them,
so that Israel might pass by with the visit of the glory of their God.

notes.text: Zion is the hill of Jerusalem on which the temple stood, and in poetry stands for the city itself.
Compare Baruch 4:36–5:9, which is very close to this psalm; the two probably share a source, or one is based on the other.

chapters.title: Of Solomon: against the tongue of lawless men.

verses.text:
Lord, rescue my soul from the lawless and wicked man,
from the lawless tongue that slanders and speaks falsehood and deceit.
The words of a wicked man’s tongue twist and turn in many ways.

It throws the houses of the lawless into confusion, with a war of whispering lips.
May God keep the lips of the lawless far away from the innocent, in their helplessness,
and may the bones of the slanderers be scattered far from those who fear the Lord.
May the slanderer’s tongue perish in a flaming fire, away from the devout.
May the Lord guard the soul of the man who makes peace in his house.
The salvation of the Lord is on Israel his servant forever,

and may the sinners perish from the face of the Lord all at once,
and may the devout of the Lord inherit his promises.

notes.text: The Greek of this verse is rough and the text may be damaged. The sense is that slander is a fire that burns first the speaker and then every household it enters.

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon, a comfort for the righteous.

verses.text:
The Lord’s right hand sheltered me;
his right hand showed us pity.

The Lord’s arm rescued us from the sword sweeping by,
from hunger and from the sinners’ death.

Wild beasts rushed upon them, vicious ones;
with their teeth they tore at their flesh,
and with their molars they ground their bones.
And from all these the Lord rescued us.

The ungodly man was troubled because of his offenses,
lest he be carried off with the sinners.

For the sinner’s ruin is terrible,
and none of this will touch the righteous.

For the correction of the righteous, done in ignorance,
is not like the ruin of the sinner.

The righteous man is disciplined in secret,
so that the sinner will not rejoice over him.

For he will admonish the righteous like a dearly loved son,
and his correction is that given to a firstborn.

For the Lord will spare his devout ones,
and wipe out their offenses by discipline.
The life of the righteous is forever.

But sinners will be taken away to destruction,
and no memory of them will be found any more.

The Lord’s mercy is on the devout,
and his mercy is on those who fear him.

chapters.title: A hymn of Solomon.

verses.text:
The Lord is faithful to those who love him in truth,
to those who endure his discipline,
to those who walk in righteousness by his commandments,
in the Law that he gave us for our life.

The devout of the Lord will live by it forever.
The Lord’s paradise, the trees of life, are his devout ones.

For this reason their inheritance is Hades and darkness and destruction,
and they will not be found on the day when the righteous receive mercy.
But the devout of the Lord will inherit life in gladness.

notes.text: The Greek is difficult. The idea seems to be that the pleasures of the wicked are brief and rotten.

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon, with a song.

verses.text:
In my distress I called on the Lord,
when I was pressed hard by the sinners, and I was saved.
For you are the hope and the refuge of the poor, God.
For who is strong, God, if not to give you thanks in truth?
And what is a man’s power, if not to give thanks to your name?

With a new psalm and song, in the gladness of the heart,
lips bearing fruit, with the tongue a well-tuned instrument,
the first offering of lips from a devout and righteous heart—

the one who does these things will never be shaken by evil;
the flame of fire and the anger of the unjust will not touch him,

when it goes out against sinners from the Lord’s presence,
to wipe out all that sinners stand on.

For the mark of God is on the righteous, for their salvation;
famine and sword and death are far from the righteous.

For they will flee from the devout as from an enemy chasing them,
but they will be pursued and caught, the sinners;
and those who do lawless things will not escape the Lord’s judgment,
but will be overtaken as by skilled enemies.
For the mark of destruction is on their foreheads.

And what sinners inherit is destruction and darkness,
and their lawless acts will chase them down to Hades below.
Their inheritance will not be found for their children.
For sins will leave the houses of sinners empty.

And sinners will perish forever on the day of the Lord’s judgment,
when God visits the earth with his judgment.

notes.text: The “mark” of verses 8 and 10 recalls the sign on the forehead in Ezek 9:4–6, and the mark of the beast in Rev 13:16–17 and 14:9. In the Psalms of Solomon, the righteous bear God’s mark for protection and the sinners bear a mark of destruction.

chapters.title: A hymn of Solomon, for the support of the devout.

verses.text:
When my soul was drowsy, away from the Lord,
I almost slipped into the deep sleep of falling.

When I was far from God, my soul was almost poured out to death,
near the gates of Hades, with the sinner.

When my soul was torn away from the Lord, the God of Israel,
it would have been so, had the Lord not taken hold of me, in his lasting mercy.

He pricked me like a horseman’s spur, to wake me up;
my savior and helper in every time saved me.

I will give thanks to you, God, that you took hold of me for salvation,
and did not count me with the sinners to my ruin.

Do not take your mercy away from me, God,
or your remembrance from my heart, until death.

Master me, God, away from evil sin
and from every wicked woman who trips up the foolish.

And do not let the beauty of a lawless woman deceive me,
nor anyone lying under the power of useless sin.

Make straight the works of my hands according to your pattern,
and watch over my steps with your remembrance.

Hold in check my tongue and my lips with words of truth;
put anger and unreasoning rage far away from me.

Take grumbling and faint-heartedness in distress away from me,
even if I sin when you discipline me to bring me back.

But in your good pleasure, with cheerfulness, strengthen my soul;
when you give strength to my soul, what is given will be enough for me.
For if you do not give strength, who will endure discipline in poverty?

When the soul is poured into the hand of its decay,
your test is in his flesh and in the distress of poverty.
If the righteous endures in these things, he will receive mercy from the Lord.

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon, with a song, to the king.{a}

verses.text:
Lord, you are our king forever and ever,
for in you, God, our soul will boast.

And how long is the span of a man’s life on earth?
His hope is as long as his time.

But we will hope in God our savior,
for the might of our God is forever, with mercy,
and our God’s kingdom lasts forever, ruling the nations.

You, Lord, chose David as king over Israel,
and you swore to him about his descendants forever,
that his kingdom would not fail before you.

and did not glorify your honored name.
They set up a royal house in glory, in place of their height;
they laid waste David’s throne with the arrogance of a war cry.{b}

But you, God, will throw them down and remove their offspring from the earth,
when a man foreign to our race rises up against them.

According to their sins you will repay them, God,
so that they find themselves treated as their deeds deserve.

God will have no pity on them;
he searched out their offspring and let not one of them go.

The Lord is faithful in all his judgments
that he carries out on the earth.

The lawless man laid our land waste, taking away its inhabitants;
they destroyed young and old and their children together.

In the anger of his splendor he sent them away to the west,
and made the rulers of the land a laughingstock, and showed no pity.

In his hostility the enemy acted with arrogance,
and his heart was foreign to our God.
And everything he did in Jerusalem was like what the nations do in their cities for their gods.

And the sons of the covenant, living among the mixed peoples, gave way to them;
there was no one among them in Jerusalem who practiced mercy and truth.

Those who loved the gatherings of the devout fled from them;
like sparrows they were scattered from their nests.

They wandered in the deserts to save their souls from evil,
and in the eyes of those who lived abroad a life that had been saved from them was precious.
Their dispersion came upon the whole earth, from lawless men.

For the heaven held back from letting rain fall on the earth,
and the ever-flowing springs were stopped, from the deeps, from the high mountains,
because there was no one among them who did righteousness and justice;
from their ruler to the least of the people, all were in every sin.
The king was in lawlessness, the judge in disobedience, and the people in sin.
Gird him with strength to shatter unjust rulers,
to cleanse Jerusalem from the nations who trample her to ruin,

to wipe out lawless nations by a word from his mouth,
so that nations run from his presence when he threatens them,
and to convict sinners by the word of their own hearts.

And he will gather a holy people, whom he will lead in righteousness,
and will judge the tribes of the people who have been made holy by the Lord their God.

And he will not allow wrong to lodge among them any longer,
and no man who knows evil will live with them.

For he will know them, that they are all sons of their God,
and he will divide them up by their tribes on the land.

And no foreigner or stranger will live among them anymore.
He will judge peoples and nations with the wisdom of his righteousness. Pause.{d}

And he will have the peoples of the nations serve him under his yoke,
and he will glorify the Lord in a place marked out for all the earth to see.
And he will cleanse Jerusalem in holiness, as it was from the beginning,

so that nations come from the end of the earth to see his glory,
carrying her exhausted sons as presents,

and to see the glory of the Lord, with which God has glorified her.
And he is a righteous king, taught by God, over them.

There will be no injustice among them in his days,
for all will be holy, and their king will be the Lord’s anointed.{e}

For he will not put his hope in horse or rider or bow,
nor will he pile up gold or silver for war,
nor will he gather hopes in the numbers of men for the day of war.
For he will smite the land with a word from his mouth, for all time,
he will bless the Lord’s people with wisdom and with gladness.

And he himself is free from sin, so as to rule a great people,
to convict rulers and remove sinners by the strength of his word.
And the Lord’s blessing goes with him, with power,

he shepherds the Lord’s flock in faith and righteousness,
and will not let any of them grow weak in their pasture.

He will lead them all in equality,
and there will be no arrogance among them, so that anyone is oppressed.

This is the glory of Israel’s king, as God foresaw,
to set him over the house of Israel and train it.

His words are refined, more than fine gold, the most precious;
in the assemblies he will judge the tribes of the people made holy.
His words are like the words of the holy ones among sanctified peoples.

Blessed are those who will live in those days,
to see the good things of Israel in the gathering of the tribes,
which God will do.

notes.text: The Greek *meta ōdēs* (“with a song”) is a heading also found on Psalms 15 and 17. “To the king” may refer to the Lord as king, or to the Davidic king expected in the psalm. This psalm is the most important description of the Messiah in the literature of the time.
The Hasmonean rulers (from 104 BC they took the title “king”) were priests, not descendants of David. The psalmist regards them as usurpers.
“Son of David” is a title here for the future king. The hope of a king from David’s line rests on 2 Sam 7:12–16.
Greek *diapsalma*, as in the Greek Psalms (Hebrew *selah*), a mark whose meaning is not known; it may signal a musical interlude or a pause.

Greek *christos kyrios*. Most scholars read “the Lord’s anointed” (*christos kyriou*, as in 18:6 and 18:8); some think the original was a Hebrew phrase “the Lord’s anointed” and that “Lord Messiah” arose in translation, or that a Christian hand altered it. “Anointed” and “Messiah” are the same word (Hebrew *mashiach*, Greek *christos*).

chapters.title: A psalm of Solomon, still about the Lord’s anointed.{a}

verses.text: Lord, your mercy is over the works of your hands forever.

Your kindness is on Israel in a rich gift.
Your eyes look on them, and none of them will lack anything.

Your ears listen to the prayer of the poor who hope;
your judgments over all the earth are with mercy,

and your love is over the descendants of Abraham, the sons of Israel.
Your discipline is on us as on a firstborn, an only son,
to turn a listening soul away from foolishness and ignorance.

May God cleanse Israel for the day of mercy, with blessing,
for the day of choice, when his anointed one is brought in.

Blessed are those who will be born in those days,
to see the good things of the Lord which he will do for the coming generation,

under the rod of discipline of the Lord’s anointed,
in reverence for his God, in the wisdom of the spirit and of righteousness and strength,

to set men straight in works of righteousness in the fear of God,
to set them all before the Lord.
A good generation, living in reverence for God, in the days of mercy. Pause.{b}
Great is our God and glorious, living on high,

who set the lights in their courses to mark the seasons of the hours from day to day,
and they have not left the road you ordered them to follow.

In the fear of God their path goes on each day,
from the day God made them and to the end of time.

notes.text: Greek *eti peri tou christou kyriou*. As in 17:36 some read “the Lord’s anointed” and others “the Lord Messiah”.
Greek *diapsalma*; see the note at 17:31.

books.name: Psalms 152–155
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Syriac text of the four apocryphal psalms numbered 152, 153, 154, and 155 in the Mosul manuscript of the Syriac Psalter (12th century AD; now Baghdad, Library of the Chaldean Patriarchate, no. 1113, Peshitta Institute siglum 12t4), in the transcription printed by the Peshitta Institute (ed. W. Baars, 1972) and available in the Comprehensive Aramaic Lexicon database. The English edition of W. Wright (*Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology* 9, 1887; public domain) was consulted for obscure words; the English here is new. Syriac *maryā* is rendered “Lord.” Readings of the Dead Sea Scrolls are cited “as reported.” **Numbering.** The Mosul manuscript numbers these four psalms 152–155 (Psalm 151 is the psalm of David and Goliath already known from the Greek Psalter). In the manuscripts of the *Book of Discipline* by Elias of al-Anbar (about the 10th century AD) the five psalms stand in a different order and without numbers: they are Psalm I (151), II (154), III (155), IV (152), and V (153). Verse numbers here follow the Mosul manuscript, and the verse counts of Psalms 154 and 155 (20 and 21) are higher than in Wright’s edition (17 and 20), which was made from a later group of manuscripts and has a shorter, somewhat different text. **About the book.** These are four short Hebrew-style psalms ascribed to David (152 and 153, which concern his fight with the lion and the wolf) and to King Hezekiah or the returning exiles (154 and 155, headings that differ among manuscripts). They survive only in Syriac. Psalms 154 and 155 also appear in Hebrew in the Great Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11QPs-a), a scroll usually dated to the 1st century AD; the Hebrew of Psalm 154 is also found in part in a fragment from Cave 4 (4Q448), as reported. The Syriac translation of these two psalms is thus based on a Hebrew text close to the Qumran one, but with a good many differences. No Hebrew text of Psalms 152 and 153 has been found, and scholars disagree about whether they were translated from a lost Hebrew original or composed in Syriac. A letter of the Catholicos Timothy I (died AD 823) mentions Hebrew manuscripts with extra “psalms of David” found near Jericho, which may explain how such psalms reached the Syriac church. The Syriac texts were first printed in the 18th century and edited by Wright in 1887 and by Baars in 1972. These psalms are not in the Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox, or Protestant canons. The Syriac Orthodox and Church of the East traditions copy them mostly as an appendix to the Psalter, and the Mosul scribe notes that they are not found in the Greek or Hebrew reckoning. Dates are given as BC/AD. CJT draft.

chapters.heading: Psalm 152
chapters.title: Spoken by David when he was fighting with a lion and a wolf that were carrying off sheep from his flock.{a}

verses.text:
Shall I go down to Sheol at the lion’s mouth,
or shall the wolf throw me into confusion?{c}

Did they not have enough, lurking near my father’s sheep
and ripping one away from his fold?
Must they also try to destroy my soul?

Have pity, Lord, on your chosen one,
and rescue your devout servant from destruction,
so that he may stand firm in praising you at all times
and give glory to the name of your greatness.{d}

Once you have freed him from the grip of the lion that destroys
and the wolf that tears,
and have taken my captive life out of the mouth of the wild beasts,

quickly, my Adonai,
send a savior from your presence,
and lift me out of the gaping pit
that wants to shut me up in its depths.{e}

notes.text: Syriac *maryā*, “Lord,” is the word the Syriac Bible uses for Yahweh, and it is rendered “Lord” throughout these psalms. In the Mosul manuscript this psalm is preceded by a note saying that these four psalms (152–155) have no explanatory introductions from Eusebius, Athanasius, or Theodore the Interpreter, and are simply written out.
Syriac *ʾel*, a short form of the divine name “God,” appears twice here.
The Syriac of this verse is run together and uncertain in the manuscript; the sense given is the likeliest, and the last words are read “as reported.”
Another reading, found in some manuscripts, is “so that he may recount your praises at all times.”
Syriac *ʾadonayhi*, a form of the Hebrew *Adonay*, “my Lord,” left in a Hebrew form in the Syriac.

chapters.heading: Psalm 153
chapters.title: Spoken by David when he received God’s kindness, when God rescued him from the lion and the wolf and he killed both of them with his own hands.

verses.text:
Praise the Lord, all you nations;
praise him, and bless his name.

For he rescued the soul of his chosen one from the hands of death,
and saved his devout servant from destruction.

He delivered me from the snares of Sheol,
and drew my soul out of the pit that cannot be fathomed.

For just before my rescue came out from his presence,
I had become two portions for two beasts.{a}

But he sent his angel,
shut up the gaping mouths against me,
and saved my life from destruction.

notes.text: Literally “two portions for two beasts.” The idea is that each animal had a share of him, as though he were already divided between them.

chapters.heading: Psalm 154
chapters.title: The prayer of Hezekiah when the Assyrians were surrounding him and he was asking God for relief from them, like a people who had obtained leave from Cyrus to go back to their own place and who ask God that their hope be fulfilled.{a}

verses.text:
With a loud voice praise God;
in the assembly of the many, make his glory heard.

Among the throng of the upright, praise him;
with the righteous, recount his majesty.

Unite your soul with the good and the whole-hearted,
so as to praise the Most High.
So that the Lord’s honor may be known, wisdom was given.{c}
So that his works may be recounted, she was made known to people.{d}

She was given to make his strength known to the simple,
and to make those who lack heart understand his glory,

who are far from her entrances
and far away from her gates.

For the Most High is the Lord of Jacob,
and his splendor is over all his works.

And the person who praises the Most High,
he will take pleasure in him,
like one who offers fine flour,

From the gates of the upright his voice is heard,
and out of the upright’s own voice comes his meditation.{f}

At their meal there is plenty, in truth,
and at their drink they drink together.

Their conversation dwells on the Most High’s Law,
and they speak in order to declare his strength.

How far from the wicked is speaking of him,
and from all the unjust, knowing him!
See, the Lord’s eye looks with pity on the good,

and on those who praise him he will multiply mercies,
and from the time of evil he will rescue their souls.

Blessed be the Lord, who rescued the afflicted from the hand of foreigners,
and delivered the blameless from the hand of the wicked,

who raises up a strong horn from Jacob,
a judge for the nations from Israel,

that he may make his dwelling long in Zion,
and that it may be planted in Jerusalem for all ages.{g}

notes.text: Hezekiah, king of Judah about 715–686 BC, was besieged by the Assyrian king Sennacherib in 701 BC (2 Kings 18–19; Isaiah 36–37). The name means “Yahweh strengthens.” Cyrus the Persian allowed the exiles to return in 538 BC (Ezra 1). The heading joins the two situations and does not fit the psalm well; in other Syriac manuscripts, the Hezekiah heading belongs to Psalm 154 and the Cyrus heading to Psalm 155, as reported.
The Syriac word is uncertain; it means something like “the simple” or “the untaught.” Wright’s 1887 English has “babes.” The same word is used in verse 7.
In the Hebrew text from Qumran (11QPs-a, as reported), wisdom is a woman and is called “she” and “her” through verse 8; the Syriac pronouns are less clear. “Her” in verse 8 follows the likely sense.

In the Hebrew text from Qumran (as reported), wisdom is a woman, and she is addressed as “she” and “her” through the rest of the psalm. The Syriac pronouns are not always clear, so “her” in verse 8 follows the likely sense.
Syriac *bsāmē*, “spices.” Wright’s 1887 text, from a later family of manuscripts, has “incense.”
Syriac *martīnūteh*. The word is uncertain and could also mean “his murmured prayer.” Wright has “admonition.” Whose voice is meant is also unclear.
Some manuscripts read “and may beautify our age in Jerusalem,” a different line.

chapters.heading: Psalm 155
chapters.title: The prayer of Hezekiah when the Assyrians were surrounding him, and he asked God for relief from them.

verses.text: Lord, I called to you; hear me.
I spread out my hands toward the dwelling places of your holiness.
Bend your ear to me and grant me my request.
Do not hold back my petition from me.

Build up my soul,
and do not tear it down.
Do not lay it bare before the wicked.

Turn away from me those who repay evil,
O judge of truth.{a}

Lord, do not judge me according to my sins,
for no one living is righteous before you.

Make me wise, Lord, in your Law,
and teach me your judgments.{b}

So that many may hear of your works,
and the nations may confess your glory.{c}

Remember me and do not forget me,
and do not bring me into what is too hard for me.

Pass away from me the sins of my youth,
and do not remember my rebellion against me.

Cleanse me, Lord, from the evil scab,
and let it not return to me again.

Dry up its roots from me,
and do not let its leaves sprout in me.

Mighty and great are you, Lord;
therefore my petition is granted before you.

To whom shall I appeal, so that he may give to me?
And what more can human might supply?

From before you, Lord, comes my confidence.
I called to the Lord, and he answered me,
and healed the break in my heart.

I dozed and fell asleep;
I dreamed, and then was woken.{d}

You held me up, Lord,
and I accept it, because the Lord has delivered me.{e}

Now I will look on their shame.
I put my hope in you and was not put to shame.
Give honor forever and ever.

Redeem Israel, your chosen,
and the house of Jacob, your tested one.{f}

notes.text: Syriac *dīnā d-qushtā*, “judge of truth.” The first words, *parʿay bīshtā*, “repayers of evil,” are not entirely certain.
The manuscript has a damaged letter at the end of this line, and the Syriac text printed by its editors marks the end of the verse as uncertain.
Syriac *ʿabdayk*. The consonants can be read as “your works” or “your servants.” “Works” is followed because the line is about what is heard and fits the parallel clause about confessing his glory.
Another reading is “I was helped.”
Syriac *ʾeqbal*, “I receive” or “I accept.” This is an uncertain readingWright’s 1887 English has “I will return thanks,” which may reflect a different reading.

At this point the Mosul manuscript closes the Psalter with a note: “Finished, with the help of our Lord: the book of the Psalms of the blessed David, prophet and king, together with five psalms that are not in the Greek reckoning or the Hebrew. But, as people say, they were found in Syriac, and I wrote them for those who look for them.”

books.name: Odes of Solomon
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Syriac text of the Odes of Solomon as transcribed in the Digital Syriac Corpus, which follows the edition of J. H. Charlesworth, *The Odes of Solomon* (1973) and the Syriac manuscripts H and N. The English here is new. The Syriac word *maryā* is rendered “Lord” and *peṯgāmā* “Word.” The English translation of J. Rendel Harris and A. Mingana, *The Odes and Psalms of Solomon* (1916–1920; public domain), and the Nuhra Version were consulted for comparison. Readings of the Coptic text (Odes 1, 5 and 6, in the *Pistis Sophia*), of the Greek text of Ode 11 (Bodmer Papyrus XI), and of the Latin quotation of Ode 19 in Lactantius, which I have not checked directly, are cited “as reported.” **Numbering.** Odes 1–2 and the beginning of Ode 3 are missing from manuscript H, so Ode 1 is given here from the Coptic, Ode 2 is lost, and Ode 3 is incomplete. The verse numbers follow the Digital Syriac Corpus, which is based on Charlesworth’s: for example, Ode 7 has 26 verses and Ode 8 has 23. Harris and Mingana, and translations based on them, divide the verses differently in places (for example, Ode 17 has 17 verses here and 16 in their edition), so references from other books may differ by a few verses. **About the book.** The Odes of Solomon are forty-two short hymns, praising God and telling of the believer’s rebirth, knowledge and joy. Though ascribed to Solomon, they were written long after his time, probably in the early 2nd century AD, perhaps in Syria; whether they were first composed in Syriac or in Greek, and whether the author was Jewish or Christian, are still debated. They have echoes of the Gospel of John, and some of them seem to speak in the voice of the Messiah (for example, Odes 22, 28, 31 and 42). The Syriac survives in two manuscripts: H (Rylands Syriac 9, 13th–15th century AD) and N (Codex Nitriensis, British Library Add. 14534, 9th–10th century AD; Odes 17:7–42:20 only), the second of which has been the basis for the readings of the damaged places. H was found and published by J. Rendel Harris in 1909; the Greek of Ode 11 was published in 1959 from a 3rd-century AD papyrus, and Odes 5 and 6 and the first Ode are also known from the Coptic *Pistis Sophia*. Ode 19 is quoted in Latin by Lactantius (about AD 310). The Odes are not part of any biblical canon, and were mostly lost to the churches until 1909. Note that several verses are damaged or doubtful in the manuscripts, and are marked in notes. Dates are given as BC/AD. CJT draft.

verses.text: The Lord is on my head as a crown, and I will never be left without him.{a}

A crown of truth was woven for me,
and it made your branches sprout in me.
For it is not like a withered crown that puts out no buds;

but you are alive on my head,
and you have blossomed on me.

Your fruit is ripe and whole,
brimming with your salvation.

notes.text: Ode 1 is not in the Syriac manuscripts, which have lost their opening pages. It survives in Coptic, quoted in the *Pistis Sophia* (3rd–4th century AD), where it is called the nineteenth ode of Solomon. The English here is translated from the Coptic “as reported” in the English translation of J. R. Harris and A. Mingana (1920), checked against the Syriac idiom of the other odes; no Coptic manuscript was read directly.

verses.text: [This ode is lost.]{a}

notes.text: Both the Syriac manuscripts break off before Ode 3, so Ode 2 has not survived in Syriac, and no Coptic quotation of it is known. Some scholars think that a few lines of the Greek text of Ode 11 in Papyrus Bodmer XI (verse 16, and a line after verse 22) that are not in the Syriac may be borrowed from this lost ode (as reported); they are given in a note at Ode 11.

verses.text: [I put on the love of the Lord.]{a}

And his limbs are with him, and I hang upon them,
and he loves me.{b}

I could never have learned to love the Lord,
unless he had first loved me.

Who can tell what love is,
except the one who is loved?

I love the Beloved, and my own soul loves him;
and wherever his rest is, I am there too.

And I will be no stranger,
for with the Lord, the Most High and Merciful, there is no grudging.

I have been mingled with him, for the lover has found the beloved;
and because I love the Son, I will become a son.

For whoever joins himself to the one who does not die
will himself become undying;

and whoever delights in the Living One
will become living.

This is the spirit of the Lord, which does not lie,
which teaches people to know his ways.
Be wise, and understanding, and watchful. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The first words of this ode are lost in the manuscript; the Syriac that is left reads “… I put on.” The words in square brackets are supplied from the sense of the next lines, as in the first edition by Harris and Mingana.
The Syriac says “with him.” Some editors change it to “with me.”

verses.text:
No one, my God, can change your holy place;
no one can alter it and set it in another place,

because they have no authority over it.
For you planned your sanctuary before you made the other places.

What is older will not be changed by what is lesser than itself.
You have given your heart, Lord, to those who are faithful to you.

You will never be idle,
and you will never be without fruit.

For one hour of faithfulness to you
is worth more than all days and years.

For who could put on your goodness
and be wronged?{a}

For your seal is known,
and your creatures are acquainted with it.{b}

Your hosts take hold of it,
and the great and chosen angels are clothed with it.

Pour out your drops upon us,
and open your rich springs, which pour out milk and honey for us.

For there is no changing of mind in you,
so that you would change your mind about anything you have promised.
And the end was plain to you.

What you gave you gave as a free gift,
so that you would never go back and take it again.

For everything was plain to you, as God,
and was set in order from the beginning in front of you.
And you, Lord, made all things. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac verb means “be wronged” or “be treated unjustly”; some translators render it “be condemned.”
The Syriac can mean “know it” or “are known to it.” A letter of the word “known” is damaged in the manuscript.

verses.text:
I give you thanks,
Lord, for I love you.

Most High, do not abandon me,
for you are my hope.

Freely I have received your goodness;
by it I will live.
Let my persecutors come and not see me.

Let a cloud of gloom fall over their eyes,
and a haze of darkness make them black.

And let there be no light for them to see,
so that they cannot seize me.

Let their plan be dulled,
and let what they have schemed come back on their own heads.{a}

For they planned a plan,
and it did not come about for them.

They made themselves ready for evil,
and were found empty.

My hope is in the Lord,
so I will not fear.

And because the Lord is my deliverer,
I will not be afraid.

He is a crown on my head,
and I will not be shaken.

And if everything is shaken,
I stand.

And if everything that is seen perishes,
I will not die.

The Lord is with me,
and I with him. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac word used for “dulled” is *ʿubāyē*, which normally means “thick” or “heavy”; it is unclear in this place. Some editors emend it to “weak.” The Coptic form of this ode, in the *Pistis Sophia*, reads “powerless,” as reported.

verses.text:
As the wind moves over the harp,
and the strings speak,

so the Spirit of the Lord speaks in my limbs,
and I speak by his love.

For he destroys everything that is foreign,
and everything belongs to the Lord.

For so it was from the beginning,
and so it will be to the end,

so that nothing may be against him,
and nothing stand up to oppose him.

The Lord has made the knowledge of himself greater,
and he is eager that those things be known which have been given to us through his goodness.

And he has given us his praise for the sake of his name;
our spirits praise his Holy Spirit.

And the dam-builders among people could not hold it back,
nor could the skill of those who hold back waters.

For it came over the face of the whole earth,
and filled everything.

And all the thirsty on the earth drank,
and thirst was loosened and put out;
for the drink was given from the Most High.

Blessed, then, are the servants of that drink,
those to whom his water has been entrusted.

They have refreshed dry lips,
and raised up the will that had gone slack.

And souls that were about to leave,
they seized from death.

They set limbs that had collapsed straight
and upright again.

They put strength into their coming,
and light into their eyes.

Everyone recognized them as the Lord’s,
and they lived by the living water that lasts for ever. Hallelujah.

notes.text: “Temple” here is the Syriac word *haykla*. The Coptic version of this ode (in the *Pistis Sophia*) has a different sentence for this verse, as reported.

verses.text:
My joy is the Lord, and my running is toward him;
this is my beautiful way.

For I have the Lord as my helper.
He made himself known to me freely, in his simplicity, because his kindness made his greatness small.

He became like me, so that I could take him in;
he was counted like me in his appearance, so that I could put him on.

I did not tremble at the sight of him,
because he was gracious to me.

He became like my nature, so that I could learn him;
like my form, so that I would not turn away from him.

The Father of knowledge
is the Word of knowledge.

He who created wisdom
is wiser than his works.

And he who made me before I was
knew what I would do when I came to be.

So he was gracious to me in his great graciousness,
and gave me to ask of him,
and to receive from his sacrifice.

For he is the one who does not decay,
the fullness of the ages and their Father.

He let himself be seen by his own,
so that they might know their maker,
and not imagine that they came from themselves.

And he set the footprints of his light upon it,
and it went on from the beginning to the end.

For through him it was served,
and it rested in the Son.

And by his salvation he will lay hold of everything,
and the Most High will be made known among his holy ones,

to carry word to those who have songs about the Lord’s coming,
so that they may go out to meet him,
singing to him with joy and with a harp of many voices.

The seers will go before him,
and will be seen before him.

They will praise the Lord for his love,
because he is near, and he sees.

And hatred will be lifted from the earth,
and will be drowned together with jealousy.

Ignorance has been destroyed,
now that the knowledge of the Lord has come.

Those who sing will sing of the goodness of the Lord, the Most High,
and bring their psalms.

Their heart will be bright as day,
and their sweet voices will match the greatness of the Lord’s majesty.

And nothing will be without life,
or without knowledge, or without speech.

He gave his creation a mouth,
to open the voice of the mouth toward him
and praise him.

Declare his power,
and show his goodness. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac reads “anger” (*ḥemtā*) and “wrongdoing” (*ʿawlūtā*). Several scholars change these words to “love” and “infancy” or “childhood,” because the first half of the comparison then matches the second. The Syriac is translated as it stands.

verses.text:
Open, open your hearts to the rejoicing of the Lord,
and let your love flow from the heart to the lips,

to bring the Lord fruit, a holy life,
and to speak watchfully in his light.

Rise and stand upright,
you who were once bowed down.

You who have been silent, speak,
for your mouth is now opened.

You who were despised, be lifted up,
for your righteousness has been lifted up.{a}

The Lord’s right hand is with you,
and he will help you.

And peace was made ready for you
before your war ever took place.

Listen to the word of truth,
and take in the knowledge of the Most High.

Your flesh does not understand what I am telling you,
nor your clothing what I am showing you.

Guard my secret,
you who are guarded by it.
Guard my faith, you who are guarded by it.

And understand my knowledge,
you who know me in truth.
Love me with love, you who love.

For I do not turn my face away from my own,
because I know them.

And before they came to be, I knew them,
and I sealed their faces.{b}

I delighted in them,
and I do not blush for them.

For they are my work,
and the power of my thoughts.

Who then will stand against my work,
or who will not be subject to them?

I wanted them, and made mind and heart; and they are mine;
and at my right hand I set my chosen ones.

My righteousness goes ahead of them,
and they will not be cut off from my name,
since it is with them.

Ask, and increase, and stay in the love of the Lord,
beloved ones in the Beloved,
the ones guarded in the Living One,
and the redeemed in the one who was redeemed.

And you will be found incorruptible in all the ages,
for the name of your Father. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Digital Syriac Corpus transcription marks a gap here. The verse is given as in Harris and Mingana (1916–1920), “as reported.”

The numbering of the second half of this ode differs between editions. Harris and Mingana number this part 11 to 14 and end the ode at verse 14; this book uses the 23-verse numbering of the Digital Syriac Corpus.

verses.text:
Open your ears,
and I will speak to you.

Give me your soul,
so that I may give you my soul too.

The word of the Lord and what he desires
is a holy thought that he thought concerning his Messiah.

For your lives are by the will of the Lord,
and his purpose is life for ever,
and your completion is without decay.

Be enriched in God the Father,
and receive the purpose of the Most High.
Be made strong and be redeemed by his goodness.

For I announce peace to you, his holy ones,
so that none who hear will fall in battle,

and so that those who have come to know him will not perish,
and those who accept him will not be put to shame.

Truth is an everlasting crown;
blessed are those who place it on their heads.

It is a precious stone,
for there have been wars over the crown.

And Righteousness took it,
and gave it to you.{a}

Put on the crown through the true covenant of the Lord,
and all who have conquered will be written in his book.

notes.text: The Syriac reads *zadiqūtā*, “Righteousness.” Some scholars read *zākūtā*, “Victory,” which suits verses 11–12, where the same word appears for the victory the readers have won.

verses.text:
The Lord shaped my mouth by his word,
and opened my heart by his light.

And he made his deathless life dwell in me,
and let me speak the fruit of his peace,

to turn back the souls of those who want to come to him,
and to take a good captivity captive, for freedom.

I was made strong and mighty, and I took the world captive;
and this became for me a praise of the Most High, and of God my Father.

And the footprints of light were set upon their heart,
and they walked in my life and were redeemed,
and became my people for ever and ever. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac word *ḥawbay* can mean “my sins,” “my debts,” or “what I owe.”

verses.text:
For the Most High circumcised me with his Holy Spirit.
He uncovered my inmost being to himself,
and filled me with his love.

His circumcision of me became my redemption.
I ran on the road, in his peace, the road of truth,

from the beginning to the end,
and I received his knowledge.

And I was set firm on the rock of truth,
where he himself had stood me up.

And speaking waters came near my lips from the Lord’s spring,
which has no envy.

So I drank
and was drunk with the living water that does not die.

Yet my drunkenness was not the drunkenness of ignorance,
for I left behind what is empty

and turned to the Most High, my God,
and was made rich by his gift.

I abandoned the folly that is scattered over the earth;
I stripped it off and threw it away from me.

And the Lord renewed me with his own clothing,
and took me as his own with his light.

From above he gave me rest that cannot decay,
and I became like a land that blossoms and rejoices in its fruit.
And the Lord was like the sun shining on the face of the land.

My eyes were lit,
and my face received the dew.
My breath was sweetened by the pleasant fragrance of the Lord.

And he took me into his paradise,
where the Lord’s pleasure is richly stored.{a}
And I bowed down to the Lord because of his glory,

and I said: Blessed are those,
Lord, who are planted in your land,
and have their place in your paradise,

and who grow with the growth of your trees,
and have passed from darkness into light.

… Look, all your workers are good, doing good works,
(and turning from wickedness to your sweetness.){b}

(And they turned the bitterness of the trees away from them,
when they were planted in your land.)
… and the everlasting memorial of your faithful servants.{c}

For the place of your paradise is wide,
and nothing in it is idle,
but everything is full of fruit.
Glory to you, God, for the endless delight of paradise. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Greek text of this ode (Papyrus Bodmer XI), as reported, has here six further lines that the Syriac does not have: “I saw trees, flourishing and full of fruit; their crown grew of itself; their wood blossomed and their fruits laughed. Their roots were from deathless ground, and a river of gladness watered them all around, in the land of everlasting life.” They are given here as reported and are not part of the Syriac text translated in this book.

In the Syriac, verses 20 to 22 are damaged. The Digital Syriac Corpus marks gaps with “…” at the start of verses 20 and 22 and puts all of verse 21 and part of verse 20 in round brackets, which signals that these words are supplied or uncertain. They are translated here as they stand, with the gaps shown as “…” and the bracketed words in round brackets.
As reported, the Greek of this ode has a longer text here and a blessing on “those who see your waters”. The Syriac, as far as it survives, has the shorter form translated here.

verses.text:
He filled me with words of truth,
so that I could speak them.

As water flows, truth flowed from my mouth,
and my lips revealed its fruit.

He caused his knowledge to overflow in me,
because the Lord’s mouth is the true Word,
and the doorway of his light.

The Most High gave it to his worlds, who are the interpreters of his beauty,
the tellers of his glory,
the confessors of his thought,
the heralds of his mind,
and the teachers of his works.

For the swiftness of the Word cannot be told,
and as it is said, so are its speed
and its sharpness; its course has no limit.

It never fails but stands firm,
and it does not know descent or the way down.{a}

For as its work is, so is its aim;
for it is light and the dawning of thought.

Through it the worlds speak to one another,
and those who were silent gained speech.

Love and harmony came from it,
and they told one another what they had.

They were stirred by the Word
and knew the one who made them,
because they were in harmony.

The mouth of the Most High addressed them,
and his explanation ran swiftly through it.

For the dwelling place of the Word is the son of man,
and its truth is love.{b}

Blessed are those who have understood everything through it,
and have known the Lord in his truth. Hallelujah.

notes.text: Syriac *peṯgāmā*, “word, utterance”, is the same word used for “Word” in Ode 7:7. It is not the Greek *Logos* of John 1.
Syriac *bar nāšā*, “son of man”, can mean simply “a human being”.

verses.text:
See, the Lord is our mirror. Open your eyes,
and look at yourselves in him,

and learn what your faces are like,
and speak praises to his spirit.

Wipe the paint off your faces,{a}
love his holiness and put it on.
Then you will be without blemish before him at all times. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac word *ṣīdātā* is rare, and its sense is uncertain. “Paint” is a likely guess, since the verse is about faces.

verses.text:
As a son’s eyes are on his father,
so my eyes, Lord, are on you at all times.
For with you are my breasts and my nourishment.{a}

Do not turn your mercies away from me,
Lord, and do not take your kindness from me.

Stretch out your right hand to me at all times,
and be my guide to the end, as you please.

Let me be pleasing before you for your glory, and
for your name’s sake let me be rescued from evil.

May your gentleness, Lord, stay with me,
and the fruits of your love.

Teach me the psalms of your truth,
so that I may bear fruit in you.

Open for me the harp of your Holy Spirit,
that I may praise you, Lord, with every note of it.

And as great as your mercies are,
so give to me, and hurry to grant what we ask.
You are able to supply all our needs. Hallelujah.

notes.text: Literally “my breasts”, the image of a nursing mother, together with the word for refreshment or sustenance.

verses.text:
As the sun is a joy to those who look
for its day, so the Lord is my joy.

In him I gained eyes,
and I saw his holy day.

Ears were given to me,
and I heard his truth.

The thought of knowledge came to me,
and I was refreshed in him.

I left the way of error and went to him,
and I received salvation from him without grudging.

He gave to me as his own gift,
and he made me as his great beauty.

I put on incorruption by his name,
and took off corruption by his kindness.

Death was destroyed before my face,
and Sheol was ended by my word.

And deathless life rose in the Lord’s land,
and was made known to his faithful,
and was given without limit to all who trust in him. Hallelujah.

As the farmer’s work is the plow,
and the helmsman’s work is steering the ship,
so the psalm of the Lord, in his praises, is my work.

The Lord is my love,
and so I will sing to him.

For I am strong in praising him,
and I have faith in him.

I will open my mouth,
and his Spirit will speak within me the Lord’s glory
and his beauty,

the deed of his hands
and the toil of his fingers,

the greatness of his mercies
and the strength of his word.

For the word of the Lord searches out what is not seen,
and examines his thought.{a}

The eye sees what he has made,
and the ear hears his thought.

He spread out the earth
and set the waters in the sea.

He stretched out the heavens
and fixed the stars.

He established the creation and set it up,
and then rested from his works.

Created things run their courses
and do their work,
and they do not know how to stand still or be idle.
And the heavenly hosts are subject to his word.

The treasury of light is the sun,
and the treasury of darkness is the night.

He made the sun for the day, to make it bright;
but night brings darkness across the surface of the earth.

Their turns, one after the other,
declare the beauty of God.

And nothing exists apart from the Lord,
for he was before anything came to be.

The worlds came into being through his word,
and through the thought of his heart.
Praise and honor to his name. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The meaning of the second half is disputed, since it is not clear whose “thought” is meant.

verses.text:
My God crowned me,
and my crown is alive.

I was made righteous by my Lord,
and my salvation does not decay.

I was set free from empty things,
and I am not condemned.

My bonds were cut by her hands.{a} I took the face
and shape of a new person,
and walked in it, and was redeemed.

And the thought of truth led me,
and I followed it and did not stray.

All who saw me were amazed,
and to them I seemed a stranger.

And he who knew me and raised me is the Most High,
in all his fullness.{b}

He glorified me by his kindness,
and lifted my knowledge to the height of truth.

There he gave me the path of his footsteps,
and I opened doors that were shut,

and broke the iron bars in pieces;
but my own iron grew hot and melted before me.

Nothing seemed shut against me,
since I was the door for all things.

I went to all my captives to free them,
so that I would leave no one bound, and none to bind.

And I gave my knowledge without grudging,
and my request in my love.

I sowed my fruits in hearts,
and changed them into myself.

They received my blessing and lived;
they gathered to me and were redeemed.

For they became my limbs,
and I was their head.
Praise to you, our head, Lord Messiah. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac has “her hands”; the feminine word has no clear antecedent in the surviving text.
The Digital Syriac Corpus numbers this ode in 17 verses and gives Harris and Mingana’s numbering, one lower from here on, in brackets. This book follows the 17-verse numbering.

verses.text:
My heart was raised up by the love of the Most High,
and grew wide, so that I might praise him for his name.

My limbs were strengthened
so that they would not fall from his power.

Sicknesses drew away from my body,
and it stood before the Lord by his will,
for his kingdom is sure.

Lord, because of those who are lacking,
do not take your word from me.

And do not, because of their works,
hold back your perfection from me.

Do not let light be overcome by darkness,
or truth flee from falsehood.

You are my God. Falsehood
and death are not in your mouth; perfection is your will.

You do not know emptiness,
because it does not know you either.

You do not know error,
because it does not know you either.

And ignorance appeared like dust,
and like the foam of the sea.

The empty-minded thought it great,
and they too became like it, and were emptied.

But those who knew, and who thought it through,
knew, and were not defiled by their thoughts.

They were in the Most High’s mind,
and they laughed at those who walk in error.

These spoke truth,
out of the breath the Most High had breathed into them.
Praise and great majesty to his name. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The sense of this verse is uncertain in the Syriac.

verses.text:
I was offered a cup of milk,
and I drank it in the sweet kindness of the Lord.

The Son is the cup, and the one who was milked is the Father,
and the Holy Spirit milked him,

because his breasts were full,
and it was not right that his milk be poured out for nothing.

The Holy Spirit opened her womb,
and mixed the milk from the Father’s two breasts,{a}

and gave the mixture to the world,
though they did not know it. And those who take it in its fullness are on the right hand.

(The womb of the virgin took it,
and she conceived and gave birth.
And the virgin became a mother with many mercies.){b}

She was in labor and bore a son, and had no pain,
because it did not happen without purpose.

And she did not need a midwife,
because he delivered her.

She gave birth like a man,
by her own will; she gave birth openly,
and took firm possession of him with a great hold.

She loved him in redemption,
and guarded him in kindness,
and showed him in majesty. Hallelujah.

notes.text: In Syriac the word for “Spirit”, *rūḥā*, can be feminine, which is why the Spirit is “her” here.
Verses 6 and 7 are in round brackets in the Digital Syriac Corpus, which marks words that are damaged or supplied.

verses.text:
I am a priest of the Lord,
and I serve him as a priest.
And I offer to him the sacrifice of his own thought.

For his thought is not like the world,
nor like the flesh, nor like those who serve in the way of the flesh.

The sacrifice of the Lord is righteousness,
and a pure heart and pure lips.

Offer your inmost parts without blemish. Let your affections not press upon affections,
and let your own self not press upon another self.

Do not buy a stranger with the blood of your own life,{a}
and do not strip him of the covering of his shame.

But put on the Lord’s kindness,
without grudging, and come to his paradise,
and make yourself a crown from his tree.

Put it on your head and be glad,
and lean on his rest.

His glory will go ahead of you,
and you will receive from his kindness and goodness,
and be anointed with truth in the glory of his holiness.
Praise and honor to his name. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Digital Syriac Corpus shows that a line is missing here. Other editions supply a line about not cheating a neighbor, which is given here only “as reported” and is not translated.

verses.text:
I lifted up my arms to the height,
to the mercy of the Lord,

because he had thrown my bonds off me,
and my helper lifted me up to his mercy and to his salvation.

I put off darkness
and put on light.

And I gained limbs besides my soul,
and there was no sickness or affliction or suffering in them.

And above all the thought of the Lord was a help to me,
and his fellowship, which does not decay.

I was lifted up into the light,
and I passed before his face.
I kept near him, praising and confessing him. …

My heart overflowed and appeared in my mouth,
and rose upon my lips.
And the gladness of the Lord and his praise grew on my face. Hallelujah.

He who brought me down from on high,
and brought me up from the regions below,

who gathers what is in the middle
and throws them to me,

who scattered my enemies
and my opponents,

who gave me power over bonds,
to loose them,

who with my hands struck down the seven-headed dragon,
and set me over its roots to destroy its seed.

You were there to help me,
and everywhere your name was around me.

Your right hand destroyed (the poison of evil),
and your hand made the way smooth for those who trust in you.

(You chose them) from the graves,
(and you separated them) from the dead.

You took dead bones
and covered them with bodies.

They were motionless,
and you gave the power to work to the living.

Your way was without decay,
and so was your face. You brought your world to incorruption,
so that everything might be dissolved and made new,

and that your rock might be the foundation of everything. Upon it you built your kingdom,
and it became the dwelling place of the holy ones. Hallelujah.

Joy is for the holy ones,
and who can put it on but they alone?

Grace belongs to the chosen,
and who will receive it except those who have trusted in it from the beginning?

Love belongs to the chosen,
and who will put it on except those who have owned it from the beginning?

Walk in the knowledge of the Most High,
and you will know the Lord’s kindness without grudging,
and for his gladness, and for the perfection of his knowledge.

His thought was like a letter,
and his will came down from the height,
and it was sent like an arrow shot from a bow with force.

And many hands rushed to the letter,
to snatch it and take it and read it.

But it escaped from their fingers,
and they were afraid of it and of the seal on it,

because they were not allowed to break its seal,
for the power over the seal was greater than they.

But those who saw it went after the letter,
to know where it would land,
and who would read it,
and who would hear it.

But a wheel received it,
and it came upon the wheel.

And with it was a sign of kingship
and of government.

And everything that disturbed the wheel it mowed down
and cut off.

It gathered a crowd of adversaries,
and spanned rivers,
and uprooted many forests,
and made a broad road.

The head came down to the feet,
because the wheel ran as far as the feet,
and whatever had come upon it.

The letter was a command,
because all the places were gathered together.

And a head was seen, the head that was revealed,
the Son of truth from the Father, the Most High.

And he inherited everything
and took it. And the plan of the many was brought to an end.

Then all the rebels grew hot and fled,
and those who persecuted and hated were put out.

And the letter was a great tablet,
written completely by the finger of God.

The name of the Father was upon it,
and also of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
to reign for ever and ever. Hallelujah.

The dove fluttered over the head of our Lord Messiah,
because he was her head.

She sang over him,
and her voice could be heard.

The inhabitants were afraid,
and the settlers were shaken.

The bird gave up its wings,
and every creeping thing died in its hole.

The depths were opened and covered again,
and they cried to the Lord like women in labor.

And no food was given to them,
because it was not theirs.

And the depths sank in the Lord’s sinking,{a}
and they perished in the thought they had held from the beginning.

For they had been corrupt from the beginning,
and the end of their corruption was life.

And everything about them that was lacking perished,
because they had no word to speak so that they might live.
And the Lord destroyed the thoughts of all those who had no truth.

For those who were lifted up in their hearts lacked wisdom,
and so were rejected, because truth was not with them.

And they were removed,
because truth was not with them.

For the Lord revealed his way
and spread out his kindness,
and those who recognized it know his holiness. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac uses the same root twice, “sank” and “sinking”, and the word can also mean “sealing”. The sense of the verse is uncertain.

verses.text:
I was set free from my bonds,
and I ran to you, my God.

(For you were the right hand of salvation)
and my helper.

You held back those who stood against me,
and (they were not seen again).

For your face was with me,
and it saved me by your kindness.

But in the eyes of many I was despised
and rejected, and in their sight I was like lead.

And strength came to me from you,
and help.

You set a lamp for me on my right and on my left,
so that nothing in me would be without light.

I was covered with the cover of your Spirit,
and I took off the garments of skin.

For your right hand lifted me up
and took sickness away from me.

I became strong in your truth,
and holy in your righteousness.

(All my enemies were afraid of me,)
and I became the Lord’s, in the Lord’s name.

By his kindness I was made righteous,
and his rest lasts for ever and ever. Hallelujah.

I poured out praise to the Lord,
because I belong to him.

I will speak his holy song,
because my heart is with him.

For his harp is in my hands,
and the songs of his rest will not be silent.

I will cry to him with my whole heart;
with every limb I will praise and exalt him.
His praise reaches from the east to the west,
and his thanksgiving from the south to the north,
and his perfection from the summit of the hills to their farthest edge.

Who can write down the psalms of the Lord,
or who can read them?

Or who can train his soul for life,
so that his soul may be saved?

Or who can rest on the Most High,
so that he may speak from his mouth?
