Who can interpret the Lord’s wonders? For the one who interprets will be dissolved,
and what is interpreted will remain.

It is enough to know, and to rest,
for the singers stand in rest,

like a river that has an abundant spring
and flows to help those who seek it. Hallelujah.

I stretched out my hands
and hallowed my Lord,
for the stretching of my hands is his sign,
and my spreading out is the upright wood. Hallelujah.

As the wings of doves over their young,
and the mouths of their young toward their mouths,
so are the wings of the Spirit over my heart.

My heart is glad and leaps,
like the baby that leaps in its mother’s womb.

I believed, and so I was at rest,
because he in whom I believed is faithful.

He has richly blessed me,
and my head is with him.

And the sword will not separate me from him,
nor the blade.

For I was made ready before destruction came,
and was set on his wings that do not decay.{a}

Deathless life embraced me
and kissed me,

and from it comes the Spirit that is in me,
and it cannot die, for it is alive.

Those who saw me were amazed,
because I was being hunted,

and they thought I had been swallowed up,
since to them I looked like one of the lost.
But my oppression became my salvation.

I became their reproach,
because there was no envy in me.

Because I did good to every person,
I was hated.

And they surrounded me like mad dogs,
who in ignorance attack their masters,

for their thinking is corrupt,
and they twist their understanding.

But I held waters in my right hand,
and I bore their bitterness with my sweetness.

I did not perish, because I was not their brother,
and my birth was not like theirs.

They sought my death and did not find it,
because I was older than the memory of them,
and in vain they cast lots against me.
And those who came after me tried in vain to wipe out the memory of him who was before them.

The mind of the Most High cannot be forestalled,
and his heart is greater than all wisdom. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Digital Syriac Corpus numbers this ode in 20 verses and gives Harris and Mingana’s numbers, one lower from here on, in brackets. This book follows the 20-verse numbering.

verses.text:
The Lord is my hope;
I will not be ashamed in him.

For he made me according to his glory,
and in the same way he gave to me according to his kindness.

He raised me according to his mercies,
and lifted me up according to his great beauty.

He brought me up from the depths of Sheol,
and drew me out of the mouth of death.
And I laid my enemies low,
and he made me righteous by his kindness. For I believed in the Lord’s Messiah,
and I came to see that he is the Lord. And he showed me his sign,

and led me by his light. He gave me the rod of his power,
to bring down the thoughts of the nations
and to humble the strength of the mighty,

to wage war with his word,
and to win the victory by his power.

The Lord threw down my enemy with his word,
and he became like dust that the wind carries away.

I praised the Most High, because he has lifted up his servant
and the son of his maidservant. Hallelujah.

Fill yourselves with water from the Lord’s living spring,
because it has been opened for you.

And come, all you who are thirsty,
and take the drink, and rest by the Lord’s spring.

For it is lovely and pure,
and gives rest to the soul.

Its waters are far sweeter than honey,
and the honeycomb of bees cannot be compared with it.

It flows from the Lord’s lips,
and its name came from the Lord’s heart.

It came without limit and unseen, and
until it was set in the middle, no one knew it.

Blessed are those who have drunk of it
and found rest in it. Hallelujah.

The depths were dissolved before the Lord,
and darkness vanished at the sight of him.

Error went astray and perished
because of him, and folly (found no path,
and sank) before the Lord’s truth.

He opened his mouth and spoke kindness
and joy, and he spoke a new song to his name.

He lifted his voice to the Most High,
and presented to him the sons who were in his hand.

And his face was made righteous,
because his holy Father had given it to him so.

Come out, you who were afflicted,
and receive joy.

Take possession of your souls through kindness,
and take for yourselves deathless life.

They condemned me when I stood up,
though I was not guilty.

They divided my spoil,
though nothing was owed to them.

But I endured, and was silent, and was still,
as though I were not moved by them.

I stood firm, not shaken,
like a solid rock that is beaten by waves and stands.

And I bore their bitterness for the sake of gentleness,
to redeem my people and make them heirs,

so that I would not cancel my promises to the patriarchs,
to whom I had pledged the redemption of their seed. Hallelujah.

The blessed have joy from their hearts,
and light from him who dwells in them,
and the Word from the truth, who came to be from himself.

For the Most High’s holy power made him strong,
and he is unmoved for ever and ever. Hallelujah.

Again grace ran, and left corruption,
and came down upon it to empty it.

And he destroyed perdition before her,
and ruined all its order.

He stood on a high place and lifted his voice,
from the far end of the earth to the other.

He drew to himself all who obeyed him,
and he did not look like an evil one.

But a perfect virgin stood,
who was proclaiming, and calling out, and saying:

Children of men, turn back,
and you their daughters, come,

and leave the ways of this corruption,
and draw near to me.

I will enter into you
and bring you out of destruction,
and make you wise in the ways of truth.

Do not be corrupted,
and do not perish.

Listen to me and be redeemed,
for the kindness of God is what I speak among you.

Through me you will be redeemed
and blessed. I am your judge.

Those who put me on will not be wronged,
but will gain a new world without corruption.

My chosen ones walked in me,
and I will make my ways known to those who seek me,
and I will make them trust in my name. Hallelujah.

No path is hard where the heart is simple,
nor is there any wound among upright thoughts.
Nor is there a storm in the depth of the shining thought.

Where a person is surrounded on every side by beauty,
there is nothing divided.
The pattern of what is below is what is above.

Everything is above,
and below there is nothing,
though those without knowledge imagine it.

Grace was revealed for your salvation. Believe,
and you will live, and be saved. Hallelujah.

The dew of the Lord settled on me in rest,
and he raised a cloud of peace over my head,

which guarded me at all times,
and became salvation to me.

Everything was shaken and frightened,
and smoke and judgment came out from them.

But I was quiet under the Lord’s decree,
and he was more to me than a shelter, and more than a foundation.

I was carried like a child on its mother’s lap,
and he gave me milk, the Lord’s dew.

And I grew by his gift,
and found rest in his perfection.

And I stretched out my hands as my soul rose up,
and I was made straight toward the Most High,
and was redeemed to him. Hallelujah.

I rested in the Spirit of the Lord,
and she lifted me up to the height.

She set me on my feet in the Lord’s height,
before his perfection and his glory,
while I praised him with the composition of his songs.

She bore me before the Lord’s face,
and though I was a son of man,
I was named the Shining One, the Son of God.

For I was glorified among the glorious,
and great among the great.

For as great as the Most High is,
so she made me, and by his newness he renewed me.

He anointed me out of his perfection,
and I became one of his near ones.

My mouth was opened like a dewy cloud,
and my heart poured out a stream of righteousness.

I came near in peace,
and was established in the Spirit of guidance. Hallelujah.

I stretched out my hands to my Lord,
and to the Most High I raised my voice.

I spoke with my heart’s lips,
and he heard me as soon as my voice reached him.

His word came to me,
and gave me the fruits of my labors,
and gave me rest by the kindness of the Lord. Hallelujah.

I went up into the light of truth as into a chariot,
and truth guided me and carried me.

It carried me across pits and chasms,
and rescued me from cliffs and waves.

It became a harbor of salvation for me,
and set me on the step of life that has no death.

And it went with me, and gave me rest,
and did not let me go astray, because it was truth, and it is.

I had no danger, because I walked with it;
and I did not go wrong in anything, because I listened to it.

For error ran away from it,
and never met it.

And truth walked on the upright road,
and whatever I did not know it showed me,

all the poisons of error,
and the scourges which are thought to be death’s sweetness.{a}

And I saw the destroyer of corruption,
when the corrupting bride was being adorned,
and the bridegroom who corrupts and is corrupted.

And I asked the truth, “Who are these?” And it said to me,
“This is the Deceiver and Error.”

They mimic the Beloved and his bride,
and mislead the world and corrupt it.

They invite many to the banquet,
and give them the wine of their drunkenness to drink,

and make them vomit up their wisdom
and knowledge, and leave them without sense.

Then they abandon them,
and these go about raving and ruined,

since they have no heart,
and do not look for one.

And I became wise, so as not to fall into the deceivers’ hands,
and I rejoiced in myself that truth went with me.{b}

I was made firm, and lived,
and was redeemed,
and my foundations were laid on the Lord’s hand,

because he planted me. He set the root,
watered it, secured it,
and blessed it,

and its fruits are for ever. (It went deep, and rose,
and spread out,) and was full and grew great.

The Lord alone was glorified,
in his planting and his farming,

in his care, and in the blessing of his lips,
in the fair planting by his right hand,

and in the skill of his planting,
and in the knowledge of his mind. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The Syriac word translated “scourges” (*nāgdē*) can also mean “cords” or “goads”.

From here to the end of the ode the Digital Syriac Corpus also gives Harris and Mingana’s numbers in brackets, one lower than those used here; Ode 38 therefore has 22 verses in this book but 21 in their edition.

verses.text:
Mighty rivers are the power of the Lord,
which carry away headlong those who despise him,

and tangle their paths,
and ruin their crossings,

and snatch their bodies,
and destroy their souls.

For they are faster than lightning,
and swifter.
But those who cross them in faith will not be shaken,
and those who walk through them blamelessly will not fear.

For the Lord is the sign in them, and the sign becomes the way
for those who cross in the name of the Lord.

So clothe yourselves in the name of the Most High, and know him, and you will cross safely,
since the rivers will be subject to you.

The Lord bridged them with his word,
then walked over them and crossed on foot.

And his footprints stand on the water
and were not harmed, but are like wood fixed in truth.

On this side and on that the waves rose,
but the footprints of our Lord the Messiah stand,

and are not blotted out
and are not destroyed.

A road has been laid down for those who cross after him, and for those who keep to the way of his faith
and worship his name. Hallelujah.

As honey drips from the combs of bees, and milk runs from a woman who loves her children,
so is my hope on you, my God.

As a spring pours out its waters,
so my heart pours forth the Lord’s praise,
and my lips bring out praise to him.

My tongue is sweet with his words,
and my limbs are made sweet by his songs.{a}

My face rejoices in his gladness,
my spirit exults in his love,
and my soul is radiant in him.

One who fears will trust in him,
and in him salvation will be sure.

His gain is life that does not die,
and those who receive it are without corruption. Hallelujah.

notes.text: In the Digital Syriac Corpus some letters of “my limbs” are damaged and supplied by the editors.

verses.text:
Let all his children praise the Lord,
and let them take up the truth of his faith.

Let his sons be known to him;
therefore let us sing in his love.

We live in the Lord by his kindness,
and we receive life by his Messiah.

For a great day has dawned on us,
and wonderful is he who gave us of his glory.

So let us all together be united in the name of the Lord,
and honor him in his goodness.

May our faces shine in his light,
and our hearts reflect on his love,
night and day.
Let us rejoice with the joy of the Lord.

Let everyone who sees me be astonished,
because I come from a different race.

The Father of truth remembered me,
who acquired me from the beginning.

For his riches bore me,
and the thought of his heart.

His Word is with us on all our road,
the Savior who gives life and does not cast out our souls.

He is the man who humbled himself,
and was lifted up by his own righteousness.
The Son of the Most High was seen in his Father’s perfection,
and light dawned from the Word who was in him from of old.

The Messiah is truly one,
and was known before the foundations of the world, …{a}
so that he might give souls life for ever through the truth of his name. A new song of praise to the Lord from those who love him. Hallelujah.

notes.text: The corpus text marks a gap in the manuscript after “foundations of the world”.

verses.text:
I stretched out my hands and came near to my Lord,
for the stretching of my hands is his sign.

And my spreading out is the upright wood,
that was hung on the way of the Upright One.

And I was of no use to those who knew me,
because I was hidden from those who did not hold me.{a}
But I will be with those who love me.

All my persecutors are dead, and they sought me,
those who had put their hope in me, because I live.

I rose, and I am with them,
and I will speak through their mouths.

For they put away those who pursued them,
and I laid on them the yoke of my love.

As the bridegroom’s arm rests over the bride,
so my yoke rests over those who know me.

And as the bridal chamber is spread out in the house of the bridegrooms,
so is my love over those who believe in me.

I was not cast out, though they thought so;
and I did not perish, though they planned it against me.

Sheol saw me and was afflicted,
and death gave me up, and many with me.

I was gall and bitterness to it,
and I descended with it to the limit of its depth.

And I let go its feet and head,
because they could not bear my face.

And I made a congregation of the living among its dead,
and spoke with them with living lips,
so that my word would not be in vain.

And those who had died ran to me, and cried out
and said, “Have pity on us, Son of God,

and act toward us in your kindness,
and bring us out from the chains of darkness,

and open
for us the door through which we may come out to you. For we see that death has not touched you.

May we also be redeemed with you,
for you are our Redeemer.”

And I heard their voice,
and set their faith in my heart,

and set my name on their heads,
for they are free and are mine. Hallelujah.

notes.text: Verses 3 and 7 are difficult in the Syriac, and the sense given here is uncertain.

books.name: Life of Adam and Eve
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Latin *Vita Adae et Evae* in the critical edition of Wilhelm Meyer (Abhandlungen der Bayerischen Akademie der Wissenschaften 14.3, Munich, 1878; public domain), as digitized in the Online Critical Pseudepigrapha, with variants and additions from other Latin manuscripts given in round brackets as they stand in that printed text. Readings of the Greek *Apocalypse of Moses* (Tischendorf, 1866; public domain) were looked up directly for the few notes that cite them. The English here is new, made directly from the Latin. The Latin *dominus deus* is rendered “the Lord God,” and the one occurrence of *Jehova* is rendered “Yahweh.” **Chapters and verses.** The Latin edition is divided into 51 chapters; it has no verse numbers, so the verses here are numbered sections made for this edition. The additional passages that Meyer prints at the end of chapters 29 and 51 are included as further verses of those chapters. The chapter numbers differ from those of the Greek *Apocalypse of Moses*, whose chapters follow a different order and length. Numbers in the text are given as numerals, and the Latin chronology is kept as written. **About the book.** The *Life of Adam and Eve* is a retelling of the story of Adam and Eve after their expulsion from paradise: their penance in the rivers, Satan’s account of why he fell (he refused to bow down to Adam), the birth of Cain, Abel, and Seth, Seth’s journey to paradise for the oil of mercy, Adam’s death and burial by angels, and Eve’s last words. Most scholars think that the original was a Jewish work written in Hebrew or Aramaic, probably in the 1st century AD, and later translated into Greek (the *Apocalypse of Moses*, which tells the story differently and ends with Eve’s death), then into Latin, Armenian, Georgian, Slavonic, and other languages. The Latin version is later than the Greek and contains some Christian additions (for example, the prophecy of Christ’s baptism in chapter 42). The oldest Latin manuscripts date from the 9th century AD (Munich), and over seventy are known. The book is not in the Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox, or Protestant canons, but it was widely read in the Middle Ages and shaped later legends, such as that of the wood of the cross. Dates are given as BC/AD. CJT draft.

verses.text: After they were driven out of paradise, they built themselves a hut and spent seven days mourning and wailing in deep sorrow.
When the seven days were over, they began to feel hungry, and they looked for something to eat, but could find nothing.
Then Eve spoke to Adam: “Master, I am starving. Go and find us something to eat.
Perhaps the Lord God will look on us again and take pity, and call us back to the place where we used to be.”
So Adam got up and walked for seven days across the whole country, and he found no food like the food they had had in paradise.

Then Eve said to Adam, “My lord, you would do better to kill me, so that I die. Perhaps then the Lord God will bring you back into paradise, because it was on my account that the Lord God was angry with you.
Do you want to put me to death? Perhaps the Lord God will bring you into paradise again, since it was because of me that you were driven out.”
Adam answered, “Eve, do not talk like that, or the Lord God may bring another curse on us. How could I raise my hand against my own flesh?
No, let us get up and look for something to live on, so that we do not waste away.”
So they set out and went on searching for nine days, and found nothing like what they had had in paradise. They found only what the animals ate.
Then Adam said to Eve, “The Lord gave this food to the animals and wild beasts to eat. We used to have the food of angels.
It is right and proper that we should grieve before the face of God who made us. Let us do great penance. Perhaps the Lord God will forgive us, take pity on us, and provide a way for us to live.”

Eve said to Adam, “My lord, tell me what penance is and how I should do it. I am afraid we may take on a burden we cannot bear, and then he will not hear our prayers, and the Lord will turn his face away from us, because we have not kept what we promised.
My lord, you have thought how much you are willing to bear in penance, because I brought this toil and trouble on you.”
Adam said to Eve, “You cannot do as much as I can. Do only as much as will save you.
I will fast for forty days. You must get up and go to the river Tigris, find a stone, step onto it in the current, and stay where the river is deep enough to reach your neck.
No word is to come out of your mouth, because we are not fit to pray to the Lord; our lips are unclean from the forbidden tree we were told not to touch.
Stand in the water of the river for thirty-seven days. I will stand in the water of the Jordan for forty days. Perhaps the Lord God will take pity on us.”
Eve went to the river Tigris and did what Adam had told her.
Adam in the same way went to the Jordan and took his stand on a stone, the water reaching his neck.
Adam said, “Waters of the Jordan, I am speaking to you: suffer with me. Gather to me all the creatures that swim in you, so that they surround me and mourn with me.
Let them not lament for themselves, but for me, because it was not they who sinned, but I.”
Immediately all the living creatures came and crowded around him, and from that hour the Jordan’s water halted and did not flow.
When eighteen days had passed, Satan became angry. He changed himself into the brightness of the angels, went to the river Tigris, to Eve, and found her weeping.
The devil himself, as if he grieved for her, began to cry and told her, “Leave the river, and stop your weeping. Stop your sadness and your groaning now.
Why are you so anxious, you and your husband Adam? The Lord God has heard your groaning and accepted your penance, and all of us angels have begged the Lord on your behalf.
He has sent me to lead you from the water and to give you the food you used to have in paradise, the food you have been mourning for.
So come out of the water now, and I will lead you to the place where your food is ready.”
When Eve heard this, she believed him. She left the river, and her skin looked like grass shriveled by the chill of the water.
As she climbed out she collapsed on the ground; the devil lifted her to her feet and took her to Adam.
When Adam saw her and the devil with her, he cried out in tears, “Oh, Eve, Eve! Where is the work of your penance?
How have you been deceived again by our enemy, the one who caused us to be shut out of our home in paradise and from its spiritual joy?”
When Eve heard this, she realized that the devil had talked her into leaving the river. She fell on her face on the ground, and her grief and groaning and lamenting were doubled.

She cried out, “Curse you, devil! Why do you attack us for nothing? What do you have against us? What have we done to you, that you pursue us so cunningly? What does your wickedness have to do with us?
Did we take your glory away and leave you without honor? Why do you hound us to death, you wicked and spiteful enemy?”

The devil groaned and said, “Adam, all my hostility and envy and pain are aimed at you. Because of you I was driven out and cut off from the glory that I had in heaven among the angels, and because of you I was thrown down to earth.”
Adam answered, “What have I done to you? What is my fault against you? You have not been harmed or hurt by us, so why do you hunt us down?”

The devil answered, “Adam, what are you saying to me? It is because of you that I was thrown out. When you were formed, I was thrown out from God’s presence and sent away from the company of the angels.

When God breathed the breath of life into you, and your face and likeness were made in the image of God, Michael brought you and made you bow down in the sight of God. And the Lord God said, ‘See, Adam, I have made you in our image and likeness.’”

“Michael went out and summoned every angel: ‘Bow down to the image of the Lord God, as the Lord God has ordered.’ Michael was the first to bow. Next he summoned me and said, ‘Bow down to the image of God, Yahweh.’

My answer was, ‘Worshiping Adam is not something I have to do.’ But Michael kept urging me to bow, and I said to him, ‘Why are you forcing me? I will not worship one who is lower than I am and came after me. In creation I am older than he is. Before he was made, I had already been made. He ought to worship me.’”
“The other angels who served under me heard this, and they also refused to bow to him. Michael said, ‘Worship the image of God. If you do not, the Lord God will be angry with you.’
And I said, ‘If he is angry with me, I will set my throne above the stars of heaven and be like the Most High.’”
“The Lord God was angry with me, and sent me out with my angels from our glory. Because of you we were driven out of our homes into this world and thrown down on the earth.
At once we were in pain, because we had been stripped of such great glory. And it hurt us to see you in such great delight.
So I tricked your wife by deceit, and through her I had you driven out of your joyful delights, just as I was driven out of my glory.”

When Adam heard this from the devil, he cried out in great tears and said, “Lord my God, my life is in your hands. Keep this enemy of mine far from me, he who is trying to destroy my soul, and give me the glory that he himself has lost.”
At once the devil disappeared from his sight. And Adam stayed on, standing in penance in the water of the Jordan for forty days.

Eve said to Adam, “Live, my lord. Life has been granted to you, because you were not guilty of the first or the second transgression. It was I who broke the commandment and was led astray, because I did not keep the command of God.
Now send me away from the light of this life. I will go to the west, where the sun sets, and stay there until I die.”
She began to walk toward the western regions, and she began to mourn and weep bitterly with loud groaning. There she made herself a shelter, carrying a child of three months in her womb.
When the time of her delivery came near, she began to be tormented by pains. She cried out to the Lord, “Have mercy on me, Lord; help me.” But she was not heard, and God’s mercy did not come to her.
Then she said to herself, “Who will tell my lord Adam? I beg you, lights of heaven, when you return to the east, tell my lord Adam.”
At that very hour Adam said, “I hear Eve crying out. Perhaps the serpent is fighting with her again.”
He walked on and came upon her in terrible distress. Eve said, “From the moment I saw you, my lord, my soul, caught in its pains, was refreshed.
Now pray to the Lord God for me, so that he will hear you and look on me and free me from these terrible pains.” And Adam prayed to the Lord for Eve.

Then twelve angels came, with two powers, who stood on the right and left of Eve. Michael stood on her right, touched her face down to her breast, and said to her, “You are blessed, Eve, because of Adam. His prayers and entreaties are great, and I have been sent to you so that you can receive our help.
Get up now and prepare for the birth.” She gave birth to a son, and he shone with light.
The baby at once rose and ran; he plucked some grass with his own hands and handed it to his mother. His name was called Cain.
Adam took Eve and the boy and led them to the east.

The Lord God sent the angel Michael with seeds of various kinds. He handed them to Adam and taught him to till the soil and tend it, so that they would have fruit to live on, they and all their descendants.
After that Eve conceived again and bore a son named Abel. Cain stayed together with Abel.
Eve said to Adam, “My lord, I had a vision in my sleep: I saw the blood of our son Abel in Cain’s hand, and Cain was swallowing it down with his mouth. That is why I am troubled.”
Adam said, “Oh no! May Cain not kill Abel! Let us separate them from each other and give each of them a separate home.”
They made Cain a farmer and Abel a shepherd, to keep them apart. But after this Cain killed Abel. Adam was then 130 years old, and Abel was 122 when he was killed.
After this Adam knew his wife and she bore a son, and he named him Seth. Adam said to Eve, “See, I have had a son to replace Abel, the one Cain killed.”
After Seth was born, Adam lived another eight hundred years and had thirty sons and thirty daughters, sixty-three in all.{a} They multiplied over the earth, in their nations.

notes.text: The Latin says “sixty-three” (*LXIII*), but thirty sons and thirty daughters make sixty; the figure is kept as the manuscripts give it.

verses.text: Adam said to Seth, “Listen, my son Seth, and I will tell you what I heard and saw. After my wife, your mother, and I were driven out of paradise, while we were praying, the archangel Michael, a messenger of God, came to me.
I saw a chariot that moved like the wind, with wheels of fire, and I was carried off to the paradise of righteousness.
I saw the Lord seated, and his appearance was a blazing fire, unbearable. And many thousands of angels stood to the right and left of his chariot.”
“When I saw this, I was terrified. Fear seized me, and I bowed down before God, face to the ground.

God said to me, ‘See, you will die, because you went against God’s command: you listened to your wife’s voice more than to mine, though I gave her into your power to have her at your will. You listened to her, and my words you disregarded.’”
“At these words of God I fell to the ground, bowed to the Lord, and said, ‘My Lord, almighty God, merciful, holy, and loving, do not let the name of your majesty’s memory be wiped out.

Turn my soul back, for I am dying and my breath will leave my mouth. Do not cast me from your presence, I whom you formed from the clay of the earth, and do not put aside your grace for the one you nourished.

See, your word comes to me.’ And the Lord said to me, ‘Because your days are numbered, you have become a lover of knowledge; for this reason it will not be taken away from your seed for ever, to serve me.’”{a}

notes.text: The Latin of the last clause is obscure (*quoniam figurantur dies tui factus es diligens scientiam*), and the translation is a best guess at its sense.

verses.text: “After hearing this I lay face down on the ground and bowed before the Lord God, saying, ‘You are the eternal and most high God, and all creatures give you honor and praise.
You are the true light, shining above every light, the living life, a power of incomprehensible greatness. The spiritual powers give you honor and praise.
You work the great wonders of your mercy with the human race.’”
“After I worshiped the Lord, the archangel Michael at once took my hand and led me out of the paradise of God’s visitation and command.
Michael had a rod in his hand. He touched the waters around paradise, and they turned to ice. I crossed over, and Michael crossed with me, and brought me back to the place from which he had taken me.

Listen, my son Seth, to the other mysteries and secrets of what is to come, which were revealed to me, who ate from the tree of knowledge and came to know and understand what will happen in this world.”

… what will happen in this age, what God will do for his creature, the human race. The Lord will appear in a blaze of fire. Out of his majestic mouth he will give everyone commands and rules (from his mouth a sword will come, sharp on both sides), and in the house where his majesty dwells they will hallow him. And he will show them the wonderful place of his majesty.{a}

Then they will build a house for the Lord their God on the earth, in the land where he fed them (the land he will prepare for them). There they will disobey his commands, their sanctuary will be set on fire, and their land will be left desolate, and they themselves will be scattered, because they have angered God. Yet again (on the third day, or the seventh) he will save them from their scattering, and they will build the house of God once more, and at the last that house will be lifted higher than it was before. And again wickedness will overcome justice.

After that God will live among people on earth, to be seen. Then justice will begin to shine. The house of God will be honored for ever, and hostile powers will no longer be able to harm those who believe in God. For himself God will bring forth a loyal people, and he will keep them safe for all ages. The wicked who refused to love his law will be punished by God their king. Heaven and earth, night and day, and all creatures will obey him; they will not go beyond his command or change their works. But people will change, abandoning the law of the Lord.

For this the Lord will drive the wicked away from himself, and the righteous will gleam like the sun before God’s eyes. At that time people will be cleansed of their sins by water; but those who refuse to be cleansed by water will be condemned. Happy will be the person who has set his soul right, when the judgments and great deeds of God take place among people, and their actions are examined by God, the righteous judge.

notes.text: Verses 4–7 (marked “a–d” in Meyer’s edition) are an addition found in only some of the Latin manuscripts. The Latin of this passage is uneven, and words in round brackets are variants or additions printed in the Latin text itself.

verses.text: In the 930th year of his life, Adam knew that his days were running out, and he said, “Gather all my sons around me, so that I may speak with them and give them my blessing before I die.”

They gathered in three groups before him, in front of the prayer house where they used to worship the Lord God. They asked him, “Father, what is wrong? Why did you call us together, and why are you lying in your bed?”
Adam answered, “My children, I am in pain and I am ill.” All his sons said to him, “Father, what does it mean to be ill with pain?”

Then his son Seth said, “Lord, perhaps you are longing for the fruit of paradise that you used to eat, and that is why you are lying here grieved? Say the word, and I will go to the gates of paradise nearest us, sprinkle dust on my head, lie on the ground in front of the gates, and cry out in great lament, pleading with the Lord. Perhaps he will listen and send his angel to fetch me some of the fruit you crave.”
Adam answered, “No, my son, that is not what I want. What I have is an illness, and a great pain in my body.”
Seth said, “Father and lord, I do not know what pain is. Do not hide it from us, but tell us.”

Adam answered, “Listen to me, my children. At our creation, mine and your mother’s, God placed us in paradise. Every fruit tree there was given to us for food, but he forbade us: ‘Do not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which stands in the middle of paradise.’
He shared out paradise between your mother and me. I received the eastern trees and those of the northern side, which faces the north wind; to your mother he gave the southern part and the western.”
“The Lord God gave us two angels to guard us. When the hour came for the angels to go up to worship in the sight of God, the enemy, the devil, found his chance, while the angels were absent.
The devil deceived your mother into eating from the forbidden tree we were told not to touch. She ate, and gave to me.”

“The Lord God grew angry with us at once. He told me, ‘You abandoned my commandment and did not obey the word I laid on you, I will bring seventy blows on your body. You will be tormented in every limb with different pains, from the top of the head, and the eyes and ears, to the nails of the feet.’
He appointed these as a scourge … together with the trees.{a}
The Lord sent all these things on me and on all our generations.”

notes.text: The Latin of this sentence is corrupt: Meyer marks *dolori* with crosses (*Haec deputavit in flagellationem + dolori + uno cum arboribus*), and no sure sense can be recovered. The Greek *Apocalypse of Moses* (ch. 8) also speaks of seventy blows, each affecting a different part of the body.

verses.text: After saying this to all his children, Adam was seized by great pains. He cried out loudly: “What shall I do, wretched as I am, caught in such pain?”
When Eve saw him weeping, she too began to weep, saying, “Lord my God, put his pain on me, because I am the one who sinned.”
Eve said to Adam, “My master, let me carry part of your pains, because this guilt came to you through me.”
Adam said to Eve, “Get up and go with my son Seth to the edge of paradise. Put dust on your heads, throw yourselves on the ground, and mourn in the sight of God.

Perhaps he will take pity and send his angel to the tree of his mercy, from which the oil of life flows, and give you a little of it, so that you can anoint me with it and I can rest from these pains that are wearing me away.”
Seth and his mother set out toward the gates of paradise. As they were walking, suddenly a beast, a serpent, came, rushed at Seth, and bit him.
When Eve saw it, she wept and said, “Woe to me, wretched woman, for I am cursed, because I did not keep the Lord’s commandments.”
Eve shouted at the serpent, “Cursed beast, how were you not afraid to throw yourself at the image of God, but dared to fight with it? How did your teeth prevail?”

The beast answered in a human voice, “Eve, is our wickedness not aimed at you? Is our rage not against you? Tell me, Eve, how was your mouth opened to eat the fruit that the Lord God commanded you not to eat? If I begin to reproach you now, can you bear it?”

Then Seth said to the beast, “The Lord God rebuke you. Be silent, be dumb, shut your mouth, you cursed enemy of the truth, confusion of destruction. Stay clear of God’s image until the day the Lord God commands that you be brought to trial.”
The beast said to Seth, “See, as you say, I am leaving the presence of the image of God.” At once the wound left Seth’s flesh from the bite.
Seth and his mother kept going toward the edges of paradise, to fetch the oil of mercy and rub it on the ailing Adam.

When they reached the gates of paradise, they picked up dust from the ground and put it on their heads. They threw themselves on the ground, face down, and began to wail with loud groaning, asking the Lord God to have mercy on Adam in his agony and to send his angel with oil from the tree of his mercy.
After they had been praying and begging for many hours, the angel Michael appeared before them. “The Lord has sent me to you,” he said. “I am the one appointed by the Lord over the human body.
I tell you, Seth, man of God, stop weeping and pleading for the oil of the tree of mercy, which you want in order to soothe your father Adam’s bodily pains.”
“I tell you that you will not be able to get any of it, except in the last days, when five thousand five hundred years have passed.

Then the most loving king, Christ, the Son of God, will come on the earth to raise up Adam’s body and with it to raise the bodies of the dead. On his coming, the Son of God himself will be baptized in the river Jordan, and as he rises out of the Jordan’s water he will anoint with the oil of his mercy all who believe in him.

The oil of mercy will be for generation after generation for those who are to be born again of water and the Holy Spirit into eternal life. Then the most loving Son of God, Christ, coming down to earth, will lead your father Adam into paradise, to the tree of mercy.”{a}

notes.text: This prophecy is a Christian addition: it speaks of Christ’s baptism and of the world lasting five thousand five hundred years before his coming, a count common in early Christian chronology. The Greek *Apocalypse of Moses* (ch. 13) also says that Seth cannot have the oil now, only at the end.

verses.text: “But you, Seth, go to your father Adam, because the time of his life is complete. Six more days, and then his soul will leave his body. When it leaves, you will see great wonders in heaven and on earth and in the lights of heaven.”
After saying this, Michael left Seth at once. Eve and Seth turned back. They took spices with them: nard, saffron, calamint, and cinnamon.

When Seth and his mother came to Adam, they told him that the serpent beast had bitten Seth. Adam said to Eve, “What have you done? You have brought a great plague on us, guilt and sin on all our generations.

And what you have done will fall on your children after my death … because those who rise from us will labor and not be strong enough, but will fail, and will curse us, saying, ‘Our parents, who lived at the beginning, brought all these evils on us.’”{a}
When Eve heard this, she began to weep and groan.

notes.text: The Latin has *+ refert +* between crosses here, meaning that the word is corrupt; the translation leaves the gap marked.

verses.text: Just as the archangel Michael had foretold, Adam’s death came after six days. When Adam realized that the hour of his death had come, he said to all his sons, “See, I am 930 years old. If I die, bury me toward the east, in … the great dwelling-place of God.”{a}
When he had finished all his words, he gave up his spirit.

notes.text: The Latin reads *contra + ortum + dei magnum habitationibus*; the word *ortum* is marked as corrupt (it could mean “sunrise” or “garden”).

verses.text: The sun, the moon, and the stars were darkened for seven days. Seth lay over his father’s body, embracing it and mourning. Eve stood looking at the ground, with her hands clasped over her head and her head bent down on her knees, and all his children wept with bitter tears.

Then the angel Michael appeared, standing at Adam’s head, and said to Seth, “Get up from your father’s body and come to me, and see what the Lord God has decided about him. He is his creature, and God has pitied him.”
All the angels sounded their trumpets and said, “Blessed are you, Lord, because you have taken pity on what you formed.”

Then Seth saw the hand of the Lord stretched out, holding Adam, and the Lord handed him to Michael, saying, “Let him be in your keeping until the day of the dispensation, in the punishments, for the last years, when I will turn his mourning to joy. Then he will sit on the throne of the one who tripped him up.”{a}

notes.text: “The one who tripped him up” (Latin *qui eum supplantavit*) is the devil. The sense is that Adam will take the place that the devil lost.

verses.text: Then the Lord said again to the angels Michael and Uriel, “Bring me three linen cloths and spread them over Adam. And bring others for his son Abel, and bury Adam and his son.”

All the powers of the angels went before Adam, and the resting of the dead was made holy. Michael and Uriel buried Adam and Abel in the regions of paradise, while Seth and his mother watched, and no one else.
And Michael and Uriel said, “As you have seen, bury your dead the same way.”

Six days after Adam died, Eve knew that her own death was near. She called all her sons and daughters together, who were Seth with his thirty brothers and thirty sisters, and she said to them all, “Listen to me, my children, and I will tell you what happened: your father and I broke God’s command.

The archangel Michael told us, ‘Because of your transgressions our Lord will bring the anger of his judgment on your race, first by water and then by fire. By these two the Lord will judge the whole human race.’”
“But listen to me, my children. Make tablets of stone and others of clay, and write on them all my life and your father’s life, everything you heard and saw from us.
If he judges our race by water, the clay tablets will dissolve and the stone ones will stay. If he judges our race by fire, the stone tablets will break up and the clay ones will be baked hard.”{a}
When Eve had said all this to her children, she stretched her hands toward heaven in prayer, bent her knees to the ground, worshiped the Lord, and gave thanks, and she gave up her spirit.

notes.text: The Latin has the nonsense word *nosbllum* in both places, which I read as *nostrum*, “our.”

verses.text: After that all her sons buried her with great weeping. When they had mourned for four days, the archangel Michael appeared to them and said to Seth, “Man of God, do not mourn for your dead more than six days. The seventh day is the sign of the resurrection and of the rest of the age to come; for on the seventh day the Lord rested from all his works.”
Then Seth made the tablets.

Then Seth made (two) tablets of stone and (two) of clay, (and he set out the letters), and he wrote on them the life of his father Adam and his mother Eve, which he had heard from them and seen with his own eyes. He put the tablets in the middle of his father’s house, in the prayer house where he prayed to the Lord. After the flood many people saw those written tablets, but no one could read them.{a}

Solomon the wise saw the writing, and he prayed to the Lord, and an angel of the Lord appeared to him and said, “I am the one who held Seth’s hand while he wrote these stones with his finger. You will understand the writing, so that you know and understand what all these stones contain, and where the prayer house was, where Adam and Eve worshiped the Lord God. You must build a temple of the Lord there, that is, a house of prayer.”

Then Solomon completed the temple of the Lord God, and he called those letters *achiliacas*, “written without words to teach them,” (written) with Seth’s finger, with the angel of the Lord holding his hand.{b}

And on those same stones was found what Enoch, the seventh from Adam, prophesied before the flood about the coming of Christ: “See, the Lord will come with his holy ones to carry out judgment on all, and to convict the wicked of all the works they have done against him, the sinners and the wicked, the grumblers and the ungodly, who walk after their own desires, and whose mouths speak arrogance.”{c}

notes.text: Verses 3–6 (marked “a–d” in Meyer’s edition) are an ending found in only some of the Latin manuscripts; it is included here as part of the text that Meyer prints.
The Latin *achiliacas* may be a corruption of a Greek word; the Latin itself explains it as “written without the teaching of words.”
This is the prophecy of Enoch quoted in the New Testament letter of Jude, verses 14–16; compare 1 Enoch 1:9.

books.name: Joseph and Aseneth
books.sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of *Joseph and Aseneth* as printed in the Online Critical Pseudepigrapha text (the Greek edition of the shorter form of the book, which follows the Greek manuscript tradition; the Greek text is public domain). Where the Greek is damaged or missing, as in chapter 11, the sense was taken from the public-domain English translation by E. W. Brooks (*Joseph and Asenath*, SPCK, London, 1918). Phrases that stand in square brackets in the printed Greek, because some manuscripts lack them, are translated here without brackets. The English here is new, made directly from the Greek, and it was not taken from the translations in *The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha* or from any other copyrighted translation. The Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God,” since no Hebrew name of God stands in the Greek text. **Chapters and verses.** The Greek is divided into 29 chapters, and the verse numbers here follow those of the Greek text as printed, with two exceptions: the long Greek chapter 23 is divided into chapters 23 and 24 here, as in the usual chapter numbering of this book, and the verses of chapter 11 are numbered for this edition. Months are given as the Greek numbers them, with the nearest modern months; times and numbers are given in modern form where the original gives them differently. **About the book.** *Joseph and Aseneth* is a Jewish romance that fills in a gap in Genesis 41:45, which says that Pharaoh gave Joseph “Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On” as his wife. It tells how the proud Egyptian virgin Aseneth, who despised men, saw Joseph, repented of her idols, was visited by a heavenly man who gave her honey of immortality, and married Joseph, and how Pharaoh’s son plotted to take her by force and was defeated. The book is usually dated between the 1st century BC and the 2nd century AD and was probably written in Greek, in Egypt. Some scholars see Christian reworking in it, and the oldest manuscripts are Byzantine and later; more than ninety are known, with versions in Syriac, Armenian, Latin, Slavonic, and other languages. It is not in the Jewish, Catholic, Orthodox, or Protestant canons. Dates are given as BC/AD. CJT draft.

verses.text: During the first of the seven plentiful years, in the second month (April–May),{a} on the fifth day of the month, Pharaoh{b} sent Joseph{c} out to make a circuit of the whole land of Egypt.{d}
In the fourth month (June–July), on the eighteenth day of the month, in that first year, Joseph came to the territory of Heliopolis.{e}
He was gathering in the grain of that region, and it was piled up like the sand of the sea.
Now in that city there was a man who was a satrap of Pharaoh, the chief of all Pharaoh’s satraps and nobles.
This man was very rich, wise, and gentle; he was a counselor to Pharaoh. His name was Pentephres,{f} and he was a priest of Heliopolis.
Pentephres had a daughter, a virgin about eighteen years old, tall and lovely, and more strikingly beautiful than any other virgin on earth.
She was not at all like the daughters of the Egyptians; in every way she was like the daughters of the Hebrews.
She was tall like Sarah,{g} lovely like Rebecca,{h} and beautiful like Rachel.{i} The name of this virgin was Aseneth.{j}
The report of her beauty spread through that whole country and to its farthest edges, and all the sons of the nobles, the satraps, and the kings wanted to marry her; they were all young men.
There was bitter rivalry among them over her, and they tried to make war on one another because of Aseneth.
The firstborn son of Pharaoh heard about her, and he kept begging his father to give her to him as his wife.
He would say to him, “Give me Aseneth, the daughter of Pentephres, the priest of Heliopolis, to be my wife.”
His father Pharaoh answered him, “Why are you looking for a wife beneath you? Are you not king of the whole world?
Look, the daughter of King Joakim{k} is already promised to you, and she is a queen of great beauty. Take her for your wife.”

notes.text: The Greek counts months by number, as the Hebrew calendar does, and gives no month name. The Hebrew year is lunar, so each month falls across two months of our calendar. The book does not say whether it counts from the spring or from another starting point; the spring-start count is used here. “Second month” corresponds to Iyyar (April–May) and “fourth month” (verse 2) to Tammuz (June–July).
“Pharaoh” is the Egyptian royal title *per-aa*, “great house.”
Hebrew *Yosef*, “may he add” (Genesis 30:24).
Hebrew *Mitsrayim*; the meaning of the name is unknown.
Greek *Heliopolis* means “city of the sun.” The Egyptian name was *Iunu*, and the Bible calls it On (Genesis 41:45).
Greek form of the Egyptian name that appears in Genesis as Potiphera; it is usually explained as “the one whom (the sun god) Re has given.”
Hebrew *Sarah*, “princess.”
Hebrew *Rivqah*; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “tied” or “a rope.”
Hebrew *Rachel*, “ewe.”
Greek *Asenet*, from the Egyptian name given in Genesis 41:45 as Asenath. It is usually explained as “she belongs to (the goddess) Neith.”
Greek form of Jehoiakim, Hebrew *Yehoyaqim*, “Yahweh raises up.” The book places him anachronistically at Pharaoh’s court; the passage may be a later insertion.

verses.text: Aseneth despised every man and spat on them, and no man had ever seen her. For next to Pentephres’ house there stood a tower, very large and very high.
On top of the tower was an upper floor containing ten rooms.
The first room was large and handsome. Its floor was paved with purple stone, and its walls were faced with costly stones of many colors.
The ceiling of that room was gold. Inside it stood countless gods of the Egyptians, made of gold and silver.
Aseneth revered all of them, and feared them, and offered sacrifices to them.
The second room held all of Aseneth’s ornaments and her chests.
In it there was a great deal of gold and silver, clothing woven with gold thread, precious chosen stones, and fine linen.
There lay all the finery of her maidenhood.
The third room was full of all the good things of the earth; it was Aseneth’s storeroom.
The other seven rooms were occupied by seven virgins, one to each room.

These waited on Aseneth. They were all of her age, because they had been born on the same night as Aseneth, and they were as beautiful as the stars of heaven. No man had ever spoken with them, nor even a male child.
There were three windows in the large room of Aseneth where her maidenhood was kept.
One window looked out on the courtyard to the east, the second looked north to the street, and the third faced south.
A golden couch stood in the room, facing east.
The couch was spread with a purple covering woven with gold thread, in blue and fine linen.
On this couch Aseneth slept alone, and no man or woman ever sat on it except Aseneth herself.
A great courtyard lay all around the house, with a very high wall around the courtyard, built of great squared stones.
The courtyard had four iron-plated gates, and each was guarded by eighteen strong young armed men.
Along the wall inside the courtyard were planted fine fruit trees of every kind, and all their fruit was ripe, for it was harvest time.

On the right side of the courtyard was a rich spring of water. Below the spring was a great basin that received its water, and from there a stream ran through the middle of the courtyard and watered all the trees in it.
In the fourth month (June–July), on the eighteenth day of the month, Joseph came to the territory of Heliopolis.
When he drew near the city, Joseph sent twelve men ahead of him to Pentephres, the priest of Heliopolis, with this message:
“I will stay with you today, since it is midday, the time for the noon meal, and the heat of the sun is great, and I would like to rest under your roof.”
Pentephres heard this and was overjoyed, and said, “Blessed be the Lord,{a} the God of Joseph.”
He called the steward of his house and said to him,
“Hurry and get my house ready, and prepare a great banquet, because Joseph, the mighty one of God, is coming to us today.”
Aseneth heard that her parents had come back from the fields of their estate, and she was glad, and said,
“I must go and see my father and mother, since they have come back from the fields of our estate.”
Aseneth hurried and put on a robe of fine linen, blue and woven with gold. She tied on a golden belt, put bracelets on her arms and ankles, wore golden trousers, and hung a necklace around her neck.
Costly stones were set all over these things, with the names of the Egyptian gods carved everywhere on the bracelets and the stones; and the faces of the idols were engraved in the stones.
On her head she put a tiara and a diadem, and bound it tight around her temples, and wrapped her head in a veil.

notes.text: The Greek text always says *kyrios*, “Lord,” and *theos*, “God.” No Hebrew name of God appears in it, so the CJT keeps “Lord” and “God” here and does not write “Yahweh.” In the Jewish Bible the God of Joseph is Yahweh.

verses.text: She hurried down the stairs from her upper floor, went to her father and mother, and greeted them.
Pentephres and his wife were filled with joy over their daughter Aseneth, because her parents saw her dressed like a bride of God.
They brought out all the good things they had carried back from their estate in the fields, and gave them to their daughter.
Aseneth was delighted with the produce, the grapes, the dates, the pigeons, the pomegranates, and the figs, because they were all beautiful.
Pentephres said to his daughter Aseneth, “Child.” She said, “Here I am, my lord.” He said to her, “Sit between us, and I will tell you what I have to say.”
Aseneth sat down between her father and mother.
Her father Pentephres took her right hand in his right hand and said, “Child.” Aseneth said, “Let my lord and father speak.”

Pentephres said to her, “Look, Joseph, the mighty one of God, is coming to us today. He is the ruler of the whole land of Egypt; Pharaoh appointed him ruler over our whole land, and he distributes grain to the whole country and saves it from the famine that is coming.
Joseph is a man who reveres God, self-controlled, and a virgin as you are today. He is a man powerful in wisdom and knowledge, the spirit of God is on him, and the favor of the Lord is with him.
Come now, my child, and I will give you to him as his wife; you will be his bride, and he will be your bridegroom forever.”
When Aseneth heard her father’s words, a great red sweat poured over her; she flared up in a great rage, looked at her father with a sideways glare, and said,
“Why does my lord and father speak like this? Does he want to hand me over, like a captive, to a foreigner, a fugitive, and a man who was sold?
Is he not the shepherd’s son out of the land of Canaan,{a} who was himself abandoned by his father?
Is he not the one who slept with his mistress, and his master threw him into the dark prison, and Pharaoh brought him out of prison because he interpreted his dream?
No! I will marry the king’s firstborn son, because he is king of the whole earth.”
When Pentephres heard this, he was ashamed to say anything more to his daughter about Joseph, since she had answered him with such arrogance and anger.

notes.text: Hebrew *Kena‘an*; the meaning is uncertain, possibly “lowland” or “merchant.”

verses.text: Just then a young man ran out from Pentephres’ servants and said, “Look, Joseph is at the doors of our courtyard.”
Aseneth fled from the sight of her parents, and went up to the upper floor and into her room, and stood at the great window that looked east, to see the one who was coming into her father’s house.
Pentephres and his wife and all his relatives went out to meet Joseph.
The gates of the courtyard that face east were opened, and Joseph came in, riding in Pharaoh’s second chariot.
Four horses were yoked to it, white as snow, with golden bridles, and the chariot was canopied in gold.

Joseph was dressed in a splendid white tunic, and the robe he wore over it was purple linen woven with gold. A golden crown was on his head, and around the crown were twelve chosen stones, and over the stones rose twelve golden rays; and a royal scepter was in his right hand.
He also held out an olive branch, heavy with fruit.
Joseph entered the courtyard, and the gates were shut.
Any man or woman who was a stranger stayed outside, because the gatekeepers had closed the doors.
Pentephres, his wife, and all his relatives came, all but their daughter Aseneth, and bowed to Joseph with their faces to the ground.
Joseph stepped down from his chariot and gave them his right hand in greeting.
When Aseneth saw Joseph, she was pierced to the soul; her insides twisted, her knees went slack, and her whole body shook. She was seized with great fear, and she groaned and said,
“Where can I go, and where can I hide from his face? How will Joseph, the son of God,{a} ever look at me, since I have spoken evil of him?
Where can I flee and hide? He sees every hiding place, and nothing hidden escapes him, because of the great light within him.
Now may the God of Joseph be merciful to me, because I spoke wicked words in ignorance.

What am I to do, wretched as I am? Did I not say, ‘Here comes Joseph, the shepherd’s son from the land of Canaan’? And now, look, the sun has come down from heaven to us in his chariot and entered our house today.
What a fool I was, and how reckless, to despise him and to say wicked things about him, not knowing that Joseph is a son of God.
For what man will ever father such beauty, and what womb will bear such light? Wretched fool that I am, who said wicked words to my father.
Now let my father give me to Joseph as a maidservant and a slave, and I will serve him forever.”

notes.text: Joseph is called a “son of God” as a man close to God. Compare 21:3.

verses.text: Joseph entered the house of Pentephres and sat on a chair and washed his feet. A table was set for him separately, because he did not eat with the Egyptians; it was an abomination to him.
Joseph said to Pentephres and to all his relatives, “Who is that woman standing in the upper room by the window? Let her leave this house.”
He was afraid she might also pester him, because all the women and daughters of the nobles and satraps of the whole land of Egypt pestered him, wanting to sleep with him.
Many Egyptian women and daughters who saw Joseph suffered terribly over his beauty, and they sent their envoys to him with gold and silver and costly gifts.
Joseph sent all of it back with threats and insults, saying, “I will not sin before the God of Israel.”{a}

He kept the face of Jacob,{b} his father, always before his eyes, and he remembered his father’s commands. For Jacob used to say to Joseph and his brothers, “Children, guard yourselves carefully against any foreign woman; do not unite with her, for that is ruin and corruption.”
This is why Joseph said, “Let that woman leave this house.”
Pentephres said to him, “My lord, the woman you saw in the upper room is not a stranger, but our daughter, a virgin who hates every man. No other man has ever seen her except you, alone, today.
If you like, she will come and greet you, for our daughter is your sister.”
Joseph was overjoyed, because Pentephres had said, “She is a virgin who hates every man.”
Joseph answered Pentephres and his wife, “If she is really your daughter, let her come, for she is my sister, and from today I will love her as my sister.”

notes.text: Hebrew *Yisra’el*, “he strives with God” or “God strives” (Genesis 32:28), the name God gave to Jacob.
Hebrew *Ya‘aqov*, “he grasps the heel,” and so “he supplants” (Genesis 25:26; 27:36).

verses.text: Aseneth’s mother went up to the upper floor and brought Aseneth to Joseph. Pentephres said to his daughter Aseneth, “Greet your brother, for he is a virgin as you are today, and he hates every foreign woman as you hate every foreign man.”
Aseneth said to Joseph, “Greetings, my lord, blessed by God Most High.”{a} Joseph said to her, “May God, who gives life to everything, bless you.”
Pentephres said to Aseneth, “Go to him and kiss your brother.”
But when she came forward to kiss Joseph, he stretched out his right hand, laid it against her chest, and said,

“It is not fitting for a man who fears God, who blesses the living God with his mouth, eats the blessed bread of life, drinks the blessed cup of immortality, and is anointed with the blessed oil of incorruption, to kiss a foreign woman, one who blesses dead and deaf idols with her mouth, eats the bread of strangling from their table, drinks the cup of ambush from their libation, and is anointed with the oil of destruction.
A man who fears God may kiss his mother, and the sister from his own tribe and family, and the wife who shares his bed, all of whom bless the living God with their mouths.
In the same way, it is not fitting for a woman who fears God to kiss a foreign man, because that is an abomination before God.”
When Aseneth heard Joseph’s words, she was deeply grieved. She sighed, staring at Joseph, and her eyes filled with tears.
Joseph saw her and felt great pity for her, because Joseph was gentle and merciful and feared the Lord. He raised his right hand over her head and said,

“Lord God of my father Israel, Most High, Mighty One, who gives life to all things and called them out of darkness into light, out of error into truth, and out of death into life: you yourself, Lord, give life to this virgin and bless her.

Renew her by your Spirit, remold her with your hidden hand, and bring her to life again with your life. Let her eat your bread of life and drink your cup of blessing, she whom you chose before she was born, and let her enter your resting place, which you have prepared for your chosen ones.”

notes.text: Greek *Hypsistos*, “Most High,” which translates the Hebrew *El Elyon*, “God Most High” (Genesis 14:18–20).

verses.text: Aseneth was very happy at Joseph’s blessing. She hurried up to her room and collapsed on her couch, sick, for joy, grief, and great fear were all mixed in her, and a steady sweat poured over her at hearing the words Joseph had spoken to her, in the name of the Most High God.
She wept bitterly and at length, and she repented of her gods, whom she had worshiped, and waited for evening to come.
Meanwhile Joseph ate and drank, and said to his servants, “Harness the horses to the chariot,” for he said, “I will go and make the circuit of the whole city and the land.”
Pentephres said to Joseph, “My lord, please stay the night here today, and go on your way in the morning.”
Joseph answered, “No, I will leave today, because this is the very day when God began his works, and on the eighth day I will come back to you again and stay here.”{a}

notes.text: “The eighth day” is counted from the day of the visit, so that Joseph returns after one full week.

verses.text: Then Pentephres and his family left for their own estate.
Aseneth was left alone with her virgins. She was despondent and wept until the sun set. She ate no bread and drank no water, but while everyone else slept, she alone stayed awake.
She opened her door, went down to the gate, and found the gatekeeper asleep with her children.
Aseneth hurried, took down the skin curtain from the door, filled it with ashes, carried it up to her room, and set it on the floor.
She shut the door securely, laid the iron bar across it, and groaned with loud lament and weeping.
The virgin whom Aseneth loved best of all the virgins heard her mistress groaning, woke the other virgins, came, and found the door shut.
She listened to the groaning and weeping of Aseneth and said, “Why are you so downcast, my lady? What is troubling you? Open to us, and let us see you.”

Aseneth, shut inside, said to them, “I have a terrible pain in my head, and I am resting on my bed. I cannot get up to open to you now, because I am weak in all my limbs. Go, each of you, to your own room.”
Then Aseneth got up, quietly opened the door, and went to her second room, where her chests of ornaments were. She opened her chest and took out a black, dark tunic.
This was the tunic of her mourning, which she had worn when her eldest brother died.

Aseneth stripped off her royal robe and dressed in the black one. She undid her golden belt and tied a rope around herself. She took the tiara off her head, and the diadem, and the bracelets from her arms.
She took all her choice clothing and threw it out of the window to the poor.
She took all her gods, the gold ones and the silver ones, without number, smashed them to pieces, and threw them to the poor and needy.

Aseneth took her royal dinner, the fattened animals, the fish, the meats, every sacrifice to her gods, and the jars of their libation wine, and threw everything out of the window to the dogs for food.
After that she took the ashes and poured them out on the floor.
She took sackcloth, tied it around her waist, took the net off her hair, scattered ashes over her head, and fell down on the ashes.
She beat her breast over and over with both hands, and wept bitterly all night with groaning until morning.
When she looked in the morning, the ashes under her had turned to mud from her tears.
Aseneth fell on her face on the ashes again until the sun set.
She did this for seven days, tasting nothing at all.

On the eighth day, at dawn, when the birds had begun to chirp and the dogs to bark at passersby, Aseneth lifted her head a little from the floor where she lay, for she was paralyzed in her limbs from so much self-humbling.{a}

She turned toward the wall, and sat under the window that looked east. She rested her head on her chest, wove her fingers together over her right knee, and kept her mouth shut. She had not opened it during the seven days and seven nights of her self-humbling.

She spoke in her heart, without opening her mouth: “What shall I do, wretched as I am? Where shall I go, and with whom shall I find shelter? Whom shall I speak to, an orphan virgin, desolate, abandoned by everyone, and hated?

Now they all hate me, and even my father and mother, because I loathed the gods, destroyed them, and gave them to the poor to be broken up. My father and mother said, ‘Aseneth is not our daughter.’ And all my relatives hate me too, and all people, because I destroyed their gods.
I hated every man who sought me in marriage, and now, in this humiliation, everyone hates me, and they enjoy my suffering.

But the Lord, the God of mighty Joseph, hates all who worship idols, for he is a jealous and terrifying God, as I have heard, toward all who worship foreign gods. That is why he hates me too, because I worshiped dead and deaf idols and blessed them.

Now I have turned away from their sacrifices, and my mouth has become a stranger to their table. I have no courage to call on the Lord, the God of heaven, the Most High, the powerful God of mighty Joseph, because my mouth is polluted with the sacrifices of the idols.

But I have heard many people say that the Hebrews’ God is a true and living God, merciful, compassionate, patient, full of mercy, and kind. He does not count the sin of a humble person, and especially of someone who sins in ignorance, and he does not prosecute lawlessness when a person is in the time of distress.
So I too, humble as I am, will be bold. I will turn to him and take refuge in him; I will admit all my sins to him and empty out my plea before him, and he may take pity on my misery.

Who knows whether he will see this humiliation of mine and the emptiness of my soul, and feel sorrow for me, and see how wretched and orphaned I am, and my virginity, and shield me? I hear that he is himself a father of orphans, a consolation for the afflicted, and an aid to the persecuted.
In any case, humble as I am, I will be bold and cry out to him.”
Then Aseneth rose from the wall where she sat, knelt, directed her eyes toward heaven, opened her mouth, and said to God:

notes.text: The Greek text here is damaged. Chapter 11 of the CJT follows the sense of the Greek, which has only a few broken lines left (“counting the sin of a humble person,” “I will confess all my sins to him”), together with the fuller reading of the Greek tradition as translated by E. W. Brooks in 1918. Verse numbers here are those of this edition.

verses.text: She spread out her hands toward the east and lifted her eyes toward heaven, and said:
“Lord God of the ages, who gave the breath of life to all, who brought the unseen into the light, who made everything and made the hidden things appear,
who raised up the heavens and founded the earth on the waters, who fixed the great stones upon the deep of the water, stones that will never sink but remain until the end, doing your will:
Lord my God, I cry out to you. Listen to my plea; I confess my sins to you and uncover my lawless deeds before you.

I have sinned, Lord; I have sinned. I have broken your law, been godless, and spoken evil in your presence. My mouth, Lord, has been polluted by the sacrifices to idols and from the table of the gods of the Egyptians.
I have sinned, Lord, before you. I have been godless, because I worshiped idols that are dead and deaf, and wretch that I am, I am not fit to open my mouth to you.

I have sinned, Lord, before you, I, the daughter of Pentephres the priest, who was proud and arrogant. I bring my plea to you, Lord, and cry out to you. Rescue me from those who pursue me, because I have fled to you like a child to its father and mother.
You, Lord, stretch out your hands over me like a father who loves his children, and tenderly, and snatch me from the hand of the enemy.
For look, the fierce old lion is chasing me, and his cubs are the gods of the Egyptians, whom I threw away and destroyed; and their father, the devil, is trying to swallow me.

But you, Lord, save me from his hands, and pull me out of his mouth, so that he does not seize me like a wolf and tear me apart and throw me into the abyss of fire, into the storm of the sea, and so that the great sea monster does not swallow me.

Save me, Lord, in my desolation, for my father and mother have disowned me because I destroyed and smashed their gods. Now I am an orphan, alone, and I have no hope but you, Lord. For you are the father of orphans, the defender of the persecuted, and the helper of the oppressed.
Look, all the wealth of my father Pentephres is temporary and fading, but the dwellings of your inheritance, Lord, are incorruptible and eternal.
Visit my orphaned state, Lord, because I have fled to you.
Look, I have laid aside my royal robe woven with gold, and put on a black tunic.
Look, I have loosened my golden belt and tied on a rope and sackcloth.
Look, I have thrown the diadem off my head and covered myself with ashes.
Look, the floor of my room, which was paved with colored and purple stone and sprinkled with perfumes, is now sprinkled with my tears and covered with dust.
Look, my Lord, from the ashes and my tears there is a great deal of mud in my room, as on a wide road.
Look, Lord, I have given my royal dinner and the fattened food to the dogs.

Look, for seven days and seven nights I have eaten no bread and drunk no water, and my mouth is as dry as a drum, my tongue is like a horn, and my lips like a piece of broken pottery. My face has sunk in, and my eyes have failed from the burning of my tears.
But, Lord, forgive me, because I sinned against you in ignorance and spoke blasphemies against my lord Joseph.

I did not know, wretch that I am, that he is your son, Lord, because people told me that Joseph was the shepherd’s son from the country of Canaan, and I believed them, and I was deceived. I despised your chosen one, Joseph, and spoke evil of him, not knowing that he is your son.
What man has ever fathered such beauty, and who else is as wise and strong as Joseph? But, my Lord, I place him in your care, because I love him more than my own soul.
Keep him in the wisdom of your grace, and place me with him as a maidservant, so that I may wash his feet, wait on him, and serve him all the days of my life.”
When Aseneth had finished her confession to the Lord, the Morning Star{a} rose in the sky in the east. Aseneth saw it and was glad, and said,
“Then the Lord God has heard me, because this star is the messenger and herald of the light of the great day.”
And look, near the Morning Star the heaven was torn open, and a light appeared that no one can describe.
Aseneth fell on her face in the ashes, and a man came to her from heaven. He stood over her head and called her: “Aseneth.”
She said, “Who is calling me? The door of my room is shut, and the tower is high. How did he get into my room?”
The man called her a second time and said, “Aseneth, Aseneth.” She said, “Here I am, my lord. Tell me who you are.”
The man said, “I am the commander of the house of the Lord and chief captain of all the army of the Most High.{b} Stand up on your feet, and I will speak to you.”
She lifted her eyes and saw a man who was like Joseph in every way, in his robe, his crown, and his royal rod,
except that his face was like lightning, his eyes like the shining of the sun, the hair on his head like a flame of fire, and his hands and feet like iron glowing from the fire.
Aseneth saw him and fell on her face at his feet in great fear and trembling.
The man said to her, “Take heart, Aseneth, and do not be afraid. Stand up on your feet, and I will speak to you.”
Aseneth stood up, and the man said to her, “Take off the black tunic you are wearing, and the sackcloth from your waist. Shake the ashes off your head and wash your face with living water,
and put on a new, untouched robe, and tie around your waist your bright double belt of virginity,
and come to me again, and I will tell you the words that have been sent to you.”
Aseneth went into her room where the chests of her ornaments were, opened her chest, and took out a new, splendid robe. She took off the black one and put on the new, bright one.
She untied the rope and the sackcloth from her waist and put on a bright double belt of virginity, one belt around her waist and one over her chest.
She shook the ashes off her head, washed her face with clean water, and covered her head with a fine, splendid veil.

notes.text: Greek *heosphoros*, “dawn-bringer,” the planet Venus when it rises before the sun (Hebrew *Helel*, “shining one,” in Isaiah 14:12).

Compare Joshua 5:14–15, where the figure who meets Joshua calls himself the “commander of the army of Yahweh.” Jewish tradition identified this figure with the archangel Michael (Hebrew *Mikha’el*, “Who is like God?”), but the Greek text here does not give his name.

verses.text: She came to the man, and when he saw her he said, “Take the veil off your head, because you are a pure virgin today, and your head is like a young man’s.”
She took it off her head. The man said to her, “Take heart, Aseneth, because the Lord has heard the words of your confession.
Take heart, Aseneth. Your name has been recorded in the book of life, and it will not be erased.
From today you will be renewed, and formed anew, and brought to life again; you will eat the bread of life, drink the cup of immortality, and be anointed with the oil of incorruption.
Take heart, Aseneth. The Lord has given you to Joseph as a bride, and he will be your bridegroom.

You will no longer be called Aseneth, but your name will be City of Refuge,{a} because many nations will take refuge in you, many peoples will shelter under your wings, and those who attach themselves to God through repentance will be guarded within your wall.

For Repentance is the daughter of the Most High, and she begs the Most High on your behalf at every hour, and on behalf of all who repent, since he is the father of Repentance, and she is the mother of virgins and pleads with him at every hour for those who repent. For he has prepared a heavenly bridal chamber for those who love her, and she will serve them forever.
Repentance is a very beautiful virgin, pure, chaste, and gentle. God Most High loves her, and all the angels respect her.
Look, I am going to Joseph, and I will speak to him about you, and he will come to you today, and see you, and be glad about you, and be your bridegroom.

Now listen to me, Aseneth, and put on your wedding robe, the old, first robe that is stored in your room, and put on all your choice jewelry, and adorn yourself like a bride, and be ready to meet him.
For look, he is coming to you today, and he will see you and be glad.”
When the man had finished speaking to Aseneth, she was filled with great joy, fell at his feet, and said to him,
“Blessed be the Lord God, who sent you to rescue me from the darkness and lead me up to the light, and blessed be his name forever.

If I have found favor in your sight, my lord, please sit on the couch a little while, and I will set a table and bread, and you will eat. I will bring you good wine, whose fragrance reaches heaven, and you will drink and go on your way.”

notes.text: Greek *polis katafyges*. The Hebrew Bible has “cities of refuge” (Numbers 35:6–15) where those who had killed accidentally could flee. Here the name describes what Aseneth will be for repentant nations.

verses.text: The man said to her, “Bring me a honeycomb too.”
Aseneth said, “Lord, I will send to the field of my estate and bring you a honeycomb.”
The man said to her, “Go into your room, and you will find a honeycomb.”
Aseneth went into her room and found a honeycomb lying on the table. The comb was white as snow and full of honey, and its aroma was the fragrance of life.
Aseneth took the comb and brought it to him. The man said to her, “Why did you say there was no honeycomb in my house? Look, you have brought me one.”
Aseneth said, “Lord, I had no honeycomb in my house, but it has come to be as you said. Perhaps it came out of your mouth, because its scent is like the scent of perfume.”

The man stretched out his hand and gripped her head and said, “You are blessed, Aseneth, because the secrets of God have been revealed to you, and blessed are those who attach themselves to the Lord God in repentance, for they will eat from this comb.
The bees of the paradise of delight{a} made this honey, and the angels of God eat from it, and whoever eats of it will never die.”
