He said, “Isaiah and those with him prophesy that Jerusalem and the cities of Judah will be laid waste, that the people of Judah and Benjamin{e} will go into captivity, and that you too, my lord the king, will be led off bound with hooks and iron chains.”
“But they are prophesying falsely against Israel and Judah.
Isaiah has said, ‘I see more than Moses{f} the prophet.’
Moses said, ‘No one can see God and live,’ yet Isaiah says, ‘I have seen God, and look, I am alive.’

“So know this, O king, that he is lying. He has also called Jerusalem Sodom,{g} and he has declared that the leaders of Judah and Jerusalem are the people of Gomorrah.” He brought many charges against Isaiah and the prophets before Manasseh.
Meanwhile Beliar lived in Manasseh’s heart, and in the hearts of the princes of Judah and Benjamin, the eunuchs, and the king’s counselors.
Belchira’s words pleased Manasseh greatly, and he sent men and seized Isaiah.

For Beliar was furious with Isaiah because of his vision, and because Isaiah had exposed Sammael, and because Isaiah had revealed that the Beloved would go out from the seventh heaven. Isaiah had revealed his transformation and descent and the human likeness he would take, the persecution he would suffer, and the tortures with which the children of Israel would torture him. He had foretold the arrival of his twelve disciples and their teaching, and that he would be crucified on a tree before the Sabbath, crucified together with evildoers, and buried in a tomb.
He had foretold that the twelve who were with him would stumble because of him, and that guards would watch the tomb.
He had also foretold how the angel of the Christian church would come down, the one who is in the heavens and whom the Lord will call in the last days.
And on the third day Gabriel,{h} the angel of the Holy Spirit, with Michael,{i} the chief of the holy angels, would open the tomb.
The Beloved, sitting on their shoulders, would come out and send out his twelve disciples.

They would teach all nations and every language about the resurrection of the Beloved. Those who believed in his cross would be saved, and also in his ascension to the seventh heaven, from which he came.
Many who believed in him would speak through the Holy Spirit.
And many signs and wonders would be done in those days.
Afterward, as his coming drew near, his disciples would abandon the teaching of the twelve apostles, along with their faith, their love, and their purity.
There would be much quarreling as his coming drew near.
In those days many would be fond of high office although they had no wisdom.
There would be many lawless elders and shepherds who treated their own sheep unjustly, and they would plunder them because they had no holy shepherds.
Many would trade the honor of the saints’ garments for the garments of the greedy. There would be much favoritism in those days, and many who loved the honor of this world.
There would be much slander and boasting as the Lord’s coming drew near, and the Holy Spirit would leave many.
In those days there would not be many prophets or people speaking trustworthy words, except one here and there in different places,
because of the spirit of error, immorality, boasting, and greed that would be found among those called servants of that One, and among those who would welcome that One.
There would be great hatred between the shepherds and elders.
For in the last days there would be great jealousy, and everyone would say whatever seemed right to him.
They would cancel the prophecy of the prophets who were before me, and they would cancel these visions of mine too, so as to speak whatever their own hearts urged.

notes.text: Ethiopic *Alagar Zagâr*, a corrupt form of Shalmaneser (see 2:14).
Hebrew *Ashshur*, named for the city and god Ashur; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *Madai*; the meaning is unknown.
Ethiopic *Tâzôn*, the same as Gozan (2 Kings 17:6); the meaning is unknown.
Hebrew *Binyamin*, “son of the right hand” or “son of the south.”
Hebrew *Mosheh*, which the Bible links with “drawn out” (Exodus 2:10); it is probably an Egyptian word meaning “child.”
Hebrew *Sedom*; the meaning is unknown.
Hebrew *Gavri’el*, “mighty one of God” or “God is my strong one.”
Hebrew *Mikha’el*, “who is like God?”

verses.text: Listen, Hezekiah, and you, Josab my son: these are the days when the world is being brought to its end.

When that end has come, Beliar, the great ruler and king of this world, who has governed it from its beginning, will descend from his firmament looking like a man: a lawless king, the killer of his own mother. This same king
will persecute the plant that the twelve apostles of the Beloved planted. One of the twelve will be handed over into his hands.
This ruler will arrive in the shape of that king, and every power of this world will come with him and obey him in all that he wishes.
At his command the sun will rise in the night, and he will bring out the moon at noon.{a}
He will carry out in the world whatever he wishes. He will act and talk like the Beloved, and he will announce, “I am God, and no one existed before me.”
Everyone on earth will put their faith in him.
They will sacrifice to him and serve him, saying, “This is God, and there is no other beside him.”
Most of those who had united to welcome the Beloved he will draw over to himself.
His miraculous power will show itself in every city and district.
In every city he will have his image set up in front of him.
He will hold power for three years, seven months, and twenty-seven days.{b}
Of those who believed in him, a few will remain in those days as his servants; they will run from wilderness to wilderness, awaiting the Beloved’s coming.

When 1,332 days have passed,{c} the Lord will arrive with his angels and the hosts of the holy ones out of the seventh heaven, in the splendor of that heaven, and he will haul Beliar down into Gehenna, together with his armies.
He will give relief to the devout he finds still alive on earth, and the sun will be put to shame,

and also to all who, out of faith in him, have cursed Beliar and his kings. The saints will accompany the Lord, wearing the garments that are now kept on high in the seventh heaven. They will come with him, their spirits clothed, and take up their presence in the world. He will give strength to those still living in the body, along with the saints, clothing them in the saints’ garments, and the Lord will wait on those who kept watch in this world.
Afterward they will turn upward in their garments, and their bodies will be left behind in the world.

Then the Beloved’s voice will rebuke in anger everything in heaven and on earth: the mountains and hills, the cities, the wilderness and the woods, the angel of the sun and the angel of the moon, and everything through which Beliar appeared and worked openly in this world. A resurrection and a judgment will take place among them in those days, and the Beloved will send fire out from himself to consume all the godless, so that it will be as if they had never been made.
The remainder of this vision is written down in the vision of Babylon.{d}
The rest of the vision about the Lord is written in the parables, in my words, in the book that I prophesied in public.

As for the Beloved’s descent into Sheol,{e} you will find it in the passage where the Lord says, “Look, my Son will understand.” All of this is written in the Psalms, among the parables of David{f} son of Jesse,{g} in the Proverbs of his son Solomon,{h} in the sayings of Korah{i} and of Ethan{j} the Israelite, in the words of Asaph,{k} and in the other Psalms that the angel of the Spirit inspired,

namely, those with no name attached to them. They are written also in the words of my father Amos{l} and of the prophets Hosea,{m} Micah,{n} Joel, Nahum,{o} Jonah,{p} Obadiah,{q} Habakkuk, Haggai,{r} Zephaniah,{s} Zechariah,{t} and Malachi,{u} and in what Joseph{v} the Just said, and in the sayings of Daniel.{w}

notes.text: Literally “the sixth hour.” The Jews counted the hours of daylight from about 6 a.m., so the sixth hour is about noon.

This adds up to about 1,335 days, the number in Daniel 12:12, and it recalls the “time, times, and half a time” of Daniel 7:25 and Revelation 12:14. The Ethiopic text of the rest of this verse is broken and is not clear in the sources used here. It seems to say that many of the faithful, who had been hoping for the One who was crucified, Jesus the Lord Christ, will be left, after Isaiah has seen him who was crucified and ascended.
The Ethiopic gives only “three hundred and thirty-two,” and the “one thousand” is supplied from the other versions. It is close to the 1,335 days of Daniel 12:12.

Hebrew *Bavel*, from Akkadian *Bab-ili*, “gate of the god”; Genesis 11:9 links it with the Hebrew word for “confuse.” The writing meant is uncertain; it may refer to Isaiah’s oracles against Babylon (Isaiah 13–14 and 21) or to a lost work.
Hebrew *She’ol*, the place of the dead; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *David*, probably “beloved.”
Hebrew *Yishay*; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *Shelomoh*, “peaceful.”
Hebrew *Qorach*, perhaps “bald.”
Hebrew *Eytan*, “enduring.”
Hebrew *Asaf*, “he gathers.”
Hebrew *Amos*, “carried” or “borne.”
Hebrew *Hoshea*, “salvation.”
A short form of Micaiah, “who is like Yahweh?”
Hebrew *Nachum*, “comfort.”
Hebrew *Yonah*, “dove.”
Hebrew *Ovadyah*, “servant of Yahweh.”
Hebrew *Haggai*, “festival.”
Hebrew *Tsefanyah*, “Yahweh has hidden” or “Yahweh has treasured.”
Hebrew *Zekharyah*, “Yahweh remembers.”
Hebrew *Mal’akhi*, “my messenger.”
Hebrew *Yosef*, “may he add” (Genesis 30:24).
Hebrew *Daniyye’l*, “God is my judge.”

verses.text: Because of these visions Beliar raged against Isaiah. He took up residence in Manasseh’s heart, and Manasseh had Isaiah cut in half with a wooden saw.
As Isaiah was being sawn, Belchira stood and denounced him, and all the false prophets stood by, laughing and gloating over Isaiah.
With the help of Mechembechus,{a} Belchira stood before Isaiah and mocked him.
Belchira told Isaiah, “Say this: ‘All that I have spoken was a lie, and Manasseh’s ways are good and just.
The ways of Belchira and his companions are good too.’”
He said this to him as the sawing began.
But Isaiah was absorbed in a vision from the Lord; his eyes were open, yet he did not see them.
Belchira spoke to Isaiah again: “Say what I tell you, and I will change their minds. I will make Manasseh, the leaders of Judah, the people, and all Jerusalem show you respect.”
Isaiah answered, “As far as I am able to speak, I say: Damned and cursed be you, and all your powers, and all your house.
For you cannot take anything from me except the skin of my body.”
So they seized Isaiah son of Amoz and sawed him in two with a wooden saw.
Manasseh, Belchira, the false prophets, the leaders, and all the people stood watching.
Before the sawing, Isaiah had said to the prophets who were with him, “Go to the region of Tyre{b} and Sidon,{c} for God has mixed the cup for me alone.”
While he was being sawn, Isaiah neither shouted nor wept; his lips spoke with the Holy Spirit until he was cut through.
Beliar did this to Isaiah through Belchira and Manasseh. For Sammael had been seething against Isaiah ever since the time of Hezekiah, king of Judah, over what Isaiah had seen concerning the Beloved,
and over the destruction of Sammael, which Isaiah had seen through the Lord while Manasseh’s father Hezekiah was still king. Manasseh acted according to the will of Satan.

notes.text: Ethiopic *Mechembêchûs*, the same figure as Matanbuchus (2:4); the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *Tsor*, “rock.”
Hebrew *Tsidon*; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “fishing.”

verses.text: In Hezekiah’s twentieth year as king of Judah, Isaiah son of Amoz came from Gilgal{a} to Jerusalem with his son Josab, to see Hezekiah.
Isaiah went in and sat on the king’s couch. A seat was brought to him, but he would not sit on it.

As Isaiah began to speak words of faith and truth with the king, all the leaders of Israel were seated, with the eunuchs and the royal counselors. Forty prophets and sons of prophets were also there, who had come from the villages, the hill country, and the lowlands on hearing that Isaiah was coming from Gilgal to Hezekiah.
They had come to greet him and to hear his words.
They wanted him to lay his hands on them so that they would prophesy, and so that he could hear their prophecy. They all stood before Isaiah.
While Isaiah was telling Hezekiah these words of truth and faith, everyone heard a door being opened, and heard the Holy Spirit speak.
The king gathered every prophet and every person present, and they came. Micaiah, aged Ananias, Joel, and Josab took seats at his right and at his left.

When all of them heard the Holy Spirit’s voice, they knelt and bowed down, and gave glory to the true God, the Most High, who dwells in the upper world and sits on high, the Holy One who rests among his holy ones.
They gave glory to him because he had opened a door in a foreign world, and had opened it to a man.
As Isaiah was speaking by the Holy Spirit for everyone to hear, he suddenly went quiet. His mind was lifted out of him, and he no longer saw the men who stood before him,
though his eyes were open. His lips were still, and the mind within his body had been taken out of him.
Yet he was still breathing, because he was watching a vision.
The angel who had been sent to show it to him was not from this firmament, and he was not one of the glorious angels of this world, but had come from the seventh heaven.
The bystanders did not think so, but the company of the prophets believed the holy Isaiah had been carried up.
The vision the holy Isaiah beheld did not belong to this world; it came from the world kept hidden from flesh.
When Isaiah had seen the vision, he described it to Hezekiah, to his son Josab, and to the other prophets who had gathered.

But the leaders, the eunuchs, and the people heard nothing. Only Samnas the scribe, Joachim,{b} and Asaph the recorder heard, for they too did what is right, and the sweet fragrance of the Spirit rested on them. The people heard nothing, since Micaiah and his son Josab had sent them outside once the wisdom of this world was taken from Isaiah and he lay like a dead man.

notes.text: Greek *Galgala*, Hebrew *Gilgal*, “circle” or “rolling.”
Ethiopic *Ijôaqêm*, Hebrew *Yehoyaqim*, “Yahweh raises up.”

verses.text: Isaiah described the vision he had seen to Hezekiah, his son Josab, Micaiah, and the other prophets. He said:

“A moment ago, while I was prophesying about the things you heard, I saw a glorious angel unlike the angels of glory that I used to see all the time. He had such glory and rank that I cannot describe his glory.
He took me by the hand and lifted me up, and I said to him, ‘Who are you? What is your name? And where are you taking me up to?’ I was given strength to speak with him.
He said to me, ‘When I have lifted you up through the different levels and shown you the vision I was sent to show, then you will understand who I am. But you do not know my name.
You will return to this body of yours, but you will see where I am lifting you up to, for I was sent for this purpose.’
I was glad that he spoke so kindly to me.
He said to me, ‘Are you glad because I have spoken kindly to you?’ And he said, ‘You will see how one greater than I am will speak with you kindly and peacefully.
You will also see his Father, who is greater, for I was sent from the seventh heaven to explain all these things to you.’
The two of us ascended to the firmament, and there I saw Sammael with his hosts. A great struggle was going on there, and Satan’s angels envied each other.
As it is above, so it is on the earth too, for what is on the earth is a likeness of what is in the firmament.
I asked the angel beside me, ‘What is the meaning of this war, and of this envy?’
He answered, ‘It has been this way ever since the world was created, and this war will last until the one you will see arrives and destroys him.’
Then he took me up above the firmament, to the first heaven.
There I saw a throne in the center, and angels stood to the right of it and to the left.

The angels on the left were unlike those standing at the right. The ones on the right had greater glory, and they praised together in a single voice. A throne stood between them, and those on the left praised after them, but their voice was different from the right-hand angels’ voice, and their praise was different too.
I asked the angel who was leading me, ‘Who is this praise sent to?’
He said, ‘It is offered to the One who sits in the seventh heaven, who rests in the holy world, together with his Beloved, who sent me to you. That is where it goes.’
Then he carried me up to the second heaven. That heaven is as high above the first as the heaven is above the earth and the firmament.

As in the first heaven, I saw angels on the right and the left, a throne in the center, and angels praising in the second heaven. The one seated on the throne in the second heaven shone more brightly than all the others.
The glory in the second heaven was immense, and its praise was not like the praise of the first heaven.

I fell on my face to bow before him, but the angel who guided me would not allow it. He said, ‘Do not worship any throne or angel of the six heavens—that is why I was sent to guide you—until I say so in the seventh heaven.
Your throne has been placed above every heaven and their angels, and so have your garments and your crown, which you will see.’
Great joy filled me, because the lovers of the Most High and of his Beloved will one day rise to that place under the guidance of the angel of the Holy Spirit.
Next he took me up to the third heaven, and again I saw the angels at the right and the left, with a throne in the center. But there the memory of this world is never heard.
I spoke to the angel with me (my appearance was shining ever more brightly as I rose from heaven to heaven): ‘Not even a trace of the emptiness of that world is spoken of here.’
He replied, ‘Nothing is spoken of, because of its weakness; yet nothing that is done there stays hidden.’

I wanted to learn how it all becomes known, and he replied, ‘When I have brought you to the seventh heaven, the one above these, from which I was sent, then you will know that nothing is concealed from the thrones, from the dwellers in the heavens, or from the angels.’ The praise they offered and the glory of the one on the throne were great, and the angels standing right and left had glory surpassing that of the heaven beneath.
Then he carried me up once more, to the fourth heaven; the distance from the third heaven to the fourth was larger than the distance from the earth to the firmament.
Once more I saw the angels at the right and the left, with the one seated on the throne between them, and they too were praising.
The right-hand angels’ praise and glory were higher than those of the left-hand angels.
The glory of the one seated on the throne exceeded that of the right-hand angels, and their glory exceeded that of the ones below.
He lifted me to the fifth heaven.
Once more I saw the right and left, and the one on the throne, whose glory was higher than that of the fourth heaven’s occupants.
The glory of the right-hand angels was higher than that of the left-hand ones,
and the one on the throne had more glory than the angels at his right.
Their praise was more splendid than the fourth heaven’s.

I praised the one who has no name, the Only-begotten, who lives in the heavens and whose name no flesh knows, who has given each heaven its glory, who makes the glory of the angels great and increases still more the glory of the one who sits on the throne.
“Then he lifted me once more, into the sixth heaven’s atmosphere, and I beheld a splendor unlike any I had seen in the five lower heavens.
I saw angels with great glory.
The praise there was holy and marvelous.
I asked the angel who guided me, ‘What am I looking at, my lord?’
He said, ‘I am not your lord, but your fellow servant.’
I asked him again, ‘Why are there no angels on the left, as there are fellow servants of ours elsewhere?’

He replied, ‘From the sixth heaven upward there are no more angels at the left, and no throne set in the center. They are ruled by the might of the seventh heaven, where the One without a name dwells, and the Chosen One, whose name has not been revealed, and no heaven can find out his name.
For he alone is the one whom all the heavens and thrones obey when he speaks. That is why I was given power and sent to bring you here, so that you could see this glory
and see the Lord of all those heavens, along with these thrones,
as he alters his shape, stage by stage, until he looks like you in form and likeness.
I tell you, Isaiah: no one who is about to return into a body in that world has gone up or seen what you see, or understood what you have understood and what you will see.
You have been granted, by the Lord’s allotment, to come here, and from here flows the power of the sixth heaven and the air.’
I praised my Lord, because through his allotment I was to come here.

He said, ‘Hear this too, then, from your fellow servant: when, by God’s will, you have left the body behind and gone up, you will be given the garment you see, and you will see other garments too, counted and kept there,
and then you will be the equal of the angels in the seventh heaven.’
He took me up to the sixth heaven, where there were no angels at the left and no throne in the center, but all looked alike, and their praise was the same.
Power was given to me too, and I praised with them, and that angel too, and our praise was like theirs.
There they all spoke the name of the first Father and of his Beloved, the Christ,{a} and of the Holy Spirit, all in one voice.
Their voice was unlike that of the angels in the five lower heavens,
or like their speech, but the voice there was different, and there was much light.
Once I was in the sixth heaven, I took the light I had seen in the lower five to be just darkness.
I was glad, and I praised him who has given such lights to those who wait for his promise.
I begged the angel who was leading me not to send me back to the fleshly world.
I tell you, Hezekiah, my son Josab, and Micaiah, that the darkness here is deep.

The angel guiding me knew my thoughts and said, ‘If this light makes you rejoice, how much more you will rejoice when you see the light in the seventh heaven, where the Lord and his Beloved are, who sent me, and who is to be named “Son” in this world. He has not yet been revealed—he who will live in the perishing world—
and the garments, thrones, and crowns kept for the righteous, for those who put their trust in that Lord who will come down in your form. The light there is vast and marvelous.
As for your not returning to the body, your days are not yet complete for coming here.’
On hearing this I was troubled, and he told me, ‘Let it not trouble you.’

notes.text: Greek *Christos*, “anointed one,” the Greek for the Hebrew *mashiach* (Messiah).

verses.text: “He brought me to the seventh heaven’s air, and I heard a voice say, ‘How high will a being of flesh climb?’ I was terrified and shook.
While I was trembling, I heard another voice sent from there saying, ‘The holy Isaiah is permitted to come up here, for his garment is here.’
I asked the angel beside me, ‘Who was it that forbade me, and who was it that permitted me to come up?’
He said to me, ‘The one who forbade you is the one in charge of the praise of the sixth heaven.
The one who permitted it is your Lord God, the Lord Christ, who will go by the name Jesus{a} in the world. But his name you cannot hear until you have left your body behind.’
He raised me to the seventh heaven, and there I saw a marvelous light and countless angels.
There I saw all the righteous ever since Adam.{b}
There I saw the holy Abel{c} and all the righteous.
There I saw Enoch{d} and everyone with him, stripped of the garments of flesh. They wore their garments of the upper world and stood like angels in great glory.
But they were not sitting on their thrones, and their crowns of glory were not on them.
I asked the angel who accompanied me, ‘Why have they received the garments, but not the thrones and the crowns?’

He said, ‘They are not given crowns and thrones of glory until the Beloved descends in the form you will see him take when he comes into the world at the end of days—the Lord who will be given the name Christ.
Even so, they see and know whose thrones and crowns these will be when he has come down and been made in your form. They will think he is only flesh and a man.
The god of that world will reach out a hand against the Son, and they will nail him to a tree and kill him without knowing who he is.
So his descent, as you will see it, will be concealed even from the heavens, so that nobody will know who he is.
After he has plundered the angel of death, he will rise on the third day and remain in that world five hundred forty-five days.{e}
Then many of the righteous will rise along with him; their spirits are not given their garments until the Lord Christ goes up and they go up with him.
Then they will receive their garments, thrones, and crowns, when he has gone up into the seventh heaven.’
I put to him the question I had asked in the third heaven:
‘Show me how everything that is done in that world is made known here.’
While I was still speaking with him, one of the angels who stood near, more glorious than the angel who had brought me up from the world,

showed me a book. He opened it, and it contained writing, but not like any book of this world. He handed it to me, and I read it: it recorded the deeds of the people of Israel, and of others unknown to me, my son Josab.
I said, ‘Truly nothing that is done in this world is hidden in the seventh heaven.’
There I saw many garments laid up, with many thrones and many crowns.
I said to the angel, ‘Whose are these garments, thrones, and crowns?’

He answered, ‘Many from that world will be given these garments because they believed in the words of the One who will be named, as I told you; they will keep his commands, trust them, and trust in his cross. These are kept for them.’
I saw One standing there whose glory surpassed all the others. His glory was vast and wonderful.

When I had seen him, all the righteous I had seen, and the angels as well, drew near to him. Adam, Abel, and Seth{f} and all the righteous came forward first and bowed to him, and all of them praised him in one voice. I praised along with them, and my praise matched theirs.
Then all the angels came near, worshiped, and praised.
I was changed again and became like an angel.
Then the angel who was leading me said to me, ‘Worship this One,’ and I worshiped and praised.
The angel said to me, ‘This is the Lord of all the praises that you have seen.’
As he was still speaking, I saw a second glorious One, similar to the first, and the righteous drew near, bowed, and praised, and I praised with them. But my glory was not changed to resemble theirs.
Then the angels came near and worshiped him.
There I saw the Lord with the second angel, both standing.
The second stood at my Lord’s left. I asked, ‘Who is this?’ and he told me, ‘Worship him. This is the Holy Spirit’s angel, the one who speaks in you and in the other righteous.’
I saw the great glory with the eyes of my spirit open, and then I could not see, nor could my guiding angel, nor any of the angels I had watched worship my Lord.
But I saw the righteous looking with great power on the glory of that One.
My Lord approached me, together with the angel of the Spirit, and said, ‘See that it has been granted you to look on God, and that power has been given, for your sake, to the angel who is with you.’
I saw my Lord and the Spirit’s angel bow down, and the two of them praised God together.
Then all the righteous came near and worshiped.
The angels came near and worshiped, and all the angels praised.

notes.text: Greek *Iesous*, from Hebrew *Yeshua* (Joshua), “Yahweh saves.”
Hebrew *Adam*, “human being,” from *adamah*, “ground.”
Hebrew *Hevel*, “breath” or “vapor.”
Hebrew *Chanokh*, “dedicated.”
The words about the third day are found in the Greek Legend and the Ethiopic, but are missing in the Latin and Slavonic. The number 545 is found only in the Ethiopic.
Hebrew *Shet*, “appointed” (Genesis 4:25).

verses.text: “Then I heard the voices and the praise that I had heard in each of the lower six heavens, rising up and sounding there.
All of it was being sent up to that Glorious One, on whose glory I could not gaze.
I myself was hearing and seeing the praise given to him.
The Lord and the Spirit’s angel watched all this and listened to it all.
All the praises sent up from the six heavens can be seen as well as heard.

I heard my guiding angel say, ‘This is the Most High among the high ones, who dwells in the holy world and rests among his holy ones, and whom the Holy Spirit, speaking through the lips of the righteous, will call “the Father of the Lord.”’
I heard the Most High, my Lord’s Father, speak to my Lord Christ, who will take the name Jesus:
‘Go out and descend through all the heavens. You will descend to the firmament and to that world, to the angel in Sheol, but you will not go as far as Haguel.{a}
You will take on the likeness of everyone in the five heavens.
You will take care to look like the angels of the firmament, and like those in Sheol.
None of the angels of that world will know that you are Lord with me over the seven heavens and their angels.

They will not know you are with me until I call out to the heavens, their angels, and their lights, as low as the sixth heaven, in a loud voice, so that you may judge and destroy the rulers, angels, and gods who belong to that world, and the realm under their rule.
For they have denied me, saying, “We alone exist, and no one is beside us.”
After that you will rise from the angels of death to your own place, and you will not be changed in each heaven, but ascend in glory and sit at my right side.
Then the rulers and powers of that world will bow down to you.’
I heard the Great Glory giving these commands to my Lord.
I watched my Lord leave the seventh heaven for the sixth.
The angel guiding me told me, ‘Pay attention, Isaiah, and watch how the Lord’s transformation and descent will appear.’
I looked, and when the angels in the sixth heaven saw him, they praised and honored him, for he had not been changed into the shape of the angels there. They praised him, and I praised with them.
I saw him descend to the fifth heaven, and there he took the shape of that heaven’s angels. They neither praised nor worshiped him, because he looked just as they did.
Then he descended to the fourth heaven and took the shape of its angels.
When they saw him, they gave him no praise or honor, since he looked like them.
Again I saw him descend, to the third heaven, where he took the form of the angels there.

The keepers of the third heaven’s gate asked for the password, and the Lord gave it so that he would not be recognized. When they saw him, they offered no praise or honor, since his appearance matched theirs.
Again I saw him descend to the second heaven, and there too he gave the password. The gatekeepers kept demanding it, and the Lord kept giving it.
I saw him make himself like the second heaven’s angels, and they looked at him and did not praise him, because he looked like them.

Again I saw him descend to the first heaven, and there too he gave the password to the gatekeepers and made himself like the angels who stood at the left of that throne. They neither praised nor honored him, since he looked like them.
But no one questioned me, because of the angel who was leading me.

Next he descended into the firmament, where this world’s ruler lives, and told the password to those at the left. He looked like them, and they did not praise him there. Instead they envied one another and fought, for evil has power there, and they quarrel over trifles.
I saw him descend and make himself resemble the angels of the air, so that he looked like one of them.
He gave no password, for there one was plundering and mistreating another.

notes.text: Ethiopic *Haguêl*, probably for Abaddon (Hebrew *Avaddon*, “destruction”), the final place of the lost; it is named only here.

verses.text: “After this the angel who spoke with me and led me said, ‘Understand, Isaiah son of Amoz, for I was sent from God for this purpose.’

I saw a woman from the family of the prophet David, named Mary,{a} a virgin, engaged to a man called Joseph,{b} a carpenter, who also belonged to the line and household of the righteous David of Bethlehem in Judah.
He came into his allotment. When she was engaged, she was found to be with child, and Joseph the carpenter wanted to send her away.
But the Spirit’s angel appeared in this world, and afterward Joseph did not divorce her; he kept Mary and told no one.
Joseph never went near Mary; he kept her a holy virgin even though she was pregnant.
For two months he did not live with her.
After two months, while Joseph was in his house with his wife Mary, the two of them alone,
it happened that when they were alone, Mary at once looked up and saw a small baby, and she was amazed.
After she was amazed, her womb was found as it had been before she conceived.
When her husband Joseph asked her, ‘What has astonished you?’ his eyes were opened; he saw the baby and praised God, for God had come into his portion.
A voice reached them: ‘Do not tell anyone about this vision.’
The news about the baby spread in Bethlehem.
Some said, ‘The virgin Mary has had a baby before she had been married two months.’

Many said, ‘She has not had a baby, and no midwife went up to her, and we have not heard the cries of labor.’ They were all blind about him, and they all knew about him, though they did not know where he was from.
They took him and went to Nazareth{c} in Galilee.{d}
Hezekiah and my son Josab, I saw this, and I tell it to the other prophets standing here: it escaped all the heavens, all the rulers, and all the gods of this world.
I saw that in Nazareth he nursed at the breast as a baby, as is usual, so that he would not be recognized.
When he was grown he performed great signs and wonders in Israel’s land and in Jerusalem.
After this the adversary grew jealous of him and roused the people of Israel against him, unaware of who he was; they delivered him to the king, crucified him, and he went down to the angel of Sheol.
I saw him in Jerusalem, crucified on a tree,
and likewise, after the third day, rising again and staying for days.
The angel who was leading me said, ‘Understand, Isaiah.’ And I saw him send out the twelve apostles and go up.
I saw him in the firmament, but he had not taken on their form; all the angels in the firmament, with the Satans, saw him and worshiped.
There was great grief there as they said, ‘How did our Lord descend among us without our seeing the glory upon him—the glory we see has been on him since the sixth heaven?’
He went up to the second heaven without changing himself, and all the angels at the right and the left, and the throne in the center,
worshiped him and praised him, saying, ‘How did our Lord pass us by on his way down, and we never noticed?’
In the same way he ascended to the third heaven, and they praised him and spoke as the others had.
In the fourth heaven and the fifth they spoke in just the same way.
But there was one glory, and he did not change himself from it.
I saw him ascend to the sixth heaven, and they bowed to him and glorified him.
But in every heaven the praise swelled louder.

I saw him go up to the seventh heaven, and every righteous person and every angel praised him. Then I saw him take his seat at the right of the Great Glory, on whose glory, as I told you, I could not look.
I also saw the angel of the Holy Spirit sitting at the left hand.
This angel said to me, ‘Isaiah son of Amoz, that is enough for you, for these are great matters, since you have seen what no child of flesh has ever seen.
You will return into your garment of flesh until your days are completed. Then you will come here.’”
Isaiah saw these things and told them to everyone who stood before him, and they praised. He said to King Hezekiah, “I have spoken these things.”
Both the end of this world,
and all this vision will be completed in the last generations.
Isaiah made Hezekiah vow that he would not tell the people of Israel, nor give anyone these words to copy.
. . . You will read such things. Stay awake in the Holy Spirit so that you may receive your garments, thrones, and crowns of glory that are stored up in the seventh heaven.
Because of these visions and prophecies, Sammael Satan cut Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, in two with a saw, by Manasseh’s hand.
Hezekiah handed all this over to Manasseh in the twenty-sixth year.
But Manasseh did not remember them or take them to heart; he became the servant of Satan and was destroyed. Here ends the vision of the prophet Isaiah, with his ascension.

notes.text: Greek *Maria*, from Hebrew *Miryam*; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *Yosef*, “may he add” (see the note at 4:22).
Greek *Nazaret*, perhaps from Hebrew *netser*, “branch,” or *notsrah*, “watcher”; the meaning is uncertain.
Hebrew *Galil*, “circle” or “district.”

books.name: Letter of Aristeas
books.sourceNote: Translated fresh from the Greek text of the Letter of Aristeas as edited by H. St. J. Thackeray for H. B. Swete, *An Introduction to the Old Testament in Greek* (Cambridge, 1900), which is public domain, in new English wording. The text used lacks sections 43 and 271, so chapters are broken at those gaps: chapter 1 is sections 1–11, chapter 2 is 12–27, chapter 3 is 28–42, chapter 4 is 44–82, chapter 5 is 83–120, chapter 6 is 121–171, chapter 7 is 172–186, chapter 8 is 187–223, chapter 9 is 224–270, chapter 10 is 272–294, and chapter 11 is 295–322. The verse numbers inside each chapter count from 1, and the traditional section number is the verse number plus the number of the last section before the chapter began. Where the Greek is corrupt or doubtful, the notes say so. The English translation of Thackeray (1904), which is also public domain, was used only as a check against over-close wording. The modern English translations in *The Old Testament Pseudepigrapha* and elsewhere, and the OCP English, were not used for wording. CJT draft.

verses.text: Philocrates,{a} the account of our meeting with Eleazar,{b} the high priest of the Jews, is worth telling. You have set great store by hearing it, by my going over each point and explaining why we were sent and for what purpose, and so I have tried to set it out plainly for you, knowing how much you love learning,

which is the highest good a person can have: to keep learning, and to keep taking in something further, whether through histories or through living the events oneself. For in this way a pure disposition is formed in the soul. It takes up what is finest, and, turning to piety, the most commanding thing of all, it governs itself by a rule that never misleads.

We were set on examining divine matters with care, and so we offered ourselves for an embassy to the man I mentioned. He is held in the highest honor for his nobility and good name by his citizens and by others, and he has won very great benefits for those with him and for his fellow citizens elsewhere. Our purpose was the translation of the divine law, since it is written among them on skins in Hebrew letters.

We carried this out eagerly, once we had found an opening with the king about the people who had been moved to Egypt from Judea{c} by the king’s father, who had been the first to take possession of the city{d} and to take over Egypt.{e} It is worth telling you this as well.

I am convinced that you lean strongly toward reverence and toward the character of people who live by the holy law, and so you will gladly hear what we intend to tell. You have only lately come to us from the island,{f} and you wish to hear whatever helps to renew the soul.
I also sent you an account earlier of matters I thought worth remembering, which we received from the high priests of Egypt, that most learned land, about the people of the Jews.

You love learning, and so it is right to share with you whatever can benefit the mind. It is right to share it with all who are like you, and much more with you, who hold such an honest conviction. You are not only my brother by kinship in character; you are also the same as I am in your eagerness for what is good.

For the charm of gold, or any other costly possession prized by the vain, does not bring the same benefit as the discipline of education and the care taken over it. But so that we do not become tiresome by dragging out the preliminaries, I will go back to the continuous course of the account.

Demetrius of Phalerum,{g} who had been put in charge of the king’s library, was given large and varied sums in order to gather together, if he could, all the books in the inhabited world. By purchases and by copying, he carried the king’s purpose as far toward its end as was in his power.

We were present when he was asked, “About how many tens of thousands of books are there?” He said, “More than two hundred thousand,{h} O king. I will take pains, within a short time, to bring the rest up to five hundred thousand.{i} I have been told that the laws of the Jews are also worth copying and worth a place in your library.”

“What is stopping you from doing this?” the king asked. “Everything you need has been put at your disposal.” Demetrius said, “They need translation. They use letters of their own, as the Egyptians have their own arrangement of letters, and they have a language of their own as well. They are assumed to use Syriac,{j} but that is not so; theirs is a different kind.” The king took in each point and gave orders that a letter should go to the Jews’ high priest, so that what had been said might be carried out.

notes.text: Greek *Philokrates*, “lover of power” or “lover of rule.” He is the narrator’s brother (verse 7).
Hebrew *Elazar*, “God has helped.”
Greek *Ioudaia*, from Hebrew *Yehudah*, “praised.”
The city is Alexandria, named for Alexander the Great (Greek *Alexandros*, “defender of men”).
Greek *Aigyptos*; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
The text does not say which island is meant.
Greek *Demetrios*, “devoted to Demeter,” the goddess of grain; *Phaleron* was a harbor of Athens, and the meaning of its name is uncertain.
Greek: “twenty myriads”; a myriad is ten thousand.
Greek: “fifty myriads.”
Greek *Syriake*; here it probably means Aramaic, the language of Syria, which Jews of that time also spoke.

verses.text: I thought the moment had come to press what I had often asked of Sosibius{a} of Tarentum{b} and Andreas,{c} the chiefs of the bodyguard: the release of those who had been moved out of Judea by the king’s father. For that king had gone through all of Coele-Syria{d} and Phoenicia,{e} using his success together with courage. Some people he deported, and others he took captive, bringing everything under his hand by fear. In the course of this he carried off to Egypt about a hundred thousand people{f} from the land of the Jews.

Of these he armed about thirty thousand{g} picked men and settled them in the country in the garrisons. (Many had already come in earlier, with the Persian{h}, and others before them had been sent as allies to fight the king of the Ethiopians{i} with Psammetichus.{j} But those were not as many as the ones Ptolemy{k} son of Lagus{l} brought over.)

As I said, he chose those who were best in age and outstanding in strength and armed them. The rest of the crowd, older and younger and women as well, he left in servitude. This was not what he really wanted in his heart; he was overruled by his soldiers because of the services they had rendered in the struggles of war. When we found a pretext for their release, as I have already explained, we spoke to the king in these words.

“It would be absurd, O king, to be proved wrong by the facts themselves. A body of law lies before all the Jews, and we intend not only to copy it but to translate it. What reason could we give for sending it, while great numbers of the same people are in servitude in your kingdom? No, with a perfect and generous spirit, release those who are held in misery. For the God who gave them their law is guiding your kingdom, as I have found by inquiry.{m}

They worship the God who oversees all things and created them, whom all people worship, and we as well, O king, though under other names, Zeus and Dios.{n} The first people to name him this way did so fittingly: that by which everything receives life and comes into being is the guide and lord of all. You surpass all people in the brightness of your mind, so release those who are held in servitude.”

After a short time, as we prayed in our hearts to God that he would shape the king’s mind toward the release of them all (for the human race is God’s creation, and God changes and turns it as he wishes; so in many and various ways I called on the one who rules the heart, that he might be compelled, as I asked, to do it),

for I had great hope, as I made my plea for the rescue of human beings, that God would bring about what was asked. What people believe they are doing in holiness, for justice and the care of good works, is directed in its deeds and plans by God, who rules over all.

The king looked up, glanced at me with a cheerful face, and said, “About how many tens of thousands do you think they will number?” Andreas, who was standing by, answered, “A little over a hundred thousand.” “A small thing indeed,” the king said, “that Aristeas{o} asks of us.” Sosibius and some of those present said, “It is also worthy of your generosity to present their release to the most high God as an offering of thanks. You have been honored supremely by the one who rules all things, and made more glorious than your ancestors. So if you make very great thank offerings, it is fitting for you.”

The king was greatly delighted. He ordered that the soldiers’ pay be increased, that twenty drachmas{p} be paid for each person, and that an order be issued about this, with the registrations made at once. He acted with generous eagerness, since God was bringing to completion our whole purpose and forcing the king to ransom not only the men who had arrived along with his father’s army but also anyone who had been there before or was brought into the kingdom afterward. They reckoned the payment at more than four hundred talents (about 30,000 pounds of silver).{q}
I think it is useful to include a copy of the order as well. The king’s generosity will be far clearer and more obvious, since God was strengthening him to bring rescue to so many multitudes.

It read as follows. “By order of the king: All those who served in the army with our father in the regions of Syria{r} and Phoenicia, and who entered the land of the Jews and gained possession of Jewish persons and brought them to the city and the country, or sold them to others, and likewise anyone who had them earlier or has had them brought in since, are to release them at once, for money. Each owner is to receive twenty drachmas for each person: soldiers as an addition to their pay, and the others from the royal bank.

We consider that these people were taken captive against our father’s wish and contrary to what is right, and that, because of the recklessness of soldiers, their land was laid waste and the removal of the Jews to Egypt took place. The gain the soldiers made in the field was enough. Therefore the oppression of human beings is altogether unreasonable.

We acknowledge that justice is owed to all people, and much more to those who are wrongly oppressed. We seek in every way what is right toward justice and toward piety for all. We therefore order that all Jewish persons who are in servitude anywhere in the kingdom, in whatever way, are to be released by those who hold them, on receipt of the stated sum, and that no one is to handle these matters with malicious delay. The registrations are to be made within three days from the day this order is posted, before those appointed for the purpose, and the persons are to be produced at once.

We judge that this will serve us and our affairs. Whoever wishes to report those who disobey may do so, on the understanding that he will gain control of the one found guilty. The property of such people will be taken into the royal treasury.”

The order was brought in to be read to the king, and it contained all of this except the words “and anyone who had them earlier or has had them brought in since.” The king added this himself, in his generosity and greatness of spirit. He also ordered that the whole sum of the payments be divided up among the officers’ attendants in the divisions and the royal bankers.

So it was decided and confirmed within seven days. The payment came to more than six hundred sixty talents (about 49,500 pounds of silver).{s} Many nursing infants were set free with their mothers, too. When the king was asked whether the twenty drachmas would be paid for these as well, he ordered that this too be done, carrying out completely what he had decided.

notes.text: Greek *Sosibios*, “life-saving.”
Greek *Taras*, a Greek city of southern Italy; the meaning of the name is uncertain.
Greek *Andreas*, “manly.”
Greek *Koile Syria*, “Hollow Syria,” the valley country between the Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon ranges, later used for all of southern Syria.
Greek *Phoinike*, perhaps “land of purple.”
Greek: “ten myriads.”
Greek: “three myriads.”
Greek *Persēs*; the Persian king Cambyses (reigned 530–522 BC) conquered Egypt. The name is Old Persian, perhaps from *Pārsa*, the land of Persia.
Greek *Aithiopes*, “burnt-faced.”
Greek *Psammitichos*, from the Egyptian royal name Psamtik; the meaning is uncertain.
Greek *Ptolemaios*, “warlike.”
Greek *Lagos*, “hare.”
The Greek of the last clause is awkward, and the sentence may be damaged.
Greek *Zeus* and *Dios* are the nominative and genitive forms of the same Greek name; the two forms were read as meaning “through whom” (*di’ hon*) life comes.
Greek *Aristeas*, “best” or “excellent.”
A drachma was a Greek silver coin; the amount is left unconverted because its buying power varied.
Greek: “over four hundred talents.” A talent is taken here as about 75 pounds (34 kg); the weights used for talents varied. The text does not name the metal, and silver is assumed.
Greek *Syria*, probably a shortened form of *Assyria*.
Greek: “more than six hundred sixty talents.” A talent is taken here as about 75 pounds (34 kg).

verses.text: When this had been accomplished, the king ordered Demetrius to submit a proposal about the copying of the Jewish books. Everything under these kings was handled by written orders and with great care, and nothing was done carelessly or at random. For this reason I have included the text of the proposal and copies of the letters, the number of the gifts sent, and the workmanship of each, since every one of them stood out for its lavishness and skill. This is a copy of the proposal.

“To the great king, from Demetrius. You gave orders, O king, that the books still missing to complete the library be gathered in, and that those that have fallen into disrepair receive proper restoration. I have given careful attention to these matters, and I now report the following to you.

The books of the law of the Jews are missing, along with a few others. They happen to be written in Hebrew letters and language, but they have been set down rather carelessly and not as they really stand, as those who know them report; for they have never had the king’s care.

It is necessary that these too be in your possession in an exact form, since this legislation is wiser and unspoiled, as one would expect of a divine law. For that reason, writers, poets, and the whole crowd of historians have kept their distance from mentioning these books and the men who have lived and still live by them, because the thinking in them is pure and solemn, as Hecataeus of Abdera{a} says.

If it seems good to you, O king, a letter will be written to the high priest in Jerusalem{b} to send elderly men whose lives have been the best, experienced in their own law, six from each tribe. We will then examine what the majority agree on, obtain an accurate translation, and set it down clearly, in a way worthy of the matter and of your purpose. May you prosper always.”

When this proposal had been presented, the king ordered a letter to be written to Eleazar about these matters, reporting also the release of the captives that had taken place. He gave, too, for the making of mixing bowls, cups, a table, and bowls for pouring offerings, fifty talents’ weight of gold (about 3,750 pounds){c} and seventy talents of silver (about 5,250 pounds), along with a great quantity of precious stones. He ordered the keepers of the treasure chests to let the craftsmen choose whichever stones they preferred. He also gave coined money for sacrifices and other needs, nearly a hundred talents (about 7,500 pounds of silver).
I will tell you about the workmanship once I have gone through the copies of the letters. The king’s letter was in this form.

“King Ptolemy sends Eleazar the high priest greetings, and wishes him health. It has happened that many Jews have been settled in our country, having been carried off from Jerusalem by the Persians during the time they ruled, and that others came to Egypt with our father as captives.

Of these our father enrolled many in the army on higher pay. He also judged those who were there earlier to be trustworthy, built forts, and handed these over to them, so that the nation of the Egyptians would be afraid because of them. Now that we have taken over the kingdom, we deal with everyone more kindly, and much more so with your fellow citizens.

We have set free more than a hundred thousand captives, giving their owners the silver they were owed, and putting right whatever was done wrongly through the rush of the crowds. We have judged that this was a pious thing to do, and we offer it in thanks to the greatest God, who has held our realm in peace and raised it to the height of glory throughout the whole inhabited world. We have placed those in the prime of life in the army, and those who are able to be near us and are worthy of trust at court we have set over our affairs.

We wish to show favor both to these people and to all the Jews in the world, and to those who come after them. We have therefore decided that your law be translated into Greek letters from the Hebrew letters, as they are called among you, so that these books too may be in our library with the other royal books.

You will do well, and in a manner worthy of our eagerness, to choose elderly men who have lived good lives, who are experienced in the law and able to translate it, six from each tribe, so that agreement may be found among the larger number, since the inquiry concerns weighty matters. For we believe that when this is finished we will win great fame.

We have sent Andreas, of the chiefs of the bodyguard, and Aristeas, who are held in honor among us, to talk with you. They are bringing first offerings of dedicated gifts for the temple, and a hundred talents of silver (about 7,500 pounds) for sacrifices and other needs. If you write to us about whatever you wish, you will please us and do something worthy of friendship, and what you choose will be carried out as quickly as possible. Farewell.”

Eleazar answered this letter, in suitable terms. It went like this: “Eleazar, high priest, to King Ptolemy, his true friend: greetings. May you be well, and the queen Arsinoe,{d} your sister, and your children; it would be as we wish. We are well also.

When we received your letter, we rejoiced greatly over your purpose and your good plan. We gathered the whole community and read it aloud to them, so that they would learn how devout you are toward our God. We also showed them the gifts you sent: bowls, twenty of gold and thirty of silver, with five mixing bowls, and a table for dedication, and a hundred talents of silver (about 7,500 pounds) for bringing sacrifices and for repairs of whatever the temple needs,

notes.text: Greek *Hekataios*, perhaps “far-shooter,” a title of the god Apollo; *Abdera* was a Greek city on the coast of Thrace, and the meaning of its name is uncertain.
Greek *Hierosolyma*, from Hebrew *Yerushalayim*, perhaps “foundation of peace.”
Greek: “fifty talents.” A talent is taken here as about 75 pounds (34 kg); the weights used for talents varied.
Greek *Arsinoe*, perhaps “man-minded.” She was the king’s sister and wife.

verses.text: for we will obey in everything that is to your advantage, even if it goes against our nature, since this is a sign of friendship and affection. You, too, have done great and unforgettable good to our citizens in many ways.

Immediately, then, we offered sacrifices for you, for your sister, your children, and your friends. The whole community prayed that all you intend may always come to you, that God, who rules over all, may keep your kingdom safe in peace and glory, and that the copying of the holy law may be carried out to your benefit and in safety.

In the presence of everyone we chose good and fine elderly men, six from each tribe, and we have sent them with the law. You will do well, righteous king, to give orders that when the copying of the books is finished, the men are brought back to us again in safety. Farewell.”

These are the men. From the first tribe: Joseph, Hezekiah, Zechariah, John, Hezekiah, Elisha.{a} From the second: Judah, Simon, Samuel, Adaeus, Mattathias, Eschlemias.{b} From the third: Nehemiah, Joseph, Theodosius, Baseas, Ornias, Dakis.{c}

From the fourth: Jonathan, Abaeus, Elisha, Hananiah, Chabrias, Chelkias (this last name is doubtful in the Greek).{d} From the fifth: Isaac, Jacob, Jesus, Sabbataeus, Simon, Levi.{e} From the sixth: Judah, Joseph, Simon, Zechariah, Samuel, Selemias.{f}

From the seventh: Sabbataeus, Zedekiah, Jacob, Isaac, Jesias, Natthaeus.{g} From the eighth: Theodosius, Jason, Jesus, Theodotus, John, Jonathan.{h} From the ninth: Theophilus, Abram, Arsamus, Jason, Endemias, Daniel.{i}

From the tenth: Jeremiah, Eleazar, Zechariah, Baneas, Elisha, Dathaeus.{j} From the eleventh: Samuel, Joseph, Judah, Jonathan, Chabeu, Dositheus.{k} From the twelfth: Isael, John, Theodosius, Arsamus, Abietes, Ezekiel.{l} In all they were seventy-two.

Such was the reply that Eleazar and those with him made to the king’s letter. I will now do as I promised and describe the works of craftsmanship. They were completed with outstanding skill, since the king contributed lavishly and looked in on the craftsmen at every stage. So they could not overlook anything or finish anything carelessly. First I will explain to you what concerns the table.
The king was eager to make the piece enormous in its measurements. He ordered inquiry to be made of people in that region about how large the table already standing in the temple in Jerusalem was.

When they told him the measurements, he asked whether he should also make a larger one. Some of the priests, and others, said that nothing prevented it. He said he wished to make it five times the size, but he was afraid it might become useless for the services.

For he did not want what came from him merely to sit in that place. He would be far more pleased if the proper services were carried out correctly on the pieces he had made, by those to whom that duty fell.

“The earlier pieces are small,” he said, “not for lack of gold; it appears that they were made to these measures for some reason. If there had been an instruction to make them larger, nothing would have been withheld. So what has been rightly done must not be overstepped or set aside.”

He ordered them to use as much variety of craftsmanship as possible, planning everything with dignity and having a fine natural sense for the expressiveness of things. Where nothing was prescribed in writing, he ordered them to make it beautiful; where it was prescribed in writing, the measures were to follow it.

They made it two cubits (3 feet) long and a cubit and a half (27 inches) high,{m} working it in tested gold, solid all the way through. I mean that the gold was not wrapped around some other material; the hammered plate itself was joined together.

They made a rim a palm (about 3 inches) wide{n} all around. The moldings were twisted, carved in relief with a pattern of cords, and wonderful in their run when seen from the three sides, for the piece was three-cornered.

On each side the design of the work had the same arrangement, so that whichever side was turned, the appearance was the same. With the molding laid along the rim, the slope toward the table itself held the pattern of beauty, and the outward slope faced the view of the person approaching.

So the ridge between the two slopes came to a sharp edge, standing up, as we said, because it was built three-cornered whichever side was turned. Settings of costly stones lay in it between the cords, one beside another, with a weaving that no one could imitate.
All were held through drilled holes by gold pins for security. At the corners, clasps drew them tight to hold them together.

At the sides, around the rim, on the part facing upward, a pattern of eggs was made with stones set in it, with a design that drew the eye in continuous fluted reliefs, set close together all around the table.

Beneath the stone-set pattern of eggs the craftsmen made a wreath of every kind of fruit, standing out clearly in relief: bunches of grapes and heads of grain, with dates, apples, olives, pomegranates, and the like. They cut the stones to the shapes of these fruits, each kind in its own color, and bound them in the gold, all around the whole edge of the table.

After the arrangement of the wreath, the same pattern was made as for the eggs, and the rest of the fluting and carving was done in the same way. This was because the table was made usable on both sides, whichever side was lifted, so that the placing of the moldings and of the rim was also at the end where the legs were.

They made a solid plate four fingers (about 3 inches) thick{o} across the whole width of the table, so that the legs could be set into it, fastened with pins and clasps at the rim. That way, whichever side was lifted would be the one in use. This can be seen on the surface, since the piece was made to be used either way up.
On the table itself they made a meander in relief, with costly stones standing out in the middle of it, of various kinds: carbuncles and emeralds, onyx, and other kinds outstanding in beauty.

After the arrangement of the meander lay a latticework, wonderful to see, making a diamond pattern in the middle. On it a crystal stone and what is called electrum{p} were set in relief, making a sight that no one could imitate.
They made the legs with capitals shaped like lilies, with the lilies bending back beneath the table, and the face toward the inside had its petals standing straight.

The base on which the leg rested on the floor was a palm (about 3 inches) high on every side and made of stone, set like a plinth in appearance, and eight fingers (about 6 inches) wide. On it rested the whole plate of the leg.{q}

They made ivy growing out of the stone, interwoven with acanthus, winding with a vine around the leg, with clusters of grapes, which were also worked in stone, up to the top. The same arrangement was used on all four legs. Everything was made so lifelike and fitted so well that the skill of the craftsmen matched the real thing exactly. Even when a breath of wind stirred the air, the leaves would move, since everything was modeled on the living thing.

They made the top of the table in three parts, like a three-leaved panel, fitted to one another with dovetail joints through the thickness of the piece, and they made the joining of the seams so that it could not be seen or found. The thickness of the whole table was not less than half a cubit (about 9 inches), so that the whole piece was worth many talents.

For the king had decided not to add anything to the size, and what would have had to be spent on making larger pieces he gave instead for these, in greater amount. According to his plan, everything was completed wonderfully and notably, inimitable in its craftsmanship and outstanding in beauty.
Of the mixing bowls, two were made of gold. They had a scale pattern that ran from the base to the middle, and between the scales stones were set with great skill.

Then came a meander a cubit (18 inches) high, with its relief in varied stonework, showing with beauty the painstaking labor of the craft. Above this was fluting, and above that an interweaving of diamond shapes with a net-like face, all the way up to the mouth.

In the middle were little shields of stones, one beside another, each of a different kind, not less than four fingers (about 3 inches) across, and they filled out the clear beauty of the piece. On the rim of the body a relief of lilies with honeysuckle ornaments, and twisting cords of grape clusters, were modeled all around.

The gold ones had this construction, and each held more than two measures (more than 20 gallons).{r} The silver ones had a smooth surface that served as a mirror, wonderful for this purpose, so that anything brought near was reflected more clearly than in ordinary mirrors.

It is not possible to describe what was accomplished for the sake of lifelike effect. When the pieces were finished and set one beside another (I mean first a silver bowl, then a gold one, then silver and gold again), the effect on the eye was altogether indescribable, and those who came to look could not tear themselves away, because of the dazzling light and the pleasure of the sight.

The effect of the surface was varied. Those who looked at the gold work felt a spell of wonder, as the mind turned continually to each piece of craft. And when someone wished to look at the arrangement of the silver pieces, everything shone around from every side, wherever one stood, and increased the delight of those who watched. So the many arts used in them were beyond description.

The gold cups they engraved with wreaths of vine in the middle, and around the rims they wove a wreath in relief of ivy, myrtle, and olive, setting costly stones in them. The rest of the work they finished in different ways, all of them striving to add to the king’s glory.
All in all, no work of such expense and craftsmanship existed in the royal treasuries or anywhere else. The king took no small care, since he loved glory in fine things.

He often put aside public business and sat attentively beside the craftsmen, so that they would finish the works in a way fitting to the place to which they were being sent. So everything was done with dignity, and worthy of the king who sent it and of the high priest who presided over the place.

The number of stones was lavish, and they were large, not fewer than five thousand, and all were of the highest craftsmanship, so that the gift of the stones and the work of the craftsmen were worth five times the gold.

notes.text: Greek forms of Hebrew names. In order: Joseph (*Yosef*), “may he add”; Hezekiah (*Chizqiyah*), “Yahweh strengthens”; Zechariah (*Zekharyah*), “Yahweh remembers”; John (*Yochanan*), “Yahweh is gracious”; Hezekiah again; Elisha (*Elisha*), “God saves.” The Greek text gives the tribes by number, not by name.

In order: Judah (*Yehudah*), “praised”; Simon (Greek form of *Shim’on*, Simeon), “he has heard”; Samuel (*Shemu’el*), “name of God” or “God has heard”; Adaeus, perhaps from *Adayah*, “Yahweh has adorned”; Mattathias (*Mattityah*), “gift of Yahweh”; Eschlemias, perhaps from *Shelemyah*, “Yahweh repays,” but the name is uncertain.
In order: Nehemiah (*Nechemyah*), “Yahweh comforts”; Joseph; Theodosius, a Greek name meaning “gift of God”; Baseas, Ornias, and Dakis, whose meanings are uncertain.

In order: Jonathan (*Yehonatan*), “Yahweh has given”; Abaeus, meaning uncertain; Elisha; Hananiah (*Chananyah*), “Yahweh has been gracious”; Chabrias, a Greek name, perhaps “graceful”; Chelkias, perhaps for Hilkiah (*Chilqiyah*), “Yahweh is my portion.”

In order: Isaac (*Yitschaq*), “he laughs”; Jacob (*Ya’aqov*), “he grasps the heel” or “may God protect”; Jesus, the Greek form of *Yeshua*, Joshua, “Yahweh saves”; Sabbataeus, “born on the Sabbath”; Simon; Levi (*Levi*), “joined.”
Selemias, perhaps for Shelemiah (*Shelemyah*), “Yahweh repays” or “Yahweh is peace.” The other names are explained above.
In order: Sabbataeus; Zedekiah (*Tsidqiyah*), “Yahweh is my righteousness”; Jacob; Isaac; Jesias, perhaps for Isaiah or Joshua; Natthaeus, meaning uncertain.
Jason, a Greek name meaning “healer,” often used by Jews in place of Joshua; Theodotus, a Greek name meaning “given by God.”

In order: Theophilus, “friend of God”; Abram (*Avram*), “exalted father”; Arsamus, a name of Persian or Semitic origin, meaning uncertain; Jason; Endemias, meaning uncertain; Daniel (*Daniyel*), “God is my judge.”
Jeremiah (*Yirmeyahu*), “Yahweh lifts up” or “Yahweh loosens”; Baneas, perhaps for Benaiah (*Benayahu*), “Yahweh has built”; Dathaeus, meaning uncertain.
Chabeu, meaning uncertain; Dositheus, a Greek name meaning “gift of God.”
Isael, perhaps for Israel (*Yisra’el*), “he struggles with God”; Abietes, perhaps for Abiah (*Aviyah*), “Yahweh is my father”; Ezekiel (*Yechezqel*), “God strengthens.”
Greek: “two cubits” and “a cubit and a half”; a cubit is taken as 18 inches (45 cm).
Greek: a “palm,” one-fourth of a cubit’s measure of six palms, taken here as about 3 inches (7.5 cm).
Greek: “four fingers”; a finger is taken as about three-quarters of an inch (1.9 cm).
Greek *elektron*, which can mean either amber or an alloy of gold and silver.
The Greek of this verse is damaged, and the sense is uncertain.
Greek: “more than two *metretai*.” A *metretes* is taken here as about 10 gallons (39 L); the size varied from place to place.

verses.text: I thought a record of these things was also necessary, and so I have made them plain to you. Next comes the account of our trip to Eleazar; before that, I will describe the lie of the whole country. When we reached those parts, we saw the city lying in the middle of all Judea, on a mountain rising to a great height.

On the summit the temple had been built, splendid to look at. It had three enclosing walls, each more than seventy cubits (about 105 feet) in size,{a} and the breadth and length matched the design of the house itself. Everything was built with a grandeur and lavishness that surpassed all else.
The doorway, the fastenings around it along the doorposts, and the strength of the lintels made it plain that money had been spent without stint.

The curtain was made very much like the doorway in every respect. Because the air moved beneath it, the woven fabric was kept in constant motion, as the billowing, which began at the floor, stretched all the way up to the top. The sight was pleasant and hard to turn away from.

The altar was built to suit the place, and the sacrifices that were burned up by fire were offered on it. The approach to the altar was laid out for good order, and the priests who served were covered down to the ankles in tunics of fine linen.

The house faces east, with its back to the west. The whole floor is paved with stone and slopes toward suitable places so that water can be carried off, which is needed to wash away the blood of the sacrifices; for tens of thousands of animals are brought in on feast days.

The supply of water never fails. A spring with abundant flow wells up naturally from within, and there are also wonderful and indescribable reservoirs underground, reaching, as they showed us, five stadia (about 3,000 feet) around the foundation of the temple.{b} From each of these run countless pipes, where the streams join together on every side.

All of these were lined with lead on the floor and the wall, and a great quantity of plaster had been poured over them, everything done with care. There were many openings at the base, invisible to everyone except those who perform the service, so that at a signal all the blood of the great mass of sacrifices that collects can be washed away.

I will describe the construction of the reservoirs as I myself became convinced of it. They led me out of the city more than four stadia (about half a mile), and at one place they told me to bend down and listen to the noise of the waters meeting. In this way the size of the vessels became clear to me, as I have said.

The service of the priests is in every respect unsurpassed in strength and in orderly, silent arrangement. All work hard of their own accord, though it is very toilsome, and each one cares for what has been assigned to him. They serve without pause, some bringing wood, others oil, others fine flour, others spices, and others burning the flesh of the offerings, using exceptional strength.

They take hold of the calves’ legs with both hands (each calf weighs about two talents or more, about 150 pounds){c} and fling them up to a wonderful height, one with each hand, and never miss the placing. The sheep and goats, too, are remarkable for weight and fat. Those in charge always choose animals without blemish and outstanding in plumpness, and so what I have described is accomplished.
A place is set aside for their rest, where those who are taking a break sit. When that happens, those of the others who have stopped rise up eagerly, with no one giving orders for the service.

Complete silence prevails, so that one would suppose no human being was present in the place, though the ministers there number about seven hundred, besides a great crowd of those bringing offerings. Yet everything is carried out with reverence, in a way worthy of great divinity.

It caused us great astonishment when we saw Eleazar at his service, with the splendor of his dress and the glory that comes from the robe he wears and the stones about him. Golden bells hang around his ankle-length robe, giving out a distinctive sound of melody, and beside each of these are little pomegranates embroidered with flowers, wonderful in color.

He was girded with a splendid belt of unusual make, woven through with the loveliest colors. On his chest he wears what is called the breastpiece, in which twelve stones of different kinds are fastened, set in gold, with the names of the tribal leaders in the order established from the beginning. Each one flashes out the natural color proper to it, beyond description.

He wears on his head the so-called turban, and on that the inimitable headband, the consecrated royal emblem, with the name of God{d} stamped in sacred letters on a gold plate in the middle of his brow. He is full of glory, since he was judged worthy of these things for the services.

The sight of all this brings fear and confusion, so that one thinks one has come into another world outside this one. I assure you that every person who comes near to see the things I have described will be filled with amazement and indescribable wonder, his mind changed by the holy arrangement of every part.

To get to know everything, we climbed to the citadel beside the city and looked around. It stands in a very high place, secured by many towers, which were built up to the top with long stones, as we learned, to guard the places around the temple,

so that if there should be an attack, an uprising, or an assault by enemies, no one could force a way into the enclosures around the house. Arrow-shooting engines stood on the towers of the citadel, and engines of various kinds, and the place lay above the enclosures I have described,

and the towers were guarded by the most trustworthy men, who had given great proofs of loyalty to their country. They had no authority to leave the citadel except on feast days, and then only some of them, and they allowed no one to come in.

They were very strict even when an order came through the one in command to admit certain people to see the place, as happened in our own case. They barely admitted the two of us, unarmed, to observe the sacrifices.

They said that this was also confirmed by oaths. All of them had sworn, under the compulsion of their religion, to keep the rule: since there were five hundred of them, no more than five persons could be let in together. For the whole guarding of the temple is the citadel, and whoever is in charge of it is made secure in this way against the dangers I have mentioned.

The extent of the city is proportionate, with a circuit of about forty stadia (about 4½ miles), as far as one can estimate. The towers are arranged like the rows of a theater, and passages can be seen, some lower down and some above, with ways through them. The ground slopes because the city is built on a mountain, and stairways lead up to the passages.

Some people take their road on the upper level and others beneath, and they keep well away from the road, because of those who are in states of purification, so that they touch nothing they should not.

It was not without reason that the first builders laid out the city in fitting proportion; they planned it wisely. The country is large and fine. Some of it is plain, the part around what is called Samaria{e} and the parts adjoining the land of the Idumeans,{f} and some is mountainous, the part adjoining the land of the Jews. These regions need constant attention to farming and the care of the soil, so that the people may have good harvests. This is what is done, and all of it is farmed with great abundance in the whole country I have described.

As for the cities, those of great size and a matching prosperity tend to be well populated while the countryside is neglected, since everyone is inclined toward cheerfulness of spirit, and by their very make-up all human beings are prone to pleasures.

That is what happened around Alexandria, which surpasses all cities in size and prosperity. People who came into it from the country as visitors stayed on for a long time and caused farming to decline.

So, to keep them from staying, the king ordered that no one remain as a visitor for more than twenty days. He also gave written instructions to the officials, that if it was necessary to summon anyone, they should decide the matter within five days.

He gave great weight also to the revenue officers and their assistants, and he appointed them by districts, so that the farmers and the city’s leading men, by making profit, would not run down the storehouses, I mean the produce of farming.

We have gone off on this subject because Eleazar showed us the things above so well. The industry of those who farm is great. The country is full of olive trees in large numbers, of grain crops and pulses, and also of vines and abundant honey. Other tree fruits and dates are not even counted among them.
There are many mixed herds, and abundant pasture for them. For that reason they saw rightly that the region needs a large population, and they laid out the city and the villages accordingly.

A great quantity of spices, costly stones, and gold is brought to the place through the Arabs.{g} The country is made for working and trade, the city is rich in crafts, and nothing brought by sea is lacking.
